items.part:
There are two tanks on a property, Tank $A$ and Tank $B$. Initially, Tank $A$ holds 1000 litres of water and Tank $B$ is empty.
Tank $B$ remains empty until $t=15$ when water is added to it at a constant rate of 30 litres per minute.

By drawing a line on the grid on the previous page, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ when the two tanks contain the same volume of water.
items.sol:
Tank $B$: $V=30(t-15)$ for $t\ge15$. This line starts at $(15,0)$ and rises $30$ litres each minute; drawn on the grid in part (a), it meets the Tank $A$ line at $t=29$.

\exfigure{33_q11_1}

Check algebraically:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000-20t &= 30(t-15)\\ 1000-20t &= 30t-450\\ 1450 &= 50t\\ t &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The tanks hold the same volume after $29$ minutes.

items.part:
There are two tanks on a property, Tank $A$ and Tank $B$. Initially, Tank $A$ holds 1000 litres of water and Tank $B$ is empty.
Using the graphs drawn, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ (where $t>0$) when the total volume of water in the two tanks is 1000 litres.
items.sol:
For $t\ge15$, the total volume is
$$\begin{aligned} (1000-20t)+30(t-15) &= 1000\\ 10t-450 &= 0\\ t &= 45 \end{aligned}$$
(For $0<t<15$ the total is $1000-20t<1000$.) Tank $A$ is not yet empty at $t=45$ ($V=100$), so the model still applies.

$\therefore$ $t=45$ minutes.

items.part: Calculate the sum of the arithmetic series $4+10+16+\cdots+1354$.
Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sec^2 x\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} &\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sec^2 x\,dx \\ &= \Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \Big[\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \tan 0\Big] \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the graph of the curve $y=-x^3+3x^2-1$, labelling the stationary points and point of inflection. Do NOT determine the $x$ intercepts of the curve.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -x^3 + 3x^2 - 1 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -3x^2 + 6x \\ &= 3x(2 - x) \end{aligned}$$
When $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, we have $3x(2-x) = 0$.
$$x = 0, \qquad x = 2$$
$$y = -1 \qquad y = -2^3 + 3(2)^2 - 1 = 3$$
Stationary points are $(0, -1)$ and $(2, 3)$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -6x + 6$$
When $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$, we have $6(1-x) = 0$.
$$x = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -1^3 + 3\times 1^2 - 1 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The point of inflection is $(1, 1)$.

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{4+x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{x}{4 + x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{2x}{4 + x^2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(4 + x^2\right) + c \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $e^{2x}(2x+1)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=2x+1\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{2x}(2x+1)\right] &= 2e^{2x}(2x+1) + 2e^{2x} \\ &= 2e^{2x}(2x + 2) \\ &= 4e^{2x}(x + 1) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int(x+1)e^{2x}\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} &\int (x+1)e^{2x}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\int 4(x+1)e^{2x}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}e^{2x}(2x+1) + c \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove that $\sec\theta-\cos\theta=\sin\theta\tan\theta$.
items.sol:
$$\sec\theta - \cos\theta = \sin\theta\tan\theta$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} - \cos\theta \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sin\theta \times \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sin\theta \times \tan\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
$$\dfrac{dT}{dt} = 70(1.5)^{-0.4t}(-0.4)\ln(1.5)$$

items.part:
Hot tea is poured into a cup. The temperature of tea can be modelled by $T=25+70(1.5)^{-0.4t}$, where $T$ is the temperature of the tea, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after it is poured.
How long after the tea is poured will it take for its temperature to reach $55^\circ\text{C}$?
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} 55 &= 25 + 70(1.5)^{-0.4t} \\ \dfrac{30}{70} &= 1.5^{-0.4t} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right) &= -0.4t\ln(1.5) \\ t &= -\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)}{0.4\ln(1.5)} \\ &\approx 5.22 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ it takes approximately $5.22$ minutes.

A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\sin x & \text{for } 0\le x\le k\\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
Find the value of $k$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k \sin x\,dx &= 1 \\ \Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^k &= 1 \\ -\cos k + \cos 0 &= 1 \\ \cos k &= 0 \\ k &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$

A landscape gardener wants to build a garden bed in the shape of a rectangle attached to a quarter-circle. Let $x$ and $y$ be the dimensions of the rectangle in metres, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{34_q25_1}

The garden bed is required to have an area of $36\text{ m}^2$ and to have a perimeter which is as small as possible. Let $P$ metres be the perimeter of the garden bed.
Show that $P=2x+\dfrac{72}{x}$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} xy + \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x^2 &= 36 \\ xy &= 36 - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x^2 \\ y &= \dfrac{36}{x} - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 2y + 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\times 2\pi x \\ &= 2\left(\dfrac{36}{x} - \dfrac{1}{4}\pi x\right) + 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x \\ &= \dfrac{72}{x} - \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x + 2x + \dfrac{1}{2}\pi x \\ &= 2x + \dfrac{72}{x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A landscape gardener wants to build a garden bed in the shape of a rectangle attached to a quarter-circle. Let $x$ and $y$ be the dimensions of the rectangle in metres, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{34_q25_1}

The garden bed is required to have an area of $36\text{ m}^2$ and to have a perimeter which is as small as possible. Let $P$ metres be the perimeter of the garden bed.
Find the smallest possible perimeter of the garden bed, showing why this is the minimum perimeter.
items.sol:
$$\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 2 - \dfrac{72}{x^2}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dP}{dx} = 0$, we have
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= \dfrac{72}{x^2} \\ x^2 &= 36 \\ x &= 6 \quad (\text{since } x > 0) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2} = \dfrac{144}{x^3}$$
When $x = 6$,
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2} = \dfrac{144}{6^3} \text{ which is greater than zero.}$$
$\therefore$ $P$ is a minimum when $x = 6$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{The minimum perimeter} &= 2\times 6 + \dfrac{72}{6} \\ &= 12 + 12 \\ &= 24 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

A cricket is an insect. The male cricket produces a chirping sound.

A scientist wants to explore the relationship between the temperature in degrees Celsius and the number of cricket chirps heard in a 15-second time interval.

Once a day for 20 days, the scientist collects data. Based on the 20 data points, the scientist provides the information below.

\begin{itemize}
\item A box-plot of the temperature data is shown.

\exfigure{34_q27_1}
\item The mean temperature in the dataset is $0.525^\circ\text{C}$ below the median temperature in the dataset.
\item A total of 684 chirps was counted when collecting the 20 data points.
\end{itemize}

The scientist fits a least-squares regression line using the data $(x,y)$, where $x$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius and $y$ is the number of chirps heard in a 15-second time interval. The equation of this line is

$$y=-10.6063+bx,$$

where $b$ is the slope of the regression line.

The least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$ where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the temperature data and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the chirp data.

Calculate the number of chirps expected in a 15-second interval when the temperature is $19^\circ$ Celsius. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= 22 - 0.525 \\ &= 21.475 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{y} &= \dfrac{684}{20} \\ &= 34.2 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ into the regression equation, we have
$$\begin{aligned} 34.2 &= -10.6063 + b(21.475) \\ \dfrac{44.8063}{21.475} &= b \\ b &= 2.08644\ldots \end{aligned}$$
When $x = 19$,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -10.6063 + 2.08644\ldots \times 19 \\ &= 29.03606\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 29 chirps are expected.

The diagram shows the graph of $y=c\ln x$, $c>0$.

\exfigure{34_q29_1}
Show that the equation of the tangent to $y=c\ln x$ at $x=p$, where $p>0$, is

$$y=\dfrac{c}{p}x-c+c\ln p.$$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= c\ln x \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{c}{x} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent at $x = p$ is $\dfrac{c}{p}$.

At $x = p$, $y = c\ln p$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ y - c\ln p &= \dfrac{c}{p}(x - p) \\ y - c\ln p &= \dfrac{c}{p}x - c \\ y &= \dfrac{c}{p}x - c + c\ln p \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{c}{p} = 1 \quad (\text{since the tangent has a gradient of } 1)$$
$$\therefore\ c = p$$
$$-c + c\ln p = 0 \quad (\text{since the tangent passes through the origin})$$
$$\begin{aligned} -c + c\ln c &= 0 \\ c(-1 + \ln c) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$c = 0 \text{ or } \ln c = 1$$
$$\therefore\ c = e \quad (\text{as } c > 0)$$

$$\begin{aligned} (a+1)x &= 4 \\ x &= \dfrac{4}{a+1} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=x\tan x$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
items.sol:

items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y(t) &= -5t^2 + 70t + 100 \\ y'(t) &= -10t + 70 \end{aligned}$$
When $y'(t) = 0$,
$$\begin{aligned} -10t + 70 &= 0 \\ t &= 7 \end{aligned}$$
At $t = 7$,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -5(7)^2 + 70(7) + 100 \\ &= 345 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
To find when the particle hits the ground, we solve
$$\begin{aligned} -5t^2 + 70t + 100 &= 0 \\ t^2 - 14t - 20 &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{14 \pm \sqrt{196 + 80}}{2} \\ &= 7 \pm \sqrt{69} \end{aligned}$$
$t = 7 + \sqrt{69}$, since $t > 0$
$$\begin{aligned} y'(7+\sqrt{69}) &= -10(7+\sqrt{69}) + 70 \\ &= -10\sqrt{69} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ a = -10$ and $b = 69$

items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} 300 &= \dfrac{4800}{\pi}\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{12} - \cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12}\right) \\ \dfrac{\pi}{16} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12} \\ \cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{\pi}{16} \\ b &= \dfrac{12}{\pi}\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{\pi}{16}\right) \\ b &= 3.95 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ He needs to wait $0.95\times 60 = 57$ minutes (to the nearest minute).

The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is translated $m$ units to the right, dilated vertically by a scale factor of $k$ and then translated 5 units down. The equation of the transformed function is $g(x)=3x^2-12x+7$.

Find the values of $m$ and $k$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &= k(x - m)^2 - 5 \\ &= k\left(x^2 - 2xm + m^2\right) - 5 \\ &= kx^2 - 2mkx + m^2k - 5 \end{aligned}$$
By inspection $k = 3$.

By equating coefficient of $x$,
$$\begin{aligned} 2mk &= 12 \\ 6m &= 12 \\ m &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
Alternate solution
$$g(x) = k(x - m)^2 - 5$$
$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &= 3x^2 - 12x + 7 \\ &= 3\left(x^2 - 4x\right) + 7 \\ &= 3\left(x^2 - 4x + 4\right) + 7 - 12 \\ &= 3(x - 2)^2 - 5 \end{aligned}$$
So $k = 3$ and $m = 2$.

items.part: Find the global maximum and minimum values of $y=x^3-6x^2+8$, where $-1\le x\le 7$.
items.sol:
Global maximum and minimum values occur at local maximum and minimum or end points of the interval.
$$y = x^3 - 6x^2 + 8$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 12x$$
When $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$,
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2 - 12x &= 0 \\ 3x(x - 4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points at $x = 0$ and $x = 4$

When $x = 0$, $y = 8$

When $x = 4$, $y = -24$

End points of interval

When $x = -1$, $y = 1$

When $x = 7$, $y = 57$

Global minimum value $= -24$

Global maximum value $= 57$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=\sin(2x)$.

Find the value of $x$, for $0<x<\pi$, for which $f'(x)=-\sqrt{3}$ AND $f''(x)=2$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \sin 2x \\ f'(x) &= 2\cos 2x \\ f''(x) &= -4\sin 2x \end{aligned}$$
When $f'(x) = -\sqrt{3}$,
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos 2x &= -\sqrt{3} \\ \cos 2x &= \dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{2} \qquad 0 < 2x < 2\pi \\ 2x &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
When $f''(x) = 2$,
$$\begin{aligned} -4\sin 2x &= 2 \\ \sin 2x &= \dfrac{-1}{2} \qquad 0 < 2x < 2\pi \\ 2x &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ for } 0 < x < \pi$$

items.sol:
Stationary points where $f'(x) = 0$
$$(1 - 2x)e^{-2x} = 0$$
$$x = \dfrac{1}{2}, \qquad \text{since } e^{-2x} \neq 0$$
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2}e^{-1} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2e} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &= 4 \times -\dfrac{1}{2} \times e^{-1} \\ &= -2e^{-1} \\ &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2e}\right) \text{ is a local maximum.}$$

A continuous random variable $X$ has cumulative distribution function given by

$$F(x)=\begin{cases} 1 & x>e^3 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{k}\ln x & 1\le x\le e^3 \\[6pt] 0 & x<1 \end{cases}.$$

items.sol:
We need $F\left(e^3\right) = 1$, since $F(x)$ is a CDF.
$$\begin{aligned} F\left(e^3\right) &= \dfrac{1}{k}\ln e^3 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{k} \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{3}{k} = 1$.
$$\therefore\ k = 3$$

items.part:
The fourth term of a geometric sequence is 48.

The eighth term of the same sequence is $\dfrac{3}{16}$.

Find the possible value(s) of the common ratio and the corresponding first term(s).
items.sol:
Let $a$ be the first term and $r$ the common ratio.

Then
$$ar^3=48 \qquad (1)$$
and
$$ar^7=\dfrac{3}{16} \qquad (2)$$
Dividing (2) by (1),
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{ar^7}{ar^3}&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{16}}{48}\\\therefore\ r^4&=\dfrac{1}{256}\\\therefore\ r&=\pm\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
If $r=\dfrac{1}{4}$,
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3&=48\\\therefore\ a&=3072\end{aligned}$$

Stationary point at $x=12$.

A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by
$$f(x)=\begin{cases} 12x^2(1-x), & \text{for } 0\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}.$$
Find the mode of $X$.
items.sol:
Mode of $X$ will be when $f(x)$ has a maximum.
$$f(x)=12x^2-12x^3,\qquad0\le x\le1$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=24x-36x^2\\&=12x(2-3x)\end{aligned}$$
$f'(x)=0$ when $x=0$ and when $2-3x=0$, $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Discard $x=0$ since $f(0)=0$, so the mode of $X$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

items.sol: $$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x12t^2(1-t)\,dt\\&=\int_0^x\left(12t^2-12t^3\right)dt\\&=\left[4t^3-3t^4\right]_0^x\\&=4x^3-3x^4\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line with acceleration $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=1-2t$, for $0\le t\le 2$.

The particle was initially at rest at the origin.
Determine $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ as a function of $t$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= \int (1 - 2t)\,dt \\ &= t - t^2 + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = C = 0$.
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dx}{dt} = t - t^2$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line with acceleration $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=1-2t$, for $0\le t\le 2$.

The particle was initially at rest at the origin.
Find the distance travelled over the first two seconds.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} x_1 &= \int_0^1 \left(t - t^2\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{2} - \dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \int_1^2 \left(t - t^2\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{2} - \dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_1^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{4}{2} - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \text{Total distance} &= \dfrac{1}{6} + \left|-\dfrac{5}{6}\right| \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the geometric series: $\sin^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\cos^4\theta+\cdots$, where $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Show that the limiting sum of the series exists for the given domain.
items.sol:
The common ratio is $r = \cos^2\theta$.

Since $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$,
$$\begin{aligned} 0 < \cos\theta &< 1 \\ 0 < \cos^2\theta &< 1 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ |r| < 1$, so the limiting sum exists.

items.part:
Consider the geometric series: $\sin^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\cos^4\theta+\cdots$, where $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Find the limiting sum of the series.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{1-\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

Working:

When $x > 2$: $y = 3 - x$ and $y = 2x - 4$.

When $x = \dfrac{7}{3}$, $y = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= a - 2 \\ a &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=xe^{-x^2}$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$. You do NOT need to check the nature of the stationary points.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2xe^{-x^2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= x\left(-2xe^{-x^2}\right) + e^{-x^2} \\ &= (1-2x^2)e^{-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} (1-2x^2)e^{-x^2} &= 0 \\ 1 - 2x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ x &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \text{ or } x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$f\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}$$
When $x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$f\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}$$
$\therefore$ The stationary points are
$$\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}\right)$$
and
$$\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}\right)$$

Interest on the loan is charged at 6% per annum, compounded monthly. Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after the $n$th monthly repayment.
Show that the monthly repayment is \$2998, correct to the nearest dollar.

Jackie took a loan of \$500 000, which is to be repaid over 30 years, by 360 equal monthly repayments of $\text{\textdollar}M$. The first repayment will be made one month after the loan is taken out. Interest on the loan is charged at 6% per annum, compounded monthly. Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after the $n$th monthly repayment.
After how many more months will the amount owing be completely repaid?
items.sol:
She needs to repay for $n$ more months:
$$\begin{aligned} 350000(1.005)^n - 2998\left(\dfrac{1.005^n - 1}{0.005}\right) &= 0 \\ 350000(1.005)^n - 2998\times 200\left(1.005^n - 1\right) &= 0 \\ (350000 - 2998\times 200)\,1.005^n &= -2998\times 200 \\ 1.005^n &= \dfrac{1499}{624} \\ n &= \log_{1.005}\left(\dfrac{1499}{624}\right) \\ n &= 175.72 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The loan is repaid after $176$ more months.

items.part:
Jackie took a loan of \$500 000, which is to be repaid over 30 years, by 360 equal monthly repayments of $\text{\textdollar}M$. The first repayment will be made one month after the loan is taken out. Interest on the loan is charged at 6% per annum, compounded monthly. Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after the $n$th monthly repayment.
Find the amount of the last repayment. Give your answer correct to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
When $n = 175$:
$$350000(1.005)^{175} - 2998\times 200\left(1.005^{175} - 1\right) = 2144.74\ldots$$
After one month, the last repayment is
$$2144.74\times 1.005 = 2155.46\ldots \approx \$2156$$
Method 2: when $n = 176$:
$$350000(1.005)^{176} - 2998\times 200\left(1.005^{176} - 1\right) \approx -842.54$$
$$2998 + (-842.54) \approx \$2156$$
$\therefore$ The last repayment is $\$2156$.

items.part:
The lamp shown in the diagram below can move along the vertical line $OB$ using a pulley system. The point $A$ lies on the horizontal line $OA$ at a distance of $d$ from $O$. The intensity $I$ of light from the lamp at point $A$ is inversely proportional to the square of its distance $r$ from the lamp. The intensity $I$ is also directly proportional to $\sin\phi$, where $\phi$ is the angle of elevation from $A$ to the lamp. Hence, the formula for $I$ can be expressed as:
$$I=\dfrac{C\sin\phi}{r^2}, \quad \text{where } C \text{ is a positive constant.}$$
Determine the height $h$ of the lamp above the line $OA$ that maximizes the intensity of light at the point $A$. Express your answer in terms of $d$.

\exfigure{408_q31_1}
items.sol:
The lamp is $h$ above $O$ and $A$ is $d$ from $O$, so $O$, $A$ and the lamp form a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $r$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$r^2 = h^2 + d^2$$
$\phi$ is the angle at $A$, and the side opposite it is $h$:
$$\sin\phi = \dfrac{h}{r} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}$$
Substitute both into $I = \dfrac{C\sin\phi}{r^2}$ to write $I$ in terms of $h$ only:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= C\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+d^2}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{h^2+d^2}\right) \\ &= Ch(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate using the product rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dh} &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} + Ch\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)(2h)(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}} \\ &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}\left[(h^2+d^2) - 3h^2\right] \\ &= C(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}(d^2 - 2h^2) \end{aligned}$$
Since $C>0$ and $(h^2+d^2)^{-\frac{5}{2}}>0$, $\dfrac{dI}{dh}=0$ when
$$\begin{aligned} d^2 - 2h^2 &= 0 \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{d^2}{2} \\ h &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}d \quad (h>0) \end{aligned}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dI}{dh}$ is the sign of $d^2-2h^2$. Test either side:
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{d}{2}: & d^2-2\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{d^2}{2} > 0 \\ h &= d: & d^2-2d^2 &= -d^2 < 0 \end{aligned}$$
$I$ increases then decreases, so the stationary point is a maximum.

$\therefore$ The intensity at $A$ is greatest when $h = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}d$.

items.part:
Consider the functions $f(x)=2^x$ and $g(x)=3^x$.
Find a single transformation that transforms the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the graph of $y=g(x)$.
items.sol:
$$f(x) = 2^x$$
$$g(x) = \left(2^{\log_2 3}\right)^x = 2^{(\log_2 3)x}$$
$\therefore$ Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{\log_2 3}$ (or $\log_3 2$).
items.final: Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{\log_2 3}$ (or $\log_3 2$)

items.part:
Consider the functions $f(x)=2^x$ and $g(x)=3^x$.
A new function $h(x)$ is found by taking the graph of $y=-g(-x)$ and translating it up by $b$ units, where $b>1$.

Sketch the graph of $y=h(x)$ showing the $x$-intercept and the asymptote in terms of $b$.
items.sol:
$$-g(-x) = -3^{-x}$$
$$h(x) = -3^{-x} + b = -\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^x + b$$
For the $y$-intercept, $x = 0$: $h(0) = b - 1$.

For the $x$-intercept:
$$\begin{aligned} -\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^x + b &= 0 \\ b &= \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^x \\ x &= \log_{\frac{1}{3}} b = -\log_3 b \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{408_q32_s1}

items.part:
Consider the functions $f(x)=2^x$ and $g(x)=3^x$.
Hence find the value of $b$ such that the area bounded by the curve $y=h(x)$, the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis is exactly $\dfrac{1}{\ln 3}$ square units.
items.sol:
$$\int_{-\log_3 b}^{0} \left(-3^{-x} + b\right)dx = \dfrac{1}{\ln 3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left[\dfrac{3^{-x}}{\ln 3} + bx\right]_{-\log_3 b}^{0} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} + 0\right) - \left(\dfrac{3^{\log_3 b}}{\ln 3} - b\log_3 b\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b \end{aligned}$$
LHS = RHS:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ -\dfrac{b}{\ln 3} + b\log_3 b &= 0 \\ b\log_3 b &= \dfrac{b}{\ln 3} \end{aligned}$$
Since $b \ne 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_3 b &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ \dfrac{\ln b}{\ln 3} &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \\ \ln b &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b = e$$

Read $\log_e(2x-1)^4$ as $\ln\big[(2x-1)^4\big]$. By the log laws,
$$y = 4\ln(2x-1)$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 4\times\dfrac{2}{2x-1} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{2x-1} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: $y=\dfrac{x}{\sin^2 x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin^2 x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2\sin x\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{vu' - uv'}{v^2} = \dfrac{\sin^2 x - 2x\sin x\cos x}{\sin^4 x}$$
Cancel a factor of $\sin x$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\sin x - 2x\cos x}{\sin^3 x}$$

Using the standard form $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^x = a^x\ln a$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3^x\ln 3$$

items.part:
Integrate the following
$$\int 3e^{5x+1}-\dfrac{1}{x^3}\,dx$$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int\left(3e^{5x+1} - x^{-3}\right)dx &= \dfrac{3}{5}e^{5x+1} - \dfrac{x^{-2}}{-2} + C \\ &= \dfrac{3}{5}e^{5x+1} + \dfrac{1}{2x^2} + C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{8}} \sec^2 2x\,dx$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{8}}\sec^2 2x\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\tan 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{8}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\tan 0 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1) - 0 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the area bounded by $y=\ln x$ and the y-axis from $y=0$ to $y=\ln 3$.
items.sol:
The region lies between the curve and the $y$-axis, so integrate with respect to $y$.

From $y = \ln x$, $x = e^y$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{\ln 3}e^y\,dy \\ &= \Big[e^y\Big]_0^{\ln 3} \\ &= e^{\ln 3} - e^0 \\ &= 3 - 1 \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The area is $2$ square units.

items.part: Differentiate $\cos 3x^3$
items.sol:
Let $u = 3x^3$, so $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 9x^2$. By the chain rule,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\cos 3x^3 &= -\sin(3x^3)\cdot 9x^2 \\ &= -9x^2\sin 3x^3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle \int x^2\sin 3x^3\,dx$
items.sol:
From (i),
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos 3x^3 = -9x^2\sin 3x^3$$
so
$$\begin{aligned} \int x^2\sin 3x^3\,dx &= -\dfrac{1}{9}\int -9x^2\sin 3x^3\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{9}\cos 3x^3 + C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation given by $2\ln x=\ln(3-2x)$
items.sol:
We need $x > 0$ and $3 - 2x > 0$, so $0 < x < \dfrac{3}{2}$.

Using log laws, $2\ln x = \ln x^2$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \ln x^2 &= \ln(3 - 2x) \\ x^2 &= 3 - 2x \\ x^2 + 2x - 3 &= 0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \text{ or } x = -3 \end{aligned}$$
$x = -3$ is rejected because $\ln(-3)$ is undefined.
$$\therefore\ x = 1$$

Read the features of $f'(x)$ from $y = f(x)$.

$f$ has stationary points at $x = -a$ (minimum), $x = 0$ (maximum) and $x = a$ (minimum), so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$ at $x = -a, 0, a$.

Sign of $f'(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &< 0 &&\text{for } x < -a &&\text{decreasing}\\ f'(x) &> 0 &&\text{for } -a < x < 0 &&\text{increasing}\\ f'(x) &< 0 &&\text{for } 0 < x < a &&\text{decreasing}\\ f'(x) &> 0 &&\text{for } x > a &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
Because $f$ is even, $f'$ is odd: the graph has point symmetry about the origin. Its turning points are at the $x$-values of the two points of inflection of $f$.

items.part:
Water is flowing out of a pool at a rate given by $R=4t-t^2$ cubic metres/minute.

If the volume of water in the pool is initially 20 cubic metres, find the amount of the water in the pool after 4 minutes.
items.sol:
Let $V$ be the volume of water in m$^3$. Water flows out, so
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-(4t-t^2)$$
Volume that flows out in the first $4$ minutes:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4(4t-t^2)\,dt&=\left[2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^4\\ &=32-\dfrac{64}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$$
Volume left after $4$ minutes:
$$\begin{aligned}V(4)&=20-\dfrac{32}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{28}{3}\approx9.33\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the curve given by $f(x)=2xe^{-x}$
Show that $f'(x)=2e^{-x}(1-x)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=2 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2e^{-x} + 2x(-e^{-x}) \\ &= 2e^{-x} - 2xe^{-x} \\ &= 2e^{-x}(1-x) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the curve given by $f(x)=2xe^{-x}$
Hence or otherwise find any stationary point(s) and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x) = 0$.

Since $2e^{-x} > 0$ for all $x$, we need $1 - x = 0$, so $x = 1$.

$f(1) = 2e^{-1} = \dfrac{2}{e}$.

Nature:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= -2e^{-x}(1-x) - 2e^{-x} \\ &= 2e^{-x}(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$f''(1) = 2e^{-1}(-1) = -\dfrac{2}{e} < 0$, so the curve is concave down there.

$\therefore$ $\left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.

items.part:
For the curve given by $f(x)=2xe^{-x}$
Determine $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to\infty} f(x)$.
items.sol:
$f(x) = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$. As $x \to \infty$, $e^x$ grows much faster than $2x$, so
$$\lim_{x \to \infty} 2xe^{-x} = 0$$

items.sol:

$$x(0) = 0, \qquad x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 1 - 2\cos 0 = -1, \qquad x(\pi) = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = 1 + 1 = 2$$
Distance for $0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{3}$: $|-1 - 0| = 1$ m.

Distance for $\dfrac{\pi}{3} \le t \le \pi$: $|2 - (-1)| = 3$ m.

$\therefore$ Total distance $= 1 + 3 = 4$ m.

items.part:
An isosceles trapezium $ABCD$ is drawn with its vertices on a semicircle centre $O$ and diameter 20 cm. Perpendiculars $BE$ and $CF$ are drawn to meet the diameter $AD$ as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{568_q16_1}
Show that the area of the trapezium $ABCD$ is given by
$$A=\dfrac{1}{4}(x+20)\sqrt{400-x^2}.$$
items.sol:
$BCFE$ is a rectangle, so $BC = EF = EO + OF = x$. The parallel sides are $AD = 20$ and $BC = x$, and the height is $BE$.

Area of a trapezium:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}(AD + BC)\times BE \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(20 + x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{400 - x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}(x + 20)\sqrt{400 - x^2} \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, on $(x+20)\sqrt{400-x^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+20 & v&=\sqrt{400-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{400-x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\sqrt{400 - x^2} + (x + 20)\cdot\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{400 - x^2}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{400 - x^2 - x^2 - 20x}{4\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \\ &= \dfrac{-2(x^2 + 10x - 200)}{4\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \\ &= -\dfrac{(x + 20)(x - 10)}{2\sqrt{400 - x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$: since $0 < x < 20$, $x + 20 \neq 0$, so $x = 10$.

Nature:
$$\begin{aligned} x &< 10 &&\text{(just below)}: & \dfrac{dA}{dx} &> 0\\ x &> 10 &&\text{(just above)}: & \dfrac{dA}{dx} &< 0\end{aligned}$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ changes from $+$ to $-$, so $x = 10$ gives a maximum.

$\therefore$ Since $BC = x$, the area is maximised when $BC = 10$ cm. (The maximum area is $75\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}^2$.)

items.part: In any set of tennis between two players A and B, the probability that player A wins the set is $\dfrac{2}{3}$ and the probability that player B wins the set is $\dfrac{1}{3}$. items.part:
The ages of the $80\,000$ residents of Bayview are normally distributed with mean 50 years and standard deviation 15 years.
Find the expected number of residents of Bayview who are either younger than 20 or older than 65.
items.sol:
Let the random variable $X$ be the age of a resident, and $Z$ the standard normal random variable.

Then $P(X<20\text{ or }X>65)=1-P(20<X<65)$.

Using $z=\dfrac{x-50}{15}$, this probability is
$$\begin{aligned}1-P(-2<Z<1)&\approx 1-\dfrac{1}{2}(0.95+0.68)\\ &=0.185\end{aligned}$$
Hence the required expected number is $0.185\times 80\,000=14\,800$.

items.part:

items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>80\,|\,X>65)&=P(Z>2\,|\,Z>1)\\ &=\dfrac{P(Z>2)}{P(Z>1)}\\ &\approx\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}(1-0.95)}{\frac{1}{2}(1-0.68)}\\ &=0.15625\end{aligned}$$
Hence the required probability is approximately $0.156$.

items.sol:
Since
$$\int_0^2 f(x)\,dx=1$$

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{10}\int_0^2(k^2x-kx^2)\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{1}{10}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}k^2x^2-\dfrac{1}{3}kx^3\right]_0^2&=1\\ \dfrac{1}{10}\left\{\dfrac{1}{2}k^2(4-0)-\dfrac{1}{3}k(8-0)\right\}&=1\\ \dfrac{1}{5}k^2-\dfrac{4}{15}k&=1\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ 3k^2-4k-15=0$

$(3k+5)(k-3)=0$

Since $k>0$, $k=3$.

items.part: If $y=\ln(1+\sin x)$ for $0\le x\le \pi$, show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+e^{-y}=0$ .
items.sol:
$y=\ln(1+\sin x)$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=\dfrac{-\sin x(1+\sin x)-\cos x\cdot\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-(\sin^2x+\cos^2x)-\sin x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-(1+\sin x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{(1+\sin x)}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{e^y}\\ &=-e^{-y}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+e^{-y}=0$$

items.part: Use the result in part (a) to determine the concavity of the curve for $0\le x\le \pi$.
items.sol:
$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-e^{-y}<0$ for all $y$ and hence for all $x$ in the domain $0\le x\le\pi$.

Hence the curve is always concave down.
items.final: The curve is always concave down for $0\le x\le\pi$.

items.part: Find the coordinates and nature of any stationary points on the curve $y=\dfrac{a}{x}+\ln x$ for $x>0$, where $a>0$ is a constant.
items.sol:
$y=\dfrac{a}{x}+\ln x$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{-a}{x^2}+\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=\dfrac{x-a}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=0 &&\text{when } x=a &&\text{stationary}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&<0 &&\text{for } 0<x<a &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&>0 &&\text{for } x>a &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ (a,\ 1+\ln a)$ is a minimum turning point.
items.final: $(a,\ 1+\ln a)$ is a minimum turning point

A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $a=2e^{-t}\text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Initially it is 2 metres to the right of $O$ and is moving towards $O$ with speed $1\text{ ms}^{-1}$.
Show that $v=1-2e^{-t}$ and $x=t+2e^{-t}$.
items.sol:
$a=2e^{-t}$

$v=-2e^{-t}+c$

When $t=0$, $v=-1$, so $-1=-2+c$.

$\therefore\ c=1$

$\therefore\ v=1-2e^{-t}$

$x=t+2e^{-t}+d$

When $t=0$, $x=2$, so $2=2+d$.

$\therefore\ d=0$

$\therefore\ x=t+2e^{-t}$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $a=2e^{-t}\text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Initially it is 2 metres to the right of $O$ and is moving towards $O$ with speed $1\text{ ms}^{-1}$.
Find in simplest exact form when and where the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
When $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^{-t}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ e^t&=2\\ \therefore\ t&=\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=t+2e^{-t}\\ &=\ln 2+2\times\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=1+\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
At rest $(1+\ln 2)$ m to the right of $O$ at time $\ln 2$ seconds.
items.final: At rest $(1+\ln 2)$ m to the right of $O$ at time $\ln 2$ seconds

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $a=2e^{-t}\text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Initially it is 2 metres to the right of $O$ and is moving towards $O$ with speed $1\text{ ms}^{-1}$.
Find in simplest exact form the distance travelled by the particle in the first $\ln 8$ seconds of its motion.
items.sol:
When $t=\ln 8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\ln 8+2e^{\ln\frac{1}{8}}\\ &=3\ln 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Hence in the first $\ln 8$ seconds:

the particle travels left $2-(1+\ln 2)$ metres,

then is instantaneously at rest before moving off to the right (since $a>0$),

travelling a further $\left(3\ln 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)-(1+\ln 2)$ metres.

Required distance is $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}+\ln 2\right)$ metres.

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$ .
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)&=\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\cdot x-(\ln x)\cdot 1}{x^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Use the result in part (a) to show that $\displaystyle\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx=\ln 2-1$ .
items.sol:
If $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$, then
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}&=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\times\dfrac{x}{\ln x}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx&=\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)\right]_e^{e^2}\\ &=\left[\ln(\ln x)-\ln x\right]_e^{e^2}\\ &=\ln 2-\ln 1-(2-1)\\ &=\ln 2-1\end{aligned}$$

The letters of the word ALGEBRA are written on seven separate cards. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{A} & \text{L} & \text{G} & \text{E} & \text{B} & \text{R} & \text{A}\\\hline\end{array}$$ Two cards are chosen at random without replacement.
What is the probability that only one of the cards chosen is the letter A?
items.sol:

$$P(\text{first card is not A and second card is A})=\dfrac{5}{7}\times\dfrac{2}{6}=\dfrac{5}{21}$$

items.sol:
Let radius $r=OX=OZ$.
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times r^2\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=12\pi$$
Hence $r=6\text{ cm}$.
$$\text{Arc length of shaded region}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\times 6=8\pi\text{ cm}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Perimeter of shaded region}&=OX+OZ+8\pi\\ &=6+6+8\pi\\ &=12+8\pi\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$

Katrina runs a business refurbishing old computers.

The cost, $C$ dollars, of refurbishing $n$ computers is given by $C=3n^2+100$.

The income, $I$ dollars, received from selling $n$ computers is given by $I=80n$.

Determine the minimum and maximum number of computers that Katrina can refurbish and sell to make a profit.
items.sol:
Solve $3n^2+100=80n$.
$$\begin{aligned}3n^2-80n+100&=0\\ n&=\dfrac{80\pm\sqrt{(-80)^2-4\times 3\times 100}}{2\times 3}\\ n&=1.315,\ 25.352\end{aligned}$$
Katrina will make a profit when $I>C$ and this occurs for $2\le n\le 25$, where $n$ represents the number of computers refurbished and sold.

Hence, the minimum number is 2 and the maximum number is 25 in order to make a profit.

items.part: The following table shows the probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$. \extable{Tp70_1} Given that $E(X)=2.08$, find the values of $p$ and $q$.
items.sol:
Sum of probabilities equals 1:
$$\begin{aligned}0.05+p+p+q+0.01&=1\\ 2p+q&=0.94\quad(1)\end{aligned}$$
$E(X)=2.08$:
$$\begin{aligned}(0\times 0.05)+(1\times p)+(2\times p)+(3\times q)+(4\times 0.01)&=2.08\\ 3p+3q&=2.04\\ p+q&=0.68\quad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Solve (1) and (2) simultaneously.

From (1): $q=0.94-2p$.

Substitute for $q$ in (2):
$$\begin{aligned}p+0.94-2p&=0.68\\ -p&=-0.26\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ p=0.26$ and $q=0.42$

items.part:
The shoe size of women in a town is normally distributed with a mean size of 8 and a standard deviation of 1.

A shoe shop in the town sells women's shoes ranging from size 5 to size 10.

Given that there are 4000 women in the town, how many would be expected to find shoes that fit them in this shop?
items.sol:
$z$-score corresponding to size 5:
$$z=\dfrac{5-8}{1}=-3$$
$z$-score corresponding to size 10:
$$z=\dfrac{10-8}{1}=2$$
By the empirical rule, the area under the standard normal curve from $z=-3$ to $z=2$ is
$$\dfrac{99.7\%}{2}+\dfrac{95\%}{2}=97.35\%$$
$$4000\times 97.35\%=3894$$
3894 women in the town can be expected to buy shoes that fit them.

$$-f(x)=-2x+\sin x$$

items.part:
Ashford ($A$), Brookdale ($B$) and Carlton ($C$) are three country towns.

Brookdale is 85 km east and 33 km north of Ashford.

Carlton is on a bearing of $026^\circ$ from Ashford and $321^\circ$ from Brookdale.

Jo completes a cross-country drive which starts and finishes in Ashford and passes through Brookdale and Carlton.

Calculate the total distance that Jo travelled, correct to the nearest kilometre. \exfigure{1346_q22_1}
items.sol:
By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$AB=\sqrt{85^2+33^2}=91.181\ldots$$
$$\text{Angle }DAB=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{33}{85}\right)=21^\circ 13'$$
$$\text{Angle }CAB=90^\circ-26^\circ-21^\circ 13'=42^\circ 47'$$
$$\text{Angle }ACB=(360^\circ-321^\circ)+26^\circ=65^\circ\quad\text{(angles at a point and alternate angles)}$$
$$\text{Angle }ABC=180^\circ-65^\circ-42^\circ 47'=72^\circ 13'\quad\text{(angle sum of triangle }ABC\text{)}$$
By the sine rule:
$$AC=\dfrac{\sin 72^\circ 13'\times 91.181}{\sin 65^\circ}=95.800$$
$$BC=\dfrac{\sin 42^\circ 47'\times 91.181}{\sin 65^\circ}=68.335$$
Alternatively, $BC$ may be determined using the cosine rule:
$$BC=\sqrt{91.181^2+95.800^2-2\times 91.181\times 95.800\times\cos 42^\circ 47'}=68.335$$
Perimeter of triangle $ABC$:
$$91.181+95.800+68.335=255.316$$
The total distance travelled is 255 km, correct to the nearest kilometre.

A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function given by $$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right), & \text{for }0\le x\le\pi\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of }x\end{cases}.$$
Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$.
items.sol:
Solve for $k$:
$$\begin{aligned}k\int_0^{\pi}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)dx&=1\\ 3k\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{\pi}&=1\\ 3k\left(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\tan\left(\dfrac{0}{3}\right)\right)&=1\\ 3k\times\sqrt{3}&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function given by $$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right), & \text{for }0\le x\le\pi\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of }x\end{cases}.$$
Find the median of $X$, correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
From part (a), solve for $t$:
$$3k\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{t}=0.5,\text{ where }k=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$$
$$\begin{aligned}3\times\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\right]_0^{t}&=0.5\\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan\left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right)-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan\left(\dfrac{0}{3}\right)&=0.5\\ \tan\left(\dfrac{t}{3}\right)&=0.5\times\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=3\tan^{-1}(0.5\times\sqrt{3})=2.14\text{ (correct to two decimal places)}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x-2}}$.

Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=\sqrt{x-2}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x-2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\dfrac{4\sqrt{x-2}-\frac{4x}{2\sqrt{x-2}}}{x-2}\\ &=\dfrac{4\sqrt{x-2}-\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x-2}}}{x-2}\end{aligned}$$
Solve $f'(x)=0$ to find any stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned}4\sqrt{x-2}-\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{x-2}}&=0\\ 4(x-2)-2x&=0\\ 4x-8-2x&=0\\ 2x&=8\end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=4$.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{4\times 4}{\sqrt{4-2}}=8\sqrt{2}$$
A stationary point exists at $(4,8\sqrt{2})$.

Using a table of gradients to determine the nature of the stationary point:

\extable{Ts71_1}

Hence the stationary point is a local minimum.
items.final: Stationary point at $(4, 8\sqrt{2})$, a local minimum

The rate of fuel consumption of a particular vehicle may be modelled by the formula

$$R=5+4e^{-0.5t},$$

where $R$ is the rate of fuel consumption, in litres per hour, after $t$ hours of travel.

In the first hour of travel, the vehicle consumed 25 litres of fuel.

Determine the amount of fuel consumed after 4 hours of travel, correct to the nearest litre.
items.sol:
The amount of fuel, $F(t)$ litres, consumed at time $t$ hours is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int R\,dt \\ &= \int 5+4e^{-0.5t}\,dt \\ &= 5t-8e^{-0.5t}+c \end{aligned}$$
At time $t=1$, the vehicle has consumed 25 litres of fuel since the start of the journey.

Finding the constant of integration, $c$:
$$\begin{aligned} 25 &= 5(1)-8e^{-0.5(1)}+c \\ 20 &= -8e^{-0.5}+c \\ c &= 20+8e^{-0.5} \end{aligned}$$
At time $t=4$, the amount of fuel the vehicle consumed is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F &= 5(4)-8e^{-0.5(4)}+20+8e^{-0.5} \\ &= 43.7695\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ After 4 hours of travel, the vehicle has consumed 44 litres of fuel.

Maroun deposits \$500 000 into a retirement fund which earns compound interest at the rate of 0.3\% per month.

Maroun withdraws spending money from the retirement fund at the end of each month.

The incomplete table below shows the account activity for the first four months and the balance at the end of the fifth month. \exfigure{1346_q28_1}
Calculate the amount of money that Maroun withdrew at the end of the fifth month.
items.sol:
Balance at the end of the fourth month:
$$496994.00+1490.98-3800=494684.98$$
$\therefore$ Balance at the end of the fourth month is $\$494\,684.98$.

Interest earned at the end of the fifth month:
$$494684.98\times 0.003=1484.05$$
$\therefore$ Interest earned at the end of the fifth month is $\$1484.05$.

Amount Maroun withdrew at the end of the fifth month:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Balance} &= P+I-M \\ M &= P+I-\text{Balance} \\ &= 494684.98+1484.05-491969.03 \\ &= 4200 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Maroun withdrew $\$4200$ at the end of the fifth month.

Maroun deposits \$500 000 into a retirement fund which earns compound interest at the rate of 0.3\% per month.

Maroun withdraws spending money from the retirement fund at the end of each month.

The incomplete table below shows the account activity for the first four months and the balance at the end of the fifth month. \exfigure{1346_q28_1}
Maroun is going to withdraw \$7500 at the end of each month, starting from the end of the sixth month.

The recurrence relation $A_n=A_{n-1}\times 1.003-7500$ models this situation, where $A_n$ is the balance in the retirement fund at the end of the $n$th month.

Determine the balance in Maroun's retirement fund at the end of the seventh month.

Maroun deposits \$500 000 into a retirement fund which earns compound interest at the rate of 0.3\% per month.

Maroun withdraws spending money from the retirement fund at the end of each month.

The incomplete table below shows the account activity for the first four months and the balance at the end of the fifth month. \exfigure{1346_q28_1}
Maroun is offered an alternative retirement fund, where interest is paid at 3.2\% per annum, compounded daily.

By calculating the effective annual rate of interest for both retirement funds, or otherwise, determine whether Maroun should remain with the current retirement fund or change to the alternative retirement fund.
items.sol:
Effective annual rate of interest for the current retirement fund:
$$\begin{aligned} (1+0.003)^{12}-1 &= 0.036599\ldots \\ &\approx 3.66\%\text{ p.a.} \end{aligned}$$
Effective annual rate of interest for the alternative retirement fund:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(1+\dfrac{0.032}{365}\right)^{365}-1 &= 0.032516\ldots \\ &\approx 3.25\%\text{ p.a.} \end{aligned}$$
The effective annual rate of interest for the alternative retirement fund is less than Maroun's current retirement fund, hence Maroun should stay with his current retirement fund.

Alternatively, compare the future value (FV) of one dollar invested in both funds.

Current fund:
$$\text{FV}=(1+0.3\%)^{12}=\$1.03659998$$
Alternative fund:
$$\text{FV}=\left(1+\dfrac{3.2\%}{365}\right)^{365}=\$1.032516057$$
The FV of the alternative fund is less than the FV of the current fund, hence Maroun should stay with his current retirement fund.
items.final: Maroun should stay with his current retirement fund (3.66% p.a. vs 3.25% p.a. effective rate).

items.part:
A rocket is returning back to Earth after completing a space mission.

Its distance from Earth can be modelled by the equation

$$S=55000\times 3^{-0.182t},$$

where $S$ is the distance from Earth in kilometres at time $t$ hours after it begins its return journey.
Find the speed of the rocket after 2 hours on its return journey.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} S'(t)=\dfrac{dS}{dt} &= -0.182\times\ln 3\times 55000\times 3^{-0.182t} \\ &= -10010\ln 3\times 3^{-0.182t} \end{aligned}$$
Speed of the rocket at time $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} S'(2) &= -10010\ln 3\times 3^{-0.182\times 2} \\ &= -7372.3576\ldots \\ \text{speed} &= |S'(2)| \approx 7372 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The speed of the rocket 2 hours after it begins its return journey is $7372 \text{ km/h}$.

items.part:
A rocket is returning back to Earth after completing a space mission.

Its distance from Earth can be modelled by the equation

$$S=55000\times 3^{-0.182t},$$

where $S$ is the distance from Earth in kilometres at time $t$ hours after it begins its return journey.
When the rocket reaches a distance of 1000 km from Earth, a parachute is released.

How long, in hours, after the rocket begins its return journey does it release its parachute? Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Let $S=1000$ and solve the equation for $t$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000 &= 55000\times 3^{-0.182t} \\ \dfrac{1}{55} &= 3^{-0.182t} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{55}\right) &= -0.182t\times\ln 3 \\ t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{55}\right)\div(-0.182\times\ln 3) \\ &= 20.0419\ldots \\ &\approx 20.04 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The rocket deploys its parachute 20.04 hours after it begins its return journey.

items.part:
The graph below shows the curve $y=x^3-3x^2+3x+4$.

Using two applications of the Trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$, determine how much the Trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve. \exfigure{1346_q30_1}
items.sol:
Exact area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^3 x^3-3x^2+3x+4\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^3+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^3 \\ &= \dfrac{75}{4}\text{ or }18.75 \end{aligned}$$
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule from $x=0$ to $x=3$ means two strips, each of width
$$h=\dfrac{3-0}{2}=1.5$$
so the function values are needed at $x=0,\ 1.5,\ 3$:
$$f(0)=4,\qquad f(1.5)=5.125,\qquad f(3)=13$$
Estimate using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+f(x_2)\right\}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1.5}{2}[4+2\times 5.125+13] \\ &\approx 20.4375 \end{aligned}$$
$$20.4375-18.75=1.6875$$
$\therefore$ The trapezoidal rule overestimates the exact area under the curve by $1.6875 \text{ units}^2$.

items.part:
A ball is dropped from a height $H$ metres above the ground. Each time it strikes the ground, it rebounds to a lower height which is $q\%$ of its previous height.

Let $h_n$ be the height reached by the ball after the $n$th bounce.
Show that, after the second bounce, the ball rebounds to a height given by

$$h_2=\dfrac{q^2H}{(100)^2}.$$
items.sol:
Initial height of the ball is $H$ metres.

The height after the $n$th bounce is the $n$th term of the geometric progression with first term $a=\dfrac{qH}{100}$ (the first rebound) and common ratio $r=\dfrac{q}{100}$, $0<q<100$.

Height after the second bounce:
$$\begin{aligned} h_n &= T_n=ar^{n-1} \\ h_2 &= \dfrac{qH}{100}\times\dfrac{q}{100} \\ &= \dfrac{q^2H}{(100)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A ball is dropped from a height $H$ metres above the ground. Each time it strikes the ground, it rebounds to a lower height which is $q\%$ of its previous height.

Let $h_n$ be the height reached by the ball after the $n$th bounce.
Show that the total distance, $D$, travelled by the ball is given by

$$D=\dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q}.$$
items.sol:
Total distance travelled may be modelled as the limiting sum of a geometric series, since $0<r<1$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= H+2(h_1+h_2+h_3+\cdots) \\ &= H+2\left(\dfrac{\frac{qH}{100}}{1-\frac{q}{100}}\right) \\ &= H+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100-q)}{100-q}+\dfrac{2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H-qH+2qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{100H+qH}{100-q} \\ &= \dfrac{H(100+q)}{100-q} \end{aligned}$$

A rectangular canvas sheet is folded to form the cover of a tent with a pentagonal cross-section, as shown in the following diagrams. \exfigure{1346_q32_1} The vertical heights on the sides of the tent are $y$ metres and the slant lengths are $4x$ metres. The horizontal distance between the vertical sides is $5x$ metres and the width of the tent is 6 metres.
Show that $y=10-4x$, given the area of the canvas sheet is $120\text{ m}^2$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} 6\times(2y+8x) &= 120 \\ 2y+8x &= 20 \\ y+4x &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=10-4x$$

items.part:
A rectangular canvas sheet is folded to form the cover of a tent with a pentagonal cross-section, as shown in the following diagrams. \exfigure{1346_q32_1} The vertical heights on the sides of the tent are $y$ metres and the slant lengths are $4x$ metres. The horizontal distance between the vertical sides is $5x$ metres and the width of the tent is 6 metres.
The following diagram shows the cross-section of the tent, where $h$ is the height of the top of the tent from the vertical sides. \exfigure{1346_q32_2} Show that $h=\dfrac{\sqrt{39}x}{2}$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} h^2 &= (4x)^2-\left(\dfrac{5x}{2}\right)^2 \\ &= 16x^2-\dfrac{25x^2}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{64x^2}{4}-\dfrac{25x^2}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{39x^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \sqrt{\dfrac{39x^2}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{39}\,x}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rectangular canvas sheet is folded to form the cover of a tent with a pentagonal cross-section, as shown in the following diagrams. \exfigure{1346_q32_1} The vertical heights on the sides of the tent are $y$ metres and the slant lengths are $4x$ metres. The horizontal distance between the vertical sides is $5x$ metres and the width of the tent is 6 metres.
Find the value of $x$ which maximises the volume of the tent.
items.sol:
Maximise the volume by maximising the area of the cross-section, since the depth is constant.

Let $A$ be the area of the cross-section of the tent.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5xy+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 5x\times h \\ &= 5xy+\dfrac{5xh}{2} \end{aligned}$$
From parts (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5x(10-4x)+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4} \\ &= 50x-20x^2+\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}x^2}{4} \\ &= 50x-\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x^2 \end{aligned}$$
Determine the stationary point and its nature:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=50-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x$$
$$\begin{aligned} 50-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x &= 0 \\ \left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x &= 25 \\ x &= 25\div\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right) \\ &= 2.05 \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=-2\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)=-24.387\ldots<0$$
$\therefore$ Maximum volume at $x=2.05$.

items.part:
A rectangular canvas sheet is folded to form the cover of a tent with a pentagonal cross-section, as shown in the following diagrams. \exfigure{1346_q32_1} The vertical heights on the sides of the tent are $y$ metres and the slant lengths are $4x$ metres. The horizontal distance between the vertical sides is $5x$ metres and the width of the tent is 6 metres.
Hence, find the maximum volume of the tent, correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
Maximum volume of tent $=$ maximum area of cross-section $\times$ depth.

From part (c):
$$V=6\times\left(50x-\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)x^2\right),\quad x=2.05$$
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 6\times\left(50\times 2.05-\left(20-\dfrac{5\sqrt{39}}{4}\right)\times 2.05^2\right) \\ &= 307.5345\ldots \\ &\approx 307.5\text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows the graphs of $y=x^3-2x$ and $y=x^2$. \exfigure{1346_q33_1} The graphs intersect at $A$, $B$ and the origin, $O$.

By finding the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$, show that the area of the shaded region is $\dfrac{37}{12}$.
items.sol:
Find the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ by equating $y=x^3-2x$ with $y=x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-2x &= x^2 \\ x^3-x^2-2x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-x-2) &= 0 \\ x(x+1)(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $-1$ and the $x$-coordinate of $B$ is $2$.

Area between the two curves is given by
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\int_{-1}^{0}x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_0^2 x^3-x^2-2x\,dx\right| \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|+\left|4-\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right| \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{12} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove that $\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\cos(90^\circ-\theta)}(1+\tan^2\theta)+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}[1+\tan^2(90^\circ-\theta)]=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\cos(90^\circ-\theta)}(1+\tan^2\theta)+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}[1+\tan^2(90^\circ-\theta)] \\ &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\sec^2\theta+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}(1+\cot^2\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} \\ &= 2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
It is known that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$. (Do NOT prove this.)

Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Divide the numerator and denominator of the integrand by $x^2$ such that:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{x\ln x}{x^2}}\,dx \\ &= \int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx \end{aligned}$$
Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$$
and
$$\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$$

$$\int\dfrac{\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}}{\frac{\ln x}{x}}\,dx\text{ is in the form }\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$$
Hence,
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x\ln x}\,dx &= \ln\left|\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right|+c \\ &= \ln|\ln x|-\ln|x|+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $x$ when $x=\log_{31}32\times\log_{30}31\times\log_{29}30\times\ldots\times\log_2 3$ for $x\in\mathbb{Z}$.
items.sol:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$, to each factor:
$$x=\dfrac{\ln32}{\ln31}\times\dfrac{\ln31}{\ln30}\times\dfrac{\ln30}{\ln29}\times\cdots\times\dfrac{\ln4}{\ln3}\times\dfrac{\ln3}{\ln2}$$
Each numerator cancels with the next denominator, leaving
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{\ln32}{\ln2} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln2^5}{\ln2} \\ &= \dfrac{5\ln2}{\ln2} \\ &= 5 \end{aligned}$$

The ages of 26 million residents of Australia are normally distributed with mean of 45 years and standard deviation of 11 years.
Determine the percentage, rounded to the nearest whole number, of individuals under 56 who are also younger than 34.
items.sol:
Method 1:
$$\dfrac{P(34)}{P(56)}=\dfrac{16\%}{84\%}=19\%$$
Method 2:
$$\begin{aligned} P(x<34\mid x<56) &= \dfrac{P(x<34\cap x<56)}{P(x<56)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.1587}{0.8413} \\ &\approx 19\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $3\sin^2 x-\sqrt{3}\sin x=0$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$ to 3 decimal places.
items.sol:
$$\sin x(3\sin x-\sqrt3)=0$$
$\sin x=0$:
$$\therefore\ x=-\pi,\ 0,\ \pi$$
$3\sin x=\sqrt3$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \sin^{-1}\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} \\ &= 0.615,\ 2.526 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-\pi,\ 0,\ 0.615,\ 2.526,\ \pi$$

It is known that the number of students in the group that take Statistics is twice the number of students that take Business. Find the values of $x$ and $y$ in the Venn diagram above.
items.sol:
$$x+y+0.24+0.1=1 \quad\text{or}\quad x+y+0.24=0.9$$

$S=2B$:

Substitute (ii) into (i):

Substitute $y$ into (i):
$$\therefore\ x=0.52$$

items.part:
The derivative of a function is given by: $f'(x)=e^x\sin x$.
Differentiate and simplify $g(x)=e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, on each term. For $e^x\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
For $e^x\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x) &= \sin x\cdot e^x+e^x\cos x-[\cos x\cdot e^x+e^x(-\sin x)] \\ &= e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x-e^x\cos x+e^x\sin x \\ &= 2e^x\sin x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The derivative of a function is given by: $f'(x)=e^x\sin x$.
Hence or otherwise, find $f(x)$ if it is known that $f(\pi)=\dfrac{e^{\pi}}{2}$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \int f'(x)\,dx &= \int e^x\sin x\,dx \\ &= \dfrac12\int2e^x\sin x\,dx \end{aligned}$$
$$f(x)=\dfrac12[e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x]+C$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(\pi) &= \dfrac12(e^\pi\sin\pi-e^\pi\cos\pi)+C \\ \dfrac{e^\pi}{2} &= \dfrac12(0+e^\pi)+C \\ C &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac12(e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x)$$

items.part:
Given the series $1\dfrac{1}{3}+2\dfrac{1}{9}+4\dfrac{1}{27}+8\dfrac{1}{81}\ \ldots$ . Find the expression of the:
general term.
items.sol:
Each term is a whole number plus a fraction:
$$1+\dfrac13,\quad 2+\dfrac19,\quad 4+\dfrac1{27},\quad 8+\dfrac1{81},\ \ldots$$
The whole numbers $1,2,4,8,\ldots$ form a GP with $a_1=1$, $r_1=2$.

The fractions $\dfrac13,\dfrac19,\dfrac1{27},\dfrac1{81},\ldots$ form a second GP with $a_2=\dfrac13$, $r_2=\dfrac13$.

So the general term is the sum of the general terms of the two GPs:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a_1r_1^{n-1}+a_2r_2^{n-1} \\ &= 1(2)^{n-1}+\dfrac13\left(\dfrac13\right)^{n-1} \\ &= 2^{n-1}+\dfrac{1}{3^n} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Given the series $1\dfrac{1}{3}+2\dfrac{1}{9}+4\dfrac{1}{27}+8\dfrac{1}{81}\ \ldots$ . Find the expression of the:
sum.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1}+\dfrac{a_2(1-r^n)}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1(2^n-1)}{2-1}+\dfrac{\frac13\left(1-\frac{1}{3^n}\right)}{1-\frac13} \\ &= 2^n-1+\dfrac12\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \\ &= 2^n-1+\dfrac12-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right) \\ &= 2^n-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)-\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_n=2^n-\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{1}{3^n}\right)-\dfrac12 \text{ or } \dfrac{2^{n+1}-3^{-n}-1}{2}$$

A chocolate making machine produces a sound with intensity of $2.5\times10^{-5}\ W/m^2$.

Calculate the sound level of the machine to 4 decimal places.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} L &= 10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{2.5\times10^{-5}}{10^{-12}}\right) \\ &= 73.9794 \text{ dB} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The decibel level of a sound is given by the formula: $$L=10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)$$ Where $L$ is the sound level in decibels, $I$ is the intensity of the sound in watts per square meter.
A nearby industrial coffee grinder produced a sound that is 20 decibels louder than the chocolate making machine. What is the percentage increase in sound intensity produced by the coffee grinder compared to the chocolate making machine? Leave your answer to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
Coffee $=93.9794$ (i.e. 20 dB louder than the chocolate machine).

Find $I$:
$$\begin{aligned} 93.9794\ldots &= 10\log_{10}\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \\ \dfrac{93.9794\ldots}{10} &= \log_{10}\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \\ 10^{9.39794\ldots} &= \dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \\ I &= 2.5\times10^{-3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \%\text{ increase} &= \dfrac{2.5\times10^{-3}-2.5\times10^{-5}}{2.5\times10^{-5}}\times100\% \\ &= 9900\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1$.
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2-12x+9 \\ &= 3(x-3)(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(x)=6x-12$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(3) &= 18-12=6>0, & f(3) &= 1 &&\text{minimum} \\ f''(1) &= 6-12=-6<0, & f(1) &= 5 &&\text{maximum} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Minimum at $(3,1)$, maximum at $(1,5)$.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1$.
Find any points of inflexion.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)=6x-12 &= 0 \\ x &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
Testing the concavity on either side of $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(1) &= -6<0 &&\text{concave down} \\ f''(3) &= 6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Let the equation of a curve be $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{e^x+1}$. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where $x=1$ in general form.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{(e^x+1)-e^xx}{(e^x+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(1-x)+1}{(e^x+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f'(1)=\dfrac{1}{(e+1)^2}$$
$$m_{\text{normal}}=-(e+1)^2$$
$$f(1)=\dfrac{1}{e+1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{1}{e+1} &= -(e+1)^2(x-1) \\ (e+1)y-1 &= -(e+1)^3x+(e+1)^3 \\ (e+1)^3x+(e+1)y-(1+(e+1)^3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using $y=mx+c$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{e+1} &= -(e+1)^2(1)+c \\ c &= \dfrac{1}{e+1}+(e+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=-(e+1)^2x+\dfrac{1}{e+1}+(e+1)^2$$
$$\therefore\ (e+1)^3x+(e+1)y-1-(e+1)^3=0$$

A right circular cone has height, $H$, and a base of radius $R$. A square prism is inscribed in the cone so that the base of the prism is on the cone's base. The prism has height, $h$, and a square base of side length $x$. \exfigure{1365_q30_1}
By using similar triangles, show that $x=2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)$.
items.sol:
In the cross-section, the triangle above the prism (height $H-h$, base $\dfrac{x}{2}$) is similar to the whole right-angled triangle (height $H$, base $R$): common angle at the apex, both right-angled (equiangular).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{H-h}{H} &= \dfrac{\frac{x}{2}}{R} \\ x &= 2R\left(\dfrac{H-h}{H}\right) \\ &= 2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A right circular cone has height, $H$, and a base of radius $R$. A square prism is inscribed in the cone so that the base of the prism is on the cone's base. The prism has height, $h$, and a square base of side length $x$. \exfigure{1365_q30_1}
Determine the height of the prism, in terms of $H$, that will maximise the volume of the prism.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= x^2h \\ &= \left(2R\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)\right)^2h \\ &= 4R^2h\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)^2 \\ &= 4R^2h\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{H}+\dfrac{h^2}{H^2}\right) \\ &= 4R^2h-\dfrac{8R^2h^2}{H}+\dfrac{4R^2h^3}{H^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dh}=4R^2-\dfrac{16R^2h}{H}+\dfrac{12R^2h^2}{H^2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4R^2\left(1-\dfrac{4h}{H}+\dfrac{3h^2}{H^2}\right) &= 0 \\ 4R^2\left(1-\dfrac{h}{H}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{3h}{H}\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=H \text{ or } h=\dfrac{H}{3}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=-\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{24R^2h}{H^2}$$
At $h=H$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=\dfrac{8R^2}{H}>0$$
$\therefore$ concave up.

At $h=\dfrac{H}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2} &= -\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{24R^2(\frac{H}{3})}{H^2} \\ &= -\dfrac{16R^2}{H}+\dfrac{8R^2}{H} \\ &= -\dfrac{8R^2}{H}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ concave down.

$\therefore\ h=\dfrac{H}{3}$ is a maximum.

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 15x^2+4x^{-3} \\ y' &= 15x^2+\dfrac{4}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$
At $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 15(1)+\dfrac{4}{(1)} \\ y' &= 19 \end{aligned}$$
Using the point–gradient form:
$$\begin{aligned} y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1) \\ y+6 &= 19(x-1) \\ y+6 &= 19x-19 \\ y &= 19x-25 \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{e^x}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{2xe^x-x^2e^x}{e^{2x}}\\ &= \dfrac{xe^x(2-x)}{e^{2x}} \\ &= \dfrac{x(2-x)}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $f'(x)=0$. Since $e^x>0$:
$$x=0 \text{ or } x=2$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= 0\\ f(2) &= \dfrac{4}{e^2}=0.541\ldots\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts602_1}
$$\therefore\ \text{Minimum at } (0,0) \text{ and maximum at } \left(2,\dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$$
