A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} 0 & x<1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{x} & 1\le x\le e\,. \\[6pt] 0 & x>e \end{cases}$$
Calculate the value of the 25th percentile $(Q_1)$ of this distribution. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
items.sol:
$Q_1$ is the value with $P(X\le Q_1)=0.25$:
$$\int_1^{Q_1}\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx=0.25$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^{Q_1}\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx &= \Big[\ln x\Big]_1^{Q_1}\\ &= \ln Q_1-\ln 1 \\ &= \ln Q_1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \ln Q_1 &= 0.25\\ Q_1 &= e^{0.25}\\ &= 1.284\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Prove that

$$\dfrac{\sin^4\theta+\cos^4\theta}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}+2=\sec^2\theta\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta.$$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sin^4\theta+\cos^4\theta}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}+2 \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^4\theta+\cos^4\theta+2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)^2}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1)^2}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta} \qquad (\text{as } \sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \sec^2\theta\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In a flock of $12\,600$ sheep, the ratio of males to females is $1:20$.

The weights of the male sheep are normally distributed with a mean of $76.2$ kg and a standard deviation of $6.8$ kg.

In the flock, 15 of the male sheep each weigh more than $x$ kg.

Find the value of $x$.
items.sol:
$$\text{Number of male sheep}=\dfrac{12\,600}{21}=600$$
$$\text{Percentage of males weighing more than } x \text{ kg}=\dfrac{15}{600}\times 100=2.5\%$$
\exfigure{1630_q23_s1}

By the empirical rule, $2.5\%$ of values lie above $z=2$.

$\therefore$ $z$-score $=2$
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 76.2+2\times 6.8 \\ x &= 76.2+13.6 \\ x &= 89.8 \text{ kg} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The weights of the female sheep are also normally distributed but have a smaller mean and smaller standard deviation than the weights of male sheep.

Explain whether it could be expected that 300 of the females from the flock each weigh more than $x$ kg, where $x$ is the value found in part (a).
items.sol:
$z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ will be larger than 2 as the mean and standard deviation for females are smaller.

The percentage of female sheep with weight greater than $x$ kg will be smaller than $2.5\%$.

There are $12\,000$ females and $2.5\%$ of $12\,000$ is $300$.

So fewer than 300 females will weigh more than $x$ kg.

Answers could include:

\exfigure{1630_q23_s2}
items.final: No; fewer than 300 females would be expected to weigh more than $x$ kg (less than 2.5% of 12 000).

items.sol:
The gradients of $y=e\ln x$ and $y=ax^2+c$ at point of intersection are both equal to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(e\ln x) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{e}{x} &= 1 \\ x &= e \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ y=e$, so $y=ax^2+c$ has gradient of 1 at point $(e,e)$.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[ax^2+c\right]=2ax$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2ax &= 1 \quad\text{at } x=e \\ 2a\cdot e &= 1 \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2e} \end{aligned}$$
and $y=ax^2+c=e$ at $x=e$:
$$\begin{aligned} e &= \dfrac{1}{2e}\cdot e^2+c \\ e &= \dfrac{e}{2}+c \\ c &= \dfrac{e}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2e},\ c=\dfrac{e}{2}$$

items.part:
Show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x-x\cos x)=x\sin x.$$
items.sol:
Using the product rule on $x\cos x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x-x\cos x) &= \cos x-\left[x\times(-\sin x)+\cos x\right] \\ &= \cos x+x\sin x-\cos x \\ &= x\sin x \quad\text{as required} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{2025\pi}x\sin x\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $\sin x-x\cos x$ is a primitive of $x\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{2025\pi}x\sin x\,dx &= \Big[\sin x-x\cos x\Big]_0^{2025\pi} \\ &= (\sin 2025\pi-2025\pi\cos 2025\pi)-(0) \\ &= 0-2025\pi\times(-1) \\ &= 2025\pi \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The regions bounded by the $x$-axis and the graph of $y=x\sin x$ for $x\ge 0$ are shown.

\exfigure{1630_q25_1}

Let $A_n=\displaystyle\int_{(n-1)\pi}^{n\pi}x\sin x\,dx$, where $n$ is a positive integer.

It can be shown that $\left|A_n\right|=(2n-1)\pi$. (Do NOT prove this.)

Find the exact total area of the regions bounded by the curve $y=x\sin x$, and the $x$-axis between $x=0$ and $x=2025\pi$.
items.sol:
The total area is $|A_1|+|A_2|+\cdots+|A_{2025}|$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Exact area of regions} &= \pi+3\pi+5\pi+\cdots+(2\times 2025-1)\pi \\ &= \pi+3\pi+5\pi+\cdots+4049\pi \end{aligned}$$
This is an arithmetic series with $a=\pi$, $d=2\pi$, $n=2025$ and $l=4049\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}(a+l) \\ S_n &= \dfrac{2025}{2}(\pi+4049\pi) \\ &= 2025\times 2025\times\pi \\ &= (2025)^2\pi \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A piece of wire is 100 cm long. Some of the wire is to be used to make a circle of radius $r$ cm. The remainder of the wire is used to make an equilateral triangle of side length $x$ cm.
Show that the combined area of the circle and equilateral triangle is given by

$$A(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}x^2+\dfrac{(100-3x)^2}{\pi}\right).$$
items.sol:
The circumference of the circle and the perimeter of the triangle add to 100 cm:
$$2\pi r+3x=100$$
$$r=\dfrac{100-3x}{2\pi}$$
Area of circle $\pi r^2$; area of the equilateral triangle $\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} A(x) &= \text{Area of circle}+\text{area of equilateral triangle} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x^2 \\ &= \pi\left(\dfrac{100-3x}{2\pi}\right)^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}\,x^2+\dfrac{(100-3x)^2}{\pi}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A piece of wire is 100 cm long. Some of the wire is to be used to make a circle of radius $r$ cm. The remainder of the wire is used to make an equilateral triangle of side length $x$ cm.
By considering the quadratic function in part (a), show that the maximum value of $A(x)$ occurs when all the wire is used for the circle.
items.sol:
$A(x)$ is a quadratic with positive coefficient of $x^2$, so $A$ has a minimum stationary point.

The maximum will therefore occur at an endpoint of the domain.

When $x=0$ (all wire used for the circle):
$$r=\dfrac{50}{\pi}$$
$$\text{Area}=\pi r^2=\dfrac{50^2}{\pi}\approx 796$$
When $r=0$ (all wire used for the triangle):
$$x=33\dfrac{1}{3}$$
$$\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times 33.333^2\approx 481$$
\exfigure{1630_q26_s1}

$\therefore$ The maximum value of $A(x)$ occurs when all wire is used for the circle.

Two applications of the trapezoidal rule use $n=2$ strips:
$$h=\dfrac{2-0}{2}=1$$
so $x_0=0$, $x_1=1$, $x_2=2$, with
$$f(0)=1, \quad f(1)=\dfrac{1}{2}, \quad f(2)=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{b-a}{2n}\Big\{f(a)+f(b)+2\left[f(x_1)\right]\Big\} \\ &= \dfrac{2-0}{2\times 2}\left\{1+\dfrac{1}{4}+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{4}+1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{8} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^x dx &= \left[\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^0}{\ln\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{-\frac{3}{4}}{-\ln 2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$

The function is concave up, so the exact value is less than the trapezoidal approximation:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4\ln 2} &< \dfrac{9}{8} \\ 24 &< 36\ln 2 \\ 2 &< 3\ln 2 \\ 2 &< \ln 8 \\ e^2 &< 8 \\ e &< \sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ e<2\sqrt{2}$$

Area of shaded segment $=$ area of sector $-$ area of triangle, and the segment is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the paddock:
$$\text{area of sector}-\text{area of triangle}=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\text{area of circle}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^2\sin\theta &= \dfrac{10^2\pi}{4} \\ 50\theta-50\sin\theta &= 25\pi \\ 50(\theta-\sin\theta) &= 25\pi \\ \theta-\sin\theta &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ \theta &= \sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{1630_q28_s1}

From part (a), $\theta=\sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $\theta$ is the $\theta$-coordinate of the point of intersection of $y=\theta$ and $y=\sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

From the graph:
$$\theta\approx 2.3 \text{ radians}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Arc length} &= r\theta \\ &= 10\times 2.3\\ &= 23 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The point $T$ is the peak of a mountain and the point $O$ is directly below the mountain's peak. The point $Y$ is due east of $O$ and the angle of elevation of $T$ from $Y$ is $60^\circ$. The point $F$ is 4 km south-west of $Y$. The points $O$, $Y$ and $F$ are on level ground. The angle of elevation of $T$ from $F$ is $45^\circ$.

\exfigure{1630_q29_1}
Let the height of the mountain be $h$.

Show that $OY=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$.
items.sol:
In $\triangle TYO$, right-angled at $O$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{OY} \\ \therefore\ OY &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
The exact value $\tan 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}$ comes from the $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$–$90^\circ$ triangle:

\exfigure{1630_q29_s1}

In $\triangle TFO$, $\angle TFO=45^\circ$, $\angle TOF=90^\circ$

$\therefore\ \angle OTF=45^\circ$

$\therefore\ \triangle TFO$ is isosceles and $OF=h$

In $\triangle FOY$, $\angle OYF=45^\circ$ ($F$ is south-west of $Y$ and $O$ is due west of $Y$). By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} h^2 &= \left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+4^2-2\times 4\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\cos 45^\circ \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{h^2}{3}+16-\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{2h^2}{3}+\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}}-16=0$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{-\frac{8}{\sqrt{6}}\pm\sqrt{\frac{64}{6}+4\times\frac{2}{3}\times 16}}{\frac{4}{3}} \\ &= 3.03 \quad\text{since } h>0 \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{1630_q29_s2}

In $\triangle FOY$, let $\theta=\angle OFY$. By the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}} &= \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{h} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3}} \\ \theta &= 24.09\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 24^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$Y$ is on a bearing of $045^\circ$ from $F$, and $O$ is $\theta$ further anticlockwise:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 45^\circ-24^\circ \\ &\approx 021^\circ \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The parabola with equation $y=(x-1)(x-5)$ is translated both horizontally to the right and vertically up by $k$ units, where $k$ is positive.

The translated parabola passes through the point $(6,11)$.

Find the value of $k$.
items.sol:
Translating right by $k$ and up by $k$: replace $x$ with $x-k$ and $y$ with $y-k$. Then substitute the point $(6,11)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-k &= (x-k-1)(x-k-5) \\ 11-k &= (6-k-1)(6-k-5) \\ 11-k &= (5-k)(1-k) \\ 11-k &= 5-6k+k^2 \\ k^2-5k-6 &= 0 \\ (k-6)(k+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$k$ is positive, so
$$k=6$$

items.part:
The equation $\cos px=\dfrac{1}{2}$ has 2 solutions where $0\le x\le 2\pi$ and $p>0$.

Find all possible values of $p$.
items.sol:
Solve $\cos x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $x\ge 0$ first:
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \ldots$$
\exfigure{1630_q31_s1}

$y=\cos px$ is a horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{p}$, so its solutions are these values multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{p}$.

Lowest value of $p$ to get 2 solutions (second solution at $x=2\pi$):

\exfigure{1630_q31_s2}
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{p} &= 2\pi \\ p &= \dfrac{5\pi}{3\times 2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Highest value of $p$ (at this value a third solution appears at $x=2\pi$, so it is excluded):

\exfigure{1630_q31_s3}
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{7\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{p} &= 2\pi \\ p &= \dfrac{7\pi}{3\times 2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{7}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{5}{6}\le p<\dfrac{7}{6}$$

items.part: Find the gradient of the tangent to $y=x^3+3x$ at $x=-1$.
items.sol:
Differentiating,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+3$$
At $x=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3(-1)^2+3\\ &=6 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the gradient of the tangent is $6$.

items.part:
The number of cars parked in a carpark is recorded each day for thirteen days. The dataset is listed in ascending order:

$$12,\ 15,\ 15,\ 17,\ 19,\ 20,\ 22,\ 24,\ 25,\ 27,\ 28,\ 30 \text{ and } m.$$
What is the interquartile range of this dataset?
items.sol:
There are $13$ values, so the median is the 7th value, $22$.

The lower half is $12, 15, 15, 17, 19, 20$, so
$$Q_1=\dfrac{15+17}{2}=16$$
The upper half is $24, 25, 27, 28, 30, m$ (since $m\ge 30$), so
$$Q_3=\dfrac{27+28}{2}=27.5$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR}&=27.5-16\\ &=11.5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of cars parked in a carpark is recorded each day for thirteen days. The dataset is listed in ascending order:

$$12,\ 15,\ 15,\ 17,\ 19,\ 20,\ 22,\ 24,\ 25,\ 27,\ 28,\ 30 \text{ and } m.$$
What is the greatest value of $m$ such that this dataset has no outlier?
items.sol:
An outlier is greater than $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$ (or less than $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$).
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}&=27.5+1.5\times 11.5\\ &=27.5+17.25\\ &=44.75 \end{aligned}$$
The lower bound is $16-17.25=-1.25$, so $12$ is not an outlier.

$m$ is a number of cars, so it is a whole number with $m\le 44.75$.

$\therefore$ the greatest value of $m$ is $44$.

items.part:
In a theatre, starting from the stage, the number of seats in each row forms an arithmetic sequence.

The theatre has 30 seats in the 3rd row and 42 seats in the 6th row.

\exfigure{1632_q13_1}
How many seats are in the first row?
items.sol:
The number of seats in row $n$ is $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_3&=a+2d=30\\ T_6&=a+5d=42 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting, $3d=12$, so $d=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} a&=30-2(4)\\ &=22 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ there are $22$ seats in the first row.

items.part:
In a theatre, starting from the stage, the number of seats in each row forms an arithmetic sequence.

The theatre has 30 seats in the 3rd row and 42 seats in the 6th row.

\exfigure{1632_q13_1}
How many seats will this theatre have if there are 9 rows?
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $a=22$, $d=4$ and $n=9$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_9&=\dfrac{9}{2}\big(2(22)+8(4)\big)\\ &=\dfrac{9}{2}\times 76\\ &=342 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the theatre has $342$ seats.

items.part: Find the range and period of the function $h(x)=3\cos(2x)+1$.
items.sol:
Range: since $-1\le\cos(2x)\le 1$,
$$\begin{aligned} -1&\le \cos(2x)\le 1\\ -3&\le 3\cos(2x)\le 3 &&(\text{multiply by } 3)\\ -2&\le 3\cos(2x)+1\le 4 &&(\text{add } 1)\end{aligned}$$
So the range is $-2\le h(x)\le 4$.

Period: for $\cos(nx)$ the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$, with $n=2$:
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y=4^{x^2+3}$.
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(a^{f(x)}\right)=f'(x)\,a^{f(x)}\ln a$ (chain rule), with $f(x)=x^2+3$ and $f'(x)=2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x\cdot 4^{x^2+3}\ln 4\\ &=2x\ln 4\cdot 4^{x^2+3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Researchers were interested in whether the critics’ scores for movies could be used to predict the general public’s scores for movies.

A random sample of movies was selected, and the average score from the critics and the average score from the public were recorded.

A scatterplot of the dataset and the least-squares regression line are shown.

\exfigure{1632_q16_1}
What was the lowest score given by the public for a movie, correct to 1 decimal place?
items.sol:
The lowest point on the scatterplot is at a critics' score of $7.4$, with a public's score of $6.1$.

$\therefore$ the lowest score given by the public was $6.1$.

items.part:
Researchers were interested in whether the critics’ scores for movies could be used to predict the general public’s scores for movies.

A random sample of movies was selected, and the average score from the critics and the average score from the public were recorded.

A scatterplot of the dataset and the least-squares regression line are shown.

\exfigure{1632_q16_1}
The gradient of the least-squares regression line for the dataset is $0.54$.

Interpret the gradient in the context of the dataset.
items.sol:
The gradient is the change in the public's score for each increase of $1$ in the critics' score.

For each $1$ point increase in the critics' score, the public's score increases by $0.54$ points on average (predicted).

items.part:
Researchers were interested in whether the critics’ scores for movies could be used to predict the general public’s scores for movies.

A random sample of movies was selected, and the average score from the critics and the average score from the public were recorded.

A scatterplot of the dataset and the least-squares regression line are shown.

\exfigure{1632_q16_1}
A new data point is included in the dataset. The critics’ score is $7.2$ and the public’s score is $6$.

Identify ONE effect this would have on the least-squares regression line.
items.sol:
At a critics' score of $7.2$ the regression line gives a public's score of about $6.65$, so the new point $(7.2,\ 6)$ lies well below the line at the left end of the data.

Including it pulls the left end of the line down, so the gradient of the least-squares regression line increases (the line becomes steeper) and the $y$-intercept decreases.
items.final: The gradient of the regression line increases (steeper) and the $y$-intercept decreases.

items.part:
A large rechargeable battery has a maximum storage capacity of 40 kWh when new.

After 1 year, the maximum storage capacity is 32 kWh.

The process of decay can be modelled by the function

$$y=ka^t$$

where $y$ is the maximum storage capacity of the battery, in kWh, $t$ years after it starts being used.
What are the values of $k$ and $a$?

A large rechargeable battery has a maximum storage capacity of 40 kWh when new.

After 1 year, the maximum storage capacity is 32 kWh.

The process of decay can be modelled by the function

$$y=ka^t$$

where $y$ is the maximum storage capacity of the battery, in kWh, $t$ years after it starts being used.
Interpret the value of $a$ in this context.
items.sol:
Each year the maximum storage capacity is multiplied by $a=0.8$.

So each year the maximum storage capacity is $80\%$ of what it was the year before: it decreases by $20\%$ per year.
items.final: Each year the capacity is multiplied by $a=0.8$, i.e. it decreases by 20% per year

items.sol:
At the points of intersection the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 7-3x&=-x^2+x+12\\ x^2-4x-5&=0\\ (x-5)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-1 \text{ or } x=5$$

Between $x=-1$ and $x=5$ the parabola is above the line (at $x=0$: $12>7$), so the area is the integral of (parabola $-$ line):
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-1}^{5}\big((-x^2+x+12)-(7-3x)\big)\,dx\\ &=\int_{-1}^{5}(-x^2+4x+5)\,dx\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2+5x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{125}{3}+50+25\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+2-5\right)\\ &=\dfrac{100}{3}+\dfrac{8}{3}\\ &=36\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=36 \text{ units}^2$$

$f'(x)$ is the gradient of $y=f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } 0\le x<2 &&f \text{ decreasing}\\ f'(2)&=0 &&\text{local minimum}\\ f'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } x>2 &&f \text{ increasing}\end{aligned}$$
$f$ is concave up for $x<5$ and concave down for $x>5$, so $f'$ increases up to $x=5$ and then decreases: $f'(x)$ is greatest at the point of inflection $x=5$.

As $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to5$ (horizontal asymptote), so $f'(x)\to0$ from above: the $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote of $y=f'(x)$.

items.part:
At a particular school, the probability that a student walks to school is $\dfrac{3}{10}$ and the probability that a student wears the correct school uniform is $\dfrac{9}{10}$.

The probability tree shows this information.

\exfigure{1632_q20_1}
One student at the school is selected at random.

What is the probability that this student walks to school and is not wearing the correct school uniform?
items.sol:
Walks and not wearing the correct uniform (multiply along the branches):
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{3}{10}\times\dfrac{1}{10}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{100}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
At a particular school, the probability that a student walks to school is $\dfrac{3}{10}$ and the probability that a student wears the correct school uniform is $\dfrac{9}{10}$.

The probability tree shows this information.

\exfigure{1632_q20_1}
Two students at the school are selected at random.

What is the probability that at least one of these students walks to school and is not wearing the correct school uniform?
items.sol:
From (a), each student independently walks and is not wearing the correct uniform with probability $\dfrac{3}{100}$, so the probability that a student does not is $\dfrac{97}{100}$.

At least one is the complement of neither:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one})&=1-\left(\dfrac{97}{100}\right)^2\\ &=1-\dfrac{9409}{10\,000}\\ &=\dfrac{591}{10\,000}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that the first derivative of $g(x)=\dfrac{x}{\ln x}$ is $g'(x)=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&=\dfrac{1\cdot\ln x-x\cdot\frac{1}{x}}{(\ln x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: What is the global maximum of $g(x)$ on the interval $[2,5]$?
items.sol:
Stationary points: $g'(x)=0$ when $\ln x-1=0$, so $x=e$, which lies in $[2,5]$.

The denominator $(\ln x)^2>0$, so the sign of $g'(x)$ is decided by $\ln x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } 2\le x<e &&\text{decreasing}\\ g'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } e<x\le5 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
So $x=e$ is a local minimum, and the global maximum is at an endpoint:
$$\begin{aligned} g(2)&=\dfrac{2}{\ln2}\approx2.885\\ g(5)&=\dfrac{5}{\ln5}\approx3.107\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the global maximum is } \dfrac{5}{\ln5}\approx3.11 \text{ (at } x=5)$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}=1+\dfrac{1}{x+1}$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x+2}{x+1}&=\dfrac{(x+1)+1}{x+1}\\ &=\dfrac{x+1}{x+1}+\dfrac{1}{x+1}\\ &=1+\dfrac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Describe the transformations required to obtain the graph $y=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}$ from the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$.
items.sol:
From (a), $y=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}=\dfrac{1}{x+1}+1$.

Replacing $x$ by $x+1$ in $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ gives $y=\dfrac{1}{x+1}$: a translation $1$ unit to the left.

Adding $1$ gives $y=\dfrac{1}{x+1}+1$: a translation $1$ unit up.

$\therefore$ Translate the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ $1$ unit to the left and $1$ unit up.
items.final: Translate $y=\frac{1}{x}$ 1 unit to the left and 1 unit up.

items.part:
The diagram shows a block of land $ABCD$. It also shows the bearing of each of the points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, from point $O$.

\exfigure{1632_q23_1}

The distance from $O$ to $C$ is 25 km, $OA=OB$ and $\angle AOB=45^\circ$.

The area of the shaded triangle $AOB$ is $80\text{ km}^2$.

What is the distance from $B$ to $C$, to the nearest kilometre?
items.sol:
\exfigure{1632_q23_s1}

Let $OA=OB=x$ km. The area of triangle $AOB$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin45^\circ&=80\\ x^2&=\dfrac{160}{\sin45^\circ}\\ &=160\sqrt2\\ x&\approx15.04\end{aligned}$$
From the bearings of $B$ and $C$:
$$\angle BOC=253^\circ-101^\circ=152^\circ$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $BOC$:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2&=x^2+25^2-2\times x\times25\cos152^\circ\\ &\approx226.27+625-2\times15.04\times25\cos152^\circ\\ &\approx1515.4\\ BC&\approx38.9\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BC\approx39 \text{ km}$$

items.part:
Radioactive cobalt-60 decays to become nickel-60. A 1000 g block of radioactive cobalt-60 is placed in a container.

After a period of 10.54 years, $75\%$ of the cobalt-60 has decayed to become nickel-60.

The decay process can be modelled by the exponential relationship

$$A=1000e^{kt}$$

where $A$ is the amount of cobalt-60 remaining (in grams) at time $t$ (in years).
Find the value of $k$, correct to 4 decimal places.

Radioactive cobalt-60 decays to become nickel-60. A 1000 g block of radioactive cobalt-60 is placed in a container.

After a period of 10.54 years, $75\%$ of the cobalt-60 has decayed to become nickel-60.

The decay process can be modelled by the exponential relationship

$$A=1000e^{kt}$$

where $A$ is the amount of cobalt-60 remaining (in grams) at time $t$ (in years).
Find the value of $t$ when the rate of change of $A$ is $-9.48$ g/year, correct to the nearest year.
items.sol:
Differentiating $A=1000e^{kt}$:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=-9.48$ with $k=-0.1315$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000(-0.1315)e^{-0.1315t}&=-9.48\\ e^{-0.1315t}&=\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\\ -0.1315t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\right)\\ t&\approx20.0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx20 \text{ years}$$

items.part:
The weights of watermelons produced by a certain farm are normally distributed with a mean of 4.82 kg. Long-term quality control data show that when a watermelon from this farm is randomly selected, the probability that it weighs less than 3.75 kg is $0.116$.

A watermelon is labelled as being the ideal size if it weighs between 4.82 kg and 5.89 kg.

What is the probability that a watermelon selected at random is the ideal size?
items.sol:
The normal distribution is symmetric about the mean $4.82$, and $3.75$ and $5.89$ are the same distance from it:
$$4.82-3.75=1.07=5.89-4.82$$
So, by symmetry, $P(X>5.89)=P(X<3.75)=0.116$.

Half of the distribution lies above the mean, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(4.82<X<5.89)&=0.5-P(X>5.89)\\ &=0.5-0.116\\ &=0.384\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity, $v$ m/s, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the function

$$v(t)=1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}$$

where $0\le t\le 1.25$ is the time in seconds. The graph of $v(t)$ is shown.

\exfigure{1632_q26_1}
At what value(s) of $t$ does the particle change direction in this interval?
items.sol:
The particle changes direction when $v$ changes sign.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}&=0\\ e^{\cos(\pi t)}&=1\\ \cos(\pi t)&=0\\ \pi t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2} &&(0\le\pi t\le1.25\pi)\\ t&=0.5\end{aligned}$$
The graph crosses the $t$-axis there ($v<0$ before, $v>0$ after).
$$\therefore\ t=0.5$$

items.part:
The velocity, $v$ m/s, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the function

$$v(t)=1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}$$

where $0\le t\le 1.25$ is the time in seconds. The graph of $v(t)$ is shown.

\exfigure{1632_q26_1}
Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=0.5$.
items.sol:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{f(t)}=f'(t)e^{f(t)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\ &=-\big(-\pi\sin(\pi t)\big)e^{\cos(\pi t)}\\ &=\pi\sin(\pi t)\,e^{\cos(\pi t)}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\pi\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)e^{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}\\ &=\pi\times1\times e^0\\ &=\pi \text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity, $v$ m/s, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the function

$$v(t)=1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}$$

where $0\le t\le 1.25$ is the time in seconds. The graph of $v(t)$ is shown.

\exfigure{1632_q26_1}
The table provides five function values for $v$, correct to 2 decimal places.

\extable{Tp879_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule with four subintervals, find the approximate distance travelled by the particle in the interval $0\le t\le 1$.
items.sol:
Distance is the area between the graph and the $t$-axis, so use $|v|$ ($v\le0$ for $0\le t\le0.5$ and $v\ge0$ for $0.5\le t\le1$):
$$\text{distance}=\int_0^1|v|\,dt$$
Four subintervals of $[0,1]$: $h=\dfrac{1-0}{4}=0.25$, with $t=0,\ 0.25,\ 0.5,\ 0.75,\ 1$ as in the table.

Trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(t_0)+2\big(f(t_1)+f(t_2)+f(t_3)\big)+f(t_4)\big]$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1|v|\,dt&\approx\dfrac{0.25}{2}\big[1.72+2(1.03+0+0.51)+0.63\big]\\ &=0.125\times5.43\\ &=0.67875\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance}\approx0.68 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
Maya plans to go on an overseas trip in 5 years’ time. Maya expects that the trip will cost \$14 000. To save for the trip, Maya began by contributing \$750 every 6 months into an annuity. After making a number of payments, Maya realised that the annuity would not reach \$14 000 in 5 years. Maya decides to double the contribution until the trip.

The interest rate was $2\%$ per annum compounding half yearly.

\exfigure{1632_q27_1}

What is the maximum number of \$750 contributions Maya could make before she will need to double her payments to reach \$14 000?
items.sol:
Contributions are every 6 months for 5 years, so $n=5\times2=10$ periods, at $r=\dfrac{2\%}{2}=1\%=0.01$ per period.

If all $10$ contributions were $\$750$, the future value (table: rate $0.01$, period $10$) would be
$$750\times10.4622=\$7846.65$$
Doubling a contribution adds another $\$750$, so if the last $m$ contributions are doubled, the extra amount is $\$750$ times the future value of an annuity of $\$1$ for $m$ periods, $\text{FV}_m$. We need
$$\begin{aligned} 7846.65+750\times\text{FV}_m&\ge14\,000\\ \text{FV}_m&\ge\dfrac{14\,000-7846.65}{750}\\ \text{FV}_m&\ge8.2045\end{aligned}$$
From the table, $\text{FV}_8=8.2857\ge8.2045$, while $\text{FV}_7=\dfrac{1.01^7-1}{0.01}\approx7.2135<8.2045$.

So at least the last $8$ contributions must be doubled, leaving at most $10-8=2$ contributions of $\$750$.

Check: $750\times10.4622+750\times8.2857=\$14\,060.93\ge\$14\,000$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum number of } \$750 \text{ contributions}=2$$

items.part:
Let $y=4x^3-3x^2-6x+d$, where $d$ is a real number.

Use differential calculus to find the values of $d$ for which this curve has exactly three $x$-intercepts. (Note: You do NOT need to find the $x$-intercepts.)
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=12x^2-6x-6\\ &=6(2x+1)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$: $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} y\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=4\left(-\dfrac{1}{8}\right)-3\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+3+d=d+\dfrac{7}{4}\\ y(1)&=4-3-6+d=d-5\end{aligned}$$
Nature, using $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=24x-6$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-\dfrac{1}{2}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-18<0 &&\text{local maximum}\\ x&=1: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=18>0 &&\text{local minimum}\end{aligned}$$
The cubic has exactly three $x$-intercepts when its local maximum is above the $x$-axis and its local minimum is below it:
$$\begin{aligned} d+\dfrac{7}{4}&>0 &&\text{so } d>-\dfrac{7}{4}\\ d-5&<0 &&\text{so } d<5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{7}{4}<d<5$$

items.part:
Sketch the graph of $y=\cot x$ on the axes provided for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

\exfigure{1632_q29_1}
items.sol:
$\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$.

Vertical asymptotes where $\sin x=0$: $x=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$.

$x$-intercepts where $\cos x=0$: $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

$\cot x$ is decreasing on each branch, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cot x=-\operatorname{cosec}^2x<0$.

\exfigure{1632_q29_s1}

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find the values of $x$ for which $y=\ln(\cot x)$ is defined in the interval $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
$\ln(\cot x)$ is defined only when $\cot x>0$.

From the graph in (a), $\cot x>0$ when
$$0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2} \quad\text{or}\quad \pi<x<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$

items.part: Prove that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(\ln(\cot x)\big)=-\operatorname{cosec} x\sec x$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cot x=-\operatorname{cosec}^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\big(\ln(\cot x)\big)&=\dfrac{-\operatorname{cosec}^2x}{\cot x}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\times\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sin x\cos x}\\ &=-\operatorname{cosec}x\sec x\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A pyramid $MABCD$ has its vertex $M$ vertically above $O$, the centre of its square base $ABCD$, as shown. $AM=\ell$ cm and makes an angle of $\theta$ with the base.

\exfigure{1632_q30_1}
Let $V$ be the volume of the pyramid.

Show that $V=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\sin\theta\cos^2\theta$.
items.sol:
In triangle $AOM$ (right angle at $O$, $\angle MAO=\theta$), using the sine and cosine ratios:
$$\begin{aligned} MO&=\ell\sin\theta\\ AO&=\ell\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is the centre of the square, so the diagonal $AC=2AO=2\ell\cos\theta$.

By Pythagoras' theorem, a square with side $s$ has $s^2+s^2=AC^2$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{base area}=s^2&=\dfrac{(2\ell\cos\theta)^2}{2}\\ &=2\ell^2\cos^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
The volume of a pyramid is $\dfrac{1}{3}\times\text{base area}\times\text{height}$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times2\ell^2\cos^2\theta\times\ell\sin\theta\\ &=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\sin\theta\cos^2\theta\end{aligned}$$

Here $\ell$ is constant and $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=\cos^2\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-2\cos\theta\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{d\theta}&=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\left(\cos^3\theta-2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\cos\theta\left(\cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta\right)\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $\cos\theta\ne0$ when $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta&=0\\ \tan^2\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} &&(\tan\theta>0)\\ \theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\approx0.6155\end{aligned}$$
Nature: $\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\cos\theta>0$, so the sign of $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ is decided by
$$\cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\left(1-2\tan^2\theta\right)$$
that is, by $1-2\tan^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta&=0.5: &1-2\tan^2\theta&\approx0.40>0 &&V \text{ increasing}\\ \theta&=0.7: &1-2\tan^2\theta&\approx-0.42<0 &&V \text{ decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the stationary point is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \theta\approx0.62$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos 2x\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\int\cos2x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin2x+C$$

items.part:
It is given

$$\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\int \cos 2x\,dx$$

where $f(0)=1$ and $f(x)>0$ for all real $x$.

Find $f(x)$.
items.sol:
The left side is a standard integral, $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+C$, and $f(x)>0$, so using (a):
$$\ln f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin2x+C$$
Using $f(0)=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln1&=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin0+C\\ C&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\ln f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin2x$, and
$$f(x)=e^{\frac{1}{2}\sin2x}$$

items.part:
Let

$$g(x)=\int_{x^3}^{1}\sqrt{\tan(t)}\,dt$$

and let $F(t)$ be an antiderivative of $\sqrt{\tan(t)}$, where $0\le x\le 1$. (Do NOT try to find $F(t)$.)
Find an expression for $g(x)$ in terms of $F$.
items.sol:
$F$ is an antiderivative of $\sqrt{\tan t}$, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus, $\displaystyle\int_a^b\sqrt{\tan t}\,dt=F(b)-F(a)$:
$$g(x)=F(1)-F(x^3)$$

items.part:
Let

$$g(x)=\int_{x^3}^{1}\sqrt{\tan(t)}\,dt$$

and let $F(t)$ be an antiderivative of $\sqrt{\tan(t)}$, where $0\le x\le 1$. (Do NOT try to find $F(t)$.)
Hence find $g'(x)$.
items.sol:
$F(1)$ is a constant and $F'(t)=\sqrt{\tan t}$. Using the chain rule on $F(x^3)$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&=0-F'(x^3)\times3x^2\\ &=-3x^2\sqrt{\tan(x^3)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Peyton borrows \$83 000. Any amount owing on the loan attracts interest at an annual rate of $6\%$, compounded monthly.

The repayments are made at the end of each month after the interest is added to the account.

Peyton makes a first monthly repayment of \$760 and then increases the value of the repayment by $10\%$ each month.

Let $A_n$ = Amount owing after the $n$th repayment.
Show that $A_3=83\,000(1.005)^3-760\big((1.005)^2+(1.005)(1.1)+(1.1)^2\big)$.

Peyton borrows \$83 000. Any amount owing on the loan attracts interest at an annual rate of $6\%$, compounded monthly.

The repayments are made at the end of each month after the interest is added to the account.

Peyton makes a first monthly repayment of \$760 and then increases the value of the repayment by $10\%$ each month.

Let $A_n$ = Amount owing after the $n$th repayment.
Show that $A_n=91\,000(1.005)^n-8000(1.1)^n$.

Peyton borrows \$83 000. Any amount owing on the loan attracts interest at an annual rate of $6\%$, compounded monthly.

The repayments are made at the end of each month after the interest is added to the account.

Peyton makes a first monthly repayment of \$760 and then increases the value of the repayment by $10\%$ each month.

Let $A_n$ = Amount owing after the $n$th repayment.
Find the amount of the final payment.
items.sol:
The loan is repaid when $A_n\le0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 91\,000(1.005)^n&\le8000(1.1)^n\\ \left(\dfrac{1.1}{1.005}\right)^n&\ge\dfrac{91}{8}\\ n&\ge\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{91}{8}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{1.1}{1.005}\right)}\approx26.9\end{aligned}$$
So $A_{26}>0$ and $A_{27}<0$: the final payment is the $27$th, and it is smaller than the scheduled $760(1.1)^{26}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{26}&=91\,000(1.005)^{26}-8000(1.1)^{26}\\ &\approx8254.41\end{aligned}$$
The final payment clears $A_{26}$ plus one month's interest:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{final payment}&=A_{26}\times1.005\\ &\approx\$8295.68\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $|2x-1|=3$.

For a geometric series the third term ($T_3$) is $20$ and the sixth term ($T_6$) is $-160$.
Find the common ratio and the first term.
items.sol:
Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_3:&\quad ar^2=20 &&(1) \\ T_6:&\quad ar^5=-160 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
$(2)\div(1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} r^3&=-8 \\ r&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $r=-2$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a(-2)^2&=20 \\ a&=5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=5,\ r=-2$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Reverse chain rule, since $2x$ is the derivative of $x^2+1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x\left(x^2+1\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\left(x^2+1\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}+C\\ &=\sqrt{x^2+1}+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A courier company tracks the delivery times (in days) for packages sent across the country. Packages arrive in 1 to 5 days. During a morning system check, the data analyst found that some of the delivery time probabilities were missing due to a database error.

The partial probability distribution is shown below:

\extable{Tq610_1}

The analyst recalls that the expected value for the delivery time is 3.2 days.
By first forming two equations, calculate the missing probabilities $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
Probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned}0.1+a+b+0.2+0.2&=1\\ a+b&=0.5\quad(1)\end{aligned}$$
Expected value is 3.2:
$$\begin{aligned}1\times 0.1+2a+3b+4\times 0.2+5\times 0.2&=3.2\\ 2a+3b&=1.3\quad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Rearrange (1): $a=0.5-b$

Substitute in (2):
$$\begin{aligned}2(0.5-b)+3b&=1.3\\ 1-2b+3b&=1.3\\ b&=0.3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=0.2,\ b=0.3$$

items.part:
A courier company tracks the delivery times (in days) for packages sent across the country. Packages arrive in 1 to 5 days. During a morning system check, the data analyst found that some of the delivery time probabilities were missing due to a database error.

The partial probability distribution is shown below:

Later that day, the full dataset was recovered from a backup, and the corrected distribution was confirmed to be:

\extable{Tp984_1}

Using the corrected distribution, calculate the variance of the delivery time.
items.sol:
$$\mathrm{Var}(X)=E\left(X^2\right)-\mu^2$$
$$\begin{aligned}E\left(X^2\right)&=0.1+4\times 0.2+9\times 0.3+16\times 0.2+25\times 0.2\\ &=11.8\end{aligned}$$
With $\mu=3.2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(X)&=11.8-3.2^2\\ &=1.56\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\left(x+\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^2$ when $x=2$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$y'=2\left(x+\dfrac{2}{x}\right)\times\left(1-\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)$$
When $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\left(2+\dfrac{2}{2}\right)^2\\ &=9\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=2\left(2+\dfrac{2}{2}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{2}{2^2}\right)\\ &=2\times 3\times\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m_N=-\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Equation of normal:
$$\begin{aligned}y-9&=-\dfrac{1}{3}(x-2)\\ -3y+27&=x-2\\ x+3y-29&=0\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$ of a moving particle is given after $t$ seconds by $v=8t-16$.

Initially the particle is located at the origin.
How far does the particle travel in the first 5 seconds?

A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vacy.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Woodville.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{1369_q19_1}
The helicopter then plans to fly directly to Underwood.

Calculate, to the nearest km, the distance that it will fly.

items.part:
A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vacy.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Woodville.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{1369_q19_1}
Determine the bearing (from Woodville) on which it should fly to return to Underwood.

Give your answer to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Let $\angle UWV=\theta$. By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{103^2+82^2-70^2}{2\times 103\times 82}\\ &=0.736\ldots\\ \theta&=42.605\ldots^\circ\\ &\approx 43^\circ\ \text{(nearest degree)}\end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $V$ from $W$ is $360^\circ-30^\circ$, and $U$ is a further $43^\circ$ anticlockwise, so the bearing from $W$ to $U$ is
$$360^\circ-30^\circ-43^\circ=287^\circ\text{T}$$

items.part:
It is given that a quantity $y$ varies inversely with the square of $x$.

When $x=4$, $y=10$.

Find the value of $y$ when $x=5$.
items.sol:
$y$ varies inversely with the square of $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&\propto\dfrac{1}{x^2}\\ y&=\dfrac{k}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute $x=4$, $y=10$ to find $k$:
$$\begin{aligned}10&=\dfrac{k}{4^2}\\ k&=160\end{aligned}$$
$$y=\dfrac{160}{x^2}$$
Substitute $x=5$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{160}{5^2}\\ &=6.4\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}=\sec 3x\operatorname{cosec}3x$
items.sol:
Write the left-hand side in terms of sine and cosine:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 3x}\times\dfrac{\cos 3x}{\sin 3x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos 3x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin 3x}\\ &=\sec 3x\operatorname{cosec}3x\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int\sec 3x\operatorname{cosec}3x\,dx$
items.sol:
Using part (a), the integrand has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ with $f(x)=\tan 3x$ and $f'(x)=3\sec^2 3x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\sec 3x\operatorname{cosec}3x\,dx&=\int\dfrac{\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln|\tan 3x|+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of two towns Melbtown and Brisbay are given by $P_M=1200e^{0.04t}$ and $P_B=1500e^{0.025t}$ respectively, where $t$ is the number of years elapsed since January 2010.
In which year will the population of Melbtown exceed 1500?
items.sol:
The population of Melbtown exceeds 1500 when
$$\begin{aligned}1200e^{0.04t}&>1500\\ e^{0.04t}&>\dfrac{5}{4}\\ 0.04t&>\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)\\ t&>5.57\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from January 2010, so $t=5.57\ldots$ is during 2015.

$\therefore$ In 2015 the population will exceed 1500.

items.part:
The population of two towns Melbtown and Brisbay are given by $P_M=1200e^{0.04t}$ and $P_B=1500e^{0.025t}$ respectively, where $t$ is the number of years elapsed since January 2010.
In which year will the rate of growth of the population in Melbtown be double the rate of growth of Brisbay?
items.sol:
Differentiate each population:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP_M}{dt}&=0.04\times 1200e^{0.04t}\\ &=48e^{0.04t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP_B}{dt}&=0.025\times 1500e^{0.025t}\\ &=37.5e^{0.025t}\end{aligned}$$
Find $t$ when $\dfrac{dP_M}{dt}=2\dfrac{dP_B}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned}48e^{0.04t}&=75e^{0.025t}\\ e^{(0.04-0.025)t}&=\dfrac{75}{48}\\ e^{0.015t}&=1.5625\\ 0.015t&=\ln(1.5625)\\ t&=\dfrac{1}{0.015}\ln(1.5625)\\ &=29.75247\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from January 2010, so $t=29.75\ldots$ is during 2039.

$\therefore$ During 2039 the rate of growth of Melbtown will be double that of Brisbay.
items.final: During 2039 the rate of growth of Melbtown will be double that of Brisbay.

items.part:
Ben sketched the curve shown below to model a tidal experiment in his Science class.

Ben knows the curve is in the form $y=k\cos(ax+b)$ where $k>0$, $a>0$ and $0\le b\le\pi$.

By finding $k$, $a$ and $b$, write the equation for Ben’s tidal experiment.

\exfigure{1369_q23_1}
items.sol:
From the graph, 3 cycles take $2\pi$, so the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{a}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\ a&=3\end{aligned}$$
The amplitude is $2$ and $k>0$, so $k=2$:
$$y=2\cos(3x+b)$$
The curve passes through $(0,-2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}-2&=2\cos b\\ \cos b&=-1\\ b&=\pi\quad(\text{since }0\le b\le\pi)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=2\cos(3x+\pi)$$

The probability of a book being ready for collection between 2 pm and 3 pm is 0.2.
Determine the value of $k$.
items.sol:
The probability between 2 pm and 3 pm is $0.2$ over one unit, so the constant section has height $0.2$.

The total area under the density function is 1 (a rectangle from 1 to 4 and a trapezium from 4 to 5):
$$\begin{aligned}3\times 0.2+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 1\times(0.2+k)&=1\\ \dfrac{0.2+k}{2}&=0.4\\ 0.2+k&=0.8\\ k&=0.6\end{aligned}$$

The diagram shows a sector with radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ where $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<\theta\le\pi$.

The arc length is $\dfrac{10\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{1369_q26_1}
Find the range of possible values for $r$, expressing your answer in interval notation.
items.sol:
The arc length of a sector is $r\theta$:
$$r\theta=\dfrac{10\pi}{3}$$
so $r=\dfrac{10\pi}{3\theta}$, which decreases as $\theta$ increases. Find $r$ at each end of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<\theta\le\pi$.

When $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (not included):
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{2}r&=\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\\ r&=\dfrac{20}{3}\end{aligned}$$
When $\theta=\pi$ (included):
$$\begin{aligned}\pi r&=\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\\ r&=\dfrac{10}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r\in\left[\dfrac{10}{3},\dfrac{20}{3}\right)$$

items.part:
The diagram shows a sector with radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ where $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<\theta\le\pi$.

The arc length is $\dfrac{10\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{1369_q26_1}
Calculate the area of the sector when $r=4$.
items.sol:
The area of a sector is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, and $r\theta=\dfrac{10\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}r\times r\theta\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The numbers $4e^{-k}$, $5$, $4e^{k}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.
Show that $2e^k-5+2e^{-k}=0$.
items.sol:
Consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence have a common difference:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3-T_2&=T_2-T_1\\ 4e^k-5&=5-4e^{-k}\\ 4e^k-10+4e^{-k}&=0\\ 2e^k-5+2e^{-k}&=0\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The numbers $4e^{-k}$, $5$, $4e^{k}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.
Hence find in exact form any possible values of $k$.
items.sol:
Multiply by $e^k$ to form a quadratic in $e^k$:
$$\begin{aligned}2e^k-5+\dfrac{2}{e^k}&=0\\ 2e^{2k}-5e^k+2&=0\end{aligned}$$
Let $u=e^k$:
$$\begin{aligned}2u^2-5u+2&=0\\ (2u-1)(u-2)&=0\\ u&=\dfrac{1}{2},\ 2\\ e^k&=\dfrac{1}{2},\ 2\\ k&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right),\ \ln 2\end{aligned}$$

Show that the perimeter, $L$, of the rectangle is given by

$$L=2x+2\sqrt{36-4x^2}$$
items.sol:
The rectangle has sides $QR=2x$ and $RS=y$:
$$\begin{aligned}L&=2x+2x+y+y\\ &=4x+2y\\ &=2x+2(x+y)\end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $(x+y)^2=36-4x^2$ and $x+y>0$, so $x+y=\sqrt{36-4x^2}$.
$$\therefore\ L=2x+2\sqrt{36-4x^2}$$

Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dL}{dx}&=2+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\left(36-4x^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(-8x)\\ &=2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{36-4x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{36-4x^2}}&=0\\ \dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{36-4x^2}}&=2\\ 8x&=2\sqrt{36-4x^2}\\ 4x&=\sqrt{36-4x^2}\\ 16x^2&=36-4x^2\\ 20x^2&=36\\ x^2&=\dfrac{36}{20}\\ x^2&=\dfrac{9}{5}\\ x&=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}}\quad(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Check the sign of $\dfrac{dL}{dx}$ either side of $x=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}}$:

\extable{Ts750_1}

$\therefore$ Maximum $L$ when $x=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}}$ m.

items.part:
Let $g(t)$ be a function defined for all $t\ge 0$. The gradient function is given by

$$g'(t)=\dfrac{33}{10}te^{-kt}.$$

where $k$ is a positive constant. The diagram below shows a sketch of $g'(t)$ against $t$.

It is given that $g'(t)$ attains the greatest value at $t=7.5$ and $g(0)=0$.

\exfigure{1369_q30_1}
Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{15}$.
items.sol:
$g'(t)$ has its greatest value at $t=7.5$, so $g''(7.5)=0$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=t & v&=e^{-kt}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-ke^{-kt}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}g''(t)&=\dfrac{33}{10}\left(e^{-kt}+t(-k)e^{-kt}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{33}{10}e^{-kt}(1-kt)\end{aligned}$$
When $t=7.5$, $g''(t)=0$:
$$\dfrac{33}{10}e^{-7.5k}(1-7.5k)=0$$
Since $e^{-7.5k}\ne 0$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-7.5k&=0\\ 7.5k&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{1}{7.5}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{15}\end{aligned}$$

Let $g(t)$ be a function defined for all $t\ge 0$. The gradient function is given by

$$g'(t)=\dfrac{33}{10}te^{-kt}.$$

where $k$ is a positive constant. The diagram below shows a sketch of $g'(t)$ against $t$.

$$\begin{aligned}85.43&\approx\int_0^{12}g'(t)\,dt\\ &=\Big[g(t)\Big]_0^{12}\\ &=g(12)-g(0)\\ &=g(12)\quad(\text{since } g(0)=0)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 85.43 is an estimate for $g(12)$.

items.part:
ng wave-shaped window that stretches across the main lobby wall, inspired by the rolling surf of the nearby beaches. The top edge of this window is modelled mathematically to reflect both a smooth curve and a gentle wave.

The height, $h(x)$, of the top edge of the window above ground level, in metres, is described by the piecewise function:

$$h(x)=\begin{cases}a\left(1-(x-1)^2\right), & 0\le x\le 1\\ 2\cos(x-1)+2, & 1<x\le d\end{cases}$$

where $a$ and $d$ are constants and $x$ is the horizontal distance from the leftmost point of the window (which is at ground level).

\exfigure{1369_q31_1}
Determine the value of $a$ in the function $h(x)$.
items.sol:
$h(x)$ is continuous at $x=1$, so the two pieces agree there:
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(1-(1-1)^2\right)&=2\cos(1-1)+2\\ a\times 1&=2\cos 0+2\\ a&=2\times 1+2\\ a&=4\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
ng wave-shaped window that stretches across the main lobby wall, inspired by the rolling surf of the nearby beaches. The top edge of this window is modelled mathematically to reflect both a smooth curve and a gentle wave.

The height, $h(x)$, of the top edge of the window above ground level, in metres, is described by the piecewise function:

$$h(x)=\begin{cases}a\left(1-(x-1)^2\right), & 0\le x\le 1\\ 2\cos(x-1)+2, & 1<x\le d\end{cases}$$

where $a$ and $d$ are constants and $x$ is the horizontal distance from the leftmost point of the window (which is at ground level).

\exfigure{1369_q31_1}
By first showing that the length of the bottom edge of the window $d$ is $(\pi+1)$ metres, determine the area of the window.
items.sol:
The right end of the window is at ground level, so $h(d)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos(d-1)+2&=0\\ 2\cos(d-1)&=-2\\ \cos(d-1)&=-1\\ d-1&=\pi\quad(\text{first solution})\\ d&=\pi+1\end{aligned}$$
The area of the window is the area under each piece of $h(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^1 4\left(1-(x-1)^2\right)dx+\int_1^{\pi+1}\left(2\cos(x-1)+2\right)dx\\ &=4\int_0^1\left(2x-x^2\right)dx+2\int_1^{\pi+1}\left(\cos(x-1)+1\right)dx\\ &=4\left[\dfrac{2x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1+2\Big[\sin(x-1)+x\Big]_1^{\pi+1}\\ &=4\left[\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-(0-0)\right]+2\left[\sin\pi+\pi+1-(\sin 0+1)\right]\\ &=\left(\dfrac{8}{3}+2\pi\right)\text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
ng wave-shaped window that stretches across the main lobby wall, inspired by the rolling surf of the nearby beaches. The top edge of this window is modelled mathematically to reflect both a smooth curve and a gentle wave.

The height, $h(x)$, of the top edge of the window above ground level, in metres, is described by the piecewise function:

$$h(x)=\begin{cases}a\left(1-(x-1)^2\right), & 0\le x\le 1\\ 2\cos(x-1)+2, & 1<x\le d\end{cases}$$

where $a$ and $d$ are constants and $x$ is the horizontal distance from the leftmost point of the window (which is at ground level).

\exfigure{1369_q31_1}
The top edge of the wall, shown as the line $AB$ below, is to just touch the window at point $C$ as shown below.

The wall is 1.39 m higher at point $A$ than point $B$. How high is point $C$ above the ground?

\exfigure{1369_q31_2}
items.sol:
$A$ is above $x=0$, $B$ is above $x=d=\pi+1$, and $A$ is 1.39 m higher than $B$:
$$m_{AB}=\dfrac{-1.39}{\pi+1}$$
$AB$ touches the window at $C$, so the gradient of the curve at $C$ equals $m_{AB}$. For $x>1$, $h'(x)=-2\sin(x-1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}-2\sin(x-1)&=\dfrac{-1.39}{\pi+1}\\ \sin(x-1)&=\dfrac{1.39}{2(\pi+1)}\\ x-1&=0.1686\ldots\quad(\text{first solution})\\ x&=1.1686\ldots\end{aligned}$$
When $x=1.1686\ldots$:
$$\begin{aligned}h(1.1686\ldots)&=2\cos(1.1686\ldots-1)+2\\ &=3.97\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $C$ is 3.97 m above the ground.

Eric is organising a gala dinner. The function centre will charge him \$2 000 to hire the room and he needs to pay a catering company \$80 per person for food.
What is the profit if 75 people attend the dinner?
items.sol:
From the graph, when 75 people attend, the income is $\$9000$ and the costs are $\$8000$:
$$9000-8000=1000$$
$\therefore$ The profit is $\$1000$ when 75 people attend.

items.part:
A saucepan of hot water at a temperature of $T^\circ$ Celsius loses heat when taken off the stove. It cools according to the equation $T=T_0+Ae^{kt}$ where $t$ is the time elapsed in minutes, $T_0$ is the room temperature measured in degrees Celsius and $k$ is a constant.
A saucepan of hot water of temperature $95^\circ$ is removed from the stove. It cools to a temperature of $90^\circ$ five minutes later in a room with a temperature of $27^\circ$. By finding the value of the constants $T_0$ and $A$, write an equation for $T$ in terms of $t$.
items.sol:
$T_0$ is the room temperature, so $T_0=27$.

Initially ($t=0$), $T=95$:
$$\begin{aligned}95&=27+Ae^{k(0)}\\A&=68\end{aligned}$$
When $t=5$, $T=90$:
$$\begin{aligned}90&=27+68e^{5k}\\63&=68e^{5k}\\e^{5k}&=\dfrac{63}{68}\\5k&=\ln\dfrac{63}{68}\\k&=\dfrac{1}{5}\ln\dfrac{63}{68}\\&=-0.01527459576\\&=-0.0153\ (3\text{ significant figures})\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T=27+68e^{-0.0153t}\quad(\text{or equivalent})$$

items.part:
A saucepan of hot water at a temperature of $T^\circ$ Celsius loses heat when taken off the stove. It cools according to the equation $T=T_0+Ae^{kt}$ where $t$ is the time elapsed in minutes, $T_0$ is the room temperature measured in degrees Celsius and $k$ is a constant.
How hot will the water be after 10 minutes?
items.sol:
When $t=10$, with $k=\dfrac{1}{5}\ln\dfrac{63}{68}=-0.01527\ldots$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=27+68e^{10k}\\&=85.36764706\\&\approx 85^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The water will be about $85^\circ$ after 10 minutes.

\extable{Tq640_1}

You may assume for the following questions that a higher number gives a better result.
In which test did Nathan perform best in relative to the population? Justify your answer with suitable calculations.
items.sol:
Compare $z$-scores, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$: a higher $z$-score is a better result relative to the population.

Muscular strength:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{93-84}{6}\\&=1.5\end{aligned}$$
Agility:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{78-70}{5}\\&=1.6\end{aligned}$$
Agility has the higher $z$-score, so Nathan performed best in agility.

Students who score above 93 or above for muscular strength will be recommended for an elite training program. By using the $z$-tables provided or otherwise, find how many people you would expect to be recommended for the program if 200 people are tested?
items.sol:
A score of 93 has $z=1.5$ (part (a)). From the $z$-table, $0.9332$ of all people have a $z$-score below $1.5$, so the expected number above it is
$$(1-0.9332)\times 200=13.36$$
$\therefore$ Approximately 13 people will be recommended for the program.

items.part: Find the gradient of the normal to the curve $y=\dfrac{x}{\tan x}$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\tan x-x\sec^2 x}{\tan^2 x}$$
When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned}m_T&=\dfrac{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{4}\sec^2\frac{\pi}{4}}{\tan^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\\&=\dfrac{1-\frac{\pi}{4}\times 2}{1}\\&=1-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-\dfrac{1}{m_T}$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_N&=\dfrac{-1}{1-\frac{\pi}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{2}{\pi-2}\\&=1.751938394\ldots\\&\approx 1.752\ (3\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the points of intersection of $y=4x+7$ and $y=x^3-3x^2+7$.
items.sol:
Solve the two equations simultaneously:
$$\begin{aligned}x^3-3x^2+7&=4x+7\\x^3-3x^2-4x&=0\\x(x^2-3x-4)&=0\\x(x-4)(x+1)&=0\\x&=0,\ -1\text{ or }4\end{aligned}$$
Substitute each value into $y=x^3-3x^2+7$:
$$\begin{aligned}x=0:\quad y&=7\\ x=-1:\quad y&=(-1)^3-3(-1)^2+7=3\\ x=4:\quad y&=(4)^3-3(4)^2+7=23\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The points of intersection are $(-1,3)$, $(0,7)$ and $(4,23)$.

items.part:
Sketch the function $y=x^3-3x^2+7$, by first finding all stationary points and determining their nature. Do NOT find the $x$-intercepts and points of inflection.

\exfigure{1356_q18_1}
items.sol:
The curve cuts the $y$-axis at $(0,7)$.

Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=3x^2-6x\\3x^2-6x&=0\\3x(x-2)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }x=2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=2^3-3\times 2^2+7\\&=3\end{aligned}$$
Determine the nature using $y''=6x-6$:
$$\begin{aligned} x=0:\quad y''&=-6<0 &&\text{maximum turning point}\\ x=2:\quad y''&=6>0 &&\text{minimum turning point}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $(0,7)$ is a maximum turning point and $(2,3)$ is a minimum turning point.

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $a=5e^{-2t}$. Initially the particle is at rest.
Write an equation for the velocity.
items.sol:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int 5e^{-2t}\,dt\\&=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2t}+c\end{aligned}$$
The particle is initially at rest, so $v=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2(0)}+c\\c&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ v=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2t}+\dfrac{5}{2}$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $a=5e^{-2t}$. Initially the particle is at rest.
Explain why the particle is always speeding up for $t>0$.
items.sol:
$a=5e^{-2t}>0$ for all $t$, since $e^{-2t}>0$.

For $t>0$, $e^{-2t}<1$, so $v=\dfrac{5}{2}\left(1-e^{-2t}\right)>0$.

Velocity and acceleration are both positive for $t>0$, so the particle is always speeding up.

items.part: The function $y=e^x\cos 2x$ has a stationary point at $x=0.23$ and $x=1.80$ (correct to 2 decimal places). Find the point of inflection of the function $y=e^x\cos 2x$ for $0.23<x<1.80$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2e^x\sin 2x+e^x\cos 2x$$
Differentiate each term with the product rule again. For $-2e^x\sin 2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-2e^x & v&=\sin 2x\\ u'&=-2e^x & v'&=2\cos 2x\end{aligned}$$
For $e^x\cos 2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4e^x\cos 2x-2e^x\sin 2x-2e^x\sin 2x+e^x\cos 2x\\&=-3e^x\cos 2x-4e^x\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection occur when $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3e^x\cos 2x-4e^x\sin 2x&=0\\-e^x(3\cos 2x+4\sin 2x)&=0\\3\cos 2x+4\sin 2x&=0\quad\text{since } e^x>0\\3\cos 2x&=-4\sin 2x\\\dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}&=\dfrac{-3}{4}\\\tan 2x&=\dfrac{-3}{4}\end{aligned}$$
For $0.23<x<1.80$, $0.46<2x<3.60$, and $\tan 2x<0$, so $2x$ is in the second quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{reference angle}&=0.6435011088\\2x&=\pi-0.6435011088\\&=2.498091545\\x&=1.249045772\\&=1.25\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e^{1.249045772}\cos(2\times1.249045772)\\&=-2.789611172\\&=-2.79\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
Check that the concavity changes either side of $x=1.25$:

\exfigure{1356_q21_s1}

$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ changes sign, so there is a point of inflection at $(1.25,-2.79)$.
\exfigure{1356_q22_s1}

items.part:
Joshua and Fahim leave base camp ($C$) together and walk on a bearing of $100^\circ T$ for 10 km to a waterfall ($W$). Joshua stays at the waterfall and Fahim continues his journey by walking 6 km on a bearing of $258^\circ T$ to a lookout ($L$).
Find the distance between the lookout and base camp. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The bearing of $L$ from $W$ is $258^\circ$, so measured anticlockwise from north:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle NWL+258^\circ&=360^\circ\\\angle NWL&=102^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $C$ from $W$ is $280^\circ$, so $\angle NWC=80^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle CWL&=102^\circ-80^\circ\\&=22^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle CWL$, $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$:
$$\begin{aligned}CL^2&=10^2+6^2-2\times 10\times 6\cos 22^\circ\\&=24.73793745\\CL&=4.973724706\\&\approx 4.97\text{ km}\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Joshua and Fahim leave base camp ($C$) together and walk on a bearing of $100^\circ T$ for 10 km to a waterfall ($W$). Joshua stays at the waterfall and Fahim continues his journey by walking 6 km on a bearing of $258^\circ T$ to a lookout ($L$).
Hence, or otherwise find the bearing that Fahim must walk on, to return to the base camp.
items.sol:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle CWL$ to find $\angle WLC$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\angle WLC&=\dfrac{CL^2+WL^2-CW^2}{2\times CL\times WL}\\&=\dfrac{4.97\ldots^2+6^2-10^2}{2\times 4.97\ldots\times 6}\\&=-0.6578246162\\\angle WLC&=131.1341759^\circ\\&\approx 131^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$\angle NWL=102^\circ$ (part (b)), and the north lines at $W$ and $L$ are parallel:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle WLN&=180^\circ-102^\circ\\&=78^\circ\quad(\text{co-interior angles})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle NLC&=131^\circ-78^\circ\\&=53^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$C$ is $53^\circ$ anticlockwise from north at $L$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-53^\circ\\&=307^\circ T\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $\log_8 x+\log_4 x=5$.
items.sol:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$, with base 2:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_8 x+\log_4 x&=5\\\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 8}+\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 4}&=5\\\dfrac{\log_2 x}{3}+\dfrac{\log_2 x}{2}&=5\\2\log_2 x+3\log_2 x&=30\\5\log_2 x&=30\\\log_2 x&=6\\x&=2^6\\&=64\end{aligned}$$

The curve lies above the line for $0<x<3$, so the area is the integral of the difference:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^3\left(\dfrac{4x}{x^2+3}-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)dx\\&=2\int_0^3\dfrac{2x}{x^2+3}\,dx-\int_0^3\dfrac{x}{3}\,dx\\&=\left[2\ln(x^2+3)-\dfrac{x^2}{6}\right]_0^3\\&=\left(2\ln(3^2+3)-\dfrac{3^2}{6}\right)-\left(2\ln(0^2+3)-\dfrac{0^2}{6}\right)\\&=2\ln 12-\dfrac{9}{6}-2\ln 3\\&=2(\ln 12-\ln 3)-\dfrac{3}{2}\\&=2\ln 4-\dfrac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of hours of daylight ($H$) in Sydney can be modelled by the trigonometric function $H=2.3\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)+13.1$ where $t$ is the number of days after 1$^{\text{st}}$ January, 2025.
What is the maximum number of hours of daylight in Sydney in a year?
items.sol:
$H$ is greatest when the sine term equals 1:
$$\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)=1$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{Maximum number of daylight hours}&=2.3\times 1+13.1\\&=15.4\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of hours of daylight ($H$) in Sydney can be modelled by the trigonometric function $H=2.3\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)+13.1$ where $t$ is the number of days after 1$^{\text{st}}$ January, 2025.
How quickly are the number of hours of daylight increasing when $t=10$?
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}H&=2.3\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))+13.1\\\dfrac{dH}{dt}&=0.0115\pi\cos(0.005(\pi t-265))\end{aligned}$$
When $t=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dH}{dt}&=0.0115\pi\cos(0.005(\pi\times 10-265))\\&=0.01416467195\\&\approx 0.0142\text{ hours/day}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{x^2} & 2\le x\le 10\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
Find the value of $a$ such that $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
items.sol:
The total area under a probability density function is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^{10}\dfrac{a}{x^2}\,dx&=1\\\int_2^{10}ax^{-2}\,dx&=1\\\Big[-ax^{-1}\Big]_2^{10}&=1\\\left[\dfrac{-a}{x}\right]_2^{10}&=1\\\dfrac{-a}{10}-\left(\dfrac{-a}{2}\right)&=1\\-a+5a&=10\\4a&=10\\a&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{x^2} & 2\le x\le 10\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
Find $P(X>8)$
items.sol:
With $a=\dfrac{5}{2}$, $f(x)=\dfrac{5}{2x^2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>8)&=\int_8^{10}\dfrac{5}{2x^2}\,dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{-5}{2x}\right]_8^{10}\\&=\left(\dfrac{-5}{2\times 10}\right)-\left(\dfrac{-5}{2\times 8}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{16}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{x^2} & 2\le x\le 10\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
Find the median of $X$.
items.sol:
The median $x$ satisfies $P(X\le x)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^x\dfrac{5}{2t^2}\,dt&=0.5\\\left[-\dfrac{5}{2t}\right]_2^x&=0.5\\\left(-\dfrac{5}{2x}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{5}{2\times 2}\right)&=0.5\\\dfrac{-5}{2x}+\dfrac{5}{4}&=0.5\\-10+5x&=2x\\3x&=10\\x&=\dfrac{10}{3}\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1356_q27_s1}

The curve is above the $x$-axis for $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and below it for $\dfrac{\pi}{4}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so
$$A=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\cos 2x\sin^4 2x\,dx+\left|\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cos 2x\sin^4 2x\,dx\right|$$
Using the reverse chain rule with $f(x)=\sin 2x$, $f'(x)=2\cos 2x$ and $n=4$:
$$\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx=\dfrac{1}{n+1}[f(x)]^{n+1}+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}2\cos 2x\sin^4 2x\,dx+\left|\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\cos 2x\sin^4 2x\,dx\right|\\&=\left[\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}+\left|\left[\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5 2x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\right|\\&=\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5\dfrac{2\times\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5 0+\left|\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5\dfrac{2\times\pi}{2}-\dfrac{1}{10}\sin^5\dfrac{2\times\pi}{4}\right|\\&=\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{1}{10}\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Nila builds furniture to order. The amount of time that it takes between placing an order and it leaving the warehouse follows a normal distribution.

Nila knows that $2.5\%$ of all her orders are made and leave her warehouse within 10 days of being placed. In total, last year, Nila received 35 orders and customers waited a combined total of 1610 days for their orders to leave the warehouse.

Nila decides that she will give a discount to at most $5\%$ of her customers who have to wait a long time for their orders and would like to advertise this.

What is the minimum waiting time a customer must exceed in order to qualify for the discount? You may use the $z$-tables provided.
items.sol:
The mean waiting time is the total wait divided by the number of orders:
$$\begin{aligned}\mu&=\dfrac{1610}{35}\\&=46\end{aligned}$$
$2.5\%$ of orders leave within 10 days, and $2.5\%$ of a normal distribution lies below $z=-2$, so 10 days has a $z$-score of $-2$:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\-2&=\dfrac{10-46}{\sigma}\\-2\sigma&=-36\\\sigma&=18\end{aligned}$$
The discount goes to the $5\%$ of customers who wait longest, so we need the score corresponding to a $z$-score of $1.65$:
$$\begin{aligned}1.65&=\dfrac{x-46}{18}\\29.7&=x-46\\x&=75.7\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Customers who wait more than 76 days will receive a discount.
items.final: Customers who wait more than 76 days will receive a discount.

items.sol:
From the spinner:
$$P(B)=\dfrac{3}{10}$$

Jonathan can win on the first, second, third, … spin; each extra green spin multiplies the probability by $\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$P(\text{Jonathan wins})=\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{10}+\ldots$$
This is the limiting sum of a geometric series with $a=\dfrac{3}{10}$ and $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{10}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{3}{5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: The common difference of an arithmetic sequence is $-4$. The sum of the first 30 terms is $23940$ and the sum of the last 30 terms is $-1980$. Find how many terms are in the sequence.
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $n=30$ and $d=-4$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{30}&=\dfrac{30}{2}\big(2a+(30-1)\times(-4)\big)\\23940&=15(2a-116)\\1596&=2a-116\\1712&=2a\\a&=856\end{aligned}$$
Let $n$ be the number of terms. The last 30 terms are
$$a+(n-1)d,\ a+(n-2)d,\ a+(n-3)d,\ \ldots,\ a+(n-30)d$$
and their sum is $-1980$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Sum}&=a+(n-1)d+a+(n-2)d+a+(n-3)d+\ldots+a+(n-30)d\\&=30a+30dn-d(1+2+3+\ldots+30)\\&=30a+30dn-d\times\dfrac{30}{2}(1+30)\\&=30a+30dn-465d\\-1980&=30\times 856+30\times(-4)n-465(-4)\\-1980&=27540-120n\\120n&=29520\\n&=246\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Ella borrows \$820 000 to purchase a house. She is being charged $8.4\%$ per annum and plans to making equal monthly repayments of \$6248 over 30 years.
Show that the amount owing after 10 years is \$724 960.57

Ella borrows \$820 000 to purchase a house. She is being charged $8.4\%$ per annum and plans to making equal monthly repayments of \$6248 over 30 years.
After paying the home loan off for 10 years, Ella gets a pay rise. Immediately after making the 120$^{\text{th}}$ payment, Ella makes a one-off payment to reduce the balance owing to \$720 000. She then increases her monthly repayments so that the loan is paid off 25 years after the initial loan. Calculate the amount of her new monthly payment.
items.sol:
After the one-off payment the balance is $\$720\,000$. The loan is paid off 25 years after it began, so $25-10=15$ years, or $180$ months, remain. Let $M$ be the new monthly repayment.

After $n$ more months the amount owing is
$$A_n=1.007^n\times 720000-M-M\times 1.007-M\times 1.007^2-\ldots-M\times 1.007^{n-1}$$
The repayments form a GP with first term $M$ and ratio $1.007$, and the loan is repaid when $A_{180}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=1.007^{180}\times 720000-\dfrac{M(1.007^{180}-1)}{1.007-1}\\0&=1.007^{180}\times 720000-\dfrac{M(1.007^{180}-1)}{0.007}\\1.007^{180}\times 720000&=\dfrac{M(1.007^{180}-1)}{0.007}\\1.007^{180}\times 720000\times 0.007&=M(1.007^{180}-1)\\M&=\dfrac{1.007^{180}\times 720000\times 0.007}{1.007^{180}-1}\\&=7047.983754\\&=\$7047.98\end{aligned}$$

The diagram shows a farmhouse $F$ that is located 300 metres from a straight section of road. The road begins at the shops $S$, which is situated 4 000 metres from the front gate $G$ of the farmhouse. The school bus leaves the shops at 8 am and travels along the road at a speed of 20m/s. Lucas lives in the farmhouse and he can cycle across the open paddock between the house and the road at a speed of 8 m/s. The bus will stop for Lucas anywhere on the road but will not wait for him.

Assume that Lucas catches the bus at the point $P$ on the road where $\angle GFP=\theta$.
Find two expressions in terms of $\theta$, one expression for the time taken for the bus to travel from $S$ to $P$ and the other expression for the time taken by Lucas to cycle from $F$ to $P$.
items.sol:
In right-angled $\triangle FGP$, $FG=300$ and $\angle GFP=\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=\dfrac{GP}{FG}\\&=\dfrac{GP}{300}\\GP&=300\tan\theta\end{aligned}$$
The bus travels $SP=4000+GP$ at 20 m/s, and time $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_B&=\dfrac{4000+300\tan\theta}{20}\\&=200+15\tan\theta\end{aligned}$$
Lucas cycles $FP$ at 8 m/s:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{FG}{FP}\\&=\dfrac{300}{FP}\\FP&=\dfrac{300}{\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}T_L&=\dfrac{300}{\cos\theta}\div 8\\&=\dfrac{75}{2\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$$

Lucas can leave home $T=T_B-T_L$ seconds after 8 am and still reach $P$ in time, so the latest departure is when this difference is a maximum.
$$T=200+15\tan\theta-\dfrac{75}{2\cos\theta}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dT}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=200+15\tan\theta-\dfrac{75}{2}(\cos\theta)^{-1}\\T'&=15\sec^2\theta+\dfrac{75}{2}(\cos\theta)^{-2}\times(-\sin\theta)\\&=\dfrac{15}{\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{75\sin\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}\\0&=\dfrac{15}{\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{75\sin\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}\\0&=15-\dfrac{75}{2}\sin\theta\\\dfrac{75}{2}\sin\theta&=15\\\sin\theta&=\dfrac{30}{75}\\\theta&=0.4115168461\end{aligned}$$

items.part: For which values of $k$ does the equation $x^2+(k+2)x+4=0$ have one solution?
items.sol:
One solution means equal roots, so the discriminant is zero:
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta&=b^2-4ac\\ &=(k+2)^2-4\times1\times4\\ &=k^2+4k-12 \end{aligned}$$
For equal roots, $\Delta=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} k^2+4k-12&=0\\ (k+6)(k-2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=-6\text{ or }k=2$$

If one ball is drawn from each bag, what is the probability that they are different colours?
items.sol:
The colours differ if white from $A$ and black from $B$, or black from $A$ and white from $B$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{different})&=P(WB)+P(BW)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5}+\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{13}{25} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x^2-9x$ at the point $(1,-8)$.
items.sol:
Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x-9$$
At $(1,-8)$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} m_T&=2\times1-9\\ &=-7 \end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-\dfrac{1}{m_T}=\dfrac{1}{7}$.

Using the point–gradient formula $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-(-8)&=\dfrac{1}{7}(x-1)\\ y&=\dfrac{x}{7}-\dfrac{57}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The tenth term of an arithmetic series is 29 and the fifteenth term is 44.
Find the value of the common difference and the value of the first term.
items.sol:
Use $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ for the two given terms:
$$\begin{aligned} a+9d&=29 &&\text{(1)}\\ a+14d&=44 &&\text{(2)} \end{aligned}$$
Subtract (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 5d&=15\\ d&=3 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $d=3$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a+27&=29\\ a&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=2,\ d=3$$

items.sol:

items.part: Differentiate $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+4x}{x+2}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2+4x & v&=x+2\\ u'&=2x+4 & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{(2x+4)(x+2)-(x^2+4x)}{(x+2)^2}$$

items.part: Differentiate $f(x)=e^{x\sin 3x}$
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 3x}\right)=e^{x\sin 3x}\times\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)$$
To find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)$, use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin 3x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)=\sin 3x\,(1)+x\cdot 3\cos 3x$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 3x}\right)=e^{x\sin 3x}\times(\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x)$$

items.part: Show that the derivative of $\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)$ is $\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$.

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=x^3-12x^2+36x$.
Find the $x$ and $y$ intercepts.
items.sol:
For the $y$ intercept, $x=0$, so $y=0$.

For the $x$ intercepts, $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=x^3-12x^2+36x\\ 0&=x(x^2-12x+36)\\ 0&=x(x-6)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the $x$ intercepts are $x=0$ and $x=6$.

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=x^3-12x^2+36x$.
Find the location and nature of any stationary points.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=3x^2-24x+36\\ y''&=6x-24 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-24x+36&=0\\ x^2-8x+12&=0\\ (x-2)(x-6)&=0\\ x&=2\text{ or }x=6 \end{aligned}$$
For $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2^3-12(2)^2+36(2)\\ &=32\\ y''&=6(2)-24\\ &=-12<0 \end{aligned}$$
so the curve is concave down at $x=2$.

For $x=6$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=6^3-12(6)^2+36(6)\\ &=0\\ y''&=6(6)-24\\ &=12>0 \end{aligned}$$
so the curve is concave up at $x=6$.

$\therefore$ $(2,32)$ is a local maximum and $(6,0)$ is a local minimum.
items.final: $(2,32)$ is a local maximum and $(6,0)$ is a local minimum

Find Dan's completion time if he finished ahead of 84% of competitors.
items.sol:
Dan finished ahead of $84\%$ of competitors, so $84\%$ of times are greater than his.

By the empirical rule, $68\%$ of times lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so the percentage of times greater than $\mu-\sigma$ is
$$50\%+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 68\%=84\%$$

items.part: Prove that $\sin x+1+\cos x\cot x-\operatorname{cosec}x=1$
items.sol:
Write everything in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, then use $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\sin x+1+\cos x\cot x-\operatorname{cosec}x\\ &=\sin x+1+\cos x\times\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}-\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x+\sin x+\cos^2x-1}{\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x+\sin x-1}{\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{1+\sin x-1}{\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x}\\ &=1\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x\ \text{ for }\ 0\le x\le\pi.$$
Find the cumulative distribution function.
items.sol:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^x\dfrac{1}{2}\sin t\,dt&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\big[\cos t\big]_0^x\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos x-1) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x),\qquad 0\le x\le\pi$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x\ \text{ for }\ 0\le x\le\pi.$$
Find the first quartile of the distribution.
items.sol:
The first quartile $x$ satisfies $F(x)=0.25$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x)&=0.25\\ 1-\cos x&=0.5\\ \cos x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le x\le\pi$:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
The first quartile is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

items.part:
The population of a certain bacteria culture grows exponentially. At 12:00 pm, the population is 1000 bacteria. After 3 hours, the population reaches 2500 bacteria.
The exponential function modelling the bacteria culture growth is of the form

$$P(t)=P_0a^t$$

where $P(t)$ is the population and $t$ is the time in hours since 12:00 pm.

$P_0$ and $a$ are constants.

Find the value of $P_0$ and $a$.
items.sol:
At $t=0$ (12:00 pm) the population is 1000, so $P_0=1000$ and $P(t)=1000(a)^t$.

Given $P(3)=2500$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2500&=1000(a)^3\\ a^3&=2.5\\ a&\approx1.3572 \end{aligned}$$
So the function is $P(t)=1000(1.3572)^t$.
