items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} P(1)&=1000(1.3572)^1\\ &=1357.2\\ P(4)&=1000(1.3572)^4\\ &\approx 3392.93 \end{aligned}$$
The average rate of change is the gradient of the chord from $t=1$ to $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Average rate}&=\dfrac{P(4)-P(1)}{4-1}\\ &\approx\dfrac{3392.93-1357.2}{3}\\ &\approx\dfrac{2035.73}{3}\\ &\approx 678.58\text{ bacteria/hour} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of a certain bacteria culture grows exponentially. At 12:00 pm, the population is 1000 bacteria. After 3 hours, the population reaches 2500 bacteria.
Find the instantaneous rate of change of the population at $t=2$ hours.
items.sol:
Differentiate using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^t\right)=a^t\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(t)&=1000(1.3572)^t\\ P'(t)&=1000(1.3572)^t\ln 1.3572\\ P'(2)&=1000(1.3572)^2\ln 1.3572\\ &\approx 562.6 \end{aligned}$$
At 2 hours, the population is increasing at approximately $562.6$ bacteria/hour.

items.part:
Initially there are 350 litres of water in a tank. Water starts flowing into the tank.

The rate of increase of the volume $V$ of water in litres is given by $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=300-7.5t$, where $t$ is the time in hours.

Find the volume of water in the tank when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$.
items.sol:
Integrating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 300-7.5t\\ V &= 300t-\dfrac{7.5t^2}{2}+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $V=350$:
$$350=0-0+C$$
$$\therefore\ V=300t-3.75t^2+350$$
When $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 300-7.5t &= 0\\ 7.5t &= 300\\ t &= 40\end{aligned}$$
When $t=40$:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 300\times 40-3.75\times 40^2+350\\ &= 6350 \text{ L}\end{aligned}$$

$$V(t)=6.5\left(1-e^{-kt}\right),$$

where $k$ is a positive constant and $t$ is the number of seconds after the circuit is switched on.
Draw a sketch of the graph of $V(t)$, showing its behaviour as $t$ increases.

In a particular electrical circuit, the voltage $V$ (volts) across a capacitor is given by

$$V(t)=6.5\left(1-e^{-kt}\right),$$

where $k$ is a positive constant and $t$ is the number of seconds after the circuit is switched on.
When $t=1$, the voltage across the capacitor is 2.6 volts.

Find the value of $k$, correct to 3 decimal places.
items.sol:
When $t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2.6 &= 6.5\left(1-e^{-k}\right)\\ 1-e^{-k} &= \dfrac{2.6}{6.5}\\ 1-e^{-k} &= 0.4\\ e^{-k} &= 0.6\\ k &= -\ln(0.6)\\ &= 0.511 \quad (\text{3 decimal places})\end{aligned}$$

where $k$ is a positive constant and $t$ is the number of seconds after the circuit is switched on.

items.sol:
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=6.5ke^{-kt}$$
When $t=2$, using $k=-\ln 0.6$ from part (b):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 6.5ke^{-2k}\\ &= 1.195 \text{ volts/second}\end{aligned}$$

In a game, the probability that a particular player scores a goal at each attempt is $0.15$.
What is the probability that this player does NOT score a goal in the first two attempts?
items.sol:
$$\text{Probability (player misses in 1 attempt)}=1-0.15=0.85$$
$$\text{Probability (player misses in both attempts)}=(0.85)^2=0.7225$$

items.part:
In a game, the probability that a particular player scores a goal at each attempt is $0.15$.
Determine the least number of attempts that this player must make so that the probability of scoring at least one goal is greater than $0.8$.
items.sol:
The player scores at least one goal unless every one of the $n$ attempts misses:
$$P(\text{at least one goal})=1-(0.85)^n$$
We need
$$\begin{aligned} 1-(0.85)^n &> 0.8\\ (0.85)^n &< 0.2\end{aligned}$$
Taking logs (and dividing by $\ln(0.85)<0$ reverses the inequality):
$$\begin{aligned} n\ln(0.85) &< \ln(0.2)\\ n &> \dfrac{\ln(0.2)}{\ln(0.85)}\\ &\approx 9.90\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The player needs 10 attempts.

The denominator is always positive, so $f''(x)>0$ when

items.part:
Jack intends to deposit \$80 into a savings account on the first day of each month for 24 months. The interest rate during this time is 6\% per annum, compounded monthly.
Calculate how much money Jack will have in his account at the end of the 24 months.
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{6\%}{12}=0.5\%$, so each month the balance is multiplied by $1.005$.

The first deposit accrues interest for 24 months.

$\therefore$ Its future value is $80(1.005)^{24}$.

The next deposit accrues interest for 23 months, and so on, down to 1 month for the last deposit.

Summing the geometric series ($a=1.005$, $r=1.005$, 24 terms):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 80(1.005)^{24}+80(1.005)^{23}+\cdots+80(1.005)^{1}\\ &= 80\left[(1.005)^1+(1.005)^2+\cdots+(1.005)^{24}\right]\\ &= 80\times(1.005)\left[\dfrac{(1.005)^{24}-1}{1.005-1}\right]\\ &= 2044.73\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Jack will have $\$2044.73$.

A function $f(x)$ is defined as

$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & \text{for } x<0\\[6pt] x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}, & \text{for } 0\le x\le 2\\[6pt] 1, & \text{for } x>2\end{cases}$$

The median $t$ satisfies $F(t)=\dfrac{1}{2}$:

Using the quadratic formula:

The median lies in $0\le t\le 2$, so we need $t<2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ t &= 2-\sqrt{2}\\ &\approx 0.586\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the derivative of $x^2\tan x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\tan x\right) &= 2x\tan x+x^2\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int (x\tan x+1)^2\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$ and part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \int (x\tan x+1)^2\,dx &= \int \left(x^2\tan^2 x+2x\tan x+1\right)dx\\ &= \int \left(x^2\left(\sec^2 x-1\right)+2x\tan x+1\right)dx\\ &= \int \left(x^2\sec^2 x+2x\tan x-x^2+1\right)dx\\ &= x^2\tan x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+x+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Anna is sitting in a carriage of a Ferris wheel which is revolving. The height, $A(t)$, in metres above the ground of the top of her carriage is given by

$$A(t)=c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{24}\right),$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds after Anna's carriage first reaches the bottom of its revolution and $c$ and $k$ are constants.

\exfigure{1628_q28_1}

The top of each carriage reaches a greatest height of 39 metres and a smallest height of 3 metres.
Billie is in another carriage. The height, $B(t)$, in metres above the ground of the top of her carriage is given by

$$B(t)=c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right),$$

where $c$ and $k$ are as found in part (a).

During each revolution, there are two occasions when Anna's and Billie's carriages are at the same heights. At what two heights does this occur? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The carriages are at the same height when $A(t)=B(t)$:
$$c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}t\right)=c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right)$$
$$\therefore\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}t\right)=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right)$$
Two angles have equal cosines when they are equal, opposite, or add to $2\pi$ (within one revolution).

Equal angles:
$$\dfrac{\pi}{24}t=\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)$$
which is impossible.

Opposite angles:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\\ -\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}t-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ \dfrac{\pi}{12}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ t &= 3\end{aligned}$$
Angles adding to $2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\\ -\dfrac{2\pi}{24}t &= -2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ \dfrac{\pi t}{12} &= \dfrac{9\pi}{4}\\ t &= 27\end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$\text{height}=21-18\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{24}=4.37 \text{ m}$$
When $t=27$:
$$\text{height}=21-18\cos\dfrac{27\pi}{24}=37.63 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=ax^2+bx+c$, where $a\ne 0$.

At a particular point, the tangent and normal to the curve are given by $t(x)=2x+3$ and $n(x)=-\dfrac{1}{2}x-2$ respectively.

The curve has a minimum turning point at $x=-4$.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
items.sol:
The tangent and normal meet where
$$\begin{aligned} 2x+3 &= -\dfrac{1}{2}x-2\\ \dfrac{5x}{2} &= -5\\ x &= -2\\ y &= 2(-2)+3\\ y &= -1\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ They meet at $(-2,-1)$.

If $y=ax^2+bx+c$, then $y'=2ax+b$.

When $x=-4$, $y'=0$ (minimum turning point):
$$\begin{aligned} -8a+b &= 0\\ \therefore\ b &= 8a\end{aligned}$$
When $x=-2$, $y'=2$ (gradient of the tangent):
$$\begin{aligned} -4a+b &= 2\\ -4a+8a &= 2\\ \therefore\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ \therefore\ b &= 4\end{aligned}$$
When $x=-2$, $y=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} a(-2)^2+b(-2)+c &= -1\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\times 4+4\times(-2)+c &= -1\\ -6+c &= -1\\ \therefore\ c &= 5\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Suppose the geometric series $x+x^2+x^3+\cdots$ has a limiting sum, $S$.

By considering the graph $y=-1-\dfrac{1}{x-1}$, or otherwise, find the range of possible values of $S$.
items.sol:
The limiting sum of a geometric series with $a=x$, $r=x$ is
$$\begin{aligned} S &= x+x^2+x^3+\cdots\\ &= \dfrac{x}{1-x} \qquad \text{where } -1<x<1\end{aligned}$$
Rewriting the given function:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -1-\dfrac{1}{x-1}=\dfrac{-(x-1)-1}{x-1}\\ &= \dfrac{-x}{x-1}=\dfrac{x}{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
So, the graph of $y=\dfrac{x}{1-x}$ is as shown.

\exfigure{1628_q30_s1}

When $x=-1$, $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

From the graph, when $-1<x<1$, $y>-\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\therefore\ S>-\dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part:
Two circles have the same centre $O$. The smaller circle has radius 1 cm, while the larger circle has radius $(1+x)$ cm. The circles enclose a region $QRST$, which is subtended by an angle $\theta$ at $O$, as shaded.

The area of $QRST$ is $A\text{ cm}^2$, where $A$ is a constant and $A>0$.

\exfigure{1628_q31_1}

Let $P$ cm be the perimeter of $QRST$.
By finding expressions for the area and perimeter of $QRST$, show that $P(x)=2x+\dfrac{2A}{x}$.
items.sol:
The perimeter is two arcs ($l=r\theta$) and two straight edges of length $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1\theta+(1+x)\theta+2x\\ &= (2+x)\theta+2x\end{aligned}$$
The area is the difference of two sectors ($A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1+x)^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1^2\theta\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta\left[1+2x+x^2-1\right]\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta\left(2x+x^2\right)\\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\theta x(2+x) \qquad (1)\end{aligned}$$
From (1):
$$(2+x)\theta=\dfrac{2A}{x}$$
Substituting into $P=(2+x)\theta+2x$:
$$\therefore\ P(x)=2x+\dfrac{2A}{x}$$

items.part:
Two circles have the same centre $O$. The smaller circle has radius 1 cm, while the larger circle has radius $(1+x)$ cm. The circles enclose a region $QRST$, which is subtended by an angle $\theta$ at $O$, as shaded.

The area of $QRST$ is $A\text{ cm}^2$, where $A$ is a constant and $A>0$.

\exfigure{1628_q31_1}

Let $P$ cm be the perimeter of $QRST$.
Show that if the perimeter, $P(x)$, is minimised, then $\theta$ must be less than 2.
items.sol:
For a stationary point, $P'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} P' &= 2-\dfrac{2A}{x^2}=0\\ x^2 &= A\\ x &= \sqrt{A} \quad (x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$P''=\dfrac{4A}{x^3}>0 \text{ when } x=\sqrt{A}$$
$\therefore$ This gives a minimum value.

Using (1) with $x=\sqrt{A}$:
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}\theta\sqrt{A}\left(2+\sqrt{A}\right)$$
$$\theta=\dfrac{2A}{\sqrt{A}\left(2+\sqrt{A}\right)}=\dfrac{2\sqrt{A}}{2+\sqrt{A}}$$
Since $2+\sqrt{A}>\sqrt{A}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta &< \dfrac{2\sqrt{A}}{\sqrt{A}}\\ &= 2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ If $P(x)$ is minimised, $\theta<2$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 0\times 0.1+1\times 0.2+2\times 0.25+3\times 0.3+4\times 0.15 \\ &= 2.2 \end{aligned}$$

Using $E(X)=2.2$ and $E(X^2)=6.3$ from parts (c) and (d):
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(X) &= E(X^2)-\mu^2 \\ &= 6.3-2.2^2 \\ &= 1.46 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the values of $x$ such that the following limiting sum exists.

$$1+(1-2x)+(1-2x)^2+(1-2x)^3+\cdots.$$
items.sol:
The limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$, with $r=1-2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1&<1-2x<1 \\ -2&<-2x<0 &&(\text{subtract } 1) \\ 1&>x>0 &&(\text{divide by } -2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0<x<1$$

items.part:
A team has a $\dfrac{1}{3}$ chance of winning any given game. If they played $3$ games, find the probability of them winning:
at least one game.
items.sol:
$P(\text{at least one})=1-P(\text{none})$:
$$1-\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^3=\dfrac{19}{27}$$

items.part:
A team has a $\dfrac{1}{3}$ chance of winning any given game. If they played $3$ games, find the probability of them winning:
exactly one game.
items.sol:
Exactly one win: $3$ choices for the game won, each with probability $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2$:
$$3\times\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2=\dfrac{4}{9}$$

items.part:
Find the value of the following arithmetic series:

$$1+5+9+\cdots+2025.$$
items.sol:
Arithmetic series with $a=1$, $d=4$ and last term $2025$. Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2025&=1+(n-1)\times 4 \\ 2024&=4(n-1) \\ 506&=n-1 \\ n&=507 \end{aligned}$$
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{507}&=\dfrac{507}{2}(1+2025) \\ &=513591 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the equation $y=2\sin 3t+4$.
State its period.
items.sol:
For $y=a\sin nt+c$ the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$, with $n=3$:

items.part:
Consider the equation $y=2\sin 3t+4$.
State its range.
items.sol:
Since $-1\le\sin 3t\le 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} -2&\le 2\sin 3t\le 2 &&(\text{multiply by } 2) \\ 2&\le 2\sin 3t+4\le 6 &&(\text{add } 4) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 2\le y\le 6$$

items.part:
Consider the graph of the curve given by $y=\dfrac{1}{27}x^3-x+2$.
Find the coordinates of its stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1}{9}x^2-1 \\ 0&=\dfrac{1}{9}x^2-1 \\ x^2&=9 \\ x&=-3 \text{ or } x=3 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $y=\dfrac{1}{27}x^3-x+2$, the stationary points are $(-3,4)$ and $(3,0)$.

Nature, using $y''=\dfrac{2}{9}x$:
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-3)&=-\dfrac{2}{3}<0 &&\text{local maximum at } (-3,4) \\ y''(3)&=\dfrac{2}{3}>0 &&\text{local minimum at } (3,0) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the graph of the curve given by $y=\dfrac{1}{27}x^3-x+2$.
Find any points of inflection.
items.sol:
Possible points of inflection occur where $y''=\dfrac{2}{9}x=0$, so $x=0$ and the point is $(0,2)$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-1)&=-\dfrac{2}{9}<0 &&\text{concave down} \\ y''(1)&=\dfrac{2}{9}>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at $x=0$.

$\therefore$ $(0,2)$ is a point of inflexion.

Find:
$\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}-\cos 3x\right)dx$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}-\cos 3x\right)dx &= \int\left(x^{-2}-\cos 3x\right)dx \\ &= -x^{-1}-\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x+C \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{x}-\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find:
$\displaystyle\int(1-2x)^5\,dx$
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int(ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int(1-2x)^5\,dx &= \dfrac{(1-2x)^6}{6\times(-2)}+C \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{12}(1-2x)^6+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Alex takes out a loan at an interest rate of $5\%$ per annum, compounded annually. At the end of each year, interest is charged and then Alex makes a repayment.
Find $A_1$ and hence $A_2$ in terms of $M$.
items.sol:
Each year interest is added (multiply by $1.05$) and then $M$ is repaid:
$$A_1=10000(1.05)-M$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1(1.05)-M \\ &=\left[10000(1.05)-M\right](1.05)-M \\ &=10000(1.05)^2-M(1.05)-M \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Alex takes out a loan at an interest rate of $5\%$ per annum, compounded annually. At the end of each year, interest is charged and then Alex makes a repayment.
Find $A_n$ in terms of $M$ and $n$.
items.sol:
Continuing the pattern from part (i):
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=10000(1.05)^2-M(1+1.05) \\ A_n&=10000(1.05)^n-M\left(1+1.05+1.05^2+\cdots+1.05^{n-1}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Alex takes out a loan at an interest rate of $5\%$ per annum, compounded annually. At the end of each year, interest is charged and then Alex makes a repayment.
Find $M$ correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.05$, $n$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned} A_n&=10000(1.05)^n-M\times\dfrac{1.05^n-1}{0.05} \\ &=10000(1.05)^n-20M(1.05^n-1) \end{aligned}$$
The loan is repaid after $10$ years, so $A_{10}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=10000(1.05)^{10}-20M(1.05^{10}-1) \\ M&=\dfrac{10000(1.05)^{10}}{20(1.05^{10}-1)} \\ &=\$1295.05 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Alex takes out a loan at an interest rate of $5\%$ per annum, compounded annually. At the end of each year, interest is charged and then Alex makes a repayment.
If Alex only wants to repay $\$350$ each year in order to pay off his loan in $20$ years, what is the maximum amount he would be able to borrow under the same interest rate? Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

Suppose $f(x)=e^x(x+1)$.
Find the first derivative of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=x+1 \\ u'&=e^x & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f'(x)=e^x(x+1)+e^x$$

items.part:
Suppose $f(x)=e^x(x+1)$.
Hence, find the second derivative of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Differentiate $f'(x)=e^x(x+1)+e^x$, using part (a) for the first term:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=e^x(x+1)+e^x+e^x \\ &=e^x(x+1)+2e^x \\ &=e^x(x+3) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Suppose $f(x)=e^x(x+1)$.
By identifying a pattern, write down an expression for the $n$th derivative of $f(x)$, where $n$ is a positive integer.
items.sol:
Each derivative adds another $e^x$: $f'(x)=e^x(x+2)$, $f''(x)=e^x(x+3)$, so
$$\dfrac{d^n}{dx^n}\,e^x(x+1)=e^x(x+n+1)$$

The shaded area is the rectangle $10\times\ln 10$ minus the region between the curve and the $y$-axis for $0\le y\le\ln 10$. On the curve, $x=e^y$:

items.part: Find the area bounded between the graphs of $y=\sqrt{x-1}$ and $y=x-1$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1374_q26_s1}

Intersections (square both sides):
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x-1}&=x-1 \\ x-1&=x^2-2x+1 \\ x^2-3x+2&=0 \\ (x-1)(x-2)&=0 \\ x&=1 \text{ or } x=2 \end{aligned}$$
The curve is above the line for $1<x<2$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_1^2\left(\sqrt{x-1}-(x-1)\right)dx \\ &=\int_1^2\left((x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-x+1\right)dx \\ &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}(x-1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_1^2 \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}-2+2-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}+1\right) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The mass of a decaying radioactive substance, in kg, at time $t$ years is given by $M=2e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a positive constant.
State the initial mass of the radioactive substance.
items.sol: $2\text{ kg}$

items.part:
The mass of a decaying radioactive substance, in kg, at time $t$ years is given by $M=2e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a positive constant.
Find the half-life of the radioactive substance. Give your answer as an exact value in terms of $k$.
items.sol:
Half-life: the mass halves to $1$ kg:
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=2e^{-kt} \\ e^{kt}&=2 \\ kt&=\ln 2 \\ t&=\dfrac{1}{k}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The mass of a decaying radioactive substance, in kg, at time $t$ years is given by $M=2e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a positive constant.
Find $\dfrac{dM}{dt}$.
items.sol: $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-2ke^{-kt}$

items.part:
The mass of a decaying radioactive substance, in kg, at time $t$ years is given by $M=2e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a positive constant.
A biomaterial is also decaying simultaneously, but at every instance in time its rate of decay is twice as fast as the radioactive substance. Find an expression for the mass of the biomaterial, in terms of $k$ and $t$, given that its initial mass is $3$ kg.
items.sol:
The biomaterial decays twice as fast, so $\dfrac{dB}{dt}=2\times\dfrac{dM}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dB}{dt}&=-4ke^{-kt} \\ B&=\int -4ke^{-kt}\,dt \\ &=4e^{-kt}+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $B=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=4+C \\ C&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ B=4e^{-kt}-1$$

items.part:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis. Its velocity in metres per second, at time $t$ seconds, is given by

$$v=\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1.$$
Find the time at which the particle is stationary.
items.sol:
Stationary when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{t+1}-1&=0 \\ \dfrac{2}{t+1}&=1 \\ 2&=t+1 \\ t&=1\text{ second} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis. Its velocity in metres per second, at time $t$ seconds, is given by

$$v=\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1.$$
Find the acceleration of the particle when it is stationary.
items.sol:
Acceleration $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, with $v=2(t+1)^{-1}-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-2(t+1)^{-2} \\ &=-\dfrac{2}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
At $t=1$ (from part (a)):
$$a(1)=-\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ ms}^{-2}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis. Its velocity in metres per second, at time $t$ seconds, is given by

$$v=\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1.$$
The total distance travelled by the particle in the first two seconds is $\ln b$ metres, for some constant $b>0$. Find the value of $b$.
items.sol:
$a<0$ for all $t$ and $v=0$ at $t=1$, so
$$\begin{aligned} v&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving right} \\ v&<0 &&\text{for } 1<t\le 2 &&\text{moving left} \end{aligned}$$
Distance in the first second:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\left(\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1\right)dt&=\Big[2\ln|t+1|-t\Big]_0^1 \\ &=2\ln 2-1 \end{aligned}$$
Distance in the next second (velocity negative):
$$\begin{aligned} \Big[t-2\ln|t+1|\Big]_1^2&=2-2\ln 3-(1-2\ln 2) \\ &=1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Total distance:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\ln 2-1+1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2&=4\ln 2-2\ln 3 \\ &=\ln 2^4-\ln 3^2 \\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b=\dfrac{16}{9}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,x\sin x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\,x\sin x=\sin x+x\cos x$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Integrate both sides of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \int(\sin x+x\cos x)\,dx&=x\sin x \\ \int\sin x\,dx+\int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x \\ -\cos x+\int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x \\ \int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x+\cos x+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} x\cos x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using part (b):
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\pi}x\cos x\,dx&=\Big[x\sin x+\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In early planetary models, planets orbit the sun in circular orbits. Suppose a planet completes its orbit of radius $r$ around the sun in time $T$, while moving at a constant speed $v$.
Express $v$ in terms of $r$ and $T$ by using:

$$\text{constant speed}=\dfrac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{time}}.$$
items.sol:
In time $T$ the planet travels one circumference, $2\pi r$:
$$v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$$

items.part:
In early planetary models, planets orbit the sun in circular orbits. Suppose a planet completes its orbit of radius $r$ around the sun in time $T$, while moving at a constant speed $v$.
By examining astronomical data made in the 1600's, Kepler noticed that $r^3$ is always directly proportional to $T^2$ for all orbits, that is, $r^3=kT^2$, for some fixed positive constant $k$. By finding an appropriate derivative, determine whether planets further from the sun move faster or slower.
items.sol:
Make $\dfrac{1}{T}$ the subject of $r^3=kT^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{T^2}&=\dfrac{k}{r^3} \\ \dfrac{1}{T}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{k}}{r^{\frac{3}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$
Substituting into part (a):
$$v=2\pi\sqrt{k}\,r^{-\frac{1}{2}}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dv}{dr}&=-\pi\sqrt{k}\,r^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\ &=-\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{k}}{r\sqrt{r}} \end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{dv}{dr}<0$ for $r>0$, so $v$ is a decreasing function of $r$.

$\therefore$ Planets further from the sun move slower.
items.final: Planets further from the sun move slower.

items.part:
A patient is undergoing a treatment involving repeated injections of $M$ milliliters of medicine, separated by regular time intervals of $t$ hours. Let $A_n$ be the amount of medicine in the body immediately after the $n^{\text{th}}$ injection, so $A_1=M$. While in the body, the medicine decays exponentially such that the amount left in the body right before the $(n+1)^{\text{th}}$ injection is given by $A_ne^{-t}$.
Find an expression for $A_2$, and show that $A_3=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t})$.
items.sol:
Before each injection the amount is multiplied by $e^{-t}$, then $M$ is added:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1e^{-t}+M \\ &=Me^{-t}+M \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_3&=A_2e^{-t}+M \\ &=(Me^{-t}+M)e^{-t}+M \\ &=M+Me^{-t}+Me^{-2t} \\ &=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t}) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A patient is undergoing a treatment involving repeated injections of $M$ milliliters of medicine, separated by regular time intervals of $t$ hours. Let $A_n$ be the amount of medicine in the body immediately after the $n^{\text{th}}$ injection, so $A_1=M$. While in the body, the medicine decays exponentially such that the amount left in the body right before the $(n+1)^{\text{th}}$ injection is given by $A_ne^{-t}$.
The patient is safe from side effects as long as the amount of medication in the body stays below $2M$ milliliters. Find the minimum value of $t$, to nearest minute, such that the patient is always safe as this treatment continues indefinitely.
items.sol:
$A_n$ is increasing in $n$, so for the treatment to be always safe we need $A_\infty<2M$.

$A_\infty$ exists since $0<e^{-t}<1$ for $t>0$ (geometric series, $r=e^{-t}$):
$$\begin{aligned} A_\infty&=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t}+e^{-3t}+\cdots) \\ &=M\times\dfrac{1}{1-e^{-t}} \\ &=\dfrac{M}{1-e^{-t}} \end{aligned}$$
We require $A_\infty<2M$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{M}{1-e^{-t}}&<2M \\ \dfrac{1}{1-e^{-t}}&<2 \\ \dfrac{e^t}{e^t-1}&<2 \\ e^t&<2e^t-2 \\ e^t&>2 \\ t&>\ln 2\text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
In minutes:
$$\begin{aligned} t&>\ln 2\times 60 \\ &=41.588\cdots\text{ mins} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=42\text{ mins}$$

The six-day cycle runs across five-day weeks. There is an A day every week except weeks $6,12,18,24,30,36$, so $34$ A days in $200$ school days:
$$P(\text{A})=\dfrac{34}{200}=\dfrac{17}{100}=17\%$$

Of the $40$ Mondays, $7$ are A days:
$$P(\text{A}\,|\,\text{Monday})=\dfrac{|\text{A}\cap\text{Monday}|}{|\text{Mondays}|}=\dfrac{7}{40}=17.5\%$$
This is not equal to $P(\text{A})=17\%$ from part (a), so the events are not independent.
items.final: $P(A|Monday)=\frac{7}{40}=17.5\%\ne17\%$, so the events are not independent.

items.sol:
Day types on the $40$ Mondays:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{A}\,|\,\text{Mon})&=P(\text{D}\,|\,\text{Mon})=P(\text{E}\,|\,\text{Mon})=P(\text{F}\,|\,\text{Mon})=\dfrac{7}{40} \\ P(\text{B}\,|\,\text{Mon})&=P(\text{C}\,|\,\text{Mon})=\dfrac{6}{40}=\dfrac{3}{20}=15\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0\times\dfrac{7}{40}+1\times\dfrac{6}{40}+2\times\dfrac{7}{40}\times 3+3\times\dfrac{6}{40} \\ &=1.65 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
_q34_1}

Alice wants to move from point $A$ to point $B$, which are two points on the circumference of a circular pond with centre $O$ and radius $R$, such that $AB$ is a diameter. She can do so by swimming directly across the pond, or run the arc $AB$. Alternatively, she also has the option of first swimming in a straight line to a chosen point $P$ on the circumference, then running arc $PB$.

Let $\angle PAB=\theta$, where $0\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Alice swims and runs at constants speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$ respectively, where $0<v_1<v_2$. Let $t$ be the time it takes for her to reach $B$.
If $M$ is the midpoint of $AP$ then $\angle OMA=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. (Do NOT show this)

Find $AM$ in terms of $R$ and $\theta$.
items.sol:
In right-angled $\triangle OMA$, $OA=R$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta&=\dfrac{AM}{R} \\ AM&=R\cos\theta \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
_q34_1}

Alice wants to move from point $A$ to point $B$, which are two points on the circumference of a circular pond with centre $O$ and radius $R$, such that $AB$ is a diameter. She can do so by swimming directly across the pond, or run the arc $AB$. Alternatively, she also has the option of first swimming in a straight line to a chosen point $P$ on the circumference, then running arc $PB$.

Let $\angle PAB=\theta$, where $0\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Alice swims and runs at constants speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$ respectively, where $0<v_1<v_2$. Let $t$ be the time it takes for her to reach $B$.
Find an expression, in terms of $v_1$ and $v_2$, for the angle $\theta$ which maximises $t$.
items.sol:
Swim $AP=2AM=2R\cos\theta$. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so $\angle POB=2\theta$ and arc $PB=2R\theta$:
$$t=\dfrac{2R\cos\theta}{v_1}+\dfrac{2R\theta}{v_2}$$
$$\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=-\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\sin\theta+\dfrac{2R}{v_2}$$
Stationary when $\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2R}{v_1}\sin\theta&=\dfrac{2R}{v_2} \\ \sin\theta&=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} \\ \theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2t}{d\theta^2}=-\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\cos\theta$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2t}{d\theta^2}\le 0$ on the whole domain, $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$ is a local maximum.

It is the only turning point between the end points, so the maximum cannot occur at an end point.

$\therefore$ $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$ gives the global maximum.

items.part:
_q34_1}

Alice wants to move from point $A$ to point $B$, which are two points on the circumference of a circular pond with centre $O$ and radius $R$, such that $AB$ is a diameter. She can do so by swimming directly across the pond, or run the arc $AB$. Alternatively, she also has the option of first swimming in a straight line to a chosen point $P$ on the circumference, then running arc $PB$.

Let $\angle PAB=\theta$, where $0\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Alice swims and runs at constants speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$ respectively, where $0<v_1<v_2$. Let $t$ be the time it takes for her to reach $B$.
Find the condition on $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}$ so that the minimum value of $t$ is achieved by only running.
items.sol:
$t$ is concave down with only a maximum turning point, so the minimum occurs at an end point, $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta&=0: &t&=\dfrac{2R}{v_1} &&\text{only swimming} \\ \theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}: &t&=\dfrac{\pi R}{v_2} &&\text{only running} \end{aligned}$$
For the minimum to occur by only running:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi R}{v_2}&<\dfrac{2R}{v_1} \\ \dfrac{v_2}{v_1}&>\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Evaluate

$$\int_2^4\dfrac{2x^2-1}{x}\,dx$$
items.sol:
Split the integrand into separate terms:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_2^4\dfrac{2x^2-1}{x}\,dx&=\int_2^4\left(2x-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx\\ &=\Big[x^2-\ln|x|\Big]_2^4\\ &=(4^2-\ln 4)-(2^2-\ln 2)\\ &=12-\ln 4+\ln 2\\ &=12-2\ln 2+\ln 2\\ &=12-\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
(Allow $12+\ln\dfrac{1}{2}$.)

items.part:
Show that

$$\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}=2\sec^2 x$$
items.sol:
Write over a common denominator, then use $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{(1+\sin x)+(1-\sin x)}{(1-\sin x)(1+\sin x)}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{1-\sin^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x}\\ &=2\sec^2 x\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence, solve

$$\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}=8,\qquad\text{for }\ 0^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ$$
items.sol:
From (a), the equation becomes $2\sec^2 x=8$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sec^2 x&=8\\ \sec^2 x&=4\\ \cos^2 x&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \cos x&=\pm\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\cos x$ is positive in the first and fourth quadrants and negative in the second and third, and the related angle is $60^\circ$:
$$\therefore\ x=60^\circ,\ 120^\circ,\ 240^\circ,\ 300^\circ$$

items.part:
Find the sum of the terms in the arithmetic series:

$$71+64+57+\cdots+(-48)$$
items.sol:
$a=71$ and $d=64-71=-7$.

Find the number of terms using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} -48&=71+(n-1)(-7)\\ -48&=71-7n+7\\ 7n&=126\\ n&=18 \end{aligned}$$
Sum using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ with last term $l=-48$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{18}&=\dfrac{18}{2}\big(71+(-48)\big)\\ &=207 \end{aligned}$$

The sum of the probabilities is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} k^2-0.1k+0.66+0.22&=1\\ k^2-0.1k-0.12&=0\\ (k-0.4)(k+0.3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $k=0.4$ or $k=-0.3$.

But $P(X=2)=-0.1k$ and $P(X=2)\ge 0$, so $k\le 0$.
$$\therefore\ k=-0.3 \text{ only}$$

Using $E(X)=\displaystyle\sum xP(X=x)$ with $k=-0.3$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0\times 0.22+1\times 0.66+2\times 0.03+3\times(-0.3)^2\\ &=0.99 \end{aligned}$$

\extable{Ts829_1}
$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2)&=0\times 0.22+1\times 0.66+4\times 0.03+9\times 0.09\\ &=1.59 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X)&=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2\\ &=1.59-(0.99)^2\\ &=0.6099 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma&=\sqrt{0.6099}\\ &=0.78096094\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the standard deviation is $0.8$ (1 decimal place).

items.part:
A particle moves along the $x$ axis with a displacement at time $t$ seconds given by

$$x=\dfrac{32}{(t+1)^2}+t-12$$
Where is the particle initially?
items.sol:
When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{32}{(0+1)^2}+0-12\\ &=20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ initially the particle is 20 m to the right of the origin.
items.final: Initially the particle is 20 m to the right of the origin ($x=20$).

items.part:
A particle moves along the $x$ axis with a displacement at time $t$ seconds given by

$$x=\dfrac{32}{(t+1)^2}+t-12$$
Show that the particle comes to rest when $t=3$.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=(-2)(32)(1)(t+1)^{-3}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{64}{(t+1)^3}+1 \end{aligned}$$
At rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-\dfrac{64}{(t+1)^3}+1\\ (t+1)^3&=64\\ t+1&=4\\ t&=3 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle comes to rest when $t=3$.

items.part:
A particle moves along the $x$ axis with a displacement at time $t$ seconds given by

$$x=\dfrac{32}{(t+1)^2}+t-12$$
Find the total distance the particle travels in the first 5 seconds.

Answer correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
At $t=3$ (at rest):
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{32}{(3+1)^2}+3-12\\ &=-7 \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate $v$ to find the acceleration:
$$a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-64(-3)(1)(t+1)^{-4}$$
At $t=3$, $a=\dfrac{192}{4^4}>0$, so the particle moves to the right after $t=3$.

At $t=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{32}{(5+1)^2}+5-12\\ &=-\dfrac{55}{9} \end{aligned}$$
The particle moves left from $x=20$ to $x=-7$, then right to $x=-\dfrac{55}{9}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance travelled}&=20+7+\left(7-\dfrac{55}{9}\right)\\ &\approx 27.9\text{ m (1 decimal place)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Elsa borrows $\$720{,}000$ from the Bank of Arendelle at an interest rate of 6% per annum. She makes a monthly repayment of $\$M$. Let the amount of money owing directly after her $n^{th}$ repayment be denoted by $A_n$.
Show that after her second repayment Elsa owes

$$A_2=720\,000(1.005)^2-M(1.005+1)$$
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{6\%}{12}=0.005$. Each month interest is added, then $M$ is repaid:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=720\,000(1.005)-M\\ A_2&=A_1(1.005)-M\\ &=\big(720\,000(1.005)-M\big)(1.005)-M\\ &=720\,000(1.005)^2-M(1.005+1) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Elsa borrows $\$720{,}000$ from the Bank of Arendelle at an interest rate of 6% per annum. She makes a monthly repayment of $\$M$. Let the amount of money owing directly after her $n^{th}$ repayment be denoted by $A_n$.
If Elsa wants to repay the loan after 30 years find the value of her monthly repayment $M$ to the nearest cent.

Elsa borrows $\$720{,}000$ from the Bank of Arendelle at an interest rate of 6% per annum. She makes a monthly repayment of $\$M$. Let the amount of money owing directly after her $n^{th}$ repayment be denoted by $A_n$.
Elsa instead decides to repay $\$4{,}500$ per month. How many months faster will she repay her loan? Answer to the nearest month.
Differentiate $x^2\ln x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\ln x\right)&=2x\ln x+x^2\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=x+2x\ln x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence, evaluate

$$\int_1^e x\ln x\,dx$$
items.sol:
Rearrange so the integrand uses the derivative from (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\ln x\right)=x+2x\ln x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^e x\ln x\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e 2x\ln x\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e\big((2x\ln x+x)-x\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[x^2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^e\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(e^2\ln e-\dfrac{e^2}{2}\right)-\left(1\ln 1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{e^2}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right]\\ &=\dfrac{e^2+1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A group of 40 adults were surveyed as to whether they paid a subscription fee to watch sport or television series online.

The following answers were given:

\begin{itemize}
\item 12 adults only pay for sport
\item 6 adults pay for both
\item 8 adults pay for neither
\end{itemize}
By drawing a Venn diagram below find the probability that an adult surveyed pays for television shows.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1370_q18_s1}

Let $x$ be the number who pay for TV only. The four regions total 40:
$$\begin{aligned} x+6+8+12&=40\\ x&=14 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{pay for TV})&=\dfrac{14+6}{40}\\ &=\dfrac{20}{40}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A group of 40 adults were surveyed as to whether they paid a subscription fee to watch sport or television series online.

The following answers were given:

\begin{itemize}
\item 12 adults only pay for sport
\item 6 adults pay for both
\item 8 adults pay for neither
\end{itemize}
An adult is chosen at random. If it is known that they pay for television series, what is the probability that they also pay for sport?
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(\text{sport}\mid\text{TV})&=\dfrac{6}{20}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{10} \end{aligned}$$

Two adults are chosen without replacement from all 40. Two adults who both pay for neither do not count, so they pay the same if both are TV only, both sport only, or both pay for both:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both TV only})&=\dfrac{14}{40}\times\dfrac{13}{39}=\dfrac{182}{1560}\\ P(\text{both sport only})&=\dfrac{12}{40}\times\dfrac{11}{39}=\dfrac{132}{1560}\\ P(\text{both TV and sport})&=\dfrac{6}{40}\times\dfrac{5}{39}=\dfrac{30}{1560} \end{aligned}$$
Adding the three cases:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both pay same})&=\dfrac{182+132+30}{1560}\\ &=\dfrac{43}{195} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An expedition leaves camp $A$ and walks 10km on a bearing of $050^\circ T$ to camp $B$. They then walk 8km on a bearing of $200^\circ T$ until they reach camp $C$.
How far to the nearest km do they need to walk from camp $C$ to camp $A$?
items.sol:
The north lines at $A$ and $B$ are parallel (co-interior angles), then angles at a point at $B$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ABN_2&=180^\circ-50^\circ=130^\circ\\ \angle ABC&=360^\circ-200^\circ-130^\circ=30^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2&=10^2+8^2-2(10)(8)\cos 30^\circ\\ &=164-80\sqrt{3}\\ AC&=\sqrt{164-80\sqrt{3}}\quad(AC>0)\\ &\approx 5\text{ km (nearest km)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An expedition leaves camp $A$ and walks 10km on a bearing of $050^\circ T$ to camp $B$. They then walk 8km on a bearing of $200^\circ T$ until they reach camp $C$.
By using the cosine rule to first find $\angle ACB$, find the bearing they need to walk on from camp $C$ to reach camp $A$.
items.sol:
Using $AC=5$, the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle ACB&=\dfrac{5^2+8^2-10^2}{2(5)(8)}\\ \angle ACB&=97.9032077\ldots^\circ\\ &\approx 97^\circ 54' \end{aligned}$$
(Using $AC=\sqrt{164-80\sqrt{3}}$ gives $\angle ACB=97.5224315\ldots^\circ\approx 97^\circ 31'$.)

Angles at a point at $B$, then co-interior angles with the parallel north lines at $B$ and $C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle CBN_2&=360^\circ-200^\circ=160^\circ\\ \angle BCN_3&=180^\circ-160^\circ=20^\circ\\ \angle ACN_3&=\angle ACB-20^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $A$ from $C$ is measured clockwise from $N_3$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-\angle ACN_3\\ &=360^\circ-(\angle ACB-20^\circ)\\ &=380^\circ-\angle ACB\\ &=282^\circ 6' T\ \text{ or }\ 282^\circ T\ \text{ or }\ 282^\circ 29' T \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $|x|=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3$
items.sol:
For $x\ge 0$, $|x|=x$; for $x<0$, $|x|=-x$:
$$x=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3\quad\text{or}\quad -x=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3$$
Multiply by 2:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=x+6 & -2x&=x+6\\ x&=6 & -3x&=6\\ & & x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Each root satisfies its case ($6\ge 0$, $-2<0$):
$$\therefore\ x=-2,\ 6$$

items.part:
An area between $y=|x|$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3$ is bounded by $x=-2$ and $x=k$, where $k>0$.

Find the value of $k$ such that the area is 10 square units.
items.sol:
The region from $x=-2$ to $x=0$ (between the line and $y=-x$):
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=\int_{-2}^0\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x+3-(-x)\right)dx\\ &=\int_{-2}^0\left(\dfrac{3}{2}x+3\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{4}+3x\right]_{-2}^0\\ &=0-\left(\dfrac{3(-2)^2}{4}+3(-2)\right)\\ &=3 \end{aligned}$$
(Or as a triangle, $A_1=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 2=3$.)

So $7$ square units more are needed for $x$ from $0$ to $k$.

The whole triangle from $x=0$ to $x=6$ has area $\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 6=9>7$, so $k<6$.

For $0\le x\le k$, the region lies between the line and $y=x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7&=\int_0^k\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x+3-x\right)dx\\ 7&=\int_0^k\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3\right)dx\\ 7&=\left[-\dfrac{1}{4}x^2+3x\right]_0^k\\ 7&=-\dfrac{1}{4}k^2+3k\\ k^2-12k+28&=0\\ (k-6)^2&=8\\ k&=6\pm 2\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
But $k<6$:
$$\therefore\ k=6-2\sqrt{2}$$

items.part:
The water depth $d$ in Penrith harbour $t$ hours after the first low tide of the day can be modelled with the equation:

$$d=5.2-0.8\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$$
What is the depth of the water at low tide?
items.sol:
At $t=0$ (first low tide):
$$\begin{aligned} d&=5.2-0.8\\ &=4.4\text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The water depth $d$ in Penrith harbour $t$ hours after the first low tide of the day can be modelled with the equation:

$$d=5.2-0.8\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$$
If the first low tide of the day occurred at 6am, what time does the next low tide occur at?
items.sol:
The period of $\cos nt$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$, here with $n=\dfrac{4\pi}{25}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{4\pi}{25}}\\ &=12.5\text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the next low tide is 12.5 hours after 6 am, at 6:30 pm.

Alternatively, solve $d=4.4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4.4&=5.2-0.8\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)\\ \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)&=1\\ \dfrac{4\pi}{25}t&=0,\ 2\pi\\ t&=0,\ 12.5 \end{aligned}$$
giving 6:30 pm.

The function $h$ is defined as $h(x)=f\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)+2$ with $f(x)$ defined for $-\infty\le x\le\infty$.

Aneeka and Brian are investigating areas $A$ and $B$ respectively on either side of the graph of $y=\ln x$ as shown on the diagram below:

\exfigure{1370_q24_1}
Brian uses the trapezoidal rule with 3 function values to estimate the area $B$. He approximates all of the values used in his working out to 2 decimal places where necessary.

What is his estimate for the area of $B$?
items.sol:
\exfigure{1370_q24_s1}

Three function values means two trapezia ($n=2$) on $[1,e^2]$, so the strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{e^2-1}{2}$$
\extable{Ts855_1}

Applying the trapezoidal rule to each strip:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&\approx\dfrac{e^2-1}{2(2)}(0+1.43)+\dfrac{e^2-1}{2(2)}(1.43+2)\\ &=7.76\ \text{(2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, in one formula:
$$\text{Area}\approx\dfrac{e^2-1}{2(2)}\left(0+2\times 1.43+2\right)=7.76$$

items.part:
Aneeka and Brian are investigating areas $A$ and $B$ respectively on either side of the graph of $y=\ln x$ as shown on the diagram below:

\exfigure{1370_q24_1}
Brian considers the area $A+B$ and uses his estimate of the area $B$ from part (b) and Aneeka’s answer in part (c) to find an approximation for the value of $e$.

What is his approximation to 2 decimal places?
items.sol:
The rectangle of width $e^2$ and height $2$ has area $e^2\times 2$, and it is made up of $A+B$:
$$\begin{aligned} e^2\times 2&\approx(e^2-1)+7.76\\ 2e^2&\approx e^2-1+7.76\\ e^2&\approx 6.76\\ e&\approx\sqrt{6.76}\quad(e>0)\\ e&\approx 2.60 \end{aligned}$$

Since the graph of $y=\ln x$ is concave down, the trapezoidal rule gives an underestimate of the area below the curve.

Hence, the estimation of $e$ is an underestimate.
items.final: Since $y=\ln x$ is concave down, the trapezoidal rule underestimates the area, so the estimate of $e$ is an underestimate.

items.part: Draw a neat sketch of $y=x^3-6x^2+9x-3$ on page 37 showing the $y$ intercept, all turning points and all points of inflexion. You need to determine the nature of any stationary points that you find. You do not need to find the $x$ intercepts.
items.sol:
For the $y$ intercept, substitute $x=0$: $y=-3$.
$$y'=3x^2-12x+9$$
For stationary points, $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-12x+9&=0\\ x^2-4x+3&=0\\ (x-3)(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=3$, $y=-3$ or $x=1$, $y=1$.

The sign of $y''$ decides the nature:
$$y''=6x-12$$
When $x=3$, $y''=6(3)-12=6>0$ (concave up), so there is a minimum turning point at $(3,-3)$.

When $x=1$, $y''=6(1)-12=-6<0$ (concave down), so there is a maximum turning point at $(1,1)$.

For possible points of inflection, $y''=0$: $6x-12=0$, so $x=2$, $y=-1$.

Check for concavity:

\extable{Ts859_1}

Concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $(2,-1)$.

\exfigure{1370_q25_s1}

items.part: For what values of $k$ does $x^3-6x^2+9x-3=k$ have 3 solutions?
items.sol:
From the sketch, the horizontal line $y=k$ cuts the curve three times between the minimum value $-3$ and the maximum value $1$:
$$-3<k<1$$
(Only two solutions when $k=-3$ or $k=1$.)

items.part:
The tangent to $y=\tan x$ at the point where $x=c$, $c\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is drawn on the diagram below. The value $c$ is chosen so that the $y$ intercept of the tangent is $-c$.

\exfigure{1370_q26_1}
Show that the equation of the tangent is

$$y=x\sec^2 c-c\sec^2 c+\tan c$$
items.sol:
Differentiate, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x$:
$$y'=\sec^2 x$$
When $x=c$: $y=\tan c$ and $y'=\sec^2 c$.

Equation of the tangent, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-\tan c&=\sec^2 c\,(x-c)\\ y&=x\sec^2 c-c\sec^2 c+\tan c \end{aligned}$$

The tangent passes through $(0,-c)$; use $\sec^2 c=1+\tan^2 c$:
$$\begin{aligned} -c&=-c\sec^2 c+\tan c\\ -c&=-c(1+\tan^2 c)+\tan c\\ -c&=-c-c\tan^2 c+\tan c\\ c\tan^2 c-\tan c&=0\\ \tan c\,(c\tan c-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$\tan c=0$ gives $c=0$, not possible since $c\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. So $\tan c=\dfrac{1}{c}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan^2 c&=\dfrac{1}{c^2}\\ 1+\tan^2 c&=\dfrac{1}{c^2}+1\\ \sec^2 c&=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient}=\dfrac{c^2+1}{c^2}$$
Alternative: from $\tan c=\dfrac{1}{c}$ and the points $(0,-c)$, $(c,\tan c)$,
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{\tan c+c}{c-0}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{c}+c}{c}\\ &=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c}\times\dfrac{1}{c}\\ &=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population $P$ of bin chickens on the main oval $t$ days after school starts for the year

$$P(t)=200-\dfrac{44}{1+10e^{-0.2t}}$$
Show that the rate of growth of the size of the population is

$$P'(t)=\dfrac{-88e^{-0.2t}}{(1+10e^{-0.2t})^2}$$
items.sol:
Write $P$ with a negative power:
$$P(t)=200-44\left(1+10e^{-0.2t}\right)^{-1}$$
Chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P'(t)&=44\left(-2e^{-0.2t}\right)\left(1+10e^{-0.2t}\right)^{-2}\\ &=\dfrac{-88e^{-0.2t}}{\left(1+10e^{-0.2t}\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population $P$ of bin chickens on the main oval $t$ days after school starts for the year

$$P(t)=200-\dfrac{44}{1+10e^{-0.2t}}$$
Find the range of $P(t)$ by considering the value of $P$ as $t\to\infty$.
items.sol:
Since $P'(t)<0$ for all $t\ge 0$, $P(t)$ is a decreasing function, so $P(t)$ is a maximum when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(0)&=200-\dfrac{44}{1+10e^0}\\ &=196 \end{aligned}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.2t}\to 0$, so $P(t)\to 200-44=156$.
$$\therefore\ 156<P(t)\le 196$$

items.part:
The population $P$ of bin chickens on the main oval $t$ days after school starts for the year

$$P(t)=200-\dfrac{44}{1+10e^{-0.2t}}$$
Show that the rate of change of the population can be written as

$$P'(t)=\dfrac{1}{220}(P-156)(P-200)$$

The population $P$ of bin chickens on the main oval $t$ days after school starts for the year

$$P(t)=200-\dfrac{44}{1+10e^{-0.2t}}$$
Hence find the population of bin chickens when the population is decreasing at its fastest rate.
items.sol:
From (c), $P'(t)$ is a quadratic in $P$:
$$P'(t)=\dfrac{1}{220}(P-156)(P-200)$$
Its graph against $P$ is a concave-up parabola with $P$-intercepts $156$ and $200$, so the minimum value of $P'(t)$ (fastest decrease) occurs midway between them:
$$P=\dfrac{156+200}{2}=178$$
$\therefore$ the population is decreasing at the fastest rate when $P=178$.

items.part: Solve $\sin x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, where $0 \le x \le 2\pi$. Giving the answer in exact form in radians
items.sol:
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ (one solution is $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$).

Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Use two applications of the Trapezoidal rule to find an approximate value, correct to 2 decimal places for, $\displaystyle \int_1^3 \ln(x^2+1)\,dx$.
items.sol:
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule on $[1, 3]$ use $n = 2$ strips:
$$h = \dfrac{3-1}{2} = 1$$
so the $x$ values are $1, 2, 3$.

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3 \ln(x^2+1)\,dx &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln(1^2+1) + \ln(3^2+1) + 2\ln(2^2+1)\right] \\ &= 3.11 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
Or, applying the rule to each strip:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln(1^2+1) + \ln(2^2+1)\right] + \dfrac{3-2}{2}\left[\ln(2^2+1) + \ln(3^2+1)\right] = 3.11$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle \int 10^{5x-1}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using the standard integral
$$\int a^{f(x)} f'(x)\,dx = \dfrac{a^{f(x)}}{\ln a} + c$$
with $f(x) = 5x - 1$ and $f'(x) = 5$:
$$\int 10^{5x-1}\,dx = \dfrac{10^{5x-1}}{5\ln 10} + c$$

items.part:
At 9 am, Brooklyn is 11 km due north of camp, while Milan is 12 km due east of camp. Their positions are shown on the diagram below.

\exfigure{1357_q14_1}

They both start walking directly towards camp at a speed of 4 kilometres per hour.

Find the distance between Brooklyn and Milan at 11 am.
items.sol:
In 2 hours each walks $2 \times 4 = 8$ km towards camp.

At 11 am Brooklyn is $11 - 8 = 3$ km from camp and Milan is $12 - 8 = 4$ km from camp.

By Pythagoras' theorem (north and east are at right angles):
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} \\ &= 5 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x) = e^{5x^3 - 10x}$ is increasing.
items.sol:
The function is increasing where $f'(x) > 0$.

By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{g(x)} = g'(x)e^{g(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= (15x^2 - 10)e^{5x^3 - 10x} \\ &= 5(3x^2 - 2)e^{5x^3 - 10x} \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{5x^3 - 10x} > 0$ for all $x$, only the factor $3x^2 - 2$ decides the sign, so we need
$$3x^2 - 2 > 0$$
The roots of $3x^2 - 2 = 0$ are $x = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$, and the parabola is positive outside its roots:
$$\therefore\ x \in \left(-\infty, -\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}\right) \cup \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}, \infty\right)$$

items.part: Evaluate in simplest form $\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin 2x\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin 2x\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos \pi - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 0\right) \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respects to $x$.
$\dfrac{3x+2}{x+4}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x+2 & v&=x+4\\ u'&=3 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{3x+2}{x+4}\right) &= \dfrac{3(x+4) - (3x+2)}{(x+4)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{3x + 12 - 3x - 2}{(x+4)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{10}{(x+4)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respects to $x$.
$x(1+2x)^4$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=(1+2x)^4\\ u'&=1 & v'&=8(1+2x)^3\end{aligned}$$
($v'$ by the chain rule.)
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x(1+2x)^4\right] &= 8x(1+2x)^3 + (1+2x)^4 \\ &= (1+2x)^3(8x + 1 + 2x) \\ &= (10x+1)(1+2x)^3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
s working in the garden when he has an accident and puts a hole in the bottom of his rainwater tank. At the time of the accident, the tank contained 10 200 litres of water.

In the first hour after the accident, Finn noticed that the volume of water in the tank decreased by 200 litres.

In the second hour, he noticed that the volume of water in the tank decreased by a further 250 litres.

Finn is concerned that the leak is growing, but he is not sure what will happen next. He wonders if the amount of water leaking from the tank each hour might form an arithmetic sequence or geometric sequence.
If the amount of water that leaks out of the tank each hour forms an arithmetic sequence, how many hours will it take until the tank is empty?
items.sol:
The leak each hour is arithmetic with $a = 200$, $d = 50$, and the tank is empty when $S_n = 10\,200$.

Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\,200 &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(200) + (n-1) \times 50\right] \\ 20\,400 &= n(400 + 50n - 50) \\ 20\,400 &= 350n + 50n^2 \\ n^2 + 7n - 408 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{-7 \pm \sqrt{7^2 - 4 \times 1 \times (-408)}}{2} \\ &= -24 \text{ or } 17 \end{aligned}$$
$n > 0$, so $n = 17$.

$\therefore$ Tank empty after 17 hours.

items.part:
s working in the garden when he has an accident and puts a hole in the bottom of his rainwater tank. At the time of the accident, the tank contained 10 200 litres of water.

In the first hour after the accident, Finn noticed that the volume of water in the tank decreased by 200 litres.

In the second hour, he noticed that the volume of water in the tank decreased by a further 250 litres.

Finn is concerned that the leak is growing, but he is not sure what will happen next. He wonders if the amount of water leaking from the tank each hour might form an arithmetic sequence or geometric sequence.
If the amount of water that leaks out of the tank each hour forms a geometric sequence, show that eight hours after the leak, over 60% of the water remains in the tank
items.sol:
The leak each hour is geometric with $a = 200$, $r = \dfrac{250}{200} = 1.25$, $n = 8$.

Using $S_n = \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_8 &= \dfrac{200(1.25^8 - 1)}{1.25 - 1} \\ &= 3968.37 \text{ L has leaked out} \end{aligned}$$
$$10\,200 - 3968.37 = 6231.63 \text{ L}$$
$$\dfrac{6231.63}{10\,200} \times 100 = 61.09\%$$
$\therefore$ After 8 hours more than $60\%$ of water remains.

items.part: Prove that $\sec x + \tan x = \dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x}$.
items.sol:
Using $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} + \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin x)(1 - \sin x)}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\cos x\,(1 - \sin x)} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x} = \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find the exact value of $\displaystyle \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sec x + \tan x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using part (a), the numerator $\cos x$ is $-1$ times the derivative of the denominator $1 - \sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x}\,dx &= -\Big[\ln|1 - \sin x|\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= -\ln\left|1 - \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right| + \ln|1 - \sin 0| \\ &= -\ln\dfrac{2 - \sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= \ln\dfrac{2}{2 - \sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$

A survey of all the Zoology students at the local university showed that $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of them had a pet cat, $\dfrac{3}{8}$ of them had a pet dog and $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of them had both a pet cat and a pet dog. 25 of the students had either a pet cat or a pet dog but not both types of pet.
Show that a total of 40 Zoology students where surveyed
items.sol:
\exfigure{1357_q22_s1}

Cat only: $\dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Dog only: $\dfrac{3}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

With $n$ students, the number with a cat or a dog but not both is
$$\left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{8}\right)n = \dfrac{5}{8}n$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5}{8}n &= 25 \\ n &= 25 \times \dfrac{8}{5} = 40 \text{ students} \end{aligned}$$

The lifetime, $X$, in tens of hours, of a battery has a cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ that is given by

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{25}{116}\left(x^2 + 3x - 4\right) & 1 < x < 1.8 \\[6pt] 1 & x \ge 1.8 \end{cases}$$
Sketch the cumulative distribution function.

\exfigure{1357_q24_1}

The lifetime, $X$, in tens of hours, of a battery has a cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ that is given by

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{25}{116}\left(x^2 + 3x - 4\right) & 1 < x < 1.8 \\[6pt] 1 & x \ge 1.8 \end{cases}$$
An outdoor lantern requires three batteries, all of which must be working, to operate. Three new batteries are inserted into the lantern.

Find the probability that the lantern will still be working after 15 hours. Give your answer as a percentage, rounded to two decimal places.
items.sol:
15 hours is $x = 1.5$ (tens of hours). A battery still working after 15 hours has $X > 1.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X > 1.5) &= 1 - P(X \le 1.5) = 1 - F(1.5) \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{25}{116}\left(1.5^2 + 3 \times 1.5 - 4\right) \\ &= \dfrac{189}{464} \end{aligned}$$
All three batteries must still be working (independent):
$$\left(\dfrac{189}{464}\right)^3 = 6.76\%$$

items.part:
The lifetime, $X$, in tens of hours, of a battery has a cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ that is given by

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{25}{116}\left(x^2 + 3x - 4\right) & 1 < x < 1.8 \\[6pt] 1 & x \ge 1.8 \end{cases}$$
Find the probability density function of the random variable $X$.
items.sol:
The probability density function is the derivative of the cumulative distribution function:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}F(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{25}{116}\left(x^2 + 3x - 4\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{25}{116}(2x + 3) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{25}{116}(2x + 3) & 1 < x < 1.8 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}$$

items.part:
Point $P(-1, -2)$ lies on $f(x)$. Point $P'$ is the image of point $P$ on the function $g(x) = 2f(3x - 1)$.
By clearly stating the transformations required to produce $g(x)$ from $f(x)$, show that the coordinates of point $P'$ are $(0, -4)$.
items.sol:
$2f(x)$: vertical dilation, scale factor 2. New point $(-1, -4)$.

$2f(x - 1)$: translation right 1. New point $(0, -4)$.

$2f(3x - 1)$: horizontal dilation, scale factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$. New point $(0, -4)$.

items.part:
Point $P(-1, -2)$ lies on $f(x)$. Point $P'$ is the image of point $P$ on the function $g(x) = 2f(3x - 1)$.
If the equation of the tangent at point $P$ on $f(x)$ is $y = x - 1$, find the equation of the tangent at point $P'$ on $g(x)$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x) &= 2f'(3x - 1) \times 3 \\ &= 6f'(3x - 1) \end{aligned}$$
The tangent at $P$, $y = x - 1$, has gradient 1, so $f'(-1) = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'(0) &= 6f'(-1) \\ &= 6 \times 1 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
Using $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ at $(0, -4)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - (-4) &= 6x \\ y &= 6x - 4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle moves along the $x$-axis, where left is in a positive direction. After $t$ seconds its displacement, $x$ metres, is given by the equation $x = (t^2 - 1)^2$.
Show that the acceleration of the particle is given by the equation

$$\ddot{x} = 12t^2 - 4$$
items.sol:
Expanding:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= (t^2 - 1)^2 \\ &= t^4 - 2t^2 + 1 \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= 4t^3 - 4t \\ \ddot{x} &= 12t^2 - 4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle moves along the $x$-axis, where left is in a positive direction. After $t$ seconds its displacement, $x$ metres, is given by the equation $x = (t^2 - 1)^2$.
The particle initially moves left, before turning around and moving to the right.

Find the particle's acceleration when it returns to its initial position.
items.sol:
When $t = 0$, $x = 1$, so the particle returns to its initial position when $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= (t^2 - 1)^2 \\ t^2 - 1 &= \pm 1 \\ t^2 &= 0,\ 2 \\ t &= 0 \text{ or } \sqrt{2} \quad (t \ge 0) \end{aligned}$$
It returns at $t = \sqrt{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x} &= 12\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^2 - 4 \\ &= 20 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(\ln x)$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(\ln x) &= -\sin(\ln x) \times \dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= \dfrac{-\sin(\ln x)}{x} \end{aligned}$$

At an $x$-intercept $y = 0$:
$$\dfrac{-\sin(\ln x)}{x} = 0$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin(\ln x) &= 0 \\ \ln x &= -\pi,\ 0 \\ x &= e^{-\pi},\ 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $k = 2$.
items.sol:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{e^{-\pi}}^{1} \dfrac{-\sin(\ln x)}{kx}\,dx &= 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{k}\int_{e^{-\pi}}^{1} \dfrac{-\sin(\ln x)}{x}\,dx &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
By part (a), the integrand is the derivative of $\cos(\ln x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{k}\Big[\cos(\ln x)\Big]_{e^{-\pi}}^{1} &= 1 \\ k &= \cos(\ln 1) - \cos\left(\ln e^{-\pi}\right) \\ &= 1 - (-1) = 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $P\left(x < \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$. Give your answer correct to three decimal places.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P\left(x < \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= \int_{e^{-\pi}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{-\sin(\ln x)}{2x}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\Big[\cos(\ln x)\Big]_{e^{-\pi}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\cos\left(\ln\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - \cos\left(\ln e^{-\pi}\right)\right) \\ &= 0.985 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: The parabola $y = x^2 - 8x + 17$ is dilated vertically by a factor of 2 and reflected about the $y$-axis. Find the equation of the transformed parabola in the form $y = a(x + b)^2 + c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.
items.sol:
Vertically dilated by a factor of 2:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{y}{2} &= x^2 - 8x + 17 \\ y &= 2x^2 - 16x + 34 \end{aligned}$$
Reflected about the $y$-axis (replace $x$ by $-x$):
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2(-x)^2 - 16(-x) + 34 \\ &= 2x^2 + 16x + 34 \end{aligned}$$
Completing the square:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2\left(x^2 + 8x + 17\right) \\ &= 2\left((x + 4)^2 + 1\right) \\ &= 2(x + 4)^2 + 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The curve $y = \sqrt{x}$ intersects the curve $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$ at $(4, 2)$.

The region bounded by the curve $y = \sqrt{x}$, the curve $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$, the line $x = 8$ and the $x$-axis is shaded in the diagram.

items.sol:
The upper boundary is $y = \sqrt{x}$ for $0 \le x \le 4$ and $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$ for $4 \le x \le 8$, so split the region at $x = 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^4 x^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx + \int_4^8 \dfrac{8}{x}\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^4 + 8\Big[\ln x\Big]_4^8 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}(8 - 0) + 8(\ln 8 - \ln 4) \\ &= \dfrac{16}{3} + 8\ln 2 \\ &= \dfrac{16 + 24\ln 2}{3} = \dfrac{8(2 + 3\ln 2)}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows two circles, one with radius $r$ and the other with radius $r\sqrt{r}$ units.

The shaded segment has an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ subtended at the centre of the circle.

\exfigure{1357_q33_1}
Given that $0 < r < 1$, show that the area of the shaded region is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}r^2 - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^3$ square units.
items.sol:
Shaded area = sector of the large circle (radius $r$) minus the triangle with two sides $r\sqrt{r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta - \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}r^2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{1}{2} \times r\sqrt{r} \times r\sqrt{r} \times \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{r^2}{2} \times \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{1}{2} \times r^3 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}r^2 - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

items.sol:
