$r = 0$ or $r = \dfrac{4\pi}{9\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}\pi}{27} \approx 0.81$; since $0 < r < 1$, $r = \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}\pi}{27}$.

Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$A'' = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}r$$
When $r = \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}\pi}{27}$:
$$A'' = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(\dfrac{4\sqrt{3}\pi}{27}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} < 0$$
$\therefore$ maximum at $r = \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}\pi}{27}$.

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$y=\ln(x^2+5x-7)$
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x) = \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= x^2+5x-7 \\ f'(x) &= 2x+5 \end{aligned}$$
$$y' = \dfrac{2x+5}{x^2+5x-7}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$y=e^x\tan x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=e^x(\sec^2 x)+\tan x\times e^x\\ &=e^x(\sec^2 x+\tan x)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$y=2^{x+3}$
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^{f(x)} = f'(x)\,a^{f(x)}\ln a$:
$$y'=2^{x+3}\ln 2$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$y=\sqrt{e^{3x}-x}$
items.sol:
Writing the root as a power and using the chain rule:
$$y=(e^{3x}-x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=(3e^{3x}-1)(e^{3x}-x)^{\frac{1}{2}-1}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{3e^{3x}-1}{2\sqrt{e^{3x}-x}}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $2\cos 2x=\sqrt{3}$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.
items.sol:
Dividing by 2:
$$\cos 2x=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} -\pi &\le x \le \pi \\ -2\pi &\le 2x \le 2\pi &&(\text{multiply by } 2) \end{aligned}$$
The related acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ (cosine is positive in quadrants 1 and 4).

\exfigure{644_q9_s1}
$$\begin{aligned} 2x &= \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\left(2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{11\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12},\ -\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ -\dfrac{11\pi}{12}$$

items.part:
Prove that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}\right)=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^2 x}$$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1+\sin x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}\right)&=\dfrac{\cos x(\cos x)-(-\sin x)(1+\sin x)}{\cos^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2 x+\sin x+\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence, or otherwise, show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(\sec x+\tan x)\right]=\sec x$$
items.sol:
$$\sec x+\tan x=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}$$
From part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x} \\ f'(x)&=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^2 x} \end{aligned}$$
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sec x+\tan x)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\times\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}=\sec x\end{aligned}$$
Hence proved.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-5x^2+7x-3$

For what values of $x$ is $f(x)$ decreasing.
items.sol:
For $f(x)$ to be decreasing, $f'(x)<0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=3x^2-10x+7\\ &=3x^2-3x-7x+7\\ &=3x(x-1)-7(x-1)\\ &=(3x-7)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)<0$ when
$$(3x-7)(x-1)<0$$
\exfigure{644_q11_s1}

The parabola is concave up, so it is negative between its roots:
$$\therefore\ 1<x<\dfrac{7}{3}$$

items.part: Sketch the curve of $y=3\sin 2x+1$ for the domain $[0,2\pi]$
items.sol:
Amplitude: $A=3$

Period: $P=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$

Shifted up 1 unit.

\exfigure{644_q12_s1}

items.part:
Without using calculus, sketch the graph of $y=2-\dfrac{3}{1-x}$,

showing the asymptotes and $x$ and $y$ intercepts.
items.sol:
$y$-intercept, when $x=0$:
$$y=2-\dfrac{3}{1-0}=-1$$
$x$-intercept, when $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=2-\dfrac{3}{1-x}\\ 1-x&=\dfrac{3}{2}\\ x&=1-\dfrac{3}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Vertical asymptote: $1-x\ne 0$, so $x\ne 1$.

Horizontal asymptote: as $x\to\infty$, $\dfrac{3}{1-x}\to 0$, so $y\to 2$.

\exfigure{644_q13_s1}

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=-x^3+6x^2-1$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$f'(x)=-3x^2+12x$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -3x^2+12x&=0\\ -3x(x-4)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$f''(x)=-6x+12$$
At $x=0$, $f(0)=-1$, so the point is $(0,-1)$.
$$f''(0)=12>0 \text{ (concave up)}$$
$\therefore$ $(0,-1)$ is a minimum turning point.

At $x=4$:
$$f(4)=-4^3+6\times4^2-1=31$$
$$f''(4)=-6\times4+12=-12<0 \text{ (concave down)}$$
$\therefore$ $(4,31)$ is a maximum turning point.
items.final: $(0,-1)$ is a minimum turning point; $(4,31)$ is a maximum turning point

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=-x^3+6x^2-1$.
Find the coordinates of the point of inflection of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Possible points of inflection occur where $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)=-6x+12&=0\\ -6x&=-12\\ x&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$f(2)=-(2)^3+6(2)^2-1=15$$
Check the concavity either side of $x=2$:

\extable{Ts1043_1}
$$\begin{aligned} f''(1)&=-6+12=6 &&\text{concave up}\\ f''(3)&=-6\times3+12=-6 &&\text{concave down}\end{aligned}$$
Since the concavity changes at $x=2$, $(2,15)$ is a point of inflection.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=-x^3+6x^2-1$.
Sketch the curve $y=f(x)$ showing the stationary points, the point of inflection and $y$-intercept.
items.sol:
\exfigure{644_q14_s1}

Point of inflection at $(2,15)$, where the curve changes from concave up to concave down.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=-x^3+6x^2-1$.
What is the maximum value of $f(x)$ for $-3\le x\le 5$?
items.sol:
The maximum on $-3\le x\le 5$ occurs at the local maximum $(4,31)$ or at an endpoint:
$$f(-3)=-(-3)^3+6(-3)^2-1=80$$
$$f(5)=-(5)^3+6(5)^2-1=24$$
For $-3\le x\le 5$ the maximum value of $f(x)$ is 80.

items.part:
A biologist is studying the growth of a population of ants in a colony. The biologist models the number of ants, $N$, with the equation $N(t)=600e^{0.02t}$, where $t$ is the number of weeks after starting the observation.

What is the rate of increase in the number of ants 40 weeks after starting the observation?

Express your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Differentiating $N(t)=600e^{0.02t}$:
$$\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0.02\times600e^{0.02t}$$
When $t=40$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dN}{dt}&=0.02\times600\times e^{0.02\times40}\\ &=12e^{0.8}\ \text{ants/week}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The tide in a harbour can be modelled using the equation $d(t)=A\cos(Bt)+C$,

where $d$ represents the depth of the water in metres and $t$ is the time, in hours after 7:00 am.

High tide occurs at 7:00 am when the water's depth is 60 m.

Low tide occurs at 2:00 pm when the water's depth is 20 m.
Find the values of $A$, $B$ and $C$, and hence write the completed function $d(t)$.
items.sol:
The depth varies between 60 m and 20 m:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{60-20}{2}=20 &&\text{(amplitude)}\\ C&=\dfrac{60+20}{2}=40 &&\text{(centre)}\end{aligned}$$
High tide (7:00 am) to low tide (2:00 pm) is 7 hours, half a period, so the period is 14:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2\pi}{B}&=14\\ B&=\dfrac{2\pi}{14}=\dfrac{\pi}{7}\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{644_q16_s1}
$$\therefore\ d(t)=20\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{7}+40$$

items.part:
The tide in a harbour can be modelled using the equation $d(t)=A\cos(Bt)+C$,

where $d$ represents the depth of the water in metres and $t$ is the time, in hours after 7:00 am.

High tide occurs at 7:00 am when the water's depth is 60 m.

Low tide occurs at 2:00 pm when the water's depth is 20 m.
A ship enters the harbour only if the height of the tide is at least 50 m. Find all the times between 7:00 am and 7:00 pm during which the ship is able to enter the harbour.
items.sol:
The ship can enter while $d(t)\ge 50$. The boundary times are when $d(t)=50$:
$$\begin{aligned} 20\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{7}+40&=50\\ \cos\dfrac{\pi t}{7}&=\dfrac{10}{20}=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le t\le 12\\ 0&\le\dfrac{\pi t}{7}\le\dfrac{12\pi}{7} &&\left(\text{multiply by } \dfrac{\pi}{7}\right)\end{aligned}$$
($\dfrac{12\pi}{7}$ is $5.39$ radians or $308.57^\circ$.)

The related acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{644_q16_s2}
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{7}=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{7}{\pi},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{7}{\pi}\\ &=2 \cdot \dot{3},\ 11.67\end{aligned}$$
So $t=2$ h 20 min or 11 h 40 min after 7:00 am, that is 9:20 am and 6:40 pm.

The depth starts at its maximum, 60 m, at $t=0$, so $d(t)\ge 50$ for
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le t\le 2 \cdot \dot{3} &&\text{7:00 am to 9:20 am}\\ 11.67&\le t\le 12 &&\text{6:40 pm to 7:00 pm}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is dilated vertically by a factor of $q^2$ and then

translated 81 units down, the transformed function is given as

$$g(x)=q^2x^2-81$$
When the transformed function $g(x)$ is translated $p$ units to the left, the resulting function is denoted as $h(x)$. Write an expression for $h(x)$.
items.sol:
Translating $p$ units to the left replaces $x$ with $x+p$:
$$h(x)=q^2(x+p)^2-81$$

items.part:
The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is dilated vertically by a factor of $q^2$ and then

translated 81 units down, the transformed function is given as

$$g(x)=q^2x^2-81$$
Find all possible values of $p$ and $q$ if $h(x)=9x^2+36x-45$.
items.sol:
Equate $h(x)$ from (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} q^2(x+p)^2-81&=9x^2+36x-45\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9x^2+36x-45+81\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9x^2+36x+36\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9(x^2+4x+4)\\ q^2(x+p)^2&=9(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
Comparing both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} q^2&=9 & x+p&=x+2\\ q&=\pm3 & p&=2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Carlos wishes to build a large aquarium to house three different species of fish which cannot live together. The top view of the water tank is shown in the diagram below. The aquarium is to be split into three sections, where the outside sections are semicircles with a diameter, $s$ metres, and the middle section, a rectangle with width, $w$ metres.

\exfigure{644_q18_1}

The aquarium is to be built using glass walls, including the interior dividers to split up the aquarium into three sections.
Carlos' budget has allowed for a total 200 m length of glass walls and dividers for the project.

Show that $w=100-s\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{2}\right)$
items.sol:
The glass is the two semicircular arcs (together $\pi s$), the two sides of length $w$ and the two dividers of length $s$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2s+2w+\pi s&=200\\ 2w&=200-2s-\pi s\\ w&=100-s\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Carlos wishes to build a large aquarium to house three different species of fish which cannot live together. The top view of the water tank is shown in the diagram below. The aquarium is to be split into three sections, where the outside sections are semicircles with a diameter, $s$ metres, and the middle section, a rectangle with width, $w$ metres.

\exfigure{644_q18_1}

The aquarium is to be built using glass walls, including the interior dividers to split up the aquarium into three sections.
Hence or otherwise, show that

$$A=100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{4+\pi}{4}\right)$$

where $A$ is the area of the entire cross section of the water tank.
items.sol:
The area is two semicircles of diameter $s$ (one circle) plus the rectangle:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{s}{2}\right)^2+w\times s\\ &=\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}+s\left(100-s\left(\dfrac{\pi+2}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}+100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+2}{2}\right)\\ &=100s+\dfrac{\pi s^2}{4}-\dfrac{\pi s^2}{2}-\dfrac{2s^2}{2}\\ &=100s-\dfrac{\pi}{4}s^2-s^2\\ &=100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1\right)\\ A&=100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Carlos wishes to build a large aquarium to house three different species of fish which cannot live together. The top view of the water tank is shown in the diagram below. The aquarium is to be split into three sections, where the outside sections are semicircles with a diameter, $s$ metres, and the middle section, a rectangle with width, $w$ metres.

\exfigure{644_q18_1}

The aquarium is to be built using glass walls, including the interior dividers to split up the aquarium into three sections.
Carlos decides that the aquarium is to be $s$ units high so that the volume of the aquarium can be found using $V=As$.

Calculate the value of $s$, such that the capacity of the water tank is a maximum.

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Using $V=As$ with part (b):
$$\begin{aligned} V&=s\left(100s-s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\right)\\ &=100s^2-s^3\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{ds}=200s-3s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dV}{ds}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 200s-3s^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)&=0\\ s\left(200-3s\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$s=0$ gives no tank, so
$$\begin{aligned} 3s\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)&=200\\ s&=\dfrac{200\times4}{3(\pi+4)}\\ &\approx 37.34\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{ds^2}=200-6s\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}\right)$$
At $s=37.34$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{ds^2}\approx-200<0$$
so the curve is concave down and this is a maximum turning point.

$\therefore$ $s=37.34$ will give maximum volume.

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=ax^2+bx+c$, where $a\ne 0$.

At a particular point, the tangent and normal to the curve are given by

$t(x)=5(x+1)$ and $n(x)=-\dfrac{x}{5}-\dfrac{1}{5}$ respectively.

The curve has a maximum turning point at $x=\dfrac{1}{4}$
Show that the point of intersection of the tangent and the normal is $(-1,0)$
items.sol:
The tangent and normal meet where $t(x)=n(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5(x+1)&=-\dfrac{x}{5}-\dfrac{1}{5}\\ 5(5x+5)&=-x-1\\ 25x+25&=-x-1\\ 25x+x&=-1-25\\ 26x&=-26\\ x&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$t(-1)=5(-1+1)=0$$
$\therefore$ the point of intersection of the tangent and the normal is $(-1,0)$.

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=ax^2+bx+c$, where $a\ne 0$.

At a particular point, the tangent and normal to the curve are given by

$t(x)=5(x+1)$ and $n(x)=-\dfrac{x}{5}-\dfrac{1}{5}$ respectively.

The curve has a maximum turning point at $x=\dfrac{1}{4}$
Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=ax^2+bx+c\\ y'&=2ax+b\end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent and the curve is the same at $(-1,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2a(-1)+b&=5\\ -2a+b&=5 &&(1)\end{aligned}$$
The maximum turning point is at $x=\dfrac{1}{4}$, so $y'\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2a\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+b&=0\\ \dfrac{a}{2}+b&=0 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a}{2}+2a&=-5\\ \dfrac{5a}{2}&=-5\\ a&=-\dfrac{5\times2}{5}=-2\end{aligned}$$
From (2):
$$b=-\dfrac{a}{2}=1$$
For $c$, substitute the point $(-1,0)$, $a$ and $b$ into $y=ax^2+bx+c$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-2(-1)^2+1(-1)+c\\ c-1-2&=0\\ c&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=-2,\ b=1,\ c=3$$

items.part:
Find an expression, in simplest form, for the general term of the arithmetic series:

$$257+246+235+\dots$$
Find the 125th term of the series above.
items.sol:
Using $T_n=268-11n$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} T_{125}&=268-11(125)\\ &=-1107\end{aligned}$$

The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.1+0.25+n+0.35&=1\\ n&=0.3\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The shaded segment shown is formed by an arc $BC$ of a circle with radius 1.6m.

The arc subtends an angle of $\dfrac{4\pi}{9}$ radians at its centre, $A$.

\exfigure{1358_q13_1}

Find the area of the shaded segment, correct to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
The segment is the sector minus the triangle $ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{segment}}&=A_{\text{sector}}-A_{\text{triangle}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(1.6)^2\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{9}-\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{9}\right)\\ &\approx 0.527\text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given $\log_5 2=a$ and $\log_5 3=b$, express $\log_5\left(\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
Using the log law $\log_a xy=\log_a x+\log_a y$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_5\left(\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{2}}\right)&=\log_5\left(6\sqrt{2}\right)\\ &=\log_5\left(2\times 3\times 2^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\\ &=\log_5\left(2^{\frac{3}{2}}\times 3\right)\\ &=\log_5\left(2^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)+\log_5 3\\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}a+b\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate with respect to $x$.
$y=(3x^2-7)^6$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=6(3x^2-7)^5\times(6x)\\ &=36x(3x^2-7)^5\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate with respect to $x$.
$y=\dfrac{2x-1}{x+8}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x-1 & v&=x+8\\ u'&=2 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{2(x+8)-(2x-1)}{(x+8)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{2x+16-2x+1}{(x+8)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{17}{(x+8)^2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=x^3+\ln x+5$ at the point $(1,6)$.
If $\sin x=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5}$, $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, find the value of $\sin^4 x-\cos^4 x$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1358_q17_s1}

By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle (hypotenuse 5, opposite side $\sqrt{5}$):
$$\text{Adjacent side}=\sqrt{25-5}=\sqrt{20}$$
Since $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\cos x>0$:
$$\cos x=\dfrac{\sqrt{20}}{5}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin^4 x-\cos^4 x&=\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\right)^4-\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{20}}{5}\right)^4\\ &=-\dfrac{3}{5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve for $x$ where $0\le x\le 2\pi$, $\quad\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\sqrt{2}$
items.sol:
Since $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)}&=\sqrt{2}\\ \sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le x\le 2\pi\\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}&\le x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le\dfrac{7\pi}{3} &&\left(\text{add } \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{4} &&\text{(invalid)}\\ &=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{9\pi}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{11\pi}{4} &&\text{(invalid)}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ x&=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ or } \dfrac{9\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{5\pi}{12} \text{ or } \dfrac{23\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
John and Robert each played equal number of computer games.

Their scores in these games are analysed to create the box plots as shown below.

\exfigure{1358_q19_1}

Robert claims that his scores were better than John's scores. Is he correct?

Support your answer by referring to the box plots' skewness of the distributions, measures of the central tendencies and the measures of the spreads.
items.sol:
Skewness: John's scores are positively skewed; Robert's scores are almost symmetrical.

John: median score 130, IQR 12, range 20.

Robert: median score 136, IQR 8, range 14.

Robert is correct because his scores are more consistent (smaller range and IQR) and more than $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of his scores are above John's median (higher median).

items.part: Show that: $\quad\sec^2 A\equiv\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} A}{\operatorname{cosec} A-\sin A}$
items.sol:
Using $\operatorname{cosec} A=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\sin A}}{\frac{1}{\sin A}-\sin A}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\sin A}}{\frac{1-\sin^2 A}{\sin A}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin^2 A}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A}\\ &=\sec^2 A=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Given $f(x)=x-2$ and $g(x)=(x+2)(x^2-4)$.
Find all points of intersection between $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.
items.sol:
The graphs meet where $f(x)=g(x)$. Factorising $x^2-4=(x+2)(x-2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} x-2&=(x+2)(x^2-4)\\ &=(x+2)(x+2)(x-2)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} (x+2)^2(x-2)-(x-2)&=0\\ (x-2)\left[(x+2)^2-1\right]&=0\end{aligned}$$
$x-2=0$ gives $x=2$.

$(x+2)^2=1$ gives $x+2=\pm1$, so $x=-1$ or $x=-3$.

Using $y=x-2$, the points of intersection are $(2,0)$, $(-1,-3)$, $(-3,-5)$.

\exfigure{1358_q21_s1}

Since $g(x)=(x+2)^2(x-2)$, the cubic has a double root at $x=-2$ (touches the $x$-axis) and crosses at $x=2$.

items.part:
Given $f(x)=x-2$ and $g(x)=(x+2)(x^2-4)$.

items.part:
A company produces resistors with resistance being normally distributed ($\mu=50\,\Omega$, $\sigma=2\,\Omega$).

Resistors below $48\,\Omega$ or exceeds $52\,\Omega$ are defective.
Find the percentage of defective resistors.
items.sol:
Defective resistors lie more than one standard deviation from the mean ($48=50-2$, $52=50+2$). By the empirical rule, $68\%$ lie within one standard deviation:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{defective}) &= P(X<48)+P(X>52)\\ &= 1-68\%\\ &= 32\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A company produces resistors with resistance being normally distributed ($\mu=50\,\Omega$, $\sigma=2\,\Omega$).

Resistors below $48\,\Omega$ or exceeds $52\,\Omega$ are defective.
In a batch of 1000 resistors, how many are expected to be non-defective?
items.sol:
From (a), $100\%-32\%=68\%$ are non-defective:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000(1-32\%) &= 1000\times 0.68\\ &= 680 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 680 resistors are expected to be non-defective.

items.part:
Show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\tan x\right)=e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)$$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
Then, using $\sec^2 x=\tan^2 x+1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\tan x\right) &= e^x\tan x+e^x\sec^2 x\\ &= e^x\left(\sec^2 x+\tan x\right)\\ &= e^x\left(\tan^2 x+1+\tan x\right)\\ &= e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Hence evaluate

$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)\,dx$$
items.sol:
From (a), $e^x\tan x$ is a primitive of $e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)dx &= \Big[e^x\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &= e^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-e^0\tan 0\\ &= \sqrt{3}\,e^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \end{aligned}$$

Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac{3k}{4}$, $P(B)=k$ and $P(\overline{A}\cap B)=k^2$ where $0<k<1$.
Find the expression of $P(A\cap B)$ in terms of $k$.

Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac{3k}{4}$, $P(B)=k$ and $P(\overline{A}\cap B)=k^2$ where $0<k<1$.
Given that the two events are independent, find the value of $k$.
items.sol:
The events are independent, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$. Using (a):
$$\begin{aligned} k-k^2 &= \dfrac{3k}{4}\cdot k\\ 4k-4k^2 &= 3k^2\\ 7k^2-4k &= 0\\ k(7k-4) &= 0\\ k &= 0 \text{ or } k=\dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$k=0$ is not allowed since $0<k<1$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{4}{7}$$

items.part:
The amount of time for Opstra Telecom. to respond to a customer query follows the probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{(5x-1)^2}, & x\ge 1\\[6pt] 0, & 0<x<1\end{cases}\qquad\text{where } x \text{ is time in hours.}$$
Show that $k=20$.
items.sol:
The total area under a probability density function is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^{\infty}\dfrac{k}{(5x-1)^2}\,dx &= 1\\ k\int_1^{\infty}(5x-1)^{-2}\,dx &= 1\\ k\left[\dfrac{(5x-1)^{-1}}{-1\times 5}\right]_1^{\infty} &= 1\\ -\dfrac{k}{5}\left[0-\dfrac{1}{4}\right] &= 1\\ \dfrac{k}{20} &= 1\\ k &= 20 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The amount of time for Opstra Telecom. to respond to a customer query follows the probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{(5x-1)^2}, & x\ge 1\\[6pt] 0, & 0<x<1\end{cases}\qquad\text{where } x \text{ is time in hours.}$$
Calculate the median response time.
items.sol:
Let the median be $m$. Half the probability lies below the median:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^m\dfrac{20}{(5x-1)^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ -4\left[\dfrac{1}{5x-1}\right]_1^m &= 0.5\\ -\dfrac{4}{5m-1}+1 &= 0.5\\ \dfrac{4}{5m-1} &= 0.5\\ m &= \dfrac{9}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The median response time is $\dfrac{9}{5}$ hours ($1.8$ hours).

The velocity of a particle is given by $\dot{x}(t)=8t^3e^{t^4}$, where $\dot{x}(t)$ is velocity in metres per second and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin.
Determine the times(s) the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$8t^3e^{t^4}=0$$
$e^{t^4}>0$ for all $t$, so $t^3=0$.
$$\therefore\ t=0$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle is given by $\dot{x}(t)=8t^3e^{t^4}$, where $\dot{x}(t)$ is velocity in metres per second and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin.
Show that the displacement function is $x(t)=2e^{t^4}-2$.
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity. The derivative of $t^4$ is $4t^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 8t^3e^{t^4}\,dt\\ &= 2\int 4t^3e^{t^4}\,dt\\ &= 2e^{t^4}+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle is at the origin: when $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^0+C &= 0\\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=2e^{t^4}-2$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle is given by $\dot{x}(t)=8t^3e^{t^4}$, where $\dot{x}(t)$ is velocity in metres per second and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin.
At what time does the particle reach a displacement of 100 metres? (Give your answer to 2 d.p.)
items.sol:
Let $x(t)=100$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{t^4}-2 &= 100\\ e^{t^4} &= 51\\ t^4 &= \ln 51\\ t &\approx 1.41 \text{ s} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The mass of oranges at Fruit King farm are normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

It is known that 25.78% of these oranges have mass more than 190 g and 34.46% of them have mass more than 180 g.

Using the table of z scores below, answer the following questions.

\extable{1358_q28_t1}
Find the mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.
items.sol:
$25.78\%$ of oranges are heavier than 190 g, so $100\%-25.78\%=74.22\%$ are lighter. From the table, this corresponds to $z=0.65$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.65 &= \dfrac{190-\mu}{\sigma}\\ 0.65\sigma &= 190-\mu \quad (1) \end{aligned}$$
Similarly, $100\%-34.46\%=65.54\%$ corresponds to $z=0.4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.4 &= \dfrac{180-\mu}{\sigma}\\ 0.4\sigma &= 180-\mu \quad (2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtract (2) from (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 0.25\sigma &= 10\\ \sigma &= 40 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $\sigma=40$ into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 0.4(40) &= 180-\mu\\ \mu &= 164 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The mean is 164 g and the standard deviation is 40 g.

items.part:
The mass of oranges at Fruit King farm are normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

It is known that 25.78% of these oranges have mass more than 190 g and 34.46% of them have mass more than 180 g.

Using the table of z scores below, answer the following questions.

\extable{1358_q28_t1}
Two oranges from Fruit King farm are chosen at random.

Given that the mass of both oranges is greater than 180 grams, what is the probability that both of them have a mass less than 194 g. Give your answer as a percentage to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
$z$-score for 194 g, using $\mu=164$ and $\sigma=40$ from (a):
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{194-164}{40}\\ &= 0.75 \end{aligned}$$
From the table, $77.34\%$ of the oranges have mass less than 194 g.

Let the mass of an orange be $X$. For one orange, by conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<194\mid X>180) &= \dfrac{P(180<X<194)}{P(X>180)}\\ &= \dfrac{77.34\%-65.54\%}{34.46\%}\\ &= 34.24\% \end{aligned}$$
The two oranges are independent:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both}) &= (34.24\%)^2\\ &= 11.73\% \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x+1)e^x$.
Show that $f''(x)=(x+3)e^x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+1 & v&=e^x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= e^x+(x+1)e^x\\ &= e^x(x+2) \end{aligned}$$
Again with the product rule, $u=x+2$, $v=e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= e^x+(x+2)e^x\\ &= e^x(x+3) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x+1)e^x$.
Find any stationary points of $f(x)$, determine their nature, and find any points of inflection.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$. From (a), $f'(x)=e^x(x+2)$:
$$e^x(x+2)=0$$
$e^x>0$ for all $x$, so $x+2=0$, $x=-2$.
$$f(-2)=(-2+1)e^{-2}=-e^{-2}$$
Nature: $f''(-2)=e^{-2}>0$, so the curve is concave up.

$\therefore$ $\left(-2,-e^{-2}\right)$ is a local minimum turning point.

Possible points of inflection occur when $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} e^x(x+3) &= 0\\ x &= -3 \end{aligned}$$
$$f(-3)=-2e^{-3}$$
Check the concavity either side of $x=-3$:

\extable{Ts1102_1}

Concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $\left(-3,-2e^{-3}\right)$.
items.final: Local minimum at $\left(-2,-e^{-2}\right)$; point of inflection at $\left(-3,-2e^{-3}\right)$

items.part:
Consider the two curves $L_1:\ y=-x^2+1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $L_2:\ y=ax^2$ for $x\ge 0$.

The diagram below shows the area enclosed by these two curves, and the $x$- and $y$-axis.

\exfigure{1358_q31_1}
Show that the two curves intersect at the point $\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{1+a}},\dfrac{a}{1+a}\right)$.
items.sol:
The curves intersect where the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} -x^2+1 &= ax^2\\ (a+1)x^2 &= 1\\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{a+1}\\ x &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}} \end{aligned}$$
$x\ge 0$ is given, so $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= a\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}\right)^2\\ &= \dfrac{a}{a+1} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Consider the two curves $L_1:\ y=-x^2+1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $L_2:\ y=ax^2$ for $x\ge 0$.

The diagram below shows the area enclosed by these two curves, and the $x$- and $y$-axis.

\exfigure{1358_q31_1}
Find the value of $a$ such that the areas of the two regions are equal.
items.sol:
Method 1

$S_1+S_2$ is the area under $L_1$ from $x=0$ to $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_1+S_2 &= \int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx\\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\ &= \left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-(0-0)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
But $S_1=S_2$, so $2S_1=\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $S_1=S_2=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

$S_1$ lies between $L_1$ (above) and $L_2$ (below), from $x=0$ to the intersection in (a):
$$\begin{aligned} S_1 &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}(-x^2+1-ax^2)\,dx\\ &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}\left(1-(1+a)x^2\right)dx\\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{1+a}{3}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}\\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}-\dfrac{1+a}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\right)-0\\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}\left(1-\dfrac{1+a}{3(1+a)}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $S_1=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}\left(1-\dfrac{1+a}{3(1+a)}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{3}\\ 2(1+a) &= (1+a)\sqrt{1+a}\\ 4(1+a)^2 &= (1+a)^2(1+a)\\ (1+a)^2(1+a)-4(1+a)^2 &= 0\\ (1+a)^2(1+a-4) &= 0\\ a &= -1 \text{ or } a=3 \end{aligned}$$
$a>0$, so $a=3$.

Method 2

$S_2=\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx-S_1$ and $S_1=S_2$, so
$$S_1=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx$$
then continue as in Method 1.

Method 3

From Method 1:
$$S_1=\dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}$$
$S_2$ is the area under $L_2$ up to the intersection, plus the area under $L_1$ from the intersection to $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_2 &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}ax^2\,dx+\int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}^1(1-x^2)\,dx\\ &= \left[\dfrac{a}{3}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}+\left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}^1\\ &= \dfrac{a}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}+\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}-\dfrac{1}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2+2a}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} \end{aligned}$$
Equating $S_1$ and $S_2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} &= \dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\\ \dfrac{2(1+a)}{(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} &= 1\\ 2(1+a) &= (1+a)\sqrt{1+a}\\ 4(1+a)^2 &= (1+a)^3\\ (1+a)^2(a-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$a=-1$ is outside the domain.
$$\therefore\ a=3$$

items.part: Differentiate: $\dfrac{5x^2 - 7}{x + 2}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=5x^2-7 & v&=x+2\\ u'&=10x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{10x(x + 2) - (5x^2 - 7)}{(x + 2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{10x^2 + 20x - 5x^2 + 7}{(x + 2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{5x^2 + 20x + 7}{(x + 2)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation: $|2x - 3| = 9x$
items.sol:
$|2x-3|=9x$ means $2x-3=9x$ or $-(2x-3)=9x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x - 3 &= 9x & \qquad -2x + 3 &= 9x \\ -3 &= 7x & 3 &= 11x \\ x &= -\dfrac{3}{7} & x &= \dfrac{3}{11} \end{aligned}$$
Test the solutions in the original equation.

$x=-\dfrac{3}{7}$:
$$\left|2 \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{7}\right) - 3\right| = \dfrac{27}{7},\qquad 9 \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{7}\right)=-\dfrac{27}{7}$$
These are not equal, so $x = -\dfrac{3}{7}$ is not a solution.

$x=\dfrac{3}{11}$:
$$\left|2 \times \dfrac{3}{11} - 3\right| = \dfrac{27}{11},\qquad 9 \times \dfrac{3}{11}=\dfrac{27}{11}$$
These are equal.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{3}{11}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 5 red, 6 green and 3 white jellybeans.

Two jellybeans are chosen at random without replacement.
Find the probability of selecting at least 1 red jellybean.
items.sol:
"At least 1 red" is the complement of "no red":
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least 1 } R) &= 1 - P(\bar{R}\bar{R}) \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{9}{14} \times \dfrac{8}{13} \\ &= \dfrac{55}{91} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the coordinates of the point on the curve $y = x^2 - 2x - 3$, where the tangent is perpendicular to the line $x + 4y - 1 = 0$.
items.sol:
Rearrange the line to gradient–intercept form:
$$\begin{aligned} 4y &= -x + 1 \\ y &= -\dfrac{1}{4}x + \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $m = -\dfrac{1}{4}$. Perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$, so $m_\perp = 4$.

The tangent has gradient $y'$, so set $y'=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 2x - 2 \\ 4 &= 2x - 2 \\ 6 &= 2x \\ x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$y = 3^2 - 2 \times 3 - 3 = 0$$
$\therefore$ The point is $(3, 0)$.

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \cos 2x\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \cos 2x\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\left(2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 0 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

A ship ($S$) observes a lighthouse ($L$) to be on a bearing of $N26^\circ E$ and a tower ($T$) to be on a bearing of $N70^\circ E$. The bearing of the lighthouse from the tower is $N15^\circ E$ and the distance from the lighthouse to the tower is 6.8 km.
Find the distance of the ship to the tower, correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
Using the sine rule in $\triangle SLT$, with $ST=x$ opposite $\angle SLT=11^\circ$ and $LT=6.8$ km opposite $\angle LST=44^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{\sin 11^\circ} &= \dfrac{6.8}{\sin 44^\circ} \\ x &= \dfrac{6.8 \times \sin 11^\circ}{\sin 44^\circ} \\ &= 1.867826\ldots \\ &\approx 1.9 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

Horizontal dilation by a factor of 3 replaces $x$ with $\dfrac{x}{3}$:
$$y=f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) = \left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)^3$$
Reflection in the $y$-axis replaces $x$ with $-x$:
$$y=f\left(-\dfrac{x}{3}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)^3 = -\dfrac{x^3}{27}$$
Translation 1 unit left replaces $x$ with $x+1$:
$$\therefore\ y=f\left(-\dfrac{x + 1}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{(x + 1)^3}{27}$$

The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} m &= 1 - 0.7 - 0.2 \\ &= 0.1 \end{aligned}$$

Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 1 \times 0.7 + 2 \times 0.1 + 3 \times 0.2 \\ &= 1.5 \end{aligned}$$

From (b), $\mu = 1.5$, so $\mu^2 = 2.25$.
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X) &= E(X^2) - \mu^2 \\ &= \left[1^2 \times 0.7 + 2^2 \times 0.1 + 3^2 \times 0.2\right] - 2.25 \\ &= 0.65 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{0.65} \\ &\approx 0.81 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Cailey produces and sells tubs of slime. The weights of the tubs of slime are normally distributed. 84% of her tubs weigh more than 152 grams and 16% of her tubs weigh more than 200 grams.
Find the mean, $\mu$, and the standard deviation, $\sigma$, of the distribution.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1359_q21_s1}

$84\%$ lie above 152 and $16\%$ lie above 200. By the empirical rule, $16\%$ lie more than one standard deviation above the mean, so 152 and 200 are at $z = -1$ and $z = 1$.

The mean is halfway between them:
$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= \dfrac{152 + 200}{2} \\ &= 176 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= 200-176\\ &= 24 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Cailey produces and sells tubs of slime. The weights of the tubs of slime are normally distributed. 84% of her tubs weigh more than 152 grams and 16% of her tubs weigh more than 200 grams.
Find the percentage of tubs of slime that weigh between 152 grams and 224 grams.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} z_{152} &= \dfrac{152-176}{24} = -1\\ z_{224} &= \dfrac{224-176}{24} = 2 \end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule, $34\%$ lie between $z=-1$ and $z=0$, and $47.5\%$ between $z=0$ and $z=2$:
$$34\% + 47.5\% = 81.5\%$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{\tan\theta\,\sec\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \sin\theta$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \times \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\right) \div \sec^2\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \div \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \times \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1} \\ &= \sin\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous probability distribution is given by $f(x) = \dfrac{3x^2}{279}$, defined in the domain $[4, 7]$.
Find the cumulative distribution function.
items.sol:
The cumulative distribution function is the area under $f$ from 4 to $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_4^x \dfrac{3t^2}{279}\,dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^3}{279}\right]_4^x \\ &= \dfrac{x^3}{279} - \dfrac{4^3}{279} \\ &= \dfrac{x^3 - 64}{279} \end{aligned}$$
for $4\le x\le 7$.

items.part:
A continuous probability distribution is given by $f(x) = \dfrac{3x^2}{279}$, defined in the domain $[4, 7]$.
Find the median of the continuous probability distribution to 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
The median $x$ satisfies $F(x)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x^3 - 64}{279} &= 0.5 \\ x^3 - 64 &= 139.5 \\ x^3 &= 203.5 \\ x &= \sqrt[3]{203.5} \\ &= 5.881951\ldots \\ &\approx 5.9 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The median is approximately 5.9.

items.part:
Consider the function $y = (1 + x)e^{-2x}$.
Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1+x & v&=e^{-2x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2e^{-2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= e^{-2x} - 2(1 + x)e^{-2x} \\ &= e^{-2x}\left(1 - 2(1 + x)\right) \\ &= e^{-2x}(-1 - 2x) \\ &= -e^{-2x}(1 + 2x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y' = 0$:
$$-e^{-2x}(1 + 2x)=0$$
$e^{-2x}>0$ for all $x$, so $1+2x=0$ and $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-2 \times \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}\\ &= \dfrac{e}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{e}{2}\right)$ is a stationary point.

Only $1+2x$ decides the sign of $y'$. Testing either side:

\extable{Ts1140_1}

$\therefore$ Maximum turning point at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{e}{2}\right)$.

items.part:
Consider the function $y = (1 + x)e^{-2x}$.
Find the point of inflection.
items.sol:
Differentiate $y'=-e^{-2x}(1+2x)$ with the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-e^{-2x} & v&=1+2x\\ u'&=2e^{-2x} & v'&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'' &= 2e^{-2x}(1 + 2x)-2e^{-2x} \\ &= 2e^{-2x}(-1 + 1 + 2x) \\ &= 4xe^{-2x} \end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection occur when $y'' = 0$:
$$4xe^{-2x}=0$$
$e^{-2x}>0$ for all $x$, so $x = 0$.

At $x = 0$, $y = 1$, so $(0, 1)$ is a possible point of inflection.

Only $4x$ decides the sign of $y''$. Testing either side:

\extable{Ts1141_1}

Concavity changes, so $(0, 1)$ is a point of inflection.

items.part:
Consider the function $y = (1 + x)e^{-2x}$.
Describe the behaviour of the curve as $x \to \pm\infty$.
items.sol:
As $x \to \infty$, $e^{-2x} \to 0$ much faster than $1+x$ grows, so $y \to 0$.

As $x \to -\infty$, $e^{-2x} \to \infty$ and $(1 + x) \to -\infty$, so $y \to -\infty$.

items.part:
A particle moves with velocity given by $v = 12\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2}$, where $v$ and $t$ are measured in cm/s and seconds respectively. The particle was initially at rest at $x = \dfrac{-24}{\pi}$.
Find the equation for displacement, $x$, in terms of $t$.
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 12\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2}\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{-12\cos\frac{\pi t}{2}}{\frac{\pi}{2}} + C \\ &= -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{2} + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $x = -\dfrac{24}{\pi}$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{24}{\pi} &= -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 0\right) + C \\ C &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{2}$$

items.part:
A particle moves with velocity given by $v = 12\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2}$, where $v$ and $t$ are measured in cm/s and seconds respectively. The particle was initially at rest at $x = \dfrac{-24}{\pi}$.
Find distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction only when it is at rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2} &= 0\\ \sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2} &= 0\\ \dfrac{\pi t}{2} &= 0, \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi, \ldots\\ t &= 0, 2, 4, 6, \ldots \end{aligned}$$
Positions using (a):
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:&\quad x = -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\\ t=2:&\quad x = -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\cos\pi = \dfrac{24}{\pi}\\ t=3:&\quad x = -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2} = 0 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1359_q25_s1}
$$\begin{aligned} \text{distance} &= \dfrac{24}{\pi} \times 2 + \dfrac{24}{\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{72}{\pi} \text{ cm} \\ &\approx 22.9 \text{ cm (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

Points of intersection, where the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x^2 &= -10x + 12 \\ 2x^2 + 10x - 12 &= 0 \\ x^2 + 5x - 6 &= 0 \\ (x - 1)(x + 6) &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \text{ or } x=-6 \end{aligned}$$
The line is above the parabola between them:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-6}^{1} \left(-10x + 12 - 2x^2\right) dx \\ &= \left[-5x^2 + 12x - \dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{-6}^{1} \\ &= \left(-5 \times 1^2 + 12 \times 1 - \dfrac{2 \times 1^3}{3}\right) - \left(-5 \times (-6)^2 + 12 \times (-6) - \dfrac{2 \times (-6)^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{19}{3} - (-108) \\ &= \dfrac{343}{3} \\ &\approx 114.3 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A company produces 40 tonnes of rice in the first year of production, 80 tonnes in the second year and 120 tonnes in its third year of production. The company continues to increase its rice production by this same amount each year thereafter.
In which year of production did the amount of rice produced for that year equal 2000 tonnes?
items.sol:
$40 + 80 + 120 + \ldots$ is an arithmetic sequence with $a = 40$, $d = 40$. Using $T_n = a + (n - 1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2000 &= 40 + (n - 1) \times 40 \\ n - 1 &= \dfrac{1960}{40} \\ &= 49 \\ n &= 50 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ In the 50th year.

items.part:
A company produces 40 tonnes of rice in the first year of production, 80 tonnes in the second year and 120 tonnes in its third year of production. The company continues to increase its rice production by this same amount each year thereafter.
What was the total amount of rice produced in the first 20 years of production?
items.sol:
Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$ with $a=40$, $d=40$, $n=20$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{20} &= \dfrac{20}{2}\left(2 \times 40 + (20 - 1) \times 40\right) \\ &= 8400 \text{ tonnes} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $\sqrt{3} + 2\cos\theta = 0$ in the domain $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos\theta &= -\sqrt{3} \\ \cos\theta &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\cos\theta < 0$, so $\theta$ is in the second or third quadrant.

Related angle: $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \theta &= \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \ \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \ \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A vertical tower of height $h$ metres stands on horizontal ground. From a point $P$ on the ground due east of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $45^\circ$. From a point $Q$ on the ground due south of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $30^\circ$. If the distance $PQ$ is 40 metres, find the exact height of the tower.

\exfigure{1359_q29_1}
items.sol:
Let $R$ be the base of the tower. In right-angled triangles $PRT$ and $QRT$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 45^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \qquad \tan 30^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ 1 &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ PR &= h & QR &= \sqrt{3}h \end{aligned}$$
$P$ is due east and $Q$ due south of $R$, so $\angle PRQ = 90^\circ$. Using Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle PRQ$:
$$\begin{aligned} 40^2 &= h^2 + \left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2 \\ 1600 &= 4h^2 \\ h^2 &= 400 \\ h &= \pm 20 \end{aligned}$$
$h > 0$, so $h = 20$ m.

items.part:
A population of insects varies according to the formula $P = 3000n^{\frac{t}{10}}$, where $n$ is a positive constant and $t$ is the time in days.

The initial population was 3000. After 20 days the population had grown to 12 000.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of increase is 6000 insects per day.
items.sol:
Initially $P=3000$; after 20 days $P=12\,000$. Find $n$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12000 &= 3000n^{\frac{20}{10}} \\ n^2 &= 4 \\ n &= \pm 2 \end{aligned}$$
$n > 0$, so $n = 2$ and $P=3000\times 2^{\frac{t}{10}}$.

Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=k\ln a\cdot a^{kt}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 3000 \times \ln 2 \times \dfrac{1}{10} \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 6000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6000 &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{20}{\ln 2} \\ \dfrac{t}{10} &= \log_2\left(\dfrac{20}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \log_2 20 - \log_2(\ln 2) \\ t &= 10\left(\dfrac{\ln 20}{\ln 2} - \dfrac{\ln(\ln 2)}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &\approx 48.5 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: When the limiting sum exists, find an expression for the limiting sum in simplest form.
items.sol:
Each term is $-\tan^2\theta$ times the one before, so the series is geometric with $a = 1$ and $r = -\tan^2\theta$. Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{1}{1 + \tan^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta} \\ &= \cos^2\theta \end{aligned}$$

items.part: For what values of $\theta$ in the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ does the limiting sum of the series exist?
items.sol:
The limiting sum exists when $|r| < 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 &< -\tan^2\theta < 1\\ 1 &> \tan^2\theta > -1 &&(\text{multiply by } -1)\\ -1 &< \tan^2\theta < 1 &&(\text{rewrite}) \end{aligned}$$
$\tan^2\theta\ge 0$, so this means $\tan^2\theta<1$, that is $-1<\tan\theta<1$.

$\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$ and $\tan\theta$ is increasing on $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{\pi}{4} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

items.part:
Jackson inherits \$200 000. He invests it into an account earning interest at a rate of 6% p.a. compounding monthly. At the end of each month, immediately after the interest has been paid, Jackson withdraws \$2000.
Find the total amount that is in the account immediately after the 3$^{\text{rd}}$ withdrawal.

Jackson inherits \$200 000. He invests it into an account earning interest at a rate of 6% p.a. compounding monthly. At the end of each month, immediately after the interest has been paid, Jackson withdraws \$2000.
How much interest was earned in the first three months?
items.sol:
Interest is the final balance minus what was deposited less what was withdrawn, $P-M$:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= A_3 - (P - M) \\ &= 196984.98 - (200000 - 3 \times 2000) \\ &= 196984.98 - 194000 \\ &= \$2984.98 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jackson inherits \$200 000. He invests it into an account earning interest at a rate of 6% p.a. compounding monthly. At the end of each month, immediately after the interest has been paid, Jackson withdraws \$2000.
Calculate the amount of money in the account immediately after the 70$^{\text{th}}$ withdrawal.

items.sol:
In the right-angled triangle formed by the light, the centre and a point on the circumference, using the sine ratio:
$$\sin\alpha = \dfrac{y}{d}$$
Using Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} d^2 &= y^2 + a^2 \\ d &= \left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \quad \text{as } d > 0 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into the given formula:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= \dfrac{k\sin\alpha}{d^2} \\ &= \dfrac{k \times \frac{y}{d}}{d^2} \\ &= \dfrac{ky}{d^3} \\ &= \dfrac{ky}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dy}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=ky & v&=\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\\ u'&=k & v'&=3y\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dy} &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} - ky \times 3y\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\left(\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\left(y^2 + a^2\right) - 3y^2\right]}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right)}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right)}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dI}{dy} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} k\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right) &= 0 \\ 2y^2 &= a^2 \\ y^2 &= \dfrac{a^2}{2} \\ y &= \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \text{as } y > 0 \end{aligned}$$
Only $a^2-2y^2$ decides the sign of $\dfrac{dI}{dy}$. Testing either side:

\extable{Ts1158_1}

$\therefore$ The intensity is a maximum when the light is at height $y = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ m.

items.part: Find the vertex of the parabola $y=x^2-6x+10$.
items.sol:
The vertex lies on the axis of symmetry, $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=-\dfrac{-6}{2\times 1}\\&=3\end{aligned}$$
$y$-coordinate:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=(3)^2-6(3)+10\\&=1\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The vertex is $(3,1)$.

items.part: Solve the equation $\cos x=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
$\cos x>0$, so the solutions are in the first and fourth quadrants. The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $\log_2(1-x)+\log_2(3-x)=3$.
items.sol:
The logarithms need $1-x>0$ and $3-x>0$, so $x<1$.

Using the log law $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2[(1-x)(3-x)]&=3\\(1-x)(3-x)&=2^3\\x^2-4x+3&=8\\x^2-4x-5&=0\\(x-5)(x+1)&=0\\x&=5 \text{ or } x=-1\end{aligned}$$
$x=5$ does not satisfy $x<1$.
$$\therefore\ x=-1$$

Using the cosine rule, $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$, with sides 7 and 9 and included angle $47^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2&=7^2+9^2-2(7)(9)\cos47^\circ\\x&=\sqrt{7^2+9^2-2(7)(9)\cos47^\circ}\\&=6.638388858\ldots\\&\approx6.6\text{ cm (2 significant figures)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $x^2(3x+5)^3$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=(3x+5)^3\\ u'&=2x & v'&=9(3x+5)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x^2(3x+5)^3\right]&=2x(3x+5)^3+x^2\left(3(3x+5)^2\times3\right)\\&=2x(3x+5)^3+9x^2(3x+5)^2\\&=x(3x+5)^2\left(9x+2(3x+5)\right)\\&=x(3x+5)^2(15x+10)\\&=5x(3x+5)^2(3x+2)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find in simplest general form the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=e^x+\log_e(2x-1)$ at the point where $x=1$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e^x+\log_e(2x-1)\\y'&=e^x+\dfrac{2}{2x-1}\end{aligned}$$
Gradient of the tangent when $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}m&=y'(1)\\&=e+2\end{aligned}$$
$y$-coordinate:
$$\begin{aligned}y(1)&=e+\log_e1\\&=e\end{aligned}$$
Equation of the tangent, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-e&=(e+2)(x-1)\\y-e&=(e+2)x-e-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (e+2)x-y-2=0$$

The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned}a+0.1+b+0.3&=1\\a+b&=0.6\quad\text{(1)}\end{aligned}$$
The expected value is 2, using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}0\times a+1\times0.1+2\times b+3\times0.3&=2\\2b+1&=2\\b&=0.5\end{aligned}$$
Substitute $b=0.5$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}a+0.5&=0.6\\a&=0.1\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A probability density function is given by $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3x^2}{117} & 2\le x\le k\\[2pt] 0 & \text{for all other } x\end{cases}$.

Find the value of $k$.
items.sol:
The total area under a probability density function is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^k\dfrac{3x^2}{117}\,dx&=1\\\left[\dfrac{x^3}{117}\right]_2^k&=1\\\dfrac{k^3-8}{117}&=1\\k^3-8&=117\\k^3&=125\\k&=5\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of years of teaching experience of the 4800 secondary teachers teaching in Australia are normally distributed with mean 20 years and standard deviation 6 years.
Use the Empirical Rules to determine how many more teachers with at most 14 years of experience there are than teachers with at least 32 years of experience.
items.sol:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ with $\mu=20$, $\sigma=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}z_{14}&=\dfrac{14-20}{6}=-1\\z_{32}&=\dfrac{32-20}{6}=2\end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule:
$$\begin{aligned}P(z\le-1)&=16\%\\P(z\ge2)&=2.5\%\end{aligned}$$
Teachers with at most 14 years' experience:
$$0.16\times4800=768$$
Teachers with at least 32 years' experience:
$$0.025\times4800=120$$
$$768-120=648$$
$\therefore$ There are 648 more teachers with at most 14 years' experience than with at least 32 years' experience.
items.final: 648 more teachers with at most 14 years' experience than with at least 32 years'

items.part:
The number of years of teaching experience of the 4800 secondary teachers teaching in Australia are normally distributed with mean 20 years and standard deviation 6 years.
Teachers with more than 14 years of teaching experience are known as highly accomplished teachers. Use the Empirical rule to find, to the nearest whole number, the percentage of highly accomplished teachers who have more than 26 years teaching experience.
items.sol:
26 years has $z=\dfrac{26-20}{6}=1$, and 14 years has $z=-1$.

The highly accomplished teachers are those with $z>-1$. The required percentage is a conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned}P(z>1\mid z>-1)&=\dfrac{P(z>1)}{P(z>-1)}\\&=\dfrac{16}{84}\\&\approx19\%\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 11 blue lollies and 9 green lollies.

David takes out a lolly from the bag without looking and eats it. He then takes out another lolly without looking and eats it.
What is the probability of David choosing a blue lolly in his first selection?
items.sol:
11 of the 20 lollies are blue:
$$P(\text{Blue})=\dfrac{11}{20}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 11 blue lollies and 9 green lollies.

David takes out a lolly from the bag without looking and eats it. He then takes out another lolly without looking and eats it.
By drawing a tree diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that David eats two lollies of different colours.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1361_q20_s1}
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{different colours})&=P(BG)+P(GB)\\&=\dfrac{11}{20}\times\dfrac{9}{19}+\dfrac{9}{20}\times\dfrac{11}{19}\\&=\dfrac{99}{190}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 11 blue lollies and 9 green lollies.

David takes out a lolly from the bag without looking and eats it. He then takes out another lolly without looking and eats it.
David opens a different bag of blue and green lollies. He notices that it contains 10 green lollies but does not count the blue lollies. He then eats two lollies without looking at their colour. If the probability that David eats two green lollies is $\dfrac{3}{8}$, how many blue lollies were in the bag?
items.sol:
Let $x$ be the number of blue lollies in the bag. There are 10 green lollies, and $P(GG)=\dfrac{3}{8}$.

First selection: $P(G)=\dfrac{10}{x+10}$.

Second selection (one green eaten): $P(G)=\dfrac{9}{x+9}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{10}{x+10}\times\dfrac{9}{x+9}&=\dfrac{3}{8}\\\dfrac{90}{(x+10)(x+9)}&=\dfrac{3}{8}\\720&=3(x+10)(x+9)\\(x+10)(x+9)&=240\\x^2+19x+90&=240\\x^2+19x-150&=0\\(x+25)(x-6)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$x>0$, so $x=6$.

$\therefore$ There are 6 blue lollies in the bag.

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-3x^2$ for $-1\le x\le 3.5$.
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=3x^2-6x\\y''&=6x-6\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3x^2-6x&=0\\3x(x-2)&=0\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=2\end{aligned}$$
For the nature of the stationary points, consider the sign of $y''$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=0: && y''=-6<0,\ y=0 && \text{maximum}\\ x&=2: && y''=6>0,\ y=-4 && \text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Maximum turning point at $(0,0)$.

$\therefore$ Minimum turning point at $(2,-4)$.
items.final: Maximum turning point at $(0,0)$; minimum turning point at $(2,-4)$

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-3x^2$ for $-1\le x\le 3.5$.
Find any points of inflection.
items.sol:
Points of inflection occur where $y''=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned}y''&=0\\6x-6&=0\\x&=1\end{aligned}$$
There is a possible point of inflection at $x=1$. Test the concavity:

\extable{Ts1183_1}

The concavity changes either side of $x=1$, so there is a point of inflection there.
$$\begin{aligned}y(1)&=1^3-3(1)^2\\&=-2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Point of inflection at $(1,-2)$.
\exfigure{1361_q21_s1}

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-3x^2$ for $-1\le x\le 3.5$.
Hence state the global maximum for $y=x^3-3x^2$ in the domain $-1\le x\le 3.5$.
items.sol:
Compare the local maximum $y=0$ at $x=0$ with the end points:
$$\begin{aligned}y(-1)&=-1-3=-4\\y(3.5)&=3.5^3-3(3.5)^2=6.125\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The global maximum is $y=6.125$, at $x=3.5$.
\extable{Ts1186_1}

items.part:
Given that $y=\log_e(3^x-2x)$
Using the table above and the trapezoidal rule, find an approximation for the value of $\displaystyle\int_1^3\log_e(3^x-2x)\,dx$ correct to three decimal places.
items.sol:
Using the trapezoidal rule with $n=4$ strips, $h=\dfrac{b-a}{n}=\dfrac{3-1}{4}=0.5$, and the $y$-values at $x=1,1.5,2,2.5,3$ from (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^3\log_e(3^x-2x)\,dx&\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left[y_0+y_4+2(y_1+y_2+y_3)\right]\\&=\dfrac{3-1}{2(4)}[0+3.045+2(0.787+1.609+2.360)]\\&=3.13925\\&\approx3.139\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $(\tan\theta-1)\left(\sqrt{3}\sin\theta-\cos\theta\right)\left(\sqrt{3}\sin\theta+\cos\theta\right)=0$

Find all solutions for $(\tan\theta-1)\left(\sqrt{3}\sin\theta-\cos\theta\right)\left(\sqrt{3}\sin\theta+\cos\theta\right)=0$, where $0\le\theta\le\pi$.
items.sol:
A product is zero when one of its factors is zero:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta-1&=0\\\sqrt{3}\sin\theta-\cos\theta&=0\\\sqrt{3}\sin\theta+\cos\theta&=0\end{aligned}$$
First factor:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=1\\\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Second factor (divide by $\cos\theta$):
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\sin\theta&=\cos\theta\\\tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
Third factor ($\tan\theta<0$, so $\theta$ is in the second quadrant):
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\sin\theta&=-\cos\theta\\\tan\theta&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\\theta&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\&=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

items.part: Find the values of any constant $A$ such that $\displaystyle\int_0^3\left(x^2+A\right)dx=2A^2$.

A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v(t)=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. The particle starts at $O$.
Show that $x(t)=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} v(t)&=3\sqrt{t+1}-9\\ &=3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\\ x(t)&=\int\left(3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\right)dt\\ &=\dfrac{3(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C\\ &=2\sqrt{(t+1)^3}-9t+C\\ &=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t+C \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at $O$, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=2(1)\sqrt{1}-9(0)+C\\ \therefore\ C&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2 \text{ as required}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v(t)=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. The particle starts at $O$.
Find when and where the particle is at rest in relation to the fixed point $O$.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9&=0\\ \sqrt{t+1}&=3\\ t+1&=9\\ \therefore\ t&=8 \end{aligned}$$
Using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} x(8)&=2(8+1)\sqrt{8+1}-9(8)-2\\ &=-20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The particle is at rest after 8 seconds, 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of motion.
items.final: The particle is at rest after 8 seconds, 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of motion ($x=-20$).

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v(t)=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. The particle starts at $O$.
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 24 seconds.
items.sol:
Using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} x(24)&=2(25)\sqrt{25}-9(24)-2\\ &=32 \end{aligned}$$
The particle travels from $x=0$ to $x=-20$ (at rest at $t=8$), then to $x=32$ in the first 24 seconds.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=20+20+32\\ &=72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove that $(1+\tan x)^2=2\tan x+\sec^2 x$.
items.sol:
Using $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=(1+\tan x)^2\\ &=1+2\tan x+\tan^2x\\ &=2\tan x+1+\tan^2x\\ &=2\tan x+\sec^2x\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find the area bounded by $y=(1+\tan x)^2$ and the $x$-axis between $-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ with a rational denominator.
items.sol:
$y=(1+\tan x)^2\ge 0$ for all $x$, so the area is the integral.

By part (a), $y=2\tan x+\sec^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left(2\tan x+\sec^2x\right)dx\\ &=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left(\dfrac{2\sin x}{\cos x}+\sec^2x\right)dx\\ &=\Big[-2\ln|\cos x|+\tan x\Big]_{-\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\ &=\left(-2\ln\left|\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right|+\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\left(-2\ln\left|\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right|+\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\\ &=-2\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-\left(-2\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\\ &=-2\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+2\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

By the angle sum of triangle $ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ABC&=180^\circ-120^\circ-40^\circ\\ &=20^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Using the sine rule in triangle $ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{AC}{\sin20^\circ}&=\dfrac{20}{\sin120^\circ}\\ AC&=\dfrac{20\sin20^\circ}{\sin120^\circ}\\ &=7.898616873\ldots\\ &\approx7.9\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

$P$ is vertically above $C$, so triangle $PCA$ is right-angled at $C$, with hypotenuse $PA=9.12$ km.

Let $\theta$ be the angle of elevation of $P$ from $A$. Using the cosine ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta&=\dfrac{7.9}{9.12}\\ \theta&=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7.9}{9.12}\right)\\ \therefore\ \theta&\approx29^\circ59' \end{aligned}$$

Let $\alpha=\angle APB$. Using the cosine rule in triangle $PAB$ with $PA=9.12$, $PB=15.52$ and $AB=20$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\alpha&=\dfrac{(9.12)^2+(15.52)^2-20^2}{2\times9.12\times15.52}\\ \alpha&=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{(9.12)^2+(15.52)^2-20^2}{2\times9.12\times15.52}\right)\\ &\approx105^\circ34' \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3 x\right)=3\cos x-3\cos^3 x$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule and $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)\\ &=3\sin^2x\cos x\\ &=3\cos x\left(1-\cos^2x\right)\\ &=3\cos x-3\cos^3x\\ &=\text{RHS as required} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos^3 x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Rearranging part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)&=3\cos x-3\cos^3x\\ \therefore\ \cos^3x&=\cos x-\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)\right] \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos^3x\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left(\cos x-\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)\right]\right)dx\\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos x\,dx-\dfrac{1}{3}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)\right]dx\\ &=\Big[\sin x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}-\dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\sin^3x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\ &=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin(0)-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\sin^3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin^3(0)\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}-0-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{8}-0\right)\\ &=\dfrac{11}{24} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The weight, in grams, of beans in a tin is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation 7.8. It is known that 10.03% of tins contains less than 200 g of beans.

Probability table for calculating the standard normal distribution. The values represent the area to the left of (or less than) the $z$-score.

\exfigure{1361_q30_1}
Use the probability table above to find the mean weight, $\mu$, of beans in a tin. Answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<200)&=10.03\%\\ &=0.1003 \end{aligned}$$
From the table, this corresponds to $z=-1.28$.

Using the $z$-score formula, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1.28&=\dfrac{200-\mu}{7.8}\\ \mu&=200+1.28\times7.8\\ \therefore\ \mu&\approx209.98\text{ g} \end{aligned}$$

Given that 97.5% of tins contain between 200 g and 210 g of beans, draw a normal distribution graph to illustrate this information. Use the probability table on page 27 to find the value of the standard deviation, $\sigma$, that can be achieved with the new setting. Answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:

By symmetry about the mean 205, each tail outside $200\le X\le210$ holds $\dfrac{1-0.975}{2}=0.0125$:

items.part: Solve the equation $x^{\ln(2)}=8$.
items.sol:
Taking natural logs of both sides and using the log law $\ln a^n=n\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^{\ln 2}&=8\\ x^{\ln 2}&=2^3\\ \ln\left(x^{\ln 2}\right)&=\ln\left(2^3\right)\\ \ln 2\,\ln x&=3\ln 2\\ \ln x&=3\\ x&=e^3 \end{aligned}$$

At the points of intersection the two equations are equal. Dividing both sides by $\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{3}\sin x&=\cos x\\ \sqrt{3}\tan x&=1\\ \tan x&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$

$\tan x>0$ in the first and third quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan x&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Between these points $y=\sqrt{3}\sin x$ is above $y=\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{7\pi}{6}}\left(\sqrt{3}\sin x-\cos x\right)dx\\ &=\Big[-\sqrt{3}\cos x-\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{7\pi}{6}}\\ &=\left(-\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)-\sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\right)-\left(-\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\\ &=\left(\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)-\left(-\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\\ &=\left(\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\left(-\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{8}{2}\\ &=4\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The volume is a hemisphere plus a cylinder:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3+\pi r^2h&=0.66\pi\\ \dfrac{2}{3}r^3+r^2h&=0.66\\ 2r^3+3r^2h&=\dfrac{99}{50}\\ 3r^2h&=\dfrac{99}{50}-2r^3\\ h&=\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The metal is a hemispherical shell, the base circle and the curved side of the cylinder:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\pi r^2+\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\ &=2\pi r^2+\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\ &=3\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)\\ &=3\pi r^2+\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}-\dfrac{4\pi r^2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}+\dfrac{5\pi r^2}{3}\ \text{as required} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}+\dfrac{5\pi r^2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{33\pi}{25}r^{-1}+\dfrac{5\pi}{3}r^2\\ A'&=-\dfrac{33\pi}{25}r^{-2}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3}r\\ A''&=\dfrac{66\pi}{25}r^{-3}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{10\pi r}{3}-\dfrac{33\pi}{25r^2}&=0\\ \dfrac{10\pi r^3}{3}-\dfrac{33\pi}{25}&=0\\ \dfrac{10\pi r^3}{3}&=\dfrac{33\pi}{25}\\ r^3&=\dfrac{99}{250}\\ \therefore\ r&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$
Second derivative test:
$$\begin{aligned} A''&=\dfrac{66\pi}{25}\left(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}\right)^{-3}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\\ &=10\pi \end{aligned}$$
$A''>0$, so $A$ is a minimum at $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}$.

Using $h$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} h&=\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100r^3}{150r^2}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^3}{150\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100\left(\frac{99}{250}\right)}{150\left(\frac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\\ &=\dfrac{99-\frac{990}{25}}{150}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{297}{750}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^1\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\ \therefore\ h&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The dimensions are $r=h=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}$ m.

Alternative end of solution, from the volume equation in part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} 2r^3+3r^2h&=1.98\\ h&=\dfrac{1.98-2r^3}{3r^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1.98-2\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^3}{3\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1.98-\frac{99}{125}}{3}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{99}{250}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\ \therefore\ h&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The first three terms of an arithmetic sequence are $x+6$, $2x-5$ and $4x-11$.

Find the value of $x$.
items.sol:
In an arithmetic sequence the common difference is constant, so $T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1$ (or $T_3+T_1=2T_2$):
$$\begin{aligned} 4x-11-(2x-5)&=2x-5-(x+6)\\ 4x-11-2x+5&=2x-5-x-6\\ 2x-6&=x-11\\ x&=-5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=\sum x\,p(x)\\ &=1\times 0+2\times 0.2+3\times 0.5+4\times 0.2+5\times 0.1\\ &=0+0.4+1.5+0.8+0.5\\ &=3.2=\mu \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2)&=\sum x^2p(x)\\ &=0+0.8+4.5+3.2+2.5\\ &=11 \end{aligned}$$
Using $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Standard deviation}&=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\\ &=\sqrt{E(X^2)-\mu^2}\\ &=\sqrt{11-3.2^2}\\ &=\sqrt{0.76}\\ &=0.871779\ldots\\ &=0.87 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $P(t)$ be a function such that $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=900e^{3t}$.

When $t=0$, $P=2000$.

Find an expression for $P(t)$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} P(t)&=\int 900e^{3t}\,dt\\ &=900\int e^{3t}\,dt\\ &=900\times\dfrac{e^{3t}}{3}+c \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $P=2000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2000&=900\times\dfrac{e^0}{3}+c\\ 2000&=300+c\\ c&=1700 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(t)=300e^{3t}+1700$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$y=\ln(\sin x)$
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\ &=\cot x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A ball is dropped from a height of 2 metres onto a hard floor and bounces. After each bounce, the maximum height reached by the ball is 75\% of the previous maximum height. Thus, after it first hits the floor, it reaches a height of 1.5 metres before falling again, and after the second bounce, it reaches a height of 1.125 metres before falling again. Correct answers to 4 significant figures.
Find the maximum height reached after the fifth bounce.
items.sol:
Let $h_n$ be the height after the $n$th bounce. Each bounce multiplies the height by $0.75$:
$$\begin{aligned} h_1&=2\times 0.75=1.5\\ h_2&=2\times 0.75^2=1.125\\ h_3&=2\times 0.75^3\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ h_5&=2\times 0.75^5\\ &=0.474609375\\ &=0.4746 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A ball is dropped from a height of 2 metres onto a hard floor and bounces. After each bounce, the maximum height reached by the ball is 75\% of the previous maximum height. Thus, after it first hits the floor, it reaches a height of 1.5 metres before falling again, and after the second bounce, it reaches a height of 1.125 metres before falling again. Correct answers to 4 significant figures.
Find the total distance travelled by the ball from the time \underline{after} reaching the maximum height with the 5\textsuperscript{th} bounce.
items.sol:
Downward motion:
$$2+2\times 0.75+2\times 0.75^2+\dots+2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6+\dots$$
From $2\times 0.75^5$ on, this is a geometric series with $a=2\times 0.75^5$ and $r=0.75$; $|r|<1$, so the limiting sum exists.

Upward motion:
$$2\times 0.75+2\times 0.75^2+\dots+2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6+\dots$$
From $2\times 0.75^6$ on, this is a geometric series with $a=2\times 0.75^6$ and $r=0.75$; $|r|<1$, so the limiting sum exists.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance after 5th bounce}&=\dfrac{2\times 0.75^5}{1-0.75}+\dfrac{2\times 0.75^6}{1-0.75}\\ &=\dfrac{2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6}{0.25}\\ &=3.3222\ldots\\ &\approx 3.322 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows a shape $APQBCD$. The shape consists of a rectangle $ABCD$ with an arc $PQ$ on the side $AB$. $BC=4.6\,\text{m}$ and $DC=7.0\,\text{m}$.

The arc $PQ$ is an arc of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $2.1\,\text{m}$ and $\angle POQ=120^{\circ}$.

\exfigure{1362_q16_1}

What is the area of the shape $APQBCD$? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
The segment is the sector minus triangle $OPQ$, with $\angle POQ=120^\circ=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{segment}}&=A_{\text{sector }OPQ}-A_{\triangle OPQ}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.1^2\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.1^2\times\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\ &=4.618\ldots-1.909586\\ &=2.708555185 \end{aligned}$$
In degrees, the same area is
$$\dfrac{120}{360}\times\pi\times 2.1^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.1^2\times\sin 120^{\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_{APQBCD}&=A_{\text{rectangle}}+A_{\text{segment}}\\ &=4.6\times 7+2.708555185\\ &=34.90855519\\ &=34.9\,\text{m}^2 \text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\sin x\cos^3 x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Let $f(x)=\cos x$, so $f'(x)=-\sin x$, and use
$$\int f'(x)\left[f(x)\right]^n\,dx=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left[f(x)\right]^{n+1}+c$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, solve the inequality $x-3>(3-x)(x+1)$.

The points of intersection are where $x-3=(3-x)(x+1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} x-3&=(3-x)(x+1)\\ (x-3)&=-(x-3)(x+1)\\ (x-3)+(x-3)(x+1)&=0\\ (x-3)\left[1+x+1\right]&=0\\ (x-3)(x+2)&=0\\ x&=3,\ -2 \end{aligned}$$
