For the function:

$$f(x)=xe^x$$
Hence or otherwise, find the value(s) of $k$, where $k$ is a real number for which the equation $xe^x=k$ has $2$ solutions.
items.sol:
The line $y=k$ meets $y=xe^x$ twice when it lies between the minimum value $-\dfrac{1}{e}$ and the asymptote $y=0$:
$$-\dfrac{1}{e}<k<0$$

Using $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2\mid X<4)&=\dfrac{P(X\ge 2\cap X<4)}{P(X<4)}\\ &=\dfrac{0.1+0.25}{0.2+0.1+0.25}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{11}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E\left(X^2\right)-\left[E(X)\right]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}E\left(X^2\right)&=0.2+2^2\times 0.1+3^2\times 0.25+4^2\times 0.3+5^2\times 0.15\\ &=11.4\\ E(X)&=0.2+2\times 0.1+3\times 0.25+4\times 0.3+5\times 0.15\\ &=3.1\\ \mathrm{Var}(X)&=11.4-3.1^2\\ &=1.79\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Joe plays soccer, a sport where a team can win, lose or draw.

Joe is prone to injury, and misses $20\%$ of his team's games.

When Joe plays, his team has a $77\%$ chance of winning and a $10\%$ chance of losing.

When Joe does not play, his team has a $53\%$ chance of winning and a $25\%$ chance of losing.
Calculate the probability that Joe's team loses any given game.

Joe plays soccer, a sport where a team can win, lose or draw.

Joe is prone to injury, and misses $20\%$ of his team's games.

When Joe plays, his team has a $77\%$ chance of winning and a $10\%$ chance of losing.

When Joe does not play, his team has a $53\%$ chance of winning and a $25\%$ chance of losing.
Given that Joe's team does not lose in a particular match, what is the probability that Joe played in that match?
items.sol:
When Joe plays, the team does not lose with probability $0.77+0.13=0.9$ (win or draw).

Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(J\mid\bar{L}\right)&=\dfrac{P\left(J\cap\bar{L}\right)}{P\left(\bar{L}\right)}\\ &=\dfrac{0.8\times(0.77+0.13)}{1-0.13}\\ &=\dfrac{24}{29}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Prove the following identity:

$$\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)}\left(1+\tan^2\theta\right)+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\left(1+\tan^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\right)=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta$$
items.sol:
Using $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\sin\theta$, $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$ and $\sec\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\operatorname{cosec}\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\sec^2\theta+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\sec^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\\ &=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of concert tickets sold, $N$, is given by

$$N=1000\times 1.6^{kt}$$

Where $t$ is the number of weeks after being available for sale, and $k$ is a constant. Initially, 1000 tickets were sold, and after 2 weeks, the total number of tickets sold was doubled.
Calculate the value of $k$, leaving your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Initially $N=1000$, and after $2$ weeks $N=2000$, so when $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}1000\times 1.6^{2k}&=2000\\ 1.6^{2k}&=2\\ 2k&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.6}\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of concert tickets sold, $N$, is given by

$$N=1000\times 1.6^{kt}$$

Where $t$ is the number of weeks after being available for sale, and $k$ is a constant. Initially, 1000 tickets were sold, and after 2 weeks, the total number of tickets sold was doubled.
At what rate was the number of tickets sold increasing after 4 weeks? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=ka^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dN}{dt}&=1000\times k\times 1.6^{kt}\times\ln 1.6\\ &=1000k\ln(1.6)\times 1.6^{kt}\end{aligned}$$
When $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dN}{dt}&=1000\times\dfrac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\times\ln 1.6\times 1.6^{\frac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\times 4}\\ &=1386.29\ldots\\ &\approx 1386\text{ tickets/week}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A fisherman's boat is trying to reach the open sea, however, it is heavily affected by the ocean tides. To reach the open sea, the boat must cross a sandbar which requires the water to be at least 4 metres deep. On a particular day, high tide occurred at midnight, and the depth, $D$, of water over the sandbar on the ensuing day is given by $D=2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+3$, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight.
Sketch the graph of $D=2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+3$, for $0\le t\le 25$, showing all key features.

A fisherman's boat is trying to reach the open sea, however, it is heavily affected by the ocean tides. To reach the open sea, the boat must cross a sandbar which requires the water to be at least 4 metres deep. On a particular day, high tide occurred at midnight, and the depth, $D$, of water over the sandbar on the ensuing day is given by $D=2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+3$, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight.
Find the times when the fisherman would not be able to cross the sandbar in his boat.
items.sol:
The boat can cross only when $D\ge 4$. Solving $D=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+3&=4\\ \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and for $0\le t\le 25$, $0\le\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\le 4\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 4\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}\\ 4t&=\dfrac{25}{3},\ \dfrac{125}{3},\ \dfrac{175}{3},\ \dfrac{275}{3}\\ t&=\dfrac{25}{12},\ \dfrac{125}{12},\ \dfrac{175}{12},\ \dfrac{275}{12}\end{aligned}$$
From the graph in part (a), $D<4$ between the first and second, and between the third and fourth, of these times:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{25}{12}&<t<\dfrac{125}{12} &&\text{0205 to 1025 hrs}\\ \dfrac{175}{12}&<t<\dfrac{275}{12} &&\text{1435 to 2255 hrs}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the boat cannot cross between 0205 and 1025 hrs, and between 1435 and 2255 hrs (exclusive of these times).
items.final: The boat cannot cross between 0205 and 1025 hrs, and between 1435 and 2255 hrs

items.part: Show that $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\,dx=1$.
items.sol:
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^x$ gives $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ form:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{e^x}\,dx&=\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}\,dx\\ &=\Big[\ln\left|1+e^x\right|\Big]_{-1}^{1}\\ &=\ln|1+e|-\ln\left|1+e^{-1}\right|\\ &=\ln\left|\dfrac{1+e}{1+\frac{1}{e}}\cdot\dfrac{e}{e}\right|\\ &=\ln\left|\dfrac{e(1+e)}{1+e}\right|\\ &=\ln e\\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, rewrite the integrand:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}&=\dfrac{1+e^{-x}-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\\ &=\dfrac{1+e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}-\dfrac{e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\\ &=1+\dfrac{-e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\end{aligned}$$
and integrate to obtain the primitive
$$x+\ln\left|1+e^{-x}\right|$$

items.part:
It is known that $T_1=1+\cos A$, $T_2=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $T_3=1-\cos A$ form the first three consecutive terms of a geometric sequence, with $T_1>T_2>T_3$.
Find the value of $A$, given $\angle A$ is an angle within a triangle.
items.sol:
$T_1$, $T_2$, $T_3$ are geometric, so $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos A}&=\dfrac{1-\cos A}{\frac{1}{2}}\\ 1-\cos^2 A&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \cos^2 A&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\ \cos A&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$A$ is an angle in a triangle, so $0<A<\pi$:
$$A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ or } A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
Since $T_1>T_2>T_3$, the ratio $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}<1$.

If $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{6}}=\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}}\approx 0.2679<1$$
If $A=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$:
$$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}}=\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{3}}\approx 3.73>1$$
$$\therefore A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ only}$$

items.part:
It is known that $T_1=1+\cos A$, $T_2=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $T_3=1-\cos A$ form the first three consecutive terms of a geometric sequence, with $T_1>T_2>T_3$.
Using the value of $A$ found in part (a), show that the series

$$\Big(1+\cos A\Big)+\dfrac{1}{2}+\Big(1-\cos A\Big)+\cdots$$

has a limiting sum.
items.sol:
With $A=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=1+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\ T_2&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}}\\ &\approx 0.2679<1\end{aligned}$$
Since $|r|<1$, a limiting sum exists.

items.part: If $y^2=(2m-y)\,(2n-y)$, show that $\dfrac{1}{m},\dfrac{1}{y},\dfrac{1}{n}$ (in this order) forms the terms of an arithmetic sequence.
items.sol:
Expanding and making $y$ the subject:
$$\begin{aligned}y^2&=(2m-y)(2n-y)\\ y^2&=4mn-2my-2ny+y^2\\ 2my+2ny&=4mn\\ y&=\dfrac{2mn}{m+n}\\ \dfrac{1}{y}&=\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}\end{aligned}$$
Checking $T_2-T_1$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_2-T_1&=\dfrac{1}{y}-\dfrac{1}{m}\\ &=\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}-\dfrac{1}{m}\cdot\dfrac{2n}{2n}\\ &=\dfrac{m+n-2n}{2mn}\\ &=\dfrac{m-n}{2mn}\end{aligned}$$
Checking $T_3-T_2$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3-T_2&=\dfrac{1}{n}-\dfrac{1}{y}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{n}\cdot\dfrac{2m}{2m}-\dfrac{m+n}{2mn}\\ &=\dfrac{2m-m-n}{2mn}\\ &=\dfrac{m-n}{2mn}\\ &=T_2-T_1\end{aligned}$$
As $T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1$, the three terms form an arithmetic sequence.

In right-angled triangle $AOT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos 60^\circ&=\dfrac{AO}{3\sqrt{3}}\\ AO&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$A$ is due west of $O$ (bearing $270^\circ$) and $B$ is on a bearing of $240^\circ$ from $O$:
$$\angle AOB=270^\circ-240^\circ=30^\circ$$
Applying the cosine rule in triangle $AOB$:
$$\begin{aligned}10^2&=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2+(OB)^2-2\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(OB)\cos 30^\circ\\ 100&=\dfrac{27}{4}+(OB)^2-3\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(OB)\\ (OB)^2-\dfrac{9}{2}(OB)-\dfrac{373}{4}&=0\\ 4(OB)^2-18(OB)-373&=0\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned}OB&=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{18^2-4\times 4\times(-373)}}{2\times 4}\\ &=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{6292}}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{18\pm 22\sqrt{13}}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{9\pm 11\sqrt{13}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Since $OB>0$:
$$OB=\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\text{ metres}$$

items.part:
A tall pole $OT$ is held in place vertically by ropes anchored by two pegs in the ground 10 metres apart at $A$ and $B$ as shown. $A$ is due west of $O$, and $B$ is at a bearing of $240^\circ\text{T}$ from $O$. The rope connecting the top of the pole $T$ to the peg at $A$ is $3\sqrt{3}$ metres long and makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ground.

\exfigure{1367_q24_1}
Hence or otherwise, find the length of the rope, $\ell$, connecting $T$ and $B$.

Give your answer to the nearest metre.
items.sol:
In right-angled triangle $AOT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin 60^\circ&=\dfrac{OT}{3\sqrt{3}}\\ OT&=\dfrac{9}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Applying Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangle $BOT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\ell^2&=OB^2+OT^2\\ &=\left(\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right)^2\\ \ell&=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right)^2}\quad(\ell>0)\\ &=12.97\ldots\\ &\approx 13\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The line $y=mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y=\ln(kx)$, where $k>0$.

Find the value of $m$, in terms of $k$.
items.sol:
The gradient of the tangent is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at the point of contact:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln(kx)\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{k}{kx}=\dfrac{1}{x}\\ m&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
At the point of contact the line and the curve meet:
$$mx=\ln(kx)$$
Substituting $m=\dfrac{1}{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\ln(kx)&=\dfrac{1}{x}\times x\\ \ln(kx)&=1\\ kx&=e\\ x&=\dfrac{e}{k}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore m=\dfrac{1}{\frac{e}{k}}=\dfrac{k}{e}$$

At $P$ the curves meet; multiplying by $e^x$ gives a quadratic in $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^x-1&=2e^{-x}\\ e^{2x}-e^x-2&=0\\ \left(e^x-2\right)\left(e^x+1\right)&=0\\ e^x&=-1\text{ or } e^x=2\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^x>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^x&=2\\ x&=\ln 2\\ y&=e^{\ln 2}-1\\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore P(\ln 2,1)$$

For $0\le x\le\ln 2$, $y=2e^{-x}$ lies above $y=e^x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^{\ln 2}\left(2e^{-x}-e^x+1\right)dx\\ &=\Big[-2e^{-x}-e^x+x\Big]_0^{\ln 2}\\ &=-2e^{-\ln 2}-e^{\ln 2}+\ln 2-\left(-2e^0-e^0+0\right)\\ &=-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-2+\ln 2-(-2-1)\\ &=\ln 2-3+3\\ &=\ln 2\end{aligned}$$

Four function values give three strips:
$$\begin{aligned}h&=\dfrac{7-1}{3}\\ &=2\end{aligned}$$
so $x=1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$:

\extable{Ts1403_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned}A&\approx\dfrac{2}{2}\left[0+\ln 7+2(\ln 3+\ln 5)\right]\\ &=2\ln 3+2\ln 5+\ln 7\end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)&=\ln x+\dfrac{1}{x}\times x\\ &=\ln x+1\end{aligned}$$

Integrating both sides of the result from part (b):
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^7(\ln x+1)\,dx&=\int_1^7\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)\,dx\\ \int_1^7\ln x\,dx+\int_1^7dx&=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7\\ \int_1^7\ln x\,dx&=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\Big[x\Big]_1^7\\ &=7\ln 7-0-(7-1)\\ &=7\ln 7-6\end{aligned}$$

The trapezoidal estimate in part (a) approximates the integral in part (c), so
$$\begin{aligned}7\ln 7-6&\approx 2\ln 3+2\ln 5+\ln 7\\ 6\ln 7&\approx 2\ln 3+2\ln 5+6\\ \ln 7&\approx\dfrac{1}{3}(\ln 3+\ln 5)+1\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by $\ddot{x}=4\sin 2t$, where $x$ is the displacement of the particle from the origin in metres, and $t$ is the time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin moving to the left at 1 metre per second.
Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}=1-2\cos 2t$.
items.sol:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=\int 4\sin 2t\,dt\\ &=-2\cos 2t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle moves left at $1$ m/s, so $\dot{x}=-1$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-1&=-2\cos 0+C\\ C&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\dot{x}=1-2\cos 2t$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by $\ddot{x}=4\sin 2t$, where $x$ is the displacement of the particle from the origin in metres, and $t$ is the time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin moving to the left at 1 metre per second.
Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-2\cos 2t&=0\\ \cos 2t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\quad(\text{smallest positive solution})\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by $\ddot{x}=4\sin 2t$, where $x$ is the displacement of the particle from the origin in metres, and $t$ is the time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin moving to the left at 1 metre per second.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds.

The diagram shows a rectangle $PQRS$ drawn in a sector $OAB$ with radius 5 metres.

It is given that $\angle AOB=\theta$, $OR=x$, $RS=y$ and $\tan\theta=2$.

\exfigure{1367_q29_1}
Show that the perimeter of the rectangle is given by:

$$2x+2\sqrt{25-4x^2}$$
items.sol:
In right-angled triangle $QOR$, with $\tan\theta=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=\dfrac{QR}{x}\\ QR&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$PS=QR=2x$ (opposite sides of the rectangle). Applying Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangle $POS$ (hypotenuse $OP=5$, the radius):
$$\begin{aligned}(x+y)^2+PS^2&=OP^2\\ (x+y)^2+(2x)^2&=5^2\\ (x+y)^2&=25-4x^2\end{aligned}$$
Since $x+y>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x+y&=\sqrt{25-4x^2}\\ y&=-x+\sqrt{25-4x^2}\end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is $2QR+2RS$:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2(2x)+2\left(-x+\sqrt{25-4x^2}\right)\\ &=2x+2\sqrt{25-4x^2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows a rectangle $PQRS$ drawn in a sector $OAB$ with radius 5 metres.

It is given that $\angle AOB=\theta$, $OR=x$, $RS=y$ and $\tan\theta=2$.

\exfigure{1367_q29_1}
Find the maximum perimeter of the rectangle. Leave your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2x+2\left(25-4x^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ \dfrac{dP}{dx}&=2+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\left(25-4x^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(-8x)\\ &=2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}&=0\\ \dfrac{8x}{\sqrt{25-4x^2}}&=2\\ 4x&=\sqrt{25-4x^2}\\ 16x^2&=25-4x^2\\ 20x^2&=25\\ x^2&=\dfrac{5}{4}\\ x&=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\quad(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts1411_1}

$\therefore$ the maximum is at $x=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}+2\sqrt{25-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^2}\\ &=\sqrt{5}+2\sqrt{20}\\ &=5\sqrt{5}\text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $5-x=\dfrac{2x}{3}$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} 5-x&=\dfrac{2x}{3}\\ 3(5-x)&=2x\\ 15-3x&=2x\\ 15&=5x\\ \therefore\ x&=3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=3x^2+5x$.

Use the definition $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ to find the derivative of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Expanding $f(x+h)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x+h)&=3(x+h)^2+5(x+h)\\ &=3x^2+6hx+3h^2+5x+5h \end{aligned}$$
so
$$\begin{aligned} f(x+h)-f(x)&=3x^2+6hx+3h^2+5x+5h-(3x^2+5x)\\ &=6xh+3h^2+5h \end{aligned}$$
Using the definition:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{6xh+3h^2+5h}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\,(6x+3h+5) \end{aligned}$$
Apply the limit by letting $h=0$:
$$\therefore \dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x+5$$

items.part:
Trish is planning a function. The cost per person to attend the function varies inversely with the number of people attending.

The cost per person is \$70 when 50 people attend.

What is the cost per person if 125 people attend the function?
items.sol:
Let $x$ be the number of people and $y$ the cost per person in dollars.

Inverse variation has the form
$$y=\dfrac{k}{x}$$
When $x=50$, $y=70$, hence
$$\begin{aligned} k&=xy\\ &=50\times70\\ &=3500 \end{aligned}$$
When $x=125$:
$$y=\dfrac{3500}{125}=28$$
$\therefore$ The cost is \$28 per person if 125 people attend.

items.part: Find the derivative of the function $y=\tan(x^2)$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\sec^2(x^2)\times\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2)\\ &=2x\sec^2(x^2) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: By using an appropriate trigonometric identity, find $\displaystyle\int x\tan^2(x^2)\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using the Pythagorean identity $\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int x\tan^2(x^2)\,dx&=\int x\left(\sec^2(x^2)-1\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x\left(\sec^2(x^2)-1\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int\left(2x\sec^2(x^2)-2x\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\tan(x^2)-x^2\right)+C &&(\text{using part (a)}) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Amy and Beth are members of a cricket team.

The parallel box-plot below summarises their batting scores for the season.

Compare the sets of scores by interpreting the summary statistics and the shape of the distributions.

\exfigure{641_q16_1}
items.sol:
Sample answer should include a reference to the shape of the distribution, for example:

\begin{itemize}
\item Shapes of distributions for Amy and Beth are symmetrical and positively skewed respectively.
\end{itemize}

Sample answer should include at least two points from those shown below:

\begin{itemize}
\item Median score for Amy is 40, which is 10 higher than the median for Beth
\item Range of scores for Beth is 95, which is 35 higher than the range of scores for Amy
\item Interquartile range (IQR) for Beth is 30, which is 10 higher than the IQR for Amy
\item Half of Beth's scores are below the first quartile for Amy
\item One quarter of Amy's and Beth's scores are above 50
\end{itemize}

Other points may be accepted if they adequately interpret and compare any summary statistic that may be found from the box-plots.

Points that are unacceptable include references to the mean, mode, standard deviation etc., as they cannot be calculated or interpreted from a box-plot.

items.part:
The weight of boxes of cereal that are produced in a factory are normally distributed with a mean of 650 grams and a standard deviation of 5 grams.

Boxes of cereal are fit for sale if they weigh more than 640 grams.

If the factory produces one million boxes, how many would you expect to be fit for sale?
items.sol:
$\mu=650$, $\sigma=5$

The $z$-score of 640 g is
$$z=\dfrac{640-650}{5}=-2$$
Using the empirical rule, $47.5\%$ of scores lie between $z=-2$ and the mean:
$$\begin{aligned} P(z>-2)&=47.5\%+50\%\\ &=97.5\% \end{aligned}$$
$$97.5\%\times1\,000\,000=975\,000$$
$\therefore$ The expected number of boxes that are fit for sale is 975 000.

items.part:
The table below shows the monthly repayments on loans of various amounts over a number of different loan periods.

\extable{641_q18_t1}
Spiro is borrowing \$30 000, to be repaid with monthly repayments over 5 years.

How much interest will be paid on the loan?
items.sol:
From the table, the monthly repayment is \$683.

Total repayments over 5 years:
$$683\times12\times5=40\,980$$
Interest paid:
$$40\,980-30\,000=10\,980$$
$\therefore$ The interest paid on the loan is \$10 980.

Using the flat-rate interest formula $I=Prn$ with $I=10\,980$, $P=30\,000$ and $n=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\,980&=30\,000\times r\times5\\ r&=10\,980\div30\,000\div5\\ &=0.0732\\ &=7.32\% \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The flat rate of interest is $7.32\%$ per annum.

items.part:
A yacht race takes a triangular course. Yachts leave from $A$ and travel on a bearing of $294^\circ$ for 18 km to a buoy at $B$.

From $B$ the yachts travel due south to another buoy at $C$.

The final leg of the race is on a bearing of $030^\circ$ from $C$ back to finish at $A$.

\exfigure{641_q19_1}

What is the total length of the race, in kilometres, correct to three significant figures?
items.sol:
$\angle BCA=30^\circ$ ($CB$ points due north and the bearing of $A$ from $C$ is $030^\circ$)

At $A$, $AC$ makes $30^\circ$ with due south (alternate angles, $BC$ parallel to the north line), so
$$\angle BAC=294^\circ-180^\circ-30^\circ=84^\circ$$
$\angle CBA=180^\circ-84^\circ-30^\circ=66^\circ$ (angle sum of $\triangle ABC$)

Using the sine rule, with $AB=18$ opposite the $30^\circ$ angle:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{AC}{\sin66^\circ}&=\dfrac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\\ AC&=\dfrac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\times\sin66^\circ\\ &=32.88763648 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{BC}{\sin84^\circ}&=\dfrac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\\ BC&=\dfrac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\times\sin84^\circ\\ &=35.80278823 \end{aligned}$$
Perimeter of the triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=18+32.88763648+35.80278823\\ &=86.6904\ldots\\ &\approx86.7 \text{ (3 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The total length of the race is 86.7 km, correct to three significant figures.

items.part:
A plane is flying through clouds to drop a water quality monitoring system onto a lake.

The lake is surrounded by forest as shown below, with all measurements in metres.

\exfigure{641_q21_1}

Estimate the probability that the plane will drop the monitoring system onto the lake.

Use the Trapezoidal rule in your calculations.
items.sol:
The rectangle is 450 m wide and 700 m long.

The centre measurement of the lake is
$$450-70-80=300$$
Using the trapezoidal rule with 2 strips along the 700 m length, $h=\dfrac{700}{2}=350$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of lake}&\approx\dfrac{350}{2}(80+2\times300+100)\\ &=136\,500 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Area of rectangle}=700\times450=315\,000 \text{ m}^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{success})&=\dfrac{\text{Area of lake}}{\text{Area of rectangle}}\\ &=\dfrac{136\,500}{315\,000}\\ &=\dfrac{13}{30} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The probability that the monitoring system will drop onto the lake is $\dfrac{13}{30}$, or about $43.3\%$.

items.part:
A robot is programmed to draw a pattern consisting of squares in increasing sizes with no overlapping lines, as shown.

\exfigure{641_q22_1}

The side length of each square follows an arithmetic sequence. The first three squares have side lengths 5 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm respectively.
What is the perimeter of the 24th square in this sequence?
items.sol:
The side lengths form the arithmetic sequence $5, 8, 11, \ldots$ with first term $a=5$ and common difference $d=3$.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $n=24$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{24}&=5+(24-1)\times3\\ &=74 \end{aligned}$$
The side length of the 24th square is 74 cm, and its perimeter is 4 times the side length:
$$4\times74=296$$
$\therefore$ The perimeter of the 24th square is 296 cm.

items.part:
A robot is programmed to draw a pattern consisting of squares in increasing sizes with no overlapping lines, as shown.

\exfigure{641_q22_1}

The side length of each square follows an arithmetic sequence. The first three squares have side lengths 5 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm respectively.
Find the total perimeter of all the squares after the robot draws the 24th square.
items.sol:
The perimeter of the first square is $4\times5=20$ cm and the perimeter of the 24th square is 296 cm.

Using the arithmetic series formula $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{24}&=\dfrac{24}{2}(20+296)\\ &=3792 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The total perimeter of the first 24 squares is 3792 cm.

items.part:
A robot is programmed to draw a pattern consisting of squares in increasing sizes with no overlapping lines, as shown.

\exfigure{641_q22_1}

The side length of each square follows an arithmetic sequence. The first three squares have side lengths 5 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm respectively.
The amount of ink in the robot's pen can only draw up to a maximum of 12 000 cm. How many complete squares can the robot draw using the one pen?
items.sol:
12 000 cm is the total perimeter the robot can draw. Dividing by 4 gives the series in terms of side length instead of perimeter:
$$12\,000\div4=3000$$
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $S_n=3000$, $a=5$ and $d=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3000&=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2\times5+(n-1)3\big)\\ 6000&=n(10+3n-3)\\ 6000&=3n^2+7n\\ 0&=3n^2+7n-6000 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$n=-45.9 \text{ or } n=43.6$$
$n>0$, so the negative answer is invalid.

$n=43.6$ means the robot draws 43 complete squares plus part of the 44th square.

$\therefore$ The robot can draw 43 complete squares with one pen.

items.part:
Steve produces videos on remote control cars and shares them on a YouTube channel.

The actual view times, in hours, on the YouTube channel over a 5-year period was recorded.

Steve suspects that the bivariate relationship between $x$ and $y$ is exponential. He decides to transform the data to make the relationship appear linear by finding the natural logarithm of the view times, and recording those values in the table shown.

\extable{641_q23_t1}

Let $n$ represent the year and $\ln(t)$ represent the transformed view time.

By finding the equation of the least-squares regression line of the transformed data, predict the actual view time on the YouTube channel in the 7th year. Give your answer correct to the nearest hour.
items.sol:
Using REG mode on the calculator with the transformed data, the least-squares regression line is
$$\ln(y)=1.124x+2.85$$
In the 7th year, $x=7$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln(y)&=1.124\times7+2.85\\ &=10.718 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} y&=e^{10.718}\\ &=45161.48948 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Steve predicts that the YouTube channel will achieve 45 161 hours of view time in the 7th year, correct to the nearest hour.

items.part:
Consider the gradient function $f'(x)=3(x+3)(x-1)$.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ passes through the point $(2,-8)$.
Show that $f(x)=x^3+3x^2-9x-10$.
items.sol:
Expanding:
$$f'(x)=3(x^2+2x-3)=3x^2+6x-9$$
Integrating:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int\left(3x^2+6x-9\right)dx\\ &=x^3+3x^2-9x+C \end{aligned}$$
Apply the condition $f(2)=-8$ to find $C$:
$$\begin{aligned} -8&=(2)^3+3(2)^2-9(2)+C\\ -8&=2+C\\ C&=-10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f(x)=x^3+3x^2-9x-10$$

items.part:
Consider the gradient function $f'(x)=3(x+3)(x-1)$.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ passes through the point $(2,-8)$.
Find the minimum and maximum values of $f(x)$ in the interval $-4\le x\le4$.

You do not need to determine the nature of the stationary points.
items.sol:
The maximum and minimum values on $-4\le x\le4$ occur at the endpoints or at the stationary points $x=-3$ and $x=1$ (where $f'(x)=0$).
$$\begin{aligned} f(-4)&=10 &&\text{endpoint}\\ f(4)&=66 &&\text{endpoint}\\ f(-3)&=17 &&\text{stationary point}\\ f(1)&=-15 &&\text{stationary point} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The minimum value is $-15$ and the maximum value is 66.
items.final: The minimum value is $-15$ and the maximum value is 66.

items.part:
Consider the gradient function $f'(x)=3(x+3)(x-1)$.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ passes through the point $(2,-8)$.
Show that a point of inflection exists at $(-1,1)$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=3x^2+6x-9\\ f''(x)&=6x+6 \end{aligned}$$
$f''(-1)=0$, hence a point of inflection may exist at $x=-1$.

Testing for a change in sign of $f''(x)$ around $x=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-2)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(0)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, hence a point of inflection exists at $x=-1$.
$$f(-1)=-1+3+9-10=1$$
$\therefore$ The point of inflection is at $(-1,1)$.

items.part:
Consider the gradient function $f'(x)=3(x+3)(x-1)$.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ passes through the point $(2,-8)$.
Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the interval $-4\le x\le4$, showing the locations of the endpoints, the stationary points and the point of inflection.
items.sol: \exfigure{641_q24_s1}

The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.3+a+b+0.1&=1\\ a+b&=0.6 &&(1) \end{aligned}$$
$E(X)=\mu=3.1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.6+3a+4b+0.5&=3.1\\ 3a+4b&=2 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
Solving (1) and (2) simultaneously:
$$a=0.4,\quad b=0.2$$

items.part:
An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation

$$C=100\left(1-2^{-kt}\right).$$

The battery is charged to 35\% capacity after 50 minutes.
Show that the value of $k$ is 0.01243, correct to 4 significant figures.
items.sol:
Substituting $C=35$ and $t=50$:
$$\begin{aligned} 35&=100\left(1-2^{-50k}\right)\\ 0.35&=1-2^{-50k}\\ 2^{-50k}&=0.65\\ -50k\ln(2)&=\ln(0.65) &&(\text{take } \ln \text{ of both sides})\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln(0.65)}{-50\ln(2)}\\ &=0.0124297\ldots\\ \therefore\ k&=0.01243 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation

$$C=100\left(1-2^{-kt}\right).$$

The battery is charged to 35\% capacity after 50 minutes.
To prolong the service life of the battery, the charger may be set to switch off when the battery reaches 90\% capacity.

For how long will the battery be on charge until it reaches 90\% capacity?
items.sol:
Substituting $C=90$ and $k=0.01243$:
$$\begin{aligned} 90&=100\left(1-2^{-0.01243t}\right)\\ 0.1&=2^{-0.01243t}\\ -0.01243t\ln(2)&=\ln(0.1) &&(\text{take } \ln \text{ of both sides})\\ t&=\dfrac{\ln(0.1)}{-0.01243\ln(2)}\\ &=267.2508\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The battery will be on charge for 267.25 minutes (2 dec. pl.), or 4 hours 27 minutes.

items.part:
An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation

$$C=100\left(1-2^{-kt}\right).$$

The battery is charged to 35\% capacity after 50 minutes.
By considering the first and second derivatives, describe the behaviour of $C$ for $t\ge0$ if the battery is left on charge indefinitely.
items.sol:
Initially ($t=0$), $C=0$.

For $k>0$, $2^{-kt}\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, hence $C\to100$ as $t\to\infty$.

Describing the rate of change using the first and second derivatives:
$$\begin{aligned} C'&=100k\ln(2)\times2^{-kt}\\ C''&=-100k^2(\ln2)^2\times2^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Given $k>0$, for all $t>0$:
$$\begin{aligned} C'&>0 &&\text{capacity increasing}\\ C''&<0 &&\text{rate of increase decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the battery charge capacity increases from 0 at a decreasing rate over time, but can never (theoretically) reach $100\%$ charge.

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{3x+1}} & 1\le x\le5\ (\text{where } A>0)\\[2mm] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Show that the value of $A$ is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.
items.sol:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} A\int_1^5(3x+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{2A}{3}\left[\sqrt{3x+1}\right]_1^5&=1\\ \dfrac{2A}{3}(4-2)&=1\\ \dfrac{4A}{3}&=1\\ \therefore\ A&=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{3x+1}} & 1\le x\le5\ (\text{where } A>0)\\[2mm] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Given that $P(X<c)=3P(X>c)$, find the value of $c$.
items.sol:
For $1\le x\le5$, using $A=\dfrac{3}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_1^x\dfrac{3}{4}(3t+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{3t+1}\right]_1^x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3x+1}-1 \end{aligned}$$
$P(X<c)=F(c)$ and $P(X>c)=1-F(c)$, so solve
$$\begin{aligned} F(c)&=3\big(1-F(c)\big)\\ F(c)&=3-3F(c)\\ 4F(c)&=3\\ F(c)&=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3c+1}-1&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\ \sqrt{3c+1}&=\dfrac{7}{2}\\ 3c+1&=\dfrac{49}{4}\\ 3c&=\dfrac{45}{4}\\ \therefore\ c&=\dfrac{15}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A factory produces boxes in the shape of rectangular prisms as shown below.

\exfigure{641_q28_1}

The length, height and width of the box are $l$ cm, $x$ cm and $2x$ cm respectively.

The factory uses $k$ cm$^2$ of sheet metal to make the box, where $k$ is a constant.
Show that $l=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x}$, given that the box is open at the top.
items.sol:
The box is open at the top, so the sheet metal forms the base and the 4 sides, with total area $k$ cm$^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} k&=2lx+lx+lx+2x^2+2x^2\\ &=4lx+4x^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 4lx&=k-4x^2\\ \therefore\ l&=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A factory produces boxes in the shape of rectangular prisms as shown below.

\exfigure{641_q28_1}

The length, height and width of the box are $l$ cm, $x$ cm and $2x$ cm respectively.

The factory uses $k$ cm$^2$ of sheet metal to make the box, where $k$ is a constant.
Hence find the maximum volume of the box that can be produced from a sheet of metal with an area of 1200 cm$^2$.
items.sol:
Let $V$ be the volume of the prism. Using $V=lwh$ and part (a) with $k=1200$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=2x^2l\\ &=2x^2\left(\dfrac{1200-4x^2}{4x}\right)\\ &=600x-2x^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} V'&=600-6x^2\\ V''&=-12x \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $V'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6x^2&=600\\ x&=\pm10 \end{aligned}$$
$x>0$ since it represents a side length, so $x=10$.

$V''<0$ when $x=10$, hence the volume is maximised when $x=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=2\times(10)^2\times\left(\dfrac{1200-4\times(10)^2}{4\times(10)}\right)\\ &=4000 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The maximum volume of the box is 4000 cm$^3$.

items.part:
The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{641_q30_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function

$$v_P=3t^2-6t+4,$$

where $v_P$ is the velocity in metres per second.

The velocity of car $Q$ is accelerating at a constant rate. Both cars start at the same point and have the same velocity at times $t=0$ and $t=4$
Show that the equation for the velocity, $v_Q$, of car $Q$ is given by $v_Q=6t+4$.
items.sol:
Car $Q$ has constant acceleration, so its velocity is linear in $t$: $v_Q=mt+c$.

At $t=0$: $v_Q=v_P=4$

At $t=4$:
$$v_Q=v_P=3(4)^2-6(4)+4=28$$
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{28-4}{4-0}=6\\ c&=4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v_Q=6t+4$$

items.part:
The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{641_q30_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function

$$v_P=3t^2-6t+4,$$

where $v_P$ is the velocity in metres per second.

The velocity of car $Q$ is accelerating at a constant rate. Both cars start at the same point and have the same velocity at times $t=0$ and $t=4$
Both cars start the race from the same point.

Find the earliest time when car $P$ will pass car $Q$ after the race starts.
items.sol:
The signed area between curves $P$ and $Q$ represents the relative displacement between the cars.

The cars are at the same displacement from the start when the displacement between them is zero, so solve for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a\big(3t^2-6t+4-(6t+4)\big)\,dt&=0\\ \int_0^a\left(3t^2-12t\right)dt&=0\\ \Big[t^3-6t^2\Big]_0^a&=0\\ a^3-6a^2&=0\\ a^2(a-6)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$a>0$, so $a=6$: the cars are the same distance from the start at $t=6$.

The integrand $3t^2-12t$ is the velocity of $P$ relative to $Q$, and $v_P>v_Q$ for $t>4$.

Hence car $P$ passes car $Q$ 6 seconds after the start of the race.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=1-x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\cdots$, where $0<x<1$.

By considering $f'(x)$, show that $f(a)-f(b)=\ln\left(\dfrac{1+b}{1+a}\right)$.
items.sol:
$$f'(x)=-1+x-x^2+x^3-\cdots$$
This is a geometric series with first term $-1$ and common ratio $-x$.

Since $0<x<1$, the geometric series has a limiting sum:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=S_\infty\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{1-(-x)}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{1+x} \end{aligned}$$
Integrating:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=-\int\dfrac{1}{1+x}\,dx\\ &=-\ln(1+x)+C \end{aligned}$$
The constant $C$ cancels in the difference:
$$\begin{aligned} f(a)-f(b)&=-\ln(1+a)-\big(-\ln(1+b)\big)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\right)-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+b}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\div\dfrac{1}{1+b}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{1+a}\times\dfrac{1+b}{1}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{1+b}{1+a}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $C$ be the circle with equation $(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$, and $\ell$ the line given by the equation $y=x+d$ for some real constant $d$.
Show that if $2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$, then $\ell$ intersects $C$ at exactly two points.
items.sol:
Solve $y=x+d$ and $(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$ simultaneously. By substitution:
$$\begin{aligned} (x-1)^2+(x+d-3)^2&=9\\ (x-1)^2+\big(x+(d-3)\big)^2&=9\\ x^2-2x+1+x^2+2x(d-3)+(d-3)^2&=9\\ x^2-2x+1+x^2+2dx-6x+d^2-6d+9&=9\\ 2x^2+2dx-8x+d^2-6d+1&=0\\ 2x^2+(2d-8)x+(d^2-6d+1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
This non-monic quadratic has 2 distinct real solutions if its discriminant $D>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} D&=(2d-8)^2-4(2)(d^2-6d+1)\\ &=4d^2-32d+64-8d^2+48d-8\\ &=-4d^2+16d+56 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula to find the values of $d$ when $D=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} d&=\dfrac{-16\pm\sqrt{(16)^2+4(4)(56)}}{2(-4)}\\ &=\dfrac{-16\pm\sqrt{1152}}{-8}\\ &=\dfrac{-16\pm24\sqrt{2}}{-8}\\ &=2\pm3\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
$D$ is a concave-down quadratic in $d$ with roots $2\pm3\sqrt{2}$, hence $D>0$ for
$$2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$$
$\therefore$ $\ell$ intersects $C$ at exactly two points if $2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$.

items.part:
Let $C$ be the circle with equation $(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$, and $\ell$ the line given by the equation $y=x+d$ for some real constant $d$.
Let $A$ and $B$ be the two points of intersection in part (a).

It is given that the distance between $A$ and $B$ is $2\sqrt{3}$ units.

By determining the coordinates of $A$ and $B$, find a possible value of $d$, leaving your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Solving the equation from part (a) with the quadratic formula gives the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$:
$$2x^2+(2d-8)x+d^2-6d+1=0$$
$$\begin{aligned} x_1&=\dfrac{8-2d-\sqrt{D}}{4}=2-\dfrac{d}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4}\\ x_2&=\dfrac{8-2d+\sqrt{D}}{4}=2-\dfrac{d}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Using $y=x+d$ for the corresponding $y$-coordinates:
$$\begin{aligned} y_1&=2+\dfrac{d}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4}\\ y_2&=2+\dfrac{d}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
So $x_2-x_1=y_2-y_1=\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}$. Using the distance formula with $AB=2\sqrt{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2}&=2\sqrt{3}\\ \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2&=12\\ D&=24 \end{aligned}$$
Solving $-4d^2+16d+56=24$, first dividing all terms by $-4$:
$$\begin{aligned} d^2-4d-8&=0\\ d&=2\pm2\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Possible values of $d$ are $2-2\sqrt{3}$ or $2+2\sqrt{3}$.

items.part: $ABC$ is a triangle in which $\cos A=-\dfrac{2}{5}$. Find the exact value of $\tan A$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{335_q11_s1}

$\cos A=-\dfrac{2}{5}$, so the reference triangle has adjacent side 2 and hypotenuse 5.

Using Pythagoras' theorem in the reference triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2&=5^2-2^2\\ x&=\sqrt{21} \end{aligned}$$
$\cos A<0$, so $A$ is obtuse and $\tan A<0$.
$$\therefore \tan A=-\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{2}$$

items.part: Solve $|3x+2|=4$
items.sol:
$|3x+2|=4$ means $3x+2=4$ or $3x+2=-4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x+2&=4\\ 3x&=2\\ x&=\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
or
$$\begin{aligned} 3x+2&=-4\\ 3x&=-6\\ x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ or } x=-2$$

items.part: Find the exact equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\log_2 x$ at the point where $x=4$.
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_a x=\dfrac{1}{x\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1}{(\ln 2)x}\\ m_T&=\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2} &&(x=4) \end{aligned}$$
At $x=4$, $y=\log_2 4=2$.

Using the point-gradient formula:
$$\begin{aligned} y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\ y-2&=\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}(x-4)\\ y&=\dfrac{x}{4\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}+2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the calculator's linear regression ($y=A+Bx$):
$$A=-44.3975\ldots,\quad B=2.3722\ldots$$
Rounding to 2 decimal places:
$$y=2.37x-44.40$$

Substituting $x=30$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2.37\times 30-44.40\\ &=26.7\\ &\approx 27\text{ ice creams} \end{aligned}$$
The $y$-intercept is $-44.40$, the number of ice creams sold at $0^\circ$C, and Barry can't sell a negative number of ice creams.

items.part: Differentiate $\dfrac{(2x+1)^2}{4+x}$ with respect to $x$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(2x+1)^2 & v&=4+x\\ u'&=2(2x+1)\times 2 & v'&=1\\ &=8x+4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{(2x+1)^2}{4+x}\right]&=\dfrac{(4+x)(8x+4)-(2x+1)^2(1)}{(4+x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{32x+16+8x^2+4x-\left(4x^2+4x+1\right)}{(4+x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{4x^2+32x+15}{(4+x)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2e^{x^2}\right)=2xe^{x^2}\left(1+x^2\right)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{x^2}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=2xe^{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2e^{x^2}\right)&=e^{x^2}\times 2x+x^2\times 2xe^{x^2}\\ &=2xe^{x^2}+2x^3e^{x^2}\\ &=2xe^{x^2}\left(1+x^2\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence show that $y=x^2e^{x^2}$ is decreasing for all $x<0$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $y'=2xe^{x^2}\left(1+x^2\right)$. When $x<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&<0\\ e^{x^2}&>0\\ 1+x^2&>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\text{negative}\times\text{positive}\times\text{positive}\\ &=\text{negative} \end{aligned}$$
Hence $y$ is decreasing for all $x<0$.

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x-3}{x^2-6x}\,dx$
items.sol:
The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator, so the integral has the form $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x-3}{x^2-6x}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{2x-6}{x^2-6x}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|x^2-6x\right|+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag of potatoes is labelled as having a net weight of 2 kilograms. The packaging process produces bags of potatoes whose weights are normally distributed with a mean of 2.05 kilograms and a standard deviation of 0.05 kilograms.
In a supermarket selling 2000 of these bags of potatoes, how many bags will contain less than the labelled weight?
items.sol:
\exfigure{335_q19_s1}

The labelled weight is 2 kg:
$$z=\dfrac{2-2.05}{0.05}=-1$$
By the empirical rule, $34\%$ of bags lie between $z=-1$ and the mean, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(z<-1)&=50\%-34\%\\ &=16\% \end{aligned}$$
$$16\%\times 2000=320$$
$\therefore$ 320 bags contain less than the labelled weight.

The heaviest $20\%$ lie above the weight with $P(Z<z)=0.8$.

From the table, $z=0.84$.

Converting back using $x=\mu+z\sigma$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2.05+0.84\times 0.05\\ &=2.092\text{ kg} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The heaviest $20\%$ of bags weigh more than 2.092 kg.
\extable{Ts2175_1}

items.part:
Sixty people visited a swimming pool one afternoon. Thirteen out of the twenty-three people who wore goggles were adults. There were nineteen children.
If an adult is selected at random, what is the probability they were wearing goggles?
items.sol:
There are $60-19=41$ adults, 13 of whom wore goggles.
$$P(\text{goggles}\mid\text{adult})=\dfrac{13}{41}$$

items.part:
Sixty people visited a swimming pool one afternoon. Thirteen out of the twenty-three people who wore goggles were adults. There were nineteen children.
An additional group of adults, not wearing goggles, arrived at the pool.

The probability that a person selected at random is an adult who is not wearing goggles is now 0.6.

How many additional adults arrived?
items.sol:
Let $x$ be the number of additional adults.

There are $41-13=28$ adults not wearing goggles, and $60+x$ people in total.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{adult not wearing goggles})&=\dfrac{28+x}{60+x}\\ \dfrac{3}{5}&=\dfrac{28+x}{60+x}\\ 3(60+x)&=5(28+x)\\ 180+3x&=140+5x\\ 40&=2x\\ x&=20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 20 additional adults arrived.

items.part:
The derivative of a function $y=f(x)$ is given by $f'(x)=3x^2-4x+1$
Find the $x$-coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine the nature of the stationary points.
items.sol:
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-4x+1&=0\\ (3x-1)(x-1)&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{3},\ 1 \end{aligned}$$
For the nature of the stationary points, consider the sign of $f''(x)$.
$$f''(x)=6x-4$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=6\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-4=-2<0 &&\text{maximum turning point at } x=\dfrac{1}{3}\\ f''(1)&=6(1)-4=2>0 &&\text{minimum turning point at } x=1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The derivative of a function $y=f(x)$ is given by $f'(x)=3x^2-4x+1$
The curve $y=f(x)$ has a $y$-intercept at $y=-2$.

Find an expression for $f(x)$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int\left(3x^2-4x+1\right)dx\\ &=x^3-2x^2+x+c \end{aligned}$$
The $y$-intercept is $-2$, so $f(0)=-2$ and $c=-2$.
$$\therefore f(x)=x^3-2x^2+x-2$$

items.part:
The derivative of a function $y=f(x)$ is given by $f'(x)=3x^2-4x+1$
Sketch the curve, clearly indicating the stationary points and intercepts on the axes.
items.sol:
Factorising to find the $x$-intercept:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^3-2x^2+x-2\\ &=x^2(x-2)+1(x-2)\\ &=\left(x^2+1\right)(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$x^2+1>0$, so the only $x$-intercept is $x=2$.

The $y$-values of the stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^3-2\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-2\\ &=-\dfrac{50}{27} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(1)&=(1)^3-2(1)^2+(1)-2\\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{335_q21_s1}

items.part:
The derivative of a function $y=f(x)$ is given by $f'(x)=3x^2-4x+1$
For what values of $x$ is the curve concave down?
items.sol:
The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$. From part (a), $f''(x)=6x-4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-4&<0\\ 6x&<4\\ x&<\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A)=0.3$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A|B)=0.4$.
Show that $P(A\cup B)=0.6$
items.sol:
Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B)&=P(A|B)\times P(B)\\ &=0.4\times 0.5\\ &=0.2 \end{aligned}$$
Using the addition rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\\ &=0.3+0.5-0.2\\ &=0.6 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A)=0.3$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A|B)=0.4$.
Find $P(\text{neither } A \text{ nor } B)$
items.sol:
Using the complement of $A\cup B$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither } A \text{ nor } B)&=1-P(A\cup B)\\ &=1-0.6\\ &=0.4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find two possible equations of a semi-circle with range $[3,5]$, given that it is an even function.
items.sol:
\exfigure{335_q23_s1}

The function is even, so the centre lies on the $y$-axis, and the range $[3,5]$ gives radius $5-3=2$.

Option 1: centre $(0,3)$, concave down (top half of the circle)
$$y=3+\sqrt{4-x^2}$$
Option 2: centre $(0,5)$, concave up (bottom half of the circle)
$$y=5-\sqrt{4-x^2}$$

items.part:
A lift accelerates from rest at a constant rate until it reaches a speed of 5 metres per second. It continues at this speed for 12 seconds and then decelerates at a constant rate before coming to rest. The total travel time for the lift is 30 seconds.

Find the total distance, in metres, travelled by the lift.

items.sol:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} p^2+p+p^2+p+2p^2+p&=1\\ 4p^2+3p-1&=0\\ (4p-1)(p+1)&=0\\ p&=\dfrac{1}{4}\text{ or }-1 \end{aligned}$$
But $p\ge 0$ (it is a probability), thus $p=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

With $p=\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=\sum x\cdot p(x)\\ &=0\left(\dfrac{5}{16}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{1}{16}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+3\left(2\times\dfrac{1}{16}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{31}{16} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\log_e(1+\sin x)-\log_e(1-\sin x)=2\log_e(\sec x+\tan x)$
items.sol:
Starting from the right-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\log_e(\sec x+\tan x)&=\log_e(\sec x+\tan x)^2\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right)^2\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{(1+\sin x)^2}{\cos^2 x}\right)\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{(1+\sin x)^2}{1-\sin^2 x}\right) &&(\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x)\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{(1+\sin x)^2}{(1+\sin x)(1-\sin x)}\right)\\ &=\log_e\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{1-\sin x}\right)\\ &=\log_e(1+\sin x)-\log_e(1-\sin x) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sketch the graphs of the functions $y=\dfrac{4}{x}$ and $y=|x+1|-4$ on the number plane below. Clearly show their point(s) of intersection and any intercepts on the axes.

\exfigure{335_q27_1}
items.sol: \exfigure{335_q27_s1}

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, solve $|x+1|-4\le\dfrac{4}{x}$
items.sol:
From the graphs in part (a), $y=|x+1|-4$ is on or below $y=\dfrac{4}{x}$ for
$$[-4,-1]\cup(0,4]$$

items.part:
Consider $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$
Use the trapezoidal rule with 4 subintervals to estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
The strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{1-0}{4}=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
so the $x$ values are $0,\ \dfrac{1}{4},\ \dfrac{1}{2},\ \dfrac{3}{4},\ 1$.

\extable{Ts2191_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{1}{8}\left[1+0+2\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{15}{16}}+\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4}}+\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{16}}\right)\right]\\ &\approx 0.748927\ldots \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$
Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$ and hence find an approximation for $\pi$ correct to 3 decimal places.
items.sol:
\exfigure{335_q28_s1}

$y=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ for $0\le x\le1$ is the quarter of the unit circle in the first quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx&=\text{area of quadrant}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\pi\times 1^2\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Using the estimate from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{4}&\approx 0.748927\ldots\\ \pi&\approx 2.99570\ldots\\ &\approx 2.996 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$
Explain why this value under-estimates the exact value of $\pi$.
items.sol: The curve is concave down, so all trapeziums used to estimate its area sit entirely below the curve, and the estimate of $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, and hence of $\pi$, is too small.

Using the cosine rule for $C$, opposite $AB=9$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos C&=\dfrac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\\ &=\dfrac{15^2+8^2-9^2}{2\times 15\times 8}\\ &=\dfrac{13}{15}\\ C&=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{13}{15}\right)\\ &=29^\circ 56' \end{aligned}$$
Using $\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8\times 15\times\sin 29^\circ 56'\\ &=29.9332\ldots\\ &\approx 29.9\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}\equiv\sec^2 x$.
items.sol:
Writing $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ and multiplying numerator and denominator by $\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\sin x}}{\frac{1}{\sin x}-\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} &&(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1)\\ &=\sec^2 x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan^2 x\left(\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}\right)dx$
items.sol:
Using part (a), the integrand is $\tan^2 x\sec^2 x$, which has the form $f'(x)\big[f(x)\big]^2$ with $f(x)=\tan x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan^2 x\left(\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\operatorname{cosec}x-\sin x}\right)dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan^2 x\sec^2 x\,dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{1}{3}\tan^3 x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\tan^3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\tan^3(0)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\left(\sqrt{3}\right)^3-0\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(3\sqrt{3}\right)\\ &=\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For a given discrete probability distribution, $E(X)=5$ and $\text{Var}(X)=3$.

Find the value of $E(2X+1)$.
items.sol:
Using $E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(2X+1)&=2\times 5+1\\ &=11 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A wire of length $L$ is bent to form a sector with radius $r$ and angle $\theta$.
Show that $\theta=\dfrac{L-2r}{r}$.

A wire of length $L$ is bent to form a sector with radius $r$ and angle $\theta$.
Show that the area $A$ of the sector is maximised when $r=\dfrac{L}{4}$.
items.sol:
Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ with $\theta$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\left(\dfrac{L-2r}{r}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{Lr}{2}-r^2 \end{aligned}$$
For maximum area, need
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=0\\ \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}&<0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=\dfrac{L}{2}-2r\\ 0&=\dfrac{L}{2}-2r\\ 2r&=\dfrac{L}{2}\\ r&=\dfrac{L}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=-2<0$$
Thus area is maximised when $r=\dfrac{L}{4}$.

items.part:
Part of each of the curves $y=3\tan x$ and $y=\cot x$ are shown on the graph below.

The curve $y=\cot x$ cuts the $x$ axis at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and the two curves intersect at the point $A$.

\exfigure{335_q33_1}
Show that the $x$ coordinate of $A$ is $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
items.sol:
At $A$, the curves are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\tan x&=\cot x\\ 3\tan^2 x&=1\\ \tan^2 x&=\dfrac{1}{3}\\ \tan x&=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ \ldots \end{aligned}$$
But at $A$, $x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, thus $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

items.part:
Part of each of the curves $y=3\tan x$ and $y=\cot x$ are shown on the graph below.

The curve $y=\cot x$ cuts the $x$ axis at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and the two curves intersect at the point $A$.

\exfigure{335_q33_1}
By considering $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+c$, find the exact area enclosed by the curves and the $x$ axis between $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
items.sol:
The region lies under $y=3\tan x$ from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and under $y=\cot x$ from $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}3\tan x\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cot x\,dx\\ &=3\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx\\ &=-3\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx\\ &=-3\Big[\ln|\cos x|\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}+\Big[\ln|\sin x|\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=-3\left[\ln\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\ln(\cos 0)\right]+\left[\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]\\ &=-3\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\ln(1)\right]+\left[\ln(1)-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\\ &=-3\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{8}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)+\ln 2\\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A farming company harvests oranges to sell to grocery stores. Oranges that weigh less than 150 grams are rejected and used for juicing instead. Typically, 16% of all oranges are rejected. Also, oranges that are larger than 300 grams are reserved for restaurants. Typically, 2.5% of all oranges are sold to restaurants.

If the weights of the oranges are normally distributed, find the mean and standard deviation of the normal distribution.
items.sol:
\exfigure{335_q34_s1}

Using the empirical rule:

$16\%$ lies below 150 g, so 150 g is one standard deviation below the mean.

$2.5\%$ lies above 300 g, so 300 g is two standard deviations above the mean.

So 150 g to 300 g spans 3 standard deviations:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Standard deviation}&=(300-150)\div 3\\ &=50\text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Mean}&=150+50\\ &=200\text{ g} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} k(\sin(\pi x)+2x), & \text{for } 0\le x\le 3\\ 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
Show that $k=\dfrac{\pi}{2+9\pi}$.
items.sol:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^3 k\big(\sin(\pi x)+2x\big)\,dx&=k\left[-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(\pi x)+x^2\right]_0^3\\ 1&=k\left[-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(3\pi)+3^2-\left(-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(0)+0^2\right)\right]\\ 1&=k\left[-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(-1)+9+\dfrac{1}{\pi}(1)-0\right]\\ 1&=k\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}+9\right)\\ 1&=k\left(\dfrac{2+9\pi}{\pi}\right)\\ k&=\dfrac{\pi}{2+9\pi} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} k(\sin(\pi x)+2x), & \text{for } 0\le x\le 3\\ 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
The graph of the density function is given below.

\exfigure{335_q35_1}

Without any calculation, explain why the mode must be greater than the median.
items.sol:
\exfigure{335_q35_s1}

The mode occurs at the maximum value on the graph.

The median occurs at the point which divides the area under the curve in half.

From the graph, the area to the left of the mode is clearly greater than half the total area.

Thus the median must be to the left of the mode, i.e. $\text{mode}>\text{median}$.

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} k(\sin(\pi x)+2x), & \text{for } 0\le x\le 3\\ 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
Find the mode of $X$. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
The mode occurs at a maximum turning point. For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\dfrac{\pi}{2+9\pi}\big(\sin(\pi x)+2x\big)\\ f'(x)&=\dfrac{\pi}{2+9\pi}\big(\pi\cos(\pi x)+2\big)\\ 0&=\pi\cos(\pi x)+2\\ \cos(\pi x)&=-\dfrac{2}{\pi}\\ \pi x&=\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right) \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{335_q35_s2}
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Reference }\angle&=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)\\ &=0.88068\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\cos(\pi x)<0$, so $\pi x$ is in the second or third quadrant of each revolution:
$$\begin{aligned} \pi x&=\pi-0.88,\ \pi+0.88,\ 3\pi-0.88,\ 3\pi+0.88,\ \ldots\\ &=2.2609,\ 4.0222,\ 8.5440,\ 10.3054,\ \ldots\\ x&=0.72,\ 1.28,\ 2.72,\ 3.28,\ \ldots \end{aligned}$$
But $0\le x\le 3$, and from the graph the mode is the third stationary point.

$\therefore$ The mode is $x=2.72$.

items.part:
The $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is given by $T_n=5n-3$.
Write down the first 3 terms of the sequence.
items.sol:
Substituting $n=1,2,3$ into $T_n=5n-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=5\times1-3=2\\T_2&=5\times2-3=7\\T_3&=5\times3-3=12\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the first 3 terms are $2,7,12$.

items.part:
The $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is given by $T_n=5n-3$.
Find the sum of the first 50 terms.
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$ with $a=2$, $d=5$, $n=50$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{50}&=\dfrac{50}{2}\left[2\times2+(50-1)\times5\right]\\&=25\times(4+245)\\&=6225\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
If $f(x)=-x^2-2x+3$ and $g(x)=2x+1$,
Write a simplified expression for $f\big(g(x)\big)$.

If $f(x)=-x^2-2x+3$ and $g(x)=2x+1$,
What is the axis of symmetry of $y=f\big(g(x)\big)$?
items.sol:
From part (a), $f(g(x))=-4x(x+2)$, a parabola with $x$-intercepts $x=0$ and $x=-2$.

The axis of symmetry is midway between the intercepts:
$$\therefore x=-1$$
Or, using $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$ with $a=-4$, $b=-8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{-(-8)}{2(-4)}\\&=\dfrac{8}{-8}\\&=-1\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$y=5x^2-\dfrac{4}{x}$

Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$f(x)=4x(6-x)^3$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=4x & v&=(6-x)^3\\u'&=4 & v'&=-3(6-x)^2\end{aligned}$$
($v'$ by the chain rule.)
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=4(6-x)^3+4x\times\big(-3(6-x)^2\big)\\&=4(6-x)^3-12x(6-x)^2\\&=4(6-x)^2(6-x-3x)\\&=4(6-x)^2(6-4x)\\&=8(6-x)^2(3-2x)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$f(x)=\tan(x^2-2)$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan f(x)=f'(x)\sec^2f(x)$:
$$f'(x)=2x\sec^2(x^2-2)$$

items.part:
Determine the following with respect to $x$.
$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x^2-3x+4}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$
items.sol:
Dividing each term by $\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{1}{2}}$ (index laws):
$$\begin{aligned}&\int\dfrac{x^2-3x+4}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx\\&=\int\dfrac{x^2}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}-\dfrac{3x}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}+\dfrac{4}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}\,dx\\&=\int x^{\frac{3}{2}}-3x^{\frac{1}{2}}+4x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{\frac{5}{2}}-\dfrac{3x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}+\dfrac{4x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}}+C\\&=\dfrac{2x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}-2x^{\frac{3}{2}}+8x^{\frac{1}{2}}+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Determine the following with respect to $x$.
$\displaystyle\int16\cos(2x-1)\,dx$
items.sol:
Using
$$\int\cos(ax+b)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{a}\sin(ax+b)+C$$
$$\begin{aligned}&\int16\cos(2x-1)\,dx\\&=16\times\dfrac{1}{2}\int2\cos(2x-1)\,dx\\&=8\sin(2x-1)+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Brendan is sitting in a cabin of a Ferris wheel which is revolving. The height, $B(t)$, in metres above the ground of her cabin is given by

$$B(t)=c-k\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{28}\right),$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds after Brendan's cabin first reaches the bottom of its revolution and $c$ and $k$ are constants.

\exfigure{1371_q15_1}

The top of each carriage reaches a greatest height of 28 metres and a smallest height of 4 metres.
Find the value of $c$ and $k$.
items.sol:
Rearranging:
$$B(t)=-k\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{28}\right)+c$$
so $c$ is the centre and $k$ is the amplitude.

The centre is midway between the greatest and smallest heights:
$$c=\dfrac{28+4}{2}=16$$
The amplitude is the distance from the centre to the greatest height:
$$k=28-16=12$$
$$\therefore c=16,\ k=12$$

items.part:
Brendan is sitting in a cabin of a Ferris wheel which is revolving. The height, $B(t)$, in metres above the ground of her cabin is given by

$$B(t)=c-k\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{28}\right),$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds after Brendan's cabin first reaches the bottom of its revolution and $c$ and $k$ are constants.

\exfigure{1371_q15_1}

The top of each carriage reaches a greatest height of 28 metres and a smallest height of 4 metres.
How many seconds does it take for one complete revolution of the Ferris wheel?
items.sol:
One complete revolution is one period. Using period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{\pi}{28}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{28}}\\&=2\pi\times\dfrac{28}{\pi}\\&=56\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}k+2k+3k+4k&=1\\10k&=1\\k&=\dfrac{1}{10}\text{ or }0.1\end{aligned}$$

From the calculator, $\sigma=1$.

Or, by hand:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)=\mu&=\sum\left[x\times p(x)\right]\\&=1\times0.1+2\times0.2+3\times0.3+4\times0.4\\&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma^2=\text{Var}(X)&=\sum\left[x^2p(x)\right]-\mu^2\\&=\left[1^2\times0.1+2^2\times0.2+3^2\times0.3+4^2\times0.4\right]-3^2\\&=10-9\\\sigma^2&=1\\\therefore\sigma&=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}$$
Or, using $\text{Var}(X)=\sum(x-\mu)^2p(x)$:

items.part:
Determine the last term under 100 in the sequence below.

$$-11,\quad-4,\quad3,\quad10,\quad17,\quad\ldots$$
items.sol:
The sequence is arithmetic with $a=-11$, $d=7$. Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=-11+7(n-1)\\&=-11+7n-7\\&=7n-18\end{aligned}$$
For the terms under 100:
$$\begin{aligned}7n-18&<100\\7n&<118\\n&<16.857\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The largest whole number is $n=16$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_{16}&=7(16)-18\\&=94\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the last term under 100 is the 16th term, $94$.

items.part: Differentiate $\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Method 1, using the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\log_e(x+1)-\log_e(x-2)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{x+1}-\dfrac{1}{x-2}\end{aligned}$$
Method 2, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x+1 & v&=x-2\\u'&=1 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{x+1}{x-2}}\times\dfrac{(x-2)\times1-(x+1)\times1}{(x-2)^2}\\&=\dfrac{x-2}{x+1}\times\dfrac{x-2-x-1}{(x-2)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-3}{(x+1)(x-2)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $3\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)=-1$ to the nearest minute for $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$.
items.sol:
Since $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$:
$$0^\circ\le\dfrac{x}{2}\le180^\circ$$
$\tan\dfrac{x}{2}<0$, so $\dfrac{x}{2}$ is in the 2nd quadrant.

\exfigure{1371_q19_s1}
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\\\dfrac{x}{2}&=161^\circ33'54.1''\\&\approx161^\circ34'\\\therefore x&=323^\circ8'\end{aligned}$$
Or:
$$\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=-18^\circ26'$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=2\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\\&=-36^\circ52'\end{aligned}$$
Adding $360^\circ$ to bring $x$ into the domain:
$$x=-36^\circ52'+360^\circ=323^\circ8'$$

items.part: Show that $1+\dfrac{10}{x-3}=\dfrac{x+7}{x-3}$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=1+\dfrac{10}{x-3}\\&=\dfrac{x-3+10}{x-3}\\&=\dfrac{x+7}{x-3}\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_4^{e+3}\dfrac{x+7}{x-3}\,dx$. Leave your answer in exact form.

Determine the sum of the geometric series below.

$$2+6+18+\cdots+39\,366$$
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $a=2$, $r=3$.

Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$ to find the number of terms:
$$\begin{aligned}2\times3^{n-1}&=39\,366\\3^{n-1}&=19\,683\\3^{n-1}&=3^9\\\therefore n-1&=9\\n&=10\end{aligned}$$
Or: $n-1=\log_3 19\,683=9$, so $n=10$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{10}&=\dfrac{2(3^{10}-1)}{3-1}\\&=\dfrac{2(3^{10}-1)}{2}\\&=3^{10}-1\\&=59\,048\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The following sequence is geometric.

$$6-x,\qquad x-8,\qquad x+4$$

Determine the possible values of the common ratio.
items.sol:
For a geometric sequence the ratio of consecutive terms is constant:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x-8}{6-x}&=\dfrac{x+4}{x-8}\\(x-8)^2&=(6-x)(x+4)\\x^2-16x+64&=6x+24-x^2-4x\\x^2-16x+64&=-x^2+2x+24\\2x^2-18x+40&=0\\2(x^2-9x+20)&=0\\2(x-4)(x-5)&=0\\\therefore x&=4\text{ or }5\end{aligned}$$
When $x=4$:
$$r=\dfrac{4-8}{6-4}=-2$$
When $x=5$:
$$r=\dfrac{5-8}{6-5}=-3$$
$\therefore$ the possible common ratios are $-2$ and $-3$.

items.part:
Anthony plays a game involving two standard dice.

The two dice are rolled. If the sum is

\begin{itemize}
\item a prime number, he receives \$5
\item a square number, he receives \$10
\item anything else, he loses \$5.
\end{itemize}
Is Anthony expected to gain or lose money in the long run? Justify your answer with relevant working.
items.sol:
From the array in part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{prime})&=\dfrac{15}{36}\\P(\text{square})&=\dfrac{7}{36}\\P(\text{anything else})&=\dfrac{14}{36}\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts1445_1}
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=5\times\dfrac{15}{36}+10\times\dfrac{7}{36}+(-5)\times\dfrac{14}{36}\\&\approx\$2.08\end{aligned}$$
Since $E(X)>0$, Anthony is expected to gain money in the long run.
items.final: Since $E(X)\approx\$2.08>0$, Anthony is expected to gain money in the long run.

items.part:
Point $P(3,-5)$ lies on the function $y=f(x)$.

The function is transformed to $y=f(1-x)+2$.

What are the coordinates of the image of $P$?
items.sol:
Writing the function as $y=f\big(-(x-1)\big)+2$, the transformations are:
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{horizontal dilation by factor } -1 &&\text{(reflect in the } y\text{-axis)}\\&\text{horizontal translation 1 unit right}\\&\text{vertical translation 2 units up}\end{aligned}$$
The horizontal dilation must happen before the horizontal translation; the vertical translation can come at any stage:
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{Option 1:} &&\text{dilation, horizontal translation, vertical translation}\\&\text{Option 2:} &&\text{vertical translation, dilation, horizontal translation}\\&\text{Option 3:} &&\text{dilation, vertical translation, horizontal translation}\end{aligned}$$
Using Option 1:
$$\begin{aligned}P(3,-5)&\mapsto(-3,-5) &&\text{reflect in the } y\text{-axis}\\&\mapsto(-2,-5) &&\text{translate 1 unit right}\\&\mapsto(-2,-3) &&\text{translate 2 units up}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the image is $P'(-2,-3)$.

The quick way: $P(x,y)\mapsto P'(1-x,\,y+2)$, so
$$P(3,-5)\mapsto P'(1-3,\,-5+2)=P'(-2,-3)$$

items.part: Differentiate $x\ln x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\ln x\\u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=x\times\dfrac{1}{x}+1\times\ln x\\&=1+\ln x\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int\ln x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Method 1, integrating the result of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\int(1+\ln x)\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\\int1\,dx+\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\x+\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x-x+C\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: from part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)=\ln x+1$, so
$$\ln x=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int\ln x\,dx&=\int\left(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1\right)dx\\&=x\ln x-x+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A toy racetrack consists of multiple track pieces which join together.

The first and longest piece of the track is 35 cm long, and each piece of track after the longest is 2 centimetres shorter than the previous piece.

The total length of the completed track is 2.6 metres.

Find the length of the shortest piece of track.
items.sol:
The track lengths form an arithmetic sequence with $a=35$, $d=-2$ and $S_n=260$ cm (2.6 m).

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2(35)+(n-1)(-2)\big)&=260\\n(70-2n+2)&=520\\n(72-2n)&=520\\72n-2n^2&=520\\2n^2-72n+520&=0\\n^2-36n+260&=0\\n&=\dfrac{36\pm\sqrt{36^2-4(1)(260)}}{2}\\&=26\text{ or }10\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}T_{26}&=35+(26-1)(-2)\\&=35+25(-2)\\&=-15\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
Lengths cannot be negative, so $n\ne26$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_{10}&=35+(10-1)(-2)\\&=17\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the length of the shortest piece is 17 cm.

items.part:
Given $x^2+y^2=14xy$,
Show that $\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}$ simplifies to $xy$.
items.sol:
Expanding and substituting the given $x^2+y^2=14xy$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{x^2+2xy+y^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{14xy+2xy}{16}\\&=\dfrac{16xy}{16}\\&=xy\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Given $x^2+y^2=14xy$,
Hence or otherwise, show that $\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)$.
items.sol:
Using the log laws $\log a+\log b=\log ab$ and $n\log a=\log a^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\right)\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ LHS $=$ RHS, as required.

Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\sqrt{xy}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(x+y)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\log16\\&=\log(x+y)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}-\log16^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log(x+y)-\log4\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log x+\dfrac{1}{2}\log y\\&=\log x^{\frac{1}{2}}+\log y^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\times y^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Determine the area of the region bounded by $y=x^2-3x-3$ and $y=x+2$.
items.sol:
Sketch the two graphs to see the region:

\exfigure{1371_q30_s1}

Points of intersection:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-3x-3&=x+2\\x^2-4x-5&=0\\(x-5)(x+1)&=0\\x=5\text{ or }x&=-1\end{aligned}$$
The line $y=x+2$ is above the parabola on $[-1,5]$, so the area is
$$\int_{-1}^{5}(\text{top curve}-\text{bottom curve})\,dx$$
Note: the area between the curves does not change if the region is translated, so no absolute value is needed as long as one graph is above the other throughout the interval, even if some of the region is below the $x$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned}&\int_{-1}^{5}\big((x+2)-(x^2-3x-3)\big)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{5}(x+2-x^2+3x+3)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{5}(-x^2+4x+5)\,dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2+5x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{5^3}{3}+2(5)^2+5(5)\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+2-5\right)\\&=36\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the infinite series below.

$$S=\sin^2x\cos^2x+2\sin^2x\cos^4x+4\sin^2x\cos^6x+\cdots$$
Given that the limiting sum of $S$ exists, show that it is $\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}$.
items.sol:
Using the limiting sum $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\sin^2x\cos^2x\\r&=\dfrac{2\sin^2x\cos^4x}{\sin^2x\cos^2x}\\&=2\cos^2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore S&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-2\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-\cos^2x-\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}&&(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x)\end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Consider the infinite series below.

$$S=\sin^2x\cos^2x+2\sin^2x\cos^4x+4\sin^2x\cos^6x+\cdots$$
Hence, show that $\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x\,(\tan^2x-1)}$ can also be expressed as the limiting sum of $S$.
items.sol:
Dividing the numerator and denominator by $\cos^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x\div\cos^2x}{(\sin^2x-\cos^2x)\div\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\tan^2x-1}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x(\tan^2x-1)}&&\text{since }\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x(\tan^2x-1)}&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\sin^2x}\left(\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1\right)}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\frac{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{\cos^2x}}\times\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x(\tan^2x-1)}&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\sin^2x}\left(\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1\right)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\cos^2x}-\frac{1}{\sin^2x}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{\cos^2x\sin^2x}}\times\dfrac{\cos^2x\sin^2x}{\cos^2x\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider $y=x^2e^{-x}$.

This will have the following derivatives (do NOT prove this).

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x(2-x)}{e^x}$$

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{x^2-4x+2}{e^x}$$
Determine any stationary points and their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\dfrac{x(2-x)}{e^x}=0$$
$e^x>0$, so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$; when $x=2$, $y=4e^{-2}$.

At $(0,0)$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2}{1}=2>0$$
so the curve is concave up and $(0,0)$ is a local minimum.

At $(2,4e^{-2})$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{4-8+2}{e^2}=-\dfrac{2}{e^2}<0$$
so the curve is concave down and $(2,4e^{-2})$ is a local maximum.
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a local minimum; $(2,4e^{-2})$ is a local maximum
