items.part: Sketch the curve $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2-12x+10$ by first finding the coordinates of all the stationary points, checking their nature, and finding the point of inflection.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)=6x^2-6x-12&=0\\6(x-2)(x+1)&=0\\x=2\ &\text{ or }\ x=-1\end{aligned}$$
$f(2)=-10$ and $f(-1)=17$.

Testing the nature with the first derivative:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -2 & -1 & 0\\ \hline f'(x) & + & 0 & -12 \end{array}\qquad\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 0 & 2 & 3\\ \hline f'(x) & - & 0 & + \end{array}$$
$\therefore$ $(-1,17)$ is a local maximum turning point.

$\therefore$ $(2,-10)$ is a local minimum turning point.

Possible inflexion where $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)=12x-6&=0\\x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\y&=\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Checking the change in concavity:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(0)&=-6 &&\text{concave down}\\f''\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=0\\f''(1)&=6 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ point of inflexion at $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{7}{2}\right)$ (concavity changes).

\exfigure{1375_q30_s1}
items.final: Local max $(-1,17)$, local min $(2,-10)$, point of inflexion $\left(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{7}{2}\right)$

items.part:
A new curve with equation $g(x)=10-f(x+2)$ is to be drawn.

What is the minimum value of this curve in the domain $-5\le x\le 1$?
items.sol:
$g(x)=-f(x+2)+10$: the graph of $f$ is reflected in the $x$-axis, translated 2 units left, then translated 10 units up.

For $-5\le x\le 1$, $x+2$ runs over $-3\le x+2\le 3$, which contains the maximum turning point $(-1,17)$ of $f$; the reflection turns this maximum into the minimum of $g$.

Reflecting in the $x$-axis: $(-1,17)$ becomes $(-1,-17)$.

Translating 2 units left: $(-3,-17)$.

Translating 10 units up: $(-3,-7)$.
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum value}=-7$$

items.part:
Use the trapezoidal rule with three function values to evaluate the integral $\int_0^1 3e^x\sin x\,dx$.

Answer to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
The trapezoidal rule with three function values uses $n=2$ strips on $[0,1]$, so $h=\dfrac{1-0}{2}=0.5$ (radians used):

\extable{Ts1627_1}

With $a=0$, $b=1$, $n=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1 3e^x\sin x\,dx&\approx\dfrac{b-a}{2n}\left[f(a)+f(b)+2f(0.5)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1-0}{2(2)}\left[0+3e\sin 1+2\times 3e^{\frac{1}{2}}\sin\dfrac{1}{2}\right]\\&=2.901\ldots\\&\approx 2.90\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Daniel grows tomatoes.

Some are grown inside a greenhouse while others are grown outside the greenhouse in the garden, with the other vegetables he grows.

The box and whisker plots shown below show the distribution of the heights of the tomato plants inside and outside the greenhouse.

\exfigure{1375_q32_1}

Write down two comparisons, supported with mathematical reasoning, about the heights of the plants grown inside the greenhouse to those grown outside the greenhouse and make a justified recommendation for future plantings.
items.sol:
Comparing the box plots.

Inside the greenhouse:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{median}&=148\text{ cm}\\ \text{range}&=190-114=76\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
Outside the greenhouse:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{median}&=138\text{ cm}\\ \text{range}&=194-102=92\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
The median is higher inside, so the plants inside are taller.

The range is larger outside, so there is more variation in heights outside.

$\therefore$ the recommendation for future plantings is to grow them inside.

items.part:
A particle moves along the $x$-axis with the acceleration at time $t$ equal to $a=12(t+3)^2$.

If the particle is initially at rest at the origin find the position of the particle after one second of motion.
items.sol:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$v=\int 12(t+3)^2\,dt=4(t+3)^3+C$$
Initially at rest, so $v=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4(3)^3+C\\C&=-108\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v=4(t+3)^3-108$$
Integrating the velocity:
$$x=\int\left(4(t+3)^3-108\right)dt=(t+3)^4-108t+C_2$$
Starting at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=81-0+C_2\\C_2&=-81\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=(t+3)^4-108t-81$$
When $t=1$:
$$x=67$$

items.part:
A die is loaded such that in a roll of a single die the chance of rolling a 1 is $\dfrac{x}{4}$, the chance of rolling a 2 is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and the chance of rolling a 6 is $\dfrac{1}{4}(1-x)$. The chance of rolling the other numbers (3,4 or 5) remain one in 6.

Two such dice are rolled together and the numbers on the uppermost faces are added to obtain a total score for the roll.

The probability of the total score of the two dice being 7 can be expressed as $y=f(x)$

Find the probability of rolling a 1 in a single roll of a die if the probability of rolling a total of 7 with two dice is $\dfrac{5}{36}$.
items.sol:
A total of 7 comes from $(1,6)$, $(6,1)$, $(2,5)$, $(5,2)$, $(3,4)$ or $(4,3)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=2\times\dfrac{x}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{4}(1-x)+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{6}\times 2+\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}\times 2\\&=\dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}+\dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{1}{18}\end{aligned}$$
Setting $f(x)=\dfrac{5}{36}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{5}{36}&=\dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}+\dfrac{5}{36}\\ \dfrac{x(1-x)}{8}&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

$x\ne 0$, as $P(1)$ exists.
$$\therefore x=1$$
$$\therefore P(1)=\dfrac{1}{4}$$

items.part:
A drain is made by folding up a rectangular sheet of metal, with cross- sectional length of 6 m, to form a cross-sectional area in the shape of an isosceles trapezium, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1375_q35_1}
Show that the area of the trapezoidal cross section of the drain can be expressed as

$A=\sin\vartheta(4+4\cos\vartheta)$ where $\vartheta$ is the angle in radians that the metal sheet is bent to form the drain.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1375_q35_s1}

From the diagram, the base and each sloping side are $2$ m, so the height is $2\sin\theta$ and each side adds $2\cos\theta$ to the top width.

Using the area of a trapezium, $A=\dfrac{1}{2}h(a+b)$ (or a rectangle plus two triangles):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}(2\sin\theta)(2+2+4\cos\theta)\\&=\sin\theta(4+4\cos\theta)\end{aligned}$$

Expanding the area from part (i):
$$A=4\sin\theta+4\sin\theta\cos\theta$$
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, on $4\sin\theta\cos\theta$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=4\sin\theta & v&=\cos\theta\\u'&=4\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=4\cos\theta+4\sin\theta(-\sin\theta)+4\cos\theta\cos\theta\\&=4\cos\theta-4(1-\cos^2\theta)+4\cos^2\theta\\&=8\cos^2\theta+4\cos\theta-4\end{aligned}$$
For a maximum or minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1)&=0\\(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

$\theta$ is an angle in a right-angled triangle, so $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ only:
$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
Testing with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}=16\cos\theta(-\sin\theta)-4\sin\theta$$
At $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=16\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\times\left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=16\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-4\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=-4\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{3}\\&=-6\sqrt{3}<0\end{aligned}$$
So the area is a maximum when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

$\therefore$ the angle that maximises the area is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (or $60^\circ$).

items.part: Solve the inequation $4x-13\le 11x+15$.
items.sol:
Collecting the $x$ terms on the left:
$$\begin{aligned}4x-11x&\le 15+13\\-7x&\le 28\end{aligned}$$
Dividing by $-7$ reverses the inequality:
$$\begin{aligned}x&\ge\dfrac{28}{-7}\\x&\ge -4\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The first term of an arithmetic sequence is 29. The sum of the first 16 terms is 2024.

What is the common difference of the sequence?
items.sol:
An arithmetic sequence with $a=29$ and $S_{16}=2024$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned}2024&=\dfrac{16}{2}\left[2\times 29+(16-1)d\right]\\253&=58+15d\\15d&=195\\d&=13\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the number of terms in the series.
items.sol:
The first and last terms are known, so use $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[a+l\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned}3535&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[10+60\right]\\7070&=n(70)\\n&=\dfrac{7070}{70}\\&=101\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the common difference.
items.sol:
The last term is $T_{101}=60$. Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned}60&=10+(101-1)d\\50&=100d\\d&=\dfrac{50}{100}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
OR, as the 100 equal steps go from $10$ to $60$:
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\dfrac{60-10}{100}\\&=\dfrac{50}{100}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find two equations in terms of $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}0.3+0.45+a+b&=1\\a+b&=0.25\qquad(1)\end{aligned}$$
The mean is $2$, so $E(X)=\displaystyle\sum xP(X=x)=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}1\times 0.3+2\times 0.45+3a+4b&=2\\0.3+0.9+3a+4b&=2\\3a+4b&=0.8\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find the values of $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
From $(1)$:
$$a=0.25-b\qquad(3)$$
Substituting $(3)$ into $(2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}3(0.25-b)+4b&=0.8\\0.75-3b+4b&=0.8\\b&=0.05\end{aligned}$$
Substituting $b=0.05$ into $(3)$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=0.25-0.05\\&=0.20\end{aligned}$$
So $a=0.20$ and $b=0.05$.

items.part: Find the values of $x$ for which $|2x-1|\le 5$.
items.sol:
$|2x-1|\le 5$ means $2x-1$ lies between $-5$ and $5$:
$$\begin{aligned}-5&\le 2x-1\le 5\\-4&\le 2x\le 6&&(\text{add }1)\\-2&\le x\le 3&&(\text{divide by }2)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Determine the number of squares required to construct $F_{15}$.
items.sol:
From the diagram, the numbers of squares form an arithmetic sequence with $a=1$ and $d=2$. Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_{15}&=1+(15-1)\times 2\\&=1+28\\&=29\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Is it possible for a figure in the sequence to have 175 squares?
items.sol:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $T_n=175$:
$$\begin{aligned}175&=1+(n-1)\times 2\\174&=2n-2\\2n&=176\\n&=\dfrac{176}{2}\\&=88\end{aligned}$$
$n$ is an integer.

$\therefore$ a figure with 175 squares is possible.
items.final: Yes, a figure with 175 squares is possible (n = 88).

items.part: Determine the number of squares required to make the first 50 figures.
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$ with $a=1$ and $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{50}&=\dfrac{50}{2}\left[2\times 1+(50-1)\times 2\right]\\&=25(2+98)\\&=25\times 100\\&=2500\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Complete a possible sequence of transformations that maps $f(x)$ to $g(x)$.
items.sol:
Rewriting $g(x)$:
$$g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}f\big(-(x-2)\big)$$
So a possible sequence is:

Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Reflection in the $y$-axis.

Translation of 2 units to the right.
items.final: Vertical dilation by factor $\frac12$; reflection in the $y$-axis; translation 2 units right.

items.part:
On the same set of axes sketch a graph of $g(x)$ below. Label the vertex and intercepts of $g(x)$.

\exfigure{163_q7_2}
items.sol:
\exfigure{163_q7_s1}

Writing $g(x)$ in vertex form:
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\big((-x+2)-3\big)^2-1\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(-x-1)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(-(x+1)\big)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(x+1)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the vertex is $\left(-1,-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

The $x$-intercepts are where $g(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=\dfrac{1}{2}(x+1)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(x+1)^2\\1&=(x+1)^2\\ \pm 1&=x+1\\x&=0\text{ or }x=-2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the common ratio.
items.sol:
Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3=ar^2&=1\\a&=\dfrac{1}{r^2}\qquad(1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}T_6=ar^5&=27\\a&=\dfrac{27}{r^5}\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Equating $(1)$ and $(2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{r^2}&=\dfrac{27}{r^5}\\ \dfrac{r^5}{r^2}&=27\\r^3&=27\\r&=3\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $(1)$:
$$a=\dfrac{1}{3^2}=\dfrac{1}{9}$$

items.part: Find the sum of the terms from $T_{10}$ to $T_{20}$ inclusive.
items.sol:
The terms from $T_{10}$ to $T_{20}$ sum to $S_{20}-S_9$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{a\left(r^n-1\right)}{r-1}$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{9}$ and $r=3$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}S_{20}-S_9&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{9}\left(3^{20}-1\right)}{3-1}-\dfrac{\frac{1}{9}\left(3^{9}-1\right)}{3-1}\\&=\dfrac{3^{20}-1-3^9+1}{2\times 9}\\&=\dfrac{3^{20}-3^9}{18}\\&=193\,709\,151\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the graph of $y=x^2-6$, labelling all intercepts.
items.sol:
\exfigure{163_q8_s1}

$x$-intercepts, where $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=x^2-6\\x^2&=6\\x&=\pm\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}$$
$y$-intercept, where $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=0-6\\&=-6\end{aligned}$$

items.part: On the same set of axes as in part (a), sketch the graph of $y=-2x-3$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{163_q8_s1}

$y$-intercept: $y=-3$.

$x$-intercept, where $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-2x-3\\2x&=-3\\x&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find algebraically the $x$-coordinates of the two points where the graphs intersect.
items.sol:
The graphs intersect where the $y$ values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-6&=-2x-3\\x^2+2x-3&=0\\(x+3)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=-3\text{ or }x=1$$

items.part: Hence solve the inequality $x^2-6<-2x-3$.
items.sol:
The parabola is below the line between the points of intersection:
$$-3<x<1$$

items.part:
Consider the geometric series $1+\left(\sqrt{5}-2\right)+\left(\sqrt{5}-2\right)^2+\ldots$.

Find the exact value of the limiting sum, expressing your answer with a rational denominator.
items.sol:
A GP with $a=1$ and $r=\sqrt{5}-2\approx 0.236\ldots$

$|r|<1$, so the limiting sum exists.

Using $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ and rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}S&=\dfrac{1}{1-(\sqrt{5}-2)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt{5}+2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{3-\sqrt{5}}\times\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{3+\sqrt{5}}\\&=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{9-5}\\&=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{4}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the value of $m$.
items.sol:
The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}m&=1-(0.75+0.03+0.002+0.001+0.0001)\\&=0.2169\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that Jessica is expected to lose \$5.66 every time she plays this lottery.
items.sol:
Using $E(X)=\displaystyle\sum xP(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=(0\times 0.75)+(20\times 0.2169)+(100\times 0.03)\\&\quad+(500\times 0.002)+(5000\times 0.001)+(10000\times 0.0001)\\&=14.338\end{aligned}$$
Tickets cost $\$20$ each, so Jessica's expected loss is
$$\begin{aligned}\$20-\$14.338&=\$5.662\\&\approx\$5.66\end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part: Find the variance of this discrete distribution. Show all working.
Show that $f(x)$ is an even function.
items.sol:
An even function satisfies $f(-x)=f(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=\dfrac{-3(-x)^2}{4+(-x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-3x^2}{4+x^2}\\&=f(x)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore f(x)$ is even, as required.

items.part: Find the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Dividing the numerator and denominator by $x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\dfrac{\frac{-3x^2}{x^2}}{\frac{4}{x^2}+\frac{x^2}{x^2}}\\&=\dfrac{-3}{\frac{4}{x^2}+1}\end{aligned}$$
As $x\to\infty$, $y\to -3$.

As $x\to -\infty$, $y\to -3$.

$\therefore$ the horizontal asymptote is $y=-3$.

items.part: Sketch the graph of $f(x)$ showing the asymptote identified in part (b) and any intercepts.
items.sol:
\exfigure{163_q9_s1}

From parts (a) and (b), the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis with horizontal asymptote $y=-3$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$.

$x^2\ge 0$, so $f(x)\le 0$ for all $x$.

items.part:
Sketch the graph of $f(x)=2+\dfrac{3}{x-1}$.

Label the axis intercepts with their coordinates and label any asymptotes with the appropriate equation.
items.sol:
\exfigure{163_q9_s2}

$x\ne 1$, so the vertical asymptote is $x=1$.

As $x\to\infty$, $\dfrac{3}{x-1}\to 0$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y=2$.

$y$-intercept, where $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=2+\dfrac{3}{0-1}\\&=2-3\\&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$x$-intercept, where $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2+\dfrac{3}{x-1}\\x-1&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\\x&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $6d=5a$.
items.sol:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$, the 3rd, 7th and 16th terms are $a+2d$, $a+6d$ and $a+15d$.

They are the first three terms of a GP, so the ratios of consecutive terms are equal:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{a+6d}{a+2d}&=\dfrac{a+15d}{a+6d}\\(a+6d)(a+6d)&=(a+2d)(a+15d)\\a^2+6ad+6ad+36d^2&=a^2+15ad+2ad+30d^2\\a^2+12ad+36d^2&=a^2+17ad+30d^2\\6d^2&=5ad\end{aligned}$$
$d\ne 0$, so dividing by $d$:
$$6d=5a\text{ as required}$$

items.part: Find the value of $r$.
items.sol:
The common ratio is the 7th term divided by the 3rd term:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{a+6d}{a+2d}\\&=\dfrac{a+6d}{\frac{1}{3}(3a+6d)}\\&=3\times\dfrac{a+6d}{3a+6d}\end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $6d=5a$:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=3\times\dfrac{a+5a}{3a+5a}\\&=3\times\dfrac{6a}{8a}\\&=\dfrac{18}{8}\\&=\dfrac{9}{4}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Complete the probability distribution table of $X$.

\extable{163_q10_t1}
items.sol:
\extable{Ts1666_1}

A sum of 6 is $2+4$ or $3+3$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X=6)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{8}+\dfrac{1}{8}\\&=\dfrac{2}{8}\\&=\dfrac{4}{16}\end{aligned}$$
A sum of 7 is $3+4$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X=7)&=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\&=\dfrac{1}{16}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Determine the standard deviation of the discrete distribution, correct to 2 decimal places. Show all working.
items.sol:
Using $E(X)=\displaystyle\sum xP(X=x)$ with the table from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=\left(3\times\dfrac{1}{16}\right)+\left(4\times\dfrac{4}{16}\right)+\left(5\times\dfrac{6}{16}\right)+\left(6\times\dfrac{4}{16}\right)+\left(7\times\dfrac{1}{16}\right)\\&=\dfrac{3}{16}+\dfrac{16}{16}+\dfrac{30}{16}+\dfrac{24}{16}+\dfrac{7}{16}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
The standard deviation is $\sigma=\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}$, where $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\big(E(X)\big)^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma&=\sqrt{\left(3^2\times\dfrac{1}{16}\right)+\left(4^2\times\dfrac{4}{16}\right)+\left(5^2\times\dfrac{6}{16}\right)+\left(6^2\times\dfrac{4}{16}\right)+\left(7^2\times\dfrac{1}{16}\right)-5^2}\\&=\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{16}+\dfrac{64}{16}+\dfrac{150}{16}+\dfrac{144}{16}+\dfrac{49}{16}-25}\\&=\sqrt{26-25}\\&=1.00\ (2\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The following transformations were applied to the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the order shown below.

\begin{itemize}
\item Horizontal translation to the right by 4 units.
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{4}{3}$
\item Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item Vertical translation down by 3 units
\item Reflection in the $x$-axis
\end{itemize}

Find the equation of the transformed function.
items.sol:
Horizontal transformations first.

Translation right 4 units:
$$y=(x+1-4)^2=(x-3)^2$$
Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{4}{3}$:
$$y=\left(\dfrac{x}{\frac{4}{3}}-3\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2$$
Then the vertical transformations.

Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2$$
Translation down 3 units:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2-3$$
Reflection in the $x$-axis:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2-3\right)\\&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2+3\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Using a suitable scale, sketch the graph of the transformed function, showing the location of the vertex and the axis intercepts.
items.sol:
\exfigure{163_q10_s1}

Writing the function from part (a) in vertex form:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2+3\\&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}(x-4)\right)^2+3\\&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{9}{16}(x-4)^2+3\\&=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2+3\end{aligned}$$
So the vertex is $(4,3)$.

$x$-intercepts, where $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2+3\\-3&=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2\\16&=(x-4)^2\\x-4&=\pm 4\\x&=0\text{ or }x=8\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the derivative of $y=\cos^4x$
items.sol:
By the chain rule, differentiating $(\cos x)^4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=4\cos^3x\times(-\sin x)\\&=-4\sin x\cos^3x\end{aligned}$$

items.part: $\dfrac{3e}{x^4}$
items.sol:
Writing with a negative index:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{3e}{x^4}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3ex^{-4}\right)\\&=-12ex^{-5}\\&=\dfrac{-12e}{x^5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: $x^2\tan x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x^2 & v&=\tan x\\u'&=2x & v'&=\sec^2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\tan x\right)&=x^2\cdot\sec^2x+\tan x\cdot 2x\\&=x^2\sec^2x+2x\tan x\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int5\sin2x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int\sin ax\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{a}\cos ax+C$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int5\sin2x\,dx&=\dfrac{-5\cos2x}{2}+C\\&=-\dfrac{5}{2}\cos2x+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^4 2\sqrt{x}+\dfrac{3}{x}\,dx$. Leave your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Writing the integrand with powers of $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}I&=\int_1^4\left(2x^{\frac{1}{2}}+3x^{-1}\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}+3\ln|x|\right]_1^4\\&=\left[\dfrac{4x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}+3\ln|x|\right]_1^4\\&=\dfrac{32}{3}+3\ln4-\left(\dfrac{4}{3}+3\ln1\right)\\&=\dfrac{28}{3}+3\ln4\end{aligned}$$
Since $3\ln 4=\ln 64$, this is also $\dfrac{28}{3}+\ln64$.

items.part:
The function $y=\sin x$ undergoes a series of graphical transformations and becomes

$$y=3\sin\left(3x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$$

Outline the transformations that were applied to $y=\sin x$, \textbf{in the correct order}.
items.sol:
Factorising inside the sine:
$$y=3\sin\left(3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)$$
In order:

First, a horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Then a horizontal translation $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ units left.

Then a vertical dilation by a factor of 3.
items.final: Horizontal dilation by factor $\frac13$, then translation $\frac{\pi}{6}$ units left, then vertical dilation by factor 3.

items.part:
The graph below shows an area enclosed between $y=-\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$.

The graphs intersect at the points $A\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4},-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$ and $B\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{4},\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$ as shown on the diagram.

\exfigure{165_q10_1}

Find the exact value of the shaded area.
items.sol:
On $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{7\pi}{4}$, $y=-\sin x$ is the upper curve:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{\frac{3\pi}{4}}^{\frac{7\pi}{4}}\left(-\sin x-\cos x\right)dx\\&=\Big[\cos x-\sin x\Big]_{\frac{3\pi}{4}}^{\frac{7\pi}{4}}\\&=\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}-\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{4}-\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt2}\\&=2\sqrt2\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=e^x+\log_e(4x-3)$ at the point where $x=1$.
items.sol:
$$y=e^x+\ln(4x-3)$$
Differentiating, with the chain rule for $\ln(4x-3)$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x+\dfrac{1}{4x-3}\times4$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e+\ln(4-3)\\&=e\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e+\dfrac{4}{4-3}\\&=e+4\end{aligned}$$
The tangent passes through $(1,e)$ with gradient $m=e+4$. Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-e&=(e+4)(x-1)\\y&=(e+4)x-e-4+e\\&=(e+4)x-4\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given $y=(\ln x)^2$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2(\ln x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\&=\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_1^e\dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{2x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\ln x^2=2\ln x$, then part (a): $\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}$ is the derivative of $(\ln x)^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^e\dfrac{\ln x^2}{2x}\,dx&=\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{2x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[(\ln x)^2\Big]_1^e\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left((\ln e)^2-(\ln1)^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1^2-0^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $y=\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$, show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=\cos x & v&=1+\sin x\\u'&=-\sin x & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
Simplifying with $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(1+\sin x)(-\sin x)-\cos x(\cos x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-\sin x-\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-(1+\sin x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\end{aligned}$$
Writing $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-(1+\sin x)^{-1}$ and using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-(-(1+\sin x)^{-2})\cdot(\cos x)\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into the left-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}+\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\cdot\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x-\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Sketch the graph of $y=3e^{(x-1)}-3$ in the box below. Show any intercepts and asymptotes.

\textbf{DO NOT USE CALCULUS.}
items.sol:
\exfigure{165_q11_s1}

This is the graph of $y=e^x$ transformed.

$y=e^{x-1}$: translated right 1 unit.

$y=3e^{x-1}$: dilated vertically by a factor of 3.

$y=3e^{(x-1)}-3$: translated down 3 units, so the asymptote $y=0$ moves to $y=-3$.

When $x=1$, $y=0$.

When $x=0$, $y=\dfrac{3}{e}-3\approx-1.9$.

items.part: At what time is the velocity of the particle a minimum? Justify your answer.
items.sol:
Velocity is a minimum when the acceleration is zero and changes from negative to positive.

From the graph, this happens at $t=2$.
$$\therefore t=2$$

items.part: At what time does the particle come to rest? Justify your answer.
items.sol:
The particle starts at rest, so it is next at rest when the velocity is $0$, that is, when the area under the acceleration–time graph is $0$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times(-2)+\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times2=0$$
$$\therefore t=4$$

items.part: Describe the motion of the particle.
items.sol:
The particle is initially moving to the left, reaching its maximum speed after 2 seconds, then slowing to a stop after 4 seconds.

It then moves to the right until it reaches a speed of $2\text{ ms}^{-1}$ after 6 seconds:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times(6-4)\times2=2$$
It then continues to the right at a constant speed of $2\text{ ms}^{-1}$.

items.part: Find the derivative of $y=\ln\sqrt{\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}}$, giving your answer in simplest form.
items.sol:
Using log laws to expand before differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[\ln(x+1)-\ln(x-1)\Big]\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{x+1}-\dfrac{1}{x-1}\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{x-1-(x+1)}{x^2-1}\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{-2}{x^2-1}\right]\\&=\dfrac{-1}{x^2-1}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: What is the \textbf{maximum} and \textbf{minimum} prices of petrol during the year?
items.sol:
The sine term lies between $-1$ and $1$:
$$-1\le\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)\le 1$$

The maximum price occurs when $\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=180+44\\&=224\text{ cents/litre}\end{aligned}$$
The minimum price occurs when $\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=180-44\\&=136\text{ cents/litre}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the function $P(t)=180+44\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)$ for $0\le t\le366$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{165_q12_s1}

The period is
$$\begin{aligned}T&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{2\pi}{183}}\\&=183\end{aligned}$$
so $0\le t\le366$ covers two cycles of the graph.

At $t=0$, $P=180$.

items.part: What is the value of $t$ when the petrol FIRST costs 202 cents per litre?
items.sol:
Setting $P=202$:
$$\begin{aligned}202&=180+44\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)\\22&=44\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)\\\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \ldots$, and the first time is the smallest solution:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\t&=\dfrac{183}{12}\\&=\dfrac{61}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Petrol first costs 202 c/L when $t=\dfrac{61}{4}$ days ($15.25$ days).

items.part: Show that the particle begins its journey at the origin.
items.sol:
For $0\le t\le1$, $x=5t$:
$$\begin{aligned}x(0)&=5(0)\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ at $t=0$, $x=0$: the particle starts at the origin.

items.part: Show that the particle is never at rest.
items.sol:
For $0\le t\le1$, $x=5t$, so the displacement increases linearly (at $5$ m/s).

At $t=1$, the second piece gives
$$\begin{aligned}x(1)&=6\sqrt{1}-\dfrac{1}{1}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
which matches $5t$, so the displacement is continuous at $t=1$.

For $t>1$:
$$x'(t)=3t^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\dfrac{1}{t^2}$$
Both terms are positive, so $x'(t)>0$ and $x(t)$ is increasing for $t>1$.

$\therefore$ the displacement is increasing for $t>0$.

$\therefore$ the particle never comes to rest.

Alternatively, as $t\to\infty$, $x'(t)\to0^+$ (an asymptote), so $x'(t)$ is never $0$.

items.part: Find the distance travelled in the first 4 seconds of the particle's journey.
items.sol:
From part (b), the graph is continuous at $t=1$ and increasing for $t>0$, so the particle does not turn and the distance is $x(4)-x(0)=x(4)$:
$$\begin{aligned}x(4)&=6\sqrt4-\dfrac{1}{4}\\&=12-\dfrac{1}{4}\\&=11\dfrac{3}{4}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Show that

$$\dfrac{\sec^23x}{\tan3x}=\sec3x\ \text{cosec}\,3x.$$
items.sol:
Writing $\sec 3x=\dfrac{1}{\cos 3x}$ and $\tan 3x=\dfrac{\sin 3x}{\cos 3x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sec3x\sec3x}{\tan3x}\\&=\sec3x\times\dfrac{1}{\cos3x}\times\dfrac{\cos3x}{\sin3x}\\&=\sec3x\times\dfrac{1}{\sin3x}\\&=\sec3x\,\text{cosec}\,3x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int\sec3x\ \text{cosec}\,3x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using part (a); the numerator $3\sec^23x$ is the derivative of $\tan3x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\sec3x\,\text{cosec}\,3x\,dx&=\int\dfrac{\sec^23x}{\tan3x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{3\sec^23x}{\tan3x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left|\tan3x\right|+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the two curves are the solutions of the equation $\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$, and solve this equation.
items.sol:
The curves intersect where $2\cos x=\cot x$, for $0\le x\le2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos x&=\cot x\\2\cos x&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\2\sin x\cos x&=\cos x\\2\sin x\cos x-\cos x&=0\\\cos x(2\sin x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Either $\cos x=0$:
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
or $2\sin x-1=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)=\cot x$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)&=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\times\cos x\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find, in simplest form, the total area of the region enclosed by the two curves for $0\le x\le\pi$.
items.sol:
For $0\le x\le\pi$ the curves enclose two regions between $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, equal in area by symmetry about $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$.

On $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $2\cos x\ge\cot x$. Using part (b) for the primitive of $\cot x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(2\cos x-\cot x\right)dx\\&=2\Big[2\sin x-\ln(\sin x)\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\&=2\left[2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\right]\\&=2\left[2-\ln1-1+\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\\&=2+2\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=2-2\ln2\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: What is the initial temperature of the oven?
items.sol:
The oven is switched on at $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^0\\&=25^\circ\text{C}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Calculate the average rate at which the temperature changes per minute from $t=25$ to $t=75$, correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
At $t=25$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2(25)}\\&=86.4265\end{aligned}$$
At $t=75$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2(75)}\\&=144.1163\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The average rate of change is the change in $T$ divided by the change in $t$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Average rate}&=\dfrac{144.1163\ldots-86.4265}{75-25}\\&=1.15\ ^\circ\text{C/min (2 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Ian can place the pizza in the oven when the instantaneous rate of change of temperature is less than or equal to $1^\circ C$ per minute.

After turning on the oven, how long must Ian wait before he can place the pizza in the oven, correct to the nearest minute?
items.sol:
The instantaneous rate is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}a^{kt}=k\ln a\cdot a^{kt}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-150\times0.2\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}\\&=-30\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}\end{aligned}$$
Require $\dfrac{dT}{dt}<1$:
$$\begin{aligned}-30\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}&<1\\(0.9)^{0.2t}&<\dfrac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\\\ln(0.9)^{0.2t}&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Dividing by $\ln(0.9)<0$ reverses the inequality:
$$\begin{aligned}0.2t&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\right)}{\ln(0.9)}\\0.2t&>10.9227\\t&>54.6\\t&>55\text{ min (nearest min)}\end{aligned}$$
Ian must wait 55 minutes.

items.part:
Show that the displacement of the particle is given by

$$x=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+4.$$
items.sol:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=\int\ddot{x}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{12e^{-2t}}{-2}+\dfrac{e^{-t}}{-1}+C\\&=-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+C\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $\dot{x}=-6$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6&=-6-1+C\\C&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+1$$
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int\dot{x}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{-6e^{-2t}}{-2}-\dfrac{e^{-t}}{-1}+t+C_2\\&=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+C_2\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $x=8$:
$$\begin{aligned}8&=3+1+0+C_2\\C_2&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+4$$

items.part: Show that the particle comes to rest after $t=\ln3$ seconds.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+1=0$$
Multiplying by $e^{2t}$ gives a quadratic in $e^t$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6-e^t+e^{2t}&=0\\(e^t)^2-e^t-6&=0\\(e^t+2)(e^t-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $e^t=-2$ or $e^t=3$.

$e^t>0$, so $e^t=-2$ has no solution.
$$\begin{aligned}e^t&=3\\t&=\ln3\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest after $t=\ln3$ seconds.

items.part:
Find the displacement when the particle comes to rest.

Give a simplified, exact answer.
Solve $\log_2 9=5\log_2 3-\log_2 x$.
items.sol:
Using the log laws $n\log_a b=\log_a b^n$ and $\log_a b-\log_a c=\log_a\dfrac{b}{c}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 9&=\log_2 3^5-\log_2 x\\ \log_2 9&=\log_2\dfrac{243}{x}\\ 9&=\dfrac{243}{x}\\ x&=27\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{5}{13}$ and $\tan\alpha<0$, find the exact value of $\cos\alpha$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{166_q11_s1}

From the right-angled triangle with sides $5$, $12$, $13$ (Pythagoras' theorem), the related acute angle $\theta$ has
$$\cos\theta=\dfrac{12}{13}$$
$\sin\alpha>0$ and $\tan\alpha<0$, so $\alpha$ is in the 2nd quadrant, where cosine is negative.
$$\therefore\ \cos\alpha=-\dfrac{12}{13}$$

items.part: Show that the length of $BC$ is $4\sqrt{6}\text{ cm}$.
items.sol:
By the angle sum of a triangle, $\angle C=180^\circ-45^\circ-75^\circ=60^\circ$.

Using the sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{BC}{\sin 45^\circ}&=\dfrac{12}{\sin 60^\circ}\\ BC&=\dfrac{12\sin 45^\circ}{\sin 60^\circ}\\ BC&=\dfrac{12\times\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\\ &=6\sqrt{2}\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{12\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{12\sqrt{6}}{3}\\ &=4\sqrt{6}\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence or otherwise, find the area of the triangle to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ with $AB=12$, $BC=4\sqrt{6}$ and the included angle $\angle B=75^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 12\times 4\sqrt{6}\times\sin 75^\circ\\ &\approx 56.78\text{ cm}^2\ (2\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $f(x)=(1-\cos x)^5$, find $f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=5(1-\cos x)^4\times\sin x\\ &=5\sin x(1-\cos x)^4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)&=5\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\left(1-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^4\\ &=5\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the derivative of the function $f(x)=x^2e^{5x}$. Give your answer in factorised form.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x^2 & v&=e^{5x}\\u'&=2x & v'&=5e^{5x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=2xe^{5x}+5x^2e^{5x}\\ &=xe^{5x}(2+5x)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $(\sin x+3)(2\sin x+1)=0$ in the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
Either $\sin x+3=0$ or $2\sin x+1=0$.

$\sin x+3=0$ gives $\sin x=-3$: no solutions, as $-1\le\sin x\le 1$.

$2\sin x+1=0$ gives $\sin x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

\exfigure{166_q11_s2}

Sine is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants, and the related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\ x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3\dfrac{27x^2-21}{3x^3-7x+8}\,dx$, leaving your answer in exact simplified form.
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3x^3-7x+8\right)=9x^2-7$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^3\dfrac{27x^2-21}{3x^3-7x+8}\,dx&=3\int_1^3\dfrac{9x^2-7}{3x^3-7x+8}\,dx\\ &=3\Big[\ln\left|3x^3-7x+8\right|\Big]_1^3\\ &=3\left[\ln\left|3(3)^3-7(3)+8\right|-\ln\left|3(1)^3-7(1)+8\right|\right]\\ &=3\left[\ln 68-\ln 4\right]\\ &=3\ln 17\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show with calculations why this geometric series has a limiting sum.
items.sol:
Each term is the previous term multiplied by $\sqrt{11}-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\sqrt{11}-3\\ &=0.31662\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$-1<0.31662\ldots<1$, so $|r|<1$.

$\therefore$ the GP has a limiting sum.

items.part: Determine the exact value of the limiting sum. Express your answer with a rational denominator.
items.sol:
Using $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=1$ and $r=\sqrt{11}-3$, then rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\left(\sqrt{11}-3\right)}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4-\sqrt{11}}\times\dfrac{4+\sqrt{11}}{4+\sqrt{11}}\\ &=\dfrac{4+\sqrt{11}}{5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Isabella plans to deposit \$7500 at the end of each year into an annuity paying 5.0% p.a. compounding annually. What is the value of her investment after 10 years?
items.sol:
Using the future value interest factor for $5\%$ p.a. over 10 years from the table, $12.578$:
$$\begin{aligned}FV&=\text{amount}\times\text{interest factor}\\ &=7500\times 12.578\\ &=\$94\,335\end{aligned}$$

items.part: What amount could Isabella invest now at 5.0% p.a. compounding annually, to achieve the same financial outcome as the annuity after 10 years?
items.sol:
Using the present value interest factor for $5\%$ p.a. over 10 years from the table, $7.722$:
$$\begin{aligned}PV&=\text{amount}\times\text{interest factor}\\ &=7500\times 7.722\\ &=\$57\,915\end{aligned}$$
OR, discounting the future value from part (a):
$$94\,335\div(1.05)^{10}=\$57\,913.51$$

items.part: Find the primitive function of $\sec^2(5x)-\sin(x)+5^x$.
items.sol:
Integrating term by term:
$$\begin{aligned}&\int\left(\sec^2(5x)-\sin x+5^x\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}\tan 5x+\cos x+\dfrac{5^x}{\ln 5}+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Determine the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\ln\left(3x^2+2\right)$ at the point $(2,\ \ln 14)$. Express your answer in general form $ax+by+c=0$.
items.sol:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln\left(3x^2+2\right)\\ y'&=\dfrac{6x}{3x^2+2}\end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{6(2)}{3(2)^2+2}\\ &=\dfrac{6}{7}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ m=\dfrac{6}{7}$ at $(2,\ln 14)$.

Using the point-gradient form $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-\ln 14&=\dfrac{6}{7}(x-2)\\ 7y-7\ln 14&=6x-12\\ 6x-7y+7\ln 14-12&=0\end{aligned}$$

items.part: When $x=9$, $y=3$. Determine the equation relating $x$ in terms of $y$.
items.sol:
For inverse proportion, $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$.

Substituting $x=9$, $y=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}3&=\dfrac{k}{9}\\ k&=27\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{27}{x}$$

items.part: If the value of $x$ is increased from 2 to 18, determine the change in the value of $y$.
items.sol:
At $x=2$, $y=\dfrac{27}{2}$.

At $x=18$, $y=\dfrac{3}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{change in }y&=\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{27}{2}\\ &=-12\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence graph the relationship between $x$ and $y$ using the values you have found previously.
items.sol: \exfigure{166_q12_s1}

$y=f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}(x-2)\right)$ is $y=f(x)$ dilated horizontally by a factor of 2, then translated 2 units right.

\exfigure{166_q13_s1}

items.part: Find the value of $k$ correct to 1 significant figure, given that there are 1660 bacteria present after 2 hours.
items.sol:
Substituting $P(120)=1660$ ($t=120$ minutes):
$$\begin{aligned}1660&=500e^{120k}\\ \dfrac{83}{25}&=e^{120k}\\ 120k&=\ln\dfrac{83}{25}\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}\\ &\approx 0.01\ (1\text{ sig. fig.})\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Determine the rate of change of the population with respect to time after 2 hours. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
Differentiating $P(t)=500e^{kt}$, where $k=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&=500ke^{kt}\\ P'(120)&=500ke^{k\times 120}\\ &=16.6\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the population is increasing at approximately 17 bacteria/min at $t=120$.

items.part:
Ava is concerned about the growth of the bacteria and wants to determine if she needs to introduce a control mechanism.

Interpret the nature of the population growth with reference to the derivatives $P'(t)$ and $P''(t)$, and hence determine if a control would be needed.
items.sol:
Differentiating $P(t)=500e^{kt}$, where $k=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&=500ke^{kt}\\ P''(t)&=500k^2e^{kt}\end{aligned}$$
$e^{kt}>0$ for all $t$, so
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&>0 &&\text{for all } t &&P(t)\text{ is increasing}\\ P''(t)&>0 &&\text{for all } t &&P'(t)\text{ is increasing}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ P(t)$ is increasing at an increasing rate, so a control mechanism should be introduced.
items.final: $P(t)$ is increasing at an increasing rate, so a control mechanism should be introduced.

items.part: Determine the expected value of the number of sales that Lara makes on a particular day.
items.sol:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=0\times 0.14+1\times 0.15+2\times 0.25+3\times 0.3+4\times 0.11+5\times 0.05\\ &=2.24\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Another sales representative, Rebecca, has an expected number of sales of 2.5 and a standard deviation in the number of sales of 1.2.

The CEO of the company would like to promote a sales representative to be the leader of the sales team.

If the CEO bases her decision on sales performance, are they more likely to promote Lara or Rebecca? Justify your answer with appropriate statistical reasoning.
items.sol:
Using $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=2.24$:
$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(X)&=0^2\times 0.14+1^2\times 0.15+2^2\times 0.25+3^2\times 0.3+4^2\times 0.11+5^2\times 0.05-2.24^2\\ &=1.8424\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma&=\sqrt{1.8424}\\ &\approx 1.36\ (2\text{ dp})\end{aligned}$$
Rebecca has a higher mean and a smaller standard deviation, so she has higher sales on average and is more consistent.

$\therefore$ Rebecca is more likely to be promoted.
items.final: Rebecca is more likely to be promoted (higher mean, smaller standard deviation: $\sigma\approx1.36$ for Lara).

items.part:
Find all the values of $\theta$ where $-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$ such that

$$\cos\left(\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$$
items.sol:
Adjusting the domain:
$$\begin{aligned}-\pi&\le\theta\le\pi\\ -\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}&\le\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6} &&\left(\text{subtract }\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\\ -\dfrac{7\pi}{6}&\le\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}&=-\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\ \theta-\dfrac{\pi}{6}&=-\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\\ \theta&=-\pi,\ -\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \pi\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Calculate the fifteenth term in this series.
items.sol:
The series is arithmetic with $a=3$, $d=6$, $n=15$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=a+(n-1)d\\ T_{15}&=3+14\times 6\\ &=87\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The sum of the first $n$ consecutive terms of the series is 243.

What is the value of $n$?
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $a=3$, $d=6$ and $S_n=243$:
$$\begin{aligned}243&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(6+6(n-1)\right)\\ 243&=\dfrac{n}{2}(6n)\\ 243&=3n^2\\ n^2&=81\\ n&=9\quad(n>0)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag contains eight cards that are each printed with one of the following sets of characters.

$$\text{aaa}\qquad\text{aab}\qquad\text{aba}\qquad\text{baa}\qquad\text{abb}\qquad\text{bab}\qquad\text{bba}\qquad\text{bbb}$$

A student chooses one card at random.

Let $N_1$ be the event that the first character printed on the card is an ‘a’ and $N_2$ be the event that the first and second characters printed on the card are both an ‘a’.

Determine whether $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events.
items.sol:
$N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent if $P(N_1\cap N_2)=P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(N_1)&=\dfrac{4}{8}=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ P(N_2)&=\dfrac{2}{8}=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ P(N_1\cap N_2)&=\dfrac{2}{8}=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ P(N_1)\times P(N_2)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{8}\end{aligned}$$
$P(N_1)\times P(N_2)\ne P(N_1\cap N_2)$

$\therefore\ N_1$ and $N_2$ are not independent.

items.part: Show that the amount $A_3$ remaining in the account after the third withdrawal of \$7000 is $A_3=P(1.005)^3-7000\left[(1.005)^2+1.005+1\right]$
Find the amount $P$ that will need to be invested if he is to withdraw \$7000 each month for the next 20 years. Express your answer to the nearest cent.
Show that $\angle CBS=52^\circ$.
Find the distance between Catherine and Sarah. Give your answer to the nearest metre.
items.sol:
\exfigure{166_q14_s2}

In right-angled triangle $MBC$ (angle of elevation $5^\circ$, $MB=105$):
$$\begin{aligned}\tan 5^\circ&=\dfrac{105}{BC}\\ BC&=\dfrac{105}{\tan 5^\circ}\\ &=105\cot 5^\circ\end{aligned}$$
In right-angled triangle $MBS$ (angle of elevation $7^\circ$):
$$\begin{aligned}\tan 7^\circ&=\dfrac{105}{BS}\\ BS&=\dfrac{105}{\tan 7^\circ}\\ &=105\cot 7^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $CBS$ with $\angle CBS=52^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}CS^2&=(105\cot 5^\circ)^2+(105\cot 7^\circ)^2-2(105\cot 5^\circ)(105\cot 7^\circ)\cos 52^\circ\\ &=\dfrac{105^2}{\tan^2 5^\circ}+\dfrac{105^2}{\tan^2 7^\circ}-\dfrac{2\times 105^2\cos 52^\circ}{\tan 5^\circ\tan 7^\circ}\\ &\approx 907\,933.4963\ldots\\ CS&=952.8554\ldots\\ &\approx 953\text{ m (nearest metre)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate the definite integral $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}3\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)dx$. Express your answer with a rational denominator.
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int\sin(ax)\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{a}\cos(ax)+C$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\pi}3\sin\dfrac{x}{4}\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{-3\cos\frac{x}{4}}{\frac{1}{4}}\right]_0^{\pi}\\ &=\left[-12\cos\dfrac{x}{4}\right]_0^{\pi}\\ &=-12\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\left(-12\cos 0\right)\\ &=-12\times\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+12\\ &=12-6\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the particle’s maximum and minimum velocity.
items.sol:
Since $-1\le\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)\le 1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Max}&=2+5=7\text{ m/s}\\ \text{Min}&=2-5=-3\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
items.final: Maximum velocity $7$ m/s, minimum velocity $-3$ m/s

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, sketch the graph of the particle’s velocity, labelling all important features (you do not need to find $x$-intercepts).

Determine how many times the particle changes its direction.

Explain your answer with reference to the graph in part (b).
items.sol:
The particle changes direction when $v(t)$ changes sign (positive to negative or negative to positive), that is, when $v(t)=0$.

For $0\le t\le 8$, the graph of $v(t)$ crosses the $t$-axis twice.

$\therefore$ the particle changes direction twice.

items.part: If the radius of each congruent circle is $r$ centimetres, show that the total area of the three shapes is given by $A=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2$
items.sol:
Let the side length of the square be $x$. The wire forms two circles (circumference $2\pi r$ each) and the square (perimeter $4x$):
$$\begin{aligned}40&=2\pi r+2\pi r+4x\\ 40&=4\pi r+4x\\ 10&=\pi r+x\\ x&=10-\pi r\end{aligned}$$
The total area is two circles ($\pi r^2$ each) and the square ($x^2$):
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ A&=2\pi r^2+(10-\pi r)^2\\ &=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find the length of the side of the square and the value of $r$ that will minimise the total area of the three shapes.
items.sol:
Differentiating (chain rule on $(10-\pi r)^2$):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=(10-\pi r)^2+2\pi r^2\\ \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=2(10-\pi r)\times(-\pi)+4\pi r\\ &=-20\pi+2\pi^2r+4\pi r\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points when $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-20\pi+2\pi^2r+4\pi r\\ 20\pi&=2\pi^2r+4\pi r\\ 10&=\pi r+2r\\ 10&=r(\pi+2)\\ r&=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}\end{aligned}$$
Checking the nature using $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=2\pi^2+4\pi>0\text{ for all }r$$
$\therefore\ A$ is always concave up, so there is a minimum at $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$.

At $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=10-\pi\left(\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{10(\pi+2)-10\pi}{\pi+2}\\ &=\dfrac{20}{\pi+2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the area is minimised when $r=\dfrac{10}{\pi+2}$ cm and the side of the square is $\dfrac{20}{\pi+2}$ cm.

items.part: If 1200 bags of jelly babies are produced, how many bags would be expected to contain less than the labelled weight?
items.sol:
\exfigure{166_q16_s1}

Standardising, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{220-224.7}{2.35}\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule, $95\%$ of weights lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<220)&=0.5\times(1-0.95)\\ &=0.025\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Expected number}&=1200\times 0.025\\ &=30\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 30 bags would be expected to be below 220 g.

Standardising, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{231-224.7}{2.35}\\ &=2.68\end{aligned}$$
Using the table:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>231)&=1-P(X\le 231)\\ &=1-\Phi(2.68)\\ &=1-0.9963\\ &=0.0037\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Expected number}&=0.0037\times 1200\\ &=4.44\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 4 bags would be expected to be over 231 g.
items.final: 4 bags would be expected to be over 231 g

items.part: Show that the area of the 4 rectangles is $\dfrac{p^4-1}{p-1}$ square units.
items.sol:
Each rectangle has width 1 and height $p^x$ at its left end ($x=0,1,2,3$):
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{rect}}&=1\times p^0+1\times p^1+1\times p^2+1\times p^3\\ &=1+p+p^2+p^3\end{aligned}$$
This is a GP with $a=1$, $r=p$, $n=4$, using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{rect}}&=\dfrac{1\left(p^4-1\right)}{p-1}\\ &=\dfrac{p^4-1}{p-1}\text{ u}^2\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: By finding the area under the curve $y=p^x$ between $x=0$ and $x=4$, and using the result in part (a), prove that $\ln p<p-1$.
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{curve}}&=\int_0^4 p^x\,dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{p^x}{\ln p}\right]_0^4\\ &=\dfrac{p^4}{\ln p}-\dfrac{p^0}{\ln p}\\ &=\dfrac{p^4-1}{\ln p}\end{aligned}$$
From the diagram, the rectangles lie under the curve, so $A_{\text{rect}}<A_{\text{curve}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{p^4-1}{p-1}&<\dfrac{p^4-1}{\ln p}\\ \dfrac{1}{p-1}&<\dfrac{1}{\ln p}\\ \ln p&<p-1\quad\text{as }p>1\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{324}$
items.sol:
Since $f(t)$ is a PDF, the total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^6 f(t)\,dt&=1\\ k\int_0^6 \left(36t-t^3\right)dt&=1\\ k\left[18t^2-\dfrac{t^4}{4}\right]_0^6&=1\\ k\left(18(6)^2-\dfrac{6^4}{4}-0\right)&=1\\ 648k-324k&=1\\ 324k&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{1}{324}\text{ as required}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Determine the mode waiting time.
items.sol:
The mode is where $f(t)$ is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}f(t)&=36kt-kt^3\\ &=\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}\\ f'(t)&=\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{3t^2}{324}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points when $f'(t)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{3t^2}{324}\\ \dfrac{3t^2}{324}&=\dfrac{1}{9}\\ t^2&=12\\ t&=\sqrt{12}\quad(t>0)\\ &=2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
Checking the nature:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(t)&=-\dfrac{6t}{324}\\ f''(2\sqrt{3})&=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{27}\end{aligned}$$
$f''(2\sqrt{3})<0$, so there is a maximum at $t=2\sqrt{3}$.

$\therefore$ the mode is $2\sqrt{3}$ minutes.

items.part: What is the probability that a candidate must wait for more than 3 minutes for a calculator check to take place, given that they have already waited for 1 minute.
items.sol:
Using conditional probability, $P(A\,|\,B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X>3\,|\,X\ge 1)&=\dfrac{P(X>3)}{P(X\ge 1)}\\ &=\dfrac{1-P(X\le 3)}{1-P(X<1)}\end{aligned}$$
With $f(t)=\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<3)&=\int_0^3\left(\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}\right)dt\\ &=\left[\dfrac{t^2}{18}-\dfrac{t^4}{1296}\right]_0^3\\ &=\dfrac{3^2}{18}-\dfrac{3^4}{1296}-0\\ &=\dfrac{7}{16}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P(X<1)&=\int_0^1\left(\dfrac{t}{9}-\dfrac{t^3}{324}\right)dt\\ &=\left[\dfrac{t^2}{18}-\dfrac{t^4}{1296}\right]_0^1\\ &=\dfrac{1^2}{18}-\dfrac{1^4}{1296}-0\\ &=\dfrac{71}{1296}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ P(X>3\,|\,X\ge 1)&=\dfrac{1-\frac{7}{16}}{1-\frac{71}{1296}}\\ &=\dfrac{729}{1225}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: A parabola with vertex $(2,-5)$ has a $y$-intercept of 11. Find the equation of the parabola.
items.sol:
Vertex form with vertex $(2,-5)$:
$$y=a(x-2)^2-5$$
When $x=0$, $y=11$:
$$\begin{aligned} 11 &= a(0-2)^2-5 \\ 11 &= 4a-5 \\ 16 &= 4a \\ a &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=4(x-2)^2-5$$
(Expanded form $y=4x^2-16x+11$ is also acceptable.)

items.part: If $3+\dfrac{1}{x}=\sqrt{15}$, find the exact value of $x$. Express your answer with a rational denominator.
items.sol:
Subtracting 3, then rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{x} &= \sqrt{15}-3 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{15}-3} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{15}+3}{15-9} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{15}+3}{6} \end{aligned}$$

The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 0.15+(3a+b)+0+(a-b)+0.05 \\ &= 0.2+4a \\ 4a &= 0.8 \\ a &= 0.2 \end{aligned}$$
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)=2.2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2.2 &= 0.15+2(3\times 0.2+b)+4(0.2-b)+5\times 0.05 \\ &= 2.4+2b-4b \\ -0.2 &= -2b \\ b &= 0.1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=0.2 \text{ and } b=0.1$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=\ln\left(\dfrac{x^2}{2x+1}\right)$.
items.sol:
Using log laws:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \ln(x^2)-\ln(2x+1) \\ &= 2\ln x-\ln(2x+1) \end{aligned}$$
$$y'=\dfrac{2}{x}-\dfrac{2}{2x+1}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int x^2(1-x^3)^5\,dx$.
items.sol:
Reverse chain rule, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(1-x^3)=-3x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int x^2(1-x^3)^5\,dx &= -\dfrac{1}{3}\int -3x^2(1-x^3)^5\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{(1-x^3)^6}{6}+C \\ &= -\dfrac{(1-x^3)^6}{18}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Use 3 applications of the trapezoidal rule to estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^{12}\sqrt{x}\,dx$. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
Three strips of width $h=\dfrac{12-0}{3}=4$:

\extable{309_q16_s_t1}

Using the trapezoidal rule with the function values from the table:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{12}\sqrt{x}\,dx &\approx \dfrac{12-0}{2\times 3}\big(0+2\sqrt{3}+2(2+2\sqrt{2})\big) \\ &= 26.24\ldots \\ &\approx 26.2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
When Alexia plugs her phone in to charge, the battery percentage displayed on her phone is given by the equation $B=-50e^{-0.6t}+92$. $B$ is the battery percentage and $t$ is the number of hours the phone has been charging for.
Sketch the graph of $B$ for $t\ge 0$.

When Alexia plugs her phone in to charge, the battery percentage displayed on her phone is given by the equation $B=-50e^{-0.6t}+92$. $B$ is the battery percentage and $t$ is the number of hours the phone has been charging for.
What is the maximum charge capacity of Alexia’s phone battery?
items.sol: $B\to 92$ as $t\to\infty$, so the maximum charge capacity is $92\%$.

items.part:
When Alexia plugs her phone in to charge, the battery percentage displayed on her phone is given by the equation $B=-50e^{-0.6t}+92$. $B$ is the battery percentage and $t$ is the number of hours the phone has been charging for.
At what rate is Alexia’s phone charging after being plugged in for 2 hours? Give your answer rounded to the nearest whole.
items.sol:
Differentiating $B=-50e^{-0.6t}+92$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dB}{dt} &= -0.6\times(-50e^{-0.6t}) \\ &= 30e^{-0.6t} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dB}{dt} &= 30e^{-0.6\times 2} \\ &= 9.0\ldots \\ &\approx 9 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ charging at $9\%$ per hour.

items.part:
The graph of $y=f'(x)$ is shown below. Sketch a graph of $y=f(x)$ on the same axes, given that $f(0)=20$.

\exfigure{309_q18_1}

On the axes below, graph the function $y=|2x+1|-3$ labelling all important features.

\exfigure{309_q19_1}
Hence, or otherwise, solve $|2x+1|-3\le 0$.
items.sol:
From the graph, $|2x+1|-3\le 0$ between the $x$-intercepts:
$$-2\le x\le 1$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx &= 2\int\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx \\ &= -2\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Amalie is bouncing on a trampoline. Her first bounce takes her to a height of 30 cm above the trampoline. She then lands on the trampoline and continues to bounce. Each time Amalie bounces, she rises to 70% of her previous height above the trampoline. Find the total distance Amalie will cover eventually.
items.sol:
\exfigure{309_q21_s1}

The heights $30, 21, \ldots$ form a geometric sequence with $a=30$, $r=0.7$, and each height is travelled up and down:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total distance} &= 2S_\infty \\ &= 2\times\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= 2\times\dfrac{30}{1-0.7} \\ &= 200 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Amalie eventually travels 200 cm.

items.part:
A function $y=f(x)$ undergoes the following transformations:

\begin{itemize}
\item A reflection in the $x$ axis
\item Then a horizontal dilation with scale factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item Then a horizontal translation 7 units left
\end{itemize}

The point $P(x,y)$ lies on $y=f(x)$. The image of $P$ on the transformed function is $P'(-2,1)$. Find the coordinates of $P$.
items.sol:
Dilation factor $\dfrac{1}{a}$ with $a=3$, translation $b=7$ left, reflection factor $k=-1$.

$x$-coordinate:
$$\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \dfrac{1}{a}x-b \\ -2 &= \dfrac{1}{3}x-7 \\ 5 &= \dfrac{1}{3}x \\ x &= 15 \end{aligned}$$
$y$-coordinate:
$$\begin{aligned} y_2 &= ky \\ 1 &= -y \\ y &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(15,-1)$$

items.part:
Consider the functions $f(x)=x^2-6x$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{x+5}$.
Find an equation for the composite function $g(f(x))$.

Consider the functions $f(x)=x^2-6x$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{x+5}$.
Hence find the domain of $g(f(x))$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-6x+5 &\ge 0 \\ (x-5)(x-1) &\ge 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x\le 1 \text{ or } x\ge 5$$

items.part:
In the diagram below, the length of minor arc $XY$ is $\dfrac{5\pi}{2}$ cm, $\theta$ is the angle subtended by that arc, and the area of shaded sector $XOY$ is $\dfrac{15\pi}{4}\text{ cm}^2$. Find the exact value of $\theta$ in radians.

\exfigure{309_q24_1}
items.sol:
Arc length $l=r\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5\pi}{2} &= r\theta \\ r &= \dfrac{5\pi}{2\theta} \quad (1) \end{aligned}$$
Sector area $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:
$$\dfrac{15\pi}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta \quad (2)$$
Substitute (1) into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{15\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{2\theta}\right)^2\theta \\ \dfrac{15\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{25\pi^2}{4\theta} \\ 30 &= \dfrac{25\pi}{\theta} \\ \theta &= \dfrac{25\pi}{30} \\ &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows plane $XYZ$ inside a rectangular prism. $M$ is the midpoint of the base diagonal $YZ$. Find, correct to the nearest degree, the size of angle $WMX$.

\exfigure{309_q25_1}
items.sol:
\exfigure{309_q25_s1}

Pythagoras' theorem in the base:
$$\begin{aligned} YZ^2 &= 8^2+6^2 \\ &= 100 \\ YZ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$M$ is the midpoint of the diagonal of the rectangle, so $MZ=5$ and $WM=5$.

In right-angled triangle $WMX$ ($WX=3$):
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{3}{5} \\ \theta &= 30.9\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 31^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle WMX\approx 31^\circ$$

items.part: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=\dfrac{\sqrt{x-1}}{x^2}$ at the point where $x=2$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=(x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}} & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{2}(x-1)^{-\frac{1}{2}} & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}x^2(x-1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-2x(x-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{x^4} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}(2)^2(2-1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-2(2)(2-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2^4} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m_T=-\dfrac{1}{8}$$

items.part:
A bullet train is travelling from Sendai to Tokyo. The train leaves Sendai and accelerates at a constant rate until it reaches 304 km/h. It continues at this speed for 45 minutes before decelerating at a constant rate and coming to a stop in Tokyo. The total travel time is $1\dfrac{1}{2}$ hours. By considering the velocity-time graph shown below, find the total distance the train travelled.

\exfigure{309_q27_1}
items.sol:
Distance is the area of the trapezium, with parallel sides $0.75$ h and $1.5$ h and height 304:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{h}{2}(a+b) \\ &= \dfrac{304}{2}(0.75+1.5) \\ &= 342 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The train travelled 342 km.

items.part:

If Tish produces 400 packets of stickers per month, how many of these can she sell?
items.sol:
$198$ is 1 standard deviation below the mean and $204$ is 2 standard deviations above.

items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(\text{too few}\mid\text{can't sell}) &= \dfrac{P(\text{too few}\cap\text{can't sell})}{P(\text{can't sell})} \\ &= \dfrac{0.5-0.5\times 0.68}{1-0.815} \\ &= 0.864\ldots \\ &\approx 86\% \end{aligned}$$

Show that the number of mangoes, $M$, produced by May’s orchard each year is given by $M=-10x^2+200x+8000$ where $x$ is the number of additional trees planted.
items.sol:
Number of trees $=20+x$; mangoes per tree $=400-10x$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= (20+x)(400-10x) \\ &= 8000-200x+400x-10x^2 \\ &= -10x^2+200x+8000 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

How many \$400 withdrawals can Hannah make from her travel fund?
items.sol:
The fund runs out when $A_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3776.76(1.005)^n-80400(1.005)^n+80400 \\ &= -76623.24(1.005)^n+80400 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The time in minutes taken for Claudia to score her first point in a tennis match can be represented by a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function given by:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} ke^x & \text{for } 0\le x\le 4\\ ke & \text{for } 4<x\le 10\\ 0 & \text{for all other } x\end{cases}$$
Find the exact value of the constant $k$.
items.sol:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= \int_0^4 ke^x\,dx+\int_4^{10} ke\,dx \\ &= \Big[ke^x\Big]_0^4+\Big[kex\Big]_4^{10} \\ &= ke^4-ke^0+10ke-4ke \\ &= ke^4-k+6ke \\ &= k(e^4+6e-1) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{e^4+6e-1}$$

items.part:
The time in minutes taken for Claudia to score her first point in a tennis match can be represented by a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function given by:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} ke^x & \text{for } 0\le x\le 4\\ ke & \text{for } 4<x\le 10\\ 0 & \text{for all other } x\end{cases}$$
The median time taken for Claudia to score her first point is less than 4 minutes. Find this median time, giving your answer correct to the nearest second.
items.sol:
The median $x$ satisfies:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5 &= \int_0^x \dfrac{1}{e^4+6e-1}e^t\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{1}{e^4+6e-1}\Big[e^t\Big]_0^x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 34.9\ldots &= e^x-e^0 \\ &= e^x-1 \\ e^x &= 35.9\ldots \\ x &= \ln 35.9\ldots \\ &= 3.582\ldots \text{ minutes} \\ &\approx 3 \text{ min } 35 \text{ s} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Claudia's median time to score a point is 3 minutes 35 seconds.

items.part:

\exfigure{309_q33_1}
items.sol:
The parabola is above $y=-\sqrt{2x+16}$ for $0\le x\le 10$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{10}\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{x}{5}-4-\left(-(2x+16)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\right)dx \\ &= \int_0^{10}\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{x}{5}-4\right)dx+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{10}2(2x+16)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{x^3}{75}+\dfrac{x^2}{10}-4x\right]_0^{10}+\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{2(2x+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_0^{10} \\ &= \left(-\dfrac{10^3}{75}+\dfrac{10^2}{10}-4(10)-0\right)+\left(\dfrac{(2(10)+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-\dfrac{(2(0)+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{130}{3}+\dfrac{152}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{22}{3}\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=10e^{-x}(1-x)$.
Find the exact coordinates of any stationary points on $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=10e^{-x} & v&=1-x\\ u'&=-10e^{-x} & v'&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= u'v+uv' \\ &= -10e^{-x}(1-x)-10e^{-x} \\ &= -10e^{-x}(1-x+1) \\ &= -10e^{-x}(2-x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points when $f'(x)=0$.

$-10e^{-x}=0$ has no solutions, so $2-x=0$:
$$x=2$$
Using the product rule on $f'(x)=-10e^{-x}(2-x)$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=-10e^{-x} & v&=2-x\\ u'&=10e^{-x} & v'&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= u'v+uv' \\ &= 10e^{-x}(2-x)+10e^{-x} \\ &= 10e^{-x}(3-x) \end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature at $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(2) &= 10e^{-2}(3-2) \\ &= 1.3\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$f''(2)>0$, so a local minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} f(2) &= 10e^{-2}(1-2) \\ &= -10e^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $(2,-10e^{-2})$ is a local minimum.

items.part:

items.sol:
Possible points of inflection when $f''(x)=0$:
$$0=10e^{-x}(3-x)$$
$10e^{-x}=0$ has no solutions, so $x=3$.

\extable{309_q34_s_t1}

Concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $x=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(3) &= 10e^{-3}(1-3) \\ &= -20e^{-3} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $(3,-20e^{-3})$ is a point of inflection.

items.part:
Matty and Charlie are playing a game where they take turns tossing their own coin. Matty’s coin is a fair coin, while Charlie’s coin has a $\dfrac{1}{3}$ chance of showing heads. Matty goes first and the first person whose coin toss shows a head wins the game.
By drawing a probability tree or otherwise, find the probability that Charlie wins the game on her first or second toss.

Matty and Charlie are playing a game where they take turns tossing their own coin. Matty’s coin is a fair coin, while Charlie’s coin has a $\dfrac{1}{3}$ chance of showing heads. Matty goes first and the first person whose coin toss shows a head wins the game.
What is the probability that Charlie will win the game?
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Charlie wins}) &= P(\bar{M}C)+P(\bar{M}\bar{C}\bar{M}C)+P(\bar{M}\bar{C}\bar{M}\bar{C}\bar{M}C)+\cdots \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\cdots \end{aligned}$$
This is an infinite geometric series with $a=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $r=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\div\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

$f'(x)=0$ at the stationary points $x=-4,\,-2,\,3$.

The sign of $f'(x)$ follows where $f$ increases or decreases:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } x<-4 &&f\text{ decreasing}\\ f'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } -4<x<-2 &&f\text{ increasing}\\ f'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } -2<x<3 &&f\text{ decreasing}\\ f'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } x>3 &&f\text{ increasing}\end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
The jump lengths are $180,\ 135,\ 101.25,\ \ldots$

Testing for a common ratio:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}&=\dfrac{135}{180}\\&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}&=\dfrac{101.25}{135}\\&=\dfrac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$, the sequence is geometric.

items.part:
A frog jumps 180 cm to a lily pad.  It then jumps 135 cm to the next lily pad, 101.25 cm to the next lily pad and so on.
The first and final lily pad are 8 metres apart.  Following this pattern, can the frog jump from the first lily pad to the last lily pad?  Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.
items.sol:
The frog's first jump lands on the first lily pad, and the last lily pad is 800 cm further, so the frog can reach it only if its total distance reaches $180+800=980$ cm.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=180$, $r=0.75$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{180}{1-0.75}\\&=720\end{aligned}$$
$S_\infty=720<980$

$\therefore$ the frog will not be able to jump from the first to the last lily pad.
items.final: The frog will not be able to jump from the first to the last lily pad (S_\infty = 720 < 980).

items.part: A farmer is monitoring the salinity of a dam on his property.  On the first day of observations, the salinity is measured as 0.15 ppt (parts per thousand).  Each subsequent day, the salinity increases by 2% of the previous day’s measurement.  When the measurement exceeds 10 ppt, the water will no longer be suitable for livestock and the farmer will begin to treat the dam.  On which day will the farmer need to start treating his dam?
items.sol:
The measurements $0.15,\ 0.153,\ 0.15606,\ \ldots$ form a geometric sequence with $a=0.15$, $r=1.02$.

The salinity reaches 10 ppt when $T_n=ar^{n-1}=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}10&=0.15(1.02)^{n-1}\\\dfrac{200}{3}&=(1.02)^{n-1}\\\log_{1.02}\left(\dfrac{200}{3}\right)&=n-1\\n-1&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{200}{3}\right)}{\ln(1.02)} &&(\text{change of base})\\n&=213.078176\end{aligned}$$
$n$ is a whole number, so the salinity first exceeds 10 ppt on day 214.

$\therefore$ the farmer needs to start treating the dam on the $214$th day.
items.final: The farmer needs to start treating the dam on the 214th day.

items.part: The first 3 terms of a geometric series are $2x+3,\ x,\ 2x-3$.  Find the value(s) of $x$.
items.sol:
Since the series is geometric, $\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x}{2x+3}&=\dfrac{2x-3}{x}\\x^2&=(2x-3)(2x+3)\\4x^2-9&=x^2\\3x^2&=9\\x&=\pm\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}$.
Prove that $f(x)$ is an even function.
items.sol:
A function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=\dfrac{8}{(-x)^2+4}\\&=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}\\&=f(x)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}$ is an even function.

items.part:

items.sol:
$x^2+4\ge 4>0$ for all $x$, so the denominator is never zero.

$\therefore$ the domain is all real $x$.

The minimum value of $x^2+4$ is 4 (when $x=0$), so the maximum value of $y=\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}$ is 2.

As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{8}{x^2+4}\to 0$.

$\therefore$ the range is $0<y\le 2$.

$$T_n=200+0.9\times T_{n-1}$$
where $T_0=200$ and $n\ge 1$.

items.part:
A company starts a page on social media.  Initially, the page has 200 followers $(ie\ T_0=200)$.  Each day the page gains an extra 200 followers but loses 10% of the number of followers on the previous day.

Let $T_n$ be the number of followers on the $n$th day.
Show that $T_n=2000\left(1-(0.9)^{n+1}\right)$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}T_0&=200\\T_1&=200+0.9\times T_0\\&=200+0.9\times 200\\T_2&=200+0.9\times T_1\\&=200+0.9\times(200+0.9\times 200)\\&=200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2\\T_3&=200+0.9\times T_2\\&=200+0.9\times(200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2)\\&=200+200\times 0.9+200\times 0.9^2+200\times 0.9^3\end{aligned}$$
Each term is the sum of a geometric series with $a=200$, $r=0.9$ and $n+1$ terms, using $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ T_n&=\dfrac{200(1-(0.9)^{n+1})}{1-0.9}\\&=2000(1-(0.9)^{n+1})\end{aligned}$$

items.part: The sum of the first ten terms of an arithmetic sequence is $(-50)$.  The next ten terms of this sequence add to $(-450)$.  Find the first term and common difference of the sequence.
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $S_{10}=-50$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{10}{2}\big(2a+(10-1)d\big)&=-50\\5(2a+9d)&=-50\\2a+9d&=-10 &&(1)\end{aligned}$$
The first 20 terms add to $(-50)+(-450)=-500$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{20}{2}\big(2a+(20-1)d\big)&=-500\\10(2a+19d)&=-500\\2a+19d&=-50 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
$(2)-(1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}10d&=-40\\d&=-4\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}2a+9(-4)&=-10\\2a&=26\\a&=13\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the first term is $13$ and the common difference is $-4$.

$y=\dfrac{3x}{\cos 4x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=3x & v&=\cos4x\\u'&=3 & v'&=-4\sin4x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{3\cos4x-3x\times(-4\sin4x)}{\cos^2 4x}\\&=\dfrac{3\cos4x+12x\sin4x}{\cos^2 4x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find:
$\displaystyle\int 5x^2+8x-3\,dx$
items.sol:
Integrating term by term:
$$\begin{aligned}\int(5x^2+8x-3)\,dx&=\dfrac{5x^3}{3}+\dfrac{8x^2}{2}-3x+c\\&=\dfrac{5x^3}{3}+4x^2-3x+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find:
$\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{(8x-1)^3}\,dx$
items.sol:
Writing with a negative index and using
$$\int(ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{1}{(8x-1)^3}\,dx&=\int(8x-1)^{-3}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{(8x-1)^{-2}}{8\times(-2)}+c\\&=\dfrac{1}{-16}(8x-1)^{-2}+c\\&=\dfrac{-1}{16(8x-1)^2}+c\end{aligned}$$
