Find:
$\displaystyle\int \cos x\sin^5 x\,dx$
items.sol:
Let $f(x)=\sin x$, so $f'(x)=\cos x$ and the integrand is $f'(x)[f(x)]^5$.

Using the reverse chain rule:
$$\int\cos x\sin^5x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{6}\sin^6x+c$$

items.part:
Calculate the following definite integrals. Leave your answers in exact form where necessary.
$\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0} \dfrac{6}{x+3}\,dx$
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{x+a}\,dx=\ln|x+a|+c$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{6}{x+3}\,dx&=6\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{1}{x+3}\,dx\\&=\Big[6\ln|x+3|\Big]_{-2}^{0}\\&=6\ln|0+3|-6\ln|(-2)+3|\\&=6\ln3-6\ln1\\&=6\ln3\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Calculate the following definite integrals. Leave your answers in exact form where necessary.
$\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sec^2 3x\,dx$
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int\sec^2 ax\,dx=\dfrac{1}{a}\tan ax+c$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\sec^2 3x\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{1}{3}\tan3x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\tan\left(3\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\dfrac{1}{3}\tan\left(3\times\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times0-\dfrac{1}{3}\times(-1)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=x^3-3x^2+4$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^3-3x^2+4\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3x^2-6x\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3x^2-6x&=0\\3x(x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$x=0$ or $x=2$

When $x=0$, $y=0^3-3\times0^2+4=4$

When $x=2$, $y=2^3-3\times2^2+4=0$

$\therefore$ Stationary points are $(0,4)$ and $(2,0)$

items.part: For which values of $x$ is the curve $y=5x^3-2x^2+6x-1$ concave up?
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=5x^3-2x^2+6x-1\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=15x^2-4x+6\\\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=30x-4\end{aligned}$$
Concave up when $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}30x-4&>0\\30x&>4\\x&>\dfrac{4}{30}\\x&>\dfrac{2}{15}\end{aligned}$$

The curve is below the $x$-axis for $0<x<2$, so take the absolute value of the integral:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\left|\int_0^2(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx\right|\\&=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{2x^2}{2}\right]_0^2\right|\\&=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right|\\&=\left|\dfrac{2^4}{4}-\dfrac{2^3}{3}-2^2-\left(\dfrac{0^4}{4}-\dfrac{0^3}{3}-0^2\right)\right|\\&=\dfrac{8}{3}\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$

Test $(2,4)$ in $y=2^x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=4\\\text{RHS}&=2^2\\&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore(2,4)$ lies on $y=2^x$.

Test $(2,4)$ in $y=-2x^2+8x-4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=4\\\text{RHS}&=-2(2)^2+8\times2-4\\&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore(2,4)$ lies on $y=-2x^2+8x-4$.

$\therefore(2,4)$ is a point of intersection of $y=-2x^2+8x-4$ and $y=2^x$.

The vertex lies on the axis of symmetry, $x=\dfrac{-b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{-8}{2\times(-2)}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
From (a), $y=4$ when $x=2$.

$\therefore$ Vertex is $(2,4)$

\exfigure{572_q18_s1}

From the graph, the parabola is above $y=2^x$ between the points of intersection $x=1$ and $x=2$:
$$\therefore 1<x<2$$

Equating $y=2x^2+x-9$ and $y=3x-5$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x^2+x-9&=3x-5\\2x^2-2x-4&=0\\x^2-x-2&=0\\(x-2)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x=2$ or $x=-1$

The line is above the parabola for $-1<x<2$, so
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-1}^{2}\big(3x-5-(2x^2+x-9)\big)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{2}(-2x^2+2x+4)\,dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{-2x^3}{3}+\dfrac{2x^2}{2}+4x\right]_{-1}^{2}\\&=\left[\dfrac{-2x^3}{3}+x^2+4x\right]_{-1}^{2}\\&=\left(\dfrac{-2(2)^3}{3}+2^2+4\times2\right)-\left(\dfrac{-2(-1)^3}{3}+(-1)^2+4\times(-1)\right)\\&=9\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=x\sin x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\sin x\\u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x\cos x+\sin x$$

items.part: Hence or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$
items.sol:
From (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin x)=x\cos x+\sin x$, so integrating both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}\int(x\cos x+\sin x)\,dx&=x\sin x\\\int x\cos x\,dx+\int\sin x\,dx&=x\sin x\\\int x\cos x\,dx-\cos x&=x\sin x+c\\\int x\cos x\,dx&=x\sin x+\cos x+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A certain radioactive isotope element decays exponentially according to the model $A=A_0e^{kt}$ where $A$ is the number of grams of the isotope at the end of $t$ days and $A_0$ is the number of grams present initially.

Initially there are 200 grams of this isotope. After 10 days, 16 grams of this substance remain. What is the rate of decay after 5 days? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
Using the model $A=A_0e^{kt}$.

When $t=0$, $A=200$, so $A_0=200$:
$$A=200e^{kt}$$
When $t=10$, $A=16$:
$$\begin{aligned}16&=200e^{10k}\\\dfrac{16}{200}&=e^{10k}\\\ln\dfrac{16}{200}&=10k\\k&=\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{16}{200}\end{aligned}$$
Differentiating,
$$\dfrac{dA}{dt}=200ke^{kt}$$
When $t=5$, with $k=\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{16}{200}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{dt}&=200ke^{5k}\\&=-14.28767882\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Rate of decay is $14.29\text{ grams/day}$

items.part: Show that the sequence $\log 3,\log 9,\log 27,\log 81,\ldots$ is an arithmetic sequence.
items.sol:
Using the log law $\log a^n=n\log a$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\log3,\log9,\log27,\log81,\ldots\\&=\log3,\log3^2,\log3^3,\log3^4,\ldots\\&=\log3,2\log3,3\log3,4\log3,\ldots\end{aligned}$$
Testing for a common difference:
$$\begin{aligned}T_2-T_1&=2\log3-\log3\\&=\log3\\T_3-T_2&=3\log3-2\log3\\&=\log3\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ AP where $a=\log3$, $d=\log3$

items.part: Hence or otherwise find the sum to 10 terms of the sequence $\log 3,\log 9,\log 27,\log 81,\ldots$ Leave your answer in simplest exact form.
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$ with $a=\log3$, $d=\log3$, $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{10}&=\dfrac{10}{2}\big[2\log3+(10-1)\log3\big]\\&=5(2\log3+9\log3)\\&=5(11\log3)\\&=55\log3\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ in the domain $0\le x\le \pi$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. For $0\le x\le\pi$, $2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lies between $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{7\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\\2x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=1$$
When $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{7\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-1$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-4<0 &&\text{maximum}\\x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{7\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=4>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12},1\right)$ is a relative maximum turning point and $\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12},-1\right)$ is a relative minimum turning point.
items.final: $\left(\frac{\pi}{12},1\right)$ is a relative maximum and $\left(\frac{7\pi}{12},-1\right)$ is a relative minimum

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ in the domain $0\le x\le \pi$.
Find the coordinates of the points of inflection.
items.sol:
Points of inflection can occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=0,\pi,2\pi\end{aligned}$$
For $0\le x\le\pi$, $2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\ge\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $0$ is rejected:
$$\begin{aligned}2x&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\text{ or }2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\2x&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\text{ or }\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\\x&=\dfrac{2\pi}{6}\left(=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\text{ or }\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$\sin\theta$ changes sign at $\theta=\pi$ and $\theta=2\pi$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ changes sign at both values: the concavity changes.

When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$$
When $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$$
$\therefore$ Points of inflection are $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},0\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6},0\right)$
\exfigure{572_q23_s1}

items.part: A sequence is defined by the rule $T_n=5^n-5n$ where $n\ge 1$. Find the sum of the first 20 terms. Leave your answer in simplest index form.
items.sol:
Each term is a power of $5$ minus a multiple of $5$, so the sum splits into two series:
$$\begin{aligned}\sum_{n=1}^{20}(5^n-5n)&=5^1-5\times1+5^2-5\times2+5^3-5\times3+\ldots+5^{20}-5\times20\\&=5^1+5^2+5^3+\ldots+5^{20}-(5\times1+5\times2+5\times3+\ldots+5\times20)\end{aligned}$$
Geometric series where $a=5$, $r=5$, $n=20$

Arithmetic series where $a=5$, $d=5$, $n=20$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ and $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{20}&=\dfrac{5(5^{20}-1)}{5-1}-\dfrac{20}{2}\big(2\times5+(20-1)\times5\big)\\&=\dfrac{5(5^{20}-1)}{4}-1050\end{aligned}$$

Let $d$ km be Feifei's rowing distance. The river is $800\text{ m}=0.8\text{ km}$ wide, so by Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with legs $0.8$ and $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}d^2&=0.8^2+x^2\\&=0.64+x^2\\d&=\sqrt{0.64+x^2}\end{aligned}$$
She rows $d$ km at $5$ km/h and runs $(2.5-x)$ km at $7$ km/h. Using time $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$t=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{5}$$

Writing the square root as a power and differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{5}\\t&=\dfrac{2.5-x}{7}+\dfrac{1}{5}(0.64+x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\\dfrac{dt}{dx}&=-\dfrac{1}{7}+\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times2x(0.64+x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=-\dfrac{1}{7}+\dfrac{x}{5\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dt}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{1}{7}+\dfrac{x}{5\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}&=0\\\dfrac{x}{5\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}&=\dfrac{1}{7}\\\dfrac{x}{5}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{0.64+x^2}}{7}\\\dfrac{7x}{5}&=\sqrt{0.64+x^2}\\\dfrac{49x^2}{25}&=x^2+0.64\\49x^2&=25x^2+16\\24x^2&=16\\x^2&=\dfrac{16}{24}\\x&=\pm0.8164965809\ldots\end{aligned}$$
Since $x>0$ (a distance),
$$x=0.8164965809\ldots\approx0.82\ (2\text{ d.p.})$$
Testing the nature with the first derivative:

\extable{572_q25_t1}

$\therefore$ When $x=0.816\ldots$ the minimum amount of time is taken for Feifei to reach Airi.

Feifei must run
$$\begin{aligned}2.5-0.816\ldots&=1.683503419\ldots\\&\approx1.68\text{ km (2 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=2e^t+4e^{-t}$, $t$ is in seconds and $v$ m/s. Initially, the particle is at the origin $O$.
Is the particle ever at rest? Give reasons.
items.sol:
Since $2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all values of $t$,
$$2e^t+4e^{-t}>0$$
for all values of $t$.

$\therefore$ The particle will never be at rest.
items.final: No, the particle is never at rest, since $2e^t+4e^{-t}>0$ for all $t$.

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=2e^t+4e^{-t}$, $t$ is in seconds and $v$ m/s. Initially, the particle is at the origin $O$.
Find the displacement function, $x$, of the particle, at time $t$ seconds.
items.sol:
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int(2e^t+4e^{-t})\,dt\\&=2e^t-4e^{-t}+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2e^0-4e^0+C\\C&=-2+4\\\therefore C&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=2e^t-4e^{-t}+2$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=2e^t+4e^{-t}$, $t$ is in seconds and $v$ m/s. Initially, the particle is at the origin $O$.
Find the time when the particle is at $x=4$.(Give your answer in exact form)
items.sol:
When $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}2e^t-4e^{-t}+2&=4\\2(e^t-2e^{-t}-1)&=0\\e^t-\dfrac{2}{e^t}-1&=0\\e^{2t}-e^t-2&=0 &&(\times e^t)\\(e^t-2)(e^t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^t+1>0$, $e^t-2=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^t&=2\\t&=\ln2\end{aligned}$$

When Fred was born, his parents opened a new savings account and made a deposit of \$300. At the start of each subsequent six-month period, his parents make a deposit of \$300. The account earns an interest rate of 6% per annum, compounded half-yearly.

Let $A_n$ be the amount (in dollars) in the account at the end of $n^{th}$ half-year.
Show that $A_2=300\times(1.03)^2+300\times(1.03)$.
items.sol:
$r=\dfrac{6\%}{2}=3\%$ per half-year.

Each deposit is made at the start of a half-year and earns interest for that half-year:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=300(1.03)\\A_2&=(A_1+300)\times1.03\\&=(300\times1.03+300)\times1.03\\&=300\times1.03^2+300\times1.03\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
When Fred was born, his parents opened a new savings account and made a deposit of \$300. At the start of each subsequent six-month period, his parents make a deposit of \$300. The account earns an interest rate of 6% per annum, compounded half-yearly.

Let $A_n$ be the amount (in dollars) in the account at the end of $n^{th}$ half-year.
Show that $A_n=10300(1.03^n-1)$.
items.sol:
Continuing the pattern, the bracket is a GP with $a=1.03$, $r=1.03$ and $n$ terms, summed with $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=300(1.03)\\A_2&=300\times1.03^2+300\times1.03\\&\;\;\vdots\\A_n&=300\times1.03^n+300\times1.03^{n-1}+\dots+300\times1.03\\&=300(1.03^n+1.03^{n-1}+\dots+1.03)\\&=300\times1.03\times\dfrac{1.03^n-1}{1.03-1}\\&=10300(1.03^n-1)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
When Fred was born, his parents opened a new savings account and made a deposit of \$300. At the start of each subsequent six-month period, his parents make a deposit of \$300. The account earns an interest rate of 6% per annum, compounded half-yearly.

$18$ years $=36$ half-years, so $n=36$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{36}&=10300(1.03^{36}-1)\\&=\$19\,552\text{ (nearest dollar)}\end{aligned}$$

An object that was initially at the origin moves with velocity ($v$ m/s) given by $v=24+10t-t^2$.
Find the maximum speed of the object.
items.sol:
$v=-t^2+10t+24$

The maximum speed is at the turning point of this concave down parabola, $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=-\dfrac{10}{2\times(-1)}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}v_{\max}&=24+10\times5-5^2\\&=49\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An object that was initially at the origin moves with velocity ($v$ m/s) given by $v=24+10t-t^2$.
Find the acceleration when the object is at rest.
items.sol:
The object is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-t^2+10t+24&=0\\t^2-10t-24&=0\\(t-12)(t+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $t\ge0$, $t=12$.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:

items.part:
An object that was initially at the origin moves with velocity ($v$ m/s) given by $v=24+10t-t^2$.
Find the total distance travelled by the object during the first 15 seconds.
items.sol:
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int v\,dt\\&=\int(-t^2+10t+24)\,dt\\&=-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+5t^2+24t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially at the origin: $t=0$, $x=0$ gives $0=0+0+0+C$, so $C=0$.
$$x=-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+5t^2+24t$$
The object is at rest at $t=12$ (from (b)) and changes direction there, so find the displacement at $t=0$, $12$ and $15$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=0: & x&=0\\t&=12: & x&=-\dfrac{12^3}{3}+5\times12^2+24\times12=432\\t&=15: & x&=-\dfrac{15^3}{3}+5\times15^2+24\times15=360\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance travelled}&=432+(432-360)\\&=504\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:

Let \$$A_n$ be the amount owing after the $n^{th}$ repayment has been made.
Show that $A_n=(1000000-200M)(1.005)^n+200M$.
items.sol:
Continuing the pattern, the bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.005$ and $n$ terms, summed with $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_2&=1000000\times1.005^2-M\times1.005-M\\&\;\;\vdots\\A_n&=1000000\times1.005^n-M\times1.005^{n-1}-M\times1.005^{n-2}-\dots-M\\&=1000000\times1.005^n-M(1.005^{n-1}+1.005^{n-2}+\dots+1)\\&=1000000\times1.005^n-M\times\dfrac{1.005^n-1}{1.005-1}\\&=1000000\times1.005^n-200M(1.005^n-1)\\&=(1000000-200M)\times1.005^n+200M\end{aligned}$$

The acceleration ($a$ m/s$^2$) of an object at time $t$ seconds is given by $a=\dfrac{-1}{(5t+1)^2}$. The object is initially 3 metres to the left of the origin travelling with velocity 1 m/s.
Find an expression for the object's velocity ($v$) at time $t$.
items.sol:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int a\,dt\\&=\int-(5t+1)^{-2}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{-(5t+1)^{-2+1}}{(-2+1)\times5}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $v=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}1&=\dfrac{1}{5(5\times0+1)}+C\\C&=0.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$$

items.part:
The acceleration ($a$ m/s$^2$) of an object at time $t$ seconds is given by $a=\dfrac{-1}{(5t+1)^2}$. The object is initially 3 metres to the left of the origin travelling with velocity 1 m/s.
Find the limiting speed of the object.
items.sol:
$v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$

As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}\to0$, so
$$v\to0.8$$
$\therefore$ The limiting speed of the object is $0.8$ m/s.

items.part:
The acceleration ($a$ m/s$^2$) of an object at time $t$ seconds is given by $a=\dfrac{-1}{(5t+1)^2}$. The object is initially 3 metres to the left of the origin travelling with velocity 1 m/s.
Find the position of the object at the end of the 10$^{\text{th}}$ second. (Answer to the nearest metre)
items.sol:
Integrating $v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int v\,dt\\&=\int\left(\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8\right)dt\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{\ln(5t+1)}{5}+0.8t+C\\&=\dfrac{\ln(5t+1)}{25}+0.8t+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3&=\dfrac{\ln(5\times0+1)}{25}+0.8\times0+C\\\therefore C&=-3\end{aligned}$$
$$x=\dfrac{1}{25}\ln(5t+1)+0.8t-3$$
When $t=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{1}{25}\ln(5\times10+1)+0.8\times10-3\\&=5.157\ldots\\&\approx5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The object is about $5$ m to the right of the origin.
items.final: about $5$ m to the right of the origin

items.part:
Seats in a theatre are arranged in rows. The number of seats in this theatre form the terms of an arithmetic series.

The sixth row has 23 seats, and the fifteenth row has 50 seats. If the theatre has 20 rows, how many seats are in the theatre?
items.sol:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $T_6=23$ and $T_{15}=50$:
$$\begin{aligned}a+5d&=23\\a+14d&=50\end{aligned}$$
Solving simultaneously (subtract the first equation from the second):
$$\begin{aligned}9d&=27\\d&=3\\a&=8\end{aligned}$$
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a+(n-1)d\big]$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{20}&=\dfrac{20}{2}\big[2\times 8+19\times 3\big]\\&=730\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ There are a total of 730 seats.

items.part: Prove $\dfrac{1}{\sec x-\tan x}+\dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}=2\sec x$.
items.sol:
Adding the fractions and using $\sec^2 x-\tan^2 x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{\sec x-\tan x}+\dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\\&=\dfrac{\sec x+\tan x+\sec x-\tan x}{\sec^2 x-\tan^2 x}\\&=\dfrac{2\sec x}{1}\\&=2\sec x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

Determine the probability that Andrew will arrive late to his next winter business meeting.
items.sol:
Andrew is late on each branch with probability $1-P(\text{on time})$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{late})&=P(\text{dry, late})+P(\text{rain, late})+P(\text{snow, late})\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{5}+\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{9}{10}\\&=\dfrac{9}{20}\end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{rain}\mid\text{late})&=\dfrac{P(\text{rain and late})}{P(\text{late})}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{3}{5}}{\frac{9}{20}}\\&=\dfrac{4}{9}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A random variable is normally distributed with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. The table provided at the back of this exam gives the probability that this random variable lies below $z$ for some positive values of $z$.

The weekly mileages covered by a sales rep, $M$ miles, are normally distributed with a mean of 365 and variance of 600.

Find the probability that in a random week the rep will cover a mileage between 380 and 410.
items.sol:
The variance is 600, so $\sigma=\sqrt{600}$. Standardising with $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ and reading the table:
$$\begin{aligned}P(380<M<410)&=P(M<410)-P(M<380)\\&=P\left(z<\dfrac{410-365}{\sqrt{600}}\right)-P\left(z<\dfrac{380-365}{\sqrt{600}}\right)\\&=P(z<1.83712\ldots)-P(z<0.61237\ldots)\\&=0.9671-0.7291\\&=0.238\end{aligned}$$

In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $OA=10$ and side 5 (the distance from $O$ to the garden bed), let $\theta$ be the angle at $O$, half of $\angle AOB$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{5}{10}\\\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
By symmetry:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle AOB&=2\theta\\&=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{major }\angle AOB&=2\pi-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Using the arc length $l=r\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Arc length}&=10\times\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{40\pi}{3}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

The lawn covered is the circle minus the minor segment cut off by $AB$. Using segment area $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\pi r^2-\left[\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)\right]\\&=\pi\times 10^2-\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right]\\&=100\pi-\dfrac{100\pi}{3}+50\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{200\pi}{3}+50\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{200\pi}{3}+25\sqrt{3}\text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$.
items.sol:
$$y=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=\ln x & v&=x\\u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{x\times\frac{1}{x}-\ln x}{x^2}\\&=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{2-\ln x^2}{x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\ln x^2=2\ln x$ and the result of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{2-\ln x^2}{x^2}\,dx&=\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{2-2\ln x}{x^2}\,dx\\&=2\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\,dx\\&=2\left[\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\right]_e^{e^2}\\&=2\left[\dfrac{\ln e^2}{e^2}-\dfrac{\ln e}{e}\right]\\&=2\left[\dfrac{2}{e^2}-\dfrac{1}{e}\right]\end{aligned}$$

Consider $f(x)=e^{2x+1}x^4$.

items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^{2x+1} & v&=x^4\\u'&=2e^{2x+1} & v'&=4x^3\end{aligned}$$
$$f'(x)=2e^{2x+1}x^4+4x^3e^{2x+1}$$
Applying the product rule to each term again:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=4e^{2x+1}x^4+8x^3e^{2x+1}+12x^2e^{2x+1}+8x^3e^{2x+1}\\&=4e^{2x+1}x^4+16x^3e^{2x+1}+12x^2e^{2x+1}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x^3e^{2x+1}(x+2)&=0\\x&=0,\ -2\end{aligned}$$
Testing with the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(-2)&=-0.79\ldots<0 &&\text{maximum}\\f''(0)&=0 &&\text{possible point of inflection, test further}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ maximum point at $(-2,\ 0.79\ldots)$

Test $(0,0)$ with the sign of $f'(x)$ either side:

\extable{317_q28_t1}

$\therefore$ $(0,0)$ is a minimum stationary point.

The total metal used to make the jar and its lid is $190\pi\text{ cm}^2$.
Show that the volume of the jar, $V\text{ cm}^3$, is given by $V=\pi(95x-2x^2-x^3)$.
items.sol:
The metal is the curved surfaces of the jar (height $h$) and the lid (height 2), plus the base and the top of the lid:
$$\begin{aligned}2\pi x(h+2)+2(\pi x^2)&=190\pi\\2x(h+2)+2x^2&=190\\x(h+2)+x^2&=95\\xh+2x+x^2&=95\\xh&=95-2x-x^2\end{aligned}$$
Using the cylinder volume $V=\pi r^2h$ with $r=x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\pi x^2h\\&=\pi x(xh)\\&=\pi x(95-2x-x^2)\\&=\pi(95x-2x^2-x^3)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{2x-1}$ and $f(g(x))=\dfrac{3x+2}{3x-5}$, find $g(x)$.
items.sol:
Substituting $g(x)$ into $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{2x-1}$:
$$f(g(x))=\dfrac{g(x)+1}{2g(x)-1}$$
Equating with $f(g(x))=\dfrac{3x+2}{3x-5}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{g(x)+1}{2g(x)-1}&=\dfrac{3x+2}{3x-5}\\(g(x)+1)(3x-5)&=(3x+2)(2g(x)-1)\\3xg(x)-5g(x)+3x-5&=6xg(x)-3x+4g(x)-2\\9g(x)+3xg(x)&=6x-3\\g(x)(3x+9)&=6x-3\\g(x)&=\dfrac{6x-3}{3x+9}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ g(x)=\dfrac{2x-1}{x+3}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^{\frac{3}{2}}+5x}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^{\frac{3}{2}}+5x}}\,dx&=\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)}}\,dx\\&=\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5}}\,dx\\&=\int x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\end{aligned}$$
By the reverse chain rule, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx&=2\int\dfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=4\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+5\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and hence evaluate $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\times\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.
items.sol:
$\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ is in the fourth quadrant with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, where $\tan$ is negative:
$$\begin{aligned}\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{1}{\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{-\sqrt{3}}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
With $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ (fourth quadrant, related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$):
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\times\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times\dfrac{1}{\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=(4x+2)^3$ at the point $(1,216)$.
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3\times4(4x+2)^2\\ &=12(4x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
At $(1,216)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=12(4(1)+2)^2\\ &=12(6)^2\\ &=432\end{aligned}$$
$m_{\text{tangent}}=432$

Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-216&=432(x-1)\\ y&=432x-216\\ 432x-y-216&=0\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $e^{3x}(1+3x)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^{3x} & v&=1+3x\\u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{3x}(1+3x)\right]&=3e^{3x}+3e^{3x}(1+3x)\\ &=3e^{3x}\big(1+(1+3x)\big)\\ &=3e^{3x}(2+3x)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int(2+3x)e^{3x}\,dx$
items.sol:
From part (a), $3e^{3x}(2+3x)$ is the derivative of $e^{3x}(1+3x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int(2+3x)e^{3x}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int 3e^{3x}(2+3x)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x}(1+3x)+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A farm has a watering system which repeatedly fills a storage tank then empties its’ contents to water different sections of the farm. The volume of water $V$ (in cubic metres) in the tank at a time $t$ is given by the equation

$$V=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos t-2\sin t$$

where $t$ is measured in minutes.
Determine whether the tank is initially filling or emptying, showing all calculations.
items.sol:
The tank is emptying when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}<0$.

When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dV}{dt}&=2\sqrt{3}\sin(0)-2\cos(0)\\ &=2\sqrt{3}(0)-2(1)\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ tank is emptying at this time
items.final: The tank is emptying initially (dV/dt = -2 < 0 at t=0).

items.part:
A farm has a watering system which repeatedly fills a storage tank then empties its’ contents to water different sections of the farm. The volume of water $V$ (in cubic metres) in the tank at a time $t$ is given by the equation

$$V=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos t-2\sin t$$

where $t$ is measured in minutes.
At what time does the tank first become completely full and what is its capacity when it is full?
items.sol:
The tank is full or empty when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\sin t-2\cos t&=0\\ 2\sqrt{3}\sin t&=2\cos t\\ \dfrac{\sin t}{\cos t}&=\dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{3}}\\ \tan t&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \ldots\end{aligned}$$
As the tank is initially emptying, the first value is when it is empty and the second is when it is full.

Tank first full when $t=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ minutes.
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)-2\sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\\ &=6\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$$
items.final: Tank first full at $t=\frac{7\pi}{6}$ minutes, with capacity $6\text{ m}^3$.

Given that the least squares regression line of marks lost on lessons missed passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$, find the mean number of lessons missed and marks lost.
items.sol:
$y=1.5x+6$

Total marks lost $=25\bar{y}$

Total lessons missed $=25\bar{x}$

The total marks lost is 230 more than the total lessons missed:
$$25\bar{x}+230=25\bar{y}\quad(1)$$
The line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$:
$$\bar{y}=1.5\bar{x}+6\quad(2)$$
Substituting (2) into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}25\bar{x}+230&=25(1.5\bar{x}+6)\\ 25\bar{x}+230&=37.5\bar{x}+150\\ 80&=12.5\bar{x}\\ \bar{x}&=6.4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{y}&=1.5(6.4)+6\\ &=15.6\end{aligned}$$
items.final: Mean lessons missed $\bar{x}=6.4$; mean marks lost $\bar{y}=15.6$

Since the test is out of 40, marks gained $=40-y$.

$\therefore$ least squares regression line for marks gained on lessons missed:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Marks gained}&=40-(1.5x+6)\\ &=40-6-1.5x\\ &=-1.5x+34\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $y=-x^3+12x-7$, for $-5\le x\le 5$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=-3x^2+12\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-6x\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3x^2+12&=0\\ 3x^2&=12\\ x^2&=4\\ x&=\pm2\end{aligned}$$
At $x=-2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-(-2)^3+12(-2)-7\\ &=-(-8)+(-24)-7\\ &=-23\end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-(2)^3+12(2)-7\\ &=-8+24-7\\ &=9\end{aligned}$$
Nature, using the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned}(-2,-23)&: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-6(-2)=12>0 &&\text{concave up, minimum turning point}\\ (2,9)&: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-6(2)=-12<0 &&\text{concave down, maximum turning point}\end{aligned}$$
items.final: $(-2,-23)$ is a minimum turning point; $(2,9)$ is a maximum turning point

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $a=14$, $d=6$, $S_n=6020$:
$$\begin{aligned}6020&=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2(14)+(n-1)6\big)\\ 12\,040&=n(28+6n-6)\\ 12\,040&=28n+6n^2-6n\\ 6n^2+22n-12\,040&=0\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned}n&=\dfrac{-22\pm\sqrt{22^2-4(6)(-12\,040)}}{2(6)}\\ &=\dfrac{-22\pm\sqrt{289\,444}}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{-22\pm538}{12}\end{aligned}$$
$n>0$, so $n=43$.

$\therefore$ there are 43 rows.

The diagram below shows a sketch of the curve $C$ with equation

The point $P$ lies on the curve and has $x$-coordinate 4. The line $l$ is the normal to the curve at $P$.

items.sol:
\exfigure{320_q27_s1}

$R$ is the area under the curve from $x=1$ to $x=4$ plus the triangle under the normal from $P$ to its $x$-intercept.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{16}{x^2}+3x-4\\ &=16x^{-2}+3x-4\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=-32x^{-3}+3\end{aligned}$$
At $P(4,9)$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{tangent}}&=-32(4)^{-3}+3\\ &=2.5\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_1m_2=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{normal}}&=-\dfrac{1}{2.5}\\ &=-\dfrac{2}{5}\end{aligned}$$
Equation of normal, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-9&=-\dfrac{2}{5}(x-4)\\ 5y-45&=-2x+8\\ 2x+5y-53&=0\end{aligned}$$
$x$-intercept ($y=0$):
$$\begin{aligned}2x+5(0)-53&=0\\ 2x&=53\\ x&=26.5\end{aligned}$$
The triangle has base $26.5-4=22.5$ and height 9:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_1^4\left(\dfrac{16}{x^2}+3x-4\right)dx+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times22.5\times9\right)\\ &=\int_1^4\left(16x^{-2}+3x-4\right)dx+101.25\\ &=\left[\dfrac{16x^{-1}}{-1}+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-4x\right]_1^4+101.25\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{16}{x}+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-4x\right]_1^4+101.25\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{16}{4}+\dfrac{3(4)^2}{2}-4(4)\right)-\left(-\dfrac{16}{1}+\dfrac{3(1)^2}{2}-4(1)\right)+101.25\\ &=22.5+101.25\\ &=123.75\text{ u}^2\end{aligned}$$

Find the value of $a$ such that $P(X<a)=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{3\pi}^{a}\dfrac{1}{4}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}\\ \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right]_{3\pi}^{a}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{a}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{a}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}+2}{4}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{a}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}+\dfrac{2}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{a}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\\ \sin\dfrac{a}{2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Since $3\pi\le a\le 5\pi$, $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\le\dfrac{a}{2}\le\dfrac{5\pi}{2}$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{a}{2}&=\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\\ a&=\dfrac{14\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v\ m/s$. The displacement is given by $x=5\log_e(2t+1)-3t$.
Find an expression for the velocity $v$.
items.sol:
Velocity is $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=5\left(\dfrac{2}{2t+1}\right)-3\\ &=\dfrac{10}{2t+1}-3\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v\ m/s$. The displacement is given by $x=5\log_e(2t+1)-3t$.
When does the particle come to rest?

A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v\ m/s$. The displacement is given by $x=5\log_e(2t+1)-3t$.
Find the initial acceleration.
items.sol:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$; by the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=10(2t+1)^{-1}-3\\ a&=-10\times2(2t+1)^{-2}\\ &=-\dfrac{20}{(2t+1)^2}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{-20}{(2(0)+1)^2}\\ &=-20\text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v\ m/s$. The displacement is given by $x=5\log_e(2t+1)-3t$.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds. Answer correct to four decimal places.
items.sol:
The particle starts at the origin, is at rest at $t=\dfrac{7}{6}$ and then turns back.

At $t=\dfrac{7}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=5\ln\left(2\left(\dfrac{7}{6}\right)+1\right)-3\left(\dfrac{7}{6}\right)\\ &=5\ln\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)-\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=5\ln(2(3)+1)-3(3)\\ &=5\ln7-9\end{aligned}$$
So the distance is out to $x\left(\dfrac{7}{6}\right)$ and back to $x(3)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total distance travelled}&=2\left(5\ln\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)-\dfrac{7}{2}\right)-(5\ln7-9)\\ &=4.310177\ldots\\ &=4.3102\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
5 people want to adopt an animal at the local shelter. All 5 people have the same probability of adopting a dog $P(D)$ and the same probability of adopting a cat $P(C)$.

It is given that $P(D)=\dfrac{9}{14}$, $P(D|C)=\dfrac{6}{13}$, and $P(C|D)=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Dev is one of the five people looking to adopt a pet.
Show that the probability of Dev adopting a cat is $\dfrac{13}{28}$.
items.sol:
Using $P(C|D)=\dfrac{P(C\cap D)}{P(D)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{3}&=\dfrac{P(C\cap D)}{\frac{9}{14}}\\ P(C\cap D)&=\dfrac{3}{14}\end{aligned}$$
Using $P(D|C)=\dfrac{P(D\cap C)}{P(C)}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{6}{13}&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{14}}{P(C)}\\ P(C)&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{14}}{\frac{6}{13}}\\ &=\dfrac{13}{28}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
5 people want to adopt an animal at the local shelter. All 5 people have the same probability of adopting a dog $P(D)$ and the same probability of adopting a cat $P(C)$.

It is given that $P(D)=\dfrac{9}{14}$, $P(D|C)=\dfrac{6}{13}$, and $P(C|D)=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Dev is one of the five people looking to adopt a pet.
What is the probability that at least one of the 5 people will NOT adopt a dog. Give your answer correct to two decimal places
items.sol:
At least one not adopting a dog is the complement of all five adopting dogs:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least 1 not a dog})&=1-P(\text{all dogs})\\ &=1-\left(\dfrac{9}{14}\right)^5\\ &=0.890207\ldots\\ &=0.89\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Calvin borrows \$470 000 to purchase a property at 7.1% p.a. where interest is compounded monthly. He makes repayments of \$3300 per month. Interest is calculated just before each payment.
Find the amount owing after the first 2 years.
items.sol:
The monthly interest rate:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=7.1\%\text{ p.a.}\\ &=\dfrac{7.1}{12}\%\text{ per month}\\ &=\dfrac{71}{12\,000}\text{ per month}\end{aligned}$$
Each month interest is added to the amount owing, then the $\$3300$ repayment is subtracted:
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=470\,000\left(1+\dfrac{71}{12\,000}\right)^1-3300\\ &=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ A_2&=A_1\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ &=\left[470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\right]\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ &=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^2-3300\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ &=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^2-3300\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}+1\right)\\ A_3&=A_2\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)-3300\\ &=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^3-3300\left(\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^2+\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}+1\right)\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ A_n&=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-3300\left(1+\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}+\cdots+\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^{n-1}\right)\end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$ and $r=\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}$, so by $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$A_n=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-\dfrac{3300\left(\left(\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-1\right)}{\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}-1}$$
After 2 years, $n=24$ months:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{24}&=470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^{24}-\dfrac{3300\left(\left(\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^{24}-1\right)}{\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}-1}\\ &=456\,654.2456\\ &=\$456\,654.25\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $\$456\,654.25$ is still owing after 2 years.

items.part:
Calvin borrows \$470 000 to purchase a property at 7.1% p.a. where interest is compounded monthly. He makes repayments of \$3300 per month. Interest is calculated just before each payment.
Find the number of months required to repay the loan.
items.sol:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$. Using $A_n$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-\dfrac{3300\left(\left(\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-1\right)}{\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}-1}&=0\\ 470\,000\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n\times\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}-1\right)&=3300\left(\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-1\right)\\ \dfrac{16\,685}{6}\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n&=3300\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n-3300\\ -\dfrac{3115}{6}\left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n&=-3300\\ \left(\dfrac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)^n&=\dfrac{3960}{623}\\ n&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{3960}{623}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{12\,071}{12\,000}\right)}\\ &=313.50738\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The loan is not repaid after 313 months, so round up:
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore n&=314\text{ months}\\ &=26\text{ years }2\text{ months}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rectangular pyramid is placed in a bowl of depth d which is part of a sphere with centre $O$ and radius $r$. The apex of the pyramid coincides with $O$. The vertices of the base, $ABCD$, lie on the bowl’s inner surface as shown in the diagram. The perpendicular from $O$ meets the diagonal $DB$ in its midpoint $M$.

Let $OM=x$, $CB=b$, and $AB=3b$.

\exfigure{320_q33_1}
Show that $DB=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$
items.sol:
$M$ is the midpoint of $DB$:
$$DB=2MB$$
In right-angled $\triangle OMB$, $OB=r$ (radius) and $OM=x$, so by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned}MB^2&=r^2-x^2\\ MB&=\sqrt{r^2-x^2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore DB=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$$

items.part:
A rectangular pyramid is placed in a bowl of depth d which is part of a sphere with centre $O$ and radius $r$. The apex of the pyramid coincides with $O$. The vertices of the base, $ABCD$, lie on the bowl’s inner surface as shown in the diagram. The perpendicular from $O$ meets the diagonal $DB$ in its midpoint $M$.

Let $OM=x$, $CB=b$, and $AB=3b$.

\exfigure{320_q33_1}
Show that the volume of the pyramid is $V=\dfrac{2}{5}x(r^2-x^2)$.
items.sol:
Volume of a pyramid, $V=\dfrac{1}{3}Ah$, with base $3b\times b$ and height $OM=x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{1}{3}Ah\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}(3b\times b)x\\ &=b^2x\end{aligned}$$
$DB$ is a diagonal of the rectangular base, so by Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle DAB$:
$$\begin{aligned}DB^2&=b^2+(3b)^2\\ DB&=\sqrt{b^2+9b^2}\\ &=\sqrt{10b^2}\end{aligned}$$
Equating with $DB=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10b^2}&=2\sqrt{r^2-x^2}\\ 10b^2&=4(r^2-x^2)\\ b^2&=\dfrac{4(r^2-x^2)}{10}\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $V=b^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{2}{5}(r^2-x^2)x\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}x(r^2-x^2)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rectangular pyramid is placed in a bowl of depth d which is part of a sphere with centre $O$ and radius $r$. The apex of the pyramid coincides with $O$. The vertices of the base, $ABCD$, lie on the bowl’s inner surface as shown in the diagram. The perpendicular from $O$ meets the diagonal $DB$ in its midpoint $M$.

Let $OM=x$, $CB=b$, and $AB=3b$.

\exfigure{320_q33_1}
Find the value of $x$ that will maximise the volume of the pyramid.
items.sol:
Expanding and differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{2}{5}xr^2-\dfrac{2}{5}x^3\\ \dfrac{dV}{dx}&=\dfrac{2}{5}(r^2-3x^2)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=\dfrac{2}{5}(r^2-3x^2)\\ 3x^2&=r^2\\ x^2&=\dfrac{r^2}{3}\\ x&=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{3}}\\ x&=\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}\quad(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ either side of $x=\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}$.

At $x=\dfrac{r}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dV}{dx}&=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(r^2-3\left(\dfrac{r}{3}\right)^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(r^2-\dfrac{r^2}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2r^2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{4r^2}{15}>0\end{aligned}$$
At $x=\dfrac{2r}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dV}{dx}&=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(r^2-3\left(\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(r^2-\dfrac{4}{3}r^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}r^2\right)\\ &=-\dfrac{2r^2}{15}<0\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts2020_1}

$\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ changes from positive to negative.

$\therefore$ maximum at $x=\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}$

items.part:
A rectangular pyramid is placed in a bowl of depth d which is part of a sphere with centre $O$ and radius $r$. The apex of the pyramid coincides with $O$. The vertices of the base, $ABCD$, lie on the bowl’s inner surface as shown in the diagram. The perpendicular from $O$ meets the diagonal $DB$ in its midpoint $M$.

Let $OM=x$, $CB=b$, and $AB=3b$.

\exfigure{320_q33_1}
If the depth of the bowl is $\dfrac{r}{3}$ units deep, explain why the maximum volume from part (c) cannot be achieved and hence find the greatest volume now possible.
items.sol:
The base of the pyramid must lie inside the bowl. From the diagram, the depth of the bowl plus $OM$ is at least the radius:
$$\begin{aligned}d+x&\ge r\\ \dfrac{r}{3}+x&\ge r\\ x&\ge r-\dfrac{r}{3}\\ x&\ge\dfrac{2r}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}<\dfrac{2r}{3}$, $x\ne\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}$, so the maximum from part (c) cannot be achieved.

At $x=\dfrac{2r}{3}$, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}<0$ (volume decreasing).

$\therefore$ the maximum under these conditions is at $x=\dfrac{2r}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)\left(r^2-\left(\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{4r}{15}\left(r^2-\dfrac{4r^2}{9}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{4r}{15}\left(\dfrac{9r^2}{9}-\dfrac{4r^2}{9}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{4r}{15}\left(\dfrac{5r^2}{9}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{4r^3}{27}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y = xe^{7x}$, expressing your answer in factorised form.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{7x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=7e^{7x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=x(7e^{7x})+e^{7x}(1)\\ &=e^{7x}(7x+1)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact gradient of the tangent to the curve $y = e^{2x + 3}$ at the point where $x = 0$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{f(x)}=f'(x)e^{f(x)}$:
$$y'=2e^{2x+3}$$
When $x=0$, $y'=2e^{3}$.

$\therefore m_T=2e^3$

items.part: Solve the equation $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} x}{5} - 2 = 0$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, correct to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{5}-2&=0\\ \operatorname{cosec}x&=10\\ \dfrac{1}{\sin x}&=10\\ \sin x&=\dfrac{1}{10}\end{aligned}$$
$\sin x>0$, so $x$ is in the first or second quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)=5^\circ 44'\\ x&=180^\circ-5^\circ 44'=174^\circ 16'\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=5^\circ 44' \text{ and } 174^\circ 16'$$

items.part:
A bag contains six cards that are each printed with one of the following numbers.

$$111,\ 121,\ 122,\ 211,\ 221,\ 222$$

A student chooses one card at random.

Let $N_1$ be the event that the first digit of the number on the card is 1, and $N_2$ be the event that the second digit of the number on the card is 1.

Determine whether $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}N_1&=\{111,121,122\}\\ N_2&=\{111,211\}\\ N_1\cap N_2&=\{111\}\end{aligned}$$
Each of the 6 cards is equally likely:
$$P(N_1)=\dfrac{1}{2},\quad P(N_2)=\dfrac{1}{3},\quad P(N_1\cap N_2)=\dfrac{1}{6}$$
If $N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent events, then $P(N_1\cap N_2)=P(N_1)\times P(N_2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(N_1)\times P(N_2)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\\ &=P(N_1\cap N_2)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore N_1$ and $N_2$ are independent.

items.part:
s Eve to watch the fireworks.

Darren is standing outside the Sydney Opera House and Sylvia is on a yacht in the harbour. They can both see the fireworks at the top of the Sydney Harbour Bridge.

\exfigure{323_q16_1}

From Darren’s position ($D$), the Sydney Harbour Bridge ($B$) is at a bearing of $78^\circ$, and the angle of elevation to the top of the bridge ($T$) is $35^\circ$.

From Sylvia’s position ($S$), the Sydney Harbour Bridge is at a bearing of $140^\circ$, and the angle of elevation to the top of the bridge is $48^\circ$.

The top of the bridge is 50 m above the base of the bridge.
Using appropriate diagrams and reasoning, show that $\angle SBD = 62^\circ$.

\exfigure{323_q16_2}
items.sol:
\exfigure{323_q16_s1}

The north lines at $S$ and $B$ are parallel, so co-interior angles are supplementary:
$$\angle SBN=180^\circ-140^\circ=40^\circ$$
The angle between south at $B$ and $BD$ is $78^\circ$ (alternate angles with the bearing at $D$, parallel north lines).

The north and south lines at $B$ form a straight angle:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle SBD&=180^\circ-40^\circ-78^\circ\\ &=62^\circ\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
s Eve to watch the fireworks.

Darren is standing outside the Sydney Opera House and Sylvia is on a yacht in the harbour. They can both see the fireworks at the top of the Sydney Harbour Bridge.

\exfigure{323_q16_1}

From Darren’s position ($D$), the Sydney Harbour Bridge ($B$) is at a bearing of $78^\circ$, and the angle of elevation to the top of the bridge ($T$) is $35^\circ$.

From Sylvia’s position ($S$), the Sydney Harbour Bridge is at a bearing of $140^\circ$, and the angle of elevation to the top of the bridge is $48^\circ$.

The top of the bridge is 50 m above the base of the bridge.
Hence, find the distance between Sylvia and Darren, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
\exfigure{323_q16_s2}

In right-angled $\triangle TSB$, $\angle STB=42^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 42^\circ&=\dfrac{SB}{50}\\ SB&=50\tan 42^\circ \end{aligned}$$
In right-angled $\triangle TDB$, $\angle DTB=55^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 55^\circ&=\dfrac{BD}{50}\\ BD&=50\tan 55^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Cosine rule in $\triangle SBD$ with $\angle SBD=62^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} SD^2&=(50\tan 55^\circ)^2+(50\tan 42^\circ)^2-2(50\tan 55^\circ)(50\tan 42^\circ)\cos 62^\circ\\ &=4107.3439\ldots\\ SD&=\sqrt{4107.3439\ldots}\\ \therefore SD&=64.09 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y = \dfrac{\ln(x - 1)}{x - 1}$ at the point $(2,0)$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln(x-1) & v&=x-1\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x-1} & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{(x-1)\left(\frac{1}{x-1}\right)-\ln(x-1)(1)}{(x-1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\ln(x-1)}{(x-1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1-\ln(2-1)}{(2-1)^2}\\ &=1-\ln 1\\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore m_T=1$ and $m_N=-1$

Equation of the normal:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=-1(x-2)\\ y&=-x+2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{323_q18_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function $v_P = 3t^2 - 6t + 4$, where $v_P$ is the velocity in metres per second.

The velocity of car $Q$ is accelerating at a constant rate. Both cars start at the same point and have the same velocity at times where $t = 0$ and $t = 4$.
Show that the equation for the velocity of car $Q$, $v_Q$, is given by $v_Q = 6t + 4$.
items.sol:
At $t=0$, $v_Q=v_P=4$

At $t=4$, $v_Q=v_P=3(4)^2-6(4)+4=28$

$Q$ accelerates at a constant rate, so $v_Q$ is linear through $(0,4)$ and $(4,28)$:
$$m=\dfrac{28-4}{4-0}=6$$
$$\therefore v_Q=6t+4$$

items.part:
The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{323_q18_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function $v_P = 3t^2 - 6t + 4$, where $v_P$ is the velocity in metres per second.

The velocity of car $Q$ is accelerating at a constant rate. Both cars start at the same point and have the same velocity at times where $t = 0$ and $t = 4$.
Both cars start the race from the same point.

Find the earliest time when car $P$ will pass car $Q$ after the race starts.
items.sol:
Both cars start at the same point, so $P$ passes $Q$ at the time $a>0$ when their displacements are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a \big(3t^2-6t+4-(6t+4)\big)\,dt&=0\\ \int_0^a (3t^2-12t)\,dt&=0\\ \Big[t^3-6t^2\Big]_0^a&=0\\ a^3-6a^2&=0\\ a^2(a-6)&=0\\ a&=0,\ 6 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ car $P$ will pass $Q$ after 6 seconds from the start of the race.

items.part: Find the derivative of $y = \tan(x^2)$.
Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int x\tan^2(x^2)\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1$, and part (a) for the primitive of $2x\sec^2(x^2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int x\tan^2(x^2)\,dx&=\int x\big(\sec^2(x^2)-1\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x\big(\sec^2(x^2)-1\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int \big(2x\sec^2(x^2)-2x\big)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\tan(x^2)-x^2\big)+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Use two applications of the trapezoidal rule to find an approximate value of $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \ln x\,dx$.

Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
Two applications of the trapezoidal rule use 2 strips, so $h=\dfrac{b-a}{n}=\dfrac{2-1}{2}=0.5$ and the $x$ values are $1$, $1.5$, $2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 \ln x\,dx&\approx\dfrac{0.5}{2}\big[(\ln 1+\ln 2)+2\ln 1.5\big]\\ &=\dfrac{0.5}{2}\big[(0+\ln 2)+2\ln 1.5\big]\\ &=0.3760\ldots\\ &\approx 0.38 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{1}{\sec\theta - \tan\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\sec\theta + \tan\theta} = 2\tan\theta$
items.sol:
Combining the fractions and using $\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{\sec\theta-\tan\theta}-\dfrac{1}{\sec\theta+\tan\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{\sec\theta+\tan\theta-(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)}{\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{\sec\theta+\tan\theta-\sec\theta+\tan\theta}{1}\\ &=2\tan\theta\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{\sec\theta - \tan\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\sec\theta + \tan\theta}\,d\theta$
items.sol:
Using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \int 2\tan\theta\,d\theta&=-2\int \dfrac{-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\,d\theta\\ &=-2\ln|\cos\theta|+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{kx}{5 - x^2} & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$
Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}$.
items.sol:
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 f(x)\,dx&=1\\ \int_0^2 \dfrac{kx}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\int_0^2 \dfrac{-2x}{5-x^2}\,dx&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln|5-x^2|\Big]_0^2&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\big[\ln|5-4|-\ln|5-0|\big]&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}\big[\ln 1-\ln 5\big]&=1\\ -\dfrac{k}{2}(0-\ln 5)&=1\\ \dfrac{k\ln 5}{2}&=1\\ k&=\dfrac{2}{\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{kx}{5 - x^2} & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$
Show that the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ is given by:

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \\ 1 - \log_5(5 - x^2) & 0 \le x \le 2 \\ 1 & x > 2 \end{cases}$$
items.sol:
For $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_0^x \dfrac{2}{\ln 5}\left(\dfrac{x}{5-x^2}\right)dx\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\int_0^x \dfrac{-2x}{5-x^2}\,dx\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\Big[\ln|5-x^2|\Big]_0^x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\big[\ln|5|-\ln|5-x^2|\big]\\ &=1-\dfrac{\ln|5-x^2|}{\ln 5}\end{aligned}$$
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$, and $5-x^2>0$ for $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=1-\log_5|5-x^2|\\ &=1-\log_5(5-x^2)\end{aligned}$$
Outside $0\le x\le 2$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=0 &&\text{for } x<0\\ F(x)&=1 &&\text{for } x>2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{kx}{5 - x^2} & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$
Hence, or otherwise, show that the median is $\sqrt{5 - \sqrt{5}}$.
items.sol:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-\log_5(5-x^2)&=0.5\\ \log_5(5-x^2)&=0.5\\ 5-x^2&=5^{0.5}\\ 5-x^2&=\sqrt{5}\\ x^2&=5-\sqrt{5}\\ x&=\pm\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x=\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$, since $0\le x\le 2$.

items.part:
A factory produces boxes in the shape of an open rectangular prism (without a lid).

\exfigure{323_q23_1}

The length, height and width of the box are $l$ cm, $x$ cm and $2x$ cm respectively.

The factory uses $k \text{ cm}^2$ of sheet metal to make the box, where $k$ is a constant.
Show that $l = \dfrac{k - 4x^2}{4x}$.
items.sol:
The open box has a base $l\times 2x$, two sides $l\times x$ and two ends $2x\times x$:
$$\begin{aligned} k&=2lx+2lx+2(2x^2)\\ k&=4lx+4x^2\\ 4lx&=k-4x^2\\ l&=\dfrac{k-4x^2}{4x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A factory produces boxes in the shape of an open rectangular prism (without a lid).

\exfigure{323_q23_1}

The length, height and width of the box are $l$ cm, $x$ cm and $2x$ cm respectively.

The factory uses $k \text{ cm}^2$ of sheet metal to make the box, where $k$ is a constant.
Hence, find the maximum volume of the box that can be produced from a sheet of metal with an area of $1200 \text{ cm}^2$.
items.sol:
Volume $=$ length $\times$ width $\times$ height, with $l$ from part (a) and $k=1200$:
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2x^2l\\ &=2x^2\left(\dfrac{1200-4x^2}{4x}\right)\\ &=600x-2x^3\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $V'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}V'&=600-6x^2\\ 600-6x^2&=0\\ 6x^2&=600\\ x^2&=100\\ x&=\pm 10\end{aligned}$$
Nature, using $V''=-12x$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=10: & V''&=-120<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ x&=-10: & V''&=120>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{max volume}&=2\times 10^2\times\dfrac{1200-4(10)^2}{40}\\ &=4000 \text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the series $\ln x - 3(\ln x)^2 + 9(\ln x)^3 - 27(\ln x)^4 + \ldots$
Show that this series is a geometric series.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{T_2}{T_1}&=\dfrac{-3(\ln x)^2}{\ln x} & \dfrac{T_3}{T_2}&=\dfrac{9(\ln x)^3}{-3(\ln x)^2}\\ &=-3\ln x & &=-3\ln x \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ there is a common ratio $r=-3\ln x$, so the series is geometric.
\exfigure{323_q24_s1}

items.part:
Consider the series $\ln x - 3(\ln x)^2 + 9(\ln x)^3 - 27(\ln x)^4 + \ldots$
Hence, or otherwise, find the values of $x$ for which the series has a limiting sum.
items.sol:
The limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$:
$$|-3\ln x|<1$$
$$\begin{aligned} -3\ln x&<1 & 3\ln x&<1\\ \ln x&>-\dfrac{1}{3} & \ln x&<\dfrac{1}{3}\\ x&>e^{-\frac{1}{3}} & x&<e^{\frac{1}{3}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore e^{-\frac{1}{3}}<x<e^{\frac{1}{3}}$$

items.part:
The graph $y = \sin x$ is vertically dilated by a scale factor of 2 and horizontally dilated such that it has a period of $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the transformed sine curve and the line $y = \sqrt{2}$ for $x \in [0,2\pi]$.
items.sol:
Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so $n=3$.

A vertical dilation by a factor of 2 gives an amplitude of 2, so $y=2\sin 3x$ for $0\le 3x\le 6\pi$.

Substitute $y=\sqrt{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin 3x&=\sqrt{2}\\ \sin 3x&=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\sin 3x>0$, so $3x$ is in the first or second quadrant:
$$3x=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{9\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{4}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{12}$$

items.part:
For a sample of fifteen high school students, their age in years, $x$, and the length of their right foot in centimetres, $y$, were recorded.

\exfigure{323_q26_1}

The graph shows the data as well as a regression line which passes through $(12, 22.5)$ and $(19, 27.5)$.
Find the equation of the regression line in the form $y = mx + c$.
items.sol:
Using $(12,22.5)$ and $(19,27.5)$:
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{27.5-22.5}{19-12}\\ &=\dfrac{5}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y-22.5&=\dfrac{5}{7}(x-12)\\ y-22.5&=\dfrac{5}{7}x-\dfrac{60}{7}\\ y&=\dfrac{5}{7}x+\dfrac{195}{14} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For a sample of fifteen high school students, their age in years, $x$, and the length of their right foot in centimetres, $y$, were recorded.

\exfigure{323_q26_1}

The graph shows the data as well as a regression line which passes through $(12, 22.5)$ and $(19, 27.5)$.
Layton has a five-year old brother whose right foot is 13 cm in length.

He extends the line of best fit and notes that it predicts that a five-year old should have a foot length of approximately 17.5 cm.

Give TWO reasons why Layton is incorrect to assume from the bivariate data that his brother has smaller than normal feet for a five-year old.
items.sol:
Layton is extrapolating well outside the data set, as the students measured were aged from 12 to 18; this is always problematic as it assumes a linear relationship which may not be true.

The strength of the relationship between age and foot length is low (the correlation coefficient is close to 0), so even interpolating within the correct age range would be unreliable.

$$\therefore A\left(\sqrt[3]{b},b\right)$$

Area between the curve and the $y$-axis: $y=x^3$, so $x=y^{\frac{1}{3}}$.

items.part:
An astronomer is attempting to predict the height of a satellite above the ground as it orbits around the Earth. Using precise measurements, the height of the satellite can be modelled with the function:

$$h(t) = 6\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t - 15)\right) + 8$$

where $h(t)$ is the height of the satellite in thousands of kilometres at time $t$ hours since midnight on any day of the year.
Find the minimum and maximum height reached by the satellite.
items.sol:
The sine term ranges from $-6$ to $6$, so $h$ ranges from $8-6$ to $8+6$ thousand km.
$$\begin{aligned} \min&=(8-6)\times 1000=2000 \text{ km}\\ \max&=(8+6)\times 1000=14\,000 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An astronomer is attempting to predict the height of a satellite above the ground as it orbits around the Earth. Using precise measurements, the height of the satellite can be modelled with the function:

$$h(t) = 6\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t - 15)\right) + 8$$

where $h(t)$ is the height of the satellite in thousands of kilometres at time $t$ hours since midnight on any day of the year.
The satellite is out of range if it is higher than 11 000 km above the ground.

Use algebraic techniques to find how many hours in the day the satellite is out of range.
items.sol:
Out of range when $h(t)>11$; first solve $h(t)=11$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\right)+8&=11\\ 6\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\right)&=3\\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le t\le 24$, $-\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)\le\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-15)&=-\dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\\ t-15&=-11,\ -7,\ 1,\ 5\\ \therefore t&=4,\ 8,\ 16,\ 20 \end{aligned}$$
From the graph, the satellite is above 11 000 km for $4<t<8$ and $16<t<20$.

$\therefore$ the satellite is out of range for 8 hours each day.

items.part:
The graph of a cumulative distribution function is shown below.

\exfigure{323_q30_1}

The curved section of the graph is part of the function $y = \dfrac{(x - 1)^3}{6}$
Show that the value of $A$ is $\sqrt[3]{6} + 1$.
items.sol:
$F(A)=1$ (the curve meets the horizontal line $y=1$ at $x=A$):
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=\dfrac{(A-1)^3}{6}\\ (A-1)^3&=6\\ A-1&=\sqrt[3]{6}\\ A&=\sqrt[3]{6}+1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The graph of a cumulative distribution function is shown below.

\exfigure{323_q30_1}

The curved section of the graph is part of the function $y = \dfrac{(x - 1)^3}{6}$
Find the probability density function for the given cumulative distribution function, including any restrictions on the domain.
items.sol:
For $1\le x\le\sqrt[3]{6}+1$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(F(x)\big)\\ &=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{6}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{(x-1)^2}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f(x)=\begin{cases} \dfrac{(x-1)^2}{2}, & 1\le x\le\sqrt[3]{6}+1\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

items.part:
Consider the gradient function $f'(x) = 3(x + 3)(x - 1)$.
The graph of $y = f(x)$ passes through the point $(2,-8)$. Show that $f(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 - 9x - 10$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=3\int (x^2+2x-3)\,dx\\ &=3\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}+x^2-3x\right]+C\\ \therefore f(x)&=x^3+3x^2-9x+C \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $(2,-8)$:
$$\begin{aligned} -8&=2^3+3(2)^2-9(2)+C\\ -8&=2+C\\ C&=-10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f(x)=x^3+3x^2-9x-10$$

items.part:
Consider the gradient function $f'(x) = 3(x + 3)(x - 1)$.
Find the coordinates of the minimum and maximum values in the interval $-4 \le x \le 4$.

You DO NOT need to determine the nature of the stationary points.
items.sol:
Stationary points are at $x=-3$ and $x=1$ (where $f'(x)=0$). Compare these with the endpoints:
$$f(-4)=10,\quad f(-3)=17,\quad f(1)=-15,\quad f(4)=66$$
$\therefore$ the minimum value is at $(1,-15)$ and the maximum value is at $(4,66)$.

items.sol:

A point of inflection is possible where $f''(x)=0$:

$f(-1)=1$, so $(-1,1)$ is a possible inflection point. Check concavity:

items.part:
An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation:

$$C = 100(1 - 2^{-kt})$$

The battery is charged at $35\%$ capacity after 50 minutes.
Show that the value of $k$ is $0.01243$, correct to 4 significant figures.

An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation:

$$C = 100(1 - 2^{-kt})$$

The battery is charged at $35\%$ capacity after 50 minutes.
To prolong the life of the battery, the charger may be set to switch off when the battery reaches $90\%$ capacity. For how long will the battery be on charge until it reaches $90\%$ capacity?

An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation:

$$C = 100(1 - 2^{-kt})$$

The battery is charged at $35\%$ capacity after 50 minutes.
By considering the first and second derivative, describe the behaviour of $C$ for $t \ge 0$ if the battery is left on charge indefinitely.
items.sol:
Initially $C=0$. Since $k>0$, $2^{-kt}\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$, so $C\to 100$ as $t\to\infty$.
$$\begin{aligned} C'&=100k\ln 2\times 2^{-kt}\\ C''&=-100k^2(\ln 2)^2\times 2^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Since $k>0$, $C'>0$ and $C''<0$ for all $t\ge 0$.

Hence, the battery charge capacity increases from 0 at a decreasing rate over time, but can never reach $100\%$ charge.

items.part: If the initial function were $y=x^2$, what transformations, stated in order, have occurred to yield the function $y=-5(x+8)^2+7$?
items.sol:
Write $-5(x+8)^2$ as a square times $-1$:
$$y=-\left(\sqrt{5}(x+8)\right)^2+7$$
Either order of description is accepted.

Method I:

1. Horizontally translated to the left by 8.

2. Vertically reflected about the $x$-axis and dilated by scale factor 5.

3. Translated up by 7.

Method II:

1. Horizontally dilated by $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$.

2. Horizontally shifted to the left by 8.

3. Vertically reflected about the $x$-axis.

4. Vertically shifted up by 7.
items.final: Translate left 8; reflect in x-axis and dilate vertically by factor 5; translate up 7.

items.part: Solve $\tan\left(x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$
items.sol:
Adjust the domain to match the angle:
$$\begin{aligned}-\pi&\le x\le\pi\\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6}&\le x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&\left(\text{add } \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Reference angle: $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$\tan$ is positive in the first and third quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\\ x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\\ &=-\dfrac{4\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{6}\\ &=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$\ln\left(\dfrac{4x^2-9}{2x-3}\right)$
items.sol:
Factorise and simplify the fraction first:
$$\dfrac{4x^2-9}{2x-3}=\dfrac{(2x+3)(2x-3)}{2x-3}=2x+3$$
Using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{4x^2-9}{2x-3}\right)\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(2x+3)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2x+3}\times 2\\ &=\dfrac{2}{2x+3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$\sin(e^{x})$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(e^{x})&=\cos(e^{x})\times e^{x}\\ &=e^{x}\cos(e^{x})\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.
$x^2\tan 3x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x^2 & v&=\tan 3x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=3\sec^2 3x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2\tan 3x)&=2x\tan 3x+3x^2\sec^2 3x\\ &=x\left[2\tan 3x+3x\sec^2 3x\right]\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\cos x$ at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$.
items.sol:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\sin x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_{\text{tangent}}&=-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, $m_{\text{tangent}}\times m_{\text{normal}}=-1$:
$$m_{\text{normal}}=\sqrt{2}$$
Equation of the normal through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&=\sqrt{2}\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\\ y&=\sqrt{2}x-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\ y&=\sqrt{2}x-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-1\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=1+3x-x^3$, defined for $-2\le x\le 3$.
Find the stationary points of the curve and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3-3x^2\\ 3-3x^2&=0\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(-1)&=1+3\times(-1)-(-1)^3=1-3+1=-1\\ f(1)&=1+3\times1-(1)^3=1+3-1=3\end{aligned}$$
So the stationary points are $(-1,-1)$ and $(1,3)$.

Nature, using $f''(x)=-6x$:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(-1)&=-6\times(-1)=6>0 &&\text{concave up} &&(-1,-1)\text{ local minimum}\\ f''(1)&=-6\times1=-6<0 &&\text{concave down} &&(1,3)\text{ local maximum}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=1+3x-x^3$, defined for $-2\le x\le 3$.
Find the point of inflection of $y=f(x)$.
items.sol:
A point of inflection is possible where $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6x&=0\\ x&=0\\ y&=1+3\times0-0^3=1\end{aligned}$$
So the possible point is $(0,1)$. Check concavity:

\extable{Ts2090_1}

The concavity changes, so $(0,1)$ is a point of inflection.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=1+3x-x^3$, defined for $-2\le x\le 3$.
Hence sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$ for $-2\le x\le 3$, showing the turning points, the point of inflection, the point(s) where the curve meets the $y$-axis.
items.sol:
Endpoints:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-2)&=1+3\times(-2)-(-2)^3\\ &=1-6+8\\ &=3\end{aligned}$$
so the endpoint is $(-2,3)$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(3)&=1+3\times3-3^3\\ &=1+9-27\\ &=-17\end{aligned}$$
so the endpoint is $(3,-17)$.

Consider the function $f(x)=1+3x-x^3$, defined for $-2\le x\le 3$.

items.sol:
