items.part:
The temperature of hot tea poured into a cup can be represented by the equation $T=25+70e^{-0.4t}$ where $T$ is the temperature of the sea in degrees Celsius, $t$ is the time in minutes after it is poured. Give your answers correct to 2 decimal places.
What is the temperature of the tea four minutes after it has been poured? Give your answer to the nearest degree Celcius.
items.sol:
Substitute $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=25+70\times e^{-0.4\times4}\\ &\approx39.13^{\circ}\text{C}\\ &\approx39^{\circ}\text{C}\ \text{(nearest degree)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The temperature of hot tea poured into a cup can be represented by the equation $T=25+70e^{-0.4t}$ where $T$ is the temperature of the sea in degrees Celsius, $t$ is the time in minutes after it is poured. Give your answers correct to 2 decimal places.
What is the rate at which the tea is cooling four minutes after it has been poured? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dT}{dt}&=70\times(-0.4)e^{-0.4t}\\ &=-28e^{-0.4t}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=4$:
$$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-28e^{-0.4\times4}\approx-5.65\ ^{\circ}\text{C/min}$$
$\therefore$ the temperature is decreasing at the rate of $5.65\ ^{\circ}\text{C/min}$.

items.part:
The temperature of hot tea poured into a cup can be represented by the equation $T=25+70e^{-0.4t}$ where $T$ is the temperature of the sea in degrees Celsius, $t$ is the time in minutes after it is poured. Give your answers correct to 2 decimal places.
How long after the tea is poured will it take for its temperature to reach $55^{\circ}\text{C}$ ? Give your answer correct to the nearest second.
items.sol:
Substitute $T=55$:
$$\begin{aligned}55&=25+70e^{-0.4t}\\ 70e^{-0.4t}&=30\\ e^{-0.4t}&=\dfrac{3}{7}\\ -0.4t&=\ln\dfrac{3}{7}\\ t&=\left(\ln\dfrac{3}{7}\right)\div(-0.4)\\ &=2.1182\ldots\text{ minutes}\\ &\approx2\text{ min }7\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In Canberra, the average daily temperature $T$ in degree Celsius $(^{\circ}\text{C})$ in Canberra is represented by the formula $T=7\sin(nx+1.5)+13$, where $n$ is a constant value and $x$ is the number of the month of the year (i.e. January = 1, February = 2 ,….)
As per this model, what are the highest and lowest average monthly temperatures in Canberra?
items.sol:
The sine function lies between $-1$ and $1$:
$$-1\le\sin(nx+1.5)\le1$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{Lowest average temp.}&=7\times(-1)+13=6^{\circ}\text{C}\\ \text{Highest average temp.}&=7\times1+13=20^{\circ}\text{C}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In Canberra, the average daily temperature $T$ in degree Celsius $(^{\circ}\text{C})$ in Canberra is represented by the formula $T=7\sin(nx+1.5)+13$, where $n$ is a constant value and $x$ is the number of the month of the year (i.e. January = 1, February = 2 ,….)
Find the exact value of $n$, given that the function has a period of 12.
items.sol:
The period of $\sin(nx+1.5)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{n}&=12\\ n&=\dfrac{2\pi}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\ &\approx0.52\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In Canberra, the average daily temperature $T$ in degree Celsius $(^{\circ}\text{C})$ in Canberra is represented by the formula $T=7\sin(nx+1.5)+13$, where $n$ is a constant value and $x$ is the number of the month of the year (i.e. January = 1, February = 2 ,….)
Which month experiences the lowest average monthly temperature?
items.sol:
The lowest temperature occurs when $\sin(nx+1.5)=-1$. With $n=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ from part (b):
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}x+1.5\right)&=-1\\ \dfrac{\pi}{6}x+1.5&=\dfrac{3}{2}\pi,\ \dfrac{3}{2}\pi+2\pi,\ \dfrac{3}{2}\pi+4\pi,\ \ldots\\ &\approx4.71,\ 10.99557\ldots,\ 17.28\\ \dfrac{\pi}{6}x&\approx3.21,\ 9.49557\\ x&\approx6.13\quad(1\le x\le 12)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the $6^{\text{th}}$ month, June, experiences the lowest average monthly temperature.
items.final: June (the 6th month) has the lowest average monthly temperature

items.part:
In Canberra, the average daily temperature $T$ in degree Celsius $(^{\circ}\text{C})$ in Canberra is represented by the formula $T=7\sin(nx+1.5)+13$, where $n$ is a constant value and $x$ is the number of the month of the year (i.e. January = 1, February = 2 ,….)
Sketch the graph of the function $T=7\sin(nx+1.5)+13$ for $1\le x\le 12$.

The diagram below shows a part of the circle described by the equation $x^2+y^2=25$. The point $P(x,y)$ lies on the circle, and with $O$ representing the origin. Point $M$ is located at coordinates $(2,0)$, while point $N$ is at coordinates $(0,4)$ and $\angle MOP$ is measured in radians.

\exfigure{640_q15_1}
Show that the area, $A$, of the quadrilateral $OMPN$ is given by

$A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$.
items.sol:
Using area $=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ in $\triangle OMP$, with $OP=5$ (radius) and $OM=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle OMP&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times5\times\sin\theta\\ &=5\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle ONP$, $OP=5$, $ON=4$ and $\angle NOP=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle ONP&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\times5\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\\ &=10\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore A&=\text{Area of }\triangle OMP+\text{Area of }\triangle ONP\\ &=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$

A maximum may occur where $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}&=5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta\\ 5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta&=0\\ 10\sin\theta&=5\cos\theta\\ \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
With $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ (right-angled triangle with sides $1$, $2$, $\sqrt{5}$):
$$\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\quad \cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=-5\sin\theta-10\cos\theta\\ &=-5\sin\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-10\cos\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=-5\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-10\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}<0\end{aligned}$$
Concave down, so $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives the maximum area.

For maximum area, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$.

$P$ is on the circle of radius $5$, so $\dfrac{x}{5}=\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=5\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\\ &=2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$$
From $x^2+y^2=25$, with $y>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sqrt{25-x^2}\\ &=\sqrt{25-20}\\ &=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore P\left(2\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}\right)$

items.part: Sketch the curve $y=(x+1)e^{1-x}$ showing all important features including finding and classifying stationary points, points of inflection, intercepts and showing what happens to the curve as $x\to\pm\infty$.
items.sol:
$y$-intercept: when $x=0$, $y=e^{1}=e$.

$x$-intercept: $e^{1-x}\ne0$, so $(x+1)e^{1-x}=0$ gives $x+1=0$, that is $x=-1$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x+1 & v&=e^{1-x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e^{1-x}+(x+1)e^{1-x}\times(-1)\\ &=e^{1-x}(1-x-1)\\ &=-xe^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$: $x=0$, $y=e$.

Product rule again, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=-x & v&=e^{1-x}\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=-e^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-1\times e^{1-x}-x\times e^{1-x}\times(-1)\\ &=e^{1-x}(-1+x)\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-1\times e^{1}<0$, concave down.

$\therefore (0,e)$ is a local maximum turning point.

Points of inflection are possible where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$: $x=1$, $y=2\times e^{0}=2$, that is $(1,2)$.

\extable{Ts2103_1}

The concavity changes, so $(1,2)$ is a point of inflection.

Behaviour as $x\to\pm\infty$:
$$\begin{aligned}&x\to+\infty: && x+1\to+\infty,\ e^{1-x}\to0 && \therefore y\to0\\ &x\to-\infty: && x+1\to-\infty,\ e^{1-x}\to\infty && \therefore y\to-\infty\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{640_q16_s1}

Revenue is the hiring fee plus $\$20$ per guest:

$$R=1000+20x$$

items.part:
The incoming revenue for a catering company, $R$, is based on a \$1 000 hiring fee plus \$20 per person where $x$ is the number of guests. The graph of the revenue model has been provided on the grid below.

\exfigure{339_q11_1}
The cost for operating the catering company is modelled by $C=1200+10x$, where $C$ is the cost and $x$ is the number of guests.

On the grid on the previous page, draw the graph of this cost model and label it as $C$.
items.sol: \exfigure{339_q11_s1}

Break-even occurs where $R=C$.

From the graph, the two lines intersect at $x=20$.

Algebraically:

$$\begin{aligned} R &= C \\ 1000+20x &= 1200+10x \\ 10x &= 200 \\ x &= 20 \end{aligned}$$

Profit is revenue minus cost, so a profit of $\$500$ needs $R-C=500$.

$$\begin{aligned} R-C &= 500 \\ 1000+20x-(1200+10x) &= 500 \\ 10x &= 700 \\ x &= 70 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}\dfrac{5x^3-6x^2+3}{x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Divide each term of the numerator by $x^2$, then integrate:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{1}^{3}\dfrac{5x^3-6x^2+3}{x^2}\,dx &= \int_{1}^{3}\left(\dfrac{5x^3}{x^2}-\dfrac{6x^2}{x^2}+\dfrac{3}{x^2}\right)dx \\ &= \int_{1}^{3}\left(5x-6+3x^{-2}\right)dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-6x+\dfrac{3x^{-1}}{-1}\right]_{1}^{3} \\ &= \left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-6x-\dfrac{3}{x}\right]_{1}^{3} \\ &= \left[\dfrac{5(3)^2}{2}-6(3)-\dfrac{3}{(3)}\right]-\left[\dfrac{5(1)^2}{2}-6(1)-\dfrac{3}{(1)}\right] \\ &= \left[22\dfrac{1}{2}-18-1\right]-\left[2\dfrac{1}{2}-6-3\right] \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts2223_1}

items.part:
The table shows the results of a survey of 300 people who have been vaccinated against a new virus.
Find the probability that the selected person is infected.
items.sol: $$P(\text{Infected})=\dfrac{\text{number infected}}{\text{total}}=\dfrac{147}{300}$$

items.part:
The table shows the results of a survey of 300 people who have been vaccinated against a new virus.
Find the probability that the selected person is not vaccinated, given that they are infected.
items.sol: $$P(\text{Not vaccinated}\mid\text{Infected})=\dfrac{\text{not vaccinated and infected}}{\text{infected}}=\dfrac{120}{147}$$

items.part:
A car leaves a petrol station and drives $N30^\circ W$ at 80 km/h. At the same time, a motor bike leaves the petrol station and travels due east at 60 km/h.
Show that after one hour, the distance between the car and the motor bike is $20\sqrt{37}$ km.
items.sol:
\exfigure{339_q15_s1}

The car's bearing is $N30^\circ W$ and the motor bike travels due east, so

$$\angle COM=30^\circ+90^\circ=120^\circ$$

After one hour, $OC=80$ km and $OM=60$ km.

By the cosine rule in $\triangle COM$:

$$\begin{aligned} CM^2 &= OC^2+OM^2-2\,OC\times OM\cos\angle COM \\ &= 80^2+60^2-2\times 80\times 60\cos 120^\circ \\ &= 80^2+60^2-2\times 80\times 60\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= 14800 \end{aligned}$$

Since $CM>0$:

$$\begin{aligned} CM &= \sqrt{14800} \\ &= \sqrt{400\times 37} \\ &= 20\sqrt{37}\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A car leaves a petrol station and drives $N30^\circ W$ at 80 km/h. At the same time, a motor bike leaves the petrol station and travels due east at 60 km/h.
Find the bearing of the car from the motor bike.

Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
By the sine rule in $\triangle COM$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\angle CMO}{OC} &= \dfrac{\sin\angle COM}{CM} \\ \dfrac{\sin\angle CMO}{80} &= \dfrac{\sin 120^\circ}{20\sqrt{37}} \\ \sin\angle CMO &= \dfrac{80\sin 120^\circ}{20\sqrt{37}} \\ \angle CMO &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{80\sin 120^\circ}{20\sqrt{37}}\right) \\ &= 34.71500\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 35^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Since $\angle COM=120^\circ$ is obtuse, $\angle CMO$ must be acute.

The motor bike is due east of $O$, so $O$ is due west of $M$ (bearing $270^\circ$), and $C$ lies north of $OM$.

$$\text{Bearing}=270^\circ+35^\circ=305^\circ$$

$$\therefore \text{ the bearing of the car from the motor bike is approximately } 305^\circ\text{T } (N55^\circ W)$$

Alternatively, use the cosine rule to find $\angle CMO$.

items.part: Find the coordinates and nature of the stationary points on the curve $y=\dfrac{x^2}{x-2}$.
items.sol:
The curve is undefined at $x=2$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x^2 & v &= x-2 \\ u' &= 2x & v' &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{2x(x-2)-x^2(1)}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^2-4x-x^2}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2-4x}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2} \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $y'=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=4$.

$$\begin{aligned} x=0: &\quad y=0 \\ x=4: &\quad y=8 \end{aligned}$$

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(4,8)$.

The denominator $(x-2)^2$ is positive, so the sign of $y'$ is the sign of $x(x-4)$. Testing the nature:

\exfigure{339_q16_s1}

Hence $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(4,8)$ is a minimum turning point.
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(4,8)$ is a minimum turning point.

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x-1}{2x+1}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Write the numerator as $(2x+1)-2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{2x-1}{2x+1}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{(2x+1)-2}{2x+1}\,dx \\ &= \int\left(1-\dfrac{2}{2x+1}\right)dx \\ &= x-\ln|2x+1|+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=x\log_e x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x & v &= \ln x \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= \dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= (1)(\ln x)+x\times\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= \ln x+1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int(\log_e x+1)\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)=\ln x+1$, so

$$\int(\ln x+1)\,dx=x\ln x+C$$

items.part: Which term of the arithmetic sequence $3, 16, 29, \ldots$ is $224$?
items.sol:
The terms increase by $16-3=13$, so $a=3$ and $d=13$.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:

$$\begin{aligned} 224 &= 3+(n-1)\times 13 \\ 13(n-1) &= 221 \\ n-1 &= 17 \\ n &= 18 \end{aligned}$$

So $224$ is the $18^{\text{th}}$ term.

items.part:
The table below shows points on a continuous curve $y=f(x)$.

\extable{339_q20_t1}

Use the trapezoidal rule to find the approximate value, correct to 2 decimal places, of

$$\int_{3}^{3.4} f(x)\,dx.$$
items.sol:
The table gives $f(x)$ at $x=3,\ 3.2,\ 3.4$, so there are $n=2$ strips of width $\dfrac{3.4-3}{2}=0.2$.

By the trapezoidal rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{3}^{3.4} f(x)\,dx &\approx \dfrac{b-a}{2n}\left[f(3)+2f(3.2)+f(3.4)\right] \\ &\approx \dfrac{3.4-3}{2\times 2}\left[7.19+2(7.62)+8.41\right] \\ &\approx 3.084 \\ &\approx 3.08 \text{ (to 2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Trout are released into a lake for the first time. The size of the population, $P$, of the trout can be modelled by the function $P=\dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5t}}$, where $t$ is the time in months after the trout are introduced into the lake.
Initially, 250 trout were released into the pond. Show that $A=4\,000$.
items.sol:
Initially $t=0$ and $P=250$:

$$\begin{aligned} 250 &= \dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5(0)}} \\ 250 &= \dfrac{A}{16} \\ A &= 4000 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Trout are released into a lake for the first time. The size of the population, $P$, of the trout can be modelled by the function $P=\dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5t}}$, where $t$ is the time in months after the trout are introduced into the lake.
Find the range of the function $P$.
items.sol:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.5t}\to 0$, so $P\to\dfrac{4000}{1+15(0)}=4000$.

Since $1+15e^{-0.5t}>1$, $P$ never reaches $4000$.

Since $t\ge 0$, the smallest value is $P=250$, at $t=0$.

$$\therefore\ 250\le P<4000$$

items.part:
Trout are released into a lake for the first time. The size of the population, $P$, of the trout can be modelled by the function $P=\dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5t}}$, where $t$ is the time in months after the trout are introduced into the lake.
At what rate is the population growing two months after the trout were released into the Lake? Give your answer correct to the nearest number of trout.
items.sol:
Rewrite $P=4000\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^{-1}$ and differentiate (chain rule):

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 4000(-1)\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^{-2}(-0.5)(15e^{-0.5t}) \\ &= \dfrac{30000e^{-0.5t}}{\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$

When $t=2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= \dfrac{30000e^{-0.5(2)}}{\left(1+15e^{-0.5(2)}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{30000}{e\left(1+15e^{-1}\right)^2} \\ &= 259.7601\ldots \\ &\approx 260 \text{ trout per month} \end{aligned}$$

So the population is increasing at approximately $260$ trout per month.

items.part:
Trout are released into a lake for the first time. The size of the population, $P$, of the trout can be modelled by the function $P=\dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5t}}$, where $t$ is the time in months after the trout are introduced into the lake.
How many months will it take for the population of trout to exceed $3\,000$?

Give your answer as a whole number.
items.sol:
Find when $P=3000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3000 &= \dfrac{4000}{1+15e^{-0.5t}} \\ 1+15e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{4}{3} \\ 15e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{1}{45} \\ -0.5t &= \ln\dfrac{1}{45} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 45}{0.5} \\ &= 7.613324\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$P$ is increasing, so it exceeds $3000$ after $7.61$ months, which is $8$ months as a whole number.

$OP=OQ=8$ cm (radii) and $PQ=8$ cm (given), so $\triangle POQ$ is equilateral.

Hence all its angles are $60^\circ$:

$$\angle POQ=60^\circ=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

The area of the bat is the area of the circle minus the area of the minor segment.

The minor segment has angle $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and its area is $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \pi\times 8^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 64\pi-32\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= 64\pi-\dfrac{32\pi}{3}+16\sqrt{3} \\ &= \dfrac{192\pi-32\pi}{3}+16\sqrt{3} \\ &= \dfrac{160\pi}{3}+16\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove that $(1+\sec x+\tan x)(1-\sec x+\tan x)=2\tan x$.
items.sol:
Group the terms as a difference of squares:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= (1+\sec x+\tan x)(1-\sec x+\tan x) \\ &= \left[(1+\tan x)+\sec x\right]\left[(1+\tan x)-\sec x\right] \\ &= (1+\tan x)^2-\sec^2 x \\ &= 1+2\tan x+\tan^2 x-\sec^2 x \\ &= (1+\tan^2 x)+2\tan x-\sec^2 x \\ &= \sec^2 x+2\tan x-\sec^2 x \quad (1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x) \\ &= 2\tan x \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the limiting sum of the geometric series $3+\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}+1}+\dfrac{3}{\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right)^2}+\ldots$.
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $a=3$ and $r=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}+1}$.

Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ exists.

$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{3}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}+1}} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{\frac{\sqrt{3}+1-1}{\sqrt{3}+1}} \\ &= 3\div\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}+1} \\ &= \dfrac{3(\sqrt{3}+1)}{\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= 3+\sqrt{3} \\ &= 4.73205\ldots \end{aligned}$$

A decimal answer was accepted.

items.part: Explain why the geometric series $3+\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}-1}+\dfrac{3}{\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)^2}+\ldots$ does not have a limiting sum.
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $a=3$ and

$$r=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}-1}=1.3660\ldots$$

Since $|r|>1$, the series does not converge.

Hence the limiting sum does not exist.
items.final: Since $|r|=1.366\ldots>1$, the series does not converge, so no limiting sum exists.

items.sol:
The probabilities sum to $1$:

$$\begin{aligned} 4p+3p+2p+p &= 1 \\ 10p &= 1 \\ p &= \dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}$$

Given $E(X)=\sum x\,p(x)=4$:

$$\begin{aligned} 4ap+6ap+6ap+4ap &= 4 \\ 20ap &= 4 \\ 20a\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right) &= 4 \\ 2a &= 4 \\ a &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= \sum x^2p(x) \\ &= 4a^2p+12a^2p+18a^2p+16a^2p \\ &= 50a^2p \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X) &= E(X^2)-\left[E(X)\right]^2 \\ &= 50a^2p-4^2 \\ &= 50(4)\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)-16 \\ &= 20-16 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 6\mid X>3) &= \dfrac{P(3<X\le 6)}{P(X>3)} \\ &= \dfrac{3p+2p}{3p+2p+p} \\ &= \dfrac{5p}{6p} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, using $p=\dfrac{1}{10}$:

$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 6\mid X>3) &= \dfrac{\frac{3}{10}+\frac{2}{10}}{\frac{3}{10}+\frac{2}{10}+\frac{1}{10}} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{5}{10}}{\frac{6}{10}} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The circle $x^2+ax+y^2+by+c=0$ with a radius of 3 units, is shifted to the right by 1 unit.

After the shifting, the circle has the centre at $(3,4)$. Find the value of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
items.sol:
Complete the square in $x$ and $y$:

$$\begin{aligned} x^2+ax+y^2+by+c &= 0 \\ \left(x+\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^2-\dfrac{a^2}{4}+\left(y+\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2-\dfrac{b^2}{4}+c &= 0 \\ \left(x+\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^2+\left(y+\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{a^2}{4}+\dfrac{b^2}{4}-c \end{aligned}$$

Shifting right by $1$ replaces $x$ with $x-1$:

$$\left(x-1+\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^2+\left(y+\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2=\dfrac{a^2}{4}+\dfrac{b^2}{4}-c$$

The new centre is $(3,4)$:

$$\begin{aligned} 1-\dfrac{a}{2} &= 3 \\ -\dfrac{b}{2} &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

So $a=-4$ and $b=-8$.

The radius is $3$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a^2}{4}+\dfrac{b^2}{4}-c &= 3^2 \\ \dfrac{(-4)^2}{4}+\dfrac{(-8)^2}{4}-c &= 9 \\ c &= 4+16-9 \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, the original centre is $(2,4)$ (one unit left of $(3,4)$):

$$\begin{aligned} (x-2)^2+(y-4)^2 &= 9 \\ x^2-4x+4+y^2-8y+16-9 &= 0 \\ x^2-4x+y^2-8y+11 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ a=-4,\quad b=-8,\quad c=11$$

items.part: Evaluate the sum of the geometric series $4+12+36+\ldots+26\,244$.
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $a=4$ and $r=\dfrac{12}{4}=3$.

Find the number of terms from $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:

$$\begin{aligned} 4\cdot 3^{n-1} &= 26244 \\ 3^{n-1} &= 6561 \\ 3^{n-1} &= 3^8 \end{aligned}$$

Equating powers, $n-1=8$, so $n=9$.

(Or $n-1=\log_3 6561=\dfrac{\ln 6561}{\ln 3}=8$, so $n=9$.)

$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1} \\ S_9 &= \dfrac{4(3^9-1)}{3-1} \\ &= 2(3^9-1) \\ &= 39\,364 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A truck travels between two towns. The distance between the towns is $B$ km.

The trucker has the following costs:

The hourly fuel costs are proportional to the square of the speed.

The hourly fuel cost is \$2000 when the speed is 40 km/h.

All other costs are \$4800 per hour. Let $x$ be the speed in km/h and $C$ be the total cost.
Show that $C=B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right)$.
items.sol:
The hourly fuel cost is proportional to $x^2$, so it is $kx^2$.

When $x=40$ the hourly fuel cost is $\$2000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2000 &= k\times 40^2 \\ k &= \dfrac{2000}{1600} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{4} \end{aligned}$$

Hourly cost $=$ fuel cost $+$ other costs:

$$\text{Hourly cost}=\dfrac{5}{4}x^2+4800$$

Since speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$, the time for the trip is $\dfrac{B}{x}$ hours.

$$\begin{aligned} C &= \left(\dfrac{5}{4}x^2+4800\right)\times\dfrac{B}{x} \\ &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A truck travels between two towns. The distance between the towns is $B$ km.

The trucker has the following costs:

The hourly fuel costs are proportional to the square of the speed.

The hourly fuel cost is \$2000 when the speed is 40 km/h.

All other costs are \$4800 per hour. Let $x$ be the speed in km/h and $C$ be the total cost.
What is the most economical speed?
items.sol:
The most economical speed minimises $C$.

$$\begin{aligned} C &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}x+\dfrac{4800}{x}\right) \\ \dfrac{dC}{dx} &= B\left(\dfrac{5}{4}-\dfrac{4800}{x^2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5}{4}-\dfrac{4800}{x^2} &= 0 \\ 5x^2 &= 4800\times 4 \\ x^2 &= 3840 \\ x &= \pm 61.96773\ldots \end{aligned}$$

Speed is positive, so $x=\sqrt{3840}\approx 61.97$.

Test the nature with the second derivative:

$$\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}=B\times\dfrac{9600}{x^3}$$

At $x=61.97$, $\dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}>0$ since $B>0$ (a distance).

So the cost is a minimum.

$$\therefore\ \text{the most economical speed is } x=\sqrt{3840}\approx 61.97 \text{ km/h}$$

items.part:
A teacher is interested in the relationship between how much time their class of 10 students spends on their phone with that of their laptop.

The teacher collected the results over the month of June and the average number of hours spent per day for each student is outlined in the table below.

\extable{339_q29_t1}
Find the equation of the Least-Squares Regression Line.

Give each coefficient to 3 decimal places.
items.sol:
Using the calculator to find the least-squares regression line $y=A+Bx$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 8.375821\ldots \approx 8.376 \\ B &= -0.875156\ldots \approx -0.875 \end{aligned}$$

$$y=8.376-0.875x$$

items.part:
A teacher is interested in the relationship between how much time their class of 10 students spends on their phone with that of their laptop.

The teacher collected the results over the month of June and the average number of hours spent per day for each student is outlined in the table below.

\extable{339_q29_t1}
Calculate Pearson's Correlation Coefficient, correct to 3 decimal places.

What conclusion can be made about the time students spend on their phone compared to their laptops?
items.sol:
$$r=-0.96229\ldots\approx -0.962 \text{ (3 decimal places)}$$

This is a strong negative correlation.

The more time a person spends on their phone, the less time they spend on their laptop.
items.final: $r\approx -0.962$; strong negative correlation: more phone time, less laptop time.

items.part:
A moving particle has an acceleration of $a\ \text{m/s}^2$ at time $t$ seconds $(t\ge 0)$.

The acceleration is given by the equation

$$a=15-6t.$$

Initially the particle is at the origin and has a velocity of $v=-12$ m/s.
Find the velocity, $v$, and displacement, $x$, in terms of $t$.
items.sol:
Integrate the acceleration, using $x=0$ and $v=-12$ when $t=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} v &= \int(15-6t)\,dt \\ &= 15t-3t^2+c \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} -12 &= 0-0+c \\ c &= -12 \end{aligned}$$

$$v=15t-3t^2-12$$

Integrate again:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(15t-3t^2-12\right)dt \\ &= \dfrac{15t^2}{2}-t^3-12t+d \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 0-0-0+d \\ d &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$x=\dfrac{15t^2}{2}-t^3-12t$$

items.part:
A moving particle has an acceleration of $a\ \text{m/s}^2$ at time $t$ seconds $(t\ge 0)$.

The acceleration is given by the equation

$$a=15-6t.$$

Initially the particle is at the origin and has a velocity of $v=-12$ m/s.
Find the time(s) when the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} -3t^2+15t-12 &= 0 \\ t^2-5t+4 &= 0 \\ (t-1)(t-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{at rest when } t=1 \text{ and } t=4 \text{ seconds}$$

items.part:
A moving particle has an acceleration of $a\ \text{m/s}^2$ at time $t$ seconds $(t\ge 0)$.

The acceleration is given by the equation

$$a=15-6t.$$

Initially the particle is at the origin and has a velocity of $v=-12$ m/s.
Find the distance travelled during the first 4 seconds.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$, at $t=1$ and $t=4$.

Find the position at $t=0,\ 1,\ 4$ using $x=\dfrac{15t^2}{2}-t^3-12t$:

$$\begin{aligned} t=0: &\quad x=0 \\ t=1: &\quad x=-5.5 \\ t=4: &\quad x=8 \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{339_q30_s1}

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 5.5+5.5+8 \\ &= 19 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A sailing club has designed a new logo which is the shaded regions shown in the diagram below.

The shaded regions are bounded by $y=\sin x$ and $y=x\sin x$ in the interval $0\le x\le\pi$.

\exfigure{339_q31_1}
Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)$ and hence show $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x & v &= \cos x \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)=\cos x-x\sin x$$

Integrate both sides:

$$\begin{aligned} \int(\cos x-x\sin x)\,dx &= x\cos x \\ \int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx &= x\cos x \\ \int x\sin x\,dx &= \int\cos x\,dx-x\cos x \\ &= \sin x-x\cos x+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A sailing club has designed a new logo which is the shaded regions shown in the diagram below.

The shaded regions are bounded by $y=\sin x$ and $y=x\sin x$ in the interval $0\le x\le\pi$.

\exfigure{339_q31_1}
Find the area of the logo. Give your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Find the intersection points:

$$\begin{aligned} \sin x &= x\sin x \\ \sin x(1-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $\sin x=0$ or $x=1$.

In $0\le x\le\pi$, the curves meet at $x=0,\ 1,\ \pi$.

The intersection at $x=1$ lies between $0$ and $\pi$, so split the area there.

Using part (a), $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x+C$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx+\int_1^{\pi}(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x-(\sin x-x\cos x)\Big]_0^1+\Big[(\sin x-x\cos x)+\cos x\Big]_1^{\pi} \\ &= (-\cos 1-\sin 1+\cos 1)-(-\cos 0-\sin 0+0)+\Big[(\sin\pi-\pi\cos\pi+\cos\pi)-(\sin 1-\cos 1+\cos 1)\Big] \\ &= (1-\sin 1)+(\pi-1-\sin 1) \\ &= \pi-2\sin 1\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=e^{-kx}+3x$, where $k$ is a positive real number.
Find, in terms of $k$, the $x$-coordinate of the stationary point of the graph of $y=f(x)$.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -ke^{-kx}+3 = 0 \\ ke^{-kx} &= 3 \\ e^{-kx} &= \dfrac{3}{k} \\ -kx &= \ln\dfrac{3}{k} \\ x &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{3}{k}}{-k} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{k}{3}}{k} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=e^{-kx}+3x$, where $k$ is a positive real number.
State the values of $k$ such that the $x$-coordinate of this stationary point is a positive real number.
items.sol:
Since $k>0$, $x>0$ when $\ln\dfrac{3}{k}<0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \ln 3-\ln k &< 0 \\ \ln 3 &< \ln k \\ k &> 3 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, $\ln\dfrac{3}{k}$ is defined when $\dfrac{3}{k}>0$ and is negative when $\dfrac{3}{k}<1$:

$$\begin{aligned} 0 < \dfrac{3}{k} &< 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{3} &> 1 \\ k &> 3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
David is in a life raft, $D$, and Anna is in a cabin cruiser, $A$, searching for him.

They are in contact by mobile telephone. David tells Anna that he can see the top of the mountain Mt Hope, $H$.

From David's position, the mountain has a bearing of $340^\circ$ and the angle of elevation to the top of the mountain is $12^\circ$.

Anna can also see Mt Hope. From her position, the mountain has a bearing of $070^\circ$ and the top of the mountain has an angle of elevation of $19^\circ$. The top of Mt Hope is $1\,244$ m above sea level.

\exfigure{339_q33_1}

Find the distance of the life raft from Anna's position.

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
\exfigure{339_q33_s1}

Let $B$ be the point at sea level directly below $H$, so $HB=1244$ m.

In $\triangle ABH$, right-angled at $B$, $\angle AHB=90^\circ-19^\circ=71^\circ$:

\exfigure{339_q33_s2}

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 71^\circ &= \dfrac{AB}{1244} \\ AB &= 1244\tan 71^\circ \end{aligned}$$

In $\triangle BDH$, right-angled at $B$, $\angle BHD=90^\circ-12^\circ=78^\circ$:

\exfigure{339_q33_s3}

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 78^\circ &= \dfrac{BD}{1244} \\ BD &= 1244\tan 78^\circ \end{aligned}$$

The bearings of $B$ from $A$ ($070^\circ$) and from $D$ ($340^\circ$) differ by $70^\circ+20^\circ=90^\circ$, so $\angle ABD=90^\circ$.

By Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle ABD$:

$$\begin{aligned} AD^2 &= AB^2+BD^2 \\ &= (1244\tan 71^\circ)^2+(1244\tan 78^\circ)^2 \\ &= 47\,305\,057.68 \end{aligned}$$

Since $AD>0$:

$$\begin{aligned} AD &= \sqrt{47\,305\,057.68} \\ &= 6877.867\ldots \\ &\approx 6877.87\text{ m (2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
On a particular day, the depth, $D$ metres, of water in Blue Harbour is given by the function $D=8+2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$ for $0\le t\le 24$, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight.
Find the amplitude and period of the function.
items.sol:
For $D=8+2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$, the amplitude is $2$.

The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{4\pi}{25}$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= 2\pi\div\dfrac{4\pi}{25} \\ &= 2\pi\times\dfrac{25}{4\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{amplitude } 2 \text{ m, period } 12\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ hours}$$

items.part:
On a particular day, the depth, $D$ metres, of water in Blue Harbour is given by the function $D=8+2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$ for $0\le t\le 24$, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight.
Find the first time when the water depth is 7 metres.
items.sol:
Set the depth equal to $7$:

$$\begin{aligned} 8+2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) &= 7 \\ 2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) &= -1 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{339_q34_s1}

The first positive solution is where the angle is $\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4\pi}{25}t &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \\ t &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\div\dfrac{4\pi}{25} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{6} \\ &= 4\text{ h }10\text{ min} \end{aligned}$$

So the water depth is first $7$ m at $4{:}10$ am.

items.part: Calculate the sum of the infinite geometric series $81-27+9-3+\cdots$.
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $a=81$ and $r=-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ exists.

$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{81}{1-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{243}{4} \end{aligned}$$

$$S=\dfrac{243}{4}=60\dfrac{3}{4}=60.75$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}e^{3x}\,dx$ in exact form.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^{1}e^{3x}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x}\right]_{-1}^{1} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}e^3-\dfrac{1}{3}e^{-3} \\ &= \dfrac{e^3}{3}-\dfrac{1}{3e^3} \end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts2274_1}

items.part:
Jeremy has three \$5 notes, two \$10 notes, four \$20 notes and one \$50 note. He decides to give one at random to his friend as a birthday present.
Show that the expected value $E(X)=16.5$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \sum x\,p(x) \\ &= 1.5+2+8+5 \\ &= 16.5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jeremy has three \$5 notes, two \$10 notes, four \$20 notes and one \$50 note. He decides to give one at random to his friend as a birthday present.
Hence or otherwise, calculate the standard deviation, correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X) &= E(X^2)-\left[E(X)\right]^2 \\ &= 437.5-16.5^2 \\ &= 165.25 \end{aligned}$$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance:

$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{165.25} \\ &= 12.85496\ldots \\ &\approx 12.9 \text{ (1 decimal place)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 17 marbles. Eight of them are red, and the others are white. Sarah randomly takes out one marble from the bag, and without replacing it, selects a second marble.
A partially completed tree diagram is shown.

Complete the probability tree diagram, by including all outcomes and probabilities on the branches.

\exfigure{347_q14_1}

A bag contains 17 marbles. Eight of them are red, and the others are white. Sarah randomly takes out one marble from the bag, and without replacing it, selects a second marble.
Find the probability that both marbles are red.
items.sol:
Both marbles are red, so $P(RR)$ is read from the tree:

$$P(RR)=\dfrac{8}{17}\times\dfrac{7}{16}=\dfrac{7}{34}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 17 marbles. Eight of them are red, and the others are white. Sarah randomly takes out one marble from the bag, and without replacing it, selects a second marble.
Find the probability that both marbles selected are different colours.
items.sol:
Different colours means red then white, or white then red:

$$\begin{aligned} P(RW\cup WR) &= \dfrac{9}{34}+\dfrac{9}{34} \\ &= \dfrac{18}{34} \\ &= \dfrac{9}{17} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $\dfrac{x^2-x}{x+2}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x^2-x & v &= x+2 \\ u' &= 2x-1 & v' &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{(2x-1)(x+2)-(x^2-x)(1)}{(x+2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^2+4x-x-2-x^2+x}{(x+2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2+4x-2}{(x+2)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Show that the derivative of $f(x)=(x-1)\sin 2x$ is

$$f'(x)=\sin 2x+2(x-1)\cos 2x.$$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x-1 & v &= \sin 2x \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= 2\cos 2x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= u'v+uv' \\ &= \sin 2x+(x-1)(2\cos 2x) \\ &= \sin 2x+2(x-1)\cos 2x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x+(x-1)\cos 2x\right)dx$.
items.sol:
By part (a), $f'(x)=\sin 2x+2(x-1)\cos 2x$, so the integrand is $\dfrac{1}{2}f'(x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x+(x-1)\cos 2x\right)dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\sin 2x+2(x-1)\cos 2x\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\Big[(x-1)\sin 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-1\right)\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-(0-1)\sin 0\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{8}-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove $\sin x\tan x+\cos x=\sec x$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \sin x\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right)+\cos x\left(\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} \\ &= \sec x \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=(2x-1)^3$ at the point where $x=1$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= (2x-1)^3 \\ y' &= 2.3(2x-1)^2 \\ &= 6(2x-1)^2 \end{aligned}$$

At $x=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= (2(1)-1)^3 = 1 \\ y' &= 6(2(1)-1)^2 = 6 \end{aligned}$$

The gradient of the normal is

$$m_2=-\dfrac{1}{m_1}=-\dfrac{1}{6}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= -\dfrac{1}{6}(x-1) \\ y &= -\dfrac{1}{6}x+1\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Equivalently, $x+6y-7=0$.

items.part:
A company records the reasons for its employees arriving late to work.

The results are shown in the Pareto chart below.

\exfigure{347_q19_1}

Approximately what percentage of issues were due to “Childcare” or “Overslept”?
items.sol:
Total frequency:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 70+40+25+15+10 \\ &= 160 \end{aligned}$$

Childcare is $40$ and Overslept is $25$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{40+25}{160} &= 0.40625 \\ &= 40.625\% \end{aligned}$$

So approximately $40\%$ of issues were due to Childcare or Overslept.

Alternatively, reading the cumulative percentage line, Traffic is at about $44\%$ and Overslept is at about $84\%$:

$$84\%-44\%=40\%$$

So approximately $40\%$.

items.part:
The diagram below shows a compass survey of the field $ABCD$.

\exfigure{347_q20_1}

A surveyor was unable to measure the distance $OD$, but was able to locate the area of the park sections.

If the area of $\Delta DOA$ is $24\text{ m}^2$, what is the length $OD$? Give your answer correct to the nearest metre.
items.sol:
\exfigure{347_q20_s1}

From the bearings, the angle at $O$ is

$$\begin{aligned} \angle DOA &= (360^\circ-304^\circ)+40^\circ \\ &= 96^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Using the area formula for $\triangle DOA$, with the other side $8$ m:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C \\ 24 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times OD\times 8\sin 96^\circ \\ 6 &= OD\sin 96^\circ \\ OD &= \dfrac{6}{\sin 96^\circ} \\ &= 6.033049677\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ OD=6\text{ m (nearest metre)}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Trial group} &: 108 \\ \text{Control group} &: 129 \end{aligned}$$

The control group has the higher centre.

The trial group is positively skewed, while the control group is negatively skewed.

Both have the same interquartile range, $12$.

items.part: Find the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of $y=\dfrac{3x-3}{(x+3)(x-2)}$.
items.sol:
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero:

$$(x+3)(x-2)=0$$

$$\therefore\ x=-3,\ x=2$$

For the horizontal asymptote, divide the numerator and denominator by $x^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{(3x-3)\div x^2}{(x^2+x-6)\div x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{3}{x}-\frac{3}{x^2}}{1+\frac{1}{x}-\frac{6}{x^2}} \end{aligned}$$

As $x\to\pm\infty$, $y\to 0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{asymptotes } x=-3,\ x=2 \text{ and } y=0$$

items.part: Hence sketch the graph of $y=\dfrac{3x-3}{(x+3)(x-2)}$, showing all intercepts and asymptotes.
items.sol:
\exfigure{347_q22_s1}

\extable{Ts2289_1}

items.part:
Hence or otherwise, find all values $x$ for which

$$\dfrac{3x-3}{(x+3)(x-2)}\ge 1.$$
items.sol:
Find where the curve meets the line $y=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3x-3}{(x+3)(x-2)} &= 1 \\ 3x-3 &= (x+3)(x-2) \\ &= x^2+x-6 \\ 0 &= x^2-2x-3 \\ &= (x-3)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$

So the curve meets $y=1$ at $x=3$ and $x=-1$ (see the green line on the sketch from part (b)).

The curve is on or above the line $y=1$ for:

$$\begin{aligned} -3 &< x \le -1 \\ 2 &< x \le 3 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x\in(-3,-1]\cup(2,3]$$

items.part:
A probability density function is defined as:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}hx(5-x), & 0\le x\le 5\\ 0 & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$
Show that $h=\dfrac{6}{125}$.
items.sol:
The area under a probability density function is $1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^5\left(5hx-hx^2\right)dx &= 1 \\ \left[\dfrac{5h}{2}x^2-\dfrac{h}{3}x^3\right]_0^5 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{125}{6}h-0 &= 1 \\ h &= \dfrac{6}{125} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A probability density function is defined as:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}hx(5-x), & 0\le x\le 5\\ 0 & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$
Find the mode of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
The mode is where $f(x)$ is a maximum, so solve $f'(x)=0$.

$$f(x)=\dfrac{6}{125}\cdot 5x-\dfrac{6}{125}x^2$$

$$f'(x)=\dfrac{6}{25}-\dfrac{12}{125}x$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12}{125}x &= \dfrac{6}{25} \\ x &= 2.5 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the mode is } x=2.5$$

items.part: Find the sum of the first 15 terms of the arithmetic series $124+117.5+111+104.5+\cdots$
items.sol:
The common difference is $d=117.5-124=-6.5$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$ with $n=15$, $a=124$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left[2(124)+(15-1)(-6.5)\right] \\ &= 1177.5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $a=\log_2 7$ and $b=\log_7 16$, show that $ab=4$.
items.sol:
Using the change of base rule, $\log_7 16=\dfrac{\log_2 16}{\log_2 7}$:

$$\begin{aligned} ab &= \log_2 7\times\log_7 16 \\ &= \log_2 7\times\dfrac{\log_2 16}{\log_2 7} \\ &= \log_2 16 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find all solutions of $2\sin^2 x+\sin x-1=0$, where $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
Let $u=\sin x$ to factorise the quadratic:

$$\begin{aligned} 2u^2+u-1 &= 0 \\ 2u^2+2u-u-1 &= 0 \\ 2u(u+1)-(u+1) &= 0 \\ (2u-1)(u+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} u=\dfrac{1}{2}: &\quad \sin x=\dfrac{1}{2},\ \ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ u=-1: &\quad \sin x=-1,\ \ x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{347_q26_s1}

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$

items.part:
The diagram below is divided into three regions, $I$, $II$ and $III$ by the curves

$$y=\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\text{ and }y=x^2.$$

\exfigure{347_q27_1}

Find the areas of each of the three regions correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Region $III$ is under $y=x^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} A_{III} &= \int_0^1 x^2\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &\approx 0.33 \end{aligned}$$

Region $II$ is under $y=\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2}$ and above $y=x^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} A_{II} &= \int_0^1\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\,dx-\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right]_0^1-\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= 0-\left(-\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)-\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= 0.303\ldots \\ &\approx 0.30 \end{aligned}$$

Region $I$ is the rest of the unit square:

$$\begin{aligned} A_I &= 1-\dfrac{2}{\pi} \\ &= 0.363\ldots \\ &\approx 0.36 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A company wanted to investigate the strength of the relationship between the amount of money spent on advertising each week and the number of visitors the company’s website receives each week. Data was collected over a 15-week period.
Pearson’s correlation coefficient for the data set is $r=0.8895$. Describe the strength and direction of this linear correlation.
items.sol:
$r=0.8895$ is close to $1$ and positive.

It is a strong, positive correlation.

items.part:
A company wanted to investigate the strength of the relationship between the amount of money spent on advertising each week and the number of visitors the company’s website receives each week. Data was collected over a 15-week period.
The graph below shows a scatterplot and the regression line for the data.

\exfigure{347_q28_1}

Use the graph to calculate the equation of the regression line.

A company wanted to investigate the strength of the relationship between the amount of money spent on advertising each week and the number of visitors the company’s website receives each week. Data was collected over a 15-week period.
Predict the number of visitors the website will receive for a week in which \$3000 was spent on advertising.
items.sol:
Substitute $x=3000$ into the regression line:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= 125(3000)-212\,500 \\ &= 162\,500 \text{ visitors} \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, reading from the graph gives between $160\,000$ and $165\,000$.

items.part:
A company wanted to investigate the strength of the relationship between the amount of money spent on advertising each week and the number of visitors the company’s website receives each week. Data was collected over a 15-week period.
Explain why the model is not useful for predicting the number of visitors for weeks in which \$1500 was spent on advertising.
items.sol:
Substitute $x=1500$ into the regression line:

$$\begin{aligned} y &= 125(1500)-212\,500 \\ &= -25\,000 \text{ visitors} \end{aligned}$$

There cannot be a negative number of visitors, so the model is not valid at $\$1500$.

items.part:
Sketch the curve $y=3e^{-x}+1$.

\exfigure{347_q29_1}
items.sol:
\exfigure{347_q29_s1}

When $x=0$:

A game involves flipping a coin, then rolling two six-sided dice. If the coin lands heads, the sum of the dice is recorded. If the coin lands tails, the difference between the dice is recorded instead.

To win the game, the number recorded must be less than 4.
What is the probability of winning given the coin landed tails?

A game involves flipping a coin, then rolling two six-sided dice. If the coin lands heads, the sum of the dice is recorded. If the coin lands tails, the difference between the dice is recorded instead.

To win the game, the number recorded must be less than 4.
What is the probability of winning the game?
items.sol:
\exfigure{347_q31_s2}

When the coin lands heads, a win needs a sum less than $4$, which occurs in $3$ of the $36$ outcomes, so $P(\text{win}\mid H)=\dfrac{3}{36}$.

Heads and tails are equally likely:

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{win}) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{30}{36}\right)+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{36}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{11}{24} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A game involves flipping a coin, then rolling two six-sided dice. If the coin lands heads, the sum of the dice is recorded. If the coin lands tails, the difference between the dice is recorded instead.

To win the game, the number recorded must be less than 4.
Given the recorded number is 4, what is the probability that the coin landed heads?
items.sol:
A recorded $4$ arises from a sum of $4$ ($3$ ways after heads) or a difference of $4$ ($4$ ways after tails).

$$\begin{aligned} P(H\mid 4) &= \dfrac{P(H\cap 4)}{P(4)} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{36}\right)}{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{36}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{36}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A homeowner intends to construct a rectangular pool in their backyard with a length of $x$ m and a width of $y$ m.

The depth will steadily increase from 1 m to $\dfrac{2x}{3}$ m, as seen in the diagram below.

The homeowner wishes to put tiles around the edge of the surface of the pool, and has enough to tile a perimeter of 27 m.

\exfigure{347_q32_1}
Show that the volume of the pool is $V(x)=-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+4x^2+\dfrac{27}{4}x$.
items.sol:
From the diagram, the volume is the average depth times the length and width:

$$V=\dfrac{x}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)y \qquad (1)$$

The perimeter is $27$ m:

$$\begin{aligned} 2x+2y &= 27 \\ y &= \dfrac{27}{2}-x \qquad (2) \end{aligned}$$

Substitute (2) into (1):

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{27}{2}-x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(\dfrac{27}{2}-x+9x-\dfrac{2x^2}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2}\left(\dfrac{27}{2}+8x-\dfrac{2x^2}{3}\right) \\ V(x) &= -\dfrac{x^3}{3}+4x^2+\dfrac{27}{4}x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A homeowner intends to construct a rectangular pool in their backyard with a length of $x$ m and a width of $y$ m.

The homeowner wishes to put tiles around the edge of the surface of the pool, and has enough to tile a perimeter of 27 m.

\exfigure{347_q32_1}
Hence, find the maximum volume of the pool.
items.sol:
The maximum occurs where $V'(x)=0$:

$$V'(x)=-x^2+8x+\dfrac{27}{4}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= x^2-8x-\dfrac{27}{4} \\ x &= \dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{64-4(1)\left(-\frac{27}{4}\right)}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{91}}{2} \\ &\approx 8.7697 \text{ or } -0.77 \end{aligned}$$

Length is positive, so ignore the negative value.

$$\begin{aligned} V(8.7697) &= -\dfrac{(8.7697)^3}{3}+4(8.7697)^2+\dfrac{27}{4}(8.7697) \\ &= 142\text{ m}^3 \text{ (3 significant figures)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of daylight hours on the $t^{th}$ day of the year in Sydney can be modelled by the following equation.

$$L(t)=12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]$$
Given that there were 14 hours of daylight 10 days before the start of the year, show that $k=2$.
items.sol:
When $t=-10$, $L=14$:

$$\begin{aligned} 14 &= 12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(-10+10)\right] \\ &= 12+k \\ k &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of daylight hours on the $t^{th}$ day of the year in Sydney can be modelled by the following equation.

$$L(t)=12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]$$
How many days into the year will the number of daylight hours be increasing the fastest? (Answer to the nearest day)
items.sol:
The daylight hours increase fastest where $L'(t)$ is a maximum, so solve $L''(t)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} L'(t) &= -\dfrac{4\pi}{365}\sin\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] \\ L''(t) &= -\dfrac{8\pi^2}{365^2}\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] &= 0 \\ \dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10) &= \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \\ t+10 &= 91.25,\ 273.75 \\ t &= 81.25,\ 263.75 \end{aligned}$$

Test which gives the maximum rate:

$$\begin{aligned} L'(81.25) &\approx -0.03 \\ L'(263.75) &\approx 0.03 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{daylight hours increase fastest } 264 \text{ days into the year}$$

items.part:
The number of daylight hours on the $t^{th}$ day of the year in Sydney can be modelled by the following equation.

$$L(t)=12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]$$
Hence, find the number of daylight hours from that day until the end of the year.
items.sol:
Daylight hours from day $264$ to the end of the year ($t=365$):

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{264}^{365}\left(12+2\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]\right)dt &= \left[12t+\dfrac{365}{\pi}\sin\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]\right]_{264}^{365} \\ &= 4399.90137-3051.81796 \\ &= 1348\text{ hours (nearest hour)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Solve the equation:

$$\log_e(x+2)=\log_e(2x)$$
items.sol:
Both logarithms must be defined:
$$\begin{aligned}x+2&>0 &&\text{so } x>-2\\2x&>0 &&\text{so } x>0\end{aligned}$$
Together these give $x>0$.

Since the logarithms are equal, their arguments are equal:
$$\begin{aligned}x+2&=2x\\x&=2\end{aligned}$$
This satisfies $x>0$, so $x=2$.

The positive multiples of 7 are $7,\,14,\,21,\,\ldots$ .

Find the sum of all positive multiples of 7 less than 1000.
items.sol:
The multiples of 7 form an arithmetic series with $a=7$ and $d=7$.

First find how many terms are less than 1000:
$$\begin{aligned}7+(n-1)\times7&<1000\\n&<142.9\ldots\end{aligned}$$
So there are 142 multiples of 7 less than 1000.
$$\begin{aligned}S_{142}&=\dfrac{142}{2}\big(2\times7+(142-1)\times7\big)\\&=71071\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, $\dfrac{1000}{7}\approx142.9$, and rounding down gives $n=142$, so $S_{142}$ is found as above.

items.part:
Find the limiting sum of the geometric series

$$2+\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}+1}+\dfrac{2}{\left(\sqrt{2}+1\right)^2}+\cdots$$

Leave your answer as an exact value with a rational denominator.
items.sol:
The common ratio is the second term divided by the first:
$$r=\dfrac{\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}+1}}{2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}+1}$$
Since $|r|<1$ the limiting sum exists, $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{2}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}+1}}\\&=\dfrac{2}{\frac{\sqrt{2}+1-1}{\sqrt{2}+1}}\\&=\dfrac{2(\sqrt{2}+1)}{\sqrt{2}}\\&=2+\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.sol:

Since $r>1$, the series does not have a limiting sum.

Here $\ln3>0$, $3^{-x}>0$ and $\left(2+3^{-x}\right)^2>0$, so $f'(x)>0$ for all $x$.

items.sol:
Integrate both sides of the given result:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)\,dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx\\x\cos x&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx\\\int x\sin x\,dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-x\cos x\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jason is a digital designer with GraphicsAI.

He designed the logo, shown below, for CEO of QuantumVerse, Saifan.

James calculated that the logo is the region bounded by the curves $y=\sin x$ and $y=x\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.
Hence, calculate the area (shaded in orange) of the logo, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The curves intersect when
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&=x\sin x\\\sin x-x\sin x&=0\\\sin x(1-x)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $\sin x=0$ or $1-x=0$, giving $x=0,\ \pi$ or $x=1$.

As $\sin x>0$ for $0<x<\pi$, the upper curve changes at $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin x&>x\sin x &&\text{for } 0<x<1\\x\sin x&>\sin x &&\text{for } 1<x<\pi\end{aligned}$$
Using $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=\int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx\\&=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x+x\cos x\Big]_0^1\\&=-\cos1-\sin1+\cos1-(-\cos0-\sin0+0)\\&=1-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A_2&=\int_1^\pi(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx\\&=\Big[\sin x-x\cos x+\cos x\Big]_1^\pi\\&=\sin\pi-\pi\cos\pi+\cos\pi-(\sin1-\cos1+\cos1)\\&=-1+\pi-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total shaded area}&=1-\sin1+(-1+\pi-\sin1)\\&=\pi-2\sin1\\&\approx1.46\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

'At least one correct' is the complement of 'none correct', and each digit is wrong with probability $\dfrac{9}{10}$:

Using calculations, decide whether 220 push ups was an outlier.
items.sol:
From the table, $Q_1=100$ and $Q_3=140$.
$$\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1=140-100=40$$
A score $x$ is an outlier if $x>Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$:
$$\begin{aligned}Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}&=140+1.5\times40\\&=200\end{aligned}$$
Since $220>200$, 220 push ups is an outlier.
items.final: Since $220>200$, 220 push ups is an outlier.

items.part: Solve $\sqrt{3}\sin2x=-\cos2x$ for the domain $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
items.sol:
Divide both sides by $\sqrt{3}\cos2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin2x}{\cos2x}&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\\tan2x&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$\tan2x$ is negative in the 2nd and 4th quadrants.

The domain $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ becomes $-\pi\le2x\le\pi$ for $2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6} &&\text{2nd quadrant}\\2x&=-\dfrac{\pi}{6} &&\text{4th quadrant } \left(2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ less one revolution}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\ \text{ or }\ x=-\dfrac{\pi}{12}$$

items.part:
Prove that

$$\dfrac{\sin x+\tan x}{1+\sec x}=\sin x$$
items.sol:
Write in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, then multiply the numerator and denominator by $\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sin x+\tan x}{1+\sec x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x+\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}}{1+\frac{1}{\cos x}}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x\cos x+\sin x}{\cos x+1}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x(\cos x+1)}{\cos x+1}\\&=\sin x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:

items.sol:

$$\begin{aligned}-1&\le\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\le1\\-1&\le-\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\le1 &&(\text{multiply by } -1)\\0&\le1-\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\le2 &&(\text{add } 1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{range}=[0,2]$$

items.part:
Natalie and her friends have made a post-HSC adventure bucket list. One of their bucket list items is to visit the Figure Eight rock pools and a visit to Figure Eight rock pools requires extreme caution. At all times it is very important to check the depth of water before entering the pools.

The depth of water at Figure Eight rock pools can be modelled by the equation

$$d=2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\,,\ \text{for } 0\le t\le12$$

where $d$ is in metres and $t$ is time after 7 am.
What is the depth of the water at high tide?
items.sol:
High tide is when $d$ is greatest, that is when $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}d&=2+\dfrac{1}{2}(1)\\&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The depth of water at high tide is $2.5$ m.

items.part:
Natalie and her friends have made a post-HSC adventure bucket list. One of their bucket list items is to visit the Figure Eight rock pools and a visit to Figure Eight rock pools requires extreme caution. At all times it is very important to check the depth of water before entering the pools.

The depth of water at Figure Eight rock pools can be modelled by the equation

$$d=2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\,,\ \text{for } 0\le t\le12$$

where $d$ is in metres and $t$ is time after 7 am.
Figure Eight rock pools is only safe to visit when the depth of the water is below 1.75 m.

Between what times is it safe to visit the pools?
items.sol:
The pools are safe when $d<1.75$:
$$\begin{aligned}2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<1.75\\\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<-0.25\\\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<-0.5\end{aligned}$$
Solve $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t=-0.5$. The related angle is $\sin^{-1}(0.5)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and sine is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6} &&\text{so } t=7\\\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&\text{so } t=11\end{aligned}$$
By checking the graph or testing values, $d<1.75$ for $7<t<11$.

As $t$ is the number of hours after 7 am, $t=7$ is 2 pm and $t=11$ is 6 pm.

$\therefore$ It is safe to visit the pools between 2 pm and 6 pm.
items.final: It is safe to visit the pools between 2 pm and 6 pm.

items.part:
A wire of length 28 m is to be cut into two pieces. One of the pieces is to be made into a square and the other into a circle.

Let $r$ metres be the radius of the circle and $x$ metres be the length of each side of the square.

The combined perimeter is given as $2\pi r+4x=28$ and the combined area, $A$, is given by:

$$A=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\ \ (\textbf{DO NOT PROVE THIS})$$

What should be the lengths of each piece so that the combined area of the circle and the square is minimum? Leave your answer in simplest exact form.
items.sol:
Differentiate the given area to find the stationary point:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\\A'&=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot2(14-2x)(-2)+2x\\&=-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x\\A''&=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2\end{aligned}$$
Set $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x&=0\\-\dfrac{56}{\pi}+\dfrac{8x}{\pi}+2x&=0\\-56+8x+2\pi x&=0\\2x(4+\pi)&=56\\x&=\dfrac{28}{4+\pi}\end{aligned}$$
$A''=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2>0$ for all $x$ (concave up), so $x=\dfrac{28}{4+\pi}$ gives a minimum.

The square has perimeter $4x$ and the circle has the rest of the wire, so the lengths of the two pieces are
$$4x=\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}\text{ m}$$
and
$$\begin{aligned}28-4x&=28-\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}\\&=\dfrac{28\pi}{4+\pi}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
items.final: Square piece: $\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}$ m; circle piece: $\dfrac{28\pi}{4+\pi}$ m

items.part:
The population size $P$ of a species of birds living at a wildlife preserve increases at a rate of

$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t\quad for\ t\ge0,$$

where $t$ is the time in months. It is known that the initial population of birds is 34.
You are given $\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt\approx22.26$, show that $P=218$ to the nearest integer at $t=4$.
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t$, the change in the population from $t=0$ to $t=4$ is
$$\begin{aligned}P(4)-P(0)&=\int_0^4\left(9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t\right)dt\\&=9\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt-\int_0^42t\,dt\end{aligned}$$
With $P(0)=34$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(4)&=9\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt-\Big[t^2\Big]_0^4+P(0)\\&=9(22.26)-16+34\\&=218.34\ldots\\&\approx218\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population size $P$ of a species of birds living at a wildlife preserve increases at a rate of

$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t\quad for\ t\ge0,$$

where $t$ is the time in months. It is known that the initial population of birds is 34.
A coal mine was recently built near the wildlife preserve and pollution from the mine affects the population of the birds from $t=4$ onwards. Kevin who works as an environmentalist, models that the population size of the birds can then be approximated by $P=Ate^{-0.05t}-100,\ (t\ge4)$.

Using part (a), show that $A=97$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $P=218$ when $t=4$. Substitute into $P=Ate^{-0.05t}-100$:
$$\begin{aligned}218&=A(4)e^{-0.05\times4}-100\\318&=4Ae^{-0.2}\\A&=\dfrac{318}{4e^{-0.2}}\\&=97.10151927\ldots\\&\approx97\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population size $P$ of a species of birds living at a wildlife preserve increases at a rate of

$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t\quad for\ t\ge0,$$

where $t$ is the time in months. It is known that the initial population of birds is 34.
Determine the maximum population size, leave your answer as an integer.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=t & v&=e^{-0.05t}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-0.05e^{-0.05t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P&=97te^{-0.05t}-100\\P'&=97\left(1\times e^{-0.05t}-0.05te^{-0.05t}\right)\\&=97e^{-0.05t}(1-0.05t)\end{aligned}$$
For a maximum, $P'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}97e^{-0.05t}(1-0.05t)&=0\\e^{-0.05t}\left(1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-0.05t}\ne0$, $1-\dfrac{t}{20}=0$, so $t=20$.

Since $97e^{-0.05t}>0$, the factor $1-0.05t$ decides the sign of $P'$. Test either side of $t=20$:

\extable{Ts2365_1}

$\therefore\ t=20$ is a maximum.

When $t=20$:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=97(20)e^{-1}-100\\&=613.6861159\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum population}=613$$

The probabilities sum to 1 for every $\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sum P(X=x)&=\dfrac{3(1-\theta)}{6}+\dfrac{3(1+\theta)}{6}\\&=1\end{aligned}$$
So this gives no restriction on $\theta$.

Each probability must also satisfy $0\le P(X=x)\le1$:
$$\begin{aligned}0\le\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}\le1 &&\text{gives}&& -5\le\theta\le1\\0\le\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}\le1 &&\text{gives}&& -1\le\theta\le5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -1\le\theta\le1$$

The even outcomes are $2$, $4$ and $6$:

items.part: Prove: $\dfrac{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}{\tan x+\sin x}=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x$
items.sol:
Method 1: multiply the numerator and denominator by $\sin x\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}+\frac{1}{\sin x}}{\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}+\frac{\sin x}{1}}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x(\cos x+1)}{\sin^2x+\sin^2x\cos x}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x(1+\cos x)}{\sin^2x(1+\cos x)}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: write the numerator using $\cot x=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan x}+\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right)\times\dfrac{1}{\tan x+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x+\tan x}{\tan x\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\tan x+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $2\cos^2 x-3\cos x=2$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Rearrange to a quadratic in $\cos x$ and factorise:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2x-3\cos x-2&=0\\(2\cos x+1)(\cos x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos x=2$.

$\cos x=2$ has no solution, since $-1\le\cos x\le1$.

For $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ the related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is negative in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$

items.part: Solve $3\sin x+\sqrt{3}\cos x=0$ over the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
Divide both sides by $\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned}3\sin x&=-\sqrt{3}\cos x\\3\tan x&=-\sqrt{3}\\\tan x&=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and tangent is negative in the 2nd and 4th quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$

A circle with centre $O$ and radius 10m is drawn on a vertical wall, standing on a horizontal floor. Point $A$ is vertically below $O$ and $\angle AOB=90^\circ$ as shown in the diagram below.

A laser pointer is aimed from a point $D$ on the ground. The angles of elevation of $A$ and $B$ from $D$ are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ respectively. Let $A$ be $h$ metres above the ground and $\angle ADB=30^\circ$.
Write expressions for $AD$ and $BD$ in terms of $h$.
items.sol:
In the right-angled triangle with the angle of elevation $30^\circ$ at $D$ and height $h$ at $A$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin30^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{AD}\\AD&=\dfrac{h}{\sin30^\circ}=2h\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is $10$ m above $A$ and $OB$ is horizontal, so $B$ is $h+10$ m above the ground:
$$BD=\dfrac{h+10}{\sin60^\circ}=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$$

items.part:
A circle with centre $O$ and radius 10m is drawn on a vertical wall, standing on a horizontal floor. Point $A$ is vertically below $O$ and $\angle AOB=90^\circ$ as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{355_q16_1}

A laser pointer is aimed from a point $D$ on the ground. The angles of elevation of $A$ and $B$ from $D$ are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ respectively. Let $A$ be $h$ metres above the ground and $\angle ADB=30^\circ$.
Hence find the exact value of $h$.
items.sol:
In $\triangle OAB$, $OA=OB=10$ and $\angle AOB=90^\circ$, so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$AB=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt{2}$$
In $\triangle ABD$, use the cosine rule with $\angle ADB=30^\circ$:
$$\left(10\sqrt{2}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+(2h)^2-2\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)(2h)\cos30^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned}200&=\dfrac{4h^2+80h+400}{3}+4h^2-4h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2+80h+400+12h^2-12h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2-40h+400\\0&=4h^2-40h-200\\&=4\left(h^2-10h-50\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$h=\dfrac{10\pm\sqrt{300}}{2}=5\pm5\sqrt{3}$$
Since $h>0$:
$$\therefore\ h=5+5\sqrt{3}\approx13.66$$

items.part: Differentiate $xe^{5x}$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{5x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=5e^{5x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{5x}\right)&=e^{5x}+x\cdot5e^{5x}\\&=e^{5x}(5x+1)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{10} 5xe^{5x}\,dx$
items.sol:
From part (a), $5xe^{5x}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{5x}\right)-e^{5x}$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{10}5xe^{5x}\,dx&=\int_0^{10}\left(5xe^{5x}+e^{5x}-e^{5x}\right)dx\\&=\left[xe^{5x}-\dfrac{e^{5x}}{5}\right]_0^{10}\\&=10e^{50}-\dfrac{e^{50}}{5}-\left(0-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)\\&=\dfrac{49e^{50}+1}{5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $f(x)=x^2-4x+5$ from first principles.
items.sol:
From first principles:
$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{(x+h)^2-4(x+h)+5-\left(x^2-4x+5\right)}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{(x+h-x)(x+h+x)-4h}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{h(2x+h)-4h}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to0}(2x+h-4)\\&=2x-4\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling on the $x$ axis is given by $v(t)=\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $t\ge 0$.
Show that the particle is stationary when $t=1$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}v(1)&=\dfrac{1}{1+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
So the particle is stationary at $t=1$.

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling on the $x$ axis is given by $v(t)=\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $t\ge 0$.
Explain why the particle is moving to the left for all times $t>1$.
items.sol:
$$a(t)=v'(t)=-\dfrac{1}{(t+1)^2}$$
$a(t)<0$ for all $t\ge0$, so $v$ is decreasing.

Since $v(1)=0$ and $v$ is decreasing, $v<0$ for all $t>1$, so the particle always moves to the left for $t>1$.

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling on the $x$ axis is given by $v(t)=\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $t\ge 0$.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds, correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
$v(0)=\dfrac{1}{2}>0$, $v(1)=0$ and $v$ is decreasing, so the direction changes at $t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving right}\\v&<0 &&\text{for } t>1 &&\text{moving left}\end{aligned}$$
So the distance is
$$d=\int_0^1\left(\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt+\left|\int_1^3\left(\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\left[\ln|t+1|-\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_0^1+\left|\left[\ln|t+1|-\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_1^3\right|\\&=\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}-(0-0)+\left|\ln4-\dfrac{3}{2}-\ln2+\dfrac{1}{2}\right|\\&=\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}+\ln2-\ln4+1\\&=\ln\dfrac{2\times2}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The distance travelled is $0.5$ m.

items.part:
Find:

$$\int\dfrac{1-x}{x^3}\,dx$$
items.sol:
Split into powers of $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{1-x}{x^3}\,dx&=\int\left(x^{-3}-x^{-2}\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{x^{-2}}{-2}+x^{-1}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{x}-\dfrac{1}{2x^2}+C\end{aligned}$$

Each term of $E(X)$ is $x\times P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=r\cdot r^n+r^2\cdot r^{n-1}+r^3\cdot r^{n-2}+\cdots\\&\quad+r^k\cdot r^{n-k+1}+\cdots+r^n\cdot r\\&=r^{n+1}+r^{n+1}+\cdots+r^{n+1}\\&=nr^{n+1} &&(1)\end{aligned}$$
The probabilities sum to 1, and they form a geometric series with first term $r$, common ratio $r$ and $n$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned}r^n+r^{n-1}+r^{n-2}+\cdots+r&=1\\\dfrac{r(r^n-1)}{r-1}&=1\\r^{n+1}-r&=r-1\\r^{n+1}&=2r-1\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$E(X)=n(2r-1)\quad\text{as required}$$

items.sol:
The boat can operate when the depth is at least 10 m. Find when $d=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}12+4\cos\left(\dfrac{t}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)&=10\\\cos\left(\dfrac{t}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{t}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{3},\ \ldots$$
Multiply by 3 and add $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:

$$t=7.85\ldots,\ 14.137\ldots$$
which are 7:51 am and 2:08 pm.

The boat can re-enter the harbour at 2:08 pm, and returns to the dock at 2:20 pm.

It needs fuel from 7:30 am to 2:20 pm, which is 6 h 50 min:
$$6\dfrac{5}{6}\times6=41\text{ L (minimum)}$$
$r=0.45$, so there is a weak (or moderate) positive correlation.

A long rectangular sheet of metal 28cm wide is to be made into a gutter by turning up sides of equal height $x$cm, perpendicular to the base as shown below:

Turning up two sides of height $x$ leaves a base of

and the cross-section is a rectangle of height $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=x(28-2x)\\&=28x-2x^2\end{aligned}$$

The height $x$ must be positive, and the base $28-2x$ must be positive:
$$\begin{aligned}x&>0 &&\text{if } x=0 \text{ there is no height}\\28-2x&>0 &&\text{if } x=14 \text{ there is no base, so } x<14\end{aligned}$$

A toxic substance in a lake is degrading naturally according to the formula $A(t)=3000m^{-0.2t}$, where $A$ is the number of grams of the substance remaining at $t$ years and $m>0$ is a constant.

items.sol:
Substitute $t=6$ and $A=2400$:
$$\begin{aligned}2400&=3000m^{-0.2(6)}\\\dfrac{4}{5}&=m^{-\frac{6}{5}}\\m&=\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{-\frac{5}{6}}\\&=1.2\text{ (1 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A toxic substance in a lake is degrading naturally according to the formula $A(t)=3000m^{-0.2t}$, where $A$ is the number of grams of the substance remaining at $t$ years and $m>0$ is a constant.
Fish can be reintroduced to the lake once the rate of change of the toxic substance is greater than $-20$. After how many years can fish be reintroduced? Answer to one decimal place.
items.sol:
With $m=1.2$, $A(t)=3000(1.2)^{-0.2t}$. Fish can be reintroduced when $A'(t)>-20$:
$$\begin{aligned}3000\ln(1.2)\times(-0.2)(1.2)^{-0.2t}&>-20\\-600\ln(1.2)(1.2)^{-0.2t}&>-20\\(1.2)^{-0.2t}&<\dfrac{1}{30\ln1.2}\end{aligned}$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}-0.2t\ln1.2&<-\ln(30\ln1.2)\\t&>\dfrac{\ln(30\ln1.2)}{0.2\ln1.2}\\&=46.5993724\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Fish can be reintroduced after $46.6$ years (1 d.p.).

items.part:

items.sol:
The amount is less than 50 when
$$\begin{aligned}3000(1.2)^{-0.2t}&<50\\-0.2t\ln1.2&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{60}\right)\\t&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{60}\right)}{-0.2\ln1.2}\\&=112.283611\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ It is safe to swim after 113 years.

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln 2)\sqrt{x^3}} & \text{for } k\le x\le 8\\[2ex] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \text{ in } \mathbb{R}\end{cases}$$
Find the value of $k$. Leave your answer as an exact value.
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^3}}=\dfrac{1}{x}$, the density is $\dfrac{3}{2(\ln2)x}$, and
$$\int\dfrac{3}{2(\ln2)x}\,dx=\dfrac{3}{2}\log_2x=\log_2\sqrt{x^3}$$
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_k^8\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln2)\sqrt{x^3}}\,dx&=1\\\left[\log_2\sqrt{x^3}\right]_k^8&=1\\\log_2\sqrt{8^3}-\log_2\sqrt{k^3}&=\log_22\\\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{8}{k}\right)^3}&=2\\\dfrac{8}{k}&=\sqrt[3]{4}\\k&=\dfrac{8}{\sqrt[3]{4}}=4\sqrt[3]{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln 2)\sqrt{x^3}} & \text{for } k\le x\le 8\\[2ex] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \text{ in } \mathbb{R}\end{cases}$$
Find the median value of $X$ as an exact value.
items.sol:
The median $m$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_k^mf(x)\,dx=0.5$, with $k=4\sqrt[3]{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{4\sqrt[3]{2}}^{m}\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln2)\sqrt{x^3}}\,dx&=0.5\\\log_2\sqrt{m^3}-\log_2\sqrt{\left(4\sqrt[3]{2}\right)^3}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\\log_2m^3-\log_2\left(2\times4^3\right)&=\log_22\\\dfrac{m^3}{2\times4^3}&=2\\m&=4\sqrt[3]{4}\end{aligned}$$
The median value is $4\sqrt[3]{4}\approx6.3496$.

items.part: The first term of an arithmetic series is 7, the common difference is 2 and the sum of the first $n$ terms is 247. Find the value of $n$.
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$ with $a=7$ and $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\times247&=n\left(14+2(n-1)\right) \\ 494&=14n+2n^2-2n \\ 2n^2+12n-494&=0 \\ n^2+6n-247&=0 \\ (n+19)(n-13)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

A population of bacteria is modelled by the function $P(t)=P_0\times e^{kt}$, where $P(t)$ is the population at time $t$ (in hours), $P_0$ is the initial population, and $k$ is the constant growth rate.
Given that the initial population $P_0$ is 100 bacteria and the population triples every 4 hours, show that value of $k=\dfrac{\ln 3}{4}$.
items.sol:
The population triples every $4$ hours, so $P(4)=3\times100=300$:
$$\begin{aligned} 300&=100e^{4k} \\ 3&=e^{4k} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(12)&=100e^{12\times\frac{\ln 3}{4}} \\ &=100\times e^{\ln 3^3} \\ &=2700 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A population of bacteria is modelled by the function $P(t)=P_0\times e^{kt}$, where $P(t)$ is the population at time $t$ (in hours), $P_0$ is the initial population, and $k$ is the constant growth rate.
Find the time it takes for the population to reach 100,000 bacteria. Leave your answer to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
Setting $P(t)=100\,000$ and using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 100\,000&=100e^{\frac{t\ln 3}{4}} \\ 1000&=e^{\ln 3^{\frac{t}{4}}} \\ 1000&=3^{\frac{t}{4}} \\ \dfrac{t}{4}&=\log_3 1000 \\ t&=\dfrac{4\ln 1000}{\ln 3} \\ &\approx25.15 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
Converting the decimal part to minutes:
$$\begin{aligned} t&\approx25+0.15\times60 \\ &=25 \text{ hours } 9 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given the function $f(x)=2x^3-\dfrac{5}{2}x^2-4x+2$. Determine the interval(s) where $f(x)$ is decreasing.
items.sol:
Decreasing where $f'(x)<0$. Find the stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-5x-4 \\ f'(x)=0:\ x&=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{25+4\times6\times4}}{12} \\ &=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{121}}{12} \\ &=\dfrac{5\pm11}{12} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{4}{3} \text{ or } x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$$
Test the nature using $f''(x)=12x-5$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=-6-5=-11<0 &&\text{maximum} \\ f''\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)&=16-5=11>0 &&\text{minimum} \end{aligned}$$
So $f(x)$ is decreasing between the maximum and the minimum:
$$-\dfrac{1}{2}<x<\dfrac{4}{3}$$

items.part:
Given the following two functions $f(x)=x^2-3$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{2-x}$.

Find the domain and range of $f(g(x))$.
items.sol:
Substitute $g(x)=\sqrt{2-x}$ into $f(x)=x^2-3$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(g(x))&=\left(\sqrt{2-x}\right)^2-3 \\ &=2-x-3 \\ &=-x-1 \end{aligned}$$
The square root needs $2-x\ge0$, so the domain is $x\le2$.

For the range, work from the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} x&\le2 \\ -x&\ge-2 &&(\text{multiply by } -1) \\ -x-1&\ge-3 &&(\text{subtract } 1) \end{aligned}$$
So the range is $[-3,\infty)$.

items.part:
Prove

$$\dfrac{\sec^2(2\theta)}{\sec^2(2\theta)-1}=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta).$$
items.sol:
Using $\sec^2(2\theta)=\tan^2(2\theta)+1$, so that $\sec^2(2\theta)-1=\tan^2(2\theta)$, and $1+\cot^2(2\theta)=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\tan^2(2\theta)+1}{\tan^2(2\theta)} \\ &=1+\dfrac{1}{\tan^2(2\theta)} \\ &=1+\cot^2(2\theta) \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta) \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, writing $\sec$ in terms of $\cos$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}}{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}-1} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}}{\frac{1-\cos^2(2\theta)}{\cos^2(2\theta)}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\cos^2(2\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2(2\theta)} \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta) \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, solve $\dfrac{\sec^2(2\theta)}{\sec^2(2\theta)-1}=2$ where $0\le\theta\le\pi$.
items.sol:
From part (a) the equation becomes $\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta)=2$. The domain is
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le\theta\le\pi \\ 0&\le2\theta\le2\pi &&(\text{multiply by } 2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta)&=2 \\ \operatorname{cosec}(2\theta)&=\pm\sqrt{2} \\ \sin(2\theta)&=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so in $0\le2\theta\le2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \\ \theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{8} \end{aligned}$$
