items.part:
Solve the following equation:

$$x-2x^2+x^3-2x^4+x^5-2x^6+\cdots=-\dfrac{2}{5}$$

Where $-1\le x\le 1$
items.sol:
Group the terms in pairs; each pair is a term of a geometric series:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=x-2x^2 \\ T_2&=x^3-2x^4 \\ T_3&=x^5-2x^6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} r&=\dfrac{x^3-2x^4}{x-2x^2} \\ &=\dfrac{x^3(1-2x)}{x(1-2x)} \\ &=x^2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $-1\le x\le1$, $r<1$, so the series has a limiting sum:
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{x-2x^2}{1-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x-2x^2}{1-x^2}&=-\dfrac{2}{5} \\ 5x-10x^2&=-2+2x^2 \\ 12x^2-5x-2&=0 \\ (3x-2)(4x+1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ or } x=-\dfrac{1}{4}$$

items.part: Given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and $y=2$ when $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, find $y$ in terms of $x$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\int\cos\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)dx \\ &=\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, $y=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+C \\ 2&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+C \\ C&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore y=\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+1$$

Each point $(x,y)$ on $y=f(x)$ moves to $\left(-2x,\,2y\right)$ on $y=2f\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}x\right)$.

items.part:
The quantity Q in mL of a certain chemical in the body varies during the day and is given by the formula $Q(t)=4+3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$

where $t$ measures hours from midnight.
Find the period in hours of the function Q.
items.sol:
The period of $\cos(nt)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$; here $n=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} T&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &=8 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The quantity Q in mL of a certain chemical in the body varies during the day and is given by the formula $Q(t)=4+3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$

where $t$ measures hours from midnight.
At what time or times of the day is the quantity a minimum?
items.sol:
\exfigure{361_q30_s1}

The minimum occurs where $Q'(t)=0$, at $t=4$ hours. The period is $8$ hours, so the minimum recurs every $8$ hours:
$$t=4,\ 12,\ 20$$
that is, at 4 am, 12 pm and 8 pm.

items.part:
The quantity Q in mL of a certain chemical in the body varies during the day and is given by the formula $Q(t)=4+3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$

where $t$ measures hours from midnight.
What is the minimum quantity of the chemical the body will contain?
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} Q(4)&=4+3\cos\pi \\ &=4-3 \\ &=1 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The quantity Q in mL of a certain chemical in the body varies during the day and is given by the formula $Q(t)=4+3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$

where $t$ measures hours from midnight.
A hospital patient requires a pill to temporarily boost the amount of the chemical whenever the quantity in his body falls to 1.5 units. At what time will a nurse have to wake the patient to give him his first pill of the day? Give your answer to nearest minute.
items.sol:
Set $Q(t)=1.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1.5&=4+3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{2.5}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Cosine is negative, so take the second-quadrant angle (the first time the quantity falls to $1.5$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=\pi-\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right) \\ &=2.5559\ldots \\ t&=2.5559\ldots\times\dfrac{4}{\pi} \\ &=3.254\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So the nurse wakes the patient at $3$ h $15$ min, that is 3:15 am.

items.part:
Given that $y=x^2\ln(x)$
Show that

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x\ln(x)+x$$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln(x) \\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x\ln(x)+x^2\times\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &=2x\ln(x)+x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Given that $y=x^2\ln(x)$
Hence, show that

$$\int x\ln(x)\,dx=\dfrac{x^2\ln(x)}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{4}+C$$
items.sol:
Integrating the result of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \int\left(2x\ln(x)+x\right)dx&=x^2\ln(x) \\ 2\int x\ln(x)\,dx+\int x\,dx&=x^2\ln(x) \\ 2\int x\ln(x)\,dx&=x^2\ln(x)-\int x\,dx \\ \int x\ln(x)\,dx&=\dfrac{x^2\ln(x)}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\int x\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{x^2\ln(x)}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{x^2}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{x^2\ln(x)}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{4}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The first two terms of an infinite geometric sequence are $T_1=20$ and $T_2=16\sin^2\theta$, where $0<\theta<2\pi$, $\theta\ne\pi$.
Find the range of the ratio $(r)$ in this geometric sequence.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} r&=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} \\ &=\dfrac{16\sin^2\theta}{20} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{5}\sin^2\theta \end{aligned}$$
For $0<\theta<2\pi$ with $\theta\ne\pi$, $\sin\theta\ne0$, so $0<\sin^2\theta\le1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&<\sin^2\theta\le1 \\ 0&<\dfrac{4}{5}\sin^2\theta\le\dfrac{4}{5} &&\left(\text{multiply by } \dfrac{4}{5}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore 0<r\le\dfrac{4}{5}$$

items.part:
The first two terms of an infinite geometric sequence are $T_1=20$ and $T_2=16\sin^2\theta$, where $0<\theta<2\pi$, $\theta\ne\pi$.
By developing an expression for the sum of the infinite sequence, find the values of $\theta$ which give the greatest sum.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{20}{1-\frac{4}{5}\sin^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{20\times5}{5-4\sin^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{100}{5-4\sin^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=100 & v&=5-4\sin^2\theta \\ u'&=0 & v'&=-8\sin\theta\cos\theta \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dS}{d\theta}=\dfrac{-100\left(-8\sin\theta\cos\theta\right)}{\left(5-4\sin^2\theta\right)^2}$$
$\dfrac{dS}{d\theta}=0$ when $\sin\theta\cos\theta=0$. In the domain $\sin\theta\ne0$, so $\cos\theta=0$:
$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \text{ or } \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
Test the values of $S$ just either side of each:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\theta&\dfrac{\pi}{2}-0.01&\dfrac{\pi}{2}&\dfrac{\pi}{2}+0.01\\\hline S&99.96&100&99.96\end{array}$$
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\theta&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}-0.01&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+0.01\\\hline S&99.96&100&99.96\end{array}$$
$\therefore$ the sum is greatest at $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ or $\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graphs of the functions $y=2\cos x$ and $y=\sqrt{2}\sin 2x$ between $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

The two graphs intersect at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

\exfigure{361_q33_1}

Find the area of the shaded region. Leave your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
The shaded region is under $y=\sqrt{2}\sin 2x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and under $y=2\cos x$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sqrt{2}\sin 2x\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\cos x\,dx \\ &=\left[-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cos 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}+\Big[2\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &=\left[-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\times0-\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\right]+\left[2\times1-2\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+2-\sqrt{2} \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\dfrac{4}{2}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{4-\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A flood insurance company determines that N, the number of claims received in a month, is a random variable with

$$P(N=n)=\dfrac{2}{3^{n+1}},\ \text{for } n=0,1,2,\ldots.$$

The numbers of claims received in different months are independent.

In any consecutive two-month period, calculate the probability that more than one claim will be received, given that zero claims were received at least one of the two months.
items.sol:
From $P(N=n)=\dfrac{2}{3^{n+1}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(N=0)&=\dfrac{2}{3} \\ P(N=1)&=\dfrac{2}{9} \\ P(N\ge2)&=\dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Solution 1:

\exfigure{361_q34_s1}
$$P(\text{at least one month with zero claims})=1-\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
More than one claim in total, given a zero month, means one month has zero claims and the other has $2$ or more:
$$\begin{aligned} P(N>1\mid\text{at least one zero month})&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{9}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{9}}{\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{4}{27}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Solution 2:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-\dfrac{P(0)P(0)+P(0)P(1)+P(1)P(0)}{P(0,0)+P(0,n)+P(n,0)} \\ &=1-\dfrac{\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{9}+\frac{2}{9}\times\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=1-\dfrac{\frac{4}{9}+\frac{8}{27}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=1-\dfrac{5}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Melinda visits a bank and makes a single deposit of \$$Q$. The annual interest rate is 3.5%.
Melinda wishes to withdraw \$8000 at the end of each year for a period of $n$ years. Show that an expression for the minimum value of $Q$ is

$$\dfrac{8000}{1.035}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^2}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^3}+\cdots+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^n}$$
items.sol:
Let $A_n$ be the balance after the $n$th withdrawal. Each year the balance is multiplied by $1.035$, then $\$8000$ is withdrawn:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=Q\times1.035-8000 \\ A_2&=A_1\times1.035-8000 \\ &=\left(Q\times1.035-8000\right)1.035-8000 \\ &=Q\times1.035^2-8000\times1.035-8000 \\ A_3&=A_2\times1.035-8000 \\ &=Q\times1.035^3-8000\times1.035^2-8000\times1.035-8000 \\ &=Q\times1.035^3-8000\left(1.035^2+1.035+1\right) \end{aligned}$$
Continuing the pattern,
$$A_n=Q\times1.035^n-8000\left(1+1.035+\cdots+1.035^{n-1}\right)$$
The minimum value of $Q$ leaves nothing after $n$ withdrawals, $A_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} Q\times1.035^n&=8000\left(1+1.035+1.035^2+1.035^3+\cdots+1.035^{n-1}\right) \\ Q&=\dfrac{8000}{1.035^n}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^{n-1}}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^{n-2}}+\cdots+\dfrac{8000}{1.035} \\ &=\dfrac{8000}{1.035}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^2}+\cdots+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^n} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Melinda visits a bank and makes a single deposit of \$$Q$. The annual interest rate is 3.5%.
Hence, or otherwise, find the minimum value $Q$ that would permit Melinda to withdraw annual amounts of \$8000 indefinitely. Give your answer to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
The expression in part (a) is a geometric series with
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{8000}{1.035} \\ r&=\dfrac{1}{1.035} \end{aligned}$$
Withdrawing indefinitely means $n\to\infty$, so the minimum value is the limiting sum (as $|r|<1$):
$$\begin{aligned} Q&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{8000}{1.035}}{1-\frac{1}{1.035}} \\ &=\$228\,571.43 \\ &\approx\$228\,571 \text{ (nearest dollar)} \end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution: the yearly interest must cover the withdrawal, so
$$\begin{aligned} Q\times3.5\%&=8000 \\ Q&=\dfrac{8000}{3.5\%} \\ &=\$228\,571.43 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows a large bio-diversity precinct the council is planning to build inside a large park. $OAB$ is a sector with centre $O$, and radius $x$ kilometres. Arc $AB$ subtends an angle of $\theta$ radians at $O$. The equilateral triangle $BCO$ adjoins the sector.

\exfigure{361_q36_1}
The perimeter of the precinct as shown in the diagram is given to be $\left(12-2\sqrt{3}\right)$ kilometres.

Calculate the maximum area of the precinct $(OABC)$. Leave your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
The perimeter is $OA+\text{arc }AB+BC+CO$, where $OA=BC=CO=x$ (radius, and equilateral triangle $BCO$), so
$$\text{Arc } AB=12-2\sqrt{3}-3x$$
Arc length is $x\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} x\theta&=12-2\sqrt{3}-3x \\ \theta&=\dfrac{12}{x}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{x}-3 \end{aligned}$$
Triangle $BCO$ is equilateral, so $\angle BOC=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area } \triangle OBC&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x^2\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x^2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Area of sector}=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\theta=\dfrac{x^2}{2}\theta$$
Area of the precinct is the area of the triangle plus the area of the sector:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4}+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\left(\dfrac{12}{x}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{x}-3\right) \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4}+6x-\sqrt{3}x-\dfrac{3x^2}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x^2}{4}+(6-\sqrt{3})x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x}{2}+(6-\sqrt{3})$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x}{2}+(6-\sqrt{3})&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{-2(6-\sqrt{3})}{\sqrt{3}-6} \\ &=\dfrac{2(\sqrt{3}-6)}{\sqrt{3}-6} \\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{2}<0$, $x=2$ gives a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{4(\sqrt{3}-6)}{4}+2(6-\sqrt{3}) \\ &=6-\sqrt{3} \text{ km}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Without using calculus, sketch the graph of $y=2+\dfrac{1}{x+4}$, showing any asymptote(s) and the $x$ and $y$-intercepts. Sketch you answer on the number plane provided below.

\exfigure{1601_q1_2}
items.sol:
The denominator is zero when $x+4=0$, so the vertical asymptote is $x=-4$.

As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{1}{x+4}\to0$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y=2$.

For the $x$-intercept, $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2+\dfrac{1}{x+4}&=0 \\ x+4&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ x&=-4.5 \end{aligned}$$
For the $y$-intercept, $x=0$:
$$y=2+\dfrac{1}{4}=2.25$$
\exfigure{1601_q1_s1}

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_0^2 \sqrt{4-2x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Write the root as a power and use $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2\sqrt{4-2x}\,dx&=\int_0^2(4-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx \\ &=\left[\dfrac{(4-2x)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}\times(-2)}\right]_0^2 \\ &=[0]-\left[\dfrac{4^{\frac{3}{2}}}{-3}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{8}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sketch the curve $y=-2\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

\exfigure{1601_q1_3}

Consider the curve $y=x^3-3x^2-9x+4$.
Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=x^3-3x^2-9x+4 \\ y'&=3x^2-6x-9 \\ &=3(x^2-2x-3) \\ &=3(x-3)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y''&=6x-6 \\ &=6(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3(x-3)(x+1)&=0 \\ x&=3 \text{ or } x=-1 \end{aligned}$$
These give the points $(-1,\,9)$ and $(3,\,-23)$. Test the nature using $y''$:
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-1)&=6(-1-1)=-12<0 &&\text{local maximum at } (-1,\,9) \\ y''(3)&=6(3-1)=12>0 &&\text{local minimum at } (3,\,-23) \end{aligned}$$
items.final: Local maximum at $(-1,9)$; local minimum at $(3,-23)$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=x^3-3x^2-9x+4$.
Find any point(s) of inflection.
items.sol:
For possible inflections, $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6(x-1)&=0 \\ x&=1 \end{aligned}$$
so the possible point is $(1,\,-7)$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2480_1}

The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $(1,\,-7)$.
\exfigure{1601_q2_s1}

items.part: The gradient of a curve, $y=f(x)$ is given by $f'(x)=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{x}}$. The curve passes through the point $(4,5)$. Find the equation of the curve.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{x}} \\ &=\dfrac{x}{2}+4x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\dfrac{x^2}{4}+8x^{\frac{1}{2}}+c \\ &=\dfrac{x^2}{4}+8\sqrt{x}+c \end{aligned}$$
Since $f(4)=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5&=\dfrac{4^2}{4}+8\sqrt{4}+c \\ c&=-15 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{4}+8\sqrt{x}-15$$

items.part:
A $100$ cm length of wire is cut into two pieces at point P, as shown in the diagram, where $x$ is the length of one of the two pieces of wire.

\exfigure{1601_q3_2}
The piece that is length $x$ is used to form a circle and the other is used to form a square. Show that the total area of the circle and square can be given by:

$$A=\dfrac{x^2}{4\pi}+\dfrac{(100-x)^2}{16}$$
items.sol:
The piece of length $x$ is the circumference of the circle:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi r&=x \\ r&=\dfrac{x}{2\pi} \end{aligned}$$
The other piece has length $100-x$ and is the perimeter of the square, so each side is $\dfrac{100-x}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{circle}}&=\pi\left(\dfrac{x}{2\pi}\right)^2 \\ A_{\text{square}}&=\left(\dfrac{100-x}{4}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total area}&=\dfrac{\pi x^2}{4\pi^2}+\left(\dfrac{100-x}{4}\right)^2 \\ &=\dfrac{x^2}{4\pi}+\dfrac{(100-x)^2}{16} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{x^2}{4\pi}+\dfrac{(100-x)^2}{16} \\ A'&=\dfrac{2x}{4\pi}-\dfrac{2(100-x)}{16} \\ &=\dfrac{x}{2\pi}-\dfrac{100-x}{8} \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{2\pi}-\dfrac{100-x}{8}&=0 \\ \dfrac{4x-\pi(100-x)}{8\pi}&=0 \\ 4x-100\pi+\pi x&=0 \\ x(4+\pi)&=100\pi \\ x&=\dfrac{100\pi}{4+\pi} \\ &=43.99\ldots \\ &\approx44 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Check that $44$ cm gives a minimum:
$$\begin{aligned} A''&=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}+\dfrac{1}{8} \\ &=0.28\ldots \\ &>0 \text{ for all } x \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $44$ cm is a minimum, so the wire should be cut at $44$ cm to minimise the total area of the square and the circle.

items.part:
Solve the following inequation:

$$x-1<2x-2x^2$$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} x-1&<2x-2x^2 \\ 2x^2-x-1&<0 \\ (2x+1)(x-1)&<0 \end{aligned}$$
The parabola $y=(2x+1)(x-1)$ opens upwards, so it is negative between its roots $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $1$:
$$\therefore -\dfrac{1}{2}<x<1 \quad\text{or}\quad \left(-\dfrac{1}{2},\,1\right)$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle \int 2x(4+3x^2)^7\,dx$
items.sol:
The derivative of $4+3x^2$ is $6x$, so multiply and divide by $3$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int 2x(4+3x^2)^7\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int 6x(4+3x^2)^7\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\dfrac{(4+3x^2)^8}{8}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{(4+3x^2)^8}{24}+C \end{aligned}$$

Let $B$ be the area of the blue region, $W$ the area of the small rectangle and $A$ the area of the big rectangle.
$$\begin{aligned} B&=\int_a^b x^n\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left[x^{n+1}\right]_a^b \\ &=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} W&=a\times a^n \\ &=a^{n+1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=b\times b^n \\ &=b^{n+1} \end{aligned}$$
The big rectangle is made up of the blue region, the red region ($3B$) and the small rectangle:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=B+3B+W \\ &=4B+W \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} b^{n+1}&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right)+a^{n+1} \\ b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right) \\ 1&=\dfrac{4}{n+1} \\ 4&=n+1 \\ n&=3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the graph of $y=|x-1|$ for $x\in[-4,4]$.
items.sol: \exfigure{373_q11_s1}

items.part:
Using the sketch from part (i) or otherwise, solve

$$|x-1|=2x+4$$
items.sol:
Graphically, the line $y=2x+4$ meets $y=|x-1|$ at $x=-1$ (the line must be sketched on the graph from part (a)).

Alternatively, solve algebraically in two cases.

Case 1, $x-1\ge0$, so $|x-1|=x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x-1&=2x+4 \\ -x&=5 \\ x&=-5 \end{aligned}$$
This does not satisfy $x\ge1$, so reject.

Case 2, $x-1<0$, so $|x-1|=-(x-1)=1-x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-x&=2x+4 \\ -3x&=3 \\ x&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $-1<1$, so this satisfies $x-1<0$.
$$\therefore x=-1$$

items.part:
Given $f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-9}$ and $g(x)=x+5$
Find positive integers $c$ and $d$ such that $f\Big(g(x)\Big)=\sqrt{(x+c)(x+d)}$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f\Big(g(x)\Big)&=\sqrt{(x+5)^2-9} \\ &=\sqrt{x^2+10x+25-9} \\ &=\sqrt{x^2+10x+16} \\ &=\sqrt{(x+8)(x+2)} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore c=8,\ d=2$ (or vice-versa)

items.part:
Given $f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-9}$ and $g(x)=x+5$
State the domain for which $f\Big(g(x)\Big)$ is defined.
Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\operatorname{cosec}x\right)=\operatorname{cosec}x-x\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x$
items.sol:
Write $x\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{x}{\sin x}$ and use the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\operatorname{cosec}x\right)&=\dfrac{\sin x-x\cos x}{\sin^2x} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}-\dfrac{x\cos x}{\sin^2x} \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}x-x\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence find:

$$\int 2\Big(\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right)\Big)\,dx$$
items.sol:
By part (a), $\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right)$ is the derivative of $x\operatorname{cosec}x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int 2\Big(\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right)\Big)\,dx&=2\int\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right)\,dx \\ &=2x\operatorname{cosec}x+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\left(x+\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^2$ at the point where $x=2$.

Write the equation of the normal using general form.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\left(x+2x^{-1}\right)^2 \\ &=x^2+4+4x^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=2$:
$$y=\left(2+\dfrac{2}{2}\right)^2=9$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x-8x^{-3} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent at $x=2$ is
$$m=2(2)-8(2)^{-3}=3$$
so the gradient of the normal is $-\dfrac{1}{3}$ (perpendicular lines have $m_1m_2=-1$).

The equation of the normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-9&=-\dfrac{1}{3}(x-2) \\ 3y-27&=-x+2 \\ x+3y-29&=0 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A)=0.3$, $P(B)=0.2$ and $P(A|B)=0.5$
Show that $P(A\cup B)=0.4$.
items.sol:
Using the conditional probability formula, $P(A|B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{0.2} \\ P(A\cap B)&=0.1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &=0.3+0.2-0.1 \\ &=0.4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

$$P\left(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\right)$$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P\left(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\right)&=1-P(A\cup B) \\ &=0.6 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 0.1+5a^2+0.2+0.2+2.5+11a&=1 \\ 5a^2+11a+3&=1 \\ 5a^2+11a+2&=0 \\ 5a^2+10a+a+2&=0 \\ 5a(a+2)+(a+2)&=0 \\ (5a+1)(a+2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$a=-\dfrac{1}{5} \text{ or } a=-2$$
For $a=-2$, $2.5+11\times(-2)=-19.5$, which is not allowed since $0\le P(X=x)\le1$.
$$\therefore a=-\dfrac{1}{5}$$

There are 4 red and 3 black discs in a bag. Ms Kim and Ms Lee are playing a game in which they take turns drawing a disc from the bag and then replacing it.

To win the game, Ms Kim must draw a red disc and for Ms Lee to win, she must draw a black disc. They continue taking turns until there is a winner. Ms Kim draws a disc first.
Find the probability that Ms Kim wins on her first draw.
items.sol: Ms Kim wins on her first draw if she draws a red disc, so $P=\dfrac{4}{7}$.

items.part:

To win the game, Ms Kim must draw a red disc and for Ms Lee to win, she must draw a black disc. They continue taking turns until there is a winner. Ms Kim draws a disc first.
Find the probability that Ms Kim wins in three or less of her turns.

There are 4 red and 3 black discs in a bag. Ms Kim and Ms Lee are playing a game in which they take turns drawing a disc from the bag and then replacing it.

To win the game, Ms Kim must draw a red disc and for Ms Lee to win, she must draw a black disc. They continue taking turns until there is a winner. Ms Kim draws a disc first.
Find the probability that Ms Kim wins the game.
items.sol:
\exfigure{373_q17_s2}

Ms Kim wins by drawing red ($\dfrac{4}{7}$); each earlier round has her draw black ($\dfrac{3}{7}$) and Ms Lee draw red ($\dfrac{4}{7}$):
$$\begin{aligned} P(1 \text{ turn})&=\dfrac{4}{7} \\ P(2 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2 \\ P(3 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^3 \\ P(4 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^3+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^3\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^4 \end{aligned}$$
So for $n$ turns,
$$P(n \text{ turns or less})=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\cdots+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^n$$
This is a GP with $a=\dfrac{4}{7}$ and $r=\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}$. The probability that Ms Kim wins the game is its limiting sum:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{4}{7}}{1-\frac{3}{7}\times\frac{4}{7}} \\ &=\dfrac{28}{37} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Prove the following identity:

$$\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=2\sec\theta.$$
items.sol:
Combine the fractions over the common denominator $\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)$, and use $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\cos^2\theta+(1+\sin\theta)^2}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta+1+2\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2+2\sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2(1+\sin\theta)}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{\cos\theta} \\ &=2\sec\theta \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving such that its displacement in metres after $t$ seconds is given by the equation

$$x=-1.5+3\sin 2t$$
State the maximum displacement of the particle.
items.sol:
The maximum value of $\sin(2t)$ is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x_{\max}&=-1.5+3\times1 \\ &=1.5 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving such that its displacement in metres after $t$ seconds is given by the equation

$$x=-1.5+3\sin 2t$$
Find the first four times when the particle is at the origin.
items.sol:
\exfigure{373_q21_s1}

The particle is at the origin when $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1.5+3\sin(2t)&=0 \\ 3\sin(2t)&=1.5 \\ \sin(2t)&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$; sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, and the pattern repeats every $2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 3\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the first four times the particle is at the origin are
$$t=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{12} \text{ seconds}$$

items.part:
A particle travels in a straight line. Its velocity $\dot{x}$ at time $t$ is given by

$$\dot{x}=\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)\ \text{metres per second}$$
Find the expression for the particle's displacement $x$ in terms of $t$, if the particle was initially at $x=2$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int\dot{x}\,dt \\ &=\int\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt \\ &=t^3-6t^2+9t+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially ($t=0$) $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=0^3-6(0)^2+9(0)+C \\ C&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=t^3-6t^2+9t+2 \text{ metres}$$

items.part:
A particle travels in a straight line. Its velocity $\dot{x}$ at time $t$ is given by

$$\dot{x}=\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)\ \text{metres per second}$$
Find an expression for the particle's acceleration in terms of $t$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=\dfrac{d}{dt}(\dot{x}) \\ &=6t-12 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle travels in a straight line. Its velocity $\dot{x}$ at time $t$ is given by

$$\dot{x}=\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)\ \text{metres per second}$$
At what times is the particle at rest?
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3t^2-12t+9&=0 \\ t^2-4t+3&=0 \\ (t-3)(t-1)&=0 \\ t&=1 \text{ or } 3 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

A particle travels in a straight line. Its velocity $\dot{x}$ at time $t$ is given by

$$\dot{x}=\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)\ \text{metres per second}$$
Find the total distance travelled between $t=0$ to $t=3$.
items.sol:
The distance is the area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, so split where the velocity changes sign ($t=1$, part (c)):
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x}&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving in the positive direction} \\ \dot{x}&<0 &&\text{for } 1<t\le3 &&\text{moving in the negative direction} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=\int_0^1\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt+\left|\int_1^3\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt\right| \\ &=\Big[t^3-6t^2+9t\Big]_0^1+\left|\Big[t^3-6t^2+9t\Big]_1^3\right| \\ &=(1-6+9)-(0)+\Big|(27-54+27)-(1-6+9)\Big| \\ &=4+|-4| \\ &=8 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given $\sin^2 x=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x$ and using only translations, reflections and dilations, carefully state all of the transformations required to transform the function $y=\sin x$ to obtain the function $y=\sin^2 x$.
items.sol:
First, $y=\cos x$ is $y=\sin x$ translated horizontally to the left by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, since $\cos x=\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

Next, $y=\cos(2x)$ is $y=\cos x$ with a horizontal compression by a factor of $2$.

Then, $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x)$ is $y=\cos(2x)$ with a reflection in the $x$-axis and a vertical compression by a factor of $2$.

Finally, $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x)$ is $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x)$ with a vertical translation of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ upwards.
items.final: Translate left by $\frac{\pi}{2}$; horizontal compression by factor 2; reflect in $x$-axis and vertical compression by factor 2; translate up $\frac12$.

items.part:
Consider the function:

$$f(x)=\log_e\left(x^2+1\right)$$
Find the stationary point(s) of $f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln g(x)=\dfrac{g'(x)}{g(x)}$, $f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$. For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}&=0 \\ 2x&=0 \\ x&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$f(0)=\ln(1)=0$, so the stationary point is $(0,0)$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=x^2+1 \\ u'&=2 & v'&=2x \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{2(x^2+1)-4x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$$
Test the nature at $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=\dfrac{2(0+1)-0}{(0+1)^2} \\ &=2>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore(0,0)$ is a local minimum stationary point.
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a local minimum stationary point.

items.part:
Consider the function:

$$f(x)=\log_e\left(x^2+1\right)$$
Find the coordinates of the point(s) of inflecion of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Using $f''(x)$ from part (a), $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2(x^2+1)-4x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}&=0 \\ -2x^2+2&=0 \\ 2x^2&=2 \\ x^2&=1 \\ x&=\pm1 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\pm1$ are possible points of inflection, with $f(1)=\ln2$ and $f(-1)=\ln2$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2529_1}

$\therefore(-1,\ln2)$ and $(1,\ln2)$ are points of inflection.

$$\int_1^3\log_e\left(x^2+1\right)\,dx$$

items.sol:
Four subintervals on $[1,3]$ give $h=\dfrac{3-1}{4}=0.5$, so the $x$ values are $1,\,1.5,\,2,\,2.5,\,3$:

\extable{Ts2531_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:

items.part:
Consider the function:

$$f(x)=\log_e\left(x^2+1\right)$$
State whether the approximation found in part (d) is greater or less than the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^3\log_e\left(x^2+1\right)\,dx$. Use your sketch in part (c) to provide a brief justification for your answer.
items.sol:
The approximation is less than the exact value.

The curve is concave down after $x=1$ ($f''(x)<0$ for $x>1$), so on each subinterval the trapezium has slightly less area than the area under the curve.
items.final: The approximation is less than the exact value (curve concave down for $x>1$).

items.part:
An open-topped fish tank of volume $90\,\text{m}^3$ is to be made in the shape of a rectangular prism of length $2x$ metres, width $x$ metres, and height $h$ metres. Materials cost \$15 per square metre for the base of the tank and \$20 per square metre for the sides of the tank.

Show that the total cost \$$C$ of making the fish tank is given by

$$C=30x^2+\dfrac{5\,400}{x}$$

and hence find the dimensions of the fish tank with the least total cost.
items.sol:
\exfigure{373_q25_s1}

The base is $2x$ by $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of base}&=2x\times x=2x^2 \\ \text{Cost of base}&=15\times2x^2=\$30x^2 \end{aligned}$$
The volume is $90\text{ m}^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=h\times2x\times x \\ 90&=2x^2h \\ h&=\dfrac{45}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
The four sides have total area
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of sides}&=2\times h\times2x+2\times x\times h \\ &=4xh+2xh \\ &=6xh \\ &=6x\times\dfrac{45}{x^2} \\ &=\dfrac{270}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost of sides}&=20\times\dfrac{270}{x} \\ &=\$\dfrac{5400}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore C=30x^2+\dfrac{5400}{x}$$
To minimise the cost, let $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dC}{dx}&=60x-\dfrac{5400}{x^2}=0 \\ 60x&=\dfrac{5400}{x^2} \\ x^3&=90 \\ x&=\sqrt[3]{90} \end{aligned}$$
Check that $x=\sqrt[3]{90}$ is a minimum:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2C}{dx^2}&=60+\dfrac{10800}{x^3} \\ &=60+\dfrac{10800}{90} &&(x^3=90) \\ &=180>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the cost is least when $x=\sqrt[3]{90}$, and the dimensions of the tank are
$$\begin{aligned} \text{length}&=2\sqrt[3]{90} \text{ m} \\ \text{width}&=\sqrt[3]{90} \text{ m} \\ \text{height}&=\dfrac{45}{\left(\sqrt[3]{90}\right)^2}=\dfrac{45}{90^{\frac{2}{3}}} \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
items.final: Length $2\sqrt[3]{90}$ m, width $\sqrt[3]{90}$ m, height $\dfrac{45}{90^{2/3}}$ m

items.sol:
\exfigure{373_q28_s1}

Find $P$ where the curves meet:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\tan x-1&=\tan x \\ \tan x&=1 \\ x&=\dfrac{\pi}{4} &&\text{(first solution)} \end{aligned}$$
The area between the curves is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\tan x-(2\tan x-1)\,dx \\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(-\tan x+1\right)dx \\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}+1\right)dx \end{aligned}$$
Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$ with $f(x)=\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\Big[\ln(\cos x)+x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &=\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)-\left(\ln(1)-0\right) \\ &=\ln\left(2^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The level of a local dam is being monitored. After $t$ days, the rate at which the volume of water in the dam is changing is given by

$$R=\dfrac{1\,000}{1+t}-500$$

where $R$ is the rate of change of the volume of water in the dam, measured in megalitres per day.

The volume of water in the dam at the end of the fifth day of monitoring was half the volume at the end of the fourth day.

Find an expression for the volume of water $V$ in the dam, $t$ days after the monitoring began.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\int R\,dt \\ &=\int\left(\dfrac{1000}{1+t}-500\right)dt \\ &=1000\ln|1+t|-500t+C \end{aligned}$$
The volume at the end of day $5$ is half that at the end of day $4$, so $V(4)=2V(5)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000\ln5-2000+C&=2\left(1000\ln6-2500+C\right) \\ 1000\ln5-2000+C&=2000\ln6-5000+2C \\ C&=1000\ln5-2000-2000\ln6+5000 \\ &=1000\left(\ln5-2\ln6\right)+3000 \\ &=1000\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3000 \\ &=1000\left(\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore V=1000\ln|1+t|-500t+1000\left(\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3\right)$$

items.part: Solve the equation $|2x-3|=18$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-3 &= 18 &&\text{or} & 2x-3 &= -18 \\ 2x &= 21 & & & 2x &= -15 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{21}{2} \text{ or } x=-\dfrac{15}{2}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $\tan(2x)=\sqrt{3}$ in the domain $0\le x\le\pi$.
items.sol:
For $0\le x\le\pi$ we need $0\le 2x\le 2\pi$.

Since $\tan 2x=\sqrt{3}$ and tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants,
$$2x=\dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ or } \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ or } \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$

items.part: A standard pack of cards consists of four suits (Diamonds, Hearts, Clubs and Spades) with 13 cards in each suit. If four cards are chosen at random from the pack and placed side by side on a table, what is the probability that they are all from different suits?
items.sol:
Each card must come from a different suit than those already chosen.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{all different suits}) &= \dfrac{52}{52}\times\dfrac{39}{51}\times\dfrac{26}{50}\times\dfrac{13}{49} \\ &= \dfrac{685\,464}{6\,497\,400} \\ &= \dfrac{2197}{20\,825} \\ &\approx 0.1055 \text{ (4 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Volodymyr likes Tic Tacs(R). On Monday he eats 2, on Tuesday he eats 4, on Wednesday he eats 6, and so on in this patern. After how many days will he have eaten a total of 132 Tic Tacs ?
items.sol:
The days form an arithmetic series $2,4,6,8,\ldots$ with $a=2$ and $d=2$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$ with $S_n=132$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{n}{2}(4+2n-2) &= 132 \\ \dfrac{n}{2}(2+2n) &= 132 \\ n(1+n) &= 132 \\ n^2+n-132 &= 0 \\ (n+12)(n-11) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$n=-12$ or $n=11$, and $n>0$.
$$\therefore\ n=11 \text{ days}$$

The bearing of landmark A from landmark O is 248T and the distance between them is 24km. The distance between landmark A and point B is 40km, and the distance from B to O is 35km.
Show that $\angle AOB=83^\circ$ to the nearest degree.

A section of land has been earmarked for a new national park. The shape of the land is shown below.

The bearing of landmark A from landmark O is 248T and the distance between them is 24km. The distance between landmark A and point B is 40km, and the distance from B to O is 35km.
Calculate the area of the planned national park, correct to the nearest square km.

items.part: Find the integral $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{10x}{x^2-8}\,dx$
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2-8)=2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} I &= 5\int\dfrac{2x}{x^2-8}\,dx \\ &= 5\ln|x^2-8|+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_2^6 2^{x-1}\,dx$
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^{kx+b}\,dx=\dfrac{a^{kx+b}}{k\ln a}$ with $k=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} I &= \left[\dfrac{2^{x-1}}{\ln 2}\right]_2^6 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 2}\left(2^5-2^1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{30}{\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ \ln\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}$
items.sol:
Using the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\dfrac{x+1}{x-2} &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\big[\ln(x+1)-\ln(x-2)\big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x+1}-\dfrac{1}{x-2} \\ &= \dfrac{(x-2)-(x+1)}{(x+1)(x-2)} \\ &= \dfrac{-3}{(x+1)(x-2)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A train wheel of radius 40 cm and centre $O$ rolls along a horizontal track (as shown below).

$M$ is a point on the wheel where the wheel touches the track before it starts to roll.

\exfigure{377_q18_1}
Through what angle does $M$ rotate about $O$ (in radians) after the wheel rolls 1 metre ?
items.sol:
Using the arc length formula $l=r\theta$, with $l=100$ cm and $r=40$ cm:
$$\begin{aligned} 100 &= 40\theta \\ \theta &= \dfrac{5}{2} \text{ radians} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A train wheel of radius 40 cm and centre $O$ rolls along a horizontal track (as shown below).

$M$ is a point on the wheel where the wheel touches the track before it starts to roll.

\exfigure{377_q18_1}
After the wheel rolls 1 metre, what is the vertical height of $M$ above the track? (answer to the nearest cm)
items.sol:
\exfigure{377_q18_s1}

$M'$ is where $M$ rolls to, and $h$ is the height of $M'$ above the track.

The angle in the right-angled triangle is $\dfrac{5}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}$ radians.

In this triangle, $\sin\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}=\dfrac{x}{40}$, so
$$x=40\sin\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= 40+x \\ &= 40+40\sin\left(\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}\right) \\ &\approx 72.0457 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=72 \text{ cm (nearest cm)}$$

items.part:
In Glenrowan, the probability that it rains on any Monday is $0.21$. If it rains on Monday, then the probability that it rains on Tuesday is $0.83$. If it does not rain on Monday, then the probability of rain on Tuesday is $0.3$.
Draw a probability tree diagram to show this scenario.

In Glenrowan, the probability that it rains on any Monday is $0.21$. If it rains on Monday, then the probability that it rains on Tuesday is $0.83$. If it does not rain on Monday, then the probability of rain on Tuesday is $0.3$.
Calculate the probability that it rains on a Tuesday in any given week.
items.sol:
Rain on Tuesday follows either rain or no rain on Monday.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{rain on Tuesday}) &= (0.21)(0.83)+(0.79)(0.3) \\ &= \dfrac{4113}{10\,000} \\ &= 0.4113 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In Glenrowan, the probability that it rains on any Monday is $0.21$. If it rains on Monday, then the probability that it rains on Tuesday is $0.83$. If it does not rain on Monday, then the probability of rain on Tuesday is $0.3$.
Given that it rains on a Tuesday, find the chance it did not rain on the Monday.
items.sol:
Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\bar M\,|\,T) &= \dfrac{P(\bar M\cap T)}{P(T)} \\ &= \dfrac{(0.79)(0.3)}{0.4113} \\ &= \dfrac{790}{1371} \\ &\approx 0.57622\ldots \\ &= 0.576 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the curve $y=4e^{-2x}$
items.sol: \exfigure{377_q20_s1}

items.part: Show that this series is geometric
items.sol:
Find the ratio of consecutive terms.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} &= \dfrac{8e^{-x}}{2e^x}=4e^{-2x} \\ \dfrac{T_3}{T_2} &= \dfrac{32e^{-3x}}{8e^{-x}}=4e^{-2x} \end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so the series is geometric with $a=2e^x$ and $r=4e^{-2x}$.

items.part: Find the values of $x$ for which this series has a limiting sum.
items.sol:
A limiting sum exists when $-1<r<1$, with $r=4e^{-2x}$.
$$-1<4e^{-2x}<1$$
From the graph in (a), this holds for $x>\ln 2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the limiting sum exists when } x>\ln 2$$

items.part: Find the limiting sum of this series in terms of $x$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{2e^x}{1-4e^{-2x}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that the curves $y=\sin 2x$ and $y=\cos x$ meet at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
items.sol:
Substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ into each curve.
$$\begin{aligned} y=\sin 2x &: & \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y=\cos x &: & \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The values are equal, so the curves meet at $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.

items.part: Sketch, on the same set of axes, the curves $y=\sin 2x$ and $y=\cos x$ in the domain $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and shade the region bounded only by those curves.
items.sol: \exfigure{377_q21_s1}

items.part: Find the area of this shaded region.
items.sol:
Between $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ the curve $y=\sin 2x$ is above $y=\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(\sin 2x-\cos x)\,dx \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x-\sin x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\pi-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}-1\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{1}{4} \text{ u}^2$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{63}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{r+1}+\sqrt{r}}$
items.sol:
Rationalise the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \sum_{r=1}^{63}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{r+1}+\sqrt{r}} &= \sum_{r=1}^{63}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{r+1}+\sqrt{r}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{r+1}-\sqrt{r}}{\sqrt{r+1}-\sqrt{r}}\right) \\ &= \sum_{r=1}^{63}\left(\sqrt{r+1}-\sqrt{r}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The terms telescope.
$$\begin{aligned} \sum_{r=1}^{63}\left(\sqrt{r+1}-\sqrt{r}\right) &= (\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{1})+(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})+\cdots+(\sqrt{63}-\sqrt{62})+(\sqrt{64}-\sqrt{63}) \\ &= -1+\sqrt{64} \\ &= 7 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A tank contains 200 litres of petrol. More petrol is pumped into the tank for 20 minutes, until it is full.

The volume flow rate $R$ of petrol, in litres per minute, is given by

$$R=4\,(20-t)$$
Find a formula for the volume $V$ of petrol in the tank after $t$ minutes, where $t\le 20$.
items.sol:
The flow rate is the rate of change of volume.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=R=4(20-t)=80-4t$$
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \int(80-4t)\,dt \\ &= 80t-2t^2+C \end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $V=200$, so $C=200$.
$$\therefore\ V=80t-2t^2+200$$

items.part:
A tank contains 200 litres of petrol. More petrol is pumped into the tank for 20 minutes, until it is full.

The volume flow rate $R$ of petrol, in litres per minute, is given by

$$R=4\,(20-t)$$
How many litres of petrol were in the tank when it was full?
items.sol:
The tank is full when the flow stops, so $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4(20-t) &= 0 \\ t &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} V(20) &= 80(20)-2(20)^2+200 \\ &= 1000 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A tank contains 200 litres of petrol. More petrol is pumped into the tank for 20 minutes, until it is full.

The volume flow rate $R$ of petrol, in litres per minute, is given by

$$R=4\,(20-t)$$
How long did it take to half fill the tank? (answer in minutes)
items.sol:
Half of the full volume of $1000$ L is $500$ L.
$$\begin{aligned} 80t-2t^2+200 &= 500 \\ 2t^2-80t+300 &= 0 \\ t^2-40t+150 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{40\pm\sqrt{1600-600}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{40\pm\sqrt{1000}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$t=35.811$ or $t=4.1886$.

The tank is full at $t=20$, so $t=35.811$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ t=4.1886 \text{ minutes (4 min 11 s)}$$

items.part: If $log_a(xy^3)=1$ and $log_a(x^2y)=1$ what is the value of $log_a(xy)$ ?
items.sol:
Using the log laws $\log_a(uv)=\log_a u+\log_a v$ and $\log_a u^n=n\log_a u$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_a x+3\log_a y &= 1 &&(1) \\ 2\log_a x+\log_a y &= 1 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2\log_a x+6\log_a y &= 2 &&2\times(1) \\ 5\log_a y &= 1 &&(3)-(2) \\ \log_a y &= \dfrac{1}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\log_a x=1-3\log_a y=1-\dfrac{3}{5}=\dfrac{2}{5}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \log_a(xy) &= \log_a x+\log_a y \\ &= \dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{2}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Isis and Layla catch a train to school each day but they get on at different stations.

The probability that Isis gets a seat each morning is $\dfrac{1}{8}$.

The probability that Layla gets a seat each morning is $\dfrac{1}{21}$.

What is the probability that, on the next three mornings, at least one girl gets a seat?
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Isis does not get a seat}) &= 1-\dfrac{1}{8}=\dfrac{7}{8} \\ P(\text{Layla does not get a seat}) &= 1-\dfrac{1}{21}=\dfrac{20}{21} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither gets a seat}) &= \dfrac{7}{8}\times\dfrac{20}{21} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither gets a seat, 3 days in a row}) &= \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^3 \\ &= \dfrac{125}{216} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one gets a seat in 3 days}) &= 1-\dfrac{125}{216} \\ &= \dfrac{91}{216} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=x^3+3x^2-9x-5$.
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3x^2+6x-9 \\ &= 3(x^2+2x-3) \\ &= 3(x+3)(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'' &= 6x+6 \\ &= 6(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= -3 &&\text{and} & y &= 22 \\ x &= 1 &&\text{and} & y &= -10 \end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $y''$ at each point:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } (-3,22): & & y'' &= 6(-3+1)=-12<0 &&\text{maximum turning point} \\ \text{At } (1,-10): & & y'' &= 6(1+1)=12>0 &&\text{minimum turning point} \end{aligned}$$
items.final: $(-3,22)$ is a maximum turning point; $(1,-10)$ is a minimum turning point

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=x^3+3x^2-9x-5$.
Sketch the curve in the domain $-5\le x\le 3$

(inflection and $x$-intercepts are not required)

Consider the curve $y=x^3+3x^2-9x-5$.
By drawing an appropriate line on your graph, or otherwise, solve

$$x^3+3x^2-9x+5=0$$

The line $y=-10$ meets the sketch from (ii) at $x=-5$ and $x=1$.

Using the trapezoidal rule:

\exfigure{377_q27_s1}

Make $x$ the subject of $y=\ln(x^2)$:
$$x^2=e^y \quad\text{so}\quad x=e^{\frac{y}{2}} \text{ (as } x>0\text{)}$$
The area under the curve is the area of the rectangle minus the shaded area.

items.part: Find $f'(x)$ if it is known that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,[f(2x)]=x^2$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[f(2x)\big]=2f'(2x)=x^2$$
$$f'(2x)=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2=\dfrac{1}{8}(2x)^2$$
Letting $u=2x$ gives $f'(u)=\dfrac{1}{8}u^2$.
$$\therefore\ f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{8}x^2$$

items.part:
$ABCD$ is a quadrilateral inscribed in a quarter of a circle centred at $A$, radius 100 m.

The points $B$ and $D$ lie on the $x$ and $y$ axes and the point $C$ moves on the circle such that $\angle CAB=\alpha$ as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{377_q29_1}
Solve the equation $\sin(x+15^\circ)=\cos 24^\circ$ for $0^\circ\le x\le 90^\circ$
items.sol:
Write $\cos 24^\circ$ as a sine using $\cos\theta=\sin(90^\circ-\theta)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \sin(x+15^\circ) &= \cos 24^\circ \\ &= \sin(90^\circ-24^\circ) \\ &= \sin 66^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x+15^\circ &= 66^\circ\ \text{ or }\ 180^\circ-66^\circ \\ x &= 51^\circ\ \text{ or }\ 99^\circ \end{aligned}$$
As $0^\circ\le x\le 90^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 51^\circ \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$ABCD$ is a quadrilateral inscribed in a quarter of a circle centred at $A$, radius 100 m.

The points $B$ and $D$ lie on the $x$ and $y$ axes and the point $C$ moves on the circle such that $\angle CAB=\alpha$ as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{377_q29_1}
Show that the area of the quadrilateral ABCD can be expressed as

$$A=5000\,(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha)$$
items.sol:
Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ in each triangle, where $AC=AB=AD=100$ (radii) and $\angle CAD=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\triangle CAB} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 100.100\sin\alpha \\ &= 5000\sin\alpha \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\triangle CAD} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 100.100\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\right) \\ &= 5000\cos\alpha \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ A_{ABCD} &= 5000\sin\alpha+5000\cos\alpha \\ &= 5000(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$ABCD$ is a quadrilateral inscribed in a quarter of a circle centred at $A$, radius 100 m.

The points $B$ and $D$ lie on the $x$ and $y$ axes and the point $C$ moves on the circle such that $\angle CAB=\alpha$ as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{377_q29_1}
Using calculus, show that the maximum area of this quadrilateral is $5000\sqrt{2}\,m^2$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 5000(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha) \\ \dfrac{dA}{d\alpha} &= 5000(\cos\alpha-\sin\alpha) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\alpha-\sin\alpha &= 0 \\ \tan\alpha &= 1 \\ \alpha &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2} &= 5000(-\sin\alpha-\cos\alpha) \\ &= 5000\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) &&\left(\text{at } \alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= -5000\sqrt{2}<0 \end{aligned}$$
So the area is a maximum when $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\max} &= 5000\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= 5000\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \\ &= 5000\sqrt{2} \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=x^2-4x$.

Sketch the graph of $y=2f(1-x)+6$, showing the location of the vertex and the intercepts.
items.sol:
Substitute $f(x)=x^2-4x$ with $x$ replaced by $1-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2f(1-x)+6 \\ &= 2\big[(1-x)^2-4(1-x)\big]+6 \\ &= 2\big[1-2x+x^2-4+4x\big]+6 \\ &= 2(x^2+2x-3)+6 \\ &= 2x^2+4x \\ &= 2x(x+2) \end{aligned}$$
The $x$-intercepts are $0$ and $-2$, so the axis of symmetry is $x=-1$ and the vertex is $(-1,-2)$.

Check by transformations: $2f(1-x)+6=2f\big(-(x-1)\big)+6$ reflects in the $y$-axis, shifts right by $1$, dilates by a factor of $2$ vertically and shifts up by $6$, so the vertex $(2,-4)$ of $f$ becomes $(-1,-2)$.

\exfigure{377_q30_s1}

For a region, the line and curve must meet at $3$ points.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{x^2+1} &= mx \\ x &= mx^3+mx \\ mx^3+(m-1)x &= 0 \\ x\big(mx^2+(m-1)\big) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
One solution is $x=0$.

The other two need $x^2=\dfrac{1-m}{m}=\dfrac{1}{m}-1$, so $x=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{m}-1}$.

For two solutions:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{m}-1 &> 0 \\ \dfrac{1}{m} &> 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0<m<1$$
Alternatively, $mx^2+(m-1)=0$ needs a positive discriminant.
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta=-4m(m-1) &> 0 \\ 4m(m-1) &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0<m<1$$

items.part:
The function $y=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ is shown below. It is an odd function.
Find the area of the region (in terms of $m$).
items.sol:
Both $y=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ and $y=mx$ are odd, so the shaded area is twice the area for $x\ge 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\times\int_0^{\sqrt{\frac{1}{m}-1}}\left(\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}-mx\right)dx \\ &= 2\times\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|x^2+1|-\dfrac{mx^2}{2}\right]_0^{\sqrt{\frac{1}{m}-1}} \\ &= \ln\left|\dfrac{1}{m}-1+1\right|-m\left(\dfrac{1}{m}-1\right)-(\ln 1-0) \\ &= \ln\left|\dfrac{1}{m}\right|+m-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\ln\left|\dfrac{1}{m}\right|+m-1 \text{ u}^2$$

items.part:
Show that $e^x\ge 1+x$ if $x\ge 0$.

(Hint: show that the function $f(x)=e^x-(1+x)$ is increasing for $x\ge 0$.)
items.sol:
Let $f(x)=e^x-1-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= e^0-1-0=0 \\ f'(x) &= e^x-1>0 \text{ for } x>0 \end{aligned}$$
So $f(x)$ is increasing for $x\ge 0$ and $f(0)=0$, hence $f(x)\ge 0$ for $x\ge 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x-1-x &\ge 0 \\ e^x &\ge 1+x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Deduce that $\displaystyle\dfrac{4}{3}\le\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le e$
items.sol:
For $0\le x\le 1$ we have $x^2\le x$, so $e^{x^2}\le e^x$ (as $e^x$ is increasing).

Using (i) with $x^2$ in place of $x$:
$$1+x^2\le e^{x^2}\le e^x$$
Integrate over $0\le x\le 1$.
$$\int_0^1(1+x^2)\,dx\le\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le\int_0^1 e^x\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[x+\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 &\le \int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx \le \Big[e^x\Big]_0^1 \\ \left(1+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-0 &\le \int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx \le e^1-e^0 \\ \dfrac{4}{3} &\le \int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx \le e-1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e-1<e$:
$$\dfrac{4}{3}\le\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le e$$

items.part: Differentiate $\dfrac{x^3}{\ln x}$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^3 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=3x^2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{\ln x}\right) &= \dfrac{3x^2\ln x-x^3\cdot\frac{1}{x}}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{3x^2\ln x-x^2}{(\ln x)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by $S_n=\dfrac{1}{2}n(3n+2)$.
Find the first three terms of the series.
items.sol:
The first term is $T_1=S_1$, and each later term is $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$ (the sum of $n$ terms less the sum of $n-1$ terms).
$$\begin{aligned} S_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1)\big(3(1)+2\big)=\dfrac{5}{2} \\ S_2 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(2)\big(3(2)+2\big)=8 \\ S_3 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(3)\big(3(3)+2\big)=\dfrac{33}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T_1 &= S_1=\dfrac{5}{2} \\ T_2 &= S_2-S_1=8-\dfrac{5}{2}=\dfrac{11}{2} \\ T_3 &= S_3-S_2=\dfrac{33}{2}-8=\dfrac{17}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first three terms are $\dfrac{5}{2}$, $\dfrac{11}{2}$ and $\dfrac{17}{2}$.

items.part:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by $S_n=\dfrac{1}{2}n(3n+2)$.
Find an expression for the $n$th term of the series.
items.sol:
From part (a), $a=\dfrac{5}{2}$ and $d=\dfrac{11}{2}-\dfrac{5}{2}=3$. Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= \dfrac{5}{2}+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\ &= \dfrac{5}{2}+3n-3 \\ &= 3n-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= \dfrac{1}{2}n(3n+2)-\dfrac{1}{2}(n-1)\big(3(n-1)+2\big) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\big[3n^2+2n-(n-1)(3n-1)\big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\big[3n^2+2n-(3n^2-4n+1)\big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(6n-1) \\ &= 3n-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=e^{\cos(\pi x)}$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{u}\right)=u'e^{u}$ with $u=\cos\pi x$:
$$y'=-\pi\sin\pi x\cdot e^{\cos\pi x}$$
At $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} m_T &= -\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot e^{\cos\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\pi(1)e^0 \\ &= -\pi \end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent:
$$\begin{aligned} m_N &= -\dfrac{1}{m_T} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $y=e^{\cos\frac{\pi}{2}}=e^0=1$, so the point is $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},1\right)$. The normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi}\left(x-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ \pi y-\pi &= x-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ 2x-2\pi y+2\pi-1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Equivalently, $y=\dfrac{1}{\pi}x-\dfrac{1}{2\pi}+1$.

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{\sec\theta-\sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta}=\sin\theta\tan\theta$.
items.sol:
Factorise the numerator using $1-\cos^4\theta=\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)$ and $1-\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^4\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \sec\theta\sin^2\theta &&(\text{cancel } 1+\cos^2\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\cdot\sin^2\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\sin\theta \\ &= \tan\theta\sin\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $\tan\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$
items.sol:
Let $x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ be the angle to solve for; its range is found from the range of $x$, one operation per line.
$$\begin{aligned} -\pi &\le x\le\pi \\ -\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{4} &\le x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{4} &&(\text{add }\dfrac{\pi}{4}) \\ -\dfrac{3\pi}{4} &\le x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le\dfrac{5\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. Tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants, and $\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\pi=-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is outside the range, so
$$\begin{aligned} x+\dfrac{\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= -\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A random variable is normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

The table gives the probability that this random variable is less than $z$ for different values of $z$.

\extable{382_q20_t1}

In a particular city, the weekly rents for apartments are normally distributed with a mean of \$750 and a standard deviation of \$100.
Find the probability that the weekly rent of an apartment chosen at random is less than \$600.
items.sol:
Standardise using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}=\dfrac{600-750}{100}=-1.5$, then use the symmetry of the normal curve, $P(Z<-1.5)=1-P(Z<1.5)$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<600) &= P(Z<-1.5) \\ &= 1-P(Z<1.5) \\ &= 1-0.933 \\ &= 0.067 \\ &= 6.7\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A random variable is normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

The table gives the probability that this random variable is less than $z$ for different values of $z$.

\extable{382_q20_t1}

In a particular city, the weekly rents for apartments are normally distributed with a mean of \$750 and a standard deviation of \$100.
Sam’s budget for the weekly rent is \$600. She has refined her searches and produced a list such that she is only looking at properties which are less than the mean weekly rent. Find the probability that an apartment that Sam chooses at random from this list is within her budget.
items.sol:
The mean is $750$, so by symmetry $P(X<750)=0.5$. Using conditional probability, $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<600\mid X<750) &= \dfrac{P(X<600\cap X<750)}{P(X<750)} \\ &= \dfrac{P(X<600)}{P(X<750)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.067}{0.5} \\ &= 0.134 \\ &= 13.4\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two identical right pyramids with square bases and equilateral triangular faces are joined to form a regular octahedron.

The following diagram shows a regular octahedron with edge length 6 cm and centre at $O$. $AM$ and $ME$ are perpendicular heights of $\Delta ABC$ and $\Delta BCE$ respectively and point $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

\exfigure{382_q21_1}

Find the size of $\angle AME$, to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
By symmetry $\triangle AMO\cong\triangle EMO$ (SSS: $AM=EM$, $AO=EO$, $MO$ common), so
$$\angle AME=2\times\angle AMO$$
In $\triangle AMC$ ($\angle AMC=90^\circ$, $AC=6$, $MC=3$), by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} AM &= \sqrt{6^2-3^2} \\ &= \sqrt{27} \\ &= 3\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle AMO$ (right angle at $O$, with $MO=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6=3$, half the side of the square base):
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle AMO &= \dfrac{MO}{AM} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \angle AMO &= \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle AME &= 2\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\ &= 109.4712\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 109^\circ \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{kx}{x^2+1}, & \text{for } 1\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 13}$.
items.sol:
Since $f(x)$ is a probability density function, the total area under it is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5\dfrac{kx}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\int_1^5\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 1 &&(\text{the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, up to the factor }2) \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln\left(x^2+1\right)\Big]_1^5 &= 1 \\ k(\ln 26-\ln 2) &= 2 \\ k\ln 13 &= 2 &&(\text{log law}: \ln 26-\ln 2=\ln 13) \\ k &= \dfrac{2}{\ln 13} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{kx}{x^2+1}, & \text{for } 1\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
Find the median $m$.
items.sol:
The median $m$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_1^m f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}$, using $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 13}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{\ln 13}\int_1^m\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx &= 0.5 \\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 13}\Big[\ln\left(x^2+1\right)\Big]_1^m &= 0.5 \\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 13}\left(\ln\left(m^2+1\right)-\ln 2\right) &= 0.5 \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{m^2+1}{2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 13 \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{m^2+1}{2}\right) &= \ln 13^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ \dfrac{m^2+1}{2} &= \sqrt{13} \\ m^2+1 &= 2\sqrt{13} \\ m^2 &= 2\sqrt{13}-1 \\ m &= \sqrt{2\sqrt{13}-1} &&(1\le m\le 5,\text{ so the positive root}) \end{aligned}$$
So $m=2.492208\ldots$

items.part:
The motion of a particle is given by $x=10t+4e^{-3.5t}-4$, where $x$ is the displacement from the starting position in metres and $t$ is time after the initial position in seconds.
Find the initial velocity.
items.sol:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-3.5t}\right)=-3.5e^{-3.5t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 10+4\times(-3.5)e^{-3.5t} \\ &= 10-14e^{-3.5t} \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 10-14e^0 \\ &= -4\text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
From part (a), the velocity is $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=10-14e^{-3.5t}$.

As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-3.5t}\to 0$, so $v\to 10$: the graph has the horizontal asymptote $v=10$.

The $t$-intercept is where $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10-14e^{-3.5t} &= 0 \\ e^{-3.5t} &= \dfrac{5}{7} \\ -3.5t &= \ln\dfrac{5}{7} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{5}{7}}{-3.5} \\ &= -\dfrac{2\ln\frac{5}{7}}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Let $f(x)$ be an even function. If $\displaystyle\int_0^6 f(x)\,dx=12$ and $\displaystyle\int_4^6 f(x)\,dx=-5$ evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4} 2f(x)\,dx$.
items.sol:
Split the integral from $0$ to $6$ at $4$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx &= \int_0^6 f(x)\,dx-\int_4^6 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 12-(-5) \\ &= 17 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-4}^{4}2f(x)\,dx &= 2\int_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,dx \\ &= 2\times 2\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 2\times 2\times 17 \\ &= 68 \end{aligned}$$

Using the quadratic formula on $2k^2-k+0.12=0$:
