items.sol:
The probabilities in a discrete probability distribution sum to 1.
$$\dfrac{1}{9}+k+\dfrac{k}{3}+\dfrac{5}{9}+\dfrac{1}{9}=1$$
Multiplying both sides by 9:
$$\begin{aligned} 1+9k+3k+5+1 &= 9 \\ 12k &= 2 \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Writing $a$ for the vertical dilation factor (so $k$ stays the letter of the required form).

Reflecting in the $x$-axis and dilating vertically by a factor of $a$ replaces $y$ by $\dfrac{-y}{a}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{-y}{a} &= x^2 \\ y &= -ax^2 \end{aligned}$$
Moving the turning point right 1 and up 3 replaces $x$ by $x-1$ and $y$ by $y-3$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-3 &= -a(x-1)^2 \\ y &= -a(x-1)^2+3 \end{aligned}$$
The graph passes through $(0,2)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= -a(0-1)^2+3 \\ -1 &= -a \\ a &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$g(x)=-(x-1)^2+3$$
$\therefore\ k=-1,\ b=-1,\ c=3$

Using $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$, where $X>2$ and $X\le4$ together mean $X=3$ or $X=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>2\mid X\le4) &= \dfrac{P(X>2\cap X\le4)}{P(X\le4)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.25+0.15}{0.1+0.15+0.3+0.25+0.15} \\ &= \dfrac{0.4}{0.95} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{19} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $f(x)=|x|$ and $g(x)$ is the new function after $f(x)$ is dilated horizontally by factor $\dfrac{1}{5}$ and shifted down 2 units, what is the range of $g(x)$?
items.sol:
A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{5}$ replaces $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{\frac{1}{5}}=5x$; a shift down 2 replaces $y$ by $y+2$.
$$\begin{aligned} g(x)+2 &= |5x| \\ g(x) &= |5x|-2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $|5x|\ge0$:
$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &\ge 0-2 \\ g(x) &\ge -2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the range is $g(x)\ge-2$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= 0+0.15+0.8+1.35+0.8 = 3.1 \\ E(X) &= 0+0.15+0.4+0.45+0.2 = 1.2 \end{aligned}$$

Piano in total is the overlap plus piano only, so $P(P)=m+0.25$.

Multiplying both sides by 10:

items.sol:
Violin only is the violin probability less the overlap found in part (c).
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{violin only}) &= 0.35-\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= 0.2875 \end{aligned}$$

Sums of 8 on the table: $(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2)$, which is 5 of the 36 equally likely outcomes.
$$P(\text{score }8)=\dfrac{5}{36}$$

The two throws are independent.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both score }8) &= \dfrac{5}{36}\cdot\dfrac{5}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{1296} \end{aligned}$$

The table is symmetric about the sum 7, so $P(2)=P(12)$, $P(3)=P(11)$, and so on. The sums $2$ to $6$ each have a matching sum from $12$ down to $8$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same}) &= 2\left[P(2\ \&\ 2)+P(3\ \&\ 3)+P(4\ \&\ 4)+P(5\ \&\ 5)+P(6\ \&\ 6)\right]+P(7\ \&\ 7) \\ &= 2\left[\dfrac{1^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{2^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{3^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{4^2}{36^2}+\dfrac{5^2}{36^2}\right]+\dfrac{6^2}{36^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2(55)+36}{1296} \\ &= \dfrac{146}{1296} \\ &= \dfrac{73}{648} \end{aligned}$$

Barbie's score is greater than, less than, or equal to Ken's, so these probabilities sum to 1.
$$P(B>K)+P(K>B)+P(B=K)=1$$
The game is fair, so $P(B>K)=P(K>B)$ and $P(B=K)=\dfrac{73}{648}$ from part (c).
$$\begin{aligned} 2P(B>K)+\dfrac{73}{648} &= 1 \\ 2P(B>K) &= \dfrac{575}{648} \\ P(B>K) &= \dfrac{575}{1296} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Describe a set of transformations to convert $f(x)=x^2$ into $g(x)=12+12x-3x^2$.
items.sol:
Reflect in the $x$-axis: replace $y$ by $-y$.
$$y=-x^2$$
Dilate vertically by a factor of 3: replace $y$ by $\dfrac{y}{3}$.
$$\dfrac{y}{3}=-x^2,\qquad y=-3x^2$$
Translate 2 units right: replace $x$ by $x-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -3(x-2)^2 \\ &= -3x^2+12x-12 \end{aligned}$$
Translate 24 units up: replace $y$ by $y-24$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-24 &= -3x^2+12x-12 \\ y &= 12+12x-3x^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ reflect in the $x$-axis, dilate vertically by a factor of 3, translate 2 units right, then 24 units up.
items.final: Reflect in the $x$-axis, dilate vertically by a factor of 3, translate 2 units right, then 24 units up.

items.part: Using a graph or otherwise determine how many real solutions there are to the equation $\sqrt{x}=(x-3)(x-1)(x+2)$.
items.sol:
The solutions are the intersections of $y=\sqrt{x}$ (for $x\ge0$) and $y=(x-3)(x-1)(x+2)$.

The cubic has $x$-intercepts $-2,\ 1,\ 3$ and, at $x=0$, $y=(-3)(-1)(2)=6$.

For $0\le x\le1$: at $x=0$ the cubic ($6$) is above $\sqrt{x}$ ($0$), and at $x=1$ it is below ($0<1$), so the graphs cross once.

For $1\le x\le3$: the cubic is $\le0$, below $\sqrt{x}$, so they do not meet.

For $x>3$: the cubic is below $\sqrt{x}$ at $x=3$ ($0<\sqrt{3}$) and above it at $x=4$ ($18>2$), so the graphs cross once.

Two points of intersection, therefore two solutions.

items.part: Hence evaluate $2\displaystyle\int_0^2 x\sqrt{2x^2+1}\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (i), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2x^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}=6x\sqrt{2x^2+1}$, so $\left(2x^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}$ is a primitive of $6x\sqrt{2x^2+1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\int_0^2 x\sqrt{2x^2+1}\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{6}\int_0^2 6x\sqrt{2x^2+1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\left(2x^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\Big]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\left\{9^{\frac{3}{2}}-1^{\frac{3}{2}}\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\{27-1\} \\ &= \dfrac{26}{3} \end{aligned}$$

For $y=\sec^2 x$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sec^2\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
For $y=2\cot x$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{1} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
Both give $y=2$, so $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},2\right)$ lies on both curves.

Using the chain rule, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x) &= \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\cos x \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} \\ &= \cot x \end{aligned}$$

The curves meet at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. The upper boundary of the region is $y=\sec^2 x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $y=2\cot x$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\text{Area}=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sec^2 x\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\cot x\,dx$$
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sin x)=\cot x$ from part (ii):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}+2\Big[\ln(\sin x)\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan 0+2\left[\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\ln\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right] \\ &= 1-0+2\left[\ln 1-\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right] \\ &= 1+2\left[0-\ln 2^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right] \\ &= 1+\ln 2 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A function is defined by the rule,

$$g(x)=\begin{cases}3 & \text{for } x\le 0\\ 3\cos x & \text{for } x>0\end{cases}$$
State the domain of $g(x)$.
items.sol:
$g(x)$ is defined for $x\le0$ and for $x>0$, so for every real $x$.
$$\text{domain: } (-\infty,\infty)$$

items.part:
A function is defined by the rule,

$$g(x)=\begin{cases}3 & \text{for } x\le 0\\ 3\cos x & \text{for } x>0\end{cases}$$
State the range of $g(x)$.
items.sol:
For $x\le0$, $g(x)=3$. For $x>0$, $3\cos x$ takes every value from $-3$ to $3$.
$$\text{range: } [-3,3]$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\log_e(x)}{x^2}$.
Find $f'(x)$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{x^2\cdot\frac{1}{x}-\ln x\cdot 2x}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{x-2x\ln x}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{1-2\ln x}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\log_e(x)}{x^2}$.
Evaluate $f'(1)$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} f'(1) &= \dfrac{1-2\ln 1}{1^3} \\ &= \dfrac{1-2\cdot 0}{1} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f'(x)=1-\dfrac{3}{x},\ $ where $x\ne 0$.

Given that $f(e)=-2$, find $f(x)$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \int\left(1-\dfrac{3}{x}\right)dx \\ &= x-3\ln|x|+c \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $f(e)=-2$:
$$\begin{aligned} -2 &= e-3\ln e+c \\ -2 &= e-3\cdot 1+c \\ c &= 1-e \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x-3\ln|x|+1-e$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=\left(x^2+1\right)e^{-x}$.

The first derivative and second derivatives of this function are:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-e^{-x}(x-1)^2$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=e^{-x}(x^2-4x+3)$ (You DO NOT need to show these).
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points are where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$-e^{-x}(1-x)^2=0$$
Since $e^{-x}>0$, $x=1$, and $y=\left(1^2+1\right)e^{-1}=\dfrac{2}{e}$.

At $x=1$ the second derivative is $0$, so the second derivative test does not decide the nature.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=e^{-1}\left(1^2-4(1)+3\right)=0$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of $x=1$.

\extable{Ts3072_1}

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-e^{-x}(x-1)^2\le0$: the gradient is negative on both sides of $x=1$.

$\therefore$ a horizontal point of inflexion at $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$
items.final: a horizontal point of inflexion at $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=\left(x^2+1\right)e^{-x}$.

The first derivative and second derivatives of this function are:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-e^{-x}(x-1)^2$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=e^{-x}(x^2-4x+3)$ (You DO NOT need to show these).
Find the points of inflexion.
items.sol:
Possible points of inflexion are where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{-x}\left(x^2-4x+3\right) &= 0 \\ e^{-x}(x-3)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$x=3$ or $x=1$ ($x=1$ is the point found in part (i)).

Test whether the concavity changes at $x=3$.

\extable{Ts3073_1}
$$y=\left(3^2+1\right)e^{-3}=\dfrac{10}{e^3}$$
$\therefore$ a point of inflexion at $\left(3,\dfrac{10}{e^3}\right)$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x+x}\,dx$, expressing the answer in the form $\ln a$ for some constant $a$.
items.sol:
The numerator $e^x+1$ is the derivative of the denominator $e^x+x$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$ applies with $f(x)=e^x+x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x+x}\,dx &= \Big[\ln|e^x+x|\Big]_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4} \\ &= \ln|e^{\ln 4}+\ln 4|-\ln|e^{\ln 2}+\ln 2| \\ &= \ln|4+\ln 4|-\ln|2+\ln 2| \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{4+\ln 4}{2+\ln 2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Using $\ln 4=2\ln 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{4+2\ln 2}{2+\ln 2}\right) &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2(2+\ln 2)}{2+\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A coffee company is designing a new logo which is initially based on the functions.

$$f(x)=2\sin(x)\ \text{ and }\ g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x),\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

These graphs are shown in the diagram below, in which the measurements in the $x$ and $y$ directions are in metres.

\exfigure{161_q13_1}

The logo is to be painted onto a large sign with the area enclosed by the graphs of the two functions (shaded in the diagram) to be painted in blue.
The total area of the shaded regions, in squares metres, can be calculated as $a\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin(x)\,dx$. What is the value of $a$?
items.sol:
By the symmetry of the graphs about $(\pi,0)$, the two shaded regions have equal area.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\left(2\sin x-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right)dx \end{aligned}$$
Since $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\,dx=0$ (a whole number of periods):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}2\sin x\,dx \\ &= 4\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore a=4$

items.part:
A coffee company is designing a new logo which is initially based on the functions.

$$f(x)=2\sin(x)\ \text{ and }\ g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x),\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

These graphs are shown in the diagram below, in which the measurements in the $x$ and $y$ directions are in metres.

\exfigure{161_q13_1}

The logo is to be painted onto a large sign with the area enclosed by the graphs of the two functions (shaded in the diagram) to be painted in blue.
The coffee company considers changing the functions used in the design of the logo.

Its next attempt used the graphs of the functions,

$$f(x)=2\sin(x)\ \text{ and }\ h(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3x),\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

On the axes below, the graph of $y=f(x)$ has been drawn.

On the same axes, draw the graph of $y=h(x)$.

A coffee company is designing a new logo which is initially based on the functions.

$$f(x)=2\sin(x)\ \text{ and }\ g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x),\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

These graphs are shown in the diagram below, in which the measurements in the $x$ and $y$ directions are in metres.

\exfigure{161_q13_1}

The logo is to be painted onto a large sign with the area enclosed by the graphs of the two functions (shaded in the diagram) to be painted in blue.
State a sequence of two transformations that maps the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the graph of $y=h(x)$.
items.sol:
Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{6}$:
$$2\sin x\ \text{becomes}\ \dfrac{2}{6}\sin x=\dfrac{1}{3}\sin x$$
Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ replaces $x$ by $3x$:
$$\dfrac{1}{3}\sin x\ \text{becomes}\ \dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x$$
items.final: Vertical dilation by factor $\frac{1}{6}$, then horizontal dilation by factor $\frac{1}{3}$ (giving $y=\frac{1}{3}\sin 3x$)

items.part:
A coffee company is designing a new logo which is initially based on the functions.

$$f(x)=2\sin(x)\ \text{ and }\ g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x),\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

These graphs are shown in the diagram below, in which the measurements in the $x$ and $y$ directions are in metres.

\exfigure{161_q13_1}

The logo is to be painted onto a large sign with the area enclosed by the graphs of the two functions (shaded in the diagram) to be painted in blue.
The coffee company now considers using the graphs of the functions $k(x)=m\sin(x)$ and $q(x)=\dfrac{1}{n}\sin(n(x))$, where $m$ and $n$ are positive integers with $m\ge 2$ and $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

Give a simplified expression for the area enclosed by the graphs of $y=k(x)$ and $y=q(x)$ in terms of $m$ and $n$ \textbf{if} $\boldsymbol{n}$ \textbf{is even.}
items.sol:
Both graphs have the same shape each side of $x=\pi$, so the area is twice the area for $0\le x\le\pi$. For even $n$, $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{n}\sin nx\,dx=0$ (a whole number of periods).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}m\sin x\,dx \\ &= 2m\Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2m\left(-\cos\pi+\cos 0\right) \\ &= 2m(1+1) \\ &= 4m \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A coffee company is designing a new logo which is initially based on the functions.

$$f(x)=2\sin(x)\ \text{ and }\ g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x),\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 2\pi.$$

These graphs are shown in the diagram below, in which the measurements in the $x$ and $y$ directions are in metres.

\exfigure{161_q13_1}

The logo is to be painted onto a large sign with the area enclosed by the graphs of the two functions (shaded in the diagram) to be painted in blue.
Find the area enclosed by the graphs of $y=k(x)$ and $y=q(x)$ in terms of $m$ and $n$ \textbf{if} $\boldsymbol{n}$ \textbf{is odd.}

Give your answer in the form $am+\dfrac{b}{n^2}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.
items.sol:
For odd $n$, $\cos(n\pi)=-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\left(m\sin x-\dfrac{1}{n}\sin nx\right)dx \\ &= 2\left[-m\cos x+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos nx\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left\{\left(-m\cos\pi+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos n\pi\right)-\left(-m\cos 0+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos 0\right)\right\} \\ &= 2\left\{\left(m-\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)-\left(-m+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)\right\} \\ &= 2\left\{2m-\dfrac{2}{n^2}\right\} \\ &= 4m-\dfrac{4}{n^2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore a=4$ and $b=-4$

items.part: What is the derivative of $\sqrt{3+x^2}$?
items.sol:
Write the function as a power and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \left(3+x^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ y' &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3+x^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot 2x \\ &= \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3+x^2}} \end{aligned}$$

How much does every 100 bread rolls made add to the cost of production?
items.sol:
Each roll adds $\$0.20$ to the cost.

A bakery shop sells bread rolls for \$0.60 each. The cost, $C$ dollars, of making $n$ bread rolls is given by $C=200+0.2n$.
On the grid below, draw the graphs of the cost, $C$, and the income, $I$.

items.sol:

items.part:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$.
Find $f'(x)$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\left(x^2+1\right)\cdot 1-x\cdot 2x}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2+1-2x^2}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1-x^2}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$.
Hence, or otherwise, find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $y=f(x)$ at the point where $x=2$, in general form.
items.sol:
Using $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ and $f'(x)$ from part (a), at $x=2$:
$$f(2)=\dfrac{2}{2^2+1}=\dfrac{2}{5},\qquad f'(2)=\dfrac{1-2^2}{\left(2^2+1\right)^2}=-\dfrac{3}{25}$$
The point is $\left(2,\dfrac{2}{5}\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{2}{5} &= -\dfrac{3}{25}(x-2) \\ 25y-10 &= -3(x-2) \\ 25y-10 &= -3x+6 \\ 3x+25y-16 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

The probabilities sum to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} k+2k+3k+2k+k &= 1 \\ 9k &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $\ln a-\ln b=\ln(a-b)$, where $a>b>1$, show that $a=\dfrac{b^2}{b-1}$.
items.sol:
Combine the logarithms on the left using $\ln a-\ln b=\ln\dfrac{a}{b}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\dfrac{a}{b} &= \ln(a-b) \\ \dfrac{a}{b} &= a-b \\ a &= ab-b^2 \\ a-ab &= -b^2 \\ a(1-b) &= -b^2 \\ a &= \dfrac{-b^2}{1-b} \\ &= \dfrac{b^2}{b-1} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the graph of $y=2|x+1|$.
items.sol:
The graph is a V shape, so find the vertex and the $y$-intercept.

The vertex is where $2|x+1|=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2|x+1| \\ x+1 &= 0 \\ x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
The $y$-intercept ($x=0$):
$$y=2|0+1|=2$$
\exfigure{162_q11_s2}

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{0} 2|x+1|\,dx$.
items.sol:
From $x=-4$ to $x=0$ the region is two triangles either side of the vertex $(-1,0)$.

At $x=-4$:
$$y=2|-4+1|=6$$
The triangle from $x=-4$ to $x=-1$ has base $3$ and height $6$. The triangle from $x=-1$ to $x=0$ has base $1$ and height $2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-4}^{0}2|x+1|\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 6+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 1\times 2 \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_{-4}^{0}2|x+1|\,dx=10$$

items.part:
Let $f'(x)=x^2+kx$.

The line $y=2x+1$ is a tangent to the graph of $y=f(x)$ at the point where $x=-1$.

Find $f(x)$.
items.sol:
The tangent has gradient $2$ at $x=-1$, so $f'(-1)=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} (-1)^2+k\times(-1) &= 2 \\ 1-k &= 2 \\ k &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=x^2-x$. Integrate to find $f(x)$.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$$
The tangent touches the curve where $x=-1$, so $f(-1)=2(-1)+1=-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} -1 &= \dfrac{(-1)^3}{3}-\dfrac{(-1)^2}{2}+C \\ -1 &= -\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}+C \\ C &= -\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{1}{6}$$

items.part:
Helga is training for a marathon. Her training includes a run every Sunday, starting with a run of 3 km on the first Sunday. Each Sunday she increases the length of her run from the previous Sunday by 2 km.
Show that on the 5$^{\text{th}}$ Sunday of training, she runs 11 km.
items.sol:
The lengths form an arithmetic sequence with first term $a=3$ and common difference $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ T_5 &= 3+(5-1)\times 2 \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 9,\ 11$ (adding $2$ each time).

So on the $5^{\text{th}}$ Sunday she runs $11$ km.

items.part:
Helga is training for a marathon. Her training includes a run every Sunday, starting with a run of 3 km on the first Sunday. Each Sunday she increases the length of her run from the previous Sunday by 2 km.
Find a simplified expression for length of her training run on the $n$th Sunday.
items.sol:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $a=3$ and $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= 3+(n-1)\times 2 \\ &= 2n+1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Helga is training for a marathon. Her training includes a run every Sunday, starting with a run of 3 km on the first Sunday. Each Sunday she increases the length of her run from the previous Sunday by 2 km.
On the $n$th Sunday, Helga runs 43 km. Find the value of $n$.
items.sol:
Put $T_n=43$ using $T_n=2n+1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2n+1 &= 43 \\ 2n &= 42 \\ n &= 21 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Helga is training for a marathon. Her training includes a run every Sunday, starting with a run of 3 km on the first Sunday. Each Sunday she increases the length of her run from the previous Sunday by 2 km.
Find the total distance she runs on Sundays, in 15 weeks of training.
items.sol:
The sum of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$, with $a=3$, $d=2$, $n=15$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left(2\times 3+(15-1)\times 2\right) \\ &= 255 \end{aligned}$$
So she runs $255$ km in total.

Each frequency is the difference of consecutive cumulative frequencies, and the cumulative frequencies are running totals.

\extable{Ts3105_1}

The modal class has the highest frequency, $14$.
$$\text{Modal class: } 1.7\text{-}2.0 \text{ m}$$

The heights from $0.45$ m up to $1.25$ m are the trees with height less than $1.25$ m, minus those less than $0.45$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{15-2}{43} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{43} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the classes $0.5\text{-}0.8$ and $0.9\text{-}1.2$ have frequencies $6$ and $7$:
$$P=\dfrac{6+7}{43}=\dfrac{13}{43}$$

items.part: Let $f(x)=x^3-x^2-x$. Find the stationary points on the graph of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate and factorise.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2-2x-1 \\ &= (3x+1)(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$, so $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $x=1$.

Test the sign of the gradient either side of each point.

\extable{Ts3108_1}

The gradient goes from positive to zero to negative at $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$, so it is a maximum. The gradient goes from negative to zero to positive at $x=1$, so it is a minimum.

Find the $y$-coordinates.
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) &= \dfrac{5}{27} \\ f(1) &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(-\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{5}{27}\right)\text{ is a maximum turning point and }(1,-1)\text{ is a minimum turning point}$$
items.final: $\left(-\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{5}{27}\right)$ is a maximum turning point and $(1,-1)$ is a minimum turning point

items.part:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two events such that $P(A)=0.4$, $P(B)=0.55$ and $P(B\mid A)=0.6$.
Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent events.
items.sol:
Two events are independent if $P(B\mid A)=P(B)$.
$$P(B\mid A)=0.6 \ne 0.55=P(B)$$
$\therefore$ $A$ and $B$ are not independent.

items.part:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two events such that $P(A)=0.4$, $P(B)=0.55$ and $P(B\mid A)=0.6$.
Find $P(A\cup B)$.
items.sol:
Use $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. First find $P(A\cap B)$ from the conditional probability.
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B) &= P(B\mid A)\times P(A) \\ &= 0.6\times 0.4 \\ &= 0.24 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B) &= 0.4+0.55-0.24 \\ &= 0.71 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the geometric series below.

$$\left(\dfrac{2}{x+3}\right)+\left(\dfrac{2}{x+3}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{2}{x+3}\right)^3+\ldots$$

Show that the series will have a limiting sum when $x=2$, but not when $x=-2$.
items.sol:
The series is geometric with common ratio $r=\dfrac{2}{x+3}$. A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.

For $x=2$:
$$|r|=\left|\dfrac{2}{5}\right|<1$$
$\therefore$ the series has a limiting sum.

For $x=-2$:
$$|r|=\left|\dfrac{2}{1}\right|=2\ge 1$$
$\therefore$ the series has no limiting sum.

items.part: For what values of $x$, in the interval $0\le x\le 2\pi$, does the line $y=-1$ intersect the graph of $y=2\cos 3x$?
items.sol:
Set the function equal to $-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos 3x &= -1 \\ \cos 3x &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$3x=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
Since $0\le x\le 2\pi$, we need $0\le 3x\le 6\pi$, so add $2\pi$ and $4\pi$ to these angles.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}+2\pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+2\pi,\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}+4\pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+4\pi \\ &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{14\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{16\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The next angle, $\dfrac{20\pi}{3}$, is greater than $6\pi$, so it is too big. Divide by $3$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{14\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{16\pi}{9}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=3x-\sin x$.
Show that $f(x)$ is an odd function.
items.sol:
A function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= 3(-x)-\sin(-x) \\ &= -3x+\sin x \\ &= -(3x-\sin x) \\ &= -f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $f(x)$ is an odd function.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=3x-\sin x$.
Given that $f(x)\ge 0$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, find the area bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis, from $x=-\pi$ to $x=\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
$f(x)$ is odd, so the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin and the area from $-\pi$ to $0$ equals the area from $0$ to $\pi$.
$$A=2\int_0^{\pi}(3x-\sin x)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+\cos x\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left[\left(\dfrac{3\pi^2}{2}+\cos\pi\right)-(0+\cos 0)\right] \\ &= 2\left[\dfrac{3\pi^2}{2}-2\right] \\ &= 3\pi^2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=(3\pi^2-4)\text{ units}^2$$

Add the two column heights.
$$225+145=370$$
So $370$ students said their favourite pet is a dog or a cat.

Dog and cat together make $74\%$ of the students, which is $370$ students.
$$\begin{aligned} 74\% &= 370 \\ 1\% &= 5 \\ 100\% &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
The cumulative percentage rises from $74\%$ to $90\%$ when fish is added.
$$\text{Fish}: 90\%-74\%=16\%$$
$$16\%\text{ of }500=80$$
So $80$ students said fish.

items.part:
A ship ($S$) leaves Port ($P$) travelling on a bearing of $072^\circ$.

After travelling 25 kilometres, the ship is due South of a lighthouse ($L$).

The ship continues on this bearing for a further 4 kilometres, then measures the bearing of the lighthouse to be $316^\circ$.

\exfigure{162_q13_2}
Show that $\angle PSL=64^\circ$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{162_q13_s1}

The bearing of $L$ from $S$ is $316^\circ$, so $L$ is $360^\circ-316^\circ=44^\circ$ west of north from $S$.

The north lines at $P$ and $S$ are parallel, so co-interior angles give the angle between north at $S$ and $SP$.
$$180^\circ-72^\circ=108^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle PSL &= 108^\circ-44^\circ \\ &= 64^\circ \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A ship ($S$) leaves Port ($P$) travelling on a bearing of $072^\circ$.

After travelling 25 kilometres, the ship is due South of a lighthouse ($L$).

The ship continues on this bearing for a further 4 kilometres, then measures the bearing of the lighthouse to be $316^\circ$.

\exfigure{162_q13_2}
Calculate the distance $LS$ from the ship to the lighthouse at this time.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
Let $M$ be the point due south of $L$, where the ship had travelled $25$ km, so $MS=4$ km. In $\triangle LMS$:
$$\angle LMS=72^\circ,\qquad \angle MLS=44^\circ$$
$\angle LMS=72^\circ$ because $LM$ is a north line and $S$ is on bearing $072^\circ$ from $M$. $\angle MLS=44^\circ$ because $LS$ is $44^\circ$ from the south line $LM$ (the back bearing of $316^\circ$ is $136^\circ$). Use the sine rule.
$$\dfrac{LS}{\sin 72^\circ}=\dfrac{4}{\sin 44^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} LS &= \dfrac{4\sin 72^\circ}{\sin 44^\circ} \\ &= 5.5 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)$ shown below.

\exfigure{162_q13_3}

Evaluate the following integrals.
$\displaystyle\int_0^6 f(x)\,dx$
items.sol:
Split the area under the graph into regions, counting area below the $x$-axis as negative.

From $x=0$ to $x=3$ the region is a trapezium with parallel sides $3$ and $2$ and height $2$. From $x=3$ to $x=4$ the region is a $1\times 1$ rectangle below the axis. From $x=4$ to $x=6$ the region is a triangle with base $2$ and height $2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6 f(x)\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{2}(3+2)-1\times 1+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 2 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)$ shown below.

\exfigure{162_q13_3}

Evaluate the following integrals.
$\displaystyle\int_0^4 \left[f(x)-2\right]\,dx$
items.sol:
Split the integral. From part (a) and the graph, $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx=5-1=4$ (trapezium minus the rectangle below the axis).
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4\left(f(x)-2\right)dx &= \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx-\int_0^4 2\,dx \\ &= 4-\left[2x\right]_0^4 \\ &= 4-(2\times 4-0) \\ &= -4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)$ shown below.

\exfigure{162_q13_3}

Evaluate the following integrals.
$\displaystyle\int_5^6 f'(x)\,dx$
items.sol:
By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(a)$, with $f(6)=0$ and $f(5)=1$ read from the graph.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_5^6 f'(x)\,dx&=\Big[f(x)\Big]_5^6\\&=f(6)-f(5)\\&=0-1\\&=-1\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx$.
items.sol:
Expand the integrand, then integrate each term.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int\cos x\sin^2 x\,dx\\&=\sin x-\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3}+C\end{aligned}$$
The second integral has the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=\sin x$, $n=2$.
$$\therefore\ \int\cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx=\sin x-\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3}+C$$

items.part:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by the formula

$S_n=3n^2-17n$, where $n>0$. Find an expression for the $n$th term of the series.
items.sol:
For any series, the $n$th term is the difference of consecutive sums, $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=S_n-S_{n-1}\\&=3n^2-17n-\left[3(n-1)^2-17(n-1)\right]\\&=3n^2-17n-3\left(n^2-2n+1\right)+17n-17\\&=3n^2-17n-3n^2+6n-3+17n-17\\&=6n-20\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_n=6n-20$$

items.part:
The population of parrots, $P$, is modelled by the function $P=P_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is time in years since May 2004.

In May 2004, there were 2500 parrots and by May 2014 the population had decreased to 1750.
Show that $P_0=2500$.
items.sol:
At $t=0$ the population is $P=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}2500&=P_0e^{-k\cdot 0}\\&=P_0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P_0=2500$$

items.part:
The population of parrots, $P$, is modelled by the function $P=P_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is time in years since May 2004.

In May 2004, there were 2500 parrots and by May 2014 the population had decreased to 1750.
Find the value of $k$. (Answer correct to four decimal places).
items.sol:
In May 2014, $t=10$ and $P=1750$, with $P_0=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}1750&=2500e^{-10k}\\\dfrac{7}{10}&=e^{-10k}\\\ln\dfrac{7}{10}&=-10k\\k&=-\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{7}{10}\\&=0.0357\ \text{(to 4 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of parrots, $P$, is modelled by the function $P=P_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is time in years since May 2004.

In May 2004, there were 2500 parrots and by May 2014 the population had decreased to 1750.
If the population continues to decrease in this manner, what will be the expected population in May 2024? Answer to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
May 2024 is $t=20$. Since $e^{-10k}=\dfrac{7}{10}$, we have $e^{-20k}=\left(\dfrac{7}{10}\right)^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2500e^{-20k}\\&=2500\times 0.49\\&=1225\ \text{parrots}\end{aligned}$$
Strong negative correlation.

items.part:
A scatter plot below shows the relationship between Age and Balance Score.

\exfigure{162_q14_1}
The least squares regression line for this data is $y=11.1249-0.1025x$.

Using this regression line, predict the Balance Score of a 65 year old.
items.sol:
Substitute $x=65$ into the regression line.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=11.1249-0.1025\times 65\\&=4.4624\end{aligned}$$
Yes, the correlation is strong and the prediction is an interpolation.
items.final: Yes, reliable: the correlation is strong and the prediction is an interpolation.

items.part:
The diagram below shows a shaded sector in a circle with radius $r$ and centre $O$.

The sector subtends an angle of $\theta$ at the centre of the circle.

The area of the sector is $49\ \text{cm}^2$.

\exfigure{162_q14_2}

Show that $\theta=\dfrac{98}{r^2}$ and hence show that the minimum perimeter of the sector will occur when the arc length of the sector is equal to the diameter of the circle.
items.sol:
The sector area is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta=49$.
$$\begin{aligned}r^2\theta&=98\\\theta&=\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is two radii plus the arc $r\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2r+r\theta\\&=2r+r\cdot\dfrac{98}{r^2}\\&=2r+98r^{-1}\\\dfrac{dP}{dr}&=2-98r^{-2}\\&=2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$
A stationary point occurs when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}&=0\\2r^2&=98\\r^2&=49\end{aligned}$$
Since $r>0$, $r=7$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=196r^{-3}=\dfrac{196}{r^3}$$
When $r=7$, $\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{196}{343}=\dfrac{4}{7}>0$, so $P$ is a minimum.

Then the arc length is
$$r\theta=7\times\dfrac{98}{7^2}=14=2\times 7.$$
$\therefore$ the perimeter is a minimum when the arc length equals the diameter of the circle.

items.part:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.
Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.
items.sol:
The velocity $v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$ is a concave-down parabola, so its maximum is at the turning point, where $v'(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}v'(t)&=-4t+2\\0&=-4t+2\\t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ s}$$

items.part:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.
Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2t^2+2t+4&=0\\-2\left(t^2-t-2\right)&=0\\-2(t-2)(t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=2$ or $t=-1$; since $t\ge 0$, $t=2$.

Integrate the velocity to find the position.
$$x(t)=\int v\,dt=-\dfrac{2t^3}{3}+t^2+4t+C$$
Initially $x(0)=4$, so $C=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}x(2)&=-\dfrac{2\times 2^3}{3}+2^2+4\times 2+4\\&=\dfrac{32}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is }\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m to the right of the origin}$$
items.final: $\tfrac{32}{3}$ m to the right of the origin

items.part:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$, at $t=2$ (part (b)), so the distance is the total area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, counting the part below the axis as positive.

\exfigure{162_q15_s1}

$$\int_0^2 v\,dt+\left|\int_2^3 v\,dt\right|$$
Using the antiderivative $F(t)=-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3+t^2+4t$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance}&=F(2)-F(0)+\big|F(3)-F(2)\big|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}-0+\left|3-\dfrac{20}{3}\right|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}+\dfrac{11}{3}\\&=\dfrac{31}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance travelled is }\dfrac{31}{3}\text{ m}$$

items.part:
The point $A(4,21)$ lies on the graph of $y=g(x)$.

It is known that the graph of $y=g(x)$ is obtained from transforming the graph of $y=f(x)$ such that $g(x)=-2f(4x+4)+1$.

Find the coordinates of the point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ which is mapped to the point $A$.

The function $y=f(x)$ is defined as

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}1 & \text{for } -3\le x\le 0\\ -x^2+1 & \text{for } x>0\end{cases}$$

Determine whether $y=f(x)$ is both continuous $\textbf{and}$ differentiable at $x=0$.

Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.
items.sol:
Check continuity at $x=0$: both pieces must give the same value.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{left: } f(0)&=1\\\text{right: } -0^2+1&=1\end{aligned}$$
So $f$ is continuous at $x=0$.

Check the gradients from each side. Each piece is differentiable for all real $x$ on its own.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{left: } f'(x)&=0\\\text{right: } y&=-x^2+1\\y'&=-2x,\ \text{so } y'(0)=0\end{aligned}$$
The gradients agree ($0=0$), so $f$ is differentiable at $x=0$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)\text{ is both continuous and differentiable at } x=0$$
items.final: $f(x)$ is both continuous and differentiable at $x=0$

items.part:
On a given day, the height of the water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right),$$

where $h$ is the height of the water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 12 am.
What is the height of the water at 12 am?
items.sol:
At 12 am, $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}h(0)&=5+2\sin 0\\&=5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
On a given day, the height of the water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right),$$

where $h$ is the height of the water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 12 am.
Sketch the graph of $h(t)=5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$, in the domain $[0,16]$.

On a given day, the height of the water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right),$$

where $h$ is the height of the water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 12 am.
A family decides to go on a picnic by the river from 12 pm to 2 pm.

It is only safe to swim in the river if the height of the water is less than 4 metres.

When is the earliest time the family can swim in the river after 12 pm?

Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
The water is safe when $h<4$. Find when $h=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)&=4\\\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{4}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{23\pi}{6},\ \ldots$$
Multiplying by $\dfrac{4}{\pi}$:
$$t=\dfrac{14}{3},\ \dfrac{22}{3},\ \dfrac{38}{3},\ \dfrac{46}{3},\ \ldots$$
At 12 pm ($t=12$), $h=5>4$, and the first solution with $t\ge 12$ is $t=\dfrac{38}{3}=12\dfrac{2}{3}$ hours. After this the height is below $4$ m.
$$\therefore\ \text{the earliest time is } 12{:}40\text{ pm}$$

items.part: Solve $\dfrac{3x}{x+2}=4$.
items.sol:
Since $x\ne -2$, multiply both sides by $x+2$.
$$\begin{aligned}3x&=4(x+2)\\3x&=4x+8\\x&=-8\end{aligned}$$
Check: $\dfrac{3(-8)}{-8+2}=\dfrac{-24}{-6}=4$.

items.part:
Evaluate the following expressions.
$\log_2 4x+\log_2 8x-2\log_2 x$
items.sol:
Use the log laws to combine the terms.
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 4x+\log_2 8x-2\log_2 x&=\log_2\left(32x^2\right)-\log_2 x^2\\&=\log_2\left(\dfrac{32x^2}{x^2}\right)\\&=\log_2 32\\&=5\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Evaluate the following expressions.
$\dfrac{25^x\times 3^{2x+5}}{15^{2x+1}}$
items.sol:
Write every base as a power of $5$ or $3$, using $25=5^2$ and $15=5\cdot 3$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{25^x\times 3^{2x+5}}{15^{2x+1}}&=\dfrac{5^{2x}\times 3^{2x+5}}{5^{2x+1}\times 3^{2x+1}}\\&=5^{2x-(2x+1)}\times 3^{2x+5-(2x+1)}\\&=5^{-1}\times 3^4\\&=\dfrac{81}{5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{(2-x^2)^3}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Adjust the integrand to the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=2-x^2$, $f'(x)=-2x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{x}{(2-x^2)^3}\,dx&=\int x(2-x^2)^{-3}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\int-2x(2-x^2)^{-3}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{(2-x^2)^{-2}}{-2}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}(2-x^2)^{-2}+C\end{aligned}$$

Total $150$, neither $15$, so $150-15=135$ like swimming or surfing or both.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{both}&=113+55-135=33\\\text{swimming only}&=113-33=80\\\text{surfing only}&=55-33=22\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{292_q14_s1}

Swimming only $80$, both $33$, surfing only $22$, neither $15$.
items.final: Swimming only 80, both 33, surfing only 22, neither 15

items.part:
A survey of 150 people found that 113 people liked swimming, 55 liked surfing and 15 liked neither.
If 2 people are selected at random, find the probability that both people like swimming only.
items.sol:
Both people are chosen from the $80$ who like swimming only, without replacement.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{80}{150}\times\dfrac{79}{149}\\&=\dfrac{632}{2235}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: For what values of $x$ is the function $f(x)=x^4-4x^3-48x^2$ concave down?
items.sol:
A function is concave down where $f''(x)<0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=4x^3-12x^2-96x\\f''(x)&=12x^2-24x-96\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}12x^2-24x-96&<0\\x^2-2x-8&<0\\(x-4)(x+2)&<0\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{292_q15_s1}

$$\therefore\ -2<x<4$$

items.part: Chloe sits a marine biology test and receives a mark of 60. The mean mark on the test was 50 with a standard deviation of 10. What percentage of her cohort did she score higher than?
items.sol:
The $z$-score measures how many standard deviations the mark is above the mean.
$$z=\dfrac{60-50}{10}=1$$
By the empirical (68-95-99.7) rule, $68\%$ of scores lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so $34\%$ lie between the mean and $z=1$.

\exfigure{292_q16_s1}

$$P(z<1)=50\%+34\%=84\%$$
So Chloe scored higher than $84\%$ of her cohort.

items.part: Chloe also sits a test on mythological creatures. The mean mark is 57 with a standard deviation of 13. Chloe received a mark of 71. Which test did she do better in compared with her cohort? Justify your answer.
items.sol:
Compare the $z$-scores of the two tests.
$$\begin{aligned}z_{\text{marine biology}}&=1\\z_{\text{mythological creatures}}&=\dfrac{71-57}{13}=\dfrac{14}{13}\approx 1.08\end{aligned}$$
Since $1.08>1$, she did better in mythological creatures because her $z$-score is higher.
items.final: She did better in mythological creatures, since her z-score (≈1.08) is higher than 1.

items.sol:
Instalments are made every 6 months for 8 years: $16$ instalments, at $\dfrac{4}{2}=2\%$ per period. The table factor for $2\%$ and $16$ periods is $18.63929$.
$$\begin{aligned}10000&=18.63929\times m\\m&=\dfrac{10000}{18.63929}\\&=\$536.50\end{aligned}$$

After 2 years there have been $4$ instalments at $2\%$ per period, with table factor $4.12161$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=536.50\times 4.12161\\&=\$2211.24\end{aligned}$$

For the remaining 6 years there are $6\times 4=24$ quarters at $\dfrac{4}{4}=1\%$ per quarter. The balance after 2 years grows by compound interest, and the new instalments are an annuity with table factor $26.97346$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2211.24\times(1.01)^{24}+536.50\times 26.97346\\&=\$17278.95\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Excess}&=17278.95-10000\\&=\$7278.95\end{aligned}$$
So she has $\$7278.95$ more than her goal.

items.part: Solve the equation $(2\cos x)^2=3$ in the domain $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.
items.sol:
Take the square root of both sides, remembering both signs.
$$\begin{aligned}(2\cos x)^2&=3\\2\cos x&=\pm\sqrt{3}\\\cos x&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

\exfigure{292_q18_s1}

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

Each point moves $1$ unit right and its $y$-coordinate is multiplied by $3$.

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=-x^2+4x-1$ at the point $(1,2)$.
items.sol:
The gradient of the tangent is $y'$ at $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=-2x+4\\y'(1)&=-2+4=2\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}y-2&=-\dfrac{1}{2}(x-1)\\y-2&=-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\y&=-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: The normal intersects $y=-x^2+4x-1$ again at point $P$. Find the coordinates of point $P$.
items.sol:
Equate the normal and the curve.
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{5}{2}&=-x^2+4x-1\\-x+5&=-2x^2+8x-2\\2x^2-9x+7&=0\\(x-1)(2x-7)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=1$ (the given point) or $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$.

When $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$, $y=-\dfrac{7}{4}+\dfrac{5}{2}=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$\therefore\ P=\left(\dfrac{7}{2},\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{1-\tan^2 x}{1+\tan^2 x}=1-2\sin^2 x$.
items.sol:
Use the identity $1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x$ in the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1-\tan^2 x}{\sec^2 x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sec^2 x}-\dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\sec^2 x}\\&=\cos^2 x-\dfrac{\frac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}}{\frac{1}{\cos^2 x}}\\&=\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x\\&=\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)-\sin^2 x\\&=1-2\sin^2 x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A geometric sequence is formed by

$$f(x)+f'(x)+f''(x)+f'''(x)+\cdots$$

where $f(x)=e^{\frac{1}{2}x}$. Find the limiting sum in terms of $x$.
items.sol:
Differentiate to find the first terms.
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=e^{\frac{1}{2}x}\\f'(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{1}{2}x}\\f''(x)&=\dfrac{1}{4}e^{\frac{1}{2}x}\end{aligned}$$
Each term is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ of the one before, so the series is geometric with $a=e^{\frac{1}{2}x}$ and $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$. Since $|r|<1$ the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\&=\dfrac{e^{\frac{1}{2}x}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=2e^{\frac{1}{2}x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:

items.part:
A ball is thrown upwards from the edge of a cliff and hits the ground below. Its vertical height ($h$) in metres above the ground is given by the formula $h=-t^2+2t+3$ where $t$ is the time in seconds.
At what time does the ball hit the ground?
items.sol:
The ball hits the ground when $h=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-t^2+2t+3&=0\\t^2-2t-3&=0\\(t-3)(t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=3$ or $t=-1$; since $t>0$, $t=3$ seconds.

items.part:
A ball is thrown upwards from the edge of a cliff and hits the ground below. Its vertical height ($h$) in metres above the ground is given by the formula $h=-t^2+2t+3$ where $t$ is the time in seconds.
At what time is the ball stationary?
items.sol:
The ball is stationary when its velocity $h'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}h'&=-2t+2\\0&=-2t+2\\t&=1\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A ball is thrown upwards from the edge of a cliff and hits the ground below. Its vertical height ($h$) in metres above the ground is given by the formula $h=-t^2+2t+3$ where $t$ is the time in seconds.
Find the total vertical distance travelled by the ball.
items.sol:
The distance is the total area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, taken as positive: the triangle above the axis ($0\le t\le 1$) and the triangle below it ($1\le t\le 3$).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 1\times 2+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 4\\&=1+4\\&=5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

The tail is the circle plus the triangle, less the removed quarter-sector and less the sector of the circle that the triangle overlaps (its apex is at the centre, angle $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$).
$$A=\text{circle}+\text{triangle}-\text{sector}-\text{sector}$$
Using $A_{\text{triangle}}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ and $A_{\text{sector}}=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\pi\cdot 30^2+\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 120^2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 30^2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{5}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 30^2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\&\approx 6069.9\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The cross section of a treasure chest is in the shape of a rectangle and a semicircle. The total perimeter of the cross section is 250 cm.

\exfigure{292_q26_1}
Show that the area of the of the cross section is given by:

$$A=125x-x^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right).$$
items.sol:
The perimeter is the base $x$, two sides $y$, and a semicircular arc of radius $\dfrac{x}{2}$, length $\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x$.
$$\begin{aligned}250&=2y+x+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x\\2y&=250-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{2}\\y&=125-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{4}\end{aligned}$$
The area is a rectangle plus a semicircle of radius $\dfrac{x}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=xy+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2\\&=x\left(125-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{4}\right)+\dfrac{\pi x^2}{8}\\&=125x-\dfrac{4x^2+2\pi x^2}{8}+\dfrac{\pi x^2}{8}\\&=125x-x^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)\end{aligned}$$

For a maximum, solve $A'=0$ and test the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned}A'&=125-2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)x\\0&=125-\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}x\\x&=\dfrac{500}{\pi+4}\approx 70.012\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$A''=-\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}<0$$
So $A$ is a maximum at this value of $x$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\max}&=125(70.012\ldots)-(70.012\ldots)^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)\\&\approx 4375.8\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the area between the graphs of $y=2x^2$ and $y=\sqrt{32x}$.

\exfigure{292_q27_1}
items.sol:
Find where the curves meet.
$$\begin{aligned}2x^2&=\sqrt{32x}\\4x^4&=32x\\x^4-8x&=0\\x\left(x^3-8\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=2$. On $0\le x\le 2$ the square-root curve is above the parabola.

$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^2\left(\sqrt{32x}-2x^2\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{2\sqrt{32}}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{2}{3}x^3\right]_0^2\\&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{32}}{3}\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^3-\dfrac{2\cdot 2^3}{3}\\&=\dfrac{32}{3}-\dfrac{16}{3}\\&=\dfrac{16}{3}\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Eugene deposits a sum of money into a bank account at the start of each year. The bank offers interest of $4\%$ p.a. compounded every 6 months. Let $A_n$ be the value of the account after $n$ years and $P$ be the value of each deposit.
Show that the total value in the account after 3 years is given by:

$$A_3=P(1.02)^6+P(1.02)^4+P(1.02)^2.$$
items.sol:
Interest is $\dfrac{4}{2}=2\%$ per 6 months, so each year the balance is multiplied by $(1.02)^2$. A deposit $P$ is made at the start of each year.
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=P(1.02)^2\\A_2&=\left(P(1.02)^2+P\right)(1.02)^2\\&=P(1.02)^4+P(1.02)^2\\A_3&=\left(P(1.02)^4+P(1.02)^2+P\right)(1.02)^2\\&=P(1.02)^6+P(1.02)^4+P(1.02)^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Eugene deposits a sum of money into a bank account at the start of each year. The bank offers interest of $4\%$ p.a. compounded every 6 months. Let $A_n$ be the value of the account after $n$ years and $P$ be the value of each deposit.
Show that $A_n=\dfrac{2601}{101}P\left(1.02^{2n}-1\right)$.
items.sol:
From part (a), the pattern of the terms continues, with $n$ deposits.
$$\begin{aligned}A_n&=P(1.02)^{2n}+P(1.02)^{2n-2}+\cdots+P(1.02)^2\\&=P(1.02)^2\left[1+1.02^2+1.02^4+\cdots+1.02^{2n-2}\right]\end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.02^2$ and $n$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{r^n-1}{r-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_n&=P(1.02)^2\times\dfrac{\left(1.02^2\right)^n-1}{1.02^2-1}\\&=P\cdot\dfrac{1.0404}{0.0404}\left(1.02^{2n}-1\right)\\&=\dfrac{2601}{101}P\left(1.02^{2n}-1\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Eugene deposits a sum of money into a bank account at the start of each year. The bank offers interest of $4\%$ p.a. compounded every 6 months. Let $A_n$ be the value of the account after $n$ years and $P$ be the value of each deposit.
If Eugene saves \$500 000 dollars at the end of 25 years, find the size of his deposits.
Differentiate $(x-1)(\sin x)$.
items.sol:
Use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x-1 & v&=\sin x\\u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[(x-1)\sin x\big]&=\sin x+(x-1)\cos x\\&=\sin x+x\cos x-\cos x\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Integrate both sides of the result of part (a).
$$\int\left(\sin x+x\cos x-\cos x\right)dx=(x-1)\sin x+C$$
$$-\cos x+\int x\cos x\,dx-\sin x=(x-1)\sin x+C$$
Make $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$ the subject.
$$\begin{aligned}\int x\cos x\,dx&=(x-1)\sin x+\cos x+\sin x+C\\&=x\sin x-\sin x+\cos x+\sin x+C\\&=x\sin x+\cos x+C\end{aligned}$$

A player picks 2 tiles from the bag (1 at a time without replacement), and their score ($X$) is the sum of the numbers on the tiles.
What is the expected score from playing this game?
items.sol:
The expected score is $E(X)=\sum x\cdot p(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=2\times\dfrac{2}{42}+3\times\dfrac{8}{42}+4\times\dfrac{10}{42}+5\times\dfrac{12}{42}+6\times\dfrac{6}{42}+7\times\dfrac{4}{42}\\&=\dfrac{4+24+40+60+36+28}{42}\\&=\dfrac{192}{42}\\&=\dfrac{32}{7}\end{aligned}$$

Seven scrabble tiles labelled with the letters A to G are placed in a bag. Each letter has a value assigned to it as shown in the photo below.

items.sol:
This is a conditional probability. Given $X=5$, the sample space is the $12$ pairs that score $5$. Of these, $4$ contain a vowel.
$$P=\dfrac{4}{12}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

items.part:
The depth ($d$) in metres of the water in a wave pool varies as waves are sent out. The depth is measured from the floor and can be modelled by the equation $d=\dfrac{4}{5}\sin at+\dfrac{3}{2}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds and $a$ is a constant. Each wave has a period of 2.5 seconds measured from the peak of the wave to the peak of the next wave.

items.sol:
The period is $2.5$ seconds, and the period of $\sin at$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{a}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{a}&=2.5\\a&=\dfrac{2\pi}{2.5}=\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\end{aligned}$$

The depth ($d$) in metres of the water in a wave pool varies as waves are sent out. Sandy can only touch the bottom of the pool when the height of the wave is less than 1.7m. For what percentage of the first 5 seconds can she touch the bottom of the pool? Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
She can touch the bottom when $d<1.7$. First find when $d=1.7$.
$$\begin{aligned}0.8\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{5}t+1.5&=1.7\\\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{5}t&=\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{292_q31_s2}

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{4\pi}{5}t&=0.2526\ldots,\ \pi-0.2526\ldots\\t&=0.1005,\ 1.149\end{aligned}$$
So $d>1.7$ for $0.1005<t<1.149$ in each $2.5$-second period, and the same proportion holds over the first $5$ seconds (two periods).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{proportion above }1.7\text{ m}&=\dfrac{1.149-0.1005}{2.5}\\&=42.0\%\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The lengths of fish in metres in the harbour are distributed according to the equation,

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-2x(x^2-1)^3+0.5 & \text{for } 0<x\le 1\\[4pt] -\dfrac{x-2}{2} & \text{for } 1<x<2\\[4pt] 0 & \text{for } x>2\end{cases}$$

People are only permitted to catch a fish whose length is between 0.45 m and $L$ m long. If 60\% of fish in the harbour are within this legal limit, find the value of $L$ correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The probability of a length between $0.45$ and $L$ is the area under $f$, so we need $\displaystyle\int_{0.45}^{L}f(x)\,dx=0.6$.

Total probability on $0<x\le1$: use the substitution $u=x^2-1$, $du=2x\,dx$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \big(-2x(x^2-1)^3+0.5\big)dx &= \left[-\dfrac{(x^2-1)^4}{4}+0.5x\right]_0^1 \\ &= \left(0+0.5\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \\ &= 0.75 \end{aligned}$$
Probability from $0.45$ to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{0.45}^1 f(x)\,dx &= 0.75-\int_0^{0.45} f(x)\,dx\\ &= 0.75-\left[-\dfrac{(x^2-1)^4}{4}+0.5x\right]_0^{0.45} \\ &= 0.75-0.37387\ldots \\ &= 0.37613\ldots \end{aligned}$$
This is less than $0.6$, so $L>1$ and we need a further $0.6-0.37613=0.22387$ from the second piece.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^L -\dfrac{x-2}{2}\,dx &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right]_1^L \\ &= L-\dfrac{L^2}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} L-\dfrac{L^2}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4}&=0.22387 \\ L^2-4L+3.8955&=0 \\ L&=2\pm\sqrt{4-3.8955} \\ &=2\pm 0.3233 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1<L<2$, take the smaller root.
$$\therefore\ L\approx 1.68 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by $S_n=25n-2n^2$.
Find the first term.
items.sol:
The first term is $T_1=S_1$.
$$\begin{aligned}S_1&=25(1)-2(1)^2\\&=23\end{aligned}$$
So the first term is $23$.

items.part:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by $S_n=25n-2n^2$.
Find the common difference.
items.sol:
Find the first three terms from the sums, using $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=23\\S_2&=25(2)-2(2)^2=42,&T_2&=S_2-S_1=19\\S_3&=25(3)-2(3)^2=57,&T_3&=S_3-S_2=15\end{aligned}$$
The terms are $23,\ 19,\ 15,\ \ldots$
$$d=19-23=-4$$

items.part:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by $S_n=25n-2n^2$.
Show that the general term is given by $T_n=27-4n$.
items.sol:
Use $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $a=23$ and $d=-4$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=23+(n-1)\times(-4)\\&=23-4n+4\\&=27-4n\end{aligned}$$

items.part: The circle $x^2+4x+y^2-6y+12=0$ is transformed by a vertical translation 3 units down and a horizontal translation 5 units right. What are the coordinates of the new centre of the transformed circle?
items.sol:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned}x^2+4x+y^2-6y+12&=0\\(x+2)^2-4+(y-3)^2-9+12&=0\\(x+2)^2+(y-3)^2&=1\end{aligned}$$
The original centre is $(-2,3)$.

Moving $5$ units right and $3$ units down gives the equation
$$(x-3)^2+y^2=1$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the new centre is }(3,0)$$

items.part: A factory gets permission to dispose, at the start of every day, 600kg of waste into a stream of water. The running stream removes 40% of any waste present, by the end of the day. Show that the amount of waste present in the stream at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ day is $900(1-0.6^n)$.
items.sol:
The stream removes $40\%$, leaving $60\%$ at the end of each day. Let $W_n$ be the amount at the end of day $n$.
$$\begin{aligned}W_1&=0.6\times 600=360\\W_2&=0.6\left(W_1+600\right)=360+360\times 0.6\\W_3&=0.6\left(W_2+600\right)=360+360\times 0.6+360\times 0.6^2\end{aligned}$$
So
$$W_n=360+360\times 0.6+360\times 0.6^2+\cdots+360\times 0.6^{n-1}$$
This is a geometric series with $a=360$, $r=0.6$ and $n$ terms.
$$\begin{aligned}W_n&=\dfrac{360\left(1-0.6^n\right)}{1-0.6}\\&=\dfrac{360}{0.4}\left(1-0.6^n\right)\\&=900\left(1-0.6^n\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the functions $f(x)=x^2-x-2$ and $g(x)=x+1$.
Find the points of intersection of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$.
items.sol:
At the points of intersection $f(x)=g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-x-2&=x+1\\x^2-2x-3&=0\\(x-3)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=3$ or $x=-1$. Substituting into $y=x+1$ gives $y=4$ and $y=0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the points of intersection are }(3,4)\text{ and }(-1,0)$$

items.part:
A square chess board contains alternating black and white squares with eight squares along each side. Andrew places one grain of rice on the first square, two grains of rice on the second square, four grains on the third, eight on the fourth, and so on, until every square is covered.
Show that the number of grains of rice in each subsequent square form a geometric sequence.
items.sol:
The numbers of grains are $1,\ 2,\ 2^2,\ 2^3,\ \ldots$ with $a=1$. The ratio of consecutive terms is constant:
$$\dfrac{2}{1}=2,\qquad\dfrac{2^2}{2}=2$$
$\therefore$ the number of grains forms a geometric sequence with $r=2$.

items.part:
A square chess board contains alternating black and white squares with eight squares along each side. Andrew places one grain of rice on the first square, two grains of rice on the second square, four grains on the third, eight on the fourth, and so on, until every square is covered.

items.sol:
The board has $8\times 8=64$ squares, so the last square is the $64^{\text{th}}$ term.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=ar^{n-1}\\T_{64}&=1\times 2^{63}\\&=2^{63}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A square chess board contains alternating black and white squares with eight squares along each side. Andrew places one grain of rice on the first square, two grains of rice on the second square, four grains on the third, eight on the fourth, and so on, until every square is covered.

The total is the sum of the first $64$ terms.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=-\dfrac{1}{x^2-1}$.
Show that $f(x)$ is an even function.
items.sol:
A function is even when $f(-x)=f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=-\dfrac{1}{(-x)^2-1}\\&=-\dfrac{1}{x^2-1}\\&=f(x)\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ f(x)$ is an even function.

items.sol:
The vertical asymptotes are where the denominator is zero: $x=\pm 1$.

items.part: The third and fifth terms of a geometric progression are 6 and $\dfrac{3}{2}$ respectively. Find the common ratio and first term for this progression.
items.sol:
Use $T_n=ar^{n-1}$ for the third and fifth terms.
$$\begin{aligned}T_3&=ar^2=6 & T_5&=ar^4=\dfrac{3}{2}\\a&=\dfrac{6}{r^2} & a&=\dfrac{3}{2r^4}\end{aligned}$$
Equate the two expressions for $a$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{6}{r^2}&=\dfrac{3}{2r^4}\\12r^4&=3r^2\\3r^2\left(4r^2-1\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $r=0$ or $r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}$. But $r=0$ gives $ar^2=0\ne 6$, so $r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Then $a=\dfrac{6}{r^2}=\dfrac{6}{\frac{1}{4}}=24$.
$$\therefore\ r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ and }a=24$$

items.part: If $4,\ x,\ y$ form a geometric sequence and $x,\ y,\ 12$ form an arithmetic sequence, find the values of $x$ and $y$.
items.sol:
For the geometric sequence $4,\ x,\ y$ the ratios are equal.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x}{4}&=\dfrac{y}{x}\\x^2&=4y\\y&=\dfrac{x^2}{4}\qquad(1)\end{aligned}$$
For the arithmetic sequence $x,\ y,\ 12$ the differences are equal.
$$\begin{aligned}y-x&=12-y\\2y-x&=12\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Substitute (1) into (2).
$$\begin{aligned}2\left(\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right)-x&=12\\\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x&=12\\x^2-2x-24&=0\\(x-6)(x+4)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=6$ or $x=-4$.

When $x=6$, $y=9$. When $x=-4$, $y=4$.
$$\therefore\ (x,y)=(6,9)\text{ or }(-4,4)$$
