items.part:
$A$ and $B$ are two arithmetic series, where all the terms are positive.

In series $A$, the first term is $a$ and common difference is $d$. In series $B$, the first term is $M$ and the common difference is $D$.

Let $P=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $A$ and let $Q=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $B$.
Show $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}$.
items.sol:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]\\Q&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2M+(n-1)D\right]\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{P}{Q}&=\dfrac{\frac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]}{\frac{n}{2}\left[2M+(n-1)D\right]}\\&=\dfrac{2a+(n-1)d}{2M+(n-1)D}\\&=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$A$ and $B$ are two arithmetic series, where all the terms are positive.

In series $A$, the first term is $a$ and common difference is $d$. In series $B$, the first term is $M$ and the common difference is $D$.

Let $P=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $A$ and let $Q=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $B$.
Express $\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}$ in terms of $a,\ d,\ M$ and $D$.
items.sol:
The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of each series is $a+(n-1)d$ and $M+(n-1)D$. For $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}&=\dfrac{a+(10-1)d}{M+(10-1)D}\\&=\dfrac{a+9d}{M+9D}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$A$ and $B$ are two arithmetic series, where all the terms are positive.

In series $A$, the first term is $a$ and common difference is $d$. In series $B$, the first term is $M$ and the common difference is $D$.

Let $P=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $A$ and let $Q=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $B$.
Given that $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{5n+4}{9n+6}$, evaluate $\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}$. This matches the ratio of the $10^{\text{th}}$ terms in part (b) when $\dfrac{n-1}{2}=9$, so $n=19$.

Substitute $n=19$ into the given ratio.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{a+9d}{M+9D}&=\dfrac{5(19)+4}{9(19)+6}\\&=\dfrac{99}{177}\\&=\dfrac{33}{59}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$
$y=\tan(3x-4)$
items.sol:
Use the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan u=\sec^2 u\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}$, with $u=3x-4$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3\sec^2(3x-4)$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$
$y=\log_e(\sin x)$
items.sol:
Use the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$, with $u=\sin x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$
$y=\dfrac{\cos 3x}{x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=\cos 3x & v&=x\\u'&=-3\sin 3x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{-3x\sin 3x-\cos 3x}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$
$y=(2x-1)e^{2x}$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=2x-1 & v&=e^{2x}\\u'&=2 & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=2e^{2x}+2(2x-1)e^{2x}\\&=2e^{2x}+4xe^{2x}-2e^{2x}\\&=4xe^{2x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{5x}$
items.sol:
Rewrite so the limit takes the standard form $\displaystyle\lim_{\theta\to 0}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{5x}&=\dfrac{4}{5}\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{4x}\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}\times 1\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=x^4+x^3+kx^2-3x-5$, where $k$ is a constant.

Find the values of $k$ for which $f(x)$ is always concave up.
items.sol:
A function is concave up when $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=4x^3+3x^2+2kx-3\\f''(x)&=12x^2+6x+2k\end{aligned}$$
$f''(x)>0$ for all $x$ requires the quadratic $2\left(6x^2+3x+k\right)$ to have positive leading coefficient ($6>0$) and $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{aligned}3^2-4\times 6\times k&<0\\9-24k&<0\\k&>\dfrac{3}{8}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows a vertical cross-section of a creek which is 10.8 metres wide.

At this location the depth of the river, in metres, has been measured at 2.7 metre intervals.

\exfigure{571_q9_1}

Use the trapezoidal rule with the five depth measurements to calculate the approximate area of the cross-section.
items.sol:
Use the trapezoidal rule with the five depths $0,\ 3.5,\ 1.3,\ 2.3,\ 0$ at spacing $h=2.7$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&\approx\dfrac{2.7}{2}\Big[0+2(3.5+1.3+2.3)+0\Big]\\&=1.35\times 14.2\\&=19.17\text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the curve passing through the point $(2,5)$ with gradient function $f'(x)=3x^2-4x+1$.
items.sol:
Integrate the gradient function, then use the point $(2,5)$ to find the constant.
$$f(x)=\int\left(3x^2-4x+1\right)dx=x^3-2x^2+x+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(2)&=5\\2^3-2\times 2^2+2+c&=5\\2+c&=5\\c&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-2x^2+x+3$$

items.part: Find the exact area of the region bounded by the curve $y=\dfrac{2}{3x}$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=2$ and $x=4$.
items.sol:
The area is the integral of $y$ from $x=2$ to $x=4$ (the curve is above the $x$-axis there).
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_2^4\dfrac{2}{3x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[\ln x\Big]_2^4\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}(\ln 4-\ln 2)\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using the primitive $\ln 3x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[\ln 3x\Big]_2^4\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}(\ln 12-\ln 6)\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln 2\text{ units}^2$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=e^x\sin x$ at the point $(\pi,0)$.
items.sol:
The gradient of the tangent comes from the product rule applied to $y=e^x\sin x$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x$$
At $x=\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_T&=e^{\pi}\sin\pi+e^{\pi}\cos\pi\\&=-e^{\pi}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_N=-\dfrac{1}{m_T}=\dfrac{1}{e^{\pi}}$$
The normal through $(\pi,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-0&=\dfrac{1}{e^{\pi}}(x-\pi)\\e^{\pi}y&=x-\pi\\e^{\pi}y-x+\pi&=0\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the following equations, solve for $x$
$2^{2x+3}-4\times 2^{x}=0$
items.sol:
Rewrite in terms of $2^x$ and factorise.
$$\begin{aligned}2^{2x+3}-4\times 2^x&=0\\2^{2x}\times 2^3-4\times 2^x&=0\\4\times 2^x\left(2\times 2^x-1\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$2^x=0$ has no solution, so $2\times 2^x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}2^x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\x&=-1\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the following equations, solve for $x$
$2\log_5 3=\log_5 x-\log_5 6$
items.sol:
Collect the logarithms using the log laws, $n\log_a b=\log_a b^n$ and $\log_a b-\log_a c=\log_a\dfrac{b}{c}$.
$$\begin{aligned}2\log_5 3&=\log_5 x-\log_5 6\\\log_5 3^2&=\log_5\left(\dfrac{x}{6}\right)\\3^2&=\dfrac{x}{6}\\x&=54\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{(2x+1)^2}$.
items.sol:
Write $\dfrac{1}{(2x+1)^2}=(2x+1)^{-2}$ and use $\displaystyle\int(ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+c$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int(2x+1)^{-2}\,dx&=\dfrac{(2x+1)^{-1}}{-1\times 2}+c\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2(2x+1)}+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{5x^2+3}\,dx$.
items.sol:
The numerator is a constant multiple of the derivative of the denominator, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(5x^2+3)=10x$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{x}{5x^2+3}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{10}\int\dfrac{10x}{5x^2+3}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{10}\ln|5x^2+3|+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{3x^2+4}{x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Divide each term of the numerator by $x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{3x^2+4}{x}\,dx&=\int\left(3x+\dfrac{4}{x}\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}x^2+4\ln|x|+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{e^{3x}}{e^{x}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
By the index laws, $\dfrac{e^{3x}}{e^{x}}=e^{2x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{e^{3x}}{e^{x}}\,dx&=\int e^{2x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\sin(4x-3)\,dx$.
items.sol:
The derivative of $4x-3$ is $4$, so the primitive of $\sin(4x-3)$ has a factor $\dfrac{1}{4}$.
$$\int\sin(4x-3)\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{4}\cos(4x-3)+c$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int 5^{x+1}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Write $5^{x+1}=5\cdot 5^x$ and use $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int 5^{x+1}\,dx&=5\int 5^x\,dx\\&=5\cdot\dfrac{5^x}{\ln 5}+c\\&=\dfrac{5^{x+1}}{\ln 5}+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\dfrac{2}{1-\sin^2 x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Use $1-\sin^2 x=\cos^2 x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x}=\sec^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{2}{1-\sin^2 x}\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x}\,dx\\&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}2\sec^2 x\,dx\\&=2\Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\&=2\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan 0\right)\\&=2\end{aligned}$$

Equate the line and the parabola.
$$\begin{aligned}2x&=-4x^2+16x\\0&=-4x^2+14x\\0&=2x(7-2x)\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The root $x=0$ is the origin, so A has
$$x=\dfrac{7}{2}$$

Between the intersection points the parabola is above the line, so the area is the integral of (parabola $-$ line) from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$ (part (a)).
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^{\frac{7}{2}}\left(-4x^2+16x-2x\right)dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{4}{3}x^3+7x^2\right]_0^{\frac{7}{2}}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\times\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^3+7\times\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^2\right)-0\\&=\dfrac{343}{12}\\&\approx 28.583\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

Reading the given graph, the curve is concave down for
$$x<1\ \text{or}\ x>9$$
\exfigure{571_q16_s1}

items.part: Differentiate $y=\sqrt{3x^2+6}$.
items.sol:
Write $y$ as a power and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=(3x^2+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(3x^2+6)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 6x\\&=\dfrac{3x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (i), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{3x^2+6}=\dfrac{3x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}$, so $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}$ is $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of that derivative.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\sqrt{3x^2+6}\Big]_0^1\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\sqrt{9}-\sqrt{6}\right)\\&=1-\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=\sin^5(2x)$
items.sol:
Apply the chain rule twice: the power, then $\sin(2x)$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=[\sin(2x)]^5\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=5[\sin(2x)]^4\cdot\cos(2x)\cdot 2\\&=10\cos(2x)\sin^4(2x)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=\sin x^{\circ}$.
items.sol:
Convert degrees to radians: $x^{\circ}=\dfrac{\pi}{180}x$ radians.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}x\right)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}x\right)\end{aligned}$$
or equivalently $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos x^{\circ}$.

items.part: Differentiate $y=\log_e\sqrt{e^{x}(2x+1)}$
items.sol:
Simplify first with the log laws $\ln\sqrt{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln A$ and $\ln(AB)=\ln A+\ln B$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left[e^x(2x+1)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln e^x+\ln(2x+1)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[x+\ln(2x+1)\right]\end{aligned}$$
Now differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{2x+1}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2x+1}\\&=\dfrac{(2x+1)+2}{2(2x+1)}\\&=\dfrac{2x+3}{4x+2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The curve $y=\dfrac{3}{x-1}$ intersects the line $y=\dfrac{3}{2}x$ at the point $(2,3)$.

The region bound by the curve $y=\dfrac{3}{x-1}$, the line $y=\dfrac{3}{2}x$, the $y$-axis and the line $y=5$ is shaded in the diagram.

\exfigure{571_q18_1}

Find the exact area of the shaded region.
items.sol:
Rewrite the curve with $x$ as the subject: $y=\dfrac{3}{x-1}$ gives $x=\dfrac{3}{y}+1$.

The shaded region is a triangle (base $2$, height $3$, up to the point $(2,3)$) together with the region between the curve and the $y$-axis for $3\le y\le 5$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 3+\int_3^5\left(\dfrac{3}{y}+1\right)dy\\&=3+\Big[3\ln y+y\Big]_3^5\\&=3+\Big[(3\ln 5+5)-(3\ln 3+3)\Big]\\&=5+3\ln\dfrac{5}{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-\dfrac{1}{4}x^4$.
Find any stationary points of the curve $y=f(x)$, and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate and solve $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3x^2-x^3\\0&=x^2(3-x)\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(0)&=0\\f(3)&=27-\dfrac{81}{4}=6.75\end{aligned}$$
Testing either side of each stationary point:

\exfigure{571_q19_s1}

$\therefore$ horizontal inflection point at $(0,0)$ and maximum point at $(3,6.75)$.
items.final: Horizontal inflection point at $(0,0)$ and maximum point at $(3,6.75)$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-\dfrac{1}{4}x^4$.
Find any points of inflection of the curve $y=f(x)$.
items.sol:
Possible points of inflection occur where $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=6x-3x^2\\0&=3x(2-x)\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=2\end{aligned}$$
Testing the concavity either side of each:

\exfigure{571_q19_s2}

$$f(2)=8-\dfrac{16}{4}=4$$
$\therefore$ points of inflection at $(0,0)$ and $(2,4)$.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-\dfrac{1}{4}x^4$.
State the range of the function for the given domain.
items.sol:
Over $-2\le x\le 5$ the greatest value is the maximum $f(3)=6.75$ (part (a)). The least value is at an end point: $f(-2)=-12$ and $f(5)=-31.25$, so the least is $-31.25$.
$$-31.25\le y\le 6.75$$
\exfigure{571_q20_s1}

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graph of the function $f(x)=\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.

The points $P(0,0)$ and $Q\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ both lie on the curve.

The point $R(t,\sin t)$ is also a point on the curve between $P$ and $Q$, such that $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{571_q21_1}
Show that $A$, the area of $\triangle PQR$, is given by

$$A=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\text{ when }t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$$
items.sol:
\exfigure{571_q21_s1}

The area of $\triangle PQR$ is the area under $PR$ plus the area under $RQ$, minus the area under $PQ$ (each a trapezium on the $x$-axis).
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}\,t\sin t+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-t\right)\left(\sin t+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
Expand and simplify.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}t\sin t+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin t+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi}{3}-t\sin t-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}t\right)-\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{6}\\&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\sin t-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}t\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graph of the function $f(x)=\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.

The points $P(0,0)$ and $Q\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ both lie on the curve.

The point $R(t,\sin t)$ is also a point on the curve between $P$ and $Q$, such that $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{571_q21_1}
Find the maximum value of $A$, the area of $\triangle PQR$.

Justify your answer, leaving your answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Differentiate and find the stationary point.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\\\dfrac{dA}{dt}&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\cos t-3\sqrt{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary point where $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=0$:
$$\cos t=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{4\pi}$$
so $t=1.145\ldots$, which lies in $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dt^2}=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(-4\pi\sin t\right)$$
When $t=1.145$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dt^2}=-0.9534<0$, so the curve is concave down and this is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin 1.145-3\sqrt{3}\times 1.145\right)\\&\approx 0.46\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum } A\approx 0.46$$

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ for the following and write it in simplified form.
$y=\tan 3x$
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan(ax)=a\sec^2(ax)$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3\sec^2 3x$$

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ for the following and write it in simplified form.
$y=e^{\cos x}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule with $u=\cos x$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\sin x\cdot e^{\cos x}$$

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ for the following and write it in simplified form.
$y=\ln\sqrt{4x^2-1}$
items.sol:
Use the log laws first: $\ln\sqrt{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln A$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln\left(4x^2-1\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(4x^2-1\right)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{8x}{4x^2-1}\\&=\dfrac{4x}{4x^2-1}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \left(e^{2x}+e^{-x}\right)dx$
items.sol: $$\int\left(e^{2x}+e^{-x}\right)dx=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}-e^{-x}+C$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int x\left(5-3x^2\right)^5dx$
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(5-3x^2\right)=-6x$, insert a factor of $-6$ and compensate with $-\dfrac{1}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int x\left(5-3x^2\right)^5dx&=-\dfrac{1}{6}\int-6x\left(5-3x^2\right)^5dx\\&=-\dfrac{1}{6}\left[\dfrac{\left(5-3x^2\right)^6}{6}\right]+C\\&=-\dfrac{1}{36}\left(5-3x^2\right)^6+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_2^3\dfrac{5x}{x^2-1}\,dx$
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2-1\right)=2x$, the integrand is $\dfrac{5}{2}$ times $\dfrac{2x}{x^2-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^3\dfrac{5x}{x^2-1}\,dx&=\dfrac{5}{2}\int_2^3\dfrac{2x}{x^2-1}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{5}{2}\Big[\ln\left|x^2-1\right|\Big]_2^3\\&=\dfrac{5}{2}(\ln 8-\ln 3)\\&=\dfrac{5}{2}\ln\dfrac{8}{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=e^{2x}(x+2)$ at the point $(1,3e^2)$.

Give your answer in general form, with exact values.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^{2x}&v&=x+2\\u'&=2e^{2x}&v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e^{2x}\cdot 1+2e^{2x}(x+2)\\&=e^{2x}\left(1+2(x+2)\right)\\&=e^{2x}(2x+5)\end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=7e^2$, the gradient of the tangent.

The tangent through $(1,3e^2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-3e^2&=7e^2(x-1)\\y-3e^2&=7e^2x-7e^2\\0&=7e^2x-y-4e^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 7e^2x-y-4e^2=0$$

items.part: Solve $\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ in the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
$\sin$ is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants, and the reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Find the range of $2x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, one operation per line.
$$\begin{aligned}0&\le x\le 2\pi\\0&\le 2x\le 4\pi&&(\text{multiply by }2)\\\dfrac{\pi}{6}&\le 2x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{25\pi}{6}&&(\text{add }\dfrac{\pi}{6})\end{aligned}$$
Solutions in this range:
$$\begin{aligned}2x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 3\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 4\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}\\2x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{2}&&(\text{subtract }\dfrac{\pi}{6})\\x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{4}&&(\text{divide by }2)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch $y=5\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ for $-2\pi\le x\le 2\pi$
Hence, state how many solutions there are to the equation $5\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)=3$ in the domain $-2\pi\le x\le 2\pi$
items.sol: The line $y=3$ meets the graph of $y=5\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ twice in $-2\pi\le x\le 2\pi$, so there are 2 solutions.
\exfigure{637_q16_s1}

items.part: The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is translated $m$ units to the left, dilated vertically by a scale factor of $k$ and then translated 7 units up. The equation of the transformed function is $g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{3}+2x+10$. Find $m$ and $k$.
items.sol:
The transformed function is $g(x)=k(x+m)^2+7$ (translate $m$ units left, dilate by $k$, translate 7 up).
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=k\left(x^2+2mx+m^2\right)+7\\&=kx^2+2mkx+m^2k+7\end{aligned}$$
Equate coefficients with $g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{3}+2x+10$.

Coefficient of $x^2$: $k=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned}2mk&=2\\2\times m\times\dfrac{1}{3}&=2\\m&=3\end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution: complete the square.
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(x^2+6x+30\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(x^2+6x+3^2+30-3^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[(x+3)^2+21\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}(x+3)^2+7\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=3,\ k=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=3+4x^3-x^4$.
Find the stationary point(s) and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate, and solve $f'(x)=0$ for the stationary points.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=12x^2-4x^3\\f''(x)&=24x-12x^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}12x^2-4x^3&=0\\4x^2(3-x)&=0\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=3\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$: $y=3$ and $f''(0)=0$, so the second derivative test is inconclusive. Test the concavity either side of $x=0$:

\extable{Ts3278_1}

The concavity changes, so $(0,3)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

When $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3+4(3)^3-3^4=30\\f''(3)&=24(3)-12(3)^2=-36<0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore(3,30)$ is a local maximum turning point.
items.final: $(0,3)$ is a horizontal point of inflection; $(3,30)$ is a local maximum turning point

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=3+4x^3-x^4$.
Show that there is a point of inflection at $(2,19)$ on the curve.
items.sol:
Possible points of inflection occur where $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}24x-12x^2&=0\\12x(2-x)&=0\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=2\end{aligned}$$
Test the concavity either side of each:

\extable{Ts3279_1}

At $x=0$ the concavity changes (the horizontal point of inflection of part (a)).

When $x=2$:
$$y=3+4(2)^3-2^4=19$$
The concavity changes at $x=2$, so $(2,19)$ is a point of inflection.

items.part: Differentiate $x^2\ln x$ .
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x^2&v&=\ln x\\u'&=2x&v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\ln x\right)&=x^2\times\dfrac{1}{x}+2x\ln x\\&=x+2x\ln x\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find the primitive of $2x+4x\ln x$.
items.sol:
By part (a), $x^2\ln x$ is a primitive of $x+2x\ln x$. Since $2x+4x\ln x=2\left(x+2x\ln x\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\left(2x+4x\ln x\right)dx&=2\int\left(x+2x\ln x\right)dx\\&=2x^2\ln x+C\end{aligned}$$

Five function values give four strips, so $h=\dfrac{5-1}{4}=1$.

Trapezoidal rule: $\displaystyle\int_1^5 f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left[f_{\text{first}}+f_{\text{last}}+2\left(\text{sum of the others}\right)\right]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^5 f(x)\,dx&\approx\dfrac{1}{2}\left[0+2(1.20+4.29+9.63)+17.47\right]\\&=23.855\\&\approx 23.86\end{aligned}$$

The limits are where the curves meet:
$$\begin{aligned}x^3-2x&=x^2\\x^3-x^2-2x&=0\\x(x-2)(x+1)&=0\\x&=-1,\ 0,\ 2\end{aligned}$$
On $-1\le x\le 0$ the cubic is above the parabola; on $0\le x\le 2$ the parabola is above the cubic.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-1}^{0}\left(x^3-2x-x^2\right)dx+\int_0^2\left(x^2-\left(x^3-2x\right)\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2\right]_0^2\\&=(0)-\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-1+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\left(\dfrac{8}{3}-4+4\right)-(0)\\&=\dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3}\\&=\dfrac{37}{12}\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Ms Iacona notices that the number of emails she receives per week from students is cyclical. Every 12 weeks she receives the highest number of emails.

The number of emails Ms Iacona receives each week, $f(t)$, is modelled by the function

$$f(t)=a\cos(bt)+c$$

where $t$ is the number of weeks after 1 January 2023 and $0\le t\le 52$.

The lowest number of emails Ms Iacona receives is 15 per week and the highest number of emails per week is 45.

The number of emails is at a maximum on 1st January 2023 i.e., when $t=0$.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
items.sol:
The amplitude is half the difference between the highest and lowest values.
$$a=\dfrac{45-15}{2}=15$$
The period is $12$ weeks.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{b}&=12\\b&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
So $f(t)=15\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+c$. The maximum is at $t=0$, so $f(0)=45$.
$$\begin{aligned}45&=15+c\\c&=30\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=15,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ c=30$$

The area is a rectangle ($2r$ by $y$) plus a semicircle, using $y$ from part (a).
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2r\cdot y+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2\\&=2r\left(10-r-\dfrac{\pi r}{2}\right)+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2\\&=20r-2r^2-\pi r^2+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2\\&=20r-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2-2r^2\end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dA}{dr}=20-\pi r-4r$$
Stationary point where $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}20-\pi r-4r&=0\\r(\pi+4)&=20\\r&=\dfrac{20}{\pi+4}\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=-\pi-4<0$$
so this is a local maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum area occurs when } r=\dfrac{20}{\pi+4}$$

items.part: Simplify $\dfrac{1-\sin^2 x}{\cot x}$ .
items.sol:
Use $1-\sin^2 x=\cos^2 x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cot x}=\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1-\sin^2 x}{\cot x}&=\cos^2 x\times\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\\&=\sin x\cos x\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the geometric series $64-16a+4a^2-\ldots$
For what values of $a$ does this series have a limiting sum?
items.sol:
The common ratio is
$$r=\dfrac{-16a}{64}=-\dfrac{a}{4}\qquad\left(\text{check: }\dfrac{4a^2}{-16a}=-\dfrac{a}{4}\right)$$
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$, that is $-1<r<1$. One operation per line:
$$\begin{aligned}-1&<-\dfrac{a}{4}<1\\-4&<-a<4&&(\text{multiply by }4)\\4&>a>-4&&(\text{multiply by }-1,\text{ reversing the inequalities})\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -4<a<4$$

items.part:
Consider the geometric series $64-16a+4a^2-\ldots$
It is known that the limiting sum of the series is 256. Find the value of $a$.
items.sol:
Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{T_1}{1-r}$ with first term $T_1=64$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{64}{1-r}&=256\\1-r&=\dfrac{64}{256}\\r&=1-\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $r=-\dfrac{a}{4}$, so
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{a}{4}&=\dfrac{3}{4}\\a&=-3\end{aligned}$$
This lies in the range $-4<a<4$ from part (a).

items.part: A circle is divided into $n$ sectors in such a way that the angles of the sectors are in arithmetic progression. The smallest two angles are $3^\circ$ and $5^\circ$. Find the value of $n$.
items.sol:
The sector angles form an arithmetic series with $a=3^\circ$ and $d=2^\circ$, and they add to a full circle, so $S_n=360$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2\times 3+(n-1)\times 2\right]&=360\\n\left(2n+4\right)&=720\\2n^2+4n-720&=0\\n^2+2n-360&=0\\(n+20)(n-18)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=18$.

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+2x}}\,dx$ .
items.sol:
The derivative of $1+2x$ is $2$, so insert a factor of $2$ and compensate with $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+2x}}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2(1+2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{(1+2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}}+C\\&=\sqrt{1+2x}+C\end{aligned}$$

Three function values on $[0,1]$ give two strips, so $h=\dfrac{1-0}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}$, with
$$f(0)=1,\quad f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=2^{\frac{3}{2}},\quad f(1)=8$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1 2^{3x}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{2}\left[1+8+2\times 2^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(9+2\times 2^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\\&=3.66421\ldots\\&\approx 3.66\text{ (2 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$$
It is an over-approximation: the graph is concave up on $0\le x\le 1$, so the trapeziums lie above the curve and their total area is more than the area under the curve.
items.final: Over-approximation, since the graph is concave up so the trapeziums lie above the curve.

items.part:
In the diagram, $CD$ is an arc of a circle with radius 8 cm and centre $O$.

T is the midpoint of $OC$. It is given that $\angle COD=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ .

\exfigure{638_q19_1}

Calculate the perimeter of $CTD$ in exact form.
items.sol:
The perimeter of $CTD$ is the arc $CD$ plus $CT$ plus $TD$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Arc }CD&=r\theta\\&=8\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{16\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$T$ is the midpoint of $OC$, so $CT=OT=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8=4$.

In $\triangle OTD$, $OT=4$, $OD=8$ and $\angle TOD=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned}TD&=\sqrt{4^2+8^2-2\times 4\times 8\times\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}}\\&=\sqrt{80-64\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}\\&=\sqrt{112}\\&=4\sqrt{7}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P=\dfrac{16\pi}{3}+4+4\sqrt{7}\text{ cm}$$

items.part:
The population of ants is growing exponentially according to the equation $P=50e^{kt}$ , where $t$ is the time in days after the insect is first counted. After four days, it is observed that the population has doubled from the initial amount.
Find the initial number of ants and show that $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$
items.sol:
At $t=0$, $P_0=50e^0=50$, so the initial number of ants is $50$.

After four days the population has doubled, so $P=100$ when $t=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}100&=50e^{4k}\\e^{4k}&=2\\4k&=\ln 2\\k&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of ants is growing exponentially according to the equation $P=50e^{kt}$ , where $t$ is the time in days after the insect is first counted. After four days, it is observed that the population has doubled from the initial amount.
At what rate (to the nearest whole number) is the population increasing at day 15?
items.sol:
Differentiate $P=50e^{kt}$ with $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=50k\,e^{kt}$$
At $t=15$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=50\times\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\times e^{\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\times 15}\\&\approx 117\text{ ants per day}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of ants is growing exponentially according to the equation $P=50e^{kt}$ , where $t$ is the time in days after the insect is first counted. After four days, it is observed that the population has doubled from the initial amount.
How many days will it take for the number of ants to first reach 1500?
items.sol:
Put $P=1500$ with $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$ and take natural logs.
$$\begin{aligned}1500&=50e^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t}\\30&=e^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t}\\\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t&=\ln 30\\t&=\dfrac{\ln 30}{\frac{1}{4}\ln 2}\\&\approx 19.6\\&\approx 20\text{ days}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The probability density function for the continuous random variable $X$ is given by:

$$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}kx(4-x), & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{array}\right\}$$
Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{9}$
items.sol:
The total probability is $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^4 kx(4-x)\,dx&=1\\k\int_1^4\left(4x-x^2\right)dx&=1\\k\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4&=1\\k\left(\left(32-\dfrac{64}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)&=1\\9k&=1\\k&=\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:

$$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}kx(4-x), & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{array}\right\}$$

items.sol:
The mode is the value of $x$ where $f(x)$ is greatest. With $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{9}x(4-x)$:

\exfigure{638_q24_s1}

The maximum is at $x=2$, which lies in $1\le x\le 4$, so the mode is $2$.

Alternatively, use calculus.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\dfrac{4}{9}-\dfrac{2x}{9}\\f'(x)&=0\ \text{when}\ x=2\\f''(x)&=-\dfrac{2}{9}<0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=2$ is a maximum, and the mode is $2$.

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x-x)=\ln x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x&v&=\ln x\\u'&=1&v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x-x)&=1\times\ln x+x\times\dfrac{1}{x}-1\\&=\ln x+1-1\\&=\ln x\end{aligned}$$
which is the right-hand side.

items.part: Hence, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^e \ln x^2\,dx$ .
items.sol:
From part (a), $x\ln x-x$ is a primitive of $\ln x$. Also $\ln x^2=2\ln x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^e\ln x^2\,dx&=2\int_1^e\ln x\,dx\\&=2\Big[x\ln x-x\Big]_1^e\\&=2\Big[(e\ln e-e)-(1\cdot\ln 1-1)\Big]\\&=2\Big[(e-e)-(0-1)\Big]\\&=2\end{aligned}$$

Yes, Sharon did really well, as her score is $3$ standard deviations above the mean.

By the empirical rule, $47.5\%$ lies between $z=-2$ and the mean, and $49.85\%$ between the mean and $z=3$.
$$47.5\%+49.85\%=97.35\%$$
So $97.35\%$ of students scored between 44 and 64.

A small school has counted the number of Year 12 students in Mathematics and Physics. They found that:

\item 5 students study Physics only

By first drawing a Venn diagram, determine the value of $x$ such that events $M$ and $P$ are independent.
items.sol:
\exfigure{638_q29_s1}

The total number of students is $12+5+3+x=20+x$. $M$ includes the students studying both, so $n(M)=12+x$ and $n(P)=5+x$.

$M$ and $P$ are independent when $P(M\cap P)=P(M)\,P(P)$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x}{20+x}&=\dfrac{12+x}{20+x}\times\dfrac{5+x}{20+x}\\x(20+x)&=(12+x)(5+x)\\20x+x^2&=60+17x+x^2\\3x&=60\\x&=20\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $f(x)=3x^2-x^3$ .
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate and solve $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=6x-3x^2\\0&=3x(2-x)\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(0)&=0\\f(2)&=3(2)^2-2^3=4\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$f''(x)=6-6x$$
$f''(0)=6>0$ (concave up), so $(0,0)$ is a local minimum turning point.

$f''(2)=6-12=-6<0$ (concave down), so $(2,4)$ is a local maximum turning point.
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a local minimum; $(2,4)$ is a local maximum

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $f(x)=3x^2-x^3$ .
Find any points of inflection.

items.sol:

items.part: The curve $y=px^3+qx$ passes through the point $(1, 4)$. The tangent at this point is parallel to the line $y=2x-6$. Find the values of $p$ and $q$.
items.sol:
The curve passes through $(1,4)$:
$$p+q=4\qquad(1)$$
Differentiate: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3px^2+q$. The gradient of the tangent at $(1,4)$ is $3p+q$. The tangent is parallel to $y=2x-6$, so its gradient is $2$:
$$3p+q=2\qquad(2)$$
From (1), $q=4-p$. Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{aligned}3p+4-p&=2\\2p&=-2\\p&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}q&=4-(-1)\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p=-1,\ q=5$$

items.part:
\exfigure{638_q33_1}

The shaded region $OAB$ is bounded by the parabolas $y=x^2$, $y=3-2x^2$

and the $x$-axis. It is given that point $A$ has the coordinates $(1, 1)$ and $O$ is the origin.
Find the coordinates of $B$.
items.sol:
$B$ is on the positive $x$-axis, so put $y=0$ in $y=3-2x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}3-2x^2&=0\\x^2&=\dfrac{3}{2}\\x&=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ B\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},0\right)$$

items.part:
\exfigure{638_q33_1}

The shaded region $OAB$ is bounded by the parabolas $y=x^2$, $y=3-2x^2$

and the $x$-axis. It is given that point $A$ has the coordinates $(1, 1)$ and $O$ is the origin.
Show that the exact area of the shaded region $OAB$ is given by:

$\left(2\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}-2\right)$ square units.
items.sol:
Split the area at $x=1$: under $y=x^2$ from $O$ to $A$, then under $y=3-2x^2$ from $A$ to $B$. Let $s=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$, so $s^3=\dfrac{3}{2}s$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_0^1 x^2\,dx+\int_1^{s}\left(3-2x^2\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\Big[x^3\Big]_0^1+\left[3x-\dfrac{2}{3}x^3\right]_1^{s}\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}+\left(3s-\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{2}s\right)-\left(3-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}+2s-\dfrac{7}{3}\\&=2s-2\\&=2\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}-2\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
John borrowed an amount \$$P$ at a rate of $3.6\%$ per annum compounded monthly on a reducing balance. At the end of each month, he repays an amount of \$$M$.
Show that the amount owing at the end of the second month is

$A_2=P(1.003)^2-M(1.003)-M$ .
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{3.6\%}{12}=0.003$, so each month the balance is multiplied by $1.003$ and then $M$ is paid.
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=P(1.003)-M\\A_2&=A_1(1.003)-M\\&=\left[P(1.003)-M\right](1.003)-M\\&=P(1.003)^2-M(1.003)-M\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
John borrowed an amount \$$P$ at a rate of $3.6\%$ per annum compounded monthly on a reducing balance. At the end of each month, he repays an amount of \$$M$.
It is now given that the amount borrowed is \$50 000 and his monthly repayment is \$350. Show that the amount owing after one year is approximately \$47 560.

John borrowed an amount \$$P$ at a rate of $3.6\%$ per annum compounded monthly on a reducing balance. At the end of each month, he repays an amount of \$$M$.
Find how many months it will take for John to fully repay the loan.
items.sol:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$. Use the geometric series sum with $a=1$, $r=1.003$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=50\,000(1.003)^n-350\times\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}\\&=50\,000(1.003)^n-\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n+\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\\&=-\dfrac{200\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n+\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{200\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n&=\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\\1.003^n&=\dfrac{7}{4}\\n\log 1.003&=\log\dfrac{7}{4}\\n&=\dfrac{\log\frac{7}{4}}{\log 1.003}\\&=186.818\ldots\\&\approx 187\text{ months}\end{aligned}$$
It takes $187$ months, that is $15$ years and $7$ months, to pay off the loan.

items.part:
\exfigure{638_q35_1}

The diagram above shows the circle $x^2+y^2=36$ . The point $S(x,y)$ lies on the circle in the first quadrant. $R(4,0)$ lies on the $x$-axis and $T(0,2)$ lies on the $y$-axis and $O$ is the origin. The size of $\angle SOR=\alpha$ where $0<\alpha<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ .
Hence, show that the area of the quadrilateral $ORST$ is given by:

$A=6\cos\alpha(2\tan\alpha+1)$
items.sol:
$T$ is on the $y$-axis, so $\angle ROT=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\angle TOS=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha$. With $OT=2$ and $OS=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle TOS&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6\times 2\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\right)\\&=6\cos\alpha\end{aligned}$$
The quadrilateral $ORST$ is $\triangle SOR$ and $\triangle TOS$ together.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=12\sin\alpha+6\cos\alpha\\&=6\cos\alpha\left(2\cdot\dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}+1\right)\\&=6\cos\alpha(2\tan\alpha+1)\end{aligned}$$

Use $A=12\sin\alpha+6\cos\alpha$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=12\cos\alpha-6\sin\alpha$$
Stationary point where $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}12\cos\alpha&=6\sin\alpha\\\tan\alpha&=2\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}=-12\sin\alpha-6\cos\alpha$$
When $\tan\alpha=2$, $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ (right-angled triangle with sides $1$, $2$, $\sqrt{5}$).
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}&=-\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{5}}-\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\\&=-6\sqrt{5}\\&\approx-13.42<0\end{aligned}$$
so the area is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \tan\alpha=2\text{ gives the maximum area}$$

\exfigure{638_q35_s1}

From part (c), $\tan\alpha=2$. For $S(x,y)$ on the circle, $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{y}{x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{y}{x}&=2\\y&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$S$ lies on $x^2+y^2=36$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2+4x^2&=36\\5x^2&=36\\x&=\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5}}=\dfrac{6\sqrt{5}}{5}&&(x>0)\end{aligned}$$
and $y=2x=\dfrac{12\sqrt{5}}{5}$.
$$S\left(\dfrac{6\sqrt{5}}{5},\dfrac{12\sqrt{5}}{5}\right)$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x^3-2x$ at the point $(-1,1)$.
items.sol:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-2$$
The gradient of the tangent at $(-1,1)$ is
$$m_1=3(-1)^2-2=1$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_2=-\dfrac{1}{m_1}=-1$.

Equation of the normal:
$$\begin{aligned} y-y_1 &= m_2(x-x_1) \\ y-1 &= -1(x+1) \\ y-1 &= -x-1 \\ y &= -x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The time it takes to complete a task varies inversely with the number of people assigned.

It takes 5 people to complete a task in 4 hours.

Find the amount of time it would take 8 people to complete the same task.
items.sol:
The time varies inversely with the number of people, so $T=\dfrac{k}{n}$ where $n$ is the number of people.

For 5 people, $T=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= \dfrac{k}{5} \\ k &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
(The task takes 20 hours for one person.) For 8 people:
$$\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{20}{8} \\ &= 2\dfrac{1}{2}\ \text{hours} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, given $y=(\ln x)^2$.
items.sol:
Let $y=u^2$ where $u=\ln x$. By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dy}{du}=2u \quad\text{and}\quad \dfrac{du}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{dy}{du}\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx} \\ &= 2u\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= \dfrac{2\ln x}{x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e}\dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{2x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\ln\left(x^2\right)=2\ln x$ and the result of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^e\dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{2x}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\Big[(\ln x)^2\Big]_1^e \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[(\ln e)^2-(\ln1)^2\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[1^2-0^2\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The graph of the primitive function of $f(x)=\tan^2x$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Find the primitive function, leaving all values in exact form.
items.sol:
Use the identity $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int\tan^2x\,dx \\ &= \int\left(\sec^2x-1\right)dx \\ &= \tan x-x+C \end{aligned}$$
The graph crosses the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}+C \\ 0 &= \sqrt{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}+C \\ C &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\tan x-x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=-\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{2}(x-\pi)\right)$.
Show that $f(x)$ is even.
items.sol:
Simplify using $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= -\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ &= \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \\ &= \cos\dfrac{x}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= \cos\left(\dfrac{-x}{2}\right) \\ &= \cos\dfrac{x}{2} \\ &= f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ f(x)$ is even.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=-\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{2}(x-\pi)\right)$.
Hence, or otherwise, find the area bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis in the interval $[-\pi,\pi]$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{515_q17_s1}

From part (a), $f(x)=\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$, which is $\ge0$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$ (since $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le\dfrac{x}{2}\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$), so the area lies above the $x$-axis.

$f$ is even, so the area is symmetrical about the $y$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx \\ &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx \\ &= 2\Big[2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left(2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2\sin0\right) \\ &= 4\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Ben is cooking a pizza. The temperature of the pizza oven is modelled by the equation

$$T=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the oven ($^\circ$C) at time $t$ minutes since the oven was switched on.
What was the initial temperature of the oven?
items.sol:
At the start, $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 175-150\times(0.9)^{0} \\ &= 175-150 \\ &= 25^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Ben is cooking a pizza. The temperature of the pizza oven is modelled by the equation

$$T=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the oven ($^\circ$C) at time $t$ minutes since the oven was switched on.
Calculate the average rate at which the temperature changes per minute from $t=25$ to $t=75$, correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
The average rate of change is $\dfrac{T(75)-T(25)}{75-25}$.
$$\begin{aligned} T(25) &= 175-150\times0.9^{0.2\times25} \\ &\approx 86.4265 \\ T(75) &= 175-150\times0.9^{0.2\times75} \\ &\approx 144.11633 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Average rate} &= \dfrac{144.11633-86.4265}{75-25} \\ &\approx 1.15^\circ\text{C/minute} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Ben is cooking a pizza. The temperature of the pizza oven is modelled by the equation

$$T=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the oven ($^\circ$C) at time $t$ minutes since the oven was switched on.
Ben can place the pizza in the oven when the instantaneous rate of change of temperature is less than or equal to $1^\circ$C per minute.

Given that Ben turned the oven on at 10:30 am, find the earliest time that Ben can place the pizza in the oven, correct to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
The instantaneous rate of change is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Differentiating with $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=ka^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -150\times0.2\times(0.9)^{0.2t}\times\ln0.9 \\ &= -30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t} \end{aligned}$$
The cut-off is where $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} -30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t} &= 1 \\ (0.9)^{0.2t} &\approx 0.316374 \\ 0.2t &\approx \log_{0.9}0.316374 \\ t &\approx \dfrac{5\ln0.316374}{\ln0.9} \\ &\approx 54.6\ \text{minutes} \end{aligned}$$
The rate $-30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t}$ decreases as $t$ increases, so it is $\le1$ for $t\ge54.6$. To the nearest minute this is $55$ minutes after $10{:}30$ am.
$$\text{Time}=10{:}30\ \text{am}+55\ \text{min}=11{:}25\ \text{am}$$

A group of students were surveyed on the type of pets they own.

The results are summarised in the following incomplete two-way table.

Given that a student owns a dog, the probability that they also own a cat is 60%.

Find the probability that a student chosen at random owns both a cat and a dog.
items.sol:
Given that a student owns a dog, the probability of also owning a cat is $60\%=\dfrac{3}{5}$. The number of dog owners is $A+32$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{A}{A+32} &= \dfrac{3}{5} \\ 5A &= 3(A+32) \\ 5A &= 3A+96 \\ 2A &= 96 \\ A &= 48 \end{aligned}$$
The total number of students is $48+32+45+35=160$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{cat and dog}) &= \dfrac{48}{160} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{10} \\ &= 30\% \end{aligned}$$

The relative level of a noise compared to a reference level is calculated by the formula

$$R=20\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N}{N_0}\right),$$

where $R$ is the relative noise level measured in decibels (dB), $N$ is the level of a noise and $N_0$ is the maximum noise level permitted.

The relative noise level at a construction site when operating machinery was found to be 8 dB higher than the maximum noise level permitted.

Show that the level of noise produced by the machinery was approximately 2.5 times greater than the maximum noise level permitted.
items.sol:
Put $R=8$ in the formula.
$$\begin{aligned} 8 &= 20\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N}{N_0}\right) \\ \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N}{N_0}\right) &= \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{N}{N_0} &= 10^{0.4} \\ &\approx 2.51 \end{aligned}$$
So $N\approx2.51\times N_0$: the noise level is approximately 2.5 times the maximum permitted level.
