A deflated weather balloon at a scientific research station is being inflated such that the rate of air flow can be modelled by the equation $V=10e^{-\sqrt{t}}$, where $V$ is the rate of air flow at time $t$.

The graph of $V=10e^{-\sqrt{t}}$ is shown below with the flow rates at hourly intervals.

\exfigure{515_q24_1}
Using three applications of the Trapezoidal rule, estimate the volume of air in the balloon at time $t=3$.

A deflated weather balloon at a scientific research station is being inflated such that the rate of air flow can be modelled by the equation $V=10e^{-\sqrt{t}}$, where $V$ is the rate of air flow at time $t$.

The graph of $V=10e^{-\sqrt{t}}$ is shown below with the flow rates at hourly intervals.

\exfigure{515_q24_1}
A safety shutoff valve is programmed to be activated before the balloon reaches its maximum volume, after which the balloon will burst.

By referring to the graph, or otherwise, explain why the Trapezoidal rule is a valid method of estimation in this context.
items.sol:
The graph of $V=10e^{-\sqrt{t}}$ is concave up for all $t>0$ (it curves above each chord joining points on the graph), so each trapezium lies above the curve and the trapezoidal rule over-estimates the volume.

An over-estimate means the true volume is never more than the estimate, so a safety valve set using the estimate will activate before the balloon reaches its maximum volume. The rule is therefore a valid, safe method here.

items.part:
A closed water tank in the shape of a half-cylinder with diameter $2r$ metres and height $h$ metres is to be made from sheet metal as shown below.

\exfigure{515_q25_1}

The surface area of the tank is $A$ square metres and the volume of the tank is $V$ cubic metres.
Show $A=\pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{r}\right)$, given that $V=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2h$.
items.sol:
The volume is $V=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2h$, so
$$h=\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2}$$
The closed tank has two half-discs (together $\pi r^2$), half of the curved cylinder surface ($\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot2\pi rh$) and a flat rectangular top ($2r\times h$).
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \pi r^2+\pi rh+2rh \\ &= \pi r^2+\pi r\cdot\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2}+2r\cdot\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi r} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{r}+\dfrac{2}{r}\right] \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{r}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A closed water tank in the shape of a half-cylinder with diameter $2r$ metres and height $h$ metres is to be made from sheet metal as shown below.

\exfigure{515_q25_1}

The surface area of the tank is $A$ square metres and the volume of the tank is $V$ cubic metres.
Show that the amount of sheet metal used is minimised when $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(2+\pi)}{\pi^2}}$.
items.sol:
Write $A$ with negative powers of $r$ so that it can be differentiated.
$$A=\pi r^2+2Vr^{-1}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi}r^{-1}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dr}=2\pi r-2Vr^{-2}-\dfrac{4V}{\pi}r^{-2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi r &= \dfrac{2V}{r^2}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi r^2} \\ 2\pi^2r^3 &= 2\pi V+4V \quad(\text{multiplying through by } \pi r^2) \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{2\pi V+4V}{2\pi^2} \\ &= \dfrac{V(\pi+2)}{\pi^2} \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(\pi+2)}{\pi^2}} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative, for $r>0$:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=2\pi+4Vr^{-3}+\dfrac{8V}{\pi}r^{-3}>0$$
The graph of $A$ is concave up for all $r>0$, so this stationary point is a minimum. It is the only stationary point for $r>0$, so it is the absolute minimum, and the amount of sheet metal is minimised when $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(2+\pi)}{\pi^2}}$.

items.part:
A closed water tank in the shape of a half-cylinder with diameter $2r$ metres and height $h$ metres is to be made from sheet metal as shown below.

\exfigure{515_q25_1}

The surface area of the tank is $A$ square metres and the volume of the tank is $V$ cubic metres.
Hence find the height of the tank, given that the volume of the tank is 10 cubic metres.
items.sol:
With $V=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10(\pi+2)}{\pi^2}} \\ &\approx 1.7335\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$
From $V=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2h$:
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{2\times10}{\pi r^2} \\ &\approx 2.118\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Michael installs a vertical radio mast on level ground at $M$. Two pegs are installed on the ground at $A$ and $B$ on bearings of $045^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ respectively from $M$.

The distance from $A$ to $M$ is 100 m and the area of triangle $AMB$ is 10 432 m$^2$.

\exfigure{515_q26_1}
Find the distance between the base of the mast, $M$, and the peg at $B$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{515_q26_s1}

The bearings of $A$ and $B$ from $M$ are $045^\circ$ and $120^\circ$, so
$$\angle AMB=120^\circ-45^\circ=75^\circ$$
Let $MB=x$. Using the area formula $\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ in triangle $AMB$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\,432 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times100\times x\times\sin75^\circ \\ x &= \dfrac{2\times10\,432}{100\sin75^\circ} \\ &\approx 216\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Michael installs a vertical radio mast on level ground at $M$. Two pegs are installed on the ground at $A$ and $B$ on bearings of $045^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ respectively from $M$.

The distance from $A$ to $M$ is 100 m and the area of triangle $AMB$ is 10 432 m$^2$.

\exfigure{515_q26_1}
Supporting wires are connected from each peg to the top of the mast at $T$.

By considering triangle $AMT$ and triangle $BMT$, find the height of the mast, given that the total length of the supporting wires is 380 m.
items.sol:
The mast is vertical, so triangles $AMT$ and $BMT$ are right-angled at $M$. Let $MT=h$ and use Pythagoras' theorem with $MA=100$ and $MB=216$:
$$TA=\sqrt{h^2+100^2} \quad\text{and}\quad TB=\sqrt{h^2+216^2}$$
The total length of the wires is $380$ m.
$$\sqrt{h^2+100^2}+\sqrt{h^2+216^2}=380$$
Isolate one root and square both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} h^2+100^2+2\sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)}+h^2+216^2 &= 380^2 \\ 2\sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)} &= 380^2-216^2-100^2-2h^2 \\ &= 87\,744-2h^2 \\ \sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)} &= 43\,872-h^2 \end{aligned}$$
Square both sides again and let $u=h^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} (u+100^2)(u+216^2) &= (43\,872-u)^2 \\ u^2+100^2u+216^2u+100^2\times216^2 &= 43\,872^2-87\,744u+u^2 \\ 100^2u+216^2u+87\,744u &= 43\,872^2-100^2\times216^2 \\ 144\,400u &= 1\,458\,192\,384 \\ u &\approx 10\,098.285 \\ h &= \sqrt{10\,098.285} \\ &\approx 100.49\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=(x+1)^2$.

The following transformations were applied to the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the order shown below.

\begin{itemize}
\item Horizontal translation to the right by 4 units
\item Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{4}{3}$
\item Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item Vertical translation down by 3 units
\item Reflection in the $x$-axis
\end{itemize}

Find the equation of the transformed function and sketch its graph, showing the location of the vertex and the axis intercepts.
items.sol:
Apply each transformation to $y=(x+1)^2$ in turn.

Translate right by 4 (replace $x$ with $x-4$):
$$y=(x-4+1)^2=(x-3)^2$$
Horizontal dilation by factor $\dfrac{4}{3}$ (replace $x$ with $\dfrac{3x}{4}$):
$$y=\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2=\dfrac{9}{16}(x-4)^2$$
Vertical dilation by factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$ (multiply $y$ by $\dfrac{1}{3}$):
$$y=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{9}{16}(x-4)^2=\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2$$
Translate down by 3:
$$y=\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2-3$$
Reflect in the $x$-axis (replace $y$ with $-y$):
$$y=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2+3$$
For the intercepts, put $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2 &= 3 \\ (x-4)^2 &= 16 \\ x-4 &= \pm4 \\ x &= 0 \text{ or } x=8 \end{aligned}$$
The $x$-intercepts are $(0,0)$ and $(8,0)$, so the $y$-intercept (at $x=0$) is also $(0,0)$.

As a check, $y=kx(x-8)$ through the vertex $(4,3)$ gives $3=-16k$, so $k=-\dfrac{3}{16}$ and $y=-\dfrac{3}{16}x(x-8)$.

\exfigure{515_q27_s1}

items.part:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis so that its position, in metres, at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$x=2\ln(t^2+3)-t$$
Determine the times when the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
Velocity is the derivative of position, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln\left(t^2+3\right)=\dfrac{2t}{t^2+3}$.
$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2\times\dfrac{2t}{t^2+3}-1=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4t}{t^2+3} &= 1 \\ 4t &= t^2+3 \\ t^2-4t+3 &= 0 \\ (t-1)(t-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=1 \text{ or } t=3\ \text{seconds}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis so that its position, in metres, at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$x=2\ln(t^2+3)-t$$
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first second.

Leave your answer in the form $\ln\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)-c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.
items.sol:
Factorise the velocity to see whether the particle changes direction in the first second.
$$v=\dfrac{4t-t^2-3}{t^2+3}=-\dfrac{(t-1)(t-3)}{t^2+3}$$
For $0\le t<1$ both $(t-1)$ and $(t-3)$ are negative, so $v<0$. The particle moves in one direction only (it is at rest at $t=1$), so the distance is $x(0)-x(1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 2\ln3 \\ x(1) &= 2\ln4-1=4\ln2-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 2\ln3-(4\ln2-1) \\ &= \ln3^2-\ln2^4+1 \\ &= \ln9-\ln16+1 \\ &= \ln\dfrac{9}{16}+1 \\ &\approx 0.42\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis so that its position, in metres, at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$x=2\ln(t^2+3)-t$$
Find the maximum velocity of the particle.
items.sol:
The acceleration is the derivative of velocity, using the quotient rule on $v=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$.
$$a=\dfrac{4(t^2+3)-4t\times2t}{(t^2+3)^2}=\dfrac{12-4t^2}{(t^2+3)^2}$$
Maximum velocity occurs where $a=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12-4t^2 &= 0 \\ t^2 &= 3 \\ t &= \sqrt{3} \quad(t\ge0) \end{aligned}$$
Test: $a>0$ for $0\le t<\sqrt{3}$ and $a<0$ for $t>\sqrt{3}$, so $v$ increases then decreases and has a maximum at $t=\sqrt{3}$ (between the rest times $t=1$ and $t=3$).
$$\begin{aligned} v_{\max} &= \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3+3}-1 \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}-1 \\ &\approx 0.1547\ \text{m/s} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{515_q28_s1}

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=3x\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3+1$.
By showing that $f'(x)=3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2(1-x)$, find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 3x & v &= \left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3 \\ u' &= 3 & v' &= -\dfrac{3}{4}\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
where $v'$ comes from the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3-\dfrac{9x}{4}\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2 \\ &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2\left[\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)-\dfrac{3x}{4}\right] \\ &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $f'(x)=0$, so $x=4$ or $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 3\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^3+1 = 2\dfrac{17}{64} \\ f(4) &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The stationary points are $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$ and $(4,1)$.

Nature of $x=1$: the factor $(1-x)$ decides the sign of $f'$ near $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(0) &= 3>0 \\ f'(2) &= -\dfrac{3}{4}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$f'$ changes from positive to negative, so $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$ is a local maximum.

Nature of $x=4$: the squared factor does not change sign.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(3) &= -\dfrac{3}{8}<0 \\ f'(5) &= -\dfrac{3}{4}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$f'$ is negative on both sides of $x=4$, so $(4,1)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
items.final: $\left(1,2\tfrac{17}{64}\right)$ is a local maximum; $(4,1)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=3x\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3+1$.
Explain why the graph of $y=f(x)$ must cross the $x$-axis at least once between $x=5$ and $x=6$.
items.sol:
Evaluate $f$ at the two ends.
$$\begin{aligned} f(5) &= 15\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3+1=\dfrac{49}{64}>0 \\ f(6) &= 18\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3+1=-\dfrac{5}{4}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$f$ is continuous and changes sign between $x=5$ and $x=6$, so there is at least one $x$-intercept in that interval (Intermediate Value Theorem).

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=3x\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3+1$.
Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the interval $[0,6]$, showing the stationary points, the $y$-intercept and the approximate location of the $x$-intercept.
items.sol:
The end points come from $f(0)$ and $f(6)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= 1 \\ f(6) &= -1\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The $x$-intercept lies between $x=5$ and $x=6$, from part (b).

\exfigure{515_q29_s1}

items.part:
Aida has \$500 000 in an investment account earning interest at a rate of 3% per annum compounded annually.

At the end of the first year, Aida withdraws \$25 000 for expenses.

Each subsequent year, the amount that Aida withdraws increases by 5% due to rising expenses.

Let $A_n$ be the balance of Aida’s investment account at the end of the $n$th year.
Show that $A_3=500000(1.03)^3-25000\left(1.05^2+(1.05)(1.03)+1.03^2\right)$.

Aida has \$500 000 in an investment account earning interest at a rate of 3% per annum compounded annually.

At the end of the first year, Aida withdraws \$25 000 for expenses.

Each subsequent year, the amount that Aida withdraws increases by 5% due to rising expenses.

Let $A_n$ be the balance of Aida’s investment account at the end of the $n$th year.
For how many complete years will Aida be able to withdraw money from this account in order to meet her expenses?
items.sol:
Continuing the pattern of part (a), after $n$ years
$$A_n=500\,000(1.03)^n-25\,000\left[(1.05)^{n-1}+(1.05)^{n-2}(1.03)+\cdots+(1.03)^{n-1}\right]$$
The money runs out when $A_n=0$.
$$25\,000\left[(1.05)^{n-1}+(1.05)^{n-2}(1.03)+\cdots+(1.03)^{n-1}\right]=500\,000(1.03)^n$$
Divide both sides by $25\,000(1.03)^{n-1}$:
$$\left(\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^{n-1}+\cdots+\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}+1=20(1.03)=20.6$$
The left side is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}$ and $n$ terms, so
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n-1}{\frac{1.05}{1.03}-1} &= 20.6 \\ \left(\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n-1 &= 0.4 \\ \left(\dfrac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n &= 1.4 \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln1.4}{\ln\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)} \\ &\approx 17.496 \end{aligned}$$
The balance is still positive after 17 withdrawals and cannot cover the 18th, so Aida can withdraw money for 17 complete years.

items.part:
The time taken, $t$ minutes, for a machine to produce car parts can be modelled by a continuous random variable with probability density function given by

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}k(t-1)^2, & 1\le t\le2\\[6pt] k\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right), & 2<t\le4\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.
items.sol:
The total area under the density function is 1.
$$\displaystyle k\int_1^2(t-1)^2\,dt+k\int_2^4\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right)dt=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} k\left[\dfrac{(t-1)^3}{3}\right]_1^2+k\left[2t-\dfrac{t^2}{4}\right]_2^4 &= 1 \\ k\left[\dfrac{1}{3}-0\right]+k\left[(8-4)-(4-1)\right] &= 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{3}k+k &= 1 \\ \dfrac{4}{3}k &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The time taken, $t$ minutes, for a machine to produce car parts can be modelled by a continuous random variable with probability density function given by

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}k(t-1)^2, & 1\le t\le2\\[6pt] k\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right), & 2<t\le4\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Let $F(t)$ be the cumulative distribution function of $f(t)$, where $F(2.16)=0.3652$.

Find the least amount of time taken to produce 88% of the parts.
items.sol:
The first piece gives the probability up to $t=2$.
$$F(2)=\dfrac{1}{3}k=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{4}=\dfrac{1}{4}=0.25$$
Since $0.25<0.88$, the required time lies in the second piece, and we still need $0.88-0.25=0.63$. Call the time $x$.
$$\dfrac{3}{4}\displaystyle\int_2^x\left(2-\dfrac{t}{2}\right)dt=0.63$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[2t-\dfrac{t^2}{4}\right]_2^x &= 0.84 \\ \left(2x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right)-(4-1) &= 0.84 \\ 0 &= \dfrac{1}{4}x^2-2x+3.84 \\ x^2-8x &= -15.36 \\ (x-4)^2 &= 0.64 \\ x-4 &= \pm0.8 \\ x &= 3.2 \text{ or } 4.8 \end{aligned}$$
$x=4.8$ is outside the domain $2<t\le4$, so $x=3.2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Time}=3.2\ \text{minutes}\ (3\text{ min }12\text{ s})$$

items.part:
A heater converts electrical power, measured in watts, into heat in such a way that the heat produced is given by the function $h(x)=\left(f(x)\right)^2$.

The heater is plugged into a faulty socket which outputs $x=g(t)$ watts at time $t$ seconds.

The power output at time $t=1$ is 3 watts and is increasing at a rate of 4 watts per second.

By considering $h'(x)$ and using the fact that $\dfrac{d}{dt}f\left(g(t)\right)=f'\left(g(t)\right)\times g'(t)$, find the rate of change of the heat produced at time $t=1$, given that $f(3)=5$ and $f'(3)=2$.
items.sol:
Given $h(x)=\left[f(x)\right]^2$, differentiate with the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dh}{dx}=2f(x)f'(x)$$
The power output is $x=g(t)$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=g'(t)$.

Given: $g(1)=3$ (so $x=3$ when $t=1$), $g'(1)=4$, $f(3)=5$ and $f'(3)=2$.

By the chain rule, $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{dh}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 2f(x)f'(x)\,g'(t) \end{aligned}$$
At $t=1$, $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 2f(3)f'(3)g'(1) \\ &= 2\times5\times2\times4 \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find an expression for the $n$th term of the arithmetic sequence $100, 92, 84, \dots$?
items.sol:
The sequence is arithmetic with first term and common difference
$$a=100,\quad d=-8$$
Using the formula for the $n$th term:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ &= 100+(n-1)(-8) \\ &= 108-8n \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_n = 108-8n$$

items.part: Find the limiting sum of the geometric series $1-\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{1}{27}+\dots$.
items.sol:
The series is geometric with
$$a=1,\quad r=-\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_\infty = \dfrac{3}{4}$$

items.part:
Two identical coins with the same bias are tossed together, and the outcome is recorded. After a large number of trials, it is observed that the probability that both coins land showing tails is $0.49$.

What is the probability that both coins land showing heads?
items.sol:
Both coins have the same bias, so
$$P(T)\times P(T)=0.49$$
$$P(T)=\sqrt{0.49}=0.7$$
Hence
$$P(H)=1-0.7=0.3$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(HH) &= 0.3\times 0.3 \\ &= 0.09 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(HH)=0.09$$

The probabilities sum to 1:
$$0.1+0.3+n+0.2=1$$
so $n=0.4$.

The expected value is
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 4(0.1)+5(0.3)+6(0.4)+7(0.2) \\ &= 5.7 \end{aligned}$$
The variance is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= 4^2(0.1)+5^2(0.3)+6^2(0.4)+7^2(0.2)-5.7^2 \\ &= 33.3-32.49 \\ &= 0.81 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ E(X)=5.7,\quad \text{Var}(X)=0.81$$

items.part:
A standard six-sided die is marked with the numbers $1, 2, \dots, 6$. A game is played by rolling the die until a 6 appears on the uppermost face. At this point the game ends.
Using a tree diagram, or otherwise, explain why the probability of the game ending before the fourth roll is:

$$\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^2\times\dfrac{1}{6}$$
items.sol:
On each roll, $P(6)=\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $P(\text{not } 6)=\dfrac{5}{6}$.

In the tree diagram, at each roll the game ends with probability $\dfrac{1}{6}$ or continues with probability $\dfrac{5}{6}$.

The game ends before the 4th roll if it ends on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd roll:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{ends before 4th roll}) &= \dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^2\times\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
A standard six-sided die is marked with the numbers $1, 2, \dots, 6$. A game is played by rolling the die until a 6 appears on the uppermost face. At this point the game ends.
What is the smallest value of $n$ for which the probability of the game ending before the $n$th roll is more than $90\%$?
items.sol:
The game ends before the $n$th roll if it ends on one of rolls $1$ to $n-1$:
$$P(\text{ends before } n\text{th roll})=\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^0\dfrac{1}{6}+\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^1\dfrac{1}{6}+\dots+\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{n-2}\dfrac{1}{6}$$
This is a geometric series with $a=\dfrac{1}{6}$, $r=\dfrac{5}{6}$ and $n-1$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{n-1} &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{6}\left(1-\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{n-1}\right)}{1-\frac{5}{6}} \\ &= 1-\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{n-1} \end{aligned}$$
We need this to exceed $0.9$. Solve the equality first:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.9 &= 1-\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{n-1} \\ \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{n-1} &= 0.1 \\ (n-1)\log\dfrac{5}{6} &= \log 0.1 \\ n-1 &= \dfrac{\log 0.1}{\log\frac{5}{6}} = 12.629\dots \\ n &= 13.629\dots \end{aligned}$$
$n$ must be a whole number, so we round up.
$$\therefore\ \text{the smallest value of } n \text{ is } 14$$

items.part: Elizabeth is a teacher. At the school where she works, $80\%$ of the teachers own a car, $15\%$ of the teachers own a motorbike and $8\%$ of the teachers do not own a car or a motorbike. What is the probability that Elizabeth owns a car given that she owns a motorbike?
items.sol:
Let $C$ = owns a car and $M$ = owns a motorbike. The proportion owning neither is $0.08$, so
$$P(C\cup M)=1-0.08=0.92$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} P(C\cap M) &= P(C)+P(M)-P(C\cup M) \\ &= 0.80+0.15-0.92 \\ &= 0.03 \end{aligned}$$
The two-way table of proportions is

\extable{Ts3417_1}

$$\begin{aligned} P(C\mid M) &= \dfrac{P(C\cap M)}{P(M)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.03}{0.15} \\ &= 0.2 = 20\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(C\mid M)=20\%$$

items.part:
In a reducing balance loan, an amount $\$P$ is borrowed for a period of $n$ months at an interest rate of $0.4\%$ per month, compounded monthly. At the end of each month a repayment of $\$M$ is made. After the $n$th repayment has been made the amount owing, $\$A_n$ is given by:

$$A_n = P(1.004)^n - M\left(1+(1.004)^1+(1.004)^2+\dots+(1.004)^{n-1}\right)$$

(Do NOT prove this.)
Celeste borrows \$500 000 in a reducing balance loan as described. The loan is to be repaid in 240 monthly repayments.

Show that $M = \$3244.79$, when rounded to the nearest cent.

In a reducing balance loan, an amount $\$P$ is borrowed for a period of $n$ months at an interest rate of $0.4\%$ per month, compounded monthly. At the end of each month a repayment of $\$M$ is made. After the $n$th repayment has been made the amount owing, $\$A_n$ is given by:

$$A_n = P(1.004)^n - M\left(1+(1.004)^1+(1.004)^2+\dots+(1.004)^{n-1}\right)$$

(Do NOT prove this.)
After 150 repayments of \$3244.79 have been made, the interest rate changes to $0.5\%$ per month.

At this stage the amount owing to the nearest dollar is \$244 837. (Do NOT prove this.)

Celeste increases her monthly repayments to \$3500.

For how many months will Celeste need to make full monthly repayments of \$3500?
items.sol:
The new rate is $0.5\%$ per month, so the monthly factor is $1.005$. Starting from $\$244\,837$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 244\,837\times 1.005-3500 \\ A_2 &= 244\,837\times 1.005^2-3500\times 1.005-3500 \end{aligned}$$
Continuing, and summing the geometric series:
$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= 244\,837\times 1.005^n-3500\left(1+1.005+\dots+1.005^{n-1}\right) \\ &= 244\,837\times 1.005^n-\dfrac{3500(1.005^n-1)}{0.005} \end{aligned}$$
Set $A_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3500(1.005^n-1) &= 244\,837\times 1.005^n\times 0.005 \\ 3500\times 1.005^n-3500 &= 1224.185\times 1.005^n \\ 2275.815\times 1.005^n &= 3500 \\ 1.005^n &= \dfrac{3500}{2275.815} \\ n &= \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{3500}{2275.815}\right)}{\log 1.005} = 86.299\dots \end{aligned}$$
The loan is not cleared after 86 repayments, so the last payment is smaller.
$$\therefore\ \text{86 full payments of } \$3500 \text{ are made}$$

items.part: If $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $P(B)=\dfrac{3}{5}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{5}{6}$, find $P(A\cap B)$
items.sol:
Using the addition rule:
$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B) &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{5}-\dfrac{5}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{15} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{4}{15}$$

items.part:
A table of future value interest factors for an annuity of \$1 is shown.

\exfigure{1585_q4c_1}

Adelaide deposits \$2000 into a savings account at the end of each quarter for 5 years. The interest rate for these 5 years is $8\%$ per annum compounded quarterly. After the final deposit in the 5th year, Adelaide stops making deposits but leaves the money in the savings account. The money in her savings account then earns interest at $5\%$ per annum, compounded annually for a further 3 years.

Find the amount of money in Adelaide's savings account at the end of the 8 years.
items.sol:
First stage: $8\%$ p.a. compounded quarterly is $2\%$ per quarter, so $r=0.02$, and 5 years is $N=20$ quarters.

From the table ($N=20$, $r=0.02$) the factor is $24.29737$:
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= 2000\times 24.29737 \\ &= \$48\,594.74 \end{aligned}$$
Second stage: this amount earns $5\%$ p.a. compounded annually for 3 years.
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= PV(1+r)^n \\ &= 48\,594.74(1+0.05)^3 \\ &= 56\,254.485\dots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the savings account holds } \$56\,254.49$$

The probabilities sum to 1:
$$r+r^2+r^3+\dots+r^{n-1}+r^n=1$$
This is a geometric series with $a=r$, ratio $r$ and $n$ terms:
$$S_n=\dfrac{r(r^n-1)}{r-1}=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} r^{n+1}-r &= r-1 \\ r^{n+1} &= 2r-1 \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$
The expected value pairs each value with its probability:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \sum xP(X=x) \\ &= r\cdot r^n+r^2\cdot r^{n-1}+r^3\cdot r^{n-2}+\dots+r^n\cdot r \\ &= r^{n+1}+r^{n+1}+\dots+r^{n+1} \\ &= nr^{n+1} \end{aligned}$$
Using (1):
$$E(X)=n(2r-1)$$
as required.

items.part: Calculate the area under $y=|2x-4|$ bounded by the $x$–axis over the domain $[0,6]$.
items.sol:
The graph of $y=|2x-4|$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=2$, so split the area at $x=2$.

For $0\le x\le 2$, $|2x-4|=4-2x$. For $2\le x\le 6$, $|2x-4|=2x-4$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^2 (4-2x)\,dx+\int_2^6 (2x-4)\,dx \\ &= \Big[4x-x^2\Big]_0^2+\Big[x^2-4x\Big]_2^6 \\ &= 4+12-(-4) \\ &= 20 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, from the graph the area is two triangles:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 4+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 8 \\ &= 20 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Write an expression using integration that would calculate the area between the curves $y=x^2$ and $y=x$ over the domain $[0,2]$. DO NOT integrate your expression or evaluate area.
items.sol:
The curves meet where $x^2=x$, that is $x=0$ or $x=1$, and the line is above the parabola on $[0,1]$ and below it on $[1,2]$.

$$\text{Area}=\int_0^1 (x-x^2)\,dx+\int_1^2 (x^2-x)\,dx$$

items.part:
An even function $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

The area of the shaded region $A$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}u^2$ and shaded region $B$ is $\dfrac{3}{2}u^2$.

\exfigure{1597_q1d_1}

Find the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx$.
items.sol:
Split the integral at $x=0$ and $x=1$.

$$\int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx=\int_{-1}^{0} f(x)\,dx+\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_1^2 f(x)\,dx$$

Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0} f(x)\,dx=\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx &= 2\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_1^2 f(x)\,dx \\ &= 2\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The graph of the function $f(x)=8x^2$ is translated $b$ units to the left, then dilated horizontally by a scale factor of $a$ with $a>0$ and then translated $c$ units up. The equation of the transformed function is $g(x)=2x^2+4x+21$.

Find possible values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
items.sol:
Translating $b$ units left gives $8(x+b)^2$.

Dilating horizontally by factor $a$ replaces $x$ with $\dfrac{x}{a}$, giving $8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2$.

Translating $c$ units up gives $8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2+c$.

Equate to $g(x)$ and expand:

$$8\left(\dfrac{x}{a}+b\right)^2+c\equiv 2x^2+4x+21$$

$$\dfrac{8}{a^2}x^2+\dfrac{16b}{a}x+(8b^2+c)\equiv 2x^2+4x+21$$

Equating coefficients of $x^2$:

$$\dfrac{8}{a^2}=2$$

so $a=2$, since $a>0$.

Equating coefficients of $x$:

$$\dfrac{16b}{a}=4$$

so $b=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Equating constants: $8b^2+c=21$, so $c=19$.

$$\therefore\ a=2,\ b=\dfrac{1}{2},\ c=19$$

The alternative working with a translation $b$ to the right gives $a=2$, $b=-\dfrac{1}{2}$, $c=19$.

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int_0^5 \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x+1}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Rewrite the integrand as a power and integrate using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^5 (3x+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{(3x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{3\cdot\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^5 \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{3x+1}\right]_0^5 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\sqrt{16}-\sqrt{1}\right) \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=\sqrt{4-x^2}$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule with $y=(4-x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(4-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times\dfrac{d}{dx}(4-x^2) \\ &= -x(4-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (i), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{4-x^2}=\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,dx &= -2\int\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,dx \\ &= -2\sqrt{4-x^2}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the curve $y=4-2\cos 2x$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$ stating its period and amplitude.
items.sol:
For $y=4-2\cos 2x$ the amplitude is $2$ and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$.

The curve oscillates between $2$ and $6$ about $y=4$.

\exfigure{1597_q2c_s1}

$$\therefore\ \text{period}=\pi,\ \text{amplitude}=2$$

items.part: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-12x=6x(x-2)=0$$

So $x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=2$, $y=2(8)-6(4)=-8$.

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(2,-8)$.

Test the nature using the second derivative:

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x-12$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=0:\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= -12<0 &&\text{maximum turning point}\\ \text{At } x=2:\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 12>0 &&\text{minimum turning point} \end{aligned}$$

A table of values of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of each point is an equivalent justification.

$$\therefore\ (0,0)\text{ is a maximum and }(2,-8)\text{ is a minimum}$$
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a maximum and $(2,-8)$ is a minimum

items.part: Find any points of inflection. Make sure you justify your answer(s).
items.sol:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and a change in concavity.

$$12x-12=0$$

So $x=1$, and $y=2-6=-4$.

Test the concavity either side of $x=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &< 0 &&\text{for } x<1 &&\text{concave down}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>1 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$

The concavity changes at $x=1$.

$$\therefore\ (1,-4)\text{ is a point of inflection}$$

items.part: Sketch the curve showing the stationary points and the point of inflection.
Show that the functions intersect at $x=-1$ and $x=2$.
items.sol:
Equate the two functions:

$$x^2-2x=-x^2+4$$

$$2x^2-2x-4=0$$

$$2(x-2)(x+1)=0$$

Hence $x=-1$ or $x=2$, as required.

Equivalently, substitute $x=-1$ and $x=2$ into both equations to show common $y$-coordinates.

items.part: Find the exact area bounded by the two curves between $x=-1$ and $x=2$.
items.sol:
Between $x=-1$ and $x=2$ the curve $y=-x^2+4$ is above $y=x^2-2x$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-1}^{2}\left[(4-x^2)-(x^2-2x)\right]dx \\ &= \int_{-1}^2(4+2x-2x^2)\,dx \\ &= \left[4x+x^2-\dfrac{2}{3}x^3\right]_{-1}^2 \\ &= \left(8+4-\dfrac{16}{3}\right)-\left(-4+1+\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{20}{3}-\left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right) \\ &= 9 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Without using calculus, sketch the graph of $y=\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}$, showing any asymptotes and $x$ and $y$ intercepts. Sketch you answer on the number plane provided.
items.sol:
Rewrite the function by dividing:

$$y=\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}=\dfrac{(x-1)+2}{x-1}=1+\dfrac{2}{x-1}$$

The denominator is zero at $x=1$, so $x=1$ is a vertical asymptote.

As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{2}{x-1}\to 0$, so $y=1$ is a horizontal asymptote.

When $x=0$, $y=-1$. When $y=0$, $x=-1$.

\exfigure{1597_q4b_s1}

items.part: Use the trapezoidal rule with five subintervals to find the approximate value of $\displaystyle\int_1^6 \dfrac{2}{x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
With five subintervals on $[1,6]$, the width is $h=\dfrac{6-1}{5}=1$, so the $x$ values are $1,2,3,4,5,6$.

For $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x}$ the function values are $2,\ 1,\ \dfrac{2}{3},\ \dfrac{1}{2},\ \dfrac{2}{5},\ \dfrac{1}{3}$.

Using the trapezoidal rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left[f_0+f_n+2(f_1+\dots+f_{n-1})\right]$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^6\dfrac{2}{x}\,dx &\approx \dfrac{6-1}{2\times 5}\left[\left(2+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+2\left(1+\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{2}{5}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{7}{3}+\dfrac{77}{15}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{56}{15} \\ &\approx 3.73 \end{aligned}$$

Any valid rounding is accepted.

items.part: Write an expression for the total price (\$$P$) of laying the cable from $A$ to $B$ via $C$ in terms of $x$.
items.sol:
The land section is $AC=10-x$ km at \$4000/km, and the ocean section $CB$ is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with sides $6$ and $x$, so $CB=\sqrt{36+x^2}$ km at \$5000/km (Pythagoras' theorem).

$$P=4000(10-x)+5000\sqrt{36+x^2}$$

items.part: Find the length for $x$ that will minimise the total price (\$$P$) of laying the whole pipe from $A$ to $B$ via $C$.
items.sol:
$P$ is minimised where $\dfrac{dP}{dx}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dx} &= -4000+5000\times\dfrac{1}{2}(36+x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 2x \\ &= \dfrac{5000x}{\sqrt{36+x^2}}-4000 \end{aligned}$$

Set this to zero:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5x}{\sqrt{36+x^2}} &= 4 \\ 25x^2 &= 16(36+x^2) \\ 9x^2 &= 576 \\ x^2 &= 64 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=\pm 8$. Since $0\le x\le 10$, $x=8$ only.

First derivative test:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=7:\ \dfrac{dP}{dx} &\approx -204<0 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \text{At } x=9:\ \dfrac{dP}{dx} &\approx 160>0 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$

So a relative minimum occurs at $x=8$.

Check against the end points:

$$\begin{aligned} P(0) &= \$70\,000 \\ P(10) &\approx \$58\,310 \\ P(8) &= \$58\,000 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=8$ gives the absolute minimum on $[0,10]$.

Alternatively, by the second derivative test:

$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dx^2}=\dfrac{180\,000}{(36+x^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$$

which equals $180>0$ at $x=8$.

$$\therefore\ CD=8 \text{ km}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{6}{3x+1}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln f(x)+C$ with $f(x)=3x+1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{6}{3x+1}\,dx &= 2\int \dfrac{3}{3x+1}\,dx \\ &= 2\ln(3x+1) + C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the mass present.

The rate of change is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, where $k$ is a positive constant and $M$ grams is the mass present at any time, $t$ years.
Show that $M = 75e^{-kt}$ is a solution to this equation.
items.sol:
Differentiate $M = 75e^{-kt}$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -k\cdot 75e^{-kt}$$
But $75e^{-kt} = M$, so
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$$
Hence $M = 75e^{-kt}$ is a solution.

items.part:
A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the mass present.

The rate of change is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, where $k$ is a positive constant and $M$ grams is the mass present at any time, $t$ years.
If $68$g remains after a period of $2$ years, find $k$ correct to two significant figures.
items.sol:
Substitute $M=68$ and $t=2$ into $M = 75e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 68 &= 75e^{-2k} \\ \dfrac{68}{75} &= e^{-2k} \\ -2k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{68}{75}\right) \\ k &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{68}{75}\right) \\ &\approx 0.049 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.049$$

items.part:
A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the mass present.

The rate of change is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, where $k$ is a positive constant and $M$ grams is the mass present at any time, $t$ years.
Find the mass of the substance that remains after $6$ years.

Give your answer to one decimal place.
items.sol:
Substitute $t=6$ and $k \approx 0.049$ into $M = 75e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 75e^{-6k} \\ &\approx 55.9 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ M \approx 55.9 \text{ g}$$

items.part:
A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the mass present.

The rate of change is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, where $k$ is a positive constant and $M$ grams is the mass present at any time, $t$ years.
At what rate is the substance decaying after $6$ years ?
items.sol:
The rate of decay is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, with $k \approx 0.049$ and $M \approx 55.9$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt} &= -kM \\ &\approx -2.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the substance is decaying at approximately } 2.7 \text{ g/year}$$

items.part:
The velocity, $\dot{x}$, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $\dot{x} = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the initial velocity.
items.sol:
Substitute $t=0$ into the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\cdot 0\right) \\ &= \cos 0 \\ &= 1 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity, $\dot{x}$, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $\dot{x} = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find an expression for the displacement of the particle, $x$, in terms of $t$.
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$x = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$, so $C = 0$.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$$

items.part:
The velocity, $\dot{x}$, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $\dot{x} = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find when the particle first comes to rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x} = 0$.
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) = 0$$
The first positive solution of $\cos\theta=0$ is $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 3 \text{ seconds}$$

items.part:
The velocity, $\dot{x}$, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $\dot{x} = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first $7$ seconds.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest at $t=3$ and then reverses, so find the distance in two stages.
$$\begin{aligned} x(3) &= \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x(7) &= \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{\pi}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{3}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance travelled} &= \dfrac{6}{\pi} + \left(\dfrac{6}{\pi} + \dfrac{3}{\pi}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{15}{\pi} \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the $x$ coordinate(s) of any stationary point(s) on the graph of $y = e^{2x}(1 - x)$. You do not need to determine the nature.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=1-x\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= -e^{2x} + 2e^{2x}(1-x) \\ &= -e^{2x} + 2e^{2x} - 2xe^{2x} \\ &= e^{2x}(1-2x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$. Since $e^{2x} \neq 0$, we need $1-2x=0$.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows the graph of $f(x) = 4 - 2^{-\frac{x}{2}}$.

\exfigure{1608_q3c_1}

The area bounded by the graph, the axes and the line $x = 4$ has been shaded.

If the area is $a - \dfrac{b}{c\ln 2}$, find $a$, $b$ and $c$.
items.sol:
The shaded area is the integral of the curve from $x=0$ to $x=4$. Use $\displaystyle\int a^{kx}\,dx = \dfrac{a^{kx}}{k\ln a}$ with $a=2$, $k=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4 \left(4 - 2^{-\frac{x}{2}}\right)dx &= \left[4x + \dfrac{2}{\ln 2}\left(2^{-\frac{x}{2}}\right)\right]_0^4\\ &= \left(16 + \dfrac{2}{\ln 2}\cdot 2^{-2}\right) - \left(0 + \dfrac{2}{\ln 2}\cdot 2^0\right)\\ &= 16 + \dfrac{1}{2\ln 2} - \dfrac{2}{\ln 2}\\ &= 16 - \dfrac{3}{2\ln 2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = 16,\ b = 3,\ c = 2$$

items.part:
An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off automatically after a period of inactivity.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation $T = 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}$, where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.
What is the temperature of the iron $8$ minutes after it has switched off ?

Give your answer to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Substitute $t=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4(8)} \\ &\approx 106^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off automatically after a period of inactivity.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation $T = 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}$, where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.
At what rate is the temperature of the iron's surface changing after $8$ minutes ?

(Give your answer to one decimal place.)
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}a^{kt} = k a^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -0.4\left(155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\right)\ln(1.2) \\ &= -62(1.2)^{-0.4t}\ln(1.2) \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -62(1.2)^{-3.2}\ln(1.2) \\ &\approx -6.3^\circ\text{C/min} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off automatically after a period of inactivity.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation $T = 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}$, where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.
How long, to the nearest minute, will it take for the iron to cool to $36^\circ\text{C}$ ?
items.sol:
Set $T=36$ and solve for $t$, taking logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned}36 &= 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\\ 16 &= 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\\ \dfrac{16}{155} &= 1.2^{-0.4t}\\ \ln\left(\dfrac{16}{155}\right) &= -0.4t\ln(1.2)\\ t &= \dfrac{-\ln\left(\frac{16}{155}\right)}{0.4\ln 1.2} \\ &\approx 31\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t \approx 31 \text{ minutes}$$

items.part:
An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off automatically after a period of inactivity.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation $T = 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}$, where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.
What will be the eventual temperature of the iron ?
items.sol:
As $t \to \infty$, $(1.2)^{-0.4t} \to 0$, so $T \to 20$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the eventual temperature is } 20^\circ\text{C}$$

items.part: Show that, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\cos 2x\right) = \cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos 2x) &= x(-2\sin 2x) + \cos 2x(1)\\ &= -2x\sin 2x + \cos 2x\\ &= \cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 2x\sin 2x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Integrate the result of part (a) over the interval, since integration reverses differentiation.
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(\cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x)\,dx = \Big[x\cos 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}$$
Rearranging,
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 2x\sin 2x\,dx = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos 2x\,dx - \Big[x\cos 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}$$
$$\begin{aligned}&= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} - \Big[x\cos 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 0\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} - 0\right)\\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{12}\\ &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3} - \pi}{12}\end{aligned}$$

What percentage of the annual rainfall occurs in the two driest seasons?

Give your answer as a whole percentage.
items.sol:
From the graph:
$$100\%-61\%=39\% \text{ (or } 40\%)$$
Alternatively, the total is $380+320+260+200=1160$ and the two driest seasons give $260+200=460$.
$$\dfrac{460}{1160}\times100\%\approx39.7\%\approx40\%$$

items.part: Find the primitive of $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2x-3}$
items.sol: $$\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\log_e|2x-3|+C$$

items.part: Calculate $\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{2\ln 2} e^{2x}\,dx$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{\ln2}^{2\ln2}e^{2x}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[e^{2x}\right]_{\ln2}^{2\ln2} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[e^{4\ln2}-e^{2\ln2}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[e^{\ln16}-e^{\ln4}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}[16-4] \\ &=6 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
It is given that $f''(x)=6x$ and that $f(x)$ has a stationary point at $(-1,2)$.

Find $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Integrating $f''(x)$:
$$f'(x)=\displaystyle\int6x\,dx=3x^2+C$$
The stationary point at $x=-1$ gives $f'(-1)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3(-1)^2+C&=0 \\ C&=-3 \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=3x^2-3$.

Integrating again:
$$f(x)=\displaystyle\int(3x^2-3)\,dx=x^3-3x+D$$
Using $f(-1)=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=(-1)^3-3(-1)+D \\ D&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-3x$$

items.part:
It is given that $1+2x-3x^2\ge 0$ in the domain $[0,1]$.

Prove that $f(x)=1+2x-3x^2$ is a probability density function for $[0,1]$.
items.sol:
For a probability density function, $f(x)\ge0$ on $[0,1]$ (given) and $\displaystyle\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^1(1+2x-3x^2)\,dx&=\left[x+x^2-x^3\right]_0^1 \\ &=(1+1-1)-0 \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f(x)\ge0$ on $[0,1]$ and the integral equals 1, $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

items.part: A normally distributed variable, $X$, has a mean of 2 and a standard deviation of 0.5. Use the empirical rule to find $P(0.5\le X\le 3)$.
items.sol:
Convert to $z$-scores using $z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} X=0.5:\ z&=\dfrac{0.5-2}{0.5}=-3 \\ X=3:\ z&=\dfrac{3-2}{0.5}=2 \end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(0.5\le X\le3)&=P(-3\le Z\le2) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(0.95+0.997) \\ &=0.9735 \end{aligned}$$
That is, $97.35\%$.

items.part: Find the second derivative of $y=x\left(x+1\right)^3$, leaving your answer in fully factorised form.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=(x+1)^3\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3(x+1)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=(x+1)^3\times1+3(x+1)^2\times x \\ &=(x+1)^2\left[(x+1)+3x\right] \\ &=(x+1)^2(4x+1) \end{aligned}$$
Applying the product rule again, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x+1)^2 & v&=4x+1\\ u'&=2(x+1) & v'&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y''&=(4x+1)\times2(x+1)+(x+1)^2\times4 \\ &=2(x+1)\left[4x+1+2(x+1)\right] \\ &=2(x+1)(6x+3) \\ &=6(x+1)(2x+1) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The circle $x^2+y^2-6x+8y-11=0$ is transformed by a horizontal translation to the left by 4 units and a vertical translation up 3 units.

What is the centre and radius of the new circle?
items.sol:
Complete the square:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-6x+9+y^2+8y+16&=11+9+16 \\ (x-3)^2+(y+4)^2&=36 \end{aligned}$$
So the centre is $(3,-4)$ and the radius is $6$.

After translating 4 units left and 3 units up, the centre is $(-1,-1)$ and the radius is unchanged.

$$\therefore\ \text{centre } (-1,-1),\ \text{radius } 6 \text{ units}$$

The probabilities sum to 1. By substitution:
$$(0.2)^2+0.16+0.18+0.3+0.2+0.12=1$$
Or by equation:
$$\begin{aligned} k^2+k+0.76&=1 \\ k^2+k-0.24&=0 \\ (k-0.2)(k+1.2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $k>0$, $k=0.2$.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0\times0.2^2+2\times0.16+4\times0.18+5\times0.3+8\times0.2+9\times0.12 \\ &=5.22 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\log_e x-x\right)=\log_e x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule on $x\log_ex$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\log_ex-x\right)&=\log_ex\times1+x\times\dfrac{1}{x}-1 \\ &=\log_ex+1-1 \\ &=\log_ex \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int_1^e \log_e x\,dx$ as an exact value.
items.sol:
By part (a), a primitive of $\log_ex$ is $x\log_ex-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^e\log_ex\,dx&=\left[x\log_ex-x\right]_1^e \\ &=(e\log_ee-e)-(1\log_e1-1) \\ &=(e-e)-(0-1) \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rainwater tank manufacturer wants to make a new storage tank that has a standard height, to reduce the obstruction of views. The manufacturer decides that it will be a 2 metre high rectangular prism with all faces made from sheet metal, including the top and bottom, and needs to hold 6000 litres of water,

Let the other dimensions be $x$ metres and $y$ metres, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1614_q13_1}

For cost reasons, the manufacturer wants to use the least amount of area of sheet metal possible.
Show that for the given capacity of the tank, $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$
items.sol:
Convert the capacity: $6000\text{ L}=6\text{ m}^3$.

The volume of the prism is length $\times$ width $\times$ height:
$$\begin{aligned} x\times y\times2&=6 \\ 2xy&=6 \\ y&=\dfrac{6}{2x} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rainwater tank manufacturer wants to make a new storage tank that has a standard height, to reduce the obstruction of views. The manufacturer decides that it will be a 2 metre high rectangular prism with all faces made from sheet metal, including the top and bottom, and needs to hold 6000 litres of water,

Let the other dimensions be $x$ metres and $y$ metres, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1614_q13_1}

For cost reasons, the manufacturer wants to use the least amount of area of sheet metal possible.
Hence, calculate the exact dimensions of the tank that uses the least amount of area of sheet metal as possible. Show all reasoning.
items.sol:
The surface area is the top and bottom plus four sides:
$$A=2(xy+2x+2y)=2xy+4x+4y$$
Substituting $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$:
$$A=4x+\dfrac{12}{x}+6$$
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=4-\dfrac{12}{x^2}$$
For a minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x^2&=12 \\ x^2&=3 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\sqrt{3}$, since $x>0$.

Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{24}{x^3}>0 \text{ for all } x>0$$
So the curve is concave up and the area is a minimum at $x=\sqrt{3}$.

Then $y=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{dimensions } \sqrt{3}\text{ m}\times\sqrt{3}\text{ m}\times2\text{ m}$$
$$\angle ABC=40^\circ+20^\circ=60^\circ$$

By the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, with $AB=37$, $BC=45$ and $\angle ABC=60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= 37^2+45^2-2\times37\times45\times\cos60^\circ \\ &= 1729 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} AC &= \sqrt{1729} \\ &= 41.5812\ldots \\ &\approx 41.6 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
The distance from $A$ to $C$ is $41.6$ km (no penalty for incorrect rounding).

By the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, find $\angle BAC$:
$$\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac{37^2+1729-45^2}{2\times37\times\sqrt{1729}}$$
so $\angle BAC=70^\circ$ (nearest degree; no penalty for using $41.6$ km).

The bearing of $C$ from $A$ is $110^\circ$T.

The bearing of $A$ from $C$ is the reverse bearing:
$$110^\circ+180^\circ=290^\circ\text{T}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of } A \text{ from } C \text{ is } 290^\circ\text{T}$$

items.part: Show that $f(x)=x^3-5x+\dfrac{xe^{-x^2}}{1+x^4}$ is an odd function.
items.sol:
Replace $x$ by $-a$ in $f(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-a) &= (-a)^3-5(-a)+\dfrac{-ae^{-(-a)^2}}{1+(-a)^4} \\ &= -a^3+5a-\dfrac{ae^{-a^2}}{1+a^4} \\ &= -\left(a^3-5a+\dfrac{ae^{-a^2}}{1+a^4}\right) \\ &= -f(a) \end{aligned}$$
Hence $f$ is an odd function.

items.part: Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{5}\left(x^3-5x+\dfrac{xe^{-x^2}}{1+x^4}\right)dx$.
items.sol:
Since $f$ is odd, the areas either side of the origin cancel.
$$\int_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,dx=0$$

items.part:
A quantity $Q$ of the radioactive isotope Carbon-14 decays according the equation of natural decay $Q=Q_0e^{-kt}$ where $Q_0$ is the initial mass of Carbon-14, $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the time in years.

The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time it takes to reduce to half its original mass. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years.
Find the exact value of $k$.
items.sol:
After one half-life, $Q=\dfrac{Q_0}{2}$ when $t=5730$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{Q_0}{2} &= Q_0e^{-5730k} \\ 0.5 &= e^{-5730k} \\ \ln0.5 &= -5730k \\ k &= -\dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln2}{5730} \end{aligned}$$
No penalty for writing $k=0.0001$ to 4 d.p.

items.part:
A quantity $Q$ of the radioactive isotope Carbon-14 decays according the equation of natural decay $Q=Q_0e^{-kt}$ where $Q_0$ is the initial mass of Carbon-14, $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the time in years.

The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time it takes to reduce to half its original mass. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years.
A fossilised leaf contains $9\%$ of its original amount of Carbon-14.

How old is the fossilised leaf? Give your answer correct to the nearest year.
items.sol:
The leaf has $9\%$ of its original amount, so $Q=0.09Q_0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.09Q_0 &= Q_0e^{-kt} \\ 0.09 &= e^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Using $k=-\dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730}$, this is
$$0.09=e^{\frac{\ln0.5}{5730}t}$$
Taking logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln0.09 &= \dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730}\,t \\ t &= \dfrac{5730\ln0.09}{\ln0.5} \\ &\approx 19\,906 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the leaf is about } 19\,906 \text{ years old}$$
No penalty for incorrect rounding.

items.part: Simplify $\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1-\sin\theta}-\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1+\sin\theta}$
items.sol:
Combine over the common denominator $(1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\cos^2\theta(1+\sin\theta)-\cos^2\theta(1-\sin\theta)}{(1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\theta\sin\theta}{1-\sin^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{2\cos^2\theta\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &=2\sin\theta \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, solve $\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1-\sin\theta}-\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1+\sin\theta}=1$ for $0\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
items.sol:
By part (a), the equation becomes
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin\theta &= 1 \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

The period is $T=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$.
$$b=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{2}}=4$$
The amplitude is $A=2$.
$$\therefore\ A=2,\ b=4$$

The graph of $y=\sin2x+1$ passes through $(0,1)$, $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},2\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right)$.

\exfigure{1614_q14_s1}

items.part: Simplify $\sqrt{x^2+2x+1}-\sqrt{x^2-2x+1}$ for $x \ge 1$.
items.sol:
Factorise each expression under the roots as a perfect square:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x^2+2x+1}-\sqrt{x^2-2x+1} &= \sqrt{(x+1)^2}-\sqrt{(x-1)^2} \\ &= (x+1)-(x-1) \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $\ln\left(2\sin^2\theta-\cos\theta\right)=0$ for $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
Since $\ln X=0$ when $X=1$:
$$2\sin^2\theta-\cos\theta=1$$
Using $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2(1-\cos^2\theta)-\cos\theta-1 &= 0 \\ 2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1 &= 0 \\ (2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

For $0\le\theta\le2\pi$:
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$

items.part: Find the stationary points and determine their nature, and any points of inflection for $y=x^4-2x^3+1$, showing all reasoning.
items.sol:
Differentiate:
$$y'=4x^3-6x^2,\qquad y''=12x^2-12x$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x^3-6x^2 &= 0 \\ 2x^2(2x-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

At $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$, $y''=9>0$, so the curve is concave up: a minimum turning point at $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},-\dfrac{11}{16}\right)$.

At $x=0$, $y''=0$, so the test is inconclusive and this is a possible horizontal point of inflexion.

Possible points of inflexion occur when $y''=0$:
$$12x(x-1)=0$$
so $x=0$ or $x=1$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} y''&=24>0 &&\text{at } x=-1 &&\text{concave up}\\ y''&=0 &&\text{at } x=0 &&\\ y''&=-3<0 &&\text{at } x=0.5 &&\text{concave down}\\ y''&=0 &&\text{at } x=1 &&\\ y''&=24>0 &&\text{at } x=2 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at both $x=0$ and $x=1$.

Since $y'=0$ at $x=0$, there is a horizontal point of inflexion at $(0,1)$. There is also a point of inflexion at $(1,0)$.
items.final: Minimum turning point at $\left(\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{11}{16}\right)$; horizontal point of inflexion at $(0,1)$; point of inflexion at $(1,0)$.

items.sol:
The sketch shows the horizontal point of inflexion at $(0,1)$, the point of inflexion at $(1,0)$ and the minimum turning point at $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},-\dfrac{11}{16}\right)$.

items.part:
The Moon has a lower gravity than Earth, and there is no atmosphere to cause air resistance, so a ball would bounce higher and for much longer on the Moon than on Earth.

When a ball is dropped on the Moon, each bounce is $95\%$ as high as the previous bounce. When an identical ball is dropped on Earth, each bounce is $50\%$ as high as the previous bounce.

\exfigure{1614_q15_2}

Two identical balls are dropped on the Moon and on Earth, each from a height of two metres, and they both eventually stop bouncing.

Calculate the difference in the total vertical distance travelled by these balls.
items.sol:
Each ball falls 2 m, then each bounce goes up and down, so the distance is a limiting sum of a G.P. with the initial 2 m subtracted.

Moon: $a=2$, $r=0.95$.
$$\begin{aligned} D_{\text{Moon}} &= \dfrac{2\times2}{1-0.95}-2 \\ &= 78 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Earth: $a=2$, $r=0.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} D_{\text{Earth}} &= \dfrac{2\times2}{1-0.5}-2 \\ &= 6 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Difference} &= 78-6 \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, a student who neglects the initial drop and finds $80-8=72$ m is awarded full marks (with correct working).

items.part:
The graph $y=\sin x$ only has one tangent in the domain $[\pi,2\pi]$ that passes through the origin as shown in the diagram below.

Let the point of contact of this tangent be $P(h,\sin h)$.

\exfigure{1614_q16_1}

Prove that $h=\tan h$.
items.sol:
Differentiate $y=\sin x$:
$$y'=\cos x$$
At $x=h$ the gradient is $\cos h$.

The tangent at $P(h,\sin h)$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\sin h &= \cos h\,(x-h) \\ y &= (\cos h)x-h\cos h+\sin h \end{aligned}$$
The tangent passes through the origin $(0,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -h\cos h+\sin h \\ h\cos h &= \sin h \\ h &= \dfrac{\sin h}{\cos h} \\ &= \tan h \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=\tan h$$

$$r=3\%\div12=0.0025,\qquad n=6\times12=72$$
The table factor for $r=0.0025$, $n=72$ is $65.81686$.
$$\begin{aligned} PV &= 65.81686\times200 \\ &= \$13\,163.37 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ PV\approx\$13\,163$$

The quarterly rate and number of periods are

The table factor is $48.87800$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\,000\,000 &= PMT\times48.878 \\ PMT &= \dfrac{2\,000\,000}{48.878} \\ &= \$40\,918 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{each quarterly repayment is } \$40\,918$$

items.part: Give the simplest exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^1 3^x\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 3^x\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{3^x}{\ln3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{\ln3}-\dfrac{1}{\ln3} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\ln3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Use the trapezoidal rule, with 3 function values, to find the area between the curve $y=x\sin^2 x$, the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ leaving your answer in exact terms.
items.sol:
With 3 function values on $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, there are 2 strips, so $h=\dfrac{\pi/2-0}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, and the $x$ values are $0$, $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

For $f(x)=x\sin^2x$:
$$f(0)=0,\qquad f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^2=\dfrac{\pi}{8},\qquad f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$
By the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(0)+2f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi/4}{2}\left\{0+2\times\dfrac{\pi}{8}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{8}\times\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{3\pi^2}{32} \end{aligned}$$

The line is above the curve on $[0,1]$, so the shaded area is
$$A=\int_0^1\left((e-1)x-(e^x-1)\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \left[\dfrac{(e-1)x^2}{2}-e^x+x\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{e-1}{2}-e+1-(0-1+0) \\ &= \dfrac{e-1}{2}-e+2 \\ &= \dfrac{3-e}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The equation $f(x)=\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ is a probability density function for $\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le x\le\pi$.

(DO NOT PROVE THIS)
Using the definition of a cumulative distribution function

$$F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\ \text{ for } a\le x\le b$$

prove that the cumulative distribution function for the given domain is:

$$F(x)=2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-1\qquad \dfrac{\pi}{3}\le x\le\pi$$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_{\pi/3}^x\cos\dfrac{t}{2}\,dt \\ &= \left[2\sin\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_{\pi/3}^x \\ &= 2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}-2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= 2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}-1 \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
The equation $f(x)=\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ is a probability density function for $\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le x\le\pi$.

(DO NOT PROVE THIS)
Hence, or otherwise, find the median of this data, correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
At the median, $F(x)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}-1 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \sin\dfrac{x}{2} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ x &= 2\sin^{-1}\dfrac{3}{4} \\ &\approx 1.7 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sergio decides to buy a top-of-the-line gaming laptop for \$12 500 from the retailer Jay-Bee. Jay-Bee offers the following terms:

\begin{itemize}
\item The customer pays for the laptop with equal monthly repayments of \$$R$ at the end of each month for 5 years.
\item The first six months are interest free. After six months, interest is charged on the balance owing at $9\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.
\item The equal monthly repayment is still made at the end of each month during the first six months.
\end{itemize}
Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.

Show that after seven months, the total amount Sergio owes is:

$$A_7=12500\times1.0075-R(6\times1.0075+1)$$
items.sol:
In the first six months no interest is charged, so each repayment reduces the balance by $R$:
$$A_1=12\,500-R,\quad A_2=12\,500-2R,\quad A_3=12\,500-3R$$
so $A_6=12\,500-6R$.

The monthly rate is $r=\dfrac{0.09}{12}=0.0075$.

In month 7, interest is added and then $R$ is paid:
$$\begin{aligned} A_7 &= A_6\times1.0075-R \\ &= (12\,500-6R)\times1.0075-R \\ &= 12\,500\times1.0075-6R\times1.0075-R \\ &= 12\,500\times1.0075-R(6\times1.0075+1) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Sergio decides to buy a top-of-the-line gaming laptop for \$12 500 from the retailer Jay-Bee. Jay-Bee offers the following terms:

\begin{itemize}
\item The customer pays for the laptop with equal monthly repayments of \$$R$ at the end of each month for 5 years.
\item The first six months are interest free. After six months, interest is charged on the balance owing at $9\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.
\item The equal monthly repayment is still made at the end of each month during the first six months.
\end{itemize}
Calculate the monthly repayment \$$R$ required to pay back the loan, correct to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
Continue the pattern, interest then repayment each month:
$$A_8=A_7\times1.0075-R=12\,500\times1.0075^2-R(6\times1.0075^2+1.0075+1)$$
$$A_9=12\,500\times1.0075^3-R(6\times1.0075^3+1.0075^2+1.0075+1)$$
Hence
$$A_n=12\,500\times1.0075^{n-6}-R\left(6\times1.0075^{n-6}+1+1.0075+\cdots+1.0075^{n-7}\right)$$
The loan lasts $n=5\times12=60$ months:
$$A_{60}=12\,500\times1.0075^{54}-R\left(6\times1.0075^{54}+\left(1+1.0075+\cdots+1.0075^{53}\right)\right)$$
The bracketed sum is a G.P. with $a=1$, $r=1.0075$ and $54$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{1.0075^{54}-1}{1.0075-1}$.

The loan is repaid, so $A_{60}=0$:
$$12\,500\times1.0075^{54}=R\left(6\times1.0075^{54}+\dfrac{1.0075^{54}-1}{0.0075}\right)$$

Upper and lower rectangles of width $0.5$ units are drawn from the $x$-axis to the curve between $x=1$ and $x=2$ as shown in the diagram.

By considering the areas of the rectangles, show that $\dfrac{7}{24}<\ln\sqrt{2}<\dfrac{5}{12}$.
items.sol:
The curve $y=\dfrac{1}{2x}$ is decreasing, so the lower rectangles have area less than the integral and the upper rectangles have area greater than it.

The heights are $y=\dfrac{1}{2}$ at $x=1$, $y=\dfrac{1}{3}$ at $x=1.5$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{4}$ at $x=2$.

Lower rectangles:
$$\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{7}{24}$$
Upper rectangles:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{5}{12}$$
The exact area is
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\dfrac{dx}{2x} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln x\right]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(\ln2-\ln1) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln2 \\ &= \ln\sqrt2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{7}{24}<\ln\sqrt2<\dfrac{5}{12}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2-1}$.
Find $f'(x)$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=x^2-1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{x^2 - 1 - 2x^2}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-x^2 - 1}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f'(x) = \dfrac{-x^2 - 1}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2}$$

The sum of the first $n$ terms in an arithmetic series is given by the formula

$$S_n = 3n^2 - 17n$$

where $n > 0$.
Show that the common difference is 6.
items.sol:
The series is arithmetic, so $a = S_1$ and $T_2 = S_2 - S_1$.
$$S_1 = 3(1)^2 - 17(1) = -14$$
so $a=-14$.
$$S_2 = 3(2)^2 - 17(2) = -22$$
$$T_2 = -22 - (-14) = -8$$
The common difference is
$$\begin{aligned} d &= T_2 - T_1 \\ &= -8 - (-14) \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$

At a local fast food restaurant, the probability, $W$, of the ice cream machine working on any given day is $40\%$. Ronald visits the restaurant on three consecutive days attempting to order an ice cream.
How many days must Ronald visit in order to be $95\%$ confident that he will eventually visit the restaurant when the ice cream machine is working?
items.sol:
The machine works on at least one of $n$ days unless it fails on every day.
$$P(W \text{ eventually}) = 1 - (0.6)^n$$
Set this equal to $0.95$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.95 &= 1 - (0.6)^n \\ (0.6)^n &= 0.05 \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln 0.05}{\ln 0.6} \\ &= 5.864\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ must be a whole number, Ronald must visit for $6$ days.

items.part:
Let $f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - x$.
Find the stationary points on the graph of $y = f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiating,
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2 + 2x - 1 \\ f''(x) &= 6x + 2 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2 + 2x - 1 &= 0 \\ (3x - 1)(x + 1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x = \dfrac{1}{3} \text{ or } x = -1$$
Test the nature using the sign of $f''(x)$.

When $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$: $f\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{5}{27}$ and $f''\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) > 0$.

So $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, -\dfrac{5}{27}\right)$ is a minimum turning point.

When $x = -1$: $f(-1) = 1$ and $f''(-1) < 0$.

So $(-1, 1)$ is a maximum turning point.
items.final: $\left(\tfrac{1}{3}, -\tfrac{5}{27}\right)$ is a minimum turning point; $(-1, 1)$ is a maximum turning point

items.part:
Solve $2\sin^2 x - 5\sin x\cos x + 3\cos^2 x = 0$, for $x \in [0, 2\pi]$.

Leave your answer in exact form
items.sol:
Factorise the left side.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin^2 x - 5\sin x\cos x + 3\cos^2 x &= 0 \\ (2\sin x - 3\cos x)(\sin x - \cos x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Case 1: $2\sin x = 3\cos x$, so $\tan x = \dfrac{3}{2}$.
$$x = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \text{ or } x = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$$
Case 2: $\sin x = \cos x$, so $\tan x = 1$.
$$x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } x = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$$

Sienna wishes to save \$50\,000 for a holiday around the world. She deposits \$500 at the beginning of every month into an account earning $4.2\%$ per annum, compounding monthly.

Find the time, to the nearest whole month, that it takes for Sienna to reach her savings goal.
items.sol:
Build up the balance month by month.
$$A_1 = 500\times 1.0035$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= \left(500(1.0035) + 500\right)\times 1.0035 \\ &= 500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_3 &= \left(500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) + 500\right)\times 1.0035 \\ &= 500(1.0035)^3 + 500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) \\ &= 500(1.0035)\left(1 + 1.0035 + 1.0035^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
Continuing the pattern, the bracket is a geometric series with $a = 1$, $r = 1.0035$ and $n$ terms.
$$A_n = 500(1.0035)\left(1 + 1.0035 + 1.0035^2 + \cdots + 1.0035^{n-1}\right)$$
Set $A_n = 50\,000$ and use the sum of a GP.
$$\begin{aligned} 50\,000 &= 500(1.0035)\times\dfrac{1.0035^n - 1}{0.0035} \\ \dfrac{2707}{2007} &= 1.0035^n \\ n &= \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{2707}{2007}\right)}{\log 1.0035} \\ &\approx 85.64 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore it will take 86 months for Sienna to reach her savings goal.

$$h = \dfrac{1.5 - 8r^3}{\pi r^2}$$
The coated surface is the 6 faces of the cube plus the curved surface of the cylinder. Let $S$ be this area.

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has a median value of $m$ and a probability density function given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx & \text{if } 0 \leq x < 1 \\ kx^2 & \text{if } 1 \leq x \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Show that $k = \dfrac{6}{55}$.
items.sol:
The total probability is 1.
$$\displaystyle\int_0^1 kx\,dx + \int_1^3 kx^2\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k}{2}x^2\right]_0^1 + \left[\dfrac{k}{3}x^3\right]_1^3 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2} + \left(9k - \dfrac{k}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{55}{6}k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k = \dfrac{6}{55}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has a median value of $m$ and a probability density function given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx & \text{if } 0 \leq x < 1 \\ kx^2 & \text{if } 1 \leq x \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Find the cumulative distribution function of $X$.
items.sol:
For $0 \le x < 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \dfrac{6}{55}\displaystyle\int_0^x t\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{6}{55}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}t^2\right]_0^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55}x^2 \end{aligned}$$
For $1 \le x \le 3$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}\displaystyle\int_1^x t^2\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}\left[\dfrac{1}{3}t^3\right]_1^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 - \dfrac{2}{55} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$F(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{55}x^2 & \text{if } 0 \le x < 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 & \text{if } 1 \le x \le 3 \end{cases}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has a median value of $m$ and a probability density function given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx & \text{if } 0 \leq x < 1 \\ kx^2 & \text{if } 1 \leq x \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Find the value of $m$, correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Since $F(1) = \dfrac{3}{55} < 0.5$, the median satisfies $1 \le m < 3$, so use the second piece with $F(m) = 0.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}m^3 &= 0.5 \\ 2 + 4m^3 &= 55 \\ m &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{53}{4}} \\ &\approx 2.37 \end{aligned}$$
The median is $m \approx 2.37$ (to 2 d.p.).

items.part:
Two surveyors, $A$ and $B$, stand on level ground to observe a large tree. The tree is directly north of surveyor $A$ who sights the top of the tree at an angle of elevation of $52^\circ$.

Surveyor $B$ is 27 metres away from Surveyor $A$ on a bearing of $043^\circ$ and sights the top of the tree at an angle of elevation of $46^\circ$.

Find the height, $h$, of the tree correct to the nearest metre.
items.sol:
\exfigure{833_q29_s1}

Let $C$ be the point at the base of the tree. Using the tangent ratio in the two right-angled triangles,
$$AC = \dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}, \qquad BC = \dfrac{h}{\tan 46^\circ}$$
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 27$ and $\angle CAB = 43^\circ$ (the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $043^\circ$ and $C$ is due north of $A$). Apply the cosine rule.
$$\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 46^\circ}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}\right)^2 + 27^2 - 2\times\dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}\times 27\times\cos 43^\circ$$
Rearranging,
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\tan^2 52^\circ} - \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 46^\circ}\right)h^2 - \dfrac{54\cos 43^\circ}{\tan 52^\circ}h + 27^2 \\ 0 &\approx -0.32215h^2 - 30.85539h + 729 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula, with $h > 0$,
$$h = \dfrac{30.855\ldots - \sqrt{30.855\ldots^2 - 4\times(-0.322\ldots)\times 729}}{2\times(-0.322\ldots)} \approx 19.6$$
$$\therefore h \approx 20 \text{ metres (to the nearest metre)}$$

items.part: Find the amplitude and period of the function $y = 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)x - 8$ .
items.sol:
The amplitude is the absolute value of the coefficient of $\sin$:
$$\text{Amplitude}=|3|=3$$
The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$ with $b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} T&=2\pi\div\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &=2\pi\times\dfrac{4}{\pi} \\ &=8 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $\sqrt{3}\tan 2x = 1$ for the domain $[-\pi, \pi]$.
items.sol:
Since $x\in[-\pi,\pi]$, we have $2x\in[-2\pi,2\pi]$, which is 2 revolutions.
$$\tan 2x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$$
Tangent is positive in quadrants 1 and 3.

Positive revolution:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6} &&(\text{Q1})\\ 2x&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6} &&(\text{Q3})\end{aligned}$$
Negative revolution:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}-2\pi=-\dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&(\text{Q1})\\ 2x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}-2\pi=-\dfrac{5\pi}{6} &&(\text{Q3})\end{aligned}$$
Dividing by 2:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{12},\ -\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\ -\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$$

items.part: Explain why the graph of $y = \tan x$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ .
items.sol:
Since $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, and at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ we have $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}=0$ while $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1$.

So $\tan x$ would be $\dfrac{1}{0}$, which is undefined.

Hence $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is a vertical asymptote.

items.part:
The velocity of a particle is given by

$$v = 2 - 4\cos t \quad \text{for } 0 \le t \le 2\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and $t$ is measured in seconds.
Find the times during the period at which the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-4\cos t&=0 \\ \cos t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Cosine is positive in quadrants 1 and 4.
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3} &&(\text{Q1})\\ t&=2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{5\pi}{3} &&(\text{Q4})\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\text{ s or } t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\text{ s}$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle is given by

$$v = 2 - 4\cos t \quad \text{for } 0 \le t \le 2\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and $t$ is measured in seconds.
When does the particle reach its maximum velocity, and what is the maximum velocity?
items.sol:
$v=2-4\cos t$ is greatest when $\cos t=-1$, that is, at $t=\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} v&=2-4(-1) \\ &=6 \text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
The particle reaches a maximum velocity of $6$ m/s at $t=\pi$ seconds.

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{2x-5}{x-3} = \dfrac{1}{x-3} + 2$
items.sol:
Method 1: write the fraction in the form $\dfrac{a}{x-3}+b$.
$$\dfrac{2x-5}{x-3}=\dfrac{a+b(x-3)}{x-3}$$
Equating numerators, $bx+(a-3b)=2x-5$, so $b=2$ and $a-3b=-5$.
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-5+6 \\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{2x-5}{x-3}=\dfrac{1}{x-3}+2$$
Method 2: start from the right-hand side.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{x-3}+2&=\dfrac{1+2(x-3)}{x-3} \\ &=\dfrac{2x-5}{x-3}\end{aligned}$$
So LHS $=$ RHS.

items.part:
Hence, sketch the function $y = \dfrac{2x-5}{x-3}$, showing all intercepts and asymptotes.

\exfigure{461_q10_1}
items.sol:
From $y=\dfrac{1}{x-3}+2$, the vertical asymptote is $x=3$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y=2$.

The $y$-intercept (put $x=0$):
$$y=\dfrac{-5}{-3}=\dfrac{5}{3}$$
The $x$-intercept (put $y=0$):
$$2x-5=0,\quad x=\dfrac{5}{2}$$
Also $(4,3)$ lies on the curve.

\exfigure{461_q10_s1}

items.part: Solve the inequality $\dfrac{2x-5}{x-3} < 2$
items.sol:
From the graph, $y<2$ where the curve lies below the asymptote $y=2$, which is for $x<3$.

$$\therefore\ x<3\text{, i.e. } x\in(-\infty,3)$$

items.part:
Given: $f(x) = x^2 - 1$

The function $g(x)$ is produced by making the following transformations to $f(x)$:

\begin{itemize}
\item reflecting on the $x$-axis
\item translating 3 units to the left
\item translating 2 units upwards
\end{itemize}
Find the equation of $g(x)$.
items.sol:
The transformations are applied in order.
$$\begin{aligned} h(x)&=-f(x)=-x^2+1 &&(\text{reflect in the } x\text{-axis})\\ k(x)&=h(x+3)=-(x+3)^2+1 &&(\text{3 units left})\\ g(x)&=k(x)+2=-(x+3)^2+3 &&(\text{2 units up})\end{aligned}$$
Expanded:
$$\begin{aligned} g(x)&=-(x^2+6x+9)+3 \\ &=-x^2-6x-6\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Given: $f(x) = x^2 - 1$

The function $g(x)$ is produced by making the following transformations to $f(x)$:

\begin{itemize}
\item reflecting on the $x$-axis
\item translating 3 units to the left
\item translating 2 units upwards
\end{itemize}
The point $A(3,8)$ lies on $f(x)$. Determine coordinates of this point after the above transformations have occurred.
items.sol:
Horizontal: translating 3 units left changes $x=3$ to $3-3=0$.

Vertical: reflecting then moving up 2 changes $y=8$ to
$$8\times(-1)+2=-6$$
$$\therefore\ (3,8)\text{ becomes }(0,-6)$$
Check: $g(0)=-6$.

items.part:
Given the parabola $y = (x-3)^2 - 16$.

The equation is in vertex form $y=(x-h)^2+k$, so the vertex is

items.part:
Given the parabola $y = (x-3)^2 - 16$.
For what range of values of $k$ will $(x-3)^2 - 16 + k = 0$ have no solutions?
items.sol:
$(x-3)^2-16+k=0$ has no solutions when the parabola $y=(x-3)^2-16+k$ has no $x$-intercepts.

The vertex $(3,-16+k)$ must be above the $x$-axis, so $-16+k>0$.
$$\therefore\ k>16$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graphs of $f(x) = a \times 2^x + c$ and $g(x) = \log_2 x$.

The two graphs meet at the point $(1,0)$ and $(2,1)$.

The asymptote of $f(x)=a\times2^x+c$ is $y=c$. From the graph it has moved down by 1, so $c=-1$.

The curve passes through $(1,0)$:
