items.part:
The temperature $T(t)$ in $^\circ C$ during an average day in May in Katherine NT, can be modelled by the function $T(t)=27.5+8.5\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)$, where $t$ is the number of hours after 9am.
Jimmy lives in Katherine, and his air conditioning unit is only set to be turned on if the outside temperature is above $33^\circ\text{C}$. Between what times during the day is his air conditioning on? Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
The air conditioning is on when $T>33$. First solve $T=33$.
$$\begin{aligned} 33&=27.5+8.5\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) \\ \dfrac{11}{17}&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $0.7037\ldots$, and sine is positive in the first and second quadrants.
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{12}=0.7037\ldots,\ 2.4378\ldots$$
$$t=2.688\ldots,\ 9.3119\ldots$$
That is 2 h 41 min and 9 h 19 min after 9 am (nearest minute), i.e. 11:41 am and 6:19 pm.

Between these times the curve is above $33^\circ\text{C}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the air conditioning is on between 11:41 am and 6:19 pm}$$
items.final: the air conditioning is on between 11:41 am and 6:19 pm

items.part:
A car travelling at a constant speed of $v$ km/h consumes fuel at the rate of $\dfrac{1}{20}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right)$ litres per hour.

Hai hires this car for a rental fee of \$10 per hour. Fuel costs \$2.12/litre and his total trip has a distance of 550 km.
Show that the total cost of the trip in dollars is given by $C=\dfrac{55583}{10v}+\dfrac{583v}{600}$.
items.sol:
Total cost is rental plus fuel, both over the time $t=\dfrac{d}{v}=\dfrac{550}{v}$ hours.
$$\text{Cost}=10t+2.12\times\left[\dfrac{1}{20}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right)\right]t$$
$$\begin{aligned} C&=10\times\dfrac{550}{v}+2.12\times\dfrac{1}{20}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right)\times\dfrac{550}{v} \\ &=\dfrac{5500}{v}+\dfrac{583}{10v}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{5500}{v}+\dfrac{583}{10v}+\dfrac{583v}{600} \\ &=\dfrac{55583}{10v}+\dfrac{583v}{600} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A car travelling at a constant speed of $v$ km/h consumes fuel at the rate of $\dfrac{1}{20}\left(1+\dfrac{v^2}{60}\right)$ litres per hour.

Hai hires this car for a rental fee of \$10 per hour. Fuel costs \$2.12/litre and his total trip has a distance of 550 km.
Find the minimum cost Hai will have to pay for his trip.
items.sol:
Write $C=\dfrac{55583}{10}v^{-1}+\dfrac{583v}{600}$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dC}{dv}=-\dfrac{55583}{10}v^{-2}+\dfrac{583}{600}$$
Stationary point: $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{583}{600}&=\dfrac{55583}{10v^2} \\ v^2&=\dfrac{55583\times 600}{10\times 583} \\ &=5720.377\ldots \end{aligned}$$
so $v=75.633\ldots$ km/h (since $v>0$).

Nature: the sign of $C''$ decides.
$$C''=\dfrac{111166}{10}v^{-3}=\dfrac{111166}{10v^3}>0 \text{ for all } v>0$$
so $v=75.633\ldots$ km/h gives the minimum cost.
$$\begin{aligned} C_{\min}&=\dfrac{55583}{10\times 75.633\ldots}+\dfrac{583\times 75.633\ldots}{600} \\ &=\$146.98 \text{ (nearest cent)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum cost is } \$146.98$$

items.part:
Differentiate each of the following with respect to $x$:
$x\log_e x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\log_e x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 1\times\log_e x + x\times\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= \log_e x + 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate each of the following with respect to $x$:
$\dfrac{\cos x}{x-2}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\cos x & v&=x-2\\ u'&=-\sin x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{-\sin x\,(x-2) - \cos x}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-x\sin x + 2\sin x - \cos x}{(x-2)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate each of the following with respect to $x$:
$(e^{2x}+1)^{-4}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule with inner function $e^{2x}+1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= -4(e^{2x}+1)^{-5}\times (e^{2x}+1)' \\ &= -4(e^{2x}+1)^{-5}\times 2e^{2x} \\ &= \dfrac{-8e^{2x}}{(e^{2x}+1)^5} \end{aligned}$$
Equivalently, $y'=-8e^{2x}(e^{2x}+1)^{-5}$.

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = \sin 2x$ at the point $x = \dfrac{\pi}{12}$.
items.sol:
Differentiate to find the gradient:
$$y' = 2\cos 2x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$, the point and gradient are
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2} \\ m &= 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = 2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} y - \dfrac{1}{2} &= \sqrt{3}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{12}\right) \\ y &= \sqrt{3}\,x - \dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{12} + \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: For what values of $x$ is the function $y = \dfrac{1}{x^2+1}$ decreasing?
items.sol:
Differentiate using the quotient rule (or the chain rule):
$$y' = \dfrac{-2x}{(x^2+1)^2}$$
The denominator is always positive, so the sign of $y'$ is the sign of $-2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &< 0 &&\text{for } x>0 &&\text{decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y \text{ is decreasing for } x>0$$

items.part: Differentiate $y = \sin^4 x$
items.sol:
By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4\sin^3 x\cos x$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 4\cos x \sin^3 x\,dx$
items.sol:
By part (a), a primitive of $4\cos x\sin^3 x$ is $\sin^4 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 4\cos x\sin^3 x\,dx &= \Big[\sin^4 x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \sin^4\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin^4 0 \\ &= 1 - 0 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $\log_e(4x-5) - \log_e 3 = 2$ , giving your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Combine the logarithms using the quotient law:
$$\log_e\dfrac{4x-5}{3} = 2$$
Convert to exponential form:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4x-5}{3} &= e^2 \\ 4x - 5 &= 3e^2 \\ x &= \dfrac{3e^2 + 5}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Use the trapezoidal rule with 3 function values to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_2^4 x\log_e x\,dx$, expressing your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
Three function values on $2\le x\le 4$ give two strips, so $h=\dfrac{4-2}{2}=1$ and the $x$ values are $2, 3, 4$.

For $f(x)=x\log_e x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(2) &= 1.38629 \\ f(3) &= 3.29584 \\ f(4) &= 5.54518 \end{aligned}$$
Applying the trapezoidal rule to each strip:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_2^4 x\log_e x\,dx &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\times 1\times(1.38629 + 3.29584) + \dfrac{1}{2}\times 1\times(3.29584 + 5.54518) \\ &\approx 6.76 \end{aligned}$$

Area above the $x$-axis counts as positive and area below as negative. From the diagram, $B$ lies below the axis and $A$, $C$ above.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-2}^{4} f(x)\,dx &= 10 - 4 + 8 \\ &= 14 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $\log_e(\sin x)$ with respect to $x$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule with inner function $\sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\times\cos x \\ &= \cot x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise , evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \cot x\,dx$, giving answer in exact form.
items.sol:
By part (a), a primitive of $\cot x$ is $\log_e|\sin x|$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cot x\,dx &= \Big[\log_e|\sin x|\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \log_e 1 - \log_e\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ &= 0 - \log_e 2^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 2 \end{aligned}$$

The $x$-intercepts of $y=f'(x)$ are at the turning points of $y=f(x)$, at $x=a$ and $x=b$.

\exfigure{570_q17_s2}

items.part: Find the equation of the curve $y = f(x)$ given that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6x - 4$ , and $y = f(x)$ has a stationary point at $(1, 2)$
items.sol:
Integrate $y''$:
$$y' = \int(6x-4)\,dx = 3x^2 - 4x + C_1$$
The stationary point at $(1,2)$ means $f'(1)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3 - 4 + C_1 &= 0 \\ C_1 &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4x + 1$. Integrate again:
$$f(x) = \int(3x^2 - 4x + 1)\,dx = x^3 - 2x^2 + x + C_2$$
The curve passes through $(1,2)$, so $f(1)=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 - 2 + 1 + C_2 &= 2 \\ C_2 &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + x + 2$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1+x}{x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Split the fraction and write each term as a power of $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1+x}{x^2}\,dx &= \int\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2} + \dfrac{x}{x^2}\right)dx \\ &= \int\left(x^{-2} + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} + \ln|x| + C \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{x} + \ln|x| + C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos\left(\dfrac{x^\circ}{2}\right)$
items.sol:
Convert to radians: $x^\circ = \dfrac{\pi x}{180}$ radians.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\cos\left(\dfrac{x^\circ}{2}\right)dx &= \int\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{360}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{360}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{360}\right) + C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{3}e^{2x-5}\,dx$.

items.sol:
The curves $y = e^x$ and $y = e^{-x}$ cross at $(0, 1)$, and the region lies between them from $x = 0$ to the line $x = 5$.

\exfigure{570_q20_s1}

items.part:
Hence calculate the area of the region bounded by curve

$y = e^x,\ y = e^{-x}$ and $x = 5$
items.sol:
The region lies between the curves from $x=0$ to $x=5$, with $e^x \ge e^{-x}$ there.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^5\left(e^x - e^{-x}\right)dx \\ &= \Big[e^x + e^{-x}\Big]_0^5 \\ &= e^5 + e^{-5} - \left(e^0 + e^0\right) \\ &= e^5 + \dfrac{1}{e^5} - 2 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Evaluate:
Given $f(x) = \log_e\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\right)$, show that $f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on the logarithm and then simplifying:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^2+1}}\times\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}(x^2+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 2x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^2+1}}\times\left(1 + \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^2+1}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2+1} + x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Evaluate:
Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$, leaving your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
By part (a), a primitive of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$ is $\ln\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} &= \Big[\ln\left|x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\right|\Big]_0^1 \\ &= \ln\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right) - \ln(0 + 1) \\ &= \ln\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$:
$5^{x+2}$
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(a^{u}\right) = a^{u}\ln a \cdot u'$ with $u = x+2$:
$$y' = 5^{x+2}\ln 5$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$:
$\log_4(3x)$
items.sol:
Split using the log law $\log_a(xy)=\log_a x+\log_a y$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \log_4(3x) = \log_4 3 + \log_4 x \\ y' &= 0 + \dfrac{1}{x\ln 4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x\ln 4} \end{aligned}$$

The fence is two radii plus the arc, and the arc length is $r\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 2r + r\theta \\ &= r(\theta + 2) \end{aligned}$$

The area of a sector is
$$A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta \qquad (1)$$
From part (a), $M = 2r + r\theta$, so
$$\theta = \dfrac{M - 2r}{r}$$
Substituting into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\times\dfrac{M - 2r}{r} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}Mr - r^2 \end{aligned}$$

Here $M$ is fixed and $A$ is a function of $r$.
$$A = \dfrac{1}{2}Mr - r^2$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dr} = \dfrac{1}{2}M - 2r$$
For a stationary point:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}M - 2r &= 0 \\ M &= 4r \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} = -2 < 0$$
so this is a maximum.

Then
$$\begin{aligned} \theta &= \dfrac{M - 2r}{r} \\ &= \dfrac{4r - 2r}{r} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta = 2 \text{ radians gives the maximum area}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 - x + 1$ .
Find the stationary points on this curve and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Find the stationary points.
$$y' = x^2 - 1$$
Set $y'=0$:
$$x^2 - 1 = 0 \quad\text{so}\quad x = \pm 1$$
The second derivative is
$$y'' = 2x$$
At $x = 1$: $y'' = 2 > 0$, so a minimum, with
$$f(1) = \dfrac{1}{3} - 1 + 1 = \dfrac{1}{3}$$
At $x=-1$: $y'' = -2 < 0$, so a maximum, with
$$f(-1) = -\dfrac{1}{3} + 1 + 1 = \dfrac{5}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum at } \left(1, \dfrac{1}{3}\right),\ \text{maximum at } \left(-1, \dfrac{5}{3}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 - x + 1$ .
Show that there is a point of inflexion at point where $x = 0$ .
items.sol:
$$y'' = 2x, \qquad y'' = 0 \text{ when } x = 0$$
Test the concavity either side of $x=0$:

\extable{Ts3881_1}

The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflexion at $x = 0$.
\exfigure{570_q24_s1}
\exfigure{570_q25_s1}

Substitute each $x$ value into both functions.

When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}, \qquad \cos\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$
When $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -1, \qquad \cos\left(2\times\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) = \cos(-\pi) = -1$$
The values agree in each case, so the two graphs intersect at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Between $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $\cos 2x \ge \sin x$, so the curve $y=\cos 2x$ is the upper one.
$$\text{Area} = \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(\cos 2x - \sin x)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x + \cos x\right]_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(-\pi) + \cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 0 - 0 \\ &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{4} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y = e^{\sin x}$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
Find all the stationary points on the curve in the given domain.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$y' = e^{\sin x}\cos x$$
Set $y'=0$. Since $e^{\sin x} > 0$, we need $\cos x = 0$, so
$$x = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
The $y$ values are
$$f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = e^{1} = e, \qquad f\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = e^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{e}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{stationary points } \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, e\right) \text{ and } \left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{1}{e}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y = e^{\sin x}$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
By finding the second derivative or otherwise, determine the nature of stationary points.
items.sol:
Differentiate $y'=e^{\sin x}\cos x$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{\sin x} & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=e^{\sin x}\cos x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'' &= e^{\sin x}\cos^2 x - e^{\sin x}\sin x \\ &= e^{\sin x}\left(\cos^2 x - \sin x\right) \end{aligned}$$
Note $e^{\sin x} > 0$.

At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$y'' = e^{1}(0 - 1) = -e < 0$$
so a maximum at $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, e\right)$.

At $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$:
$$y'' = e^{-1}(0 + 1) = e^{-1} > 0$$
so a minimum at $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{1}{e}\right)$.

items.part:
Consider the function $y = e^{\sin x}$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
Find the $x-$values of points of inflexion, correct to 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
Points of inflexion occur where $y''=0$:
$$e^{\sin x}\left(\cos^2 x - \sin x\right) = 0$$
Since $e^{\sin x} > 0$, $\cos^2 x - \sin x = 0$. Using $\cos^2 x = 1-\sin^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 - \sin^2 x - \sin x &= 0 \\ \sin^2 x + \sin x - 1 &= 0 \\ \sin x &= \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{-1-\sqrt{5}}{2}<-1$ has no solution, so $\sin x=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$.

Hence $x \approx 0.7$ or $x \approx 2.5$ (radians). Concavity changes at both (checked with a table of $y''$ values), giving points of inflexion at about $(0.7, 1.9)$ and $(2.5, 1.9)$ (both have $y=e^{\sin x}=e^{0.618\ldots}\approx1.86$).
\exfigure{570_q26_s1}

The total number of jackets is $100$, and $20$ of them are size 12.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage} &= \dfrac{20}{100} \times 100\% \\ &= 20\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 20\% \text{ of the jackets were size 12}$$

The modal size is the size with the highest frequency.
$$\text{Modal size} = 10$$
There are $100$ jackets, so the median is the mean of the 50th and 51st sizes.
$$\text{Median} = \dfrac{\text{50th size} + \text{51st size}}{2} = 12$$
$$\therefore\ \text{modal size } 10 \text{ and median size } 12$$

The upper quartile is
$$Q_3 = 14$$
The lower quartile is
$$Q_1 = 10$$
The interquartile range is
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 14 - 10 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ Q_3 = 14,\ Q_1 = 10,\ IQR = 4$$

items.part:
Bianca started a new job on 1st January 2022 with a salary of \$115 500. Her salary increases by 4.5% on January 1st each year thereafter.
Calculate her salary in the eighth year.
items.sol:
Her salary forms a geometric sequence with first term $115\,500$ and common ratio $1 + \dfrac{4.5}{100} = 1.045$.

The eighth year has $7$ increments, so
$$\begin{aligned} T_8 &= 115500(1.045)^{8-1} \\ &\approx \$157\,179.54 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{her salary in the eighth year is } \$157\,179.54$$

items.part:
Bianca started a new job on 1st January 2022 with a salary of \$115 500. Her salary increases by 4.5% on January 1st each year thereafter.
In which year will her salary first exceed \$200 000?
items.sol:
Using the geometric sequence from part (a), the salary in year $n$ is $115500(1.045)^{n-1}$. We need
$$115500(1.045)^{n-1} > 200000$$
Divide both sides by $115500$.
$$1.045^{n-1} > \dfrac{200000}{115500} = \dfrac{400}{231}$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides.
$$\ln 1.045^{n-1} > \ln\dfrac{400}{231}$$
Apply the power law.
$$(n-1)\ln 1.045 > \ln\dfrac{400}{231}$$
Divide by $\ln 1.045 > 0$.
$$n - 1 > \dfrac{\ln\frac{400}{231}}{\ln 1.045} \approx 12.47$$
$n$ is a whole number, so the smallest value is
$$n - 1 = 13$$
The salary first exceeds \$200 000 after $13$ increments, so the year is
$$2022 + 13 = 2035$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the year is } 2035$$

items.part:
A set of bivariate data is given below:

For this set of data:
Find the equation of the least-squares regression line.
items.sol:
From the calculator, the regression line is $y = A + Bx$ with
$$A = 16.99, \qquad B = -0.9429$$
Therefore the least-squares regression line is

The rate at which a certain compound is formed during a nuclear reaction, in $R$ grams per minute, is given by the formula:

$$R = 20 + \dfrac{5}{t+1}$$

where $t$ is time in minutes since the beginning of the reaction.
At what rate is the compound being formed at the end of 4 minutes?
items.sol:
Substitute $t = 4$ into the formula.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 20 + \dfrac{5}{4+1} \\ &= 21 \text{ g/min} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the rate is } 21 \text{ g/min}$$

items.part:
The rate at which a certain compound is formed during a nuclear reaction, in $R$ grams per minute, is given by the formula:

$$R = 20 + \dfrac{5}{t+1}$$

where $t$ is time in minutes since the beginning of the reaction.
What value does $R$ approach as $t$ approaches infinity?
items.sol:
As $t \to \infty$, the term $\dfrac{5}{t+1} \to 0$.
$$R \to 20 + 0 = 20$$
$$\therefore\ R \text{ approaches } 20 \text{ g/min}$$

The rate at which a certain compound is formed during a nuclear reaction, in $R$ grams per minute, is given by the formula:

$$R = 20 + \dfrac{5}{t+1}$$

where $t$ is time in minutes since the beginning of the reaction.
How many grams of the compound are formed in the first 4 minutes? Express you answer in exact form.
items.sol:
The amount formed is the integral of the rate over the first 4 minutes.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total grams} &= \int_0^4 \left(20 + \dfrac{5}{t+1}\right) dt \\ &= \Big[20t + 5\ln|t+1|\Big]_0^4 \\ &= 80 + 5\ln 5 - (0 + 5\ln 1) \\ &= 80 + 5\ln 5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (80 + 5\ln 5) \text{ grams}$$

items.part:
The velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x} = 3\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ metres per second for $0 \le t \le 2\pi$.
Find the equation of the acceleration $\ddot{x}$ of the particle as a function of time.
items.sol:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$\ddot{x} = 3\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

items.part:
The velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x} = 3\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ metres per second for $0 \le t \le 2\pi$.
Calculate the maximum speed of the particle and the times at which it occurs in the given domain.
items.sol:
The maximum speed is the amplitude of $\dot{x}$, so it is $3$ m/s.

Speed is $|\dot{x}|$, so it is greatest when $\dot{x} = \pm 3$, which is when the acceleration is zero.
$$\ddot{x} = 3\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$$
$$\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$$

For $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, we have $-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \le t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} \le \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, so
$$t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \text{ or } \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
$$t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \text{ or } \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$

The maximum speed is $3$ m/s, at $t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $t = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ seconds.
items.final: Maximum speed $3$ m/s, at $t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $t = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ seconds

items.part:
The velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x} = 3\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ metres per second for $0 \le t \le 2\pi$.
Find the equation of the displacement of the particle, $x$, as a function of time if the particle was initially 3 metres to the left of the origin.
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int \dot{x}\,dt \\ &= \int 3\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) dt \\ &= -3\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C \end{aligned}$$

Initially $x = -3$ (to the left of the origin), so at $t = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -3 &= -3\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C \\ C &= -1.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = -3\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - 1.5$$

items.part:
The population of the suburb of Baulkham Hills has been growing over the last few years. At the beginning of January 2019, the population was 32500 and at the beginning of January 2022 it is estimated at 37700.
Assume that the population $P$ obeys the law of natural growth $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP$, for some positive constant $k$, where $t$ is number of years since the beginning of January 2019. Show that $P = 32500e^{kt}$ satisfies the equation $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP$.
items.sol:
Differentiate $P = 32500e^{kt}$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = k \times 32500e^{kt}$$

Since $P = 32500e^{kt}$, this gives
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP$$

Hence $P = 32500e^{kt}$ satisfies the equation.

items.part:
The population of the suburb of Baulkham Hills has been growing over the last few years. At the beginning of January 2019, the population was 32500 and at the beginning of January 2022 it is estimated at 37700.
Find the value of the positive constant $k$. Leave your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
At the beginning of January 2019, $t = 0$ and $P = 32500$.

At the beginning of January 2022, $t = 3$ and $P = 37700$.

Substitute into $P = 32500e^{kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 37700 &= 32500e^{3k} \\ \dfrac{37700}{32500} &= e^{3k} \\ 3k &= \ln\dfrac{37700}{32500} \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln\dfrac{377}{325} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 1.16 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of the suburb of Baulkham Hills has been growing over the last few years. At the beginning of January 2019, the population was 32500 and at the beginning of January 2022 it is estimated at 37700.
Calculate the size of the population at the beginning of January 2027.
items.sol:
January 2027 is $8$ years after January 2019, so $t = 8$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 32500e^{\frac{1}{3}\ln 1.16 \times 8} \\ &= 48280.45\ldots \\ &\approx 48280 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of the suburb of Baulkham Hills has been growing over the last few years. At the beginning of January 2019, the population was 32500 and at the beginning of January 2022 it is estimated at 37700.
During which year will the population first exceed 55000?
items.sol:
We need $P > 55000$.
$$32500e^{\frac{1}{3}\ln 1.16\, t} > 55000$$
$$\dfrac{55000}{32500} < e^{\frac{1}{3}\ln 1.16\, t}$$
$$t > 10.63$$

Check by trial: at $t = 10$, $P = 53301$; at $t = 11$, $P = 56005$.

The population first exceeds $55000$ during the year $2019 + 10 = 2029$.
$$\therefore\ \text{During } 2029$$

Peter borrows \$480 000 from a bank. The loan is to be repaid over 20 years in equal monthly instalments of \$$M$ at the end of each month, after the interest has been added. Reducible interest is charged at 4.8% p.a., calculated monthly.

Let \$$A_n$ be the amount owing at the end of $n$ months after the repayment has been made.
Show that $A_n = 480000 \times 1.004^n - M\left(\dfrac{1.004^n - 1}{0.004}\right)$.
items.sol:
Continuing the pattern from part (a):
$$A_3 = 480000(1.004)^3 - M(1.004)^2 - M(1.004) - M$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= 480000(1.004)^n - M(1.004)^{n-1} - \cdots - M(1.004) - M \\ &= 480000(1.004)^n - M\left[1.004^{n-1} + \cdots + 1.004 + 1\right] \end{aligned}$$

The bracket is a geometric series with $a = 1$, $r = 1.004$ and $n$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= 480000(1.004)^n - M\left[1 \times \dfrac{1.004^n - 1}{1.004 - 1}\right] \\ &= 480000 \times 1.004^n - M\left[\dfrac{1.004^n - 1}{0.004}\right] \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Edric deposits \$1000 into a saving account at the beginning of each year. He makes his first deposit on January 1, 2000. The investment earns compound interest at a rate of 9% p.a., compounded yearly. He makes the last deposit of \$1000 on January 1, 2025 and he withdraws all his savings at the end of 2025.
Show that the total amount in the account, in dollars, at the end of 2025 is given by:

$$1000 \times \dfrac{1.09(1.09^{26} - 1)}{0.09}$$
items.sol:
Adding the values of all $26$ deposits at the end of 2025:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= A_1 + A_2 + \cdots + A_{26} \\ &= 1000(1.09)^{26} + 1000(1.09)^{25} + \cdots + 1000(1.09)^1 \\ &= 1000\left[1.09^{26} + 1.09^{25} + \cdots + 1.09^1\right] \end{aligned}$$

The bracket is a geometric series with $n = 26$, $a = 1.09$, $r = 1.09$, with sum $a\,\dfrac{r^n - 1}{r - 1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 1000 \times 1.09\,\dfrac{(1.09)^{26} - 1}{1.09 - 1} \\ &= 1000 \times \dfrac{1.09(1.09^{26} - 1)}{0.09} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Simplify $2 + \dfrac{t^2}{t+1} - \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{t+1}\right)$.
items.sol:
Write everything over the common denominator $t+1$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2+\dfrac{t^2}{t+1}-\left(1+\dfrac{1}{t+1}\right) &= \dfrac{2(t+1)+t^2-(t+1)-1}{t+1} \\ &= \dfrac{2t+2+t^2-t-1-1}{t+1} \\ &= \dfrac{t^2+t}{t+1} \\ &= \dfrac{t(t+1)}{t+1} \\ &= t \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove $\tan\theta(1 - \cot^2\theta) + \cot\theta(1 - \tan^2\theta) = 0$.
items.sol:
Rewrite using $\cot\theta=\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \tan\theta(1-\cot^2\theta)+\cot\theta(1-\tan^2\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{\tan\theta(\tan^2\theta-1)}{\tan^2\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}(1-\tan^2\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{\tan^2\theta-1+1-\tan^2\theta}{\tan\theta} \\ &= 0 \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

For a $6$-period annuity, the number of periods is $3\times 2=6$ and the rate per period is $8\%\div 2=4\%$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= 3\times 2 \\ &= 6 \text{ half-years} \\ \text{Rate} &= 8\%\div 2 \\ &= 4\% \text{ per half-year} \\ \text{Future value} &= 700\times 6.6330 \\ &= \$4643.10 \end{aligned}$$

The table factor for $6$ periods at $4\%$ is $6.6330$.

Grace needs a future value of $\$6000$, with the same table factor $6.6330$.

$$\begin{aligned} 6000 &= x\times 6.6330 \\ x &= \$904.57 \end{aligned}$$

The extra contribution needed is

$$\begin{aligned} \$904.57-\$700 &= \$204.57 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Grace must contribute } \$204.57 \text{ more each half-year.}$$

items.part: Find the second derivative of $y = \ln(4x - 1)$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on $y=\ln(4x-1)$:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{4}{4x-1}=4(4x-1)^{-1}$$

Differentiating again:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= -4(4x-1)^{-2}\times 4 \\ &= -\dfrac{16}{(4x-1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y = x^2 e^{6x}$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{6x}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=6e^{6x}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= u'v+uv' \\ &= 2xe^{6x}+6x^2e^{6x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y = \dfrac{\sin 5x}{x^4}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin 5x & v&=x^4\\ u'&=5\cos 5x & v'&=4x^3\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2} \\ &= \dfrac{5x^4\cos 5x-4x^3\sin 5x}{x^8} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In a raffle 50 tickets are sold, and there is one first prize and one second prize. Jody buys 15 tickets in the raffle. The first prize is drawn then the second prize.
What is the probability that Jody wins the first prize, but not the second prize?
items.sol:
Jody wins the first prize (probability $\dfrac{15}{50}$), then does not win the second (probability $\dfrac{35}{49}$).

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{15}{50}\times\dfrac{35}{49} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{14} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In a raffle 50 tickets are sold, and there is one first prize and one second prize. Jody buys 15 tickets in the raffle. The first prize is drawn then the second prize.
Find the probability that Jody wins at least one prize?
items.sol:
Use the complement: $P(\text{at least one prize})=1-P(\text{no prize})$.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-\left(\dfrac{35}{50}\times\dfrac{34}{49}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{18}{35} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Determine the angle of inclination $\theta$ of the line $x + y + 1 = 0$.

\exfigure{1321_q18_1}
items.sol:
Rearrange to gradient form.

$$y=-x-1,\qquad m=-1$$

The angle of inclination satisfies $\tan\theta=m$.

$$\tan^{-1}(-1)=-45^\circ$$

The angle of inclination must lie between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, so add $180^\circ$.

$$\therefore\ \theta=135^\circ$$

items.part: Differentiate $f(x) = 5x^2 - 3x$ from first principles.
items.sol:
Using the definition of the derivative from first principles:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{5(x+h)^2-3(x+h)-(5x^2-3x)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{5x^2+10xh+5h^2-3x-3h-5x^2+3x}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{10xh+5h^2-3h}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{h(10x+5h-3)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}(10x+5h-3) \\ &= 10x-3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the area bounded by the curve $y = 3e^{2x}$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = 1$ and $x = 5$.

Leave your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
The area is found by integrating from $x=1$ to $x=5$ (the curve is above the $x$-axis).

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5 3e^{2x}\,dx &= \dfrac{3}{2}\left[e^{2x}\right]_1^5 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{2}\left(e^{10}-e^{2}\right) \\ &\approx 33028.6 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $\log_5(x+1) - \log_5 x = 2$.
items.sol:
Combine the logs using $\log_a m-\log_a n=\log_a\dfrac{m}{n}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \log_5(x+1)-\log_5 x &= 2 \\ \log_5\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x}\right) &= 2 \\ \dfrac{x+1}{x} &= 5^2 \\ x+1 &= 25x \\ 24x &= 1 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{24} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3 \dfrac{2\,dx}{5x - 2}$ correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The integrand is $\dfrac{2}{5x-2}$. Write it so the numerator is the derivative of $5x-2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3\dfrac{2}{5x-2}\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{5}\int_1^3\dfrac{5}{5x-2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{2}{5}\Big[\ln(5x-2)\Big]_1^3 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{5}\Big[\ln(5(3)-2)-\ln(5(1)-2)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{2}{5}(\ln 13-\ln 3) \\ &\approx 0.59 \text{ (2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Fill in the following table and use the trapezoidal rule with 4 function values to approximate $\displaystyle\int_4^7 2^x \, dx$.

\extable{1321_q24_t1}
items.sol:
The table of values has $4$ function values, so there are $3$ strips of width $h = \dfrac{7-4}{3} = 1$.

\extable{Ts3954_1}

Applying the trapezoidal rule with the first and last values, and the two middle values doubled:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_4^7 2^x\,dx &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left(16 + 128 + 2(32 + 64)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(336) \\ &= 168 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \int_4^7 2^x\,dx \approx 168 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y = x\cos x$ at the point where $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
items.sol:
Differentiating using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$

$$y' = \cos x - x\sin x$$

When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $y = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0$.

The gradient of the tangent is

$$m_1 = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_1 m_2 = -1$:

$$m_2 = \dfrac{2}{\pi}$$

The normal passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$:

$$\begin{aligned} y - y_1 &= m_2(x - x_1) \\ y - 0 &= \dfrac{2}{\pi}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ y &= \dfrac{2x}{\pi} - 1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ y = \dfrac{2x}{\pi} - 1$$

items.part:
The weights of metal drums are normally distributed with a mean of 8.1kg and a standard deviation of 2kg.

\exfigure{1321_q26_1}
Use the $z$-score table provided at the back of the paper to answer this question.

Find $P(8.4 \le X \le 11)$, where $X$ is a random variable, representing the weight of the drums?
items.sol:
Convert each weight to a $z$-score using $z = \dfrac{x - \bar{x}}{\sigma}$.

$$z = \dfrac{8.4 - 8.1}{2} = 0.15 \qquad z = \dfrac{11 - 8.1}{2} = 1.45$$

Using the $z$-score table:

$$\begin{aligned} P(0.15 \le z \le 1.45) &= P(z \le 1.45) - P(z \le 0.15) \\ &= 0.9265 - 0.5596 \\ &= 0.3669 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P(8.4 \le X \le 11) = 0.3669$$

items.part:
Consider $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3$ in the domain $-1 \le x < 3$.
Find the stationary point(s) and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= x^3 - 3x^2 + 3 \\ f'(x) &= 3x^2 - 6x \\ f''(x) &= 6x - 6 \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2 - 6x &= 0 \\ 3x(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x = 0$ or $x = 2$, both in the domain $-1 \le x < 3$.

When $x = 0$, $y = 3$. When $x = 2$, $y = 8 - 12 + 3 = -1$.

The second derivative decides the nature:

$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -6 < 0 &&\text{maximum turning point}\\ f''(2) &= 6 > 0 &&\text{minimum turning point}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ (0, 3) \text{ is a maximum and } (2, -1) \text{ is a minimum turning point}$$
items.final: $(0,3)$ is a maximum and $(2,-1)$ is a minimum turning point

items.part:

items.sol:

$$\begin{aligned} 6x - 6 &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

When $x = 1$, $y = 1 - 3 + 3 = 1$.

Test for a change in concavity:

The concavity changes at $x = 1$.

$$\therefore\ (1, 1) \text{ is a point of inflection}$$

Write each term with base $2$: $4^x = 2^{2x} = (2^x)^2$ and $2^{x+2} = 2^2\cdot 2^x$.

$$(2^x)^2 - 4(2^x) = 32$$

Let $u = 2^x$.

$$\begin{aligned} u^2 - 4u - 32 &= 0 \\ (u - 8)(u + 4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $u = 8$ or $u = -4$.

$2^x > 0$ for all $x$, so $2^x = -4$ has no solution.

$$2^x = 8 = 2^3$$

$$\therefore\ x = 3$$

The curves meet where $\sin x = 1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x$, so $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ in the shaded region.

On $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]$ the curve $f$ is above $g$. On $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ the curve $g$ is above $f$.

$$A = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \big(\sin x - 1 + \cos 2x\big)\,dx + \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \big(1 - \cos 2x - \sin x\big)\,dx$$

$$A = \left[-\cos x - x + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} + \left[x - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x + \cos x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}$$

First integral:

$$\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - \left(-\cos 0 - 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 0\right)$$

Second integral:

$$\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\pi + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

Adding the two integrals:

$$A \approx 0.66 \text{ units}^2 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 3^x & \text{for } 0 \le x \le k \\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$
Find the value of $k$ correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
For a probability density function, the total area is $1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k 3^x\,dx &= 1 \\ \left[\dfrac{3^x}{\ln 3}\right]_0^k &= 1 \\ \dfrac{3^k}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} &= 1 \\ 3^k &= \ln 3 + 1 \\ k &= \log_3(\ln 3 + 1) \\ &\approx 0.67 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.67$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 3^x & \text{for } 0 \le x \le k \\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$
Evaluate the $8^{\text{th}}$ decile correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The $8^{\text{th}}$ decile is the value $x$ with $F(x) = 0.8$, where $F$ is the cumulative distribution function.

$$F(x) = \int 3^x\,dx = \dfrac{3^x}{\ln 3} + C$$

Since $F(0) = 0$:

$$0 = \dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} + C, \quad \text{so } C = -\dfrac{1}{\ln 3}$$

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \le 0 \\[6pt] \dfrac{3^x - 1}{\ln 3}, & 0 \le x \le 0.67 \\[6pt] 1, & x > 0.67 \end{cases}$$

Solve $F(x) = 0.8$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3^x - 1}{\ln 3} &= 0.8 \\ 3^x &= 0.8\ln 3 + 1 \\ x &= \log_3(0.8\ln 3 + 1) \\ &\approx 0.57 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the } 8^{\text{th}} \text{ decile is } 0.57$$

items.part: Given $f''(t) = t + \sqrt{t}$, find the equation of the curve $f(t)$, given $f(1) = 1$ and $f'(1) = 2$.
items.sol:
Integrate $f''(t) = t + t^{\frac{1}{2}}$:

$$f'(t) = \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \dfrac{2}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}} + C$$

Using $f'(1) = 2$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{2}{3} + C \\ C &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$f'(t) = \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \dfrac{2}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}} + \dfrac{5}{6}$$

Integrate again:

$$f(t) = \dfrac{t^3}{6} + \dfrac{4}{15}t^{\frac{5}{2}} + \dfrac{5}{6}t + D$$

Using $f(1) = 1$:

$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{4}{15} + \dfrac{5}{6} + D \\ D &= -\dfrac{4}{15} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f(t) = \dfrac{t^3}{6} + \dfrac{4}{15}t^{\frac{5}{2}} + \dfrac{5}{6}t - \dfrac{4}{15}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that its distance $x$ metres from the origin is given by $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$.
Where is the particle initially?
items.sol:
Initially $t = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is initially } 2 \text{ m from the origin}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that its distance $x$ metres from the origin is given by $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$.
When does the particle first come to rest?
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v = 0$.

$$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -4\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first comes to rest when } t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that its distance $x$ metres from the origin is given by $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$.
When does the particle first pass through the origin?
items.sol:
The particle is at the origin when $x = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first passes through the origin when } t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that its distance $x$ metres from the origin is given by $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$.
Find when the rate of change of velocity is zero.
items.sol:
The rate of change of velocity is the acceleration $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$.

$$a = -4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

Set $a = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ a = 0 \text{ when } t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
\exfigure{1321_q32_s1}

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that its distance $x$ metres from the origin is given by $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$.
Calculate the total distance travelled between $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $t = \dfrac{6\pi}{7}$.
items.sol:
From the graph, the particle moves towards the maximum at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ ($x = 4$), then reverses and moves back towards the origin. Split the motion at the turning point.

At $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:

$$x = 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

At $t = \dfrac{6\pi}{7}$, $t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{11\pi}{21}$:

$$x = 4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)$$

From $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ the particle travels $4 - 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

From $x = 4$ to the final position (which is negative, as $\dfrac{6\pi}{7} > \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$) it travels $4 + \left|4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)\right|$.

$$\text{Total distance} = \left(4 - 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right) + 4 + \left|4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)\right|$$

$$\therefore\ \text{total distance} \approx 4.835 \text{ m (3 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
A radioactive substance is decaying such that its mass, $m$ grams, at a time $t$ years after initial observation is given by

$$m = 60e^{kt}, \text{ where } k \text{ is a constant.}$$

After 100 years, the mass of radioactive substance is 42 grams.
Find the value of $k$, leaving your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Substitute $t = 100$ and $m = 42$ into $m = 60e^{kt}$.

$$\begin{aligned} 42 &= 60e^{100k} \\ 0.7 &= e^{100k} \\ 100k &= \ln 0.7 \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k = \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7$$

items.part:
A radioactive substance is decaying such that its mass, $m$ grams, at a time $t$ years after initial observation is given by

$$m = 60e^{kt}, \text{ where } k \text{ is a constant.}$$

After 100 years, the mass of radioactive substance is 42 grams.
Find the value of $t$ when $m = 30$.
items.sol:
Using $k = \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7$ and $m = 30$:

$$\begin{aligned} 30 &= 60e^{\frac{t}{100}\ln 0.7} \\ 0.5 &= e^{\frac{t}{100}\ln 0.7} \\ \ln 0.5 &= \dfrac{t}{100}\ln 0.7 \\ t &= 100\times\dfrac{\ln 0.5}{\ln 0.7} \\ &\approx 194.34 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ t \approx 194.34 \text{ years}$$

items.part:
\$2000 is invested into a credit union account at the beginning of each year and interest is paid at the end of each year, at a rate of $6.5\%$ per annum, on the balance in the account at that time.
Show that the value of the investment at the end of the 3 years is \$6814.35.
items.sol:
Each \$2000 earns interest at the end of each year it is in the account: the first deposit for $3$ years, the second for $2$ years and the third for $1$ year.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Value} &= 2000(1.065)^3 + 2000(1.065)^2 + 2000(1.065) \\ &= \$6814.35 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
\$2000 is invested into a credit union account at the beginning of each year and interest is paid at the end of each year, at a rate of $6.5\%$ per annum, on the balance in the account at that time.
At the end of how many years, before the next \$2000 is invested, would the accumulated amount in the account first exceed \$100,000?
items.sol:
At the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ year, the deposits have grown for $n, n-1, \ldots, 1$ years.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Amount} &= 2000(1.065)^n + 2000(1.065)^{n-1} + \cdots + 2000(1.065) \\ &= 2000\left(1.065 + 1.065^2 + \cdots + 1.065^n\right) \end{aligned}$$

This is a GP with $a = 1.065$, $r = 1.065$ and $n$ terms, so $S_n = \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$.

$$\text{Amount} = 2000\times\dfrac{1.065(1.065^n - 1)}{1.065 - 1} = \dfrac{2130}{0.065}\left(1.065^n - 1\right)$$

We need the amount to exceed \$100000.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2130}{0.065}\left(1.065^n - 1\right) &> 100000 \\ 1.065^n &> 4.0516 \\ n &> \dfrac{\log 4.0516}{\log 1.065} \\ n &> 22.2 \end{aligned}$$

$n$ is a whole number of years, so $n = 23$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the amount first exceeds \$100000 at the end of 23 years}$$

The disc has area $\pi R^2 = 100$, so

$$R^2 = \dfrac{100}{\pi}$$

When the sector is formed into a cone, the slant height is $R$. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with sides $h$, $r$ and hypotenuse $R$:

$$\begin{aligned} R^2 &= h^2 + r^2 \\ h &= \sqrt{R^2 - r^2} \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{\pi} - r^2} \end{aligned}$$

The volume of a cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$. Substitute $h$ from part (a).

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2\sqrt{\dfrac{100}{\pi} - r^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2\sqrt{\dfrac{100 - \pi r^2}{\pi}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}r^2\sqrt{\pi^2\times\dfrac{100 - \pi r^2}{\pi}} \\ &= \dfrac{r^2\sqrt{100\pi - \pi^2 r^2}}{3} \end{aligned}$$

Write $V$ as a single power so it can be differentiated by the chain rule.

$$V = \sqrt{\dfrac{r^4(100\pi - \pi^2 r^2)}{9}} = \left(\dfrac{100\pi r^4}{9} - \dfrac{\pi^2 r^6}{9}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

$$\begin{aligned} V' &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{100\pi r^4}{9} - \dfrac{\pi^2 r^6}{9}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times\left(\dfrac{400\pi r^3}{9} - \dfrac{6\pi^2 r^5}{9}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{400\pi r^3}{9} - \frac{6\pi^2 r^5}{9}}{2\sqrt{\frac{100\pi r^4}{9} - \frac{\pi^2 r^6}{9}}} \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $V' = 0$, that is when the numerator is zero.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{400\pi r^3}{9} - \dfrac{6\pi^2 r^5}{9} &= 0 \\ \pi r^3\left(400 - 6\pi r^2\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $r = 0$ (rejected, no cone) or $400 - 6\pi r^2 = 0$, giving

$$r = \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}}$$

Test the sign of $V'$ either side of this value; the sign is decided by the numerator, $\pi r^3(400 - 6\pi r^2)$.

\extable{Ts3978_1}

The sign of $V'$ changes from positive to negative, so the volume is a maximum.

$$\therefore\ V \text{ is maximised when } r = \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}}$$

The area of a sector of radius $R$ and angle $\theta$ is $\dfrac{\theta}{2}R^2$. Equate it to the given $A = \pi Rr$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\theta}{2}R^2 &= \pi Rr \\ \dfrac{\theta}{2}R &= \pi r \\ \theta &= \dfrac{2\pi r}{R} \end{aligned}$$

Substitute $R = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{\pi}}$ and $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}}$ (maximum volume, part (c)).

$$\begin{aligned} \theta &= \dfrac{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{200}{3\pi}}}{\sqrt{\frac{100}{\pi}}} \\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}\times\dfrac{\pi}{100}} \\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}} \\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{6}{9}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\pi\sqrt{6}}{3} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \theta = \dfrac{2\pi\sqrt{6}}{3} \text{ radians}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\cot\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\times\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.
items.sol:
Use $\cot\theta=\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}$, with $\tan\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=\sqrt3$ and $\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ (third quadrant).

$$\begin{aligned} \cot\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\times\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt6} \end{aligned}$$

The series is geometric with first term $a=2$ and common ratio $r=\dfrac{-6}{2}=-3$.

items.part:
Find the sum of the given arithmetic series.

$$9+16+23+\dots+2963$$
items.sol:
The series is arithmetic with $a=9$ and $d=7$. Find the number of terms using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2963 &= 9+(n-1)\times7 \\ n &= 423 \end{aligned}$$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_{423} &= \dfrac{423}{2}(9+2963) \\ &= 628\,578 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Let $f(x)=-x^2+2x-3$ and $g(x)=x^2+3$. Express $f\big(g(x)\big)$ in the form of $ax^4+bx^2+c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are non-zero integers.

Differentiate the following functions and simplify your answers where necessary.
$y=e^{5x}\cos 3x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{5x} & v&=\cos3x\\ u'&=5e^{5x} & v'&=-3\sin3x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= e^{5x}\times(-3\sin3x)+5e^{5x}\times\cos3x \\ &= -3e^{5x}\sin3x+5e^{5x}\cos3x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions and simplify your answers where necessary.
$y=\dfrac{10x-3}{x^2+1}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=10x-3 & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=10 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{(x^2+1)\times10-(10x-3)\times2x}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{10x^2+10-20x^2+6x}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-10x^2+6x+10}{(x^2+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: An object rolls 0.5 metres in the first second. Then each second after, it rolls by two thirds of the distance of its previous roll. How far will it roll altogether eventually?
items.sol:
The distances form a geometric series with first term $a=0.5$ and common ratio $r=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Since $|r|<1$, the sum to infinity exists:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{0.5}{1-\frac{2}{3}} \\ &=1.5\text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Leonard and Howard start jobs at the beginning of the same year. Leonard's annual salary in the first year is \$53000 and increases by $3\%$ at the beginning of each subsequent year. Howard's annual salary in the first year is \$59000 and increases by \$1500 at the beginning of each subsequent year.
Show that in the $15^{\text{th}}$ year, Leonard's annual salary is higher than Howard's annual salary.
items.sol:
Leonard's salaries form a geometric sequence with $a=53000$, $r=1.03$:
$$\begin{aligned} L_{15}&=53000\times1.03^{14} \\ &=\$80167.25542\dots \\ &\approx\$80167.26 \end{aligned}$$
Howard's salaries form an arithmetic sequence with $a=59000$, $d=1500$:
$$\begin{aligned} H_{15}&=59000+1500\times14 \\ &=\$80000 \end{aligned}$$
Since $80167.26>80000$, $L_{15}>H_{15}$.

items.part:
Leonard and Howard start jobs at the beginning of the same year. Leonard's annual salary in the first year is \$53000 and increases by $3\%$ at the beginning of each subsequent year. Howard's annual salary in the first year is \$59000 and increases by \$1500 at the beginning of each subsequent year.
In the first 15 years, how much in total, does Leonard earn?
items.sol:
Using the geometric series sum $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ with $a=53000$, $r=1.03$, $n=15$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15}&=\dfrac{53000\times(1.03^{15}-1)}{1.03-1} \\ &=\$985742.435994\dots \\ &\approx\$985742.44 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Leonard and Howard start jobs at the beginning of the same year. Leonard's annual salary in the first year is \$53000 and increases by $3\%$ at the beginning of each subsequent year. Howard's annual salary in the first year is \$59000 and increases by \$1500 at the beginning of each subsequent year.
In which year will Leonard start to earn a salary more than \$90000 a year?
items.sol:
Leonard's salary in year $n$ is $53000\times1.03^{n-1}$, so we need
$$\begin{aligned} 53000\times1.03^{n-1}&>90000 \\ 1.03^{n-1}&>\dfrac{90}{53} \\ (n-1)\ln1.03&>\ln\left(\dfrac{90}{53}\right) \\ n&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{90}{53}\right)}{\ln1.03}+1 \\ n&>18.91406\dots \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ is a whole number, $n=19$.

items.part:
A probability density function $f(x)$ is given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(5-x), & \text{if } 0\leq x\leq 5\\ 0, & \text{if } x<0,\ x>5\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.
Show that $k=\dfrac{6}{125}$.
items.sol:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^5kx(5-x)\,dx&=1 \\ k\int_0^5(5x-x^2)\,dx&=1 \\ k\left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^5&=1 \\ k\times\dfrac{125}{6}&=1 \\ k&=\dfrac{6}{125} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A probability density function $f(x)$ is given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(5-x), & \text{if } 0\leq x\leq 5\\ 0, & \text{if } x<0,\ x>5\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.
Determine the mode of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
The mode is where $f(x)$ is greatest. Here $f(x)$ is a concave down parabola with $x$-intercepts $x=0$ and $x=5$.

The vertex lies midway between the intercepts:
$$x=\dfrac{0+5}{2}=2.5$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the mode of } f(x) \text{ is } x=2.5$$

items.part:
A probability density function $f(x)$ is given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(5-x), & \text{if } 0\leq x\leq 5\\ 0, & \text{if } x<0,\ x>5\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.
Find $P(X>3)$.
items.sol:
The probability that $X>3$ is the complement of $P(X\le 3)$, using $k=\dfrac{6}{125}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>3) &= 1-P(X\le 3) \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\displaystyle\int_0^3 (5x-x^2)\,dx \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\left[\dfrac{5\times 3^2}{2}-\dfrac{3^3}{3}-0\right] \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\times\dfrac{27}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{44}{125} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X>3)=\dfrac{44}{125}$$

items.part:
On any given day, the depth of water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right),\ 0\leq t\leq 24$$

where $h$ is the depth of water, in metres and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 6 am.
Find the minimum depth of the water in the river.
items.sol:
The minimum of $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)$ is $-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} h_{\min} &= 14-8 \\ &= 6 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum depth is } 6 \text{ metres}$$

items.part:
On any given day, the depth of water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right),\ 0\leq t\leq 24$$

where $h$ is the depth of water, in metres and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 6 am.
Find the values of $t$ for which $h(t)=10$.
items.sol:
Set $h(t)=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} 14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= 10 \\ 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= -4 \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with $0\le \dfrac{\pi t}{12}\le 2\pi$.
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{12}=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ t=14 \text{ or } t=22$$

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-x^2-x+6$, for $-3\leq x\leq 3$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= x^3-x^2-x+6 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 3x^2-2x-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-2x-1 &= 0 \\ (3x+1)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $x=1$, giving $y=\dfrac{167}{27}$ and $y=5$ respectively.

The second derivative decides the nature.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-2$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=-\dfrac{1}{3}: \quad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 6\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-2=-4<0 \\ \text{At } x=1: \quad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 6\times 1-2=4>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(-\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{167}{27}\right) \text{ is a maximum turning point and } (1,5) \text{ is a minimum turning point}$$
items.final: $\left(-\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{167}{27}\right)$ is a maximum turning point and $(1,5)$ is a minimum turning point

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-x^2-x+6$, for $-3\leq x\leq 3$.
Show that there is a point of inflection at $\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{151}{27}\right)$.
items.sol:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-2$$
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-2 &= 0 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^3-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2-\dfrac{1}{3}+6 \\ &= \dfrac{151}{27} \end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts4025_1}

There is a change in concavity, therefore the point of inflection is $\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{151}{27}\right)$.

items.part:
Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-x^2-x+6$, for $-3\leq x\leq 3$.
Sketch the curve for $-3\leq x\leq 3$, showing all key features.

Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-x^2-x+6$, for $-3\leq x\leq 3$.
For what values of $x$ is the curve decreasing and concaving up?
items.sol:
The curve is decreasing for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}<0$, that is $-\dfrac{1}{3}<x<1$, and concave up for $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$, that is $x>\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Both hold together when:
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{3}<x<1$$

items.part:
A tank contains 50 litres of water. A tap at the base of the tank allows water to flow out at a rate proportional to the quantity of water still in the tank at that time, given by the equation $W=W_0e^{-kt}$, where $W$ is the amount of water in the tank and $t$ is time in minutes. After 2 minutes, 10 litres of water has been released.
Show that $k=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5}$.
items.sol:
Initially $W_0=50$, so $W=50e^{-kt}$.

After 2 minutes, 10 litres has been released, so $W=40$ when $t=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 40 &= 50e^{-2k} \\ \dfrac{4}{5} &= e^{-2k} \\ \ln\dfrac{4}{5} &= -2k \\ k &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A tank contains 50 litres of water. A tap at the base of the tank allows water to flow out at a rate proportional to the quantity of water still in the tank at that time, given by the equation $W=W_0e^{-kt}$, where $W$ is the amount of water in the tank and $t$ is time in minutes. After 2 minutes, 10 litres of water has been released.
How much water has been released from the tank after 10 minutes? Give your answer to the nearest litre.
items.sol:
When $t=10$, using $k=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5}$:
$$\begin{aligned} W &= 50e^{-10\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{4}{5}\right)} \\ &= 16.384 \end{aligned}$$
So 16.384 litres of water are in the tank.
$$\begin{aligned} 50-16.384 &= 33.616 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 34 \text{ litres of water have been released}$$

Substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into both functions.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y &= \sqrt{3}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The same $y$ value is obtained, therefore $A\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ is a point of intersection of the two functions.

At an intersection, the two functions are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} \sin x &= \sqrt{3}\cos x \\ \tan x &= \sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
Tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants.
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ B\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$$

The sine curve is above $y=\sqrt{3}\cos x$ between $A$ and $B$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\left(\sin x-\sqrt{3}\cos x\right)dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x-\sqrt{3}\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}} \\ &= \left(-\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)-\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}+3\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}-3\right) \\ &= 4 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v$ m/s. The displacement is given by $x=2t-3\log_e(t+1)$.
Find an expression for the velocity $v$.
items.sol:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2t-3\log_e(t+1) \\ v &= \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2-\dfrac{3}{t+1} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v$ m/s. The displacement is given by $x=2t-3\log_e(t+1)$.
Find the initial acceleration.
items.sol:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$v=2-3(t+1)^{-1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 3(t+1)^{-2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{3}{(0+1)^2} \\ &= 3 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v$ m/s. The displacement is given by $x=2t-3\log_e(t+1)$.
When does the particle come to rest?
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-\dfrac{3}{t+1} &= 0 \\ \dfrac{3}{t+1} &= 2 \\ t+1 &= \dfrac{3}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest when } t=\dfrac{1}{2} \text{ s}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v$ m/s. The displacement is given by $x=2t-3\log_e(t+1)$.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first three seconds. Answer correct to four decimal places.
items.sol:
The particle turns at $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ (from part (c)), so find the displacement at the end and at the turning point.
$$\begin{aligned} t=3: \quad x &= 2\times 3-3\log_e 4 \\ &= 6-3\log_e 4 \\ &\approx 1.841116 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t=\dfrac{1}{2}: \quad x &= 2\times\dfrac{1}{2}-3\log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+1\right) \\ &= 1-3\log_e\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &\approx -0.216395 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1322_q30_s1}

The particle goes from $0$ to $-0.216395$, then back past the origin to $1.841116$, so the total distance is
$$\begin{aligned} (6-3\log_e 4)+2\left|1-3\log_e\dfrac{3}{2}\right| &\approx 2.273907 \\ &\approx 2.2739 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right)=-\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x$.
items.sol:
Write $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}=(\sin x)^{-1}$ and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^{-1} \\ &= -1\times\cos x\times(\sin x)^{-2} \\ &= -\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x} \\ &= -\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x\,dx$. Give your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
From part (a), $-\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ is a primitive of $\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\left[\dfrac{1}{\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}\right] \\ &= -\left[1-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A cylinder is inscribed in a cone of radius 9 cm and perpendicular height 25 cm.

\exfigure{1322_q32_1}
Show that the perpendicular height $h$ of the cylinder is given by

$$h=\dfrac{25(9-r)}{9},$$

where $r$ is the radius of the cylinder.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1322_q32_s1}

In the cross-section, $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EDC$ are similar (common angle at $C$, both right-angled, equiangular).
$$\dfrac{EC}{AC}=\dfrac{ED}{AB}$$
with $EC=9-r$, $AC=9$, $ED=h$ and $AB=25$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{9-r}{9} &= \dfrac{h}{25} \\ h &= \dfrac{25(9-r)}{9} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A cylinder is inscribed in a cone of radius 9 cm and perpendicular height 25 cm.

\exfigure{1322_q32_1}
Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by

$$V=\dfrac{25\pi}{9}(9r^2-r^3)$$
items.sol:
The volume of a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$; substitute $h$ from part (a).
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \pi r^2\times\dfrac{25(9-r)}{9} \\ &= \dfrac{25\pi}{9}(9r^2-r^3) \end{aligned}$$

For a maximum, set $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dr}=\dfrac{25\pi}{9}(18r-3r^2)$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{25\pi}{9}(18r-3r^2) &= 0 \\ 3r(6-r) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $r=0$ or $r=6$. If $r=0$ cm, the cylinder doesn't exist, so $r=6$ cm.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2}=\dfrac{25\pi}{9}(18-6r)$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } r=6: \quad \dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2} &= \dfrac{25\pi}{9}(18-6\times 6) \\ &= -50\pi<0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $r=6$ gives the maximum volume.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{25\pi}{9}(9\times 6^2-6^3) \\ &= 300\pi \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ V_{\max}=300\pi \text{ cm}^3$$

items.part: Solve $|3x-8|=7$
items.sol:
For $|3x-8|=7$, either $3x-8=7$ or $3x-8=-7$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x-8&=7\\ 3x&=15\\ x&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3x-8&=-7\\ 3x&=1\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=5 \text{ or } x=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

items.part:
A circle has the equation $x^2-6x+y^2+4y+k=0$ for some constant $k$.

Find the set of possible values for $k$.
items.sol:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-6x+y^2+4y+k&=0\\ (x-3)^2-9+(y+2)^2-4+k&=0\\ (x-3)^2+(y+2)^2&=13-k\end{aligned}$$
This is a circle only if the right side (the radius squared) is positive.
$$13-k>0$$
$$\therefore\ k<13$$

items.part: If $\tan x=3$ and $\sin x<0$, find the exact value of $\cos x$.
items.sol:
Since $\tan x=3>0$ and $\sin x<0$, the angle $x$ is in the third quadrant, where $\cos x<0$.

Use a right-angled triangle with opposite $3$, adjacent $1$ and hypotenuse $\sqrt{1^2+3^2}=\sqrt{10}$. Then
$$\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$$

items.part:
Marios thinks about three distinct numbers $x$, $x+4$ and $9x$.

Find all possible sets of these three numbers if they are successive terms in a geometric series.
items.sol:
In a geometric series consecutive terms have equal ratios.
$$\dfrac{9x}{x+4}=\dfrac{x+4}{x}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 9x^2&=(x+4)^2\\ 9x^2&=x^2+8x+16\\ 8x^2-8x-16&=0\\ x^2-x-2&=0\\ (x-2)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=2$ or $x=-1$.

If $x=2$, the numbers are $2,\ 6,\ 18$.

If $x=-1$, the numbers are $-1,\ 3,\ -9$.

items.part:
Neve randomly selects two socks from a draw containing thirteen white socks and seven black socks without replacement.
Find the probability of selecting a matching pair of colours.
items.sol:
A matching pair is two white socks or two black socks.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{13}{20}\times\dfrac{12}{19}+\dfrac{7}{20}\times\dfrac{6}{19}\\ &=\dfrac{99}{190}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Neve randomly selects two socks from a draw containing thirteen white socks and seven black socks without replacement.
Find the probability of not selecting a pair of black socks.
items.sol:
Use the complement of selecting two black socks.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-\dfrac{7}{20}\times\dfrac{6}{19}\\ &=\dfrac{169}{190}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $2e^{2x}-e^x=0$
items.sol:
Factorise:
$$e^x\left(2e^x-1\right)=0$$
Since $e^x\ne 0$, we need $2e^x-1=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ x&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=-\ln 2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Three people play a game that involves collecting apples that are placed $4$ m apart. The first apple is placed $6$ m from point $P$. Players collect the closest apple, then return it to the bucket before collecting the next closest apple and so on.

\exfigure{1323_q17_1}
When collecting her last apple, Hannah ran $130$ m from point $P$ to the apple.

How many apples did she collect in total?
items.sol:
The distances to the apples form an arithmetic sequence with first term $a=6$ and common difference $d=4$.

The $n$th term is $T_n=a+(n-1)d$. Setting $T_n=130$:
$$\begin{aligned} 130&=6+(n-1)\times 4\\ 124&=4n-4\\ n&=32\end{aligned}$$
She collected $32$ apples.

Each apple needs a return trip, so the distances run are $12, 20, 28, \dots$, an arithmetic series with $a=12$, $d=8$ and $n=41$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{41}&=\dfrac{41}{2}\left[24+8(41-1)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{41}{2}\left[24+320\right]\\ &=7052 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

Using the same series ($a=12$, $d=8$) with sum $42\,432$:
$$\begin{aligned} 42\,432&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[24+8(n-1)\right]\\ 84\,864&=24n+8n^2-8n\\ 0&=8n^2+16n-84\,864\\ 0&=n^2+2n-10\,608\\ 0&=(n+104)(n-102)\end{aligned}$$
So $n=-104$ or $n=102$.

Since $n>0$, $n\ne -104$.

$$\therefore\ \text{Luke collected } 102 \text{ apples}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos 3x\,dx$
items.sol: $$\int \cos 3x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x+C$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{5x-1}\,dx$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned}\int_0^1 e^{5x-1}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{5}\left[e^{5x-1}\right]_0^1\\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}\left(e^4-\dfrac{1}{e}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{e^4}{5}-\dfrac{1}{5e}\\ &=\dfrac{e^5-1}{5e}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta$
items.sol:
Take the left-hand side and use the common denominator $\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)$.
$$\begin{aligned}LHS&=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}+\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta+1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}\\ &=\dfrac{2+2\cos\theta}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)} &&(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1)\\ &=\dfrac{2(1+\cos\theta)}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{\sin\theta}\\ &=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\\ &=RHS\end{aligned}$$

The area under the curve from $x=0$ to $x=1$ is
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,(1-x)\,dx\\ &=\int_0^1\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}-x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-\dfrac{2x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}\right]_0^1\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{15} \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Maddie owns a company, and has noticed that the profits have been decreasing each year, by $8\%$ of the previous years' profit. In 2013, her company made a profit of \$100\,000.
How much profit will the company make in 2022?
items.sol:
The profits form a geometric sequence with $a=100\,000$ and $r=1-0.08=0.92$.

2022 is the 10th year, so
$$\begin{aligned}T_{10}&=100\,000\,(0.92)^9\\ &\approx \$47\,216.14\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Maddie owns a company, and has noticed that the profits have been decreasing each year, by $8\%$ of the previous years' profit. In 2013, her company made a profit of \$100\,000.
In total, how much profit has been made in the ten-year period from 2013 to 2022 inclusive?
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ with $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{10}&=\dfrac{100\,000\left(1-0.92^{10}\right)}{1-0.92}\\ &\approx \$707\,014.43\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Maddie owns a company, and has noticed that the profits have been decreasing each year, by $8\%$ of the previous years' profit. In 2013, her company made a profit of \$100\,000.
If this trend continues, what is the total amount of profit the company will make?
items.sol:
Since $|r|=0.92<1$, the limiting sum exists, with $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{100\,000}{1-0.92}\\ &=\$1\,250\,000\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x\sin x$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
items.sol:
Differentiating using the product rule:
$$y'=\sin x+x\cos x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, the tangent gradient is
$$\begin{aligned} m_T &= \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-1$.

The $y$ value at this point is
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{\pi}{2} &= -1\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ y &= -x+\pi \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=-x+\pi$$

items.part:
Bowen is an archaeologist and he is excavating a rectangular site with dimensions of $150$ metres by $60$ metres, as shown below. The site is divided into $8$ equal rectangles.

\exfigure{1323_q25_1}

The shaded region indicates the portion of the site that has been excavated.

Using the trapezoidal rule in your working, calculate the percentage of the site that is yet to be excavated, to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
Trapezoidal rule with strip width $37.5$ m (the length $150$ m divided into $4$ strips) and the measured widths as shown:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Excavated} &\approx \dfrac{37.5}{2}\Big(0+0+2(42+59+36)\Big) \\ &= 5137.5 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The total area is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 60\times150 \\ &= 9000 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The area yet to be excavated is
$$\begin{aligned} 9000-5137.5 &= 3862.5 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
As a percentage of the site:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3862.5}{9000}\times100 &\approx 43\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 43\% \text{ is yet to be excavated}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{6x}{\left(3x^2+1\right)^4}\,dx$ to 3 decimal places
items.sol:
Rewrite the integrand as a power and integrate (reverse chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 6x\left(3x^2+1\right)^{-4}dx &= \left[\dfrac{\left(3x^2+1\right)^{-3}}{-3}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{13^{-3}}{-3}-\dfrac{1^{-3}}{-3} \\ &\approx 0.333 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0.333$$

Completed table: the $xp(x)$ row is $0,\ 0.15,\ 0.4,\ 0.75,\ 0.2$ and the $x^2p(x)$ row is $0,\ 0.15,\ 0.8,\ 2.25,\ 0.8$.

The mean is the sum of the $xp(x)$ row:
$$\mu=1.5$$
Using $\text{Var}(X)=\sum x^2p(x)-\mu^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= 4-1.5^2 \\ &= 1.75 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Var}(X)=1.75$$

Rishi: $\sigma=1.4$.

Jeremy: $\sigma=\sqrt{1.75}\approx1.32$.

Jeremy has the lower standard deviation, so Jeremy is more consistent.
items.final: Jeremy is more consistent (lower standard deviation, $\approx1.32<1.4$)

items.part: Julie sells lolly bags at a market stall. The bags have a mean weight of $105$ g and a standard deviation of $2.5$ g. Julie offers a money back refund for any bag under $100$ g. If the weights are normally distributed, and she sells $200$ lolly bags, how many times will she have to refund customers?
items.sol:
The $z$-score for $100$ g is
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{100-105}{2.5} \\ &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule, about $2.5\%$ of bags weigh under $100$ g.
$$\begin{aligned} 2.5\%\times200 &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 5 \text{ refunds}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=7+4x^3-3x^4$
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 12x^2-12x^3 \\ &= 12x^2(1-x)=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$, giving the points $(0,7)$ and $(1,8)$.

The second derivative is
$$y''=24x-36x^2$$
At $x=1$: $y''=-12<0$, so $(1,8)$ is a maximum turning point.

At $x=0$: $y''=0$, so test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{aligned} x=-1:&\ y''=-60 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=0:&\ y''=0 &&\\ x=\dfrac12:&\ y''=3 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at $x=0$, so $(0,7)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
$$\therefore\ (0,7)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion and }(1,8)\text{ is a maximum turning point}$$
items.final: $(0,7)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion and $(1,8)$ is a maximum turning point
