items.part:
Consider the curve $y=7+4x^3-3x^4$
Find any values of $x$ such that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}>0$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0$.
items.sol:
For $y''<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 24x-36x^2 &< 0 \\ 12x(2-3x) &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x<0$ or $x>\dfrac{2}{3}$.

For $y'>0$: $12x^2(1-x)>0$, so $x<1$ and $x\ne0$.

Combining both conditions:
$$\therefore\ x<0 \text{ or } \dfrac{2}{3}<x<1$$

items.part:
Nathan recorded the time people spent training (in hours) and the times they ran (in minutes) in the Sutherland to Surf running race.

\extable{1323_q30_t1}
Find the equation of line of best fit (regression line) in the form $y=Bx+A$.

Round the values of $A$ and $B$ to 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
Using the regression function on the data:
$$y=-0.4x+59.9$$

Substitute $x=22$ into the regression line:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -0.4\times22+59.9 \\ &\approx 51 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

Substitute $y=80$:
$$\begin{aligned} 80 &= -0.4x+59.9 \\ 20.1 &= -0.4x \\ x &= -50.25 \end{aligned}$$
Negative training hours is not possible, which suggests extrapolating the data is not valid.
items.final: $x=-50.25$ hours; negative training hours is not possible, so extrapolating is not valid

items.part:
The rate at which the depth of water changes in a bay is given by $R=4\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{6}$ m/h.
When Maya goes swimming in the bay, the depth is initially $2$ m.

Find an equation for the depth of water, $d$ metres, over time $t$ hours.
items.sol:
Depth is the integral of the rate:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \int 4\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\,dt \\ &= -\dfrac{24\pi}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+C \\ &= -24\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$ and $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= -24+C \\ C &= 26 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ d=-24\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+26$$

items.part:
The rate at which the depth of water changes in a bay is given by $R=4\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{6}$ m/h.
Georgia goes swimming $3$ hours after Maya. Find the depth of water at this time.
items.sol:
At $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= -24\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+26 \\ &= 26 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact area enclosed between the curve $y=\log_e x$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=1$ and $y=3$.
items.sol:
The area is between the curve and the $y$-axis, so integrate with respect to $y$. Since $y=\log_e x$, we have $x=e^y$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_1^3 e^y\,dy \\ &= \left[e^y\right]_1^3 \\ &= \left(e^3-e\right) \text{ units}^2 \\ &= e\left(e^2-1\right) \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Chloe records the lifespan of termites, and determines the that the number of weeks a termite lives can be modelled by the function:

$$f(x)=\dfrac{4}{5}-\dfrac{x^2}{45}\qquad \text{for } 3\le x\le 6$$
Show that $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
items.sol:
A PDF must integrate to $1$ over its domain (and $f(x)\ge0$ there).
$$\begin{aligned} \int_3^6\left(\dfrac{4}{5}-\dfrac{x^2}{45}\right)dx &= \left[\dfrac{4x}{5}-\dfrac{x^3}{135}\right]_3^6 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{24}{5}-\dfrac{216}{135}\right)-\left(\dfrac{12}{5}-\dfrac{27}{135}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{16}{5}-\dfrac{11}{5} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore $f(x)$ is a PDF.

items.part:
Chloe records the lifespan of termites, and determines the that the number of weeks a termite lives can be modelled by the function:

$$f(x)=\dfrac{4}{5}-\dfrac{x^2}{45}\qquad \text{for } 3\le x\le 6$$
Find the CDF (Cumulative Distribution Function).
items.sol:
The CDF is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_3^x f(t)\,dt$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \left[\dfrac{4t}{5}-\dfrac{t^3}{135}\right]_3^x \\ &= \dfrac{4x}{5}-\dfrac{x^3}{135}-\dfrac{11}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{108x-x^3-297}{135} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Chloe records the lifespan of termites, and determines the that the number of weeks a termite lives can be modelled by the function:

$$f(x)=\dfrac{4}{5}-\dfrac{x^2}{45}\qquad \text{for } 3\le x\le 6$$
Find the mean lifespan of a termite
items.sol:
The mean is $\mu=\displaystyle\int_3^6 xf(x)\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= \left[\dfrac{4x^2}{10}-\dfrac{x^4}{180}\right]_3^6 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{144}{10}-\dfrac{1296}{180}\right)-\left(\dfrac{36}{10}-\dfrac{81}{180}\right) \\ &= 4.05 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Pete worked in a National Park in 1942 and he introduced $18$ koalas to the park. By 2002, the number of koalas had grown to $5000$. The number of koalas has grown exponentially according to the rule $N=N_0e^{kt}$, where $t$ is the number of years since 1942. $N_0$ represents the initial amount of koalas and $k$ is a constant. By first finding these values, predict the number of koalas expected to be in the National Park in 2022.
items.sol:
The initial number is $N_0=18$.

In 2002, $t=60$ and $N=5000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5000 &= 18e^{60k} \\ \dfrac{5000}{18} &= e^{60k} \\ 60k &= \log_e\left(\dfrac{5000}{18}\right) \\ k &= 0.0937\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $N=18e^{0.0937\ldots t}$.

In 2022, $t=80$:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 18e^{0.0937\ldots\times80} \\ &\approx 32\,624 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 32\,624 \text{ koalas}$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1323_q35_1}

Kate has an irregular shaped backyard as seen in the diagram above by shape $ABCD$.

The sector $BCD$ has a centre $B$, whilst $AB=AD=3$ m.
Show that the length of $DB$ is $3\sqrt{3}$ m.
items.sol:
In triangle $ABD$, $AB=AD$, so the base angles are equal. $\angle ABD=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ (from the figure, as $\angle DBC=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$) and $\angle ADB=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Hence $\angle DAB=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $ABD$:
$$\begin{aligned} DB^2 &= 3^2+3^2-2\times3^2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \\ &= 27 \\ DB &= 3\sqrt{3} \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1323_q35_1}

Kate has an irregular shaped backyard as seen in the diagram above by shape $ABCD$.

The sector $BCD$ has a centre $B$, whilst $AB=AD=3$ m.
Find the total area of the backyard in exact form.
items.sol:
Area of triangle $ABD$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times3^2\times\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{9}{2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Area of sector $BCD$ (radius $3\sqrt{3}$, angle $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times\left(3\sqrt{3}\right)^2\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6} &= \dfrac{135\pi}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{45\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Adding:
$$\therefore\ \text{Total}=\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}+45\pi}{4} \text{ m}^2$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has a displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ m/s. Initially the particle is at $O$.
Use integration to show that $x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\right)dt \\ &= \dfrac{3(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C \\ &= 2(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$ and $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2-0+C \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has a displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ m/s. Initially the particle is at $O$.
Find when the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
At rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1} &= 9 \\ \sqrt{t+1} &= 3 \\ t+1 &= 9 \\ t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest at } t=8 \text{ seconds}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has a displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ m/s. Initially the particle is at $O$.
Find the distance travelled in the first $24$ seconds of its motion.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction at $t=8$, so find the positions at $t=8$ and $t=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(8) &= 2(9)(3)-72-2 \\ &= -20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x(24) &= 2(25)(5)-216-2 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
From $0$ to $-20$ is $20$ m, then from $-20$ to $32$ is $52$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total distance} &= 20+20+32 \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An isosceles triangle $ABC$, where $AC=BC$, is inscribed in a circle of radius $10$ cm.

$OP=x$ and $OP$ bisects $AB$ such that $AB\perp OP$.

\exfigure{1323_q37_1}
Show that $A$, the area of triangle $ABC$, is given by $A=(10+x)\sqrt{100-x^2}$
items.sol:
In right-angled triangle $OPB$, Pythagoras' theorem gives
$$\begin{aligned} PB^2 &= 10^2-x^2 \\ PB &= \sqrt{100-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Since $OP$ bisects $AB$, $AB=2\sqrt{100-x^2}$.

The height of the triangle is $x+10$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times2\sqrt{100-x^2}\times(x+10) \\ &= (10+x)\sqrt{100-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An isosceles triangle $ABC$, where $AC=BC$, is inscribed in a circle of radius $10$ cm.

$OP=x$ and $OP$ bisects $AB$ such that $AB\perp OP$.

\exfigure{1323_q37_1}
Find $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$, leaving your answer as a single simplified fraction

An isosceles triangle $ABC$, where $AC=BC$, is inscribed in a circle of radius $10$ cm.

$OP=x$ and $OP$ bisects $AB$ such that $AB\perp OP$.

\exfigure{1323_q37_1}
Prove that the triangle with a maximum area is equilateral
items.sol:
For a maximum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$-2(x+10)(x-5)=0$$
So $x=-10$ or $x=5$. Since $x>0$ is a distance, $x\ne-10$, so $x=5$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side:
$$\begin{aligned} x=4:&\ \dfrac{dA}{dx}\approx3.1 &&\text{increasing}\\ x=5:&\ \dfrac{dA}{dx}=0 &&\\ x=6:&\ \dfrac{dA}{dx}\approx-4 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=5$ gives a maximum.

When $x=5$: $AB=2\sqrt{75}=10\sqrt{3}$, $AP=5\sqrt{3}$ and the height is $15$.

In right-angled triangle $APC$:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= \left(5\sqrt{3}\right)^2+15^2 \\ &= 300 \\ AC &= 10\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
So $AC=CB=AB$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the triangle of maximum area is equilateral}$$

items.part: Find the 10th term of this sequence.
items.sol:
The sequence has $a = 7$ and common difference $d = 11 - 7 = 4$.

Using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= 7 + (10-1)\times 4 \\ &= 43 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Is $113$ a term in this sequence? Justify your answer by performing appropriate calculations.
items.sol:
Suppose $T_n = 113$, using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 7 + (n-1)\times 4 &= 113 \\ (n-1)\times 4 &= 106 \\ n - 1 &= 26.5 \\ n &= 27.5 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ must be a whole number, $113$ is not a term of the sequence.
items.final: 113 is not a term of the sequence, since $n = 27.5$ is not a whole number

items.part: Find the value of the first term and show that the common difference is $6$.
items.sol:
Using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$ for the fifth term:
$$a + 4d = 21 \qquad (1)$$
Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$ for the first five terms:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5}{2}(2a + 4d) &= 45 \\ 2a + 4d &= 18 \\ a + 2d &= 9 \qquad (2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (2) from (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 2d &= 12 \\ d &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $d = 6$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a + 4(6) &= 21 \\ a &= -3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = -3 \text{ and } d = 6$$

items.part: Hence, determine the minimum number of terms required to obtain a sum greater than $600$.
items.sol:
With $a = -3$ and $d = 6$, the sum of $n$ terms is
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(-3) + (n-1)6\right] \\ &= n(3n - 6) \\ &= 3n^2 - 6n \end{aligned}$$
We need $S_n > 600$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3n^2 - 6n &> 600 \\ n^2 - 2n - 200 &> 0 \end{aligned}$$
Solve $n^2 - 2n - 200 = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 800}}{2} \\ &= 15.18\ldots \text{ or } -13.18\ldots \end{aligned}$$
The parabola is positive for $n > 15.18\ldots$ or $n < -13.18\ldots$, and the second is impossible as $n > 0$.

Since $n$ is a whole number, the minimum number of terms is $16$.

items.part:
Consider the geometric series $1 + \left(1 - \sqrt{e}\right) + \left(1 - \sqrt{e}\right)^2 + \cdots$
Explain why this geometric series has a limiting sum?
items.sol:
The common ratio is
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{1 - \sqrt{e}}{1} \\ &= 1 - \sqrt{e} \\ &\approx -0.648 \end{aligned}$$
So $|r| \approx 0.648 < 1$.

Since $|r| < 1$, the geometric series has a limiting sum.
items.final: Since $|r| \approx 0.648 < 1$, the series has a limiting sum

items.part:
Consider the geometric series $1 + \left(1 - \sqrt{e}\right) + \left(1 - \sqrt{e}\right)^2 + \cdots$
Find the value of the limiting sum in terms of $e$.
items.sol:
Using $S = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a = 1$ and $r = 1 - \sqrt{e}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{1}{1 - (1 - \sqrt{e})} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{e}} \end{aligned}$$

The lengths above the ground form a geometric series $0.3 + 0.6 + \cdots$ with $a = 0.3$, $r = 2$ and $n = 10$.

Using $S_n = \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{0.3(2^{10} - 1)}{2 - 1} \\ &= 306.9 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Each of the $10$ posts is imbedded $0.2$ m:
$$0.2 \times 10 = 2 \text{ m}$$
Total length of steel:
$$\begin{aligned} 306.9 + 2 &= 308.9 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $\dfrac{(x+3)^2}{e^{2x}}$ and simplify your answer.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x+3)^2 & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=2(x+3) & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{e^{2x}\cdot 2(x+3) - (x+3)^2\cdot 2e^{2x}}{\left(e^{2x}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2e^{2x}(x+3)\left[1 - (x+3)\right]}{\left(e^{2x}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2(x+3)(-x-2)}{e^{2x}} \\ &= -\dfrac{2(x+3)(x+2)}{e^{2x}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $e^{2x} - 2e^x - 15 = 0$ for $x$.
items.sol:
Let $y = e^x$, so the equation becomes a quadratic in $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} y^2 - 2y - 15 &= 0 \\ (y - 5)(y + 3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $y = 5$ or $y = -3$.

That is, $e^x = 5$ or $e^x = -3$.

Since $e^x > 0$ for all $x$, $e^x = -3$ has no solution.
$$\therefore\ x = \ln 5$$

items.part: Solve the equation $2^{2x} = 5^{2x-1}$ for $x$. Leave your answer to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
Take natural logs of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x\ln 2 &= (2x - 1)\ln 5 \\ 2x\ln 2 &= 2x\ln 5 - \ln 5 \\ \ln 5 &= 2x\ln 5 - 2x\ln 2 \\ &= 2x(\ln 5 - \ln 2) \end{aligned}$$
Since $\ln 5 - \ln 2 = \ln 2.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{\ln 5}{2\ln 2.5} \\ &\approx 0.878\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \approx 0.88 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
Sketch the graph of $y = -e^x + 2$ on the axes given below. Label asymptotes with their equations and axis intercepts with their coordinates.

\exfigure{636_q12_1}
items.sol:
The graph is $y = -e^x + 2$.

As $x \to -\infty$, $e^x \to 0$, so $y \to 2$: the horizontal asymptote is $y = 2$.

When $x = 0$: $y = -1 + 2 = 1$.

When $y = 0$: $e^x = 2$, so $x = \ln 2$.

items.part:
The number of bacteria in a sample of water from an infested lake is increasing by 6% per hour. Initially, there were 2500 bacteria when testing started.
Write an equation that represents the number of bacteria after $t$ hours.
items.sol:
The number of bacteria is multiplied by $1.06$ each hour, starting from $2500$:
$$N = 2500(1.06)^t$$
where $N$ is the number of bacteria and $t$ is in hours.

items.part:
The number of bacteria in a sample of water from an infested lake is increasing by 6% per hour. Initially, there were 2500 bacteria when testing started.
How many bacteria are present after 2 days?
items.sol:
$2$ days is $48$ hours, so $t = 48$:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 2500(1.06)^{48} \\ &= 40\,984.67\ldots \\ &\approx 40\,985 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of bacteria in a sample of water from an infested lake is increasing by 6% per hour. Initially, there were 2500 bacteria when testing started.
A pesticide was introduced 10 hours after the initial count. The pesticide has a positive result in controlling the growth of bacteria. Instead of increasing, bacteria count started reducing by 8% per hour. During which hour from the initial count, will the number of bacteria be reduced to 700?
items.sol:
After $10$ hours the number is $2500(1.06)^{10}$. After that it falls by $8\%$ each hour, so it is multiplied by $0.92$ each hour:
$$N = 2500(1.06)^{10}(0.92)^n$$
where $n$ is the number of hours since the pesticide was introduced.

Set $N = 700$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2500(1.06)^{10}(0.92)^n &= 700 \\ (0.92)^n &= \dfrac{700}{2500(1.06)^{10}} \\ &= 0.28(1.06)^{-10} \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln\left[0.28(1.06)^{-10}\right]}{\ln 0.92} \\ &\approx 22.25 \end{aligned}$$
The total time from the start is $10 + 22.25 = 32.25$ hours, which is during the $33$rd hour.
$$\therefore\ \text{the } 33\text{rd hour from the start}$$

items.part: Given that $\log 4 + \log 16 + \log 64 + \cdots + \log 16384 = a\log b$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers and $b$ is a prime number.
items.sol:
Write each number as a power of $2$ and use $\log 2^k = k\log 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} &\log 4 + \log 16 + \log 64 + \cdots + \log 16384 \\ &= \log 2^2 + \log 2^4 + \log 2^6 + \cdots + \log 2^{14} \\ &= 2\log 2 + 4\log 2 + 6\log 2 + \cdots + 14\log 2 \\ &= \log 2\left[2 + 4 + 6 + \cdots + 14\right] \end{aligned}$$
The bracket is an arithmetic series with first term $2$, last term $14$ and common difference $2$, so $n = \dfrac{14}{2} = 7$.

Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_7 &= \dfrac{7}{2}(2 + 14) \\ &= 56 \end{aligned}$$
So the sum is $56\log 2$.
$$\therefore\ a = 56,\ b = 2$$

items.part: The point $A(-1, 4)$ lies on the graph of the function $f(x)$. Find the image of $A$ on $g(x) = 4f(-x) + 2$ .
items.sol:
For $g(x)=4f(-x)+2$, the point $(a,b)$ on $f$ maps to $\left(-a,\ 4b+2\right)$.

For $A(-1,4)$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= -(-1) = 1 \\ y &= 4\times 4 + 2 = 18 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the image is } (1, 18)$$

items.part: List a set of transformations that, when applied in order, would transform $y = x^3$ to the graph with equation $y = (2x-2)^3 + 3$.
items.sol:
Factorise to show the order of the transformations:
$$y=(2x-2)^3+3 = \left[2(x-1)\right]^3+3$$
The transformations, in order, are:

1. Dilate horizontally by scale factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

2. Translate right by 1 unit.

3. Translate up by 3 units.
items.final: Dilate horizontally by factor $\tfrac12$, translate right 1 unit, translate up 3 units

items.sol:
The $y$-intercept is found at $x=0$.

The point of inflection $(0,0)$ of $y=x^3$ is moved by the transformations in part (a) to $(1,3)$.

items.part: Sketch the graph of $y = 1 - \dfrac{6}{x+3}$ showing the asymptotes and the $x$ and $y$-intercepts.
items.sol:
Write $y = -\dfrac{6}{x+3}+1$.

Vertical asymptote: $x=-3$.

Horizontal asymptote: $y=1$.

The $y$-intercept is found at $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 1 - \dfrac{6}{3} \\ &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
The $x$-intercept is found at $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= \dfrac{6}{x+3} \\ x+3 &= 6 \\ x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A data analytics company is programming a system to distinguish between humans and bots in an online video game. The company gathers data on 100 human players. The average number of mouse clicks per minute for these 100 players is shown in the frequency table below.

\extable{634_q17_t1}
The company is considering flagging accounts whose number of clicks per minute qualifies as an outlier according to the data gathered.

What are the ranges of number of clicks per minute that would qualify as an outlier?
items.sol:
An outlier lies below $Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR$ or above $Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR &= 50 - 1.5\times 30 \\ &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR &= 80 + 1.5\times 30 \\ &= 125 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{outliers are scores less than } 5 \text{ or greater than } 125$$
items.final: Outliers are less than 5 or greater than 125 clicks per minute.

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$y = \tan(5x - 3)$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan u = \sec^2 u \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}$ with $u = 5x-3$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 5\sec^2(5x-3)$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$y = e^{\sin x}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u} = e^{u}\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}$ with $u = \sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= e^{\sin x}\cdot\cos x \\ &= \cos x\, e^{\sin x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$y = \ln\left(\dfrac{3x+2}{x-4}\right)$
items.sol:
Using the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b} = \ln a - \ln b$:
$$y = \ln(3x+2) - \ln(x-4)$$
Differentiating, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u = \dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{3}{3x+2} - \dfrac{1}{x-4} \\ &= \dfrac{3(x-4)-(3x+2)}{(3x+2)(x-4)} \\ &= \dfrac{-14}{(3x+2)(x-4)} \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, use $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ where $f(x) = \dfrac{3x+2}{x-4}$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x+2 & v&=x-4\\ u'&=3 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{3(x-4)-(3x+2)}{(x-4)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-14}{(x-4)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{\frac{-14}{(x-4)^2}}{\frac{3x+2}{x-4}} \\ &= \dfrac{-14}{(x-4)(3x+2)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$y = 2^x x^2$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2^x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=2^x\ln 2 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \ln(2)\,x^2\,2^x + 2x\cdot 2^x$$

items.part:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{e^{3x+4}}$.

Prove that $f'(x) = \dfrac{1-3x}{e^{3x+4}}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{3x+4}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3e^{3x+4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{e^{3x+4} - 3x\,e^{3x+4}}{\left(e^{3x+4}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^{3x+4}(1-3x)}{\left(e^{3x+4}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1-3x}{e^{3x+4}} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Let $g(x) = \cos^2\left(6x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

Find the exact value of $g'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)$.
items.sol:
Write $g(x) = \left[\cos\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]^2$ and apply the chain rule twice.
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x) &= 2\cos\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\times\left(-\sin\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\times 6 \\ &= -12\cos\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\sin\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$, where $6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right) &= -12\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= -12\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= -3\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent of $y = \dfrac{1}{e^{5x-10}}$ at $x = 2$.
items.sol:
Rewrite using index laws:
$$y = e^{-(5x-10)} = e^{-5x+10}$$
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -5e^{-5x+10}$$
At $x=2$, the gradient is
$$\begin{aligned} m &= -5e^{-5(2)+10} \\ &= -5e^0 \\ &= -5 \end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$, the $y$ value is
$$\begin{aligned} y &= e^{-5\times 2+10} \\ &= e^0 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
so the point is $(2,1)$.

Using $y - y_1 = m(x-x_1)$:
$$y - 1 = -5(x-2)$$

items.part:
The brand new u-Phone 15 was released by Orange inc. at the beginning of 2022. While the production of the u-Phone 15 started slowly, it increased at a rapid rate, and is modelled by the function $f(t) = e^{4t} + 10000$, where $t$ is the number of years after 2022 ($t = 0$ is the beginning of 2022).

While demand for the phones started quite small, the marketing campaign was quite successful, and soon more and more people wanted to get their own u-Phone 15. The demand for the u-Phone is modelled by the function $g(t)$ where $g(t) = f'(t)$, the derivative of the production of the phones.
After how many days does the demand for the u-Phone 15 overtake the number of phones that have been produced?
items.sol:
Demand overtakes production when $g(t) = f(t)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4e^{4t} &= e^{4t} + 10000 \\ 3e^{4t} &= 10000 \\ e^{4t} &= \dfrac{10000}{3} \\ 4t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{10000}{3}\right) \\ t &\approx 2.03 \text{ years} \end{aligned}$$
Converting to days:
$$2.0279\ldots\times 365 \approx 740 \text{ days}$$

items.part:
The line $y = mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$ at a point $P$.
Show that the coordinates of $P$ is $(3, -e)$.
items.sol:
The curve is $y = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$, so
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$$
At $P$ the line and curve meet, and $m$ equals the gradient of the curve:
$$mx = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x},\qquad m = -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$$
Substituting $m$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{\frac{1}{3}x}\times x &= -e^{\frac{1}{3}x} \\ -\dfrac{1}{3}x &= -1 \\ x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
(dividing by $-e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$, which is never zero).

At $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -e^{\frac{1}{3}\times 3} \\ &= -e \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the coordinates of } P \text{ are } (3,-e)$$

items.part:
The line $y = mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$ at a point $P$.
Find the exact value of $m$.
items.sol:
The point $(3,-e)$ lies on $y = mx$.
$$\begin{aligned} -e &= 3m \\ m &= -\dfrac{e}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $x+\dfrac{x-4}{3}=2$.
items.sol:
Multiply both sides by 3 to clear the fraction.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x+x-4&=6\\ 4x-4&=6\\ 4x&=10\\ x&=\dfrac{5}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5}{2}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\leq t\leq 14\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for } 0\leq t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$
Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$.
items.sol:
For a probability density function the total area is 1:
$$\displaystyle\int_1^{14}\dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k}{2}\ln|2t-1|\right]_1^{14}&=1\\ \dfrac{k}{2}\left(\ln 27-\ln 1\right)&=1\\ \dfrac{k}{2}\ln 27&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\leq t\leq 14\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for } 0\leq t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$
After how many days will a person have a 75% chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?
items.sol:
The cumulative distribution must reach $0.75$:
$$F(t)=\displaystyle\int_1^{t}f(u)\,du=0.75$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{\ln 27}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln|2t-1|-\ln 1\right]&=0.75\\ \ln|2t-1|&=0.75\ln 27\\ 2t-1&=e^{0.75\ln 27}\\ t&=\dfrac{e^{0.75\ln 27}+1}{2}\\ &\approx 6.42 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 6.42\text{ days}$$

items.part: What are the possible values of $a$ if $1+2a+4a^2+8a^3+\cdots$ is to have a limiting sum?
items.sol:
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.

Here $r=2a$, so
$$\begin{aligned} |2a|&<1\\ -1&<2a<1\\ -\dfrac{1}{2}&<a<\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{1}{2}<a<\dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x^2+4x-7$ at the point $(1,-2)$
items.sol:
Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x+4$$
At $x=1$ the tangent gradient is $6$, so the normal gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y+2&=-\dfrac{1}{6}(x-1)\\ y&=-\dfrac{1}{6}x-\dfrac{11}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x+6y+11=0$$

items.part:
A curve is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}x^4-2x^2+1$.

Sketch the graph of the curve for the domain $[-3,3]$ showing all key features including, classifying the nature of stationary points, and finding any points of inflection. Also state where the curve is concave down. You do not need to find the $x$-intercepts
items.sol:
The $y$-intercept is $f(0)=1$.

Stationary points: $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x)=x^3-4x=x(x^2-4)=0$$
So $x=0,\ \pm2$, giving $(0,1)$, $(2,-3)$ and $(-2,-3)$.

Nature, using the second derivative $f''(x)=3x^2-4$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=-4<0 &&\text{local maximum at }(0,1)\\ f''(\pm2)&=8>0 &&\text{local minima at }(\pm2,-3) \end{aligned}$$
Possible inflection: $f''(x)=0$ gives $x=\pm\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\approx\pm1.15$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&>0 &&\text{for } x<-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\text{ and } x>\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3} &&\text{concave up}\\ f''(x)&<0 &&\text{for } -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}<x<\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3} &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at both, so $\left(\pm\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3},-\dfrac{11}{9}\right)$ are points of inflection.

End points: $f(\pm3)=3.25$, so $(\pm3,3.25)$.

\exfigure{635_q15_s1}

$$\therefore\ \text{the curve is concave down for } -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}<x<\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$$

items.part:
James has some sticks that are all of the same length. He arranges them in squares and has made the following 3 rows of patterns.

\exfigure{635_q17_1}

He notices that 4 sticks are required to make the single square in the first row, 7 sticks in the second row and in the third row he needs 10 sticks to make 3 squares.
Find an expression, in terms of $n$, for the number of sticks required to make a similar arrangement of $n$ squares in the $n^{\text{th}}$ row.
items.sol:
The first row uses 4 sticks and each extra square adds 3 sticks, so this is an arithmetic sequence with $a=4$, $d=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n&=4+(n-1)\times3\\ &=3n+1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
James has some sticks that are all of the same length. He arranges them in squares and has made the following 3 rows of patterns.

\exfigure{635_q17_1}

He notices that 4 sticks are required to make the single square in the first row, 7 sticks in the second row and in the third row he needs 10 sticks to make 3 squares.
James continues to make squares following the same pattern. He makes 4 squares in the fourth row and so on until he has completed 10 rows. Find the total number of sticks James uses in making these 10 rows.
items.sol:
The total is the sum of the first 10 terms of the arithmetic sequence with $a=4$, $d=3$, $n=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10}&=\dfrac{10}{2}\left[2\times4+(10-1)\times3\right]\\ &=5(8+27)\\ &=175\text{ sticks} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
James has some sticks that are all of the same length. He arranges them in squares and has made the following 3 rows of patterns.

\exfigure{635_q17_1}

He notices that 4 sticks are required to make the single square in the first row, 7 sticks in the second row and in the third row he needs 10 sticks to make 3 squares.
James started with 1750 sticks. Given that James continues the pattern to complete $k$ rows but does not have sufficient sticks to complete the $(k+1)^{\text{th}}$ row. Show that $k$ satisfies $(3k-100)(k+35)<0$.
items.sol:
Completing $k$ rows uses $S_k$ sticks, which must be less than 1750 for the $k$ rows to be possible (and the next row cannot be completed).
$$\begin{aligned} S_k=\dfrac{k}{2}\left[2\times4+(k-1)\times3\right]&<1750\\ k(8+3k-3)&<3500\\ 3k^2+5k-3500&<0\\ 3k^2+105k-100k-3500&<0\\ 3k(k+35)-100(k+35)&<0\\ (3k-100)(k+35)&<0 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
James has some sticks that are all of the same length. He arranges them in squares and has made the following 3 rows of patterns.

\exfigure{635_q17_1}

He notices that 4 sticks are required to make the single square in the first row, 7 sticks in the second row and in the third row he needs 10 sticks to make 3 squares.
What is the value of $k$?
items.sol:
Since $k+35>0$ for $k\geq0$, the inequality $(3k-100)(k+35)<0$ needs $3k-100<0$.
$$0\leq k<\dfrac{100}{3}=33\dfrac{1}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ k=33$$

items.part:
Find the value of $k$ such that

$$\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{x^2}{x^3-2}\,dx=\ln k$$
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator $x^3-2$, so use $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3-2}\,dx&=\ln k\\ \dfrac{1}{3}\left[\ln|x^3-2|\right]_{-2}^{0}&=\ln k\\ \ln 2-\ln 10&=3\ln k\\ \ln\dfrac{2}{10}&=\ln k^3\\ k^3&=\dfrac{1}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{5}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{5}}$$

The sign for ‘Pizza $\pi$’ restaurant is in the shape of a circle with a sector cut out of it. The sector has an angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. If the area of the sign is $30\pi$, what is the radius of the circle?
items.sol:
The sign is a sector with the $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ sector removed, so its angle is
$$2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$
Using the sector area $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\times\dfrac{5\pi}{3}&=30\pi\\ r^2&=\dfrac{30\pi\times6}{5\pi}\\ &=36 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r=6\text{ units (since } r>0)$$

items.part: For what values of $k$ does the quadratic equation $5x^2-2x+(8k-15)=0$ have real roots?
items.sol:
Here $a=5$, $b=-2$, $c=8k-15$. The roots are real when the discriminant $\Delta\ge 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} (-2)^2-4\times5\times(8k-15) &\ge 0\\ 304-160k &\ge 0\\ k &\le \dfrac{304}{160}=\dfrac{19}{10}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k\le\dfrac{19}{10}$$

items.part:
Differentiate with respect to $x$
$e^{x\sin 2x}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{u}\right)=e^{u}\dfrac{du}{dx}$ with $u=x\sin 2x$. The product rule gives $\dfrac{du}{dx}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 2x}\right)&=e^{x\sin 2x}\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 2x)\\ &=e^{x\sin 2x}\left[\sin 2x+2x\cos 2x\right]\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate with respect to $x$
$\dfrac{x^2}{\ln(x)}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{\ln x}\right)=\dfrac{2x\ln x-x}{(\ln x)^2}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. Initially, it is travelling to the left at 1 cm/min. Its acceleration as a function of time($t$) is given by $a=\pi\cos\pi t+\pi\sin\pi t$ for $0\leq t\leq 2$ where time and displacement are measured in minutes and cm respectively.
Find when the particle changes its direction for the first time.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$. Integrate the acceleration, using $v=-1$ when $t=0$ (travelling left at 1 cm/min).
$$\begin{aligned} v-(-1)&=\int_0^t(\pi\cos\pi t+\pi\sin\pi t)\,dt\\ v+1&=\Big[\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t\Big]_0^t\\ v+1&=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t+1\\ v&=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t\end{aligned}$$
Set $v=0$:
$$\tan\pi t=1$$
So $\pi t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{5\pi}{4},\dots$, giving $t=\dfrac14,\dfrac54$ minutes.
$$\therefore\ \text{the first change of direction is at } t=\dfrac14 \text{ min (15 seconds)}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. Initially, it is travelling to the left at 1 cm/min. Its acceleration as a function of time($t$) is given by $a=\pi\cos\pi t+\pi\sin\pi t$ for $0\leq t\leq 2$ where time and displacement are measured in minutes and cm respectively.
Find the exact total distance travelled in the first half a minute.
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity $v=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t$ from part (a), with $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$x=\int(\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t)\,dt=-\dfrac{\cos\pi t}{\pi}-\dfrac{\sin\pi t}{\pi}+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $C=\dfrac{1}{\pi}$. Hence
$$x=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\left[\cos\pi t+\sin\pi t-1\right]$$
The particle turns at $t=\dfrac14$, so find $x$ there and at $t=\dfrac12$.
$$x\left(\dfrac14\right)=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1),\qquad x\left(\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(0+1-1)=0$$
The particle moves to $-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1)$ and then returns to $0$, so the distance travelled for $0\le t\le\dfrac12$ is
$$\therefore\ 2\times\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1) \text{ cm}$$

items.part:
Integrate the following:
$\displaystyle\int x^4(x^5-3)^2\,dx =$
items.sol:
The factor $5x^4$ is the derivative of $x^5-3$, so use the reverse chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned}\int x^4(x^5-3)^2\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{5}\int5x^4(x^5-3)^2\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}\cdot\dfrac{(x^5-3)^3}{3}+C\\ &=\dfrac{1}{15}(x^5-3)^3+C\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, expand:
$$\int x^4(x^{10}-6x^5+9)\,dx=\dfrac{x^{15}}{15}-\dfrac{3}{5}x^{10}+\dfrac{9}{5}x^5+C$$

items.part:
Integrate the following:
$\displaystyle\int\left(\sqrt{x}-\dfrac{2}{x}+3e^{-x}+1\right)dx =$
items.sol:
Write each term as a power of $x$ and integrate term by term.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}-2x^{-1}+3e^{-x}+1\right)dx&=\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-2\ln|x|-3e^{-x}+x+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx=\dfrac{10}{3},\ 0\leq a<\pi$, calculate the value of $a$.
items.sol:
Integrate, then apply the limits.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^a5\sin3x\,dx&=\left[-\dfrac{5}{3}\cos3x\right]_0^a\\ &=-\dfrac{5}{3}\left[\cos3a-\cos0\right]\end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\dfrac{10}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{5}{3}\left[\cos3a-1\right]&=\dfrac{10}{3}\\ \cos3a-1&=-2\\ \cos3a&=-1\end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le a<\pi$, we have $0\le3a<3\pi$, so $3a=\pi$.
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

items.part: Solve $2\cos\left[2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]=1$ in the domain $[0,2\pi]$.
items.sol:
Divide by $2$:
$$\cos\left[2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]=\dfrac12$$
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants.

For $0\le x\le2\pi$, the angle $2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ lies in the range
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}&\le 2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\le\dfrac{11\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 4\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
$$x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ x=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ 2\pi$$

The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}t^2+t^2+\dfrac{t}{4}+\dfrac{4t+1}{8}&=1\\ 2t^2+\dfrac{6t+1}{8}&=1\\ 16t^2+6t-7&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$t=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{36+448}}{32}=\dfrac{-6\pm22}{32}$$
Since $0\le P(X=x)\le1$, $t$ cannot be negative (as $t^2$ and $\dfrac{t}{4}$ are probabilities, $t\ge0$), so we take the positive root.
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac12$$

With $t=\dfrac12$: $P(X=-1)=P(X=0)=\dfrac14$, $P(X=1)=\dfrac18$, $P(X=2)=\dfrac38$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-1\times\dfrac14+0+1\times\dfrac18+2\times\dfrac38\\ &=-\dfrac14+\dfrac18+\dfrac34\\ &=\dfrac58\end{aligned}$$

items.part: What is the probability that at least ONE person has green eyes?
items.sol:
"At least one" is the complement of "none". Each person fails to have green eyes with probability $0.96$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one})&=1-P(\text{none})\\ &=1-0.96\times0.96\\ &=0.0784\end{aligned}$$

items.part: What is the smallest number of people that can be chosen at random so that the probability that at least ONE has green eyes is greater than $0.4$?
items.sol:
For $n$ people, $P(\text{at least one})=1-(0.96)^n$.
$$\begin{aligned}1-(0.96)^n&>0.4\\ (0.96)^n&<0.6\end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms. Since $\ln0.96<0$, the inequality reverses when dividing.
$$\begin{aligned}n\ln0.96&<\ln0.6\\ n&>\dfrac{\ln0.6}{\ln0.96}=12.51\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n=13 \text{ people}$$

items.part:
In a laboratory, a food product is heated in an oven at $210^\circ$ C in an effort to kill harmful bacteria. The number of bacteria recorded when the food product is first placed in the oven is 1800. After ten minutes the number of bacteria recorded is 550.

It is found that $N$, the number of bacteria remaining $t$ minutes after being in the oven is given by $N=Ae^{-kt}$ where $A$ and $k$ are constants.
Find the value of $A$.

In a laboratory, a food product is heated in an oven at $210^\circ$ C in an effort to kill harmful bacteria. The number of bacteria recorded when the food product is first placed in the oven is 1800. After ten minutes the number of bacteria recorded is 550.

It is found that $N$, the number of bacteria remaining $t$ minutes after being in the oven is given by $N=Ae^{-kt}$ where $A$ and $k$ are constants.
Calculate the value of $k$ correct to 4 decimal places.
items.sol:
When $t=10$, $N=550$:
$$\begin{aligned}550&=1800e^{-10k}\\ e^{-10k}&=\dfrac{55}{180}\\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\left(\dfrac{55}{180}\right)\\ &\approx0.1186\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In a laboratory, a food product is heated in an oven at $210^\circ$ C in an effort to kill harmful bacteria. The number of bacteria recorded when the food product is first placed in the oven is 1800. After ten minutes the number of bacteria recorded is 550.

It is found that $N$, the number of bacteria remaining $t$ minutes after being in the oven is given by $N=Ae^{-kt}$ where $A$ and $k$ are constants.
If an acceptable number of bacteria present is 100 or less, For how long should the food product to be in the oven? Express your answer to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
We need $N\le100$.
$$\begin{aligned}1800e^{-0.1186t}&\le100\\ e^{-0.1186t}&\le\dfrac{1}{18}\\ -0.1186t&\le\ln\dfrac{1}{18}\\ t&\ge\dfrac{\ln18}{0.1186}\approx24.37\end{aligned}$$
The inequality reverses when dividing by $-0.1186$. Rounding $24.37$ to the nearest minute gives $24$, but $N(24)\approx105>100$, so round up to the next whole minute:
$$\therefore\ t=25 \text{ minutes}$$

items.part:
After a week of heavy rain, the local dam starts to fill until at 10am on Sunday the dam overflows into the river. At time $t$ (hours after the dam begins spilling), the height ($H$) of the river changes at the rate of $\left[1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right]$ metres per hour. Initially the height of the river is 5 metres.
Show that the height of the river is given by the formula $H=-\dfrac{t^2}{40}+t+5$
items.sol:
Integrate the rate of change, with $H=5$ when $t=0$.
$$\dfrac{dH}{dt}=1-\dfrac{t}{20}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_5^H dH&=\int_0^t\left(1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right)dt\\ H-5&=\left[t-\dfrac{t^2}{40}\right]_0^t\\ H-5&=t-\dfrac{t^2}{40}\\ H&=-\dfrac{t^2}{40}+t+5\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
After a week of heavy rain, the local dam starts to fill until at 10am on Sunday the dam overflows into the river. At time $t$ (hours after the dam begins spilling), the height ($H$) of the river changes at the rate of $\left[1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right]$ metres per hour. Initially the height of the river is 5 metres.
Find the maximum height of the river during this flood.
items.sol:
$H=-\dfrac{t^2}{40}+t+5$ is a concave-down parabola, so the maximum is at the vertex.
$$t=\dfrac{-1}{2\times\left(-\frac{1}{40}\right)}=20$$
$$H(20)=-\dfrac{20^2}{40}+20+5=15$$
Alternatively, $\dfrac{dH}{dt}=0$ gives $t=20$, and $\dfrac{d^2H}{dt^2}=-\dfrac{1}{20}<0$ confirms a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum height}=15 \text{ metres}$$

items.part:
After a week of heavy rain, the local dam starts to fill until at 10am on Sunday the dam overflows into the river. At time $t$ (hours after the dam begins spilling), the height ($H$) of the river changes at the rate of $\left[1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right]$ metres per hour. Initially the height of the river is 5 metres.
A bridge over this river will be flooded and closed once the height of the river reaches 12.5 metres. At what time(s) and day(s) will the bridge be closed and reopened?
items.sol:
The bridge closes when $H=12.5$.
$$\begin{aligned}12.5&=-\dfrac{t^2}{40}+t+5\\ t^2-40t+300&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$t=\dfrac{40\pm\sqrt{1600-1200}}{2}=\dfrac{40\pm20}{2}=10 \text{ or } 30$$
The dam starts spilling at 10am Sunday.

At $t=10$: 10 hours later is 8pm Sunday, when the bridge closes.

At $t=30$: 30 hours later is 10am Monday plus 6 hours, which is 4pm Monday, when the bridge reopens.
$$\therefore\ \text{closed at 8pm Sunday and reopened at 4pm Monday}$$
items.final: closed at 8pm Sunday and reopened at 4pm Monday

items.part: Simplify fully: $\dfrac{3}{x+2}\times\dfrac{x^2+2x}{6x-3}$
items.sol:
Factorise the numerator and denominator, then cancel common factors.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{x+2}\times\dfrac{x^2+2x}{6x-3} &= \dfrac{3}{x+2}\times\dfrac{x(x+2)}{3(2x-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2x-1} \end{aligned}$$

Using the cosine rule, $x^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$, with the sides $11$ and $13$ and the included angle $80^\circ$:
$$x^2=11^2+13^2-2\times 11\times 13\times\cos 80^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \sqrt{11^2+13^2-2\times 11\times 13\times\cos 80^\circ} \\ &\approx 15.50 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $f(x)=(x-5)^2$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{x}-5$, find $g\left(f(x)\right)$
items.sol:
Substitute $f(x)$ into $g$.
$$\begin{aligned} g(f(x)) &= g\left((x-5)^2\right) \\ &= \sqrt{(x-5)^2}-5 \\ &= |x-5|-5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: The first term of an arithmetic series is 4. The fifth term is four times the third term. Find the sum of the first 10 terms.
items.sol:
Here $a=4$, and the condition is $t_5=4t_3$. Using $t_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} a+4d &= 4(a+2d) \\ a+4d &= 4a+8d \\ 3a &= -4d \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $a=4$ gives $12=-4d$, so $d=-3$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}\left[2a+9d\right] \\ &= 5\left[2\times 4+9\times(-3)\right] \\ &= -95 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $\log_e(2x+1)-\log_e 3=3$
items.sol:
Combine the logarithms using $\log_e a-\log_e b=\log_e\dfrac{a}{b}$.
$$\log_e\dfrac{2x+1}{3}=3$$
Write in exponential form.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2x+1}{3} &= e^3 \\ 2x+1 &= 3e^3 \\ 2x &= 3e^3-1 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3e^3-1\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta-1)\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$
items.sol:
Use $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ and $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}-1\right)\times\sin^2\theta \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\right)\times\sin^2\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\times\sin^2\theta \\ &= \cos^2\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise solve $(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta-1)\sin^2\theta=\dfrac{3}{4}$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$
items.sol:
By part (a), the equation becomes $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta &= \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$:
$$\theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ or } \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$
For $\cos\theta=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$:
$$\theta=-\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \text{ or } \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pm\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\sec^2 x\,dx$ giving the answer in exact form with rational denominator.
items.sol:
The antiderivative of $\sec^2 x$ is $\tan x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\sec^2 x\,dx &= \Big[\tan x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \sqrt{3}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int x^2\left(x^3-1\right)^5\,dx$
items.sol:
The derivative of the inner function $x^3-1$ is $3x^2$, so adjust by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int x^2(x^3-1)^5\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{3}\displaystyle\int 3x^2(x^3-1)^5\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{(x^3-1)^6}{6}+C \\ &= \dfrac{(x^3-1)^6}{18}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=3+4x^3-x^4$.
Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate.
$$f'(x)=12x^2-4x^3,\qquad f''(x)=24x-12x^2$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x^2-4x^3 &= 0 \\ 4x^2(3-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=3$.

At $x=3$, the second derivative decides the nature.
$$f''(3)=24\times 3-12\times 3^2=-36<0$$
So there is a maximum at $x=3$.
$$f(3)=3+4\times 3^3-3^4=30$$
Hence $(3,30)$ is a maximum.

At $x=0$, $f''(0)=0$, so test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline f''(x) & -36 & 0 & 12 \end{array}$$
The sign of $f''$ changes from negative to positive, so the concavity changes and $x=0$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
$$f(0)=3$$
$$\therefore\ (3,30) \text{ is a maximum and } (0,3) \text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion.}$$
items.final: $(3,30)$ is a maximum and $(0,3)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=3+4x^3-x^4$.
Show that there is a point of inflexion at $(2,19)$ on the curve.
items.sol:
Points of inflexion occur where $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 24x-12x^2 &= 0 \\ 12x(2-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=2$.

At $x=0$ there is a horizontal point of inflexion, shown in part (a).

At $x=2$, test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline f''(x) & 12 & 0 & -36 \end{array}$$
The concavity changes from upward to downward, so there is a point of inflexion at $x=2$.
$$f(2)=3+4\times 2^3-2^4=19$$
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a point of inflexion at } (2,19).$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x}=1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x}$
items.sol:
Rewrite the numerator as $1-e^x+2e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x+2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x}{1-e^x}+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= 1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution, starting from the right-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= 1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x+2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x}\,dx$
items.sol:
Use part (a), then write the second term as a multiple of $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ with $f(x)=1-e^x$, $f'(x)=-e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x}\,dx &= \displaystyle\int\left(1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x}\right)dx \\ &= \displaystyle\int\left(1+(-2)\left(\dfrac{-e^x}{1-e^x}\right)\right)dx \\ &= x-2\ln\left|1-e^x\right|+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: A normal to the graph of $y=2\sqrt{x}$ has the equation $y=-3x+b$. Find the value of $b$.
items.sol:
Differentiate the curve to find the gradient of the tangent.
$$y'=2\times\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$$
The gradient of the normal is the negative reciprocal.
$$m=-\sqrt{x}$$
This equals the gradient $-3$ of the given normal.
$$\begin{aligned} -\sqrt{x} &= -3 \\ x &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
When $x=9$, $y=2\sqrt{9}=6$, so the point of contact is $(9,6)$.

The normal passes through this point.
$$\begin{aligned} 6 &= -3\times 9+b \\ b &= 33 \end{aligned}$$

If they won the previous game, the probability of winning their next game is 0.8

$$\begin{aligned} P(WW' \text{ or } W'W') &= P(WW')+P(W'W') \\ &= 0.8\times 0.2+0.2\times 0.6 \\ &= 0.16+0.12 \\ &= 0.28 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the probability distribution below, find the values of $m$ and $n$ given that the expected value of the distribution is 4.8

\extable{1324_q23_t1}
items.sol:
The probabilities sum to $1$.

$$\begin{aligned} 0.1+0.3+m+0.3+0.2 &= 1 \\ m+0.9 &= 1 \\ m &= 0.1 \end{aligned}$$

The expected value is $\sum xP(x)=4.8$.

$$\begin{aligned} 0.1\times 0+0.3\times 2+m\times 3+0.3\times 7+0.2\times n &= 4.8 \\ 0.6+3m+2.1+0.2n &= 4.8 \\ 2.7+3\times 0.1+0.2n &= 4.8 \\ 2.7+0.3+0.2n &= 4.8 \\ 0.2n &= 1.8 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ m=0.1,\ n=9$$

items.part:
If $f(x)=\log_e\left(x+\sqrt{x}\right)$
Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{2x\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on $f(x)=\log_e\left(x+\sqrt{x}\right)$:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{x+\sqrt{x}}\left[1+\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x+\sqrt{x}}\times\dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{\left(x+\sqrt{x}\right)\times 2\sqrt{x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{\sqrt{x}\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)\times 2\sqrt{x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{2x\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
If $f(x)=\log_e\left(x+\sqrt{x}\right)$
Hence, when $x=2$, Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{2x\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)}$ can be written in the form $a+b\sqrt{2}$
items.sol:
Substitute $x=2$ and rationalise the denominator.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(2) &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}+1}{2\times 2\left(\sqrt{2}+1\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}+1}{4\left(\sqrt{2}+1\right)}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}-1} \\ &= \dfrac{4-2\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}-1}{4(2-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{3-\sqrt{2}}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{1}{4}\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$

Substitute into $f(x)=e^{2x}(1-x)$.

$$f(-1)=0.27,\quad f(0)=1,\quad f(1)=0$$

items.part:
Consider the function defined by $f(x)=e^{2x}(1-x)$ where $-3\le x\le 1$
Using the trapezoidal rule with five function values, approximate the area under the curve $f(x)$ for $-3\le x\le 1$.
items.sol:
There are five function values, so four strips of width $h=\dfrac{1-(-3)}{4}=1$, at $x=-3,-2,-1,0,1$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{1-(-3)}{2\times 4}\Big[f(-3)+f(1)+2\big(f(-2)+f(-1)+f(0)\big)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{4}{8}\Big[0.01+0+2(0.05+0.27+1)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.65 \\ &= 1.325 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function defined by $f(x)=e^{2x}(1-x)$ where $-3\le x\le 1$
Differentiate $f(x)=e^{2x}(1-x)$ and show that the function has only one stationary point.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=1-x \\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=-1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= e^{2x}\times(-1)+(1-x)\times 2e^{2x} \\ &= -e^{2x}+2e^{2x}-2xe^{2x} \\ &= e^{2x}(1-2x) \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $f'(x)=0$, so $e^{2x}(1-2x)=0$.

Since $e^{2x}>0$ for all $x$, $1-2x=0$, so $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$$f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=e^{1}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=\dfrac{e}{2}$$

The curve has only one stationary point, $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{e}{2}\right)$, or $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},1.36\right)$.

items.part:
Calculate the exact area of the shaded region in the diagram below enclosed by the curves $y=x^2$, $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ and the line $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$

\exfigure{1324_q26_1}
items.sol:
The curve $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ is above $y=x^2$ on the shaded region, and they meet at $x=1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}-x^2\right)dx \\ &= \left[\ln x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1} \\ &= \left(\ln 1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-\left(\ln\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{8}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{3}-\ln\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{24} \\ &= -\dfrac{7}{24}-\ln\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \ln 2-\dfrac{7}{24} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2^x+1}$
Show that $\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2^x+1}=\dfrac{2^x-1}{2(2^x+1)}$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2^x+1} \\ &= \dfrac{2^x+1-2}{2\left(2^x+1\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{2^x-1}{2\left(2^x+1\right)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2^x+1}$
Hence determine whether $f(x)$ is even, odd or neither. Show all working.
items.sol:
Find $f(-x)$ using the form from part (a), multiplying numerator and denominator by $2^x$.

$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= \dfrac{2^{-x}-1}{2\left(2^{-x}+1\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2^x}-1}{2\left(\frac{1}{2^x}+1\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{1-2^x}{2\left(1+2^x\right)} \\ &= -\dfrac{2^x-1}{2\left(2^x+1\right)} \\ &= -f(x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f(x)\text{ is an odd function.}$$

items.part:
The velocity $v$ of a particle initially at the origin is given by $v(t)=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{4}t\right)$, in metres per second.
Find the displacement function $x(t)$
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} x(t) &= \int v(t)\,dt \\ &= \int \sin\left(\dfrac{1}{4}t\right)dt \\ &= -4\cos\dfrac{1}{4}t+C \end{aligned}$$

When $t=0$, $x=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -4\cos 0+C \\ C &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x(t)=-4\cos\dfrac{1}{4}t+4$$

items.part:

Find the acceleration function $a(t)$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} a(t) &= \dfrac{d}{dt}v(t) \\ &= \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\sin\dfrac{1}{4}t\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{4}t\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The rate of fuel burn, $t$ minutes after the engine starts operation, $R$ kg per minute, is given by the relation

$$R=10+\dfrac{10}{1+2t}$$
Calculate the total amount of the fuel burnt in the first 7 minutes.
items.sol:
The total fuel burnt is the integral of the rate.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= \int_0^7 R\,dt \\ &= \int_0^7\left(10+\dfrac{10}{1+2t}\right)dt \\ &= \left[10t+10\times\dfrac{\ln|1+2t|}{2}\right]_0^7 \\ &= 5\Big[2t+\ln|1+2t|\Big]_0^7 \\ &= 5\Big[\left(2\times 7+\ln|1+2\times 7|\right)-\left(2\times 0+\ln 1\right)\Big] \\ &= 5\left[14+\ln 15\right] \text{ kg} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Carol, Mary and Manar arrive at the top of a cliff at 9:00 am on a particular Saturday morning. They are planning to explore the lower cave in the cliff.

\exfigure{1324_q30_1}

The height, $h$ metres of the seawater is given by the function $h(t)=7-4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{7}t\right)$, where $t$ is the number of hours after 9:00 am, on Saturday morning.
The girls notice that the height of the water is falling and they wait for the water to fall so that they can explore the lower cave. When the water is 4 metres and falling, they enter the lower cave. What time do the girls enter the lower cave?
items.sol:
Set the height equal to $4$.

$$\begin{aligned} 7-4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{7}t\right) &= 4 \\ -4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{7}t\right) &= -3 \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{7}t\right) &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

The water is falling when $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{7}t\right)$ is increasing, which is the first solution, so $\dfrac{\pi}{7}t=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{3}{4}$.

$$t=\dfrac{7}{\pi}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{3}{4}\approx 1 \text{ hr } 53 \text{ min}$$

The girls enter the lower cave at 10:53 am.

items.part:
A wire of length 5 metres is to be bent to form the hypotenuse and base of a right angled triangle $ABC$ with right angle at $B$. Let the length of the base $BC$ be $x$ metres.
Show that the area of the triangle $ABC$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}x\sqrt{25-10x}$ square meters.
items.sol:
By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle $ABC$:

$$\begin{aligned} AB^2 &= (5-x)^2-x^2 \\ &= 25-10x+x^2-x^2 \\ &= 25-10x \end{aligned}$$

So $AB=\sqrt{25-10x}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times BC\times AB \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}x\sqrt{25-10x} \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A wire of length 5 metres is to be bent to form the hypotenuse and base of a right angled triangle $ABC$ with right angle at $B$. Let the length of the base $BC$ be $x$ metres.
Find the maximum possible area of the triangle $ABC$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sqrt{25-10x} \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{-10}{2\sqrt{25-10x}} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{25-10x}+x\times\dfrac{-10}{2\sqrt{25-10x}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{25-10x-5x}{\sqrt{25-10x}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{25-15x}{\sqrt{25-10x}} \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 25-15x &= 0 \\ x &= \dfrac{25}{15}=\dfrac{5}{3}\approx 1.67 \end{aligned}$$

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 1 & \dfrac{5}{3} & 2 \\ \hline \dfrac{dA}{dx} & 1.29 & 0 & -1.12 \end{array}$$

The derivative changes sign from positive to negative, so $A$ is a maximum when $x=\dfrac{5}{3}$.

$$\begin{aligned} A_{\max} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{5}{3}\times\sqrt{25-\dfrac{10\times 5}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6}\sqrt{\dfrac{25}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{6\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{25\sqrt{3}}{18} \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $3^{2x-1}=5^x$, giving your answer to 2 d.p.
items.sol:
Take natural logarithms of both sides.
$$(2x-1)\ln 3=x\ln 5$$
Expand and collect the $x$ terms.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x\ln 3-\ln 3&=x\ln 5 \\ x(2\ln 3-\ln 5)&=\ln 3 \\ x&=\dfrac{\ln 3}{2\ln 3-\ln 5} \\ &\approx 1.87 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x\approx 1.87$$

items.part: Differentiate $3+\sin 2x$.
items.sol:
Differentiate $y=3+\sin 2x$ using the chain rule.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2\cos 2x$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{\cos 2x}{3+\sin 2x}\,dx$
items.sol:
From part (a), the derivative of $3+\sin 2x$ is $2\cos 2x$, so the numerator is half of this derivative.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{\cos 2x}{3+\sin 2x}\,dx&=\dfrac12\int\dfrac{2\cos 2x}{3+\sin 2x}\,dx \\ &=\dfrac12\ln|3+\sin 2x|+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^6 (x+k)\,dx=30$, and $k$ is a constant, find the value of $k$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6(x+k)\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+kx\right]_0^6 \\ &=\left(\dfrac{6^2}{2}+6k\right)-0 \\ &=18+6k \end{aligned}$$
Since the integral equals $30$:
$$\begin{aligned} 18+6k&=30 \\ 6k&=12 \\ k&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=2$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2$
Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the curve $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^3-3x^2 \\ f'(x)&=3x^2-6x \\ f''(x)&=6x-6 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x(x-2)&=0 \\ x&=0 \text{ or } x=2 \end{aligned}$$
The second derivative decides the nature.

At $x=0$: $f(0)=0$ and $f''(0)=-6<0$, so $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point.

At $x=2$: $f(2)=2^3-3\times 4=-4$ and $f''(2)=6>0$, so $(2,-4)$ is a minimum turning point.
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point; $(2,-4)$ is a minimum turning point

items.part:

items.sol:
The curve meets the $x$-axis when $f(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-3x^2&=0 \\ x^2(x-3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=3$.

The curve meets the $y$-axis at $(0,0)$, and the turning points from part (a) are $(0,0)$ and $(2,-4)$.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2$
Find the values of $x$ for which the curve $y=f(x)$ is concave up.
items.sol:
The curve is concave up when $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-6&>0 \\ 6x&>6 \\ x&>1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is concave up when } x>1$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_e^{e^3}\dfrac{5}{x}\,dx$
items.sol:
The antiderivative of $\dfrac{5}{x}$ is $5\ln x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_e^{e^3}\dfrac5x\,dx&=5\Big[\ln x\Big]_e^{e^3} \\ &=5\left(\ln e^3-\ln e\right) \\ &=5(3-1) \\ &=10 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=x^2\log_e x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln x \\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac1x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=2x\ln x+x^2\cdot\dfrac1x \\ &=x+2x\ln x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by:

$$\dot{x}=8-8e^{-2t}$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds and $x$ is the displacement in metres.
Show that the particle is initially at rest.
items.sol:
Substitute $t=0$ into $\dot x=8-8e^{-2t}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dot x&=8-8e^{0} \\ &=8-8 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$$
So the particle is initially at rest.

items.part:
The velocity of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by:

$$\dot{x}=8-8e^{-2t}$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds and $x$ is the displacement in metres.
Show that the acceleration of the particle is always positive.
items.sol:
Differentiate the velocity.
$$\ddot x=16e^{-2t}$$
Since $e^{-2t}>0$ for all $t$, $\ddot x>0$.

So the acceleration is always positive.

items.part:
The velocity of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by:

$$\dot{x}=8-8e^{-2t}$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds and $x$ is the displacement in metres.
Explain why the particle is moving in the positive direction for all $t>0$.
items.sol:
From part (a) the particle is initially at rest, so $\dot x=0$ at $t=0$.

From part (b) the acceleration is always positive, so the velocity is increasing for all $t$.

Therefore the velocity is greater than $0$ for all $t>0$, and the particle moves in the positive direction.

items.part:
The velocity of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by:

$$\dot{x}=8-8e^{-2t}$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds and $x$ is the displacement in metres.
As $t\to\infty$, the velocity of the particle approaches a constant. Find the value of the constant.
items.sol:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-2t}\to 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x &= 8-8e^{-2t} \\ &\to 8-0 \\ &= 8 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the constant is } 8$$

items.part: The circle $x^2+6x+y^2+2y=-6$ is reflected in the y-axis.Sketch the reflected circle, showing the coordinates of the centre and the radius.
items.sol:
Complete the square to find the centre and radius.

$$\begin{aligned} x^2+6x+y^2+2y &= -6 \\ x^2+6x+3^2+y^2+2y+1^2 &= -6+9+1 \\ (x+3)^2+(y+1)^2 &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

So the radius is $2$ units and the centre is $(-3,-1)$.

Reflecting in the $y$-axis changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate, so the centre becomes $(3,-1)$ and the radius is still $2$.

\exfigure{1325_q23_s1}

items.part:
A town planning committee notes that the rate of growth of the town's population since 1985 has followed the formula: $\dfrac{dp}{dt}=(1500+200t)$ people per year

where $t$ is the number of years since 1st January 1985. On 1st January 1992 the population was $25\,000$. Find the formula for the city's population from 1985 onwards.
items.sol:
Population is the integral of the rate of growth.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \int (1500+200t)\,dt \\ &= 1500t+\dfrac{200t^2}{2}+K \\ &= 1500t+100t^2+K \end{aligned}$$

On 1 January 1992, $t=7$ and $P=25\,000$.

$$\begin{aligned} 25\,000 &= 1500(7)+100(7)^2+K \\ &= 10\,500+4900+K \\ K &= 9600 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P=100t^2+1500t+9600$$

items.part: Solve $10\sin^2 x-4\sin x=5$ for $0^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ$.
items.sol:
Rearrange to a quadratic in $\sin x$.

$$10\sin^2x-4\sin x-5=0$$

Using the quadratic formula:

$$\sin x=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{216}}{20}$$

$$\sin x\approx 0.93485 \text{ or } \sin x\approx -0.534847$$

For $\sin x\approx 0.93485$, $x$ is in the first and second quadrants.

$$x\approx 69.2^\circ,\ 110.8^\circ$$

For $\sin x\approx -0.534847$, $x$ is in the third and fourth quadrants.

$$x\approx 212.3^\circ,\ 327.7^\circ$$

items.part: Differentiate $\log_e(\cos x)$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Let $y=\ln(\cos x)$. Using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= -\tan x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\tan x\,dx$
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\cos x)=-\tan x$, so $\displaystyle\int \tan x\,dx=-\ln(\cos x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\tan x\,dx &= -\Big[\ln(\cos x)\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= -\left[\ln\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)-\ln(\cos 0)\right] \\ &= -\left[\ln\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\ln 1\right] \\ &= -\ln\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \\ &\approx 0.35 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A square sheet of metal is 16cm on each side. Squares of side $x$ cm are cut from each corner. The sheet is then bent along the dotted lines to form an open box.

\exfigure{1325_q27_1}
Show that the volume of the box $V$, expressed as a function of $x$ is given by:

$V(x)=4x(x-8)^2$
items.sol:
After cutting squares of side $x$ from each corner, the base is a square of side $16-2x$ and the height is $x$.

$$\begin{aligned} V &= (16-2x)^2\,x \\ &= x\big(2(8-x)\big)^2 \\ &= 4x(8-x)^2 \\ &= 4x(x-8)^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ V(x)=4x(x-8)^2$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=(x-8)^2\\ u'&=4 & v'&=2(x-8)\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} V'(x) &= 4(x-8)^2+8x(x-8) \\ &= 4(x-8)\big[(x-8)+2x\big] \\ &= 4(x-8)(3x-8) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $V'(x)=0$, so $x=8$ or $x=\dfrac{8}{3}$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.

$$V''(x)=24x-128$$

$$\begin{aligned} V''(8) &= 24(8)-128>0 &&\text{minimum turning point}\\ V''\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) &= 24\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right)-128<0 &&\text{maximum turning point} \end{aligned}$$

The maximum volume occurs at $x=\dfrac{8}{3}$.

$$\begin{aligned} V\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) &= 4\times\dfrac{8}{3}\left(\dfrac{8}{3}-8\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{8192}{27} = 303\dfrac{11}{27} \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{maximum volume } 303\dfrac{11}{27}\text{ cm}^3 \text{ at } x=\dfrac{8}{3}$$

The shaded area is the quarter circle less the area under the parabola between $x=0$ and $x=1$.

The area of the quarter circle is:

$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= \dfrac{1}{4}\pi r^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\pi(2)^2 \\ &= \pi \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The area under the parabola is:

$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= \int_0^1 (x^2-3x+2)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+2x\right]_0^1 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{3}{2}+2\right)-0 \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Shaded area}=\left(\pi-\dfrac{5}{6}\right)\text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
In a game a six-sided dice is rolled twice.

The difference between the two results is recorded.
Find the expected value, $E(X)$, and the standard deviation $\sigma$.
items.sol:
The expected value is $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 0\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{5}{18}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{2}{9}\right)+3\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right)+5\left(\dfrac{1}{18}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{35}{18} \\ &= 1\dfrac{17}{18} \end{aligned}$$

For the standard deviation, $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= 0^2\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)+1^2\left(\dfrac{5}{18}\right)+2^2\left(\dfrac{2}{9}\right)+3^2\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)+4^2\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right)+5^2\left(\dfrac{1}{18}\right) \\ &= 5\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Since $\mu=1\dfrac{17}{18}$, $\mu^2=3\dfrac{253}{324}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= 5\dfrac{5}{6}-3\dfrac{253}{324} \\ &\approx 2.0524 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \sigma\approx 1.43 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$

items.part: The sum of the series $1+8+15+\dots$ is $396$. How many terms does the series contain?
items.sol:
This is an arithmetic series with first term $a=1$ and common difference $d=7$.

Let there be $n$ terms, so $S_n=396$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2+7(n-1)\big) &= 396 \\ n(7n-5) &= 792 \\ 7n^2-5n-792 &= 0 \\ (7n+72)(n-11) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $n=-\dfrac{72}{7}$ or $n=11$.

The number of terms must be a positive integer, so $n=11$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the series has } 11 \text{ terms}$$

items.part:
A circular clock face, centre O, has a minute hand OA and an hour hand OB.

$OA=10$ cm, $OB=7$ cm.

Calculate the length of $AB$ when the hands show 5 o'clock.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

\exfigure{1325_q31_1}
items.sol:
Each hour on the clock face is $\dfrac{360^\circ}{12}=30^\circ$, so at 5 o'clock:

$$\angle AOB=5\times 30^\circ=150^\circ$$

In triangle $AOB$, using the cosine rule with $AB=x$:

$$\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 10^2+7^2-2\times10\times7\times\cos150^\circ \\ &\approx 270.243 \\ x &\approx 16.439 \\ &\approx 16.4 \text{ cm (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ AB\approx 16.4 \text{ cm}$$

items.part:
Under certain climatic conditions the number $N$ of blue-green algae satisfies the equation

$$N(t)=Ae^{0.15t}$$

where $t$ is measured in days and $A$ is a constant.
Show that the number of algae increases at a rate proportional to the number.
items.sol:
Differentiate $N(t)=Ae^{0.15t}$.

$$\begin{aligned} N'(t) &= 0.15Ae^{0.15t} \\ &= 0.15\,N(t) \end{aligned}$$

Since $0.15$ is a constant, $N'(t)\propto N(t)$, so the number increases at a rate proportional to the number.

items.part:
Under certain climatic conditions the number $N$ of blue-green algae satisfies the equation

$$N(t)=Ae^{0.15t}$$

where $t$ is measured in days and $A$ is a constant.
When $t=3$ the number of algae was estimated to be $1.7\times10^8$. Evaluate $A$.
items.sol:
Substitute $t=3$ and $N=1.7\times10^8$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1.7\times10^8 &= Ae^{0.15(3)} \\ &= Ae^{0.45} \\ A &= \dfrac{1.7\times10^8}{e^{0.45}} \\ &\approx 1.0839\times10^8 \\ &\approx 1.1\times10^8 \text{ (2 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Under certain climatic conditions the number $N$ of blue-green algae satisfies the equation

$$N(t)=Ae^{0.15t}$$

where $t$ is measured in days and $A$ is a constant.
The number of algae doubles every $x$ days. Find the value of $x$.
items.sol:
At $t=0$, $N(0)=Ae^{0}=A$, so after $x$ days $N(x)=2A$.

$$\begin{aligned} Ae^{0.15x} &= 2A \\ e^{0.15x} &= 2 \\ 0.15x &= \ln 2 \\ x &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.15} \\ &\approx 4.6209 \\ &\approx 4.6 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$

In the diagram, triangle $ABC$ is right angled at $B$. $AB=8$ cm and $\angle BAC=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

The circular arc $BD$ has centre $A$ with radius $AB$.

items.sol:
The area of a sector is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, with $r=8$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

items.part:
In the diagram, triangle $ABC$ is right angled at $B$. $AB=8$ cm and $\angle BAC=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

The circular arc $BD$ has centre $A$ with radius $AB$.

\exfigure{1326_q11_1}
Hence find the exact area of the shaded region $BCD$.
items.sol:
In right-angled triangle $ABC$, $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{BC}{8}$, so first find $BC$.
$$BC=8\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
The shaded region is the triangle less the sector.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{shaded}}&=A_{\text{triangle}}-A_{\text{sector}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times8\times8\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{32\pi}{3} \\ &=32\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{32\pi}{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The graphs meet where $f(x)=g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} x+\sin x&=x \\ \sin x&=0 \\ x&=k\pi,\quad k\in\mathbb{Z} \end{aligned}$$
From the diagram, $A$ is at the first positive solution.
$$\therefore\ x=\pi$$

The shaded area lies between $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ from $x=0$ to $x=\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^{\pi}\big(f(x)-g(x)\big)\,dx \\ &=\int_0^{\pi}\big((x+\sin x)-x\big)\,dx \\ &=\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx \\ &=\Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &=(-\cos\pi)-(-\cos0) \\ &=1+1 \\ &=2\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x^4-x^5$.
Find $f'(x)$

Consider the function $f(x)=2x^4-x^5$.

items.sol:
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 8x^3-5x^4&=0 \\ x^3(8-5x)&=0 \\ x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=\dfrac{8}{5} \end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $f'(x)$ either side of each point.

Therefore there is a minimum turning point at $(0,0)$.

And a maximum turning point at $\left(\dfrac{8}{5},2.62\right)$.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x^4-x^5$.

items.sol:
Possible points of inflection occur when $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=24x^2-20x^3 \\ 24x^2-20x^3&=0 \\ 4x^2(6-5x)&=0 \\ x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=\dfrac{6}{5} \end{aligned}$$
Test for a change in concavity. Note $x=0$ is a minimum point, so it is not an inflection.

Since there is a change in concavity at $x=\dfrac{6}{5}$, there is a point of inflection at $\left(\dfrac{6}{5},1.659\right)$.

items.part: Given the function $f(x)=x^2-2$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{7-x}$ sketch $y=f(g(x))$ over its natural domain.

Let $\log_a 2=x$ and $\log_a 3=y$.

Find an expression for $\log_a 12$ in terms of $x$ and $y$.
items.sol:
Write $12=4\times3$ and use the log laws.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_a12&=\log_a(4\times3) \\ &=\log_a4+\log_a3 \\ &=\log_a2^2+\log_a3 \\ &=2\log_a2+\log_a3 \\ &=2x+y \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate with respect to $x$
$x\tan x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\tan x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\sec^2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x\tan x)&=x\sec^2x+\tan x\cdot1 \\ &=x\sec^2x+\tan x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate with respect to $x$
$\sin x\cos^2 x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=\cos^2x \\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=-2\sin x\cos x \end{aligned}$$
Here $v'$ comes from the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x\cos^2x)&=\cos x\cdot\cos^2x+\sin x\left(-2\sin x\cos x\right) \\ &=\cos^3x-2\sin^2x\cos x \\ &=\cos x\left(\cos^2x-2\sin^2x\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate with respect to $x$
$\dfrac{x}{e^x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{e^x}\right)&=\dfrac{e^x\cdot1-x\cdot e^x}{(e^x)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{e^x(1-x)}{e^{2x}} \\ &=\dfrac{1-x}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Coal is extracted from a mine at a rate that is proportional to the amount of coal remaining in the mine. Hence the amount $R$ remaining after $t$ years is given by $R=R_0e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a constant and $R_0$ is the initial amount of coal.

After 20 years, $50\%$ of the initial amount of coal remains.
Find the exact value of $k$.
items.sol:
When $t=20$, $R=\dfrac{1}{2}R_0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}R_0&=R_0e^{-20k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2}&=e^{-20k} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=-20k \\ -\ln2&=-20k \\ k&=\dfrac{1}{20}\ln2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Coal is extracted from a mine at a rate that is proportional to the amount of coal remaining in the mine. Hence the amount $R$ remaining after $t$ years is given by $R=R_0e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a constant and $R_0$ is the initial amount of coal.

After 20 years, $50\%$ of the initial amount of coal remains.
How many more years will elapse before only $10\%$ of the original amount remains?
items.sol:
From part (i), $k=\dfrac{1}{20}\ln 2$. Set $R=0.1R_0$ and solve for $t$.
$$\begin{aligned}0.1R_0&=R_0e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ 0.1&=e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ \ln(0.1)&=\ln e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ -\dfrac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t&=-\ln 10\\ t&=\dfrac{20\ln 10}{\ln 2}\\ &\approx 66.44\end{aligned}$$
The question asks for how many more years, so subtract the first 20 years.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{More years}&=66.44-20\\ &=46.44\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 46.44 \text{ more years}$$

items.part:
A student was asked to differentiate $f(x)=x^2-2x$ from first principles. The student began the solution as shown below. Complete the solution.

$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{(x+h)^2-2(x+h)-\left[x^2-2x\right]}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{x^2+2hx+h^2-2x-2h-x^2+2x}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{2hx+h^2-2h}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\,(2x-2+h)\\ &=2x-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f'(x)=2x-2$$

items.part:
Loudness, in decibels, is given by the formula $L=\log_e\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$, where $I$ is the intensity level and $I_0$ is the threshold sound (or sound that can barely be heard). Sounds louder than 85 dB can damage hearing.

The intensity of a vacuum cleaner is estimated to be 10 000 000 times the threshold level $I_0$. Would using a vacuum cleaner damage your hearing based on this estimate? Justify your answer with appropriate working.
items.sol:
Substitute $I=10\,000\,000I_0$ into the formula.
$$\begin{aligned}L&=\log_e\left(\dfrac{10\,000\,000\,I_0}{I_0}\right)\\ &=\ln(10\,000\,000)\\ &\approx 16.11 \text{ dB}\end{aligned}$$
Since $16.11<85$, using this vacuum cleaner would not damage your hearing.
items.final: No; $L\approx16.11$ dB, which is less than 85 dB, so it would not damage hearing.
