items.part:
At the start of year 2000 a colony of 600 animals was established in a sanctuary. Each year the population size grows at a rate of $10\%$ per year and at the end of each year 50 of the animals are released into the wild. The population size $P_n$ at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ year can be determined using the recurrence relation $P_n=1.1\times P_{n-1}-50$ where $n=1,2,3,\dots$ and $P_0=600$.
Write down expressions for $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ in terms of $P_0$ and hence show that $P_n=100\times(1.1)^n+500$.

At the start of year 2000 a colony of 600 animals was established in a sanctuary. Each year the population size grows at a rate of $10\%$ per year and at the end of each year 50 of the animals are released into the wild. The population size $P_n$ at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ year can be determined using the recurrence relation $P_n=1.1\times P_{n-1}-50$ where $n=1,2,3,\dots$ and $P_0=600$.
Find the year in which the growth in population size from the beginning of that year to the start of the next year first exceeds 100.
items.sol:
The growth over year $n$ is $P_n-P_{n-1}$. We need the least integer $n$ with $P_n-P_{n-1}>100$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100\left\{(1.1)^n-(1.1)^{n-1}\right\} &> 100 \\ (1.1)^{n-1}(1.1-1) &> 1 \\ (1.1)^{n-1} &> 10 \\ (n-1)\log_{10}(1.1) &> 1 \\ n-1 &> \dfrac{1}{\log_{10}(1.1)}\approx 24.16 \end{aligned}$$
So $n-1=25,26,27,\dots$, and the least value is $n=26$.

$$\text{Year } n \text{ is the calendar year } 1999+n \text{ (year 1 is 2000), so } n=26 \text{ is } 2025.$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the required year is } 2025$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. Initially the particle is at $O$.
Use integration to show that $x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.
items.sol:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement, so integrate $v$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9 \\ x &= 2(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+c \end{aligned}$$
Initially $x=0$ when $t=0$, so $0=2-0+c$ and $c=-2$.
$$\therefore\ x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. Initially the particle is at $O$.
Find when and where the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9 &= 0 \\ \sqrt{t+1} &= 3 \\ t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
Then $x=2(9)(3)-72-2=-20$.

Also, when $t=0$, $v=-3$, so the particle starts in the negative direction.

The particle is at rest at time 8 seconds, when it is 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of travel.
items.final: The particle is at rest at time 8 seconds, when it is 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of travel.

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. Initially the particle is at $O$.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 24 seconds of its motion.
items.sol:
At $t=24$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2(25)(5)-9(24)-2 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
The particle changes direction at $t=8$, so in the first 24 seconds it travels from $x=0$ to $x=-20$, then to $x=32$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 20+(20+32) \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance travelled is } 72 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
The cost $\$C$ per hour when employees work $x$ hours per day to complete a project is given by $C=ax^3+d$ for some constants $a$ and $d$. The time $T$ hours to complete the project is given by $T=\dfrac{120}{x}$. In order to complete the project, the cost would be $\$248$ per hour when employees work 4 hours per day on the project and $\$472$ per hour when employees work 8 hours per day on the project.
Write down two equations in $a$ and $d$ and solve these equations to find the values of $a$ and $d$.
items.sol:
Substitute each pair of values into $C=ax^3+d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 248 &= 64a+d &&(1)\\ 472 &= 512a+d &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtract (1) from (2).
$$\begin{aligned} 224 &= 448a \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 248-64\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 216 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2},\ d=216$$

items.part:
The cost $\$C$ per hour when employees work $x$ hours per day to complete a project is given by $C=ax^3+d$ for some constants $a$ and $d$. The time $T$ hours to complete the project is given by $T=\dfrac{120}{x}$. In order to complete the project, the cost would be $\$248$ per hour when employees work 4 hours per day on the project and $\$472$ per hour when employees work 8 hours per day on the project.
Show that the total cost $\$S$ of completing the project when employees work $x$ hours per day on the project is given by $S=60x^2+\dfrac{25\,920}{x}$.
items.sol:
The total cost is the time multiplied by the cost per hour, $S=TC$, with $a=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $d=216$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{120}{x}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{2}+216\right) \\ &= 60x^2+\dfrac{25\,920}{x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The cost $\$C$ per hour when employees work $x$ hours per day to complete a project is given by $C=ax^3+d$ for some constants $a$ and $d$. The time $T$ hours to complete the project is given by $T=\dfrac{120}{x}$. In order to complete the project, the cost would be $\$248$ per hour when employees work 4 hours per day on the project and $\$472$ per hour when employees work 8 hours per day on the project.
Use differentiation to find the minimum total cost of completing the project.
items.sol:
Differentiate $S=60x^2+25\,920x^{-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dS}{dx} &= 120x-\dfrac{25\,920}{x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{120}{x^2}\left(x^3-216\right) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dS}{dx}=0$, so $x^3=216$ and $x=6$.

Then $S=60(36)+\dfrac{25\,920}{6}=6480$.

Since $\dfrac{120}{x^2}>0$, the sign of $\dfrac{dS}{dx}$ is the sign of $x^3-216$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dS}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 0<x<6 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dS}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=6\\ \dfrac{dS}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>6 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
So $x=6$ gives a minimum.

$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum cost is } \$6480$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ or $x>2$.
Show that $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
items.sol:
A probability density function must satisfy $f(x)\ge0$ and $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx=1$.

For $1\le x\le2$, $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}>0$, and $f(x)=0$ elsewhere.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 f(x)\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{x}\right]_1^2 \\ &= -1+2 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Both conditions hold.

Hence $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ or $x>2$.
Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ of the random variable $X$.
items.sol:
For $1\le x\le 2$, integrate the density from 1 to $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_1^x\dfrac{2}{t^2}\,dt \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{t}\right]_1^x \\ &= 2-\dfrac{2}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<1\\[6pt] 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x}\right), & 1\le x\le2\\[6pt] 1, & x>2\end{cases}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ or $x>2$.
Show that if $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$ are the quartiles of the distribution of $X$ then $\dfrac{1}{Q_1}$, $\dfrac{1}{Q_2}$, $\dfrac{1}{Q_3}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.
items.sol:
The quartiles satisfy $F(Q_1)=\dfrac{1}{4}$, $F(Q_2)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $F(Q_3)=\dfrac{3}{4}$, using $F(x)=2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$.

For $Q_1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_1}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_1} &= \dfrac{7}{8} \end{aligned}$$
For $Q_2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_2} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
For $Q_3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_3}\right) &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_3} &= \dfrac{5}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The differences between consecutive terms are
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{Q_2}-\dfrac{1}{Q_1} &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_3}-\dfrac{1}{Q_2} &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The common difference is $-\dfrac{1}{8}$.

Hence $\dfrac{1}{Q_1},\dfrac{1}{Q_2},\dfrac{1}{Q_3}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.

Start from $y=e^x$ and build $y=6-8e^{-x}$ one step at a time.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=e^x \\ y&=8e^x &&(\text{vertical dilation, factor } 8)\\ y&=-8e^x &&(\text{reflection in the } x\text{-axis})\\ y&=-8e^{-x} &&(\text{reflection in the } y\text{-axis})\\ y&=6-8e^{-x} &&(\text{translation up 6 units})\end{aligned}$$
A vertical dilation by a factor 8, then reflections in the $x$ and $y$ axes, followed by a vertical translation upwards by 6 units.
items.final: A vertical dilation by a factor 8, then reflections in the $x$ and $y$ axes, followed by a vertical translation upwards by 6 units.

items.sol:
The curves intersect where $e^x=6-8e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{2x} &= 6e^x-8 &&(\text{multiply by } e^x)\\ e^{2x}-6e^x+8 &= 0 \\ (e^x-2)(e^x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $e^x=2$ or $e^x=4$.
$$\therefore\ x_1=\ln 2,\quad x_2=\ln 4$$

On $\ln 2\le x\le\ln 4$ the curve $y=6-8e^{-x}$ is above $y=e^x$, so the area is
$$\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\left(6-8e^{-x}-e^x\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \Big[6x+8e^{-x}-e^x\Big]_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4} \\ &= 6(\ln 4-\ln 2)+8\left(e^{-\ln 4}-e^{-\ln 2}\right)-\left(e^{\ln 4}-e^{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= 6\ln 2+8\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-(4-2) \\ &= 6\ln 2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area is } (6\ln 2-4) \text{ square units}$$

items.part: Find the largest domain for which $\sqrt{2x-3}$ is defined.
items.sol:
The square root is defined when $2x-3\ge0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-3 &\ge 0 \\ 2x &\ge 3 \\ x &\ge \dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the domain is } \left[\dfrac{3}{2},\infty\right)$$

items.part: Factorise $2x^2 + 3x - 2xy - 3y$.
items.sol:
Group in pairs and take out common factors.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x^2+3x-2xy-3y &= x(2x+3)-y(2x+3) \\ &= (2x+3)(x-y) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x) = -x^2 + x + 4$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 2$.
Find $f(3)$.

Let $f(x) = -x^2 + x + 4$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 2$.
Express $f(g(x))$ in the form $ax^4 + bx^2 + c$, where $a, b$ and $c$ are non-zero integers.

A circle is given by $x^2 + 2x + y^2 - 4y - 4 = 0$.
By completing the square, find the radius and centre of the circle.
items.sol:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+2x+y^2-4y-4 &= 0 \\ (x^2+2x+1)+(y^2-4y+4) &= 4+1+4 \\ (x+1)^2+(y-2)^2 &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
The circle has centre $(-1,2)$ and radius $3$.

items.part: Rewrite $\sqrt{7} + \sqrt{8}$ in the form $\sqrt{a + b\sqrt{c}}$ using the smallest integer values possible for $c$.
items.sol:
Let $\sqrt{a+b\sqrt c}=\sqrt7+\sqrt8$ and square both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} a+b\sqrt c &= (\sqrt7+\sqrt8)^2 \\ &= 7+2\sqrt{56}+8 \\ &= 15+2\sqrt{4\times14} \\ &= 15+4\sqrt{14} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \sqrt7+\sqrt8=\sqrt{15+4\sqrt{14}}$$

items.part:
An arithmetic sequence is given by $4, 13, 22, 31, \dots$.
Find the $25^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence.
items.sol:
For an arithmetic sequence, $a=4$, $d=9$ and $n=25$.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{25} &= 4+24\times9 \\ &= 220 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An arithmetic sequence is given by $4, 13, 22, 31, \dots$.
Find the sum to the $25^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence.
items.sol:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ with $l=220$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{25} &= \dfrac{25}{2}(4+220) \\ &= 2800 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $4, x, y, \dfrac{32}{27}$ are four consecutive terms of a geometric series. Solve for $x$ and $y$.
items.sol:
Method 1. In a geometric sequence consecutive ratios are equal, so
$$\dfrac{x}{4}=\dfrac{32}{27y} \qquad (1)$$
$$\dfrac{x}{4}=\dfrac{y}{x}, \text{ so } y=\dfrac{x^2}{4} \qquad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{4} &= \dfrac{32}{27\left(\frac{x^2}{4}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{128}{27x^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 27x^3 &= 512 \\ x^3 &= \dfrac{512}{27} \\ x &= \dfrac{8}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^2}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{64}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{16}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2. Here $a=4$ and $r=\dfrac{x}{4}$, so
$$T_4=4\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3=\dfrac{32}{27}$$
This gives $x^3=\dfrac{512}{27}$, so $x=\dfrac{8}{3}$. Then
$$y=T_3=4\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{8}{3} \text{ and } y=\dfrac{16}{9}$$

items.part: Show that the derivative of $\dfrac{x}{e^x}$ is $\dfrac{1-x}{e^x}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{e^x\cdot1-xe^x}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(1-x)}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1-x}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1-x+e^x}{2e^x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Split the fraction and use part (a).
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{1-x+e^x}{2e^x}\,dx &= \int\left(\dfrac{1-x}{2e^x}+\dfrac{e^x}{2e^x}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int\left(\dfrac{1-x}{e^x}+1\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{x}{e^x}+x\right]+c \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2e^x}+\dfrac{x}{2}+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the derivative of $x^2 - 1$ using first principles.
items.sol:
Using first principles, $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{(x+h)^2-1-(x^2-1)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{x^2+2xh+h^2-1-x^2+1}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{2xh+h^2}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to0}(2x+h) \\ &= 2x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling in a straight line is given by $v = 2t - 4$, where $t$ is time in seconds and $x$ its displacement from the origin in metres. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the expression for the particle's displacement as a function of time.
items.sol:
$$x=\displaystyle\int(2t-4)\,dt=t^2-4t+c$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $c=0$.
$$x=t^2-4t$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling in a straight line is given by $v = 2t - 4$, where $t$ is time in seconds and $x$ its displacement from the origin in metres. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the total distance travelled for the first 5 seconds.
items.sol:
When $t=5$:
$$x=5^2-4(5)=5$$
The particle may change direction when it is stationary, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2t-4 &= 0 \\ t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
When $t=2$:
$$x=2^2-4(2)=-4$$
The particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=-4$, then to $x=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{distance} &= 4+9 \\ &= 13 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the total distance is the area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times4+\dfrac{1}{2}\times3\times6=4+9=13 \text{ m}$$

items.part: Solve for $k$ such that $\displaystyle\int_2^k (-3x+1)\,dx = \int_k^6 (-3x+1)\,dx$.
items.sol:
Evaluate each side using the antiderivative $-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left[-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x\right]_2^k \\ &= -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k-(-6+2) \\ &= -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k+4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \left[-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x\right]_k^6 \\ &= (-54+6)-\left(-\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k\right) \\ &= -48+\dfrac{3k^2}{2}-k \end{aligned}$$
Equate the two sides.
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k+4 &= -48+\dfrac{3k^2}{2}-k \\ 3k^2-2k-52 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4+624}}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{628}}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{157}}{3} \end{aligned}$$

From the calculator, using the data in the table:
$$r=-0.999\ldots\approx-1.000 \text{ (to 3 decimal places)}$$

From the calculator, the least squares regression line is
$$y=-6.52x+15$$
There is a strong negative linear correlation between altitude and temperature.

The probabilities sum to 1.
$$0.15+0.15+0.2+k^2+\dfrac{k}{2}=1$$
Simplifying:
$$\begin{aligned} k^2+\dfrac{k}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2} &= 1 \\ 2k^2+k+1 &= 2 \\ 2k^2+k-1 &= 0 \\ (2k-1)(k+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $k=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $k=-1$.

Probabilities cannot be negative, so $k\ge 0$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part: At the start of the week Susie has three yellow shirts and two green shirts. She wears one clean shirt each day. On Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of that week, she randomly selects one shirt to wear. In this three day period, what is the probability that Susie does not wear a shirt of the same colour on any two successive days?
items.sol:
The colours must alternate, so the shirts worn are YGY or GYG (no replacement).
$$\begin{aligned} P &= P(YGY)+P(GYG) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{4}\times\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{60}+\dfrac{6}{60} \\ &= \dfrac{18}{60} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{10} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Georgina is training for the Tokyo Olympics. She swims 1.5km on the first day, and on each day after that she swims 200 metres more than the previous day. That is, she swims 1.7km on the second day and 1.9km on the third day and so on.
How many days of training will she require to have swum a combined total of over 100km?
items.sol:
The distances form an arithmetic series with $a=1.5$ and $d=0.2$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2\times1.5+(n-1)\times0.2\right]=100$$
$$\begin{aligned} n\left(3+\dfrac{n-1}{5}\right) &= 200 \\ 15n+n(n-1) &= 1000 \\ n^2+14n-1000 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$n=\dfrac{-14\pm\sqrt{14^2+4(1)(1000)}}{2}=\dfrac{-14\pm\sqrt{4196}}{2}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=\dfrac{-14+\sqrt{4196}}{2}\approx 25.39$.

So she needs $26$ days of training.

items.part:
Georgina is training for the Tokyo Olympics. She swims 1.5km on the first day, and on each day after that she swims 200 metres more than the previous day. That is, she swims 1.7km on the second day and 1.9km on the third day and so on.
Georgina wants to have swum over 200 km in total over 20 days. If on the first day she still swims 1.5 km but increases her swim by a distance of $x$ km per day. Find the value of $x$ so that she can reach her goal.
items.sol:
Here $a=1.5$, $n=20$ and $d=x$.
$$\dfrac{20}{2}\left[2\times1.5+(20-1)x\right]=200$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3+19x &= 20 \\ 19x &= 17 \\ x &= \dfrac{17}{19} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{17}{19}\text{ km}$$

items.part: By writing $0 \cdot \dot{7}\dot{6}$ as a geometric series, use the limiting sum formula to show that $0 \cdot \dot{7}\dot{6} = \dfrac{76}{99}$.
items.sol:
Write the decimal as a geometric series.
$$0\cdot\dot{7}\dot{6}=0.76+0.0076+0.000076+\cdots$$
Here $a=0.76$ and $r=0.01$, with $|r|<1$.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{0.76}{1-0.01} \\ &= \dfrac{0.76}{0.99} \\ &= \dfrac{76}{99} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve for $k$ such that $y = e^{kt}$ satisfies the equation $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} = \dfrac{dy}{dt} + y$.
items.sol:
Differentiate $y=e^{kt}$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dt}=ke^{kt},\qquad \dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}=k^2e^{kt}$$
Substitute into $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}=\dfrac{dy}{dt}+y$.
$$\begin{aligned} k^2e^{kt} &= ke^{kt}+e^{kt} \\ k^2 &= k+1 \\ k^2-k-1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$k=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{(-1)^2-4(1)(-1)}}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}$$

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y$ equals:
$\log_2 x$
items.sol:
Using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \log_2 x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 2} \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{x\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y$ equals:
$2^x$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} y &= 2^x \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= (\ln 2)\cdot 2^x \end{aligned}$$

The area is split at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where the graphs intersect.
$$A=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(1-\cos x)\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \Big[x-\sin x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}+\Big[-\cos x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-1\right)-(0-0)-(-1-0) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ units}^2$$

There are 6 subintervals of width $10$, so the trapezoidal rule gives:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Water} &\approx \dfrac{10}{2}\Big[500+2(400+350+280+200+180)+150\Big] \\ &= 17350 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = x(x-2)(x+1)$.
Find the coordinates of any stationary point, to 1 decimal place, and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$y=x^3-x^2-2x,\qquad \dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-2x-2$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$x=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4+24}}{6}$$
So $x\approx 1.2$ or $x\approx -0.5$.

The second derivative is $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-2$.

When $x=1.2$, $y\approx -2.1$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\approx 5.2>0$.

So there is a local minimum at $(1.2,-2.1)$.

When $x=-0.5$, $y\approx 0.6$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\approx -5<0$.

So there is a local maximum at $(-0.5,0.6)$.
items.final: Local minimum at $(1.2,-2.1)$; local maximum at $(-0.5,0.6)$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = x(x-2)(x+1)$.
Find the coordinates of any points of inflection.
items.sol:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$6x-2=0,\quad\text{so } x=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Test the concavity either side.

items.part:
On average, Silvester takes 15 mins to walk to the train station, and from there it takes an average of 45mins to get to the city by train once he is at the station. The standard deviations for the walk and the train trip are 2mins and 5 mins, respectively.
Silvester went to meet his friends today. It took him 18mins to walk to the station, and 52mins to get to the city from the station. Calculate the z-scores for the walk and the train trip respectively.
items.sol:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$z_{\text{walk}}=\dfrac{18-15}{2}=1.5$$
$$z_{\text{train}}=\dfrac{52-45}{5}=1.4$$

items.part:
On average, Silvester takes 15 mins to walk to the train station, and from there it takes an average of 45mins to get to the city by train once he is at the station. The standard deviations for the walk and the train trip are 2mins and 5 mins, respectively.
Assume that the walking time from home to the station is normally distributed. Using the empirical rule, find the number of minutes Silvester should allow himself so that he will arrive at the station faster than the allowed time 97.5% of the time?
items.sol:
By the empirical rule, $97.5\%$ of values lie below $\mu+2\sigma$, so $z=2$.
$$\dfrac{x-15}{2}=2$$
$$\therefore\ x=19\text{ min (at least 19 min)}$$

items.part:
The height of 10 people in centimetres are 170, 180, 185, 188, 192, 193, 193, 194, 196, 202.

Use the interquartile range criteria to determine if there are any outliers in this set of data.
items.sol:
The quartiles are $Q_1=185$ and $Q_3=194$, so $IQR=9$.

Outliers lie outside these boundaries.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1-1.5\times IQR &= 185-13.5=171.5 \\ Q_3+1.5\times IQR &= 194+13.5=207.5 \end{aligned}$$
Since $170<171.5$, the value $170$ is an outlier.

items.part:
A probability distribution is said to have a \textbf{memoryless property} if the probability of some future event occurring is not affected by the occurrence of past events.

In formal statistic terms, a random variable $X$ is said to follow a probability distribution with a memoryless property if for any $a, x \ge 0$ it is true that:

$$P(X > x + a \mid X > a) = P(X > x)$$

You are given that $X$ is modelled by a continuous random variable with probability density function of the form $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, for some constant $\lambda$.
Show that the corresponding cumulative distribution function is given by $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$.
items.sol:
For $x\ge 0$, the cumulative distribution function is the integral of the density.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \displaystyle\int_0^x \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt \\ &= \Big[-e^{-\lambda t}\Big]_0^x \\ &= -e^{-\lambda x}+e^{0} \\ &= 1-e^{-\lambda x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A probability distribution is said to have a \textbf{memoryless property} if the probability of some future event occurring is not affected by the occurrence of past events.

In formal statistic terms, a random variable $X$ is said to follow a probability distribution with a memoryless property if for any $a, x \ge 0$ it is true that:

$$P(X > x + a \mid X > a) = P(X > x)$$

You are given that $X$ is modelled by a continuous random variable with probability density function of the form $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, for some constant $\lambda$.
Hence, prove the memoryless property for the distribution of $X$:

$$P(X > x + a \mid X > a) = P(X > x)$$
items.sol:
Using conditional probability, and noting $X>x+a$ implies $X>a$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>x+a\mid X>a) &= \dfrac{P\big((X>x+a)\cap(X>a)\big)}{P(X>a)} \\ &= \dfrac{P(X>x+a)}{P(X>a)} \end{aligned}$$
Using $P(X>t)=1-F(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{P(X>x+a)}{P(X>a)} &= \dfrac{e^{-\lambda(x+a)}}{e^{-\lambda a}} \\ &= \dfrac{e^{-\lambda x}\cdot e^{-\lambda a}}{e^{-\lambda a}} \\ &= e^{-\lambda x} \end{aligned}$$
Also $P(X>x)=1-\left(1-e^{-\lambda x}\right)=e^{-\lambda x}$.
$$\therefore\ P(X>x+a\mid X>a)=P(X>x)$$

items.part: Solve $2\log_2 x - 9\log_x 2 = 3$.
items.sol:
Using $\log_x 2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2 x}$:
$$2\log_2 x-\dfrac{9}{\log_2 x}-3=0$$
Let $u=\log_2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2u^2-3u-9 &= 0 \\ (2u+3)(u-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $\log_2 x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$ or $\log_2 x=3$.
$$\therefore\ x=2^{-\frac{3}{2}}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\ (\approx 0.3535)\text{ or } x=8$$

items.part:
Consider the series $1 - \tan^2\theta + \tan^4\theta - \tan^6\theta \dots$.
For what values of $\theta$ in the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ does a limiting sum exist for the series?
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $r=-\tan^2\theta$.

A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan^2\theta &< 1 \\ -1 &< \tan\theta < 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{\pi}{4}<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

items.part:
Consider the series $1 - \tan^2\theta + \tan^4\theta - \tan^6\theta \dots$.
Find the expression for this limiting sum in its simplest form.
items.sol:
Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=1$ and $r=-\tan^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{1}{1+\tan^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta} \\ &= \cos^2\theta \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A barrel maker charges \$50 per hour for the time spent on each job, as well as the cost to cover the power used on machinery. Depending on the setting chosen, the machine uses power at a rate of $20 + \dfrac{v^2}{10}$ MW per hour, where $v$ barrels/hour is the speed of which the machine makes barrels. (That is, $v = 3$ means the machine can make 3 barrels in an hour). Power costs \$1.25 per MW used. A job is given to make 1200 barrels.
Show that the cost (\$$C$) to pay for this job is given by $C = \dfrac{90000}{v} + 150v$.
items.sol:
Cost is the wage plus the power cost, where the time taken is $T=\dfrac{1200}{v}$ hours.
$$C=50T+1.25\left(20+\dfrac{v^2}{10}\right)T$$
Substituting $T$:
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 50\left(\dfrac{1200}{v}\right)+1.25\left(20+\dfrac{v^2}{10}\right)\left(\dfrac{1200}{v}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{60000}{v}+\left(25+\dfrac{v^2}{8}\right)\dfrac{1200}{v} \\ &= \dfrac{60000}{v}+\dfrac{30000}{v}+150v \\ &= \dfrac{90000}{v}+150v \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A barrel maker charges \$50 per hour for the time spent on each job, as well as the cost to cover the power used on machinery. Depending on the setting chosen, the machine uses power at a rate of $20 + \dfrac{v^2}{10}$ MW per hour, where $v$ barrels/hour is the speed of which the machine makes barrels. (That is, $v = 3$ means the machine can make 3 barrels in an hour). Power costs \$1.25 per MW used. A job is given to make 1200 barrels.
Assuming that $v$ can take any non-negative values, find the speed $v$, that minimizes the cost and determine this cost.
items.sol:
Differentiate and set $C'=0$.
$$C'=-\dfrac{90000}{v^2}+150=0$$
So $v^2=600$, and $v=\sqrt{600}\approx 24.5$ since $v>0$.

Test the nature:
$$C''=\dfrac{2\times 90000}{v^3}>0 \text{ as } v>0$$
So this is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} C_{\min} &= \dfrac{90000}{\sqrt{600}}+150\sqrt{600} \\ &= \dfrac{18000}{\sqrt{6}} \\ &\approx \$7348.47 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows the graph of the function $y = \ln(x^2)$, where $x > 0$.

The points $P(1,0)$, $Q(e,2)$ and $R(t, \ln t^2)$ all lie on the curve.

The area of $\triangle PQR$ is maximum when the tangent at $R$ is parallel to the line through $P$ and $Q$.

\exfigure{1331_q39_1}
Show that $R$ has coordinates $(e-1, \ln[(e-1)^2])$ for $\triangle PQR$ to have maximum area.
items.sol:
Differentiate $f(x)=\ln(x^2)$.
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2}=\dfrac{2}{x}$$
The gradient of $PQ$ is:
$$m_{PQ}=\dfrac{2-0}{e-1}=\dfrac{2}{e-1}$$
The tangent at $R$ is parallel to $PQ$, so the gradients are equal.
$$\dfrac{2}{x}=\dfrac{2}{e-1},\quad\text{so } x=e-1$$
Then $y=\ln(e-1)^2$.
$$\therefore\ R=\left(e-1,\ln(e-1)^2\right)$$

items.part:
The diagram shows the graph of the function $y = \ln(x^2)$, where $x > 0$.

The points $P(1,0)$, $Q(e,2)$ and $R(t, \ln t^2)$ all lie on the curve.

The area of $\triangle PQR$ is maximum when the tangent at $R$ is parallel to the line through $P$ and $Q$.

\exfigure{1331_q39_1}
Hence find the size of $\angle RPQ$ correct to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the angles that $PQ$ and $PR$ make with the positive $x$-axis.
$$m_{PQ}=\dfrac{2}{e-1}=\tan\alpha,\quad \alpha=49^\circ 20'$$
$$m_{RP}=\dfrac{\ln(e-1)^2-0}{(e-1)-1}=\dfrac{\ln(e-1)^2}{e-2}=\tan\beta,\quad \beta=56^\circ 26'$$
So $\angle RPQ=\beta-\alpha=7^\circ 6'$.
$$\therefore\ \angle RPQ\approx 7^\circ$$
Alternatively, by the cosine rule:
$$\cos\theta=\dfrac{PR^2+PQ^2-RQ^2}{2\,PR\cdot PQ}=\dfrac{1.688+6.9527-1.8415}{2\sqrt{1.688\times 6.9527}}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows the graph of the function $y = \ln(x^2)$, where $x > 0$.

The points $P(1,0)$, $Q(e,2)$ and $R(t, \ln t^2)$ all lie on the curve.

The area of $\triangle PQR$ is maximum when the tangent at $R$ is parallel to the line through $P$ and $Q$.

\exfigure{1331_q39_1}
Hence or otherwise, find the maximum area of $\triangle PQR$, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}|PQ||PR|\sin\angle RPQ$ with $\angle RPQ=7^\circ$.

Find the side lengths.
$$|PQ|=\sqrt{(e-1)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{e^2-2e+5}=\sqrt{6.9527}\approx 2.6368$$
$$|PR|=\sqrt{(e-2)^2+\left(\ln(e-1)^2\right)^2}=\sqrt{1.688}\approx 1.2992$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\max} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.6368\times 1.2992\times\sin 7^\circ \\ &\approx 0.2088 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A_{\max}\approx 0.21\text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
Consider the arithmetic series $5+12+19+\ldots+292$.
Show that there are 42 terms.
items.sol:
This is an arithmetic series with
$$a=5,\quad d=7$$
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $T_n=292$:
$$\begin{aligned} 292&=5+(n-1)\times7 \\ 287&=7n-7 \\ 294&=7n \\ n&=42 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ there are 42 terms, as required.

items.part:
Consider the arithmetic series $5+12+19+\ldots+292$.
Find the sum of the series.
items.sol:
Using the sum formula for an arithmetic series, $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{42}&=\dfrac{42}{2}(5+292) \\ &=6237 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_{42}=6237$$

items.part: Show that the sequence $\dfrac{1}{2},\ \dfrac{1}{3},\ \dfrac{2}{9},\ldots$ is geometric.
items.sol:
A sequence is geometric if consecutive terms have a common ratio.
$$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\dfrac{\frac13}{\frac12}=\dfrac23$$
$$\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{\frac29}{\frac13}=\dfrac23$$
Since $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}$, the sequence is geometric.

items.part:
Mark borrowed \$22 000 to buy a diamond ring for Seiko. He will repay the loan over 4 years in equal monthly instalments. Reducible interest will be charged at a rate of 9% p.a. compounded monthly.

\extable{1583_q1e_t1}

Using the present value interest factors table, determine:
the amount Mark will repay each month.
items.sol:
The number of repayments is $4\times12=48$, and the monthly rate is
$$9\%\div12=0.75\%=0.0075$$
The present value of the loan equals the repayment times the table factor (48 periods, $0.75\%$):
$$22000=M\times40.18478$$
$$\begin{aligned} M&=\dfrac{22000}{40.18478} \\ &=547.4709\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Mark will repay } \$547.47 \text{ per month.}$$

items.part:
Mark borrowed \$22 000 to buy a diamond ring for Seiko. He will repay the loan over 4 years in equal monthly instalments. Reducible interest will be charged at a rate of 9% p.a. compounded monthly.

\extable{1583_q1e_t1}

Using the present value interest factors table, determine:
the amount of interest Mark will pay on his loan.
items.sol:
The total repaid is
$$\begin{aligned} \$547.47\times48&=\$26\,278.56 \end{aligned}$$
The interest is the total repaid less the amount borrowed:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest}&=\$26\,278.56-\$22\,000 \\ &=\$4278.56 \end{aligned}$$
Note: using the unrounded repayment, $48\times\dfrac{22000}{40.18478}-22000=\$4278.61$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Interest}=\$4278.56$$

items.part:
On the day of his daughter's birth James deposits \$1500 in a trust fund that pays interest of 3% p.a. compounded annually. He continues to deposit \$1500 in the trust fund on his daughter's birthday each year.

The amount, $A_n$, in the account immediately prior to the deposit being made on his daughter's $n^{\text{th}}$ birthday can be determined using the recurrence relation:

$$A_n=\left(A_{n-1}+1500\right)\left(1.03\right)$$

Where $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ and $A_0=0$.

Use the recurrence relation to find the amount of money in the trust fund immediately before James makes the deposit on his daughter's third birthday.
items.sol:
Using the recurrence relation $A_n=(A_{n-1}+1500)(1.03)$ with $A_0=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=(0+1500)\times1.03=1545 \\ A_2&=(1545+1500)\times1.03=3136.35 \\ A_3&=(3136.35+1500)\times1.03=4775.4405 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the amount is } \$4775.44$$

items.part:
Andrew borrows \$640 000 which is to be repaid in equal monthly instalments. The interest rate is 4.8% p.a. reducible, calculated monthly. Interest is charged and calculated just before each repayment is made.

Let the amount that Andrew repays each month be $M$ and the amount owing after the $n^{\text{th}}$ repayment be $A_n$.
Show that $A_2=640000\times1.004^2-M\times1.004-M$.
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $4.8\%\div12=0.4\%=0.004$, so the balance is multiplied by $1.004$ before each repayment.
$$A_1=640000\times1.004-M$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1\times1.004-M \\ &=(640000\times1.004-M)\times1.004-M \\ &=640000\times1.004^2-M\times1.004-M \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Andrew borrows \$640 000 which is to be repaid in equal monthly instalments. The interest rate is 4.8% p.a. reducible, calculated monthly. Interest is charged and calculated just before each repayment is made.

Let the amount that Andrew repays each month be $M$ and the amount owing after the $n^{\text{th}}$ repayment be $A_n$.
Show that $A_n=640000\times1.004^n-250M\left(1.004^n-1\right)$.
items.sol:
Continuing the pattern from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} A_3&=(640000\times1.004^2-M\times1.004-M)\times1.004-M \\ &=640000\times1.004^3-M(1+1.004+1.004^2) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$A_n=640000\times1.004^n-M\left(1+1.004+1.004^2+\ldots+1.004^{n-1}\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.004$ and $n$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{1.004^n-1}{1.004-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_n&=640000\times1.004^n-\dfrac{M\left(1.004^n-1\right)}{1.004-1} \\ &=640000\times1.004^n-\dfrac{M\left(1.004^n-1\right)}{0.004} \\ &=640000\times1.004^n-250M\left(1.004^n-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Andrew borrows \$640 000 which is to be repaid in equal monthly instalments. The interest rate is 4.8% p.a. reducible, calculated monthly. Interest is charged and calculated just before each repayment is made.

Let the amount that Andrew repays each month be $M$ and the amount owing after the $n^{\text{th}}$ repayment be $A_n$.
If Andrew makes monthly repayments of \$4000, how long will it take him to repay the loan?
items.sol:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$, with $M=4000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=640000\times1.004^n-250\times4000\left(1.004^n-1\right) \\ 0&=640000\times1.004^n-1000000\times1.004^n+1000000 \\ 360000\times1.004^n&=1000000 \\ 1.004^n&=\dfrac{25}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Taking logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned} n\ln(1.004)&=\ln\left(\dfrac{25}{9}\right) \\ n&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{25}{9}\right)}{\ln(1.004)} \\ &=255.923\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ must be a whole number of months, round up.
$$\therefore\ \text{it will take Andrew 256 months to repay the loan.}$$

items.part:
A machine produces items of which 5% are defective.
If three items are chosen at random, what is the probability they are all defective?
items.sol:
Each item is defective with probability $0.05$, independently, so
$$P(\text{all three defective})=0.05^3=\dfrac{1}{8000}=0.000125$$

items.part:
A machine produces items of which 5% are defective.
A random sample of $n$ items is taken from the machine. Find the largest possible value of $n$ in order that the probability that none of the items is defective is at least 0.6.
items.sol:
The probability an item is not defective is
$$1-\dfrac1{20}=\dfrac{19}{20}$$
We need the probability that none of $n$ items is defective to be at least $0.6$:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{19}{20}\right)^n&\ge0.6 \\ n\ln\left(\dfrac{19}{20}\right)&\ge\ln(0.6) \end{aligned}$$
Since $\ln\left(\dfrac{19}{20}\right)<0$, dividing reverses the inequality:
$$n\le\dfrac{\ln(0.6)}{\ln\left(\frac{19}{20}\right)}=9.9589\ldots$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the largest value of } n \text{ is } 9.$$

items.part:
Liz and Jo are playing a game. They take turns in tossing 2 fair coins. The first player to toss 2 heads is the winner. Jo has the first turn.
What is the probability that Jo will win the game on her first or second turn?
items.sol:
Each toss of 2 coins gives
$$P(HH)=\dfrac14,\quad P(\text{not }HH)=\dfrac34$$
Jo wins on her first turn with probability
$$P(W)=\dfrac14$$
Jo wins on her second turn if both Jo and Liz fail first, then Jo succeeds:
$$P(LLW)=\dfrac34\times\dfrac34\times\dfrac14=\dfrac{9}{64}$$
Adding the two cases:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Jo wins on first or second turn})&=\dfrac14+\dfrac{9}{64} \\ &=\dfrac{25}{64} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Liz and Jo are playing a game. They take turns in tossing 2 fair coins. The first player to toss 2 heads is the winner. Jo has the first turn.
What is the probability that Jo will eventually win the game?
items.sol:
Jo wins on turn 1, turn 2, turn 3, and so on, so
$$P(W)+P(LLW)+P(LLLLW)+\ldots=\dfrac14+\left(\dfrac34\right)^2\times\dfrac14+\left(\dfrac34\right)^4\times\dfrac14+\ldots$$
This is a geometric series with
$$a=\dfrac14,\quad r=\left(\dfrac34\right)^2=\dfrac{9}{16}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the sum to infinity exists:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac14}{1-\left(\frac34\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac47 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the probability Jo eventually wins is } \dfrac47$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = 6x^2 - x^3$.
Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate, then stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 12x - 3x^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 12x - 3x^2 \\ &= 3x(4-x) \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 0$ or $x = 4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{When } x=4,\ y &= 6\times 4^2 - 4^3 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts4660_1}

The slope is decreasing, flat, increasing, flat, decreasing, so there is a maximum turning point at $(4,32)$ and a minimum turning point at $(0,0)$.

Alternatively, use the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12 - 6x$$
At $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12>0$ (concave up), so a minimum.

At $x=4$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -12<0$ (concave down), so a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum at } (4,32),\ \text{minimum at } (0,0)$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = 6x^2 - x^3$.
Find any points of inflexion.
items.sol:
Points of inflexion occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12 - 6x$$
$$0 = 12 - 6x$$
So $x = 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{When } x=2,\ y &= 6\times 2^2 - 2^3 \\ &= 16 \end{aligned}$$
This is a possible point of inflexion at $(2,16)$. Test the concavity either side.

\extable{Ts4661_1}

The curve is concave up, then concave down, so the concavity changes.
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a point of inflexion at } (2,16)$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = 6x^2 - x^3$.
Sketch the curve, showing the stationary points, the point of inflexion and the $x$ and $y$ intercepts.
items.sol:
For the $x$-intercepts, put $y=0$.
$$0 = x^2(6-x)$$
So $x = 0$ or $x = 6$.

\exfigure{1595_q1b_s1}

The curves meet where the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 - 2x - 1 &= 3 - x^2 \\ 2x^2 - 2x - 4 &= 0 \\ 2(x^2 - x - 2) &= 0 \\ 2(x-2)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 2$ or $x = -1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the curves intersect when } x = 2 \text{ and } x = -1$$

The area is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve between the intersections $x=-1$ and $x=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-1}^{2}\left(3 - x^2 - (x^2 - 2x - 1)\right)dx \\ &= \int_{-1}^{2}\left(4 + 2x - 2x^2\right)dx \\ &= \left[4x + x^2 - \dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2} \\ &= \left(4\times 2 + 2^2 - \dfrac{2\times 2^3}{3}\right) - \left(4\times(-1) + (-1)^2 - \dfrac{2\times(-1)^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{20}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right) \\ &= 9 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x+1}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Rewrite with a negative index, then integrate using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx = \dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x+1}}\,dx &= \int (3x+1)^{-\frac12}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{(3x+1)^{\frac12}}{3\times\frac12} + C \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3x+1}}{3} + C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Use the trapezoidal rule with five function values to find, correct to 1 decimal place, the approximate value of $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \log_{10}(x+1)\,dx$.
items.sol:
There are five function values, so four strips on $[0,4]$.
$$h = \dfrac{4-0}{4} = 1$$
\extable{Ts4667_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4 \log_{10}(x+1)\,dx &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\Big(0 + \log_{10}5 + 2(\log_{10}2 + \log_{10}3 + \log_{10}4)\Big) \\ &= 1.729\ldots \\ &\approx 1.7 \text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rainwater tank is designed to be in the shape of a cylinder with radius $r$ metres and height $h$ metres.

\exfigure{1595_q3b_1}

The volume of the tank is to be 20 cubic metres. Let $A$ be the surface area of the tank, including its top and base, in square metres.
Given that $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$ and $V = \pi r^2 h$, show that $A = 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{40}{r}$.
items.sol:
Use $V=20$ in $V=\pi r^2 h$ to eliminate $h$.
$$h = \dfrac{20}{\pi r^2}$$
Substitute into $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\times\dfrac{20}{\pi r^2} \\ &= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{40}{r} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rainwater tank is designed to be in the shape of a cylinder with radius $r$ metres and height $h$ metres.

\exfigure{1595_q3b_1}

The volume of the tank is to be 20 cubic metres. Let $A$ be the surface area of the tank, including its top and base, in square metres.
Find the value of $r$ for which the surface area occurs minimum occurs and justify that it is a minimum value.
items.sol:
Write $A = 2\pi r^2 + 40r^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dr} &= 4\pi r - 40r^{-2} \\ &= 4\pi r - \dfrac{40}{r^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{40}{r^2} &= 4\pi r \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{10}{\pi} \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10}{\pi}} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} &= 4\pi + 80r^{-3} \\ &= 4\pi + \dfrac{80}{r^3} \end{aligned}$$
When $r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10}{\pi}}$, $r^3=\dfrac{10}{\pi}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} &= 4\pi + \dfrac{80\pi}{10} \\ &= 12\pi \\ &= 37.6\ldots > 0 \end{aligned}$$
So the surface area is a minimum.

Alternatively, test the slope either side.

\extable{Ts4670_1}

The slope is decreasing, flat, increasing, so there is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10}{\pi}}$$

items.part: Sketch the curve $y = -4 + 3\sin 2x$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
For $y = -4 + 3\sin 2x$:

the amplitude is $3$,

the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$,

the graph is shifted down 4.

So the range is found in steps.
$$\begin{aligned} -1 &\le \sin 2x \le 1 \\ -3 &\le 3\sin 2x \le 3 &&(\text{multiply by } 3) \\ -7 &\le -4 + 3\sin 2x \le -1 &&(\text{subtract } 4) \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1595_q3c_s1}

items.part: Given $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^3 = \dfrac{3\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^2}{2\sqrt{x}}$, find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^2}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Divide the given derivative by $\dfrac32$ to match the integrand.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^2}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx &= \dfrac23\int \dfrac{3\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^2}{2\sqrt{x}}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac23\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^3 + C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Without using calculus, sketch the graph of $y = 3 + \dfrac{1}{x+2}$, showing the asymptotes and the $x$ and $y$ intercepts.
items.sol:
Write $y = 3 + \dfrac{1}{x+2}$.

The vertical asymptote is $x=-2$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y=3$.

For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 3 + \dfrac12 \\ &= \dfrac72 \end{aligned}$$
For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3 + \dfrac{1}{x+2} \\ -3 &= \dfrac{1}{x+2} \\ -3x - 6 &= 1 \\ x &= -\dfrac73 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1595_q4c_s1}

The line $y=k$ must cut the graph of $y=f(x)$ three times.

This happens between the minimum value $-2$ and the maximum value $5$, not including those values.
$$\therefore\ -2 < k < 5$$

Rewrite the function to read the transformations.
$$y = f\left(\dfrac{x}{2} - 1\right) = f\left(\dfrac12(x-2)\right)$$
This is a horizontal dilation by a factor of 2, then a horizontal translation right 2.

Each $x$-coordinate becomes $2x+2$.

$x$-intercepts: $-6\to -10$, $0\to 2$, $4\to 10$.

Turning points: $(-4,5)\to(-6,5)$ and $(2,-2)\to(6,-2)$.

\exfigure{1595_q4d_s1}

items.part: Given that $f'(x)=3-2e^{-x}$ and $f(0)=1$, find $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Integrate term by term.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int \left(3-2e^{-x}\right)dx\\ &=3x+2e^{-x}+c\end{aligned}$$
Use $f(0)=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=0+2+c\\ c&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=3x+2e^{-x}-1$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to $y=e^{2x}+1$ at $x=1$.
items.sol:
Differentiate to find the gradient of the tangent.
$$y'=2e^{2x}$$
When $x=1$, $y=e^{2}+1$ and $m_T=2e^{2}$.

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_N=-\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}$$
Equation of the normal:
$$\begin{aligned} y-(e^{2}+1)&=-\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}(x-1)\\ y&=-\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}x+\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}+e^{2}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}x+\dfrac{1+2e^{4}+2e^{2}}{2e^{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x+2e^{2}y-\left(1+2e^{4}+2e^{2}\right)=0$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=e^{x^{2}}$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule:
$$y'=2xe^{x^{2}}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int xe^{x^{2}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x^{2}}\right)=2xe^{x^{2}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int xe^{x^{2}}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2xe^{x^{2}}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{x^{2}}+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the curve $y=e^{x}-1$.
items.sol: \exfigure{1606_q2c_s1}

items.part: Find the area between the $x$ axis and the curve $y=e^{x}-1$ between $x=-1$ and $1$.
items.sol:
The curve is below the $x$ axis for $-1\le x<0$ and above it for $0<x\le 1$, so the area is split at $x=0$.
$$A=\left|\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}(e^{x}-1)\,dx\right|+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}(e^{x}-1)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left|\left[e^{x}-x\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left[e^{x}-x\right]_{0}^{1}\\ &=\left|e^{0}-0-\left(e^{-1}+1\right)\right|+(e-1)-e^{0}\\ &=\left|1-\dfrac{1}{e}-1\right|+e-2\\ &=\dfrac{1}{e}+e-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=e+\dfrac{1}{e}-2 \text{ units}^2$$

items.part: The height of water in a tank is initially 50cm. The height is decreasing at a rate of $0.5t$ cm/min. Calculate the time for the tank to empty, to the nearest second.
items.sol:
Integrate the rate, with $h=50$ when $t=0$.
$$\dfrac{dh}{dt}=-0.5t$$
$$\begin{aligned} h&=-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}+c\\ 50&=0+c\\ h&=50-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
The tank is empty when $h=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=50-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}\\ t^{2}&=200\\ t&=\sqrt{200}\end{aligned}$$
We take the positive root since $t>0$.
$$\therefore\ t\approx 14 \text{ min } 9 \text{ s}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line from the origin, and after $t$ seconds its velocity in m/s is given by $v=4-2t$ m/s.
Find when the particle is stationary.
items.sol:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-2t&=0\\ t&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=2 \text{ seconds}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line from the origin, and after $t$ seconds its velocity in m/s is given by $v=4-2t$ m/s.
Find the distance travelled during the first 6 seconds.
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity, with $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int(4-2t)\,dt\\ &=4t-t^{2}+c\end{aligned}$$
Since $c=0$, $x=t(4-t)$.

The particle turns at $t=2$ (from part (a)), so find the positions at $t=2$ and $t=6$.
$$\begin{aligned} t=2:&\ x=4 \text{ m}\\ t=6:&\ x=-12 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The particle moves from $0$ to $4$, then back from $4$ to $-12$.
$$\text{Distance}=4+4+12=20 \text{ m}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=\ln\sqrt{4x+1}$.
items.sol:
Use the log law $\ln a^{n}=n\ln a$ first.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\ln(4x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(4x+1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{4}{4x+1}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{4x+1}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{4x+6}{x^{2}+3x}\,dx$.
items.sol:
The numerator is twice the derivative of $x^{2}+3x$, so the integrand has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{4x+6}{x^{2}+3x}\,dx&=2\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{2x+3}{x^{2}+3x}\,dx\\ &=2\Big[\ln\left(x^{2}+3x\right)\Big]_{1}^{2}\\ &=2\left[\ln 10-\ln 4\right]\\ &=2\ln\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the stationary point on the curve $y=e^{x^{2}+4x}$ and determine its nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$y'=(2x+4)e^{x^{2}+4x}$$
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$. Since $e^{x^{2}+4x}>0$, we need $2x+4=0$, so $x=-2$.

Test the nature using the second derivative, using the product rule.
$$y''=2e^{x^{2}+4x}+(2x+4)^{2}e^{x^{2}+4x}$$
At $x=-2$:
$$y''=2e^{-4}>0$$
So the stationary point is a minimum. When $x=-2$, $y=e^{-4}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum stationary point at } \left(-2,\,e^{-4}\right)$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $a=\sin 2t$.

At time $t=0$, $v=0$ m/s and $x=1$ m.
Find the velocity when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ seconds.
items.sol:
Integrate the acceleration, with $v=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\int\sin 2t\,dt\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+c\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-\dfrac{1}{2}+c\\ c&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
So $v=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}$.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$:
$$\begin{aligned} v&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{2-\sqrt{2}}{4} \text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $a=\sin 2t$.

At time $t=0$, $v=0$ m/s and $x=1$ m.
Find displacement when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ seconds.
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity from part (a), with $x=1$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}t+c\end{aligned}$$
Since $x=1$ when $t=0$, $c=1$.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{\pi}{16}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{8}+\dfrac{\pi}{16}+1\\ &=\dfrac{\pi-2\sqrt{2}+16}{16} \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The rate of change of $Q$ with respect to time is given by $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$.

If $Q=2$ when $t=1$ and $Q=5$ when $t=2$, find $Q$ when $t=3$.
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$, exponential growth gives $Q=Q_0e^{kt}$.

Substitute the two given conditions.
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=Q_0e^{k} &&(1)\\ 5&=Q_0e^{2k} &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Dividing (2) by (1):
$$\begin{aligned} e^{k}&=\dfrac{5}{2}\\ k&=\ln\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=Q_0\cdot\dfrac{5}{2}\\ Q_0&=\dfrac{4}{5}\end{aligned}$$
So $Q=\dfrac{4}{5}e^{\left(\ln\frac{5}{2}\right)t}$.

When $t=3$:
$$Q=\dfrac{4}{5}e^{3\ln\frac{5}{2}}$$
$$\therefore\ Q=\dfrac{4}{5}\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^{3}=\dfrac{25}{2}$$

Split into two cases.

Case 1: $2x - 3 = 6$

$$\begin{aligned} 2x &= 9 \\ x &= \dfrac{9}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Case 2: $2x - 3 = -6$

$$\begin{aligned} 2x &= -3 \\ x &= -\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{9}{2} \text{ or } x = -\dfrac{3}{2}$$

items.part:
The function $y = f(x)$ is defined as

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } -2 \le x \le 0 \\ -x^2 + 1 & \text{for } x \ge 0 \end{cases}$$

By sketching $y = f(x)$ or otherwise, write the domain and range of $y = f(x)$ using interval notation.
Prove that $\dfrac{\sin A}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} = 2\,\text{cosec}\,A$.
items.sol:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sin A}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} + \dfrac{(1 + \cos A)^2}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A + (1 + \cos A)^2}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A + 1 + 2\cos A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{2 + 2\cos A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} &&(\text{since } \sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1) \\ &= \dfrac{2(1 + \cos A)}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sin A} \\ &= 2\operatorname{cosec} A \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An airport scanner screens bags for prohibited items. An alarm is supposed to be triggered when a prohibited item is detected.

On a given day, $5\%$ of bags contain prohibited items. If a bag contains prohibited items, there is a $95\%$ chance that it triggers the alarm. If a bag does not contain prohibited items, there is a $2\%$ chance that it triggers the alarm.
Complete the probability tree using the information provided.

\exfigure{1612_q14_1}
items.sol: \exfigure{1612_q14_s1}

items.part:
An airport scanner screens bags for prohibited items. An alarm is supposed to be triggered when a prohibited item is detected.

On a given day, $5\%$ of bags contain prohibited items. If a bag contains prohibited items, there is a $95\%$ chance that it triggers the alarm. If a bag does not contain prohibited items, there is a $2\%$ chance that it triggers the alarm.
Given that a randomly selected bag triggers the alarm, what is the probability that it contains a prohibited item?
items.sol:
Use the conditional probability formula.

$$P(\text{prohibited} \mid \text{alarm}) = \dfrac{P(\text{prohibited} \cap \text{alarm})}{P(\text{alarm})}$$

From the tree:

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{prohibited} \mid \text{alarm}) &= \dfrac{\frac{5}{100} \times \frac{95}{100}}{\left(\frac{5}{100} \times \frac{95}{100}\right) + \left(\frac{95}{100} \times \frac{2}{100}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The heights of 30 mothers and daughters were recorded. The results are shown in the scatterplot. The least-squares regression line on the scatterplot passes through the point $(180, 184)$.

\exfigure{1612_q15_1}
Katarina calculated that the correlation coefficient for this data set is $r = -2.5$.

Without calculating the correlation coefficient, give TWO reasons why Katarina must be incorrect.
items.sol:
Reason 1: a correlation coefficient satisfies $-1 \le r \le 1$, and $r = -2.5$ lies outside this.

Reason 2: the scatterplot shows a positive correlation, so $r$ should be positive, with $0 < r < 1$.

items.part:
The heights of 30 mothers and daughters were recorded. The results are shown in the scatterplot. The least-squares regression line on the scatterplot passes through the point $(180, 184)$.

\exfigure{1612_q15_1}
The equation of the least-squares regression line for this data set is in the form

$$y = 0.8077x + A,$$

where $A$ is a constant. Katarina is 160 cm tall.

Use the equation of the least-squares regression line to estimate the height of Katarina's mother. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
The line passes through $(180, 184)$, so find $A$.

$$\begin{aligned} 184 &= 0.8077(180) + A \\ 184 &= 145.386 + A \\ A &= 38.614 \end{aligned}$$

Hence the line is $y = 0.8077x + 38.614$.

Katarina is $160$ cm tall, so $y = 160$.

$$\begin{aligned} 160 &= 0.8077x + 38.614 \\ x &\approx 150.285 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore Katarina's mother is approximately $150$ cm tall.

items.part: Evaluate $f'(\pi)$ given that $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{\cos x}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{(\cos x)(2x) - (x^2)(-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{x(2\cos x + x\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} \end{aligned}$$

Substitute $x = \pi$.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(\pi) &= \dfrac{\pi(2\cos\pi + \pi\sin\pi)}{\cos^2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi(-2 + 0)}{(-1)^2} \\ &= -2\pi \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $y = x\ln x$.
Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= (x)\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) + (\ln x)(1) \\ &= 1 + \ln x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $y = x\ln x$.
Hence, or otherwise, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^e \ln x\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a), if $y = x\ln x$ then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$.

By the fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$\int_1^e (1 + \ln x)\,dx = \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e$$

Split the left side.

$$\int_1^e 1\,dx + \int_1^e \ln x\,dx = \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e$$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^e \ln x\,dx &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e - \int_1^e 1\,dx \\ &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e - \Big[x\Big]_1^e \\ &= (e\ln e - 1\ln 1) - (e - 1) \\ &= e - (e - 1) \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the primitive function $y$ given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2x}{3x^2 + 1}$.
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, so write the integrand in the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.

$$\begin{aligned} y &= \int \dfrac{2x}{3x^2 + 1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\int \dfrac{6x}{3x^2 + 1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left|3x^2 + 1\right| + C \end{aligned}$$

The area under the curve from $0$ to $1$ is found by integrating.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,(1 - x)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^1 \left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} - x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} - \dfrac{2}{5}x^{\frac{5}{2}}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{2}{5}\right) - (0 - 0) \\ &= \dfrac{4}{15} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A basketball player shoots a ball from a height of 2 metres into a hoop 14 metres away. The hoop 3 metres from the ground. After moving 5 metres horizontally, the ball reaches a height of 4 metres from the ground. This information is shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1612_q20_1}

The path of the ball can be modelled by the quadratic function

$$y = ax^2 + bx + c,$$

where $y$ represents the height of the ball from the ground, $x$ is the horizontal displacement from the basketball player, and $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$ that best model the path of the ball.
items.sol:
Place axes with the player at the origin.

\exfigure{1612_q20_s2}

The ball passes through $(0, 2)$, $(5, 4)$ and $(14, 3)$.

Substituting $(0, 2)$ gives $c = 2$, so $y = ax^2 + bx + 2$.

Substituting $(5, 4)$:

$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= 25a + 5b + 2 \\ 2 &= 25a + 5b \\ a &= \dfrac{2 - 5b}{25} &&(1) \end{aligned}$$

Substituting $(14, 3)$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 196a + 14b + 2 \\ 1 &= 196a + 14b &&(2) \end{aligned}$$

Substituting (1) into (2):

$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 196\left(\dfrac{2 - 5b}{25}\right) + 14b \\ 25 &= 196(2 - 5b) + 350b \\ 25 &= 392 - 980b + 350b \\ -367 &= -630b \\ b &= \dfrac{367}{630} \end{aligned}$$

Substituting into (1):

$$a = \dfrac{2 - 5\left(\frac{367}{630}\right)}{25} = -\dfrac{23}{630}$$

$$\therefore\ a = -\dfrac{23}{630},\ b = \dfrac{367}{630},\ c = 2$$

Model A is a geometric sequence with first term $a = 200\,000$ (2021) and common ratio $r = 1.1$.

The general term is $T_n = 200\,000(1.1)^{n-1}$.

For 2025, $n = 5$.

$$\begin{aligned} T_5 &= 200\,000(1.1)^{4} \\ &= 292\,820 \end{aligned}$$

Model B is an arithmetic sequence with $a = 200\,000$ and $d = M$, so the general term is
$$T_n = 200\,000 + (n-1)M$$
2025 is the 5th year, so $T_5 = 292\,820$.
$$\begin{aligned} 292\,820 &= 200\,000 + (5-1)M \\ 92\,820 &= 4M \\ M &= \$23\,205 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ M = \$23\,205$$

items.part:
Archaeologists are excavating a rectangular site with dimensions of 150 metres by 60 metres.

The shaded region indicates the portion of the site that has been excavated.

\exfigure{1612_q22_1}

Use the trapezoidal rule to best approximate the total area that has been excavated. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
The shaded region is described by the table of values below.

Using the trapezoidal rule with $n = 4$ and $a = 0$, $b = 150$:

items.part:
Consider the function $y = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$.

It is known that as $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ and as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to -\infty$.
Find the $x$- and $y$-intercepts.
items.sol:
For the $x$-intercept, let $y = 0$:
$$0 = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$$
so $2x = 0$, giving $x = 0$. The $x$-intercept is $(0,0)$.

For the $y$-intercept, let $x = 0$:
$$y = \dfrac{2(0)}{e^0} = 0$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,0)$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the only intercept is at the origin}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$.

It is known that as $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ and as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to -\infty$.
Find and classify any turning points on $y = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{(e^x)(2) - (2x)(e^x)}{(e^x)^2} = \dfrac{2e^x(1-x)}{e^{2x}} = \dfrac{2(1-x)}{e^x}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{2(1-x)}{e^x} \\ 1 - x &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
When $x = 1$, $y = \dfrac{2}{e}$.

The sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of $x=1$ gives its nature:

\extable{Ts4729_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $\left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.

items.part:
Consider the function $y = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$.

It is known that as $x \to \infty$, $y \to 0$ and as $x \to -\infty$, $y \to -\infty$.
Show that a point of inflection occurs at $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$.
items.sol:
From part (b), $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2(1-x)}{e^x}$.

Using the quotient rule with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1-x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2\left[\dfrac{(e^x)(-1) - (1-x)(e^x)}{e^{2x}}\right] = 2\left(\dfrac{xe^x - 2e^x}{e^{2x}}\right) = \dfrac{2(x-2)}{e^x}$$
For a possible point of inflection, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{2(x-2)}{e^x} \\ x &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
When $x = 2$, $y = \dfrac{4}{e^2}$.

The sign of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ either side of $x=2$ tests the concavity:

\extable{Ts4730_1}

The concavity changes, so $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$ is a point of inflection.

items.part:
The time, in minutes, between the arrival of customers at an Automated Teller Machine (ATM) is represented by the variable, $t$, which is a continuous random variable modelled by the probability density function

$$f(t) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-\frac{t}{3}} & t \ge 0 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Find the median time between the arrival of customers at the ATM. Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
Let $F(x)$ be the cumulative distribution function.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_0^x \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-\frac{t}{3}}\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\left[-3e^{-\frac{t}{3}}\right]_0^x \\ &= -\left[e^{-\frac{x}{3}} - e^0\right] \\ &= 1 - e^{-\frac{x}{3}} \end{aligned}$$
The median satisfies $F(x) = 0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5 &= 1 - e^{-\frac{x}{3}} \\ 0.5 &= e^{-\frac{x}{3}} \\ \ln 0.5 &= -\dfrac{x}{3} \\ x &= -3\ln 0.5 = 2.079\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the median time is 2 minutes}$$

The triangles' perimeters form a geometric sequence with $a = p$ and $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$, since each new triangle has sides half as long. With $p_n$ the perimeter of the $n$th triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} p_n &= ar^{n-1} \\ &= p\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1} \\ &= p\left(\dfrac{1^{n-1}}{2^{n-1}}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{p}{2^{n-1}} \quad (\text{since } 1^{n-1} = 1) \end{aligned}$$

The total perimeter is the sum to infinity, valid since $|r| = \dfrac{1}{2} < 1$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{p}{1-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{p}{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= 2p \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_\infty = 2p \text{ cm}$$

Assume that all darts thrown will hit the board and no darts will land on the lines.
Paula has two attempts at throwing a dart at the board. On one of her attempts, Paula's dart lands in the centre circle. On another attempt, her dart lands in the outer section.

Show that the probability that this occurs, in any order, is $\dfrac{3}{160}$.
items.sol:
The outer section is the board minus the circle of radius 5, so
$$P(\text{outer}) = \dfrac{\pi(20)^2 - \pi(5)^2}{\pi(20)^2} = \dfrac{15}{16}$$
The two darts can land in either order, so multiply by 2.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{centre and outer, any order}) &= 2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{100} \times \dfrac{\pi(20)^2 - \pi(5)^2}{\pi(20)^2}\right) \\ &= 2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{100} \times \dfrac{15}{16}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{160} \end{aligned}$$

Show that the length of the whiteboard, $L$, is $\dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$.
items.sol:
Divide the whiteboard into two parts, $L_1$ and $L_2$, one in each corridor.

\exfigure{1612_q31_s1}

In the right-angled triangle in the 3 m corridor, by the cosine ratio:
$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{3}{L_1}, \quad\text{so}\quad L_1 = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta}$$
In the right-angled triangle in the 4 m corridor, by the sine ratio:
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{L_2}, \quad\text{so}\quad L_2 = \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$$

items.sol:
To minimise $L = \dfrac{3}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{4}{\sin\theta}$, write it with powers and differentiate.
$$L = 3(\cos\theta)^{-1} + 4(\sin\theta)^{-1}$$
$$\dfrac{dL}{d\theta} = \dfrac{3\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} - \dfrac{4\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \dfrac{3\sin^3\theta - 4\cos^3\theta}{\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin^3\theta - 4\cos^3\theta &= 0 \\ \tan^3\theta &= \dfrac{4}{3} \\ \tan\theta &= \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} \\ \theta &= \tan^{-1}\left[\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\right] = 0.833\ldots \text{ radians} \end{aligned}$$
Converting to degrees:
$$0.833\times\dfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 47.74^\circ$$
The sign of $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta}$ either side of this value tests the nature:

\extable{Ts4744_1}

The gradient changes from negative to positive, so $\theta = 47.74^\circ$ gives a minimum turning point.

items.part: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin A}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} = 2\operatorname{cosec} A$.
items.sol:
Combine the fractions over the common denominator $\sin A(1 + \cos A)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sin A}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} + \dfrac{(1 + \cos A)^2}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A + 1 + 2\cos A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{2 + 2\cos A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} &&(\text{since } \sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1) \\ &= \dfrac{2(1 + \cos A)}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sin A} \\ &= 2\operatorname{cosec} A \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}A_{\triangle ABC}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(CB)(CA)\sin C\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}h\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}h^2\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times21\\&=\dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Also, with base $AB=7$ and height $w$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\triangle ABC}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times7\times w\\\dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}&=\dfrac{7w}{2}\\w&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the width of the footpath is } \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{ metres}$$

items.sol:
Since $-1\le\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\le1$:

items.part:
An office has climate control and the temperature at any time $t$ hours is $T$ degrees Celsius, where

$$T(t)=22+3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\qquad t\in[0,24]$$

Let $t=0$ correspond to the time which Miss Kim arrives at the office (8:00 am). What is the latest time that she should finish eating the lunch, before the food is spoilt?
items.sol:
The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{12}}=24$ hours.

Find when $T=23.5$:
$$\begin{aligned}23.5&=22+3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\\\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{\pi}{12}t=\dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ or } \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
so $t=2$ or $t=10$.

The temperature is above $23.5^\circ$C from $t=2$, that is from 10 am.

$\therefore$ the latest time she should finish eating is 1 pm.

items.part: Differentiate $\ln(\tan 3x)$.
items.sol: $$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln(\tan3x)\right)=\dfrac{3\sec^23x}{\tan3x}$$

items.part: Differentiate $\dfrac{x}{e^{3x+1}}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{3x+1}\\u'&=1 & v'&=3e^{3x+1}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{e^{3x+1}}\right)&=\dfrac{e^{3x+1}(1)-x\left(3e^{3x+1}\right)}{\left(e^{3x+1}\right)^2}\\&=\dfrac{e^{3x+1}(1-3x)}{\left(e^{3x+1}\right)^2}\\&=\dfrac{1-3x}{e^{3x+1}}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\log_e\left(2x^2+1\right)$ at the point $(2,\log_e 9)$.
items.sol:
Differentiating, using the chain rule for $\ln$:
$$y'=\dfrac{4x}{2x^2+1}$$
At $x=2$:
$$y'=\dfrac{4(2)}{2(2^2)+1}=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_N=\dfrac{-1}{m_T}=-\dfrac{9}{8}$$
The equation of the normal is
$$y-\log_e 9=-\dfrac{9}{8}(x-2)$$
$$y=-\dfrac{9}{8}x+\log_e 9+\dfrac{9}{4}$$
The general form $9x+8y-18-8\log_e 9=0$ is also acceptable.

items.part: Find: $\displaystyle\int\left(1+e^{7x}\right)dx$
items.sol: $$\int\left(1+e^{7x}\right)dx=x+\dfrac{1}{7}e^{7x}+C$$

items.part: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int_0^2\dfrac{2}{5x+4}\,dx$
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(5x+4)=\dfrac{5}{5x+4}$, write the integrand with a factor of $5$ in the numerator.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2\dfrac{2}{5x+4}\,dx&=\dfrac{2}{5}\int_0^2\dfrac{5}{5x+4}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{2}{5}\Big[\ln(5x+4)\Big]_0^2\\&=\dfrac{2}{5}\left(\ln 14-\ln 4\right)\\&=\dfrac{2}{5}\ln\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{2x}\right)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{2x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{2x}\right)&=1\cdot e^{2x}+x\cdot 2e^{2x}\\&=2xe^{2x}+e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence or otherwise, find

$$\int xe^{2x}\,dx$$
items.sol:
From part (a), integrating both sides:
$$xe^{2x}+C=\displaystyle\int\left(2xe^{2x}+e^{2x}\right)dx$$
Rearranging:
$$2\int xe^{2x}\,dx=xe^{2x}-\int e^{2x}\,dx=xe^{2x}-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}+C$$
Dividing by $2$:
$$\int xe^{2x}\,dx=\dfrac{x}{2}e^{2x}-\dfrac{1}{4}e^{2x}+\dfrac{C}{2}$$

$f(x)$ intersects the axes at the points $A$ and $B$. The line joining $A$ and $B$ is also shown.

Show that the exact value of the shaded area is

$$6-\dfrac{6}{\ln 3}$$
items.sol:
When $x=0$:
$$f(0)=9-3=6$$
When $y=0$:
$$3^{x+1}=3^2,\quad x=1$$
So $A(0,6)$ and $B(1,0)$.

The shaded area is the area under the curve less the triangle under the line $AB$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_0^1\left(9-3^{x+1}\right)dx-\dfrac{1}{2}(1\times 6)\\&=\left[9x-\dfrac{3^{x+1}}{\ln 3}\right]_0^1-3\\&=\left[\left(9-\dfrac{3^2}{\ln 3}\right)-\left(0-\dfrac{3}{\ln 3}\right)\right]-3\\&=9-\dfrac{6}{\ln 3}-3\\&=6-\dfrac{6}{\ln 3}\end{aligned}$$
