items.part: Show that the derivative of $2x\log_5 x$ is $2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln5}$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=\log_5 x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2x\log_5 x\right)&=2\log_5 x+2x\left(\dfrac{1}{x\ln 5}\right)\\ &=2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln5}\right)dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a), simplify the derivative:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln 5}&=2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}\\ &=2\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right) \end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right)dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[2x\log_5 x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=\Big[x\log_5 x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
This is undefined, as $\log_5 0$ is undefined.

items.part:
Ms Alrubai and Mrs Norman are employed as doctors. They both start on the same annual salary. However, Ms Alrubai negotiated an annual salary increase of $\$5\,000$, while Mrs Norman negotiated an annual salary increase of $7\%$.

Find their starting annual salary given that after $16$ years they have both made the same amount of money in total.
items.sol:
Alrubai's salaries form an arithmetic series with $d=5000$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{16}&=\dfrac{16}{2}\left[2a+(16-1)5000\right]\\ &=8\left[2a+75\,000\right]\\ &=16a+600\,000 \end{aligned}$$
Norman's salaries form a geometric series with $r=1.07$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{16}&=\dfrac{a\left(1.07^{16}-1\right)}{1.07-1}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a \end{aligned}$$
Equate the totals and solve for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} 16a+600\,000&=\left(\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a\\ \left(16-\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a&=-600\,000\\ a&=\dfrac{-600\,000}{16-\frac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}}\\ &\approx \$50\,470.84 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the starting salary is } \$50\,470.84$$

items.part:
If Mr Ferrarin wakes up late, the probability that he exercises is $\dfrac{1}{3}$, and if he wakes up on time the probability that he exercises is $\dfrac{4}{5}$.
In a particular week, Mr Ferrarin wakes up on time on Thursday morning and late on Friday morning.

Find the probability that Mr Ferrarin exercised on at least one of these days.
items.sol:
The probability of exercising on at least one day is the complement of exercising on neither day. On time: not exercising is $\dfrac{1}{5}$; late: not exercising is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{13}{15} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
If Mr Ferrarin wakes up late, the probability that he exercises is $\dfrac{1}{3}$, and if he wakes up on time the probability that he exercises is $\dfrac{4}{5}$.
Find the probability that Mr Ferrarin exercises on any given Monday.
items.sol:
Add the probabilities of exercising after waking on time and after waking late.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exercise})&=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{4}{5}+\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=0.45 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
If Mr Ferrarin wakes up late, the probability that he exercises is $\dfrac{1}{3}$, and if he wakes up on time the probability that he exercises is $\dfrac{4}{5}$.
Hence, or otherwise, find the probability that Mr Ferrarin woke up on time on a Monday, given that he exercised that day.
items.sol:
Using the conditional probability formula, with $A$ = wakes on time and $B$ = exercises:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A|B)&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{4}\times\frac{4}{5}}{0.45}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The graphs of $f(x)=-x^2+2$ and $g(x)=x^3-x^2-kx+2$, where $k$ is a constant, are shown below.

The graphs intersect and create two closed regions, A and B.

\exfigure{1338_q33_1}

Show that these two regions have the same area.
items.sol:
The graphs meet where they are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-x^2-kx+2&=-x^2+2\\ x^3-kx&=0\\ x\left(x^2-k\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{k}$.

For region A, $g(x)$ is above $f(x)$, and $g(x)-f(x)=x^3-kx$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{k}}^{0}\left(x^3-kx\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{kx^2}{2}\right]_{-\sqrt{k}}^{0}\\ &=0-\left(\dfrac{k^2}{4}-\dfrac{k^2}{2}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
For region B, $f(x)$ is above $g(x)$, and $f(x)-g(x)=-x^3+kx$.
$$\begin{aligned} B&=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\sqrt{k}}\left(-x^3+kx\right)dx\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{x^4}{4}+\dfrac{kx^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{\sqrt{k}}\\ &=-\dfrac{k^2}{4}+\dfrac{k^2}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=B$$

items.part:
Ned Kelly, $N$, left his hideout, $H$, and walked along a straight path at $7$ km/h. At the same time that Ned left his hideout, the Police, $P$, are $20$ km away from his hideout, walking towards it along a different straight path at $5$ km/h. The two paths meet at an angle of $120^\circ$.

\exfigure{1338_q34_1}

The distance between Ned Kelly and the police at time $t$ hours is $D$ km.
Show that $D^2=39t^2-60t+400$.
items.sol:
After $t$ hours, $HP=20-5t$ and $HN=7t$, with $\angle PHN=120^\circ$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $PHN$, $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$:
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=(20-5t)^2+(7t)^2-2(20-5t)(7t)\cos 120^\circ\\ &=400-200t+25t^2+49t^2-2(20-5t)(7t)\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=400-200t+74t^2+140t-35t^2\\ &=39t^2-60t+400 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Ned Kelly, $N$, left his hideout, $H$, and walked along a straight path at $7$ km/h. At the same time that Ned left his hideout, the Police, $P$, are $20$ km away from his hideout, walking towards it along a different straight path at $5$ km/h. The two paths meet at an angle of $120^\circ$.

\exfigure{1338_q34_1}

The distance between Ned Kelly and the police at time $t$ hours is $D$ km.
Find the minimum distance, to the nearest kilometre, between the police and Ned Kelly.
items.sol:
$D$ is a minimum when $D^2$ is, so find the minimum stationary point of $D^2$.
$$\dfrac{d\left(D^2\right)}{dt}=78t-60$$
Stationary point when $78t-60=0$:
$$t=\dfrac{60}{78}=\dfrac{10}{13}$$
Test the sign of the derivative:
$$t=0.7,\ \dfrac{10}{13},\ 0.8:\ \dfrac{d\left(D^2\right)}{dt}=-5.4,\ 0,\ 2.4$$
The gradient changes from negative to positive, so this is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=39\left(\dfrac{10}{13}\right)^2-60\left(\dfrac{10}{13}\right)+400\\ &\approx 376.923 \end{aligned}$$
$$D\approx 19.41\text{ km (2 d.p.)}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum distance is about } 19\text{ km}$$

Case 2:

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\sqrt{x}\right)$.
items.sol:
Write $x\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{3}{2}}$ and use the power rule.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\sqrt{x}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}x^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, by the product rule, the derivative is $\sqrt{x}+\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{x}}$.

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}\right)\right)$.
items.sol:
Using the log laws, split the logarithm of a quotient into a difference.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln(1-3x)-\ln(1+2x)\Big]\\&=\dfrac{-3}{1-3x}-\dfrac{2}{1+2x}\\&=\dfrac{-3(1+2x)-2(1-3x)}{(1-3x)(1+2x)}\\&=\dfrac{-5}{(1-3x)(1+2x)}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, by the quotient rule:
$$\dfrac{-5}{(1+2x)^2}\div\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}=\dfrac{-5}{(1+2x)(1-3x)}$$

items.part:
A yacht leaves Port A on a bearing of $120^\circ$ and sails for three hours at an average speed of 15km/h to its destination where it stops.

At the same time, a speed boat also leaves from Port A and travels due south to Island B that is 30km from the port.

\exfigure{1340_q13_1}
Calculate the distance of the yacht from Island B to the nearest kilometre.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1340_q13_s1}

Distance sailed by the yacht: $15\times3=45$ km.

The angle at $A$ between $AB$ (due south) and $AY$ (bearing $120^\circ$) is $180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $ABY$:
$$\begin{aligned}YB^2&=30^2+45^2-2(30)(45)\cos60^\circ\\&=1575\\YB&=\sqrt{1575}\\&=39.686\ldots\\&\approx40\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A yacht leaves Port A on a bearing of $120^\circ$ and sails for three hours at an average speed of 15km/h to its destination where it stops.

At the same time, a speed boat also leaves from Port A and travels due south to Island B that is 30km from the port.

\exfigure{1340_q13_1}
Find the bearing of Island B from the yacht to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Applying the sine rule in triangle $ABY$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle YBA}{45}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{YB}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\angle YBA&=\dfrac{45\sin60^\circ}{YB}\\&=0.98198\ldots\\\angle YBA&=79.1066\ldots^\circ\\&\approx79^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Bearing of $B$ from $Y$:
$$180^\circ+79^\circ=259^\circ\text{T}$$
Using the rounded value $YB=40$ gives $\angle YBA\approx77^\circ$ and bearing $257^\circ\text{T}$. Other methods, such as the cosine rule for the angle at $Y$, also give $259^\circ\text{T}$.

items.part:
A yacht leaves Port A on a bearing of $120^\circ$ and sails for three hours at an average speed of 15km/h to its destination where it stops.

At the same time, a speed boat also leaves from Port A and travels due south to Island B that is 30km from the port.

\exfigure{1340_q13_1}
After spending several hours at the island, the speed boat travels due north back to Port A.

How far south of the port will the speed boat be when it is directly west of the yacht?
items.sol:
Let $x$ be the distance south of the port when the boat is directly west of the yacht. The yacht is 45 km from $A$ on a line making $60^\circ$ with due south.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos60^\circ&=\dfrac{x}{45}\\x&=45\cos60^\circ\\&=22.5\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
The speed boat is 22.5 km south of the port.

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int (2+5x^2)\,dx$.
Find $\displaystyle\int 5\sin x\cos^3 x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Rewrite in the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int5\sin x\cos^3x\,dx&=-5\int(-\sin x)\cos^3x\,dx\\&=-5\times\dfrac{\cos^4x}{4}+C\\&=-\dfrac{5\cos^4x}{4}+C\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, let $u=\cos x$, so $du=-\sin x\,dx$:
$$-5\int u^3\,du=-\dfrac{5u^4}{4}+C$$

items.part:
Chris and Ann are participating in a charity bicycle ride between Canberra and Liverpool.

Chris leaves Canberra and rides to Liverpool, a distance of 250 km, at an average speed of 20km/h. His distance from Liverpool is modelled by the equation $C=250-20t$, where $C$ is his distance from Liverpool and $t$ is the time in hours he has been riding.
On the grid below, sketch the graph of this model and label it ‘Chris’.

\exfigure{1340_q16_1}
items.sol:
The line has $y$-intercept $250$ and gradient $-20$. It meets the $t$-axis when $250-20t=0$, that is at $t=12.5$.

\exfigure{1340_q16_s1}

items.part:
Chris and Ann are participating in a charity bicycle ride between Canberra and Liverpool.

Chris leaves Canberra and rides to Liverpool, a distance of 250 km, at an average speed of 20km/h. His distance from Liverpool is modelled by the equation $C=250-20t$, where $C$ is his distance from Liverpool and $t$ is the time in hours he has been riding.
Ann rides in the opposite direction and leaves from Berrima, a town located 90km from Liverpool. She begins riding at the same time as Chris and rides at an average speed of 12km/h towards Canberra.

By drawing a line on the grid above, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ when Chris and Ann pass each other.
items.sol:
Ann starts 90 km from Liverpool and rides away from it at 12 km/h, so her distance from Liverpool is
$$A=90+12t$$
Chris: $C=250-20t$. They pass each other when $A=C$:
$$\begin{aligned}90+12t&=250-20t\\32t&=160\\t&=5\end{aligned}$$
Graphically, Ann's line from $(0,90)$ with gradient 12 crosses Chris's line at $t=5$.
$$\therefore\ t=5\text{ hours}$$

items.part:
Chris and Ann are participating in a charity bicycle ride between Canberra and Liverpool.

Chris leaves Canberra and rides to Liverpool, a distance of 250 km, at an average speed of 20km/h. His distance from Liverpool is modelled by the equation $C=250-20t$, where $C$ is his distance from Liverpool and $t$ is the time in hours he has been riding.
Chris and Ann are initially 160km apart. Using the graphs drawn, or otherwise, find the value of $t$ when Chris and Ann are next 160km apart.
items.sol:
The distance between them is $A-C$, so set
$$\begin{aligned}90+12t-(250-20t)&=160\\32t-160&=160\\32t&=320\\t&=10\end{aligned}$$
Graphically, at $t=10$ Chris is 50 km and Ann 210 km from Liverpool.
$$\therefore\ t=10\text{ hours}$$

items.part:
Chris and Ann are participating in a charity bicycle ride between Canberra and Liverpool.

Chris leaves Canberra and rides to Liverpool, a distance of 250 km, at an average speed of 20km/h. His distance from Liverpool is modelled by the equation $C=250-20t$, where $C$ is his distance from Liverpool and $t$ is the time in hours he has been riding.
Find the value of $t$ when the riders have ridden a total of 264km.
items.sol:
Distance ridden by Chris: $20t$. Distance ridden by Ann: $12t$.
$$\begin{aligned}20t+12t&=264\\32t&=264\\t&=8.25\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=8.25\text{ hours}$$

items.part: Without using calculus, sketch the graph of $y=2-\dfrac{1}{x+4}$, showing any intercepts and asymptotes.
items.sol:
The asymptotes are $x=-4$ and $y=2$.

$x$-intercept ($y=0$):
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{1}{x+4}&=0\\2(x+4)&=1\\x&=-\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$y$-intercept ($x=0$):
$$y=2-\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{7}{4}$$
Extra point on the left branch: at $x=-5$, $y=2+1=3$.

items.part:
A runner is training for a long-distance event.

The first week she runs 1.2 km.

The second week she runs 1.8 km.

The third week she runs 2.7 km, and so on, adding on half of the previous week.
How far does she run in the fourth week?
items.sol:
The common ratio is
$$r=\dfrac{1.8}{1.2}=\dfrac{2.7}{1.8}=1.5$$
Fourth week:
$$T_4=2.7\times1.5=4.05\text{ km}$$
Check: $T_4=1.2\times1.5^3=4.05$ km.

items.part:
A runner is training for a long-distance event.

The first week she runs 1.2 km.

The second week she runs 1.8 km.

The third week she runs 2.7 km, and so on, adding on half of the previous week.
How far does she run in \textbf{total} after the first 6 weeks?
items.sol:
The distances form a geometric series with $a=1.2$, $r=1.5$, $n=6$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_6&=\dfrac{1.2(1.5^6-1)}{1.5-1}\\&=24.9375\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
Check by adding the terms: $1.2+1.8+2.7+4.05+6.075+9.1125=24.9375$.

items.part:
A runner is training for a long-distance event.

The first week she runs 1.2 km.

The second week she runs 1.8 km.

The third week she runs 2.7 km, and so on, adding on half of the previous week.
The event she is training for is 45 km.

In which week will she first exceed this distance?
items.sol:
The $n$th term is $T_n=1.2\times1.5^{n-1}$. Set $T_n=45$:
$$\begin{aligned}45&=1.2\times1.5^{n-1}\\37.5&=1.5^{n-1}\\\ln37.5&=(n-1)\ln1.5\\n&=\dfrac{\ln37.5}{\ln1.5}+1\\&=9.93872\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The terms increase, so the first whole week with $n>9.94$ is week 10.
$$\therefore\ \text{She first exceeds 45 km in the 10th week.}$$
items.final: She first exceeds 45 km in the 10th week.

In any game, the probability that Ash wins is $\dfrac{3}{5}$ and the probability that Naomi wins is $\dfrac{2}{5}$.
Draw a probability tree showing the possible outcomes, in a series of three games.
items.sol:
Let $A$ be "Ash wins" and $N$ be "Naomi wins". Each branch has probability $\dfrac{3}{5}$ for $A$ and $\dfrac{2}{5}$ for $N$. After $AA$ or $NN$ the series stops.

\exfigure{1340_q19_s1}

items.part:
Ash and Naomi complete a series of games. The series finishes when one player has won two games.

In any game, the probability that Ash wins is $\dfrac{3}{5}$ and the probability that Naomi wins is $\dfrac{2}{5}$.
What is the probability that Naomi wins the series?
items.sol:
Naomi wins the series by $ANN$, $NAN$ or $NN$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Naomi wins}) &= P(ANN)+P(NAN)+P(NN) \\ &= 2\times\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5}\right)+\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{44}{125} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Ash and Naomi complete a series of games. The series finishes when one player has won two games.

In any game, the probability that Ash wins is $\dfrac{3}{5}$ and the probability that Naomi wins is $\dfrac{2}{5}$.
What is the probability that Naomi wins at least one game?
items.sol:
Naomi wins at least one game unless Ash wins the first two games.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one}) &= 1-P(AA) \\ &= 1-\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{16}{25} \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2-x & v&=(x+2)^3\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=3(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -(x+2)^3+(2-x)\times3(x+2)^2 \\ &= (x+2)^2\left[3(2-x)-(x+2)\right] \\ &= (x+2)^2(6-3x-x-2) \\ &= (x+2)^2(4-4x) \\ &= 4(x+2)^2(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(2-x)(x+2)^3$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature. You may use $f''(x)=-12x(x+2)$.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$, so $x=-2$ or $x=1$.
$$f(-2)=0,\quad f(1)=(2-1)(1+2)^3=27$$
The points are $(-2,0)$ and $(1,27)$.

Nature of $(1,27)$, using $f''(x)=-12x(x+2)$:
$$f''(1)=-12(1)(3)=-36<0$$
so $(1,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

Nature of $(-2,0)$: here $f''(-2)=0$, so test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-3)&=-36 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(-1)&=12 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(-2,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.
items.final: $(1,27)$ is a maximum turning point; $(-2,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(2-x)(x+2)^3$.
Find the coordinates of all points of inflection of $y=f(x)$.
items.sol:
Points of inflection need $f''(x)=0$.
$$-12x(x+2)=0$$
so $x=0$ or $x=-2$.

$$f(0)=2\times8=16$$
From part (b), $(-2,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

Test $(0,16)$ for a change in concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-1)&=12 &&\text{concave up}\\ f''(1)&=-36 &&\text{concave down}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(0,16)$ is a point of inflection.

$$\therefore\ \text{points of inflection: } (-2,0) \text{ and } (0,16)$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(2-x)(x+2)^3$.
Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$ below, showing all intercepts, stationary points, and points of inflection.

Let $f(x)=(2-x)(x+2)^3$.
Does $y=f(x)$ have a global maximum or global minimum in its natural domain? If so, specify where.
items.sol:
The curve has a maximum turning point at $(1,27)$ and both ends go down, so there is a global maximum of $27$ when $x=1$.

There is no global minimum, since $y\to-\infty$ as $x\to\pm\infty$.
items.final: Global maximum of $27$ when $x=1$; no global minimum.

items.part: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_3^4 \dfrac{x}{x^2-8}\,dx$ in simplest form.
items.sol:
The numerator is half the derivative of $x^2-8$, so write
$$\begin{aligned} \int_3^4\dfrac{x}{x^2-8}\,dx &= \dfrac12\int_3^4\dfrac{2x}{x^2-8}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac12\Big[\ln|x^2-8|\Big]_3^4 \\ &= \dfrac12\left(\ln8-\ln1\right) \\ &= \dfrac12\ln8 \\ &= \dfrac32\ln2 \end{aligned}$$

Five function values give $n=4$ strips, so $h=\dfrac{6-2}{4}=1$ and the $x$-values are $2,3,4,5,6$.

Using the trapezoidal rule, $A\approx\dfrac{b-a}{2n}\left\{f(a)+f(b)+2\left[f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3)\right]\right\}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{6-2}{2\times4}\left\{\dfrac12+\dfrac16+2\left[\dfrac13+\dfrac14+\dfrac15\right]\right\} \\ &\approx 1.117\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ sketched below.

\exfigure{1340_q22_1}
Calculate the same area by evaluating $\displaystyle\int_2^6 \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$.

Give your answer correct to three decimal places.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_2^6\dfrac1x\,dx &= \Big[\ln|x|\Big]_2^6 \\ &= \ln6-\ln2 \\ &\approx 1.099\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The trapezoidal rule gives an approximation, whereas integration gives the exact area.

The curve is concave up, so the sloping sides of the trapezia lie above the curve and the trapezoidal rule gives an overestimate.

items.part:
The function $f(t)=a\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}t\right)+b$ is drawn below, where $0\le t\le 48$.

The maximum value of $f(t)$ is 70 000 when $t=12$. The minimum value of $f(t)$ is 10 000 when $t=36$.

\exfigure{1340_q23_1}

What are the values of $a$ and $b$?
items.sol:
The amplitude is half the difference between the maximum and minimum.
$$a=\dfrac{70000-10000}{2}=30000$$
The centre line is halfway between them.
$$b=10000+30000=40000$$

items.part:
A particle starts to move from the origin along the $x$-axis.

Its velocity, measured in metres, at some time $t$ seconds, is given by $v=4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}$ m/s.
Explain why the particle is never at rest.
items.sol:
If the particle is at rest, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1} &= 0 \\ 4(3t+1) &= 2 \\ 12t &= -2 \\ t &= -\dfrac16 \end{aligned}$$
But $t\ge0$, so the particle is never at rest.

items.part:
A particle starts to move from the origin along the $x$-axis.

Its velocity, measured in metres, at some time $t$ seconds, is given by $v=4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}$ m/s.
Find the acceleration of the particle at $t=3$ seconds.
items.sol:
Write $v=4-2(3t+1)^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} a=\dfrac{dv}{dt} &= -2\times(-1)(3t+1)^{-2}\times3 \\ &= \dfrac{6}{(3t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$a=\dfrac{6}{(3\times3+1)^2}=\dfrac{6}{100}=0.06\ \text{m/s}^2$$

items.part:
A particle starts to move from the origin along the $x$-axis.

Its velocity, measured in metres, at some time $t$ seconds, is given by $v=4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}$ m/s.
Find the exact distance travelled by the particle between $t=0$ and $t=5$ seconds.
items.sol:
By part (a) the particle is never at rest and $v>0$, so it never changes direction. The distance equals the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{distance} &= \int_0^5\left(4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}\right)dt \\ &= \Big[4t-\dfrac23\ln|3t+1|\Big]_0^5 \\ &= 20-\dfrac23\ln16 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, $x=4t-\dfrac23\ln|3t+1|+C$, and $x=0$ when $t=0$ gives $C=0$. At $t=5$, $x=20-\dfrac23\ln16$.

$$\therefore\ \text{distance}=\left(20-\dfrac23\ln16\right)\text{ m}$$

items.part:
A particle starts to move from the origin along the $x$-axis.

Its velocity, measured in metres, at some time $t$ seconds, is given by $v=4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}$ m/s.
Find the particle’s limiting velocity.
items.sol:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{2}{3t+1}\to0$, so $v\to4$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the limiting velocity is } 4 \text{ m/s}$$

items.part:
At the beginning of the year 1935, 100 cane toads were introduced into Australia. Exactly 5 years later, the population had grown to 1000.

Assume that the number of cane toads is increasing exponentially and satisfies an equation of the form

$$N=N_0e^{kt}$$

where $N_0$ and $k$ are constants and $t$ is measured in years from the start of 1935.
Show that $N_0=100$ and $k=\dfrac{\ln 10}{5}$.

At the beginning of the year 1935, 100 cane toads were introduced into Australia. Exactly 5 years later, the population had grown to 1000.

Assume that the number of cane toads is increasing exponentially and satisfies an equation of the form

$$N=N_0e^{kt}$$

where $N_0$ and $k$ are constants and $t$ is measured in years from the start of 1935.
How long does it take for the population to reach 2 million? Give your answer to the nearest year.
Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln(\sec x+\tan x)\right)=\sec x$.
items.sol:
Apply the chain rule to the logarithm, with $\sec x=(\cos x)^{-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sec x+\tan x) &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\times\dfrac{d}{dx}\left((\cos x)^{-1}+\tan x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}+\sec^2x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\left(\tan x\sec x+\sec^2x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\sec x(\tan x+\sec x)}{\sec x+\tan x} \\ &= \sec x \end{aligned}$$
as required.

The curves meet where $\cos x=\dfrac12\sec x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos x &= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} \\ 2\cos^2x &= 1 \\ \cos^2x &= \dfrac12 \\ \cos x &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \end{aligned}$$
The solution in the first quadrant is $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

items.part: Hence, find the exact area of the shaded region $R$.
items.sol:
The region lies between $y=\cos x$ (above) and $y=\dfrac12\sec x$ from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Part (a) gives $\displaystyle\int\sec x\,dx=\ln(\sec x+\tan x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\cos x-\dfrac12\sec x\right)dx \\ &= \Big[\sin x-\dfrac12\ln(\sec x+\tan x)\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac12\ln\left(\sqrt2+1\right)\right)-\left(0-\dfrac12\ln1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac12\ln\left(\sqrt2+1\right)\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Use the graph below to find the value of $k$ which satisfies $\displaystyle\int_{-6}^{k} f(x)\,dx=0$.

\exfigure{1340_q27_1}
items.sol:
The area above the $x$-axis is a trapezium.
$$A_1=\dfrac12\times10\times(5+2)=35\ \text{units}^2$$
The area below the $x$-axis is a triangle-based region with base $k-4$ and height from the graph.
$$A_2=\dfrac12(k-4)(6+4)=5k-20\ \text{units}^2$$
For $\displaystyle\int_{-6}^{k}f(x)\,dx=0$ the two areas must be equal.
$$\begin{aligned} 5k-20 &= 35 \\ 5k &= 55 \\ k &= 11 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Point $A(2e,1)$ lies on the function $h(x)$. The tangent to $h(x)$ at $A$ has equation $y=\dfrac{x}{2e}$.

Point $B$ is the image of the point $A$ on the function $g(x)=3h(2x+4)$.
Show that $B$ has coordinates $(e-2,3)$.
items.sol:
Write $g(x)=3h\left(2(x+2)\right)$. A point $(x,y)$ on $h$ maps to $\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-2,\,3y\right)$ on $g$.
$$B=\left(\dfrac{2e}{2}-2,\,3\times1\right)=(e-2,\,3)$$

items.part:
Point $A(2e,1)$ lies on the function $h(x)$. The tangent to $h(x)$ at $A$ has equation $y=\dfrac{x}{2e}$.

Point $B$ is the image of the point $A$ on the function $g(x)=3h(2x+4)$.
Hence, find the equation of the tangent to $g(x)$ at point $B$, in general form.
items.sol:
Differentiate $g(x)=3h(2x+4)$ using the chain rule.
$$g'(x)=3h'(2x+4)\times2=6h'(2x+4)$$
At $B$, $x=e-2$, so $2x+4=2e$.
$$g'(e-2)=6h'(2e)$$
But $h'(2e)$ is the gradient of the tangent at $A$, which is $\dfrac{1}{2e}$.
$$g'(e-2)=6\times\dfrac{1}{2e}=\dfrac{3}{e}$$
The tangent at $B$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-3 &= \dfrac{3}{e}\left(x-(e-2)\right) \\ ey-3e &= 3x-3e+6 \\ 3x-ey+6 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1340_q29_1}

The diagram above shows a part of the circle $x^2+y^2=25$. The point $P(x,y)$ is on the circle, and point $O$ is the origin. Point $M$ has coordinates $(2,0)$, point $N$ has coordinates $(0,4)$, and $\angle MOP$ is measured in radians.
Show that the area, $A$, of the quadrilateral $OMPN$ is given by

$$A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$$
items.sol:
Triangle $OPM$ has $OP=5$ (radius), $OM=2$ and included angle $\theta$.
$$A_{\triangle OPM}=\dfrac12\times5\times2\times\sin\theta=5\sin\theta$$
Triangle $ONP$ has $ON=4$, $OP=5$ and included angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta$.
$$A_{\triangle ONP}=\dfrac12\times4\times5\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=10\cos\theta$$
Therefore
$$A=A_{\triangle OPM}+A_{\triangle ONP}=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$$
as required.

Differentiate $A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$.
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta$$
For a stationary point $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10\sin\theta &= 5\cos\theta \\ \tan\theta &= \dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right)\approx0.463$ radians.

Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}=-5\sin\theta-10\cos\theta\approx-11.18<0$$
so this is a maximum turning point.

$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum area occurs when } \tan\theta=\dfrac12$$

Since $\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac12$, we have $y=\dfrac{x}{2}$. Also $P$ lies on $x^2+y^2=25$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+\dfrac{x^2}{4} &= 25 \\ 5x^2 &= 100 \\ x^2 &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
P is in the first quadrant, so $x=2\sqrt5$ and $y=\sqrt5$.

Alternatively, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}$, so $y=5\sin\theta=\sqrt5$ and $x=5\cos\theta=2\sqrt5$.

$$\therefore\ P=\left(2\sqrt5,\ \sqrt5\right)$$

items.part: Solve $2^x = \dfrac{1}{16}$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} 2^x &= \dfrac{1}{2^4} \\ 2^x &= 2^{-4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = -4$$

items.part: Factorise $x^3 + 27$.
items.sol:
Using the sum of cubes, $a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)$, with $a=x$ and $b=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^3 + 27 &= x^3 + 3^3\\ &= (x+3)(x^2 - 3x + 3^2)\\ &= (x+3)(x^2 - 3x + 9)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Simplify $\dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{x-1}{3}$.
items.sol:
Use the common denominator 6.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{x-1}{3} &= \dfrac{3x}{6} - \dfrac{2(x-1)}{6}\\ &= \dfrac{3x - 2x + 2}{6}\\ &= \dfrac{x+2}{6}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find a primitive of $\sqrt{x}$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned}\int x^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx &= \dfrac{x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} + C\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}x\sqrt{x} + C\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
Cosine is negative, so $\theta$ is in quadrants 2 and 3.

The acute angle is
$$\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
Quadrant 2:
$$\theta = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$
Quadrant 3:
$$\theta = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \text{ or } \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$

items.part: Calculate the sum of the arithmetic series $32 + 36 + 40 + \dots + 144$.
items.sol:
The series is arithmetic with first term $a=32$, common difference $d=4$ and last term $T_n=144$.

Find the number of terms using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 144 &= 32 + (n-1)\cdot 4 \\ 4n &= 116 \\ n &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
Use $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{29} &= \dfrac{29}{2}\left[2(32) + 28\times 4\right]\\ &= 14.5\times 176\\ &= 2552\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$x\tan 2x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\tan 2x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2\sec^2 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y' &= 1\cdot\tan 2x + x\cdot 2\sec^2 2x\\ &= \tan 2x + 2x\sec^2 2x\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$\dfrac{\ln x}{x^2}$
items.sol:
Write the function as a product, $\ln x\cdot x^{-2}$, and use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x^{-2}\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=-2x^{-3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y' &= \dfrac{1}{x}\cdot x^{-2} + \ln x\cdot\left(-2x^{-3}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{1}{x^3} - \dfrac{2\ln x}{x^3}\\ &= \dfrac{1 - 2\ln x}{x^3}\end{aligned}$$
The quotient rule gives the same result.

items.part:
The parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ has a vertex at $(3, 1)$ and passes through $(0, 0)$.
Find the other $x$-intercept.
items.sol:
The parabola passes through $(0,0)$ with vertex $(3,1)$, which lies above the origin, so it is concave down.

The axis of symmetry is $x=3$, so the other $x$-intercept is the reflection of $x=0$:
$$\therefore\ x = 6$$

items.part:
The parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ has a vertex at $(3, 1)$ and passes through $(0, 0)$.
Find $a$, $b$ and $c$
items.sol:
The zeros are $x=0$ and $x=6$, so $y=a(x-0)(x-6)=ax(x-6)$.

The point $(3,1)$ satisfies the equation:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 3a(-3) \\ 1 &= -9a \\ a &= -\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y &= -\dfrac{x}{9}(x-6)\\ &= -\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{2}{3}x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = -\dfrac{1}{9},\ b = \dfrac{2}{3},\ c = 0$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1341_q19_1}

The lengths of the sides of a triangle are 4.2 cm, 5.3 cm, and 7.6 cm.
Calculate the size of the largest angle of the triangle.

Leave your answer correct to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
The largest angle $\theta$ is opposite the longest side (7.6 cm). Using the cosine rule:
$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{4.2^2 + 5.3^2 - 7.6^2}{2\times 4.2\times 5.3}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta \approx 106^\circ$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1341_q19_1}

The lengths of the sides of a triangle are 4.2 cm, 5.3 cm, and 7.6 cm.
Hence, calculate the area of the triangle.

Leave your answer correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
Using the area formula with the included angle $106^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 4.2\times 5.3\times\sin 106^\circ\\ &\approx 10.7 \text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A) = p$, $P(B) = 2p$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.42$, and $P(A \cap B) = 0.03$.
Show that $p = 0.15$
items.sol:
Using $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} p + 2p - 0.03 &= 0.42 \\ 3p &= 0.45 \\ p &= 0.15 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A) = p$, $P(B) = 2p$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.42$, and $P(A \cap B) = 0.03$.
By use of a Venn diagram, or otherwise, show that $P(A \cup \tilde{B}) = 0.73$,

where $\tilde{B}$ is the complement of $B$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $P(B)=2p=0.3$, so
$$P(\tilde{B}) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$$
$A\cup\tilde{B}$ is everything except the part of $B$ outside $A$, so it is $\tilde{B}$ together with $A\cap B$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cup\tilde{B}) &= P(\tilde{B}) + P(A\cap B)\\ &= 0.7 + 0.03\\ &= 0.73\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A) = p$, $P(B) = 2p$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.42$, and $P(A \cap B) = 0.03$.
Show that $P(A \cap \tilde{B}) = 0.12$ and hence determine, with reasoning, whether the events $A$ and $\tilde{B}$ are independent.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cap\tilde{B}) &= P(A) - P(A\cap B)\\ &= 0.15 - 0.03\\ &= 0.12\end{aligned}$$
For independence we need $P(A\cap\tilde{B}) = P(A)\,P(\tilde{B})$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(A)\times P(\tilde{B}) &= 0.15\times 0.7\\ &= 0.105\end{aligned}$$
Since $0.12\ne 0.105$, $A$ and $\tilde{B}$ are NOT independent.

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} x^2 + x\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned}\int_{-1}^{1}(x^2+x)\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_{-1}^{1}\\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$TP$ is a tower on horizontal ground, $ABP$. Note $\angle TPA = 90^\circ$

Two straight cables, $AT$ and $BT$, connect the top, $T$, of the tower to the ground.

\exfigure{1341_q22_1}

$AT$ and $BT$ make angles with the ground of $27^\circ$ and $43^\circ$ respectively.

$BT$ is 25 m closer to the foot of the tower, $P$, than $A$.

What is the length of the cable $AT$, correct to 2 significant figures?
items.sol:
In the triangle $ABT$, $\angle ABT$ is the exterior-adjacent angle at $B$:
$$\angle ABT = 180^\circ - 43^\circ = 137^\circ$$
By the angle sum of the triangle:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle ATB &= 180^\circ - 27^\circ - 137^\circ\\ &= 16^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Using the sine rule with $AB=25$:
$$\dfrac{AT}{\sin 137^\circ} = \dfrac{25}{\sin 16^\circ}$$
$$\therefore\ AT \approx 62 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
A quadrilateral has vertices $A(-1, 8)$, $B(7, 12)$, $C(8, 5)$, and $D(2, -3)$ as shown below.

\exfigure{1341_q24_1}

NOT TO SCALE
Show that the equation of diagonal $BD$ is $y = 3x - 9$.
items.sol:
The diagonal $BD$ passes through $B(7,12)$ and $D(2,-3)$.

The gradient is
$$\begin{aligned} m_{BD} &= \dfrac{-3 - 12}{2 - 7} \\ &= \dfrac{-15}{-5} \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Using point-gradient form with $B(7,12)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 12 &= 3(x - 7) \\ y - 12 &= 3x - 21 \\ y &= 3x - 9 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A quadrilateral has vertices $A(-1, 8)$, $B(7, 12)$, $C(8, 5)$, and $D(2, -3)$ as shown below.

\exfigure{1341_q24_1}

NOT TO SCALE
The equation of diagonal $AC$ is $x + 3y = 23$.

Find the coordinates of $E$, the point of intersection of the diagonals.
items.sol:
$E$ lies on both diagonals, so substitute $y = 3x - 9$ into $x + 3y = 23$.
$$\begin{aligned} x + 3(3x - 9) &= 23 \\ x + 9x - 27 &= 23 \\ 10x &= 50 \\ x &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 3\times 5 - 9 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ E = (5, 6)$$

items.part:
A quadrilateral has vertices $A(-1, 8)$, $B(7, 12)$, $C(8, 5)$, and $D(2, -3)$ as shown below.

\exfigure{1341_q24_1}

NOT TO SCALE
Show that $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
items.sol:
The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ passes through the midpoint of $AB$ with gradient perpendicular to $AB$.
$$\begin{aligned} m_{AB} &= \dfrac{12 - 8}{7 - (-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{8} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So the gradient of the perpendicular bisector is $-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Midpoint of } AB &= \left(\dfrac{-1+7}{2}, \dfrac{8+12}{2}\right) \\ &= (3, 10) \end{aligned}$$
The perpendicular bisector is
$$\begin{aligned} y - 10 &= -2(x - 3) \\ y - 10 &= -2x + 6 \\ 2x + y - 16 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Test $E(5,6)$:
$$2(5) + 6 - 16 = 0$$
Hence $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

items.part:
By drawing two appropriate graphs determine how many roots there are of the equation $e^x + 2x - 3 = 0$.

\exfigure{1341_q25_1}
items.sol:
Rearrange the equation as $e^x = 3 - 2x$. The roots are the $x$ values where $y = e^x$ meets $y = 3 - 2x$.

The line $y = 3 - 2x$ has $y$-intercept $3$ and $x$-intercept $\dfrac{3}{2}$.

\exfigure{1341_q25_s1}

The graphs intersect at one point.

$$\therefore\ \text{there is 1 root}$$

items.part: By using the Reference sheet, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^2}{\left(8 - x^3\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Write the integrand as a power and use $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x) = 8 - x^3$, $f'(x) = -3x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int x^2\left(8 - x^3\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dx &= -\dfrac{1}{3}\int -3x^2\left(8 - x^3\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{\left(8 - x^3\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}} + C \\ &= -\dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{8 - x^3} + C \end{aligned}$$

For one year, the future value factor at $5\%$ for $2$ periods is $2.0500$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Future value} &= \$24\,000 \times 2.0500 \\ &= \$49\,200 \end{aligned}$$

Interest is $4\%$ per annum compounded six-monthly, so $2\%$ per half-year. Two years gives $n = 4$ periods.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Future value} &= \$31\,800 \times 4.1216 \\ &= \$131\,066.88 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The table below shows the future value of a \$1 annuity.

\extable{1341_q27_t1}
Victoria aims to have a deposit for an apartment of at least \$92 000 in four years time by investing in an annuity. The annuity has an interest rate of 6% per annum compounded annually.

Calculate Victoria's yearly contribution, to the nearest dollar, to achieve the deposit.
items.sol:
The future value factor for $6\%$ and $4$ years is $4.3746$.
$$P \times 4.3746 \ge 92\,000$$
$$\begin{aligned} P &\ge \dfrac{92\,000}{4.3746} \\ &= \$21\,030.49 \end{aligned}$$
Round up, since the deposit must be at least $\$92\,000$.
$$\therefore\ \text{yearly contribution} = \$21\,031$$

The line is below the parabola between $x=-2$ and $x=4$, so the area is the integral of the difference (parabola minus line).
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-2}^{4}\left((-2x^2 + 6x + 11) - (2x - 5)\right)dx \\ &= \int_{-2}^{4}\left(-2x^2 + 4x + 16\right)dx \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}x^3 + 2x^2 + 16x\right]_{-2}^{4} \\ &= \left(-\dfrac{128}{3} + 32 + 64\right) - \left(\dfrac{16}{3} + 8 - 32\right) \\ &= 120 - \dfrac{144}{3} \\ &= 72 \text{ u}^2 \end{aligned}$$

$P$ and $Q$ lie on both the line and the circle. Substitute $y = 2x + 5$ into the circle equation.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 + (2x+5)^2 - 6x - 2(2x+5) - 30 &= 0 \\ x^2 + 4x^2 + 20x + 25 - 6x - 4x - 10 - 30 &= 0 \\ 5x^2 + 10x - 15 &= 0 \\ 5(x^2 + 2x - 3) &= 0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = -3$ or $x = 1$. The point $P$ has $x=-3$, so $Q$ has $x = 1$ and
$$y = 2(1) + 5 = 7$$
$$\therefore\ Q = (1, 7)$$

Complete the square on the equation from (a).
$$\begin{aligned} (x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 - 2y + 1) &= 30 + 9 + 1 \\ (x-3)^2 + (y-1)^2 &= 40 \end{aligned}$$
So the centre is $C_1 = (3, 1)$ and $r = \sqrt{40}$.

The distances from the centres $C_1$ and $C_2$ to $P$ or $Q$ are all $r$, so $PC_1QC_2$ is a rhombus and its diagonals bisect each other at $M$.

The midpoint of $PQ$ is
$$M = \left(\dfrac{1 - 3}{2}, \dfrac{7 - 1}{2}\right) = (-1, 3)$$
The midpoint of $C_1C_2$, with $C_2 = (x, y)$, is also $M$:
$$(-1, 3) = \left(\dfrac{x+3}{2}, \dfrac{y+1}{2}\right)$$
So
$$x = 2(-1) - 3 = -5, \qquad y = 2(3) - 1 = 5$$
The second circle has the same radius, so
$$\therefore\ (x+5)^2 + (y-5)^2 = 40$$

items.part:
A roof of a house has a rectangular base 7 m by 10 m.

Each of the four sloping faces make an angle of $50^\circ$ with the horizontal.

The midpoint of $EF$ lies vertically above intersection of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.

\exfigure{1341_q30_1}

Calculate the total surface area of the sloping faces, correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
Each sloping face makes $50^\circ$ with the horizontal. Half the width of the base is $3.5$ m.

In the right-angled triangle formed by the roof height $h_R$ and a horizontal run of $3.5$ m:
$$\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{h_R}{3.5}, \quad\text{so}\quad h_R = 3.5\tan 50^\circ$$
The slant height $h_\triangle$ of the sloping face satisfies
$$\begin{aligned} \sin 50^\circ &= \dfrac{h_R}{h_\triangle} \\ h_\triangle &= \dfrac{3.5\tan 50^\circ}{\sin 50^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
The horizontal run $x$ on the end faces satisfies
$$\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{h_R}{x} = \dfrac{3.5\tan 50^\circ}{x}, \quad\text{so}\quad x = 3.5$$
Then $EF = 10 - 2\times 3.5 = 3$ m.

The two triangular end faces have base $7$ and slant height $\dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ}$. The two trapezium faces have parallel sides $3$ and $10$ and the same slant height.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2 \times 7 + \dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 10)\times 2\right) \\ &\approx 108.9 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total area} \approx 108.9 \text{ m}^2 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
In an online game there are various 'power-ups' that players can discover while progressing through the game. The power-ups come in two sizes, major and minor, and they all belong to one of two categories, either combat or survival.

It is known that 85% of the power-ups in the game are minor and the rest are major.

Of the major power-ups it is known that 60 % are combat power-ups, while of the minor power-ups it is known that 30 % are combat power-ups.
Using the given information, complete the tree diagram below.

\exfigure{1341_q31_1}
items.sol:
The minor power-ups are $85\%$ and the major ones $15\%$. On the minor branch, $30\%$ are combat, so the rest are survival. On the major branch, $60\%$ are combat.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{survival}\mid\text{minor}) &= 0.7 \\ P(\text{combat}\mid\text{major}) &= 0.6 \\ P(\text{survival}\mid\text{major}) &= 0.4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In an online game there are various 'power-ups' that players can discover while progressing through the game. The power-ups come in two sizes, major and minor, and they all belong to one of two categories, either combat or survival.

It is known that 85% of the power-ups in the game are minor and the rest are major.

Of the major power-ups it is known that 60 % are combat power-ups, while of the minor power-ups it is known that 30 % are combat power-ups.
Find the probability that when a power-up is discovered it will be a combat power-up.
items.sol:
A combat power-up is either minor and combat, or major and combat.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{combat}) &= 0.85 \times 0.3 + 0.15 \times 0.6 \\ &= 0.345 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In an online game there are various 'power-ups' that players can discover while progressing through the game. The power-ups come in two sizes, major and minor, and they all belong to one of two categories, either combat or survival.

It is known that 85% of the power-ups in the game are minor and the rest are major.

Of the major power-ups it is known that 60 % are combat power-ups, while of the minor power-ups it is known that 30 % are combat power-ups.
Given that a power-up is a combat power-up, find the probability that it is a major power-up
items.sol:
Let $A$ be the event that the power-up is major and $B$ the event that it is combat. Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A \mid B) &= \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.15\times 0.6}{0.345} \\ &= \dfrac{0.09}{0.345} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{23} \\ &\approx 0.2609 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Astronomers classify the brightness of stars according to a scale of magnitudes. The difference in magnitude between two stars is defined by the formula

$$m_1 - m_2 = 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{b_2}{b_1}\right),$$

where $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the magnitudes of the two stars, and $b_1$ and $b_2$ are the corresponding apparent brightnesses measured in watts per metre squared.

The magnitude of a star is a unitless measure, and its value can be positive or negative.

The star Sirius has a magnitude of $-1.4$ and an apparent brightness of $1.04 \times 10^{-7}$ W/m$^2$.
The star Acrux has an apparent brightness of $1.42 \times 10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$.

Calculate the magnitude of Acrux, correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Take Sirius as star 1 and Acrux as star 2 in the given formula, and make $m_2$ the subject.
$$m_1 - m_2 = 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{b_2}{b_1}\right)$$
In the source working, $m_1 = -1.4$ is the Sirius magnitude and the quantity sought is the Acrux magnitude; the source writes
$$\begin{aligned} m &= -1.4 + 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1.04\times 10^{-7}}{1.42\times 10^{-8}}\right) \\ &\approx 0.76 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{magnitude of Acrux} \approx 0.76$$

items.part:
Astronomers classify the brightness of stars according to a scale of magnitudes. The difference in magnitude between two stars is defined by the formula

$$m_1 - m_2 = 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{b_2}{b_1}\right),$$

where $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the magnitudes of the two stars, and $b_1$ and $b_2$ are the corresponding apparent brightnesses measured in watts per metre squared.

The magnitude of a star is a unitless measure, and its value can be positive or negative.

The star Sirius has a magnitude of $-1.4$ and an apparent brightness of $1.04 \times 10^{-7}$ W/m$^2$.
The Sun has a magnitude of $-26.7$.

Calculate the apparent brightness of the Sun, correct to three significant figures.
items.sol:
Take the Sun as star 1 and Sirius as star 2, and make $b_1$ the subject. Let $A = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{2.5}$.

The source working gives $A = 10.12$, so
$$\begin{aligned} b_1 &= b_2 \times 10^A \\ &= 1.04 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{10.12} \\ &\approx 1370 \text{ W/m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Doctor Hopper is investigating the population of kangaroos in New South Wales.

The doctor found, based on historical data that the population of kangaroos, $P$, could be modelled by

$$P = 7500 + 500(1.09)^t,$$

where $t$ is the number of years since the start of the year 2000, $t \ge 0$.

Find the rate at which the population of kangaroos is growing at the end of 2021.

Leave your answer correct to two significant figures.
items.sol:
Differentiate using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^t\right) = a^t\ln a$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 500 \times (1.09)^t \ln 1.09$$
The end of 2021 is $t = 22$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 500 \times (1.09)^{22}\ln 1.09 \\ &\approx 290 \text{ per year} \end{aligned}$$

The trapezoidal rule with strip width $1$ gives the area $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\text{first} + \text{last} + 2\times\text{middle heights}\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Current area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2 + 2(2.38 + 2.5 + 2.38) + 2\right) \\ &= 9.26 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Proposed area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2 + 2(2.78 + 3 + 2.78) + 2\right) \\ &= 10.56 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{increase in area} = 1.3 \text{ m}^2$$

items.part:
The spiral below is formed by connecting semi-circles of increasing radii.

\exfigure{1341_q35_1}

The lengths of each spiral form a geometric sequence, with the length of the first and second spirals being $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ cm and $\pi$ cm respectively.

Show that the sum of the first $n$ spirals is $\dfrac{\pi\left(2^n - 1\right)}{2}$ cm, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.
items.sol:
The lengths form a geometric sequence with first term $a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and common ratio
$$r = \dfrac{\pi}{\frac{\pi}{2}} = 2$$
Using the sum of a geometric series:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\times\dfrac{2^n - 1}{2 - 1} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi\left(2^n - 1\right)}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{3}{2^{2t}}\,dt$
items.sol:
Write $\dfrac{3}{2^{2t}} = 3\cdot 4^{-t}$ and use $\displaystyle\int a^{kt}\,dt = \dfrac{a^{kt}}{k\ln a}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \dfrac{3}{2^{2t}}\,dt &= 3\int_0^1 4^{-t}\,dt \\ &= 3\left[\dfrac{4^{-t}}{-\ln 4}\right]_0^1 \\ &= -3\left[\dfrac{1}{4\ln 4} - \dfrac{1}{\ln 4}\right] \\ &= -3\times\left(-\dfrac{3}{4\ln 4}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{4\ln 4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Kay borrows \$60 000 to set up a clothing pop up shop.

She must pay 12% p.a. interest compounded monthly, with repayments at the end of every six months. Let $\$A_n$ be the amount still owed after the $n$th repayment of $\$M$.
Show that $A_2 = 60\,000(1.01)^{12} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6\right)$
items.sol:
$12\%$ p.a. compounded monthly is $1\%$ per month, and repayments are every $6$ months.

After the 1st month Kay owes $60\,000 \times 1.01$. This continues, so at the end of the 5th month she owes $60\,000 \times 1.01^5$.

At the end of the 6th month interest is added and then the repayment is made.
$$A_1 = 60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M$$
At the end of the 7th month Kay owes $\left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)1.01$. This continues, so at the end of the 11th month she owes $\left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)1.01^5$.

At the 12th month, the same process gives
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= A_1 \times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= \left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)\times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= 60\,000 \times 1.01^{12} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Kay borrows \$60 000 to set up a clothing pop up shop.

She must pay 12% p.a. interest compounded monthly, with repayments at the end of every six months. Let $\$A_n$ be the amount still owed after the $n$th repayment of $\$M$.
If it takes 15 years to pay off the loan, find the amount of each repayment, $M$.
items.sol:
$15$ years is $30$ repayments, so we need $A_{30}$.

The same step gives the pattern:
$$\begin{aligned} A_3 &= A_2 \times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= \left[60\,000 \times 1.01^{12} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6\right)\right]\times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= 60\,000 \times 1.01^{18} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6 + 1.01^{12}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$A_{30} = 60\,000 \times 1.01^{180} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6 + 1.01^{12} + \cdots + 1.01^{174}\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a = 1$, $r = 1.01^6$ and $n = 30$ terms:
$$A_{30} = 60\,000 \times 1.01^{180} - M \times \dfrac{\left(1.01^6\right)^{30} - 1}{1.01^6 - 1}$$
The loan is paid off, so $A_{30} = 0$.
$$M = \dfrac{60\,000 \times 1.01^{180}\left(1.01^6 - 1\right)}{1.01^{180} - 1}$$
$$\therefore\ M \approx \$4430.07$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that it is $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds. The acceleration of the particle is given by

$$\ddot{x} = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \ \text{ m/s}^2$$

Initially the particle is travelling with a velocity of 3 m/s.
Find the first two times when the particle is stationary.
items.sol:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x} &= -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \\ \dot{x} &= -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\left(-\dfrac{3}{\pi}\right)\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + C \\ &= 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $v = 3$:
$$3 = 2\cos 0 + C, \quad\text{so}\quad C = 1$$
$$\dot{x} = 1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t$$
The particle is stationary when $v = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + 1 &= 0 \\ \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}t &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 2 \text{ and } t = 4$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that it is $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds. The acceleration of the particle is given by

$$\ddot{x} = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \ \text{ m/s}^2$$

Initially the particle is travelling with a velocity of 3 m/s.
How far does the particle travel in the first four seconds.
items.sol:
From (a), $v = 1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t$ is positive for $0 \le t < 2$ and negative for $2 < t \le 4$ (it is zero at $t=2$ and $t=4$). So the particle turns at $t = 2$ and the distance is found in two parts.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \int_0^2 \left(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)dt + \left|\int_2^4 \left(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)dt\right| \\ &= \left[t + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right]_0^2 + \left|\left[t + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right]_2^4\right| \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \left|4 - \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \left(2 + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi} + \left|2 - \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right| \\ &= \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\ &\approx 4.96 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

Let $P = (x, y)$ with $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$. The rectangle has sides $6 - x$ and $12 - y$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= (6 - x)(12 - y) \\ &= 72 - 6y - 12x + xy \\ &= 72 - \dfrac{48}{x} - 12x + 8 \\ &= 80 - 12x - \dfrac{48}{x} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx} = -12 + \dfrac{48}{x^2}, \qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{96}{x^3}$$
and $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$ for $x \in [1, 4]$.

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -12 + \dfrac{48}{x^2} &= 0 \\ x^2 &= 4 \\ x &= 2 \quad (x \in [1, 4]) \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$, $x = 2$ gives a maximum, with $A = 32$.

Check the end points:
$$\begin{aligned} x = 1:&\quad A = 20 \\ x = 4:&\quad A = 20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{greatest } A = 32 \text{ at } x = 2;\ \text{least } A = 20 \text{ at } x = 1 \text{ and } x = 4$$

items.part: Solve the equation $|1-2x| = 5$.
items.sol:
Either $1-2x=5$ or $1-2x=-5$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-2x &= 5 & 1-2x &= -5 \\ x &= -2 & x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-2 \text{ or } x=3$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^2}{4x^3-6}\,dx$
items.sol:
The numerator is a constant multiple of the derivative of $4x^3-6$, which is $12x^2$, so the integral is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x^2}{4x^3-6}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{12}\int\dfrac{12x^2}{4x^3-6}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{12}\ln|4x^3-6|+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\tan x}{e^{2x}}\right)$. Answer in the simplest exact form.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\tan x & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=\sec^2 x & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\tan x}{e^{2x}}\right) &= \dfrac{e^{2x}\sec^2 x-2e^{2x}\tan x}{(e^{2x})^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\sec^2 x-2\tan x}{e^{2x}} \end{aligned}$$
Equivalently $\dfrac{(\tan x-1)^2}{e^{2x}}$, which is not required.

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \left(2\sin x - \sec^2 2x\right)dx$. Leave your answer in the simplest exact form.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(2\sin x-\sec^2 2x)\,dx &= \left[-2\cos x-\dfrac{1}{2}\tan 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &= \left(-2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt3\right)-\left(-2-0\right) \\ &= 2-\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{4-3\sqrt3}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 4}\dfrac{x^2-16}{8+2x-x^2}$
items.sol:
Factorise the numerator and denominator, then cancel the common factor $x-4$.
$$\begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{x^2-16}{8+2x-x^2} &= \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{(x-4)(x+4)}{(x-4)(-2-x)} \\ &= \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{x+4}{-(2+x)} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{-6} \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Chandra is an enthusiastic gardener. She planted a lemon tree on $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2019, when it was 80 centimetres tall. At the end of the first year after planting, it was 130 centimetres tall, that is, it grew 50 centimetres. Each year's growth was then 90% of the growth of the previous year.
How tall was the lemon tree after three years?
items.sol:
Each year's growth is $90\%$ of the previous year's, so the growths in the first three years are $50$, $50\times0.9$ and $50\times0.9^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} H &= 80+(50+50\times0.9+50\times0.9^2) \\ &= 80+(50+45+40.5) \\ &= 215.5 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Chandra is an enthusiastic gardener. She planted a lemon tree on $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2019, when it was 80 centimetres tall. At the end of the first year after planting, it was 130 centimetres tall, that is, it grew 50 centimetres. Each year's growth was then 90% of the growth of the previous year.
Assuming the present growth pattern is maintained, explain why the lemon tree will never reach a height of 10 metres?
items.sol:
The yearly growths form a geometric series with $a=50$ and $r=0.9$. Since $|r|<1$, the sum to infinity exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{50}{1-0.9} \\ &= 500 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Maximum height $=500+80=580$ cm, which is less than $10$ m.

So the tree will never reach $10$ m.

items.part:
Chandra is an enthusiastic gardener. She planted a lemon tree on $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2019, when it was 80 centimetres tall. At the end of the first year after planting, it was 130 centimetres tall, that is, it grew 50 centimetres. Each year's growth was then 90% of the growth of the previous year.
In which year will the lemon tree reach a height of 5 metres?
items.sol:
Height after $n$ years is $80$ plus the sum of $n$ terms of the series. Set this equal to $500$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} 500 &= 80+\dfrac{50(1-0.9^n)}{1-0.9} \\ 420 &= \dfrac{50(1-0.9^n)}{0.1} \\ 0.84 &= 1-0.9^n \\ 0.9^n &= 0.16 \\ n &= \dfrac{\log 0.16}{\log 0.9} \\ &\approx 17.3 \end{aligned}$$
So the height is reached during the 18th year, which is 2036.

Packets of coffee beans are labelled with a net weight of 300 g. It is found that the weight of a packet can be modelled by a normal distribution, with mean 306 g and standard deviation 3 g.
Use the Empirical rule to determine the probability that the weight of one packet of coffee beans is less than the advertised weight of 300 g.
items.sol:
The weight $300$ is two standard deviations below the mean, since $306-2\times3=300$.

By the Empirical rule, $95\%$ of weights lie within two standard deviations, so $5\%$ lie outside, split equally between the two tails.
$$P(\text{weight}<300)=\dfrac{0.05}{2}=0.025=2.5\%$$

items.part:
Packets of coffee beans are labelled with a net weight of 300 g. It is found that the weight of a packet can be modelled by a normal distribution, with mean 306 g and standard deviation 3 g.
Manufacturers aim to ensure that the expected number of underweight packets in the shipment will be less than 20. The machine is adjusted to give a mean weight of 308 g, with the standard deviation of 3 g remaining the same. Will they meet their target? Justify your answer.
items.sol:
The $z$-score for a packet of weight 300 g, with mean 308 g and standard deviation 3 g, is
$$z=\dfrac{300-308}{3}\approx-2.67$$
By symmetry of the normal distribution:
$$\begin{aligned} P(Z<-2.67)&=1-P(Z<2.67) \\ &=1-0.99621 \\ &\approx 0.0038 \ (0.38\%) \end{aligned}$$
The shipment has $40\times100=4000$ packets, so
$$\text{Expected number underweight}=0.0038\times4000\approx15.2<20$$
$$\therefore\ \text{They meet the target.}$$
items.final: Yes, they meet the target (expected about 15.2 underweight packets, which is less than 20).

items.part: Solve the equation $\sec\theta + 8\cos\theta = 6$ for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$. Answer correct to 3 decimal places, where necessary.
items.sol:
Write $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and multiply through by $\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}+8\cos\theta&=6 \\ 1+8\cos^2\theta&=6\cos\theta \\ 8\cos^2\theta-6\cos\theta+1&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $x=\cos\theta$.
$$(4x-1)(2x-1)=0$$
so $\cos\theta=\dfrac14$ or $\cos\theta=\dfrac12$.

For $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac12$ gives $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, and $\cos\theta=\dfrac14$ gives $\theta\approx1.318,\ 4.965$.
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 1.318,\ 4.965,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$

Consider the cubic function $y = x^3 + ax^2 + bx + 3$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

At the point $(1, 8)$ on the curve, the equation of the tangent is given by $y = 2x + 6$.

Determine the values of $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
The point $(1,8)$ lies on the curve.
$$\begin{aligned} 8&=1+a+b+3 \\ a+b&=4 \end{aligned}\qquad (1)$$
The gradient of the tangent is $2$, and
$$y'=3x^2+2ax+b$$
When $x=1$, $y'=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=3+2a+b \\ 2a+b&=-1 \end{aligned}\qquad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$a=-5$$
Then $-5+b=4$, so $b=9$.
$$\therefore\ a=-5,\ b=9$$

items.part:
A probability density function is given by $f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}; & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0; & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $a$ is a constant.
Show that $a = 1$.
items.sol:
The total probability must equal 1.
$$\int_0^2\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{a(1+4x)^{\frac12}}{\frac12\times4}\right]_0^2&=1 \\ \dfrac{a}{2}\sqrt9-\dfrac{a}{2}\sqrt1&=1 \\ \dfrac{3a}{2}-\dfrac{a}{2}&=1 \\ a&=1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A probability density function is given by $f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}; & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0; & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $a$ is a constant.
Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.
items.sol:
With $a=1$, and using a second variable $t$ in the integrand:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_0^x(1+4t)^{-\frac12}\,dt \\ &=\left[\dfrac{(1+4t)^{\frac12}}{\frac12\times4}\right]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{1+4x}}{2}-\dfrac12 \\ &=\dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
The complete cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<0\\[6pt] \dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right), & 0\le x\le2\\[6pt] 1, & x>2\end{cases}$$

items.part:
A probability density function is given by $f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}; & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0; & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $a$ is a constant.

items.sol:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=\dfrac12$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right)&=\dfrac12 \\ \sqrt{1+4x}&=2 \\ 1+4x&=4 \\ x&=\dfrac34 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the median is } \dfrac34$$

An open trough of depth $h$ metres and length one metre is constructed out of stainless steel sheeting. The cross-section of the trough is an isosceles trapezium with the acute angles being $45^\circ$ each. The width of the bottom of the trough is $a$ metres. The area of the cross-section measures $60\ \text{m}^2$.
Show that the amount of stainless steel, $A$, in $\text{m}^2$, required to construct the trough is given by:

$$A = \dfrac{60}{h} - h + 2h\sqrt{2} + 120.$$
items.sol:
The steel is two trapezium ends, two slanted sides and the base (length 1 m).

Each slanted side has length $\sqrt{h^2+h^2}$ by Pythagoras' theorem.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\times\left(\dfrac12h(2a+2h)\right)+2\times\left(\sqrt{h^2+h^2}\times1\right)+(a\times1) \\ &=h(2a+2h)+2\sqrt2h+a \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $a=\dfrac{60}{h}-h$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2h\left(\dfrac{60}{h}-h\right)+2h^2+2\sqrt2h+\left(\dfrac{60}{h}-h\right) \\ &=120+2h\sqrt2+\dfrac{60}{h}-h \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{60}{h}-h+2h\sqrt2+120$$

Write $A=60h^{-1}-h+2h\sqrt2+120$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dA}{dh}=-60h^{-2}-1+2\sqrt2,\qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dh^2}=\dfrac{120}{h^3}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{60}{h^2}&=2\sqrt2-1 \\ h&=\sqrt{\dfrac{60}{2\sqrt2-1}} \\ &\approx5.728 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dh^2}=\dfrac{120}{(5.728)^3}\approx0.638>0$$
so this is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ h\approx5.728 \text{ m}\ (5728 \text{ mm})$$

items.part:
The Artful Dodger has three 20 cent coins in his pocket. One of the coins has heads on both sides, another is biased such that it has a 75% chance of landing on heads and the third coin is a fair coin.

A coin is selected at random and tossed.

Given that the coin that was tossed comes up heads, what is the probability that it was the fair coin?
items.sol:
By the conditional probability formula, with each coin chosen with probability $\dfrac13$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{fair}\mid\text{heads})&=\dfrac{P(\text{fair}\cap\text{heads})}{P(\text{heads})} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac13\times\frac12}{\left(\frac13\times1\right)+\left(\frac13\times\frac34\right)+\left(\frac13\times\frac12\right)} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac16}{\frac13+\frac14+\frac16} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{4+3+2} \\ &=\dfrac29 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $\displaystyle\int_{-10}^{4}f(x)\,dx=3$ and $\displaystyle\int_{4}^{6}f(x)\,dx=5$, find the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-10}^{6}2f(x)\,dx$.
items.sol:
The integral of $2f(x)$ over $[-10,6]$ splits at $x=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-10}^{6}2f(x)\,dx&=2\left[\int_{-10}^{4}f(x)\,dx+\int_4^6f(x)\,dx\right]\\ &=2[3+5]\\ &=16\end{aligned}$$

The sign of $f''(x)=6x+2$ decides the nature.

So there is a maximum at $x=-2$. This agrees with the graph, where $A$ is left of the $y$-axis.

items.sol:
Differentiate and set the derivative to zero.

so there is a maximum turning point at $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{32}{27}\right)$.
$$f''(2)=4>0$$
so there is a minimum turning point at $(2,0)$.
items.final: Maximum turning point at $\left(\tfrac{2}{3},\tfrac{32}{27}\right)$; minimum turning point at $(2,0)$

Since $x^2+4y^2=36$, we have $y^2=\dfrac{36-x^2}{4}$.

$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=(36-x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}(36-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(-2x)=-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left[5x-\dfrac{1}{\ln2}2^x\right]_0^2+\left[-\dfrac{3}{4}(3-x)^{\frac{4}{3}}\right]_2^3 \\ &=10-\dfrac{4}{\ln2}+\dfrac{1}{\ln2}-\left(0-\dfrac{3}{4}\right) \\ &=10\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{3}{\ln2} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that the function $y=kxe^{kx}$ has exactly one stationary point and its $y$-value is independent of $k$, where $k$ is a constant.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=kx & v&=e^{kx}\\ u'&=k & v'&=ke^{kx}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=ke^{kx}+k^2xe^{kx} \\ &=ke^{kx}(1+kx) \end{aligned}$$
For $y'=0$: $ke^{kx}\ne0$, so $1+kx=0$ and $x=-\dfrac{1}{k}$ is the only stationary point.

When $x=-\dfrac{1}{k}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=k\left(-\dfrac{1}{k}\right)e^{k\left(-\frac{1}{k}\right)} \\ &=-e^{-1} \end{aligned}$$
which is independent of $k$.

items.part:
Arthur's bag contains 4 green marbles and 2 red marbles. Beatrice's bag contains 3 green marbles and 3 red marbles. One of their bags is randomly selected, and then two marbles are removed in succession without replacement.

What is the probability that Arthur's bag was selected, given that the two marbles were the same colour?
items.sol:
Using the definition of conditional probability:
$$P(A\mid\text{same colour})=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and same colour})}{P(\text{same colour})}$$
For Arthur's bag (both red or both green):
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\text{ and same})&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4}{6}\times\dfrac{3}{5} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{30} \end{aligned}$$
For Beatrice's bag:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B\text{ and same})&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{5}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{5} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{30} \end{aligned}$$
$$P(\text{same colour})=\dfrac{7}{30}+\dfrac{6}{30}=\dfrac{13}{30}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\mid\text{same colour})&=\dfrac{\frac{7}{30}}{\frac{13}{30}} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{13} \end{aligned}$$

On 1st April 2020, Ferdinand takes out a 25 year loan with reducible interest charged at a rate of $1.2\%$ per annum, compounded monthly.

The loan is to be repaid in equal monthly repayments of \$2370 at the end of each month.
On 1st April 2022, rising inflation and the outbreak of a conflict in Europe have economic impacts which cause the bank to increase the interest rate on home loans to $3.6\%$ per annum. Calculate the amount of Ferdinand's new monthly repayment, correct to the nearest dollar, if he is still to repay the loan within the 25 year term.
items.sol:
Let $B_n$ be the amount owing $n$ months after 1st April 2022, and $M$ the new monthly repayment.

The rate is $3.6\%$ p.a. $=0.3\%$ per month, so the monthly factor is $1.003$.

The remaining term is $25\times12-24=276$ months.
$$B_n=571\,367\times1.003^n-\dfrac{M(1.003^n-1)}{1.003-1}$$
When $n=276$, $B_{276}=0$:
$$0=571\,367\times1.003^{276}-\dfrac{M(1.003^{276}-1)}{0.003}$$
$$\begin{aligned} M&=\dfrac{571\,367\times1.003^{276}\times0.003}{1.003^{276}-1} \\ &=3047.09656\ldots \\ &\approx \$3047 \text{ (nearest dollar)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Solve:

$$\dfrac{243}{6\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{27}}=3^x$$
items.sol:
Simplify the denominator using $\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}$, then write each side as a power of 3.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{243}{6\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{27}}&=\dfrac{243}{6\sqrt{3}-3\sqrt{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{3^5}{3\sqrt{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{3^4}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &=3^3\sqrt{3} \\ &=3^{3\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x=3\dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part: Differentiate $(\sin x)^3$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(u^3\big)=3u^2u'$ with $u=\sin x$:

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^3=3\sin^2 x\cos x$$

items.part: Hence find the gradient of the normal at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$
items.sol:
The gradient of the tangent is the derivative from part (a) at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

$$\begin{aligned} m_T&=3\sin^2\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_Tm_N=-1$.

$$m_N=-\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\approx -0.9428\ldots$$

items.part:
Find the derivative of

$$\dfrac{e^{3x}}{x^2}$$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{3x} & v&=x^2 \\ u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=2x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{e^{3x}}{x^2}\right)&=\dfrac{3e^{3x}\times x^2-2x\,e^{3x}}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{x\,e^{3x}(3x-2)}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{e^{3x}(3x-2)}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the primitive of $\sqrt{5x+1}$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int(5x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx&=\dfrac{(5x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{5\times\frac{3}{2}}+C \\ &=\dfrac{2}{15}(5x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}+C \end{aligned}$$

The curve meets the $x$-axis at $x=-2$ and $x=6$, so the area is

$$\int_{-2}^{6}(12+4x-x^2)\,dx$$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-2}^{6}(12+4x-x^2)\,dx&=\left[12x+2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{6} \\ &=\left(12\times 6+2\times 6^2-\dfrac{6^3}{3}\right)-\left(12\times(-2)+2\times 2^2-\dfrac{(-2)^3}{3}\right) \\ &=72-\left(-\dfrac{40}{3}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{256}{3} \\ &=85\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

\extable{Ts5369_1}

Five function values give 4 strips, so

$$h=\dfrac{6-(-2)}{4}=2$$

Using the trapezoidal rule, $A\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big(y_0+y_4+2(y_1+y_2+y_3)\big)$:

$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{2}{2}\Big(0+0+2(12+16+12)\Big) \\ &=80 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The error is the exact area less the estimate.

$$\text{Error}=85\dfrac{1}{3}-80=5\dfrac{1}{3}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage error}&=\dfrac{5\frac{1}{3}}{85\frac{1}{3}}\times 100\% \\ &=6.25\% \end{aligned}$$

The estimate is an underestimate by $6.25\%$.

items.part:
Consider the function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} x^2-2x+2 & -3\le x\le 1\\ x+1 & 1<x\le 6 \end{cases}$$
Justify why the function is NOT continuous at $x=1$
items.sol:
Compare the limits at $x=1$ from each piece.

$$L^+=1+1=2$$

$$\therefore\ L^-\ne L^+,\ \text{so the function is not continuous at } x=1.$$

items.sol:

$$y=x-3x^2+x^3+C$$

items.part:
A bag contains 4 red liquorice and 6 black liquorice lollies. Reese picks a lolly at random. If it is a red liquorice lolly, she will eat it and pick another. If it is a black liquorice lolly, she will replace it in the bag and choose another.

By drawing a tree diagram or otherwise, find the probability that after two draws, she chooses a red lolly and a black lolly, in any order.
items.sol:
If the first lolly is red, it is not replaced, so the second draw is from 9 lollies (3 red, 6 black).

If the first lolly is black, it is replaced, so the second draw is from 10 lollies (4 red, 6 black).

The two orders are $RB$ and $BR$.

$$\begin{aligned} P(RB\text{ or }BR)&=\dfrac{4}{10}\times\dfrac{6}{9}+\dfrac{6}{10}\times\dfrac{4}{10} \\ &=\dfrac{38}{75} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=x\ln x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\ln x+x\times\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &=\ln x+1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence find

$$\int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx$$
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)=\ln x+1$. Integrate both sides from $e$ to $2e$:

$$\int_e^{2e}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)\,dx=\int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx+\int_e^{2e}1\,dx$$

$$\big[x\ln x\big]_e^{2e}=\int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx+\big[x\big]_e^{2e}$$

Rearranging:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_e^{2e}\ln x\,dx&=\big[x\ln x\big]_e^{2e}-\big[x\big]_e^{2e} \\ &=2e\ln 2e-e\ln e-(2e-e) \\ &=2e\ln 2e-e\ln e-e \\ &=2e\ln 2e-e-e \\ &=2e\ln 2e-2e \\ &=2e(\ln 2+\ln e)-2e \\ &=2e\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: In a circle, an arc length of 30cm subtends $80^\circ$ at the centre of that circle. Find its radius.
items.sol:
The arc length is $l = \dfrac{\theta}{360}\times 2\pi r$ with $\theta = 80$.
$$\begin{aligned} 30 &= \dfrac{80}{360}\times 2\pi r \\ &= \dfrac{4}{9}\pi r \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \pi r &= \dfrac{30\times 9}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{135}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{135}{2\pi} \\ &\approx 21.5 \text{ cm (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r \approx 21.5 \text{ cm}$$

items.part: Solve $\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$
items.sol:
Since $0\le x\le 2\pi$, adjust the range of the angle one step at a time.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le x\le 2\pi \\ 0&\le \dfrac{x}{2}\le \pi &&(\text{divide by } 2)\\ -\dfrac{\pi}{4}&\le \dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le \dfrac{3\pi}{4} &&(\text{subtract } \dfrac{\pi}{4})\end{aligned}$$
We need $\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

In the range $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le \theta\le \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ the only solution is $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4} &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ \dfrac{x}{2} &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \\ x &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x^2(k-x)$, where $k$ is a constant.
If $f(x)$ has a maximum turning point at $(2,8)$, show that $k=3$.
items.sol:
A maximum turning point at $(2,8)$ means $f'(2)=0$.

Expanding, $f(x)=2kx^2-2x^3$, so $f'(x)=4kx-6x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 4k\times 2-6\times 2^2 \\ 0 &= 8k-24 \\ k &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, use $f(2)=8$:
$$\begin{aligned} 8 &= 2\times 2^2(k-2) \\ 8 &= 8(k-2) \\ 1 &= k-2 \\ k &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=3$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x^2(k-x)$, where $k$ is a constant.
Find the minimum turning point (you do not need to test for this) and any inflexion points (prove by testing or otherwise).
items.sol:
With $k=3$, $f(x)=6x^2-2x^3$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 12x-6x^2 \\ &= 6x(2-x) \end{aligned}$$
The stationary points are at $x=0$ and $x=2$. Since $(2,8)$ is the maximum, $(0,0)$ is the minimum turning point.

For inflexions, find where $f''(x)=0$.
$$f''(x)=12-12x$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 12-12x \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Test the concavity either side of $x=1$.

\extable{Ts5383_1}

The concavity changes from concave up to concave down, so $(1,4)$ is a point of inflexion.

Alternatively, $x=1$ lies between the maximum $(2,8)$ and the minimum $(0,0)$, so the curve changes concavity there.
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum turning point } (0,0),\ \text{inflexion point } (1,4)$$

Between them the curve is above the line (at $x=-5$: $\sqrt{4}=2>\dfrac{4}{3}$).

items.part:
A survey of where students choose to read the current news revealed that, on a regular basis, 33% read the news on Instagram, 45% read the news on Facebook and 44% do not read the news at all.
By constructing a Venn Diagram, or otherwise, find the percentage of students who get their news from both Facebook and Instagram.
items.sol:
Let $F$ = Facebook and $I$ = Instagram. $P(\text{neither})=44\%$, so $P(F\cup I)=56\%$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(F\cap I) &= 33+45-56 \\ &= 22\% \end{aligned}$$
Venn diagram: Facebook only $23\%$, both $22\%$, Instagram only $11\%$, neither $44\%$.
$$\therefore\ P(F\cap I)=22\%$$

items.part:
A survey of where students choose to read the current news revealed that, on a regular basis, 33% read the news on Instagram, 45% read the news on Facebook and 44% do not read the news at all.
A student is selected at random. Given that this student does read the news on a regular basis, find the probability that this student gets their news from Facebook.
items.sol:
Using conditional probability, with $\text{News}$ meaning the student reads the news:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Fb}\mid\text{News}) &= \dfrac{P(\text{Fb}\cap\text{News})}{P(\text{News})} \\ &= \dfrac{23+22}{23+22+11} \\ &= \dfrac{45}{56} \\ &\approx 80.4\% \text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P \approx 80.4\%$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line such that at time $t$ seconds, its distance $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ of a line is given by the equation $x=1-\cos 2t$.
Hence state the times and positions where the particle is at rest in the first 3 seconds.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$, that is, at the turning points of the graph.

In the first 3 seconds these occur at $t=0$ and $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (since $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\approx 1.57<3<\pi$).

At both times the position is $x=0$ at $t=0$ and $x=2$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\therefore\ t=0 \text{ s}\ (x=0) \text{ and } t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s}\ (x=2)$$

items.part:
Rumour spreading at a school can be modelled by $N=2\times 1.61^{0.7t}$ where $N$ is the number of students who have heard the rumour and $t$ is the number of hours after it first started.
How many students would have heard the rumour 6 hours after it started?
items.sol:
Substitute $t=6$ into the model.
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 2\times 1.61^{0.7\times 6} \\ &= 14.78\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 14 \text{ or } 15 \text{ students (both accepted)}$$

items.part:
Rumour spreading at a school can be modelled by $N=2\times 1.61^{0.7t}$ where $N$ is the number of students who have heard the rumour and $t$ is the number of hours after it first started.
How long would it take all 165 Year 12 students to hear the rumour?
items.sol:
Set $N=165$ and solve for $t$.
$$\begin{aligned} 165 &= 2\times 1.61^{0.7t} \\ \dfrac{165}{2} &= 1.61^{0.7t} \end{aligned}$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{165}{2}\right) &= \ln\left(1.61^{0.7t}\right) \\ &= 0.7t\ln 1.61 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{165}{2}\right)}{0.7\ln 1.61} \\ &= 13.23\ldots \\ &\approx 13.24 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 13.24 \text{ hours}$$
