items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} 4kx(2-x^2) & 0\le x\le 1\\ 0 & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}$$
Find the value of $k$.
items.sol:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1.
$$\displaystyle \int_0^1 \left(8kx-4kx^3\right)dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[4kx^2-kx^4\right]_0^1 &= 1 \\ 4k-k-(0-0) &= 1 \\ 3k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} 4kx(2-x^2) & 0\le x\le 1\\ 0 & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}$$
Find the mode of the distribution to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
With $k=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{8}{3}x-\dfrac{4}{3}x^3$$
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{8}{3}-4x^2$$
The mode is the maximum of $f(x)$, so solve $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{8}{3}-4x^2 \\ 4x^2 &= \dfrac{8}{3} \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{2}{3} \\ x &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}} \end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le x\le 1$, $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$.

This is a maximum, as $f'(x)$ is a downward parabola, positive before and negative after $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{mode}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}\approx 0.82 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
In $\triangle PQR$ the size of $\angle QPR$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. The length of $PQ$ is $(x+3)$ units and the length of $PR$ is $(4-x)^2$ units, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1344_q35_1}
Show that the area $A$ of the triangle can be given by:

$$A=\dfrac{1}{4}(x^3-5x^2-8x+48)$$
items.sol:
Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ with $C=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}(x+3)(4-x)^2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(x+3)(16-8x+x^2)\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(16x-8x^2+x^3+48-24x+3x^2\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(x^3-5x^2-8x+48\right) \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate the area from part (a).
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(3x^2-10x-8\right)$$
For a maximum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3x^2-10x-8 \\ &= (3x+2)(x-4) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $x=4$.

As $(4-x)^2$ is a length, $x\ne 4$. Hence $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Test the nature of the stationary point.

\extable{Ts5402_1}

$\therefore$ a maximum at $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Then the sides are
$$PQ=-\dfrac{2}{3}+3=\dfrac{7}{3}$$
$$PR=\left(4+\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2=\dfrac{196}{9}$$
By the cosine rule in $\triangle PQR$:
$$\begin{aligned} QR^2 &= \left(\dfrac{7}{3}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{196}{9}\right)^2-2\times\dfrac{7}{3}\times\dfrac{196}{9}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{38857}{81}-\dfrac{2744}{27}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= 391.70\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ QR=19.79\ldots\approx 19.8 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^2-2x^3$
For what values of $x$ will $f(x)=x^2-2x^3$ be increasing?
items.sol:
For $f(x)$ increasing we need $f'(x)>0$.
$$f'(x)=2x-6x^2$$
Solve
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-6x^2&>0\\ 2x(1-3x)&>0\end{aligned}$$
The critical values are $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{3}$, and the parabola $2x-6x^2$ is concave down, so it is positive between them.
$$\therefore\ 0<x<\dfrac{1}{3}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^2-2x^3$
For what values of $x$ will $f(x)=x^2-2x^3$ be concave down?
items.sol:
For concave down we need $f''(x)<0$.
$$f''(x)=2-12x$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2-12x&<0\\ x&>\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x>\dfrac{1}{6}$$

items.part: Prove $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{cosec}x)=-\operatorname{cosec}x\cot x$
items.sol:
Write $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ and use the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1 & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=0 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{cosec}x)&=\dfrac{\sin x\times 0-\cos x}{(\sin x)^2}\\ &=-\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\ &=-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Using logarithm laws to simplify, find the derivative of the following function.

$g(x)=\log_e\left(\dfrac{e^{-x}-1}{\sqrt{e}}\right)$
items.sol:
Using the log laws,
$$g(x)=\ln(e^{-x}-1)-\ln\sqrt{e}$$
The second term is constant, so
$$g'(x)=\dfrac{-e^{-x}}{e^{-x}-1}+0$$
$$\therefore\ g'(x)=\dfrac{-e^{-x}}{e^{-x}-1}=\dfrac{1}{e^{x}-1}$$

items.part:
A piece of wire of length 24 cm is to be cut into two pieces. One piece is to be bent to form a square of side $x$ cm and the other piece is to be bent to form an equilateral triangle of side $y$ cm. Let $A_1(x)$ and $A_2(y)$ be the respective areas of the square and equilateral triangle.
With the aid of a diagram, show that $A_2(y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}y^2$.
items.sol:
The 24 cm wire is cut into lengths $4x$ (square) and $3y$ (triangle).

Diagram: a square of side $x$; an equilateral triangle of side $y$ with each angle $60^\circ$.

Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ with two sides $y$ and included angle $60^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2(y)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times y^2\times\sin 60^\circ\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times y^2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}y^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A piece of wire of length 24 cm is to be cut into two pieces. One piece is to be bent to form a square of side $x$ cm and the other piece is to be bent to form an equilateral triangle of side $y$ cm. Let $A_1(x)$ and $A_2(y)$ be the respective areas of the square and equilateral triangle.
Show that the sum $S$ of the two areas is given by $S=x^2+\dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{9}(6-x)^2$.
items.sol:
The total length of wire is 24 cm:
$$4x+3y=24$$
So $3y=24-4x$, hence
$$y=\dfrac{4}{3}(6-x)$$
Substitute into $S=A_1+A_2=x^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}y^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} S&=x^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\left[\dfrac{4}{3}(6-x)\right]^2\\ &=x^2+\dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{9}(6-x)^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A piece of wire of length 24 cm is to be cut into two pieces. One piece is to be bent to form a square of side $x$ cm and the other piece is to be bent to form an equilateral triangle of side $y$ cm. Let $A_1(x)$ and $A_2(y)$ be the respective areas of the square and equilateral triangle.
Hence, determine the exact value of $x$ so that $S$ is at its minimum.
items.sol:
$$\dfrac{dS}{dx}=2x-\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}(6-x)$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dS}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}(6-x)=\dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3}-\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}x\\ \left(2+\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}\right)x&=\dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3}\\ x&=\dfrac{24\sqrt{3}}{9+4\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2S}{dx^2}=2+\dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{9}>0$$
So $S$ is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{24\sqrt{3}}{9+4\sqrt{3}}$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x=12\ln(t+2)-2t+5$$

where $t$ is measured in seconds.
What is the inititial position of the particle? Give your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=12\ln 2-0+5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=12\ln 2+5 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x=12\ln(t+2)-2t+5$$

where $t$ is measured in seconds.
Find an expression for the velocity of the particle at time $t$.
items.sol: $$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{12}{t+2}-2$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x=12\ln(t+2)-2t+5$$

where $t$ is measured in seconds.
Find when the particle comes to rest.
items.sol:
At rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12}{t+2}&=2\\ 6&=t+2\\ t&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest after 4 seconds}$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x=12\ln(t+2)-2t+5$$

where $t$ is measured in seconds.
What happened to the acceleration eventually?
items.sol:
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\dfrac{12}{(t+2)^2}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $(t+2)^2\to\infty$, so
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}\to 0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the acceleration tends to } 0$$

items.part:
Fish are introduced into a small dam. The size of the population, $N$, of fish can be modelled can be modelled by the function

$$N=\dfrac{500}{1+24e^{-0.5t}}$$

where $t$ is the time in months after the fish are introduced into the dam.
Show that the rate of growth of the size of the population is given by

$$\dfrac{dN}{dt}=\dfrac{6000e^{-0.5t}}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}$$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=500 & v&=1+24e^{-0.5t}\\ u'&=0 & v'&=-12e^{-0.5t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt}&=\dfrac{(1+24e^{-0.5t})\cdot 0-500\times(-12e^{-0.5t})}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}\\ &=\dfrac{6000e^{-0.5t}}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Fish are introduced into a small dam. The size of the population, $N$, of fish can be modelled can be modelled by the function

$$N=\dfrac{500}{1+24e^{-0.5t}}$$

where $t$ is the time in months after the fish are introduced into the dam.
Find the range of the function $N$, justifying your answer.
items.sol:
When $t=0$:
$$N=\dfrac{500}{1+24}=20$$
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.5t}\to 0$, so
$$N\to\dfrac{500}{1+24\times 0}=500$$
Since $\dfrac{dN}{dt}>0$ for all $t$, $N$ is always increasing, so it rises from 20 towards 500 without reaching it.
$$\therefore\ 20\le N<500$$

Let $L=a+b$, where the two parts of the tube satisfy
$$a=\dfrac{3}{\cos\alpha},\qquad b=\dfrac{4}{\sin\alpha}$$
$$L=3(\cos\alpha)^{-1}+4(\sin\alpha)^{-1}$$
$$\dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}=\dfrac{3\sin\alpha}{\cos^2\alpha}-\dfrac{4\cos\alpha}{\sin^2\alpha}=\dfrac{3\sin^3\alpha-4\cos^3\alpha}{\cos^2\alpha\sin^2\alpha}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin^3\alpha-4\cos^3\alpha&=0\\ \tan^3\alpha&=\dfrac{4}{3}\\ \tan\alpha&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{4}{3}}\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}&<0 &&\text{at } \alpha=47^\circ\\ \dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}&=0 &&\text{at } \alpha\approx 47.7^\circ\\ \dfrac{dL}{d\alpha}&>0 &&\text{at } \alpha=48^\circ\end{aligned}$$
So $L$ is a minimum at $\alpha=47.74^\circ$. The longest tube that fits round the corner has this minimum length:
$$L=\dfrac{3}{\cos 47.74^\circ}+\dfrac{4}{\sin 47.74^\circ}\approx 9.87\text{ m}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum length}\approx 9.87\text{ m (2 dp)}$$

items.part:
The events $A$ and $B$ occur such that $P(A)=0.7$, $P(B')=0.8$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.8$.

Find $P(A\cap B)$.
items.sol:
Since $P(B')=0.8$,
$$P(B)=1-0.8=0.2$$
Using the addition rule, $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.8 &= 0.7+0.2-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) &= 0.9-0.8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(A\cap B)=0.1$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\left(\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-1\right)dx$
items.sol:
Integrate term by term, using $\displaystyle \int \sin(ax)\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{a}\cos(ax)$.
$$\int\left(\sin\dfrac{x}{2}-1\right)dx=-2\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-x+c$$

items.part:
Given $f(x)=x^4+2x^3+1$
Find the stationary points and points of inflection.
items.sol:
Differentiate to find stationary points.
$$f'(x)=4x^3+6x^2=2x^2(2x+3)$$
Setting $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=0$ or $x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Substituting, $f(0)=1$ and $f\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)=-\dfrac{11}{16}$.

Stationary points: $(0,1)$ and $\left(-\dfrac{3}{2},-\dfrac{11}{16}\right)$.

For points of inflection, solve $f''(x)=0$.
$$f''(x)=12x^2+12x=12x(x+1)$$
So $x=0$ or $x=-1$.

Test the sign of $f''$ either side of each root.
$$\begin{aligned} f''&>0 &&\text{for } x<-1 &&\text{concave up}\\ f''&<0 &&\text{for } -1<x<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''&>0 &&\text{for } x>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
Concavity changes at both, so $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are points of inflection.
items.final: Stationary points: $(0,1)$ and $\left(-\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{11}{16}\right)$; points of inflection: $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1)$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a horizontal straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point O on the line given by $x=t(t-3)^2$ where velocity $v$ is in $\text{ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $\ddot{x}$ is in $\text{ms}^{-2}$.
Show that $v=3(t-1)(t-3)$ and $\ddot{x}=6(t-2)$
items.sol:
Differentiate $x=t(t-3)^2$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=t & v&=(t-3)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(t-3)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=(t-3)^2+2t(t-3) \\ &=(t-3)(t-3+2t) \\ &=(t-3)(3t-3) \\ &=3(t-1)(t-3) \end{aligned}$$
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, again by the product rule with $u=t-1$, $v=t-3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=3\big((t-1)\cdot 1+(t-3)\cdot 1\big) \\ &=3(2t-4) \\ &=6(t-2) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a horizontal straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point O on the line given by $x=t(t-3)^2$ where velocity $v$ is in $\text{ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $\ddot{x}$ is in $\text{ms}^{-2}$.
Find when the particle is moving towards O.
items.sol:
Since $x=t(t-3)^2\ge 0$ for $t\ge 0$, the particle is never left of O, so it moves towards O when $v<0$.
$$3(t-1)(t-3)<0$$
This parabola opens upward, so it is negative between the roots.
$$\therefore\ 1<t<3$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a horizontal straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point O on the line given by $x=t(t-3)^2$ where velocity $v$ is in $\text{ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $\ddot{x}$ is in $\text{ms}^{-2}$.
Find when the particle is moving towards O and slowing down.
items.sol:
The particle slows down when $v$ and $\ddot{x}$ have opposite signs. Moving towards O means $v<0$, so we need $\ddot{x}>0$.
$$6(t-2)>0$$
Hence $t>2$.

From part (b), $v<0$ for $1<t<3$.

Therefore both conditions hold when
$$2<t<3$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a horizontal straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point O on the line given by $x=t(t-3)^2$ where velocity $v$ is in $\text{ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $\ddot{x}$ is in $\text{ms}^{-2}$.
How far has the particle travelled in the first 4 seconds?
items.sol:
The particle may change direction where $v=0$, so find the positions at the endpoints and turning points.
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:&\quad x=0\\ t=4:&\quad x=4 \end{aligned}$$
From $v=3(t-1)(t-3)=0$, the particle is at rest at $t=1$ and $t=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} t=1:&\quad x=4\\ t=3:&\quad x=0 \end{aligned}$$
The particle goes from $0$ to $4$, back to $0$, then to $4$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 4+4+4\\ &= 12 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given $\sec\theta=-\dfrac{37}{12}$ for $0<\theta<\pi$, find the exact value of $\text{cosec}\,\theta$.
items.sol:
Since $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$,
$$\cos\theta=-\dfrac{12}{37}$$
In a right-angled triangle with adjacent $12$ and hypotenuse $37$, Pythagoras' theorem gives opposite side $\sqrt{37^2-12^2}=35$.

For $0<\theta<\pi$, $\sin\theta>0$, and $\cos\theta<0$ places $\theta$ in the second quadrant, so
$$\sin\theta=\dfrac{35}{37}$$
Since $\text{cosec}\,\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$,
$$\therefore\ \text{cosec}\,\theta=\dfrac{37}{35}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log_3 x^4\right)$
items.sol:
Using the log law $\log_3 x^4=4\log_3 x$, then the change of base rule $\log_3 x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log_3 x^4\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(4\log_3 x\right)\\ &= 4\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 3}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{4}{\ln 3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &= \dfrac{4}{x\ln 3} \end{aligned}$$

The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.3+a+0.3+b&=1\\ a+b&=0.4 &&(1) \end{aligned}$$
The mean is $1.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0+1\cdot a+2(0.3)+3b&=1.5\\ a+3b&=0.9 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 2b&=0.5\\ b&=0.25 \end{aligned}$$
Then $a=0.4-0.25=0.15$.
$$\therefore\ a=0.15,\ b=0.25$$

items.part: Solve $e^{2\ln x}=2x+3$.
items.sol:
The logarithm needs $x>0$. Using $e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$:
$$e^{2\ln x}=e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} x^2&=2x+3\\ x^2-2x-3&=0\\ (x-3)(x+1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=3$ or $x=-1$. Since $x>0$, reject $x=-1$.
$$\therefore\ x=3$$

items.part:
On any given day, the depth of water in a lake is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right),\ 0\le t\le 24$$

where $h$ is the depth of water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 6 am.
Find the values of $t$ for which $h(t)=10$.
items.sol:
Setting $h(t)=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} 14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=10\\ 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=-4\\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le t\le 24$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\le 2\pi$. Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{12}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ t=14 \text{ or } t=22$$

items.part:
On any given day, the depth of water in a lake is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right),\ 0\le t\le 24$$

where $h$ is the depth of water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 6 am.
What rate is the depth of the river changing at 1:00 pm?
items.sol:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} h'(t)&=8\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from 6 am, so 1:00 pm is $t=7$.
$$h'(7)=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\right)\text{ m/h}$$
$$\therefore\ h'(7)\approx -0.54 \text{ m/h}$$

On any given day, the depth of water in a lake is modelled by the function

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1-x^2}{3x-x^3}\,dx$
items.sol:
The derivative of the denominator $3x-x^3$ is $3-3x^2$, so write the numerator as $\dfrac{1}{3}(3-3x^2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1-x^2}{3x-x^3}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{3-3x^2}{3x-x^3}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left|3x-x^3\right|+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt{4-x^2}$.
Find the domain and range of the function.
items.sol:
The square root needs $4-x^2\ge 0$, so $-2\le x\le 2$.

On this domain $0\le 4-x^2\le 4$, so $0\le\sqrt{4-x^2}\le 2$.
$$\text{Domain: } -2\le x\le 2,\qquad \text{Range: } 0\le y\le 2$$

items.part:
The figure below shows a baseball field which is a circular sector XAB with a radius $4r$ and subtends $\angle AXB$ at the centre X. DXC is another sector with radius $3r$ where D and C are on XA and XB respectively.

The region G is bounded by the points ABCD and has an area of $5000\ \text{m}^2$.

\exfigure{1036_q22_1}
Show that the perimeter of region G, is given by $P=2r+\dfrac{10000}{r}$.
items.sol:
The arc length of a sector of radius $R$ and angle $\theta$ is $R\theta$, so arc $AB=4r\theta$ and arc $CD=3r\theta$. Also $AD=BC=4r-3r=r$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=AD+AB+BC+CD\\ &=r+4r\theta+r+3r\theta\\ &=2r+7r\theta &&(1) \end{aligned}$$
The area of $G$ is the large sector minus the small sector, using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}R^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}(4r)^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}(3r)^2\theta&=5000\\ \dfrac{7r^2\theta}{2}&=5000\\ \theta&=\dfrac{10000}{7r^2} \end{aligned}$$
Substituting into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} P&=2r+7r\cdot\dfrac{10000}{7r^2}\\ &=2r+\dfrac{10000}{r} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The figure below shows a baseball field which is a circular sector XAB with a radius $4r$ and subtends $\angle AXB$ at the centre X. DXC is another sector with radius $3r$ where D and C are on XA and XB respectively.

The region G is bounded by the points ABCD and has an area of $5000\ \text{m}^2$.

\exfigure{1036_q22_1}
Calculate the minimum value of $P$.
items.sol:
Differentiating $P=2r+\dfrac{10000}{r}$:
$$\dfrac{dP}{dr}=2-\dfrac{10000}{r^2}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} r^2&=5000\\ r&=50\sqrt{2} &&(r>0) \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{20000}{r^3}>0 \text{ since } r>0$$
So $r=50\sqrt{2}$ gives a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} P_{\min}&=100\sqrt{2}+\dfrac{10000}{50\sqrt{2}}\\ &=100\sqrt{2}+100\sqrt{2}\\ &=200\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiating the curve:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=8(2x-1)^3$$
At $B(1,1)$ the gradient is $8$, so the tangent is
$$y-1=8(x-1)$$
When $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1&=8(x-1)\\ x&=\dfrac{7}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The curve meets the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The region $R$ is the area under the curve from $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ to $x=1$, minus the triangle under the tangent with base $1-\dfrac{7}{8}=\dfrac{1}{8}$ and height $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of } R&=\displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}(2x-1)^4\,dx-\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{8}\times 1\\ &=\left[\dfrac{(2x-1)^5}{10}\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}-\dfrac{1}{16}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{10}-0-\dfrac{1}{16}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{80} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Alice, Brett and Chris are all going to see the Eiffel Tower. Alice is due north of the tower, Chris is due east and Brett is on the line of sight between them. The angles of elevation to the top of the tower from Alice, Brett and Chris are $23^\circ$, $25^\circ$ and $32^\circ$ respectively.
Show that the angle between the Eiffel Tower, Alice and Chris is represented by

$$\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ}$$
items.sol:
Let $D$ be the base of the tower, $E$ its top and $h=DE$. Let $\theta=\angle DAC$, the angle between the tower, Alice and Chris. Since Alice is due north and Chris due east of the tower, $\angle ADC=90^\circ$.

In right-angled triangle $CDE$:
$$h=CD\tan 32^\circ,\quad\text{so } CD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 32^\circ}$$
In right-angled triangle $ADE$:
$$h=AD\tan 23^\circ,\quad\text{so } AD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}$$
In right-angled triangle $ADC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta&=\dfrac{CD}{AD}\\ &=\dfrac{h}{\tan 32^\circ}\div\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}\\ &=\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ}\approx 34.2^\circ$$

items.part:
Alice, Brett and Chris are all going to see the Eiffel Tower. Alice is due north of the tower, Chris is due east and Brett is on the line of sight between them. The angles of elevation to the top of the tower from Alice, Brett and Chris are $23^\circ$, $25^\circ$ and $32^\circ$ respectively.
What is the bearing of Brett from the Eiffel Tower?
items.sol:
In triangle $ADB$ (right-angled at the elevation triangles): $AD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}$ and $BD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 25^\circ}$. Also $\angle DAB=\theta\approx 34.2^\circ$, with $\angle ABD=\alpha$ and $\angle ADB=\beta$.

By the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{AD}&=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{BD}\\ \sin\alpha&=\sin\theta\times\dfrac{\tan 25^\circ}{\tan 23^\circ}\\ &\approx 0.61729 \end{aligned}$$
So $\alpha\approx 38^\circ$ or $\alpha\approx 142^\circ$ (ambiguous case).

If $\alpha=38^\circ$:
$$\beta=180^\circ-38^\circ-34^\circ=108^\circ$$
This is not valid, because $B$ lies between $A$ and $C$ so $0<\beta<90^\circ$.

Therefore $\alpha=142^\circ$, and
$$\beta=180^\circ-34^\circ-142^\circ\approx 4^\circ$$
Brett is $4^\circ$ east of north from the tower.
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing is about } 004^\circ\text{T}$$

Multiply both sides by 3 to clear the fraction.
$$\begin{aligned} 4x-\dfrac{2x+1}{3}&=5\\ 12x-(2x+1)&=15\\ 10x-1&=15\\ 10x&=16\\ x&=1.6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=1.6$$

Let the second cable have length $c$. In the triangle formed by the two cables, the angle between the 80 m cable and the 20 m side at $A$ is $60^\circ$, so apply the cosine rule.
$$\begin{aligned} c^2&=20^2+80^2-2\times 20\times 80\cos 60^\circ\\ &=5200\\ c&=\sqrt{5200}\\ &=72.11102551\ldots\\ &\approx 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

Let $O$ be the base of the building.

Method 1 (right-angled trigonometry). In the right-angled triangle with $A$, $O$ and the top of the building:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ&=\dfrac{69.2}{AO}\\ AO&=\dfrac{69.2}{\tan 60^\circ}\\ &=39.9526\ldots\\ &\approx 40 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using the 80 m cable as hypotenuse:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos 60^\circ&=\dfrac{AO}{80}\\ AO&=80\cos 60^\circ=40 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (Pythagoras). In the right-angled triangle with $B$ and $O$:
$$\begin{aligned} 72^2&=OB^2+69.2^2\\ OB^2&=395.36\\ OB&=19.9 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
So $AO\approx 20+19.9=39.9\approx 40$ m.

The distance from $A$ to the base of the building is approximately 40 metres.

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3x^2e^{2x+1}\right)=6xe^{2x+1}(x+1)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x^2 & v&=e^{2x+1}\\ u'&=6x & v'&=2e^{2x+1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3x^2e^{2x+1}\right)&=6x\cdot e^{2x+1}+3x^2\cdot 2e^{2x+1}\\ &=6xe^{2x+1}+6x^2e^{2x+1}\\ &=6xe^{2x+1}(1+x)\\ &=6xe^{2x+1}(x+1) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2 x(x+1)e^{2x+1}\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $6x(x+1)e^{2x+1}$ is the derivative of $3x^2e^{2x+1}$, so write the integrand with the factor 6.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 x(x+1)e^{2x+1}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{6}\int_1^2 6x(x+1)e^{2x+1}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\Big[3x^2e^{2x+1}\Big]_1^2\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\left(3(2)^2e^{5}-3(1)^2e^{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\left(12e^5-3e^3\right)\\ &=2e^5-\dfrac{1}{2}e^3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Express $\dfrac{2x}{x^2-4}-\dfrac{x+1}{x^2-x-2}$ as a single algebraic fraction, in simplest form.
items.sol:
Factorise each denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2x}{x^2-4}-\dfrac{x+1}{x^2-x-2}&=\dfrac{2x}{(x-2)(x+2)}-\dfrac{x+1}{(x-2)(x+1)}\\ &=\dfrac{2x}{(x-2)(x+2)}-\dfrac{1}{x-2}\\ &=\dfrac{2x-(x+2)}{(x+2)(x-2)}\\ &=\dfrac{x-2}{(x+2)(x-2)}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{x+2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle moves on the $x$-axis so that it’s displacement in metres from the origin at a time $t$ seconds is given by the equation $x=\ln(t^2+6)$.

The particle starts from rest at the point $x=\ln(6)$ and accelerates in a positive direction as shown in the distance-time graph below.

\exfigure{1547_q15_1}

Determine when the acceleration of the particle becomes zero and find the velocity at this time.
items.sol:
Differentiate the displacement to find the velocity.
$$\dot{x}=\dfrac{2t}{t^2+6}$$
Differentiate using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2t & v&=t^2+6\\ u'&=2 & v'&=2t \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=\dfrac{2(t^2+6)-2t\cdot 2t}{(t^2+6)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{12-2t^2}{(t^2+6)^2} \end{aligned}$$
The acceleration is zero when $12-2t^2=0$, so $t^2=6$.

Since $t\ge 0$, $t=\sqrt{6}$.

The velocity at this time is
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{(\sqrt{6})^2+6}\\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\sqrt{6}\text{ s and } v=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\text{ m/s}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x^4-3x^2+18x+24$ at the point where $x=-2$.
items.sol:
Find the point of contact.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(-2)^4-3(-2)^2+18(-2)+24\\ &=16-12-36+24\\ &=-8 \end{aligned}$$
Find the gradient of the tangent.
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=4x^3-6x+18\\ \text{at } x=-2:\ y'&=-32+12+18\\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$
The tangent has gradient $m_1=-2$, so the normal has gradient $m_2=\dfrac{1}{2}$, since $m_1m_2=-1$.

Equation of the normal through $(-2,-8)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-(-8)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(x-(-2)\big)\\ 2y+16&=x+2\\ x-2y-14&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x-2y-14=0\ \left(\text{or } y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-7\right)$$

items.part:
The results on a class task are normally distributed with a mean of 40.

Two students, Dixie and Chloe, both receive their results on the task.

Dixie is told that she scored a mark of 50 and that this converted to a $z$-score of 2.

Chloe is only told that her $z$-score was 2.5.

By first finding the standard deviation, determine what mark Chloe scored on the task.
items.sol:
Use the $z$-score formula $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ with Dixie's result to find $\sigma$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=\dfrac{50-40}{\sigma}\\ \sigma&=5 \end{aligned}$$
Now use Chloe's $z$-score.
$$\begin{aligned} 2.5&=\dfrac{x-40}{5}\\ 12.5&=x-40\\ x&=52.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Chloe scored } 52.5$$

items.part:
An artist has two boxes of paints beside his easel. The first box contains 15 tubes which contain green, red or blue paint and the second contains four tubes which have only red or blue paint.

The artist chooses one tube of paint from each box.

The tree diagram below shows the probabilities of him choosing a given colour.

\exfigure{1547_q18_1}
What is the probability that the tubes he chooses are red and blue?
items.sol:
The colours red and blue can occur in two orders, red then blue or blue then red.
$$\begin{aligned} P(R\text{ and }B)&=P(RB)+P(BR)\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{60}+\dfrac{3}{20}\\ &=\dfrac{16}{60}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{15} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An artist has two boxes of paints beside his easel. The first box contains 15 tubes which contain green, red or blue paint and the second contains four tubes which have only red or blue paint.

The artist chooses one tube of paint from each box.

The tree diagram below shows the probabilities of him choosing a given colour.

\exfigure{1547_q18_1}
What is the probability that the tubes he chooses are not the same colour?
items.sol:
Find the probability that the colours are the same, then subtract from 1.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same})&=P(RR)+P(BB)\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{3}{4}+\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{20}+\dfrac{1}{20}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{not same})&=1-\dfrac{2}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A ship leaves port travelling on a bearing of $065^\circ$. After travelling 20 kilometres, the ship is due south of a lighthouse.

The ship continues on this bearing for a further 4 kilometres, then measures the bearing of the lighthouse to be $320^\circ$.

\exfigure{1547_q19_1}
Show that $\angle PSL$ is $75^\circ$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle NSP&=180^\circ-65^\circ\\ &=115^\circ \end{aligned}$$
(co-interior angles)
$$\begin{aligned} \angle NSL&=360^\circ-320^\circ\\ &=40^\circ \end{aligned}$$
(angles in a revolution)
$$\begin{aligned} \angle LSP&=115^\circ-40^\circ\\ &=75^\circ \end{aligned}$$
(adjacent angles making up $\angle NSP$)

$\therefore\ \angle PSL=75^\circ$

items.part:
A ship leaves port travelling on a bearing of $065^\circ$. After travelling 20 kilometres, the ship is due south of a lighthouse.

The ship continues on this bearing for a further 4 kilometres, then measures the bearing of the lighthouse to be $320^\circ$.

\exfigure{1547_q19_1}
Calculate the distance from the ship to the lighthouse at this time.
items.sol:
In triangle $LPS$, use the sine rule with the 4 km side and the distance $d$ (the source gives the angles $65^\circ$ and $40^\circ$ opposite $d$ and the 4 km side respectively).
$$\dfrac{d}{\sin 65^\circ}=\dfrac{4}{\sin 40^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} d&=\dfrac{4\sin 65^\circ}{\sin 40^\circ}\\ &=5.6398\ldots\\ &\approx 5.6 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
The ship is approximately 5.6 kilometres from the lighthouse.

items.part: Find the greatest and least values of the function $f(x)=10x^2e^{-x}$ in the domain $[0,4]$.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=10x^2 & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=20x & v'&=-e^{-x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=-10x^2e^{-x}+20xe^{-x}\\ &=10xe^{-x}(2-x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $f'(x)=0$ when $x=0$ or $x=2$.

Test $x=2$ (the factor $2-x$ decides the sign, as $10xe^{-x}>0$ for $x>0$):
$$\begin{aligned} f'(1)&=10e^{-1}>0 &&\text{increasing}\\ f'(3)&=-30e^{-3}<0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=2$ is a local maximum.
$$f(2)=10(2)^2e^{-2}=\dfrac{40}{e^2}\approx 5.4$$
Compare with the end points.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0)&=0\\ f(4)&=10(4)^2e^{-4}\approx 2.93 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f(4)>0$, the least value is at $x=0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{greatest value } \dfrac{40}{e^2}\approx 5.4,\ \text{least value } 0$$

items.part: What is $\displaystyle\int(10x-15)\,(x^2-3x)^4\,dx$.
items.sol:
Factorise the numerator so that it is a multiple of the derivative of $x^2-3x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int(10x-15)(x^2-3x)^4\,dx&=\int5(2x-3)(x^2-3x)^4\,dx\\&=5\cdot\dfrac{1}{5}(x^2-3x)^5+c\\&=(x^2-3x)^5+c\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{4x^3+x^2\,dx}{3x^4+x^3}$.
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(3x^4+x^3)=12x^3+3x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^2\dfrac{4x^3+x^2}{3x^4+x^3}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int_1^2\dfrac{12x^3+3x^2}{3x^4+x^3}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\ln(3x^4+x^3)\Big]_1^2\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\ln 56-\ln 4\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln 14\end{aligned}$$

From the table, $P(-0.5<z<0.5)=0.3829$ and $P(-1.25<z<1.25)=0.7887$.

By symmetry, each half of these intervals has half the probability.
$$\begin{aligned}P(-0.5<z<1.25)&=\dfrac{0.3829}{2}+\dfrac{0.7887}{2}\\&=0.19145+0.39435\\&=0.5858\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A random variable is normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

The table gives the probability that this random variable lies between $-z$ and $z$ for different values of $z$.

\extable{1547_q22_t1}

\exfigure{1547_q22_1}

The probability values given in the table for different values of $z$ are represented by the shaded area in the diagram beside the table.
The arm span (in metres) for a group of 1200 residents of a town are normally distributed with a mean of 1.68 metres and a standard deviation of 0.24 metres.

By first calculating $z$-scores, use the table above to determine how many of the residents will have an arm span greater than 1.5 metres.
items.sol:
Calculate the $z$-score for 1.5 m.
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\&=\dfrac{1.5-1.68}{0.24}\\&=-0.75\end{aligned}$$
From the table, $P(-0.75<z<0.75)=0.5467$, so by symmetry the area to the right of $-0.75$ is this half plus the right half of the curve.
$$P(z>-0.75)=\dfrac{0.5467}{2}+0.5=0.77335 \text{ (or } 77.335\%)$$
Number of residents:
$$\begin{aligned}0.77335\times1200&=928.02\\&\approx 928\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 928 \text{ residents}$$

items.part: Use calculus to determine and verify the nature of the stationary points, find local maxima and minima and points of inflection (horizontal or otherwise) and hence sketch the graph of the function $y=12x^5-15x^4-40x^3$. Accurate values for all $x$-intercepts are not required.
items.sol:
Differentiate and factorise.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=12x^5-15x^4-40x^3\\y'&=60x^4-60x^3-120x^2\\&=60x^2(x-2)(x+1)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$, so $x=0,\ 2,\ -1$.
$$\begin{aligned}y''&=240x^3-180x^2-240x\\&=60x(4x^2-3x-4)\end{aligned}$$
Test each stationary point using $y''$.
$$\begin{aligned}x=0&: y''=0 &&\text{(possible inflection)}\\x=2&: y''=720>0 &&\text{(concave up, minimum)}\\x=-1&: y''=-180<0 &&\text{(concave down, maximum)}\end{aligned}$$
Possible inflections occur when $y''=0$: $x=0$ or $4x^2-3x-4=0$, giving
$$x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{73}}{8}\approx-0.69 \text{ or } 1.44$$
Test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{aligned}x=-0.5&: y''=45>0\\x=1&: y''=-180<0\end{aligned}$$
Concavity changes at each of these, so all are points of inflection. At $x=0$ the gradient is also zero, so it is a horizontal inflection.

Key points: local maximum $(-1,13)$, point of inflection $(-0.693,7.935)$, horizontal inflection $(0,0)$, point of inflection $(1.443,-110.143)$, local minimum $(2,-176)$.

\exfigure{1547_q23_s1}
items.final: Local max $(-1,13)$, local min $(2,-176)$, horizontal inflection $(0,0)$, inflections at $(-0.693,7.935)$ and $(1.443,-110.143)$

items.part:
Harrison received a lump sum from his superannuation fund when he retired. He deposited some of this into a new bank account, earning 2\% per annum compound interest.

The table below shows present value interest factors for an annuity of \$1 for various interest rates ($r$) and numbers of periods ($N$).

\extable{1547_q25_t1}
For the first 5 years following retirement, Harrison was able to withdraw \$36 000 at the end of each year to pay his remaining mortgage and living expenses.

Show that the present value of a \$36 000 annuity for 5 years is \$169 686.
items.sol:
The present value of an annuity is the withdrawal times the factor from the table, using $r=0.02$ and $N=5$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Present value}&=\$36\,000\times4.7135\\&=\$169\,686\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Harrison received a lump sum from his superannuation fund when he retired. He deposited some of this into a new bank account, earning 2\% per annum compound interest.

The table below shows present value interest factors for an annuity of \$1 for various interest rates ($r$) and numbers of periods ($N$).

\extable{1547_q25_t1}
Harrison wants to reduce his withdrawal to \$20 000 per year for the next 10 years, starting 5 years after his retirement.

If the amount he deposited when he opened the account was \$340 000, would he be able to make these planned withdrawals over the ten years? (Justify your answer with calculations)
items.sol:
The ten years of withdrawals start after year 5, so take the $\$20\,000$ annuity for 15 years and subtract the $\$20\,000$ annuity for 5 years.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Present value}&=20\,000\times12.8493-20\,000\times4.7135\\&=\$162\,716\end{aligned}$$
The total required is this plus the $\$169\,686$ from part (a).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total}&=\$162\,716+\$169\,686\\&=\$332\,402\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \$340\,000 \text{ would be enough}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graphs of $y=3x+\sqrt{2}$, $\;y=-\sqrt{3}\,x-\sqrt{2}$ and $y=2x^2-4\sqrt{2}$.

Use the graph to find the solution to the following inequalities, giving your answer correct to the nearest tenth.
$3x+\sqrt{2}>2x^2-4\sqrt{2}$
items.sol:
We need where the line $y=3x+\sqrt{2}$ is above the curve $y=2x^2-4\sqrt{2}$.

From the graph this is between the intersection points, approximately $x=-1.3$ and $x=2.8$.

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graphs of $y=3x+\sqrt{2}$, $\;y=-\sqrt{3}\,x-\sqrt{2}$ and $y=2x^2-4\sqrt{2}$.

\exfigure{1547_q26_1}

Use the graph to find the solution to the following inequalities, giving your answer correct to the nearest tenth.
$2x^2+\sqrt{3}\,x-3\sqrt{2}\ge 0$
items.sol:
Rearrange the inequality so both sides are given graphs.
$$\begin{aligned}2x^2+\sqrt{3}x-3\sqrt{2}&\ge0\\2x^2-3\sqrt{2}&\ge-\sqrt{3}x\\2x^2-4\sqrt{2}&\ge-\sqrt{3}x-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Daria adds together the integers, which are not multiples of 2 or 3, between 1 and 300 inclusive.

So, $1+5+7+11+\ldots\ldots\,295+299$.

Eva adds together all the powers of 2 between 1 and 10 000 inclusive.

So, $1+2+4+8+\ldots\,4\,096+8\,192$

Who will achieve the larger answer and what is the difference?
items.sol:
Daria: add all integers to 300, then remove multiples of 2 and of 3, adding back multiples of 6 (removed twice). Each is an arithmetic series.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{All integers}&=\dfrac{300}{2}(1+300)=45150\\\text{Multiples of 2}&=\dfrac{150}{2}(2+300)=22650\\\text{Multiples of 3}&=\dfrac{100}{2}(3+300)=15150\\\text{Multiples of 6}&=\dfrac{50}{2}(6+300)=7650\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Required sum}&=45150-(22650+15150-7650)\\&=15000\end{aligned}$$
Eva: the powers of 2 form a GP with $a=1$, $r=2$. Find $n$ from the last term.
$$ar^{n-1}=2^{n-1}=8192=2^{13}$$
so $n=14$.
$$\begin{aligned}S_{14}&=\dfrac{1(2^{14}-1)}{2-1}\\&=16383\end{aligned}$$
Eva's sum is larger, and the difference is
$$16383-15000=1383$$
items.final: Eva has the larger sum, by $1383$

items.sol:
The total area under a probability density function is 1.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^t(1-e^{-x})\,dx&=1\\\Big[x+e^{-x}\Big]_0^t&=1\\t+e^{-t}-1&=1\end{aligned}$$
So the cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=x+e^{-x}-1$$
Substitute $t=1.84$:
$$1.84+e^{-1.84}-1=0.99881743\approx1$$
So the area under the curve is 1, correct to 2 decimal places.

Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{-x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right)&=e^{-x}-xe^{-x}-e^{-x}\\&=-xe^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
The expected value is $E(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^{1.84}x\,f(x)\,dx$. Using the result above, $\displaystyle\int -xe^{-x}\,dx=xe^{-x}+e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(x)&=\int_0^{1.84}(x-xe^{-x})\,dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+xe^{-x}+e^{-x}\right]_0^{1.84}\\&=2.14384149-1\\&=1.14384149\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A banner is designed as an isosceles triangle, with equal sides of length $x$ cm and base of length $2y$ cm, as shown.

\exfigure{1547_q29_1}

The total perimeter of the triangle is 40 cm.
Show that the area of the triangle in terms of $x$ can written as:

$$A=(20-x)\,(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$
items.sol:
The perimeter is $2x+2y=40$, so $y=20-x$.

Let $h$ be the height. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with sides $y$, $h$, $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}h&=\sqrt{x^2-y^2}\\&=\sqrt{x^2-(20-x)^2}\\&=\sqrt{40x-400}\end{aligned}$$
The area is
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot2y\cdot h\\&=(20-x)(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A banner is designed as an isosceles triangle, with equal sides of length $x$ cm and base of length $2y$ cm, as shown.

\exfigure{1547_q29_1}

The total perimeter of the triangle is 40 cm.
Use calculus to find the values of $x$ and $y$ which give a maximum area and find this area.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=20-x & v&=(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\u'&=-1 & v'&=20(40x-400)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dA}{dx}&=(20-x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}(40x-400)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot40-(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{800-60x}{(40x-400)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary point when $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$x=\dfrac{80}{6}=13\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side.
$$\begin{aligned}x=13&: \dfrac{dA}{dx}\approx1.82>0\\x=14&: \dfrac{dA}{dx}\approx-3.16<0\end{aligned}$$
So the area is a maximum at $x=13\dfrac{1}{3}$, and then $y=20-x=6\dfrac{2}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\left(20-\dfrac{40}{3}\right)\left(40\times\dfrac{40}{3}-400\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&\approx76.98\\&\approx77\text{ cm}^2 \text{ (2 s.f.)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A blueberry farmer records the crop size in kilograms from a range of blueberry shrubs on his trial patch. The data includes shrubs which have just begun to produce berries right through to fully mature plants.

\exfigure{1547_q30_1}

Some statistical measures for the data in the Scatterplot are shown below.

Correlation Coefficient $(r)=0.874$

\extable{1547_q30_t1}
The gradient of the least-squares regression line can be found using the formula:

$$\text{gradient}=r\times\dfrac{\text{standard deviation of }y\text{ scores}}{\text{standard deviation of }x\text{ scores}}=r\dfrac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}.$$

Given that the least-squares regression line crosses the vertical axis at 0.339, find the equation of the regression line and hence predict the crop (in kg) from a 100 cm high shrub.
items.sol:
Use the given gradient formula with the statistics from the table.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{gradient}&=r\dfrac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}\\&=0.874\times\dfrac{0.61}{35.42}\\&=0.01505195\end{aligned}$$
The intercept is 0.339, so the equation is
$$y=0.01505195x+0.339$$
When $x=100$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=0.01505195\times100+0.339\\&=1.844195\\&\approx1.84\text{ kg}\end{aligned}$$
(accept 1.85 kg from the graph)

The value $r=0.874$ shows a strong positive correlation between the variables, so predictions such as that in part (a) would be very reliable.

From the data, shrubs only begin producing berries from about 30 cm in height, and the mature shrubs are no taller than about 150 cm, as neither appears in the data.

Predictions would therefore only be reliable between about $x=30$ and $x=150$.

items.part:
The graph below shows the line $y=\dfrac{x+1}{4}$ and the curve $y=\cos x$ on the same set of axes.

Note the $x$-axis has a scale which is in normal decimal numerals, but it also shows the position of multiples of the irrational number $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

\exfigure{1547_q31_1}

Draw the graph of $y=3\cos 2x$ on the same set of axes and use this to solve the equation:

$$3\cos 2x=\dfrac{x+1}{4}$$

for the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$. Give your answer as a decimal, correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:

items.part: Prove that: $\;\sin^2 x+\cot^2 x=\operatorname{cosec}^2 x-\cos^2 x$.
items.sol:
Start from the left-hand side and write $\cot^2x=\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\sin^2x+\cot^2x\\&=\sin^2x+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cdot\sin^2x+\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\end{aligned}$$
Use $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$ in the first term of the numerator.
$$\begin{aligned}&=\dfrac{\sin^2x(1-\cos^2x)+\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x-\sin^2x\cos^2x+\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x-\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\end{aligned}$$
Use $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}&=\dfrac{1-\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}-\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}\\&=\operatorname{cosec}^2x-\cos^2x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

The curves cross at $x=0,\ 2,\ 5$, so the area is found in two parts. The difference of the curves is $(x^3-4x^2+12)-(3x^2-10x+12)=x^3-7x^2+10x$, which changes sign at $x=2$.
$$\text{Area}=\left|\int_0^2(x^3-7x^2+10x)\,dx\right|+\left|\int_2^5(x^3-7x^2+10x)\,dx\right|$$
Integrate each part.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{7x^3}{3}+5x^2\right]_0^2\right|+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{7x^3}{3}+5x^2\right]_2^5\right|\\&=\left|5\dfrac{1}{3}\right|+\left|-10\dfrac{5}{12}-5\dfrac{1}{3}\right|\\&=5\dfrac{1}{3}+15\dfrac{3}{4}\\&=21\dfrac{1}{12}\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Bree borrows \$20 000 to buy a car. She is charged interest at 4.8\% pa, calculated at the end of each month, and she repays regular monthly instalments of \$$P$ after the interest is added.
Show that the amount owing after $n$ months is given by the equation

$A_n=20000\times1.004^n-P\left(1.004^{n-1}+1.004^{n-2}+\cdots\ldots+1.004^2+1.004+1\right)$.
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $r=\dfrac{0.048}{12}=0.004$, so each month the balance is multiplied by $1.004$ and then $P$ is subtracted.
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=20000\times1.004-P\\A_2&=A_1\times1.004-P\\&=20000\times1.004^2-P(1.004+1)\\A_3&=A_2\times1.004-P\\&=20000\times1.004^3-P(1.004^2+1.004+1)\end{aligned}$$
Continuing the pattern,
$$A_n=20000\times1.004^n-P\left(1.004^{n-1}+1.004^{n-2}+\cdots+1.004^2+1.004+1\right)$$

items.part:
Bree borrows \$20 000 to buy a car. She is charged interest at 4.8\% pa, calculated at the end of each month, and she repays regular monthly instalments of \$$P$ after the interest is added.
After paying the loan for 12 months, she still owes \$17 055.80 on the loan.

Find the amount of the monthly instalment, \$$P$.

Bree borrows \$20 000 to buy a car. She is charged interest at 4.8\% pa, calculated at the end of each month, and she repays regular monthly instalments of \$$P$ after the interest is added.
Determine the number of months required to pay off the loan completely (the term of the loan).
items.sol:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$, with $P=320$.
$$\begin{aligned}20000\times1.004^n-\dfrac{320(1.004^n-1)}{0.004}&=0\\20000(1.004)^n&=80000(1.004^n-1)\\60000(1.004)^n&=80000\\(1.004)^n&=\dfrac{4}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms.
$$\begin{aligned}n&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)}{\ln(1.004)}\\&\approx72.06\end{aligned}$$
Since a whole number of instalments is needed, the loan is paid completely after 73 months.

items.part: Find the area bounded by the curve $y = 1 + e^{0.5x}$, $x$-axis and the lines $x = 1$ and $x = 2$ by using the trapezoidal rule with five trapezia. Answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
For $y = 1 + e^{0.5x}$ on $[1,2]$ with five trapezia, the strip width is
$$h = \dfrac{b - a}{n} = \dfrac{2 - 1}{5} = 0.2$$
So the $x$ values are $1, 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8, 2$.

\extable{Ts5567_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left[y_0 + y_5 + 2(y_1 + y_2 + y_3 + y_4)\right] \\ &\approx \dfrac{0.2}{2}\left[2.649 + 3.718 + 2(2.822 + 3.014 + 3.226 + 3.460)\right] \\ &\approx 3.14 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Pasta boxes are labelled with a net weight of 375 g. The business selling the pasta boxes fills the boxes to a net weight of 380 g, to avoid customer complaints. The weight of the pasta boxes follows a normal distribution with a mean weight of 380 g and a standard deviation of 2.5 g.
What is the probability that a box selected randomly will contain less than 375 g of pasta?
items.sol:
Find the $z$-score of $375$.
$$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \dfrac{375 - 380}{2.5} = -2$$
About $95\%$ of scores lie between $z = -2$ and $z = 2$, so $5\%$ lie outside, split equally between the two tails.
$$5\% \div 2 = 2.5\%$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The probability a box has less than 375 g is } 2.5\%$$

items.part:
Pasta boxes are labelled with a net weight of 375 g. The business selling the pasta boxes fills the boxes to a net weight of 380 g, to avoid customer complaints. The weight of the pasta boxes follows a normal distribution with a mean weight of 380 g and a standard deviation of 2.5 g.
The business sets a target of less than $16\%$ of all boxes will contain more than 385 g of pasta. The business can change the mean weight of the boxes to meet this target. What is mean weight required to meet the target if the standard deviation remains at 2.5?
items.sol:
About $68\%$ of scores lie between $z = -1$ and $z = 1$, so $16\%$ lie above $z = 1$. This is the target, so $385$ must correspond to $z = 1$.
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \\ 1 &= \dfrac{385 - \mu}{2.5} \\ \mu &= 385 - 2.5 \\ &= 382.5 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The mean weight is } 382.5 \text{ g}$$

items.part: Solve $|5 - 3x| \ge 11$
items.sol:
For $|A| \ge k$, we need $A \ge k$ or $A \le -k$.

So $5 - 3x \ge 11$ or $5 - 3x \le -11$.

First case:
$$\begin{aligned} -3x &\ge 6 \\ x &\le -2 &&(\text{divide by } -3, \text{ reverse the inequality}) \end{aligned}$$
Second case:
$$\begin{aligned} -3x &\le -16 \\ x &\ge \dfrac{16}{3} &&(\text{divide by } -3, \text{ reverse the inequality}) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \le -2 \text{ or } x \ge \dfrac{16}{3}$$

items.part: Differentiate $x^3e^{2x}$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^3 & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=3x^2 & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^3e^{2x}\right) &= 3x^2e^{2x} + 2x^3e^{2x} \\ &= x^2e^{2x}(2x + 3) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle moves such that its velocity at a given time is given by:

$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$
What is the initial acceleration of the particle?
items.sol:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$$
$$\ddot{x} = -16\cos t$$
Initially $t = 0$:
$$\ddot{x} = -16\cos 0 = -16$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Initially the acceleration is } 16 \text{ m/s}^2 \text{ towards the left}$$
items.final: Initially the acceleration is $16 \text{ m/s}^2$ towards the left

items.part:
A particle moves such that its velocity at a given time is given by:

$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$
When is the particle first at rest?
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when the velocity is zero.
$$\begin{aligned} 8 - 16\sin t &= 0 \\ 16\sin t &= 8 \\ \sin t &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The particle is first at rest after } \dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ seconds}$$

items.part:
A particle moves such that its velocity at a given time is given by:

$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$
Given that the particle is initially at the origin, find an equation for the displacement ($x$), at a time $t$.
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$x = \displaystyle\int (8 - 16\sin t)\,dt = 8t + 16\cos t + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$ (initially at the origin):
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 8 \times 0 + 16\cos 0 + C \\ C &= -16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = 8t + 16\cos t - 16$$

items.part:
A particle moves such that its velocity at a given time is given by:

$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$
Find the distance travelled between the first two times when the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, so find the displacement at each time using the result of part (c).
$$\begin{aligned} x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) &= 8\times\dfrac{\pi}{6}+16\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}-16 \\ &= \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}-16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) &= 8\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+16\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}-16 \\ &= \dfrac{20\pi}{3}-8\sqrt{3}-16 \end{aligned}$$
The velocity is not zero between these times, so the distance is the size of the change in displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \left|\left(\dfrac{20\pi}{3}-8\sqrt{3}-16\right)-\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}-16\right)\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{16\pi}{3}-16\sqrt{3}\right| \\ &= 16\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{16\pi}{3} \ (\approx 10.96) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $e^{\cos(\pi x)}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule with $u=\cos(\pi x)$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u}=e^{u}\dfrac{du}{dx}$, where $\dfrac{du}{dx}=-\pi\sin(\pi x)$.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{\cos(\pi x)} = -\pi\sin(\pi x)\,e^{\cos(\pi x)}$$

items.part:
The probability density function for the continuous random variable $X$ is given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx(4 - x) & 1 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
What is the value of $k$?
items.sol:
The total area under a probability density function is 1.
$$\int_1^4 kx(4-x)\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^4 (4kx-kx^2)\,dx &= 1 \\ k\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4 &= 1 \\ k\left[\left(32-\dfrac{64}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right] &= 1 \\ 9k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{9}$$

items.part:
The probability density function for the continuous random variable $X$ is given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx(4 - x) & 1 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Find $F(t)$ the cumulative distribution function.
items.sol:
With $k=\dfrac{1}{9}$, the density is
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{9}x(4-x) & 1\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
For $1\le t\le 4$, $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$, so the integral starts at 1.
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int_{-\infty}^t f(x)\,dx \\ &= \int_1^t \dfrac{1}{9}x(4-x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\int_1^t (4x-x^2)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^t \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[\left(2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\left[2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}-\dfrac{5}{3}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{27}(6t^2-t^3-5) \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<1\\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{27}(6x^2-x^3-5) & 1\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 1 & x>4\end{cases}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $2\sin x + \sqrt{3} = 0$ where $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin x+\sqrt{3} &= 0 \\ \sin x &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with related acute angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\text{ or }\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$

items.part:
James has some sticks that are all of the same length. He arranges them in squares and has made the following 3 rows of patterns:

\exfigure{1302_q20_1}

He notices that 4 sticks are required to make the single square in the first row, 7 sticks to make 2 squares in the second row and in the third row he needs 10 sticks to make 3 squares.
Find an expression, in terms of $n$, for the number of sticks required to make a similar arrangement of $n$ squares in the $n$th row.
items.sol:
The numbers of sticks form the sequence $4, 7, 10, \ldots$

This is an arithmetic sequence with first term $a=4$ and common difference $d=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ &= 4+3(n-1) \\ &= 3n+1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
James has some sticks that are all of the same length. He arranges them in squares and has made the following 3 rows of patterns:

\exfigure{1302_q20_1}

He notices that 4 sticks are required to make the single square in the first row, 7 sticks to make 2 squares in the second row and in the third row he needs 10 sticks to make 3 squares.
James continues to make squares following the same pattern. He makes 4 squares in the 4th row and so on until he has completed 10 rows. Find the total number of sticks James uses in making these 10 rows.
items.sol:
The total is the sum of the first 10 terms of the arithmetic series $4, 7, 10, \ldots$ with $a=4$, $d=3$, $n=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right] \\ S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}\left[2\times 4+(10-1)\times 3\right] \\ &= 175 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 175 \text{ sticks}$$

items.part:
James has some sticks that are all of the same length. He arranges them in squares and has made the following 3 rows of patterns:

\exfigure{1302_q20_1}

He notices that 4 sticks are required to make the single square in the first row, 7 sticks to make 2 squares in the second row and in the third row he needs 10 sticks to make 3 squares.
James started with 1750 sticks. Given that James continues the pattern to complete $k$ rows but does not have sufficient sticks to complete the $(k+1)$th row, show that $k$ satisfies $(3k - 100)(k + 35) < 0$.
items.sol:
The number of sticks used in $k$ rows must be less than 1750 (there are not enough for row $k+1$ is handled in part (d)).
$$S_k<1750$$
Using the sum of an arithmetic series,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k}{2}\left[2\times 4+3(k-1)\right] &< 1750 \\ k(8+3k-3) &< 3500 \\ 3k^2+5k-3500 &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
Factorising,
$$(3k-100)(k+35)<0$$

items.part:
James has some sticks that are all of the same length. He arranges them in squares and has made the following 3 rows of patterns:

\exfigure{1302_q20_1}

He notices that 4 sticks are required to make the single square in the first row, 7 sticks to make 2 squares in the second row and in the third row he needs 10 sticks to make 3 squares.
What is the value of $k$?
items.sol:
Find where the quadratic is zero.
$$(3k-100)(k+35)=0$$
$$k=\dfrac{100}{3}\text{ or }k=-35$$
\exfigure{1302_q20_s1}

The product is negative between the roots, so $-35<k<\dfrac{100}{3}$.

The value of $k$ is a positive whole number of rows, and $\dfrac{100}{3}=33 \cdot \dot{3}$.
$$\therefore\ k=33$$

items.part:
Let $f(x) = (x + 3)(x - 1)^2$
Find the coordinates of the intercepts.
items.sol:
For the $x$-intercepts, put $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= (x+3)(x-1)^2 \\ x &= -3 \text{ or } x=1 \end{aligned}$$
For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= (0+3)(0-1)^2 \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\text{ intercepts are }(-3,0),\ (1,0)\text{ and }(0,3)$$

items.part:
Let $f(x) = (x + 3)(x - 1)^2$
Find the coordinates of the stationary points on the curve with the equation $y = f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x+3) & v&=(x-1)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= (x+3)\cdot 2(x-1)+(x-1)^2\times 1 \\ &= 3x^2+2x-5 \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(x)=6x+2$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2+2x-5 &= 0 \\ (3x+5)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$x=-\dfrac{5}{3}\text{ or }x=1$$
When $x=-\dfrac{5}{3}$, $y=\dfrac{256}{27}$. When $x=1$, $y=0$.

The stationary points are $\left(-\dfrac{5}{3},\dfrac{256}{27}\right)$ and $(1,0)$.

The sign of $f''$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=-\dfrac{5}{3}:\ f''&=6\times\left(-\dfrac{5}{3}\right)+2=-8<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ \text{At } x=1:\ f''&=6\times 1+2=8>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x) = (x + 3)(x - 1)^2$
What are the coordinates of any points of inflexion?
items.sol:
A possible point of inflexion occurs where $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x+2 &= 0 \\ x &= -\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$, $y=\dfrac{128}{27}$.

Test for a change in concavity.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-1)&=6\times(-1)+2=-4<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(0)&=6\times 0+2=2>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so
$$\therefore\text{ the point of inflexion is }\left(-\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{128}{27}\right)$$

Let $f(x) = (x + 3)(x - 1)^2$
Sketch the graph of $y = f(x)$ over a suitable domain.

In $[-4,2]$ the line segment from $(-4,0)$ to $(0,-2)$ forms a triangle with the $x$-axis, and the quarter circle of radius 2 gives a quarter-circle region.

items.part:
A continuous function $y = f(x)$ defined in the domain $[-4, 5]$. The function consists of a line segment, a quarter of a circle centred at $(0, 0)$ with radius 2 and a logarithmic function $f(x) = \ln(x - 1)$ in the domain $[2, 5]$

\exfigure{1302_q22_1}
Hence, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_2^5 \ln(x - 1)\,dx$

given that $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^5 f(x)\,dx = 4\ln 4 - 7 - \pi$
items.sol:
Split the given integral at $x=2$.
$$\int_{-4}^5 f(x)\,dx=\int_{-4}^2 f(x)\,dx+\int_2^5 f(x)\,dx$$
The region on $[-4,2]$ lies below the $x$-axis, so its integral is $-(4+\pi)$.
$$4\ln 4-7-\pi=-(4+\pi)+\int_2^5 \ln(x-1)\,dx$$
$$\therefore\ \int_2^5 \ln(x-1)\,dx=4\ln 4-3$$

items.part: Find $p$ given that $\displaystyle\int_2^3 \dfrac{1}{1 - x}\,dx = \ln p$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_2^3 \dfrac{1}{1-x}\,dx &= \Big[-\ln|1-x|\Big]_2^3 \\ &= -\ln 2+\ln 1 \\ &= -\ln 2 \\ &= \ln\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p=\dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part:
The curve $C$ has the equation $y = f(x)$, $x \ne 0$, and the point $P(2, 1)$ lies on $C$.
Find $f(x)$ given $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6 - \dfrac{8}{x^2}$.
items.sol:
Rewrite with negative powers, then integrate term by term.
$$f'(x)=3x^2-6-8x^{-2}$$
$$f(x)=x^3-6x+8x^{-1}+C$$
The point $P(2,1)$ lies on $C$, so $f(2)=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 2^3-6\times 2+8\times 2^{-1}+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-6x+\dfrac{8}{x}+1$$

items.part:
The curve $C$ has the equation $y = f(x)$, $x \ne 0$, and the point $P(2, 1)$ lies on $C$.
Find an equation for the tangent to $C$ at the point $P$. Express your answer in general form.
items.sol:
The gradient of the tangent at $P(2,1)$ is $f'(2)$.
$$\begin{aligned} m &= f'(2) \\ &= 3\times 2^2 - 6 - 8\times 2^{-2} \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
Using the point-gradient form $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= 4(x-2) \\ y - 1 &= 4x - 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 4x-y-7=0$$

items.part:
Let $X$ be a normally distributed random variable with mean 6 and variance 9 and let $Z$ be the random variable with the standard normal distribution.
Find $P(X > 6)$.
items.sol:
Here $\mu = 6$ and $\sigma^2 = 9$ (so $\sigma = 3$).

The normal distribution is symmetric about the mean, so
$$P(X>6)=P(X>\mu)=0.5$$

items.part:
Let $X$ be a normally distributed random variable with mean 6 and variance 9 and let $Z$ be the random variable with the standard normal distribution.
Find $b$ such that $P(X > 8) = P(Z < b)$.
items.sol:
By symmetry about the mean $6$, $P(X>8)=P(X<4)$.

Convert to a $z$-score:
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \\ &= \dfrac{4-6}{3} \\ &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
So $P(X>8)=P\left(Z<-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$.
$$\therefore\ b=-\dfrac{2}{3}$$

items.part:
The number of year 12 students who completed 30 minutes of exercise for each of the past ten days was as follows: 10, 11, 13, 17, 13, 15, 17, 28, 19, 15
Is 28 an outlier for this set of data? Justify your answer with calculations.
items.sol:
A value is an outlier if it is above $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Upper limit} &= Q_3+1.5\times IQR \\ &= 17+1.5\times 4 \\ &= 23 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $28$ is an outlier, as it is above the upper limit of $23$.
items.final: Yes, 28 is an outlier as it is above the upper limit of 23.

The line has the form $y=mx+c$, so
$$\text{Income}=0.8\times\text{Age}+c$$
The line of best fit passes through $(65,65)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 65 &= 0.8\times 65+c \\ c &= 13 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Income}=0.8\times\text{Age}+13$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Income} &= 0.8\times\text{Age}+13 \\ &= 0.8\times 80+13 \\ &= 77 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the income of an 80 year old person is } \$77\,000$$
People over the age of 65 often have a reduced income due to retirement, so the prediction in part (c) is not accurate.
The association is linear, positive and weak.

items.part:
The concentration of a pesticide in the soil is modelled by the equation given by:

$P = P_0e^{-kt}$

where $P_0$ and $k$ are constants, and $t$ is the number of days after the application of the pesticide.
Once in the soil, the half-life of the pesticide is the time taken for its concentration to be reduced to one half of its initial value. If the half-life of the pesticide is 25 days, find the value of $k$. Answer correct to 2 significant figures.

The concentration of a pesticide in the soil is modelled by the equation given by:

$P = P_0e^{-kt}$

where $P_0$ and $k$ are constants, and $t$ is the number of days after the application of the pesticide.
What is the percentage decrease in concentration of the pesticide after 80 days? Answer to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
With $k=0.028$ and $t=80$:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= P_0e^{-0.028\times 80} \\ &= 0.1064\ldots P_0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage decrease} &= 1-0.1064\ldots \\ &= 0.8936\ldots \\ &\approx 89\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx = \dfrac{10}{3}$, $0 \le a < \pi$, calculate the value of $a$.
items.sol:
Integrate, then apply the limits:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx &= \dfrac{10}{3} \\ \left[-\dfrac{5}{3}\cos 3x\right]_0^a &= \dfrac{10}{3} \\ -\dfrac{5}{3}(\cos 3a-\cos 0) &= \dfrac{10}{3} \\ \cos 3a-\cos 0 &= -2 \\ \cos 3a &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
So $3a=\pi, 3\pi,\ldots$, and since $0\le a<\pi$ we need $0\le 3a<3\pi$, giving $3a=\pi$.
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
\exfigure{1302_q32_s1}

items.part:
The line $y = mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$ at a point $P$.
Find the coordinates of $P$.
items.sol:
At $P$ the line and curve have the same $y$-value:
$$mx=-e^{\frac{1}{3}x} \qquad (1)$$
At $P$ the line's gradient equals the gradient of the curve:
$$m=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-e^{\frac{1}{3}x}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{3}e^{\frac{1}{3}x} \qquad (2)$$
From (1), $-e^{\frac{1}{3}x}=mx$, so substituting into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{1}{3}mx \\ x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$y=-e^{\frac{1}{3}\times 3}=-e$$
$$\therefore\ P=(3,-e)$$

items.part:
The line $y = mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$ at a point $P$.
Find the value of $m$.
items.sol:
At $P$, $mx=-e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$ with $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3m &= -e^{\frac{1}{3}\times 3} \\ 3m &= -e \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=-\dfrac{e}{3}$$

items.part:
Harvey is designing an open-ended tent as shown below.

\exfigure{1302_q33_1}

The frame of the tent is made using rods of two different lengths:

\begin{itemize}
\item $x$ metres for the top and bottom edges
\item $y$ metres for each sloping edge.
\end{itemize}

The rods cost \$9.50 per metre.

The frame is covered by one rectangular sheet of fabric whose area is $24\ \text{m}^2$.
Show that the total length, $l$ m, of rods is given by:

$$l = 3x + \dfrac{48}{x}$$
items.sol:
The sheet is a rectangle with dimensions $x$ and $2y$, so
$$\begin{aligned} x\times 2y &= 24 \\ y &= \dfrac{24}{2x} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{x} \end{aligned}$$
The frame has three rods of length $x$ and four of length $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} l &= 3x+4y \\ &= 3x+4\times\dfrac{12}{x} \\ &= 3x+\dfrac{48}{x} \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dl}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3-\dfrac{48}{x^2} &= 0 \\ x^2 &= 16 \\ x &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
Since $x$ is a length, $x=-4$ is rejected.

Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2l}{dx^2}=\dfrac{96}{x^3}=\dfrac{96}{4^3}>0 \text{ at } x=4$$
So $l$ has a minimum at $x=4$.
$$\therefore\ x=4 \text{ m}$$

The minimum length of rods occurs at $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} l &= 3\times 4+\dfrac{48}{4} \\ &= 24 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= 24\times 9.50 \\ &= \$228 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum cost of the frame is } \$228$$

items.part:
A ball thrown upwards from a building attains a height above the ground given by the function $h(t)=8t-2t^2+12$, where $t$ is the time in seconds and $h$ is in metres.

Find the value for $t$ for which $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=0$ and hence find the maximum height above the ground the ball reaches.
items.sol:
The maximum height occurs where $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 8-4t = 0\\ t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

Test the nature with the second derivative.

$$\dfrac{d^2h}{dt^2}=-4<0$$

So the graph is concave down and this is a maximum.

$$\begin{aligned} h(2) &= 8(2)-2(2)^2+12\\ &= 20 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ t=2 \text{ and the maximum height is } 20 \text{ m}$$

items.part: Find the first and second derivative of the function $f(x)=(x^2-4)^3$.
items.sol:
Use the chain rule for the first derivative.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3(x^2-4)^2\times 2x\\ &= 6x(x^2-4)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=6x & v&=(x^2-4)^2\\ u'&=6 & v'&=4x(x^2-4)\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= 6(x^2-4)^2+6x\times 4x(x^2-4)\\ &= 6(x^2-4)\left[(x^2-4)+4x^2\right]\\ &= 6(x^2-4)(5x^2-4) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f'(x)=6x(x^2-4)^2 \text{ and } f''(x)=6(x^2-4)(5x^2-4)$$

items.part:
Lucy contemplates playing a new game which involves tossing three coins simultaneously. She will receive \$10 if she obtains 3 heads, \$5 if she obtains 2 heads and \$3.00 if she obtains 1 head. However, if she obtains no heads, she must pay \$20. She must also pay \$5 for each game she plays.
What is Lucy's expected gain?
items.sol:
The gain $X$ for 0, 1, 2, 3 heads, with each probability from three tosses, is:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} X & -20 & 3 & 5 & 10\\ \hline P(X) & \dfrac{1}{8} & \dfrac{3}{8} & \dfrac{3}{8} & \dfrac{1}{8}\end{array}$$

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= -20\times\dfrac{1}{8}+3\times\dfrac{3}{8}+5\times\dfrac{3}{8}+10\times\dfrac{1}{8}\\ &= \$1.75 \end{aligned}$$

This is before the \$5 fee.

$$\therefore\ E(X)=\$1.75$$

items.part:
Lucy contemplates playing a new game which involves tossing three coins simultaneously. She will receive \$10 if she obtains 3 heads, \$5 if she obtains 2 heads and \$3.00 if she obtains 1 head. However, if she obtains no heads, she must pay \$20. She must also pay \$5 for each game she plays.
Is this a fair game? Why?
items.sol:
It costs \$5 to play, so the expected gain per game is

$$\begin{aligned} 1.75-5 &= -3.25 \end{aligned}$$

Lucy can expect to lose \$3.25 per game on average.

A fair game has an expected gain of 0.

$$\therefore\ \text{It is not a fair game, as Lucy loses money.}$$
items.final: It is not a fair game, as Lucy loses money (expected gain $-\$3.25$ per game).

items.sol:
The cone's height, radius and slant side form a right-angled triangle.

By Pythagoras' theorem, with slant side 9 and height $x$:

$$\begin{aligned} r^2+x^2 &= 9^2\\ r^2 &= 81-x^2 \end{aligned}$$

Since $r>0$,

$$\therefore\ r=\sqrt{81-x^2}$$

The volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$, with $h=x$ and $r^2=81-x^2$.

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(81-x^2)x\\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(81x-x^3\right) \end{aligned}$$

Expand and differentiate.

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 27\pi x-\dfrac{1}{3}\pi x^3\\ \dfrac{dV}{dx} &= 27\pi-\pi x^2 \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$.

$$x^2=27$$

Since $x>0$, $x=\sqrt{27}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.

$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-2\pi x=-2\pi\sqrt{27}<0$$

So this is a maximum.

$$\therefore\ \text{the height for maximum volume is } \sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}$$

items.part: If $f(x)=(x+1)^2$ and $g(x)=x-2$ then find function $F$ defined as $f(g(x))$.
items.sol:
Substitute $g(x)=x-2$ into $f$.

$$\begin{aligned} f(g(x)) &= \left((x-2)+1\right)^2\\ &= (x-1)^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ F(x)=(x-1)^2$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^4-3x^2$.
Find any stationary points.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 4x^3-6x\\ &= 2x(2x^2-3) \end{aligned}$$

So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$.

$$f(0)=0$$

$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right) &= \dfrac{9}{4}-\dfrac{9}{2}\\ &= -2\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{stationary points: } (0,0),\ \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},-2\dfrac{1}{4}\right),\ \left(-\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},-2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^4-3x^2$.
Determine their nature.
items.sol:
Use the second derivative to test the nature.

$$f''(x)=12x^2-6$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -6<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ f''\left(\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right) &= 12>0 &&\text{minimum} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{maximum turning point at } (0,0);\ \text{minimum turning points at } \left(\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},-2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$$
items.final: maximum turning point at $(0,0)$; minimum turning points at $\left(\pm\sqrt{\tfrac{3}{2}},-2\tfrac{1}{4}\right)$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^4-3x^2$.
Find any intercepts.
items.sol:
Intercepts: put $y=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} x^4-3x^2 &= 0\\ x^2(x^2-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{3}$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{intercepts: } (0,0),\ (-\sqrt{3},0),\ (\sqrt{3},0)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^4-3x^2$.
Hence, sketch the curve for the domain $[-3,3]$.

items.sol:
Substitute each value of $x$ into $P(X=x)=\dfrac{x^2}{30}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\ \hline P(X=x) & \dfrac{1}{30} & \dfrac{4}{30} & \dfrac{9}{30} & \dfrac{16}{30}\end{array}$$

items.part:
The probability distribution of $X$ is given by the formula $P(X=x)=\dfrac{x^2}{30}$, where $x=1,2,3,4$.
Find the expected value of $X$.
items.sol:
The expected value is $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 1\times\dfrac{1}{30}+2\times\dfrac{4}{30}+3\times\dfrac{9}{30}+4\times\dfrac{16}{30}\\ &= \dfrac{100}{30}\\ &= 3\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The probability distribution of $X$ is given by the formula $P(X=x)=\dfrac{x^2}{30}$, where $x=1,2,3,4$.
Find $P(X<\mu)$.
items.sol:
From part (b), $\mu=\dfrac{100}{30}=3\dfrac{1}{3}$, so $X<\mu$ means $X=1,2,3$.
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(X<3\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{30}+\dfrac{4}{30}+\dfrac{9}{30}\\ &=\dfrac{14}{30}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X<\mu)=\dfrac{7}{15}$$

Let the height be $h$ cm. The volume of a cylinder is
$$V=\pi x^2h \quad (1)$$
The can is open, so the surface area is the base plus the curved surface.
$$300=\pi x^2+2\pi xh$$
Hence
$$2\pi xh=300-\pi x^2$$
$$h=\dfrac{1}{2\pi x}\left(300-\pi x^2\right) \quad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\pi x^2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\pi x}\left(300-\pi x^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{x}{2}\left(300-\pi x^2\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(300x-\pi x^3\right) \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

Write the volume as a function of $x$ and differentiate.
$$V=150x-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x^3$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dx}=150-\dfrac{3}{2}\pi x^2$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$.
$$\pi x^2=100$$
Since $x>0$,
$$x=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{\pi}}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-3\pi x<0 \text{ for } x>0$$
So this is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3000}{\sqrt{\pi}}-\dfrac{1000}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1000}{\sqrt{\pi}} \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum volume}=\dfrac{1000}{\sqrt{\pi}} \text{ cm}^3$$

Find the general primitive, $F$, of the following functions.
$f(x)=x^8-x^7+10$
items.sol:
Increase each power by 1 and divide by the new power.

items.part:
Find the general primitive, $F$, of the following functions.
$f(t)=\dfrac{t^4-1}{t^2}$
items.sol:
Split the fraction and use index laws.
$$\begin{aligned} f(t)&=\dfrac{t^4}{t^2}-\dfrac{1}{t^2}\\ &=t^2-t^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
Integrate term by term.
$$\begin{aligned} F(t)&=\dfrac{t^3}{3}-\dfrac{t^{-1}}{-1}+c\\ &=\dfrac{t^3}{3}+\dfrac{1}{t}+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $s$ in terms of $t$ if $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=u+at$, given that $u$ and $a$ are constants and $s=0$ when $t=0$.
items.sol:
Integrate with respect to $t$.
$$s=ut+\dfrac{at^2}{2}+c$$
When $t=0$, $s=0$, so $c=0$.
$$\therefore\ s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}at^2$$

items.part:
The function $f(x)=x^4+ax^3-4x^2+bx+6$ has $x$-intercepts $(2,0)$ and $(-3,0)$.

Find the values of $a$ and $b$.

Below is a sketch of a function. On the same axes draw the curve of the first derivative.

\exfigure{154_q11e_1}
items.sol:
\exfigure{154_q11e_s1}

The derivative has $x$-intercepts at the turning points of $f$.

Complete the table with $xp(x)$ and $x^2p(x)$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} x & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9 & 10 & \text{Total}\\ \hline p(x) & \dfrac{4}{25} & \dfrac{5}{25} & \dfrac{7}{25} & \dfrac{6}{25} & \dfrac{2}{25} & \dfrac{1}{25} & 1\\ xp(x) & \dfrac{20}{25} & \dfrac{30}{25} & \dfrac{49}{25} & \dfrac{48}{25} & \dfrac{18}{25} & \dfrac{10}{25} & \dfrac{175}{25}\\ x^2p(x) & \dfrac{100}{25} & \dfrac{180}{25} & \dfrac{343}{25} & \dfrac{384}{25} & \dfrac{162}{25} & \dfrac{100}{25} & \dfrac{1269}{25}\end{array}$$
The expected value is the sum of $xp(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=\dfrac{175}{25}\\ &=7 \end{aligned}$$

Use $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$, with $E(X^2)$ the total of $x^2p(x)$ from the table.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X)&=\dfrac{1269}{25}-7^2\\ &=\dfrac{1269-1225}{25}\\ &=\dfrac{44}{25}\\ &=1.76 \end{aligned}$$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma&=\sqrt{1.76}\\ &\approx 1.33 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{9}{x^{2.}-4}$.
Is this function odd, even or neither?
items.sol:
A function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=\dfrac{9}{(-x)^2-4}\\ &=\dfrac{9}{x^2-4}\\ &=f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f \text{ is an even function}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{9}{x^{2.}-4}$.
Determine any horizontal and vertical asymptotes
items.sol:
As $x\to\pm\infty$, the denominator grows without bound, so $f(x)\to 0$.

Horizontal asymptote: $y=0$.

Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero.
$$x^2-4=0$$
$$x=\pm 2$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{9}{x^{2.}-4}$.
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=9(x^2-4)^{-1}\\ f'(x)&=-9(x^2-4)^{-2}\times 2x\\ &=\dfrac{-18x}{(x^2-4)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Solve $f'(x)=0$.
$$x=0$$
$$f(0)=-\dfrac{9}{4}$$
The stationary point is $\left(0,-\dfrac{9}{4}\right)$.

The denominator is positive, so the sign of $f'$ is decided by $-18x$. Test either side of $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(-1)&=2>0 &&\text{increasing}\\ f'(0)&=0\\ f'(1)&=-2<0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(0,-\dfrac{9}{4}\right) \text{ is a maximum turning point}$$
