items.part:
The cost of running a train at a constant speed $v$ km/h is $C=50+\dfrac{v^2}{100}$ dollars per hour.
Find the time taken for an 800 km journey in terms of $v$.
items.sol:
Use speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$.
$$v=\dfrac{800}{t}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{800}{v} \text{ hours}$$

items.part:
The cost of running a train at a constant speed $v$ km/h is $C=50+\dfrac{v^2}{100}$ dollars per hour.
Hence, find an expression for the cost of an 800 km journey.
items.sol:
The cost of the journey is the cost per hour multiplied by the time.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost}&=\left(50+\dfrac{v^2}{100}\right)\times\dfrac{800}{v}\\ &=\dfrac{40000}{v}+8v \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The cost of running a train at a constant speed $v$ km/h is $C=50+\dfrac{v^2}{100}$ dollars per hour.
Find the most economical speed for this journey.
items.sol:
Differentiate the cost with respect to $v$.
$$\text{Cost}=40000v^{-1}+8v$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dv}(\text{Cost})=-40000v^{-2}+8$$
Set the derivative to zero.
$$v^2=5000$$
Since $v>0$,
$$v=\sqrt{5000}\approx 70.71 \text{ km/h}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2}{dv^2}(\text{Cost})=\dfrac{80000}{v^3}>0 \text{ for } v>0$$
So this is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the most economical speed is about } 70.71 \text{ km/h}$$

items.part:
Janet is a biologist completing research on bee hives on the river called \textit{Bend}. The river follows the curve $y=x^2-1,\ x\ge 0$ as shown below. All lengths are measured in kilometres.

Janet's research station is located at $(0,0)$ and the Bee hive ($P$) is located at $(0,1)$.

Janet was interested in a Bee hive ($R$) located on the \textit{Bend} river.

\exfigure{154_q13b_1}
Using the distance formula, if the bee hive is at the point $R\ (s,t)$ show that the length ($L$) in kilometres in a straight line from $P$ to the bee hive located at $R$ is given by

$L=\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}$.

$\left[\text{Distance formula: }\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\right]$
items.sol:
$R$ lies on $y=x^2-1$, so $t=s^2-1$ and $R=(s,s^2-1)$.

Use the distance formula between $P(0,1)$ and $R$.
$$\begin{aligned} L&=\sqrt{(s-0)^2+\left((s^2-1)-1\right)^2}\\ &=\sqrt{s^2+(s^2-2)^2}\\ &=\sqrt{s^2+s^4-4s^2+4}\\ &=\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Janet is a biologist completing research on bee hives on the river called \textit{Bend}. The river follows the curve $y=x^2-1,\ x\ge 0$ as shown below. All lengths are measured in kilometres.

Janet's research station is located at $(0,0)$ and the Bee hive ($P$) is located at $(0,1)$.

Janet was interested in a Bee hive ($R$) located on the \textit{Bend} river.

\exfigure{154_q13b_1}
If the Bee hive ($R$) is located at a point closet to the beehive ($P$).

Find $\dfrac{dL}{ds}$ and hence find the coordinates of the Bee hive ($R$).
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} L&=(s^4-3s^2+4)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=\dfrac{4s^3-6s}{2\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}}\\ &=\dfrac{2s^3-3s}{\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}} \end{aligned}$$
The denominator is positive, so $\dfrac{dL}{ds}=0$ when the numerator is zero.
$$s(2s^2-3)=0$$
Since $s>0$,
$$s=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$$
Then
$$t=\dfrac{3}{2}-1=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
Test the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} s=1:\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<0 &&\text{decreasing}\\ s=2:\ \dfrac{dL}{ds}&=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{8}}>0 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
So $L$ is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ R=\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$

items.part:
Janet is a biologist completing research on bee hives on the river called \textit{Bend}. The river follows the curve $y=x^2-1,\ x\ge 0$ as shown below. All lengths are measured in kilometres.

Janet's research station is located at $(0,0)$ and the Bee hive ($P$) is located at $(0,1)$.

Janet was interested in a Bee hive ($R$) located on the \textit{Bend} river.

\exfigure{154_q13b_1}
Find the length ($L$), in kilometres, the direct line between the Bee hives.
items.sol:
Substitute $s^2=\dfrac{3}{2}$ into $L=\sqrt{s^4-3s^2+4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} L&=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2-3\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)+4}\\ &=\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{4}-\dfrac{18}{4}+\dfrac{16}{4}}\\ &=\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{4}}\\ &\approx 1.32 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=2x\tan x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 2\tan x + 2x\sec^2 x \\ &= 2(\tan x + x\sec^2 x) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=\dfrac{e^{2x}}{5x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=5x\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{5x(2e^{2x})-e^{2x}\times 5}{25x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{10xe^{2x}-5e^{2x}}{25x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{5e^{2x}(2x-1)}{25x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^{2x}(2x-1)}{5x^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin 2x\,dx.$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin 2x\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\pi+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 0 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: $\displaystyle\int_0^3\dfrac{3x^4-2x^3+x^2}{x^2}\,dx$
items.sol:
Divide each term by $x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^3\dfrac{3x^4-2x^3+x^2}{x^2}\,dx &= \int_0^3(3x^2-2x+1)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{3x^3}{3}-\dfrac{2x^2}{2}+x\right]_0^3 \\ &= (27-9+3)-0 \\ &= 21 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=e^x+1$ at the point $(1,\ e+1)$.
items.sol:
$$y'=e^x$$
When $x=1$, the gradient is $m=e$.

The tangent through $(1,\ e+1)$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-(e+1) &= e(x-1) \\ y-e-1 &= ex-e \\ y &= ex+1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^3 2xe^{x^2+1}\,dx.$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^3 2xe^{x^2+1}\,dx &= \left[e^{x^2+1}\right]_0^3 \\ &= e^{9+1}-e^1 \\ &= e^{10}-e \end{aligned}$$

The creek is $15$ m wide with strips of width $5$ m, so $h=5$ and the depths are $0,\ 1.4,\ 1.8,\ 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{5}{2}(0+1.4)+\dfrac{5}{2}(1.4+1.8)+\dfrac{5}{2}(1.8+0) \\ &= 3.5+8+4.5 \\ &= 16 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{4}{x^3}-\sqrt{x}\right)dx.$
items.sol:
Rewrite in index form.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\left(\dfrac{4}{x^3}-\sqrt{x}\right)dx &= \int(4x^{-3}-x^{\frac12})\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{4x^{-2}}{-2}-\dfrac{x^{\frac32}}{\frac32}+C \\ &= -2x^{-2}-\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac32}+C \\ &= -\dfrac{2}{x^2}-\dfrac{2}{3}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)^3+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2}(2x+1)^3\,dx.$

items.sol:
The curves meet where the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-x^2 &= 2x \\ x^2-4x &= 0 \\ x(x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=4$.

When $x=4$, $y=2\times 4=8$.
$$\therefore\ B=(4,8)$$

Between $x=0$ and $x=4$ the parabola is above the line.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^4(6x-x^2-2x)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^4(-x^2+4x)\,dx \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2\right]_0^4 \\ &= -\dfrac{64}{3}+32 \\ &= \dfrac{32}{3} \\ &= 10\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $y=e^{2x}+e^{8x}$, prove that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}-10\dfrac{dy}{dx}+16y=0.$
items.sol:
Differentiate twice.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2e^{2x}+8e^{8x}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4e^{2x}+64e^{8x}$$
Substitute into the left-hand side.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= 4e^{2x}+64e^{8x}-10(2e^{2x}+8e^{8x})+16(e^{2x}+e^{8x}) \\ &= 4e^{2x}+64e^{8x}-20e^{2x}-80e^{8x}+16e^{2x}+16e^{8x} \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part: Find $f(x)$ given $f'(x)=\sec^2 2x$ and the curve passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right).$
items.sol:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\tan 2x+c$$
The curve passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} &= \dfrac12\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}+c \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+c \end{aligned}$$
So $c=0$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac12\tan 2x$$

items.part:
For the function $f(x)=2\cos x+1$
State the range
items.sol:
Since $-1\le\cos x\le 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} -2&\le 2\cos x\le 2 &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\\ -1&\le 2\cos x+1\le 3 &&(\text{add } 1)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the function $f(x)=2\cos x+1$
Show that the function $f(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$
items.sol:
The curve crosses the $x$-axis when $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2\cos x+1 \\ \cos x &= -\dfrac12 \\ x &= \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

items.part:
For the function $f(x)=2\cos x+1$
Calculate the exact area of the region bounded by the curve $f(x)=2\cos x+1$ and the $x$ and $y$ axes for $0\le x\le\dfrac{2}{3}\pi.$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}(2\cos x+1)\,dx \\ &= \left[2\sin x+x\right]_0^{\frac{2\pi}{3}} \\ &= \left(2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)-0 \\ &= 2\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \\ &= \sqrt3+\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
This equals $\dfrac{3\sqrt3+2\pi}{3}$ units$^2$.

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\cos^4 x\sin x\,dx.$
items.sol:
Differentiating $\cos^5 x$ with the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos^5 x)=-5\cos^4 x\sin x$$
so
$$\int -5\cos^4 x\sin x\,dx=\cos^5 x+c$$
Dividing by $-5$:
$$\therefore\ \int\cos^4 x\sin x\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{5}\cos^5 x+c$$

There are three function values, so two strips of width $h=\dfrac{1-0}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}$, with $x=0,\ \dfrac{1}{2},\ 1$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&0&\dfrac{1}{2}&1\\\hline f(x)&1&4&16\end{array}$$
Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{2}(1+4)+\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{2}(4+16)\\ &=1.25+5\\ &=6.25\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^1 2^{4x}\,dx\approx 6.25$$

The curve is concave up, so each chord lies above the curve.

Hence the trapezia have greater area than the area under the curve.

$$\therefore\ \text{over approximation}$$
items.final: Over approximation, since the curve is concave up so the chords lie above the curve and the trapezia have greater area.

items.part: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx=\dfrac{10}{3},\quad 0\le a<\pi,$ calculate the value of $a$.
items.sol:
Integrating:
$$\left[-\dfrac{5}{3}\cos 3x\right]_0^a=\dfrac{10}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{5}{3}(\cos 3a-\cos 0)&=\dfrac{10}{3}\\ \cos 3a-1&=-2\\ \cos 3a&=-1\end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le a<\pi$, we have $0\le 3a<3\pi$, so $3a=\pi$.
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=1+e^x.$

Show that $f(x)\times f(-x)=f(x)+f(-x).$
items.sol:
Left-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=(1+e^x)(1+e^{-x})\\ &=1+e^{-x}+e^x+e^0\\ &=2+e^x+e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
Right-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=(1+e^x)+(1+e^{-x})\\ &=2+e^x+e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)\times f(-x)=f(x)+f(-x)$$

items.part:
Explain why this integral is meaningless.

$\displaystyle\int_0^4\dfrac{1}{3-3^x}\,dx.$
items.sol:
The denominator is zero when $3-3^x=0$, that is at $x=1$.

This lies inside $0\le x\le 4$, so there is a vertical asymptote there and the function is not continuous on the interval.

$$\therefore\ \text{the integral is meaningless}$$
items.final: The denominator is zero at $x=1$ (inside the interval), so there is a vertical asymptote and the integral is meaningless.

items.part:
Find the area enclosed between the curve $y=\sqrt{x+1}$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=3$.

\exfigure{155_q12c_1}
items.sol:
Make $x$ the subject:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\sqrt{x+1}\\ y^2&=x+1\\ x&=y^2-1\end{aligned}$$
The region lies between the $y$-axis and the curve for $0\le y\le 3$. For $0\le y<1$ the curve is left of the $y$-axis ($x<0$), so that part is taken as an absolute value.
$$A=\int_1^3(y^2-1)\,dy+\left|\int_0^1(y^2-1)\,dy\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left[\dfrac{y^3}{3}-y\right]_1^3+\left|\left[\dfrac{y^3}{3}-y\right]_0^1\right|\\ &=\left(\dfrac{27}{3}-3\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right)+\left|\dfrac{1}{3}-1\right|\\ &=\dfrac{20}{3}+\dfrac{2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{22}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=7\dfrac{1}{3}\text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=\dfrac{e^x}{e^x+1}.$
Find any $x$ or $y$ intercepts.
items.sol:
For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$:
$$y=\dfrac{e^0}{e^0+1}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$:
$$\dfrac{e^x}{e^x+1}=0$$
But $e^x\ne 0$ for all $x$, so there is no solution.

$$\therefore\ y\text{-intercept }\dfrac{1}{2},\ \text{no }x\text{-intercept}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=\dfrac{e^x}{e^x+1}.$
Show that there are NO stationary points.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=e^x+1\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{(e^x+1)e^x-e^x\cdot e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{e^x(e^x+1-e^x)}{(e^x+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $y'=0$:
$$\dfrac{e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}=0$$
But $e^x\ne 0$ for all $x$, so there is no solution.

$$\therefore\ \text{there are no stationary points}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=\dfrac{e^x}{e^x+1}.$
Determine the behaviour of the curve as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty.$
items.sol:
As $x\to\infty$, $e^x$ becomes very large, so $y\to 1$ from below.

As $x\to-\infty$, $e^x\to 0$, so $y\to 0$ from above.
$$\therefore\ y\to 1^{-}\text{ as }x\to\infty,\quad y\to 0^{+}\text{ as }x\to-\infty$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=\dfrac{e^x}{e^x+1}.$

The shaded area is the trapezium less the area under the curve.

$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{2}{e}\text{ units}^2$$

items.part: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \dfrac{2x}{x^2+8}\,dx$.
items.sol:
The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so the primitive is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4\dfrac{2x}{x^2+8}\,dx&=\Big[\ln(x^2+8)\Big]_0^4\\ &=\ln 24-\ln 8\\ &=\ln 3\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}\right)\right)$. Give your answer in simplest form.

(Hint: Use your log laws to help with the differentiation).
items.sol:
Using the log laws, $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$, rewrite the expression.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big(\ln(\sin x)-\ln(1+\cos x)\Big)=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}-\dfrac{-\sin x}{1+\cos x}$$
Combine over a common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} &=\dfrac{\cos x(1+\cos x)+\sin^2x}{\sin x(1+\cos x)}\\ &=\dfrac{\cos x+\cos^2x+\sin^2x}{\sin x(1+\cos x)}\\ &=\dfrac{1+\cos x}{\sin x(1+\cos x)}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\ &=\operatorname{cosec}x\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A surveyor who is $y$ metres due south of a tower sees the top of it with an angle of elevation $8^\circ$.

A second surveyor is $x$ metres due east of the tower.

From her position the angle of elevation is $10^\circ$ to the top of the tower.

The two surveyors are 940 m apart.

\exfigure{156_q11g_1}
Show that $y = \dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}$.
items.sol:
In the right-angled triangle formed by the tower (height $h$), the base and the surveyor, the angle of elevation is $8^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 8^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{y}\\ y&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A surveyor who is $y$ metres due south of a tower sees the top of it with an angle of elevation $8^\circ$.

A second surveyor is $x$ metres due east of the tower.

From her position the angle of elevation is $10^\circ$ to the top of the tower.

The two surveyors are 940 m apart.

\exfigure{156_q11g_1}
Find the height ($h$) of the tower to the nearest metre.
items.sol:
Similarly, for the second surveyor, $x=\dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ}$.

The surveyors and the base of the tower form a right-angled triangle (right angle at the base), so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$x^2+y^2=940^2$$
Substitute.
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ}\right)^2&=940^2\\ h^2\left(\cot^28^\circ+\cot^210^\circ\right)&=940^2\\ h&=\sqrt{\dfrac{940^2}{\cot^28^\circ+\cot^210^\circ}}\\ &\approx 103.3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The height of the tower is $103$ m, to the nearest metre.

items.part: If $\displaystyle\int_0^3 f(x)\,dx = 8$, find $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{-1} 2f(x+4)\,dx$.
items.sol:
The graph of $y=f(x+4)$ is the graph of $y=f(x)$ translated $4$ units to the left, so the area is unchanged.
$$\int_{-4}^{-1}f(x+4)\,dx=\int_0^3f(x)\,dx=8$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-4}^{-1}2f(x+4)\,dx&=2\int_{-4}^{-1}f(x+4)\,dx\\ &=2\times 8\\ &=16\end{aligned}$$

If one of the 30 people was randomly selected, find the probability. that they like soccer only. Give your answer in simplest form.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(\text{soccer only})&=\dfrac{5}{30}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
From a group of 15 hockey players at a game of hockey, 13 played on the field, 7 sat on the bench and 5 both played and sat on the bench. A hockey player is chosen at random from the team.

Let $A$ be the event ‘the person played on the field’ and let $B$ be the event ‘the person sat on the bench’.

Find $P(A \mid B)$.
items.sol:
Here $A\cap B$ is the event 'played and sat on the bench'.
$$P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{5}{15},\qquad P(B)=\dfrac{7}{15}$$
Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\mid B)&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{5}{15}}{\frac{7}{15}}\\ &=\dfrac{5}{7}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Twenty students sit a Geography test and the mean of their scores is 78. Two students sit the test late and their scores are 96 and 82.

What is the new mean for the Geography test?
items.sol:
The new total of scores is $20\times 78+96+82$, shared among $22$ students.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{New mean}&=\dfrac{20\times 78+96+82}{22}\\ &=79\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Describe the three transformation which, when applied in succession, change the graph of $y = \sqrt{x}$ to the graph with the equation $y = 4\sqrt{x-1} + 3$.
items.sol:
Starting from $y=\sqrt{x}$:

Dilate vertically by a factor of $4$, giving $y=4\sqrt{x}$.

Shift right by $1$ unit, giving $y=4\sqrt{x-1}$.

Shift up by $3$ units, giving $y=4\sqrt{x-1}+3$.
items.final: Dilate vertically by factor 4, shift right 1 unit, shift up 3 units

items.part:
A function is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{2x-1}{3x+2}$.

Find the gradient of the normal at the point where $x = -1$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x-1 & v&=3x+2\\ u'&=2 & v'&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{2(3x+2)-3(2x-1)}{(3x+2)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{(3x+2)^2}\end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent at $x=-1$ is
$$f'(-1)=\dfrac{7}{(3\times(-1)+2)^2}=7$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent.
$$m_{\text{normal}}=-\dfrac{1}{7}$$
The gradient of the normal at $(-1,3)$ is $-\dfrac{1}{7}$.

items.part:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution.

\extable{156_q13b_t1}

Given that $E(X) = 0.8$, then
Find the values of $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
The probabilities sum to 1, and $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0\times a+1\times b+2\times0.3 \\ 0.8&=b+0.6 \\ b&=0.2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} a+b+0.3&=1 \\ a+0.2+0.3&=1 \\ a&=0.5 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ a=0.5,\ b=0.2$$

items.part:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution.

\extable{156_q13b_t1}

Given that $E(X) = 0.8$, then
Calculate the $\text{Var}(X)$ correct to 2 decimal places. Show all working.
items.sol:
Using $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\big[E(X)\big]^2$, first find $E(X^2)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2)&=0^2\times0.5+1^2\times0.2+2^2\times0.3 \\ &=1.4 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X)&=1.4-0.8^2 \\ &=0.76 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Whilst performing some experiments, biomechanics students have found that the rate of change of the distance (in cm/s) travelled by a ball is given by $A(t) = 4\ln(1+10t)$, where $t$ is the number of seconds elapsed since the start of the experiment.

Let $D$ cm be the distance travelled by the particle from $t = 1$ to $t = 5$.
Estimate $D$ by using the trapezoidal rule with 4 sub-intervals.

Give your answer current to the nearest centimetre.
items.sol:
The distance is the integral of the rate, so $D=\displaystyle\int_1^5A(t)\,dt$.

With 4 sub-intervals, $h=\dfrac{5-1}{4}=1$, so the function values are needed at $t=1,2,3,4,5$.

$$D\approx\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[4\ln11+4\ln51+2\big(4\ln21+4\ln31+4\ln41\big)\Big]$$

$$D\approx53.4277685$$

$$\therefore\ D\approx53 \text{ cm}$$

items.part:
Whilst performing some experiments, biomechanics students have found that the rate of change of the distance (in cm/s) travelled by a ball is given by $A(t) = 4\ln(1+10t)$, where $t$ is the number of seconds elapsed since the start of the experiment.

Let $D$ cm be the distance travelled by the particle from $t = 1$ to $t = 5$.
Is $D$ an over-estimate or an under-estimate? Justify your answer using calculus to describe the concavity of the graph and compare to your answer in (a).
items.sol:
Concavity is decided by the sign of $A''(t)$.

$$A'(t)=\dfrac{40}{1+10t}$$

$$A''(t)=-\dfrac{400}{(1+10t)^2}$$

Since $(1+10t)^2>0$, $A''(t)<0$ for $t\ge0$.

So the graph is concave down, the trapezia lie under the curve, and the estimate in (a) is an under-estimate of $D$.

$$\therefore\ D \text{ is an under-estimate}$$

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x) = 4x^2 - x^4$.
By solving $f(x) = 0$ show that $x$-intercepts are $-2$, 0 and 2.
items.sol:
Solve $f(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 4x^2-x^4&=0 \\ x^2(4-x^2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x^2=0$ or $4-x^2=0$.

$$\therefore\ x=0 \text{ or } x=\pm2$$

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x) = 4x^2 - x^4$.
Prove that $f(x)$ is an even function.
items.sol:
A function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=4(-x)^2-(-x)^4 \\ &=4x^2-x^4 \\ &=f(x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is an even function}$$

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x) = 4x^2 - x^4$.
Show that $f'\left(\sqrt{2}\right) = 0$.
items.sol:
Differentiate term by term.

$$f'(x)=8x-4x^3$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'\left(\sqrt2\right)&=8\sqrt2-4\left(\sqrt2\right)^3 \\ &=8\sqrt2-4\times2\sqrt2 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x) = 4x^2 - x^4$.
Given that $\left(\sqrt{2},4\right)$ is a maximum turning point, explain in words why $\left(-\sqrt{2},4\right)$ is also a maximum turning point.
items.sol:
Since $f$ is even, its graph is a reflection of itself in the $y$-axis.

So every stationary point on the right of the $y$-axis has a matching stationary point of the same type on the left.

$$\therefore\ \left(-\sqrt2,4\right) \text{ is also a maximum turning point}$$

items.part:
A city is suffering through a drought and adopts a plan to import water from another city.

It is given that the volume of water imported in the $1^{\text{st}}$ year since the start of the plan is $1.8\times10^{9}\ \text{m}^3$. In subsequent years, the volume of water imported each year is 90% of the volume of water imported in the previous year
Find how much water was imported in the $4^{\text{th}}$ year.

Give your answer correct 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
The yearly volumes form a geometric sequence with $a=1.8\times10^9$, $r=0.9$ and $n=4$.

$$\begin{aligned} T_4&=ar^{n-1} \\ &=1.8\times10^9\times0.9^{3} \\ &\approx1.3\times10^9 \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A city is suffering through a drought and adopts a plan to import water from another city.

It is given that the volume of water imported in the $1^{\text{st}}$ year since the start of the plan is $1.8\times10^{9}\ \text{m}^3$. In subsequent years, the volume of water imported each year is 90% of the volume of water imported in the previous year
Find the total volume of water imported in the first 10 years.

Give your answer correct 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
The total is the sum of the first 10 terms of the geometric sequence, $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$, with $a=1.8\times10^9$, $r=0.9$, $n=10$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{10}&=\dfrac{1.8\times10^9\left(0.9^{10}-1\right)}{0.9-1} \\ &=1.172378808\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ S_{10}\approx1.2\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
A city is suffering through a drought and adopts a plan to import water from another city.

It is given that the volume of water imported in the $1^{\text{st}}$ year since the start of the plan is $1.8\times10^{9}\ \text{m}^3$. In subsequent years, the volume of water imported each year is 90% of the volume of water imported in the previous year
Explain why the total volume of water imported since the start of the plan will never exceed $1.9\times10^{10}\ \text{m}^3$.
items.sol:
Since $|r|=0.9<1$, the series has a limiting sum.

$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{1.8\times10^9}{1-0.9} \\ &=1.8\times10^{10} \end{aligned}$$

The total can never exceed $1.8\times10^{10}$, and $1.8\times10^{10}<1.9\times10^{10}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the total never exceeds } 1.9\times10^{10} \text{ m}^3$$

items.part: Solve $e^{2\ln x} = 4x + 21$
items.sol:
Use $e^{2\ln x}=e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$, valid for $x>0$.

$$\begin{aligned} x^2&=4x+21 \\ x^2-4x-21&=0 \\ (x-7)(x+3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=7$ or $x=-3$.

The original equation needs $x>0$ for $\ln x$, so $x=-3$ is rejected.

$$\therefore\ x=7$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 3\sin x\,dx$.
items.sol:
The function $y=3\sin x$ is odd, and the limits are symmetric about $0$.

$$\therefore\ \displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}3\sin x\,dx=0$$

items.part:
The displacement of an object measured in metres after $t$ seconds is given by $x = e^{t^2} - 2t^2$.
Given that the velocity is the rate of change of the displacement, find an expression for the velocity.
items.sol:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement.

$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(e^{t^2}-2t^2\right)$$

$$v=2te^{t^2}-4t$$

items.part:
The displacement of an object measured in metres after $t$ seconds is given by $x = e^{t^2} - 2t^2$.
Find the two times when the object is stationary.
items.sol:
The object is stationary when $v=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2te^{t^2}-4t&=0 \\ 2t\left(e^{t^2}-2\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $t=0$ or $e^{t^2}=2$.

$$\begin{aligned} e^{t^2}&=2 \\ t^2&=\ln2 \\ t&=\pm\sqrt{\ln2} \end{aligned}$$

Time cannot be negative, so $t\ge0$ and $t=-\sqrt{\ln2}$ is rejected.

$$\therefore\ t=0 \text{ s or } t=\sqrt{\ln2} \text{ s}$$

items.part:
The displacement of an object measured in metres after $t$ seconds is given by $x = e^{t^2} - 2t^2$.
Find an expression for the acceleration of the object.
items.sol:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Differentiate $2te^{t^2}$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uw)=u'w+uw'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=2t & w&=e^{t^2} \\ u'&=2 & w'&=2te^{t^2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} a&=2e^{t^2}+2t\times2te^{t^2}-4 \\ &=2e^{t^2}+4t^2e^{t^2}-4 \end{aligned}$$

The mean level is $15$, the low is $12$ and the high is $18$.

The amplitude is $3$. The curve is at its minimum when $t=0$ (7 am), so $A=-3$.

Low tide is at 7 am and high tide at 1 pm, so half a period is $6$ hours and the period is $12$.

$$b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

$$\therefore\ A=-3,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

The ship needs $h\ge13.5$. First solve $h=13.5$.

$$\begin{aligned} 13.5&=-3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+15 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)&=\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$

In one 12-hour cycle, $\dfrac{\pi t}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, so $t=2$ or $t=10$.

Between these times $\dfrac{\pi t}{6}$ lies between $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, so the cosine is below $\dfrac12$ and $h>13.5$ (check: at $t=6$, $h=18$), so the ship can sail for $2\le t\le10$.

With $t$ measured from 7 am, $t=2$ is 9 am and $t=10$ is 5 pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{the ship can sail between 9 am and 5 pm}$$

(The next window opens at 9 pm, $t=14$, as the cycle repeats.)
items.final: the ship can sail between 9 am and 5 pm

items.part:
The population of an ant colony is modelled by the equation $P = 1000e^{kt}$, where $t$ is measured in weeks.
Find the initial population.
items.sol:
The initial population is at $t=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} P&=1000e^{0} \\ &=1000 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of an ant colony is modelled by the equation $P = 1000e^{kt}$, where $t$ is measured in weeks.
After 10 weeks the population is 25 000.

Show that $k = 0.3219$, correct to 4 decimal places.

The population of an ant colony is modelled by the equation $P = 1000e^{kt}$, where $t$ is measured in weeks.
During which week will the population exceed 80 000 for the first time?
items.sol:
Solve $P=80000$ using $k=0.3219$.

$$\begin{aligned} 80000&=1000e^{0.3219t} \\ 80&=e^{0.3219t} \\ 0.3219t&=\ln80 \\ t&=\dfrac{\ln80}{0.3219} \\ &\approx13.613 \end{aligned}$$

The population passes 80 000 after 13.613 weeks, which is during the 14th week.

$$\therefore\ \text{14th week}$$

items.part:
An artist posted a song online. Each day there were $2^n + 3n$ downloads, where $n$ is the number of days after the song was posted.
Find the number of downloads on the third day after the song was posted.
items.sol:
Substitute $n=3$.

$$\begin{aligned} T_3&=2^3+3(3) \\ &=17 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ 17 \text{ downloads}$$

items.part:
An artist posted a song online. Each day there were $2^n + 3n$ downloads, where $n$ is the number of days after the song was posted.
What is the total number of times the song was downloaded in the first 20 days after it was posted?
items.sol:
The total is the sum of two parts: a geometric series from $2^n$ and an arithmetic series from $3n$.

Geometric part: $a=2$, $r=2$, $n=20$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{20}&=\dfrac{2\left(2^{20}-1\right)}{2-1} \\ &=2\,097\,150 \end{aligned}$$

Arithmetic part: $a=3$, $d=3$, $n=20$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{20}&=\dfrac{20}{2}\big(2\times3+(20-1)\times3\big) \\ &=630 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total}&=2\,097\,150+630 \\ &=2\,097\,780 \text{ downloads} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An enclosure in the shape of a right-angled triangle is to be made using 18 m of fencing, with an existing wall serving as one side of the triangle, where no fencing is required.

The area of the enclosure is $A$ square metres where the side of the triangle perpendicular to the wall is $x$ m in length.

\exfigure{156_q16b_1}
Show that the area is given by $A = 3x\sqrt{9-x}$.
items.sol:
The fencing covers the side $x$ and the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is $18-x$ m.

In the right-angled triangle, the side along the wall $h$ satisfies Pythagoras' theorem.

$$\begin{aligned} h&=\sqrt{(18-x)^2-x^2} \\ &=\sqrt{324-36x} \\ &=\sqrt{36(9-x)} \\ &=6\sqrt{9-x} \end{aligned}$$

The area is half base times height.

$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac12\times x\times6\sqrt{9-x} \\ &=3x\sqrt{9-x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An enclosure in the shape of a right-angled triangle is to be made using 18 m of fencing, with an existing wall serving as one side of the triangle, where no fencing is required.

The area of the enclosure is $A$ square metres where the side of the triangle perpendicular to the wall is $x$ m in length.

\exfigure{156_q16b_1}
Find the value of $x$ that will maximise the area, showing why this is the maximum.
items.sol:
Write $A=3x(9-x)^{\frac12}$ and use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x & v&=(9-x)^{\frac12} \\ u'&=3 & v'&=-\dfrac12(9-x)^{-\frac12} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx}&=3(9-x)^{\frac12}-\dfrac{3x}{2}(9-x)^{-\frac12} \\ &=\dfrac{6(9-x)-3x}{2\sqrt{9-x}} \\ &=\dfrac{54-9x}{2\sqrt{9-x}} \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 54-9x&=0 \\ x&=6 \end{aligned}$$

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side of $x=6$; the denominator is positive for $x<9$, so the numerator $54-9x$ decides the sign.

\extable{Ts5767_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $x=6$ gives a maximum.

Alternatively, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{-9(12-x)}{4(9-x)^{\frac32}}$, and at $x=6$ this is approximately $-2.598<0$, so a maximum.

$$\therefore\ x=6 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
A block of ice in the form of a cube melts in such a way that the block remains cubic. After a time $t$ hours the volume of the block is $V\ \text{m}^3$. Initially the cube has edge length of 4 metres and after 9 hours the cube has edge length of 1 metre.
If the rate of change of volume, $R\ \text{m}^3$ per hour, is given by $R = -k$ for some constant $k > 0$, show that $V = 64 - 7t$.
items.sol:
The rate of change of volume is constant.

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-k$$

Integrating gives

$$V=-kt+c$$

Initially the edge is $4$ m, so when $t=0$, $V=4^3=64$.

$$V=64-kt$$

After 9 hours the edge is $1$ m, so $V=1$ when $t=9$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1&=64-9k \\ 9k&=63 \\ k&=7 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ V=64-7t$$

items.part:
A block of ice in the form of a cube melts in such a way that the block remains cubic. After a time $t$ hours the volume of the block is $V\ \text{m}^3$. Initially the cube has edge length of 4 metres and after 9 hours the cube has edge length of 1 metre.
Find when the cube has edge length 2 metres.
items.sol:
An edge length of 2 m gives volume $2^3=8 \text{ m}^3$.

$$\begin{aligned} 8&=64-7t \\ 7t&=56 \\ t&=8 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the edge length is 2 m after 8 hours}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $x^2-6=x$
items.sol:
Rearranging to zero and factorising:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-x-6&=0 \\ (x-3)(x+2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3 \text{ or } x=-2$$

items.part: In the space below, sketch the graph of $y=x^2-6$ and $y=x$. Label the coordinates of any point of intersection and any $x$ or $y$ intercepts of the graph.
items.sol: \exfigure{563_q7_s1}

items.part: Find the values of $x$, for which $x^2-6>x$.
items.sol:
The parabola is above the line outside the intersection points $x=-2$ and $x=3$.
$$\therefore\ x<-2 \text{ or } x>3$$

The graph of $f(x)=|x|$ is translated right 3 units, reflected in the $x$-axis, multiplied vertically by 2, and translated up 2 units.

Hence
$$\begin{aligned} k&=-2 \\ b&=-3 \\ c&=2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch $y=3\cos x-2$ and $y=\dfrac{x}{4}-1$ in the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
items.sol: \exfigure{563_q9_s1}

items.part:
Hence or otherwise, how many solutions are there to the equation

$$3\cos x-2=\dfrac{x}{4}-1\,?$$
items.sol:
From the graphs in part (a), the curves intersect twice.
$$\therefore\ 2 \text{ solutions}$$

items.part: Express $0.4\dot{6}$ as infinite series and hence express as simplest fraction.
items.sol:
Write the decimal as a sum:
$$0.4666\dots=0.4+0.06+0.006+\cdots$$
The terms after $0.4$ form a geometric series with $a=\dfrac{6}{100}$ and $r=\dfrac{1}{10}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.4666\dots&=\dfrac{4}{10}+\dfrac{\frac{6}{100}}{1-\frac{1}{10}} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{10}+\dfrac{\frac{6}{100}}{\frac{9}{10}} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{10}+\dfrac{2}{30} \\ &=\dfrac{14}{30} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{15} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0.4\dot{6}=\dfrac{7}{15}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}$
Write down the domain.
items.sol:
The denominator cannot be zero, so $x^2-4\ne0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{domain: all real } x,\ x\neq\pm2$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}$
Find the vertical and horizontal asymptotes
items.sol:
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero: $x=\pm2$.

For the horizontal asymptote:
$$\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}=0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{vertical asymptotes } x=\pm2,\ \text{horizontal asymptote } y=0$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}$
Hence sketch the graph of $y=\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}$, showing all intercepts and asymptotes.
items.sol: \exfigure{563_q11_s1}

items.part: In a geometric progression $S_4=30$, while the sum to infinity is 32. Find the first three terms.
items.sol:
For a geometric series, $S_4=\dfrac{a(1-r^4)}{1-r}=30$ and $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=32$.

From the second, $a=32(1-r)$. Substituting into the first:
$$\begin{aligned} 30&=\dfrac{32(1-r)(1-r^4)}{1-r} \\ 1-r^4&=\dfrac{30}{32} \\ r^4&=1-\dfrac{30}{32} \\ r^4&=\dfrac{1}{16} \end{aligned}$$
So $r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}$, and both satisfy $|r|<1$.

For $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$32=\dfrac{a}{1-\frac{1}{2}}$$
so $a=16$, and the terms are $16, 8, 4,\dots$

For $r=-\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$32=\dfrac{a}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=\dfrac{2a}{3}$$
so $a=48$, and the terms are $48, -24, 12,\dots$
$$\therefore\ 16, 8, 4 \text{ or } 48, -24, 12$$

items.part:
Given the sketch of the function $y=f(x)$, sketch the graph of $y=3f(x+3)$, clearly indicating the new coordinates for $A,B,C,D$ and $E$ on the graph.

\exfigure{563_q13_1}

For a given arithmetic sequence, the ratio of the sum of the first $m$ terms to the sum of first $n$ terms is $m^2:n^2$, where $m\neq n$.

Prove that the ratio of the $m^{th}$ term to the $n^{th}$ term is $(2m-1):(2n-1)$.
items.sol:
The ratio of the sums of the first $m$ and $n$ terms, using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$, is
$$\dfrac{\frac{m}{2}\left(2a+(m-1)d\right)}{\frac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)}=\dfrac{m^2}{n^2}$$
Cancelling $\dfrac{m}{n}$ on both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2a+(m-1)d}{2a+(n-1)d}&=\dfrac{m}{n} \\ 2an+mnd-nd&=2am+mnd-md \\ 2an-2am&=nd-md \\ 2a(n-m)&=d(n-m) \end{aligned}$$
Since $m\ne n$, we may divide by $n-m$:
$$d=2a \qquad (1)$$
The ratio of the $m^{th}$ to the $n^{th}$ term is, using (1),
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a+(m-1)d}{a+(n-1)d}&=\dfrac{a+(m-1)2a}{a+(n-1)2a} \\ &=\dfrac{1+2(m-1)}{1+2(n-1)} \\ &=\dfrac{1+2m-2}{1+2n-2} \\ &=\dfrac{2m-1}{2n-1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_m:T_n=(2m-1):(2n-1)$$

items.part: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\,dx$ in exact form.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\,dx &= \Big[-2e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\Big]_0^1 \\ &= -2\left(e^{-\frac{1}{2}}-1\right) \\ &= 2-2e^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{15}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 15\cos(4x)\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_{\frac{\pi}{15}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 15\cos 4x\,dx &= \dfrac{15}{4}\Big[\sin 4x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{15}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{15}{4}\left(\sin 2\pi-\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{15}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{15}{4}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{15} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The function $f(x)$ is defined by the rule $f(x) = x^2(6-x)$ in the domain $-1 \le x \le 6$.
Find the stationary points of $f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= 6x^2-x^3 \\ f'(x) &= 12x-3x^2 \\ &= 3x(4-x) \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=0$ or $x=4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=4$, $y=4^2(6-4)=32$.

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(4,32)$.

To find their nature, use the second derivative.
$$f''(x)=12-6x$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=12>0 &&\text{so }(0,0)\text{ is a minimum}\\ f''(4)&=-12<0 &&\text{so }(4,32)\text{ is a maximum}\end{aligned}$$
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a minimum and $(4,32)$ is a maximum

items.part:
The function $f(x)$ is defined by the rule $f(x) = x^2(6-x)$ in the domain $-1 \le x \le 6$.
Sketch the graph of $y = f(x)$. Showing all intercepts and stationary points.
items.sol:
The endpoint at $x=-1$ is $f(-1)=(-1)^2(7)=7$.

\exfigure{569_q11_s1}

items.part:
The function $f(x)$ is defined by the rule $f(x) = x^2(6-x)$ in the domain $-1 \le x \le 6$.
State the range of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
On the domain $-1\le x\le 6$, the endpoint values are $f(-1)=7$ and $f(6)=0$.

The minimum value is $f(0)=0$ and the maximum value is $f(4)=32$.
$$0\le y\le 32$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{(3x-1)^2}$.
items.sol:
Rewrite the integrand as a power and integrate.
$$\begin{aligned} \int(3x-1)^{-2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{(3x-1)^{-1}}{-1}+C \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{3(3x-1)}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{3x}{x^2+1}\,dx$.
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $x^2+1$, which is $2x$, so
$$\int\dfrac{3x}{x^2+1}\,dx=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln(x^2+1)+C$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^3-x^2+1}{x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Divide each term by $x^2$, then integrate.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x^3-x^2+1}{x^2}\,dx &= \int\left(x-1+x^{-2}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{x^2}{2}-x-\dfrac{1}{x}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int_3^5 \dfrac{e^x}{e^x-7}\,dx$. State your answer as an exact value in simplest form.
items.sol:
The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so the integral is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_3^5\dfrac{e^x}{e^x-7}\,dx &= \Big[\ln\left(e^x-7\right)\Big]_3^5 \\ &= \ln\left(e^5-7\right)-\ln\left(e^3-7\right) \\ &= \ln\dfrac{e^5-7}{e^3-7} \end{aligned}$$
This is approximately $2.38$.

items.part: Differentiate $y = \ln\dfrac{x\left(x^2-1\right)}{x+1}$.
items.sol:
Factorise the numerator, $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$, and cancel $x+1$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \ln\dfrac{x(x-1)(x+1)}{x+1} \\ &= \ln\left[x(x-1)\right] \\ &= \ln x+\ln(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{x-1} \\ &= \dfrac{2x-1}{x(x-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{2x-1}{x^2-x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = x\cos x$ at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos x-x\sin x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{3-\sqrt3\pi}{6} \\ &\approx -0.407 \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is
$$y-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{3-\sqrt3\pi}{6}\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

items.part:
Use two applications of the trapezoidal rule to find an approximation to $\displaystyle\int_2^4 \ln x\,dx$.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
Two applications means $n=2$ strips, so
$$h=\dfrac{4-2}{2}=1$$
The function values at $x=2,3,4$ are
$$f(2)=\ln 2\approx 0.693,\quad f(3)=\ln 3\approx 1.097,\quad f(4)=\ln 4\approx 1.386$$
Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_2^4 \ln x\,dx &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left[f(2)+2f(3)+f(4)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[0.693+2(1.097)+1.386\right] \\ &\approx 2.14 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{x}$. Show all working.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{x} &= 4\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{4x} \\ &= 4\times 1 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove that $\tan\theta(\sec\theta-\sin\theta\tan\theta)=\sin\theta$.
items.sol:
Writing in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\left[\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}-\dfrac{\sin\theta\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \sin\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence: Solve $2\tan\theta(\sec\theta-\sin\theta\tan\theta)=1$ for $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
By part (a), the equation becomes
$$2\sin\theta=1$$
so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

In $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$, sine is positive in the first and second quadrants.
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{\cos x}{2+\sin x}\,dx$. State your answer as an exact value in simplest form.
items.sol:
The numerator is the derivative of $2+\sin x$, so the integral is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \dfrac{\cos x}{2+\sin x}\,dx &= \Big[\ln(2+\sin x)\Big]_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \ln\left(2+\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\ln\left(2+\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) \\ &= \ln 3-\ln 1 \\ &= \ln 3 \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{569_q17_s1}

Since $f'(x)=0$ at $x=-1,5,10$, these are the stationary points of $f$.

The sign of $f'$ decides the nature:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-1 &&\text{minimum}\\ x&=5 &&\text{maximum}\\ x&=10 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{569_q17_s2}

$f'(x)$ is a cubic with zeros at $x=-1,5,10$: $f'(x)=k(x+1)(x-5)(x-10)$ with $k>0$. Its turning points are where $f''(x)=0$:

$f''$ is a concave-up parabola:

The other intersections lie on the $x$-axis, so they are the zeros of $g(x)$.

items.sol:
Make $x$ the subject by taking exponentials of both sides.

So $2x=e^y+5$.

items.part:

items.part: Write the derivative of $\log_e(\tan x)$, where $\tan x > 0$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with $u=\tan x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e(\tan x) &= \dfrac{1}{\tan x}\times\sec^2 x \\ &= \text{cosec}\,x\sec x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence find $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \text{cosec}\,x\,\sec x\,dx$.

Leave your answer as an exact value in simplest form.
items.sol:
By part (a), an antiderivative of $\text{cosec}\,x\sec x$ is $\log_e(\tan x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \text{cosec}\,x\sec x\,dx &= \Big[\log_e(\tan x)\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \log_e\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\log_e\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= \log_e\sqrt3-\log_e 1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\log_e 3 \end{aligned}$$

A cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ is inscribed in the cone as sown below.

\exfigure{569_q22_1}
Show that $h = 18-2r$.
items.sol:
In the cross-section, $AB=18$ is the height of the cone, so $AD=18-h$.

In $\triangle ADE$ and $\triangle ABC$: $\angle ADE=\angle ABC=90^\circ$ and $\angle AED=\angle ACB$ (corresponding angles, $DE\parallel BC$).

Hence $\triangle ADE$ is similar to $\triangle ABC$, and corresponding sides are in proportion:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{AD}{AB} &= \dfrac{DE}{BC} \\ \dfrac{18-h}{18} &= \dfrac{r}{9} \\ 18-h &= 2r \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=18-2r$$

items.part:
The radius of the base of a cone is 9 cm and its height is 18 cm.

A cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ is inscribed in the cone as sown below.

\exfigure{569_q22_1}
Show that the volumes of the cylinder of maximum volume and the cone, are in the ratio 4:9.
items.sol:
The volume of the cylinder, using $h=18-2r$:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \pi r^2h \\ &= \pi r^2(18-2r) \\ &= 18\pi r^2-2\pi r^3 \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} V' &= 36\pi r-6\pi r^2 \\ &= 6\pi r(6-r) \end{aligned}$$
$V'=0$ gives $r=0$ or $r=6$. Since $r\ne 0$, $r=6$, and this is a maximum.

Then $h=18-2(6)=6$, so
$$V_{\text{cyl}}=\pi(6)^2(6)=216\pi$$
$$V_{\text{cone}}=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(81)(18)=486\pi$$
$$\therefore\ V_{\text{cyl}}:V_{\text{cone}}=216:486=4:9$$

Annabelle takes 2 cans, without replacement, from a refrigerator that contains 8 cans of Pepsi, 4 cans of Coke and 3 cans of Sprite. Find the probability that Annabelle gets:
2 of the same drink
items.sol:
Add the probabilities of two Pepsi, two Coke and two Sprite (15 cans in total, no replacement).
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{8}{15}\times\dfrac{7}{14} + \dfrac{4}{15}\times\dfrac{3}{14} + \dfrac{3}{15}\times\dfrac{2}{14} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{105} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Annabelle takes 2 cans, without replacement, from a refrigerator that contains 8 cans of Pepsi, 4 cans of Coke and 3 cans of Sprite. Find the probability that Annabelle gets:
At least one Pepsi
items.sol:
Use the complement: at least one Pepsi is the opposite of no Pepsi (7 of the 15 cans are not Pepsi).
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1 - P(\text{no Pepsi}) \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{6}{14} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $|7x-12|\ge 16$
items.sol:
For $|A| \ge k$, either $A \ge k$ or $A \le -k$.

Case 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 7x - 12 &\ge 16 \\ 7x &\ge 28 \\ x &\ge 4 \end{aligned}$$
Case 2:
$$\begin{aligned} 7x - 12 &\le -16 \\ 7x &\le -4 \\ x &\le -\dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \le -\dfrac{4}{7} \text{ or } x \ge 4$$

Jure owns a building supply company. They sell packets of screws which claim to have 75 screws per packet. To avoid customer complaints, the mean amount of screws in a packet is 79 and the variance is 4.
What is the probability that a packet of screws selected randomly will have less than 75 screws in it?

The standard deviation is $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
$$z = \dfrac{75 - 79}{2} = -2$$
By the 68-95-99.7 rule, 95% lie within 2 standard deviations, so 2.5% lie below $z=-2$.
$$\therefore\ P = 2.5\%$$

Convert degrees to radians: $x^{\circ} = \dfrac{\pi x}{180}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \cos x^{\circ}\,dx &= \int \cos\dfrac{\pi x}{180}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{180}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{180} + C \\ &= \dfrac{180}{\pi}\sin x^{\circ} + C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{x}{2x^2+1}\,dx$
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $2x^2+1$, which is $4x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 \dfrac{x}{2x^2+1}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{4}\int_1^2 \dfrac{4x}{2x^2+1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\Big[\ln(2x^2+1)\Big]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\ln 9 - \ln 3\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\ln 3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and leave each answer as a single simplified fraction:

$y=(3x-4)\sqrt{5-2x}$
items.sol:
Write $y = (3x-4)(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 3x - 4 & v &= (5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ u' &= 3 & v' &= -(5-2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}} - \dfrac{3x-4}{(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\ &= \dfrac{3(5-2x) - (3x-4)}{\sqrt{5-2x}} \\ &= \dfrac{19 - 9x}{\sqrt{5-2x}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and leave each answer as a single simplified fraction:

$y=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= \sin x & v &= 1 + \cos x \\ u' &= \cos x & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{(1+\cos x)\cos x - \sin x(-\sin x)}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x + \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x + 1}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1+\cos x} \end{aligned}$$

Compare $z$-scores, $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Science: } z &= \dfrac{86 - 73}{8} = 1.625 \\ \text{English: } z &= \dfrac{83 - 74}{5.5} \approx 1.636 \end{aligned}$$
The English $z$-score is higher.

$\therefore$ Luke performed better in English.
items.final: Luke performed better in English (z ≈ 1.636 vs 1.625)

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int_2^3 e^{5-2x}\,dx$, expressing your answer as a single simplified fraction
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_2^3 e^{5-2x}\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{5-2x}\right]_2^3 \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(e^{-1} - e\right) \\ &= \dfrac{e}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2e} \\ &= \dfrac{e^2 - 1}{2e} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jasmine's salary in her job increases by the same amount every year. In the $4^{\text{th}}$ year at her job she earned \$81 000. In the $9^{\text{th}}$ year of her job she earned \$98 500.
Find how much Jasmine earned in the first year of her job and by how much her pay increases each year.
items.sol:
The salary forms an arithmetic sequence with first term $a$ and common difference $d$, so $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} a + 3d &= 81\,000 \\ a + 8d &= 98\,500 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting:
$$\begin{aligned} 5d &= 17\,500 \\ d &= 3500 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} a + 10\,500 &= 81\,000 \\ a &= 70\,500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{first year pay is } \$70\,500 \text{, with an annual increase of } \$3500$$
items.final: First year pay is $\$70\,500$, with an annual increase of $\$3500$

items.part:
Jasmine's salary in her job increases by the same amount every year. In the $4^{\text{th}}$ year at her job she earned \$81 000. In the $9^{\text{th}}$ year of her job she earned \$98 500.
How much will Jasmine have earned in total after working at her job for 15 years?
items.sol:
Use the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$, with $n = 15$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left(2\times 70\,500 + 14\times 3500\right) \\ &= \$1\,425\,000 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jasmine's salary in her job increases by the same amount every year. In the $4^{\text{th}}$ year at her job she earned \$81 000. In the $9^{\text{th}}$ year of her job she earned \$98 500.
Bree started a job at the same time, and with the same starting salary as Jasmine. Bree's salary, however, increased by 2% per annum. With the use of logarithms, show in which year will her income first be greater than \$100 000?
items.sol:
Bree's salary is a geometric sequence with $a = 70\,500$ and $r = 1.02$, so $T_n = 70\,500(1.02)^{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 70\,500(1.02)^{n-1} &> 100\,000 \\ 1.02^{n-1} &> \dfrac{200}{141} \end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms of both sides (the base $1.02>1$, so the inequality is unchanged):
$$\begin{aligned} n - 1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{200}{141}\right)}{\log 1.02} \\ n - 1 &> 17.65\ldots \\ n &> 18.65\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ she first earns more than $\$100\,000$ in her 19th year at the job.
items.final: She first earns more than $\$100\,000$ in her 19th year

items.part: A school has two History classes that sit an exam. Andy's class has 16 students and has a mean mark of 65%, whilst Juliana's class has 24 students. The combined mean for the 2 classes is 68.6%. Find the mean for the Juliana's class.
items.sol:
The combined total of marks equals the sum of the class totals. Let $x$ be the mean of Juliana's class.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{16\times 65 + 24x}{40} &= 68.6 \\ 1040 + 24x &= 2744 \\ 24x &= 1704 \\ x &= 71 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the mean of Juliana's class is } 71\%$$

items.sol:
The dog covers a full circle of radius 20 m, less the minor segment cut off by the fence 10 m from the post.

The angle $\theta$ at the post subtended by the segment: half the angle satisfies
$$\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$
so $\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Using the segment area $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 400\pi - \dfrac{1}{2}\times 20^2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 400\pi - \dfrac{400\pi}{3} + 200\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &\approx 1011 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\le t\le 14\\[2mm] 0 & \text{for } 0\le t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$
Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$
items.sol:
The total probability over the domain is 1.
$$\int_1^{14} \dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k}{2}\int_1^{14} \dfrac{2}{2t-1}\,dt &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{14} &= 1 \\ k\left(\ln 27 - \ln 1\right) &= 2 \\ k\ln 27 &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k = \dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\le t\le 14\\[2mm] 0 & \text{for } 0\le t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$
After how many days will a person have a 75% chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?
items.sol:
Let $T$ days be the time at which the cumulative probability is 0.75.
$$\int_1^{T} \dfrac{\frac{2}{\ln 27}}{2t-1}\,dt = \dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\ln 27}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{T} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \ln(2T-1) &= \dfrac{3\ln 27}{4} \\ 2T - 1 &= e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} \\ T &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} + 1}{2} \\ &\approx 6.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after 7 days}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\sqrt{\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}}\right]=\dfrac{2}{4-x^2}$
items.sol:
Use the log laws to rewrite the function, then differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right] &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2+x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2-x)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2+x}+\dfrac{1}{2-x}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2-x+2+x}{(2+x)(2-x)}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{4}{4-x^2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{4-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A drug is used to control a medical condition. It is known that the quantity $Q$ milligrams of drug remaining in the body after $t$ hours satisfies an equation of the form $Q=Q_0e^{kt}$ where $Q_0$ and $k$ are constants. The initial dose is 6 milligrams and after 15 hours the amount remaining in the body is half the initial dose.
Find the values of $Q_0$ and $k$.
items.sol:
When $t=0$, $Q=Q_0$, so $Q_0=6$.

After 15 hours the amount is half the initial dose, so $Q=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 6e^{15k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= e^{15k} \\ 15k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$k = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{15}$$

items.part:
A drug is used to control a medical condition. It is known that the quantity $Q$ milligrams of drug remaining in the body after $t$ hours satisfies an equation of the form $Q=Q_0e^{kt}$ where $Q_0$ and $k$ are constants. The initial dose is 6 milligrams and after 15 hours the amount remaining in the body is half the initial dose.
After how long will one-eighth of the initial dose remain?
items.sol:
One-eighth of the initial dose is $\dfrac{6}{8}=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4} &= 6e^{kt} \\ \dfrac{1}{8} &= e^{kt} \\ kt &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $k$ from part (a).
$$t = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\div 15} = 45 \text{ hours}$$

items.part: Kloe has taken up golf, each year she plays 30 rounds of golf. In 2011 she totalled 3300 shots, in 2021 she totalled 2760 shots. The number of shots she took each year decreased by the same amount. To make it as a professional golfer she needs to get under 2115 shots in her 30 rounds. If this trend continues, in what year can she become a professional golfer?
items.sol:
The yearly totals form an arithmetic progression. From 2011 to 2021 is 10 years, so with $a=3300$:
$$\begin{aligned} a+10d &= 2760 \\ 10d &= -540 \\ d &= -54 \end{aligned}$$
She needs fewer than 2115 shots.
$$\begin{aligned} a+(n-1)d &< 2115 \\ 3300+54-54n &< 2115 \\ -54n &< -1239 \\ n &> 22.944\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $n=23$ years, and Kloe can be a professional golfer in 2033.

items.part: Show that the derivative of $y=\log_e(\tan x)$ is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\tan x+\cot x$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with $u=\tan x$.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\tan^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\tan x}+\dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \cot x+\tan x \end{aligned}$$
which is the required result.

items.part: Hence find the equation of the tangent to $y=\log_e(\tan x)$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$
items.sol:
The gradient is the derivative from part (a) at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} m &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= 1+1 \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \log_e\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= \log_e 1 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} y-0 &= 2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ y &= 2x-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{8.8} \\ &\approx 2.966 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: State the natural domain of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2-x^2}}$
items.sol:
The square root needs $2-x^2\ge 0$, and the denominator cannot be zero, so $2-x^2>0$.
$$x^2<2$$
$$\therefore\ -\sqrt{2}<x<\sqrt{2}, \text{ or } \left(-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=4x^3-x^4$
Find any stationary points and determine their nature and find any points of inflection
items.sol:
$$y'=12x^2-4x^3 \qquad y''=24x-12x^2$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x^2-4x^3 &= 0 \\ 4x^2(3-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=3$, giving the points $(0,0)$ and $(3,27)$.

At $x=0$, $y''=0$, so the test is inconclusive and $(0,0)$ is a possible point of inflexion.

At $x=3$, $y''=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

For points of inflexion, $y''=0$.
$$12x(2-x)=0$$
So $x=0$ or $x=2$. Test the concavity either side of each.
$$\begin{aligned} x=1 &: y''=12>0 \\ x=2 &: y''=0 \\ x=2.5 &: y''=-15<0 \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(2,16)$ is a point of inflexion.
$$\begin{aligned} x=-1 &: y''=-36<0 \\ x=0 &: y''=0 \\ x=1 &: y''=12>0 \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes and $y'=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
items.final: Maximum turning point $(3,27)$; horizontal point of inflexion $(0,0)$; point of inflexion $(2,16)$

items.sol: \exfigure{1303_q35_s1}

The lengths form a geometric sequence with first term $a=10$ and ratio $r=0.96$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_5 &= 10\times 0.96^4 \\ &\approx 8.49 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Using the sum of a GP, $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ with $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10(1-0.96^{10})}{1-0.96} \\ &\approx 83.8 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{10}{1-0.96} \\ &= 250 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Now $2.4 \text{ m}=240 \text{ cm}<250 \text{ cm}$.

So 2.4 m is not sufficient to make an unlimited number of rectangles.
items.final: Not sufficient: $S_\infty=250$ cm $>240$ cm, so 2.4 m cannot make an unlimited number of rectangles

items.sol:
The volume of a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$, with $V=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= \pi r^2h \\ h &= \dfrac{4}{\pi r^2} \end{aligned}$$
The closed cylinder has surface area $S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= 2\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\dfrac{4}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 2\pi r^2+\dfrac{8}{r} \\ &= 2\pi r^2+8r^{-1} \end{aligned}$$

For a minimum, set $S'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} S' &= 4\pi r-8r^{-2} = 0 \\ 4\pi r-\dfrac{8}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 4\pi r^3-8 &= 0 \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{8}{4\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{2}{\pi}}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$S''=4\pi+\dfrac{16}{r^3}$$
Since $r>0$, $S''>0$, so this is a minimum area.
$$\therefore\ r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{2}{\pi}} \text{ m}$$

items.part: Simultaneously solve the equations $\log_{10}(2-x)-\log_{10}y=1-\log_{10}2$ and $\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y$
items.sol:
Rearrange the first equation using log laws.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(2-x)+\log_{10}2-1 &= \log_{10}y \\ \log_{10}(4-2x)-1 &= \log_{10}y \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$
$$\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y \qquad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{4-2x}{2x}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{4-2x}{2x} &= 10 \\ 4-2x &= 20x \\ x &= \dfrac{2}{11} \end{aligned}$$
From (2), $y=2x=\dfrac{4}{11}$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2}{11},\ y=\dfrac{4}{11}$$

items.part:
Max borrows \$250 000 to purchase a house. He repays his loan in equal monthly instalments of \$$M$ for 25 years. Interest is charged at 3% p.a., compounded monthly.
By first finding expressions for $A_1,A_2$ and $A_3$ (the amount owing after 1 month, 2 months and 3 months), find an expression for $A_n$ (the amount owing after $n$ months).

Max borrows \$250 000 to purchase a house. He repays his loan in equal monthly instalments of \$$M$ for 25 years. Interest is charged at 3% p.a., compounded monthly.
Find the amount of each monthly instalment, \$$M$, and hence calculate the amount of interest Max pays on the loan.
items.sol:
The loan is repaid after $25\times 12=300$ months, so $A_{300}=0$.
$$250000(1.0025)^{300}-M\left(1+1.0025+\cdots+1.0025^{299}\right)=0$$
The bracket is a GP sum with $a=1$, $r=1.0025$, $n=300$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= \dfrac{250000(1.0025)^{300}}{\left(\frac{1.0025^{300}-1}{1.0025-1}\right)} \\ &= \$1185.53 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest} &= 300M-250000 \\ &= \$105\,658.49 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $\ddot{x}=4\cos 2t$, where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially the particle is at the origin with a velocity of 1 ms$^{-1}$.
Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$
items.sol:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\dot{x}=\displaystyle\int 4\cos 2t\,dt=2\sin 2t+C$$
When $t=0$, $\dot{x}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 2\sin 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $\ddot{x}=4\cos 2t$, where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially the particle is at the origin with a velocity of 1 ms$^{-1}$.
Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin 2t+1 &= 0 \\ \sin 2t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first time $2t>0$ with $\sin 2t=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ is in the third quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned} 2t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $\ddot{x}=4\cos 2t$, where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially the particle is at the origin with a velocity of 1 ms$^{-1}$.
Find the displacement, $x$, of the particle in terms of $t$.
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity.
$$x=\displaystyle\int(2\sin 2t+1)\,dt=-\cos 2t+t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -\cos 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-\cos 2t+t+1$$

items.part:
A standard die is rolled twice. The sum $X$ of the numbers that are upwards-facing is calculated.
Determine the probability that $X$ is less than or equal to 5.
items.sol:
Using a table of the 36 equally likely outcomes, 10 outcomes give $X\le 5$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 5) &= \dfrac{10}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{18} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A standard die is rolled twice. The sum $X$ of the numbers that are upwards-facing is calculated.
It is known that a 4 appears on the die at least once in the two throws. What is the probability that $X$ is greater than 9?
items.sol:
Outcomes with at least one 4: $36-25=11$.

Of these, the sums greater than 9 are $(4,6)$ and $(6,4)$, which is 2 outcomes.
$$P(X>9\mid \text{a 4 on a die})=\dfrac{2}{11}$$

items.part:
Chemistry, Physics and Biology are three of the subjects students may decide to study. For a group of 50 students, the following is known:

\begin{itemize}
\item 12 students study neither Chemistry nor Physics nor Biology
\item 20 students study Chemistry
\item 25 students study Physics
\item 15 students study Biology
\item 9 students study both Chemistry and Physics
\item 10 students study both Chemistry and Biology
\item 11 students study both Physics and Biology
\end{itemize}

A student is chosen at random. By drawing a Venn diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that the student studies all three subjects.
items.sol:
Let $x$ be the number studying all three subjects.

The number studying none is 12, so
$$n(\text{at least one subject})=50-12=38$$
Adding the three subject totals gives $20+25+15=60$, and $60-38=22$.

From the Venn diagram regions:
$$\begin{aligned} (9-x)+(10-x)+(11-x)+2x &= 22 \\ 30-x &= 22 \\ x &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$P(\text{all three})=\dfrac{8}{50}=\dfrac{4}{25}$$
Alternatively, using
$$P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-\big[P(A\cap B)+P(A\cap C)+P(B\cap C)\big]+P(A\cap B\cap C)$$
we get
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B\cap C) &= \dfrac{38}{50}-\dfrac{20+25+15}{50}+\dfrac{9+10+11}{50} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{50} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{25} \end{aligned}$$

The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.1+b+0.3 &= 1 \\ b &= 0.6 \end{aligned}$$
Using $\mu=\sum x\,P(X=x)=25$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10(0.1)+a(0.6)+30(0.3) &= 25 \\ 1+0.6a+9 &= 25 \\ 0.6a &= 15 \\ a &= 25 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag contains three white balls and four black balls. Two balls are selected at random without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of black balls drawn.
Construct the probability distribution table.

A bag contains three white balls and four black balls. Two balls are selected at random without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of black balls drawn.
the expected value of $X$.
items.sol:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 0\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{8}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag contains three white balls and four black balls. Two balls are selected at random without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of black balls drawn.
the variance of $X$.
items.sol:
Using $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X) &= 0^2\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)+1^2\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)+2^2\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)-\left(\dfrac{8}{7}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{20}{49} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag contains three white balls and four black balls. Two balls are selected at random without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of black balls drawn.
the standard deviation.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \text{Standard deviation} &= \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{49}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $\cos\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = -1$, where $0 \le x \le 2\pi$
items.sol:
From $0\le x\le 2\pi$ we get $0\le 2x\le 4\pi$, so
$$-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le 2x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le \dfrac{15\pi}{4}$$
In this range, $\cos^{-1}(-1)$ gives
$$2x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\pi,\ 3\pi$$
$$2x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{4}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{8}$$

Sketch the graph of $y = 1 + 3\cos 2x$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$

items.sol:
The graph $y=1+3\cos 2x$ has amplitude 3, period $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ and centre line $y=1$.

items.part:
The graph of $y = 2\sin x + 1$ is shown below. Use the graph to determine how many solutions exist for the equation $2\sin x + 1 = \dfrac{x}{2}$.

\exfigure{633_q13_1}
Prove that $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta}$
items.sol:
Writing in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{1-\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{(1+\sin\theta)(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{1-\sin\theta} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: What is the first term of the geometric sequence $3, 3\sqrt{2}, 6, 6\sqrt{2}, \ldots$ which exceeds 800?
items.sol:
The sequence is geometric with $a=3$ and $r=\sqrt{2}$, so $T_n=3(\sqrt{2})^{n-1}$.

We need $T_n>800$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3(\sqrt{2})^{n-1} &> 800 \\ (\sqrt{2})^{n-1} &> \dfrac{800}{3} \\ (n-1)\log(\sqrt{2}) &> \log\left(\dfrac{800}{3}\right) \\ n-1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{800}{3}\right)}{\log(\sqrt{2})} \approx 16.11 \\ n &> 17.11 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ is a whole number, the 18th term is the first to exceed 800.
items.final: The 18th term is the first to exceed 800.

items.part: In an arithmetic series, the fourth term is 6 and the sum of the first 16 terms is 120. Find the common difference.
items.sol:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(2a+(n-1)d)$.

From $T_4=6$:
$$a+3d=6,\quad\text{so}\quad 2a+6d=12 \quad (1)$$
From $S_{16}=120$:
$$\dfrac{16}{2}(2a+15d)=120,\quad\text{so}\quad 2a+15d=15 \quad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$9d=3$$
$$\therefore\ d=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

items.part:
Given that $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, show that the limiting sum of the series

$$\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos^2\theta + \sin\theta\cos^4\theta + \sin\theta\cos^6\theta + \ldots$$

is equal to $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$. Explain why you can find the limiting sum.
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $a=\sin\theta$ and $r=\cos^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} \\ &= \operatorname{cosec}\theta \end{aligned}$$
A limiting sum exists when $-1<r<1$. For $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0<\cos^2\theta<1$, so the limiting sum can be found.

items.part:
A clerk is employed at an initial salary of \$18\,320 per annum and after each year of service he receives an increase of \$780 per year.
What is his salary for the second year of employment?
items.sol:
The salary rises by $\$780$ after the first year.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Salary} &= \$18\,320 + \$780 \\ &= \$19\,100 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A clerk is employed at an initial salary of \$18\,320 per annum and after each year of service he receives an increase of \$780 per year.
What is his salary for the tenth year of employment?
items.sol:
The salaries form an arithmetic sequence with $a = 18\,320$ and $d = 780$, so the tenth term is $a + 9d$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= \$(18\,320 + 9 \times 780) \\ &= \$25\,340 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A clerk is employed at an initial salary of \$18\,320 per annum and after each year of service he receives an increase of \$780 per year.
What are his total earnings over ten years of employment?
items.sol:
Using the arithmetic series sum $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$ with $n=10$, $a = 18\,320$ and $l = 25\,340$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}(18\,320 + 25\,340) \\ &= \$218\,300 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
$x$, $x^2$ and $7x$ are the first three consecutive terms of an arithmetic series.
Show that $x(x-4) = 0$
items.sol:
In an arithmetic series the common difference is constant, so $T_2 - T_1 = T_3 - T_2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 - x &= 7x - x^2 \\ 2x^2 - 8x &= 0 \\ 2x(x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(x-4) = 0$$

items.part:
$x$, $x^2$ and $7x$ are the first three consecutive terms of an arithmetic series.
Hence, find the first 3 terms of this series if all the terms are positive integers.
items.sol:
From part (i), $x = 0$ or $x = 4$.

The terms are positive, so $x \ne 0$ and $x = 4$.

The terms are $4,\ 16,\ 28$.

items.part: Show that the sequence $\log_{10} 3,\ \log_{10} 9,\ \log_{10} 81, \dots$ is a geometric sequence.
items.sol:
A sequence is geometric if consecutive ratios are equal. Using $\log_{10} 9 = 2\log_{10} 3$ and $\log_{10} 81 = 4\log_{10} 3$:
$$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{\log_{10} 9}{\log_{10} 3} = 2$$
$$\dfrac{T_3}{T_2} = \dfrac{\log_{10} 81}{\log_{10} 9} = 2$$
Since $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{T_3}{T_2}$, the sequence is geometric.

items.part: How many terms of the series $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \cdots$ give a sum of $\dfrac{2047}{2048}$?
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $a = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Using $S_n = \dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2047}{2048} &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\right)}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{1}{2^n} \end{aligned}$$
So $2^n = 2048 = 2^{11}$, hence $n = 11$.

There are $11$ terms.

items.part: Calculate the sum of all the numbers between 100 and 400 (non-inclusive), which are not divisible by 7.
items.sol:
First find the sum of all the integers from 101 to 399, an arithmetic series with $n = 299$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{299}{2}(101 + 399) \\ &= 74\,750 \end{aligned}$$
The multiples of 7 in this range are $105, 112, 119, \cdots, 399$. Find how many there are using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 399 &= 105 + (n-1)\times 7 \\ n &= 43 \end{aligned}$$
Their sum is
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{43}{2}(105 + 399) \\ &= 10\,836 \end{aligned}$$
Subtract the multiples of 7 from the total.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum} &= 74\,750 - 10\,836 \\ &= 63\,914 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the sum is } 63\,914$$

items.part: Using the formula for the limiting sum of a geometric series, convert the recurring decimal $4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5}$ into a mixed fraction.
items.sol:
Write the decimal as a whole number plus a geometric series.
$$4.353535\ldots = 4 + 0.35 + 0.0035 + 0.000035 + \cdots$$
The terms after $4$ form a geometric series with $a = 0.35$ and $r = 0.01$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum $S = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$ applies.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5} &= 4 + \dfrac{0.35}{1 - 0.01} \\ &= 4 + \dfrac{35}{99} \\ &= 4\dfrac{35}{99} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5} = 4\dfrac{35}{99}$$

items.part: Find the exact values of $\theta$ such that $2\sin^2\theta = 1 - \sin\theta$, where $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
Rearrange to a quadratic in $\sin\theta$.
$$2\sin^2\theta + \sin\theta - 1 = 0$$
Factorising (or using the quadratic formula):
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1^2 - 4(2)(-1)}}{2\times 2} \\ &= -1 \text{ or } \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $\sin\theta = -1$:
$$\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
For $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$

items.part: Prove that $(1 + \cot^2 x)(\sec^2 x - 1) = \sec^2 x$
items.sol:
Use the identities $1 + \cot^2 x = \text{cosec}^2 x$ and $\sec^2 x - 1 = \tan^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= (1 + \cot^2 x)(\sec^2 x - 1) \\ &= \text{cosec}^2 x \times \tan^2 x \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x}\times\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \sec^2 x \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sketch the graph of $y = 2 - \cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ for $-2\pi \le x \le 2\pi$, stating its period and amplitude.

Period = ____________________

Amplitude = ____________________
items.sol:
The graph is $y = 2 - \cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$, so $b = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and the amplitude is the coefficient of the cosine.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= \dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= 4\pi \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Amplitude} = 1$$
