items.part: Solve $\cos 2x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ in the domain $[0, 360^\circ]$
items.sol:
Let $u = 2x$. Since $0 \le x \le 360^\circ$, we have $0 \le u \le 720^\circ$.
$$\cos u = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
The reference angle is $30^\circ$, and cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants. Two full rotations are covered.
$$u = 30^\circ, 330^\circ, 390^\circ, 690^\circ$$
Dividing by 2:
$$x = 15^\circ, 165^\circ, 195^\circ, 345^\circ$$

items.part:
The population of salmon in a salmon farm grows and reduces as fish are born and sold.

The population $P$ is given by $P = 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900$ where $t$ is time in days.
Determine the initial population.
items.sol:
The initial population is at $t = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 500\cos(0) + 900 \\ &= 1400 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of salmon in a salmon farm grows and reduces as fish are born and sold.

The population $P$ is given by $P = 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900$ where $t$ is time in days.
What is the minimum number of salmon in the farm at any time?
items.sol:
The minimum occurs when $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) = -1$.
$$\begin{aligned} P_{\min} &= -500 + 900 \\ &= 400 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of salmon in a salmon farm grows and reduces as fish are born and sold.

The population $P$ is given by $P = 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900$ where $t$ is time in days.
How many days will it take for salmon population to first reach 1150?
items.sol:
Set $P = 1150$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1150 &= 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For the first time, take the smallest positive angle.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{4} &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ t &= \dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ days}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$y = \tan^3 x$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on $y = (\tan x)^3$:
$$y' = 3\tan^2 x \times \sec^2 x$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$y = x^4 2^x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^4 & v&=2^x\\ u'&=4x^3 & v'&=2^x\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 4x^3 \times 2^x + (2^x \ln 2)x^4 \\ &= 2^x x^3(4 + x\ln 2) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: By first simplifying the expression, differentiate $y = \dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{2}} + e^{-x}}{e^x}$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Simplify first using index laws.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{2}}}{e^x} + \dfrac{e^{-x}}{e^x} \\ &= e^{\frac{x}{2} - x} + e^{-x-x} \\ &= e^{-\frac{x}{2}} + e^{-2x} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$y' = -\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{x}{2}} - 2e^{-2x}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$g(x) = \ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{2x-3}\right)$
items.sol:
Use the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$ first.
$$g(x) = \ln(x+1) - \ln(2x-3)$$
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{x+1} - \dfrac{2}{2x-3} \\ &= \dfrac{2x - 3 - 2x - 2}{(x+1)(2x-3)} \\ &= \dfrac{-5}{(x+1)(2x-3)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$y = (e^{2x} + 4)^3$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3(e^{2x}+4)^2 \times 2e^{2x} \\ &= 6e^{2x}(e^{2x}+4)^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.
$y = \sin(x^\circ)$
items.sol:
Convert degrees to radians, since $x^\circ = \dfrac{\pi x}{180}$ radians.
$$y = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{180}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{180}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos x^\circ \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $y = \dfrac{x}{\ln x}$, show that $y^2 - xy + x^2 y' = 0$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$y' = \dfrac{\ln x - 1}{(\ln x)^2}$$
Substitute into the left side.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= y^2 - xy + x^2 y' \\ &= \left(\dfrac{x}{\ln x}\right)^2 - x\times\dfrac{x}{\ln x} + x^2\,\dfrac{\ln x - 1}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2 - x^2\ln x + x^2\ln x - x^2}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= 0 \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Determine the equation of the normal to the curve $y = \cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ at the point where $x = \pi$.
items.sol:
Differentiate to find the tangent gradient.
$$y' = -\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$$
At $x=\pi$:
$$m_{\text{tangent}} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The normal is perpendicular, so $m_{\text{normal}} = 2$.

At $x = \pi$, $y = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y - 0 &= 2(x - \pi) \\ y &= 2x - 2\pi \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Rationalise $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}+1}{\sqrt{5}-2}$, giving your answer in simplest form.
items.sol:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sqrt{5}+1}{\sqrt{5}-2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}+1}{\sqrt{5}-2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{5}+2}{\sqrt{5}+2} \\ &=\dfrac{5+2\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5}+2}{5-2^2} \\ &=7+3\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to $f(x)=e^{2x}$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
items.sol:
The tangent has gradient $f'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=e^{2x} \\ f'(x)&=2e^{2x} \\ f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=e \\ f'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=2e\end{aligned}$$
Equation of the tangent:
$$\begin{aligned}y-e&=2e\left(x-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ y-e&=2ex-e \\ y&=2ex\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions
$f(x)=\tan 2x$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\tan 2x \\ f'(x)&=2\sec^2 2x\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions
$f(x)=\dfrac{e^x}{\cos x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^x & v&=\cos x \\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\dfrac{e^x\cos x-e^x(-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} \\ &=\dfrac{e^x(\cos x+\sin x)}{\cos^2 x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^4+3x^2+1}{x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Divide each term by $x^2$ before integrating.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{x^4+3x^2+1}{x^2}\,dx&=\int\left(x^2+3+x^{-2}\right)dx \\ &=\dfrac{x^3}{3}+3x-\dfrac{1}{x}+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{4x}{x^2+1}\,dx$.
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $x^2+1$, which is $2x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{4x}{x^2+1}\,dx&=2\int\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx \\ &=2\ln\left(x^2+1\right)+C\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A circular disc is cut into twelve sectors whose angles are in an arithmetic sequence.

The angle of the largest sector is twice the angle of the smallest sector.

Find the size of the angle, in degrees, of the smallest sector.
items.sol:
The sector angles sum to the full circle, so $S_{12}=360$. The largest angle is twice the smallest, so $T_{12}=2T_1=2a$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned}360&=\dfrac{12}{2}(a+2a) \\ 60&=3a \\ a&=20\end{aligned}$$
Therefore the smallest angle is $20^\circ$.

items.part: Given that $\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)=2$, show that $x^2-3x-4=0$.
items.sol:
Combine the logarithms using $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$.
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)&=2 \\ \log_2\big(x(x-3)\big)&=2 \\ x(x-3)&=2^2 \\ x^2-3x-4&=0\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find the solution(s) of the equation $\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)=2$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-3x-4&=0 \\ (x-4)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=4$ or $x=-1$.

The logarithms need $x>0$ and $x-3>0$, so $x>3$.

Hence $-1$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x=4$$

items.part:
In the diagram below, $OABC$ is a rectangle with sides 7 cm and 2 cm. $PQ$ is a straight line. $AP$ and $CQ$ are circular arcs, with the centre $O$ the centre of both circles, and $\angle AOP=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

\exfigure{1306_q17_1}

NOT TO SCALE
Find the exact arc length $CQ$.
items.sol:
Angles at $O$ on a straight line sum to $\pi$; $\angle AOC=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (rectangle) and $\angle AOP=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle COQ&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The radius of arc $CQ$ is $OC=2$ cm, so using $l=r\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}l_{CQ}&=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In the diagram below, $OABC$ is a rectangle with sides 7 cm and 2 cm. $PQ$ is a straight line. $AP$ and $CQ$ are circular arcs, with the centre $O$ the centre of both circles, and $\angle AOP=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

\exfigure{1306_q17_1}

NOT TO SCALE
Find the exact area of the sector $OAP$.
items.sol:
The radius of sector $OAP$ is $OA=7$ cm. Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 7^2\times\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{49\pi}{12}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In the diagram below, $OABC$ is a rectangle with sides 7 cm and 2 cm. $PQ$ is a straight line. $AP$ and $CQ$ are circular arcs, with the centre $O$ the centre of both circles, and $\angle AOP=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

\exfigure{1306_q17_1}

NOT TO SCALE
Find the exact length of interval $AP$, correct to 1 decimal place.
items.sol:
Apply the cosine rule in triangle $OAP$, where $OP=OA=7$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned}AP^2&=OP^2+OA^2-2\times OP\times OA\cos\angle AOP \\ &=7^2+7^2-2\times 7\times 7\times\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=98-98\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=98-49\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned}AP&=\sqrt{98-49\sqrt{3}} \\ &\approx 3.6234\ldots \\ &\approx 3.6\text{ cm (1 dp)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The probability that a student plays badminton is 0.3. The probability that a student plays neither table tennis or badminton is 0.5, and the probability that a student plays both sports is $x$.
Using the Venn diagram, or otherwise, complete the probabilities below.

\exfigure{1306_q18_1}

$P(B)=\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$

$P(B\cap T)=\_\_\_\_$

The probability that a student plays badminton is 0.3. The probability that a student plays neither table tennis or badminton is 0.5, and the probability that a student plays both sports is $x$.
Find the probability that a student plays table tennis but not badminton
items.sol:
The probabilities in the Venn diagram sum to $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}1&=0.5+P(B)+P(T)-P(B\cap T) \\ 0.5&=0.3+P(T)-x \\ P(T)&=0.2+x\end{aligned}$$
Table tennis but not badminton:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(T\cap\overline{B}\right)&=P(T)-P(B\cap T) \\ &=0.2+x-x \\ &=0.2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The probability that a student plays badminton is 0.3. The probability that a student plays neither table tennis or badminton is 0.5, and the probability that a student plays both sports is $x$.
It is known that if a student plays table tennis, the probability that they also play badminton is 0.5

Find the probability that a student plays both badminton and table tennis.
items.sol:
Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P(B\mid T)&=\dfrac{P(B\cap T)}{P(T)} \\ 0.5&=\dfrac{x}{0.2+x} \\ 0.1+0.5x&=x \\ 0.1&=0.5x \\ x&=0.2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(B\cap T)=0.2$$

items.part:
The probability that a student plays badminton is 0.3. The probability that a student plays neither table tennis or badminton is 0.5, and the probability that a student plays both sports is $x$.
Hence, or otherwise, determine the probability that a student plays only badminton.
items.sol:
Badminton only is badminton less both sports.
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(B\cap\overline{T}\right)&=0.3-x \\ &=0.3-0.2 \\ &=0.1\end{aligned}$$

Using the statistics function of a calculator:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=-0.854\ldots \\ &\approx -0.85\ (2\text{ dp})\end{aligned}$$

Using the calculator's linear regression, $y=A+Bx$ with
$$A\approx 863.72,\quad B\approx -57.98$$
So
$$y=-57.98x+863.72$$

Substitute $x=5.5$ into the line of best fit.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=-57.98\times 5.5+863.72 \\ &=544.83\end{aligned}$$
The estimated income per capita is $\$545$ (nearest dollar).

items.part:
A particle moves such that its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, at a time $t$ seconds is given by $\dot{x}=4-8\cos t$.

The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the two times the particle is first at rest?
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4-8\cos t \\ 8\cos t&=4 \\ \cos t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The first quadrant solution is $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is also positive in the fourth quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The first two times the particle is at rest are $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ seconds and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ seconds.

items.part:
A particle moves such that its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, at a time $t$ seconds is given by $\dot{x}=4-8\cos t$.

The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the equation for displacement $x$ in terms of time $t$.
items.sol:
Integrating the velocity gives the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int(4-8\cos t)\,dt\\&=4t-8\sin t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle is at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4(0)-8\sin 0+C\\C&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=4t-8\sin t$$

items.part:
A particle moves such that its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, at a time $t$ seconds is given by $\dot{x}=4-8\cos t$.

The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the exact distance travelled by the particle between the first two times it is at rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $4-8\cos t=0$, that is $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$. Since $v>0$ between these times, the distance travelled is the difference in displacement.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=4\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}-8\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-8\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
When $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=4\times\dfrac{5\pi}{3}-8\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+8\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}-\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-4\sqrt{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{16\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}\text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The population of an island is increasing according to the formula $P=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}$ where $P$ is the population in thousands and $t$ is the time in years after January 1st 2020.
Find the initial rate of change of the population of the island.
items.sol:
Differentiating the population formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=10\times\dfrac{1}{50}e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}e^{\frac{t}{50}}\end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{5}e^0=\dfrac{1}{5}$$
$P$ is in thousands, so initially the population is increasing at a rate of $200$ people per year.

items.part:
The population of an island is increasing according to the formula $P=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}$ where $P$ is the population in thousands and $t$ is the time in years after January 1st 2020.
Use the model to predict the population on 1st January 2040, correct to the nearest thousand.
items.sol:
On 1 January 2040, $t=20$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=20+10e^{\frac{20}{50}}\\&\approx 34.9182\end{aligned}$$
The predicted population on 1 January 2040 is $35\,000$.

items.part:
The population of an island is increasing according to the formula $P=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}$ where $P$ is the population in thousands and $t$ is the time in years after January 1st 2020.
Using the model, predict in what year will the population reach 40 000.
items.sol:
The population is $40$ thousand, so $P=40$.
$$\begin{aligned}40&=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\e^{\frac{t}{50}}&=2\\\dfrac{t}{50}&=\ln 2\\t&=50\ln 2\\&\approx 34.657\end{aligned}$$
The population will reach $40\,000$ during 2054.

items.part:
The height of water $h$ metres in a harbour can be modelled using the function below:

$h=4-A\sin(bt)$, where $t$ is the time in hours after midnight.

\exfigure{1306_q22_1}

At 2 am the height of water in the harbour is at its minimum.

At 6 am the height of water in the harbour is at its maximum.
Find the values of $A$ and $b$.
items.sol:
The minimum is at 2 am and the maximum at 6 am, so the minimum height is $2$ and the maximum is $6$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{amplitude}&=\dfrac{6-2}{2}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A=2$$
Half a period is $4$ hours (from minimum to maximum), so the period is $8$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{b}&=8\\b&=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A=2,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

items.part:
The height of water $h$ metres in a harbour can be modelled using the function below:

$h=4-A\sin(bt)$, where $t$ is the time in hours after midnight.

\exfigure{1306_q22_1}

At 2 am the height of water in the harbour is at its minimum.

At 6 am the height of water in the harbour is at its maximum.
A boat can only enter the harbour when the height of the water is more than 5 metres.

Express the information given as an equation, and solve the equation to find the first time the boat can enter the harbour.
items.sol:
The boat can enter when $h>5$, so first solve $h=5$ with $A=2$, $b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned}5&=4-2\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\\\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\\t&=\dfrac{28}{6},\ \dfrac{44}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The first time is $t=\dfrac{28}{6}=4\text{ h }40\text{ min}$.
$$\therefore\text{ the boat can first enter at } 4{:}40 \text{ am}$$
items.final: The boat can first enter at 4:40 am ($t=\frac{28}{6}$ hours)

items.part: Use the trapezoidal rule with 4 sub-intervals to estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{x}\,dx$, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
There are 4 sub-intervals on $[0,2]$, so $h=\dfrac{2-0}{4}=0.5$ and the $x$ values are $0,\ 0.5,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2\sqrt{x}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{0.5}{2}\left(\sqrt{0}+\sqrt{2}+2\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}}+\sqrt{1}+\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)\right)\\&\approx 1.8194\\&\approx 1.82\text{ (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that the equation $2\cos^2 x=4-5\sin x$ may be written as $2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2=0$.
items.sol:
Using $\cos^2 x=1-\sin^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2 x&=4-5\sin x\\2\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)&=4-5\sin x\\2-2\sin^2 x&=4-5\sin x\\2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+4-2&=0\\2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2&=0\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence solve $2\cos^2 x=4-5\sin x$, for $0^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ$.
items.sol:
From part (a), the equation is $2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2=0$. Factorise.
$$\begin{aligned}2\sin^2 x-4\sin x-\sin x+2&=0\\2\sin x(\sin x-2)-1(\sin x-2)&=0\\(2\sin x-1)(\sin x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\sin x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\sin x=2$.

Since $-1\le\sin x\le 1$, $\sin x=2$ is rejected.
$$\sin x=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ x=30^\circ,\ 150^\circ$$

items.part:
The line $y=24(x-1)$ is tangent to the curve $y=ax^3+bx^2+4$ at $x=2$.
Using the fact that the tangent meets the curve to show that $2a+b=5$.
items.sol:
When $x=2$ the tangent has
$$\begin{aligned}y&=24(2-1)\\&=24\end{aligned}$$
The point of contact is $(2,24)$, which also lies on the curve $y=ax^3+bx^2+4$.
$$\begin{aligned}24&=a\times 2^3+b\times 2^2+4\\24&=8a+4b+4\\20&=8a+4b\\5&=2a+b\quad\ldots(1)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The line $y=24(x-1)$ is tangent to the curve $y=ax^3+bx^2+4$ at $x=2$.
By finding another relationship between $a$ and $b$, find the values of $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
The gradient of the curve at $x=2$ equals the gradient of the tangent, $24$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3ax^2+2bx\\24&=3a\times 2^2+2b\times 2\\24&=12a+4b\\6&=3a+b\quad\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$a=1$$
Substituting into (1): $2+b=5$.
$$\therefore\ a=1,\ b=3$$

items.part:
Two children, Jack and Jill, each throw two fair cubical dice simultaneously.

The score for each child is the sum of the two numbers shown on their respective dice.
Complete the table below for the sum of two fair cubical dice below.

\exfigure{1306_q26_1}
items.sol: \extable{Ts6024_1}

items.part:
Two children, Jack and Jill, each throw two fair cubical dice simultaneously.

The score for each child is the sum of the two numbers shown on their respective dice.
Calculate the probability that Jack obtains a score of 9.
items.sol:
There are $4$ ways of scoring $9$ out of $36$ equally likely outcomes.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Jack gets }9)&=\dfrac{4}{36}\\&=\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two children, Jack and Jill, each throw two fair cubical dice simultaneously.

The score for each child is the sum of the two numbers shown on their respective dice.
Calculate the probability that Jack and Jill each obtain a score of 9.
items.sol:
The two children throw independently, so the probabilities multiply.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Jack and Jill both score }9)&=P(\text{Jack scores }9)\times P(\text{Jill scores }9)\\&=\dfrac{1}{9}\times\dfrac{1}{9}\\&=\dfrac{1}{81}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two children, Jack and Jill, each throw two fair cubical dice simultaneously.

The score for each child is the sum of the two numbers shown on their respective dice.
By considering the symmetry of the table in (a), show that the probability of Jack and Jill obtaining the same score is $\dfrac{73}{648}$.
items.sol:
By symmetry of the table, $P(k,k)$ for score $k$ equals $P(14-k,14-k)$, so the scores $2$ to $6$ are matched with $12$ to $8$.
$$\begin{aligned}&P(\text{same score})\\&=P(2,2)+P(3,3)+\cdots+P(12,12)\\&=2P(2,2)+2P(3,3)+2P(4,4)+2P(5,5)+2P(6,6)+P(7,7)\\&=P(7,7)+2\big[P(2,2)+P(3,3)+P(4,4)+P(5,5)+P(6,6)\big]\\&=\left(\dfrac{6}{36}\right)^2+2\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{2}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{4}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{5}{36}\right)^2\right]\\&=\dfrac{73}{648}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two children, Jack and Jill, each throw two fair cubical dice simultaneously.

The score for each child is the sum of the two numbers shown on their respective dice.
Find the probability that Jack's score exceeds Jill's score.
items.sol:
The events Jack scores more, less, or the same as Jill are exhaustive. By symmetry, $P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})=P(\text{Jack}<\text{Jill})$, and from part (d) $P(\text{Jack}=\text{Jill})=\dfrac{73}{648}$.
$$\begin{aligned}1&=P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})+P(\text{Jack}<\text{Jill})+P(\text{Jack}=\text{Jill})\\1&=2P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})+\dfrac{73}{648}\\2P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})&=1-\dfrac{73}{648}\\P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})&=\dfrac{575}{1296}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:

Show that $\dfrac{dr}{dk}=\dfrac{2k-k^3}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dk}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=k^2 & v&=\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\u'&=2k & v'&=\dfrac{4k^3-2k}{2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}\end{aligned}$$
where $v'$ comes from the chain rule:
$$v'=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(4k^3-2k\right)$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dr}{dk}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\times 2k-k^2\times\frac{4k^3-2k}{2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}}{\left(\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\right)^2}\\&=\dfrac{4k\left(\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\right)^2-k^2\left(4k^3-2k\right)}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)\times 2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}\\&=\dfrac{4k\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)-k^2\left(4k^3-2k\right)}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{4k^5-4k^3+4k-4k^5+2k^3}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{4k-2k^3}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{2k-k^3}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the coordinates of any horizontal points of inflexion on the curve with equation

$y=x^4-8x^3+18x^2+4$
items.sol:
Differentiate twice.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^4-8x^3+18x^2+4\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=4x^3-24x^2+36x\\\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=12x^2-48x+36\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflexion occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=12x^2-48x+36\\0&=x^2-4x+3\\0&=(x-3)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=1\text{ or }x=3$$
For a horizontal point of inflexion, the value of $x$ must also be a stationary point, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

When $x=1$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(1)^3-24(1)^2+36(1)=16\ne 0$$
When $x=3$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(3)^3-24(3)^2+36(3)=0$$
So only $x=3$ is stationary. Check for a change of concavity:

\extable{Ts6037_1}

When $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3^4-8(3)^3+18(3)^2+4\\&=31\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (3,31)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion}$$

The area enclosed between the curve $y=x^2$ and the line $y=mx$ is $\dfrac{32}{3}$ square units.

\exfigure{1306_q29_1}

items.sol:
Let the $x$-value of the point of intersection be $a$. The point lies on both $y=x^2$ and $y=mx$, so $a^2=ma$.
$$m=a$$
The line is above the curve between $x=0$ and $x=a$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{32}{3}&=\int_0^a\left(mx-x^2\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{mx^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^a\\&=\dfrac{ma^2}{2}-\dfrac{a^3}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying by $6$:
$$\begin{aligned}64&=3ma^2-2a^3\\&=3a^3-2a^3\quad(\text{since }m=a)\\a^3&=64\\a&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=a=4$$

Using calculus, find the coordinates of the points $A$ and $B$ in exact form.
items.sol:
Differentiate $f(x)=x^2-7x+5\ln x+8$.
$$f'(x)=2x-7+\dfrac{5}{x}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2x-7+\dfrac{5}{x}\\0&=2x^2-7x+5\\0&=2x^2-2x-5x+5\\0&=2x(x-1)-5(x-1)\\0&=(2x-5)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$x=1\text{ or }x=\dfrac{5}{2}$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(1)&=1-7+5\ln 1+8\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{5}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}f\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)&=\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^2-7\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)+5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)+8\\&=5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)-\dfrac{13}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A(1,2),\quad B\left(\dfrac{5}{2},\ 5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)-\dfrac{13}{4}\right)$$

The factor $-2$ reflects the graph in the $x$-axis, so the local maximum at $A$ becomes a local minimum.

items.sol:
\exfigure{1309_q16_s2}

A duet needs one violinist and one clarinettist. Students are chosen without replacement from the $28$.
$$P(\text{duet})=P(V,C)+P(V,\text{both})+P(C,V)+P(C,\text{both})+P(\text{both},V)+P(\text{both},C)+P(\text{both},\text{both})$$
By symmetry of order:

items.sol:
In the right-angled triangle $ABC$ (angle of inclination $36^\circ$ at $A$):
$$\tan36^\circ=\dfrac{CB}{AB}$$
$$\begin{aligned}CB&=AB\tan36^\circ\\&\approx4.950\times\tan36^\circ\\&\approx3.596\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
By the sine rule in $\triangle ABD$:
$$\dfrac{BD}{\sin15^\circ}=\dfrac{3.5}{\sin30^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned}BD&=\dfrac{3.5\sin15^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}\\&\approx1.812\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
In the right-angled triangle $CBD$:
$$\tan\angle CDB=\dfrac{CB}{BD}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle CDB&=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3.596}{1.812}\right)\\&\approx63^\circ16'\ \text{(nearest minute)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Charlie is applying for membership at a new golf club that has a strong reputation. The scores of his current club have a lower quartile of 110 and an upper quartile of 118 and Charlie’s score is not an outlier.

Given that the club he plans to join has scores with a lower quartile of 90 and an upper quartile of 106, can you assure Charlie that his score will not be an outlier in his new club? Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.
items.sol:
A score is an outlier if it lies outside $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$ and $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

Current club:
$$IQR=118-110=8$$
$$1.5\times IQR=12$$
$$\text{Upper bound}=118+12=130,\quad\text{Lower bound}=110-12=98$$
$\therefore$ Charlie's score is between $98$ and $130$.

New club:
$$IQR=106-90=16$$
$$1.5\times IQR=24$$
$$\text{Upper bound}=106+24=130,\quad\text{Lower bound}=90-24=66$$
$\therefore$ Charlie is not an outlier in the new club, as his score is not outside the bounds $66$ to $130$.
items.final: Yes; Charlie is not an outlier in the new club, as his score lies within the bounds 66 to 130.

items.sol:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_6^x f(t)\,dt$.

Mani is a fruit grower. After his oranges are picked, they are sorted by a machine, according to size. The distribution of the diameter, in centimetres, of oranges is modelled by a continuous random variable, $X$, with probability density function given below.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{3x^3}{4}+15x^2-99x+216 & 6\le x\le 8\\[6pt] 0 & \text{Otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Find the mode of the distribution.
items.sol:
The mode occurs at the global maximum, that is at a stationary point or at an end of the domain.

End points:
$$f(6)=0,\quad f(8)=0$$
To find stationary points, differentiate:
$$f'(x)=-\dfrac{3}{4}\left(3x^2-40x+132\right)$$
Set $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-40x+132 &= 0 \\ (3x-22)(x-6) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $x=6$ or $x=\dfrac{22}{3}$.

Values of $f$ at these points:
$$f(6)=0,\quad f\left(\dfrac{22}{3}\right)=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
The greatest value is $\dfrac{8}{9}$, at $x=\dfrac{22}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the mode of the distribution is } \dfrac{22}{3}$$

Therefore $a$ corresponds to a $z$-score of $-1.6$.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 134-1.6\times 16 \\ &= 108.4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given the functions $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-1}$ and $g(x)=e^x$, state the domain of $f\big(g(x)\big)$. Give your answer in \textbf{interval notation}.
items.sol:
Compose the functions:
$$f\big(g(x)\big)=\dfrac{1}{e^x-1}$$
The denominator cannot be zero:
$$\begin{aligned} e^x-1 &\ne 0 \\ e^x &\ne 1 \\ x &\ne 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the domain of } f\big(g(x)\big) \text{ is } (-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=2xe^{\frac{x}{2}}$.
Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2e^{\frac{x}{2}}+xe^{\frac{x}{2}} \\ &= (2+x)e^{\frac{x}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$. Since $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$, this needs $2+x=0$, so $x=-2$.
$$f(-2)=-\dfrac{4}{e}\approx -1.47$$
Test the sign of $f'(x)$ either side of $x=-2$:

\extable{Ts6126_1}

The gradient changes from negative to positive.
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a minimum turning point at } \left(-2,-\dfrac{4}{e}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=2xe^{\frac{x}{2}}$.
Find coordinates of any points of inflection.
items.sol:
From part (a), $f'(x)=(2+x)e^{\frac{x}{2}}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2+x & v&=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}+\dfrac{2+x}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}} \\ &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(1+\dfrac{2+x}{2}\right) \\ &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(\dfrac{4+x}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$, $f''(x)=0$ when $4+x=0$, so $x=-4$.

Test the sign of $f''(x)$ either side of $x=-4$:

\extable{Ts6127_1}

The concavity changes at $x=-4$.
$$f(-4)=-\dfrac{8}{e^2}\approx -1.083$$
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a point of inflection at } \left(-4,-\dfrac{8}{e^2}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=2xe^{\frac{x}{2}}$.
For what values of $x$ is the curve concave down?
items.sol:
From part (b), $f''(x)=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(\dfrac{4+x}{2}\right)$ and $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$.

The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$, that is when $4+x<0$.
$$\therefore\ x<-4$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y=2xe^{\frac{x}{2}}$.
Draw a sketch of the curve, showing all critical points.
items.sol:
The $y$-intercept is at $x=0$:
$$f(0)=0$$
The $x$-intercept is at $y=0$:
$$2xe^{\frac{x}{2}}=0$$
so $x=0$.

items.part:
The effectiveness of a drug is measured by its ability to reduce the number of bacteria in a culture over time. The culture is reduced according to the model $N=N_0e^{-kt}$ where $N$ is the number of bacteria and $t$ is the time since the drug was administered in minutes.

A drug is tested in a culture initially with 1200 bacteria, which reduces to 200 in 6 minutes. How many bacteria are left in the culture after 3 minutes?
items.sol:
When $t=0$, $N=1200$:
$$1200=N_0e^0,\quad N_0=1200$$
so $N=1200e^{-kt}$.

When $t=6$, $N=200$:
$$\begin{aligned} 200 &= 1200e^{-6k} \\ e^{-6k} &= \dfrac{200}{1200}=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ -6k &= \ln\dfrac{1}{6} \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{1}{6}}{-6}\approx 0.299 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
So $N=1200e^{-kt}$ with $k=\dfrac{\ln 6}{6}$ (keep $k$ exact: the rounded $0.299$ gives $489.3$).

When $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 1200e^{-\frac{\ln 6}{6}\times 3} = 1200e^{-\frac12\ln 6} = \dfrac{1200}{\sqrt6} \\ &= 489.898\ldots \approx 490 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $\sin\theta=\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{19}}$ and $\theta$ is obtuse, find the exact value of $\tan\theta$ in simplest form.
items.sol:
Since $\theta$ is obtuse, it lies in quadrant 2, so $\sin\theta>0$ and $\tan\theta<0$. Construct a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $2\sqrt{19}$ and opposite side $6+\sqrt{2}$.

\exfigure{1309_q24_s1}

Let $A$ be the adjacent side. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} A^2 &= \left(2\sqrt{19}\right)^2-\left(6+\sqrt{2}\right)^2 \\ &= 76-\left(36+12\sqrt{2}+2\right) \\ &= 76-\left(38+12\sqrt{2}\right) \\ &= 38-12\sqrt{2} \\ &= 36-12\sqrt{2}+2 \\ &= \left(6-\sqrt{2}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
so $A=6-\sqrt{2}$.

In quadrant 2 the tangent is negative:
$$\therefore\ \tan\theta=-\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{6-\sqrt{2}}$$
or equivalently
$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}-6}$$

items.part:
A tin can with a closed lid is made in the shape of a cylinder as shown below. The lid has a radius of $r$ cm and a height of $h$ cm.

\exfigure{1309_q25_1}

The volume of the can is $192\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
Show that the total surface area of the can, $A\text{ cm}^2$, is given by:

$$A=2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right)$$
items.sol:
The volume of a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$. Given $V=192\pi$:
$$h=\dfrac{192\pi}{\pi r^2}=\dfrac{192}{r^2}\qquad(1)$$
The closed can has two circular ends and a curved surface:
$$A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi\left(r^2+rh\right)\qquad(2)$$
Substitute (1) into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\pi\left(r^2+r\left(\dfrac{192}{r^2}\right)\right) \\ &= 2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A tin can with a closed lid is made in the shape of a cylinder as shown below. The lid has a radius of $r$ cm and a height of $h$ cm.

\exfigure{1309_q25_1}

The volume of the can is $192\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
Find the value of $r$ for which the tin has a minimum surface area.
items.sol:
Write the area with a negative power:
$$A=2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right)=2\pi\left(r^2+192r^{-1}\right)$$
Differentiate:
$$A'=2\pi\left(2r-192r^{-2}\right),\quad A''=2\pi\left(2+384r^{-3}\right)$$
For stationary points, $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2r-\dfrac{192}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 2r &= \dfrac{192}{r^2} \\ 2r^3 &= 192 \\ r^3 &= 96 \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{96} \end{aligned}$$
Nature: when $r=\sqrt[3]{96}$,
$$A''=2\pi\left(2+\dfrac{384}{r^3}\right)=2\pi\left(2+\dfrac{384}{96}\right)>0$$
so this is a minimum turning point.
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum surface area occurs when } r=\sqrt[3]{96}$$

items.part: Hence, determine the number of solutions of the equation $f(2(x+2))=|x+3|$.
items.sol:
From the sketch in part (a), the graph of $y=f(2(x+2))$ meets $y=|x+3|$ at three points.
$$\therefore\ \text{there are 3 solutions}$$

items.part: Differentiate $\ln\big(\cos(2x)\big)$.
items.sol:
Let $u=\cos 2x$, so $u'=-2\sin 2x$, and $y=\ln u$.

Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{-2\sin 2x}{\cos 2x} \\ &= -2\tan 2x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence, or otherwise, evaluate:

$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\tan(2x)\,dx$$
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\cos 2x)=-2\tan 2x$, so
$$\begin{aligned} I &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\tan(2x)\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}-2\tan(2x)\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[\ln(\cos 2x)\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\ln(\cos 0)\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\ln 1\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

At the intersection the two $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x} &= 2^{-x} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= 2\times 2^{-x} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= 2^{1-x} \\ 2^{-1} &= 2^{1-x} \\ -1 &= 1-x \\ x &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

Find the $x$-intercept of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x} &= 0 \\ 2^{-1} &= 2^{-x} \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The shaded area is the area under $y=2^{-x}$ from $0$ to $2$, minus the area under $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}$ from $1$ to $2$:
$$A=\int_0^2 2^{-x}\,dx-\int_1^2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= -\left[\dfrac{2^{-x}}{\ln 2}\right]_0^2-\left[\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{2^{-x}}{\ln 2}\right]_1^2 \\ &= -\left(\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}\right)-\left(\left(\dfrac{2}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2\ln 2}\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &\approx 0.9427 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Show that

$$\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$$
items.sol:
To prove: $\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$.

Using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$, with base $c=b$:
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= \log_a b \\ &= \dfrac{\log_b b}{\log_b a} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\log_b a} \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence, solve the equation

$$6\log_x 2+\log_2 x-5=0$$
items.sol:
By part (a), $\log_x 2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2 x}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 6\log_x 2+\log_2 x-5 &= 0 \\ \dfrac{6}{\log_2 x}+\log_2 x-5 &= 0 \\ 6+(\log_2 x)^2-5\log_2 x &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $u=\log_2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u^2-5u+6 &= 0 \\ (u-3)(u-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $u=3$ or $u=2$.

For $\log_2 x=3$: $x=2^3=8$.

For $\log_2 x=2$: $x=2^2=4$.
$$\therefore\ x=4 \text{ or } x=8$$

items.part:
A weight is attached to a spring that is connected to the ceiling. The weight is pulled away from the ceiling and then released so that it bounces up and down.

Let the distance of the weight from the ceiling be $x$ metres. The spring stretches and contracts such that $x$ varies sinusoidally with time, between 1.2 metres and 1.8 metres. It takes 1 second for the weight to go from its highest point to its lowest point.

The motion of the weight can be modelled using a sine wave of the form:

$$x=a\sin(bt+c)+d$$

How far from the ceiling is the weight 2.7 seconds after it is at a high point?
items.sol:
Since $x$ is the distance from the ceiling, the high point is at $x=1.2$ and the low point is at $x=1.8$.

Amplitude and centre of motion:
$$a=\dfrac{1.8-1.2}{2}=0.3,\qquad d=\dfrac{1.8+1.2}{2}=1.5$$
The time from high to low is 1 s, which is half a period:
$$\text{period}=2\times 1=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$$
so $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$.

Assuming the weight starts ($t=0$) at the centre of motion, the distance from the ceiling is modelled by
$$x=0.3\sin(\pi t)+1.5$$
The weight is at a high point when $x=1.2$, that is when $\sin(\pi t)=-1$, which first occurs at $t=1.5$.

The required time is 2.7 s after this:
$$1.5+2.7=4.2$$
When $t=4.2$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 0.3\sin(\pi\times 4.2)+1.5 \\ &\approx 1.676 \text{ m (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
As the period is 2, the same answer follows from $t=1.5+0.7$, that is $t=0.2$.

The displacement is the signed area under the velocity graph, $\displaystyle\int_0^t f(x)\,dx$. This equals $0$ when $t=2$.
$$\therefore\ t=2$$

The particle is furthest from the origin when $\left|\displaystyle\int_0^t f(x)\,dx\right|$ is largest, which is at $t=4$.
$$\therefore\ t=4$$

Since $f(x)$ is velocity, $f'(x)$ is acceleration. The greatest acceleration is where the gradient of the velocity graph is greatest.
$$\therefore\ t=4$$
\exfigure{1309_q31_s1}

items.part:
The graph of the function $y=\cos\big(2a(x-b)\big)+c$ is shown below, where $a,b$ and $c$ are constants. Point $P$ has coordinates $(b,c+1)$.

\exfigure{1309_q32_1}

On the same set of axes, sketch:

$$y=-c\sin(3ax-3ab)$$

You may use the space below for working.
items.sol:
Original function: $y=\cos\big(2a(x-b)\big)+c$.

New function: $y=-c\sin\big(3a(x-b)\big)$.

The centre of motion $c$ of the original corresponds to the amplitude of the new function.

Both functions are translated horizontally by $b$.

The ratio of the periods, original to new, is $2a:3a=2:3$. So the new function completes 3 periods in the time the original completes 2, that is 3 periods in 24 boxes, or 1 period in 8 boxes.

The new function is a negative sine curve.

\exfigure{1309_q32_s1}

items.part:
A competition is run where 400 raffle tickets are placed in a box.

There are two prizes to be won. The ticket for first prize is drawn from the box without replacement, and then the ticket for second prize is drawn from the box.

Rex has 20 tickets in the raffle. Find the probability that he wins:
no prizes.
items.sol:
Rex has 20 of the 400 tickets, so 380 tickets are not his. Without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{no prizes}) &= \dfrac{380}{400} \times \dfrac{379}{399} \\ &= \dfrac{379}{420} \\ &\approx 90.2\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A competition is run where 400 raffle tickets are placed in a box.

There are two prizes to be won. The ticket for first prize is drawn from the box without replacement, and then the ticket for second prize is drawn from the box.

Rex has 20 tickets in the raffle. Find the probability that he wins:
at least one prize.
items.sol:
Use the complement of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one prize}) &= 1 - \dfrac{379}{420} \\ &= \dfrac{41}{420} \\ &\approx 9.8\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A Lotto game is conducted where 5 balls are selected without replacement from 50 balls, which are numbered from 1 to 50.

A Lotto game is conducted and all five balls are drawn.

Find the probability that all of the balls drawn have even numbers.
items.sol:
There are 25 even numbers among the 50 balls. Without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{25}{50} \times \dfrac{24}{49} \times \dfrac{23}{48} \times \dfrac{22}{47} \times \dfrac{21}{46} \\ &= \dfrac{33}{1316} \\ &\approx 2.5\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: For two events $X$ and $Y$, find $P(X \mid Y)$ if $P(X \cap Y) = 0.3$ and $P(Y) = 0.4$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(X \mid Y) &= \dfrac{P(X \cap Y)}{P(Y)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.3}{0.4} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4} \text{ or } 75\% \end{aligned}$$

Using the complement and the addition formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\overline{A \cup B}) &= 1 - P(A \cup B) \\ &= 1 - \left[P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\right] \\ &= 1 - \left[\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right] \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{11}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A coin is tossed $n$ times, where $n > 1$.

Find the probability of obtaining $n$ tails.
items.sol:
Each toss is a tail with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$, and the tosses are independent.
$$P(n \text{ tails}) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n = \dfrac{1}{2^n}$$

items.part:
An incomplete probability distribution table is shown below:

What is the expected value $E(X)$ for the distribution?

Show your calculations.

For the random variable $X$, it is known that $E(X) = 10$ and $\text{Var}(X) = 2.25$
What is $\sigma$, the standard deviation, for this distribution?
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} \\ &= \sqrt{2.25} \\ &= 1.5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the random variable $X$, it is known that $E(X) = 10$ and $\text{Var}(X) = 2.25$
Find $E(2X)$ and $\text{Var}(2X)$ for a new distribution $2X$.
items.sol:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(2X) &= 2^2 \times 2.25 \\ &= 9 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Joseph completes two class tests, one in History and one in Science.

Joseph's mark in his History test was 67. The test mean for the class was $\mu = 60$ and the standard deviation was $\sigma = 5$.

In the Science test, the test mean for the class was $\mu = 65$ and standard deviation was $\sigma = 3.5$.

What Science mark does Joseph need to achieve to be equivalent to his History mark?
items.sol:
Find Joseph's History mark in standard deviations above the mean:
$$z = \dfrac{67-60}{5} = 1.4$$
The equivalent Science mark is $1.4$ standard deviations above the Science mean:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 65 + 1.4 \times 3.5 \\ &= 69.9 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: What is the $101^{\text{st}}$ term of the arithmetic sequence $\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\dfrac{7}{10}$, $\dfrac{9}{10}$, $\dots$ ?
items.sol:
The common difference is $d = \dfrac{7}{10}-\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a + (n-1)d \\ T_{101} &= \dfrac{1}{2} + 100 \times \dfrac{1}{5} \\ &= 20.5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In an arithmetic series, the third term is 8 and the twentieth term is 127.
Find the common difference.
items.sol:
Using $T_n = a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} a + 2d &= 8 \\ a + 19d &= 127 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting:
$$\begin{aligned} 17d &= 119 \\ d &= 7 \end{aligned}$$
Then $a = 8 - 14 = -6$.

items.part:
In an arithmetic series, the third term is 8 and the twentieth term is 127.
Find the sum of the first 20 terms.
items.sol:
Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$ with $a=-6$ and $l = T_{20} = 127$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{20} &= \dfrac{20}{2}\left[-6 + 127\right] \\ &= 10 \times 121 \\ &= 1210 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{6} (n+1)^2$
Find the $10^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence $35\,000, 28\,000, 22\,400, \dots$
items.sol:
Check for a common ratio:
$$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{28000}{35000} = \dfrac{4}{5}, \qquad \dfrac{T_3}{T_2} = \dfrac{22400}{28000} = \dfrac{4}{5}$$
So this is a G.P. with $a = 35000$ and $r = \dfrac{4}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= 35000 \times \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^9 \\ &\approx 4697.62 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Jimmy is investing in a superannuation fund to which he contributes $\$100$ at the beginning of each month for 10 years. The fund pays $2.4\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. If the fund matures at the end of the $10^{\text{th}}$ year, find the total value of the Jimmy's investment at maturity.
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{2.4\%}{12} = 0.2\%$, so each month multiplies by $r = 1.002$.

Each $\$100$ is invested at the start of a month, so the first earns interest for 120 months, the last for 1 month:
$$\begin{aligned} 1\text{st} &= 100 \times 1.002^{120} \\ 2\text{nd} &= 100 \times 1.002^{119} \\ 3\text{rd} &= 100 \times 1.002^{118} \\ &\ \vdots \\ 120\text{th} &= 100 \times 1.002 \end{aligned}$$
The total is:
$$100\left[1.002 + 1.002^2 + \cdots + 1.002^{120}\right]$$
This is a G.P. with $a = 1.002$, $r = 1.002$, $n = 120$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 100 \times 1.002\left[\dfrac{1.002^{120} - 1}{1.002 - 1}\right] \\ &= \$13\,574.32 \text{ (nearest cent)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jason borrows $\$400\,000$ at $7.2\%$ p.a. The interest is compounded monthly on the amount owing. The terms of the loan are that no repayments are made for one year and then equal monthly repayments of $\$M$ are made for another 9 years. Hence the terms of the loan are for 10 years in total.

Each repayment is deducted at the end of the month after the interest has been calculated for the month.

Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.
Show that the amount owing after 15 months from when the loan was taken out is:

$$A_{15} = 400000 \times 1.006^{15} - M\left(1 + 1.006 + 1.006^2\right)$$
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{7.2\%}{12} = 0.6\%$, so each month multiplies by $1.006$.

No repayments are made for the first 12 months:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 400000 \times 1.006 \\ A_2 &= 400000 \times 1.006^2 \\ &\ \vdots \\ A_{12} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{12} \end{aligned}$$
The first repayment is at the end of month 13:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{13} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{13} - M \\ A_{14} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{14} - 1.006M - M \\ A_{15} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{15} - 1.006^2M - 1.006M - M \\ &= 400000 \times 1.006^{15} - M\left(1 + 1.006 + 1.006^2\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jason borrows $\$400\,000$ at $7.2\%$ p.a. The interest is compounded monthly on the amount owing. The terms of the loan are that no repayments are made for one year and then equal monthly repayments of $\$M$ are made for another 9 years. Hence the terms of the loan are for 10 years in total.

Each repayment is deducted at the end of the month after the interest has been calculated for the month.

Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.
Find the value of $M$ if the loan is fully repaid at the end of 10 years.
items.sol:
Following the pattern of part (a), after $n$ months:
$$A_n = 400000 \times 1.006^n - M\left(1 + 1.006 + 1.006^2 + \cdots + 1.006^{n-13}\right)$$
So for $n = 120$:
$$A_{120} = 400000 \times 1.006^{120} - M\left(1 + 1.006 + \cdots + 1.006^{107}\right)$$
The bracket is a G.P. with $a = 1$, $r = 1.006$, $n = 108$.

The loan is repaid, so $A_{120} = 0$:
$$0 = 400000 \times 1.006^{120} - M\left(\dfrac{1.006^{108} - 1}{0.006}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 400000 \times 1.006^{120} \times \dfrac{0.006}{1.006^{108} - 1} \\ &= \$5418.46 \end{aligned}$$

The graph is a parabola with vertex $(-1,-3)$ that opens downwards, so it has the form

$$g(x)=k(x+1)^2-3,\quad k<0$$

Since $f(x)=x^2$, this is $g(x)=k\,f(x+1)-3$.

The graph passes through the $y$-intercept $(0,-5)$.

$$\begin{aligned} -5&=k(0+1)^2-3\\ k&=-2\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ g(x)=-2f(x+1)-3,\quad k=-2,\ b=1,\ c=-3$$

items.part:
Use the graph below to solve the inequality $3-2x-x^2\le 3$.

\exfigure{1593_q1c_1}
items.sol:
The inequality $3-2x-x^2\le 3$ holds where the parabola is on or below the line $y=3$.

The graph meets the line where

$$\begin{aligned} 3-2x-x^2&=3\\ -x(x+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$

so at $x=-2$ and $x=0$. The parabola is below the line outside these points.

$$\therefore\ x\le -2 \text{ or } x\ge 0$$

items.part: Given $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $g(x)=x^2-4$, find the equation of any vertical asymptotes of $f(g(x))$.
items.sol:
Substituting $g(x)$ into $f$:

$$f(g(x))=\dfrac{1}{x^2-4}$$

Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero.

$$\begin{aligned} x^2-4&=0\\ (x-2)(x+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$

The numerator is never zero, so these are asymptotes.

$$\therefore\ x=2 \text{ and } x=-2$$

items.part:
The graph of $f(x)=\cos x$ is horizontally dilated by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and then translated to the left by $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ units to give $g(x)$.
Find the equation of $g(x)$.
items.sol:
A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ replaces $x$ with $2x$:

$$y=\cos 2x$$

A translation left by $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ replaces $x$ with $x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

$$\begin{aligned} g(x)&=\cos\left(2\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)\\ &=\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\\ &=-\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ g(x)=\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=-\sin 2x$$

items.part:
The graph of $f(x)=\cos x$ is horizontally dilated by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and then translated to the left by $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ units to give $g(x)$.
Sketch the graph of $g(x)$ for $[0, 2\pi]$.

Consider the function $f(x)=4x^3-x^4$.
Find the stationary points on the curve $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiating $f(x)=4x^3-x^4$:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=12x^2-4x^3\\ &=4x^2(3-x)\end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

$$f(0)=0,\qquad f(3)=4(27)-81=27$$

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(3,27)$.

Nature: the second derivative is

$$f''(x)=24x-12x^2=12x(2-x)$$

At $x=3$: $f''(3)=12(3)(-1)=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a local maximum.

At $x=0$: $f''(0)=0$, so the test is inconclusive and we test the sign of $f'(x)=4x^2(3-x)$ either side.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(-1)&=4(1)(4)=16>0\\ f'(1)&=4(1)(2)=8>0\end{aligned}$$

The gradient is positive on both sides of $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

$$\therefore\ (3,27)\text{ is a local maximum and }(0,0)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflection}$$
items.final: $(3,27)$ is a local maximum and $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=4x^3-x^4$.
Sketch the graph, showing clearly the stationary points and any axis intercepts.

items.sol:
The function is increasing where $f'(x)>0$, and concave down where $f''(x)<0$.

From the graph of $f'(x)$ (a parabola with $x$-intercepts $-2$ and $2$):
$$f'(x)>0 \text{ for } x<-2 \text{ or } x>2$$
From the graph of $f''(x)$ (a line through the origin with positive gradient):
$$f''(x)<0 \text{ for } x<0$$
Both conditions hold only where $x<-2$.
$$\therefore\ x<-2$$

items.part:
Use the Trapezoidal Rule to find, with five function values and correct to three decimal places, an approximation for the value of:

$$\int_0^2 \sqrt{5^x+2}\;dx$$
items.sol:
Five function values give $4$ strips, so the strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{2-0}{4}=0.5$$
The $x$ values are $0,\ 0.5,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 2$, with $f(x)=\sqrt{5^x+2}$.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 0.5 & 1 & 1.5 & 2 \\ \hline f(x) & 1.7321 & 2.0582 & 2.6458 & 3.6305 & 5.1962 \\ \hline \end{array}$

Using the Trapezoidal Rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(x_0)+2(f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3))+f(x_4)\big]$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 \sqrt{5^x+2}\,dx &\approx \dfrac{0.5}{2}\big[1.7321+5.1962+2(2.0582+2.6458+3.6305)\big] \\ &\approx 5.899 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^2 \sqrt{5^x+2}\,dx\approx 5.899$$

items.part: Given that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x^2-5}}=\dfrac{-2x}{(x^2-5)\sqrt{x^2-5}}$, find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x}{4(x^2-5)\sqrt{x^2-5}}\,dx$
items.sol:
Rewrite the integrand as a multiple of the given derivative:
$$\dfrac{x}{4(x^2-5)\sqrt{x^2-5}}=-\dfrac{1}{8}\cdot\dfrac{-2x}{(x^2-5)\sqrt{x^2-5}}$$
Since the given derivative says $\dfrac{-2x}{(x^2-5)\sqrt{x^2-5}}$ integrates to $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x^2-5}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{x}{4(x^2-5)\sqrt{x^2-5}}\,dx &= -\dfrac{1}{8}\cdot\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x^2-5}}+C \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{x^2-5}}+C \end{aligned}$$

The curves intersect where the $y$ values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x-x^3 &= x \\ 3x-x^3 &= 0 \\ x(3-x^2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=0$ or $x^2=3$.
$$\therefore\ x=0 \text{ or } x=\pm\sqrt{3}$$

From the graph, $y=4x-x^3$ is above $y=x$ for $0<x<\sqrt{3}$, and below it for $-\sqrt{3}<x<0$. The region is symmetric about the origin (both functions are odd), so the two parts have equal area.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\int_0^{\sqrt{3}}\big[(4x-x^3)-x\big]\,dx \\ &= 2\int_0^{\sqrt{3}}(3x-x^3)\,dx \\ &= 2\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= 2\left(\dfrac{9}{2}-\dfrac{9}{4}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=\dfrac{9}{2} \text{ units}^2$$

items.part: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a \sqrt{4x+1}\;dx=\dfrac{13}{3}$, find $a$.
items.sol:
Integrate using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a \sqrt{4x+1}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{(4x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}\right]_0^a \\ &= \dfrac{(4a+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\dfrac{13}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} (4a+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-1 &= 26 \\ (4a+1)^{\frac{3}{2}} &= 27 \\ 4a+1 &= 9 \\ a &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=2$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows an athlete, Paul, who wishes to get from point $A$ (in the ocean) to point $Y$, located on the shore of a straight beach. $P$ is the point on the beach nearest to $A$, such that $AP=2$ km and $PY=2$ km. Paul achieves this by swimming to a point $Q$ located on the beach and running to $Y$.

He is able to swim 1 km in $5\sqrt{5}$ minutes and run 1 km in five minutes.

Let $PQ=x$ km.

\exfigure{1593_q4c_1}
Show that an expression for the time, $T$ minutes, taken by the athlete to reach $Y$ is given by:

$$T=5\sqrt{5}\left(\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)+5(2-x)$$
items.sol:
In right-angled triangle $APQ$, Pythagoras' theorem gives the swimming distance:
$$AQ=\sqrt{x^2+2^2}=\sqrt{x^2+4} \text{ km}$$
Swimming takes $5\sqrt{5}$ minutes per km, so the swimming time is $5\sqrt{5}\left(\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)$ minutes.

The running distance is $QY=PY-PQ=(2-x)$ km, at $5$ minutes per km, so the running time is $5(2-x)$ minutes.
$$\therefore\ T=5\sqrt{5}\left(\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)+5(2-x)$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows an athlete, Paul, who wishes to get from point $A$ (in the ocean) to point $Y$, located on the shore of a straight beach. $P$ is the point on the beach nearest to $A$, such that $AP=2$ km and $PY=2$ km. Paul achieves this by swimming to a point $Q$ located on the beach and running to $Y$.

He is able to swim 1 km in $5\sqrt{5}$ minutes and run 1 km in five minutes.

Let $PQ=x$ km.

\exfigure{1593_q4c_1}
Find the minimum time, in minutes, taken for the athlete to reach point $Y$.
items.sol:
Here $0\le x\le 2$. Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dT}{dx}=\dfrac{5\sqrt{5}\,x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}-5$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dT}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{5}\,x &= \sqrt{x^2+4} \\ 5x^2 &= x^2+4 \\ x^2 &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $x\ge 0$, $x=1$.

The second derivative decides the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2T}{dx^2}=\dfrac{20\sqrt{5}}{(x^2+4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}>0 \text{ for all } x$$
Hence $x=1$ gives a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} T(1) &= 5\sqrt{5}\cdot\sqrt{5}+5(1) \\ &= 25+5 \\ &= 30 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum time}=30 \text{ minutes}$$

From the graph, the curves meet at $x=1$ and $x=2$. Check: $\dfrac{2}{x} = -x+3$ gives $x^2-3x+2=0$, so $x=1$ or $x=2$.

For $1\le x\le 2$ the line is above the curve. For $2\le x\le 4$ the curve is above the line. So the area is
$$A=\int_1^2\left(-x+3-\dfrac{2}{x}\right)dx+\int_2^4\left(\dfrac{2}{x}+x-3\right)dx$$
First integral:
$$\begin{aligned} \left[-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+3x-2\ln x\right]_1^2 &= (-2+6-2\ln 2)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}+3\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{2}-2\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Second integral:
$$\begin{aligned} \left[2\ln x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}-3x\right]_2^4 &= (2\ln 4+8-12)-(2\ln 2+2-6) \\ &= 4\ln 2-4-2\ln 2+4 \\ &= 2\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Adding,
$$A=\dfrac{3}{2}-2\ln 2+2\ln 2$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{3}{2}\text{ units}^2$$

items.part: Differentiate $e^{x^2}$.
items.sol:
Use the chain rule with $u=x^2$, so $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u}=e^{u}\dfrac{du}{dx}$.
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x^2}\right)=2x\,e^{x^2}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0} x e^{x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x^2}\right)=2x\,e^{x^2}$, so $\displaystyle\int x e^{x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{x^2}+C$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^{0} x e^{x^2}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}e^{x^2}\right]_{-1}^{0} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}e^{0}-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{1} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_{-1}^{0} x e^{x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{1-e}{2}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=x^2e^{-x}$ at $x=1$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 2x e^{-x}-x^2e^{-x} \\ &= e^{-x}(2x-x^2) \end{aligned}$$
At $x=1$:
$$y=e^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{e},\qquad \dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{-1}(2-1)=\dfrac{1}{e}$$
The tangent through $\left(1,\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$ with gradient $\dfrac{1}{e}$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{1}{e} &= \dfrac{1}{e}(x-1) \\ y &= \dfrac{x}{e} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{x}{e}$$

items.part:
Find
$\displaystyle\int 40-e^{-2x+4}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{-2x+4}=-2e^{-2x+4}$, we have $\displaystyle\int e^{-2x+4}\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2x+4}$.
$$\therefore\ \int 40-e^{-2x+4}\,dx=40x+\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2x+4}+C$$

items.part:
Find
$\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^3-2x}{x^4-4x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
The derivative of the denominator is $4x^3-8x=4(x^3-2x)$, which is $4$ times the numerator.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{x^3-2x}{x^4-4x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{4}\int \dfrac{4x^3-8x}{x^4-4x^2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\ln\left|x^4-4x^2\right|+C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{4}\ln\left|x^4-4x^2\right|+C$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \tan^2 x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Use the identity $\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \tan^2 x\,dx &= \int (\sec^2 x - 1)\,dx \\ &= \tan x - x + C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int \tan^2 x\,dx = \tan x - x + C$$

items.part: Find the $x$ value of the maximum turning point on the curve $f(x)=\cos x-\sin x$ between $[0,2\pi]$.
items.sol:
Turning points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x) = -\sin x - \cos x$$
$$\begin{aligned} -\sin x - \cos x &= 0 \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
For $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, $\tan x = -1$ gives $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ or $x = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$.

The second derivative decides the nature of each point.
$$f''(x) = -\cos x + \sin x$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \sqrt{2} > 0 &&\text{minimum}\\ f''\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = -\sqrt{2} < 0 &&\text{maximum} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=\dfrac{2x}{\cos x}$, leaving your answer in terms of $\sec x$ and $\tan x$.
items.sol:
Write $y = \dfrac{2x}{\cos x} = 2x\sec x$ and use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=\sec x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\sec x\tan x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 2\sec x + 2x\sec x\tan x \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2\sec x + 2x\sec x\tan x$$

items.part:
The volume of water in a rock pool at time $t$ hours is $V$ litres. The rate of change of the volume is given by $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=40\sin(0.5t)$.

At time $t=0$, the volume of water in the pool is 100 litres.

Find the volume of water when $t=2$ to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
Integrate the rate of change to find $V$.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \int 40\sin(0.5t)\,dt \\ &= -80\cos(0.5t) + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $V=100$:
$$\begin{aligned} 100 &= -80\cos 0 + C \\ C &= 180 \end{aligned}$$
So $V = 180 - 80\cos(0.5t)$. When $t = 2$ (angle in radians):
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 180 - 80\cos 1 \\ &\approx 136.78 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ V \approx 137 \text{ litres}$$

items.part:
The amount of paracetamol $P$, in the human body, decreases from an initial amount of $P_0=400$mg according to the equation $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-0.12P$ where $P$ is measured in mg and $t$ is the time in hours.
Show that $P=400e^{-0.12t}$ is a solution to the equation $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-0.12P$
items.sol:
Differentiate $P = 400e^{-0.12t}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 400\times(-0.12)e^{-0.12t} \\ &= -0.12\left(400e^{-0.12t}\right) \\ &= -0.12P \end{aligned}$$
Also, when $t=0$, $P = 400e^{0} = 400 = P_0$.
$$\therefore\ P = 400e^{-0.12t} \text{ is a solution of } \dfrac{dP}{dt}=-0.12P$$

items.part:
The amount of paracetamol $P$, in the human body, decreases from an initial amount of $P_0=400$mg according to the equation $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-0.12P$ where $P$ is measured in mg and $t$ is the time in hours.
Find the time taken to the nearest minute to have 250mg of paracetamol left in the body.
items.sol:
Put $P = 250$ in $P = 400e^{-0.12t}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 250 &= 400e^{-0.12t} \\ e^{-0.12t} &= 0.625 \\ -0.12t &= \ln 0.625 \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 0.625}{-0.12} \\ &\approx 3.9167 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
Convert to minutes:
$$3.9167\times 60 \approx 235.0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the time is } 235 \text{ minutes}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^3 x$.
items.sol:
Use the chain rule with $u=\sin x$, so $\sin^3 x = u^3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^3 x &= 3\sin^2 x\cdot\cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^3 x = 3\sin^2 x\cos x$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int \cos x\sin^2 x\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^3 x = 3\sin^2 x\cos x$, so integrating both sides:
$$\int 3\sin^2 x\cos x\,dx = \sin^3 x + C$$
Divide by 3:
$$\therefore\ \int \cos x\sin^2 x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{3}\sin^3 x + C$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line.

Its velocity $v$ ms$^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=\dfrac{6}{t+1}-3$
Find the acceleration of the particle when the particle is stationary.
items.sol:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{6}{t+1} - 3 &= 0 \\ t + 1 &= 2 \\ t &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, with $v = 6(t+1)^{-1} - 3$.
$$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -\dfrac{6}{(t+1)^2}$$
When $t=1$:
$$a = -\dfrac{6}{4} = -\dfrac{3}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the acceleration is } -\dfrac{3}{2} \text{ ms}^{-2}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line.

Its velocity $v$ ms$^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=\dfrac{6}{t+1}-3$
Sketch a graph of $v$ against $t$ for $t\geq 0$, indicating intercepts and asymptote(s) where applicable.
items.sol:
Intercepts and asymptote:
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:\ v &= 6 - 3 = 3 \\ v=0:\ t &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
As $t \to \infty$, $\dfrac{6}{t+1} \to 0$, so $v \to -3$: the horizontal asymptote is $v=-3$.

\exfigure{1604_q5_s1}

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line.

Its velocity $v$ ms$^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=\dfrac{6}{t+1}-3$
Find the exact distance travelled by the particle in the first 5 seconds.

(answer to 2 decimal places).
items.sol:
From the graph, $v \ge 0$ for $0 \le t \le 1$ and $v < 0$ for $1 < t \le 5$. The particle turns round at $t=1$, so the two stages are found separately.

An antiderivative of $v$ is
$$x = 6\ln(t+1) - 3t$$
Distance in the first second:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 v\,dt &= \big[6\ln(t+1) - 3t\big]_0^1 \\ &= (6\ln 2 - 3) - 0 \\ &= 6\ln 2 - 3 \end{aligned}$$
Displacement from $t=1$ to $t=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5 v\,dt &= (6\ln 6 - 15) - (6\ln 2 - 3) \\ &= 6\ln 3 - 12 \end{aligned}$$
This is negative ($\approx -5.41$), so the distance in this stage is $12 - 6\ln 3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total distance} &= (6\ln 2 - 3) + (12 - 6\ln 3) \\ &= 9 + 6\ln 2 - 6\ln 3 \\ &= 9 - 6\ln\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance} = 9 - 6\ln\dfrac{3}{2} \approx 6.57 \text{ m}$$

items.part: Factorise fully, $x - xy^2$.
items.sol:
Remove the common factor $x$, then use the difference of two squares.
$$\begin{aligned} x - xy^2 &= x(1 - y^2) \\ &= x(1-y)(1+y) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{x+1}\right)$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=x+1\\ u'&=2x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{x+1}\right) &= \dfrac{(x+1)\cdot 2x - x^2\cdot 1}{(x+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^2 + 2x - x^2}{(x+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2 + 2x}{(x+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate the function, $y = x^2 e^{2x}$ leaving your answer in simplest factored form.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= x^2(2e^{2x}) + e^{2x}(2x) \\ &= 2xe^{2x}(x+1) \end{aligned}$$

The arc length formula is $l = r\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10 &= 4\theta \\ \theta &= 2.5 \text{ radians} \end{aligned}$$

The sector area formula is $A = \dfrac12 r^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac12 \times 4^2 \times 2.5 \\ &= 20 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{3}{2x+1}\, dx$.
items.sol:
Write the integrand so the numerator is the derivative of $2x+1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \int_0^2 \dfrac{3}{2x+1}\,dx &= \dfrac32\int_0^2 \dfrac{2}{2x+1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac32\Big[\ln(2x+1)\Big]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac32\ln 5 - \dfrac32\ln 1 \\ &= \dfrac32\ln 5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: The gradient function of a curve is $f'(x) = 4x + 3$. The curve passes through the point $(-2, 5)$. Find $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Integrate the gradient function.
$$f(x) = 2x^2 + 3x + C$$
The curve passes through $(-2, 5)$, so $f(-2) = 5$.
$$\begin{aligned} 5 &= 2(-2)^2 + 3(-2) + C \\ 5 &= 8 - 6 + C \\ C &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x) = 2x^2 + 3x + 3$$

items.part:
The table shows the future value of an annuity of \$1 for a selection of interest rates per period and investment terms. The contributions are made at the end of each period.

\exfigure{1310_q11g_1}
Tom invests \$750 at the end of each quarter into an account which earns $8\%$ per annum with interest compounded quarterly.

He does this for 3 years.

Find the future value of Tom's investment.
items.sol:
Interest is compounded quarterly, so the rate per period is $\dfrac{8}{4} = 2\%$ and the number of periods is $3\times 4 = 12$.

From the table, the factor for $2\%$ and $12$ periods is $13.4121$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Future value} &= 750 \times 13.4121 \\ &= \$10059.08 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The table shows the future value of an annuity of \$1 for a selection of interest rates per period and investment terms. The contributions are made at the end of each period.

\exfigure{1310_q11g_1}
His brother, Jake, finds an account that will earn him $12\%$ per annum. The interest will also be compounded quarterly.

However, Jake is only prepared to contribute for 2 years.

Find the amount that he must contribute quarterly if he is to achieve the same future value as Tom.
items.sol:
For Jake, the rate per period is $\dfrac{12}{4} = 3\%$ and the number of periods is $2\times 4 = 8$.

From the table, the factor is $8.8923$. Let his quarterly contribution be $\$M$.
$$\begin{aligned} M \times 8.8923 &= 10059.08 \\ M &= \$1131.21 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jamjet Industries produce galvanised bolts for the roofing industry. Due to manufacturing constraints, the maximum number of bolts they can produce in a month is 120 000.

The cost of production is \$50 000 plus 95 cents per bolt.

The bolts are sold for \$1.75 each and the graph that represents Jamjet's revenue, $R$, appears on the axes below.

\exfigure{1310_q12a_1}
Find the linear equation for the cost, $C$, of producing $n$ bolts.
items.sol:
The cost is a fixed \$50 000 plus \$0.95 per bolt.
$$C = 50000 + 0.95n$$

items.part:
Jamjet Industries produce galvanised bolts for the roofing industry. Due to manufacturing constraints, the maximum number of bolts they can produce in a month is 120 000.

The cost of production is \$50 000 plus 95 cents per bolt.

The bolts are sold for \$1.75 each and the graph that represents Jamjet's revenue, $R$, appears on the axes below.

\exfigure{1310_q12a_1}
What is the practical significance of the gradient of the line in (a) ?
items.sol: The gradient of the cost line is $0.95$, so it represents the cost of production per bolt (the rate at which cost increases for each extra bolt).
items.final: The gradient 0.95 is the cost of production per bolt (cost increase for each extra bolt).

items.part:
Jamjet Industries produce galvanised bolts for the roofing industry. Due to manufacturing constraints, the maximum number of bolts they can produce in a month is 120 000.

The cost of production is \$50 000 plus 95 cents per bolt.

The bolts are sold for \$1.75 each and the graph that represents Jamjet's revenue, $R$, appears on the axes below.

\exfigure{1310_q12a_1}
Find the number of bolts Jamjet must sell in a month to break even.
items.sol:
Break-even occurs when revenue equals cost, $1.75n = C$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1.75n &= 50000 + 0.95n \\ 0.8n &= 50000 \\ n &= 62500 \end{aligned}$$
Jamjet must sell 62 500 bolts.

items.part:
Jamjet Industries produce galvanised bolts for the roofing industry. Due to manufacturing constraints, the maximum number of bolts they can produce in a month is 120 000.

The cost of production is \$50 000 plus 95 cents per bolt.

The bolts are sold for \$1.75 each and the graph that represents Jamjet's revenue, $R$, appears on the axes below.

\exfigure{1310_q12a_1}
What is the maximum monthly profit attainable by Jamjet ?
items.sol:
Profit is revenue minus cost.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Profit} &= 1.75n - (50000 + 0.95n) \\ &= 0.8n - 50000 \end{aligned}$$
Profit increases with $n$, so it is greatest at the maximum production $n = 120000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Profit} &= 0.8\times 120000 - 50000 \\ &= \$46000 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number plane below shows the interval joining the points $A(-5, -4)$ and $B(-1, -3)$.

The line, $l$, is drawn through $B$ so as to be perpendicular to $AB$ and meets the $x$-axis at $C$ and the $y$-axis at $D$.

Find the area of triangle $COD$.

\exfigure{1310_q12b_1}
items.sol:
Gradient of $AB$:
$$m_{AB} = \dfrac{-3-(-4)}{-1-(-5)} = \dfrac14$$
The line $l$ is perpendicular to $AB$, so $m_l = -4$.

It passes through $B(-1,-3)$, so use $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y + 3 &= -4(x+1) \\ y &= -4x - 7 \end{aligned}$$
Point $D$ is the $y$-intercept, so $D$ is $(0,-7)$.

Point $C$ is where $y = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -4x - 7 \\ x &= -\dfrac74 \end{aligned}$$
So $C$ is $\left(-\dfrac74, 0\right)$.

Triangle $COD$ is right-angled at $O$, with $OD = 7$ and $OC = \dfrac74$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac12 \times \dfrac74 \times 7 \\ &= \dfrac{49}{8} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The total is 80 and 12 people did not holiday, so $80 - 12 = 68$ people holidayed.

Both: $42 + 36 - 68 = 10$.

Interstate only: $42 - 10 = 32$.

NSW only: $36 - 10 = 26$.

\exfigure{1310_q12c_s1}

Ten people holidayed both interstate and within NSW.
$$P(\text{I}\cap\text{N}) = \dfrac{10}{80} = \dfrac18$$

Of the 80 people, $80 - 12 = 68$ have travelled, and 36 of them holidayed within NSW.
$$P(\text{N}\mid\text{traveller}) = \dfrac{36}{68} = \dfrac{9}{17}$$

$42$ people went interstate, so $80-42 = 38$ did not. Exactly one interstate traveller means the order is (I, not I) or (not I, I), without replacement.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly one I}) &= P(\text{I},\overline{\text{I}}) + P(\overline{\text{I}},\text{I}) \\ &= \dfrac{42}{80}\times\dfrac{38}{79} + \dfrac{38}{80}\times\dfrac{42}{79} \\ &= \dfrac{399}{790} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle, initially at the origin, is moving in a straight line. Its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, after $t$ seconds is given by $v = 2 - 2t$.
Find the initial velocity.
items.sol:
Substitute $t = 0$ into $v = 2 - 2t$.
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 2 - 2(0) \\ &= 2 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle, initially at the origin, is moving in a straight line. Its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, after $t$ seconds is given by $v = 2 - 2t$.
Find when the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2-2t \\ 2t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1 \text{ second}$$

items.part:
A particle, initially at the origin, is moving in a straight line. Its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, after $t$ seconds is given by $v = 2 - 2t$.
Find when the particle is next at the origin.
items.sol:
Position is the integral of velocity, so $x=\displaystyle\int v\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int (2-2t)\,dt \\ &= 2t - t^2 + C \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$, giving $C=0$.
$$x = 2t - t^2$$
The particle is at the origin when $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2t - t^2 \\ &= t(2-t) \end{aligned}$$
So $t=0$ or $t=2$. The particle is next at the origin when $t\ne 0$.
$$\therefore\ t = 2 \text{ seconds}$$

items.part:
A particle, initially at the origin, is moving in a straight line. Its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, after $t$ seconds is given by $v = 2 - 2t$.
Find the distance travelled in the first 4 seconds.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction when it comes to rest, at $t=1$, so find $x$ at $t=0$, $1$ and $4$ using $x=2t-t^2$.

When $t=0$, $x=0$ (given in the initial conditions).

When $t=1$:
$$x = 2(1)-1^2 = 1$$
When $t=4$:
$$x = 2(4)-4^2 = -8$$
So the particle starts at the origin, moves right to $x=1$ and then travels left to $x=-8$.

Distance travelled:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 1 + (1+8) \\ &= 10 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle travels a total of } 10 \text{ m in the first 4 seconds}$$

The probabilities in a distribution sum to 1.
$$\dfrac{32}{243}+k+k+\dfrac{40}{243}+\dfrac{10}{243}+\dfrac{1}{243}=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2k+\dfrac{83}{243} &= 1 \\ 2k &= \dfrac{160}{243} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{80}{243}$$

Using $\mathrm{E}(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$ and $k=\dfrac{80}{243}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}(X) &= 0\left(\dfrac{32}{243}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+3\left(\dfrac{40}{243}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{10}{243}\right)+5\left(\dfrac{1}{243}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{405}{243} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{3} \end{aligned}$$

Using $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathrm{E}(X^2)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=\dfrac{5}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(X) &= \left[0\left(\dfrac{32}{243}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+9\left(\dfrac{40}{243}\right)+16\left(\dfrac{10}{243}\right)+25\left(\dfrac{1}{243}\right)\right]-\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{10}{9} \end{aligned}$$
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
$$\therefore\ \sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{9}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{3}$$

items.part:
A flagpole, $BD$, lies on flat level ground.

It is supported by two cables, $AD$ and $CD$ as shown below. The cable $AD$ is inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal and is tied 18 metres from the foot of the pole.

The second cable is tied at a point, $C$, 12m from $A$ and on a bearing of $210^\circ$ from $A$.

\exfigure{1310_q13c_1}

Find $\theta$, correct to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
In the right-angled triangle $BAD$, $\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{BD}{18}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &= \dfrac{BD}{18} \\ BD &= \dfrac{18}{\sqrt{3}} = 6\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB=18$, $AC=12$ and $\angle BAC=60^\circ$. By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2 &= 18^2+12^2-2(18)(12)\cos 60^\circ \\ &= 468-216 \\ &= 252 \end{aligned}$$
$$BC=\sqrt{252}=6\sqrt{7}$$
In the right-angled triangle $BCD$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{BD}{BC} \\ &= \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{6\sqrt{7}} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{7}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta\approx 33^\circ$$

items.part:
The function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{6} - \dfrac{x^2}{4} - 3x + 1$ is defined for $x$ in the domain $[-4, 6]$.
Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate to find the stationary points.
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}-3$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}-3 \\ 0 &= x^2-x-6 \\ &= (x-3)(x+2) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-2$ or $x=3$.

The $y$ values:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-2) &= \dfrac{(-2)^3}{6}-\dfrac{(-2)^2}{4}-3(-2)+1 \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{3}-1+6+1 \\ &= 4\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(3) &= \dfrac{3^3}{6}-\dfrac{3^2}{4}-3(3)+1 \\ &= \dfrac{27}{6}-\dfrac{9}{4}-9+1 \\ &= -5\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Use the second derivative to determine the nature.
$$f''(x)=x-\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-2) &= -2-\dfrac{1}{2}=-2\dfrac{1}{2}<0 \\ f''(3) &= 3-\dfrac{1}{2}=2\dfrac{1}{2}>0 \end{aligned}$$
So there is a local maximum at $\left(-2,\,4\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ and a local minimum at $\left(3,\,-5\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$.
items.final: Local maximum at $\left(-2, 4\tfrac{2}{3}\right)$; local minimum at $\left(3, -5\tfrac{3}{4}\right)$

items.part:
The function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{6} - \dfrac{x^2}{4} - 3x + 1$ is defined for $x$ in the domain $[-4, 6]$.
Find the absolute maximum of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
The absolute maximum on $[-4,6]$ is the greatest of the local maximum and the endpoint values. The local maximum is $4\dfrac{2}{3}$, so evaluate the endpoints.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-4) &= \dfrac{(-4)^3}{6}-\dfrac{(-4)^2}{4}-3(-4)+1 \\ &= -10\dfrac{2}{3}-4+12+1 \\ &= -1\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(6) &= \dfrac{6^3}{6}-\dfrac{6^2}{4}-3(6)+1 \\ &= 36-9-18+1 \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the absolute maximum of } f(x) \text{ is } 10$$
