The percentage results of a university entrance examination are normally distributed with a mean mark is 60 and the standard deviation is 8.
If Jimmy's mark corresponds to a negative $z$-score in the range, $-1 < z < 0$ give a possible value for Jimmy's mark.
items.sol:
Here $\mu=60$ and $\sigma=8$. A $z$-score between $-1$ and $0$ means the mark lies between $\mu-\sigma=52$ and $\mu=60$.

Any mark in the range $52<x<60$ is possible, for example $56$.

items.part:
The percentage results of a university entrance examination are normally distributed with a mean mark is 60 and the standard deviation is 8.
Tyler obtains a result of $72\%$. Show that his $z$-score is 1.5.
items.sol:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{72-60}{8} \\ &= 1.5 \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
The percentage results of a university entrance examination are normally distributed with a mean mark is 60 and the standard deviation is 8.
Zoe's $z$-score was 1. What was her percentage mark?
items.sol:
Rearranging the $z$-score formula, $x=\mu+z\sigma$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 60+1(8) \\ &= 68 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Zoe's mark was } 68\%$$

items.part:
The percentage results of a university entrance examination are normally distributed with a mean mark is 60 and the standard deviation is 8.
When Tyler was sent his results, he was informed that his mark was better than $93.3\%$ of candidates.

The examination was completed by 85000 students. The shaded area below represents those students whose mark was higher than Zoe's but lower than Tyler's. How many students are represented by the shaded area?

\exfigure{1310_q14c_1}
items.sol:
By the empirical rule, a $z$-score of 1 means Zoe's result is better than $50\%+34\%=84\%$ of scores.

Tyler's result is better than $93.3\%$ of scores, so the percentage between Zoe and Tyler is
$$93.3\%-84\%=9.3\%$$
Students represented by the shaded region:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 9.3\%\times 85000 \\ &= 7905 \end{aligned}$$

An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off after a period of time.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation,

$$T = 22 + 162(1.2)^{-0.5t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.
What is the temperature of the iron 6 minutes after it has switched off ? Give your answer to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Substitute $t=6$ into the model.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 22+162(1.2)^{-0.5(6)} \\ &\approx 116^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off after a period of time.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation,

$$T = 22 + 162(1.2)^{-0.5t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.
At what rate is the temperature of the iron's surface changing after 6 minutes ?
items.sol:
The rate of change is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{u}\right)=a^{u}\ln a\cdot u'$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= 162(-0.5)(1.2)^{-0.5t}(\ln 1.2) \\ &= -81(1.2)^{-0.5t}(\ln 1.2) \end{aligned}$$
When $t=6$:
$$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-81(1.2)^{-0.5(6)}(\ln 1.2)\approx -8.5^\circ\text{C per minute}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows the beginning of a series of concentric circles. The radius of the inner most circle is 1 unit. The radius of each circle moving outwards, is 1 more than the previous circle.

The area between two concentric circles is called an annulus. The area of the annulus marked $A$ is $3\pi$ square units. The area of the annulus marked $B$ is $5\pi$ square units. The area of the annulus marked $C$ is $7\pi$ square units and so on.

\exfigure{1310_q15c_1}
Find the area of the $10^{\text{th}}$ annulus.
items.sol:
The areas of the annuli moving outwards form the arithmetic sequence $3\pi,\ 5\pi,\ 7\pi,\ \ldots$ with $a=3\pi$ and $d=2\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ T_{10} &= 3\pi+(10-1)2\pi \\ &= 21\pi \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area of the } 10^{\text{th}} \text{ annulus is } 21\pi \text{ square units}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows the beginning of a series of concentric circles. The radius of the inner most circle is 1 unit. The radius of each circle moving outwards, is 1 more than the previous circle.

The area between two concentric circles is called an annulus. The area of the annulus marked $A$ is $3\pi$ square units. The area of the annulus marked $B$ is $5\pi$ square units. The area of the annulus marked $C$ is $7\pi$ square units and so on.

\exfigure{1310_q15c_1}
Show that the sum of the first $n$ annuli is found by $S_n = \pi n^2 + 2n\pi$
items.sol:
The sum of $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$, with $a=3\pi$ and $d=2\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(3\pi)+(n-1)2\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[3\pi+(n-1)\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[3\pi+n\pi-\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[n\pi+2\pi\right] \\ &= \pi n^2+2n\pi \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
The diagram shows the beginning of a series of concentric circles. The radius of the inner most circle is 1 unit. The radius of each circle moving outwards, is 1 more than the previous circle.

The area between two concentric circles is called an annulus. The area of the annulus marked $A$ is $3\pi$ square units. The area of the annulus marked $B$ is $5\pi$ square units. The area of the annulus marked $C$ is $7\pi$ square units and so on.

\exfigure{1310_q15c_1}
What is the minimum number of annuli needed for a combined area of $300\ \text{u}^2$ ?
items.sol:
We need the combined area to be at least $300$.
$$\pi n^2+2n\pi\ge 300$$
$$\pi n^2+2n\pi-300\ge 0$$
Solve $\pi n^2+2n\pi-300=0$ using the quadratic formula.
$$n=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}=\dfrac{-2\pi\pm\sqrt{4\pi^2+1200\pi}}{2\pi}$$
Since $n>0$, only the positive root applies.
$$n=\dfrac{-2\pi+\sqrt{4\pi^2+1200\pi}}{2\pi}\approx 8.8$$
The quadratic $f(n)=\pi n^2+2n\pi-300$ is an upward parabola, so $f(n)\ge 0$ for $n\ge 8.8$. Since $n$ is a whole number, the minimum is $n=9$.
$$\therefore\ 9 \text{ annuli are required for a total area of } 300 \text{ u}^2$$

items.part:
Nick chooses an integer, $x$, between 1 and 20 at random.

He reduces this number by 1, 4 and 9 in turn and then multiplies to find the product, $P$.
Show that, $P = x^3 - 14x^2 + 49x - 36$
items.sol:
Reducing $x$ by 1, 4 and 9 gives the factors, so $P=(x-1)(x-4)(x-9)$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= (x-1)(x^2-13x+36) \\ &= x^3-13x^2+36x-x^2+13x-36 \\ &= x^3-14x^2+49x-36 \end{aligned}$$
as required.

items.part:
Nick chooses an integer, $x$, between 1 and 20 at random.

He reduces this number by 1, 4 and 9 in turn and then multiplies to find the product, $P$.
Find the minimum value of $P$.
items.sol:
Minimum values occur where $P'(x)=0$.
$$P'(x)=3x^2-28x+49$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3x^2-28x+49 \\ &= (3x-7)(x-7) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac{7}{3}$ or $x=7$. Since $x$ is an integer, $x=7$ only.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$P''(x)=6x-28$$
When $x=7$, $P''=14>0$, so $x=7$ gives a minimum.

The minimum value:
$$\begin{aligned} P(7) &= (7-1)(7-4)(7-9) \\ &= -36 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum value of } P \text{ is } -36$$

Jelena retires with a balance in her superannuation account of \$700 000.

The fund earns interest at the rate of $3.6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.

At the end of each month, Jelena withdraws \$4000 from the account.

The amount, $A_n$, left in her fund after the $n^{th}$ withdrawal is given by,

$$A_n = 700000(1.003)^n - 4000\left\{1 + 1.003 + (1.003)^2 + \ldots + (1.003)^{n-1}\right\}$$

(Do NOT prove this result)

Find, correct to the nearest month, the time taken for the balance in the fund to reduce to \$400 000.
items.sol:
The balance is to reduce to $\$400\,000$. The bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.003$ and $n$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}$.
$$400000=700000(1.003)^n-4000\left(\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}\right)$$
Multiply both sides by $0.003$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1200 &= 2100(1.003)^n-4000\left(1.003^n-1\right) \\ &= 4000-1900(1.003)^n \end{aligned}$$
$$1.003^n=\dfrac{28}{19}$$
Take logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{28}{19}\right)}{\ln 1.003} \\ &\approx 129.448963 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n\approx 129 \text{ months}$$

With 3 function values the strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{7-1}{2}=3$$
so the $x$ values are $1$, $4$ and $7$. By the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{3}{2}\left[\ln 1+2(\ln 4)+\ln 7\right] \\ &\approx 7.078 \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x) &= x\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)+\ln x\,(1) \\ &= 1+\ln x \end{aligned}$$

From (b), $x\ln x$ is an antiderivative of $1+\ln x$.
$$\int_1^7(1+\ln x)\,dx=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7$$
$$\int_1^7 1\,dx+\int_1^7\ln x\,dx=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7$$
Rearranging:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^7\ln x\,dx &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\int_1^7 1\,dx \\ &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\Big[x\Big]_1^7 \\ &= (7\ln 7-0)-(7-1) \\ &= 7\ln 7-6 \end{aligned}$$

The trapezoidal estimate from (a) approximates the integral in (c).
$$\begin{aligned} 7\ln 7-6 &\approx 7.078 \\ 7\ln 7 &\approx 13.078 \\ \ln 7 &\approx 1.87 \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:

In a chess tournament, each player has a 'chess rating', which is a value from 1600 to 2000.

Danny wants to know if there is a correlation between the number of years a player has spent playing chess and their chess rating.

Danny randomly surveyed 10 players at the tournament. The results are shown in the table.

\extable{1312_q12_t1}

Beth, a competitor in the tournament, has spent 5 years playing chess.

Use the equation of the least-squares regression line for this data set to determine Beth's chess rating. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
items.sol:
The least-squares regression line has the form $y = Bx + A$.

From the calculator, $A \approx 1554.49$ and $B \approx 34.64$, so
$$y = 34.64x + 1554.49$$
When $x=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 34.64\times5+1554.49 \\ &\approx 1727.69 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore, Beth's chess rating is predicted to be $1728$.

items.part:
A tennis arena has a maximum capacity of 15000 spectators. The number of spectators, $N$, and the ticket price in dollars, $P$, are modelled using the linear relationship $N = m \times P + c$, where $m$ and $c$ are constants.

According to the arena's records, the following is known.

\begin{itemize}
\item When the price of a ticket is \$50, the attendance averages 12500 spectators.
\item When the price of a ticket is \$35, the attendance averages 14000 spectators.
\end{itemize}
By developing and solving a pair of simultaneous equations, show that the number of spectators as a function of ticket price can be expressed as $N = -100P + 17500$.
items.sol:
Substitute the two known values into $N = mP + c$.

When $P=50$, $N=12500$:
$$12500 = 50m+c \qquad (1)$$
When $P=35$, $N=14000$:
$$14000 = 35m+c \qquad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 1500 &= -15m \\ m &= -100 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 12500 &= 50(-100)+c \\ c &= 17500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ N = -100P+17500$$

items.part:
A tennis arena has a maximum capacity of 15000 spectators. The number of spectators, $N$, and the ticket price in dollars, $P$, are modelled using the linear relationship $N = m \times P + c$, where $m$ and $c$ are constants.

According to the arena's records, the following is known.

\begin{itemize}
\item When the price of a ticket is \$50, the attendance averages 12500 spectators.
\item When the price of a ticket is \$35, the attendance averages 14000 spectators.
\end{itemize}
The revenue generated from an event, $R$, is calculated using $R = N \times P$.

What is the maximum revenue generated from this event?
items.sol:
Revenue is
$$R = (-100P+17500)P = -100P^2+17500P$$
This is a concave-down quadratic, so the maximum is at the vertex:
$$P = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = \dfrac{-17500}{2(-100)} = 87.5$$
When $P=87.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} R &= -100(87.5)^2+17500(87.5) \\ &= \$765\,625 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum revenue} = \$765\,625$$

items.part:
A tennis arena has a maximum capacity of 15000 spectators. The number of spectators, $N$, and the ticket price in dollars, $P$, are modelled using the linear relationship $N = m \times P + c$, where $m$ and $c$ are constants.

According to the arena's records, the following is known.

\begin{itemize}
\item When the price of a ticket is \$50, the attendance averages 12500 spectators.
\item When the price of a ticket is \$35, the attendance averages 14000 spectators.
\end{itemize}
The manager of this event wants the tennis arena to be filled with 15000 spectators.

Show that this will result in a revenue loss of \$390625.
items.sol:
When $N=15000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 15000 &= -100P+17500 \\ P &= 25 \end{aligned}$$
Revenue at this price:
$$\begin{aligned} R &= -100(25)^2+17500(25) \\ &= \$375\,000 \end{aligned}$$
Revenue loss:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{loss} &= 765\,625-375\,000 \\ &= \$390\,625 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = \dfrac{1}{4x+1}$ at the point $(0, 1)$.
items.sol:
Write $y = (4x+1)^{-1}$ and differentiate using the chain rule:
$$y' = -4(4x+1)^{-2} = \dfrac{-4}{(4x+1)^2}$$
When $x=0$:
$$y' = \dfrac{-4}{(4\times0+1)^2} = -4$$
The tangent at $(0,1)$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= -4(x-0) \\ y &= -4x+1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(x^2\right)$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on $\ln\left(x^2\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac12\times\dfrac{2x}{x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x}{x^2} \\ &= \dfrac1x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y = \dfrac{e^x}{\sin x}$ with respect to $x$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{x} & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=e^{x} & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\sin x\cdot e^x - e^x\cos x}{\sin^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(\sin x-\cos x)}{\sin^2 x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} x + \sin x \, dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} (x+\sin x)\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\cos x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^2}{2}-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)-\left(0-\cos 0\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi^2}{32}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+1 \end{aligned}$$

The point $(-1,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection: $f'(-1)=0$ and the concavity changes from down to up.

items.part: Solve the equation $\log_{10}(x - 21) = 2 - \log_{10}x$.
items.sol:
The logarithms need $x-21>0$ and $x>0$, so $x>21$.

Collect the logs on one side:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(x-21)+\log_{10}x &= 2 \\ \log_{10}[x(x-21)] &= 2 \\ x(x-21) &= 10^2 \\ x^2-21x-100 &= 0 \\ (x-25)(x+4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-4$ or $x=25$.

Since $x>21$, $x=-4$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x = 25$$

Shirley uses her car every day. Sometimes, she needs a few attempts to start her car. Let the discrete random variable $X$ represent the number of attempts needed.

The probability function for the random variable $X$ is given by

The probabilities sum to $1$. Each term is half the previous one:

A teacher surveyed his class of 24 students about the subjects that they have chosen to study in the following year.

The results indicate that:

\begin{itemize}
\item 8 students chose to study neither Physics nor Chemistry
\item 8 students chose to study Chemistry
\item 12 students chose to study Physics.

Draw a Venn diagram showing this information.
items.sol:
Using $|\text{CHE}\cup\text{PHY}|=24-8=16$ and
$$|\text{CHE}\cup\text{PHY}|=|\text{CHE}|+|\text{PHY}|-|\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}|$$
we get $16=8+12-|\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}|$, so $|\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}|=4$.

items.part:
A teacher surveyed his class of 24 students about the subjects that they have chosen to study in the following year.

The results indicate that:

\begin{itemize}
\item 8 students chose to study neither Physics nor Chemistry
\item 8 students chose to study Chemistry
\item 12 students chose to study Physics.
\end{itemize}
A student choosing to study Chemistry is event 1. A student choosing to study Physics is event 2.

If a student is chosen at random, determine whether these events are independent of each other.
items.sol:
From the Venn diagram:
$$P(\text{PHY})=\dfrac{12}{24}=\dfrac{1}{2},\quad P(\text{CHE})=\dfrac{8}{24}=\dfrac{1}{3},\quad P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY})=\dfrac{4}{24}=\dfrac{1}{6}$$
Test for independence:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{PHY})\times P(\text{CHE}) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6} \\ &= P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}) \end{aligned}$$
Since $P(\text{CHE})\times P(\text{PHY})=P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY})$, the two events are independent.

items.part:
A teacher surveyed his class of 24 students about the subjects that they have chosen to study in the following year.

The results indicate that:

\begin{itemize}
\item 8 students chose to study neither Physics nor Chemistry
\item 8 students chose to study Chemistry
\item 12 students chose to study Physics.
\end{itemize}
The entire year group is given the same survey. The results indicate that:

\begin{itemize}
\item the probability that a student chose to study Chemistry is $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item the probability that a student chose to study Physics is $\dfrac{2}{5}$
\item given that a student chose to study Chemistry, the probability that they chose to study Physics is $\dfrac{3}{7}$.
\end{itemize}

Calculate the probability that a student picked at random has chosen to study Chemistry or Physics.
items.sol:
Using the addition rule and $P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY})=P(\text{CHE})\times P(\text{PHY}\mid\text{CHE})$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{CHE}\cup\text{PHY}) &= P(\text{CHE})+P(\text{PHY})-P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{2}{5}-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{7}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{62}{105} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with a velocity given by

$$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 8\cos\left(2t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$$

where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in metres and $t$ is time measured in seconds.

The particle is initially at rest 4 m to the right of the origin.
Show that the displacement of the particle is given by $x = 4\sin\left(2t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + 8$.
items.sol:
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 8\cos\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)dt \\ &= 8\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right]+C \\ &= 4\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=4$:
$$4=4\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+C=-4+C$$
so $C=8$.
$$\therefore\ x=4\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+8$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with a velocity given by

$$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 8\cos\left(2t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$$

where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in metres and $t$ is time measured in seconds.

The particle is initially at rest 4 m to the right of the origin.
Show that the particle comes to rest again when it is 12 m to the right of the origin and $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ s.
items.sol:
Method 1: the particle is at rest when $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$\cos\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$$
so $2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ldots$, giving $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\pi,\ldots$

Hence the particle next comes to rest at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds.

Method 2: when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=8\cos\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$x=4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+8=12 \text{ m}$$
Therefore, at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ the particle is at rest 12 m to the right of the origin.

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with a velocity given by

$$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 8\cos\left(2t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$$

where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in metres and $t$ is time measured in seconds.

The particle is initially at rest 4 m to the right of the origin.
By finding a function for acceleration, describe the motion of the particle after $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ s and before it next comes to rest.
items.sol:
Differentiating the velocity:
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-16\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$$
When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-16\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=-16$$
The acceleration is negative, so the particle moves towards the left after being stationary at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
items.final: Acceleration is $-16$ at $t=\frac{\pi}{2}$, so the particle moves to the left after being stationary

A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(t) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1 \le t \le 14 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for } 0 \le t < 1 \text{ or } t > 14 \end{cases}$$
Show that $k = \dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$.
items.sol:
Since $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)\,dt=1$:
$$\int_1^{14}\dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt=1$$
$$\dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln|2t-1|\Big]_1^{14}=1$$
$$\dfrac{k}{2}(\ln27-\ln1)=1$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{2}{\ln27}$$

After how many days will a person have a 75% chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?
items.sol:
Let $T$ be the time by which the probability of showing symptoms is $0.75$.
$$\int_1^T\dfrac{2}{\ln27}\times\dfrac{1}{2t-1}\,dt=\dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\dfrac{1}{\ln27}\Big[\ln|2t-1|\Big]_1^T=\dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\ln|2T-1|=\dfrac{3\ln27}{4}$$
$$2T-1=e^{\frac{3\ln27}{4}}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{3\ln27}{4}}+1}{2} \\ &= 6.422\ldots \\ &\approx 7 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$

The mass of two substances, $A$ and $B$, are decaying exponentially according to

$$M_A = 200e^{-0.05t}$$
$$M_B = 400 \times 3^{-0.12t},$$

where $M$ is the mass in grams and $t$ is the time in minutes.
Find the time taken for substance $A$ to decrease to half of its original value. Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
Half the original mass is $M_A=100$:
$$100=200e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\dfrac{1}{2}=e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=-0.05t$$
$$\ln2=0.05t$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln2}{0.05} \\ &= 13.86\ldots \\ &\approx 14 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The mass of two substances, $A$ and $B$, are decaying exponentially according to

$$M_A = 200e^{-0.05t}$$
$$M_B = 400 \times 3^{-0.12t},$$

where $M$ is the mass in grams and $t$ is the time in minutes.
At what instance do both particles decay at the same rate? Give your answer correct to the nearest second.
items.sol:
Differentiating each mass:
$$\dfrac{dM_A}{dt}=-0.05\times200e^{-0.05t}=-10e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\dfrac{dM_B}{dt}=400\times\ln3\times(-0.12)\times3^{-0.12t}=-48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$$
Equate the two rates:
$$-10e^{-0.05t}=-48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$$
Write both sides with base $e$, using $3^{-0.12t}=e^{(-0.12\ln3)t}$:
$$\dfrac{10}{48\ln3}=\dfrac{3^{-0.12t}}{e^{-0.05t}}=\dfrac{e^{(-0.12\ln3)t}}{e^{-0.05t}}=e^{(-0.12\ln3+0.05)t}$$
$$0.1895\ldots=e^{-0.0818\ldots t}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln0.1895\ldots}{-0.0818\ldots} \\ &= 20.317\ldots \text{ minutes} \\ &\approx 20 \text{ minutes } 19 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Therefore both substances decay at the same rate at 20 minutes and 19 seconds.

Jonathan's parents decide to set up an investment account to help pay for his university degree. Jonathan's parents deposit \$1000 into the account every year, which earns interest at 4% per annum, compounded yearly. They deposited the first \$1000 at the beginning of the year when Jonathan is born. Jonathan will receive the full amount at the end of the year he turns 18 years old.

Let $A_n$ be the value of the account after $n$ years.
The amount in the account continues to earn interest at 4% per annum. Jonathan enrols in a four-year university course, which costs $\$M$ each year, to be paid at the end of the year. As a result:

$$A_{19} = 26000\left(1.04^{18} - 1\right)(1.04) - M.$$

How much can Jonathan withdraw from the account each year if the entire amount is to be withdrawn over the four years?
items.sol:
Each year the balance grows by $1.04$ and then $M$ is withdrawn:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{20} &= \left[26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)-M\right](1.04)-M \\ &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^2-M(1+1.04) \end{aligned}$$
$$A_{21}=26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^3-M\left(1+1.04+1.04^2\right)$$
By the pattern, using the geometric series sum $\dfrac{1.04^4-1}{0.04}=25\left(1.04^4-1\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{22} &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4-M\left(1+1.04+1.04^2+1.04^3\right) \\ &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4-25M\left(1.04^4-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
The account is empty when $A_{22}=0$:
$$M=\dfrac{26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4}{25\left(1.04^4-1\right)}$$
$$\therefore\ M=\$7347.66$$

items.part:
Show that the exact value to the first two solutions to the equation $\tan 4x = 8$ in the domain $[0, \pi]$ are

$$x_1 = \dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8$$

$$\text{and } x_2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi + \tan^{-1}8\right).$$
items.sol:
The solutions of $\tan4x=8$ with $0\le4x\le4\pi$ are
$$4x=\tan^{-1}8,\ \pi+\tan^{-1}8,\ 2\pi+\tan^{-1}8$$
so
$$x=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8,\ \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right),\ \dfrac{1}{4}\left(2\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
Therefore the first two solutions are
$$x_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8 \quad\text{and}\quad x_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$

items.part: Write down the $x$-coordinates of $P_1$ and $P_2$.

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{-\frac{1}{2}x} & v&=\sin4x\\ u'&=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{1}{2}x} & v'&=4\cos4x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 10\left[\sin4x\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}+e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}\times4\cos4x\right] \\ &= 10e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x+4\cos4x\right) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $y'=0$. Since $e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}>0$, we need $-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x+4\cos4x=0$, which is $\tan4x=8$ by part (a).

Therefore:
$$X_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8,\qquad X_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$

It is known that the $y$-coordinates of the stationary points $Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, \ldots, Y_n$ form a geometric sequence.

Find the exact value of the common ratio for this geometric sequence. Express your answer in simplest form.
items.sol:
At $X_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8$:
$$Y_1=10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\tan^{-1}8}\sin\left(\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
At $X_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$, using $\sin(\pi+\theta)=-\sin\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} Y_2 &= 10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)}\sin\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right) \\ &= -10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)}\sin\left(\tan^{-1}8\right) \end{aligned}$$
The common ratio is
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{Y_2}{Y_1} \\ &= -e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)+\frac{1}{8}\tan^{-1}8} \\ &= -e^{-\frac{1}{8}\pi} \end{aligned}$$

A plumber leases equipment which is valued at \$60 000.

The salvage value of the equipment at any time can be calculated using either of the two methods of depreciation shown in the table.

\extable{300_q28_t1}

Under which method of depreciation would the salvage value of the equipment be lower at the end of 3 years? Justify your answer with appropriate mathematical calculations.
items.sol:
Straight-line method, using $S = V_0 - D_n$:
$$\begin{aligned}S &= 60\,000-3500\times 3\\ &= \$49\,500\end{aligned}$$
Declining-balance method, using $S = V_0(1-r)^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}S &= 60\,000(1-0.12)^3\\ &= 60\,000(0.88)^3\\ &= \$40\,888.32\end{aligned}$$
Since $\$40\,888.32 < \$49\,500$:
$$\therefore\ \text{the declining-balance method gives the lower salvage value.}$$
items.final: The declining-balance method gives the lower salvage value ($40\,888.32 < 49\,500$).

The following formula can be used to calculate an estimate for blood alcohol content (BAC) for males.

$$BAC_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$$

$M$ is the person's weight in kilograms

$H$ is the number of hours of drinking

Substitute $BAC=0.02$, $N=3$ and $M=75$ into the formula.

Subtract from 9:00 pm.
$$9{:}00 \text{ pm} - 2 \text{ h } 38 \text{ min} = 6{:}22 \text{ pm}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Cameron began drinking at 6:22 pm.}$$

A dam is in the shape of a triangular prism which is 50 m long, as shown.

Both ends of the dam, $ABC$ and $DEF$, are isosceles triangles with equal sides of length 25 metres. The included angles $BAC$ and $EDF$ are each $150^\circ$.

\exfigure{271_q28_1}

Calculate the number of litres of water the dam will hold when full.
items.sol:
The cross-section is a triangle with two sides of 25 m and included angle $150^\circ$, so use the area formula $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 25\times 25\times \sin 150^\circ \\ &= 156.25 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The volume is the cross-sectional area times the length.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 156.25 \times 50 \\ &= 7812.5 \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1000 \text{ L}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Litres} &= 7812.5 \times 1000 \\ &= 7\,812\,500 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the dam holds } 7\,812\,500 \text{ L}$$

items.part:
Sydney is 10 hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC $+10$) and New York is 5 hours behind Coordinated Universal Time (UTC $-5$).

Tony travels from Sydney to New York. His plane leaves Sydney at 8:20 pm on Wednesday local time and flies non-stop to New York.

The flight takes 20 hours and 24 minutes.

What time and day is it in New York when the plane lands?
items.sol:
Sydney is ahead of New York by
$$10 - (-5) = 15 \text{ hours}$$
Add the flight time to the departure time (Sydney time):
$$8{:}20 \text{ pm Wednesday} + 20\text{ h }24\text{ min} = 4{:}44 \text{ pm Thursday}$$
Subtract the time difference to get New York time:
$$4{:}44 \text{ pm} - 15 \text{ hours} = 1{:}44 \text{ am}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{it is } 1{:}44 \text{ am Thursday in New York}$$

The diagram shows a park consisting of a rectangle and a semicircle. The semicircle has a radius of 100 m. The dimensions of the rectangle are 200 m and 250 m.

A lake occupies a section of the park as shown. The rest of the park is a grassed section. Some measurements from the end of the grassed section to the edge of the lake are also shown.

\exfigure{271_q32_1}
Using two applications of the trapezoidal rule, calculate the approximate area of the grassed section.
items.sol:
The grassed section has parallel sides 160, 150 and 250 with strip width 100, so apply the trapezoidal rule twice.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 100\times(160+150) + \dfrac{1}{2}\times 100\times(150+250) \\ &= 50\times 310 + 50\times 400 \\ &= 35\,500 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lake area} &= 65\,708 - 35\,500 \\ &= 30\,208 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

How much less will Frankie pay overall by making the lump sum payment?
items.sol:
Total number of repayments:
$$50 + 146 = 196$$
Total paid with the lump sum:
$$\begin{aligned} 196\times 1485 + 40\,000 &= \$331\,060 \end{aligned}$$
Total paid under the original arrangement:
$$\begin{aligned} 23\times 12\times 1485 &= \$409\,860 \end{aligned}$$
The saving is
$$\begin{aligned} 409\,860 - 331\,060 &= \$78\,800 \end{aligned}$$

A full container has 4.8 L of a mixture of cordial and water in the ratio $1 : 3$.

After removing 1.2 L of the mixture, more water is added to refill the container.

What is the ratio of cordial to water in the final mixture?
items.sol:
After removing 1.2 L, $3.6$ L remains, still in the ratio $1:3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cordial} &= \dfrac{3.6}{4} = 0.9 \text{ L} \\ \text{Water} &= \dfrac{3.6\times 3}{4} = 2.7 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
Adding 1.2 L of water gives $2.7 + 1.2 = 3.9$ L of water.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{cordial} : \text{water} &= 0.9 : 3.9 \\ &= 3 : 13 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the ratio of cordial to water is } 3:13$$

items.part:
Consider the following dataset.

$$1 \quad 5 \quad 9 \quad 10 \quad 15$$

Suppose a new value, $x$, is added to this dataset, giving the following.

$$1 \quad 5 \quad 9 \quad 10 \quad 15 \quad x$$

It is known that $x$ is greater than 15. It is also known that the difference between the means of the two datasets is equal to ten times the difference between the medians of the two datasets.

Calculate the value of $x$.
items.sol:
For the first dataset:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{mean} &= \dfrac{1+5+9+10+15}{5} = 8 \\ \text{median} &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
For the second dataset, since $x>15$ it is the largest value:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{mean} &= \dfrac{40+x}{6} \\ \text{median} &= \dfrac{9+10}{2} = 9.5 \end{aligned}$$
The difference in means equals ten times the difference in medians:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{40+x}{6}-8 &= 10(9.5-9) \\ \dfrac{40+x}{6}-8 &= 5 \\ \dfrac{40+x}{6} &= 13 \\ 40+x &= 78 \\ x &= 38 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = 38$$

items.part:
The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) scores for adults in City $A$ are normally distributed with a mean of 108 and a standard deviation of 10.

The IQ scores for adults in City $B$ are normally distributed with a mean of 112 and a standard deviation of 16.
Yin is an adult who lives in City $A$ and has an IQ score of 128.

What percentage of the adults in this city have an IQ score higher than Yin's?
items.sol:
$$\dfrac{128-108}{10} = 2$$
So $128$ is 2 standard deviations above the mean.

About $95\%$ of scores lie within 2 standard deviations, so $5\%$ lie outside, split equally between the two tails.
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{5\%}{2} = 2.5\% \text{ have an IQ score higher than Yin's}$$

items.part:
The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) scores for adults in City $A$ are normally distributed with a mean of 108 and a standard deviation of 10.

The IQ scores for adults in City $B$ are normally distributed with a mean of 112 and a standard deviation of 16.
There are 1 000 000 adults living in City $B$.

Calculate the number of adults in City $B$ that would be expected to have an IQ score lower than Yin's.
items.sol:
Mean of City $B$ is $112$, so one standard deviation above the mean is
$$112+16 = 128$$
So Yin's score is 1 standard deviation above the mean in City $B$.

The percentage with a lower score is
$$50\%+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 68\% = 84\%$$
The expected number of adults is
$$1\,000\,000\times 0.84 = 840\,000$$

items.part:
The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) scores for adults in City $A$ are normally distributed with a mean of 108 and a standard deviation of 10.

The IQ scores for adults in City $B$ are normally distributed with a mean of 112 and a standard deviation of 16.
Simon, an adult who lives in City $A$, moves to City $B$. The $z$-score corresponding to his IQ score in City $A$ is the same as the $z$-score corresponding to his IQ score in City $B$.

By first forming an equation, calculate Simon's IQ score. Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
Let $x$ be Simon's IQ score. Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} z_A &= \dfrac{x-108}{10} \\ z_B &= \dfrac{x-112}{16} \end{aligned}$$
The $z$-scores are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x-108}{10} &= \dfrac{x-112}{16} \\ 16(x-108) &= 10(x-112) \\ 16x-1728 &= 10x-1120 \\ 6x &= 608 \\ x &\approx 101.3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Simon's IQ score is } 101.3$$

Navneet and her husband want to buy a house. Their combined gross income is $\$9836.67$ per month. They can afford $25\%$ of their gross monthly income for loan repayments. The couple are already paying off a car loan at $\$260$ per month.

The bank offers a loan with monthly repayments of $\$8.36$ per $\$1000$ borrowed.

Calculate the largest loan that this couple can afford, to the nearest thousand.
items.sol:
Find $25\%$ of the gross monthly income.
$$25\%\times 9836.67 = \$2459.17$$
Subtract the car loan repayment.
$$2459.17 - 260 = \$2199.17$$
The repayment is $\$8.36$ per $\$1000$, so divide to find the number of thousands.
$$2199.17\div 8.36 \approx 263.0586$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Maximum loan} = 263.0586\times 1000 \approx \$263\,000$$

items.part:
Michael takes a loan of $\$450\,000$ over a period of 25 years at a reducible interest rate of $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.

Repayments $R$ are made monthly.

Using the table of present value interest factors below and the recurrence relation,

$$A_{n+1} = A_n(1+r) - R$$

Calculate how much interest has been charged on the loan after the second repayment.

\extable{3314_q8_t1}
items.sol:
The monthly rate and number of repayments are
$$r = 6\%\div 12 = 0.5\% ,\qquad n = 25\times 12 = 300$$
From the table, the interest factor is $155.2069$, so
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 450\,000\div 155.2069 \\ &= \$2899.36 \end{aligned}$$
Using $A_{n+1} = A_n(1+r) - R$ with $A_0 = 450\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 450\,000(1.005) - 2899.36 = \$449\,350.64 \\ A_2 &= 449\,350.64(1.005) - 2899.36 = \$448\,698.03 \end{aligned}$$
The loan has reduced by
$$450\,000 - 448\,698.03 = \$1301.97$$
The total repayments are
$$2\times 2899.36 = \$5798.72$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest} &= 5798.72 - 1301.97 \\ &= \$4496.75 \end{aligned}$$

The distribution of children's ages in 2000 is negatively skewed.

The median is 12 (location).

The interquartile range is 8 and the range is 18 (spread).

In 2010, $25\%$ of the children were aged 0-2.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.25\times 2500 &= 625 \text{ children} \end{aligned}$$

In 2010 the children aged 12-18 are those from the upper quartile to the maximum: a quarter of the 2500 children, which is 625.

In 2000 the median is 12, so the 625 children aged 12-18 are half of the data.

Therefore there were 1250 children in 2000.
$$\therefore\ 2\times 625 = 1250 \text{ children}$$

items.part: Determine $f(x)$ given that $f'(x)=\sec^2 2x+\sin 2x$ and $f(0)=1$.
items.sol:
Integrate each term.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{\tan 2x}{2}-\dfrac{\cos 2x}{2}+C$$
Use $f(0)=1$ to find $C$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0)&=\dfrac{\tan 0}{2}-\dfrac{\cos 0}{2}+C=1 \\ 0-\dfrac{1}{2}+C&=1 \\ C&=\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\tan 2x-\cos 2x+3\right)$$

items.part:
The curve of $y=f(x)$ is given below. Sketch $y=-2f(-2x)$, indicating all key features of your sketch including intercepts, turning points and any asymptotes. The dashed line represents an asymptote and there is a turning point at $(-1,-1)$.

items.sol:

The ogive joins the upper class boundaries. Half of the 50 students is a cumulative frequency of 25, which lies on the segment from $(70,24)$ to $(80,44)$:
$$\text{median}\approx70+\dfrac{25-24}{44-24}\times10=70.5$$
$$\therefore\ \text{median}\approx70.5$$

Reading the ogive at a mark of 45, about $20\%$ of students scored below 45.
$$\therefore\ 20\%$$

The 6th and 7th deciles are at cumulative frequencies 30 and 35, which the ogive gives as about $73$ and $75.5$.
$$\therefore\ 75$$

items.part:
A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ where $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.
Explain why the particle never changes direction.
items.sol:
The range of $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ is $[0,4]$.

So $v\ge 0$ for all $t$.

Therefore the particle is only ever stationary or travelling in the positive direction, so it never changes direction.

items.part:
A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ where $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the displacement $x$ of the particle after 1 second.
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity.
$$x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=0+\dfrac{1}{\pi}+C \\ C&=-\dfrac{1}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)-\dfrac{1}{\pi}$.

When $t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2+\dfrac{1}{\pi}-\dfrac{1}{\pi} \\ &=2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ where $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.
For sufficiently large values of $t$ (as $t\to\infty$), describe the behaviour of the displacement of the particle.
items.sol:
$$x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)-\dfrac{1}{\pi}$$
The cosine term is bounded, so as $t\to\infty$, $x\to\infty$.

Therefore the displacement approaches infinity.

Students can also use the fact that the particle never changes direction from part (a).

items.part:
A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ where $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the exact acceleration of the particle at $t=4$ seconds.
items.sol:
Differentiate the velocity.
$$a=-4\pi\cos(2\pi t)$$
When $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-4\pi\cos(8\pi) \\ &=-4\pi \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right)=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule inside the logarithm, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right]&=\dfrac{\frac{(3-x)(1)-(3+x)(-1)}{(3-x)^2}}{\frac{3+x}{3-x}} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{(3-x)^2}\cdot\dfrac{3-x}{3+x} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{(3-x)(3+x)} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using log laws:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(3+x)-\ln(3-x)\right]&=\dfrac{1}{3+x}+\dfrac{1}{3-x} \\ &=\dfrac{(3-x)+(3+x)}{(3+x)(3-x)} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{9-x^2}$.
items.sol:
From part (a):
$$\int\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx=\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)+C$$
Divide by 6.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{6}\int\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact area bounded by the curve $y=x^2-2$, the $x$ axis and the line $y=4$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1305_q3b_s1}

The curve is $y=x^2-2$, so $x=\pm\sqrt{y+2}$.

By symmetry, integrate with respect to $y$ from $0$ to $4$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\int_0^4\sqrt{y+2}\,dy \\ &=2\left[\dfrac{(y+2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^4 \\ &=\dfrac{4}{3}\left[(y+2)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^4 \\ &=\dfrac{4}{3}\left(6^{\frac{3}{2}}-2^{\frac{3}{2}}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{4}{3}\left(6\sqrt{6}-2\sqrt{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{8}{3}\left(3\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}\right) \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The first term of a geometric series is $e^{x}$ and the fifth term is $81e^{9x}$.
Show that the common ratio can be expressed by $r=3e^{2x}$.
items.sol:
For a geometric series, $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, with $a=e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_5=e^x r^4&=81e^{9x} \\ r^4&=81e^{8x} \\ r&=\sqrt[4]{81e^{8x}} \\ &=3e^{2x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The first term of a geometric series is $e^{x}$ and the fifth term is $81e^{9x}$.
Find an expression for the $8^{\text{th}}$ term of the series.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} T_8&=ar^7 \\ &=e^x\left(3e^{2x}\right)^7 \\ &=e^x\cdot 2187e^{14x} \\ &=2187e^{15x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The first term of a geometric series is $e^{x}$ and the fifth term is $81e^{9x}$.
For what values of $x$ does the series have a limiting sum?
items.sol:
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$|3e^{2x}|<1$$
Since $3e^{2x}>0$ for all $x$, this becomes:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&<3e^{2x}<1 \\ 0&<e^{2x}<\dfrac{1}{3} &&(\text{divide by } 3) \\ 2x&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) &&(\text{take } \ln) \\ x&<\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) &&(\text{divide by } 2) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The first term of a geometric series is $e^{x}$ and the fifth term is $81e^{9x}$.
Find the exact value of $x$ if the limiting sum is 3.
items.sol:
Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=\dfrac{e^x}{1-3e^{2x}} \\ 3\left(1-3e^{2x}\right)&=e^x \\ 3-9e^{2x}&=e^x \\ 0&=9e^{2x}+e^x-3 \end{aligned}$$
Let $u=e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=9u^2+u-3 \\ u&=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{1-4(9)(-3)}}{18} \\ &=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{109}}{18} \end{aligned}$$
Since $u=e^x>0$, $u$ cannot be negative.
$$e^x=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{109}}{18}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\ln\left(\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{109}}{18}\right)\approx-0.65$$

items.part:
A factory located next to a lake has recently been shut down due to concerns about chemical run off. A bird's eye view of the lake is given in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1305_q5_1}

Local volunteers have begun a clean-up effort to remove these harmful chemicals from the lake. The concentration of chemicals is given by the equation:

$$C=1.5-0.4e^{kt}$$

Let $C$ be the concentration of chemicals in the lake in kg/m$^3$, where $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the number of years after the clean-up effort has started.
The initial weight of chemical run off in the lake is 38500 kg, and the average depth of the lake is 5 m. Use the trapezoidal rule to show that the initial concentration of chemical run off can be estimated as 1.1 kg/m$^3$.
items.sol:
Trapezoidal rule with width $h=25$ and the measured widths from the diagram:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{25}{2}\left(45+55+2(80+90+60)\right) \\ &=7000 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Volume $=$ area $\times$ depth:
$$V=7000\times 5=35000 \text{ m}^3$$
Concentration is weight divided by volume:
$$\dfrac{38500 \text{ kg}}{35000 \text{ m}^3}=1.1 \text{ kg/m}^3$$

items.part:
A factory located next to a lake has recently been shut down due to concerns about chemical run off. A bird's eye view of the lake is given in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1305_q5_1}

Local volunteers have begun a clean-up effort to remove these harmful chemicals from the lake. The concentration of chemicals is given by the equation:

$$C=1.5-0.4e^{kt}$$

Let $C$ be the concentration of chemicals in the lake in kg/m$^3$, where $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the number of years after the clean-up effort has started.
Find the value of $k$ to three significant figures if it takes 2.45 years to remove all chemical run off from the lake
items.sol:
All chemical is removed when $C=0$ at $t=2.45$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=1.5-0.4e^{2.45k} \\ \dfrac{1.5}{0.4}&=e^{2.45k} \\ 2.45k&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1.5}{0.4}\right) \\ k&=\dfrac{\ln(1.5\div 0.4)}{2.45} \\ &=0.539 \text{ (3 significant figures)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A factory located next to a lake has recently been shut down due to concerns about chemical run off. A bird's eye view of the lake is given in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1305_q5_1}

Local volunteers have begun a clean-up effort to remove these harmful chemicals from the lake. The concentration of chemicals is given by the equation:

$$C=1.5-0.4e^{kt}$$

Let $C$ be the concentration of chemicals in the lake in kg/m$^3$, where $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the number of years after the clean-up effort has started.
Find the rate of change in the concentration of chemical run off in the lake at $t=1.8$ years. Round your answer to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Differentiate $C=1.5-0.4e^{0.539t}$.
$$\dfrac{dC}{dt}=-0.4\times 0.539\,e^{0.539t}$$
When $t=1.8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dC}{dt}&=-0.4\times 0.539\,e^{0.539\times 1.8} \\ &=-0.5699\ldots \\ &\approx -0.57 \text{ kg/m}^3 \text{ per year} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$ start moving along the $x$ axis at time $t=0$. Particle $P$ is initially at $x=8$ and its velocity $v$ in m/s at time $t$ in seconds is given by $v=2t-4$.

The position of particle $Q$ is given by $x=4-\ln(t+1)$. The diagram shows the graph of $x=4-\ln(t+1)$.

\exfigure{1305_q6b_1}
Show that the position of particle $P$ is given by $x=(t-2)^2+4$.
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity.
$$x=t^2-4t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=8$, so $C=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=t^2-4t+8 \\ &=(t-2)^2+4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$ start moving along the $x$ axis at time $t=0$. Particle $P$ is initially at $x=8$ and its velocity $v$ in m/s at time $t$ in seconds is given by $v=2t-4$.

The position of particle $Q$ is given by $x=4-\ln(t+1)$. The diagram shows the graph of $x=4-\ln(t+1)$.

\exfigure{1305_q6b_1}
Explain why particles $P$ and $Q$ will never collide.
items.sol: The displacement-time graphs of $P$ and $Q$ never intersect, so the particles are never at the same position and never collide.

items.part:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$ start moving along the $x$ axis at time $t=0$. Particle $P$ is initially at $x=8$ and its velocity $v$ in m/s at time $t$ in seconds is given by $v=2t-4$.

The position of particle $Q$ is given by $x=4-\ln(t+1)$. The diagram shows the graph of $x=4-\ln(t+1)$.

\exfigure{1305_q6b_1}
Show that the distance between the particles can be given by $PQ=(t-2)^2+\ln(t+1)$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} PQ&=\left((t-2)^2+4\right)-\left(4-\ln(t+1)\right) \\ &=(t-2)^2+4-4+\ln(t+1) \\ &=(t-2)^2+\ln(t+1) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$ start moving along the $x$ axis at time $t=0$. Particle $P$ is initially at $x=8$ and its velocity $v$ in m/s at time $t$ in seconds is given by $v=2t-4$.

The position of particle $Q$ is given by $x=4-\ln(t+1)$. The diagram shows the graph of $x=4-\ln(t+1)$.

\exfigure{1305_q6b_1}
Find the exact time that the distance between the particles $PQ$ is a minimum.
items.sol:
Stationary values occur where $PQ'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} PQ'&=2(t-2)+\dfrac{1}{t+1}=0 \\ 2t-4&=-\dfrac{1}{t+1} \\ (2t-4)(t+1)&=-1 \\ 2t^2-2t-4+1&=0 \\ 2t^2-2t-3&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Solve using the quadratic formula.
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-4(2)(-3)}}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{28}}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{7}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Since $t\ge 0$, $t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$PQ''=2-\dfrac{1}{(1+t)^2}$$
At $t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}$:
$$PQ''=2-\dfrac{1}{\left(1+\frac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}\right)^2}\approx 1.8745>0$$
So the stationary point is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2} \text{ s}$$

items.part:
For the curve $y=x^3+6x^2+9x$,
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3x^2+12x+9 \\ &=3(x^2+4x+3) \\ &=3(x+3)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x+12$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$3(x+3)(x+1)=0$$
So $x=-3$ or $x=-1$.

For $x=-3$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6(-3)+12=-6<0$$
So there is a maximum at $(-3,0)$.

For $x=-1$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6(-1)+12=6>0$$
So there is a minimum at $(-1,-4)$.

items.part:
For the curve $y=x^3+6x^2+9x$,
Sketch the curve, showing all main features, including intercepts, stationary points and any points of inflection.
items.sol:
Points of inflection occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x+12&=0 \\ x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(-2)^3+6(-2)^2+9(-2) \\ &=-8+24-18 \\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Testing the concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-3:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=-2:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0 &&\\ x=-1:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $(-2,-2)$.

items.part:
A piece of string of length 6 metres is cut into two pieces.

One piece forms a square with sides $x$ cm and the other piece forms a circle.

\exfigure{1307_q11c_1}
Show that the radius $(r)$ of the circle in terms of $x$ is given by

$$r=\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi}.$$
items.sol:
The square has perimeter $4x$ and the circle has circumference $2\pi r$. The total length of string is $6$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4x+2\pi r&=6 \\ 2\pi r&=6-4x \\ r&=\dfrac{6-4x}{2\pi} \\ &=\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A piece of string of length 6 metres is cut into two pieces.

One piece forms a square with sides $x$ cm and the other piece forms a circle.

\exfigure{1307_q11c_1}
Hence find the lengths of the two pieces of string which obtain the minimum area. Leave your answer in terms of $\pi$.
items.sol:
The total area is the circle plus the square, using $r=\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\pi r^2+x^2 \\ &=\pi\left(\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2 \\ &=\dfrac{(3-2x)^2}{\pi}+x^2 \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot2(3-2x)(-2)+2x \\ &=\dfrac{-12+8x+2\pi x}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{8+2\pi}{\pi}>0$$
So the stationary point is a minimum.

For the minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -12+8x+2\pi x&=0 \\ x(8+2\pi)&=12 \\ x&=\dfrac{12}{8+2\pi} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{4+\pi} \end{aligned}$$
The length of string for the square is
$$4x=\dfrac{24}{4+\pi}$$
The length for the circle is
$$6-\dfrac{24}{4+\pi}=\dfrac{6\pi}{4+\pi}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{square: }\dfrac{24}{4+\pi},\quad\text{circle: }\dfrac{6\pi}{4+\pi}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3 x^{-2}\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3x^{-2}\,dx&=\left[-x^{-1}\right]_1^3 \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{3}-(-1) \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the area bounded by the $x$-axis and the curve $y=x^2-4$.
items.sol:
The $x$-intercepts satisfy $x^2-4=0$, so $x=\pm2$.

The function is even, so the area is twice the area from $0$ to $2$. The curve lies below the $x$-axis there, so take the absolute value.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left|2\int_0^2(x^2-4)\,dx\right| \\ &=2\left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-4x\right]_0^2\right| \\ &=2\left|\dfrac{8}{3}-8-0\right| \\ &=2\times\dfrac{16}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{32}{3} \\ &=10\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: By firstly differentiating $y=\sqrt{2x^2-4}$, find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2x^2-4}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{2x^2-4}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2x^2-4\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(4x)\left(2x^2-4\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{2x^2-4}} \end{aligned}$$
Hence $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{2x^2-4}}\,dx=\sqrt{2x^2-4}+c$, and dividing by $2$:
$$\int\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2x^2-4}}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2x^2-4}+c$$

items.part:
Consider the curves $y=x^3$ and $y=7x^2-10x$, that intersect at three points.
Show that two of these points of intersection are $(0,0)$ and $(2,8)$.
items.sol:
Equating the two equations:
$$\begin{aligned} x^3&=7x^2-10x \\ x^3-7x^2+10x&=0 \\ x(x^2-7x+10)&=0 \\ x(x-2)(x-5)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0,\ 2$ or $5$.

For $x=0$: $y=0^3=0$. For $x=2$: $y=2^3=8$.

Hence $(0,0)$ and $(2,8)$ are points of intersection.

items.part:
Consider the curves $y=x^3$ and $y=7x^2-10x$, that intersect at three points.
Hence or otherwise, draw a sketch and calculate the area enclosed between the curves, between the two points found in part (a)
Solve $\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$
items.sol:
For $0\le x\le2\pi$, the angle $x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ lies in $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{13\pi}{6}\right]$.

The acute related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, since $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$
Subtracting $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$

items.part:
The curve $y=f(x)$ passes through the point $(0,7)$.

If its gradient function is given by $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1-6\sin 3x$, find the equation of the curve.
items.sol:
Integrating the gradient function:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int(1-6\sin3x)\,dx \\ &=x+\dfrac{6\cos3x}{3}+C \\ &=x+2\cos3x+C \end{aligned}$$
The curve passes through $(0,7)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(0)&=0+2\cos0+C=7 \\ 2+C&=7 \\ C&=5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x+2\cos3x+5$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line.

At time $t$ seconds, its distance $x$ metres from a fixed point 0 on the line is given by $x=1-\cos 2t$.
Sketch the graph of $x$ as a function of $t$ for $0\le t\le\pi$

A particle moves in a straight line.

At time $t$ seconds, its distance $x$ metres from a fixed point 0 on the line is given by $x=1-\cos 2t$.
Using your graph, or otherwise, find the times when the particle is at rest and the position of the particle at these times.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$, that is when $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$. These are the stationary points of the graph.

The stationary points occur at
$$t=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi$$
The position at these times is
$$x=0,\ 2,\ 0 \text{ metres respectively}$$
items.final: At rest at $t=0,\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \pi$, with positions $x=0,\ 2,\ 0$ metres respectively

items.part: Differentiate $\sin^2 x$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} y&=\sin^2 x\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\cos x\sin x\ (=\sin 2x) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, calculate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\sin x+\cos x)^2\,dx$, leaving your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Expand the integrand and use $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\sin x+\cos x)^2\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\sin^2x+2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2x\right)dx\\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(1+2\sin x\cos x)\,dx \end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^2x=2\sin x\cos x$, so a primitive of $2\sin x\cos x$ is $\sin^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} &=\Big[x+\sin^2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\ &=\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^2\right]-0\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find derivatives for the following, with respect to $x$.
$\ln\left(x^2+2\right)$

Find derivatives for the following, with respect to $x$.
$3^x e^x$
items.sol:
Write $3^x=e^{x\ln3}$ and apply the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{x\ln3} & v&=e^x\\ u'&=\ln3\,e^{x\ln3} & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\ln3}e^x\right)&=e^{x\ln3}e^x+e^x\ln3\,e^{x\ln3}\\ &=3^xe^x+3^xe^x\ln3\\ &=3^xe^x(1+\ln3) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that the curve $y=2x^2-\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-4$ has a stationary point at $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\ \ln 4-3\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.
items.sol:
Differentiate:
$$y'=4x-\dfrac1x$$
At $x=\dfrac12$:
$$y'=4\times\dfrac12-2=0$$
so there is a stationary point at $x=\dfrac12$.

Substitute $x=\dfrac12$ into $y$, using the log law $-\ln\left(\dfrac14\right)=\ln4$:
$$\begin{aligned} y\left(\dfrac12\right)&=2\times\dfrac14-\ln\left(\dfrac14\right)-4\\ &=\dfrac12+\ln4-4\\ &=\ln4-3\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac12,\ \ln4-3\dfrac12\right)\text{ is a stationary point.}$$

items.part: Find the co-ordinates of the point of intersection of the line $y=3$ and the curve $y=e^x+1$.
items.sol:
The line and curve meet where $e^x+1=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x&=2\\ x&=\ln2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the point of intersection is }(\ln2,\ 3)$$

items.part: Draw a neat sketch of the area bounded by $y=3$, the $y$-axis and the curve $y=e^x+1$.
items.sol: \exfigure{1307_q14c_s1}

items.part: Calculate the exact area drawn in part (b).
items.sol:
The area is the integral of the upper function minus the lower function, from $x=0$ to $x=\ln2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^{\ln2}\left(3-\left(e^x+1\right)\right)dx\\ &=\int_0^{\ln2}\left(2-e^x\right)dx\\ &=\Big[2x-e^x\Big]_0^{\ln2}\\ &=(2\ln2-2)-(0-1)\\ &=2\ln2-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=(2\ln2-1)\text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle, $P$, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$ is $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=e^{-t}+e^{-2t}$ where $t$ is measured in seconds.

Initially, the displacement of the particle is $x=\dfrac{3}{4}$ m, travelling at a velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac{3}{2}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Show that the displacement of the particle is given by:

$$x=e^{-t}+\dfrac{1}{4}e^{-2t}-\dfrac{1}{2}.$$
items.sol:
Integrate the acceleration:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-e^{-t}-\dfrac12e^{-2t}+c_1$$
Initially $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac32$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac32&=-e^0-\dfrac12e^0+c_1\\ c_1&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dx}{dt}=-e^{-t}-\dfrac12e^{-2t}$$
Integrate again:
$$x=e^{-t}+\dfrac14e^{-2t}+c_2$$
Initially $x=\dfrac34$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac34&=e^0+\dfrac14e^0+c_2\\ c_2&=-\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=e^{-t}+\dfrac14e^{-2t}-\dfrac12$$

items.part:
The acceleration of a particle, $P$, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$ is $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=e^{-t}+e^{-2t}$ where $t$ is measured in seconds.

Initially, the displacement of the particle is $x=\dfrac{3}{4}$ m, travelling at a velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac{3}{2}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Find the limit of the displacement of $P$, and hence the limit of the distance that $P$ travels after $t=0$.
items.sol:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-t}\to0$ and $e^{-2t}\to0$.
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}x=0+\dfrac14(0)-\dfrac12=-\dfrac12$$
The particle starts at $x=\dfrac34$, so the limiting change in displacement from the starting point is
$$\dfrac34-\left(-\dfrac12\right)=1.25\text{ m}$$
items.final: limit of displacement $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ m; distance $1.25$ m

items.part:
Show that the function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right),\ [0,6]$$

is a probability density function.
items.sol:
A probability density function needs $f(x)\ge0$ on the domain and a total area of $1$.

For $0\le x\le6$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\le\pi$, so $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)\ge0$ (see graph). Hence $f(x)\ge0$.

\exfigure{1307_q16a_s1}

Now find the total area:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6\dfrac{\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)dx&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left[-\dfrac6\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)\right]_0^6\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left[-\dfrac6\pi\cos\pi+\dfrac6\pi\cos0\right]\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left(-\dfrac6\pi\times(-1)+\dfrac6\pi\times1\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\times\dfrac{12}{\pi}\\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the function is a probability density function, since }f(x)\ge0\text{ and }\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=1.$$

items.part: For a particular continuous random variable $X$, find $P(X\le 4)$ for the function described in part (a)
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(X\le4)&=\int_0^4\dfrac{\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left[-\dfrac6\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)\right]_0^4\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left(-\dfrac6\pi\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+\dfrac6\pi\cos0\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\times\left(-\dfrac6\pi\right)\times\left(-\dfrac12\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{12}\times\dfrac6\pi\\ &=\dfrac14+\dfrac12\\ &=\dfrac34 \end{aligned}$$

ect to minimum length regulations when they are caught.

ie. fish shorter than a given length must be returned to the water if caught.

Two such species are Red Snapper and Barramundi which have minimum lengths of 30 cm and 55 cm respectively.

A fishing tour operator in Northern Australia has made observations over a long period of time and found that, when measured in cm, both the variables ‘R’ (the lengths of caught Red Snapper) and ‘B’ (the lengths of caught Barramundi), are normally distributed.

‘R’ has a mean of 36 cm and standard deviation of 3 cm. ‘B’ has a standard deviation of 4 cm.
Calculate the mean length of Barramundi caught if $2.5\%$ of Barramundi caught are less than 54 cm.
items.sol:
By the empirical rule, $95\%$ of Barramundi are within $2$ standard deviations of the mean, so $5\%$ are more than $2$ standard deviations from the mean.

By symmetry, $2.5\%$ of Barramundi are more than $2$ standard deviations below the mean.

Hence
$$\begin{aligned} 54&=\mu-2s\\ \mu&=54+2\times4\\ &=62\text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
The mean length of caught Barramundi was $62$ cm.

items.part:
ect to minimum length regulations when they are caught.

ie. fish shorter than a given length must be returned to the water if caught.

Two such species are Red Snapper and Barramundi which have minimum lengths of 30 cm and 55 cm respectively.

A fishing tour operator in Northern Australia has made observations over a long period of time and found that, when measured in cm, both the variables ‘R’ (the lengths of caught Red Snapper) and ‘B’ (the lengths of caught Barramundi), are normally distributed.

‘R’ has a mean of 36 cm and standard deviation of 3 cm. ‘B’ has a standard deviation of 4 cm.
Calculate the $z$-scores for the minimum allowed lengths for both variables, R and B, and comment upon what this means in terms of which of the two species are more likely to be returned to the water after capture.
items.sol:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{s}$:

Red Snapper (minimum $30$ cm):
$$z=\dfrac{30-36}{3}=-2$$
Barramundi (minimum $55$ cm, $\mu=62$):
$$z=\dfrac{55-62}{4}=-1.75$$
By the empirical rule, only $2.5\%$ of caught Red Snapper are returned, since the minimum length is $2$ standard deviations below the mean.

The Barramundi minimum is only $1.75$ standard deviations below the mean, so more than $2.5\%$ of Barramundi are returned.

Therefore caught Barramundi are more likely to be returned to the water.
items.final: Red Snapper $z=-2$, Barramundi $z=-1.75$; caught Barramundi are more likely to be returned to the water

items.part:
Historical data for a particular aptitude test show that its completion time has a mean of 5 minutes with a standard deviation of 30 seconds.

As part of the selection process for an available job, an employer requires candidates to complete the test faster than $90\%$ of all applicants to progress to the next stage.

An extract from a probability table for the standard normal distribution is shown below.

\exfigure{1307_q16d_1}

Darcy completed the aptitude test in 4 minutes and 23 seconds.

Did Darcy qualify for the next stage of selection? Justify your answer by demonstrating your knowledge of the normal distribution and the application of $z$-scores to the problem.
items.sol:
From the table, the $z$-score for being faster than $89.97\%$ of applicants is $1.28$, and for $90.15\%$ it is $1.29$.

The qualifying time (faster means below the mean) is
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\mu-1.28s\\ &=5\text{ minutes}-1.28\times30\text{ seconds}\\ &=4\text{ minutes }21.6\text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
or, using $1.29$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\mu-1.29s\\ &=5\text{ minutes}-1.29\times30\text{ seconds}\\ &=4\text{ minutes }21.3\text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Either answer is acceptable: $1.28$ is closer to $90\%$ probability, while $1.29$ ensures the probability exceeds $90\%$.

Darcy's time of $4$ minutes $23$ seconds is slower than the qualifying time, so she does not qualify for the next stage.

Check using Darcy's $z$-score: she was $37$ seconds faster than the mean, so
$$z=\dfrac{37}{30}\approx1.23$$
which is less than the $1.28$ required.
items.final: No, Darcy did not qualify: her time of 4 min 23 s is slower than the qualifying time (about 4 min 21.6 s).

A grandstand at an oval is shown in cross-section $BCDE$.

The seating, along the interval $DE$, is angled at $\alpha^\circ$ to the horizontal and begins 4 m above ground level.

From $B$, Aiden measures the angle of elevation of $D$ to be $51^\circ$, then walks 44 m onto the field and measures the angle of elevation of $D$ to be $28^\circ$ from point $A$.

\exfigure{722_q14_1}
Show that $\angle ADB = 23^\circ$
items.sol:
Since $\angle ABD$ and the $51^\circ$ elevation angle lie on a straight line, they are supplementary.
$$\angle ABD = 180^\circ - 51^\circ = 129^\circ$$
In $\triangle ABD$, the angle at $A$ is $28^\circ$. By the angle sum of a triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ADB + 28^\circ + 129^\circ &= 180^\circ \\ \angle ADB &= 23^\circ \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

Calculate the distance $DF$ and hence find the angle of the seating, $\alpha$, to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
In right-angled $\triangle BCD$, with $BD = 53$ and angle $51^\circ$ at $B$:
$$\sin 51^\circ = \dfrac{DC}{53}$$
$$\begin{aligned} DC &= 53\sin 51^\circ \\ &\approx 41.19 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The seating begins $4$ m above ground, so
$$DF = DC - 4 = 53\sin 51^\circ - 4$$
Also
$$\cos 51^\circ = \dfrac{BC}{53}$$
$$BC = 53\cos 51^\circ$$
The seating angle satisfies
$$\tan\alpha = \dfrac{53\sin 51^\circ - 4}{53\cos 51^\circ}$$
$$\therefore\ \alpha \approx 48^\circ$$

items.part:
In triangle $DEF$, $\angle EDF = 44^\circ$, $EF = 6$ cm, and $DE = 7$ cm.

Find $\angle EFD$ to the nearest degree, given that it is obtuse.
items.sol:
Use the sine rule in $\triangle DEF$.
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle EFD}{7} = \dfrac{\sin 44^\circ}{6}$$
$$\sin\angle EFD = \dfrac{7\sin 44^\circ}{6}$$
The acute solution is $54^\circ$.
$$\angle EFD \approx 54^\circ$$
The angle is obtuse, so take the supplement.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle EFD &= 180^\circ - 54^\circ \\ &= 126^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Scarlett lives with her parents and two siblings. Every evening her parents watch television together for 2.5 hours and Scarlett and her siblings are on their devices for 4 hours.

The television consumes 270 watts per hour and each of the children's devices consumes 130 watts per hour.
How much electricity, in kilowatt-hours, is consumed by the household each week?
items.sol:
Energy is power times time. Find the Wh used in a week (7 evenings).

Television (one set, 2.5 hours):
$$\text{TV} = 270\times 7\times 2.5 = 4725 \text{ Wh}$$
Devices (3 children, 4 hours):
$$\text{Devices} = 3\times 130\times 7\times 4 = 10\,920 \text{ Wh}$$
Convert to kilowatt-hours by dividing by $1000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= \dfrac{4725 + 10\,920}{1000} \\ &= 15.645 \text{ kWh} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 15.645 \text{ kWh per week}$$

items.part:

items.sol:
There are 52 weeks in a year.
$$\text{Electricity per year} = 15.645\times 52 = 813.54 \text{ kWh}$$
The 25% discount means paying $75\%$ of the cost.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= 813.54\times 0.17\times 0.75 \\ &= \$103.73 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Cost} = \$103.73 \text{ per year}$$

items.part:

items.sol:
A decrease of $20\%$ per year is compounding, with multiplier $0.8$.

$$P = 71409 \times 0.8^n$$
We need $P = 200$, so test values of $n$.

$$\begin{aligned} n = 26:&\quad 71409 \times 0.8^{26} = 215.82 \\ n = 27:&\quad 71409 \times 0.8^{27} = 172.66 \end{aligned}$$
The population first drops below $200$ at $n=27$; at $n=26$ it is still above $200$.

$$\therefore\ \text{it takes } 27 \text{ years}$$

Median $(Q_2) = 7$

Upper quartile $(Q_3) = 10$

Highest score $= 20$

Is 20 an outlier? Justify your answer with calculations.
items.sol:
The interquartile range is
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 10 - 4 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
An outlier lies above $Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR &= 10 + 1.5\times 6 \\ &= 19 \end{aligned}$$
Since $20 > 19$, 20 is an outlier.

items.sol:

items.part:
City $A$ is in Sweden and is located at $(58^\circ\text{N}, 16^\circ\text{E})$. Sydney, in Australia, is located at $(33^\circ\text{S}, 151^\circ\text{E})$.

Robert lives in Sydney and needs to give an online presentation to his colleagues in City $A$ starting at 5:00 pm Thursday, local time in Sweden.

What time and day, in Sydney, should Robert start his presentation?

It is given that $15^\circ = 1$ hour time difference. Ignore daylight saving.
items.sol:
Both cities have longitude to the East.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Longitude difference} &= 151^\circ - 16^\circ \\ &= 135^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Time difference} &= 135\div 15 \\ &= 9 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
Sydney is further east, so it is 9 hours ahead of City $A$.

$\therefore$ The time in Sydney is 2 am Friday.

items.sol:
The probability of a head is twice that of a tail, so heads are $2$ parts and tails $1$ part out of $3$.

$$P(\text{head})=\dfrac{2}{3}$$

items.part:
A coin is biased so that it is twice as likely to show a head than a tail.
In two throws of this coin, what is the probability of obtaining at least one head?
items.sol:
The only way to get no heads is two tails, and $P(\text{tail})=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{no heads}) &= \dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ P(\text{at least 1 head}) &= 1-\dfrac{1}{9} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{9} \end{aligned}$$

The flight from Sydney to Rio de Janeiro will take 20 hours.

The flight will arrive in Rio de Janeiro at 3 pm on Wednesday 20 July.

On what day and at what time will Sakura leave Sydney?
items.sol:
Sydney is 13 hours ahead of Rio (UTC $+10$ and UTC $-3$).

Rio arrival time minus flight time:

$$3\text{ pm}-20\text{ hours}=7\text{ pm Tuesday 19 July (Rio time)}$$

Add the time difference of 13 hours:

$$7\text{ pm}+13\text{ hours}=8\text{ am Wednesday 20 July}$$

Alternative method: convert the arrival to Sydney time first.

$$3\text{ pm}+13\text{ hours}=4\text{ am Thursday 21 July}$$

$$4\text{ am}-20\text{ hours}=8\text{ am Wednesday 20 July}$$

Sakura leaves Sydney at 8 am on Wednesday 20 July.
items.final: Sakura leaves Sydney at 8 am on Wednesday 20 July.

items.part: Solve simultaneously the equations $y = \sqrt{x + 1}$ and $y = 11 - x$ and show that there is one point of intersection. Give your answer as a coordinate.
items.sol:
Equate the two expressions for $y$.
$$\sqrt{x+1} = 11 - x$$
Square both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} x + 1 &= (11-x)^2 \\ &= 121 - 22x + x^2 \\ 0 &= x^2 - 23x + 120 \\ &= (x-15)(x-8) \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 15$ or $x = 8$.

Squaring can introduce extra roots, so check each in the original equation.

For $x = 15$: $\sqrt{16} = 4 \ne -4 = 11-15$, rejected.

For $x = 8$: $\sqrt{9} = 3 = 11-8$, true.

The only point of intersection is:
$$(8, 3)$$
