\exfigure{1315_q32_1}
Let the area of triangle be $A$. Show that $A^2=-33x^2+462x-1089$.
items.sol:
Using the area formula with the sides $8$ and $x$ about angle $Z$, then $\sin^2Z=1-\cos^2Z$:

$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac12 ab\sin C\\ A^2&=\dfrac14 a^2b^2\sin^2 Z\\ A^2&=\dfrac14\,8^2x^2\left(1-\cos^2 Z\right)\\ A^2&=16x^2\left(1-\left(\dfrac{7x-33}{4x}\right)^2\right)\\ A^2&=16x^2\left(\dfrac{16x^2-\left(49x^2-462x+1089\right)}{16x^2}\right)\\ A^2&=-33x^2+462x-1089\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The triangle $XYZ$ has $XZ=8$, $YZ=x$, $XY=z$ as shown below.

The perimeter of the triangle $XYZ$ is 22.

\exfigure{1315_q32_1}
Hence, calculate the maximum area for triangle and state what type of triangle with the maximum area.
items.sol:
The maximum of $A$ occurs at the maximum of $A^2$.

$$A^2=-33x^2+462x-1089$$

Differentiate and set equal to zero.

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(A^2\right)&=-66x+462\\ -66x+462&=0\\ x&=7\end{aligned}$$

Test the nature:

$$\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\left(A^2\right)=-66<0$$

So $x=7$ gives a maximum.

Then $z=14-x=7$, so $YZ=XY=7$.

$$\begin{aligned}A^2&=-33(7)^2+462(7)-1089=528\\ A&=\sqrt{528}=4\sqrt{33}\approx22.98\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum area is } 4\sqrt{33}\text{ units}^2\text{, when triangle } XYZ \text{ is isosceles}$$
items.final: maximum area is $4\sqrt{33}$ units$^2$, when triangle XYZ is isosceles

items.part:
The graph below shows functions $f(x)=-3$ and $g(x)=x^2(x-2)$. The curves intersect at the point $(-1,-3)$. Find the area of the shaded region.

\exfigure{1315_q33_1}
items.sol:
The shaded area is the rectangle between $y=-3$ and the $x$-axis over $-1\le x\le0$, minus the area under the curve $g$ there.

$$\begin{aligned}A&=3-\left|\int_{-1}^0 g(x)\,dx\right|\\ &=3-\left|\int_{-1}^0 \left(x^3-2x^2\right)dx\right|\\ &=3-\left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^0\right|\\ &=3-\left|0-\left(\dfrac14+\dfrac23\right)\right|\\ &=\dfrac{25}{12}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{25}{12} \text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
Let $X$ be a uniform discrete random variable with possible values $X=1,2,3,\dots,n$.

Show that $\text{Var}(X)=\dfrac{n^2-1}{12}$.

You are given $1^2+2^2+3^2+\dots+n^2=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$. [DO NOT PROVE THIS]
items.sol:
Each value has probability $P(X=x)=\dfrac1n$ for $x=1,2,\dots,n$.

Expected value, using $1+2+\dots+n=\dfrac n2(1+n)$:

$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=1\times\dfrac1n+2\times\dfrac1n+\dots+n\times\dfrac1n\\&=\dfrac1n(1+2+\dots+n)\\&=\dfrac1n\cdot\dfrac n2(1+n)\\&=\dfrac{1+n}{2}\end{aligned}$$

Using the given sum of squares:

$$\begin{aligned}E\left(X^2\right)&=\dfrac1n\left(1^2+2^2+\dots+n^2\right)\\&=\dfrac1n\cdot\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\\&=\dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\text{Var}(X)=E\left(X^2\right)-\left(E(X)\right)^2$:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Var}(X)&=\dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}-\left(\dfrac{1+n}{2}\right)^2\\ &=\dfrac{(n+1)\left[2(2n+1)-3(1+n)\right]}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{(n+1)(n-1)}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{n^2-1}{12}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
From the top of a tower, which is 60 metres high, Isaac throws a stone upward and allows it to fall under gravity.

The height of the stone is modelled by the equation, $h = 20t - 5t^2 + 60$, where $h$ is the height (in metres) of the stone above ground level and $t$ is the time in seconds since the stone was thrown.
ON YOUR PAPER, NEATLY DRAW THE CURVE FOR THIS EQUATION AND LABEL IT “Stone”.

\exfigure{1316_q11_1}

From the top of a tower, which is 60 metres high, Isaac throws a stone upward and allows it to fall under gravity.

The height of the stone is modelled by the equation, $h = 20t - 5t^2 + 60$, where $h$ is the height (in metres) of the stone above ground level and $t$ is the time in seconds since the stone was thrown.
At the same time as the stone is thrown, Jay releases a toy glider from the top of the tower.

The glider drifts down, losing height at a constant rate of 5 metres per second.

items.sol:
The glider starts at the top of the tower, so the $h$-intercept is $c=60$.

It loses 5 m each second, so the gradient is

$$m=\dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}=-\dfrac{5}{1}=-5$$

The equation is

$$h=-5t+60$$

To start a game of Trouble, Noel and Jacob each roll a single die.

items.sol:
The outcomes where Jacob's number is greater than Noel's are the 15 cells on one side of the diagonal of the table.

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$:
$\dfrac{\cos 3x}{x^2}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=\cos 3x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=-3\sin 3x & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\cos 3x}{x^2}\right) &= \dfrac{-3x^2\sin 3x-2x\cos 3x}{(x^2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(-3x\sin 3x-2\cos 3x)}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{-3x\sin 3x-2\cos 3x}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$:
$\ln\sqrt{3-x}$.
items.sol:
Using log laws to simplify first:

$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \ln\sqrt{3-x} \\ &= \ln (3-x)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(3-x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{-1}{3-x} \\ &= \dfrac{-1}{2(3-x)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Ten kilograms of salt is placed into a swimming pool and begins to dissolve.

After $t$ hours the amount, $S$ kg, of undissolved salt is given by: $S = 10e^{-kt}$.

Calculate the value of $k$ to 3 significant figures, given that $S = 4.7$ when $t = 4$.
items.sol:
Substitute $S=4.7$ and $t=4$ into $S=10e^{-kt}$:

$$4.7=10e^{-4k}$$

$$\dfrac{4.7}{10}=e^{-4k}$$

Taking natural logs:

$$\begin{aligned} -4k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{4.7}{10}\right) \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{4.7}{10}\right)}{-4} \\ &= 0.1887556461\ldots \\ &\approx 0.189 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) = 1$ for the domain $[-\pi, \pi]$.
items.sol:
Rearrange first:

$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ \sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$

For $-\pi\le x\le\pi$, we need $-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le\dfrac{x}{3}\le\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

The only solutions in this interval are $\dfrac{x}{3}=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

The other solutions, $\pm\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, lie outside it (giving $x=\pm\dfrac{9\pi}{4}$, outside the domain).

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\text{ or } x=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$

items.part: By first differentiating $\ln(\cos x)$, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \tan x\,dx$.
items.sol:
Differentiating using the chain rule:

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\cos x)=\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}=-\tan x$$

So $\tan x$ has antiderivative $-\ln(\cos x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan x\,dx &= -\left[\ln\cos x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= -\left[\ln\dfrac{1}{2}-\ln 1\right] \\ &= -\ln\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x-3}{x^2-6x+5}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2-6x+5)=2x-6=2(x-3)$, the numerator is half the derivative of the denominator.

Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln f(x)+C$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x-3}{x^2-6x+5}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{2(x-3)}{x^2-6x+5}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|x^2-6x+5\right|+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two websites give reviews of books.

Both sites give each book a rating out of a possible 100.

A statistician analysed the ratings awarded by the two sites to 100 books and obtained the statistical results below.

\extable{1316_q22_t1}
The book “Moonlighting” got a rating of 78 on Bookophile and a rating of 84 on Great Reads.

Convert both these ratings to $z$-scores and determine which website rated the book higher in comparison to other books on the site.
items.sol:
Using the $z$-score formula $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} z_B&=\dfrac{78-60}{12}=\dfrac{18}{12}=1.5 \\ z_G&=\dfrac{84-76}{8}=\dfrac{8}{8}=1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1.5>1$, the rating on Bookophile is higher in comparison to other books on the site.
items.final: $z_B=1.5$, $z_G=1$; Bookophile rated the book higher in comparison to other books on the site.

items.part:
Two websites give reviews of books.

Both sites give each book a rating out of a possible 100.

A statistician analysed the ratings awarded by the two sites to 100 books and obtained the statistical results below.

\extable{1316_q22_t1}
What percentage of books would have a rating between 60 and 84 on the Bookophile website?
items.sol:
On Bookophile the $z$-scores are:
$$\begin{aligned} x=60:\ z&=\dfrac{60-60}{12}=0 \\ x=84:\ z&=\dfrac{84-60}{12}=2 \end{aligned}$$
Approximately $95\%$ of scores have $z$-scores between $-2$ and $2$, so by symmetry $47.5\%$ lie between $z=0$ and $z=2$.
$$\therefore\ 47.5\%\text{ of books}$$

items.part:
Consider the probability density function for a random variable $X$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{k}{\sqrt{9+3x}} & 0 \le x \le 9 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$
Find the value of $k$ and hence write the equation of the Cumulative Density Function.
items.sol:
For a probability density function the total area is 1:
$$\displaystyle\int_0^9\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{9+3x}}\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} k\left[\dfrac{(9+3x)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{3\times\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^9&=1 \\ \dfrac{2k}{3}\left[(9+27)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]&=1 \\ \dfrac{2k}{3}\left[6-3\right]&=1 \\ 2k&=1 \\ k&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_0^x(9+3t)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{(9+3t)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}\times 3}\right]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}(9+3x)^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{3}(9)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3x}-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{2},\qquad F(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3x}-1\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 9$$

items.part:
Consider the probability density function for a random variable $X$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{k}{\sqrt{9+3x}} & 0 \le x \le 9 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$
Find the median value of $X$.
items.sol:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3m}-1&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{9+3m}&=\dfrac{9}{2} \\ 9+3m&=\dfrac{81}{4} \\ 3m&=\dfrac{45}{4} \\ m&=\dfrac{15}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{median}=\dfrac{15}{4}$$

items.part:
Consider the geometric series

$$1 + (\sqrt{7}-2) + (\sqrt{7}-2)^2 + \cdots$$
Show with calculations why this geometric series has a limiting sum.
items.sol:
A geometric series has a limiting sum when $|r|<1$, where $r=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$.
$$r=\dfrac{\sqrt{7}-2}{1}=\sqrt{7}-2\approx 0.6$$
Since $|r|<1$, the series has a limiting sum.

items.part:
Consider the geometric series

$$1 + (\sqrt{7}-2) + (\sqrt{7}-2)^2 + \cdots$$
Find the exact value of the limiting sum with a rational denominator.
items.sol:
With $a=1$ and $r=\sqrt{7}-2$, the limiting sum formula is $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{1}{1-(\sqrt{7}-2)} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3-\sqrt{7}}\times\dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{3+\sqrt{7}} \\ &=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{9-7} \\ &=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Jamie-Lee considers two options to allow her to purchase a property worth \$250 000 within the next fifteen years.
One option is to invest an amount at the end of each year into an annuity which pays interest at 3% per annum.

This table shows the future values of an annuity of \$1 for periods between 10 and 16 years, for different annual interest rates. The contributions are made at the end of each year.

\extable{1316_q27_t1}

Use the table to determine how much she would need to invest each year to achieve her target of \$250 000 after 15 years.
items.sol:
From the table, for $3\%$ and $15$ years the interest factor is $18.5989$.

The yearly investment $A$ satisfies $18.5989A=250\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=250\,000\div 18.5989 \\ &=13\,441.655\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{yearly investment}=\$13\,441.66$$

items.part:
Jamie-Lee considers two options to allow her to purchase a property worth \$250 000 within the next fifteen years.
Her second option is to borrow \$250 000 now at the same interest rate and pay it back in monthly repayments over 15 years.

This table shows the present values of an annuity of \$1 for periods between 165 and 172 months, for different monthly interest rates.

\extable{1316_q27_t2}

Use the table to find the monthly repayment necessary to pay off the loan of \$250 000 in fifteen years.
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $3\%\div 12=0.25\%$ and the period is $15\times 12=180$ months, so the table interest factor is $144.8055$.

If $R$ is the monthly repayment, $250\,000=144.8055R$.
$$\begin{aligned} R&=250\,000\div 144.8055 \\ &=\$1726.45 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{monthly repayment}=\$1726.45$$

items.part:

items.sol:
Loan payments per year:
$$\begin{aligned} 1726.45\times 12&=\$20\,717.45 \end{aligned}$$
This is more than the yearly investment of $\$13\,441.66$.

Therefore she would pay less each year with the investment option.
items.final: The investment option costs less each year ($\$13\,441.66$ vs $\$20\,717.45$)

items.sol:
The area under the triangle is
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}bh=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 0.5=1\text{ unit}^2$$
So $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx=1$, and $f(x)=0$ outside $(0,4)$, so $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$. Also $f(x)\ge 0$, so it could be a probability density function.

For $0\le x<2$: the gradient is $m=\dfrac{0.5}{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and the $y$-intercept is $0$, so $y=\dfrac{x}{4}$.

For $2\le x\le 4$: the gradient is $m=\dfrac{-0.5}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{4}$, and $y=0$ when $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=-\dfrac{1}{4}(x-4) \\ y&=1-\dfrac{x}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{4} & 0\le x<2\\[6pt] 1-\dfrac{x}{4} & 2\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}$. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the displacement equation $x$ in terms of $t$ for this particle.
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$x=\displaystyle\int\left(1-2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right)dt=t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=0-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin 0+C \\ C&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}$. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the exact distance travelled in the first 4 seconds.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}&=0 \\ \cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{\pi t}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3},\dfrac{7\pi}{3} \\ t&=1,5,7 \end{aligned}$$
In the first 4 seconds the direction changes only at $t=1$, so find the distance for $0\le t\le 1$ and $1\le t\le 4$ separately.
$$\begin{aligned} d&=\left|\displaystyle\int_0^1 v\,dt\right|+\left|\displaystyle\int_1^4 v\,dt\right| \\ &=\left|\left[t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right]_0^1\right|+\left|\left[t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right]_1^4\right| \\ &=\left|1-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right|+\left|\left(4+\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\left(1-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &=\left|1-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right|+\left|3+\dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right| \\ &=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi}-1+3+\dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\ &=2+\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance}=\left(2+\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right)\text{ m}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}$. The particle is initially at the origin.
Find the exact acceleration of the particle at $t = 4$ seconds.
items.sol:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:
$$a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}$$
When $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi}{3}\text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

In the cone, Pythagoras' theorem gives $r^2+h^2=169$, so $r^2=169-h^2$.

Substituting into $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(169-h^2)h \\ &=\dfrac{169\pi h}{3}-\dfrac{\pi h^3}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $V'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} V'&=\dfrac{169\pi}{3}-\pi h^2=0 \\ h^2&=\dfrac{169}{3} \\ h&=\dfrac{13}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{13\sqrt{3}}{3}\approx 7.5 \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative:
$$V''=-2\pi h<0\ \text{ when } h=\dfrac{13\sqrt{3}}{3}$$
so it is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ h=\dfrac{13\sqrt{3}}{3}\text{ cm}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x) = 2x^3 - x^4$

Sketch the function for the domain $[-2,2]$, showing all key features including finding any stationary points, determining the nature and or any inflexions.

Space to draw the graph is provided on the next page.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-4x^3 \\ &=2x^2(3-2x)=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$. Then $f(0)=0$ and $f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)=\dfrac{27}{16}$.

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{27}{16}\right)$.

Nature, from the sign of $f'(x)$:

\extable{Ts7127_1}

So $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion and $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{27}{16}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.

For other inflexions, $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=12x-12x^2 \\ &=12x(1-x)=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

\extable{Ts7127_2}

The concavity changes at $x=1$ and $f(1)=1$, so $(1,1)$ is a point of inflexion. $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion, as found above.

items.part: Find the value of $p$ and $q$ such that $(1-\sqrt{3})^2=2p-\sqrt{3q}$
items.sol:
Expand the left-hand side.
$$\begin{aligned} (1-\sqrt{3})^2 &= (1-\sqrt{3})(1-\sqrt{3}) \\ &= 1-2\sqrt{3}+3 \\ &= 4-2\sqrt{3} \\ &= 2(2)-\sqrt{3\times 4} \end{aligned}$$
Comparing with $2p-\sqrt{3q}$:
$$\therefore\ p=2,\ q=4$$

items.part: Solve the equation $|3x+4|=5$.

$$3x+4=5 \quad\text{or}\quad 3x+4=-5$$
$$3x=1 \quad\text{or}\quad 3x=-9$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ or } x=-3$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{5x^2-3x}{x^3}\,dx$
items.sol:
Divide each term by $x^3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{5x^2-3x}{x^3}\,dx &= \int\left(\dfrac{5}{x}-3x^{-2}\right)dx \\ &= 5\ln|x|-\dfrac{3x^{-1}}{-1}+C \\ &= 5\ln|x|+\dfrac{3}{x}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\cos 2x}{e^x}\right)$ in simplest form.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\cos 2x & v&=e^x \\ u'&=-2\sin 2x & v'&=e^x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\cos 2x}{e^x}\right) &= \dfrac{e^x(-2\sin 2x)-\cos 2x\,(e^x)}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(-2\sin 2x-\cos 2x)}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{e^x}\left(-2\sin 2x-\cos 2x\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve for $x$: $\log_3(2x+1)+\log_3 x=1$
items.sol:
Combine the logarithms using $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$. The logarithms need $2x+1>0$ and $x>0$, so $x>0$.
$$\log_3\big(x(2x+1)\big)=1$$
Convert to index form.
$$\begin{aligned} x(2x+1) &= 3^1 \\ 2x^2+x-3 &= 0 \\ 2x^2-2x+3x-3 &= 0 \\ 2x(x-1)+3(x-1) &= 0 \\ (2x+3)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=1$ or $x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Since $x>0$, $x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x=1$$

items.part: Solve the equation $\sqrt{3}\sin\theta+\cos\theta=0$ where $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
Rearranging, $\sqrt3\sin\theta=-\cos\theta$.

Dividing by $\cos\theta$ (note $\cos\theta\ne 0$, since otherwise $\sin\theta=0$ as well):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \\ \tan\theta&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$

items.part:
The following distribution table shows the number of mobile phones in a sample of families.

\extable{1317_q12b_t1}

It is given that $k$ is a positive integer.
If the median of the distribution is $4$, write down the minimum possible value of $k$.
items.sol:
Writing the data in order from the largest value, the sample has $k+16$ values.

$$5,5,5,5,4,4,4,4,\underline{4},3,3,3,3,3,3,3,2,\dots$$
There are 8 numbers on each side of the median (the underlined $4$).

$$\therefore\ k=1$$

items.part:
The following distribution table shows the number of mobile phones in a sample of families.

\extable{1317_q12b_t1}

It is given that $k$ is a positive integer.
If the mean of the distribution is $3$, find the value of $k$.
items.sol:
The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{mean}&=\dfrac{2k+3\times 7+4\times 5+5\times 4}{k+16} \\ 3&=\dfrac{2k+61}{k+16} \\ 3k+48&=2k+61 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=13$$

items.part:
A curve $C$ has the equation $y=f(x)$ where $x\neq 0$. The point $P(1,3)$ lies on the curve.
Find $f(x)$, given $f'(x)=7-\dfrac{3}{x^2}+4x$
items.sol:
Integrating $f'(x)=7-3x^{-2}+4x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int\left(7-3x^{-2}+4x\right)dx \\ &=7x-\dfrac{3x^{-1}}{-1}+\dfrac{4x^2}{2}+c \\ &=2x^2+7x+\dfrac3x+c \end{aligned}$$
Since $P(1,3)$ lies on the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=2+7+3+c \\ c&=-9 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=2x^2+7x+\dfrac3x-9$$

items.part:
A curve $C$ has the equation $y=f(x)$ where $x\neq 0$. The point $P(1,3)$ lies on the curve.
Find the equation of the normal to curve $C$, at the point $P$.

Express your answer in general form.
items.sol:
The gradient of the tangent at $P$ is $f'(1)$:
$$m_T=7-3+4=8$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-\dfrac18$.

Equation of the normal:
$$\begin{aligned} y-3&=-\dfrac18(x-1) \\ 8y-24&=-x+1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x+8y-25=0$$

items.part:
Use the standard normal distribution table below to find the probability for a normally distributed random variable $X$, given $P(X\ge 18)$ where $\mu=5$ and $\sigma=10$.

\exfigure{1317_q12d_1}
items.sol:
Standardise using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 18)&=P\left(Z\ge\dfrac{18-5}{10}\right) \\ &=P(Z\ge 1.3) \\ &=1-P(Z<1.3) \\ &=1-0.9032 \\ &=0.0968 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X\ge 18)=0.0968=\dfrac{121}{1250}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line and its velocity is given by: $v=-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right)$ for $0\le t\le 8$.

The graph shows its velocity $v$ metres per second at time $t$ seconds.

\exfigure{1317_q13a_1}
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first $6$ seconds.
items.sol:
From the graph, $v\le 0$ for $0\le t\le 4$ and $v\ge 0$ for $4\le t\le 8$, and the graph is symmetric about $t=4$. The distance in the first 4 seconds equals the distance in the last 4, so the first 6 seconds cover $1.5$ times the first 4 seconds.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=\left|\int_0^4\left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)dt\right|\times 1.5 \\ &=\left|\left[\dfrac{4}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right]_0^4\right|\times 1.5 \\ &=\left|\dfrac4\pi\cos\pi-\dfrac4\pi\cos 0\right|\times 1.5 \\ &=\left|-\dfrac8\pi\right|\times 1.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance}=\dfrac{12}{\pi}\text{ m}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line and its velocity is given by: $v=-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right)$ for $0\le t\le 8$.

The graph shows its velocity $v$ metres per second at time $t$ seconds.

\exfigure{1317_q13a_1}
At what time does the particle reach its maximum displacement? Justify your answer.
items.sol:
Displacement is position relative to the origin.

Integrating the velocity gives $x=\dfrac{4}{\pi}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right)+c$.

Maximum displacement occurs when $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right)$ has its maximum value.

$$\therefore\ t=0 \text{ and } t=8$$

items.part:
A bag contains five red marbles and four blue marbles.

Three marbles are drawn in succession.

At each draw, if the marble is red it is replaced, and if it is blue it is not replaced.

Find the probability of drawing: one red marble.
items.sol:
Tree diagram (1st, 2nd, 3rd draw). After a red draw the marble is replaced, so the probabilities stay $\dfrac59$ red and $\dfrac49$ blue. After a blue draw there are 8 marbles ($\dfrac58$ red, $\dfrac38$ blue). After two blue draws there are 7 marbles ($\dfrac57$ red, $\dfrac27$ blue).

Exactly one red marble can occur in three ways:
$$\begin{aligned} P(RBB)&=\dfrac59\times\dfrac49\times\dfrac38=\dfrac{5}{54} \\ P(BRB)&=\dfrac49\times\dfrac58\times\dfrac38=\dfrac{5}{48} \\ P(BBR)&=\dfrac49\times\dfrac38\times\dfrac57=\dfrac{5}{42} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{1 red})=\dfrac{5}{54}+\dfrac{5}{48}+\dfrac{5}{42}=\dfrac{955}{3024}$$

items.part: Prove that $\dfrac{\tan\theta+1}{\sec\theta}-\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}\theta}{\cot\theta+\tan\theta}=\sin\theta$.
items.sol:
Express everything in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, using $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$, $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ and $\cot\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\cos\theta\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}+1\right)-\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\left(\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}+\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)} \\ &=\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\left(\frac{\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\right)} \\ &=\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\left(\frac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\right)} \\ &=\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\cos\theta \\ &=\sin\theta \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle starts from the origin and moves in a straight line with a velocity given by $v=\dfrac{3t}{5+t^2}$ metres per second, where $t$ is in seconds.
Find an expression for the acceleration. Simplify your answer.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3t & v&=5+t^2 \\ u'&=3 & v'&=2t \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{(5+t^2)(3)-(3t)(2t)}{(5+t^2)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{15+3t^2-6t^2}{(5+t^2)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{15-3t^2}{(5+t^2)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle starts from the origin and moves in a straight line with a velocity given by $v=\dfrac{3t}{5+t^2}$ metres per second, where $t$ is in seconds.
Describe the motion of the particle initially. In your answer, make reference to the velocity and to the acceleration of the particle.
items.sol:
When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} v&=0 \\ a&=\dfrac{15}{25}=\dfrac35 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the particle is initially at rest, and its velocity will increase due to the positive acceleration of $0.6\text{ m/s}^2$.

items.part:
The top of a tower $B$ is due north of Patricia ($P$) and its angle of elevation is $42^\circ$. From Queenie ($Q$) who is $80$ metres from Patricia, the tower is due west and its angle of elevation is $38^\circ$. Let the height of the tower be $h$ metres and let $C$ be the base of the tower on the ground. Calculate the height of the tower, correct to one decimal place.

\exfigure{1317_q14b_1}
items.sol:
\exfigure{1317_q14b_s1}

The angles of depression/elevation give $\angle PBC=48^\circ$ and $\angle QBC=52^\circ$ in the vertical triangles (angle sum with the right angle at $C$).

In $\triangle PBC$: $PC=h\tan 48^\circ$.

In $\triangle QBC$: $QC=h\tan 52^\circ$.

P is due south of $C$ and Q is due east of $C$, so $\triangle PCQ$ is right-angled at $C$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} PC^2+QC^2&=PQ^2 \\ h^2\tan^2 48^\circ+h^2\tan^2 52^\circ&=80^2 \\ h^2&=\dfrac{80^2}{\tan^2 48^\circ+\tan^2 52^\circ} \\ h&=\sqrt{2228.636719} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{height of tower}\approx 47.2\text{ m}$$

items.part:
The cost of riding a Harley-Davidson motor bike (in dollars per hour) depends on the speed ($v$) of the motor bike (in kilometres per hour) and is given by $C=3v^2+15v+20000$.
Show that the total cost for a trip of $90$ km is given by: $P=270v+1350+\dfrac{1800000}{v}$
items.sol:
The cost per hour is $C=3v^2+15v+20000$. A trip of $90$ km at speed $v$ takes $t=\dfrac{90}{v}$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{90}{v}\times C \\ &=\dfrac{90}{v}\left(3v^2+15v+20000\right) \\ &=270v+1350+\dfrac{1800000}{v} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The cost of riding a Harley-Davidson motor bike (in dollars per hour) depends on the speed ($v$) of the motor bike (in kilometres per hour) and is given by $C=3v^2+15v+20000$.
Find the speed, in km/h, that will minimise the cost of this trip
items.sol:
For minimum cost, $\dfrac{dP}{dv}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dv}&=270-\dfrac{1800000}{v^2}=0 \\ v^2&=\dfrac{1800000}{270}=\dfrac{20000}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Since $v>0$:
$$v=\sqrt{\dfrac{20000}{3}}\approx 81.6\text{ km/h}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dv^2}=\dfrac{3600000}{v^3}$$
When $v=81.6$:
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dv^2}=\dfrac{3600000}{81.6^3}\approx 6.6>0$$
so this is a minimum.

$$\therefore\ v\approx 81.6\text{ km/h minimises the cost}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = x^3 - x + 4$ at $x = 1$.
items.sol:
Differentiate to find the gradient:
$$y' = 3x^2 - 1$$
At $x = 1$, the gradient is $y' = 2$.

When $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 1 - 1 + 4 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
So the point is $(1, 4)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y - 4 &= 2(x - 1) \\ y &= 2x + 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y = 2x + 2$$

items.part: Differentiate $y = \sqrt{x}$.
items.sol:
Write the function as a power:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= x^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ y' &= \dfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y = \cos 2x$.
Differentiate $y = x^3 \ln x$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^3 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=3x^2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= u'v + uv' \\ &= 3x^2\ln x + x^2 \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{1318_q13_s1}

Total sales are $\$25\,000$, and Saturday plus Sunday is $\$14\,000$.

So the week days total
$$\begin{aligned} 25\,000 - 14\,000 &= 11\,000 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{11\,000}{25\,000} \times 100\% &= 44\% \end{aligned}$$
Reading the Pareto chart at Sunday gives about $56\%$ for the weekend, so $44\%$ for the week days. The chart reading is not very accurate.

Any one valid action, for example:

More staff on weekends.

A sale early in the week to encourage customers.

Close on a Monday.

Longer trading hours on weekends.
items.final: More staff on weekends (any one valid action).

items.part: If $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{3}{7}$ and $\tan\theta$ is positive, find the value of $\sin\theta$. Leave your answer in simplified form.
items.sol:
In a right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and adjacent side 3, let the opposite side be $x$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 + 3^2 &= 7^2 \\ x^2 &= 40 \\ x &= \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10} \end{aligned}$$
So the acute reference angle $\alpha$ has $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}$.

Since $\cos\theta < 0$ and $\tan\theta > 0$, $\theta$ is in Quadrant 3, where sine is negative.
$$\therefore\ \sin\theta = -\dfrac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}$$

items.part:
The graph of $y = \dfrac{2}{x}$ is translated upwards by 1 unit followed by a reflection in the $x$-axis.
State the equation of the new graph.
items.sol:
Translating up 1 unit gives $y = \dfrac{2}{x} + 1$. Reflecting in the $x$-axis negates $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -\left(\dfrac{2}{x} + 1\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{2}{x} - 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The graph of $y = \dfrac{2}{x}$ is translated upwards by 1 unit followed by a reflection in the $x$-axis.
Sketch the new graph. Clearly indicate any intercepts with the axes and any asymptotes.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1318_q15_s1}

The $x$-intercept is found by setting $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{2}{x} - 1 &= 0 \\ x &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
There is no $y$-intercept, as $x=0$ is an asymptote. The asymptotes are $x = 0$ and $y = -1$.

items.part: How many terms are there in the series $11 + 13 + 15 + \cdots$ if the sum is 375?
items.sol:
This is an arithmetic series with $a = 11$ and $d = 2$.

Using the sum formula $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 375 &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left(22 + (n-1)2\right) \\ 750 &= n(20 + 2n) \\ 2n^2 + 20n - 750 &= 0 \\ n^2 + 10n - 375 &= 0 \\ (n - 15)(n + 25) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $n = 15$ or $n = -25$.

Since $n > 0$, $n = 15$.
$$\therefore\ \text{There are 15 terms.}$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1318_q17_1}

The diagram above shows three checkpoints $A$, $B$ and $C$ in an orienteering event.

Checkpoints $A$ and $C$ are such that $C$ is 12 km due north of $A$. One participant starts from $A$ and walks in the direction of $050^\circ$ T. After 9 km the participant arrives at checkpoint $B$.
Find the distance $BC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, with $\angle BAC = 50^\circ$, $AC = 12$ and $AB = 9$:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2 &= 12^2 + 9^2 - 2 \times 12 \times 9\cos 50^\circ \\ &= 86.157\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BC \approx 9.28 \text{ km}$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1318_q17_1}

The diagram above shows three checkpoints $A$, $B$ and $C$ in an orienteering event.

Checkpoints $A$ and $C$ are such that $C$ is 12 km due north of $A$. One participant starts from $A$ and walks in the direction of $050^\circ$ T. After 9 km the participant arrives at checkpoint $B$.
What is the true bearing of $C$ from $B$? Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Let $\angle ACB = \theta$. Using the sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{9}{\sin\theta} &= \dfrac{BC}{\sin 50^\circ} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{9\sin 50^\circ}{BC} \\ &= 0.7428\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\theta \approx 48^\circ$$
Ambiguous case check: the other angle is $180^\circ - 48^\circ = 132^\circ$, and $132^\circ + 50^\circ > 180^\circ$, so $\theta$ is acute.

Since $C$ is north-west of $B$, the bearing of $C$ from $B$ is
$$360^\circ - 48^\circ = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$
Alternatively, let $\angle ABC = \alpha$:
$$\sin\alpha = \dfrac{12\sin 50^\circ}{BC} = 0.9903\ldots$$
so $\alpha = 82^\circ$, and the bearing is
$$82^\circ + 50^\circ + 180^\circ = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{bearing} = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$

items.part:
Solve the following equation for $x$ in terms of $a$:

$$3\log_a x + 4 = 5\log_a x$$
items.sol:
Collect the logarithm terms:
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= 5\log_a x - 3\log_a x \\ &= 2\log_a x \end{aligned}$$
So $\log_a x = 2$.
$$\therefore\ x = a^2$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{5}{x}\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\int \dfrac{5}{x}\,dx = 5\ln|x| + C$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1318_q19b_1}

For the diagram above, find the exact area bounded by the curve $y = 4x - e^x$ and the $x$-axis between $x = 1$ and $x = 2$.
items.sol:
The curve is above the $x$-axis on $1 \le x \le 2$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \displaystyle\int_1^2 (4x - e^x)\,dx \\ &= \left[2x^2 - e^x\right]_1^2 \\ &= (8 - e^2) - (2 - e) \\ &= 6 - e^2 + e \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area} = (6 + e - e^2) \text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
\extable{1318_q20_t1}

The table above shows the probability distribution of a spinner for a board game.

Let $X$ be the outcome of the spinner.
Find $P(X \le 3)$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(X \le 3) &= \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{4}{10} + \dfrac{2}{10} \\ &= \dfrac{9}{10} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
\extable{1318_q20_t1}

The table above shows the probability distribution of a spinner for a board game.

Let $X$ be the outcome of the spinner.
Find the expected value $E(X)$.
items.sol:
Using $E(X) = \displaystyle\sum x\,p(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 1 \times \dfrac{3}{10} + 2 \times \dfrac{4}{10} + 3 \times \dfrac{2}{10} + 4 \times \dfrac{1}{10} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{8}{10} + \dfrac{6}{10} + \dfrac{4}{10} \\ &= 2.1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
\extable{1318_q20_t1}

The table above shows the probability distribution of a spinner for a board game.

Let $X$ be the outcome of the spinner.
Find the variance $\text{Var}(X)$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= 1^2\times\dfrac{3}{10} + 2^2\times\dfrac{4}{10} + 3^2\times\dfrac{2}{10} + 4^2\times\dfrac{1}{10} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{16}{10} + \dfrac{18}{10} + \dfrac{16}{10} \\ &= 5.3 \end{aligned}$$
Using $\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \mu^2$ with $\mu = 2.1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= 5.3 - (2.1)^2 \\ &= 0.89 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$.
Find the stationary points of the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$. Determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 8x - 6x^2 = 2x(4 - 3x) \\ y'' &= 8 - 12x \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $y' = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = \dfrac{4}{3}$.

The sign of $y''$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} x = 0:\ & y'' = 8 > 0 &&\text{concave up, so } (0,0) \text{ is a minimum turning point} \\ x = \dfrac{4}{3}:\ & y'' = 8 - 12 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = -8 < 0 &&\text{concave down, so a maximum turning point} \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \dfrac{4}{3}$:
$$y = 4\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^2 - 2\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^3 = \dfrac{64}{27}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum at } (0,0),\ \text{maximum at } \left(\dfrac{4}{3}, \dfrac{64}{27}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$.
Show that there is an inflection point at $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{32}{27}\right)$ on the curve.
items.sol:
Inflection points occur where $y'' = 0$:
$$8 - 12x = 0$$
so $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

Test the concavity either side of $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

\extable{Ts7188_1}

The concavity changes at $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so there is an inflection point there, with $y = \dfrac{32}{27}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{inflection point at } \left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{32}{27}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$.
For what interval is the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$ increasing?
items.sol:
The curve is increasing where $y' > 0$, that is $2x(4-3x) > 0$.
$$\therefore\ 0 < x < \dfrac{4}{3}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$.
Hence, sketch the graph of the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$. Clearly label the stationary points, the point of inflection and any intercepts with the axes.

A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x = 12\ln(t + 2) - 2t + 5,$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds.
What is the initial position of the particle? Give your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
At $t = 0$:
$$x = 12\ln 2 + 5$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is } (12\ln 2 + 5) \text{ metres to the right of } O$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x = 12\ln(t + 2) - 2t + 5,$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds.
Find the expression for the velocity of the particle at time $t$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} v &= \dfrac{dx}{dt} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{t + 2} - 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x = 12\ln(t + 2) - 2t + 5,$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds.
Find the time when the particle is at rest.
items.sol:
At rest, $v = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12}{t+2} - 2 &= 0 \\ \dfrac{12}{t+2} &= 2 \\ 12 &= 2t + 4 \\ 2t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 4 \text{ s}$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x = 12\ln(t + 2) - 2t + 5,$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds.
What happens to the acceleration eventually?
items.sol:
Write $v = 12(t+2)^{-1} - 2$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{dv}{dt} \\ &= -12(t+2)^{-2} \\ &= -\dfrac{12}{(t+2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
As $t \to \infty$, $(t+2)^2 \to \infty$.
$$\therefore\ a \to 0$$

items.part: Solve the equation $2\sin 2x = 1$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.

Let $u = 2x$. Since $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, we have $0 \le u \le 4\pi$.

Then $2\sin u = 1$, so $\sin u = \dfrac{1}{2}$, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, over two revolutions:
$$u = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \dfrac{13\pi}{6}, \dfrac{17\pi}{6}$$
Since $x = \dfrac{u}{2}$:
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{\pi}{12}, \dfrac{5\pi}{12}, \dfrac{13\pi}{12}, \dfrac{17\pi}{12}$$

items.part: Shade the regions bounded by the curve $y = \sin x$, the $x$-axis and between $x = 0$ and $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$. Calculate the total area of these regions.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1318_q26_s2}

The curve is above the $x$-axis for $0 \le x \le \pi$ and below it for $\pi \le x \le \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, so the area is found in two parts.

Area from $0$ to $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin x \, dx &= \left[-\cos x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} - (-\cos 0) \\ &= 0 + 1 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
By symmetry the area from $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ to $\pi$ is also $1$, and the area from $\pi$ to $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is also $1$.
$$\text{Total area} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 \text{ units}^2$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^5 \dfrac{x^2 + 3}{x}\,dx$
items.sol:
Divide each term by $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5 \dfrac{x^2 + 3}{x}\,dx &= \int_1^5 \left(x + \dfrac{3}{x}\right)dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} + 3\ln x\right]_1^5 \\ &= \dfrac{25}{2} + 3\ln 5 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + 3\ln 1\right) \\ &= 12 + 3\ln 5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hugo has three years to save \$25\,000 for a holiday.
Hugo deposits a single lump sum into an account paying 8% p.a. interest compounded every 6 months. What lump sum is needed to ensure he can afford his holiday in three years time? Give your answer to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
The interest rate per period is $R = 4\%$ per 6 months, and the number of periods is $n = 3 \times 2 = 6$.

Using the compound interest formula, $FV = PV(1+R)^n$:
$$PV \times (1.04)^6 = 25\,000$$
$$\begin{aligned} PV &= \dfrac{25\,000}{1.04^6} \\ &\approx \$19\,758 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hugo has three years to save \$25\,000 for a holiday.
\extable{1318_q28_t1}

Hugo instead decides to make regular deposits to an annuity to save for his holiday. He deposits \$1800 at the end of each quarter over 3 years at 12% p.a. interest compounded quarterly.

Use the future value table above to determine if Hugo will have enough money to take his holiday. Show working to explain your answer.
items.sol:
The rate per quarter is $R = \dfrac{12\%}{4} = 3\%$, and the number of quarters is $n = 3 \times 4 = 12$.

The table value for $3\%$ and $12$ periods is $14.1920$.
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= 1800 \times 14.1920 \\ &= \$25\,546 \end{aligned}$$
Since $\$25\,546 > \$25\,000$, Hugo has enough money for his holiday.

items.part:
A closed cylindrical tank has a circular base of radius $r$ metres and a height of $h$ metres. It can hold $160\pi\ \text{m}^3$ of wheat. The material for the flat circular top and bottom costs \$10 per square metre and the material for the curved surface costs \$8 per square metre.
Show that the height of the tank is $h = \dfrac{160}{r^2}$.
items.sol:
The volume of a cylinder is $V = \pi r^2 h$, and the tank holds $160\pi \text{ m}^3$.
$$160\pi = \pi r^2 h$$
$$\therefore\ h = \dfrac{160}{r^2}$$

items.part:
A closed cylindrical tank has a circular base of radius $r$ metres and a height of $h$ metres. It can hold $160\pi\ \text{m}^3$ of wheat. The material for the flat circular top and bottom costs \$10 per square metre and the material for the curved surface costs \$8 per square metre.
Find the dimensions of the tank that minimise the cost of construction.
items.sol:
The top and bottom are two circles of area $\pi r^2$, at \$10 per square metre.
$$\text{Cost} = 2 \times \pi r^2 \times 10 = 20\pi r^2$$
The curved surface has area $2\pi r h$, and $h = \dfrac{160}{r^2}$, at \$8 per square metre.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\pi r \times \dfrac{160}{r^2} = \dfrac{320\pi}{r} \\ \text{Cost} &= \dfrac{320\pi}{r} \times 8 = \dfrac{2560\pi}{r} \end{aligned}$$
The total cost is
$$C = 20\pi r^2 + 2560\pi r^{-1}$$
Differentiating,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dC}{dr} &= 40\pi r - 2560\pi r^{-2} \\ C'' &= 40\pi + \dfrac{5120\pi}{r^3} \end{aligned}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dC}{dr} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2560\pi}{r^2} &= 40\pi r \\ r^3 &= 64 \\ r &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
When $r = 4$,
$$C'' = 40\pi + \dfrac{5120\pi}{64} > 0$$
so this is a minimum.

The height is
$$h = \dfrac{160}{4^2} = 10 \text{ m}$$
$$\therefore\ r = 4 \text{ m and } h = 10 \text{ m}$$

items.part: Prove the identity $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta}$.
items.sol:
Rewrite in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, then use $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= (\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{1 - \sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{(1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Tom invented a dice game to play on his own. He throws a pair of six-sided dice repeatedly until the difference between the dice is 2 or 3.

If the difference is 2, Tom wins and the game ends.

If the difference is 3, Tom loses and the game ends.

If the difference is any other number, he continues to throw until the difference is a 2 or 3.
Show that the probability that Tom wins on his first throw of the dice is $\dfrac{2}{9}$.
items.sol:
The difference is $2$ for the pairs $(1,3),(2,4),(3,5),(4,6)$ and their reverses, so $8$ of the $36$ equally likely outcomes.
$$P(\text{win on first throw}) = \dfrac{8}{36} = \dfrac{2}{9}$$

items.part:
Tom invented a dice game to play on his own. He throws a pair of six-sided dice repeatedly until the difference between the dice is 2 or 3.

If the difference is 2, Tom wins and the game ends.

If the difference is 3, Tom loses and the game ends.

If the difference is any other number, he continues to throw until the difference is a 2 or 3.
Calculate the probability that the game continues to a second throw.
items.sol:
The difference is $3$ for the pairs $(1,4),(2,5),(3,6)$ and their reverses, which is $6$ outcomes.
$$P(\text{difference } 2 \text{ or } 3) = \dfrac{8 + 6}{36} = \dfrac{14}{36}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{continue}) &= 1 - \dfrac{14}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{11}{18} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Tom invented a dice game to play on his own. He throws a pair of six-sided dice repeatedly until the difference between the dice is 2 or 3.

If the difference is 2, Tom wins and the game ends.

If the difference is 3, Tom loses and the game ends.

If the difference is any other number, he continues to throw until the difference is a 2 or 3.
What is the probability that Tom wins in one of the first three throws? Leave your answer in unsimplified form.
items.sol:
Tom wins on throw $1$, or continues once and wins on throw $2$, or continues twice and wins on throw $3$.
$$P = \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{2}{9}$$
This simplifies to $\dfrac{643}{1458}$.

items.part:
Tom invented a dice game to play on his own. He throws a pair of six-sided dice repeatedly until the difference between the dice is 2 or 3.

If the difference is 2, Tom wins and the game ends.

If the difference is 3, Tom loses and the game ends.

If the difference is any other number, he continues to throw until the difference is a 2 or 3.
Calculate the probability that Tom wins the game.
items.sol:
The probabilities of winning on throw $1, 2, 3, \dots$ form a geometric series with first term $a = \dfrac{2}{9}$ and common ratio $r = \dfrac{11}{18}$.

Since $|r| < 1$, the sum to infinity exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1 - r} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{2}{9}}{1 - \frac{11}{18}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{9} \times \dfrac{18}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
On the 1st January 2021, Amanda invested \$7000 into a bank account that paid interest at a rate of 6% p.a. compounded annually. Amanda decided to add \$700 to her account on the 1st January each year, beginning in 2022.

Let $A_n$ be the amount in the account on the 1st January after $n$ years, after interest and her deposit has been paid.
Show that $A_2 = A_1 \times 1.06 + 700$.
items.sol:
$A_1$ is the opening amount after one year's interest and the deposit.
$$A_1 = 7000 \times 1.06 + 700$$
In the second year the balance earns $6\%$ interest and then $\$700$ is added.
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= A_1 + 0.06A_1 + 700 \\ &= A_1 \times 1.06 + 700 \end{aligned}$$
Expanding,
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= (7000 \times 1.06 + 700) \times 1.06 + 700 \\ &= 7000 \times 1.06^2 + 700 \times 1.06 + 700 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
On the 1st January 2021, Amanda invested \$7000 into a bank account that paid interest at a rate of 6% p.a. compounded annually. Amanda decided to add \$700 to her account on the 1st January each year, beginning in 2022.

Let $A_n$ be the amount in the account on the 1st January after $n$ years, after interest and her deposit has been paid.
Hence, determine how much was in her account on 1st January 2031, after interest and her deposit has been paid. Give your answer to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
Continuing the pattern,
$$A_3 = 7000 \times 1.06^3 + 700 \times 1.06^2 + 700 \times 1.06 + 700$$
$$A_n = 7000 \times 1.06^n + 700 \times 1.06^{n-1} + \cdots + 700 \times 1.06 + 700$$
The terms after the first form a geometric series with $a = 700$, $r = 1.06$ and $n$ terms.
$$A_n = 7000 \times 1.06^n + \dfrac{700(1.06^n - 1)}{0.06}$$
1st January 2031 is $10$ years after 2021, so $n = 10$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{10} &= 7000 \times 1.06^{10} + \dfrac{700(1.06^{10} - 1)}{0.06} \\ &\approx \$21\,762 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
On the 1st January 2021, Amanda invested \$7000 into a bank account that paid interest at a rate of 6% p.a. compounded annually. Amanda decided to add \$700 to her account on the 1st January each year, beginning in 2022.

Let $A_n$ be the amount in the account on the 1st January after $n$ years, after interest and her deposit has been paid.
Amanda's friend, Bard, invested \$7000 into an account in a different bank on the 1st January 2021 and made no further payments. On 1st January 2031, Bard's balance was \$23\,417.

Calculate the annual rate of compound interest paid on Bard's account. Give your answer to 4 significant figures.
items.sol:
Bard's balance after $10$ years at $R\%$ p.a. compounded annually is given by
$$7000\left(1 + \dfrac{R}{100}\right)^{10} = 23\,417$$
Taking the tenth root,
$$\begin{aligned} 1 + \dfrac{R}{100} &= \sqrt[10]{\dfrac{23\,417}{7000}} \\ \dfrac{R}{100} &= \sqrt[10]{\dfrac{23\,417}{7000}} - 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ R \approx 12.83\%$$

items.part:
The 2021 Semester one report marks for a Year 12 Advanced Mathematics cohort at a particular selective boys high school is normally distributed with a mean of 76 and a standard deviation of 11
What is the probability that a randomly selected student from the cohort will have a mark between 54 and 98 ?
items.sol:
$54=\mu-2\sigma$ and $98=\mu+2\sigma$, so by the empirical rule the probability is the proportion within 2 standard deviations of the mean.
$$\therefore\ P(54\le X\le 98) = 95\%$$

items.part:

A student is selected randomly from the cohort. What is the probability that his mark is less than or equal to 65?
items.sol:
$65=\mu-\sigma$. By the empirical rule, $34\%$ of scores lie between $\mu-\sigma$ and $\mu$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 65) &= 50\% - 34\% \\ &= 16\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Prove that $(\sin x + \cos x)(\sec x - \operatorname{cosec} x) = \tan x - \cot x$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= (\sin x+\cos x)(\sec x - \operatorname{cosec} x) \\ &= \sin x\sec x + \cos x\sec x - \sin x\operatorname{cosec} x - \cos x\operatorname{cosec} x \\ &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} + \dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x} - \dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x} - \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} \\ &= \tan x + 1 - 1 - \cot x \\ &= \tan x - \cot x \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int x(x^2 + 5)^9\,dx$

$$\begin{aligned} \int x(x^2+5)^9\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x(x^2+5)^9\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{n+1}[f(x)]^{n+1} + C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{10}(x^2+5)^{10} + C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int x(x^2+5)^9\,dx = \dfrac{(x^2+5)^{10}}{20} + C$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 - 9x$
Show that $f(x)$ has 2 stationary points at $P\,(1,-5)$ and $Q(-3,27)$ and determine their nature
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2+6x-9 \\ &= 3(x+3)(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=-3$ or $x=1$.
$$f(-3) = (-3)^3 + 3(-3)^2 - 9(-3) = 27$$
$$f(1) = 1+3-9 = -5$$
Hence the stationary points are $(-3,27)$ and $(1,-5)$, as required.

Nature (sign of $f'(x)$ either side):

\extable{Ts7262_1}

$\therefore\ (-3,27)$ is a local maximum and $(1,-5)$ is a local minimum.
items.final: $(-3,27)$ is a local maximum and $(1,-5)$ is a local minimum.

items.part:

Find any points of inflexion
items.sol:
Points of inflexion occur where $f''(x)=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$f''(x) = 6x+6 = 0 \text{ so } x=-1$$
$$y = (-1)^3+3(-1)^2-9(-1) = 11$$
Concavity changes at $x=-1$, since $f''(x)=6(x+1)$ changes sign there.

$$\therefore\ (-1,11) \text{ is a point of inflexion}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} & \text{for } 1 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Find the cumulative distribution function
items.sol:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_1^x f(t)\,dt$ for $1\le x\le 2$.

$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_1^x\left(\dfrac{t}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{4}+\dfrac{t}{4}\right]_1^x \\ &= \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{x}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2+x-2}{4} \end{aligned}$$

For $x<1$, $F(x)=0$, and for $x>2$, $F(x)=1$.

$$\therefore\ F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x<1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{x^2+x-2}{4} & 1\le x\le 2 \\[6pt] 1 & x>2 \end{cases}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} & \text{for } 1 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Find $P(1.6 \le X \le 2)$
items.sol:
Using $P(a\le X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)$:

$$\begin{aligned} P(1.6\le X\le 2) &= F(2)-F(1.6) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{2^2}{4}+\dfrac{2}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1.6^2}{4}+\dfrac{1.6}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= 0.46 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P(1.6\le X\le 2)=0.46 \left(=\dfrac{23}{50}\right)$$

items.part:
A tank initially holds 8100 litres of Water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. A mathematical model predicts that the volume, $V$ litres, of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V = 8100\left(1 - \dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2$$
How long does the tank take to drain fully?
items.sol:
The tank is fully drained when $V=0$.

$$8100\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2=0$$

So $1-\dfrac{t}{90}=0$.

$$\therefore\ t=90 \text{ minutes}$$

items.part:
A tank initially holds 8100 litres of Water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. A mathematical model predicts that the volume, $V$ litres, of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V = 8100\left(1 - \dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2$$
What volume does the model predict will remain after 20 minutes ?
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} V &= 8100\left(1-\dfrac{20}{90}\right)^2 \\ &= 8100\times\left(\dfrac{7}{9}\right)^2 \\ &= 4900 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A tank initially holds 8100 litres of Water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. A mathematical model predicts that the volume, $V$ litres, of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V = 8100\left(1 - \dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2$$
At what rate does the model predict that the water will be draining from the tank after 30 minutes ?
items.sol:
The rate of change of volume is $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$. Differentiating using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 8100\times 2\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{90}\right) \\ &= -180\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right) \\ &= 2t-180 \text{ L/min} \end{aligned}$$

At $t=30$:

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2\times 30-180=-120 \text{ L/min}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the water drains at } 120 \text{ L/min}$$

items.part:
A tank initially holds 8100 litres of Water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. A mathematical model predicts that the volume, $V$ litres, of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V = 8100\left(1 - \dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2$$
At what time does the model predict that the water will drain from the tank at its fastest rate ?
items.sol:
The rate is $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2t-180$, so $\dfrac{d^2V}{dt^2}=2$.

Since $\dfrac{d^2V}{dt^2}\ne 0$, $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ has no stationary points and no points of inflexion. The greatest draining rate must therefore be at an endpoint of $0\le t\le 90$.

$$\begin{aligned} t=0 &: \dfrac{dV}{dt}=-180 \text{ L/min} \\ t=90 &: \dfrac{dV}{dt}=0 \text{ L/min} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the fastest draining rate is at } t=0$$

The shaded area is the area under $f(x)$ from $x=-1$ to $x=0$, plus the area under $g(x)$ from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-1}^0 (x+1)\,dx+\int_0^1 (x-1)^2\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-1}^0+\left[\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= 0-\left(\dfrac{(-1)^2}{2}-1\right)+\left(0-\dfrac{(-1)^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{5}{6} \text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$v = 2 - \dfrac{4}{t+1}$$
Show that the particle is at rest when $t = 1$
items.sol:
At $t=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} v &= 2-\dfrac{4}{1+1} \\ &= 2-2 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest when } t=1$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$v = 2 - \dfrac{4}{t+1}$$
The particle's initial displacement is 1 m. Find its displacement when at rest (3 decimal points)
items.sol:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(2-\dfrac{4}{t+1}\right)dt \\ &= 2t-4\ln(t+1)+C \end{aligned}$$

When $t=0$, $x=1$:

$$0-4\ln 1+C=1$$

So $C=1$ and $x=2t-4\ln(t+1)+1$.

At rest, $t=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2(1)-4\ln 2+1 \\ &= 3-4\ln 2 \\ &\approx 0.227 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{displacement} \approx 0.227 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$v = 2 - \dfrac{4}{t+1}$$
Find the expression for the accelaration of the particle at time $t$
items.sol:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{dv}{dt} \\ &= \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(2-4(t+1)^{-1}\right) \\ &= 4(t+1)^{-2} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$v = 2 - \dfrac{4}{t+1}$$
Explain why the displacement of the particle is always positive
items.sol:
The particle is at rest only when $t=1$, so the displacement has only one stationary point, at $t=1$.

The acceleration there is $\dfrac{4}{(1+1)^2}=1>0$, so the displacement has a local minimum at $t=1$ (concave up).

The displacement at this minimum is $0.227>0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{displacement is always} \ge 0.227, \text{ so always positive}$$

items.part:
Two straight roads meet at $R$ at an angle of $90^\circ$. At time $t = 0$ car $A$ leaves $R$ on one road, and car $B$ is 100 km from $R$ on the other road. Car $A$ travels away from $R$ at a speed of 80 km/h, and car $B$ travels towards $R$ at a speed of 60 km/h.

\exfigure{1319_q38_1}

The distance between the cars at time $t$ hours is $r$ km.
Show that $r^2 = 2000(5t^2 - 6t + 5)$
items.sol:
After $t$ hours, $RA=80t$ and $RB=100-60t$.

The roads meet at a right angle, so by Pythagoras' theorem in triangle $ARB$:

$$\begin{aligned} r^2 &= RB^2+RA^2 \\ &= (100-60t)^2+(80t)^2 \\ &= 10000-12000t+3600t^2+6400t^2 \\ &= 10000t^2-12000t+10000 \\ &= 2000(5t^2-6t+5) \end{aligned}$$

as required.

items.part:
Two straight roads meet at $R$ at an angle of $90^\circ$. At time $t = 0$ car $A$ leaves $R$ on one road, and car $B$ is 100 km from $R$ on the other road. Car $A$ travels away from $R$ at a speed of 80 km/h, and car $B$ travels towards $R$ at a speed of 60 km/h.

\exfigure{1319_q38_1}

The distance between the cars at time $t$ hours is $r$ km.
Show that $\dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt} = 20000t - 12000$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt} &= \dfrac{d}{dt}\left[2000(5t^2-6t+5)\right] \\ &= 2000(10t-6) \\ &= 20000t-12000 \end{aligned}$$

as required.

items.part:
Two straight roads meet at $R$ at an angle of $90^\circ$. At time $t = 0$ car $A$ leaves $R$ on one road, and car $B$ is 100 km from $R$ on the other road. Car $A$ travels away from $R$ at a speed of 80 km/h, and car $B$ travels towards $R$ at a speed of 60 km/h.

\exfigure{1319_q38_1}

The distance between the cars at time $t$ hours is $r$ km.
Hence or otherwise find the minimum distance ($r$) between the cars (justify your answer with relevant mathematical arguments)
items.sol:
$r$ is a minimum when $r^2$ is a minimum.

Stationary point: $\dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 20000t-12000 &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{6}{10}=0.6 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

Nature: $\dfrac{d^2(r^2)}{dt^2}=20000>0$ for all $t$, so $r^2$ is concave up and the stationary point is a minimum.

$$\begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt{2000(5\times 0.6^2-6\times 0.6+5)} \\ &= \sqrt{6400} \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum distance is } 80 \text{ km}$$

items.part:
Between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18, 2021, the height of the tide in Sydney harbour was given by

$$h(t) = 1 + 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) \text{ for } 0 \le t < 12$$

Where $h$ is the height of the tide in metres, and $t$ is in hours with $t = 0$ at 8 am
What is the period of $h(t)$
items.sol:
For $h(t)=1+0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$ with $b=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= 2\pi\div\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= 2\pi\times\dfrac{6}{\pi} \\ &= 12 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18, 2021, the height of the tide in Sydney harbour was given by

$$h(t) = 1 + 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) \text{ for } 0 \le t < 12$$

Where $h$ is the height of the tide in metres, and $t$ is in hours with $t = 0$ at 8 am
What was the height $h(t)$ at low tide, and at what time did this low tide occur
items.sol:
The minimum value of $\sin$ is $-1$, so the minimum height is $1-0.4=0.6$ m.

The sine curve reaches its minimum at $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of the period:

$$\dfrac{3}{4}\times 12=9 \text{ hours}$$

So the time is $8 \text{ am}+9 \text{ hours}=5$ pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{low tide is } 0.6 \text{ m at } 5 \text{ pm}$$
items.final: Low tide is $0.6$ m at 5 pm

items.part:
Between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18, 2021, the height of the tide in Sydney harbour was given by

$$h(t) = 1 + 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) \text{ for } 0 \le t < 12$$

Where $h$ is the height of the tide in metres, and $t$ is in hours with $t = 0$ at 8 am
A cruise ship is only able to enter the harbour if the tide is at least 1.2 m. Find all the times between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18 2021 that the cruise ship was able to enter the harbour
items.sol:
The ship can enter when $h\ge 1.2$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1+0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge 1.2 \\ 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge 0.2 &&(\text{subtract } 1) \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge \dfrac{1}{2} &&(\text{divide by } 0.4) \end{aligned}$$

For $0\le t<12$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t<2\pi$, and $\sin\theta\ge\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\theta\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t &\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ 1\le t &\le 5 \end{aligned}$$

The times are $8+1=9$ am and $8+5=13$, that is, 1 pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{the ship can enter between 9 am and 1 pm}$$
items.final: The ship can enter between 9 am and 1 pm

items.part:
Differentiate the following:
$2x\sin x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 2x & v &= \sin x \\ u' &= 2 & v' &= \cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(2x\sin x) = 2\sin x + 2x\cos x$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following:
$\sqrt{2x^3 - 4}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule with the outer function $u^{\frac12}$ and inner function $2x^3 - 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(2x^3-4)^{\frac12} &= \dfrac12\cdot 6x^2(2x^3-4)^{-\frac12} \\ &= \dfrac{3x^2}{\sqrt{2x^3-4}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following:
$e^{\tan x + 1}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x + 1) = \sec^2 x$:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{\tan x+1}\right) = \sec^2 x\, e^{\tan x+1}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following:
$\dfrac{x}{\log_{10} x}$
items.sol:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_{10} x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 10}$, so
$$\dfrac{x}{\log_{10}x} = \dfrac{\ln 10\cdot x}{\ln x}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= \ln 10\cdot x & v &= \ln x \\ u' &= \ln 10 & v' &= \dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{\log_{10}x}\right) &= \dfrac{\ln 10\cdot\ln x - \ln 10}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln 10(\ln x - 1)}{(\ln x)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2-1} \\ &= \dfrac{2(x^2-1)+2}{x^2-1} \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{2}{x^2-1} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find all asymptotes of the function $y \equiv \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2 - 1}$
items.sol:
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator of $\dfrac{2}{x^2-1}$ is zero: $x^2 - 1 = 0$, so $x = \pm 1$.

As $x \to \pm\infty$, $\dfrac{2}{x^2-1} \to 0$, so $y \to 2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{asymptotes at } x = \pm 1 \text{ and } y = 2$$

items.part: Showing working, determine whether the curve is an odd function, an even function or neither.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= \dfrac{2(-x)^2}{(-x)^2-1} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2-1} \\ &= f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the function is even}$$

items.part: Hence, sketch the curve showing all key features.
items.sol: \exfigure{1015_q7_s1}

items.part: Show $x^x \equiv e^{x \ln x}$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} x^x &= e^{\ln x^x} \\ &= e^{x\ln x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^x\right)$
items.sol:
Using the product rule on the exponent, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x) = \ln x + x\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} = 1 + \ln x$.

Then by the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\ln x}\right) &= (1+\ln x)\,e^{x\ln x} \\ &= (1+\ln x)\,x^x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x) = -x^5 + 15x^3$.
Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -5x^4 + 45x^2 \\ f''(x) &= -20x^3 + 90x \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x) = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -5x^2(x^2 - 9) &= 0 \\ -5x^2(x+3)(x-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 0, \pm 3$.

Test the nature using $f''(x)$.

At $x = 0$, $f''(0) = 0$, so test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-0.1) &= -8.98 < 0 \\ f''(0.1) &= 8.98 > 0 \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a horizontal point of inflection at $x = 0$.

At $x = 3$, $f''(3) = -270 < 0$, so a local maximum.

At $x = -3$, $f''(-3) = 270 > 0$, so a local minimum.

The $y$-values are $f(0) = 0$, $f(3) = 162$ and $f(-3) = -162$.

$$\therefore\ \text{horizontal point of inflection at } (0,0),\ \text{local minimum at } (-3,-162),\ \text{local maximum at } (3,162)$$
items.final: horizontal point of inflection at $(0,0)$, local minimum at $(-3,-162)$, local maximum at $(3,162)$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x) = -x^5 + 15x^3$.
Find the $x$-coordinates of any points of inflection.
items.sol:
For points of inflection, $f''(x) = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -20x^3 + 90x &= 0 \\ -10x(2x^2 - 9) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 0$ or $x = \pm\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$.

\extable{Ts7373_1}

The concavity changes at each of these values.

$$\therefore\ \text{points of inflection at } x = 0 \text{ and } x = \pm\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x) = -x^5 + 15x^3$.
Sketch the curve $y = f(x)$, showing all important features.

(NB: There is no need to evaluate the $x$-intercepts).

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x) = -x^5 + 15x^3$.
State the values of $x$ for which the curve is concave up.
items.sol:
The curve is concave up where $f''(x) > 0$, with $f''(x) = -10x(2x^2 - 9)$ and zeros at $x = 0, \pm\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$.

This holds for
$$x < -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2} \quad\text{and}\quad 0 < x < \dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$$

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so its displacement $x$, in metres, from a fixed point O, is given by $x = 1 - 2\sin 2t$, where the time, $t$, is measured in seconds from $t = 0$.
Where is the particle initially?
items.sol:
Initially $t = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 1 - 2\sin 0 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
So the particle is 1 m to the right of the origin.
items.final: 1 m to the right of the origin ($x = 1$)

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so its displacement $x$, in metres, from a fixed point O, is given by $x = 1 - 2\sin 2t$, where the time, $t$, is measured in seconds from $t = 0$.
When and where does the particle first come to rest?
items.sol:
Differentiating $x = 1 - 2\sin 2t$:
$$\dot x = -4\cos 2t$$
The particle is at rest when $\dot x = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -4\cos 2t &= 0 \\ 2t &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
This is the first time, as it is the smallest positive $t$.

The position then is
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 1 - 2\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
After $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ s the particle is at rest 1 m to the left of the origin.
items.final: After $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ s the particle is at rest 1 m to the left of the origin ($x=-1$)

items.part:
A particle moves along a straight line so its displacement $x$, in metres, from a fixed point O, is given by $x = 1 - 2\sin 2t$, where the time, $t$, is measured in seconds from $t = 0$.
What is the acceleration of the particle when $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$?
items.sol:
Differentiating $\dot x = -4\cos 2t$:
$$\ddot x = 8\sin 2t$$
When $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot x &= 8\sin\pi \\ &= 0 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
On a dark night, two ships, Saga and Hero, sail parallel to a straight coastline on which there are two lights of equal brightness, 16 kilometres apart.

\exfigure{1015_q11_1}

Suppose the coastline is represented by the $x$ axis where the origin $O$ is chosen to be the midpoint of the light sources. It is known that the (total) brightness from the lights on a ship a point $P(x, b)$ is

$$l = \dfrac{1}{b^2 + (x+8)^2} + \dfrac{1}{b^2 + (x-8)^2}$$
Show that $\dfrac{dl}{dx} = -\dfrac{2P}{Q}$, where

$P = \left[(x+8)\left(b^2 + (x-8)^2\right)^2 + (x-8)\left(b^2 + (x+8)^2\right)^2\right]$ AND

$Q = \left[\left(b^2 + (x+8)^2\right)^2 \left(b^2 + (x-8)^2\right)^2\right]$
items.sol:
Write $l$ using negative powers:
$$l = \left[b^2+(x+8)^2\right]^{-1} + \left[b^2+(x-8)^2\right]^{-1}$$
Differentiating each term with the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dl}{dx} = \dfrac{-2(x+8)}{\left(b^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2} + \dfrac{-2(x-8)}{\left(b^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2}$$
Combining over the common denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dl}{dx} &= \dfrac{-2\left[(x+8)\left(b^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2 + (x-8)\left(b^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2\right]}{\left(b^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2\left(b^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2} \\ &= -\dfrac{2P}{Q} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
On a dark night, two ships, Saga and Hero, sail parallel to a straight coastline on which there are two lights of equal brightness, 16 kilometres apart.

\exfigure{1015_q11_1}

Suppose the coastline is represented by the $x$ axis where the origin $O$ is chosen to be the midpoint of the light sources. It is known that the (total) brightness from the lights on a ship a point $P(x, b)$ is

$$l = \dfrac{1}{b^2 + (x+8)^2} + \dfrac{1}{b^2 + (x-8)^2}$$
To answer (b) and (c), you may assume the following factorisation:

$$P = 2x\left(x^2 + 64 + b^2 + 16\sqrt{64 + b^2}\right)\left(x^2 + 64 + b^2 - 16\sqrt{64 + b^2}\right)$$

Saga sails parallel to the coast at a distance 15 km from the coast.

By considering $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$, show that, as Saga sails from left to right, the brightness on Saga increases to a maximum when $x = 0$ and then decreases.
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{dl}{dx} = -\dfrac{2P}{Q}$ with the given factorisation of $P$ and $b = 15$ (so $64 + b^2 = 289$ and $16\sqrt{289} = 272$):
$$\dfrac{dl}{dx} = \dfrac{-4x\left(x^2+64+15^2+16\sqrt{64+15^2}\right)\left(x^2+64+15^2-16\sqrt{64+15^2}\right)}{\left(15^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2\left(15^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2}$$
The numerator simplifies, so for stationary points $\dfrac{dl}{dx} = 0$:
$$-4x(x^2+561)(x^2+17) = 0$$
So $x = 0$ is the only real solution.

The denominator is positive for all real $x$, and $(x^2+561)(x^2+17) > 0$ for all real $x$.

So the sign of $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$ is the sign of $-4x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dl}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x < 0 &&\text{increasing} \\ \dfrac{dl}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{for } x = 0 &&\text{stationary} \\ \dfrac{dl}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } x > 0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the brightness increases to a maximum at } x = 0 \text{ and then decreases}$$

items.part:
On a dark night, two ships, Saga and Hero, sail parallel to a straight coastline on which there are two lights of equal brightness, 16 kilometres apart.

\exfigure{1015_q11_1}

Suppose the coastline is represented by the $x$ axis where the origin $O$ is chosen to be the midpoint of the light sources. It is known that the (total) brightness from the lights on a ship a point $P(x, b)$ is

$$l = \dfrac{1}{b^2 + (x+8)^2} + \dfrac{1}{b^2 + (x-8)^2}$$
Hero sails parallel to the coast at a distance 6 km from the coast.

Describe how the brightness on Hero changes as Hero sails from left to right. Give clear reasons for your answer.
items.sol:
With $b = 6$ (so $64 + b^2 = 100$ and $16\sqrt{100} = 160$), from the given factorisation:
$$\dfrac{dl}{dx} = \dfrac{-4x\left(x^2+64+6^2+16\sqrt{64+6^2}\right)\left(x^2+64+6^2-16\sqrt{64+6^2}\right)}{\left(6^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2\left(6^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dl}{dx} = 0$:
$$-4x(x^2+260)(x^2-60) = 0$$
So $x = 0$ or $x = \pm\sqrt{60}$.

The denominator and $x^2 + 260$ are always positive, so the sign of $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$ is the sign of $-x(x^2-60)$.

\extable{Ts7381_1}

The signs of $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$ across the intervals are positive, negative, positive, negative (slopes: up, down, up, down).

So the brightness increases to a maximum at $x = -\sqrt{60}$, then decreases to a minimum at $x = 0$, then increases to another maximum at $x = \sqrt{60}$, then decreases.

items.part:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ given:
$y=\log_2 x$
items.sol:
Using the change of base rule, $\log_2 x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 2}$.

$$y=\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}\cdot\ln x$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{x\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$

$y=\log_e(x^2+2x)$
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2x+2}{x^2+2x}$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{4x-3}{x}=\dfrac{-3}{x}+4$
items.sol:
Method 1: start from the right-hand side.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{-3}{x}+4 \\ &=\dfrac{-3+4x}{x} \\ &=\dfrac{4x-3}{x} \\ &=\text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$

Method 2: start from the left-hand side.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{4x-3}{x} \\ &=\dfrac{4x}{x}-\dfrac{3}{x} \\ &=4-\dfrac{3}{x} \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence or otherwise, sketch the graph of $y=\dfrac{4x-3}{x}$ showing any asymptotes and the $x$-intercept.

\exfigure{1035_q11e_1}
items.sol:
Write $y=4-\dfrac{3}{x}$ from part (i).

As $x \to \infty$, $\dfrac{3}{x} \to 0$, so $y \to 4$. Also $x=0$ makes $\dfrac{3}{x}$ undefined.

Hence the asymptotes are $x=0$ and $y=4$.

For the $x$-intercept, let $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4x-3}{x}&=0 \\ 4x-3&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1035_q11e_s1}

items.part:
A function $f(x)$ is defined by $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2$.
For what values of $x$ is the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ concave up?
items.sol:
The graph is concave up when $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-6x \\ f''(x)&=12x-6 \end{aligned}$$
So $12x-6>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x&>6 \\ x&>\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{concave up when } x>\dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part:
A function $f(x)$ is defined by $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2$.
Find all the solutions for $f(x)=0$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=0 \\ 2x^3-3x^2&=0 \\ x^2(2x-3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=0 \text{ or } x=\dfrac{3}{2}$$

items.part:
A function $f(x)$ is defined by $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2$.
Find the turning points for the curve $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x^2-6x&=0 \\ 6x(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=1$, $y=2(1)^3-3(1)^2=-1$.

Hence the stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,-1)$.

To find their nature, use $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x-6$.

When $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-6<0$ (concave down), so $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point.

When $x=1$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6>0$ (concave up), so $(1,-1)$ is a minimum turning point.
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point; $(1,-1)$ is a minimum turning point

items.part:
A function $f(x)$ is defined by $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2$.
Find the coordinates of the point of inflexion.
items.sol:
A point of inflexion occurs where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x-6&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3-3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4} \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{point of inflexion is } \left(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$

NB: The concavity changes either side of $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$. There is no need to check this, since the question states there is a point of inflexion.
