items.part: If $y=\tan^2x$, find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$, such that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=ay^2+by+2$.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule, then write in terms of $\tan x$ using $\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\tan x\sec^2x \\ &=2\tan x(1+\tan^2x) \\ &=2\tan x+2\tan^3x \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate again.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=2\sec^2x+6\tan^2x\sec^2x \\ &=2(1+\tan^2x)+6\tan^2x(1+\tan^2x) \\ &=2+2\tan^2x+6\tan^2x+6\tan^4x \\ &=2+8\tan^2x+6\tan^4x \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $y=\tan^2x$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6y^2+8y+2$$
$$\therefore\ a=6,\ b=8$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.
Find the cumulative distributive function (CDF)
items.sol:
The CDF is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_0^x\dfrac{1}{2}\sin t\,dt \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos t\right]_0^x \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos x-1) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.
Find the first quartile of the distribution.
items.sol:
The first quartile satisfies $F(x)=0.25$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x)&=\dfrac{1}{4} \\ 1-\cos x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \cos x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ x&=\dfrac{\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $x\log_ex$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\log_ex \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x\log_ex)&=x\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)+\log_ex(1) \\ &=1+\log_ex \end{aligned}$$
So $\log_ex=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\log_ex)-1$.

items.part: Hence or otherwise, evaluate (in exact form), $\displaystyle\int_1^2\log_ex\,dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\log_ex=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\log_ex)-1$ from part (a), a primitive of $\log_ex$ is $x\log_ex-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\log_ex\,dx&=\left[x\log_ex-x\right]_1^2 \\ &=2\log_e2-2-(\log_e1-1) \\ &=2\log_e2-2+1 \\ &=2\log_e2-1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
At time $t$ years after it was purchased the value $\$V$ of a car is given by $V=25\,000e^{-0.5t}$.
Find the loss in value of the car during the third year.
items.sol:
$$V=25\,000e^{-0.5t}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-12\,500e^{-0.5t}$$
The third year runs from $t=2$ to $t=3$, so the loss is $V(2)-V(3)$:
$$\begin{aligned} V(2)-V(3)&=25\,000e^{-1}-25\,000e^{-1.5} \\ &=25\,000\left(e^{-1}-e^{-1.5}\right) \\ &\approx\$3618.73 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the car loses about }\$3618.73\text{ in the third year}$$

items.part:
At time $t$ years after it was purchased the value $\$V$ of a car is given by $V=25\,000e^{-0.5t}$.
Find the year in which the car is losing value at a rate of $\$100$ per year.
items.sol:
The rate of loss is $100$ per year, so $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-100$.
$$\begin{aligned} -12\,500e^{-0.5t}&=-100 \\ e^{-0.5t}&=\dfrac{1}{125} \\ -0.5t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{125}\right) \\ -0.5t&=-\ln125 \\ t&=\dfrac{\ln125}{0.5} \\ &\approx 9.6566 \end{aligned}$$
So the car is losing value at $\$100$ per year during the 10th year.
items.final: The car is losing value at $100 per year during the 10th year.

items.part:
The first term of a geometric series is 16 and the fourth term is $\dfrac{1}{4}$.
Find the common ratio.
items.sol:
For a geometric sequence, $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, with $a=16$ and $T_4=\dfrac{1}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{4}&=16r^{3} \\ r^3&=\dfrac{1}{64} \\ r&=\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The first term of a geometric series is 16 and the fourth term is $\dfrac{1}{4}$.
Find the limiting sum of the series.
items.sol:
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{16}{1-\frac{1}{4}} \\ &=21\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has a displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v$ ms$^{-1}$, and acceleration $a$ ms$^{-2}$ is given by $a=6t-12$. Initially, the particle is at rest at $O$.
Find expressions for $v$ and $x$ in terms of $t$.
items.sol:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$v=\dfrac{6t^2}{2}-12t+c=3t^2-12t+c$$
When $t=0$, $v=0$, so $c=0$ and $v=3t^2-12t$.

Integrate the velocity.
$$x=\dfrac{3t^3}{3}-\dfrac{12t^2}{2}+c=t^3-6t^2+c$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $c=0$.
$$\therefore\ v=3t^2-12t,\quad x=t^3-6t^2$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has a displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v$ ms$^{-1}$, and acceleration $a$ ms$^{-2}$ is given by $a=6t-12$. Initially, the particle is at rest at $O$.
Find when and where the particle is next at rest.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3t^2-12t&=0 \\ 3t(t-4)&=0 \\ t&=0,\ 4 \end{aligned}$$
The particle is next at rest at $t=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=4^3-6(4)^2 \\ &=-32 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is next at rest when } t=4 \text{ s, 32 m to the left of the origin}$$
items.final: The particle is next at rest when $t=4$ s, 32 m to the left of the origin ($x=-32$).

items.sol:
The area is $\displaystyle\int_0^k y\,dx$. The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so the primitive is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k\dfrac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}\,dx&=\left[\ln(e^x+e^{-x})\right]_0^k \\ &=\ln(e^k+e^{-k})-\ln(e^0+e^0) \\ &=\ln(e^k+e^{-k})-\ln2 \\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{e^k+e^{-k}}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

Set the area equal to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{e^k+e^{-k}}{2}\right)&=1 \\ \dfrac{e^k+e^{-k}}{2}&=e \\ e^k+e^{-k}&=2e \end{aligned}$$
Multiply each term by $e^k$.
$$(e^k)^2+1=2e(e^k)$$
$$(e^k)^2-2e(e^k)+1=0$$
Let $m=e^k$, so $m^2-2em+1=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{2e\pm\sqrt{(-2e)^2-4(1)(1)}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{2e\pm\sqrt{4e^2-4}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{2e\pm2\sqrt{e^2-1}}{2} \\ &=e\pm\sqrt{e^2-1} \end{aligned}$$
Since $m=e^k$:

Since $k>0$, $e^k>1$, and $e-\sqrt{e^2-1}\approx0.19<1$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ k=\ln\left(e+\sqrt{e^2-1}\right)\ (\approx1.657)$$

items.part: Show that $\log_x 5 = \dfrac{1}{\log_5 x}$
items.sol:
Using the change of base formula to base 5:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_x 5 &= \dfrac{\log_5 5}{\log_5 x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\log_5 x} \text{ since } \log_5 5 = 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, solve the equation $\log_5 x = 4\log_x 5$
items.sol:
From part (a), $\log_x 5 = \dfrac{1}{\log_5 x}$, so the equation becomes
$$\begin{aligned} \log_5 x &= \dfrac{4}{\log_5 x} \\ (\log_5 x)^2 &= 4 \\ \log_5 x &= \pm 2 \end{aligned}$$
If $\log_5 x = 2$, then $x = 5^2 = 25$.

If $\log_5 x = -2$, then $x = 5^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{25}$.
$$\therefore\ x = 25 \text{ or } x = \dfrac{1}{25}$$

items.part:
Let $y = 3e^{-x}$.
Show that the gradient of the tangent to the curve $y = 3e^{-x}$ at $x = -1$ is $m = -3e$.
items.sol:
Differentiating $y = 3e^{-x}$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -3e^{-x}$$
At $x=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -3e^{-(-1)} \\ &= -3e \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m = -3e$$

items.part:
Let $y = 3e^{-x}$.
Hence, or otherwise, find the equation of the normal to the curve $y = 3e^{-x}$ at $x = -1$.
items.sol:
The tangent gradient is $-3e$, so the normal gradient is $\dfrac{1}{3e}$.

At $x=-1$:
$$y = 3e^{-(-1)} = 3e$$
The normal passes through $(-1, 3e)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 3e &= \dfrac{1}{3e}(x+1) \\ 3e(y-3e) &= x+1 \\ x - 3ey + 9e^2 + 1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $\log_2(x-3) + \log_2(x+4) = 3,\ x > 3$
items.sol:
Using the log law for addition:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_2(x-3)(x+4) &= 3 \\ \log_2(x^2+x-12) &= 3 \\ x^2+x-12 &= 2^3 \\ x^2+x-20 &= 0 \\ (x-4)(x+5) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=4$ or $x=-5$.

Since $x>3$, reject $x=-5$.
$$\therefore\ x = 4$$

items.part:
The length of a whale species is modelled using the equation $L = 6 - 4e^{-kt}$ where $L$ is in metres, $t$ is the age of the whale in years and $k$ is a positive constant.
What is the length of the whale at birth?
items.sol:
At birth $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} L &= 6 - 4e^{-k(0)} \\ &= 6 - 4\times 1 \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
The length of the whale at birth is $2$ m.

items.part:
The length of a whale species is modelled using the equation $L = 6 - 4e^{-kt}$ where $L$ is in metres, $t$ is the age of the whale in years and $k$ is a positive constant.
If a three-year-old whale is 4.5 metres long, what is the value of $k$ (to 2 decimal places)?
items.sol:
Substitute $t=3$, $L=4.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4.5 &= 6 - 4e^{-3k} \\ 4e^{-3k} &= 1.5 \\ e^{-3k} &= \dfrac{1.5}{4} \\ -3k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1.5}{4}\right) \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1.5}{4}\right)}{-3} \\ &\approx 0.33 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.33 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
The length of a whale species is modelled using the equation $L = 6 - 4e^{-kt}$ where $L$ is in metres, $t$ is the age of the whale in years and $k$ is a positive constant.
Explain why the length of a whale from this species cannot exceed 6 metres. Justify your response with calculations.
items.sol:
For $L = 6 - 4e^{-kt}$ with $k>0$, as $t \to \infty$, $e^{-kt} \to 0$.
$$L \to 6 - 4\times 0 = 6$$
Also $4e^{-kt}>0$ for all $t$, so $L<6$.

Hence the length cannot exceed $6$ metres.

items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \cot 210^\circ + \sec(-225^\circ) &= \dfrac{1}{\tan 210^\circ} + \dfrac{1}{\cos(-225^\circ)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\tan(180^\circ+30^\circ)} + \dfrac{1}{\cos 135^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\tan 30^\circ} + \dfrac{1}{-\cos 45^\circ} \\ &= \sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Solve $3\sin\theta - 2\operatorname{cosec}\theta = 5$ for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.

Give your answer(s) to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
Using $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin\theta - \dfrac{2}{\sin\theta} &= 5 \\ 3\sin^2\theta - 2 - 5\sin\theta &= 0 \\ (3\sin\theta + 1)(\sin\theta - 2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $\sin\theta = 2$.

$\sin\theta = 2$ has no solutions as $-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1$.

The reference angle is $0.340$, and $\sin\theta<0$ in the 3rd and 4th quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta &= \pi + 0.340 = 3.48 \\ \theta &= 2\pi - 0.340 = 5.94 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta \approx 3.48 \text{ or } 5.94 \text{ radians}$$

items.part: Prove that $\tan\theta - \dfrac{\sin^3\theta}{\cos\theta} = \sin\theta\cos\theta$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \tan\theta - \dfrac{\sin^3\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} - \dfrac{\sin^3\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta(1 - \sin^2\theta)}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \quad (\text{since } \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1) \\ &= \sin\theta\cos\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In Cherry Harbour, the height of the water above sea level, $h$ (in metres), is modelled by the function $h = 6.5 - 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)$ where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight on Saturday.

Boats can safely enter the Harbour when the water is at least 7 metres above sea level.
Show that the earliest time for a boat to enter Cherry Harbour on Sunday is 6.58am.
items.sol:
Boats can enter when $h=7$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7 &= 6.5 - 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right) \\ 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right) &= -0.5 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right) &= -0.25 \end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $1.318$. For the first time after midnight, $\dfrac{\pi}{12}t = \pi - 1.318$.
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\pi - 1.318}{\frac{\pi}{12}} \\ &\approx 6.9656 \\ &\approx 6 \text{ h } 58 \text{ min} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the earliest time is } 6.58 \text{ am}$$

items.part:
In Cherry Harbour, the height of the water above sea level, $h$ (in metres), is modelled by the function $h = 6.5 - 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)$ where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight on Saturday.

Boats can safely enter the Harbour when the water is at least 7 metres above sea level.
How long can boats enter Cherry Harbour before the water is too shallow again? Give your answer to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
Boats can enter when $h \ge 7$, that is when
$$\pi - 1.318 \le \dfrac{\pi}{12}t \le \pi + 1.318$$
Multiplying by $\dfrac{12}{\pi}$:
$$\dfrac{12(\pi - 1.318)}{\pi} \le t \le \dfrac{12(\pi + 1.318)}{\pi}$$
That is, $6.58$ am $\le t \le 5.02$ pm.
$$\therefore\ \text{boats can enter for } 10 \text{ h } 4 \text{ min, between } 6.58 \text{ am and } 5.02 \text{ pm}$$

items.part:
The mean weight of 14 Year 12 students is $78.9$ kg, when a $15^{\text{th}}$ person is included, the mean increases by $1.03$ kg.

The new mean is $78.9+1.03=79.93$, so the total weight of 15 students is

The 15th person's weight is the difference:
$$\begin{aligned} 1198.95-1104.6&=94.35 \text{ kg} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the } 15^{\text{th}} \text{ person weighs } 94.35 \text{ kg}$$

items.part:
Enrico has decided to conduct a study to examine the relationship between students' English and Mathematics abilities. In order to conduct his study, Enrico requested records of all students' scores from the school.
Enrico's school is concerned with the privacy implications of his request. Give one reason why Enrico's school may be concerned and suggest a way Enrico can address these concerns and maintain students' privacy.
items.sol:
The school may be concerned because students have the right to keep their own scores private, since it is their personal data.

One way to address this concern would be to supply the scores without names or classes attached, making the data anonymous and only useful in aggregate.

items.sol:
The correlation is moderate and negative, and the gradient of the regression line is negative ($-0.2$).

Students with higher Mathematics scores tend to have lower English scores: on average, English is $0.2$ marks lower for each extra Mathematics mark. The correlation is only moderate, and it does not show that one score causes the other.

No, this line cannot be used to predict scores in other schools.

There are too many influencing factors that differ from one school context to the next, which may lead their data to look completely different and not be accurately represented by this model.

items.part: Differentiate $e^{5x}$ with respect to $x$.
If $y=\log_e 2x^2$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with $u=2x^2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{4x}{2x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: What is the derivative of $y=\dfrac{e^{3x}+4}{x^3}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{vu'-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{3x}+4 & v&=x^3\\ u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=3x^2\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{x^3(3e^{3x})-(e^{3x}+4)(3x^2)}{x^6} \\ &= \dfrac{3x^2\left(xe^{3x}-e^{3x}-4\right)}{x^6} \\ &= \dfrac{3\left(xe^{3x}-e^{3x}-4\right)}{x^4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=3\cos^4 x$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule with $u=\cos x$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 3\times4\cos^3x\times(-\sin x) \\ &= -12\sin x\cos^3x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Fully factorise $f'(x)$ if $f(x)=4x^2e^{12x}$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{12x}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=12e^{12x}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 4\left(vu'+uv'\right) \\ &= 4\left[e^{12x}(2x)+x^2(12e^{12x})\right] \\ &= 4e^{12x}(2x+12x^2) \\ &= 8xe^{12x}(1+6x) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ if $f(x)=\sin x+\cos 2x$, leaving your answer in exact form.

$$\begin{aligned} f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) &= \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}-2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-2\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Determine $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{4y^3}\,dy$
items.sol:
Rewrite the integrand using indices.

$$\begin{aligned} \int\sqrt{4y^3}\,dy &= \int(4y^3)^{\frac12}dy \\ &= \int2y^{\frac32}dy \\ &= \dfrac{2y^{\frac52}}{\frac52}+C \\ &= \dfrac{4y^{\frac52}}{5}+C \\ &= \dfrac45\sqrt{y^5}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find a primitive function for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=6^{2x}$
items.sol:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^x=a^x\ln a$, we have $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+c$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int6^{2x}dx &= \dfrac12\int2\times6^{2x}dx \\ &= \dfrac12\times\dfrac{6^{2x}}{\ln6}+C \\ &= \dfrac{6^{2x}}{2\ln6}+C \end{aligned}$$

A primitive function is $\dfrac{6^{2x}}{2\ln6}$ (that is, $C=0$).

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{3x^6-x^5+2x^3}{x^4}\,dx$
items.sol:
Divide each term by $x^4$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{3x^6-x^5+2x^3}{x^4}\,dx &= \int\left(3x^2-x+\dfrac2x\right)dx \\ &= x^3-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+2\ln|x|+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int(45x^2+100x)(3x^3+10x^2)^3\,dx$

A spherical balloon is being filled with helium at the rate given by $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2$.

$V$ is the volume of helium in the balloon after $t$ minutes and $r$ is the radius in cm.

Where $r=\dfrac{1}{4}t$, find the volume of gas that has been pumped into the balloon when $t=6$. Assume the balloon was initially deflated. Leave your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
Substitute $r=\dfrac14t$ into the given rate.

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi\left(\dfrac14t\right)^2=\dfrac{\pi t^2}{4}$$

Integrate with respect to $t$.

$$V=\int\dfrac{\pi t^2}{4}dt=\dfrac{\pi t^3}{12}+C$$

The balloon is initially deflated, so $V=0$ when $t=0$. Hence $C=0$ and $V=\dfrac{\pi t^3}{12}$.

When $t=6$:

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{\pi\times6^3}{12} \\ &= 18\pi \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the volume of gas is } 18\pi \text{ cm}^3$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following expressions. Simplify your answers, if possible.
$\dfrac{e^{3x}}{x-1}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{3x} & v&=x-1\\ u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(x-1)3e^{3x}-e^{3x}(1)}{(x-1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{3xe^{3x}-3e^{3x}-e^{3x}}{(x-1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{3xe^{3x}-4e^{3x}}{(x-1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{e^{3x}(3x-4)}{(x-1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following expressions. Simplify your answers, if possible.
$\tan x\cos x$
items.sol:
Let $y=\tan x\cos x$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\tan x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=\sec^2 x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\cos x\sec^2 x+\tan x(-\sin x) \\ &=\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos^2 x}-\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos x} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}-\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos x} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\cos x} \\ &=\cos x \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: simplify first.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\tan x\cos x \\ &=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\times\cos x \\ &=\sin x \end{aligned}$$
So
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos x$$

items.part:

items.sol:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$y=\log_4(x^2+3)=\dfrac{\ln(x^2+3)}{\ln 4}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{\ln 4}\cdot\dfrac{2x}{x^2+3} \\ &=\dfrac{2x}{(\ln 4)(x^2+3)} \\ &=\dfrac{x}{(\ln 2)(x^2+3)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the following
$\displaystyle\int x^4\left(x^5-2\right)^3\,dx$

items.part: Evaluate exactly $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{x-1}{x^2-2x+4}\,dx$ , simplify your answer fully.
items.sol:
The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator, so the integral is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x-1}{x^2-2x+4}\,dx&=\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2x-2}{x^2-2x+4}\right)dx \\ &=\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|x^2-2x+4\right|\right]_0^1 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 3-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 4 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) \\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\ln\left(\dfrac{2x-1}{x+1}\right)$ , at the point where $x=2$ .
items.sol:
Rewrite using the log laws:
$$y=\ln(2x-1)-\ln(x+1)$$
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{2x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}$$
At $x=2$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
This is the gradient of the tangent. For perpendicular lines $m_1m_2=-1$, so the gradient of the normal is $-3$.

When $x=2$:
$$y=\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{3}\right)=\ln 1=0$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=-3(x-2) \\ y&=-3x+6 \end{aligned}$$
The equation of the normal is $y=-3x+6$.

items.part: A circle is given by the equation $x^2+y^2+4x-10y=-16$ . Find the centre and radius of this circle.
items.sol:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$, adding the same amounts to both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+4x+4+y^2-10y+25&=-16+4+25 \\ (x+2)^2+(y-5)^2&=13 \end{aligned}$$
The centre is $(-2,5)$ and the radius is $\sqrt{13}$.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x+2)(x-2)^3$.
Find the $x$ and $y$ - intercepts of $y=f(x)$ .
items.sol:
For the $x$-intercepts put $y=0$:
$$(x+2)(x-2)^3=0$$
so $x=-2$ or $x=2$.

For the $y$-intercept put $x=0$:
$$y=(2)(-2)^3=-16$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+2 & v&=(x-2)^3\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3(x-2)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=(x-2)^3(1)+(x+2)\cdot 3(x-2)^2 \\ &=(x-2)^2\left[(x-2)+3(x+2)\right] \\ &=(x-2)^2(4x+4) \\ &=4(x-2)^2(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
For $f''(x)$, use the product rule again on $4(x+1)(x-2)^2$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+1 & v&=(x-2)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(x-2)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=4\left[(x+1)\cdot 2(x-2)+(x-2)^2\right] \\ &=4(x-2)\left[2(x+1)+(x-2)\right] \\ &=4(x-2)(3x) \\ &=12x(x-2) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x+2)(x-2)^3$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature. Justify your answers fully.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$:
$$4(x-2)^2(x+1)=0$$
so $x=-1$ or $x=2$.

Also $f(-1)=-27$ and $f(2)=0$, so the stationary points are $(-1,-27)$ and $(2,0)$.

Nature: the sign of $f''$ decides at $x=-1$.
$$f''(-1)=12(-1)(-3)=36>0$$
The curve is concave up, so $(-1,-27)$ is a minimum turning point.

At $x=2$:
$$f''(2)=12(2)(0)=0$$
so there is a possible horizontal inflexion at $x=2$. Testing concavity either side:

\extable{Ts7836_1}

The concavity changes (concave down to concave up), so $(2,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
items.final: $(-1,-27)$ minimum turning point; $(2,0)$ horizontal point of inflexion

items.part:
Tom planted a silky oak tree three years ago when it was 80 cm tall. At the end of the first year after planting, it was 130 cm tall, that is it grew 50 cm. Each year's growth was 90% of the previous year's.
What was the growth of the silky oak after 3 years?
items.sol:
The yearly growths form a geometric sequence:

$$50,\ 50(0.9),\ 50(0.9)^2,\dots$$

The growth after 3 years is the sum of the first three terms.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Growth} &= 50+50(0.9)+50(0.9)^2 \\ &= 135.5 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Tom planted a silky oak tree three years ago when it was 80 cm tall. At the end of the first year after planting, it was 130 cm tall, that is it grew 50 cm. Each year's growth was 90% of the previous year's.
Assuming that it maintains the present growth pattern, explain why the tree will never reach a height of 6 metres.
items.sol:
The yearly growths $50,\ 50(0.9),\ 50(0.9)^2,\dots$ form an infinite geometric series with $r=0.9$.

$S_\infty$ exists as $|r|<1$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{50}{1-0.9} \\ &= 500 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

So the limiting growth is $500$ cm and the limiting height is

$$80+500=580 \text{ cm}<600 \text{ cm}.$$

Therefore the tree will never reach a height of 6 m.

items.part:
Tom planted a silky oak tree three years ago when it was 80 cm tall. At the end of the first year after planting, it was 130 cm tall, that is it grew 50 cm. Each year's growth was 90% of the previous year's.
In which year will the silky oak reach a height of 5 metres?
items.sol:
To reach a height of 5 m the tree needs to grow $420$ cm.

Using the sum of a GP, $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$:

$$\begin{aligned} 420 &= \dfrac{50(1-0.9^n)}{1-0.9} \\ 42 &= 50(1-0.9^n) \\ \dfrac{42}{50} &= 1-0.9^n \\ 0.9^n &= \dfrac{8}{50}=0.16 \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln 0.16}{\ln 0.9} \approx 17.39344 \end{aligned}$$

The tree will reach 5 metres during the 18th year.
items.final: The tree will reach 5 metres during the 18th year.

A leak from a tanker has accidentally contaminated a farmer's paddock with a toxic chemical. The chemical concentration in the soil was 6 kL/ha immediately after the accident. One year later the concentration in the soil was measured to be 2.4 kL/ha.

It is known that the concentration, $C$, is given by:

$$C=C_0\,e^{-kt},$$

where $C_0$ and $k$ are constants and $t$ is measured in years.
Show that $C_0=6$ and $k=-\ln\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)$.

A leak from a tanker has accidentally contaminated a farmer's paddock with a toxic chemical. The chemical concentration in the soil was 6 kL/ha immediately after the accident. One year later the concentration in the soil was measured to be 2.4 kL/ha.

It is known that the concentration, $C$, is given by:

$$C=C_0\,e^{-kt},$$

where $C_0$ and $k$ are constants and $t$ is measured in years.
It will not be safe for the farmer to plant a new crop until the concentration falls below 0.2 kL/ha. How long, to the nearest month, after the spill does the farmer need to wait for the paddock to be safe to use.
items.sol:
Using $C_0=6$ and $k=-\ln\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)$:

$$C=6e^{-\left(-\ln\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)\right)t}=6e^{\ln\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)t}$$

Put $C=0.2$:

$$\begin{aligned} 0.2 &= 6e^{\ln\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)t} \\ \dfrac{1}{30} &= e^{\ln\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)t} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{30}\right) &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)t \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{30}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)} \approx 3.71191944 \end{aligned}$$

The paddock will be safe after 3 years and 9 months.

items.sol:
$$P(\text{Alice wins game})=\dfrac{1}{30}+\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{30}\right)+\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{30}\right)+\cdots$$

This is a geometric series with $a=\dfrac{1}{30}$ and $r=\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)$.

$S_\infty$ exists as $|r|<1$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{30}}{1-\left(\frac{29}{30}\right)\left(\frac{39}{40}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{40}{69} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 4e^{-x} &= e^x-3 \\ \dfrac{4}{e^x} &= e^x-3 \\ 4 &= e^x(e^x-3) \\ 4 &= e^{2x}-3e^x \end{aligned}$$

Hence $e^{2x}-3e^x-4=0$.

Let $u=e^x$, so $u^2=e^{2x}$. The equation from part (a) becomes

so $u=4$ or $u=-1$, that is $e^x=4$ or $e^x=-1$.

$e^x\neq-1$ as $e^x>0$.

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that after $t$ seconds ($t\geq 0$) its velocity $v$ is given by $v=\left(\dfrac{2}{1+t}-t\right)\ \text{m/s}$ . The displacement of the particle from the origin is given by $x$ metres.
Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=0$ .
items.sol:
Write $v=2(1+t)^{-1}-t$ and differentiate.

$$\begin{aligned} a &= -2(1+t)^{-2}-1 \\ &= -\dfrac{2}{(1+t)^2}-1 \end{aligned}$$

At $t=0$:

$$a=-2-1=-3 \text{ m/s}^2$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that after $t$ seconds ($t\geq 0$) its velocity $v$ is given by $v=\left(\dfrac{2}{1+t}-t\right)\ \text{m/s}$ . The displacement of the particle from the origin is given by $x$ metres.
If the particle is initially at the origin, find the displacement as a function of $t$ .
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \displaystyle\int v\,dt \\ &= 2\ln|1+t|-\dfrac{t^2}{2}+C \end{aligned}$$

At $t=0$, $x=0$:

$$0=2\ln 1-0+C$$

so $C=0$.

Hence

$$x=2\ln|1+t|-\dfrac{t^2}{2}.$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that after $t$ seconds ($t\geq 0$) its velocity $v$ is given by $v=\left(\dfrac{2}{1+t}-t\right)\ \text{m/s}$ . The displacement of the particle from the origin is given by $x$ metres.
When is the particle stationary?
items.sol:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{1+t}-t &= 0 \\ 2-t(1+t) &= 0 \\ 2-t-t^2 &= 0 \\ t^2+t-2 &= 0 \\ (t+2)(t-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $t=1$ (as $t\geq 0$).

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line so that after $t$ seconds ($t\geq 0$) its velocity $v$ is given by $v=\left(\dfrac{2}{1+t}-t\right)\ \text{m/s}$ . The displacement of the particle from the origin is given by $x$ metres.
How far does the particle travel in the first 2 seconds? Give your answer correct to three significant figures.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction at $t=1$, so find the displacement at $t=0,1,2$.

$$\begin{aligned} t=0:&\ x=0 \\ t=1:&\ x=2\ln 2-\dfrac{1}{2}\approx 0.88629 \\ t=2:&\ x=2\ln 3-2\approx 0.19722 \end{aligned}$$

The particle moves forward to $0.88629$ at $t=1$, then back to $0.19722$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 0.88629+(0.88629-0.19722) \\ &\approx 1.57536 \\ &\approx 1.58 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A tank initially holds 3600 litres of water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. The tank takes 60 minutes to empty. A mathematical model predicts that the volume $V$ litres of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V=3600\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)^2,\ \text{where } 0\leq t\leq 60 .$$
How long will it take for the tank to become half full (to nearest minute)?
items.sol:
Half full means $V=1800$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3600\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)^2 &= 1800 \\ \left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 1-\dfrac{t}{60} &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ t &= 60\left(1\mp\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \end{aligned}$$

So $t\approx 17.5736$ or $t\approx 102.4264$.

As $0\leq t\leq 60$, only $t\approx 17.5736$ is valid.

To the nearest minute, $t\approx 18$ minutes.

items.part:
A tank initially holds 3600 litres of water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. The tank takes 60 minutes to empty. A mathematical model predicts that the volume $V$ litres of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V=3600\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)^2,\ \text{where } 0\leq t\leq 60 .$$
At what rate does the model predict that the water will drain from the tank after twenty minutes?
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 7200\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)\left(-\dfrac{1}{60}\right) \\ &= -120\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right) \\ &= -120+2t \end{aligned}$$

At $t=20$:

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-80$$

After 20 minutes, water is draining at 80 L/min.

items.part:
A tank initially holds 3600 litres of water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. The tank takes 60 minutes to empty. A mathematical model predicts that the volume $V$ litres of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V=3600\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)^2,\ \text{where } 0\leq t\leq 60 .$$
At what time does the model predict that the water will drain from the tank at its fastest rate?
items.sol:
The draining rate is $\left|\dfrac{dV}{dt}\right|$, the steepness of the graph of $V$ against $t$.

This is greatest at $t=0$, where the tangent to the curve is steepest.

So the maximum draining rate occurs when $t=0$ (that is, 120 L/min).

items.part:
The average monthly temperature, $T^\circ$, for a town in NSW can be modeled on the formula

$$T=7\sin(nx+1.5)+13,$$

where $n=$ a constant value and

$x=$ the number of the month of the year ( i.e. January=1, February=2, …..).
The period of the function is 12. Determine the value of $n$ correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The period of $\sin(nx+1.5)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$.

$$\begin{aligned} 12 &= \dfrac{2\pi}{n} \\ 12n &= 2\pi \\ n &= \dfrac{2\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\approx 0.52 \end{aligned}$$

So $n\approx 0.52$ (2 decimal places).

In $\triangle HAB$ (right-angled at $A$, with $HA=1$):

$$\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{HB}\quad\text{and}\quad\tan\theta=\dfrac{AB}{1}$$

so $HB=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $AB=\tan\theta$.

Similarly in $\triangle SDC$: $SC=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $DC=\tan\theta$.

Distance walked $=2HB=\dfrac{2}{\cos\theta}$, so the time walked is

$$\dfrac{2}{\cos\theta}\div 4=\dfrac{1}{2\cos\theta}\text{ hours}.$$

Distance skated $=6-2\tan\theta$, so the time skated is $\dfrac{6-2\tan\theta}{12}$ hours.

$$\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{1}{2\cos\theta}+\dfrac{6-2\tan\theta}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\tan\theta}{6} \end{aligned}$$

as required.

Write $T=\dfrac{(\cos\theta)^{-1}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\tan\theta}{6}$ and differentiate.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{d\theta} &= -\dfrac{(-\sin\theta)(\cos\theta)^{-2}}{2}-\dfrac{\sec^2\theta}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{1}{6\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{3\sin\theta-1}{6\cos^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$

For a minimum, $\dfrac{dT}{d\theta}=0$. Since $\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}=\sec^2\theta\neq 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin\theta-1 &= 0 \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ \theta &\approx 19^\circ 28' \end{aligned}$$

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dT}{d\theta}$ either side:

$$\begin{aligned} \theta=10^\circ:&\ \dfrac{dT}{d\theta}<0 \\ \theta=19^\circ28':&\ \dfrac{dT}{d\theta}=0 \\ \theta=30^\circ:&\ \dfrac{dT}{d\theta}>0 \end{aligned}$$

The slope changes from negative to positive, so there is a minimum turning point.

$$\therefore\ \theta\approx 19^\circ 28'$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$ at $x=9$.
items.sol:
Differentiate $y=\sqrt{x}$.

$$y'=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$$

The gradient of the tangent at $x=9$ is

$$m=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{9}}=\dfrac{1}{6}$$

The tangent passes through $(9,3)$.

$$\begin{aligned} y-3 &= \dfrac{1}{6}(x-9) \\ 6y-18 &= x-9 \\ x-6y+9 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Using the cosine rule,

$$x^2=9^2+7^2-2\times9\times7\cos47^\circ$$

$$x\approx 6.6 \text{ cm}$$

the number of arrangements which contain 3 cherries.
items.sol:
Multiply the number of cherries on each wheel.

items.part:
A certain poker machine with 3 wheels has 10 fruit symbols on each wheel. The first wheel has 4 cherries on it, the second has 2 cherries on it and the third wheel has 5 cherries on it. Find
the probability of obtaining 3 cherries on the viewing line.
items.sol:
The total number of arrangements is $10\times10\times10=1000$.

$$\begin{aligned} P(3\text{ cherries}) &= \dfrac{40}{1000} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{10}\times\dfrac{2}{10}\times\dfrac{5}{10} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{25} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+3x$.
Find the stationary points and detemine their nature.
items.sol:
$$f'(x)=3x^2-6x+3,\qquad f''(x)=6x-6$$

Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-6x+3 &= 0 \\ x^2-2x+1 &= 0 \\ (x-1)^2 &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

When $x=1$, $y=1$.

Test the nature: $f''(1)=6(1)-6=0$, so the second derivative test fails. Check the concavity either side of $x=1$.

\extable{Ts7880_1}

The concavity changes at $x=1$.

$$\therefore \text{ there is a horizontal point of inflexion at } (1,1)$$

A mixture is to be made of two foods $A$ and $B$. The two foods $A$, $B$ contain nutrients $P$ and $Q$ as shown below:

items.part:
A mixture is to be made of two foods $A$ and $B$. The two foods $A$, $B$ contain nutrients $P$ and $Q$ as shown below:

\extable{1274_q15_t1}

The mixture contains 8 ounces of $P$ and 6 ounces of $Q$.

For example: one part of $A$ and 3 parts of $B$ will make 8 ounces of $P$ i.e.., $A+3B=8$
Solve the two equations simultaneously to find the values of $A$ and $B$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} A+3B &= 8 &&(1) \\ 2A+B &= 6 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$

Multiply (1) by 2.

$$2A+6B=16$$

Subtract (2).

$$5B=10,\ \text{so } B=2$$

Substitute $B=2$ in (2).

$$2A+2=6,\ \text{so } A=2$$

$$\therefore\ A=2 \text{ and } B=2$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=e^{\cos 2x}$
items.sol:

items.part:
Given the function $f(x)=x^2+2x$ and $g(x)=x+1$.

Find $f(g(x))$.

items.sol:
The arc length formula is $l=r\theta$, with $0<\theta\le2\pi$.

$$\dfrac{10\pi}{3}=r\theta,\ \text{so } \theta=\dfrac{10\pi}{3r}$$

Now use $0<\theta\le 2\pi$.

$$\begin{aligned} 0<\dfrac{10\pi}{3r} &\le 2\pi \\ 10\pi &\le 6\pi r &&(\text{multiply by } 3r>0) \\ \dfrac{5}{3} &\le r &&(\text{divide by } 6\pi) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ r\ge\dfrac{5}{3}$$

The area of a sector is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, where $\theta=\dfrac{10\pi}{3r}$ and $r=4$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times4^2\times\dfrac{10\pi}{3\times4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times16\times\dfrac{10\pi}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{80\pi}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{20\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

The area of the sector is $\dfrac{20\pi}{3}$ square units.

The probabilities sum to 1.

$$\begin{aligned} p+\dfrac{2}{5}+\dfrac{3}{20}+\dfrac{1}{4}+p &= 1 \\ 2p+\dfrac{4}{5} &= 1 \\ 2p &= \dfrac{1}{5} \\ p &= \dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}$$

The mean is $\mu=\sum xP(X=x)$.

$$\mu=0\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{3}{20}\right)+3\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+8\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right)=2\dfrac{1}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<\mu) &= P\left(X<2\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \\ &= P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{2}{5}+\dfrac{3}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{20} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: The function $f(x)=\sin^2(2x+1)$ is given. If $f'(x)=m\cos(2x+1)\sin(2x+1)$. Find the value of $m$.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule.

$$f'(x)=2\sin(2x+1)\cdot 2\cos(2x+1)=4\cos(2x+1)\sin(2x+1)$$

Comparing with $f'(x)=m\cos(2x+1)\sin(2x+1)$,

$$m=4$$

items.part: A circle is given by the equation $x^2+y^2-6x+2y=6$. Find the centre and radius of the circle.
items.sol:
Complete the square in $x$ and $y$.

$$\begin{aligned} x^2-6x+9+y^2+2y+1 &= 6+9+1 \\ (x-3)^2+(y+1)^2 &= 16 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{centre } (3,-1) \text{ and radius } 4$$

items.part: Given $f(x)=x^2-6x+8$ Differentiate $f(x)$ using first principles.
items.sol:
Using $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$:

$$f(x+h)=(x+h)^2-6(x+h)+8=x^2+2xh+h^2-6x-6h+8$$

$$f(x+h)-f(x)=2hx-6h+h^2$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{2hx-6h+h^2}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to0}(2x-6+h) \\ &= 2x-6 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The gradient function of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by $f'(x)=4x-5$. The curve passes through the point $(2,3)$.

items.sol:

$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \int(4x-5)\,dx \\ &= 2x^2-5x+C \end{aligned}$$

The curve passes through $(2,3)$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 2(2)^2-5(2)+C \\ 3 &= -2+C \\ C &= 5 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f(x)=2x^2-5x+5$$

Domain: $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$

Range: $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)\cup\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$

items.part: Differentiate $y=xe^{3x}$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{3x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3e^{3x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=e^{3x}+3xe^{3x}\\ &=e^{3x}(1+3x)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence find the exact value of

$$\int_0^2 e^{3x}(3+9x)\,dx$$
items.sol:
Factorise the integrand so that part (a) can be used.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2 e^{3x}(3+9x)\,dx&=3\int_0^2 e^{3x}(1+3x)\,dx\\ &=3\Big[xe^{3x}\Big]_0^2 &&(\text{from part (a)})\\ &=3\big(2e^6-0\big)\\ &=6e^6\end{aligned}$$

Starting from $f(x)=|x|$, the graph is:

translated to the right by 3 units,

reflected in the $x$-axis,

stretched vertically by a factor of 2,

translated up by 2 units.

So $y=-2|x-3|+2$, which has the form $kf(x+b)+c$.

$$\therefore\ k=-2,\ b=-3,\ c=2$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1274_q28_1}

Decaln walks 1600 metres due north along a road from point $A$ to point $B$.

The point is due east of a hill $XY$, where $X$ is the top of the hill.

The point $Y$ is directly below point $X$ and is on the same horizontal plane as the road.

Let the height of the hill above point $Y$ be $h$ metres.

From point $A$, the angle of elevation to the top of the hill is $16^o$.

From point $B$, the angle of elevation to the top of the hill is $12^o$.
Show that $BY=h\cot 12^o$.
items.sol:
In the right-angled triangle $XYB$ (right angle at $Y$), $\tan 12^\circ=\dfrac{XY}{BY}$.
$$\dfrac{h}{BY}=\tan 12^\circ$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{BY}{h}=\cot 12^\circ$$
$$\therefore\ BY=h\cot 12^\circ$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1274_q28_1}

Decaln walks 1600 metres due north along a road from point $A$ to point $B$.

The point is due east of a hill $XY$, where $X$ is the top of the hill.

The point $Y$ is directly below point $X$ and is on the same horizontal plane as the road.

Let the height of the hill above point $Y$ be $h$ metres.

From point $A$, the angle of elevation to the top of the hill is $16^o$.

From point $B$, the angle of elevation to the top of the hill is $12^o$.
Hence, find the value of $h$.
items.sol:
Similarly, in triangle $XYA$, $AY=h\cot 16^\circ$.

Using Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle $BAY$ (right angle at $A$):
$$\begin{aligned}(h\cot 12^\circ)^2&=(h\cot 16^\circ)^2+1600^2\\ h^2\cot^2 12^\circ-h^2\cot^2 16^\circ&=1600^2\\ h^2\left(\cot^2 12^\circ-\cot^2 16^\circ\right)&=1600^2\\ h^2&=\dfrac{1600^2}{\cot^2 12^\circ-\cot^2 16^\circ}\\ h&=\dfrac{1600}{\sqrt{\cot^2 12^\circ-\cot^2 16^\circ}}\\ &\approx 507\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h\approx 507 \text{ m (nearest whole number)}$$

items.part:
The length of a whale species is modelled using the equation

$$L=5.2-4.6e^{-kt}$$

where $L$ is in meters and $t$ is the age in years and $k$ is a positive constant.
What is the length of the whale at birth?
items.sol:
At birth $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}L&=5.2-4.6e^0\\ &=0.6 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The length of a whale species is modelled using the equation

$$L=5.2-4.6e^{-kt}$$

where $L$ is in meters and $t$ is the age in years and $k$ is a positive constant.
If a three year old whale has a length of $4.45$ metres, what is the value of $k$, correct to 2 decimal places?
items.sol:
Substitute $t=3$, $L=4.45$.
$$\begin{aligned}4.45&=5.2-4.6e^{-3k}\\ 4.6e^{-3k}&=0.75\\ e^{-3k}&=\dfrac{0.75}{4.6}\\ -3k&=\ln\left(\dfrac{0.75}{4.6}\right)\\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left(\dfrac{0.75}{4.6}\right)\\ &\approx 0.60\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k\approx 0.60 \text{ (2 decimal places)}$$

items.part:
The length of a whale species is modelled using the equation

$$L=5.2-4.6e^{-kt}$$

where $L$ is in meters and $t$ is the age in years and $k$ is a positive constant.
Find the limiting length of the whale species.
items.sol:
Write
$$L=5.2-\dfrac{4.6}{e^{kt}}$$
As $t\to\infty$ (with $k>0$), $e^{kt}\to\infty$, so $\dfrac{4.6}{e^{kt}}\to 0$ and $L\to 5.2$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the limiting length is } 5.2 \text{ m}$$

items.part: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+kx+8$, where $k$ is a constant. Find the values of $k$ for which $f(x)$ is an increasing function.
items.sol:
$$f'(x)=3x^2-6x+k$$
$f(x)$ is increasing when $f'(x)>0$ for all $x$. Since $a=3>0$, this needs $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{aligned}(-6)^2-4(3)(k)&<0\\ 36-12k&<0\\ 12k&>36\\ k&>3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is increasing when } k>3$$

items.part: Find integers $a$ and $b$ such that $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}-2}=a+b\sqrt{5}$.
items.sol:
Rationalise the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5-2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt5+2}{\sqrt5+2}&=\dfrac{\sqrt5+2}{(\sqrt5)^2-2^2}\\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt5+2}{5-4}\\ &=2+\sqrt5\end{aligned}$$
Comparing $2+\sqrt5=a+b\sqrt5$:
$$\therefore\ a=2,\ b=1$$

items.part:
A wire of length $28\,m$ is to be cut into two pieces. One of the piece is to be made into a square and the other into a circle. Let $r$ be the radius of the circle and $x$ meters be the length of each side of the square. The combined perimeter is given as $2\pi r+4x=28$ and the combined area, $A$, is given by:

$$A=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2$$ (\textbf{DO NOT prove this})

What should be the lengths of each piece so that the combined area of the circle and the square is minimum?
items.sol:
Simplify the area expression.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\\ &=\dfrac{4}{\pi}(7-x)^2+x^2\end{aligned}$$
Differentiate.
$$A'=-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x$$
$$A''=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2$$
Stationary points: $A'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x&=0\\ -\dfrac{56}{\pi}+\dfrac{8x}{\pi}+2x&=0\\ -56+8x+2\pi x&=0\\ -28+4x+\pi x&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{28}{\pi+4}\end{aligned}$$
Since $A''=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2>0$ for all $x$, this is a minimum.

The lengths of the two pieces are
$$4x=\dfrac{112}{\pi+4}\text{ m}$$
$$28-4x=28-\dfrac{112}{\pi+4}=\dfrac{28\pi}{\pi+4}\text{ m}$$

items.part:
Initially a car is at rest. The car then starts from a point $P$ at time $t=0$ seconds and comes to a stop at point $Q$. The distance $x$, in metres covered by the car, in $t$ seconds is given by $x=t^2\left(2-\dfrac{t}{3}\right)$. Find
the time taken by it to reach $Q$.
items.sol:
Distance is $x=2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}$, so the velocity is
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=4t-t^2$$
The car is at rest at $Q$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}4t-t^2&=0\\ t(4-t)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=0$ (start) or $t=4$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the car takes 4 seconds to reach } Q$$

the distance between $P$ and $Q$.

items.part: There is a large sheet of paper which is $0.1\,mm$ thick that is cut in half. Then one piece is placed on top of the other. This pile is again cut in half and one pile is placed on top of the other. This process is repeated 40 times. How high is the pile of the sheets?
items.sol:
After the first cut the pile is $0.2$ mm thick, and each cut doubles it. The thicknesses form a GP: $0.2,\ 0.4,\ 0.8,\ \dots$ with $a=0.2$ and $r=2$.

After 40 cuts, the thickness is the 40th term.
$$\begin{aligned}T_{40}&=0.2\times 2^{39}\\ &\approx 1.1\times 10^{11}\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the pile is } 1.1\times 10^{11}\text{ mm, or } 110\,000\text{ km, high}$$

items.part: What angle does the line $2x+3y+6=0$ make with the positive $x$-axis? Round to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
Rewrite the line as $y=-\dfrac{2}{3}x-2$, so the gradient is
$$m=-\dfrac{2}{3}$$
The angle $\alpha$ with the positive $x$-axis satisfies $\tan\alpha=m$, so $\tan\alpha=-\dfrac{2}{3}$.

The gradient is negative, so $\alpha$ is obtuse:
$$\alpha=146^\circ19'$$

Use $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$, or a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $8$ and adjacent side $1$.

The opposite side is $\sqrt{8^2-1^2}=\sqrt{63}=3\sqrt7$.
$$\sin\angle BAC=\dfrac{3\sqrt7}{8}$$

Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times5\times13\times\sin\angle BAC\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times5\times13\times\dfrac{3\sqrt7}{8}\\&=\dfrac{195\sqrt7}{16}\\&\approx 32.2\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $2\log x=\log(5x+6)$
items.sol:
The logarithms need $x>0$. Using the power law:
$$\begin{aligned}\log x^2&=\log(5x+6)\\x^2&=5x+6\\x^2-5x-6&=0\\(x-6)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=6$ or $x=-1$. Since $x>0$, reject $x=-1$.
$$\therefore\ x=6$$

items.part: Solve $\left|1-2\cos^2 x\right|=1$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$
items.sol:
Case 1: $1-2\cos^2x=1$
$$\begin{aligned}\cos^2x&=0\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Case 2: $1-2\cos^2x=-1$
$$\begin{aligned}\cos^2x&=1\\\cos x&=\pm1\\x&=0,\pi,2\pi\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=0,\dfrac{\pi}{2},\pi,\dfrac{3\pi}{2},2\pi$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following expressions.
$\log_5(\tan x)$
items.sol:
Using the change of base rule, $\log_5(\tan x)=\dfrac{\ln(\tan x)}{\ln5}$.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log_5(\tan x)\right)=\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\ln5\,\tan x}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following expressions.
$\dfrac{2^x}{e^x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=2^x & v&=e^x\\u'&=\ln2\cdot2^x & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{2^x}{e^x}\right)&=\dfrac{\ln2\cdot2^x\cdot e^x-2^x\cdot e^x}{(e^x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{e^x2^x(\ln2-1)}{e^{2x}}\\&=\dfrac{2^x(\ln2-1)}{e^x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the graph $y=f(x)$. Both arcs have a radius of four units.

\exfigure{1275_q17_1}

Using the graph of $y=f(x)$, $x\ge 0$, evaluate exactly the following integrals.
$\displaystyle\int_0^{12} f(x)\,dx$
items.sol:
The area is found from rectangles, a quarter circle of radius $4$ and a triangle.
$$\begin{aligned}\displaystyle\int_0^{12}f(x)\,dx&=(6\times6)+(4\times2)+\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\times4^2+\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times2\\&=46+4\pi\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the graph $y=f(x)$. Both arcs have a radius of four units.

\exfigure{1275_q17_1}

Using the graph of $y=f(x)$, $x\ge 0$, evaluate exactly the following integrals.
$\displaystyle\int_0^{18} f(x)\,dx$
items.sol:
Split the integral; the region from $12$ to $18$ lies below the axis, so it is subtracted.
$$\begin{aligned}\displaystyle\int_0^{18}f(x)\,dx&=\int_0^{12}f(x)\,dx+\int_{12}^{18}f(x)\,dx\\&=46+4\pi-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times2+\left(4\times6-\dfrac{1}{4}\times\pi\times4^2\right)\right)\\&=46+4\pi-(26-4\pi)\\&=20+8\pi\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution shown in the table below

\extable{1275_q18_t1}

and $E(X)=0.55$
By forming a pair of simultaneous equations, or otherwise, find the values of $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
Using $E(X)=\sum x_ip_i$:
$$E(X)=-a+0\cdot b+0.2+2(0.15)+3(0.13)$$
$$\begin{aligned}0.55&=-a+0.89\\a&=0.34\end{aligned}$$
The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}0.34+b+0.2+0.15+0.13&=1\\b&=0.18\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=0.34,\ b=0.18$$

items.part:
The discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution shown in the table below

\extable{1275_q18_t1}

and $E(X)=0.55$
Calculate $\operatorname{Var}(X)$
items.sol:
Using $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X^2)&=1(a)+0(b)+1(0.2)+4(0.15)+9(0.13)\\&=2.31\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(X)&=2.31-0.55^2\\&=2.0075\end{aligned}$$

items.part: The length of steel rods produced by a machine is normally distributed with a standard deviation of 3 mm. It is found that $2.5\%$ of all rods are less than 25 mm long. Find the mean length of rods produced by the machine.
items.sol:
$2.5\%$ of rods are below $25$ mm, so $25$ is $2$ standard deviations below the mean: $z=-2$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2&=\dfrac{25-\mu}{3}\\25-\mu&=-6\\\mu&=31\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3+6x^2+9x+4$ in the domain $-4\le x\le 1$
Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$f'(x)=3x^2+12x+9,\qquad f''(x)=6x+12$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3(x^2+4x+3)&=0\\(x+3)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=-3$ or $x=-1$.

For $x=-3$: $y=4$ and $f''(-3)=-6<0$, so there is a maximum turning point at $(-3,4)$.

For $x=-1$: $y=0$ and $f''(-1)=6>0$, so there is a minimum turning point at $(-1,0)$.
items.final: Maximum turning point at $(-3,4)$; minimum turning point at $(-1,0)$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3+6x^2+9x+4$ in the domain $-4\le x\le 1$
Determine the coordinates of its point(s) of inflexion.
items.sol:
A possible point of inflexion is where $f''(x)=0$:
$$6x+12=0$$
So $x=-2$ and $y=2$.

Test the concavity:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(-3)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\f''(-2)&=0\\f''(-1)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflexion at $(-2,2)$.

items.sol:
The endpoints are $(-4,0)$ and $(1,20)$, the $y$-intercept is $4$, and the turning points and inflexion are from parts (a) and (b).

items.part:

What is the global maximum value of the curve in the domain $-4\le x\le 1$
items.sol:
The maximum over the domain is at the endpoint $x=1$, where $f(1)=20$, which exceeds the local maximum $4$.
$$\therefore\ \text{global maximum}=20$$

$P(C)=\dfrac{3}{7}$, $P(D\mid\overline{C})=\dfrac{2}{5}$, and $P(\overline{D}\mid C)=\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Where $C$ is the event that "a person has a cat" and $D$ is the event that "a person has a dog"
a cat and a dog

Multiply along the branches $C$ then $D$.

items.part:
A pet ownership survey resulted in the following results:

$P(C)=\dfrac{3}{7}$, $P(D\mid\overline{C})=\dfrac{2}{5}$, and $P(\overline{D}\mid C)=\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Where $C$ is the event that "a person has a cat" and $D$ is the event that "a person has a dog"
at least one pet (cat or dog)
items.sol:
Use the complement: the only way to have no pet is $\overline C$ and $\overline D$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least 1 pet})&=1-P(\overline C\cap\overline D) \\ &=1-\dfrac47\times\dfrac35 \\ &=\dfrac{23}{35} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=2+\sqrt{x-3}$ for $x\ge 3$.

The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=\dfrac{12}{x}+2$ for $x>0$
Write the domain and range of the function $f$ using interval notation.
items.sol:
The square root needs $x-3\ge0$.

Domain: $x\ge3$, that is $[3,\infty)$.

Since $\sqrt{x-3}\ge0$, we have $f(x)\ge2$.

Range: $y\ge2$, that is $[2,\infty)$.

items.part:
The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=2+\sqrt{x-3}$ for $x\ge 3$.

The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=\dfrac{12}{x}+2$ for $x>0$
Write an expression for the composite function $h(x)=g(f(x))$ and hence find a value for $g(f(12))$

Then

$$\tan x=1$$
So $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ for $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$$y=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$$
$$\therefore\ A\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)$$

For $B$: $\tan x=1$ with $\pi<x<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, so $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

Between $A$ and $B$, $\sin x\ge\cos x$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{5\pi}{4}}(\sin x-\cos x)\,dx \\ &=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{5\pi}{4}} \\ &=-\Big[\cos x+\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{5\pi}{4}} \\ &=-\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\right) \\ &=2\sqrt2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=2\sqrt2\ \text{units}^2$$

Let $D=(x,y)$. $X$ is the midpoint of $BD$, so

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. Its velocity for $t\ge 0$ is given by $v=\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t$, where time is in seconds and displacement in metres.
Find when the particle changes direction.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$.
$$\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t=0$$
Multiply by $t+1$:
$$4-2t^2-2t=0$$
$$t^2+t-2=0$$
$$(t+2)(t-1)=0$$
So $t=-2$ or $t=1$. Since $t\ge0$, reject $t=-2$.
$$\therefore\ t=1\text{ second}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line. Its velocity for $t\ge 0$ is given by $v=\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t$, where time is in seconds and displacement in metres.
Find the exact distance travelled in the first 2 seconds.
items.sol:
The particle changes direction at $t=1$, so split the integral there.
$$d=\left|\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t\right)dt\right|+\left|\displaystyle\int_1^2\left(\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t\right)dt\right|$$
Integrating:
$$d=\left|\Big[4\ln|t+1|-t^2\Big]_0^1\right|+\left|\Big[4\ln|t+1|-t^2\Big]_1^2\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned} d&=|4\ln2-1|+|4\ln3-3-4\ln2| \\ &=4\ln2-1-(4\ln3-3-4\ln2) \\ &=8\ln2+2-4\ln3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ d=8\ln2+2-4\ln3\text{ metres}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\left(x^2-2x+2\right) & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Where $k$ is a constant
Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{12}$
items.sol:
The total probability is 1, so
$$\displaystyle k\int_1^4\left(x^2-2x+2\right)dx=1$$
$$k\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2+2x\right]_1^4=1$$
$$k\left(\left(\dfrac{64}{3}-16+8\right)-\left(\dfrac13-1+2\right)\right)=1$$
$$12k=1$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{12}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\left(x^2-2x+2\right) & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Where $k$ is a constant
Fully define the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.
items.sol:
For $1\le x\le4$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{12}\displaystyle\int_1^x\left(t^2-2t+2\right)dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12}\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2+2x-\dfrac43\right] \\ &=\dfrac{x^3}{36}-\dfrac{x^2}{12}+\dfrac{x}{6}-\dfrac19 \end{aligned}$$
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<1\\[6pt] \dfrac{x^3}{36}-\dfrac{x^2}{12}+\dfrac{x}{6}-\dfrac19 & 1\le x\le4\\[6pt] 1 & x>4\end{cases}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\left(x^2-2x+2\right) & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Where $k$ is a constant
Show that the median of $X$ lies between $x=3.2$ and $x=3.3$
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} F(3.2)&=\dfrac{3.2^3}{36}-\dfrac{3.2^2}{12}+\dfrac{3.2}{6}-\dfrac19 \\ &\approx0.479 \\ &<0.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} F(3.3)&=\dfrac{3.3^3}{36}-\dfrac{3.3^2}{12}+\dfrac{3.3}{6}-\dfrac19 \\ &\approx0.5296 \\ &>0.5 \end{aligned}$$
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=0.5$, and $F$ is increasing.

$\therefore$ the median lies between $x=3.2$ and $x=3.3$.

items.part:
Consider the geometric series $1+\dfrac{4}{3}\sin^2 x+\dfrac{16}{9}\sin^4 x+\dfrac{64}{27}\sin^6 x+\dots$
When the limiting sum exists, find an expression for its value.
items.sol:
The first term is $a=1$ and the common ratio is $r=\dfrac43\sin^2x$.
$$S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac43\sin^2x}$$

items.part:
Consider the geometric series $1+\dfrac{4}{3}\sin^2 x+\dfrac{16}{9}\sin^4 x+\dfrac{64}{27}\sin^6 x+\dots$
For what values of $x$ in the interval $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ does the limiting sum of this series exist?
items.sol:
The limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$\left|\dfrac43\sin^2x\right|<1$$
For $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin x>0$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 0&<\dfrac43\sin^2x<1 \\ 0&<\sin^2x<\dfrac34 &&(\text{multiply by } \dfrac34) \\ 0&<\sin x<\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} &&(\text{square root}) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \sec^2(2x)\tan^4(2x)\,dx$
items.sol:
The derivative of $\tan(2x)$ is $2\sec^2(2x)$, so insert a factor of $2$ and compensate with $\dfrac12$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\sec^2(2x)\tan^4(2x)\,dx&=\dfrac12\int2\sec^2(2x)\tan^4(2x)\,dx \\ &=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{\tan^5(2x)}{5}+c \\ &=\dfrac{\tan^5(2x)}{10}+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{5x^2}{x^3+1}\,dx$
items.sol:
The derivative of $x^3+1$ is $3x^2$, so the integrand has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{5x^2}{x^3+1}\,dx&=\dfrac53\int\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3+1}\,dx \\ &=\dfrac53\ln|x^3+1|+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the anti-derivative of $\dfrac{1}{1-2x}$ with respect to $x$.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{(x+3)(2x+1)}{\sqrt{x}},\ x>0$
Show that $f(x)$ can be written in the form

items.sol:

$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\dfrac{2x^2+7x+3}{\sqrt{x}}\\ &=2x^2\cdot x^{-\frac12}+7x\cdot x^{-\frac12}+3x^{-\frac12}\\ &=2x^{\frac32}+7x^{\frac12}+3x^{-\frac12}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the common ratio of a geometric series with a first term of 3 and a limiting sum of 1.8.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x-2)(x^2+1)$
Find where the graph of $y=f(x)$ cuts the $x$-axis and $y$ axis.
items.sol:
For the $x$-intercept, let $y=0$.
$$(x-2)(x^2+1)=0$$
Since $x^2+1\neq0$, $x=2$.

For the $y$-intercept, let $x=0$.
$$y=(-2)(1)=-2$$
So the graph cuts the $x$-axis at $(2,0)$ and the $y$-axis at $(0,-2)$.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x-2)(x^2+1)$
Find the coordinates of the stationary points on the curve with the equation $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Expand, then differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=x^3-2x^2+x-2\\ f'(x)&=3x^2-4x+1\\ f''(x)&=6x-4\end{aligned}$$

A tree grows from ground level to a height of 1.2 metres in one year. In each subsequent year, it grows $\dfrac{9}{10}$ as much as it did in the previous year.

items.sol:
The yearly growths form a geometric series with $a=1.2$ and $r=\dfrac{9}{10}$.

items.part:
Sonny repays a loan over a period of $n$ months. His monthly repayments form an arithmetic sequence. He repays \$119 in the first month, \$117 in the second month, \$115 in the third month, and so on. Sonny makes his final repayment in the $n$th month.
Find the amount Sonny repays in the 25th month.
items.sol:
The repayments form an arithmetic sequence with $a=119$ and $d=-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= 119+(n-1)(-2) \\ &= -2n+121 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T_{25} &= -2(25)+121 \\ &= 71 \end{aligned}$$
The repayment is $\$71$.

items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} (n-80)(n-40) &= 0 \\ n &= 40 \text{ or } n=80 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} n=40:\ T_{40} &= -2(40)+121=\$41 &&(\text{sensible}) \\ n=80:\ T_{80} &= -2(80)+121=-\$39 &&(\text{negative repayment}) \end{aligned}$$
Therefore $n=80$ is not a sensible solution, because the final repayment would be negative.

The average life cycle of an insect is one month. A viable nest of this insect has between 100 000 to 500 000 insects. The population $P$ of a nest of this insect grows exponentially so that:

items.sol:
Integrate the rate of growth.
$$P=\dfrac{1200}{0.3}e^{0.3t}+C=4000e^{0.3t}+C$$
When $t=1$, $P=5000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 5000 &= 4000e^{0.3}+C \\ C &\approx -399.435 \end{aligned}$$
For $P=100\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4000e^{0.3t} &= 100\,000+399.435 \\ e^{0.3t} &\approx 25.0999 \\ 0.3t &= \ln 25.0999 \\ t &\approx 10.7429 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 11 \text{ months}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^n$
items.sol:
Write out the terms:
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^n = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{5^2} + \dfrac{1}{5^3} + \cdots\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a = \dfrac{1}{5}$ and $r = \dfrac{1}{5}$, with $|r| < 1$, so it has a limiting sum $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} &= 2 \times \dfrac{\frac{1}{5}}{1 - \frac{1}{5}} \\ &= 2 \times \dfrac{1}{5} \times \dfrac{5}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate:

Gradient of the tangent at $x = 2$:
$$f'(2) = \dfrac{1}{2-1} = 1$$
The normal is perpendicular, so
$$m_\perp = \dfrac{-1}{1} = -1$$
At $x=2$, $f(2)=\ln 1+2=2$, so the point on the curve is $(2,2)$ (the paper printed $(2,0)$).

Equation of the normal through $(2, 2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 2 &= -1(x - 2) \\ y &= -x + 4 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Describe the transformations applied to $y = x^2$ in order to give the transformed function of $y = (4x + 2)^2$.
items.sol:
Rewrite the function:
$$\begin{aligned} y = (4x+2)^2 &= \left(\dfrac{x + \frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{4}}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $y = x^2$ is dilated horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and translated to the left by $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Alternatively, $y = \left(\dfrac{x}{\frac{1}{4}} + 2\right)^2$: translate to the left by $2$, then dilate horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{4}$.

Alternatively,
$$y = (2(2x+1))^2 = 4(2x+1)^2$$
so
$$\dfrac{y}{4} = \left(\dfrac{x + \frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^2$$
So $y = x^2$ is dilated horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, translated to the left by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and dilated vertically by a factor of $4$.

This gives the same curve as the first method, since $4(2x+1)^2=(4x+2)^2$.
items.final: Dilated horizontally by factor $\frac{1}{4}$ and translated left by $\frac{1}{2}$

A continuous random variable $X$ has a function $f$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x^3 - x + a, & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Find the value of $a$ which makes $f(x)$ a valid probability density function
items.sol:
The total probability is 1 and $f(x) = 0$ elsewhere, so
$$\int_0^1 (2x^3 - x + a)\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{x^4}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 + ax\right]_0^1 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} + a &= 1 \\ a &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a function $f$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x^3 - x + a, & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Find the expected value and variance of $X$.
items.sol:
Expected value:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) = \mu &= \int_0^1 x(2x^3 - x + 1)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^1 (2x^4 - x^2 + x)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{5}x^5 - \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{17}{30} \end{aligned}$$
Variance:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 &= \int_0^1 x^2 f(x)\,dx - \mu^2 \\ &= \int_0^1 (2x^5 - x^3 + x^2)\,dx - \left(\dfrac{17}{30}\right)^2 \\ &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}x^6 - \dfrac{1}{4}x^4 + \dfrac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^1 - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{375}{900} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{86}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{43}{450} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: In an arithmetic sequence, the fifth term is 25 and the eighteenth term 181. What is the smallest value of $n$ such that the sum of the first $n$ term in the sequence is at least 27365?
items.sol:
Use the arithmetic sequence $T_n = a + (n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} a + 4d &= 25 &&(1) \\ a + 17d &= 181 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtract (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 13d &= 156 \\ d &= 12 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a + 48 &= 25 \\ a &= -23 \end{aligned}$$
Sum of the first $n$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a + (n-1)d\big) \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}(12n - 58) \\ &= 6n^2 - 29n \end{aligned}$$
We need $6n^2 - 29n \ge 27365$, that is
$$6n^2 - 29n - 27365 \ge 0$$
The positive root is
$$n = \dfrac{29 + \sqrt{29^2 - 4 \times 6 \times (-27365)}}{2 \times 6} \approx 69.99$$
So $n > 69.99$ and $n$ is a whole number.
$$\therefore n = 70$$

items.sol:
The square root needs $x + 1 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -1$.

items.part:
Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}$ for $x \ge 0$
Let $g(x) = x^2 + 4x + 3$, where $x \le c$ and $c \le 0$. Find the largest possible value of $c$ such that the range of $g(x)$ is a subset of the domain of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
From part (a), the domain of $f$ is $x \ge 0$, so the range of $g$ must lie in $[0, \infty)$.

Factorise:
$$g(x) = x^2 + 4x + 3 = (x+3)(x+1)$$
We need $g(x) \ge 0$, so
$$x \ge -1 \text{ or } x \le -3$$
But $x \le c$ and $c \le 0$, so the domain of $g$ is $x \le c$ with $c \le 0$.

For $g(x) \ge 0$ on all of $x \le c$, we need $x \le -3$.
$$\therefore\ c = -3$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = \sin x + \cos x$ in the domain $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.
Find $x$-intercepts, express your answer in terms of $\pi$.
items.sol:
The $x$-intercepts occur where $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \sin x + \cos x &= 0 \\ \sin x &= -\cos x \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
In $-\pi \le x \le \pi$:
$$\therefore\ x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = \sin x + \cos x$ in the domain $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.
Find any stationary points, and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \cos x - \sin x = 0 \\ \tan x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative:
$$y'' = -\sin x - \cos x$$
At $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$y'' = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < 0 \quad \text{(maximum)}$$
At $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$:
$$y'' = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} > 0 \quad \text{(minimum)}$$
The $y$-values are:
$$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}, \qquad y\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -\sqrt{2}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \sqrt{2}\right) \text{ is a local maximum and } \left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, -\sqrt{2}\right) \text{ is a local minimum.}$$
items.final: $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \sqrt{2}\right)$ is a local maximum and $\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, -\sqrt{2}\right)$ is a local minimum

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = \sin x + \cos x$ in the domain $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.
Find any points of inflection.
items.sol:
Points of inflection occur where $y''=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} -\sin x - \cos x &= 0 \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Test concavity:

\extable{Ts8070_1}

Since the concavity changes at each value, the points $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}, 0\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, 0\right)$ are points of inflection.

items.part:
Consider the curve $y = \sin x + \cos x$ in the domain $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.
Explain why the points found in (c) are not points of horizontal inflection.
items.sol:
A horizontal point of inflection needs $y'=0$ as well as a change of concavity.
$$\begin{aligned} y'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)-\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2\ne0 \\ y'\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=-\sqrt2\ne0 \end{aligned}$$
The gradient is not zero at either point, so they are not horizontal points of inflection.

items.sol:
The triangle has base $x$ and height $f(x) = 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times x \times 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ &= xe^{-\frac{x}{5}} \end{aligned}$$

A maximum occurs where $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$ and $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= x & v &= e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= -\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= x\left(-\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\right) + e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ &= e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{5}\right) = 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-\frac{x}{5}} > 0$ for all $x$, $x = 5$.

Second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} - \dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} + \dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} = e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\left(\dfrac{x}{25}-\dfrac{2}{5}\right)$$
At $x = 5$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = e^{-1}\left(\dfrac15-\dfrac25\right) = -\dfrac{1}{5e} < 0$, so this is a maximum.

At $x = 5$:
$$A = 5e^{-1}$$
$$\therefore\ A_{\max} = \dfrac{5}{e} \text{ units}^2 \text{ at } x = 5$$

Find $S$: $f(0) = 2$, so $S(0, 2)$.

Find $T$: solve $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ e^{-\frac{x}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ x &= -5\ln\dfrac{1}{4} = 5\ln 4 \end{aligned}$$
So $T\left(5\ln 4, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

The region lies between the chord $ST$ (above) and the curve (below) for $0 \le x \le 5\ln 4$. Its area is the trapezium under $ST$ (parallel sides $2$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}$, width $5\ln 4$) minus the area under the curve.

Trapezium:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 5\ln 4\left(2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 \end{aligned}$$
Area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= \displaystyle\int_0^{5\ln 4} 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\,dx \\ &= \Big[-10e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\Big]_0^{5\ln 4} \\ &= -10e^{-\ln 4} + 10 \\ &= -10\times\dfrac{1}{4} + 10 \\ &= \dfrac{15}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Required area:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= A_1 - A_2 \\ &= \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 - \dfrac{15}{2} \\ &\approx 1.16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A = \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 - \dfrac{15}{2} \text{ units}^2$$

The population of a white-ant colony can be modelled using the equation $P = Ae^{kt}$, where $A$ and $k$ are positive constants and $t$ is time in weeks. Initially, the population is 1000. Two weeks later, the population has increased to become 1500.
Find the value of $A$ and $k$. Express your answer in exact form.

The population of a white-ant colony can be modelled using the equation $P = Ae^{kt}$, where $A$ and $k$ are positive constants and $t$ is time in weeks. Initially, the population is 1000. Two weeks later, the population has increased to become 1500.
Find the population after four week, correct to the nearest possible number of white-ants.
items.sol:
Substitute $t = 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1000e^{4 \times \frac{\ln 1.5}{2}} \\ &= 1000e^{2\ln 1.5} \\ &= 1000\times1.5^2 \\ &= 2250 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 2250 \text{ white-ants}$$

items.part:
The population of a white-ant colony can be modelled using the equation $P = Ae^{kt}$, where $A$ and $k$ are positive constants and $t$ is time in weeks. Initially, the population is 1000. Two weeks later, the population has increased to become 1500.
White-ants can cause significant structural timber damages. Assume this particular ant colony was found near a timbre structured home, using the model above to explain why the situation is getting worse. Show all mathematical calculations.
items.sol:
Differentiate the model to find the rate of growth.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= kAe^{kt} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln 1.5}{2} \times 1000 \times e^{\frac{\ln 1.5}{2}t} \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{dP}{dt} > 0$ for $t > 0$, the population is increasing, and $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ itself increases with $t$, so the population grows faster over time.

$\therefore$ the situation is getting worse.

items.part: Find the number of terms in the geometric sequence $128, 192, \ldots, 972$.
items.sol:
The first term is $a=128$ and the common ratio is $r=\dfrac{192}{128}=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Suppose there are $k$ terms, so $T_k=972$. Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 972&=128\times\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{k-1}\\ \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{k-1}&=\dfrac{243}{32}=\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^5\\ k-1&=5\\ k&=6\end{aligned}$$
There are 6 terms in the geometric sequence.

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x-2)(x^2+1)$
Find the coordinates of the stationary points on the curve with the equation $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x-2 & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=(x-2)\cdot 2x+(x^2+1)\times1\\ &=3x^2-4x+1\\ f''(x)&=6x-4\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-4x+1&=0\\ (3x-1)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=\dfrac13$ or $x=1$.

When $x=\dfrac13$, $y=-\dfrac{50}{27}$. When $x=1$, $y=-2$.

The stationary points are $\left(\dfrac13,-\dfrac{50}{27}\right)$ and $(1,-2)$.

Nature, using the sign of $f''(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=\dfrac13:\ f''&=6\times\dfrac13-4=-2<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ \text{At } x=1:\ f''&=6\times1-4=2>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
So $\left(\dfrac13,-\dfrac{50}{27}\right)$ is a maximum and $(1,-2)$ is a minimum.
items.final: $\left(\tfrac13,-\tfrac{50}{27}\right)$ is a maximum and $(1,-2)$ is a minimum

items.part:
The students in a school were surveyed on the number of hours of sleep per week. The results were normally distributed with a mean of 48 hours.
What percentage of students would have indicated they had between 51 and 57 hours of sleep per week?
items.sol:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\bar x}{s}$:
$$z=\dfrac{51-48}{3}=1 \quad\text{and}\quad z=\dfrac{57-48}{3}=3$$
Between $z=1$ and $z=3$, using the 68% and 99.7% rules,
$$\text{Percentage}=\dfrac{99.7\%}{2}-\dfrac{68\%}{2}=15.85\%$$
$$\therefore\ 15.85\% \text{ have between 51 and 57 hours of sleep per week.}$$

items.part:
The probability density function for the continuous random variable $X$ is:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}x^3-x+\dfrac{5}{4} & 0\le x\le 1\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Find $E(X)$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}xf(x)\,dx \\ &=\displaystyle\int_0^1 x\left(x^3-x+\dfrac{5}{4}\right)dx \\ &=\displaystyle\int_0^1 \left(x^4-x^2+\dfrac{5}{4}x\right)dx \\ &=\left[\dfrac{x^5}{5}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{5x^2}{8}\right]_0^1 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}-\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{5}{8} \\ &=\dfrac{59}{120} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An alarm system is made up of a number of identical components.

The alarm system below is wired in series, i.e. the system works only when both components operate properly. Find the probability that the system does not fail. (Give your answer correct to three decimal places.)

\exfigure{1280_q28_1}
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(\text{system does not fail})&=(1-0.05)(1-0.05) \\ &=0.9025 \\ &\approx0.903 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An alarm system is made up of a number of identical components.

The probability that component $X$ fails is 0.05.
Another alarm system below is wired in parallel i.e. only one component needs to work for the circuit to work. What is the minimum number of components needed so that the probability of the system working is greater than 99.999%? Clearly justify your working.

\exfigure{1280_q28_2}
items.sol:
Let the number of components be $n$. The system works if at least one component works, so
$$P(\text{system works})=1-(0.05)^n$$
Require
$$\begin{aligned} 1-(0.05)^n&>0.99999 \\ 0.00001&>(0.05)^n \\ \log 0.00001&>n\log 0.05 \\ 3.843\ldots&<n \end{aligned}$$
The inequality sign reverses because $\log 0.05$ is negative.

Since $n$ is a whole number,
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum number of components is } 4$$

items.part: If a coin is tossed $n$ times, where $n>1$, find the probability of obtaining at least one head and at least one tail.
items.sol:
Subtract the cases of no heads and no tails (which cannot overlap since $n>1$).
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-P(\text{no heads})-P(\text{no tails}) \\ &=1-\dfrac{1}{2^n}-\dfrac{1}{2^n} \\ &=1-\dfrac{2}{2^n} \\ &=1-2^{1-n} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds, its displacement from the origin is $x$ metres and is given by $x=1-\cos 2t$.
Find the velocity of the particle when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
items.sol:
$$x=1-\cos2t,\quad v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2\sin2t$$
At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

items.part:
A particle moves in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds, its displacement from the origin is $x$ metres and is given by $x=1-\cos 2t$.
When is the particle's velocity greater than 1 m/s?
items.sol:
Solve $v=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin2t&=1 \\ \sin2t&=\dfrac12 \\ 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
From the graph of $v$, it exceeds 1 between these times.
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{\pi}{12}<t<\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$$

items.part: For the curve $y=2x^2-\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-4$, find the coordinates of the minimum stationary point. Give your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
A minimum occurs where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4x-\dfrac{0.5}{\frac{x}{2}}=4x-\dfrac1x$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4x-\dfrac1x \\ 4x^2&=1 \\ x^2&=\dfrac14 \\ x&=\pm\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
The logarithm needs $x>0$, so $x=\dfrac12$.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2\left(\dfrac12\right)^2-\ln\left(\dfrac{0.5}{2}\right)-4 \\ &=\ln4-3\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4+\dfrac{1}{x^2}$$
At $x=\dfrac12$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4+4=8>0$, so it is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum point is } \left(\dfrac12,\ \ln4-\dfrac72\right)$$

items.part:
By expressing $\sec\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, show that

$$\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta=1$$
items.sol:
Use $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta&=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the largest domain for which $\sqrt{x^2-2x-8}$ is defined.
items.sol:
The square root is defined only when the expression under it is non-negative, so we need

$$x^2-2x-8\ge 0$$

$$(x-4)(x+2)\ge 0$$

Hence $x\le -2$ or $x\ge 4$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the largest domain is } (-\infty,-2]\cup[4,\infty)$$

items.part: For $x$ and $y$ rational numbers and $\left(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}\right)^2=x+y+2\sqrt{xy}$, write $\sqrt{16+2\sqrt{55}}$ in the form $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}$.
items.sol:
Compare $\sqrt{16+2\sqrt{55}}$ with $\sqrt{x+y+2\sqrt{xy}}$, so $x+y=16$ and $xy=55$.

The numbers with sum 16 and product 55 are $11$ and $5$.

$$\therefore\ \sqrt{16+2\sqrt{55}}=\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{5}$$

items.part: Find the values of $x$ and $y$ if the first four terms of a geometric sequence are $3,x,y,192$.
items.sol:
In a geometric sequence the ratio of consecutive terms is constant:

$$\dfrac{x}{3}=\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{192}{y}$$

So $x^2=3y$ (1) and $y^2=192x$ (2).

Substituting (2) into (1) gives

$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{y^2}{192}\right)^2&=3y \\ \dfrac{y^4}{36864}&=3y \end{aligned}$$

so $y=48$.

Therefore $x=12$ and $y=48$.

Alternatively, using $T_4=ar^{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned} 192&=3r^3 \\ r^3&=64 \\ r&=4 \end{aligned}$$

Then $x=3\times 4=12$ and $y=12\times 4=48$.

$$\therefore\ x=12,\ y=48$$
