items.part:
Consider the curve $y=3x^4-16x^3+24x^2-9$.
Show that the first and second derivatives are respectively

$$y'=12x(x-2)^2$$

$$y''=12(x-2)(3x-2)$$
items.sol:
Differentiate $y=3x^4-16x^3+24x^2-9$:

$$\begin{aligned} y'&=12x^3-48x^2+48x \\ &=12x(x^2-4x+4) \\ &=12x(x-2)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate again:

$$\begin{aligned} y''&=36x^2-96x+48 \\ &=12(3x^2-8x+4) \\ &=12(3x-2)(x-2) \\ &=12(x-2)(3x-2) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=3x^4-16x^3+24x^2-9$.
Find and classify all stationary points and points of inflexion.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:

$$12x(x-2)^2=0$$

so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$, $y=-9$; when $x=2$, $y=7$. The stationary points are $(0,-9)$ and $(2,7)$.

At $(0,-9)$:

$$y''=12(-2)(-2)=48>0$$

The curve is concave up, so $(0,-9)$ is a minimum.

At $(2,7)$:

$$y''=12(0)(4)=0$$

This is a possible point of inflexion, so test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts8162_1}

The concavity changes from down to up, so $(2,7)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

Other possible points of inflexion occur when $y''=0$:

$$12(x-2)(3x-2)=0$$

so $x=2$ or $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

\extable{Ts8162_2}

The concavity changes, so $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},-\dfrac{67}{27}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.
items.final: $(0,-9)$ minimum; $(2,7)$ horizontal point of inflexion; $\left(\tfrac{2}{3},-\tfrac{67}{27}\right)$ point of inflexion

items.part:
Consider the curve $y=3x^4-16x^3+24x^2-9$.
Over which interval(s) is the curve decreasing?
items.sol:
The curve is decreasing when $y'<0$:

$$12x(x-2)^2<0$$

Since $(x-2)^2\ge 0$, the sign of $y'$ is decided by $x$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the curve is decreasing for } x<0$$

Find $\tan A$ if $\operatorname{cosec} A=-\dfrac{13}{12}$ and $\sec A>0$.
items.sol:
Since $\operatorname{cosec}A=-\dfrac{13}{12}$, we have $\sin A=-\dfrac{12}{13}$.

Since $\sec A>0$, $\cos A>0$.

So $A$ is in the fourth quadrant. In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 13 and opposite side 12, the adjacent side is 5.

items.part:
Solve

$$\cos^2 2x=\dfrac{1}{2}$$

for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
items.sol:
Taking square roots:

$$\cos 2x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\ \text{ or }\ \cos 2x=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$$

For $0\le x\le 2\pi$ we need $0\le 2x\le 4\pi$.

For $\cos 2x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$:

$$2x=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{7\pi}{4},\dfrac{9\pi}{4},\dfrac{15\pi}{4}$$

For $\cos 2x=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$:

$$2x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\dfrac{5\pi}{4},\dfrac{11\pi}{4},\dfrac{13\pi}{4}$$

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{8},\dfrac{3\pi}{8},\dfrac{5\pi}{8},\dfrac{7\pi}{8},\dfrac{9\pi}{8},\dfrac{11\pi}{8},\dfrac{13\pi}{8},\dfrac{15\pi}{8}$$

items.part: Solve $3\tan\theta-\cot\theta=5$ for $0^\circ\le\theta\le 360^\circ$. Give your answers to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Since $\cot\theta=\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}$, multiply $3\tan\theta-\cot\theta=5$ by $\tan\theta$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3\tan^2\theta-1&=5\tan\theta \\ 3\tan^2\theta-5\tan\theta-1&=0 \end{aligned}$$

Using the quadratic formula:

$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{25+12}}{6}=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{37}}{6}$$

For $\tan\theta=\dfrac{5+\sqrt{37}}{6}$ (positive, first and third quadrants):

$$\theta=62^\circ,\ 180^\circ+62^\circ=242^\circ$$

For $\tan\theta=\dfrac{5-\sqrt{37}}{6}$ (negative, second and fourth quadrants), the related angle gives $-10.22^\circ$:

$$\theta=-10.22^\circ+360^\circ\approx 350^\circ,\quad \theta=-10.22^\circ+180^\circ\approx 170^\circ$$

$$\therefore\ \theta=62^\circ,\ 170^\circ,\ 242^\circ,\ 350^\circ$$

items.part:
Evaluate:

$$\int 1+e^{7x}\,dx$$

Evaluate:

$$\int_0^3 \dfrac{8x}{1+x^2}\,dx$$
items.sol:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, so

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^3\dfrac{8x}{1+x^2}\,dx&=4\int_0^3\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\,dx \\ &=4\Big[\ln(1+x^2)\Big]_0^3 \\ &=4\ln 10 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graph of $y=e^x(x+1)$.

\exfigure{1281_q22_1}

Using a graphical method, determine the number of solutions to the equation

$$2e^x(1+x)=2-3x-2x^2$$

You may use the diagram above in your solution.
items.sol:
Divide the equation by 2:

$$2e^x(1+x)=2-3x-2x^2 \iff e^x(1+x)=1-1.5x-x^2$$

Solutions occur where $y=1-1.5x-x^2$ meets $y=e^x(x+1)$.

Complete the square for the parabola:

$$y=-(x+0.75)^2+1.5625$$

It is concave down with maximum at $x=-0.75$.

\exfigure{1281_q22_s1}

Both curves pass through $(0,1)$, so $x=0$ is a solution. The parabola cuts the curve again on the negative side.

$$\therefore\ \text{there are two solutions}$$

The probabilities sum to 1:

$$0.2+0.6p^2+0.1+1-p+0.1=1$$

Simplify:

$$\begin{aligned} 0.6p^2-p+0.4&=0 \\ 3p^2-5p+2&=0 \\ (3p-2)(p-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ p=\dfrac{2}{3}\ \text{ or }\ p=1$$

Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$ with $p=\dfrac{2}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0.2\times 0+0.6\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2\times 1+0.1\times 2+\left(1-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\times 3+0.1\times 4 \\ &\approx 1.87 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 1.87)&=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4) \\ &=0.1+\left(1-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)+0.1 \\ &=0.5\dot{3} \\ &\approx 0.53 \end{aligned}$$

Using $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(X)&=0.6\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2+0.1\times 4+\dfrac{1}{3}\times 9+16\times 0.1-\left(\dfrac{28}{15}\right)^2 \\ &=5.2667-3.4844 \\ &\approx1.78 \end{aligned}$$

The mean is $\mu=4.5$.

Since $P(X>5.5)=0.0465$, we have $P(Z<z)=1-0.0465=0.9535$.

From the table, $z=1.68$.

Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5.5-4.5}{\sigma}&=1.68 \\ \sigma&=\dfrac{1}{1.68} \\ &=0.5952 \\ &\approx 0.595 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Differentiate $e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{3x} & v&=\cos x-3\sin x \\ u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=-\sin x-3\cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)\right]&=3e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)+e^{3x}(-\sin x-3\cos x) \\ &=e^{3x}(3\cos x-9\sin x-\sin x-3\cos x) \\ &=-10e^{3x}\sin x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence or otherwise, find

$$\int e^{3x}\sin x\,dx$$
items.sol:
Integrating the result of part (a):
$$\int \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)\right]dx=-10\int e^{3x}\sin x\,dx$$
The left side is $e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)$, so
$$\int e^{3x}\sin x\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{10}e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)+C$$

items.part:
A telecommunications box is to be placed at some point $Q$ along a road $PQR$, as shown in the diagram below. Two cables will connect the box to relay stations at $A$ and $B$. Let $AP=2$ km be the perpendicular distance from $A$ to the road, and similarly, let $BR=1$ km be the perpendicular distance from $B$ to the road. The distance $PR$ is 5 km.

\exfigure{1281_q26_1}
By letting $PQ=x$ kilometres, show that the total length $L$ of the cable is given by

$$L=\sqrt{x^2+4}+\sqrt{x^2-10x+26}$$
items.sol:
In right-angled triangle $APQ$, $AP=2$ and $PQ=x$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$AQ=\sqrt{x^2+2^2}$$
In right-angled triangle $BRQ$, $BR=1$ and $QR=5-x$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$QB=\sqrt{(5-x)^2+1^2}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} L&=AQ+QB \\ &=\sqrt{x^2+4}+\sqrt{x^2-10x+26} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dL}{dx}=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}+\dfrac{x-5}{\sqrt{x^2-10x+26}}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=0$:
$$\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}=\dfrac{5-x}{\sqrt{x^2-10x+26}}\qquad(*)$$
Squaring both sides (this can introduce an extra solution):
$$\dfrac{x^2}{x^2+4}=\dfrac{(5-x)^2}{x^2-10x+26}$$
$$x^4-10x^3+26x^2=25x^2-10x^3+x^4+100-40x+4x^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=3x^2-40x+100 \\ &=(3x-10)(x-10) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ or $x=10$.

But $x=10$ exceeds $PR=5$ and does not satisfy $(*)$, since the left side is positive and the right side is negative. It is the extra solution introduced by squaring.

Hence $x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ only.

\extable{Ts8183_1}

The table shows $x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ is a local minimum.

$$\therefore\ Q \text{ should be located } \dfrac{10}{3} \text{ km from } P.$$

items.part:
The equation of a circle is given by

$$x^2+y^2+4x-2y-20=0$$
Find the centre and radius of the circle.
items.sol:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+4x+4+y^2-2y+1&=20+4+1 \\ (x+2)^2+(y-1)^2&=25 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{centre } (-2,1),\ \text{radius } 5 \text{ units}$$

items.part:
The equation of a circle is given by

$$x^2+y^2+4x-2y-20=0$$
Hence evaluate

$$\int_{-7}^{3} 1+\sqrt{21-4x-x^2}\,dx$$
items.sol:
Rewrite the expression under the root:
$$\begin{aligned} 21-4x-x^2&=21-\left((x+2)^2-4\right) \\ &=25-(x+2)^2 \end{aligned}$$
From $(x+2)^2+(y-1)^2=25$, the upper half gives $y-1=\sqrt{25-(x+2)^2}$, so
$$y=1+\sqrt{21-4x-x^2}$$
This is the upper semicircle raised by 1.

\exfigure{1281_q27_s1}

Hence the integral is the area of a rectangle plus the area of a semicircle:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-7}^{3}\left(1+\sqrt{21-4x-x^2}\right)dx&=(3-(-7))\times 1+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(5)^2 \\ &=10+\dfrac{25\pi}{2} \\ &\approx 49.27 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A boat travelling in a straight line in a still lake has its engine turned off at time $t=0$ seconds. Its velocity $v$ metres per second at time $t$ seconds thereafter is given by

$$v(t)=\dfrac{100}{(t+2)^2}$$
Discuss $v(t)$ as $t\to\infty$ and hence the motion of the boat.
items.sol:
As $t\to\infty$, $(t+2)^2\to\infty$, so
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}v(t)=0^+$$
Also $v(t)>0$ for $t\ge 0$, since $(t+2)^2>0$.

So the boat forever slows, approaching zero velocity but never reaching a complete stop.

items.part:
A boat travelling in a straight line in a still lake has its engine turned off at time $t=0$ seconds. Its velocity $v$ metres per second at time $t$ seconds thereafter is given by

$$v(t)=\dfrac{100}{(t+2)^2}$$
Show that the acceleration on the boat is always oppositely directed to its motion.
items.sol:
Since $v(t)>0$ for $t\ge 0$, the boat moves in the positive direction.

Differentiating $v(t)=100(t+2)^{-2}$:
$$a(t)=v'(t)=-\dfrac{200}{(t+2)^3}$$
For $t\ge 0$, $(t+2)^3>0$, so $a(t)<0$.

Velocity is always positive and acceleration always negative, so acceleration opposes motion.

items.part:
A boat travelling in a straight line in a still lake has its engine turned off at time $t=0$ seconds. Its velocity $v$ metres per second at time $t$ seconds thereafter is given by

$$v(t)=\dfrac{100}{(t+2)^2}$$
To the nearest metre, how far does the boat travel from $t=5$ to $t=10$ seconds?
items.sol:
The distance is the integral of the (positive) velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int_5^{10}100(t+2)^{-2}\,dt \\ &=-100\Big[(t+2)^{-1}\Big]_5^{10} \\ &=-100\left(\dfrac{1}{12}-\dfrac{1}{7}\right) \\ &=5.95 \\ &\approx 6 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

The diagram below shows the area bounded between two curves, $y=\sqrt{x}$ and $y=x$.

\exfigure{1281_q29_1}

Consider the region bounded by the curves, the line $x=0$ and $x=k$, where $k>1$.

For what value of $k$ will the area to the left of point $P$ be equal to the area to the right of $P$?
items.sol:
The areas left and right of $P$ are equal when
$$\int_0^1\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}-x\right)dx=\int_1^k\left(x-x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)dx$$
$$\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_1^k$$
$$\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{k^2}{2}-\dfrac{2k^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{2}{3}$$
$$\dfrac{k^2}{2}-\dfrac{2k^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}=0$$
$$k^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\dfrac{k^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2}-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)=0$$
Since $k>1$, $k^{\frac{3}{2}}\ne 0$, so $\sqrt{k}=\dfrac{4}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{16}{9}$$

items.part:
Consider the probability density function $f$ for a random variable $X$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{9+2x}}; & 0\le x\le 8\\[1ex] 0; & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $a$ is a constant.
Find the value of $a$.
items.sol:
The total probability is 1:
$$1=\int_0^8\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{9+2x}}\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=a\int_0^8(9+2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx \\ &=a\Big[(9+2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big]_0^8 \\ &=a(5-3) \\ &=2a \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part:
Consider the probability density function $f$ for a random variable $X$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{9+2x}}; & 0\le x\le 8\\[1ex] 0; & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $a$ is a constant.
Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.
items.sol:
For $0\le x\le 8$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^x(9+2t)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[\sqrt{9+2t}\Big]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{9+2x}-3\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<0\\[1ex] \dfrac{\sqrt{9+2x}-3}{2} & 0\le x\le 8\\[1ex] 1 & x>8\end{cases}$$

items.part:
Consider the probability density function $f$ for a random variable $X$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{9+2x}}; & 0\le x\le 8\\[1ex] 0; & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $a$ is a constant.
Hence find the interquartile range, $Q_3-Q_1$.
items.sol:
Make $x$ the subject of $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{9+2x}-\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$x=\dfrac{\left[2\left(\frac{3}{2}+F(x)\right)\right]^2-9}{2}$$
$Q_3$ occurs when $F(x)=\dfrac{3}{4}$:
$$Q_3=\dfrac{\left(2\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{4}\right)\right)^2-9}{2}=\dfrac{45}{8}=5.625$$
$Q_1$ occurs when $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$Q_1=\dfrac{\left(2\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\right)\right)^2-9}{2}=\dfrac{13}{8}=1.625$$
$$\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1=4$$

$$P(-2\le X\le 2)=\int_{-2}^{2} f(x)\,dx$$
items.sol:
The graph is symmetric ($f(-x)=f(x)$), so
$$\int_{-2}^2f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^2f(x)\,dx$$
Use the trapezoidal rule with strip width $h=1$ on $x=0,1,2$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(-2\le X\le 2)&\approx 2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\left[0.3989+2\times 0.2420+0.05399\right] \\ &\approx 0.9369 \text{ (4 significant figures)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows a sphere of radius $R$ and centre $O$ circumscribing a square pyramid. The points $A,B,C,D$ and $S$ all lie on the surface of the sphere and form the vertices of the pyramid with $ABCD$ the base. The point $T$ lies directly beneath $O$ and lies in the base of the pyramid such that $AT\perp OT$.

\exfigure{1281_q32_1}
Let $x=OT$. Show that the volume of the pyramid is

$$V=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)^2(R-x)$$
items.sol:
The base $ABCD$ is a square. Since $AT\perp OT$, in right-angled triangle $OTA$ Pythagoras' theorem gives $AT=\sqrt{R^2-x^2}$.

$AT$ is half a diagonal of the square, so the diagonal is $2\sqrt{R^2-x^2}$.

Area of a square $=\dfrac{1}{2}d^2$, so
$$\text{base area}=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(2\sqrt{R^2-x^2}\right)^2=2(R^2-x^2)$$
Height $=x+R$ (from $T$ up through $O$ to $S$).
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times 2(R^2-x^2)\times(x+R) \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)(R-x)(R+x) \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)^2(R-x) \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule on $V=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)^2(R-x)$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(R+x)^2 & v&=R-x \\ u'&=2(R+x) & v'&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[2(R+x)(R-x)-(R+x)^2\right]$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=(R+x)\left[2(R-x)-(R+x)\right] \\ &=R-3x \end{aligned}$$
The factor $R+x\ne 0$, since $R,x>0$ are lengths, so $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$.

Nature test:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[2(-2x)-2(R+x)\right]=-\dfrac{4}{3}(3x+R)$$
At $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{4}{3}(R+R)<0 \text{ as } R>0$$
So $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$ gives a local maximum.

Maximum volume:
$$\begin{aligned} V\left(\dfrac{R}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{2}{3}\left(R+\dfrac{R}{3}\right)^2\left(R-\dfrac{R}{3}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{16R^2}{9}\times\dfrac{2R}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{64}{81}R^3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.

$$\dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}$$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{vu'-uv'}{v^2}\\ &=\dfrac{x^2\cos x-\sin x\cdot 2x}{x^4} \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:

$\therefore f(x)$ is an odd function.

Using $\text{Var}(X)=\sum (x-\mu)^2p(x)$ with $\mu=2$:

items.part: Koolara High School wants to sell a new sports shirt to its students at \$40 each. To manufacture the shirts, the schools pays a fixed cost of \$595, as well as \$33 per shirt. By writing a pair of simultaneous equations, calculate how many shirts the school must sell in order to break-even.
items.sol:
Let $x$ be the number of shirts.

Cost: $C=595+33x$

Revenue: $R=40x$

Break-even occurs when $C=R$.
$$\begin{aligned} 595+33x&=40x\\ 7x&=595\\ x&=85 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the school must sell 85 shirts.

items.part: Given that $\log_a b=3.14$ and $\log_a c=2.45$, find the value of $\log_a\sqrt{bc}$.
items.sol:
Using the log laws:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_a\sqrt{bc}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log_a bc\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\log_a b+\log_a c\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(3.14+2.45)\\ &=2.795 \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
Use the complement, where $LL$ means no prize on either draw.

items.part:
A swimming pool is to be emptied for maintenance. The quantity of water, $Q$ litres, remaining in the pool at a time, $t$ minutes after it starts to drain, is given by:

$$Q(t)=2000(25-t)^2,\quad t\ge 0$$
How long will it take to remove half of the water from the pool to the nearest minute?
items.sol:
At $t=0$:
$$Q(0)=2000\times25^2=1\,250\,000\ \text{L}$$
Half the quantity is $625\,000$ L.
$$\begin{aligned} 625\,000&=2000(25-t)^2\\ 312.5&=(25-t)^2\\ 25-t&=\pm\sqrt{312.5} \end{aligned}$$
Since $t\le25$, take $25-t=\sqrt{312.5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} t&=25-\sqrt{312.5}\\ &=7.3223\ldots\\ &\approx7\ \text{minutes} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A swimming pool is to be emptied for maintenance. The quantity of water, $Q$ litres, remaining in the pool at a time, $t$ minutes after it starts to drain, is given by:

$$Q(t)=2000(25-t)^2,\quad t\ge 0$$
At what time does the rate of flow of water from the pool reach 20 000 L/minute?
items.sol:
The rate of flow is the rate of change of $Q$.
$$Q'(t)=-4000(25-t)$$
The water flows out at $20\,000$ L/minute, so $Q'(t)=-20\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} -20\,000&=-4000(25-t)\\ 5&=25-t\\ t&=20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the rate reaches $20\,000$ L/minute after 20 minutes.

items.part:
The Year 12 students at Koolara High School were surveyed on the number of hours of sleep they get per week. The results are normally distributed. The survey indicated that 95% of students had between 42 and 54 hours of sleep per week.
Determine the mean number of hours of sleep per week.
items.sol:
Since 95% of scores lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, 42 to 54 spans $4\sigma$.
$$\sigma=\dfrac{54-42}{4}=3$$
The mean is the midpoint of 42 and 54.
$$\mu=48\ \text{hours}$$

What percentage of students would have indicated they had between 51 and 57 hours of sleep per week?

The Year 12 students at Koolara High School were surveyed on the number of hours of sleep they get per week. The results are normally distributed. The survey indicated that 95% of students had between 42 and 54 hours of sleep per week.
The Year 12 students at a nearby school, Chetswood High, were also surveyed. The results are also normally distributed with a mean of 50 hours and standard deviation of 2 hours.

Chetswood High boast they have a greater percentage of Year 12 students that get more than 54 hours of sleep per week. Are they correct? Justify your answer with relevant calculations.
items.sol:
Chetswood High: $\mu=50,\ \sigma=2$.
$$z=\dfrac{54-50}{2}=2$$
Koolara High: $\mu=48,\ \sigma=3$.
$$z=\dfrac{54-48}{3}=2$$
The $z$-score of 54 hours is 2 for both schools, so the same percentage of students in each school get more than 54 hours of sleep per week.

$\therefore$ Chetswood High is not correct.
items.final: No, Chetswood High is not correct; both schools have the same percentage (z-score 2).

A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=3e^{t}+6e^{-t}$ with $t$ measured in minutes and $v$ in ms$^{-1}$.

The particle begins its motion at the origin.
What is the initial velocity?
items.sol:
Initially $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 3e^0+6e^0 \\ &= 3+6 \\ &= 9 \text{ ms}^{-1} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=3e^{t}+6e^{-t}$ with $t$ measured in minutes and $v$ in ms$^{-1}$.

The particle begins its motion at the origin.
Find an equation for $x$, the displacement of the particle.
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int (3e^t+6e^{-t})\,dt \\ &= 3e^t-6e^{-t}+c \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3e^0-6e^0+c \\ c &= 6-3 = 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3e^t-6e^{-t}+3$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=3e^{t}+6e^{-t}$ with $t$ measured in minutes and $v$ in ms$^{-1}$.

The particle begins its motion at the origin.
Show that when $x=10$, $3e^{2t}-7e^{t}-6=0$.
items.sol:
Substitute $x=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10 &= 3e^t-6e^{-t}+3 \\ 3e^t-6e^{-t}-7 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Multiply both sides by $e^t$.
$$3e^{2t}-7e^t-6=0$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=3e^{t}+6e^{-t}$ with $t$ measured in minutes and $v$ in ms$^{-1}$.

The particle begins its motion at the origin.
Hence, find the value of $t$ when $x=10$.
items.sol:
Factorise the quadratic in $e^t$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3e^{2t}-7e^t-6 &= 0 \\ (3e^t+2)(e^t-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $e^t=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $e^t=3$.

The first has no solution as $e^t>0$ for all $t$.

Hence $e^t=3$.
$$\therefore\ t=\ln 3$$

items.part:
The queueing time, $X$ minutes, of a customer at the checkout of a supermarket has the probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{12}{625}x^2(k-x) & 0\le x\le k\\[1ex] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Show that the value of $k$ is 5.
items.sol:
Total probability is 1.
$$\int_0^k \dfrac{12}{625}x^2(k-x)\,dx=1$$
$$\dfrac{12}{625}\int_0^k (kx^2-x^3)\,dx=1$$
$$\left[\dfrac{kx^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^k=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
$$\dfrac{k^4}{3}-\dfrac{k^4}{4}=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
$$\dfrac{k^4}{12}=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
So $k^4=625$, and since $k\ge 0$,
$$\therefore\ k=5$$

items.part:
The queueing time, $X$ minutes, of a customer at the checkout of a supermarket has the probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{12}{625}x^2(k-x) & 0\le x\le k\\[1ex] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Is a customer more likely to wait less than 3 minutes, or more than 3 minutes? Justify your answer with calculations.
items.sol:
Find the probability of waiting at least 3 minutes.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 3) &= \int_3^5 \dfrac{12}{625}x^2(5-x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\int_3^5 (5x^2-x^3)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\dfrac{5x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_3^5 \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\left(\dfrac{625}{3}-\dfrac{625}{4}\right)-\left(45-\dfrac{81}{4}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\dfrac{625}{12}-\dfrac{99}{4}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{328}{625} \\ &= 0.5248 \end{aligned}$$
Since $0.5248>0.5$, a customer is more likely to wait more than 3 minutes.
items.final: More likely to wait more than 3 minutes, since $P(X\ge 3)=0.5248>0.5$

items.part:
A river has level parallel riverbanks $OC$ and $AB$ of width $w$ metres. $OF$ is a vertical flagpole of height $h$ metres which stands with its base $O$ on the edge of riverbank $OC$. Positions $A$ and $B$ are two points on the other riverbank such that $AB=7$ metres and $\angle AOB=60^\circ$.

The angle of elevation to the top of the flagpole form $A$ and $B$ are $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ respectively, as shown below.

\exfigure{1283_q29_1}
Show that the height of the flagpole is $\sqrt{21}$ metres.
items.sol:
In $\Delta OFB$, $\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{h}{OB}$.
$$OB=\dfrac{h}{\tan 30^\circ}=\sqrt{3}\,h$$
In $\Delta OFA$, $\tan 60^\circ=\dfrac{h}{OA}$.
$$OA=\dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\Delta OAB$.
$$\begin{aligned} 7^2 &= OA^2+OB^2-2(OA)(OB)\cos 60^\circ \\ 49 &= \dfrac{h^2}{3}+3h^2-2\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}\,h\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{10h^2}{3}-h^2 \\ &= \dfrac{7h^2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
So $h^2=21$, and since $h>0$,
$$\therefore\ h=\sqrt{21} \text{ m}$$

items.part:
A river has level parallel riverbanks $OC$ and $AB$ of width $w$ metres. $OF$ is a vertical flagpole of height $h$ metres which stands with its base $O$ on the edge of riverbank $OC$. Positions $A$ and $B$ are two points on the other riverbank such that $AB=7$ metres and $\angle AOB=60^\circ$.

The angle of elevation to the top of the flagpole form $A$ and $B$ are $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ respectively, as shown below.

\exfigure{1283_q29_1}
By finding the area of $\Delta AOB$, or otherwise, find the width of the river.
items.sol:
With $h=\sqrt{21}$, $OA=\sqrt{7}$ and $OB=3\sqrt{7}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of } \Delta AOB &= \dfrac{1}{2}(OA)(OB)\sin 60^\circ \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{7}\times 3\sqrt{7}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The width $w$ is the perpendicular height from $O$ to $AB$, so
$$\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times w\times 7$$
Equate the two areas.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{7w}{2} &= \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4} \\ 7w &= \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ w=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{ m}$$

items.part:
An isosceles triangle $ABC$, where $AB=BC$, is inscribed in a circle of radius 10 cm.

$OP=x$ and $OP$ bisects $AC$, such that $AC\perp OP$.

\exfigure{1283_q31_1}
Show that the area, $A$, of $\Delta ABC$ is given by $A=(10+x)\sqrt{100-x^2}$
items.sol:
$P$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $OP\perp AC$, so $BP=OB+OP=10+x$.

In right-angled $\Delta OPC$, by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$PC^2=OC^2-OP^2=10^2-x^2$$
so $PC=\sqrt{100-x^2}$ and
$$AC=2PC=2\sqrt{100-x^2}$$
Using area $=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times AC\times BP \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\sqrt{100-x^2}\times(10+x) \\ &= (10+x)\sqrt{100-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
An isosceles triangle $ABC$, where $AB=BC$, is inscribed in a circle of radius 10 cm.

$OP=x$ and $OP$ bisects $AC$, such that $AC\perp OP$.

\exfigure{1283_q31_1}
By first showing that the derivative is

$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\dfrac{100-10x-2x^2}{\sqrt{100-x^2}}$$

prove that the triangle with maximum area is equilateral.
items.sol:
Use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=10+x & v&=\sqrt{100-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{100-x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= \sqrt{100-x^2}+(10+x)\times\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{100-x^2}} \\ &= \dfrac{100-x^2-x(10+x)}{\sqrt{100-x^2}} \\ &= \dfrac{100-10x-2x^2}{\sqrt{100-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100-10x-2x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2+5x-50 &= 0 \\ (x+10)(x-5) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-10$ or $x=5$. Since $x>0$, $x=5$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$.
$$\begin{aligned} x=4:\ \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= 3.055\ldots>0 &&\text{increasing}\\ x=5:\ \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= 0 && \\ x=6:\ \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= -4<0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
So the area is a maximum when $x=5$ cm.

Then
$$BP=5+10=15,\qquad PC=\sqrt{100-5^2}=5\sqrt{3},\qquad AC=2\times 5\sqrt{3}=10\sqrt{3}$$
In right-angled $\Delta BPC$:
$$BC=\sqrt{15^2+(5\sqrt{3})^2}=\sqrt{300}=10\sqrt{3}$$
Since $AB=BC$, we have $AB=BC=AC=10\sqrt{3}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the triangle of maximum area is equilateral}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 100 raffle tickets. Five of these tickets are golden.

Augustus is permitted to select two tickets, consecutively, without replacement.

By drawing a tree diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that,
the first ticket is golden.
items.sol:
There are 5 golden tickets among 100.

$$P(\text{first golden})=\dfrac{5}{100}=\dfrac{1}{20}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 100 raffle tickets. Five of these tickets are golden.

Augustus is permitted to select two tickets, consecutively, without replacement.

By drawing a tree diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that,
neither ticket is golden.
items.sol:
Neither ticket golden: the first is not golden, then the second (without replacement) is not golden.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither golden}) &= \dfrac{95}{100}\times\dfrac{94}{99} \\ &= \dfrac{893}{990} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A bag contains 100 raffle tickets. Five of these tickets are golden.

Augustus is permitted to select two tickets, consecutively, without replacement.

By drawing a tree diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that,
at least one ticket is golden.
items.sol:
"At least one golden" is the complement of "neither golden".

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one golden}) &= 1-\dfrac{893}{990} \\ &= \dfrac{97}{990} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In a class of 25 students, each student is required to study at least one of French or German.

It is known that 16 students study French and 18 students study German.

Find the probability that a randomly selected student studies,
only French.
items.sol:
Everyone studies at least one language, so the number studying both is $16+18-25=9$.

The number studying only French is $16-9=7$.

$$P(\text{only French})=\dfrac{7}{25}$$

items.part:
In a class of 25 students, each student is required to study at least one of French or German.

It is known that 16 students study French and 18 students study German.

Find the probability that a randomly selected student studies,
both languages.
items.sol:
Number studying both languages: $16+18-25=9$.

$$P(\text{both})=\dfrac{9}{25}$$

items.part:
In a class of 25 students, each student is required to study at least one of French or German.

It is known that 16 students study French and 18 students study German.

Find the probability that a randomly selected student studies,
both languages given that they study French.
items.sol:
Of the 16 students who study French, 9 also study German.

$$P(\text{both}\mid\text{French})=\dfrac{9}{16}$$

items.part:
Consider the finite arithmetic series $30, 28.5, 27, \dots, -6$.
Show that the sequence contains 25 terms.
items.sol:
For an arithmetic sequence, the $n$th term is $T_n=a+(n-1)d$, with $a=30$ and $d=-1.5$. The last term is $-6$.

$$\begin{aligned} -6 &= 30+(n-1)(-1.5) \\ -36 &= -1.5n+1.5 \\ -37.5 &= -1.5n \\ n &= 25 \end{aligned}$$

So the sequence contains 25 terms.

items.part:
Consider the finite arithmetic series $30, 28.5, 27, \dots, -6$.
Find the sum of the sequence.
items.sol:
Using the sum formula $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ with $n=25$, $a=30$, $l=-6$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_{25} &= \dfrac{25}{2}(30-6) \\ &= 300 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_{25} &= \dfrac{25}{2}\left[60+24(-1.5)\right] \\ &= 300 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Max is given an old coin by his grandfather. The current value of the coin is \$600.

Each year, it is predicted that the coin's value will be 10% greater than in the previous year.
How much, to the nearest dollar, will the coin be worth after 6 years?
items.sol:
Using the compound interest formula with $P=600$, $r=0.1$, $n=6$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= P(1+r)^n \\ &= 600(1+0.1)^6 \\ &\approx \$1063 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Max is given an old coin by his grandfather. The current value of the coin is \$600.

Each year, it is predicted that the coin's value will be 10% greater than in the previous year.
Max decides that he will sell the coin when the value of the coin exceeds \$3000.

For how many complete years must Max keep the coin?
items.sol:
The value exceeds \$3000 when

$$\begin{aligned} 600(1.1)^n &> 3000 \\ 1.1^n &> 5 \end{aligned}$$

Taking logarithms of both sides (base $1.1>1$, so the inequality is preserved):

$$\begin{aligned} \log_{1.1}1.1^n &> \log_{1.1}5 \\ n &> \dfrac{\ln 5}{\ln 1.1} \\ n &> 16.88\dots \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ 17 \text{ years are required.}$$

The probabilities in a distribution sum to 1.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{4}+3k+\dfrac{5}{18}+k+\dfrac{1}{36} &= 1 \\ 4k &= \dfrac{4}{9} \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

Using $E(X)=\sum x\,p(x)$:

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \left(2\times\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+\left(3\times\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\left(4\times\dfrac{5}{18}\right)+\left(5\times\dfrac{1}{9}\right)+\left(6\times\dfrac{1}{36}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{10}{3} \end{aligned}$$

Using $Var(X)=\sum x^2p(x)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=\dfrac{10}{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned} Var(X) &= \left(4\times\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+\left(9\times\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\left(16\times\dfrac{5}{18}\right)+\left(25\times\dfrac{1}{9}\right)+\left(36\times\dfrac{1}{36}\right)-\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{10}{9} \end{aligned}$$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{9}} \\ &\approx 1.05 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: $A$ and $B$ represent a pair of mutually exclusive events. Find $P(A \cap B)$.
items.sol:
Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together.

$$P(A\cap B)=0$$

items.part:
In Victor's year group, 75% of the students pass the yearly English exam, 60% pass the yearly Science exam.

Given that 42% of the year group pass both English and Science, find the probability that Victor passes Science, given that he has passed English.
items.sol:
Using conditional probability, $P(S\mid E)=\dfrac{P(S\cap E)}{P(E)}$:

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{pass Science}\mid\text{pass English}) &= \dfrac{0.42}{0.75} \\ &= 0.56 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $P(L)=0.17$, $P(L\cap M)=0.018$ and $P(M)=0.12$, show that $L$ and $M$ are not independent.
items.sol:
For independent events, $P(L\cap M)=P(L)\times P(M)$.

$$\begin{aligned} P(L)\times P(M) &= 0.17\times0.12 \\ &= 0.0204 \\ &\neq 0.018 = P(L\cap M) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ L \text{ and } M \text{ are not independent.}$$

items.part:
A coin is biased so that the probability of the coin showing tails on any throw is $p$.

The probability that the coin shows tails exactly once in two throws is $0.32$.
Find, in terms of $p$, the probability that the coin shows heads on any throw.
items.sol:
Heads is the complement of tails.

$$P(\text{Heads})=1-p$$

items.part:
A coin is biased so that the probability of the coin showing tails on any throw is $p$.

The probability that the coin shows tails exactly once in two throws is $0.32$.
Find the possible values of $p$.
items.sol:
Exactly one tail in two throws means tail then head, or head then tail.

\exfigure{1576_q4e_s1}

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly one tail}) &= p(1-p)+(1-p)p \\ &= 2p(1-p) \end{aligned}$$

This equals $0.32$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2p(1-p) &= 0.32 \\ p(1-p) &= 0.16 \\ p-p^2 &= 0.16 \\ p^2-p+0.16 &= 0 \\ 100p^2-100p+16 &= 0 \\ 25p^2-25p+4 &= 0 \\ (5p-1)(5p-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ p=\dfrac{1}{5} \text{ or } p=\dfrac{4}{5}$$

Each square has side $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of the previous one, and $EFGH$ is the second square after the unit square.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Side length}_{EFGH} &= 1\times\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{3}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{9}{16} \text{ units} \end{aligned}$$

Each side is multiplied by $\dfrac{3}{4}$, so each area is multiplied by $\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2=\dfrac{9}{16}$.

The areas form a geometric series $1+\dfrac{9}{16}+\dfrac{81}{256}+\dots$ with $a=1$ and $r=\dfrac{9}{16}$.

Since $|r|<1$, the sum to infinity exists.

$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1-\frac{9}{16}} \\ &= \dfrac{16}{7} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Nick borrows \$380 000 to buy an apartment. The loan is repaid in equal monthly instalments. The interest, which is charged at 0.3% per month, is reducible and calculated monthly. The amount owing after $n$ months, $\$A_n$, is given by,

$$A_n = Pr^n - M(1 + r + r^2 + \dots + r^{n-1}),$$

(Do NOT prove this)

where $\$P$ is the amount borrowed, $r = 1.003$ and $\$M$ is the monthly repayment.
The loan is to be repaid over 25 years. Show that the monthly repayment is \$1923 to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
With $P=380000$, $r=1.003$, $n=25\times12=300$ and the loan fully repaid, $A_{300}=0$.

$$0=380000(1.003)^{300}-M\left(1+1.003+1.003^2+\dots+1.003^{299}\right)$$

The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, ratio $1.003$ and 300 terms.

$$0=380000(1.003)^{300}-M\left[\dfrac{1.003^{300}-1}{0.003}\right]\quad(*)$$

$$\begin{aligned} M &= 380000(1.003)^{300}\times\dfrac{0.003}{1.003^{300}-1} \\ &= 1922.810307\ \text{(by calculator)}\quad(*) \\ &\approx \$1923 \end{aligned}$$

as required.

items.part:
Nick borrows \$380 000 to buy an apartment. The loan is repaid in equal monthly instalments. The interest, which is charged at 0.3% per month, is reducible and calculated monthly. The amount owing after $n$ months, $\$A_n$, is given by,

$$A_n = Pr^n - M(1 + r + r^2 + \dots + r^{n-1}),$$

(Do NOT prove this)

where $\$P$ is the amount borrowed, $r = 1.003$ and $\$M$ is the monthly repayment.
Using the monthly repayment found in part (a), find how many months are needed for the balance of the loan to be less than half of the original amount borrowed?
items.sol:
Half the original amount is $\$190000$, so find $n$ when $A_n=190000$.

$$190000=380000(1.003)^n-1923\left[\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}\right]$$

Since $\dfrac{1923}{0.003}=641000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 190000 &= 380000(1.003)^n-641000(1.003^n-1) \\ 190000 &= 380000(1.003)^n-641000(1.003)^n+641000 \\ 261000(1.003)^n &= 451000 \\ 1.003^n &= 1.7279\dots \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln(1.7279\dots)}{\ln(1.003)} \\ &= 182.58\dots \end{aligned}$$

The balance decreases as $n$ increases, so we need the next whole month.

$$\therefore\ 183 \text{ months are required.}$$

items.part: Solve the double inequation $-3 \le 3x - 2 < 4$ and write your answer using “bracket interval notation”.
items.sol:
Do the same operation to every part of the inequality, one operation per line.
$$\begin{aligned} -3&\le 3x-2<4\\ -1&\le 3x<6 &&(\text{add } 2)\\ -\dfrac{1}{3}&\le x<2 &&(\text{divide by } 3)\end{aligned}$$
In interval notation the solution is
$$\left[-\dfrac{1}{3},\,2\right)$$

items.part: Solve $\left|2x - 5\right| = 7$ for $x$.
items.sol:
If $|A|=7$ then $A=7$ or $A=-7$, so

$2x-5=7$ or $2x-5=-7$

$2x=12$ or $2x=-2$
$$\therefore\ x=6 \text{ or } x=-1$$

items.part:
If $f(x) = x^{2} - 1$ and $g(x) = 1 - 2x$, find
$g \circ f(2)$
items.sol:
First find $f(2)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(2)&=2^{2}-1\\ &=3\end{aligned}$$
Then apply $g$.
$$\begin{aligned} g\circ f(2)&=g(3)\\ &=1-2(3)\\ &=-5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ g\circ f(2)=-5$$

items.part:
If $f(x) = x^{2} - 1$ and $g(x) = 1 - 2x$, find
$f \circ g(x)$
items.sol:
Substitute $g(x)$ into $f$.
$$\begin{aligned} f\circ g(x)&=(1-2x)^{2}-1\\ &=1-4x+4x^{2}-1\\ &=4x^{2}-4x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f\circ g(x)=4x^{2}-4x$$

items.part:
Find the centre and the radius of the circle with equation,

$$x^{2} - 4x + y^{2} + 6y - 12 = 0$$
items.sol:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^{2}-4x+y^{2}+6y-12&=0\\ x^{2}-4x+4+y^{2}+6y+9&=12+4+9\\ (x-2)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}&=25\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{centre is } (2,-3),\ \text{radius is } 5$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int (x^{3} - 2x + 3)\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\displaystyle\int (x^{3}-2x+3)\,dx=\dfrac{x^{4}}{4}-x^{2}+3x+C$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0.5}^{2} \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Write the integrand as a power of $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{0.5}^{2}\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx&=\displaystyle\int_{0.5}^{2}x^{-2}\,dx\\ &=\left[-x^{-1}\right]_{0.5}^{2}\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{0.5}^{2}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}+2\\ &=1\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graphs of $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{2}(x - 2)$ and $g(x) = 2\sqrt{x}$.

The area enclosed by the graphs has been shaded. The graphs intersect at the origin and the point $A$.

\exfigure{1591_q2d_1}
Verify that the $x$ coordinate of $A$ is 4.
items.sol:
Substitute $x=4$ into each function.
$$\begin{aligned} f(4)&=\dfrac{4}{2}(4-2)=4\\ g(4)&=2\sqrt{4}=4\end{aligned}$$
Since $f(4)=g(4)$, the graphs meet where $x=4$, so the $x$ coordinate of $A$ is $4$.

items.part:
The diagram below shows the graphs of $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{2}(x - 2)$ and $g(x) = 2\sqrt{x}$.

The area enclosed by the graphs has been shaded. The graphs intersect at the origin and the point $A$.

\exfigure{1591_q2d_1}
Find the area of the shaded region.
items.sol:
Between $x=0$ and $x=4$ the curve $g$ is above $f$, so the integrand is $g(x)-f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sqrt{x}-\dfrac{x}{2}(x-2)&=2x^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}+x\end{aligned}$$
The area is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}\left(2x^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}+x\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{4}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{6}x^{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}\right]_{0}^{4}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\cdot 8-\dfrac{1}{6}\cdot 64+8\right)-0\\ &=8\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Given that $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 5$ and that $f(x)$ is an even function, state the value of

$$\int_{-a}^{a} 2f(x)\,dx .$$
items.sol:
Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx=2(5)=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}2f(x)\,dx&=2\times 10\\ &=20\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y = 4x^{3} - x^{4}$.
Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=12x^{2}-4x^{3}\\ 0&=4x^{2}(3-x)\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=3$, $y=27$.

Test the nature using $y''=24x-12x^{2}$.

At $x=0$: $y''=0$, so the test fails and $(0,0)$ is a possible horizontal point of inflexion.

At $x=3$: $y''=24(3)-12(9)=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

Alternatively, test the nature using $y'$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline y' & 16 & 0 & 8 \end{array}$$
The gradient is positive on both sides of $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a possible point of inflexion.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline y' & 16 & 0 & -64 \end{array}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

Confirm the inflexion at $(0,0)$ by checking the concavity.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline y'' & -36 & 0 & 12 \end{array}$$
The concavity changes, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
$$\therefore\ (3,27)\text{ is a maximum turning point and }(0,0)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion}$$
items.final: $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point and $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion

items.part:
Consider the function $y = 4x^{3} - x^{4}$.
Find any points of inflexion.
items.sol:
Points of inflexion need $y''=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=24x-12x^{2}\\ &=12x(2-x)\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

The point $(0,0)$ was shown to be a horizontal point of inflexion in part (a).

When $x=2$, $y=4(2)^{3}-2^{4}=16$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline y'' & 12 & 0 & -36 \end{array}$$
The concavity changes at $x=2$.
$$\therefore\ (0,0)\text{ and }(2,16)\text{ are points of inflexion}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y = 4x^{3} - x^{4}$.
Sketch the graph of $y = 4x^{3} - x^{4}$. showing all important features including intercepts with the axes.
items.sol:
Find the intercepts with the axes.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4x^{3}-x^{4}\\ &=x^{3}(4-x)\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=4$.

\exfigure{1591_q3b_s1}

items.part: Sketch the graph of $y = \left|x + 1\right|$ for $-4 \le x \le 4$.
items.sol: \exfigure{1591_q4b_s1}

items.part:
Using the sketch from part (a), or otherwise, solve

$$\left|x + 1\right| = x + 3$$
items.sol:
Draw the line $y=x+3$ on the same axes as $y=|x+1|$.

The graphs meet where $x=-2$.
$$\therefore\ x=-2$$

items.part:
Use the Trapezoidal Rule with 5 function values to find an approximation for the definite integral

$$\int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx .$$
items.sol:
Five function values give four strips, so
$$h=\dfrac{3-1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
and the $x$ values are $1,\ \dfrac{3}{2},\ 2,\ \dfrac{5}{2},\ 3$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} x & 1 & \dfrac{3}{2} & 2 & \dfrac{5}{2} & 3 \\ \hline f(x) & 1 & \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{3} \end{array}$$
Using the trapezoidal rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f_0+2(f_1+f_2+f_3)+f_4\big]$:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{1}{4}\left[1+2\left(\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{2}{5}\right)+\dfrac{1}{3}\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{67}{15}\\ &=\dfrac{67}{60}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$ then $y'' = \dfrac{2}{x^{3}}$. Briefly explain how this implies that your approximation found in part (a) overestimates the exact value of the definite integral.
items.sol:
For $1\le x\le 3$, $y''=\dfrac{2}{x^{3}}>0$, so the curve is concave up.

On a concave up curve the chords (the tops of the trapezoids) lie above the curve.

Therefore the approximation in part (a) is an overestimate.

items.part:
Consider the function $y = \cos x$ in the domain $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
Give the equation of the function if $y = \cos x$ is subjected to the following transformations;

1. A horizontal dilation with factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$, followed by,

2. A horizontal translation to the left of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
items.sol:
A horizontal dilation by factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ replaces $x$ by $2x$.
$$y=\cos 2x$$
A translation $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the left replaces $x$ by $x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\cos 2\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\ &=\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $y = \cos x$ in the domain $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
Sketch the function after the transformations described in part (a), for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
items.sol: \exfigure{1591_q4d_s1}

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{6x}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\,dx$
items.sol:
Rewrite the integrand in the form $k\,f'(x)[f(x)]^{n}$, with $f(x)=1-x^{2}$ and $f'(x)=-2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{6x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\,dx&=\displaystyle\int 6x(1-x^{2})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\ &=-3\displaystyle\int -2x(1-x^{2})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\ &=-3\cdot\dfrac{(1-x^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}}+C\\ &=-6\sqrt{1-x^{2}}+C\end{aligned}$$

Substitute each given point into $y=\dfrac{h}{x^{2}+k}$.

The point $(0,-6)$ gives
$$-6=\dfrac{h}{k}$$
so $h=-6k$.

The point $(5,-1)$ gives
$$-1=\dfrac{h}{25+k}$$
so $h=-k-25$.

Equate the two expressions for $h$.
$$\begin{aligned} -6k&=-k-25\\ -5k&=-25\\ k&=5\end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} h&=-6k\\ &=-6(5)\\ &=-30\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=-30,\ k=5,\ \text{so } y=\dfrac{-30}{x^{2}+5}$$

$R$ lies on the curve directly below $Q$, so its $x$ coordinate is $\alpha$.

When $x=\alpha$,
$$y=\dfrac{-30}{\alpha^{2}+5}$$
$$\therefore\ R\text{ is }\left(\alpha,\ \dfrac{-30}{\alpha^{2}+5}\right)$$

The rectangle is symmetric about $x=0$, so the width is $PQ=2\alpha$.

The height is $QR=\dfrac{30}{\alpha^{2}+5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=PQ\times QR\\ &=2\alpha\cdot\dfrac{30}{\alpha^{2}+5}\\ &=\dfrac{60\alpha}{\alpha^{2}+5}\end{aligned}$$

The area is a maximum where $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=0$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\alpha}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^{2}}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=60\alpha & v&=\alpha^{2}+5\\ u'&=60 & v'&=2\alpha\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=\dfrac{60(\alpha^{2}+5)-60\alpha\cdot 2\alpha}{(\alpha^{2}+5)^{2}}$$
Set the numerator to zero.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=60\alpha^{2}+300-120\alpha^{2}\\ &=300-60\alpha^{2}\\ 0&=5-\alpha^{2}\end{aligned}$$
Since $\alpha>0$, $\alpha=\sqrt{5}$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}$ either side of $\alpha=\sqrt{5}$, where $\sqrt{5}\approx 2.24$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \alpha & 2 & \sqrt{5} & 3 \\ \hline \dfrac{dA}{d\alpha} & \dfrac{60}{81} & 0 & -\dfrac{60}{49} \end{array}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative, so this is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \alpha=\sqrt{5}\text{ gives the maximum area}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$
$\dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=x^2 \\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}\right)&=\dfrac{x^2\cos x-2x\sin x}{(x^2)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{x\cos x-2\sin x}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Fred sits his Trial exams in Modern History and Ancient History.

The marks for the Modern History class have a mean of 54 and a standard deviation of 5.6.

The marks for the Ancient History class have a mean of 76 and a standard deviation of 2.1.
Compare and contrast the distribution of marks for the two classes.
items.sol:
The Ancient History class has a higher mean and a smaller standard deviation, so its marks are grouped more closely around the mean and are more consistent.

The Modern History class has a lower mean and a larger standard deviation, so its marks are more spread out around the lower mean and are less consistent.

items.part:
Fred sits his Trial exams in Modern History and Ancient History.

The marks for the Modern History class have a mean of 54 and a standard deviation of 5.6.

The marks for the Ancient History class have a mean of 76 and a standard deviation of 2.1.
Fred scored 65 for Modern History and 80 for Ancient History.

Using $z$-score calculations, explain which subject he performed better in and why.
items.sol:
Use $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

Modern History: $x=65$, $\mu=54$, $\sigma=5.6$
$$z_{\text{MH}}=\dfrac{65-54}{5.6}\approx 1.96$$
Ancient History: $x=80$, $\mu=76$, $\sigma=2.1$
$$z_{\text{AH}}=\dfrac{80-76}{2.1}\approx 1.90$$
Fred performed better in Modern History, as his higher positive $z$-score means he was further above the mean than in Ancient History, even though his raw mark was lower.

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^{e^3}\dfrac{5}{x}\,dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_1^{e^3}\dfrac{5}{x}\,dx&=5\Big[\ln x\Big]_1^{e^3} \\ &=5(\ln e^3-\ln 1) \\ &=5(3-0) \\ &=15 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equations $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ and $y=11-x$ simultaneously and show that there is one point of intersection. Give its coordinates.
items.sol:
Set the two expressions for $y$ equal and square both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x+1}&=11-x \\ x+1&=(11-x)^2 \\ x+1&=121-22x+x^2 \\ x^2-23x+120&=0 \\ (x-8)(x-15)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=8$ or $x=15$.

When $x=8$, $y=3$. When $x=15$, $y=-4$.

The radical sign means the positive square root, so $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ is never negative. Hence $(15,-4)$ is not a solution.

The only point of intersection is $(8,3)$.

items.part:
For the curve $y=x^3-3x^2-9x+4$:
Find any stationary points and classify them.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^3-3x^2-9x+4\\ y'&=3x^2-6x-9\\ &=3(x^2-2x-3)\\ &=3(x-3)(x+1)\\ y''&=6x-6=6(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$.
$$3(x-3)(x+1)=0$$
So $x=3$ or $x=-1$.

When $x=3$: $y=-23$ and $y''=12>0$, so $(3,-23)$ is a minimum.

When $x=-1$: $y=9$ and $y''=-12<0$, so $(-1,9)$ is a maximum.
items.final: $(3,-23)$ is a minimum; $(-1,9)$ is a maximum

items.part:
John started work at 18 and at the beginning of each month he invested \$400 into a superannuation fund. Interest was paid at $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly on the investment. John retired at 63 after having contributed to the fund for 45 years.
How much did John contribute to the fund over 45 years?
items.sol:
There are 12 contributions each year for 45 years.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total}&=400\times 12\times 45\\ &=\$216\,000\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ John contributed \$216 000 over the 45 years.

items.part:
John started work at 18 and at the beginning of each month he invested \$400 into a superannuation fund. Interest was paid at $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly on the investment. John retired at 63 after having contributed to the fund for 45 years.
How much did John's investment amount to after 45 years?
items.sol:
The monthly rate is
$$r=\dfrac{0.06}{12}=0.005\text{ (that is, } 0.5\%)$$
After 1 month:
$$A_1=400\times 1.005^1$$
After 2 months:
$$A_2=400\times 1.005^2+400\times 1.005^1$$
After 45 years (540 months):
$$A_{540}=400\times 1.005^{540}+400\times 1.005^{539}+\cdots+400\times 1.005^1$$
This is a GP with first term $400\times 1.005$, ratio $1.005$ and 540 terms, so using the sum of a GP:
$$A_{540}=400\times\dfrac{1.005\left(1.005^{540}-1\right)}{1.005-1}=\$1\,107\,909.03$$
$\therefore$ John's investment is worth \$1 107 909.03 after 45 years.

items.part:
John started work at 18 and at the beginning of each month he invested \$400 into a superannuation fund. Interest was paid at $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly on the investment. John retired at 63 after having contributed to the fund for 45 years.
John plans to reinvest some of the money into an account which offers $8\%$ p.a. compound interest compounded annually. He plans to have \$300 000 at the end of the 10 year investment period. How much does John need to reinvest to achieve this amount. Answer correct to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
Using the compound interest formula:
$$\begin{aligned}FV&=PV(1+r)^n\\ 300\,000&=PV(1+0.08)^{10}\\ PV&=138\,958.0464\ldots\\ &\approx\$138\,958\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ John needs to reinvest \$138 958.

items.part:
A leak from a tanker has accidently contaminated a farmer's paddock with a toxic chemical.

The chemical concentration in the soil was 6kL/ha immediately after the accident.

One year later the concentration was measured to be 2.4kL/ha.

It is known that the concentration, $C$, is given by:

$$C=C_0e^{-kt}$$

Where $C_0$ and $k$ are constants and $t$ is measured in years.

Evaluate $C_0$ and $k$.
items.sol:
At $t=0$, $C=6$:
$$6=C_0e^0$$
So $C_0=6$ kL/ha and $C=6e^{-kt}$.

At $t=1$, $C=2.4$:
$$\begin{aligned}2.4&=6e^{-k}\\ 0.4&=e^{-k}\end{aligned}$$
Taking $\ln$ of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}k&=-\ln(0.4)\\ &=0.9162907318\ldots\\ &\approx 0.916\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given the function $f(x)=x^2-4x$ and $g(x)=x^2-9$, write an expression for $g\big(f(x)\big)$ in its simplest form.
items.sol:
Substitute $f(x)=x^2-4x$ into $g(x)=x^2-9$:
$$\begin{aligned}g\big(f(x)\big)&=g(x^2-4x)\\&=(x^2-4x)^2-9\\&=x^4-8x^3+16x^2-9\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ g\big(f(x)\big)=x^4-8x^3+16x^2-9$$

The graph is a transformation of $f(x)=x^2$, so $g(x)=k(x+b)^2+c$.

The vertex is $(5,6)$, so $b=-5$ and $c=6$:
$$y=k(x-5)^2+6$$
Substitute the $y$-intercept $\left(0,-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{7}{3}&=k(0-5)^2+6\\ 25k&=-\dfrac{25}{3}\\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ g(x)=-\dfrac{1}{3}f(x-5)+6$$

items.part:
A sequence is given by $\sqrt{8},\ \sqrt{32},\ \sqrt{72},\ \cdots$
Show that the terms form an arithmetic sequence.
items.sol:
Simplify each term:
$$\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2},\quad \sqrt{32}=4\sqrt{2},\quad \sqrt{72}=6\sqrt{2}$$
Check for a common difference:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3-T_2&=6\sqrt{2}-4\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}\\T_2-T_1&=4\sqrt{2}-2\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
So $T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1$.

Hence the terms form an arithmetic sequence.

items.part:
A sequence is given by $\sqrt{8},\ \sqrt{32},\ \sqrt{72},\ \cdots$
The sum of the first $n$ terms is $132\sqrt{2}$. Find the value of $n$.
items.sol:
From part (a), $a=2\sqrt{2}$ and $d=2\sqrt{2}$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$:
$$\begin{aligned}132\sqrt{2}&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2\times 2\sqrt{2}+(n-1)\times 2\sqrt{2}\right)\\&=n\left(2\sqrt{2}+n\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}\right)\\&=n^2\sqrt{2}+n\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
Divide by $\sqrt{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}n^2+n-132&=0\\(n-11)(n+12)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $n=11$ or $n=-12$.

But $n\ge 1$, hence $n=11$ only.
$$\therefore\ n=11$$

items.part:
An annulus sector is made with an angle $\theta$ at its centre. Its inner and outer radii are $\dfrac{1}{r}$ metres and $r$ metres respectively, as shown.

\exfigure{1286_q15_1}

The perimeter of this annulus sector is 6 metres.

Show that $\theta=\dfrac{2(-r^2+3r+1)}{r^2+1}$.
items.sol:
The perimeter is two straight edges of length $r-\dfrac{1}{r}$ plus the inner arc $\dfrac{1}{r}\theta$ and the outer arc $r\theta$ (arc $=$ radius $\times$ angle).
$$P=2\left(r-\dfrac{1}{r}\right)+\dfrac{1}{r}\theta+r\theta$$
Set $P=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2(r^2-1)}{r}+\dfrac{\theta}{r}+\dfrac{r^2\theta}{r}&=6\\2r^2-2+\theta+r^2\theta&=6r\\\theta(1+r^2)&=-2r^2+6r+2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{2(-r^2+3r+1)}{r^2+1}$$

items.part: Prove that $2\cos^2\theta+2\sec^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)+2\sin^2\theta=4+2\cot^2\theta$.
items.sol:
Use the complementary angle relationship $\sec\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\operatorname{cosec}\theta$, and $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$, $\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta=1+\cot^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)+2\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta\\&=2+2(1+\cot^2\theta)\\&=4+2\cot^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{LHS}=\text{RHS}$$

In $\triangle DCT$, right-angled at $C$, with $TC=1044$:

items.part:
A factory produces chocolate chip cookies and oatmeal cookies in both regular and sugar free variants. Each day, $\dfrac{3}{5}$ of the cookies produced are chocolate chip and the rest are oatmeal. According to demand, $\dfrac{5}{7}$ of the chocolate chip cookies are regular and the rest of the chocolate chip cookies are sugar free, while $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of the oatmeal cookies are sugar free and the rest of the oatmeal cookies are regular.
A cookie is selected at random. Given that a sugar free cookie is selected, find the probability that the cookie was chocolate-chip.
items.sol:
Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P(C\mid S)&=\dfrac{P(C\cap S)}{P(S)}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{2}{7}}{\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{2}{7}+\frac{2}{5}\times\frac{2}{3}}\\&=\dfrac{6}{35}\div\dfrac{46}{105}\\&=\dfrac{9}{23}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(C\mid S)=\dfrac{9}{23}$$

items.part:
A company tracked the number of sales made by each sales staff in a day. Using the data from a large number of days, the company estimated the probability of the number of sales made by each sales staff in a day.

Let the random variable $S$ be the number of sales made by Linda per day.

The following table shows the probability data for Linda's daily sales.

\extable{1286_q21_t1}

Linda is expected to make 5.05 sales per day. Find Linda's variance and standard deviation, correct to two decimal places.

(Hint: Add any required rows in the table using the space provided above.)
items.sol:
Variance uses $\mathrm{Var}(S)=\Sigma s^2p(s)-E(S)^2$, so add a row for $s^2p(s)$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c}s&2&3&4&5&6&7\\\hline P(S=s)&0.05&0.1&0.15&0.35&0.15&0.2\\\hline s^2&4&9&16&25&36&49\\\hline s^2p(s)&0.2&0.9&2.4&8.75&5.4&9.8\end{array}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(S)&=(0.2+0.9+2.4+8.75+5.4+9.8)-5.05^2\\&=27.45-25.5025\\&=1.9475\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \mathrm{Var}(S)\approx 1.95$$
$$\sigma=\sqrt{1.9475}\approx 1.40$$
$$\therefore\ \sigma\approx 1.40$$

items.part:
An ice cream company launches a promotion in which customers have a chance of winning a limited edition item. The probability of winning this prize is 0.07 with each individual purchase. Each person can only win the prize once.

Benjamin decides to purchase one ice block each day until he wins the prize.
Find the probability that he wins the item on the first or second day, correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Let $W$ be the event that Benjamin wins on a given day, so $P(W)=0.07$ and $P(\overline{W})=0.93$.

He wins on the first or second day if he wins on day 1, or loses on day 1 and wins on day 2:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A)&=P(W)+P(\overline{W})P(W)\\&=0.07+0.93\times 0.07\\&=0.1351\end{aligned}$$
Hence the probability that Benjamin wins on the first or second day is $0.14$.

items.part:
An ice cream company launches a promotion in which customers have a chance of winning a limited edition item. The probability of winning this prize is 0.07 with each individual purchase. Each person can only win the prize once.

Benjamin decides to purchase one ice block each day until he wins the prize.
Hence find the smallest number of days for which the probability that Benjamin will win the limited edition item, is greater than 80%.
items.sol:
The probabilities that Benjamin first wins on day $1, 2, 3,\cdots$ are
$$0.07,\ 0.93\times 0.07,\ 0.93^2\times 0.07,\ \cdots$$
This is a geometric sequence with $a=0.07$ and $r=0.93$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$, we need
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{0.07(1-0.93^n)}{1-0.93}&>0.8\\1-0.93^n&>0.8 &&(\text{since } 1-0.93=0.07)\\-0.93^n&>-0.2\\0.93^n&<0.2\end{aligned}$$
Take logs (dividing by $\log 0.93<0$ reverses the inequality):
$$\begin{aligned}n&>\log_{0.93}0.2\\&=\dfrac{\log_{10}0.2}{\log_{10}0.93}\\&\approx 22.18\end{aligned}$$
Hence the smallest number of days is $23$.

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=-(x-2)(x+2)(x-1)$.
Sketch the curve in space provided without using calculus. Show all intercepts with the axes.
items.sol: \exfigure{1286_q23_s1}

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=-(x-2)(x+2)(x-1)$.
Hence find the exact area bounded by the curve and the $x$-axis.
items.sol:
Expand the factorised form.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=-(x^2-4)(x-1)\\ &=-(x^3-x^2-4x+4) \end{aligned}$$
The curve lies below the $x$-axis for $-2\le x\le 1$ and above it for $1\le x\le 2$, so the area uses the negative of the signed area on $[-2,1]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=-\int_{-2}^{1}\left[-(x^3-x^2-4x+4)\right]dx+\int_{1}^{2}\left[-(x^3-x^2-4x+4)\right]dx\\&=\int_{-2}^{1}\left(x^3-x^2-4x+4\right)dx-\int_{1}^{2}\left(x^3-x^2-4x+4\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+4x\right]_{-2}^{1}-\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+4x\right]_{1}^{2}\\&=[F(1)-F(-2)]-[F(2)-F(1)]\\&=\left(\dfrac{23}{12}-\left(-\dfrac{28}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\dfrac{4}{3}-\dfrac{23}{12}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{71}{6}\text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=-\dfrac{1}{2}x^4+2x^3+\dfrac{3}{2}$.
Find the coordinates of stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
$$f'(x)=-2x^3+6x^2$$
$$f''(x)=-6x^2+12x$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2x^3+6x^2&=0\\ -2x^2(x-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=3$.

When $x=0$: $f(0)=\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $f''(0)=0$, so there is a potential point of inflexion at $x=0$. Test the concavity either side.

\extable{Ts8410_1}

The concavity changes, hence $\left(0,1\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

When $x=3$: $f(3)=15$ and $f''(3)=-18<0$.

Hence $(3,15)$ is a maximum stationary point.
items.final: $\left(0,1\tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion; $(3,15)$ is a maximum stationary point

items.part:
A function is given by $f(x)=-\dfrac{1}{2}x^4+2x^3+\dfrac{3}{2}$.
Show that there is another point of inflexion at $x=2$.
items.sol:
Points of inflexion occur when $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-6x^2+12x&=0\\ -6x(x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=2$.

From part (a), there is a horizontal point of inflexion at $\left(0,1\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

When $x=2$: $f(2)=\dfrac{19}{2}$. Test the concavity either side of $x=2$.

\extable{Ts8411_1}

The concavity changes at $x=2$.

Hence $\left(2,9\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.

items.part:
A company is designing a closed cylindrical container of radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm for their new product. The container is to have a surface area of $112\pi\ \text{cm}^2$.

\exfigure{1286_q25_1}
Show that the volume of the container is given by the expression:

$$V=56\pi r-\pi r^3$$
items.sol:
The surface area of a closed cylinder is $SA=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{aligned}112\pi&=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\ 112\pi-2\pi r^2&=2\pi rh\\ h&=\dfrac{56-r^2}{r}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into $V=\pi r^2h$.
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\pi r^2\left(\dfrac{56-r^2}{r}\right)\\ &=56\pi r-\pi r^3\end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dV}{dr}=56\pi-3\pi r^2$$
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2}=-6\pi r$$
Turning points occur when $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}56\pi-3\pi r^2&=0\\ r^2&=\dfrac{56}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Since $r\ge 0$, $r=\sqrt{\dfrac{56}{3}}$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2}=-6\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{56}{3}}<0$$
Hence the volume is maximised when $r\approx 4.32$ cm.

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=e^{-\sin x}$ at $x=\pi$.
items.sol:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\cos x\cdot e^{-\sin x}$$
When $x=\pi$: $y=1$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$.

So the gradient is $m=1$ at $(\pi,1)$.

Using the point-gradient form of a straight line:
$$\begin{aligned}y-1&=1\times(x-\pi)\\ y&=x-\pi+1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the tangent is } y=x-\pi+1$$

items.part:
The population $P$ of a colony of ants is given by $P(t)$, where $t$ is the time in years after a scientist first discovered the colony. The ant population changes at a rate modelled by the function:

$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=1800e^{0.6t}$$

The colony had a population of 700 ants when first discovered by the scientist. Calculate the number of years for the population to reach 79\,700 ants, correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Integrate the rate of change.
$$P=\int 1800e^{0.6t}\,dt=3000e^{0.6t}+c$$
When $t=0$, $P=700$:
$$\begin{aligned}700&=3000e^0+c\\ c&=-2300\end{aligned}$$
So $P=3000e^{0.6t}-2300$.

When $P=79\,700$:
$$\begin{aligned}79\,700&=3000e^{0.6t}-2300\\ \dfrac{82}{3}&=e^{0.6t}\\ \ln\dfrac{82}{3}&=0.6t\\ t&=\dfrac{5}{3}\ln\dfrac{82}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Hence the population reaches $79\,700$ after $t\approx 5.51$ years.

items.part: Differentiate $y=2\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^5$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on $y=2u^5$ with $u=7-e^{x^3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=10\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4\times\left(-3x^2e^{x^3}\right)\\ &=-30x^2e^{x^3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence find $\displaystyle\int 5x^2e^{x^3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4\,dx$.
items.sol:
From part (a):
$$\int-30x^2e^{x^3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4dx=2\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^5+c$$
Divide both sides by $-6$.
$$\therefore\ \int5x^2e^{x^3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4dx=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^5+c$$

Equate $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned}4e^x-3&=2-\dfrac{1}{e^x}\\ 4e^{2x}-3e^x&=2e^x-1 &&(\text{multiply by } e^x)\\ 4e^{2x}-5e^x+1&=0\end{aligned}$$

Factorise the quadratic in $e^x$.
$$(4e^x-1)(e^x-1)=0$$
So $e^x=\dfrac{1}{4}$ or $e^x=1$.

Hence $x=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}$ or $x=0$.

From the graph, $f(x)$ is above $g(x)$ between the intersections.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\left[\left(2-\dfrac{1}{e^x}\right)-(4e^x-3)\right]dx\\&=\int_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\left(5-e^{-x}-4e^x\right)dx\\&=\left[5x+e^{-x}-4e^x\right]_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\\&=\left(0+e^0-4e^0\right)-\left(5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}+e^{-\ln\frac{1}{4}}-4e^{\ln\frac{1}{4}}\right)\\&=(-3)-\left(5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}+4-1\right)\\&=-5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}-6\\&=5\ln 4-6\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A\approx 0.931 \text{ units}^2$$

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x)=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}$.
items.sol:
Write $\sec x=(\cos x)^{-1}$ and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left((\cos x)^{-1}\right)\\ &=-(\cos x)^{-2}\times(-\sin x)\\ &=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence show that the derivative of $y=\dfrac{\sec x}{\sin x+\cos x}$ can be expressed as:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\tan^2 x+2\tan x-1}{1+2\sin x\cos x}$$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, and part (a), with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=\sec x & v&=\sin x+\cos x\\ u'&=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x} & v'&=\cos x-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(\sin x+\cos x)\cdot\frac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}-\sec x(\cos x-\sin x)}{(\sin x+\cos x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{\tan^2x+\tan x-1+\tan x}{\sin^2x+\cos^2x+2\sin x\cos x}\\&=\dfrac{\tan^2x+2\tan x-1}{1+2\sin x\cos x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the primitive function $F(x)$ of the function $f(x)=\cot x$, given that $F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=3$.
items.sol:
Write the function in terms of sine and cosine.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$$
$$F(x)=\ln|\sin x|+c$$
Using $F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}3&=\ln 1+c\\ c&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\ln|\sin x|+3$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle is given by:

$$v(t)=-6\cos 2t\qquad\text{for } 0\le t\le 2\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and time is measured in seconds.

After $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds, the particle has a displacement of 4 metres.
Show that the displacement of the particle is given by:

$$x(t)=-3\sin 2t+4$$
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=\int(-6\cos 2t)\,dt\\ &=-6\times\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2t+c\\ &=-3\sin 2t+c\end{aligned}$$
When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=-3\sin\pi+c\\ c&=4\end{aligned}$$
Hence the displacement is $x(t)=-3\sin 2t+4$.

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and time is measured in seconds.

items.part:
The velocity of a particle is given by:

$$v(t)=-6\cos 2t\qquad\text{for } 0\le t\le 2\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and time is measured in seconds.

After $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds, the particle has a displacement of 4 metres.
Find the acceleration of the particle in terms of $t$, and hence state the maximum magnitude of acceleration.
items.sol:
Differentiate the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}a(t)&=\dfrac{d}{dt}(-6\cos 2t)\\ &=-6(-2\sin 2t)\\ &=12\sin 2t\end{aligned}$$
The amplitude of the acceleration is $12$.

Hence the maximum magnitude of acceleration is $12 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
items.final: $a(t)=12\sin 2t$; maximum magnitude of acceleration is $12\text{ m s}^{-2}$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle is given by:

$$v(t)=-6\cos 2t\qquad\text{for } 0\le t\le 2\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and time is measured in seconds.

After $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds, the particle has a displacement of 4 metres.
State the values of $t$ for which the displacement of the particle is increasing at an increasing rate.
items.sol:
The displacement increases at an increasing rate when $x'(t)>0$ and $x''(t)>0$, that is, when the curve is rising and concave up.

From the properties of a sine curve, the displacement graph has:

Points of inflexion at $t=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ 2\pi$.

Minimum turning points at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

\exfigure{1286_q32_s2}

Hence the displacement is increasing at an increasing rate when
$$\dfrac{\pi}{4}<t<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\dfrac{5\pi}{4}<t<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$

items.part: Factorise $2x^2+5x+2$
Rationalise the denominator: $\dfrac{2}{3-\sqrt{2}}$
items.sol:
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $3+\sqrt{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{3-\sqrt2} &= \dfrac{2}{3-\sqrt2}\times\dfrac{3+\sqrt2}{3+\sqrt2} \\ &= \dfrac{6+2\sqrt2}{9-2} \\ &= \dfrac{6+2\sqrt2}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the following integrals:

$\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1-2x^5}{x}\,dx$
items.sol:
Split the fraction and integrate each term.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{1-2x^5}{x}\,dx &= \int\left(\dfrac{1}{x}-2x^4\right)dx \\ &= \ln x-\dfrac{2x^5}{5}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Find the following integrals:

$\displaystyle\int (3x+2)^4\,dx$

Differentiate the following functions:

$y=3^{5x+2}$
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^{u}=u'\ln a\cdot a^{u}$ with $u=5x+2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \ln 3\cdot 5\cdot 3^{5x+2} \\ &= 5\ln 3\cdot 3^{5x+2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following functions:

$y=\dfrac{x}{\log_e x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\ln x\cdot 1-x\cdot\frac{1}{x}}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln x-1}{(\ln x)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Write down the domain of $g(x)=\log_e(x+\pi)$
items.sol:
The logarithm needs a positive argument.
$$\begin{aligned} x+\pi &> 0 \\ x &> -\pi \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Domain: } x>-\pi$$

items.part: Solve $2\log_e x=\log_e(2x+3)$
items.sol:
Using $n\ln a=\ln a^n$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln x^2 &= \ln(2x+3) \\ x^2 &= 2x+3 \\ x^2-2x-3 &= 0 \\ (x-3)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=3$ or $x=-1$.

But $x=-1$ cannot be substituted into $\ln x$, so it is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x=3$$

items.part: Solve the inequality $x^2\ge 3x+18$
items.sol:
Rearrange and factorise.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-3x-18 &\ge 0 \\ (x-6)(x+3) &\ge 0 \end{aligned}$$
The parabola is concave up with roots $-3$ and $6$, so it is above or on the axis outside the roots.
$$\therefore\ x\le -3 \text{ or } x\ge 6$$

items.part:
Three towns, $A$, $B$ and $C$ form a triangle.

Town $A$ is 80 km from Town $B$ and Town $C$ is 40 km from Town $A$ as shown below:

\exfigure{1300_q19_1}

The bearing of Town $B$ from Town $A$ is $130^\circ$. The bearing of Town $C$ from Town $A$ is $240^\circ$
Use this information to find the size of $\angle CAB$, and hence find the area of the triangle formed by the three towns to the nearest square kilometre.
items.sol:
The bearings of $B$ and $C$ from $A$ are $130^\circ$ and $240^\circ$, measured from north at $A$.
$$\angle CAB=240^\circ-130^\circ=110^\circ$$
Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 40\times 80\times\sin 110^\circ \\ &\approx 1503.5 \\ &\approx 1504 \text{ km}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle CAB=110^\circ \text{ and the area is } 1504 \text{ km}^2$$
items.final: $\angle CAB=110^\circ$ and the area is $1504\text{ km}^2$

items.part:
Three towns, $A$, $B$ and $C$ form a triangle.

Town $A$ is 80 km from Town $B$ and Town $C$ is 40 km from Town $A$ as shown below:

\exfigure{1300_q19_1}

The bearing of Town $B$ from Town $A$ is $130^\circ$. The bearing of Town $C$ from Town $A$ is $240^\circ$
Using the cosine rule, find the distance between Town $B$ and Town $C$, to the nearest kilometre.
items.sol:
By the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, with $\angle CAB=110^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2 &= 40^2+80^2-2(40)(80)\cos 110^\circ \\ &\approx 10188.92892\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $BC\approx 100.940224\ldots$
$$\therefore\ BC = 101 \text{ km (nearest km)}$$

items.part:
For the curve: $y=x^3-3x^2-9x+4$
Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3x^2-6x-9 \\ &= 3(x^2-2x-3) \\ &= 3(x-3)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
$$y''=6x-6=6(x-1)$$
For stationary points $y'=0$, so $x=3$ or $x=-1$.

When $x=3$, $y=-23$. When $x=-1$, $y=9$.

At $(3,-23)$, $y''=6(3-1)=12>0$, so a local minimum.

At $(-1,9)$, $y''=6(-1-1)=-12<0$, so a local maximum.

$$\therefore\ \text{local minimum at } (3,-23),\ \text{local maximum at } (-1,9)$$
items.final: local minimum at $(3,-23)$, local maximum at $(-1,9)$

items.part:
For the curve: $y=x^3-3x^2-9x+4$
Find any points of inflexion.
items.sol:
For inflexions $y''=0$, so $6(x-1)=0$, giving $x=1$ and $y=-7$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} x=0&: y''=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=2&: y''=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is an inflexion.
$$\therefore\ \text{inflexion at } (1,-7)$$
