items.part: Find the exact value of $\cot\theta$ given that $\cos\theta=0.6$ and $\sin\theta<0$.
items.sol:
$\cos\theta=0.6=\dfrac{3}{5}$, with $\cos\theta>0$ and $\sin\theta<0$, so $\theta$ is in Quadrant 4 and $\tan\theta<0$.

Using the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5:
$$\tan\theta=-\dfrac{4}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ \cot\theta=-\dfrac{3}{4}$$
Alternatively, since $\sin\theta<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= -\sqrt{1-\cos^2\theta} \\ &= -\sqrt{1-\dfrac{9}{25}} \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \cot\theta &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{3}{5}}{-\frac{4}{5}} \\ &= -\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A geometric progression has $5^{\text{th}}$ term $9$ and $13^{\text{th}}$ term $59\,049$.
Find the first term and the common ratio.
items.sol:
Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$T_5=ar^4=9,\qquad T_{13}=ar^{12}=59\,049$$
Dividing:
$$\dfrac{ar^{12}}{ar^4}=\dfrac{59\,049}{9}$$
So $r^8=6561$, giving $r=3$ or $r=-3$.

Substituting into $ar^4=9$:
$$a(81)=9$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{9},\ r=\pm 3$$

items.part:
A geometric progression has $5^{\text{th}}$ term $9$ and $13^{\text{th}}$ term $59\,049$.
Find the $19^{\text{th}}$ term.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{19} &= ar^{18} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\cdot 3^{18} \\ &= 3^{16} \\ &= 43\,046\,721 \end{aligned}$$
The same result follows from $r=-3$, since $(-3)^{18}=3^{18}$.

items.part:
The number of bacteria in a culture can be modelled by $B=120\,000\,e^{0.4t}$ where $t$ is the time in hours after the experiment started.
How many bacteria are there after 6 hours have passed?

The number of bacteria in a culture can be modelled by $B=120\,000\,e^{0.4t}$ where $t$ is the time in hours after the experiment started.
How fast was the culture growing after 6 hours?
items.sol:
The growth rate is the derivative:
$$\dfrac{dB}{dt}=0.4\times 120\,000\,e^{0.4t}=48\,000\,e^{0.4t}$$
At $t=6$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dB}{dt} &= 48\,000\,e^{2.4} \\ &= 529\,112 \text{ per hour} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of bacteria in a culture can be modelled by $B=120\,000\,e^{0.4t}$ where $t$ is the time in hours after the experiment started.
What was the average rate of increase over the first 6 hours?
items.sol:
At $t=0$, $B=120\,000e^0=120\,000$.

Average rate of increase over the first 6 hours:
$$\begin{aligned} &= \dfrac{1\,322\,781-120\,000}{6} \\ &= 200\,463 \text{ per hour} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of bacteria in a culture can be modelled by $B=120\,000\,e^{0.4t}$ where $t$ is the time in hours after the experiment started.
How long, in hours and minutes, will it take until the number of bacteria doubles?
items.sol:
Doubling means $B=240\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 240\,000 &= 120\,000\,e^{0.4t} \\ e^{0.4t} &= 2 \\ 0.4t &= \ln 2 \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.4} \\ &\approx 1.732867\ldots \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1 \text{ hour } 44 \text{ minutes (nearest minute)}$$
\extable{Ts8463_1}

items.part:
In an experiment, 2 balls are drawn at random and without replacement from an urn containing 4 red balls and 6 black balls. Let $X$ be the number of red balls selected.
What is the expected number of red balls drawn?
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \sum x\,p(x) \\ &= \dfrac{4}{15}+\dfrac{4}{15}+\dfrac{4}{15}+0 \\ &= \dfrac{12}{15} \\ &= 0.8 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
In an experiment, 2 balls are drawn at random and without replacement from an urn containing 4 red balls and 6 black balls. Let $X$ be the number of red balls selected.
What is the variance, $V(X)$, of this distribution?
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= 4\cdot\dfrac{2}{15}+1\cdot\dfrac{4}{15}+1\cdot\dfrac{4}{15}+0\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{16}{15} \end{aligned}$$
Using $V(X)=E(X^2)-(E(X))^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} V(X) &= \dfrac{16}{15}-(0.8)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{32}{75} \\ &\approx 0.427 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1300_q26_1}

The diagram above shows the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\sqrt{3}\cos x$, $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

The second point of intersection is labelled $B$.
Show, using any appropriate method, that $B$ has coordinates $\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
items.sol:
At $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$:
$$\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{3}\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3} &= \sqrt{3}\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= \sqrt{3}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So both curves pass through $\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.

Alternatively, $\sin x=\sqrt{3}\cos x$ gives $\tan x=\sqrt{3}$, so $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

The second intersection has $x>\pi$, so $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ and $y=\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

items.part:
\exfigure{1300_q26_1}

The diagram above shows the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\sqrt{3}\cos x$, $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

The second point of intersection is labelled $B$.
Find the exact area of the shaded region.
items.sol:
The shaded region lies below the $x$-axis, so each integral is taken in absolute value:
$$\text{Area}=\left|\int_{\pi}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\sin x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_{\frac{4\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}}\sqrt{3}\cos x\,dx\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= \left|\Big[-\cos x\Big]_{\pi}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\right|+\left|\Big[\sqrt{3}\sin x\Big]_{\frac{4\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}}\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{2}+(-1)\right|+\left|-\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\left|-\sqrt{3}+\dfrac{3}{2}\right| \end{aligned}$$
As $\sqrt{3}>\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &= \sqrt{3}-1 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1300_q27_1}

items.part:
For events $A$ and $B$ from a sample space, $P(A|B)=\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{3}$
Calculate $P(A\cap B)$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B)&=P(A|B)\cdot P(B) \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For events $A$ and $B$ from a sample space, $P(A|B)=\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{3}$
Calculate $P(\bar{A}\cap B)$ where $\bar{A}$ denotes the complement of $A$.
items.sol:
Using the conditional probability formula for $\bar A$ given $B$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\bar A\cap B)&=P(\bar A|B)\cdot P(B) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively,
$$\begin{aligned} P(\bar A\cap B)&=P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For events $A$ and $B$ from a sample space, $P(A|B)=\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{3}$
If $A$ and $B$ are independent, calculate $P(A\cup B)$
items.sol:
If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $P(A)=P(A|B)=\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Using the addition rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The gradient of a curve is given by $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3x}{x^2+e}$

The curve passes through $(0,2)$. What is its equation?
items.sol:
Rewrite the gradient so the numerator is the derivative of the denominator:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3x}{x^2+e}=\dfrac{3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2x}{x^2+e}$$
so
$$y=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln(x^2+e)+C$$
The curve passes through $(0,2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln e+C \\ 2&=\dfrac{3}{2}+C \\ C&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$y=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln(x^2+e)+\dfrac{1}{2}$$

items.part:
If $f(x)=\sqrt{2-x}$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{x}$, then
Find the rule for the composite function $f\circ g$
items.sol: $$f\circ g(x)=f(g(x))=\sqrt{2-\sqrt{x}}$$

items.part:
If $f(x)=\sqrt{2-x}$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{x}$, then
Find the domain of $f\circ g$
items.sol:
$\sqrt{x}$ needs $x\ge 0$.

The outer square root needs $2-\sqrt{x}\ge 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x}&\le 2 \\ x&\le 4 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore the domain is
$$0\le x\le 4 \text{ (i.e. } [0,4])$$

items.sol:

items.part:

items.sol:
By part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\cos x)=-\tan x$. By part (b), $\tan x\ge 0$ on $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan x\,dx \\ &=-\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}(-\tan x)\,dx \\ &=-\Big[\ln(\cos x)\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &=-\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\ln 1\right] \\ &=-(\ln 1-\ln 2-\ln 1) \\ &=\ln 2\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence solve the equation $|x|-2x=3$

If $|x|-2x=3$, then $|x|=2x+3$.

Subtracting $1$ from both sides gives

So the solution is where the graphs in part (a) intersect.

Therefore

items.part:
One half percent ($0.5\,\%$) of a country has a certain viral disease. A test is developed for the disease. The test gives a false positive $3\%$ of the time, and a false negative $2\%$ of the time.
Show that the probability that Andy, a randomly selected person, tests positive is $0.03475$

[Hint: in this question, let $D$ be the event that Andy has the disease, and $\overline{D}$ be the event Andy does not have it. Let $T$ be the event that Andy's test comes back positive.]
items.sol:
A person tests positive either with the disease or without it, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(T)&=P(T|D)\cdot P(D)+P(T|\bar D)\cdot P(\bar D) \\ &=(0.98)(0.005)+(0.03)(0.995) \\ &=0.03475 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
One half percent ($0.5\,\%$) of a country has a certain viral disease. A test is developed for the disease. The test gives a false positive $3\%$ of the time, and a false negative $2\%$ of the time.
Andy just got the bad news that his test came back positive.

Find the probability that Andy actually has the disease.
items.sol:
Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(D|T)&=\dfrac{P(D\cap T)}{P(T)} \\ &=\dfrac{P(T|D)\cdot P(D)}{P(T)} \\ &=\dfrac{(0.98)(0.005)}{0.03475} \\ &=0.141\ldots \\ &\approx 14\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows a sector of a circle of radius $r$ centimetres. The angle at the centre is $\theta$ radians, and the perimeter of the whole sector is $8\ \text{cm}$.

\exfigure{1300_q38_1}
Show that $A$, the area of the sector in $\text{cm}^2$, is given by

$$A=\dfrac{32\theta}{(\theta+2)^2}$$
items.sol:
Using the sector area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ and $r=\dfrac{8}{2+\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{8}{2+\theta}\right)^2\theta \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{64\theta}{(2+\theta)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{32\theta}{(2+\theta)^2} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=32\theta & v&=(\theta+2)^2 \\ u'&=32 & v'&=2(\theta+2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=\dfrac{(\theta+2)^2\cdot 32-32\theta\cdot 2(\theta+2)}{(\theta+2)^4}$$
For a stationary point $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 32(\theta+2)^2-64\theta(\theta+2)&=0 \\ 32(\theta+2)\left[\theta+2-2\theta\right]&=0 \\ 32(\theta+2)(2-\theta)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
so $\theta=-2$ or $\theta=2$.

But $0\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and both values lie outside this range, so the maximum occurs at an endpoint.

At $\theta=0$:
$$A=0$$
At $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{32\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+2\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{16\pi}{\left(\frac{\pi+4}{2}\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{64\pi}{(\pi+4)^2} \\ &\approx 3.9422\ \text{cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore the maximum area is $\dfrac{64\pi}{(\pi+4)^2}\ \text{cm}^2\approx 3.9422\ \text{cm}^2$, obtained when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radians.

items.part: Differentiate $y=\dfrac{2x}{3-5x}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=3-5x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=-5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{2(3-5x)-2x(-5)}{(3-5x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{6-10x+10x}{(3-5x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{6}{(3-5x)^2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{6}{(3-5x)^2}$$

items.part: Given that $f'(x)=3x^2-7$ and $f(3)=5$, find $f(x)$.
items.sol:
Integrate $f'(x)$:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{3x^3}{3}-7x+C=x^3-7x+C$$
Use $f(3)=5$ to find $C$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5&=3^3-7\times3+C\\ &=27-21+C\\ &=6+C\end{aligned}$$
So $C=-1$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-7x-1$$

items.part: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=3^{2x+1}\ln x$ at the point $(1,0)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3^{2x+1} & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=(2\ln3)\,3^{2x+1} & v'&=\dfrac1x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(2\ln3)\left(3^{2x+1}\right)\ln x+3^{2x+1}\times\dfrac1x$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=(2\ln3)(3^3)\ln1+3^3\times\dfrac11\\ &=27\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the gradient is } 27$$

items.part: Show that the equation $\dfrac{4\cos\theta}{\tan\theta}+15=0$ can be expressed as $4\sin^2\theta-15\sin\theta-4=0$.
items.sol:
Use $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4\cos\theta}{\tan\theta}+15&=0\\ 4\cos\theta\times\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}+15&=0\\ 4\cos^2\theta+15\sin\theta&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Use $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4(1-\sin^2\theta)+15\sin\theta&=0\\ 4-4\sin^2\theta+15\sin\theta&=0\\ 4\sin^2\theta-15\sin\theta-4&=0 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence solve the equation $\dfrac{4\cos\theta}{\tan\theta}+15=0$ for $0\leq\theta\leq2\pi$.
items.sol:
Factorise the quadratic in $\sin\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4\sin^2\theta-15\sin\theta-4&=0\\ 4\sin^2\theta-16\sin\theta+\sin\theta-4&=0\\ 4\sin\theta(\sin\theta-4)+(\sin\theta-4)&=0\\ (\sin\theta-4)(4\sin\theta+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\sin\theta=4$ (no solution, since $\sin\theta\le1$) or $\sin\theta=-\dfrac14$.

Since $\sin\theta<0$, $\theta$ is in the third or fourth quadrant.
$$\theta=3.394\ldots,\ 6.031\ldots$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=3.39 \text{ or } 6.03 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has cumulative distribution function $F$ given by

$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & \text{for } x<1,\\ k(x^2-x) & \text{for } 1\leq x\leq 2,\\ 1 & \text{for } x>2,\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a constant.
Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{2}$, and hence find the $90^{\text{th}}$ percentile value of $X$, giving your answer correct to three significant figures.
items.sol:
Since $F$ is continuous and $F(x)=1$ for $x>2$, $F(2)=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=k(2^2-2)\\ 1&=2k\\ k&=\dfrac12\end{aligned}$$
For the $90^{\text{th}}$ percentile, solve $F(x)=0.9$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.9&=\dfrac12(x^2-x)\\ 1.8&=x^2-x\\ 0&=x^2-x-1.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{-(-1)\pm\sqrt{(-1)^2-4\times1\times(-1.8)}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{8.2}}{2}\\ &=1.932,\ -0.932\end{aligned}$$
Since $1\le x\le2$, we take the positive root.
$$\therefore\ x=1.93 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$

items.part:
The continuous random variable $X$ has cumulative distribution function $F$ given by

$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & \text{for } x<1,\\ k(x^2-x) & \text{for } 1\leq x\leq 2,\\ 1 & \text{for } x>2,\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a constant.
Find an expression for $f(x)$ which represents the probability density function of $X$.
items.sol:
The density function is the derivative of $F$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=F'(x)\\ &=\dfrac12(2x-1)\\ &=x-\dfrac12\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\begin{cases}x-\dfrac12 & 1\le x\le2\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

The areas are $A_1=w^2$ and $A_2=\dfrac12w^2$.

Let the side of the second tile be $x$.
$$x^2=\dfrac12w^2$$
Since $x>0$:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}w$$

Third tile: $A_3=\dfrac14w^2$, so the side length is $\dfrac12w$.

Fourth tile: $A_4=\dfrac18w^2$, so the side length is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}w$.

The side lengths form a geometric sequence with $a=w$ and common ratio
$$r=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.707$$
Since $|r|<1$, a limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\ &=\dfrac{w}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}\\ &\approx3.414w\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{no matter how many tiles, the total length is less than } 3.5w$$

items.part:
The heights of female students at NSGHS are normally distributed with a mean of 168 cm and a standard deviation of 4.5 cm.
Find the probability that the height of a randomly selected female student attending NSGHS is between 159 cm and 163.5 cm.
items.sol:
159 cm is 2 standard deviations below the mean ($168-2\times4.5$) and 163.5 cm is 1 standard deviation below ($168-4.5$).

Using the 68%-95% rule, the probability is half the difference of the two percentages.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac12(95\%-68\%)\\ &=13.5\%\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
It is also known that the heights of male students at NSBHS are normally distributed with a mean of 170 cm and standard deviation of 6.5 cm.

Wendy is a student at NSGHS and she is 173.5 cm tall. Caleb is a student at NSBHS and he is 176 cm tall. Who is the taller student relative to their peers in their own school? Justify your answer.
items.sol:
Compare $z$-scores, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Wendy: } z&=\dfrac{173.5-168}{4.5}=\dfrac{11}{9}\approx1.22\\ \text{Caleb: } z&=\dfrac{176-170}{6.5}=\dfrac{12}{13}\approx0.92\end{aligned}$$
Since Wendy has the higher $z$-score, she is more standard deviations above the mean compared to Caleb, so she is the taller student relative to her peers.
items.final: Wendy is taller relative to her peers (z ≈ 1.22 vs Caleb's z ≈ 0.92)

items.part: What height would Caleb need to be in order to be comparable to Wendy’s height in relation to her school peers?
items.sol:
Caleb would need Wendy's $z$-score of $\dfrac{11}{9}$.
$$\begin{aligned} h&=170+\dfrac{11}{9}\times6.5\\ &=\dfrac{3203}{18}\\ &\approx177.94\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Caleb would need to be about } 178 \text{ cm}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows a circle with centre $O$ and radius $r$ cm. The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the circle and $AT$ is a tangent to the circle.

$OBT$ is a straight line and $\angle AOB=\theta$ radians.

\exfigure{1289_q22_1}
Express the area of the shaded region in terms of $r$ and $\theta$.
items.sol:
$OA\perp AT$ since $AT$ is a tangent, so in right-angled triangle $OAT$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{AT}{r}$.

Hence $AT=r\tan\theta$.

The shaded area is the triangle minus the sector.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\text{area }\triangle OAT-\text{sector }OAB\\ &=\dfrac12\times r\times r\tan\theta-\dfrac12r^2\theta\\ &=\dfrac12r^2\tan\theta-\dfrac12r^2\theta\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows a circle with centre $O$ and radius $r$ cm. The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the circle and $AT$ is a tangent to the circle.

$OBT$ is a straight line and $\angle AOB=\theta$ radians.

\exfigure{1289_q22_1}
Given that $r=3$ and $\theta=1.2$, find the perimeter of the shaded region. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The perimeter is $AT$, $BT$ and the arc $AB$.

In right-angled triangle $OAT$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac{r}{OT}$, so $OT=\dfrac{3}{\cos1.2}$, and $BT=OT-OB$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Perimeter}&=AT+BT+\text{arc }AB\\ &=3\tan1.2+(OT-OB)+3\times1.2\\ &=3\tan1.2+\left(\dfrac{3}{\cos1.2}-3\right)+3\times1.2\\ &\approx16.5955\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{perimeter}\approx16.60 \text{ cm}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\tan^2 x+\sin 2x\right)dx$.
items.sol:
Using $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\tan^2x+\sin2x\right)dx &=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\sec^2x-1+\sin2x\right)dx \\ &=\left[\tan x-x-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &=\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)-\left(\tan0-0-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos0\right) \\ &=\left(1-\dfrac{\pi}{4}-0\right)-\left(0-0-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution:

\extable{1289_q24_t1}

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

Given that $E(X)=2.85$, find the values of $a$ and $b$.
items.sol:
The probabilities sum to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.3+0.2+0.1+a+b&=1 \\ a+b&=0.4 \qquad (1) \end{aligned}$$
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,p(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=1\times0.3+2\times0.2+3\times0.1+4a+5b \\ 2.85&=1+4a+5b \\ 4a+5b&=1.85 \qquad (2) \end{aligned}$$
Multiply (1) by 4:
$$4a+4b=1.6 \qquad (3)$$
Subtract (3) from (2):
$$b=0.25$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\therefore\ a=0.15,\ b=0.25$$

items.part:
The derivative of a function is defined as $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.

Differentiate $f(x)=5x-x^2$ from first principles.
items.sol:
Using the definition with $f(x)=5x-x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{[5(x+h)-(x+h)^2]-[5x-x^2]}{h} \\ &=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{5x+5h-x^2-2xh-h^2-5x+x^2}{h} \\ &=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{5h-2xh-h^2}{h} \\ &=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}(5-2x-h) \\ &=5-2x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-kx^2+3x+3$. For what values of $k$ is $f(x)$ an increasing function?
items.sol:
$$f'(x)=3x^2-2kx+3$$
For $f(x)$ to be increasing, $f'(x)>0$ for all $x$. Since $3x^2-2kx+3$ is concave up, this needs $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{aligned} (-2k)^2-4\times3\times3&<0 \\ 4k^2&<36 \\ k^2&<9 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -3<k<3$$

items.part:
Consider the curve $f(x)=2x^3-x^2-4x+6$. Find the stationary points of $f(x)$ and determine their nature. Then sketch the curve, clearly labelling the stationary points.

You do not need to find the $x$-intercepts of $f(x)$.
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=2x^3-x^2-4x+6 \\ f'(x)&=6x^2-2x-4=2(3x^2-x-2) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$:
$$0=2(3x+2)(x-1)$$
so $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $x=1$.

items.part:
A teacher in college asks her mathematics students what other subjects they are studying. She finds that, of her 24 students, 12 study physics, 8 study geography and 4 study both.

A student is chosen at random from the class. Determine whether the event ‘the student studies physics’ and the event ‘the student studies geography’ are independent.
items.sol:
The events are independent if $P(P\cap G)=P(P)\times P(G)$.

Interpretation 1 (12 physics, 8 geography, 4 both, 8 neither):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{4}{24}=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{12}{24}\times\dfrac{8}{24}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
LHS $=$ RHS, $\therefore$ independent.

Interpretation 2 (16 physics, 12 geography, 4 both):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{4}{24}=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{16}{24}\times\dfrac{12}{24}=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
LHS $\neq$ RHS, $\therefore$ not independent.

items.part:
It is known that for the whole college:

\begin{itemize}
\item The probability of a student studying mathematics is $\dfrac{1}{5}$
\item The probability of a student studying biology is $\dfrac{1}{6}$
\item The probability of a student studying biology given that they study mathematics is $\dfrac{3}{8}$
\end{itemize}

Calculate the probability that in the whole college a student studies mathematics or biology or both.
items.sol:
Given $P(M)=\dfrac{1}{5}$, $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{6}$, $P(B|M)=\dfrac{3}{8}$. Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B|M)&=\dfrac{P(B\cap M)}{P(M)} \\ \dfrac{3}{8}&=\dfrac{P(B\cap M)}{\frac{1}{5}} \\ P(B\cap M)&=\dfrac{3}{40} \end{aligned}$$
Using the addition rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B\cup M)&=P(M)+P(B)-P(B\cap M) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{6}-\dfrac{3}{40} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{24} \end{aligned}$$

During a recent flood, the level of water in a river was measured at regular time intervals starting from midnight. The height $h$ metres, by which the water level exceeded normal levels was recorded. The rate at which $h$ increased at time $t$, is given by $R(t)$.

items.sol:
Five function values give 4 strips over $0\le t\le\dfrac{10}{3}$, so $h=\dfrac{\frac{10}{3}-0}{4}=\dfrac{5}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{\frac{5}{6}}{2}\left[0.5+2(1.1+1.6+1.5)+0\right] \\ &=\dfrac{89}{24} \\ &\approx 3.71 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\text{peak water level}=3.71+0.25=3.96 \text{ m}$$
Since this is less than 4 m, the town will not have to be evacuated.
items.final: Peak water level is $3.96$ m $<4$ m, so the town did not need to be evacuated.

The shaded area splits into a triangle $A_1$ and a region $A_2$ below the $x$-axis.
$$A_1=\dfrac{1}{2}\times1\times1=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
Since $y=\ln x$, we have $x=e^y$, so integrate with respect to $y$:

items.part:
A scientist is researching the effects of caffeine. She models the mass of caffeine in the body using $m=m_0e^{-kt}$ where $m_0$ milligrams is the initial mass of caffeine in the body and $m$ milligrams is the mass of caffeine in the body after $t$ hours.

It takes 5.7 hours for the mass of caffeine in the body to halve.

One cup of strong coffee contains 200 mg of caffeine.
The scientist drinks two strong cups of coffee at 8 am. By first finding the value of $k$, use the model to estimate the mass of caffeine in the scientist’s body at midday to the nearest gram.
items.sol:
At $t=5.7$, $m=\dfrac{m_0}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}&=e^{-5.7k} \\ \ln\dfrac{1}{2}&=-5.7k \\ -\ln2&=-5.7k \\ k&=\dfrac{\ln2}{5.7} \end{aligned}$$
Two cups at 8 am give $m_0=400$ mg, and midday is $t=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} m&=400e^{-4k} \\ &=245.929\ldots \\ &\approx 246 \text{ mg} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A scientist is researching the effects of caffeine. She models the mass of caffeine in the body using $m=m_0e^{-kt}$ where $m_0$ milligrams is the initial mass of caffeine in the body and $m$ milligrams is the mass of caffeine in the body after $t$ hours.

It takes 5.7 hours for the mass of caffeine in the body to halve.

One cup of strong coffee contains 200 mg of caffeine.
The scientist wants the mass of caffeine in her body to stay below 480 mg. Use the model to find the earliest time that she could drink another cup of strong coffee. Give your answer to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
Another cup adds 200 mg, so before it she needs $480-200=280$ mg in her body, with $m_0=400$.
$$\begin{aligned} 280&=400e^{-kt} \\ \dfrac{280}{400}&=e^{-kt} \\ \ln\dfrac{280}{400}&=-kt \\ t&=-\dfrac{1}{k}\ln\dfrac{280}{400} \\ &=2\text{ h }56\text{ min} \end{aligned}$$
The earliest time is 10:56 am.

Consider the diagram below.

\exfigure{1289_q35_1}

$OAB$ is a sector of a circle with centre at $O$ and radius $r$ such that $\angle AOB=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$RSTU$ is a rectangle drawn inside the sector and $\angle ROA=\theta$ as shown in the diagram where $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
Show that $UT=r\cos\theta-\sqrt{3}\,r\sin\theta$.
items.sol:
Since $UT=UO-OT$, find $UO$ and $OT$.

In $\triangle URO$ (right-angled at $U$):
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta&=\dfrac{UO}{OR} \\ UO&=r\cos\theta \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta&=\dfrac{UR}{OR} \\ UR&=r\sin\theta \end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle OTS$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}&=\dfrac{ST}{OT} \\ OT&=ST\div\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3\,ST \end{aligned}$$
But $ST=UR$ (opposite sides of a rectangle), so
$$OT=\sqrt3\,UR=\sqrt3\,r\sin\theta$$
$$\therefore\ UT=r\cos\theta-\sqrt3\,r\sin\theta$$

items.part:
Consider the diagram below.

\exfigure{1289_q35_1}

$OAB$ is a sector of a circle with centre at $O$ and radius $r$ such that $\angle AOB=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$RSTU$ is a rectangle drawn inside the sector and $\angle ROA=\theta$ as shown in the diagram where $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
Show that the area of the rectangle can be expressed as $A=r^2\left(\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sqrt{3}\sin^2\theta\right)$. Hence find the value of $\theta$ which will maximise the area of the rectangle.
items.sol:
The area is $A=UT\times UR$ with $UR=r\sin\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=(r\cos\theta-\sqrt3\,r\sin\theta)\,r\sin\theta \\ &=r^2\left(\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sqrt3\sin^2\theta\right) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate and set $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=r^2\left(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta-2\sqrt3\sin\theta\cos\theta\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta-2\sqrt3\sin\theta\cos\theta \\ 0&=1-\tan^2\theta-2\sqrt3\tan\theta &&(\text{divide by } \cos^2\theta) \\ 0&=\tan^2\theta+2\sqrt3\tan\theta-1 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta&=\dfrac{-2\sqrt3\pm\sqrt{(2\sqrt3)^2-4(1)(-1)}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{-2\sqrt3\pm4}{2} \\ &=-\sqrt3\pm2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $\tan\theta>0$, so $\tan\theta=2-\sqrt3$ and $\theta=15^\circ$.

Test the sign of $A'$ either side:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\theta & 14^\circ & 15^\circ & 16^\circ\\ \hline A' & 0.07r^2 & 0 & -0.07r^2\end{array}$$
Since $r^2>0$, $A'$ changes from positive to negative.
$$\therefore\ \text{the area is a maximum when } \theta=15^\circ \left(=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)$$

items.part: Differentiate $e^{x\sin x}$.
items.sol:
Use the chain rule: for $y=e^{f(x)}$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f'(x)e^{f(x)}$, with $f(x)=x\sin x$.

By the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=\sin x+x\cos x$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(\sin x+x\cos x)\,e^{x\sin x}$$

items.part: If $f(x) = \log_e(x^2 + 1)$, calculate $f'(-1)$.
items.sol:
Differentiate using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln f(x)=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$$
Substitute $x=-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(-1) &= \dfrac{-2}{2} \\ &= -1 \end{aligned}$$

How many cans would be in the $10^{\text{th}}$ row?
items.sol:
The numbers of cans form an arithmetic series with $a=3$ and $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= a+(n-1)d \\ &= 3+9\times 2 \\ &= 21 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A shop assistant is building a display of soup cans. The top row will contain 3 cans, and each subsequent row below will have 2 more cans than the previous row above.
The shop assistant has 400 cans. How many rows is the tallest display that he can build using this pattern?
items.sol:
Use the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$, with $S_n=400$.
$$\begin{aligned} 400 &= \dfrac{n}{2}[6+2n-2] \\ 800 &= 4n+2n^2 \\ 0 &= n^2+2n-400 \end{aligned}$$
By the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+4\times 400}}{2} \\ &= -1\pm\sqrt{401} \\ &\approx 19.02 \text{ or } -21.02 \end{aligned}$$
The number of rows is positive, so $n\approx 19.02$. Only whole rows can be built, so round down.
$$\therefore\ 19 \text{ rows}$$

items.part: The completion times for the Oztown triathlon race were normally distributed with mean time 60 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes. Using the empirical rule, find Ozzie's completion time if he finished ahead of 84% of competitors.
items.sol:
By the empirical rule, about $68\%$ of times lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so $16\%$ lie above $65$ minutes and $16\%$ below $55$ minutes.

To finish ahead of $84\%$ of competitors, Ozzie's time must be faster (lower) than $84\%$ of the times, so only $16\%$ are faster than him. That is one standard deviation below the mean:
$$60-5=55\text{ minutes}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Ozzie's completion time is } 55 \text{ minutes}$$

Given the series $\tan^2 x - \tan^4 x + \tan^6 x - \tan^8 x + \dots$ for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
Determine the values of $x$ such that the series has a limiting sum.
items.sol:
The series is geometric. Find the common ratio.
$$r=\dfrac{-\tan^4 x}{\tan^2 x}=-\tan^2 x$$
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$|-\tan^2 x|<1$$
So $\tan^2 x<1$, which gives $-1<\tan x<1$.
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{\pi}{4}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

items.part:
Given the series $\tan^2 x - \tan^4 x + \tan^6 x - \tan^8 x + \dots$ for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
Write a fully simplified expression in $x$ for the limiting sum of the given series.
items.sol:
The series is geometric with $a=\tan^2 x$ and $r=-\tan^2 x$.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{\tan^2 x}{1-(-\tan^2 x)} \\ &= \dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\sec^2 x} \\ &= \sin^2 x \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_\infty=\sin^2 x$$

items.part:
A particle is moving along the $x$ axis. Its displacement, $x$ metres from the origin after $t$ seconds, is given by $x = e^t - 3e^{2t}$ for $t \ge 0$ .

Explain why the particle never comes to rest.
items.sol:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=e^t-3e^{2t} \\ v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=e^t-6e^{2t} \end{aligned}$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$e^t\left(1-6e^t\right)=0$$
Since $e^t>0$ for all $t$, $e^t=0$ has no solution (it would need $t=\ln 0$).

Otherwise $1=6e^t$, so
$$\begin{aligned} e^t&=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)\approx -1.79 \end{aligned}$$
This is negative, but $t\ge 0$.

Hence $v=0$ has no solution for $t\ge 0$, so the particle never comes to rest.

items.part:
Given the function $f(x) = -x^3 + 9x^2 - 24x + 16$
Determine the coordinates of any stationary points and their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiate and factorise:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=-3x^2+18x-24 \\ &=-3\left(x^2-6x+8\right) \\ &=-3(x-4)(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(x)=-6x+18=-6(x-3)$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$, so $x=2$ or $x=4$.

At $x=4$: $f(4)=0$ and $f''(4)=-6<0$ (concave down), so there is a maximum at $(4,0)$.

At $x=2$: $f(2)=-4$ and $f''(2)=6>0$ (concave up), so there is a minimum at $(2,-4)$.

The random variable $X$ has the standard normal distribution, with probability density function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}}$ over the domain $(-\infty,\infty)$ .

In the diagram below, the region $R_{0.67}$ indicates the area under $y = f(x)$ over the domain $[0, 0.67]$.

\exfigure{1284_q31_1}

If the area of $R_{0.67}$ is 0.25, determine the range of scores that could be identified as outliers.
items.sol:
Since $R_{0.67}$ has area $0.25$, $Q_3=0.67$, and by symmetry $Q_1=-0.67$.

The interquartile range is
$$\text{IQR}=0.67-(-0.67)=1.34$$
Outliers lie below $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$ or above $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$:
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}&=-0.67-1.5\times 1.34\approx -2.68 \\ Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}&=0.67+1.5\times 1.34\approx 2.68 \end{aligned}$$
Hence outliers are scores below $-2.68$ or above $2.68$.

\exfigure{1284_q31_s1}
items.final: Outliers are scores below $-2.68$ or above $2.68$

items.part:
The diagram below shows a rectangular piece of metal, which is bent to form a gutter for the flow of water. The cross-section of a gutter is a trapezium.

\exfigure{1284_q32_1}
Show that the cross-sectional area $A(\theta)$, as a function of $\theta$, is given by

$$A(\theta) = 100\sin\theta\,(1 + \cos\theta)$$
items.sol:
The cross-section is a trapezium, so $A=\dfrac{h}{2}(a+b)$, with parallel sides $a=10$ and $b=10+2\times 10\cos\theta$ and height $h=10\sin\theta$ (from the right-angled triangle on each side, hypotenuse $10$).
$$\begin{aligned} A(\theta)&=\dfrac{10\sin\theta}{2}\left(10+\left(10+20\cos\theta\right)\right) \\ &=5\sin\theta\left(20+20\cos\theta\right) \\ &=100\sin\theta\left(1+\cos\theta\right) \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=1+\cos\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A'(\theta)&=100\left[\cos\theta(1+\cos\theta)+\sin\theta(-\sin\theta)\right] \\ &=100\left(\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\right) \\ &=100\left(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1\right) \\ &=100(\cos\theta+1)(2\cos\theta-1) \end{aligned}$$
For a stationary point $A'(\theta)=0$, so $\cos\theta=-1$ or $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Since $\theta$ is acute, $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$A''(\theta)=100\left(-4\cos\theta\sin\theta-\sin\theta\right)=-100\sin\theta(4\cos\theta+1)$$
$$A''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-150\sqrt{3}<0$$
Hence the cross-sectional area is a maximum when
$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

items.part: Prove that $\dfrac{1}{1 - \sin x} + \dfrac{1}{1 + \sin x} \equiv 2\sec^2 x$ where $\sin x \ne \pm 1$
items.sol:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator, then use $1-\sin^2 x=\cos^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x} \\ &=\dfrac{(1+\sin x)+(1-\sin x)}{1-\sin^2 x} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x} \\ &=2\sec^2 x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

The area between the curves is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve. Using part (i):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}-\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\right)dx \\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}2\sec^2 x\,dx \\ &=2\Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &=2\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-0\right) \\ &=2\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$

At what rate is the population changing 45 years later? Answer in terms of $P_0$.
items.sol:
The population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP$ with $k=-0.01$, since $P=P_0e^{-0.01t}$.

At $t=45$, $P=P_0e^{-0.45}$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-0.01P_0e^{-0.45}$$

items.part:
The lizards on Goanna Island are gradually dying out. The predicted population $P$ of lizards, $t$ years after the first observation was made, is $P = P_0\,e^{-0.01t}$ , where $P_0$ is the initial population.
When will the population decline to 10% of the original population? Leave your answer in exact form.
items.sol:
The population is $10\%$ of the original when $P=\dfrac{P_0}{10}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{P_0}{10}&=P_0e^{-0.01t} \\ 0.1&=e^{-0.01t} \\ \ln(0.1)&=-0.01t \\ t&=\dfrac{-\ln 10}{-0.01} \\ &=100\ln 10 \text{ years} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The monthly sales, $X$ (in units of \$100, 000), of a business are modelled by the two probability density functions:

$$g(x) = \begin{cases} 2x & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{Model 1}$$

OR

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx^3(1 - x^2) & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{Model 2}$$
Determine the value of $k$ in the second model.
items.sol:
For a probability density function, the total area is $1$:
$$k\int_0^1\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx=1$$
Evaluate the integral:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx&=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^6}{6}\right]_0^1 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{k}{12}=1$, giving
$$k=12$$

items.part:
The monthly sales, $X$ (in units of \$100, 000), of a business are modelled by the two probability density functions:

$$g(x) = \begin{cases} 2x & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{Model 1}$$

OR

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx^3(1 - x^2) & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{Model 2}$$
Show that the two models have the same median value.
items.sol:
Let $M$ be the median of model $g$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}&=\int_0^M 2x\,dx \\ &=\Big[x^2\Big]_0^M \\ &=M^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $M^2=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

For model $f$, with $k=12$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^M f(x)\,dx&=\int_0^M 12\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx \\ &=\Big[3x^4-2x^6\Big]_0^M \\ &=3M^4-2M^6 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $M^2=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3M^4-2M^6&=3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=M$ is also the median of model $f$, so the two models have the same median.

The graph below shows the cubic curve $y = 9x - x^3$, with domain $[0, 4.5]$.

\exfigure{1284_q36_1}

The curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.

The diagram shows two bounded regions:

$R$ bounded by $y = f(x),\ y = 0,\ x = 0$ and $x = 3$

$S$ bounded by $y = f(x),\ y = 0,\ x = 3$ and $x = a$

It is given that $a > 3$. Determine the value of $a$ such that regions $R$ and $S$ have the same area.
items.sol:
Region $R$ lies above the $x$-axis and region $S$ lies below it (the curve is negative for $x>3$). Equal areas mean the signed integrals cancel:
$$\int_0^3\left(9x-x^3\right)dx+\int_3^a\left(9x-x^3\right)dx=0$$
The two integrals combine into one:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a\left(9x-x^3\right)dx&=0 \\ \left[\dfrac{9x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^a&=0 \\ \dfrac{9a^2}{2}-\dfrac{a^4}{4}&=0 \\ 18a^2-a^4&=0 \\ a^2\left(18-a^2\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $a=0$ or $a=\pm 3\sqrt{2}$.

Since $a>3$, we take the positive root:
$$a=3\sqrt{2}$$

Sam invests \$$M$ into an account at the beginning of each month. The account earns 3% p.a. interest, compounded monthly.
Show that the total amount in the account at the end of the second month, $A_2$ is given by $A_2 = M \times (1.0025 + 1.0025^2)$
items.sol:
Interest per month is $\dfrac{3}{12}\%=0.25\%$, so each month the amount grows by a factor of $1.0025$.
$$A_1=M\times\left(1+\dfrac{3}{1200}\right)=M\times 1.0025$$
At the end of month 2, $A_1$ has grown once more and the second payment has grown for one month:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1\times 1.0025+M\times 1.0025 \\ &=M\times 1.0025^2+M\times 1.0025 \\ &=M\left(1.0025+1.0025^2\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sam invests \$$M$ into an account at the beginning of each month. The account earns 3% p.a. interest, compounded monthly.
Show that the amount in the account after $n$ months, $A_n$, is given by $A_n = 401M(1.0025^n - 1)$
items.sol:
Each payment earns interest for the months remaining, so
$$A_n=M\left(1.0025+1.0025^2+\dots+1.0025^n\right)$$
Factor out $1.0025$ to leave a geometric series with first term $1$, ratio $1.0025$ and $n$ terms:
$$A_n=M\times 1.0025\left(1+1.0025+\dots+1.0025^{n-1}\right)$$
Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_n&=M\times 1.0025\left(\dfrac{1.0025^n-1}{1.0025-1}\right) \\ &=401M\left(1.0025^n-1\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sam invests \$$M$ into an account at the beginning of each month. The account earns 3% p.a. interest, compounded monthly.

items.sol:

$$\begin{aligned} 6000&=401M\left(1.0025^{12}-1\right) \\ M&=\dfrac{6000}{401\left(1.0025^{12}-1\right)} \\ &=\$491.93 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

After the first five months of contributions, Sam increases his monthly payment to \$600. Given Sam's final contribution is less than \$600, what will be the minimum amount of this contribution (to the nearest \$5) to reach his goal of \$6000?
items.sol:
First find the amount after 5 months of contributions of $\$491.93$, using the formula from part (ii):
$$A_5=401\times 491.93\left(1.0025^5-1\right)=\$2478.16$$
Amount still to save:

Number of $\$600$ payments needed, from $3521.84=401\times 600\left(1.0025^n-1\right)$:

So $5<n<6$: five full payments of $\$600$ and a smaller sixth payment.

Five payments of $\$600$:

The first $\$2478.16$ earns interest for a further 5 months:

Combined total after 10 months:

Final contribution:
$$6000-5531.87=\$468.13\approx\$470 \text{ (to the nearest } \$5)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(3+x)-\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(3-x) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3+x}-\dfrac{-1}{3-x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3+x}+\dfrac{1}{3-x} \\ &= \dfrac{3-x+3+x}{(3+x)(3-x)} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{6}\ln\dfrac{5}{2}$ .
items.sol:
By part (a), $\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$ is the derivative of $\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{6}\int_1^2\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\left[\ln\dfrac{5}{1}-\ln\dfrac{4}{2}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}(\ln 5-\ln 2) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\ln\dfrac{5}{2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Simplify $\dfrac{\tan\theta\sec\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}$ .
items.sol:
Use $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ and $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\tan\theta\sec\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta} &= \dfrac{\tan\theta\sec\theta}{\sec^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\cos\theta \\ &= \sin\theta \end{aligned}$$

Calculate the area bounded by the curves $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ and $y=11-x$ and the $x$-axis.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1290_q22_s1}

The curve $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=-1$ and meets the line $y=11-x$ at $x=8$, where $y=3$.

The line meets the $x$-axis at $x=11$, so the triangle has base $3$ and height $3$.

The area is the area under the curve from $-1$ to $8$ plus the triangle.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-1}^{8}(x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 3 \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{3}(x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{-1}^{8}+4.5 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\left[9^{\frac{3}{2}}-0\right]+4.5 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\times 27+4.5 \\ &= 22.5 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the functions $f(x)=\ln(x)$ and $g(x)=e^{2x+1}$.
Show that the composite function, $g\big(f(x)\big)$, is a parabola.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} g(f(x)) &= e^{2\ln x+1} \\ &= e^{\ln x^2+1} \\ &= e^{\ln x^2}\times e \\ &= ex^2 \end{aligned}$$$$\text{which is a parabola.}$$

The domain of $f(x)=\ln x$ is $(0,\infty)$.

The domain of $g(x)=e^{2x+1}$ is $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Therefore the domain of $g(f(x))$ is $(0,\infty)$.

items.part:
A swimming pool is to be emptied for maintenance. The quantity of water, $Q$ litres, remaining in the pool at a time, $t$ minutes after it starts to drain, is given by:

$Q(t)=2000(25-t)^2,\ t\ge 0$.
At what rate (in litres/min) is the water being removed at any time ($t$)?
items.sol:
Differentiating using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} Q'(t) &= 2\times 2000(25-t)\times(-1) \\ &= -4000(25-t) \end{aligned}$$$$\therefore\ \text{water is removed at the rate of } 4000(25-t) \text{ litres per minute.}$$

items.part:
A swimming pool is to be emptied for maintenance. The quantity of water, $Q$ litres, remaining in the pool at a time, $t$ minutes after it starts to drain, is given by:

$Q(t)=2000(25-t)^2,\ t\ge 0$.
If the pool is completely full before being emptied, how long will it take to remove half of the water from the pool to the nearest minute?
items.sol:
The model applies for $0\le t\le 25$.

When full, $t=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} Q(0) &= 2000(25)^2 \\ &= 1\,250\,000 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$Half full means $Q(t)=625\,000$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2000(25-t)^2 &= 625\,000 \\ (25-t)^2 &= 312.5 \\ 25-t &= \sqrt{312.5} \\ t &\approx 7.32 \end{aligned}$$The other solution, $t\approx 42.67$, is outside the domain.

$$\therefore\ \text{it takes 7 minutes (to the nearest minute).}$$

items.part:
A swimming pool is to be emptied for maintenance. The quantity of water, $Q$ litres, remaining in the pool at a time, $t$ minutes after it starts to drain, is given by:

$Q(t)=2000(25-t)^2,\ t\ge 0$.
At what time does the rate of flow of water from the pool reach 20 kL/minute?
items.sol:
The rate is $20$ kL/min $=20\,000$ L/min.

$$\begin{aligned} 4000(25-t) &= 20\,000 \\ 25-t &= 5 \\ t &= 20 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that the two functions $y=4x-x^3$ and $y=x$ intersect when $x=0$ and $x=\pm\sqrt{3}$ .
items.sol:
Solve simultaneously.

$$\begin{aligned} 4x-x^3 &= x \\ 3x-x^3 &= 0 \\ x(3-x^2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$Hence $x=0$ or $x^2=3$, so $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt3$.

Therefore the functions intersect when $x=0$ and $x=\pm\sqrt3$.

items.part: Hence find the exact area between the two functions in the first quadrant.
items.sol:
In the first quadrant the curves meet at $x=0$ and $x=\sqrt3$, and $4x-x^3\ge x$ between them.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{\sqrt3}(4x-x^3)\,dx-\int_0^{\sqrt3}x\,dx \\ &= \int_0^{\sqrt3}(3x-x^3)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{\sqrt3} \\ &= \dfrac92-\dfrac94 \\ &= \dfrac94 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The displacement of a particle is described by the equation $x=4te^{-t}+3$, where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in cm and $t$ is the time in seconds.
Find the particle's initial displacement.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 4\times 0\times e^{0}+3 \\ &= 3 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The displacement of a particle is described by the equation $x=4te^{-t}+3$, where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in cm and $t$ is the time in seconds.
Find an equation for the particle's velocity.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=4t & v&=e^{-t}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=-e^{-t}\end{aligned}$$$$\begin{aligned} v&=\dfrac{dx}{dt} \\ &= 4e^{-t}+4t(-e^{-t}) \\ &= 4e^{-t}(1-t) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The displacement of a particle is described by the equation $x=4te^{-t}+3$, where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in cm and $t$ is the time in seconds.
Find when the particle is at maximum distance from the origin and what its displacement is at that time.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur when $v=0$.

$$4e^{-t}(1-t)=0$$Since $e^{-t}\neq 0$, $1-t=0$, so $t=1$ second.

Test the nature using the acceleration:

$$\dfrac{dv}{dt}=4e^{-t}(t-2)$$$$\text{At } t=1:\ \dfrac{dv}{dt}=-\dfrac{4}{e}<0$$Hence the particle is at maximum distance from the origin at $t=1$.

$$\begin{aligned} x(1) &= 4(1)e^{-1}+3 \\ &= \dfrac{4}{e}+3 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The displacement of a particle is described by the equation $x=4te^{-t}+3$, where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in cm and $t$ is the time in seconds.
Describe what happens to the particle eventually, given that as $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{t}{e^t}\to 0$ .
items.sol:
Write $x=\dfrac{4t}{e^t}+3$.

As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{t}{e^t}\to 0$, so $\dfrac{4t}{e^t}\to 0$.

Therefore the particle eventually approaches $x=3$.

items.part:
It is known for a large population that at the beginning of winter, 15% of people will be infected with a particular virus.
Four people are selected at random.

Find the probability that at least one of them has the virus.
items.sol:
Let $V$ be the event that a person has the virus.

$$P(V)=0.15,\qquad P(\overline V)=0.85$$$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one}) &= 1-P(\text{none}) \\ &= 1-(0.85)^4 \\ &= 0.47799375 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
It is known for a large population that at the beginning of winter, 15% of people will be infected with a particular virus.
What is the smallest number of people a drug company would need to test to have a greater than 95% chance that at least one of the tested people has the virus?
items.sol:
Let $n$ be the least number of people tested.

$$\begin{aligned} 1-(0.85)^n &> 0.95 \\ (0.85)^n &< 0.05 \\ n\ln 0.85 &< \ln 0.05 \\ n &> \dfrac{\ln 0.05}{\ln 0.85} &&(\text{inequality reversed as } \ln 0.85<0) \\ n &> 18.43312827\ldots \end{aligned}$$Hence 19 people would need to be tested.

items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{204+205}{830} &= \dfrac{409}{830} \\ &= 0.49277\ldots \\ &\approx 49.3\% \end{aligned}$$

Giving a reason, determine if it is worth the health authorities using this new medication.
items.sol:
Medication group: $\dfrac{204}{416}\approx 49.04\%$.

Control group: $\dfrac{205}{414}\approx 49.52\%$.

The incidence of the virus is similar in both groups (a difference of about $0.5\%$), so it is not worth using the new medication.
items.final: Not worth using the new medication, since the incidence of the virus is similar in both groups (about 49.0% vs 49.5%).

A triangular enclosure has been created by the fences PQ and PR, each of length 40 metres. A river forms the third boundary of the enclosure, as shown in the diagram.

Let $\angle PQR=\theta$.
Show that the area of $\triangle PQR$ is $A=800\sin 2\theta$.
items.sol:
Since $PQ=PR$, $\triangle PQR$ is isosceles, so $\angle QRP=\theta$.

By the angle sum of a triangle, $\angle QPR=180^\circ-2\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac12\times 40\times 40\times\sin(180^\circ-2\theta) \\ &= 800\sin(180^\circ-2\theta) \\ &= 800\sin 2\theta \end{aligned}$$since $\sin(180^\circ-2\theta)=\sin 2\theta$.

A triangular enclosure has been created by the fences PQ and PR, each of length 40 metres. A river forms the third boundary of the enclosure, as shown in the diagram.

items.sol:
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=1600\cos 2\theta$$For stationary points:

items.part: Factorise $8x^{3}+125$
items.sol:
Use the sum of cubes, $a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)\left(a^{2}-ab+b^{2}\right)$, with $a=2x$ and $b=5$.
$$\begin{aligned}8x^{3}+125&=(2x)^{3}+5^{3}\\ &=(2x+5)\left(4x^{2}-10x+25\right)\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve $\left|2x-1\right|=5$
items.sol:
The absolute value equals 5 when the inside is $5$ or $-5$.
$$2x-1=5\qquad\text{or}\qquad 2x-1=-5$$
$$\therefore\ x=3\text{ or }x=-2$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.

items.sol:

Differentiate using the power rule.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned}y'&=8e^{x}+8x\,e^{x}\\ &=8e^{x}(x+1)\end{aligned}$$

items.sol: Many-to-one: for example $\sin 0=\sin\pi=0$, so different $x$ values give the same $y$ value.

items.part:
Given that $f''(x)=6x-2$ and that there is a stationary point on $f(x)$ at $(1,2)$, find
$f(x)$
items.sol:
Integrate $f''(x)$.
$$f'(x)=\int(6x-2)\,dx=3x^{2}-2x+c$$
The stationary point at $(1,2)$ gives $f'(1)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=3-2+c\\ c&=-1\end{aligned}$$
so $f'(x)=3x^{2}-2x-1$.

Integrate again.
$$f(x)=\int\left(3x^{2}-2x-1\right)dx=x^{3}-x^{2}-x+c$$
The point $(1,2)$ lies on the curve, so $f(1)=2$.
$$\begin{aligned}2&=1-1-1+c\\ c&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^{3}-x^{2}-x+3$$

items.part:
Given that $f''(x)=6x-2$ and that there is a stationary point on $f(x)$ at $(1,2)$, find
The co-ordinates of any point(s) of inflection.
items.sol:
A point of inflection needs $f''(x)=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$\begin{aligned}6x-2&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{27}-\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{1}{3}+3\\ &=\dfrac{70}{27}\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $f''(x)$ either side.
$$\begin{aligned}f''(0)&=-2<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(1)&=4>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection.
$$\therefore\ \text{the point of inflection is }\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{70}{27}\right)$$

items.part: Differentiate $y=e^{\sin x}$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u}=u'e^{u}$ with $u=\sin x$:
$$y'=\cos x\,e^{\sin x}$$

items.part: Show $y=e^{\sin x}$ has 2 stationary points for $0\le x\le 2\pi$ and find the coordinates of these stationary points in simplest exact form.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$\cos x\,e^{\sin x}=0$$
Since $e^{\sin x}>0$ for all $x$, there is no solution to $e^{\sin x}=0$, so $\cos x=0$.
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\qquad(0\le x\le2\pi)$$
There are exactly 2 stationary points.

At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $y=e^{\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}=e$.

At $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$: $y=e^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{e}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the stationary points are }\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},e\right)\text{ and }\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$$

items.part: Find the nature of these stationary points.
items.sol:
Test the sign of $y'=\cos x\,e^{\sin x}$ either side of each stationary point.

Near $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&0&\dfrac{\pi}{2}&\pi\\\hline y'&1&0&-1\end{array}$$
The sign of $y'$ changes from positive to negative, so $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},e\right)$ is a local maximum.

Near $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&\pi&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}&2\pi\\\hline y'&-1&0&1\end{array}$$
The sign of $y'$ changes from negative to positive, so $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$ is a local minimum.

Alternatively, $y''$ is negative at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and positive at $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.
items.final: $\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2},e\right)$ is a local maximum; $\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2},\tfrac{1}{e}\right)$ is a local minimum

items.part:
Given $y=x\sqrt{x+1}$,
Show $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3x+2}{2\sqrt{x+1}}$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\sqrt{x+1}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{x+1}}+\sqrt{x+1}\\ &=\dfrac{x+2(x+1)}{2\sqrt{x+1}}\\ &=\dfrac{3x+2}{2\sqrt{x+1}}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Given $y=x\sqrt{x+1}$,
Hence, or otherwise, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_3^8\dfrac{3x+2}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx$
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{3x+2}{2\sqrt{x+1}}$ is the derivative of $x\sqrt{x+1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_3^8\dfrac{3x+2}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx&=2\int_3^8\dfrac{3x+2}{2\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx\\ &=2\left[x\sqrt{x+1}\right]_3^8\\ &=2\left(8\sqrt{9}-3\sqrt{4}\right)\\ &=36\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4}x^{3}\,dx$
items.sol:
Since $f(x)=x^{3}$ is an odd function and the limits are $-4$ and $4$, the integral is zero.

$$\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4}x^{3}\,dx=0$$

Alternatively, using the primitive:

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4}x^{3}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{x^{4}}{4}\right]_{-4}^{4} \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given that $f(x)=2x+1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}+5$, find $f\left(g(-3)\right)$.
items.sol:
Evaluate the inner function first.

$$g(-3)=(-3)^{2}+5=14$$

Then apply $f$.

$$\begin{aligned} f\left(g(-3)\right) &= 2(14)+1 \\ &= 29 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the value(s) of $k$ for which the equation $y=(k+1)x^{2}-(2+k)x+3$ is positive definite.
items.sol:
$y$ is positive definite if $\Delta<0$ and $a>0$.

For $y=(k+1)x^{2}-(2+k)x+3$:

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta &= b^{2}-4ac \\ &= (2+k)^{2}-12(k+1) \\ &= k^{2}+4k+4-12k-12 \\ &= k^{2}-8k-8 \end{aligned}$$

So $\Delta<0$ gives $k^{2}-8k-8<0$.

Solving $k^{2}-8k-8=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{64+32}}{2} \\ &= 4\pm2\sqrt6 \end{aligned}$$

Hence $4-2\sqrt6<k<4+2\sqrt6$.

Also $a>0$ means $k+1>0$, so $k>-1$. This is already satisfied, since $4-2\sqrt6\approx-0.9>-1$.

$$\therefore\ 4-2\sqrt6<k<4+2\sqrt6$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following.
$y=\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+4}{x-3}\right)$
items.sol:
Split the logarithm using the log laws.

$$\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+4}{x-3}\right)=\log_e(x+4)-\log_e(x-3)$$

Differentiating:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x+4}-\dfrac{1}{x-3}$$

Equivalently, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{-7}{(x+4)(x-3)}$.

items.part:
Differentiate the following.
$y=8\sin x\ln x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=8\sin x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=8\cos x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= uv'+vu' \\ &= \dfrac{8\sin x}{x}+8\cos x\ln x \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Determine
$\displaystyle\int 1+\tan^{2}\theta\,d\theta$
items.sol:
Use the identity $1+\tan^{2}\theta=\sec^{2}\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int(1+\tan^{2}\theta)\,d\theta &= \int\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta \\ &= \tan\theta+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Determine
$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{8x+10}{2x^{2}+5x}\,dx$
items.sol:
The derivative of the denominator $2x^{2}+5x$ is $4x+5$, and the numerator is twice this.

$$\dfrac{8x+10}{2x^{2}+5x}=2\cdot\dfrac{4x+5}{2x^{2}+5x}$$

So

$$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{8x+10}{2x^{2}+5x}\,dx=2\ln\left|2x^{2}+5x\right|+C$$

items.part:
The velocity, $v$ metres per second, of a body $t$ seconds after starting from rest, is given by $v=3t-t^{2}$.
Find how far the body has travelled when it next comes to rest.
items.sol:
The body is at rest when $v=0$.

$$0=t(3-t)$$

So $t=3$ (it next comes to rest).

Integrate the velocity to find the displacement.

$$x=\displaystyle\int(3t-t^{2})\,dt=\dfrac{3t^{2}}{2}-\dfrac{t^{3}}{3}+C$$

Since it starts from rest at the origin, $x(0)=0$, so $C=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} x(3) &= \dfrac{27}{2}-9 \\ &= 4.5 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the body has travelled } 4.5 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
The velocity, $v$ metres per second, of a body $t$ seconds after starting from rest, is given by $v=3t-t^{2}$.
Show that the acceleration of the body at this time is negative.

Interpret your answer.
items.sol:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

$$a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=3-2t$$

At $t=3$:

$$a=3-2(3)=-3<0$$

Interpretation: the body has slowed down, coming to rest. It then changes direction and speeds up.

items.part:
For the curve $y=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$
Show $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)$ lies on the curve.
items.sol:
Substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into the right-hand side.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \dfrac{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{1+\frac12} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\frac32} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} \\ &= \text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)\text{ lies on the curve}$$

items.part:
For the curve $y=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$
Show $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{1+\cos x}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^{2}}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=1+\cos x\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{\cos x(1+\cos x)+\sin^{2}x}{(1+\cos x)^{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x+\cos^{2}x+\sin^{2}x}{(1+\cos x)^{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\cos x}{(1+\cos x)^{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1+\cos x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the curve $y=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$
Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$
items.sol:
The gradient at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ comes from part (b).

$$\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{1}{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\frac32} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

The tangent passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$.

$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} &= \dfrac23\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ y &= \dfrac23x-\dfrac{2\pi}{9}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If the sum of the first 10 terms of the series $\log_2\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)+\log_2\left(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)+\log_2\left(\dfrac{1}{x^{3}}\right)+\ldots$ is $-110$, find the value of $x$.
items.sol:
Use the log laws to rewrite each term.

$$-\log_2x-2\log_2x-3\log_2x-\ldots$$

This is an arithmetic series with $a=-\log_2x$, common difference $d=-\log_2x$, $n=10$ and last term $l=-10\log_2x$.

Using $S_{n}=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:

$$\begin{aligned} -110 &= \dfrac{10}{2}\left(-\log_2x-10\log_2x\right) \\ &= -5\cdot11\log_2x \end{aligned}$$

So $\log_2x=2$.

$$\therefore\ x=2^{2}=4$$

items.part:
The probability that a certain girl wakes up late in the morning is 0.6.

When she wakes up late, the probability that she is late to work is 0.85.

When she wakes up on time, the probability that she is late to work is 0.4.
What is the probability that she is late to work on any morning?
items.sol:
She is late to work either by waking late or by waking on time, so add the two branches.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{late}) &= P(\text{wake late and late})+P(\text{wake on time and late}) \\ &= 0.6\times0.85+0.4\times0.4 \\ &= 0.67 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The probability that a certain girl wakes up late in the morning is 0.6.

When she wakes up late, the probability that she is late to work is 0.85.

When she wakes up on time, the probability that she is late to work is 0.4.
Upon seeing the girl arriving late, her boss asks her if she overslept.

What is the probability that the truthful answer is `yes'?
items.sol:
Use conditional probability.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{wakes up late}\mid\text{arrives late}) &= \dfrac{P(\text{wakes up late}\cap\text{arrives late})}{P(\text{late})} \\ &= \dfrac{0.6\times0.85}{0.67} \\ &= \dfrac{51}{67} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The rate at which liquid is flowing into a vessel after $t$ minutes is given by $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{t+1}$.

If the volume of liquid in the vessel is $(\log_e 2)$ cubic metres after 3 minutes, what is the volume after 8 minutes? Answer correct to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
Integrate the rate (with $t\ge0$, so $t+1>0$).

$$V=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{t+1}\,dt=\ln(t+1)+c$$

At $t=3$, $V=\ln2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \ln2 &= \ln4+c \\ c &= \ln2-\ln4=\ln\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$

So $V=\ln(t+1)+\ln\dfrac12$. At $t=8$:

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \ln9+\ln\dfrac12 \\ &\approx 1.50 \text{ m}^{3} \text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the area bounded by the curve $y=(x+2)^{3}$ and the $x$-axis between $x=-3$ and $x=2$.
items.sol:
The curve $y=(x+2)^{3}$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-2$, so split the area there.

\exfigure{1292_q30_s1}

A primitive is

$$\displaystyle\int(x+2)^{3}\,dx=\dfrac{(x+2)^{4}}{4}+C$$

The part from $-3$ to $-2$ is below the axis, so subtract its (negative) integral.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}(x+2)^{3}\,dx-\int_{-3}^{-2}(x+2)^{3}\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{(x+2)^{4}}{4}\right]_{-2}^{2}-\left[\dfrac{(x+2)^{4}}{4}\right]_{-3}^{-2} \\ &= 64+\dfrac14 \\ &= \dfrac{257}{4} \text{ square units} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch the curve of $y=\log_e(x+1)$ including intercept(s) and asymptotes.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1292_q31_s1}

The vertical asymptote is $x=-1$, and the curve passes through the origin $(0,0)$.

items.part: Using the trapezoidal rule with 4 sub-intervals, estimate $\displaystyle\int_1^2\ln(x+1)\,dx$, correct to 3 decimal places.
items.sol:
The strip width is

$$h=\dfrac{2-1}{4}=\dfrac14$$

So the $x$ values are $1,\ \dfrac54,\ \dfrac32,\ \dfrac74,\ 2$. With $f(x)=\ln(x+1)$, the trapezoidal rule gives

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^2\ln(x+1)\,dx &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left[f(1)+2\left(f\left(\dfrac54\right)+f\left(\dfrac32\right)+f\left(\dfrac74\right)\right)+f(2)\right] \\ &= \dfrac18\left[\ln2+2\left(\ln\dfrac94+\ln\dfrac52+\ln\dfrac{11}{4}\right)+\ln3\right] \\ &\approx 0.909 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Would the trapezoidal rule used in this instance provide a value that is greater than or less than $\displaystyle\int_1^2\ln(x+1)\,dx$? Explain your answer.
items.sol:
Over the interval the curve is concave down, so each trapezoid lies below the curve.

$$\therefore\ \text{the trapezoidal estimate is less than the exact value}$$
items.final: The trapezoidal estimate is less than the exact value (curve concave down, trapezoids lie below the curve)

items.part:
The population of a town can be estimated by using the formula $P=P_0e^{kt}$, where $t$ is the time in years after the year 2020 and $P_0$ and $k$ are constants.

The population at the beginning of the year 2020 was 300, and at the beginning of 2024 it was 450.
Find the annual growth rate, $k$, of the population correct to 3 significant figures.

The population of a town can be estimated by using the formula $P=P_0e^{kt}$, where $t$ is the time in years after the year 2020 and $P_0$ and $k$ are constants.

The population at the beginning of the year 2020 was 300, and at the beginning of 2024 it was 450.
In what year will the town's population be double that of the year 2020?
items.sol:
Double the 2020 population is $600$.

$$\begin{aligned} 600 &= 300e^{\frac{\ln3-\ln2}{4}t} \\ 2 &= e^{\frac{\ln3-\ln2}{4}t} \\ \ln2 &= \dfrac{\ln3-\ln2}{4}\,t \\ t &= \dfrac{4\ln2}{\ln3-\ln2} \\ &\approx 6.84 \text{ years} \end{aligned}$$

Hence towards the end of the year 2026 the town will have double the 2020 population.

$$\therefore\ \text{the year is } 2026$$

items.part:
The water height in an estuary fluctuates according to the tide. Flooding will occur when the water height reaches 1.5 m. One day the high tide of 1.6 m occurred at 3:00 am and the following low tide at 9:30 am. Assume that the following high tide was also 1.6 m and the height of the tide is modelled by the equation

$$h=1+0.6\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{13}(t+0.25)\right),$$

where $h$ is the height in metres and $t$ is the time in hours after midnight.

Find the time when the next flooding would be expected to occur, to the nearest minute.
items.sol:
Flooding occurs when $h=1.5$.

$$1.5=1+0.6\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{13}(t+0.25)\right)$$

$$\dfrac56=\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{13}+\dfrac{\pi}{26}\right)$$

The first solution is $t\approx1.7882$ (1:47 am), which is before the 9:30 am low tide.

The period is $13$ hours, so adding $13$ hours gives the next time the tide is rising through $1.5$ m.

$$t\approx14.7882$$

The next flooding is expected at 14:47, i.e. 2:47 pm.

Alternatively, the general solution is

$$t=\dfrac{13}{2\pi}(-1)^{k}\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac56\right)+\dfrac{13k}{2}-\dfrac14$$

Then $k=0$ gives $t\approx1.7882$ and $k=2$ gives $t\approx14.7882$.

$$\therefore\ \text{flooding is expected at } 2{:}47 \text{ pm}$$

items.part:
Michael borrows \$650 000 to buy a unit at $6\%$ per annum with interest compounded monthly.

The loan is to be repaid with equal monthly repayments of \$4200.

Let \$$A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.
Show that $A_n=840\,000-190\,000\times1.005^{n}$
items.sol:
The interest rate is $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly, which is $0.5\% = 0.005$ per month.

The amount owing grows by $0.5\%$ and then the repayment is taken off, with $A_0=650\,000$.

$$A_n=1.005A_{n-1}-4200$$

Developing the first terms:

$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 650\,000\times1.005-4200 \\ A_2 &= 650\,000\times1.005^{2}-4200(1+1.005) \\ A_3 &= 650\,000\times1.005^{3}-4200(1+1.005+1.005^{2}) \end{aligned}$$

Hence

$$A_n=650\,000\times1.005^{n}-4200\left(1+1.005+\ldots+1.005^{n-1}\right)$$

The bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.005$ and $n$ terms.

$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= 650\,000\times1.005^{n}-4200\times\dfrac{1.005^{n}-1}{1.005-1} \\ &= 650\,000\times1.005^{n}-840\,000\left(1.005^{n}-1\right) \\ &= 840\,000-190\,000\times1.005^{n} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Michael borrows \$650 000 to buy a unit at $6\%$ per annum with interest compounded monthly.

The loan is to be repaid with equal monthly repayments of \$4200.

Let \$$A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.
After 15 years, the amount owing is \$373 722 to the nearest dollar.

At this time Michael borrows a further \$200 000 to build an extension.

He adds this onto his previous mortgage. If the monthly repayments remain the same, what is the minimum remaining number of months it will take him to pay off the balance of the loan?
items.sol:
After $180$ months the amount owing is $A_{180}=373\,722$.

The new loan is

$$\$(373\,722+200\,000)=\$573\,722$$

Let $B_n$ be the amount owing after a further $n$ months. The same working as in part (a) gives

$$\begin{aligned} B_n &= 573\,722\times1.005^{n}-840\,000\left(1.005^{n}-1\right) \\ &= 840\,000-266\,278\times1.005^{n} \end{aligned}$$

The loan is paid off when $B_n=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1.005^{n} &= \dfrac{840\,000}{266\,278} \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{840\,000}{266\,278}\right)}{\ln1.005} \\ &\approx 230.35 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ 231 \text{ months are needed to pay off the loan}$$

items.part:
Find the shaded area enclosed by the curves $y=x^{2}$ and $y=9+3x-x^{2}$ and the line $y=1$.

\exfigure{1292_q35_1}
items.sol:
\exfigure{1292_q35_s1}

Find where the two curves meet.

$$\begin{aligned} x^{2} &= 9+3x-x^{2} \\ 2x^{2}-3x-9 &= 0 \\ (2x+3)(x-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=-1.5$ or $x=3$.

The line $y=1$ meets $y=x^{2}$ where $x^{2}=1$, so $x=\pm1$.

First find the area between the curves, then subtract the area between the line $y=1$ and $y=x^{2}$.

$$\displaystyle\int_{-1.5}^{3}\left(9+3x-x^{2}-x^{2}\right)dx \quad\text{and}\quad \int_{-1}^{1}\left(1-x^{2}\right)dx$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left[9x+\dfrac32x^{2}-\dfrac23x^{3}\right]_{-1.5}^{3}-\dfrac43 \\ &= 29\dfrac{1}{24} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rotating camera is formed with a cross-section as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1292_q36_1}

The cross-section consists of a semi-circle $AXC$ with centre $O$ and radius $\dfrac{r}{2}$, and a sector $ABC$ of radius $r$, centre $A$ and angle $\theta$.
Show that the perimeter, $P$, of the cross-section $ABCX$ is given by $P=r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\theta+1\right)$.
items.sol:
The semi-circle has diameter $r$, so its perimeter is $r+\dfrac{\pi r}{2}$.

The sector has two radii and an arc, with perimeter $r+r\theta$ on the boundary.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{\pi r}{2}+r+r\theta \\ &= r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+1+\theta\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rotating camera is formed with a cross-section as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1292_q36_1}

The cross-section consists of a semi-circle $AXC$ with centre $O$ and radius $\dfrac{r}{2}$, and a sector $ABC$ of radius $r$, centre $A$ and angle $\theta$.
If the area of cross-section $ABCX$ is 1 square unit, show that $P=\dfrac{2}{r}+r\left(1+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$.
items.sol:
The area is a semi-circle of radius $\dfrac{r}{2}$ plus a sector of radius $r$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac12\pi\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)^{2}+\dfrac12r^{2}\theta \\ &= \dfrac18r^{2}(\pi+4\theta) \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

So $\pi+4\theta=\dfrac{8}{r^{2}}$, giving

$$\theta=\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

Substitute into $P$.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+1+\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{r}+r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rotating camera is formed with a cross-section as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1292_q36_1}

The cross-section consists of a semi-circle $AXC$ with centre $O$ and radius $\dfrac{r}{2}$, and a sector $ABC$ of radius $r$, centre $A$ and angle $\theta$.
Show that the least perimeter occurs when $r^{2}=\dfrac{8}{\pi+4}$ and calculate $\theta$.

Write the size of this angle to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Write $P=2r^{-1}+r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1\right)$ and differentiate.

$$\dfrac{dP}{dr}=-\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}+\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1 \qquad \dfrac{d^{2}P}{dr^{2}}=4r^{-3}$$

The perimeter is stationary when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{r^{2}} &= \dfrac{\pi+4}{4} \\ r^{2} &= \dfrac{8}{\pi+4} \end{aligned}$$

For $r>0$, $\dfrac{d^{2}P}{dr^{2}}=4r^{-3}>0$, so $P$ is a minimum.

From (b), $\theta=\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, and here $\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1$.

$$\theta=1 \text{ radian}\approx57^\circ$$

Using the definition of absolute value, $2x-7=4$ or $2x-7=-4$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2x&=11 & \text{or}\quad 2x&=3\\ x&=\dfrac{11}{2}=5\dfrac{1}{2} & \text{or}\quad x&=\dfrac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x=5\dfrac{1}{2} \text{ or } x=\dfrac{3}{2}$$

items.part:
The weight $M$, in kg, of an object on the moon is directly proportional to the weight $E$ of the object on Earth. An astronaut who weighs 90 kg on Earth weighs 16.4 kg on the moon.
Find an equation for converting the weight of an object on Earth to its weight on the moon.
items.sol:
Since $M$ is directly proportional to $E$, $M=kE$.

Substitute $E=90$, $M=16.4$.

$$\begin{aligned} 16.4&=k\times90\\ k&=\dfrac{16.4}{90}=\dfrac{41}{225}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ M=\dfrac{41}{225}E$$

items.part:
The weight $M$, in kg, of an object on the moon is directly proportional to the weight $E$ of the object on Earth. An astronaut who weighs 90 kg on Earth weighs 16.4 kg on the moon.
An astronaut weighs 120 kg on Earth. How much will the astronaut weigh on the moon?
items.sol:
Substitute $E=120$ into $M=\dfrac{41}{225}E$.

$$\begin{aligned} M&=\dfrac{41}{225}\times120\\ &\approx 21.87 \text{ kg (2 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{The astronaut will weigh } 21.87 \text{ kg on the moon.}$$

items.part: Given $\cos 2\theta=0.5$ and $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\le\theta\le 2\pi$, what is the value of $\sin\theta$ ?
items.sol:
Solve $\cos2\theta=\dfrac12$ for $0\le 2\theta\le 4\pi$.

$$2\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}$$

$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$

The only value in $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\le\theta\le2\pi$ is $\theta=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$, so

$$\sin\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=-\dfrac12$$

Alternatively, use the double angle identity $\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1-2\sin^2\theta&=\dfrac12\\ 2\sin^2\theta&=\dfrac12\\ \sin^2\theta&=\dfrac14\\ \sin\theta&=\pm\dfrac12\end{aligned}$$

In the fourth quadrant, $\sin\theta<0$.

$$\therefore\ \sin\theta=-\dfrac12$$

Convert 10 months to years: $t=\dfrac{10}{12}=\dfrac56$.

$$P\left(\dfrac56\right)=\dfrac{500\times\frac56}{2\left(\frac56\right)^2+9}\approx 40.107 \text{ thousand}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{about } 40.11 \text{ thousand (2 d.p.)}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=500t & v&=2t^2+9\\ u'&=500 & v'&=4t\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P'(t)&=\dfrac{(2t^2+9)\times500-500t\times4t}{(2t^2+9)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1000t^2+4500-2000t^2}{(2t^2+9)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{4500-1000t^2}{(2t^2+9)^2}\end{aligned}$$

Substitute $t=12$ into $P'(t)$.

$$\begin{aligned} P'(12)&=\dfrac{4500-1000(12)^2}{(2\times12^2+9)^2}\\ &\approx-1.58\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the population is decreasing at about } 1.58 \text{ thousand per year}$$
items.final: $P'(12)\approx-1.58$; population decreasing at about 1.58 thousand per year

items.part: Find the $x$-values for the points on the graph of $f(x)=-x^3+6x^2$ at which the normal has slope $\dfrac{-1}{9}$.
items.sol:
Differentiate.

$$f'(x)=-3x^2+12x$$

The normal has slope $m_N=-\dfrac19$, so the tangent has slope $m_T=9$.

Set $f'(x)=9$.

$$\begin{aligned} -3x^2+12x&=9\\ 3x^2-12x+9&=0\\ x^2-4x+3&=0\\ (x-3)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x=1 \text{ or } x=3$$
