items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int 5x^2(x^3+1)^{10}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Differentiate $(x^3+1)^{11}$ using the chain rule.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+1)^{11}&=11(x^3+1)^{10}\times3x^2\\ &=33x^2(x^3+1)^{10}\end{aligned}$$

So divide by $33$ and multiply by $5$.

$$\therefore\ \int5x^2(x^3+1)^{10}\,dx=\dfrac{5}{33}(x^3+1)^{11}+c$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following:
$f(x)=e^{-2x}(1+x^2)$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{-2x} & v&=1+x^2\\ u'&=-2e^{-2x} & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=e^{-2x}\times2x+(1+x^2)\times(-2e^{-2x})\\ &=2e^{-2x}\left(x-(1+x^2)\right)\\ &=2e^{-2x}(x-1-x^2)\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following:
$f(x)=\ln\left(\dfrac{x^3+4}{6-x}\right)$
items.sol:
Use the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$ first.

$$f(x)=\ln(x^3+4)-\ln(6-x)$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3+4}-\dfrac{-1}{6-x}\\ &=\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3+4}+\dfrac{1}{6-x}\end{aligned}$$

Differentiating the quotient directly gives the equivalent form

$$f'(x)=\dfrac{2(9x^2-x^3+2)}{(x^3+4)(6-x)}$$

items.part: Show that $f(x)=-x^3-5x+1$ is always decreasing.
items.sol:
Differentiate.

$$f'(x)=-3x^2-5$$

Since $x^2\ge0$, we have $-3x^2\le0$, so $f'(x)\le-5$.

Hence $f'(x)<0$ for all $x$ (the graph of $f'(x)$ is a downward parabola with maximum value $-5$, so it lies below the $x$-axis).

$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is always decreasing.}$$

items.part: Find the area between the curve $y=x^2-3x$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $1\le x\le 5$.
items.sol:
The curve $y=x^2-3x=x(x-3)$ is below the $x$-axis for $1\le x<3$ and above it for $3<x\le5$, so the two regions are found separately.

$$\text{Area}=\left|\displaystyle\int_1^3(x^2-3x)\,dx\right|+\displaystyle\int_3^5(x^2-3x)\,dx$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}\right]_1^3\right|+\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}\right]_3^5\\ &=\left|\left(9-\dfrac{27}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac13-\dfrac32\right)\right|+\left(\dfrac{125}{3}-\dfrac{75}{2}-\left(9-\dfrac{27}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=\left|-\dfrac{10}{3}\right|+\dfrac{26}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{36}{3}\\ &=12 \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The world population was approximately 6.04 billion at the beginning of 2000. It has been estimated that the population is growing exponentially at the rate of 0.016 per year.

The world population $P$ is modelled by the equation $P=P_0e^{kt}$, where $k$ and $P_0$ are constants and $t$ is the amount of time (in years) since the beginning of 2000.
Estimate the world population at the end of 2030.
items.sol:
The model is $P=6.04e^{0.016t}$.

The end of 2030 is 31 years after the beginning of 2000, so $t=31$.

$$\begin{aligned} P_{31}&=6.04e^{0.016\times31}\\ &\approx9.9185\\ &\approx9.919 \text{ billion (3 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The world population was approximately 6.04 billion at the beginning of 2000. It has been estimated that the population is growing exponentially at the rate of 0.016 per year.

The world population $P$ is modelled by the equation $P=P_0e^{kt}$, where $k$ and $P_0$ are constants and $t$ is the amount of time (in years) since the beginning of 2000.
After how many years will the population be double the population in 2000?
items.sol:
The population doubles when $P=2P_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2P_0&=P_0e^{0.016t}\\ 2&=e^{0.016t}\\ \ln2&=\ln e^{0.016t}\\ 0.016t&=\ln2\\ t&=\dfrac{\ln2}{0.016}\\ &\approx43.32 \text{ years}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x^3-x^4$.
Find the coordinates of any stationary points on the curve $y=f(x)$.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-4x^3=0\\ 2x^2(3-2x)&=0\end{aligned}$$

So $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac32$, giving $y=0$ or $y=\dfrac{27}{16}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{stationary points are } (0,0) \text{ and } \left(\dfrac32,\dfrac{27}{16}\right)$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x^3-x^4$.
Determine their nature.
items.sol:
Test the sign of the slope $f'(x)=2x^2(3-2x)$ either side of each stationary point.

\extable{Ts8775_1}

The slope is increasing, stationary, increasing, stationary, decreasing.

At $x=0$ the slope is positive on both sides, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

At $x=\dfrac32$ the slope changes from positive to negative.

$$\therefore\ (0,0) \text{ is a horizontal point of inflection and } \left(\dfrac32,\dfrac{27}{16}\right) \text{ is a maximum turning point.}$$
items.final: $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection and $\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac{27}{16}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x^3-x^4$.
Find any points of inflection on the curve $y=f(x)$.
items.sol:
Points of inflection occur where $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= 12x-12x^2 = 0 \\ 12x(1-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

\extable{Ts8776_1}

The concavity changes at $x=1$, and $y=1$ when $x=1$.

$$\therefore\ (1,1) \text{ is a point of inflection (and } (0,0) \text{ is a horizontal point of inflection, from (b))}$$
items.final: $(1,1)$ is a point of inflection (and $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection)

items.part:
Use the standard normal distribution table on the opposite page, or otherwise, to answer the questions below.
Find $P(-1.93\le z\le 0.79)$.

Use the standard normal distribution table on the opposite page, or otherwise, to answer the questions below.
A large class takes an exam, and the students' scores are normally distributed. The mean score is $\mu=72$ and the standard deviation is $\sigma=4.5$. Students who score in the top 10% receive an A grade. What is the minimum score needed to get an A grade?
items.sol:
An A grade is a score above 90% of scores. From the table, $P(z\le 1.28)\approx 0.9$.

So the minimum score for an A grade has a $z$-score of $1.28$. Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1.28 &= \dfrac{x-72}{4.5} \\ x &= 72+4.5\times 1.28 \\ &= 77.76 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the functions $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{3-2x}$ and $g(x)=1+3x^2$.
Find $f\circ g(x)$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} f\circ g(x) &= f(g(x)) \\ &= f(1+3x^2) \\ &= \sqrt[3]{3-2(1+3x^2)} \\ &= \sqrt[3]{1-6x^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the functions $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{3-2x}$ and $g(x)=1+3x^2$.
Evaluate $g(f'(1))$
items.sol:
Write $f(x)=(3-2x)^{\frac13}$ and differentiate using the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac13(3-2x)^{-\frac23}\times(-2) \\ &= -\dfrac23(3-2x)^{-\frac23} \end{aligned}$$
$$f'(1)=-\dfrac23(3-2)^{-\frac23}=-\dfrac23$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} g\left(f'(1)\right) &= g\left(-\dfrac23\right) \\ &= 1+3\left(-\dfrac23\right)^2 \\ &= 1+\dfrac43 \\ &= \dfrac73 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $a=\log_{\frac{1}{x}}\dfrac{1}{N}$ such that $x>0$ and $N>0$, show that $a=\log_x N$.
items.sol:
Method 1: use the definition of a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \log_{\frac1x}\dfrac1N \\ \left(\dfrac1x\right)^a &= \dfrac1N &&(\text{definition of log}) \\ \dfrac{1}{x^a} &= \dfrac1N \\ x^a &= N \\ a &= \log_x N &&(\text{definition of log}) \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: use the change of base rule.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \log_{\frac1x}\dfrac1N \\ &= \dfrac{\log_x\frac1N}{\log_x\frac1x} &&(\text{change of base}) \\ &= \dfrac{\log_x(N^{-1})}{\log_x(x^{-1})} \\ &= \dfrac{-\log_x N}{-\log_x x} &&(\log_a(b^c)=c\log_a b) \\ &= \dfrac{\log_x N}{1} &&(\log_x x=1) \\ &= \log_x N \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The probability density function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}(x^2+1)$ is defined over the interval $[0,1]$.

Find the value of :
$E(X)$.
items.sol:
Using $E(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^1 x f(x)\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \dfrac13\int_0^1 x(x^2+1)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac13\int_0^1 (x^3+x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac14+\dfrac12\right] \\ &= \dfrac14 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The probability density function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}(x^2+1)$ is defined over the interval $[0,1]$.

Find the value of :
the variance.
items.sol:
Using $\text{Var}(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^2 f(x)\,dx-(E(X))^2$ with $E(X)=\dfrac14$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= \dfrac13\int_0^1 (x^4+x^2)\,dx-\left(\dfrac14\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac{x^5}{5}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1-\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac15+\dfrac13\right]-\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= \dfrac{83}{720} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The probability density function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}(x^2+1)$ is defined over the interval $[0,1]$.

Find the value of :
the standard deviation, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{83}{720}} \\ &\approx 0.34 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling along the $x$ axis is given by $v=2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds .
When is the particle stationary?
items.sol:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-\dfrac{10}{t+2} &= 0 \\ \dfrac{10}{t+2} &= 2 \\ 10 &= 2t+4 \\ 2t &= 6 \\ t &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is stationary at } t=3 \text{ seconds}$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling along the $x$ axis is given by $v=2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds .
What happens to the velocity as $t\to\infty$ ?
items.sol:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{10}{t+2}\to 0$.

So $v\to 2-0=2$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the velocity approaches } 2 \text{ ms}^{-1}$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling along the $x$ axis is given by $v=2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds .
Find the acceleration when the particle is stationary.
items.sol:
Acceleration is $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, with $v=2-10(t+2)^{-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= -10\times(-1)(t+2)^{-2} \\ &= 10(t+2)^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 10(3+2)^{-2} \\ &= 0.4 \text{ ms}^{-2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The velocity of a particle travelling along the $x$ axis is given by $v=2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds .
Find the distance travelled in the first 5 seconds, in exact form.
items.sol:
\exfigure{1293_q32_s1}

The particle moves left from $t=0$ until $t=3$, then turns around and moves right from $t=3$ until $t=5$.

Displacement is the integral of velocity, so the distance travelled in the first 5 seconds is
$$\left|\int_0^3\left(2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\right)dt\right|+\int_3^5\left(2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\right)dt$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= \Big|\big[2t-10\ln(t+2)\big]_0^3\Big|+\big[2t-10\ln(t+2)\big]_3^5 \\ &= \big|6-10\ln 5-(0-10\ln 2)\big|+10-10\ln 7-(6-10\ln 5) \\ &= -6+10\ln 5-10\ln 2+4-10\ln 7+10\ln 5 \\ &= 20\ln 5-10\ln 2-10\ln 7-2 \\ &= 10\ln\left(\dfrac{25}{14}\right)-2 \end{aligned}$$
The last step uses the log laws.

$$\therefore\ \text{distance} = 10\ln\left(\dfrac{25}{14}\right)-2 \text{ m}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^7 f(x)\,dx$, where $f(x)=3-|x-2|$.
items.sol:
Find the $x$-intercepts by solving $|x-2|=3$.

So $x-2=3$ giving $x=5$, or $x-2=-3$ giving $x=-1$.

The graph of $f(x)=3-|x-2|$ has vertex $(2,3)$, $y$-intercept $1$ and $x$-intercepts $-1$ and $5$.

The integral is the signed area: a trapezoid from $x=0$ to $x=2$, a triangle above the axis from $x=2$ to $x=5$, and a triangle below the axis from $x=5$ to $x=7$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^7\left(3-|x-2|\right)dx &= \dfrac12\times 2(1+3)+\dfrac12\times 3\times 3-\dfrac12\times 2\times 2 \\ &= 4+\dfrac92-2 \\ &= 6\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Sketch $f(x)=-3\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+2$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.
Hence, state the number of solutions to the equation $-3\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+2=0.5x+1$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.
items.sol:
Draw the line $y=0.5x+1$ on the same axes as the curve from part (a). It meets the curve 3 times.

$$\therefore\ 3 \text{ solutions}$$
$$AB=\dfrac{8}{\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$$

Write $AB=8(\sin\theta)^{-1}+(\cos\theta)^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dAB}{d\theta} &= -8(\sin\theta)^{-2}\cos\theta-(\cos\theta)^{-2}\cdot(-\sin\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{-8\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{-8\cos^3\theta+\sin^3\theta}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dAB}{d\theta}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} -8\cos^3\theta+\sin^3\theta &= 0 \\ \sin^3\theta &= 8\cos^3\theta \\ \tan^3\theta &= 8 \\ \tan\theta &= 2 \\ \theta &\approx 63.43^\circ \end{aligned}$$

\extable{Ts8797_1}

The gradient goes from negative to positive, so this is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} AB &= \dfrac{8}{\frac{2}{\sqrt5}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\sqrt5}} = 4\sqrt5+\sqrt5=5\sqrt5 \\ &\approx 11.18 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the shortest plank is about } 11.18 \text{ m}$$

items.part: Neville lives in a town where one third of the days are rainy days. If it is a rainy day, the chance of heavy traffic is $\dfrac{1}{2}$. If it is not a rainy day, the chance of heavy traffic is $\dfrac{1}{4}$. If it is a rainy day and there is heavy traffic, there is a 50% chance that Neville will arrive late to work. On the other hand , the probability of being late is reduced to $\dfrac{1}{8}$ if it is not a rainy day and there is no heavy traffic. In other situations, the probability of Neville being late to work is 0.35. On a random day, Neville arrives late to work. What is the probability that it is a rainy day?
items.sol:
\exfigure{1293_q36_s1}

Let $R$ be a rainy day and $L$ be arriving late. Using conditional probability, $P(R\mid L)=\dfrac{P(L\cap R)}{P(L)}$, with the branches from the tree diagram:
$$P(R\mid L)=\dfrac{\frac13\times\frac12\times\frac12+\frac13\times\frac12\times\frac{35}{100}}{\frac13\times\frac12\times\frac12+\frac13\times\frac12\times\frac{35}{100}+\frac23\times\frac14\times\frac{35}{100}+\frac23\times\frac34\times\frac18}$$
$$\therefore\ P(R\mid L)=\dfrac{34}{63}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x+3}{x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Split the fraction into separate terms.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{2x+3}{x^2}\,dx&=\int\left(\dfrac{2}{x}+\dfrac{3}{x^2}\right)dx\\ &=\int\left(2x^{-1}+3x^{-2}\right)dx\\ &=2\ln x+\dfrac{3x^{-1}}{-1}+c\\ &=2\ln x-\dfrac{3}{x}+c \end{aligned}$$

For $|u|>a$, either $u>a$ or $u<-a$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-1&>5 & \text{or}\quad 2x-1&<-5\\ x&>3 & x&<-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x>3 \text{ or } x<-2$$

items.part: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=\ln(2x-5)$ at $x=3$.
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$y'=\dfrac{2}{2x-5}$$
At $x=3$ the gradient is
$$m=\dfrac{2}{6-5}=2$$
When $x=3$:
$$y=\ln 1=0$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=2(x-3)\\ y&=2x-6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=2x-6$$

Using the cosine rule with the $50^\circ$ angle between the sides $8$ and $10$:
$$\begin{aligned} w^2&=8^2+10^2-2\times 8\times 10\cos 50^\circ\\ &=64+100-160\cos 50^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ w\approx 7.8 \text{ cm (2 s.f.)}$$

items.sol:

The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and tangent is negative in the 2nd and 4th quadrants.

Probabilities on each branch: the first draw is Green with probability $\dfrac{8}{14}$. After a White first draw, 8 green balls remain among 13, so Green has probability $\dfrac{8}{13}$.

Two different colours means White then Green, or Green then White.

items.part:
On his 1st birthday, Timmy was given \$5 by his Aunty Ruth. On each subsequent birthday, Aunty Ruth gave Timmy \$2 more than the previous year.
How much did Aunty Ruth give Timmy on his 20th birthday?
items.sol:
The amounts form an arithmetic sequence with $a=5$ and $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{20}&=a+(n-1)d\\ &=5+(20-1)\times 2\\ &=5+38\\ &=43 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Timmy was given } \$43.$$

items.part:
On his 1st birthday, Timmy was given \$5 by his Aunty Ruth. On each subsequent birthday, Aunty Ruth gave Timmy \$2 more than the previous year.
If Timmy saves the money every year, how old will he be when he has received over \$100 in total?
items.sol:
The total after $n$ birthdays is the sum of the arithmetic series with $a=5$, $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)>100\\ \dfrac{n}{2}\left(10+2(n-1)\right)&>100\\ n(n+4)&>100 \end{aligned}$$
By trial and error, $n>8$.

So he has received over \$100 after his 9th birthday.
$$\therefore\ \text{Timmy will be } 9.$$

items.sol:

items.part:
The bank has provided Jocelyn with the following two brief annuity tables to help her make financial decisions.

\exfigure{1295_q19_1}

Jocelyn pays \$5000 per annum into her superannuation scheme, which pays $4\%$ per annum, compounded yearly.
Sammy wins the lottery and invests all \$80\,000 at $4\%$ per annum for $20$ years, compounded annually. How much would Jocelyn need to increase her annual repayments to match Sammy's payout after $20$ years? Give your answer correct to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
Method 1 (future value table): the payment must satisfy
$$\begin{aligned} \text{payment}\times 29.7781&\ge 80\,000\times(1.04)^{20}\\ \text{payment}&\ge \$5887 \end{aligned}$$
Method 2 (present value table):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{payment}&\ge 80\,000\div 13.5903\\ &=\$5887 \end{aligned}$$
The increase is $5887-5000$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Jocelyn needs to pay } \$887 \text{ more each year.}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}$.
Determine algebraically whether the function is even, odd, or neither.
items.sol:
Find $f(-x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=\dfrac{-x}{1+(-x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-x}{1+x^2}\\ &=-f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is odd.}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}$.
Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-x^2}{\left(1+x^2\right)^2}$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=1+x^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{1\times(1+x^2)-x(2x)}{(1+x^2)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1+x^2-2x^2}{(1+x^2)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1-x^2}{(1+x^2)^2}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}$.
Determine the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and verify their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-x^2&=0\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $y=\dfrac12$; when $x=-1$, $y=-\dfrac12$.

\extable{Ts8826_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative at $x=1$, and from negative to positive at $x=-1$.

Therefore $\left(1,\dfrac12\right)$ is a local maximum and $\left(-1,-\dfrac12\right)$ is a local minimum.
items.final: $\left(1,\tfrac12\right)$ is a local maximum and $\left(-1,-\tfrac12\right)$ is a local minimum

items.part:
A concert is to be held. The number of people expected to attend $N$ varies inversely with distance $D$ metres from the concert to the city centre.

If the distance from the city centre is $300$ m then $6000$ people are expected to attend, as shown below.

\exfigure{1295_q23_1}
Find an equation for the graph in terms of $N$ and $D$ in the form $N=\dfrac{k}{D}$, where $k$ is a constant.
items.sol:
Substitute $D=300$, $N=6000$ into $N=\dfrac{k}{D}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6000&=\dfrac{k}{300}\\ k&=1\,800\,000\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ N=\dfrac{1\,800\,000}{D}$$

items.part:
A concert is to be held. The number of people expected to attend $N$ varies inversely with distance $D$ metres from the concert to the city centre.

If the distance from the city centre is $300$ m then $6000$ people are expected to attend, as shown below.

\exfigure{1295_q23_1}
The concert needs an attendance of at least $2000$ in order to make a profit. Find the maximum distance the concert can be from the city centre and still make a profit.
items.sol:
The concert makes a profit when $N\ge2000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1\,800\,000}{D}&\ge2000\\ D&\le900\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum distance is } 900 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
A concert is to be held. The number of people expected to attend $N$ varies inversely with distance $D$ metres from the concert to the city centre.

If the distance from the city centre is $300$ m then $6000$ people are expected to attend, as shown below.

\exfigure{1295_q23_1}
At a point on the graph, the number of people attending is decreasing at the rate of $5$ people per $4$ metres. Find the value of $D$ for this point.
items.sol:
Since $N=\dfrac{k}{D}$, differentiating with respect to $D$ gives
$$\dfrac{dN}{dD}=-\dfrac{k}{D^2}$$
The rate is $-\dfrac{5}{4}=-1.25$ people per metre, so
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=\dfrac{-k}{dN/dD}\\ &=\dfrac{-1\,800\,000}{-1.25}\\ &=1\,440\,000\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ D=1200 \text{ m}\ (=1.2 \text{ km})$$

items.part:
A experimenter records the following data:

$4\quad 6\quad 8\quad 8\quad 9\quad 10\quad 12\quad 12\quad 17\quad 24$
Use the standard criterion for outliers on your reference sheet to determine any outliers in the data.
items.sol:
From the ordered data, $Q_1=8$ and $Q_3=12$.
$$\begin{aligned} IQR&=12-8\\ &=4\end{aligned}$$
An outlier is a value above $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$ or below $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times4&=18\\ Q_1-1.5\times4&=2\end{aligned}$$
Only $24$ lies outside the interval from $2$ to $18$.

$$\therefore\ 24 \text{ is an outlier}$$

items.part:
A experimenter records the following data:

$4\quad 6\quad 8\quad 8\quad 9\quad 10\quad 12\quad 12\quad 17\quad 24$
Write down a dataset with the same variance but a mean of $15$.
items.sol:
Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean but leaves the variance unchanged. The mean is $11$, so add $4$ to every value:
$$8,\ 10,\ 12,\ 12,\ 13,\ 14,\ 16,\ 16,\ 21,\ 28$$

The probabilities must sum to $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2m+(1-8m)+4m+0.1&=1\\ -2m+1.1&=1\\ m&=0.05\end{aligned}$$
Then $p(x)$ is $0.1,\ 0.6,\ 0.2,\ 0.1$ for $x=1,2,3,4$, all non-negative.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=1\times0.1+2\times0.6+3\times0.2+4\times0.1\\ &=0.1+1.2+0.6+0.4\\ &=2.3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=0.05 \text{ and } E(X)=2.3$$

items.part:
A $20$ kg block of a radioactive isotope is decaying, and the amount $M$ kg remaining after $t$ years is given by the equation

$$M=20e^{-0.05t}$$
Find the mass of the isotope remaining after $2$ years. Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} M&=20e^{-0.05\times2}\\ &=20e^{-0.1}\\ &\approx18.1 \text{ kg}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A $20$ kg block of a radioactive isotope is decaying, and the amount $M$ kg remaining after $t$ years is given by the equation

$$M=20e^{-0.05t}$$
How long until half the isotope has decayed? Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.
items.sol:
Half the isotope has decayed when $M=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10&=20e^{-0.05t}\\ e^{-0.05t}&=\dfrac12\\ -0.05t&=\ln\dfrac12\\ t&=\dfrac{\ln2}{0.05}\\ &\approx13.9\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after } 13.9 \text{ years}$$

items.part:
A $20$ kg block of a radioactive isotope is decaying, and the amount $M$ kg remaining after $t$ years is given by the equation

$$M=20e^{-0.05t}$$
Show that $M$ satisfies the equation $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.05M$ and hence find the rate of decay when $5$ kg of the isotope remains. Give your answer correct to $2$ significant figures.
items.sol:
Differentiating $M=20e^{-0.05t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt}&=20\times(-0.05)e^{-0.05t}\\ &=-0.05\left(20e^{-0.05t}\right)\\ &=-0.05M\end{aligned}$$
When $M=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt}&=-0.05\times5\\ &=-0.25\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the rate of decay is } 0.25 \text{ kg/year}$$

items.part: Sketch the graphs of $y=10\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}x$ and $y=x$ for $0\le x\le 12$ in the space provided below. Mark the point of intersection at $(5,5)$.
items.sol: \exfigure{1295_q27_s1}

items.part: Find a simplified exact expression for the area bounded by the two graphs for $0\le x\le 5$.
items.sol:
The graphs meet at $(5,5)$, with the sine curve above the line for $0<x<5$, so the area is
$$\int_0^5\left(10\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{6}-x\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} &=\left[-\dfrac{60}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{6}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^5\\ &=\left(-\dfrac{60}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}-\dfrac{25}{2}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{60}{\pi}-0\right)\\ &=\dfrac{60}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-\dfrac{25}{2}+\dfrac{60}{\pi}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{30\sqrt3+60}{\pi}-\dfrac{25}{2}$$

A pupil is selected at random.
Find the probability that the pupil is right-handed.
items.sol: $$P(\text{right-handed})=\dfrac{154}{200}=\dfrac{77}{100}=0.77$$

items.part:
Data from $200$ pupils is tabulated below. The data gathered indicates which hand they write with and their favourite colour.

\extable{1295_q28_t1}

A pupil is selected at random.
Find the probability that the pupil prefers green, given that they are left-handed.
items.sol: $$P(\text{green}\mid\text{left})=\dfrac{17}{46}$$

items.part:
Data from $200$ pupils is tabulated below. The data gathered indicates which hand they write with and their favourite colour.

\extable{1295_q28_t1}

A pupil is selected at random.
Are the events of being left-handed and preferring green independent? Justify your answer with a calculation.
items.sol:
Events are independent if $P(\text{green}\mid\text{left})=P(\text{green})$.
$$P(\text{green})=\dfrac{61}{200},\qquad P(\text{green}\mid\text{left})=\dfrac{17}{46}$$
These differ, so the events are dependent.

Alternatively, independence needs $P(\text{green and left})=P(\text{green})\times P(\text{left})$.
$$P(\text{green and left})=\dfrac{17}{200},\qquad P(\text{green})\times P(\text{left})=\dfrac{61}{200}\times\dfrac{46}{200}$$
These differ, so the events are dependent.

items.part:
Janice deposits \$5000 into her savings account every year on January 1. During the year, the account receives compound interest of $6\%$ per annum, where interest is added to her account at the end of each year.

Let $J_n$ be the value of Janice's account immediately after her $n$th investment.
Show that $J_2=\$10\,300$.

Janice deposits \$5000 into her savings account every year on January 1. During the year, the account receives compound interest of $6\%$ per annum, where interest is added to her account at the end of each year.

Let $J_n$ be the value of Janice's account immediately after her $n$th investment.
Show that

$$J_n=\dfrac{250\,000\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{3}$$
items.sol:
Let $M=5000$ be the annual deposit. Each earlier deposit is multiplied by $1.06$ for each further year.
$$\begin{aligned} J_2&=1.06M+M\\ J_3&=(1.06M+M)\times1.06+M\\ &=M+1.06M+1.06^2M\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$J_n=M+1.06M+1.06^2M+\dots+1.06^{n-1}M$$
This is a geometric series with $n$ terms, first term $M$ and $r=1.06$.
$$\begin{aligned} J_n&=\dfrac{M\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{1.06-1}\\ &=\dfrac{5000\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{0.06}\\ &=\dfrac{250\,000\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{3}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Janice deposits \$5000 into her savings account every year on January 1. During the year, the account receives compound interest of $6\%$ per annum, where interest is added to her account at the end of each year.

Let $J_n$ be the value of Janice's account immediately after her $n$th investment.
Determine the minimum number of years until Janice's account contains \$100\,000.
items.sol:
Solve $J_n=100\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100\,000&=\dfrac{250\,000\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{3}\\ \dfrac{30}{25}&=1.06^n-1\\ 1.06^n&=2.2\end{aligned}$$
Taking logarithms,
$$\begin{aligned} n&=\log_{1.06}2.2\\ &=\dfrac{\log2.2}{\log1.06}\\ &\approx13.5\end{aligned}$$
$n$ must be a whole number of instalments, so round up.

$$\therefore\ n=14,\ \text{on the payment of the 14th instalment, at the start of the 14th year}$$

items.part:
Let $y=xe^{x^2-3x}$.
Show that

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\left(2x^2-3x+1\right)e^{x^2-3x}$$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{x^2-3x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=(2x-3)e^{x^2-3x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=1\times e^{x^2-3x}+x(2x-3)e^{x^2-3x}\\ &=\left(1+2x^2-3x\right)e^{x^2-3x}\\ &=\left(2x^2-3x+1\right)e^{x^2-3x}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Let $y=xe^{x^2-3x}$.
For what values of $x$ is $y$ decreasing?
items.sol:
$y$ is decreasing where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}<0$. First find where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x^2-3x+1&=0\\ (2x-1)(x-1)&=0\\ x&=\dfrac12,\ 1\end{aligned}$$
$e^{x^2-3x}>0$, so the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is the sign of the quadratic. It is an upright parabola, so it is negative between its roots.

$$\therefore\ y \text{ is decreasing for } \dfrac12<x<1$$

items.part:
A company is manufacturing barrels with a constant volume specified by the customer. The barrels are open cylinders with a circular base but no top. Each barrel has height $h$ metres, radius $r$ metres and volume $V$ cubic metres.

In the manufacturing process, the circular base and the material for the curved side are cut from flat sheets of metal, which are then folded to form the open cylinder. The metal used to construct a barrel is shown by the total area in the diagram below. After the circular base is removed, the remaining metal is wasted.

\exfigure{1295_q31_1}
Show that the area of the sheet metal required to construct a barrel is given by

$$A=\dfrac{2V}{r}+4r^2$$
items.sol:
The metal is a square of side $2r$ plus a rectangle of dimensions $2\pi r$ by $h$ for the curved side.
$$A=(2r)^2+2\pi rh$$
The volume of the cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$, so $h=\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}$. Substituting,
$$\begin{aligned} A&=4r^2+2\pi r\times\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}\\ &=4r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A company is manufacturing barrels with a constant volume specified by the customer. The barrels are open cylinders with a circular base but no top. Each barrel has height $h$ metres, radius $r$ metres and volume $V$ cubic metres.

In the manufacturing process, the circular base and the material for the curved side are cut from flat sheets of metal, which are then folded to form the open cylinder. The metal used to construct a barrel is shown by the total area in the diagram below. After the circular base is removed, the remaining metal is wasted.

\exfigure{1295_q31_1}
Find the minimum area of metal $A$ required to make a barrel. Your result will depend on $V$.
items.sol:
Differentiate $A=\dfrac{2V}{r}+4r^2$ and set $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=-\dfrac{2V}{r^2}+8r=0\\ \dfrac{2V}{r^2}&=8r\\ r^3&=\dfrac{V}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}&=\dfrac{4V}{r^3}+8\\ &=\dfrac{4V\times4}{V}+8\\ &=24>0\end{aligned}$$
The curve is concave up, so this is a local minimum.

The minimum area is
$$\begin{aligned} A&=4r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}\\ &=\dfrac{4r^3+2V}{r}\\ &=\dfrac{3V}{r}\qquad(\text{since } 4r^3=V)\\ &=\dfrac{3V}{\sqrt[3]{V/4}}\\ &=3\sqrt[3]{4}\,V^{\frac23}\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A company's new logo is the region bounded by $y=\sin x$ and $y=x\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. This region is shown shaded in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1295_q32_1}

Calculate the area of the logo, correct to $2$ decimal places.

You may wish to assume the result

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\cos x\right)=\cos x-x\sin x.$$
items.sol:
\exfigure{1295_q32_s1}

From the hint, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)=\cos x-x\sin x$. Integrating both sides,
$$x\cos x=\sin x-\int x\sin x\,dx$$
$$\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x$$
The curves meet where $x\sin x=\sin x$, that is $x=1$ (for $0<x<\pi$). For $0<x<1$, $\sin x>x\sin x$; for $1<x<\pi$, $x\sin x>\sin x$.

First region:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=\int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx\\ &=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x+x\cos x\Big]_0^1\\ &=(-\cos1-\sin1+\cos1)-(-1)\\ &=1-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
Second region:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=\int_1^{\pi}(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx\\ &=\Big[\sin x-x\cos x+\cos x\Big]_1^{\pi}\\ &=(\pi-1)-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
Total area:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=A_1+A_2\\ &=1-\sin1+\pi-1-\sin1\\ &=\pi-2\sin1\\ &\approx1.46 \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

items.part: Simplify $\dfrac{x}{x^2-4}-\dfrac{4}{x-2}$
items.sol:
Factorise $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$ and use the common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{x^2-4}-\dfrac{4}{x-2} &= \dfrac{x}{(x-2)(x+2)}-\dfrac{4}{x-2} \\ &= \dfrac{x-4(x+2)}{(x-2)(x+2)} \\ &= \dfrac{x-4x-8}{(x-2)(x+2)} \\ &= \dfrac{-3x-8}{(x-2)(x+2)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Rationalise the denominator of $\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{5}-2}$
items.sol:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{7}{\sqrt5-2} &= \dfrac{7}{\sqrt5-2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt5+2}{\sqrt5+2} \\ &= \dfrac{7(\sqrt5+2)}{5-4} \\ &= 7(\sqrt5+2) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(0,-3)$ and has an angle of inclination of $30^\circ$. Leave your answer in gradient-intercept form.
items.sol:
The gradient is the tangent of the angle of inclination.
$$m=\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$$
The line passes through $(0,-3)$, so the $y$-intercept is $-3$.
$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}x-3$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$
$f(x)=\tan 7x$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule for $\tan ax$:
$$f'(x)=7\sec^2 7x$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following with respect to $x$
$f(x)=\ln(x^2+2)$
items.sol:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+2}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int(4x+3)^9\,dx$
items.sol:
Reverse the chain rule, dividing by the derivative $4$ of the inner function.
$$\begin{aligned} \int(4x+3)^9\,dx &= \dfrac{(4x+3)^{10}}{10\times 4}+c \\ &= \dfrac{(4x+3)^{10}}{40}+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of students absent from Year 12 for the past nine days was as follows:

14, 17, 13, 16, 17, 12, 11, 28, 19
Find the standard deviation. Answer correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
Using the statistics mode of a calculator with the nine values:
$$\sigma_x\approx 4.8$$

items.part:
The number of students absent from Year 12 for the past nine days was as follows:

14, 17, 13, 16, 17, 12, 11, 28, 19
Find the lower quartile and the upper quartile
items.sol:
Ordered data: $11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 17, 19, 28$.

The median is $Q_2=16$. The lower half is $11, 12, 13, 14$, so $Q_1=\dfrac{12+13}{2}=12.5$. The upper half is $17, 17, 19, 28$, so $Q_3=\dfrac{17+19}{2}=18$.

The lower quartile is $12.5$ and the upper quartile is $18$.

items.part:
The number of students absent from Year 12 for the past nine days was as follows:

14, 17, 13, 16, 17, 12, 11, 28, 19
Find the interquartile range
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3-Q_1 \\ &= 18-12.5 \\ &= 5.5 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Solve the equation $\tan^2 x=3$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$
items.sol:
Take square roots of both sides.
$$\tan x=\pm\sqrt3$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and $\tan x$ takes both signs, so there is a solution in each quadrant.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$

items.part:
There are fifteen marbles in a jar. Five of the marbles are red, five are blue and five are yellow.

Ron randomly selects two marbles and puts them in his pocket.
What is the probability that the two marbles are red?
items.sol:
Selecting without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(2\text{ red}) &= \dfrac{5}{15}\times\dfrac{4}{14} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{21} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
There are fifteen marbles in a jar. Five of the marbles are red, five are blue and five are yellow.

Ron randomly selects two marbles and puts them in his pocket.
What is the probability that the two marbles are the same colour?
items.sol:
Each colour has five marbles, so each colour has the same probability as red.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same colour}) &= P(RR)+P(BB)+P(YY) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{21}+\dfrac{2}{21}+\dfrac{2}{21} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{7} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the following continuous probability distribution

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3x^2}{511} & \text{for } 1\le x\le 8\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Find $P(X=5)$
items.sol:
For a continuous distribution, the probability at a single point is zero.
$$P(X=5)=0$$

items.part:
For the following continuous probability distribution

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3x^2}{511} & \text{for } 1\le x\le 8\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Find $P(X\le 5)$
items.sol:
Integrate the density from $1$ to $5$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 5) &= \int_1^5 \dfrac{3x^2}{511}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{511}\Big[x^3\Big]_1^5 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{511}\left(5^3-1^3\right) \\ &= \dfrac{124}{511} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
For the following continuous probability distribution

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3x^2}{511} & \text{for } 1\le x\le 8\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Find $P(X>5)$
items.sol:
Using the complement of part (b):
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>5) &= 1-P(X\le 5) \\ &= 1-\dfrac{124}{511} \\ &= \dfrac{387}{511} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A motorist drives 35 km from Town $A$ to Town $B$ on a bearing of $030^\circ T$.

He then drives 55 km to Town $C$ that is on a bearing of $135^\circ T$ from Town $B$.

\exfigure{1297_q20_1}
Find the size of $\angle ABC$
items.sol:
The angle at $B$ is made up of the angle between $BA$ and the north line at $B$, and the angle between the north line and $BC$.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ABC &= 30^\circ+\left(180^\circ-135^\circ\right) \\ &= 75^\circ \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A motorist drives 35 km from Town $A$ to Town $B$ on a bearing of $030^\circ T$.

He then drives 55 km to Town $C$ that is on a bearing of $135^\circ T$ from Town $B$.

\exfigure{1297_q20_1}
Find the distance between $A$ and $C$ to the nearest kilometre.
items.sol:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$ with $\angle ABC=75^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= 35^2+55^2-2\times 35\times 55\cos 75^\circ \\ &= 3253.54\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} AC &\approx 57 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ AC = 57 \text{ km (to the nearest km)}$$

items.part:
In a class of 23 students, on Sunday night 12 watched The Office, 13 watched Stranger Things while 7 watched both.
Find the probability that a student chosen at random watched neither
items.sol:
Only The Office: $12-7=5$. Only Stranger Things: $13-7=6$. Both: $7$.

Watched at least one: $5+7+6=18$, so neither: $23-18=5$.
$$P(\text{neither})=\dfrac{5}{23}$$

items.part:
In a class of 23 students, on Sunday night 12 watched The Office, 13 watched Stranger Things while 7 watched both.
Find the probability that they watched The Office, given that they watched Stranger Things
items.sol:
Of the $13$ who watched Stranger Things, $7$ also watched The Office.
$$P(\text{The Office}\mid\text{Stranger Things})=\dfrac{7}{13}$$

items.part: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(1-\sec^2\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx$
items.sol:
Using $\displaystyle\int \sec^2 \dfrac{x}{2}\,dx = 2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(1-\sec^2\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx &= \left[x-2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \left[\dfrac{\pi}{3}-2\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]-\left[0-2\tan 0\right] \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=4+3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)$

State the amplitude
items.sol:
For $f(x)=a+b\cos(nx)$ the amplitude is $|b|$.
$$\text{Amplitude}=3$$

items.part: Simplify $\dfrac{\log(a^3b^2)-\log(ab^2)}{\log\sqrt{a}}$
items.sol:
Using $\log A-\log B=\log\dfrac{A}{B}$ in the numerator, and $\sqrt{a}=a^{\frac{1}{2}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\log(a^3b^2)-\log(ab^2)}{\log\sqrt{a}} &= \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{a^3b^2}{ab^2}\right)}{\log a^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\ &= \dfrac{\log(a^2)}{\log a^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\log a}{\frac{1}{2}\log a} \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

The curve crosses the $x$-axis where $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-2x-8 &= 0 \\ (x-4)(x+2) &= 0 \\ x &= 4 \text{ or } x=-2 \end{aligned}$$
From the diagram, $A$ is the positive intercept.
$$\therefore\ A=(4,0)$$

The curve is below the $x$-axis for $0\le x\le 4$ and above it for $4\le x\le 6$, so the two areas are found separately.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4 (x^2-2x-8)\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2-8x\right]_0^4 \\ &= -\dfrac{80}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_4^6 (x^2-2x-8)\,dx &= -12-\left(-\dfrac{80}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{44}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \left|-\dfrac{80}{3}\right|+\dfrac{44}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{124}{3} \\ &= 41\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+6$
Show that stationary points occur at $(-1,11)$ and $(3,-21)$ and determine their nature
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2-6x-9 \\ 3x^2-6x-9 &= 0 \\ 3(x^2-2x-3) &= 0 \\ 3(x-3)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=3$ or $x=-1$.

When $x=3$, $y=-21$. When $x=-1$, $y=11$.

The second derivative decides the nature.
$$f''(x)=6x-6$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(3) &= 12>0 &&\text{minimum turning point at } (3,-21) \\ f''(-1) &= -12<0 &&\text{maximum turning point at } (-1,11) \end{aligned}$$
items.final: Minimum turning point at $(3,-21)$; maximum turning point at $(-1,11)$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+6$
Find the coordinates of any points of inflexion
items.sol:
Possible points of inflexion occur where $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-6 &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $y=-5$, so the possible point is $(1,-5)$.

Test the concavity either side of $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -6<0 &&\text{concave down} \\ f''(1) &= 0 \\ f''(2) &= 6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflexion.
$$\therefore\ (1,-5)\text{ is a point of inflexion}$$

items.part:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+6$
Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$, labelling the stationary points and the $y$-intercept.

Do not attempt to find the $x$-intercepts.
items.sol: \exfigure{1297_q27_s1}

items.part: Differentiate $\log_3 x^3$
items.sol:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_3 x^3=\dfrac{\ln x^3}{\ln 3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\ln x^3}{\ln 3}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3}\cdot\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{x\ln 3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Determine the equation of a curve given by $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=18x+4$ if it is known that $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point on the curve.
items.sol:
Integrate once.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=9x^2+4x+c$$
The point $(1,-2)$ is stationary, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ when $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9+4+c &= 0 \\ c &= -13 \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=9x^2+4x-13$.

Integrate again.
$$y=3x^3+2x^2-13x+C$$
Substitute $x=1$, $y=-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} -2 &= 3+2-13+C \\ C &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=3x^3+2x^2-13x+6$$

items.part: Sketch $y=3\cos x$ in the domain $-2\pi\le x\le 2\pi$
items.sol: \exfigure{1297_q31_s1}

items.part: Hence or otherwise, how many solutions are there to the equation $3\cos x=1-x$?
items.sol:
Draw $y=1-x$ on the same axes as $y=3\cos x$.

A large tank of liquid which contains $L$ litres of a toxic chemical is being drained.

The amount of chemical in the tank over time $t$ minutes, is given by:

$$L=110(20-t)^2$$
At what rate is the chemical draining out of the tank after 5 minutes?
items.sol:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} L &= 110(20-t)^2 \\ \dfrac{dL}{dt} &= 220(20-t)\times(-1) \\ &= -220(20-t) \end{aligned}$$
When $t=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dL}{dt} &= -220(20-5) \\ &= -3300 \text{ L/min} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A factory is producing laptops. The annual production, $M$ laptops at time $t$ years, is given by:

$M=M_0e^{kt}$

Initially the production at the factory was 2000 laptops per annum.

Five years later it had increased to 3200 laptops per annum.
Find the values of $M_0$ and $k$ (Answer correct to three decimal places).
items.sol:
When $t=0$, $M=2000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2000 &= M_0e^0 \\ M_0 &= 2000 \end{aligned}$$
So $M=2000e^{kt}$. When $t=5$, $M=3200$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3200 &= 2000e^{5k} \\ 1.6 &= e^{5k} \\ \ln 1.6 &= 5k \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln 1.6}{5} \\ &\approx 0.094 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ M_0=2000,\quad k\approx 0.094$$

items.part:

Initially the production at the factory was 2000 laptops per annum.

Five years later it had increased to 3200 laptops per annum.
How many years will it take for the production to double its original output? Answer correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
The original output is 2000, so double is $M=4000$. Use $k=\dfrac{\ln 1.6}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4000 &= 2000e^{\frac{\ln 1.6}{5}t} \\ 2 &= e^{\frac{\ln 1.6}{5}t} \\ \ln 2 &= \dfrac{\ln 1.6}{5}t \\ t &= 7.37\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 7.4 \text{ years}$$

The graphs intersect at $x=0$ and $x=K$ for $x\ge 0$.
By solving the two equations simultaneously, show that $K=3\sqrt{2}$
items.sol:
The graphs meet where the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-9x &= 9x \\ x^3-18x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-18) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x^2=18$, giving $x=\pm\sqrt{18}=\pm3\sqrt{2}$.

Since $K>0$, we have $K=3\sqrt{2}$.

items.part: Show that $\dfrac{1}{2x-5}-\dfrac{1}{2x+5}=\dfrac{10}{4x^2-25}$
items.sol:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{2x-5}-\dfrac{1}{2x+5} \\ &= \dfrac{(2x+5)-(2x-5)}{(2x-5)(2x+5)} \\ &= \dfrac{10}{4x^2-25} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Hence find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{4x^2-25}$

Leave your answer in simplest form.
items.sol:
By part (a), $\dfrac{10}{4x^2-25}=\dfrac{1}{2x-5}-\dfrac{1}{2x+5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{dx}{4x^2-25} &= \dfrac{1}{10}\int\dfrac{10\,dx}{4x^2-25} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{10}\int\left(\dfrac{1}{2x-5}-\dfrac{1}{2x+5}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{10}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2x-5)-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2x+5)\right]+c \\ &= \dfrac{1}{20}\ln\left(\dfrac{2x-5}{2x+5}\right)+c \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A particle is moving in a straight line and its velocity is given by:

$$v=1-2\sin 2t \text{ for } 0\le t\le\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and $t$ in seconds.
At what time(s) is particle's acceleration zero?
items.sol:
The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity.
$$a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-4\cos 2t$$
Set $a=0$ for $0\le t\le\pi$, so $\cos 2t=0$ with $0\le 2t\le 2\pi$.
$$2t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$

items.part:

$$v=1-2\sin 2t \text{ for } 0\le t\le\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and $t$ in seconds.
When is the particle at rest?
items.sol:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-2\sin 2t &= 0 \\ \sin 2t &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le 2t\le 2\pi$:
$$2t=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

A particle is moving in a straight line and its velocity is given by:

$$v=1-2\sin 2t \text{ for } 0\le t\le\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and $t$ in seconds.
Initially the particle is at the origin.

Find the displacement function $x$ as a function of $t$
items.sol:
Integrate the velocity to find the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int(1-2\sin 2t)\,dt \\ &= t+\cos 2t+c \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$ and $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 0+\cos 0+c \\ c &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=t+\cos 2t-1$$

items.part:
\exfigure{1297_q40_1}

The angle at the centre $C$ of a circle of radius 2 cm is $\pi\theta$ radians, $0<\theta<2$, as shown on the diagram above.
Show that the volume of the cone is given by $V=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\sqrt{4\theta^4-\theta^6}$

(The formula for the volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2\sqrt{l^2-r^2}$ where $l$ is the slant height)
items.sol:
The slant height of the cone is the radius of the sector, so $l=2$, and $r=\theta$ from part (b).
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2\sqrt{l^2-r^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\theta^2\sqrt{2^2-\theta^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}\sqrt{\theta^4(4-\theta^2)} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}\sqrt{4\theta^4-\theta^6} \end{aligned}$$

Write $V=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\left(4\theta^4-\theta^6\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The maximum occurs where $V'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} V' &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}\left(4\theta^4-\theta^6\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(16\theta^3-6\theta^5\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi\left(16\theta^3-6\theta^5\right)}{6\sqrt{4\theta^4-\theta^6}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $V'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 16\theta^3-6\theta^5 &= 0 \\ 2\theta^3(8-3\theta^2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $\theta\ne 0$, $\theta^2=\dfrac{8}{3}$.
$$\theta=\sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}}\approx 1.63 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$
Nature test, using the sign of $V'$:
$$\begin{aligned} V'(1) &\approx 3.02>0 &&\text{increasing} \\ V'(1.63) &= 0 && \\ V'(1.8) &\approx -3.72<0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative.
$$\therefore\ \text{the volume is a maximum when } \theta\approx 1.63$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following:
$y=x^3\cos x$
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x^3 & v &= \cos x \\ u' &= 3x^2 & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= u'v + uv' \\ &= 3x^2\cos x - x^3\sin x \\ &= x^2(3\cos x - x\sin x) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Differentiate the following:
$y=\dfrac{(1-x)^3}{x^2}$ and show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ may be expressed as $-\dfrac{(x+2)(1-x)^2}{x^3}$
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= (1-x)^3 & v &= x^2 \\ u' &= -3(1-x)^2 & v' &= 2x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{-3x^2(1-x)^2 - 2x(1-x)^3}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{x(1-x)^2\left[-3x - 2(1-x)\right]}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{(1-x)^2\left[-3x - 2 + 2x\right]}{x^3} \\ &= -\dfrac{(x+2)(1-x)^2}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show $\ln(\sin^2 x)-\ln(\cos^2 x)=2\ln(\tan x)$ for $0\le x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \ln(\sin^2 x) - \ln(\cos^2 x) &= \ln\left(\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}\right) \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right)^2 \\ &= 2\ln(\tan x) \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, differentiate $\ln(\sin^2 x)-\ln(\cos^2 x)$ for $0\le x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
items.sol:
Using part (a):

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(\sin^2 x) - \ln(\cos^2 x)\right] &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[2\ln(\tan x)\right] \\ &= 2\cdot\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x \cdot \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sin x\cos x} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: If $y=\log_3(2x)$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$
items.sol:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b = \dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:

$$y = \dfrac{\ln(2x)}{\ln 3}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 3}\cdot\dfrac{2}{2x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x\ln 3} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Given $f(x)=2\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^x$, find $f'(x)$
items.sol:
Rewrite with base $e$, using $a^x = e^{x\ln a}$:

$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= 2\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^x \\ &= 2\cdot 2^{\frac{x}{2}} \\ &= 2e^{\frac{x}{2}\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\cdot e^{\frac{x}{2}\ln 2} \\ &= \ln 2\cdot 2^{\frac{x}{2}} \\ &= \ln 2\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the exact gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=\log_e(\tan x)$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on $\ln u$ with $u=\tan x$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x)=\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\tan x}$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\sec^2\frac{\pi}{3}}{\tan\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt3}\\ &=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient}=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{3}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows a Ferris wheel with a diameter of 70 metres. Passengers board the Ferris wheel when its carriages reaches its lowest point $P$, at ground level. The wheel rotates at a constant rate in a clockwise direction and completes one revolution every 20 minutes.

\exfigure{1763_q16_1}

Let $h$ be the vertical height of a carriage $t$ minutes after it passes point $P$.
It is known that $h$ can be expressed in the form $h(t)=a\cos(bt)+c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants. Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
items.sol:
The period is $20$ minutes, so
$$\dfrac{2\pi}{b}=20$$
$$b=\dfrac{2\pi}{20}=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$$
The height oscillates between $0$ and $70$, so the centre line is $c=35$ and the amplitude is $35$. The carriage starts at its lowest point ($h=0$ at $t=0$), so the cosine is reflected and $a=-35$.
$$h(t)=-35\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right)+35$$
$$\therefore\ a=-35,\quad b=\dfrac{\pi}{10},\quad c=35$$
\exfigure{1763_q16_s1}

items.part:
The diagram below shows a Ferris wheel with a diameter of 70 metres. Passengers board the Ferris wheel when its carriages reaches its lowest point $P$, at ground level. The wheel rotates at a constant rate in a clockwise direction and completes one revolution every 20 minutes.

\exfigure{1763_q16_1}

Let $h$ be the vertical height of a carriage $t$ minutes after it passes point $P$.
Let $R$ be the rate at which $h$ changes over time.

By first finding $R$, find the maximum rate of change of $R$ with respect to time.
items.sol:
The rate of change of height is the derivative of $h$.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= h'(t) \\ &= -35\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)\left(-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{7\pi}{2}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating again gives the rate of change of $R$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= \dfrac{7\pi}{2}\times\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \\ &= \dfrac{7\pi^2}{20}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \end{aligned}$$
The maximum value of the cosine is $1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum of } \dfrac{dR}{dt} = \dfrac{7\pi^2}{20}$$

Let $h$ be the vertical height of a carriage $t$ minutes after it passes point $P$.
When Leo enters the carriage, he is excited to reach a height of 50m above the ground.

Determine how long it will take him to reach this height. Give your answer to the nearest second.
items.sol:
Set $h=50$.
$$\begin{aligned} 50 &= -35\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+35 \\ 15 &= -35\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \\ -\dfrac37 &= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The first time this happens is the first solution of the cosine equation.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{10} &= \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac37\right) \\ t &= \dfrac{10}{\pi}\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac37\right) \\ &\approx 6.41\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 6 \text{ minutes } 25 \text{ seconds}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int x\sqrt{5x^2+1}\,dx$
items.sol:
Method 1: the integrand is of the form $k\,f'(x)[f(x)]^n$ with $f(x)=5x^2+1$, $f'(x)=10x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{5x^2+1}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{10}\int 10x\sqrt{5x^2+1}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{10}\times\dfrac23(5x^2+1)^{\frac32}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{15}(5x^2+1)^{\frac32}+C\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: if $y=(5x^2+1)^{\frac32}$ then
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=15x(5x^2+1)^{\frac12}$$
so
$$\int x\sqrt{5x^2+1}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{15}(5x^2+1)^{\frac32}+C$$

items.part:
When cooking oil cools down, its temperature, $T$, in degrees Celsius, after $t$ minutes is given by the formula

$$T=60+150e^{-0.1t}$$
At what temperature is the oil decreasing at a rate of $10^\circ$C per minute? Leave your answer to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
The temperature is decreasing at $10^\circ$C per minute when $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-10$.
$$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-15e^{-0.1t}$$
$$\begin{aligned} -10 &= -15e^{-0.1t} \\ \dfrac23 &= e^{-0.1t} \\ -0.1t &= \ln\left(\dfrac23\right) \\ t &= -10\ln\left(\dfrac23\right) \\ &\approx 4.0547 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $e^{-0.1t}=\dfrac23$ into $T$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 60+150\left(\dfrac23\right) \\ &= 160^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:

Given $f(x)=x-2$ and $g(x)=(x+2)(x^2-4)$
Find the $x$-coordinates of all points of intersection between $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.
items.sol:
Intersections occur where $f(x)=g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} x-2 &= (x+2)(x^2-4) \\ (x-2)-(x+2)(x+2)(x-2) &= 0 \\ (x-2)\left[1-(x+2)^2\right] &= 0 \\ (x-2)\left[(x+2)^2-1\right] &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
From $x-2=0$, $x=2$.

From $(x+2)^2=1$, $x=-1$ or $x=-3$.
$$\therefore\ x=-3,\ -1 \text{ or } 2$$

items.part:
The velocity, $\dot{x}$, in m/s of a particle moving in a horizontal straight line is given by:

$$\dot{x}=3-\dfrac{9}{t-2}\quad\text{for } t>2,$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds.
Hence, or otherwise, find the distance travelled by the particle between $t=3$ and $t=7$. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
The velocity is negative for $3\le t<5$ and positive for $5<t\le 7$, so the distance is found in two parts.
$$\text{Distance}=-\int_3^5\left(3-\dfrac{9}{t-2}\right)dt+\int_5^7\left(3-\dfrac{9}{t-2}\right)dt$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= -\Big[3t-9\ln(t-2)\Big]_3^5+\Big[3t-9\ln(t-2)\Big]_5^7 \\ &= -\Big[\big(15-9\ln 3\big)-\big(9-9\ln 1\big)\Big]+\Big[\big(21-9\ln 5\big)-\big(15-9\ln 3\big)\Big] \\ &= (9\ln 3-6)+\left(6+9\ln\dfrac35\right) \\ &\approx 5.29 \text{ m (2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
Since $P(B)=P(A\cap B)+P(\bar{A}\cap B)$, we have
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B)&=P(B)-P(\bar{A}\cap B) \\ &=k-k^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac{3k}{4}$, $P(B)=k$ and $P(\bar{A}\cap B)=k^2$ where $0<k<1$.
Given that the two events are independent, find the value of $k$.
items.sol:
If the events are independent, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

$$\begin{aligned} k-k^2&=\dfrac{3k}{4}\times k \\ 4k-4k^2&=3k^2 \\ 7k^2-4k&=0 \\ k(7k-4)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $k=0$ or $k=\dfrac{4}{7}$.

Since $0<k<1$:
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{4}{7}$$

Given a function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3x}{4}(2-x) & \text{for } 0\le x\le 2\\[2mm] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Prove that $f(x)$ represents a probability density function.
items.sol:
The values of $y=\dfrac{3x}{4}(2-x)$ are never negative for $0\le x\le 2$, as the graph shows.

\exfigure{1763_q25_s1}

Hence $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$.

Also
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx&=\dfrac{3}{4}\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left[x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left(2^2-\dfrac{2^3}{3}\right)-\dfrac{3}{4}\left(0^2-\dfrac{0^3}{3}\right) \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f(x)\ge0$ for all $x$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$, $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

items.part:
Consider the function:

$$f(x)=\log_e(x^2+1)$$
Find the stationary point(s) of $f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}\times2x=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}=0$$
so $2x=0$, giving $x=0$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=2 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=\dfrac{2(x^2+1)-2x(2x)}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{2x^2+2-4x^2}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{2(1-x^2)}{(x^2+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(0)=\dfrac{2(1-0^2)}{(0^2+1)^2}=2>0$$
So the curve is concave up at $x=0$, a minimum point.
$$f(0)=\ln(0^2+1)=0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum point is } (0,0)$$

Inflection points occur where $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 2(1-x^2)&=0 \\ x^2&=1 \\ x&=\pm1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f(\pm1)=\ln\left((\pm1)^2+1\right)=\ln2$$

\extable{Ts8990_1}

The concavity changes at both, so
$$\therefore\ (-1,\ln2)\text{ and }(1,\ln2)\text{ are points of inflection}$$

State whether the approximation found in part (b) is greater or less than the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^3\log_e(x^2+1)\,dx$. Use your sketch in part (c) to provide a brief justification for your answer.

$$\therefore\ \text{the approximation is less than the exact value}$$
items.final: the approximation is less than the exact value

The perpendicular distance from $S$ to $O$ is 2 km while the distance $OY$ is 4 km.

Time is $T=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$. Use Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle SOX$ for the swim.
$$SX=\sqrt{a^2+4}\ \text{ so } T_1=\dfrac{\sqrt{a^2+4}}{4}\text{ hours}$$
Bike ride:

Combining the three times:

$$p+5q=2.7 \quad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$4q=2$$
Hence $q=0.5$ and $p=0.2$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 5)&=0.5+0.1 \\ &=0.6 \end{aligned}$$

Using conditional probability,
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 5\mid X\ge 3)&=\dfrac{P(X\ge 5\cap X\ge 3)}{P(X\ge 3)} \\ &=\dfrac{0.5+0.1}{0.2+0.5+0.1} \\ &=\dfrac{0.6}{0.8} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

Find the sum of the terms in the arithmetic series.

$$2026+2011+1996+\cdots 271.$$
items.sol:
The series has $a=2026$, $d=-15$ and last term $l=271$.

Find the number of terms using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 271&=2026+(n-1)(-15) \\ n&=118 \end{aligned}$$
The sum is
$$\begin{aligned} S_{118}&=\dfrac{118}{2}(2026+271) \\ &=135523 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\dfrac{5e^{2x}}{5-x^2}$ at $x=1$.
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=5e^{2x} & v&=5-x^2\\ u'&=10e^{2x} & v'&=-2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(5-x^2)\times 10e^{2x}-5e^{2x}(-2x)}{(5-x^2)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{10e^{2x}(5-x^2+x)}{(5-x^2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
At $x=1$: $y=\dfrac{5e^2}{4}$, so the point is $\left(1,\dfrac{5e^2}{4}\right)$.
$$m_T=\dfrac{10e^2(5-1+1)}{16}=\dfrac{25e^2}{8},\qquad m_N=-\dfrac{8}{25e^2}$$
The normal is
$$y-\dfrac{5e^2}{4}=-\dfrac{8}{25e^2}(x-1)$$
(The school's working found the normal at $x=0$, $x+2y-2=0$, not at the $x=1$ the question asks for.)

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x+1)(x-2)^2$
Show that $f'(x)=3x(x-2)$ and find $f''(x)$.
items.sol:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+1 & v&=(x-2)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(x-2)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=(x-2)^2+2(x-2)(x+1) \\ &=(x-2)(x-2+2x+2) \\ &=3x(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
Since $f'(x)=3x^2-6x$,
$$f''(x)=6x-6$$

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x+1)(x-2)^2$
Find the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$3x(x-2)=0$$
so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

Then $y=f(0)=4$ and $y=f(2)=0$, giving the points $(0,4)$ and $(2,0)$.

The sign of $f''$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down, so } (0,4) \text{ is a maximum}\\ f''(2)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up, so } (2,0) \text{ is a minimum} \end{aligned}$$
items.final: $(0,4)$ is a maximum; $(2,0)$ is a minimum

items.part:
Let $f(x)=(x+1)(x-2)^2$
Determine the point of inflection of $y=f(x)$.
items.sol:
A point of inflexion needs $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-6&=0 \\ x&=1 \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=(1+1)(1-2)^2=2$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(2)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so the point of inflexion is $(1,2)$.

items.part: Differentiate $y=\ln\sin(2x)$
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on $y=\ln\sin(2x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{2\cos 2x}{\sin 2x} \\ &=2\cot 2x \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int(\cot(2x)+3\sec^2 x)\,dx$
items.sol:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(\ln\sin 2x\big)=2\cot 2x$, so $\displaystyle\int \cot 2x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|\sin 2x|$.

Also $\displaystyle\int \sec^2 x\,dx=\tan x$.
$$\int(\cot 2x+3\sec^2 x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|\sin 2x|+3\tan x+C$$

items.part:
A music festival is preparing a decorative light display along the main entrance. The lights are arranged in rows. The first row contains 12 lights. Each successive row contains exactly 5 more lights than the previous row.

If there are 792 lights used for this display, how many rows are there?
items.sol:
This is an arithmetic series with $a=12$, $d=5$ and $S_n=792$.

Using the sum formula:
$$S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$$
$$792=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2\times 12+(n-1)\times 5\big)$$
$$1584=24n+5n^2-5n$$
$$5n^2+19n-1584=0$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} n&=\dfrac{-19\pm\sqrt{19^2-4\times 5\times(-1584)}}{10} \\ &=\dfrac{-19\pm 179}{10} \end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=\dfrac{160}{10}=16$.
$$\therefore\ \text{there are } 16 \text{ rows}$$

items.part:
Information was collected from a group of employees at a company regarding their modes of transport to work. Each employee indicated whether they travel by train, bus or both. The results showed that 60% of the employees travel by train, 50% of the employees travel by bus, and 25% of the employees travel by both bus and train. It was also found that 36 employees travel by exactly one mode of transport mentioned.
Show that total number of employees in the company is $60$.
items.sol:
Let the total number of employees be $n$.

Employees travelling by exactly one mode are those by train only plus those by bus only. Each of these is the total for that mode minus the $25\%$ who travel by both.
$$\begin{aligned} (60\%-25\%)n+(50\%-25\%)n&=36 \\ 60\%\times n&=36 \\ n&=60 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the total number of employees is } 60$$

items.part:
Information was collected from a group of employees at a company regarding their modes of transport to work. Each employee indicated whether they travel by train, bus or both. The results showed that 60% of the employees travel by train, 50% of the employees travel by bus, and 25% of the employees travel by both bus and train. It was also found that 36 employees travel by exactly one mode of transport mentioned.
Two different employees are selected at random from the group. Find the probability that neither travel by bus.
items.sol:
Employees not travelling by bus: $50\%$ of $60=30$.

Choosing two different employees without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither})&=\dfrac{30}{60}\times\dfrac{29}{59} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{29}{59} \\ &=\dfrac{29}{118} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: In a geometric sequence, the $10th$ term is 768 and the $13th$ term is 6144. Find the first term, and the common ratio.
items.sol:
For a geometric sequence $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, so
$$ar^9=768 \quad (1)$$
$$ar^{12}=6144 \quad (2)$$
Dividing (2) by (1):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{ar^{12}}{ar^9}&=\dfrac{6144}{768} \\ r^3&=8 \\ r&=2 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{768}{2^9} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{3}{2},\ r=2$$

P$(8,32)$ lies on $y=kx$, so substitute it.

The parabola is above the line between $x=0$ and $x=8$, so the area is the integral of the difference.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^8(12x-x^2-4x)\,dx \\ &=\int_0^8(8x-x^2)\,dx \\ &=\left[4x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^8 \\ &=4(8)^2-\dfrac{8^3}{3} \\ &=256-\dfrac{512}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{256}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=\dfrac{256}{3}\text{ units}^2$$

Alex and Ben are playing a game using a two fair six-sided dice. They take turns rolling both dice with Alex going first, followed by Ben, and then continuing in this alternating pattern.

The objective of the game is to be the first player to roll a total of exactly 10 on the two dice. Once a player rolls a total of exactly 10, the game ends and that player is declared the winner.
Find the probability that Alex wins the game on his first turn.
items.sol:
Totals of $10$: $(5,5),(6,4),(4,6)$, which is 3 outcomes out of 36.
$$P=\dfrac{3}{36}=\dfrac{1}{12}$$

items.part:
Alex and Ben are playing a game using a two fair six-sided dice. They take turns rolling both dice with Alex going first, followed by Ben, and then continuing in this alternating pattern.

The objective of the game is to be the first player to roll a total of exactly 10 on the two dice. Once a player rolls a total of exactly 10, the game ends and that player is declared the winner.
Find the probability that Alex wins the game on either his first turn or second turn.
items.sol:
On each turn, $P(\text{win})=\dfrac{1}{12}$ and $P(\text{lose})=\dfrac{11}{12}$.

Alex wins on his second turn if Alex loses, Ben loses, then Alex wins.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{1}{12}+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{12}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{265}{1728} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Alex and Ben are playing a game using a two fair six-sided dice. They take turns rolling both dice with Alex going first, followed by Ben, and then continuing in this alternating pattern.

The objective of the game is to be the first player to roll a total of exactly 10 on the two dice. Once a player rolls a total of exactly 10, the game ends and that player is declared the winner.
Find the probability that Alex eventually wins the game.
items.sol:
Alex can win on turn 1, 2, 3, and so on, each time after both players have lost the earlier rounds.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{1}{12}+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^2\dfrac{1}{12}+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^4\dfrac{1}{12}+\cdots \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(1+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^4+\cdots\right) \end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$ and $r=\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^2$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{1}{12}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1-\left(\frac{11}{12}\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{12}{23} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rescue helicopter is searching for two hikers, Liam (L) and Sophia (S), who are stranded on the different sides of a flat levelled valley. Both hikers can see the top of Eagle Peak (E) and are communicating with the rescue team by radio.

Liam reports that Eagle Peak has a bearing of $072^\circ$ from his position, and the angle of elevation to the top of Eagle Peak is $18^\circ$. Sophie reports that Eagle Peak has a bearing of $118^\circ$ from her position, and the angle of elevation to the top of the peak is $27^\circ$. The top of the Eagle Peak is 1800 metres above the valley floor.

Find the distance between Liam and Sophie and determine the bearing of Liam from Sophie's position.

\exfigure{1772_q27_1}
items.sol:
Let $B$ be the point on the valley floor directly below the peak $E$. In each right-angled triangle $LBE$ and $SBE$, use the tangent ratio with $BE=1800$.
$$\tan 18^\circ=\dfrac{1800}{LB},\quad LB=5539.8\text{ m}$$
$$\tan 27^\circ=\dfrac{1800}{SB},\quad SB=3532.7\text{ m}$$
The bearings of $B$ from $L$ and $S$ differ, so
$$\angle LBS=118^\circ-72^\circ=46^\circ$$
Cosine rule in triangle $LBS$:
$$\begin{aligned} LS&=\sqrt{5539.8^2+3532.7^2-2(5539.8)(3532.7)\cos 46^\circ} \\ &=3997.47\ldots\text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Sine rule to find $\angle S$:
$$\dfrac{\sin S}{LB}=\dfrac{\sin 46^\circ}{LS}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin S&=\dfrac{LB\sin 46^\circ}{LS} \\ &=0.9964 \end{aligned}$$
$LB$ is the longest side and $LB^2\approx30.69\times10^6>LS^2+SB^2\approx28.46\times10^6$, so $S$ is obtuse (the ambiguous case): $S\approx180^\circ-85.5^\circ=94.5^\circ$.

The bearing of Liam from Sophie is
$$118^\circ+94.5^\circ\approx213^\circ$$
$$\therefore\ LS\approx 3997\text{ m and the bearing of Liam from Sophie is } 213^\circ$$
items.final: $LS\approx 3997$ m and the bearing of Liam from Sophie is $213^\circ$

items.part:
The amount of time $X$ in minutes that customers spend waiting for a ride at a theme park is modelled by the probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}, & 0\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Show that $k=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$.
items.sol:
The total probability is $1$, so
$$\int_0^5 k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx=1$$
$$\left[\dfrac{10k}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_0^5=1$$
$$\dfrac{10k}{\pi}\left(\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{10}-0\right)=1$$
Since $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1$, $\dfrac{10k}{\pi}=1$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$$

items.part:
The amount of time $X$ in minutes that customers spend waiting for a ride at a theme park is modelled by the probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}, & 0\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Find the probability that a customer waits between 2 and 4 minutes, give your answer correct to 4 decimal places.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(2\le X\le 4)&=\int_2^4\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx \\ &=\left[\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_2^4 \\ &=\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{10}-\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{10} \\ &=0.36327\ldots \\ &\approx 0.3633 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The amount of time $X$ in minutes that customers spend waiting for a ride at a theme park is modelled by the probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}, & 0\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
What is the probability that a customer waits more than 4 minutes? Give answer correct to 4 decimal places.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(X>4)&=\int_4^5\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx \\ &=\left[\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_4^5 \\ &=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{10} \\ &=0.048943\ldots \\ &\approx 0.0489 \end{aligned}$$

A rectangular water tank of width $b$ cm and height $h$ cm is designed to fit perfectly inside a cylindrical pipe with diameter of 30 cm as shown, where all vertices of the rectangular prism touch the circumference of the base circles.

\exfigure{1772_q29_1}

The length of the tank is twice its height and the volume ($V$) of the tank is given by

$$V=bhl$$
Show that $V=2b(900-b^2)$.
items.sol:
The cross-section is a rectangle inscribed in the circle of diameter $30$, so its diagonal is $30$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$b^2+h^2=30^2,\quad h=\sqrt{900-b^2}$$
The length is $l=2h$.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=bhl \\ &=b\times\sqrt{900-b^2}\times 2\sqrt{900-b^2} \\ &=2b(900-b^2) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A rectangular water tank of width $b$ cm and height $h$ cm is designed to fit perfectly inside a cylindrical pipe with diameter of 30 cm as shown, where all vertices of the rectangular prism touch the circumference of the base circles.

The length of the tank is twice its height and the volume ($V$) of the tank is given by

$$V=bhl$$
Find the dimensions of the rectangular prism that maximises the volume of the tank. Justify your answer.
items.sol:
Expand the volume, then differentiate to find stationary points.
$$V=1800b-2b^3$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{db}=1800-6b^2=0$$
$$b^2=300$$
Since $b>0$, $b=10\sqrt{3}$.

Then
$$h=\sqrt{900-300}=\sqrt{600}=10\sqrt{6},\quad l=2h=20\sqrt{6}$$
Second derivative test:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{db^2}=-12b$$
When $b=10\sqrt{3}$, $\dfrac{d^2V}{db^2}=-120\sqrt{3}<0$, so this is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{dimensions are } 10\sqrt{3}\times 10\sqrt{6}\times 20\sqrt{6}\text{ cm}$$

items.part:
A rectangular water tank of width $b$ cm and height $h$ cm is designed to fit perfectly inside a cylindrical pipe with diameter of 30 cm as shown, where all vertices of the rectangular prism touch the circumference of the base circles.

\exfigure{1772_q29_1}

The length of the tank is twice its height and the volume ($V$) of the tank is given by

$$V=bhl$$
A square based tank with a diagonal 30 cm could also be designed to fit inside the pipe. Show that the rectangular water tank is more than 5% greater in volume compared to square based tank.
items.sol:
Rectangular tank:
$$V_{\text{rect}}=10\sqrt{3}\times 10\sqrt{6}\times 20\sqrt{6}=12000\sqrt{3}$$
Square-based tank: the diagonal of the base is $30$, so
$$b^2+b^2=30^2,\quad b=\sqrt{450}=15\sqrt{2},\quad l=2b$$
$$\begin{aligned} V_{\text{sq}}&=b^2l \\ &=(15\sqrt{2})^2\times 2(15\sqrt{2}) \\ &=13500\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
Percentage increase:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12000\sqrt{3}-13500\sqrt{2}}{13500\sqrt{2}}&=0.0887\ldots \\ &=8.87\%>5\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the rectangular tank is more than } 5\% \text{ greater in volume}$$

items.part:
In a flock of 22400 sheep, the ratio of males to females is $9:15$. The weights of the female sheep are normally distributed with a mean of 78.4 kg and a standard deviation of 5.6 kg. In the flock, 13979 of the female sheep each weigh more than $x$ kg.

Find the value of $x$.
items.sol:
The ratio of males to females is $9:15$, so
$$\text{Number of females}=\dfrac{15}{24}\times 22400=14000$$
$$P(X>x)=\dfrac{13979}{14000}=0.9985$$
$$P(X<x)=1-0.9985=0.0015$$
This corresponds to $z=-3$. Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} -3&=\dfrac{x-78.4}{5.6} \\ x&=78.4+(-3)(5.6) \\ &=61.6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=61.6$$

$$T(t)=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$$

where $t$ if the time in hours after midnight, $0\le t\le 24$.
Find the temperature at midnight.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} T(0)&=22+8\cos\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{12}\right) \\ &=22+8\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=26^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The temperature, $T^\circ$ C, at a farm over the course of a day is modelled by

$$T(t)=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$$

where $t$ if the time in hours after midnight, $0\le t\le 24$.
Find $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$, leave your answer in the simplest form.
items.sol:
Using the chain rule on $T=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-\dfrac{8\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right) \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The temperature, $T^\circ$ C, at a farm over the course of a day is modelled by

$$T(t)=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$$

where $t$ if the time in hours after midnight, $0\le t\le 24$.
Determine whether the temperature is initially decreasing or increasing.
items.sol:
Initially means $t=0$. The sign of $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$ decides whether $T$ is increasing or decreasing.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{12}\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ &>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the temperature is initially increasing}$$

items.part:
The temperature, $T^\circ$ C, at a farm over the course of a day is modelled by

$$T(t)=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$$

where $t$ if the time in hours after midnight, $0\le t\le 24$.
Find the maximum temperature and determine the first time at which this occurs.
items.sol:
The maximum of cosine is $1$, so
$$T_{\max}=22+8(1)=30^\circ\text{C}$$
This occurs when
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right)=1$$
so $\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)=0$, giving $t=4$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum temperature is } 30^\circ\text{C, first at } t=4 \text{ (4 am)}$$
items.final: maximum temperature is $30^\circ\text{C}$, first at $t=4$ (4 am)

A business owner takes an reducing balance loan of \$500000 to expand their company. Interest is charged at $0.4\%$ per month, compounded monthly. At the end of each month, interest is added to the loan balance and then a repayment of \$3200 is made.

Let $A_n$ be the balance owing on the loan at the end of $n$ months.
Show that $A_2=500000(1.004)^2-3200(1.004)-3200$.
items.sol:
Interest of $0.4\%$ is added, then the repayment is made.
$$A_1=500000(1.004)-3200$$
Repeating the process:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1\times 1.004-3200 \\ &=500000(1.004)^2-3200(1.004)-3200 \end{aligned}$$

A business owner takes an reducing balance loan of \$500000 to expand their company. Interest is charged at $0.4\%$ per month, compounded monthly. At the end of each month, interest is added to the loan balance and then a repayment of \$3200 is made.

Let $A_n$ be the balance owing on the loan at the end of $n$ months.

A business owner takes an reducing balance loan of \$500000 to expand their company. Interest is charged at $0.4\%$ per month, compounded monthly. At the end of each month, interest is added to the loan balance and then a repayment of \$3200 is made.

Let $A_n$ be the balance owing on the loan at the end of $n$ months.
After how many months will the balance owing first be less than \$250000.
items.sol:
We need $A_n<250000$.
$$800000-300000(1.004)^n<250000$$
$$-300000(1.004)^n<-550000$$
Dividing by $-300000$ reverses the inequality:
