$$\begin{aligned} 26x &= 390 \\ x &= \dfrac{390}{26} = 15 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Length} &= 9 \times 15 = 135 \\ \text{Width} &= 4 \times 15 = 60 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \text{Length} \times \text{Width} \\ &= 135 \times 60 \\ &= 8100 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The blood alcohol content ($BAC$) for males can be estimated by

$$BAC_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$$

where

$N$ = number of standard drinks

$H$ = number of hours drinking

$M$ = the person’s weight in kilograms.

The number of hours for a person’s $BAC$ to reach zero is given by

$$\text{Time} = \dfrac{BAC}{0.015}.$$

Henry, a 72 kg male, consumes a total of three drinks at a family dinner.

The drinks are:

\begin{itemize}
\item two 375 mL cans of beer that hold 1.4 standard drinks each
\item one 250 mL can of mixer that holds 1.8 standard drinks.
\end{itemize}

It took 2 hours and 10 minutes for Henry’s $BAC$ to return to zero.

How many hours did Henry take to consume the three drinks, correct to the nearest hour?
items.sol:
The time for the $BAC$ to reach zero is 2 hours 10 minutes, so
$$\begin{aligned} 2\dfrac{10}{60} &= \dfrac{BAC}{0.015} \\ BAC &= 2\dfrac{10}{60} \times 0.015 \\ &= 0.0325 \end{aligned}$$
Number of drinks:
$$N = 2 \times 1.4 + 1.8 = 4.6$$
Substituting into the $BAC$ formula with $M = 72$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.0325 &= \dfrac{(10 \times 4.6) - 7.5H}{6.8 \times 72} \\ 15.912 &= 46 - 7.5H \\ -30.088 &= -7.5H \\ H &= \dfrac{-30.088}{-7.5} = 4.0117\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ H \approx 4 \text{ hours}$$

items.part:
In a typical week Kim works 36 hours and is paid \$42 per hour.

In the 2025–2026 financial year, Kim took 4 weeks annual leave and received a leave loading of $17.5\%$ of 4 weeks pay.

In the same year, Kim also had allowable deductions totalling \$4800. Use 1 year = 52 weeks.
What is Kim’s taxable income?
items.sol:
Weekly pay:
$$42 \times 36 = \$1512$$
Taxable income is annual pay plus leave loading, less deductions:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Taxable income} &= 1512 \times 52 + 4 \times 1512 \times 17.5\% - 4800 \\ &= \$74\,882.40 \end{aligned}$$

Diego flew from Sydney to Hong Kong. Diego departed Sydney at 10:15 pm Coordinated Universal Time (UTC +10) on Wednesday and travelled via Singapore.

The flight from Sydney to Singapore took 7 hours 50 minutes.

The time between arriving in Singapore and departing from Singapore was 2 hours and 15 minutes.

The flight from Singapore to Hong Kong took 3 hours 40 minutes.

Singapore and Hong Kong both operate on UTC +8.

What time and day was it when Diego arrived in Hong Kong?
items.sol:
Hong Kong is UTC $+8$ and Sydney is UTC $+10$, so the time difference is
$$10 - 8 = 2 \text{ hours}$$
Total travel time:
$$7\text{ h }50\text{ min} + 2\text{ h }15\text{ min} + 3\text{ h }40\text{ min} = 13\text{ h }45\text{ min}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Arrival} &= 10{:}15\text{ pm} + 13\text{ h }45\text{ min} - 2\text{ h} \\ &= 10{:}15\text{ pm} + 11\text{ h }45\text{ min} \\ &= 10{:}00\text{ am Thursday} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Diego arrived at 10:00 am Thursday, Hong Kong local time}$$

items.sol:

In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $AB = 8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos 20^\circ &= \dfrac{AF}{8} \\ AF &= 7.517\ldots \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

Paint is sold in two sizes at a local shop.

\begin{itemize}
\item Four-litre cans at \$90 per can
\item Ten-litre cans at \$205 per can
\end{itemize}

Mina needs to purchase 80 litres of paint.

Calculate the amount of money Mina will save by purchasing only ten-litre cans of paint rather than only four-litre cans of paint.
items.sol:
Ten-litre cans: $80 \div 10 = 8$ cans.
$$\text{Cost} = \$205 \times 8 = \$1640$$
Four-litre cans: $80 \div 4 = 20$ cans.
$$\text{Cost} = \$90 \times 20 = \$1800$$
The saving is the difference.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Savings} &= \$1800 - \$1640 \\ &= \$160 \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
The interest-free period is 45 days, so interest applies for
$$68 - 45 = 23 \text{ days}$$
Using the compound interest formula with daily rate $\dfrac{13.74\%}{365}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \$392\left(1 + \dfrac{0.1374}{365}\right)^{23} \\ &= \$395.41 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest charged} &= \$395.41 - \$392 \\ &= \$3.41 \end{aligned}$$

The volume of 30 spheres is

$$\begin{aligned} 1058.115 &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times (14 \times 14) \times h \\ h &= \dfrac{1058.115 \times 3}{14 \times 14} \\ &\approx 16.2 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Stamp duty is charged per $\$100$ or part thereof:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Monthly repayment} &= \$30\,071.10 \div 36 \\ &= \$835.31 \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
Capture-recapture: the tagged proportion in the sample equals the tagged proportion in the population $P$.

$$\dfrac{196}{P} = \dfrac{49}{130}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{130\times 196}{49} \\ &= 520 \end{aligned}$$

The estimated number of penguins in the colony is $520$.

Ensuring the rope is tight, she records the length of rope as 16.2 m, as shown in the diagram below. The angle of depression from the boat to the anchor is $49^\circ$.

\exfigure{497_q35_1}
Due to the difficulty of keeping the rope taught and the movement of the boat in the water, Jennifer estimates that the measurement of the angle has an error of $2^\circ$ and the length of the rope has an error of 0.1 m.

What is the upper and lower bound for the depth of the lake?
items.sol:
The depth is $x = L\cos\theta$, which is smallest for the largest angle and shortest rope.

Smallest: angle $41 + 2 = 43^\circ$, rope $16.2 - 0.1 = 16.1$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 16.1 \cos 43^\circ \\ &\approx 11.8 \end{aligned}$$
Largest: angle $41 - 2 = 39^\circ$, rope $16.2 + 0.1 = 16.3$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 16.3 \cos 39^\circ \\ &\approx 12.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{lower bound } 11.8 \text{ m, upper bound } 12.7 \text{ m}$$
items.final: Lower bound $11.8$ m, upper bound $12.7$ m

items.part:
Lachlan buys 8 tickets in a raffle where 240 tickets were sold. He wins first prize.

What is the probability that he wins the second prize given that Lachlan has already won first prize?
items.sol:
After Lachlan wins first prize, there are $239$ tickets left, and $7$ of them are his.
$$P(\text{wins 2nd prize}) = \dfrac{7}{239}$$

There are 12 equally likely outcomes, and one of them is 3.
$$P(3) = \dfrac{1}{12}$$

The numbers less than 10 are $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(<10) &= \dfrac{9}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

The numbers divisible by 4 are $4, 8, 12$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{divisible by } 4) &= \dfrac{3}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:

items.sol:
Both ate an apple, so multiply along the apple-apple branches.

items.part:
A bowl of fruit contains 21 pieces of fruit of which 8 are oranges and 13 are apples.

Jack takes one piece of fruit at random and eats it. Jill also takes a piece of fruit at random and eats it.
Find the probability that Jack and Jill ate different fruits.
items.sol:
Different fruits means orange then apple, or apple then orange. Add the two branch products.
$$\begin{aligned} P(OA \text{ or } AO) &= \dfrac{8}{21} \times \dfrac{13}{20} + \dfrac{13}{21} \times \dfrac{8}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{52}{105} \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:

The fuel consumption for an Audi Q2 is $8.2$ litres/$100$ km. On a road trip, this car travels a distance of $1420$ km and the fuel cost is \$1.92 per litre.

What is the total fuel cost for this trip?
items.sol:
Fuel used is the consumption rate times the distance in hundreds of km.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fuel used} &= \dfrac{8.2}{100} \times 1420 \\ &= 116.44 \text{ litres} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= 116.44 \times 1.92 \\ &\approx \$223.56 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sienna has moved into a four-bedroom unit which she will share with three friends. She is responsible for one quarter of the rent and one quarter of the utilities (electricity and water) for the unit. She has just got her first full time job, which pays \$1964 per fortnight after tax.
With her new full time job paying \$1964 per fortnight after tax, she needs to budget for these expenses. The rent on the unit is \$492 per week and the most recent quarterly bills for electricity and water were \$572 and \$260 respectively.

To safeguard against potential increases Sienna budgets an additional 20\% of these expenses.

How much should she budget from her fortnightly pay to cover her share of these expenses?
items.sol:
Sienna pays one quarter of the rent. Rent is weekly, so a fortnight is 2 weeks.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Share of rent} &= \dfrac{492}{4} \times 2 \\ &= \$246 \end{aligned}$$
Bills are quarterly, so there are 4 sets of bills a year and 26 fortnights.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Yearly utility bills} &= 4 \times (572 + 260) \\ &= \$3328 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Her share of bills} &= (3328 \div 26) \div 4 \\ &= \$32 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Current accommodation expenses} &= 246 + 32 \\ &= \$278 \end{aligned}$$
Add 20% for possible increases.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Budget} &= 1.2 \times 278 \\ &= \$333.60 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sienna has moved into a four-bedroom unit which she will share with three friends. She is responsible for one quarter of the rent and one quarter of the utilities (electricity and water) for the unit. She has just got her first full time job, which pays \$1964 per fortnight after tax.
She is also purchasing a car using a loan which has monthly payments of \$572. The car has weekly running expenses of \$48 and annual service, insurance, and registration expenses of \$ 1831.70. How much should she budget from her fortnightly pay to cover her car related expenses?
items.sol:
Monthly payments are 12 a year and there are 26 fortnights in a year.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fortnightly loan payment} &= 572 \times \dfrac{12}{26} \\ &= \$264 \end{aligned}$$
Running costs are weekly, so double them.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Running costs} &= 48 \times 2 \\ &= \$96 \end{aligned}$$
Annual expenses are divided by 26.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fortnightly bills} &= 1831.70 \div 26 \\ &\approx \$70.45 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total car budget} &= 264 + 96 + 70.45 \\ &= \$430.45 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Sienna has moved into a four-bedroom unit which she will share with three friends. She is responsible for one quarter of the rent and one quarter of the utilities (electricity and water) for the unit. She has just got her first full time job, which pays \$1964 per fortnight after tax.
Sienna pays \$145 per week toward household groceries and food and allows \$40 per day to buy lunch and other incidental daily expenses.

How much does she have left from her fortnightly pay to save for other major purchases and entertainment?
items.sol:
Groceries are weekly, so double them. Lunch is daily, so multiply by 14 days.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fortnightly food and groceries} &= 145 \times 2 \\ &= \$290 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fortnightly lunch and incidentals} &= 40 \times 14 \\ &= \$560 \end{aligned}$$
Using the results of parts (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total budget} &= 333.60 + 430.45 + 290 + 560 \\ &= \$1614.05 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Savings} &= 1964 - 1614.05 \\ &= \$349.95 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
The number of orders received in a particular week is represented by $n$. The company's costs $C$, and revenue $R$ in dollars, producing and delivering these orders, are given by the equations $C = 400 + 5n$ and $R = 25n$.
Show that the company "breaks even" when $n = 20$.
items.sol:
At the break-even point $R = C$. Substitute $n = 20$ into each equation.
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 400 + 5(20) \\ &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 25 \times 20 \\ &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
Since $R = C$, the company breaks even when $n = 20$.

items.part:
The number of orders received in a particular week is represented by $n$. The company's costs $C$, and revenue $R$ in dollars, producing and delivering these orders, are given by the equations $C = 400 + 5n$ and $R = 25n$.
The company made a profit ($P$) of \$600 last week.

Using the equation $P = R - C$, determine the number of internet orders the company delivered last week?
items.sol:
Profit is revenue minus cost.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= R - C \\ &= 25n - (5n + 400) \\ &= 20n - 400 \end{aligned}$$
Put $P = 600$.
$$\begin{aligned} 600 &= 20n - 400 \\ 1000 &= 20n \\ n &= 50 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore 50 orders were produced and delivered.

items.part:
The maximum heart rate is based on your age:

Maximum heart rate = 220 − your age

The target heart rate is generally expressed as a percentage, usually between 50% to 85% of the maximum heart rate.

Josh is 22 years old.
Sam’s target heart rate of 60% is 114 beats per minute. What is Sam’s age?
items.sol:
Let $x$ be Sam's maximum heart rate. Then 60% of $x$ is $114$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.6x &= 114 \\ x &= \dfrac{114}{0.6} \\ &= 190 \end{aligned}$$
Using $MHR = 220 - \text{age}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 190 &= 220 - \text{age} \\ \text{age} &= 220 - 190 \\ &= 30 \text{ years} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A student travels to and from university five days each week. She compares the costs of two different modes of travel.

Her motorcycle uses one litre of fuel for every 17 km travelled. The cost of fuel is \$1.47/ L and the distance from her home to the university car park is 34 km.

One way cost of travelling by a direct bus is \$4.71 per trip.

Which mode of travel is cheaper per week and by how much? Support your answer with calculations.
items.sol:
Each week she makes $5 \times 2 = 10$ one-way trips. Fuel for a 34 km trip is $\dfrac{34}{17} = 2$ litres.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Motorcycle} &= 2 \times 1.47 \times 2 \times 5 \\ &= \$29.40 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bus} &= 4.71 \times 5 \times 2 \\ &= \$47.10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Difference} &= 47.10 - 29.40 \\ &= \$17.70 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The motorcycle is cheaper by } \$17.70 \text{ per week}$$
items.final: The motorcycle is cheaper by $17.70 per week

items.part:
Amy hopes to have \$25,000 in 3 years to buy a car. She opens an account which pays interest of 4\% pa, compounded quarterly.

How much will she need to invest today to ensure she meets her savings goal?
items.sol:
Interest is compounded quarterly for 3 years, so $n = 12$ and $r = \dfrac{4\%}{4} = 1\%$.
$$\begin{aligned} 25000 &= PV\left(1 + \dfrac{4\%}{4}\right)^{12} \\ 25000 &= PV(1.01)^{12} \\ PV &= \dfrac{25000}{(1.01)^{12}} \\ &= \$22186.23 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Maximilian is in Athens, which is two hours ahead of the Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Dominic is in New York, which is five hours behind UTC.

Dominic is going to fly from New York to Athens. His flight will leave on Wednesday at 9am, New York time, and will take 11 hours.

What day and time will it be in Athens when he arrives?
items.sol:
Athens is 2 hours ahead of UTC and New York is 5 hours behind UTC, so the time difference is
$$2 - (-5) = 7 \text{ hours}$$
Arrival in New York time: $9\text{ am} + 11\text{ h} = 8\text{ pm}$ Wednesday.

Add the time difference to get Athens time.

$\therefore$ Dominic arrives in Athens at $3$ am Thursday.

The perimeter is the sum of the three sides.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 880 + 1290 + 1260 \\ &= 3430 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

Farmer Ellis has assumed the paddock has a right angle and has used side $c$ as the height, which is the wrong formula.

He should have used

$$A = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$$

Using the cosine rule for the angle opposite side $c$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos C &= \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} \\ &= \dfrac{1290^2 + 1260^2 - 880^2}{2 \times 1290 \times 1260} \\ &= 0.762\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} C &= \cos^{-1}(0.762\ldots) \\ &= 40^\circ 21' \end{aligned}$$

Using the area formula with the included angle $C$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1290 \times 1260 \times \sin(40^\circ 21') \\ &\approx 526\,200 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the sine rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin B}{1260} &= \dfrac{\sin 40^\circ 21'}{880} \\ B &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sin 40^\circ 21'}{880} \times 1260\right) \\ &= 67^\circ 59' \end{aligned}$$

Using the angle sum of a triangle:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 180^\circ - 67^\circ 59' - 40^\circ 21' \\ &= 71^\circ 40' \end{aligned}$$

The completed triangle has

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 71^\circ 40' & a &= 1290 \text{ m} \\ B &= 67^\circ 59' & b &= 1260 \text{ m} \\ C &= 40^\circ 21' & c &= 880 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{3307_q4_s1}

In right-angled triangle $ABD$, the side $BD$ is opposite the angle $71^\circ 40'$ and $AB = 880$ is the hypotenuse.

$$\sin 71^\circ 40' = \dfrac{BD}{880}$$

$$\begin{aligned} BD &= 880 \times \sin 71^\circ 40' \\ &\approx 835 \\ &\approx 840 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

Angle $C$ could be used instead.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Population} &= \dfrac{144 \times 15}{10} \\ &= 216 \text{ ducks} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The estimate is } 216 \text{ ducks.}$$

Eliza is attempting to fill her bathtub with jelly.

Water needed per $85$ g of crystals is $250$ mL, so for $10.2$ kg $= 10\,200$ g we multiply by $\dfrac{10\,200}{85} = 120$.
$$250 \times 120 = 30\,000 \text{ mL} = 30 \text{ L}$$
The urn boils $10$ L at a time, so

Route B is shorter, so it uses less fuel.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fuel} &= \dfrac{160.33 \times 9.3}{100} \\ &\approx 14.91 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$

Interest is $\dfrac{6\%}{12} = 0.5\%$ per month, over $3 \times 12 = 36$ months.

$$\begin{aligned} 11 &= \dfrac{5p + 10}{2} \\ 22 &= 5p + 10 &&(\text{multiply by } 2) \\ 12 &= 5p &&(\text{subtract } 10) \\ p &= \dfrac{12}{5} &&(\text{divide by } 5) \\ &= 2.4 \end{aligned}$$

Reading the plot, Team A has 13 scores:

The median is the 7th score, $18$.

Team B has 12 scores:
$$2, 6, 13, 17, 19, 22, 24, 25, 28, 34, 36, 37$$
The median is the mean of the 6th and 7th scores:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{22 + 24}{2} &= 23 \end{aligned}$$
Difference in medians:
$$\begin{aligned} 23 - 18 &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
The medians differ by $5$ repetitions (Team B higher).

For Team A (13 scores), the median is the 7th score. The lower half is the first six scores $5, 6, 8, 14, 17, 17$, so
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 &= \dfrac{8 + 14}{2} \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
The upper half is the last six scores $20, 22, 27, 31, 33, 40$, so
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 &= \dfrac{27 + 31}{2} \\ &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
Interquartile range of Team A:
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= 29 - 11 \\ &= 18 \end{aligned}$$
Since $18 > 16$, Team A has the larger interquartile range.

This means the middle $50\%$ of Team A's results are more spread out, so Team A is less consistent than Team B.

In particular, he has been taking note of the Brown Treecreeper, a threatened species.

The number of sightings over the last four years are shown below.

\extable{308_q18_t1}

What was the greatest percentage decrease from one year to the next and how does this compare to the greatest percentage increase?
items.sol:
Percentage change from one year to the next, using $\dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{old value}} \times 100\%$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2019 \text{ to } 2020 &: \dfrac{28 - 32}{32} \times 100 = -12.5\% \\ 2020 \text{ to } 2021 &: \dfrac{27 - 28}{28} \times 100 \approx -3.6\% \\ 2021 \text{ to } 2022 &: \dfrac{31 - 27}{27} \times 100 \approx +14.8\% \end{aligned}$$
The greatest percentage decrease was $12.5\%$ (2019 to 2020).

The greatest percentage increase was about $14.8\%$ (2021 to 2022), which is greater than the greatest decrease by about $2.3$ percentage points.
items.final: Greatest decrease 12.5% (2019 to 2020); greatest increase about 14.8% is greater by about 2.3 percentage points

$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{47-40}{5} \\ &= 1.4 \end{aligned}$$

Convert both scores to $z$-scores using $z=\dfrac{x-40}{5}$.

The table gives the percentage between $z=0$ and $z=a$, and the distribution is symmetrical, so the percentage between $z=-0.4$ and $z=0$ equals that between $z=0$ and $z=0.4$.

$$\begin{aligned} 41.92 + 15.54 &= 57.46 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vanna Beach.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Weston.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{308_q21_1}
It then plans to fly directly back to Underwood.

Calculate the distance that it will fly.
items.sol:
\exfigure{308_q21_s1}

The return flight is side $UW$ of triangle $UVW$. First find $\angle UVW$.

The bearing of $U$ from $V$ is $055^\circ+180^\circ=235^\circ$ (co-interior angles with the north lines), and the bearing of $W$ from $V$ is $150^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle UVW &= 235^\circ-150^\circ \\ &= 85^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Apply the cosine rule in triangle $UVW$.
$$\begin{aligned} UW^2 &= UV^2+VW^2-2\cdot UV\cdot VW\cos 85^\circ \\ &= 70^2+82^2-2\times 70\times 82\times\cos 85^\circ \\ &\approx 10\,623.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} UW &\approx 103.07 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the helicopter flies about } 103 \text{ km}$$

items.part:
A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vanna Beach.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Weston.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{308_q21_1}
Determine the bearing (from Weston) on which it should fly to return to Underwood.
items.sol:
\exfigure{308_q21_s1}

Find $\angle UWV$ using the sine rule in triangle $UVW$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin \angle UWV}{70} &= \dfrac{\sin 85^\circ}{103.07} \\ \sin \angle UWV &= \dfrac{70\sin 85^\circ}{103.07} \\ \angle UWV &\approx 42.6^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The angle is acute because $UV<VW$, so $\angle UWV$ is opposite the shorter side.

The bearing of $V$ from $W$ is $150^\circ+180^\circ=330^\circ$. Underwood lies anticlockwise from $WV$ (to the left when facing $V$ from $W$), so subtract.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing of } U \text{ from } W &= 330^\circ-42.6^\circ \\ &\approx 287^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the helicopter should fly on a bearing of about } 287^\circ$$

items.part:
An outdoor spa has a pump which is rated at 350 watts and a heater which is rated at 1.2 kW.

The table below shows the amount of usage that the pump and heater have at different times of the year.

\extable{308_q22_t1}

How many kWh of energy would the spa use in a year?
items.sol:
Energy $(\text{kWh})$ = power $(\text{kW})\times$ time (hours). The pump is $350 \text{ W}=0.35 \text{ kW}$.

Pump hours per day:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Warmer months} &: 3+1.5=4.5 \text{ h} \\ \text{Cooler months} &: 1.5+1.2=2.7 \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
Pump hours per year:
$$\begin{aligned} 4.5\times 182+2.7\times 183 &= 819+494.1 \\ &= 1313.1 \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
Heater hours per day:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Warmer months} &: 5\times 12=60 \text{ min}=1 \text{ h} \\ \text{Cooler months} &: 12\times 12=144 \text{ min}=2.4 \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
Heater hours per year:
$$\begin{aligned} 1\times 182+2.4\times 183 &= 182+439.2 \\ &= 621.2 \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
Total energy:
$$\begin{aligned} E &= 0.35\times 1313.1+1.2\times 621.2 \\ &= 459.585+745.44 \\ &\approx 1205 \text{ kWh} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the spa uses about } 1205 \text{ kWh in a year}$$

items.part:
The network diagram below shows the location of nine towns and the connecting roads between them, along with the length of each road in kilometres.

\exfigure{308_q23_1}

Find the shortest path joining $A$ and $H$ and give its length.

You can write values on the diagram as part of your working.
items.sol:
Work outwards from $A$, writing on each town the shortest distance found from $A$ (Dijkstra's method).
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 0 \\ E &= 8 \\ B &= 9 \\ F &= \min(12,\ 8+5)=12 \\ C &= \min(9+6,\ 12+10)=15 \\ I &= 8+8=16 \\ D &= 15+7=22 \\ G &= \min(12+13,\ 16+7)=23 \\ H &= \min(22+12,\ 23+10,\ 16+19)=33 \end{aligned}$$
The smallest value at $H$ comes via $G$, and $G$'s shortest value comes via $I$, which comes via $E$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Length} &= 8+8+7+10 \\ &= 33 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{shortest path } A\to E\to I\to G\to H \text{, length } 33 \text{ km}$$
items.final: $A\to E\to I\to G\to H$, length $33$ km

items.part:
Tahnee bought a car for use with her small business for \$24 000.

For taxation purposes she needed to work out a depreciated value of the car each year.

She initially decided to do this using the declining balance method at a rate of 25%.
Show that the depreciation of the car in the first four years is more than three times greater than the depreciation between the fourth and eighth years using this method.
items.sol:
Declining balance: $V=24\,000(0.75)^n$, since the value falls 25% each year.
$$\begin{aligned} V_4 &= 24\,000(0.75)^4 = \$7593.75 \\ V_8 &= 24\,000(0.75)^8 \approx \$2402.71 \end{aligned}$$
Depreciation in the first four years:
$$\begin{aligned} 24\,000-7593.75 &= \$16\,406.25 \end{aligned}$$
Depreciation between the fourth and eighth years:
$$\begin{aligned} 7593.75-2402.71 &= \$5191.04 \end{aligned}$$
Three times the later depreciation:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\times 5191.04 &= \$15\,573.12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 16\,406.25>15\,573.12$$
so the depreciation in the first four years is more than three times the depreciation between the fourth and eighth years.

items.part:
Tahnee bought a car for use with her small business for \$24 000.

For taxation purposes she needed to work out a depreciated value of the car each year.

She initially decided to do this using the declining balance method at a rate of 25%.
She decided to change to the straight-line method of depreciation, as calculations were easier, but wants the value after eight years to be same as she calculated using the declining balance method.

By what amount should she depreciate the car each year, and what percentage is this of the cars new value?
items.sol:
The value after eight years must be $\$2402.71$, so the total depreciation is
$$\begin{aligned} 24\,000-2402.71 &= \$21\,597.29 \end{aligned}$$
Straight-line depreciation spreads this equally over 8 years.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Yearly depreciation} &= \dfrac{21\,597.29}{8} \\ &\approx \$2699.66 \end{aligned}$$
As a percentage of the new value:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2699.66}{24\,000}\times 100 &\approx 11.25\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{she should depreciate the car by about } \$2699.66 \text{ each year, which is about } 11.25\% \text{ of its new value}$$
items.final: about $\$2699.66$ each year, about $11.25\%$ of its new value

items.part:
Abigail and Daniel use different measuring tapes to measure the dimensions of the rectangle shown below.

Abigail's tape has centimetres labelled, with millimetre markings shown in between.

Daniel's tape has centimetres labelled, with half centimetre markings shown in between.

\exfigure{308_q26_1}

They both record the length as 11.5 cm.

Abigail records the width as 6.3 cm while Daniel records it as 6.5 cm.
What is the percentage error in each of their measurements of the length?
items.sol:
The greatest possible error is half the smallest marked unit.

Abigail (millimetres): error $=\pm 0.05$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage error} &= \dfrac{0.05}{11.5}\times 100 \\ &\approx 0.43\% \end{aligned}$$
Daniel (half centimetres): error $=\pm 0.25$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage error} &= \dfrac{0.25}{11.5}\times 100 \\ &\approx 2.2\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Abigail } \approx 0.43\%,\ \text{Daniel } \approx 2.2\%$$

Abigail's tape has centimetres labelled, with millimetre markings shown in between.

Daniel's tape has centimetres labelled, with half centimetre markings shown in between.

They both record the length as 11.5 cm.

items.part:
Sandy is on holiday in San Francisco and wants to stream a Matilda's World Cup match which is played in Sydney on Monday $31^{\text{st}}$ July and starts at 3:00 pm.

San Francisco is located at UTC $-8$ and Sydney at UTC $+10$.

San Francisco is subject to daylight saving in July and August, but Sydney is not.

At what time and date in San Francisco should Sandy start streaming the match?
items.sol:
Convert the Sydney start time to UTC. Sydney is UTC $+10$, so subtract 10 hours.
$$\begin{aligned} 3{:}00 \text{ pm Monday} &= 15{:}00 \text{ Monday (Sydney)} \\ \text{UTC} &= 15{:}00-10{:}00 = 5{:}00 \text{ am Monday} \end{aligned}$$
San Francisco is UTC $-8$, but daylight saving makes it UTC $-7$ in July.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{San Francisco} &= 5{:}00 \text{ am Monday}-7 \text{ h} \\ &= 10{:}00 \text{ pm Sunday} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Sandy should start streaming at } 10{:}00 \text{ pm on Sunday } 30^{\text{th}} \text{ July}$$

items.part:
Mr Jensen records the number of days that each student in his Year 11 class is absent during Semester 1 and he also works out their average test mark as a percentage.

He draws the scatterplot below to help him in his discussions with his students in relation to their absences.

\exfigure{308_q28_1}

He calculates the correlation coefficient to be $-0.9419$.

He draws a line of best fit on the scatterplot which has an equation of $m = 96.6 - 3.84n$.

Describe and interpret the data and other information provided and explain how it could be used in discussions with students about absences.
items.sol:
Correlation: $r=-0.9419$ is close to $-1$, so there is a strong negative linear relationship. Students with more days absent tend to have lower average marks.

Strength: the coefficient of determination is
$$\begin{aligned} r^2 &= (-0.9419)^2 \\ &\approx 0.887 \end{aligned}$$
so about $88.7\%$ of the variation in average mark is explained by the number of days absent. The points on the scatterplot lie close to the line.

Line of best fit $m=96.6-3.84n$:

The gradient $-3.84$ means that, on average, each extra day absent is associated with a drop of about $3.84$ marks.

The intercept $96.6$ is the predicted mark for a student with no absences.

The line can be used for prediction within the data range (about $1.5$ to $11$ days). For example, for 5 days absent:
$$\begin{aligned} m &= 96.6-3.84\times 5 \\ &= 77.4 \end{aligned}$$
Limitations: the line should not be used far outside the range (for instance, a very large $n$ would predict a negative mark). Correlation does not prove that absence causes the lower marks, since other factors may affect both.

Use in discussions: Mr Jensen can show students that missing more days is strongly linked to lower marks, with each day missed costing nearly 4 marks on average, and encourage good attendance.

items.part:
The Discount Dapper Corporation produces cummerbunds for sale.

In any production run, the cost ($\$C$) of producing $N$ cummerbunds is given by the equation:

$$C = 8N + 2000$$

The cummerbunds are sold to retailers at the cost of \$12 each, so the equation for the revenue returned to the corporation is $R = 12N$.

Draw the lines representing the cost equation ($C$) and the revenue equation ($R$) on the axes below and use the graph to find the break-even point after which the corporation begins to make a profit on the run of cummerbunds.

\exfigure{308_q29_1}
items.sol:
Plot each line from two points, using $N=0$ and $N=1000$.
$$\begin{aligned} C=8N+2000:\quad & N=0,\ C=2000;\quad N=1000,\ C=10\,000 \\ R=12N:\quad & N=0,\ R=0;\quad N=1000,\ R=12\,000 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{308_q29_s1}

The break-even point is where the lines cross, so $C=R$.
$$\begin{aligned} 8N+2000 &= 12N \\ 2000 &= 4N \\ N &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 12\times 500 \\ &= 6000 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{break-even point is } (500,\ \$6000)\text{; a profit is made after } 500 \text{ cummerbunds}$$

An electrical circuit has a constant voltage applied and has a resistance which can be changed.

The amount of current in amps ($C$) which will flow in the circuit is inversely proportional to the resistance in Ohms ($R$) of the circuit.

The graph below shows the curve which demonstrates the relationship between $R$ and $C$ for this circuit.

\exfigure{308_q31_1}
The equation which describes the curve is of the form $C = \dfrac{K}{R}$.

Use the point $(6, 40)$ on the graph to find the value of $K$.
items.sol:
The curve has equation $C = \dfrac{K}{R}$, and passes through $(6, 40)$.

Substitute $R = 6$, $C = 40$.
$$\begin{aligned} 40 &= \dfrac{K}{6} \\ K &= 40\times 6 \\ &= 240 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ K = 240$$

items.part:
Jelena borrows \$24 000 through a reducing balance loan.

Interest is calculated monthly (with each month considered as $\dfrac{1}{12}$ of a year).

Repayments of \$800.00 are deducted each month after the interest is added.

Jelena uses the spreadsheet below, to show the progress of the loan.

\extable{308_q32_t1}
What is the annual percentage interest rate?
items.sol:
In month 1 the interest on $\$24\,000$ is $\$160$ (cell C2).

The monthly rate is
$$\dfrac{160}{24\,000} = \dfrac{1}{150} \approx 0.667\%$$
The annual rate is $12$ times the monthly rate.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{annual rate} &= 12\times \dfrac{1}{150} \\ &= 0.08 \\ &= 8\% \text{ p.a.} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the interest rate is } 8\% \text{ p.a.}$$

items.part:

Interest is calculated monthly (with each month considered as $\dfrac{1}{12}$ of a year).

Repayments of \$800.00 are deducted each month after the interest is added.

Jelena uses the spreadsheet below, to show the progress of the loan.

\extable{308_q32_t1}
Complete the next two rows to find the amount $X$, which would appear in cell E7.

items.sol:
Forward scan (earliest start time, left box): take the largest total along any path into each node.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{after } G &: 7 \\ \text{after } H &: 9 \\ \text{after } I,K &: \max(7+5,\ 9+8) = 17 \\ \text{after } M &: 17+6 = 23 \\ \text{end} &: \max(17+10,\ 23+7,\ 9+11,\ 9+13) = 30 \end{aligned}$$
Backward scan (latest start time, right box): start from the end time $30$ and take the smallest value.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{before } N &: 30-7 = 23 \\ \text{node after } I,K &: \min(30-10,\ 23-6) = 17 \\ \text{node after } H &: \min(17-8,\ 30-11,\ 30-13) = 9 \\ \text{node after } G &: 17-5 = 12 \\ \text{start} &: \min(12-7,\ 9-9) = 0 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{308_q33_s1}
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum completion time} = 30 \text{ minutes}$$

The critical path joins the nodes where the earliest and latest start times are equal.

These are the activities with no float: $H$, $K$, $M$, $N$.

Check: $9+8+6+7 = 30$.
$$\therefore\ \text{critical path: } H \to K \to M \to N$$

Activity $I$ runs from the node after $G$ to the node after $I,K$.

Float time $=$ latest finish $-$ earliest start $-$ duration.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{float} &= 17 - 7 - 5 \\ &= 5 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the float time of } I \text{ is } 5 \text{ minutes}$$

Georgia is working as a surveyor and wishes to find the perimeter and area of a field $PQRS$.

The drawing below is completed from a radial survey centred at point $A$.

\exfigure{308_q34_1}

The bearing from $A$ of $P$ is $336^\circ$ and of $Q$ is $042^\circ$, and the distance $AP$ is 260 m.
Explain why $\angle PAQ = 66^\circ$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{308_q34_s1}

North is the reference line at $A$. $P$ is on a bearing of $336^\circ$, which is $360^\circ - 336^\circ = 24^\circ$ to the west of north.

$Q$ is on a bearing of $042^\circ$, which is $42^\circ$ to the east of north.

North lies between $AP$ and $AQ$, so the angles add.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle PAQ &= 24^\circ + 42^\circ \\ &= 66^\circ \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Georgia is working as a surveyor and wishes to find the perimeter and area of a field $PQRS$.

The drawing below is completed from a radial survey centred at point $A$.

\exfigure{308_q34_1}

The bearing from $A$ of $P$ is $336^\circ$ and of $Q$ is $042^\circ$, and the distance $AP$ is 260 m.
Calculate the length of $PQ$ (to the nearest m) and hence find the perimeter of the field.
items.sol:
\exfigure{308_q34_s2}

In $\triangle PAQ$, $AP = 260$, $\angle PAQ = 66^\circ$ and $\angle PQA = 72^\circ$, so $AP$ is opposite $\angle PQA$ and $PQ$ is opposite $\angle PAQ$.

By the sine rule,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{PQ}{\sin 66^\circ} &= \dfrac{260}{\sin 72^\circ} \\ PQ &= \dfrac{260\sin 66^\circ}{\sin 72^\circ} \\ &\approx 249.7 \\ &\approx 250 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is $PQ + QR + RS + SP$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Perimeter} &= 250 + 190 + 185 + 250 \\ &= 875 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ PQ \approx 250 \text{ m and the perimeter is } 875 \text{ m}$$
items.final: $PQ \approx 250$ m and the perimeter is 875 m

Lachie and Emily are enrolled in different schools but are doing the same courses in English and Mathematics.

When they complete their Trial HSC Exams, they compare their results in Mathematics and English from their separate schools.

The statistical results for the exams at both schools are shown below.

All of the exam results were normally distributed.

\extable{308_q37_t2}
Use $z$-scores to determine which student performed best on their English exam, compared to their school cohort.
items.sol:
Use $z = \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ for each English mark.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lachie: } z &= \dfrac{68-68}{8} = 0 \\ \text{Emily: } z &= \dfrac{68-74}{6} = -1 \end{aligned}$$
Lachie's $z$-score is higher, so he is further above his school's average.
$$\therefore\ \text{Lachie performed best in English compared with his cohort}$$
items.final: Lachie performed best in English compared with his cohort

items.part:
Lachie and Emily are enrolled in different schools but are doing the same courses in English and Mathematics.

The statistical results for the exams at both schools are shown below.

All of the exam results were normally distributed.

Calculate Lachie's raw maths mark and determine who performed best on their Mathematics exam, compared to their school cohort.
items.sol:
For Lachie, $z = 2$, $\mu = 62$, $\sigma = 9$. Use $x = \mu + z\sigma$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 62 + 2\times 9 \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$
For Emily, with a mark of $79$, $\mu = 64$, $\sigma = 5$:
$$z = \dfrac{79-64}{5} = 3$$
Emily's $z$-score of $3$ is higher than Lachie's $2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Lachie's mark was } 80 \text{, and Emily performed best in Mathematics compared with her cohort}$$
items.final: Lachie's mark was 80, and Emily performed best in Mathematics compared with her cohort

The loan is the present value of all repayments. The rate per month is
$$\dfrac{6\%}{12} = 0.5\% = 0.005$$
Treat the repayments as $\$500$ for all $48$ months plus an extra $\$300$ for the last $24$ months (months $25$ to $48$).

The factor for the last $24$ months is the difference of the $48$ and $24$ period factors at $0.005$:
$$42.58032 - 22.56287 = 20.01745$$

items.part:
The network diagram shows nine towns and the fifteen roads that connect them.

The length of each road is shown, in kilometres.

All the roads need to be resurfaced after heavy rainfall.

The local council decides to initially resurface the minimum length of roads that will allow all towns to be connected by resurfaced roads.

This is equivalent to finding a minimum spanning tree.

\exfigure{308_q39_1}

Determine the minimum spanning tree and find the total length of roads to be resurfaced, then redraw the minimum spanning tree on the vertices below, showing the distances.

\exfigure{308_q39_2}

Length of roads to be resurfaced = _________ km
items.sol:
Use Kruskal's algorithm: add the shortest road that does not form a cycle, until all $9$ towns are connected ($8$ roads).
$$\begin{aligned} XY &= 7 &&\text{add} \\ SZ &= 8 &&\text{add} \\ RZ &= 9 &&\text{add} \\ UV &= 9 &&\text{add} \\ ZT &= 10 &&\text{add} \\ VW &= 10 &&\text{add} \\ RT &= 12 &&\text{rejected (cycle } R, Z, T) \\ SU &= 12 &&\text{add (joins } \{S,Z,R,T\} \text{ to } \{U,V,W\}) \\ ZV &= 13,\ TW = 14,\ RS = 15 &&\text{rejected (cycles)} \\ VY &= 15 &&\text{add (joins } \{X,Y\}) \end{aligned}$$
This gives $8$ roads, so the tree is complete.

\exfigure{308_q39_s1}
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 7+8+9+9+10+10+12+15 \\ &= 80 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{length of roads to be resurfaced} = 80 \text{ km}$$

items.part:
A loaf of bread is measured to have a mass of 700 g, to the nearest 10 g.

Calculate the percentage error of this measurement, correct to three decimal places.
items.sol:
The absolute error is half the precision of the measuring unit.
$$\text{Absolute error}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10\text{ g}=5\text{ g}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Percentage error}&=\dfrac{5}{700}\times 100\\&\approx 0.714\%\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{percentage error}\approx 0.714\%$$

Angelo bought a laptop four years ago. It depreciated by \$220 each year using the straight-line method of depreciation. The salvage value of the laptop is now \$180.

Calculate the original amount that Angelo paid for the laptop.
items.sol:
Use the straight-line depreciation formula $S=V_0-Dn$, with $S=180$, $D=220$ and $n=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}180&=V_0-220\times 4\\180&=V_0-880\\V_0&=180+880\\&=\$1060\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Angelo paid } \$1060 \text{ for the laptop.}$$

During the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney, which is located at $(35^\circ\text{S}, 150^\circ\text{E})$, the 100 m freestyle swimming final was held on a Wednesday at 2:00 pm local time. The event was broadcast live to New York, which is located at $(40^\circ\text{N}, 75^\circ\text{W})$.

What time and day was the event broadcast in New York?

It is given that $15^\circ = 1$ hour time difference. Ignore daylight saving.
items.sol:
The longitude difference is found by adding, since the cities are on opposite sides of $0^\circ$.
$$\text{Longitude difference}=75+150=225^\circ$$
$$\text{Time difference}=225\div 15=15\text{ hours}$$
New York is west of Sydney, so it is 15 hours behind Sydney.
$$2\text{ pm}-15\text{ hours}=11{:}00\text{ pm}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the event was broadcast at 11:00 pm on Tuesday.}$$

Cameron is a teacher and his gross annual income is \$108 000. He paid a total of \$26 200 in Pay As You Go (PAYG) tax during the 2022–23 financial year. His tax deductions include the purchase of teaching resources valued at \$342 and teacher union fees of \$674. Cameron must also pay a Medicare levy of 2% of his taxable income.

Given that Cameron paid \$26 200 in PAYG tax, determine whether he will receive a tax refund or owe money to the Australian Taxation Office and if he owes the ATO by how much.
items.sol:
Deductions are subtracted from gross income.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Taxable income}&=108\,000-(342+674)\\&=\$106\,984\end{aligned}$$
This income lies in the bracket above \$45 000, so
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Tax payable}&=5902+(106\,984-45\,000)\times 0.325\\&=\$26\,046.80\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Medicare levy}&=2\%\times 106\,984\\&=\$2139.68\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total taxes}&=26\,046.80+2139.68\\&=\$28\,186.48\end{aligned}$$
Cameron has paid \$26 200, which is less than \$28 186.48.
$$\therefore\ \text{Cameron owes the ATO } \$1986.48.$$

items.part:
Charlotte invested \$7000 for six years at an interest rate of 4.5% per annum.
If interest is compounded yearly, find the amount of interest that Charlotte earned after six years, correct to the nearest cent.
items.sol:
Using the compound interest formula $FV=PV(1+r)^n$ with $PV=7000$, $r=0.045$, $n=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}FV&=7000(1+0.045)^6\\&=\$9115.82\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Interest}&=9115.82-7000\\&=\$2115.82\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Charlotte invested \$7000 for six years at an interest rate of 4.5% per annum.
If the compound interest found in part (a) was earned as simple interest over the same period, determine the simple interest rate used. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
Using the simple interest formula $I=Prn$ with $I=2115.82$, $P=7000$ and $n=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}2115.82&=7000\times r\times 6\\2115.82&=42\,000r\\r&=\dfrac{2115.82}{42\,000}\\&=0.050376\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r\approx 5.04\%$$

The hexagon has been divided into two triangles $AEF$ and $BDC$, and a rectangle $ABDE$, as shown above.

Show that the area of the hexagon is approximately $65\text{ cm}^2$.
items.sol:
Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is $120^\circ$, so $\angle AFE=120^\circ$.

Using the cosine rule in $\triangle AEF$:

The hexagon is two triangles plus the rectangle.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of hexagon} &= (2\times 10.8)+43.5 \\ &\approx 65 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Olivia is a scientist who is concerned about the magpie population in her town. She collects 170 magpies and tags them. A couple of months later she collects 32 magpies and found 10 of them were tagged. What is her estimate of the magpie population, using the capture-recapture method?
items.sol:
Capture-recapture: $\dfrac{\text{tagged in second sample}}{\text{second sample}}=\dfrac{\text{tagged originally}}{\text{population}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Population} &\approx \dfrac{170\times 32}{10} \\ &= 544 \text{ magpies} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: The maximum speed ($v$), in km/h, of a truck is inversely proportional to the weight ($w$ kg) it carries. A truck carrying a weight of 1600 kg can travel at 80 km/h. What is the maximum speed of the truck if the weight is 1250 kg
items.sol:
The speed is inversely proportional to the weight.
$$v=\dfrac{k}{w}$$
Substitute $v=80$ and $w=1600$.
$$\begin{aligned} 80 &= \dfrac{k}{1600} \\ k &= 80\times 1600 \\ &= 128\,000 \end{aligned}$$
So $v=\dfrac{128\,000}{w}$.

When $w=1250$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &= \dfrac{128\,000}{1250} \\ &= 102.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the speed is } 102.4 \text{ km/h}$$

items.part:
A business produces bottles of cola whose capacity is normally distributed with a mean capacity of 600 mL and a standard deviation of 2 mL.
If 99.7% of bottles pass the quality control check, what limits will the volume of cola in each bottle almost certainly lie?
items.sol:
About $99.7\%$ of scores lie within 3 standard deviations of the mean, so between $z=-3$ and $z=3$.

Lower limit, using $z=\dfrac{x-600}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} -3 &= \dfrac{x-600}{2} \\ x &= 2\times(-3)+600 \\ &= 594 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
Upper limit:
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= \dfrac{x-600}{2} \\ x &= 3\times 2+600 \\ &= 606 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the limits are } 594 \text{ mL and } 606 \text{ mL}$$

items.part:
45% of the residents in a local community have been administered only one vaccination against a spreading virus and 30% of the residents have been administered two vaccinations (so that they are fully vaccinated).
What is the probability that a randomly chosen resident from the community has NOT been administered at least ONE vaccination?
items.sol:
The probability of no vaccination is one minus the probability of one or two vaccinations.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-(0.45+0.3) \\ &= 0.25 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 25\% \text{ or } 0.25 \text{ or } \dfrac{1}{4}$$

items.part:
45% of the residents in a local community have been administered only one vaccination against a spreading virus and 30% of the residents have been administered two vaccinations (so that they are fully vaccinated).
If TWO residents are randomly selected from the community, what is the probability that at least ONE of them has been administered at least ONE vaccination?
items.sol:
Use the complement: at least one vaccinated is one minus neither vaccinated.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-(0.25\times 0.25) \\ &= 1-0.0625 \\ &= 0.9375 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 0.9375 \text{ or } 93.75\%$$

items.part:
The Discount Dapper Corporation produces men’s ties for sale.

In any production run, the cost ($\$C$) of producing $N$ ties is given by the equation:

$$C=8N+2000$$

The ties are sold to retailers at the cost of \$12 each, so the equation for the revenue returned to the corporation is $R=12N$
Determine the break-even point. Explain the significance of this point.
items.sol:
At the break-even point, cost equals revenue.
$$\begin{aligned} 8N+2000 &= 12N \\ 2000 &= 4N \\ N &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
Then $R=12\times 500=6000$.

The break-even point is $(500, 6000)$.

This means the corporation must make and sell more than 500 ties to make a profit.
items.final: Break-even point is $(500, 6000)$; the corporation must make and sell more than 500 ties to make a profit.

The formula below is used to calculate an estimate for the blood alcohol content (BAC) of males.

$$\text{BAC}_{male}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{6.8M}$$

where $N$ is the number of standard drinks consumed, $H$ is the number of hours between the first and the last drink, and $M$ is the mass in kilograms.

Stephen weighs 98 kilograms. He consumed 6.5 standard drinks between 6:00 pm and 9:45 pm. He then stopped drinking alcohol.

His BAC reached zero at 1:15am. Calculate the rate at which his body metabolised the alcohol, in terms of BAC per hour. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.
items.sol:
Stephen drank from 6:00 pm to 9:45 pm, so $H=3.75$ hours.

Substitute into the formula with $N=6.5$ and $M=98$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{BAC}&=\dfrac{10\times 6.5-7.5\times 3.75}{6.8\times 98}\\&=0.0553346\ldots\end{aligned}$$
His BAC reached zero 3.5 hours after 9:45 pm (at 1:15 am).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Rate of metabolism}&=\dfrac{\text{BAC}}{\text{time taken}}\\&=\dfrac{0.0553346\ldots}{3.5}\\&\approx 0.0158 \text{ BAC/hour (to 4 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

Aisha used her credit card to buy 1500 shares at a price of \$7.50 per share. A brokerage fee of $1.2\%$ was also charged on the purchase.

At the end of her first year owning the shares, she collected an annual dividend at a yield of $5.5\%$. She then used this dividend to pay back part of her credit card debt.

Calculate the amount Aisha still owes on her credit card given that the interest rate on the credit card is $20\%$ per annum, compounded daily.
items.sol:
The cost of the shares includes the $1.2\%$ brokerage fee.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Cost of buying shares}&=1500\times 7.50\times 1.012\\&=\$11\,385\end{aligned}$$
The debt grows for one year at $20\%$ per annum, compounded daily.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Amount owing after one year}&=11\,385\left(1+\dfrac{20\%}{365}\right)^{365}\\&=\$13\,904.91\end{aligned}$$
The dividend is $5.5\%$ of the value of the shares.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Dividend}&=5.5\%\times 1500\times 7.50\\&=\$618.75\end{aligned}$$
The dividend is then paid off the debt.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Amount owing after repayment}&=13\,904.91-618.75\\&=\$13\,286.16\end{aligned}$$

Louie is a real estate agent earning a retainer of \$600 per week.
Every month Louie also earns a commission at a rate of $R\%$ on the first \$500 000 of his sales, and then at half of that rate on any sales above \$500 000.

Louie’s monthly income after selling \$750 000 worth of property is \$17 600.

items.sol:
Commission is $R\%$ on the first \$500 000 and $\dfrac{R}{2}\%$ on the remaining \$250 000. Add the retainer of \$2600 to equal \$17 600.
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\dfrac{R}{100}\times 500\,000\right)+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{R}{100}\times 250\,000\right)+2600&=17\,600\\5000R+1250R&=15\,000\\6250R&=15\,000\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore R=2.4$$

A parent used Young's formula to calculate the required medication dosage for their child.

Young's formula is

$$\text{Dosage} = \dfrac{\text{Age of child (years)} \times \text{Adult dose}}{\text{Age of child (years)} + 12}.$$

They found that the child's dosage was one third of the adult dose.

How old is the child?
items.sol:
Let $a$ be the child's age in years and $d$ the adult dose. Young's formula gives the child's dose as one third of the adult dose:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}d &= \dfrac{ad}{a + 12} \\ \dfrac{a}{a + 12} &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ 3a &= a + 12 \\ 2a &= 12 \\ a &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the child is 6 years old}$$

The time taken for a colony of ants to break up a sandwich and carry it away to the nest is inversely proportional to the number of ants performing the task.

If there are 20 ants, then it takes 42 minutes for the sandwich to be taken to the nest.
Calculate how long it takes for 32 ants to carry the sandwich to the nest.
items.sol:
Time is inversely proportional to the number of ants, so with $t$ the time and $n$ the number of ants,
$$t = \dfrac{k}{n}$$
Substituting $t = 42$, $n = 20$:
$$\begin{aligned} 42 &= \dfrac{k}{20} \\ k &= 840 \end{aligned}$$
So $t = \dfrac{840}{n}$. When $n = 32$:
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{840}{32} \\ &= 26.25 \text{ minutes} \\ &= 26 \text{ minutes } 15 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

Scientists perform two wildlife surveys six months apart to estimate the total koala population in a valley.

In the first survey they tagged 50 koalas and then released them back into the wild.

In the second survey six months later, they caught and checked 80 koalas. Of these 80 koalas 15 had tags.
What is the estimate for the number of koalas in the valley?
items.sol:
The proportion of tagged koalas is the same in the sample as in the whole population, so with $T$ the total population,
$$\dfrac{T}{50} = \dfrac{80}{15}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 50 \times \dfrac{80}{15} \\ &= 266 \cdot \dot{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{there are approximately 267 koalas in the valley}$$

items.part: In a normally distributed set of scores, the mean is 35 and the standard deviation is 3. What percentage of scores lie between 26 and 29?
items.sol:
Express 26 and 29 as $z$-scores, using mean $35$ and standard deviation $3$.

$$\begin{aligned} 26 &= 35 - 3\times 3 &&(z=-3)\\ 29 &= 35 - 2\times 3 &&(z=-2) \end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule, about $95\%$ of scores lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean and about $99.7\%$ lie within 3.

So the percentage between $z=-3$ and $z=-2$ and the same percentage between $z=2$ and $z=3$ together make

$$99.7\% - 95\% = 4.7\%$$
By symmetry, each side has half of this.

$$\dfrac{4.7\%}{2} = 2.35\%$$
$$\therefore\ 2.35\% \text{ of scores lie between 26 and 29.}$$

Cairo in Egypt is located at $(30^\circ\text{N},\ 31^\circ\text{E})$.

Sydney, in Australia, is located at $(33^\circ\text{S},\ 151^\circ\text{E})$.

Camilla lives in Sydney and needs to attend an online meeting with her business partners in Cairo starting at 11:00 am on Monday, local time in Cairo.

What time and day, in Sydney, does Camilla need to log on to the meeting?

Ignore daylight saving.
items.sol:
Time zones are based on longitude: each $15^\circ$ is 1 hour, and places further east are ahead.

The difference in longitude is

$$151^\circ - 31^\circ = 120^\circ$$
So the time difference is

$$\dfrac{120}{15} = 8 \text{ hours}$$
Sydney is further east, so Sydney is 8 hours ahead of Cairo.

Cairo 11:00 am Monday becomes

$$11{:}00 \text{ am} + 8 \text{ h} = 7{:}00 \text{ pm Monday}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Camilla must log on at 7:00 pm on Monday (Sydney time).}$$

The interquartile range is

$$\text{IQR} = 48 - 36 = 12$$
A score is an outlier if it lies outside the fences

$$\begin{aligned} \text{lower fence} &= Q_1 - 1.5\times \text{IQR} = 36 - 18 = 18 \\ \text{upper fence} &= Q_3 + 1.5\times \text{IQR} = 48 + 18 = 66 \end{aligned}$$
With no outliers, all scores lie between $18$ and $66$. The range is largest when the minimum is $18$ and the maximum is $66$.

$$\text{Range} = 66 - 18 = 48$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum possible range} = 48$$

items.sol:
For $n = 30$ tables:

Profit is income minus cost:

$$2700 - 2200 = \$500$$

The bearing of $A$ from $O$ is $045^\circ$ and the bearing of $D$ from $O$ is $318^\circ$.

This is greater than $180^\circ$, so the angle inside the block is

Ella contributes \$1200 per month at the start of each month into an investment which pays interest at $3.6\%$ per annum, compounded monthly.
Show that at the end of the second month, the future value of Ella’s investment will be \$2410.81.
items.sol:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{3.6\%}{12}=0.3\%=0.003$. Payments are made at the start of each month, so the first payment earns interest for 2 months and the second for 1 month.
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= 1200(1.003)^2+1200(1.003) \\ &= 1207.2108+1203.60 \\ &= 2410.8108 \\ &\approx \$2410.81 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the future value after 2 months is } \$2410.81$$

items.sol:
Beth's lump sum is invested for 18 months at $0.003$ per month, so her balance is

$$\begin{aligned} 22\,796.62-22\,226.19 &= \$570.43 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Karim has a box containing 7 blue pens and 5 red pens. He selects a pen at random from the box and places it on a table. He then selects a second pen and places it on the table next to the first pen.
What is the probability that the pens on the table are both red?
items.sol:
Both pens are red, so the outcome is $RR$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(RR) &= \dfrac{5}{12}\times\dfrac{4}{11} \\ &= \dfrac{20}{132} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{33} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{both red})=\dfrac{5}{33}$$

items.part:
Karim has a box containing 7 blue pens and 5 red pens. He selects a pen at random from the box and places it on a table. He then selects a second pen and places it on the table next to the first pen.
What is the probability that the pens on the table are different colours?
items.sol:
Different colours means $BR$ or $RB$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{different}) &= P(BR)+P(RB) \\ &= \dfrac{7}{12}\times\dfrac{5}{11}+\dfrac{5}{12}\times\dfrac{7}{11} \\ &= \dfrac{35}{132}+\dfrac{35}{132} \\ &= \dfrac{70}{132} \\ &= \dfrac{35}{66} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{different colours})=\dfrac{35}{66}$$

Activity $H$ starts after $E$, $F$ and $G$ are all finished, so its EST is the longest of the paths into the node where they meet.
$$\begin{aligned} A,F &: 3+7=10 \\ B,E &: 2+5=7 \\ B,C,D,G &: 2+4+3+5=14 \end{aligned}$$
The longest is 14 days.
$$\therefore\ \text{EST of } H = 14 \text{ days}$$

After $H$ and $I$, $J$, the finish of the project needs $K$. The activity $K$ starts when both $H$ and $J$ are complete.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{via } H &: 14+4=18 \\ \text{via } I,J &: 14+2+4=20 \end{aligned}$$
So $K$ starts at day 20 and takes 3 days.
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum completion time} = 20+3 = 23 \text{ days}$$

The critical path is the longest path from start to finish, with length 23 days.

The longest route to the node before $H$ and $I$ is $B,C,D,G$ (14 days). After that, $I,J$ (6 days) is longer than $H$ (4 days).
$$\begin{aligned} B+C+D+G+I+J+K &= 2+4+3+5+2+4+3 \\ &= 23 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{critical path: } B,C,D,G,I,J,K$$
items.final: $B, C, D, G, I, J, K$

items.sol:
Float time $=$ LST $-$ EST, or equivalently (latest finish) $-$ (EST) $-$ (duration).

$E$ starts after $B$, so its EST is 2 days. It must finish by day 14, the EST of $H$ and $I$ (the critical path reaches that node at day 14).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{float} &= 14-2-5 \\ &= 7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{float time of } E = 7 \text{ days}$$

Lauren spends \$6000 on a new photocopier for her business.

She uses the declining-balance method to calculate the depreciation of the photocopier. She claims this amount as a tax deduction each year. She can only claim the depreciation for that particular year.
If the rate of depreciation is $26\%$ per annum, show that the depreciation she can claim in the second year is equal to \$1154, rounded correct to the nearest dollar.
items.sol:
Declining-balance depreciation is $26\%$ of the value at the start of each year.

Year 1:
$$\begin{aligned} D_1 &= 0.26\times 6000 = \$1560 \\ V_1 &= 6000-1560 = \$4440 \end{aligned}$$
Year 2:
$$\begin{aligned} D_2 &= 0.26\times 4440 \\ &= \$1154.40 \\ &\approx \$1154 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the depreciation in the second year is } \$1154$$

items.part:

Using the tax table below and ignoring the Medicare levy, calculate the amount of tax she needs to pay.

\extable{819_q33_t1}
items.sol:
The only deduction is the depreciation from part (a), $\$1154$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{taxable income} &= 110\,000-1154 \\ &= \$108\,846 \end{aligned}$$
This lies in the bracket $\$90\,001-\$180\,000$: $\$20\,797$ plus $37$c for each $\$1$ over $\$90\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{tax} &= 20\,797+0.37\times(108\,846-90\,000) \\ &= 20\,797+0.37\times 18\,846 \\ &= 20\,797+6973.02 \\ &= \$27\,770.02 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{she pays } \$27\,770.02 \text{ in tax}$$

items.sol:
From the scale $1:1000$, $1 \text{ cm}$ represents $10 \text{ m}$, so the roof measures $100 \text{ m}$ by $70 \text{ m}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{area} &= 100\times 70 \\ &= 7000 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1 \text{ kL} = 1 \text{ m}^3$, the volume required is $1200 \text{ m}^3$.

Volume of water $=$ area $\times$ depth of rain.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{depth} &= \dfrac{1200}{7000} \text{ m} \\ &\approx 0.1714 \text{ m} \\ &\approx 171 \text{ mm} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 171 \text{ mm of rain must fall}$$

By the maximum-flow minimum-cut theorem, the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut.

Cut the network between $\{S,A,C,D,E\}$ and $\{B,T\}$. The edges crossing from the first set to the second are $AB$, $CB$ and $ET$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{cut} &= 10+6+18 \\ &= 34 \end{aligned}$$
A flow of 34 is achievable (see part (b)), so no smaller cut exists.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum flow} = 34 \text{ litres per minute}$$

One set of flows that gives 34 L/min:
$$\begin{aligned} SA&=16, & SC&=9, & SD&=9, \\ AB&=10, & AC&=6, & CB&=6, \\ CE&=9, & DE&=9, & BT&=16, \\ ET&=18 \end{aligned}$$
Check conservation at each vertex: at $A$, $16=10+6$; at $C$, $9+6=6+9$; at $D$, $9=9$; at $B$, $10+6=16$; at $E$, $9+9=18$. Flow out of $S$ is $16+9+9=34$.

\exfigure{819_q37_s1}

The maximum flow can only increase if an edge of the minimum cut is enlarged. The minimum cut consists of $AB$, $CB$ and $ET$.

Increasing $ET$ by 3 only raises the flow by 2, because another cut then limits the flow. Increasing $AB$ by 3 (to 13) or $CB$ by 3 (to 9) raises the maximum flow from 34 to 37, the capacity of the cut at $BT$ and $ET$ ($19+18$).
$$\therefore\ \text{increase edge } AB \text{ (or edge } CB\text{)}$$

Tom has a total of \$80 000 in an investment account earning interest at a rate of $0.6\%$ per month. Each month, immediately after the interest has been paid, Tom withdraws \$1200 from the account.

The amount in the account immediately after the $n$th withdrawal can be determined using the recurrence relation

$$A_n = A_{n-1}(1.006) - 1200$$

where $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ and $A_0 = 80\,000$
Use the recurrence relation to find the amount of money in the account immediately after the third withdrawal.
items.sol:
Apply $A_n=1.006A_{n-1}-1200$ three times, starting from $A_0=80\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 80\,000(1.006)-1200 = 79\,280 \\ A_2 &= 79\,280(1.006)-1200 = 78\,555.68 \\ A_3 &= 78\,555.68(1.006)-1200 \approx 77\,827.01 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after the third withdrawal the account holds } \$77\,827.01$$

items.part:
Tom has a total of \$80 000 in an investment account earning interest at a rate of $0.6\%$ per month. Each month, immediately after the interest has been paid, Tom withdraws \$1200 from the account.

The amount in the account immediately after the $n$th withdrawal can be determined using the recurrence relation

$$A_n = A_{n-1}(1.006) - 1200$$

where $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ and $A_0 = 80\,000$
Calculate the amount of interest earned in the first three months.
items.sol:
Interest earned $=$ (final balance) $+$ (total withdrawn) $-$ (starting balance).

Total withdrawn $=3\times1200=\$3600$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{interest} &= 77\,827.01+3600-80\,000 \\ &= \$1427.01 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{interest earned in the first three months is } \$1427.01$$

items.sol:
The box is $20 \text{ cm}$ by $30 \text{ cm}$ by $40 \text{ cm}$. Each ball has diameter $10 \text{ cm}$, so the radius is $5 \text{ cm}$. Each layer is $10 \text{ cm}$ high, so the number of layers is $\dfrac{40}{10}=4$.

Balls in the box: $6\times4=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} V_{\text{ball}} &= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi(5)^3 = \dfrac{500\pi}{3} \\ V_{\text{balls}} &= 24\times\dfrac{500\pi}{3} = 4000\pi \approx 12\,566.4 \text{ cm}^3 \\ V_{\text{box}} &= 20\times30\times40 = 24\,000 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{empty space} &= \dfrac{24\,000-12\,566.4}{24\,000}\times100\% \\ &\approx 47.6\% \\ &\approx 48\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 48\% \text{ of the box is empty}$$

items.part:
The formula for the volume of a cone is

$$V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$$

Where $V$ is the volume, $h$ is the height and $r$ is the radius.
Show that the radius of the cone is

$$r=\sqrt{\dfrac{3V}{\pi h}}$$
items.sol:
Start with the volume formula and make $r$ the subject.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h \\ 3V &= \pi r^2 h \\ \dfrac{3V}{\pi h} &= r^2 \end{aligned}$$
Taking the positive square root (a radius is positive):
$$r=\sqrt{\dfrac{3V}{\pi h}}$$

items.part:

items.sol:
Substitute $V=200$ and $h=20$.
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt{\dfrac{3\times 200}{\pi\times 20}} \\ &\approx 3.09 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Painter B: charges \$80 per hour and bases his quote on painting 20 square metres per hour.

How much will be saved by choosing the cheaper quote? Justify your answer using mathematical reasoning and /or calculations.
items.sol:
Painter A charges per $25$ square metres.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1500}{25} &= 60 \\ 60\times 90 &= \$5400 \end{aligned}$$
Painter B takes $\dfrac{1500}{20}$ hours at \$80 per hour.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1500}{20} &= 75 \\ 75\times 80 &= \$6000 \end{aligned}$$
Painter A is cheaper.
$$\text{Saving}=6000-5400=\$600$$

items.sol:
In triangle $CLM$, $\angle LCM=140^\circ$ (the bearings $65^\circ$ and $285^\circ$ differ by $220^\circ$, so the angle on the other side is $360^\circ-220^\circ=140^\circ$). Using the cosine rule:

items.sol:
Let $\theta=\angle CML$. Using the sine rule in triangle $CLM$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{16} &= \dfrac{\sin 140^\circ}{40} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{16\sin 140^\circ}{40} \\ \theta &= 14.89\ldots^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The bearing of the lake from the mountain is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 180^\circ-75^\circ-\theta \\ &\approx 90^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing is } 090^\circ$$

items.part: Zane achieved a mark of 68/80 for his Biology Assessment task 3 exam. The scores for this exam are normally distributed, with a standard deviation of 3.2% and a mean of 80%. If he wants to perform at the same level in the HSC Trial exam, and the mean increases by 5% and the standard deviation decreases by 2%, what mark must he achieve, to the nearest whole mark, if the exam is out of 70?
items.sol:
Zane's mark as a percentage:
$$\dfrac{68}{80} = 85\%$$
His $z$-score on the first exam:
$$z = \dfrac{85-80}{3.2} = 1.5625$$
New mean $=80+5=85\%$ and new standard deviation $=3.2-2=1.2\%$. Keep the same $z$-score.
$$\begin{aligned} 1.5625 &= \dfrac{x-85}{1.2} \\ x &= 86.875\% \end{aligned}$$
Convert to a mark out of 70.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{86.875}{100}\times 70 \\ &= 60.81\ldots \\ &\approx 61 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Zane needs } 61 \text{ out of } 70$$

What is the UTC of India?
items.sol:
Hawaii is UTC$-10$, so UTC time is $10$ hours ahead of Hawaii time.
$$9\text{ pm Wednesday} + 10 \text{ h} = 7\text{ am Thursday (UTC)}$$
India's time is $12:30$ pm Thursday, so India is ahead of UTC by
$$12:30 - 7:00 = 5\text{ h }30\text{ min}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the UTC of India is } +5{:}30 \text{ (UTC } +5.5)$$

The quadrant is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the circle, so its area is $\dfrac{1}{4}\pi r^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{4}\pi r^2 &= 100 \\ r^2 &= \dfrac{400}{\pi} \\ r &\approx 11.284 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
The arc $l$ is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the circumference.
$$\begin{aligned} l &= \dfrac{1}{4}\times 2\pi r \\ &\approx \dfrac{1}{4}\times 2\pi \times 11.284 \\ &\approx 17.7 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ l \approx 17.7 \text{ cm}$$

A rectangular farm shed has a roof with dimensions of 20m by 12m. All the rain that falls onto this roof is diverted into a cylindrical water tank which has a radius of 1.6m. During a storm, 35 mm of rain falls onto the roof.
Calculate the volume of water that fell onto the roof. Give your answer in $\text{m}^3$.
items.sol:
The rain forms a rectangular prism, with the roof as its base and the depth of rain as its height.

Convert the depth to metres: $35 \text{ mm} = 0.035 \text{ m}$.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 20\times 12\times 0.035 \\ &= 8.4 \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the volume of water is } 8.4 \text{ m}^3$$

items.sol:
Since $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1000$ litres:
$$\begin{aligned} 8.4\times 1000 &= 8400 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 8400 \text{ litres were diverted to the tank}$$

items.part:
A rectangular farm shed has a roof with dimensions of 20m by 12m. All the rain that falls onto this roof is diverted into a cylindrical water tank which has a radius of 1.6m. During a storm, 35 mm of rain falls onto the roof.
Use your answer from part (a) to calculate the increase in the depth of water in the tank due to the rain that falls onto the roof during the storm. Give your answer to two decimal places.

The volume of a cylinder is given by $V = \pi r^2 h$
items.sol:
The extra water in the tank forms a cylinder of volume $8.4 \text{ m}^3$ and radius $1.6$ m.

Using $V=\pi r^2 h$:
$$\begin{aligned} 8.4 &= \pi\times 1.6^2\times h \\ h &= \dfrac{8.4}{\pi\times 1.6^2} \\ &\approx 1.0444 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the depth increases by about } 1.04 \text{ m}$$

Pragyat is a huge online influencer and works for the Kardashian family. He is completing his tax return. He has a gross salary of \$210 560 from the company and an additional income from a modelling contract totalling \$20 800. He is claiming \$32 800 in allowable deductions.
Calculate Pragyat's taxable income
items.sol:
Taxable income is total income less allowable deductions.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Taxable income} &= 210\,560 + 20\,800 - 32\,800 \\ &= \$198\,560 \end{aligned}$$

The taxable income of $\$198\,560$ is in the bracket $\$180\,001$ and over, so the tax is $\$51\,667$ plus $45$ cents for each dollar over $\$180\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Tax} &= 51\,667 + 0.45\times(198\,560 - 180\,000) \\ &= 51\,667 + 0.45\times 18\,560 \\ &= 51\,667 + 8352 \\ &= \$60\,019 \end{aligned}$$

The formula $C = \dfrac{5}{9}(F - 32)$ is used to convert temperatures between degrees Fahrenheit ($F$) and degrees Celsius ($C$).

Convert $7^\circ C$ to the equivalent temperature in Fahrenheit.
items.sol:
Substitute $C = 7$ into the formula.
$$7 = \dfrac{5}{9}(F-32)$$
Multiply both sides by $\dfrac{9}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} F - 32 &= 7 \times \dfrac{9}{5} \\ &= 12.6 \\ F &= 12.6 + 32 \\ &= 44.6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 7^\circ\text{C} = 44.6^\circ\text{F}$$

On 20th July, Izabella purchased a Harry Styles concert ticket for \$480 on her credit card. No other purchases were made using this card in July. Simple interest was charged at a rate of $19.74\%$ p.a. There was no interest free period. The period for which interest was charged included the date of purchase and the date of payment.

What amount was paid when the account was paid in full on 31st July?
items.sol:
Interest is charged from 20th July to 31st July, including both dates.
$$\text{Number of days} = 31 - 20 + 1 = 12$$
Use the simple interest formula $I = Prn$ with $P = 480$, $r = 0.1974$ per year and $n = \dfrac{12}{365}$ years.
$$\begin{aligned} I &= 480 \times 0.1974 \times \dfrac{12}{365} \\ &\approx \$3.12 \end{aligned}$$
The amount paid is the purchase price plus interest.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Amount} &= 480 + 3.12 \\ &= \$483.12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Izabella paid } \$483.12$$

There are three parallel offsets (20, 90, 150) and two strips, each of width
$$h = \dfrac{220}{2} = 110 \text{ m}$$
The trapezoidal rule on each strip gives $\dfrac{h}{2}(y_{\text{first}} + y_{\text{last}})$.

The trapezoidal rule replaces the curved boundary with straight chords.

On the first strip the boundary rises steeply and then flattens (concave down), so it lies above the chord joining the $20$ m and $90$ m offsets. The trapezium leaves out the area between the chord and the curve. The second strip is closer to straight, so the effect there is small.

In a small business, the seven employees earn the following wages per week:

$\$450,\ \$735,\ \$780,\ \$885,\ \$990,\ \$1\,020,\ \$1\,455$
Is the wage of \$1 455 an outlier for this set of data? Justify your answer with calculations
items.sol:
The data are in order, with $n = 7$. The median is $\$885$, so the lower half is $450, 735, 780$ and the upper half is $990, 1020, 1455$.
$$Q_1 = 735, \qquad Q_3 = 1020$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= 1020 - 735 \\ &= 285 \end{aligned}$$
An outlier lies above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Upper fence} &= 1020 + 1.5\times 285 \\ &= 1447.5 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1455 > 1447.5$, the wage of $\$1455$ is an outlier.

items.part:

$\$450,\ \$735,\ \$780,\ \$885,\ \$990,\ \$1\,020,\ \$1\,455$
Each employee will receive a \$40 pay increase.

What effect will this have on the standard deviation. Give a reason for your answer.
items.sol:
The standard deviation will not change.

Adding \$40 to every wage shifts every score and the mean by \$40, so each score's distance from the mean is unchanged. The spread of the data is the same.
items.final: The standard deviation will not change, since every score and the mean shift by \$40 so the spread is the same.

The leftover fuel is in the ratio $40:1$, so it has $41$ parts in total.

A valid cut must separate the source $A$ from the sink $F$, so that every path from $A$ to $F$ is cut. In the diagram, both $A$ and $F$ lie on the same side (below) of the dashed line.

$$\therefore\ \text{the cut is invalid because it does not separate the source from the sink}$$

By the maximum flow, minimum cut theorem, the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut.

Consider the cut separating $\{A, B, C, D\}$ from $\{E, F\}$. It cuts the edges directed from the source side to the sink side: $D\to F$ and $C\to E$. The edge $E\to D$ points back to the source side, so it is not counted.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{capacity} &= 180+95 \\ &= 275 \text{ litres per hour} \end{aligned}$$
This flow can be achieved: send $135$ along $A\to B\to D$, $140$ along $A\to C$ (of which $95$ goes $C\to E\to F$ and $45$ goes $C\to D$), and $D\to F$ carries $135+45=180$. Total into $F$ is $180+95=275$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum flow is } 275 \text{ litres per hour}$$

items.sol:
The initial volume is the $V$-intercept, found by putting $t = 0$.
$$V = 360 - 12(0) = 360$$

items.part:

Half the initial volume is $\dfrac{360}{2} = 180$ litres, so put $V = 180$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the tank has half its initial volume after } 15 \text{ minutes}$$

items.part:
The marks in a class test are normally distributed. The mean is 100 and the standard deviation is 10.
What percentage of marks lie between 80 and 110?
items.sol:
Find the $z$-scores of the two marks.
$$\begin{aligned} z_{110} &= \dfrac{110-100}{10} = 1 \\ z_{80} &= \dfrac{80-100}{10} = -2 \end{aligned}$$
So 110 is $+1\sigma$ and 80 is $-2\sigma$.

Using the 68% and 95% rules, the percentage between $-2\sigma$ and $+1\sigma$ is
$$\begin{aligned} 68+(95-68)\times\dfrac{1}{2} &= 81.5\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 81.5\%$$

$$\therefore\ A \approx 6.928 \text{ cm}^2$$

When it is a time at $P$, the time at $R$ is found by adding the flight time and the 7 hour difference.

$$\text{Time at } P + 10.5 + 7 = \text{Time at } R$$
$5{:}30\text{ am}$ at $P$ is $11\text{ pm}$ at $R$.

The masses of a group of men are normally distributed with mean 78 kg and standard deviation 5 kg. Find the probability, as a percentage, that a man, chosen at random from the group, will have a mass which is:
less than 68 kg?
items.sol:
Convert to a $z$-score.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<68) &= P\left(z<\dfrac{68-78}{5}\right) \\ &= P(z<-2) \\ &= 0.025 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{probability} = 2.5\%$$

items.part:
The masses of a group of men are normally distributed with mean 78 kg and standard deviation 5 kg. Find the probability, as a percentage, that a man, chosen at random from the group, will have a mass which is:
between 73 kg and 88 kg?
items.sol:
Convert to $z$-scores, then use the $68\%$ and $95\%$ rules.
$$\begin{aligned} P(73<X<88) &= P\left(\dfrac{73-78}{5}<z<\dfrac{88-78}{5}\right) \\ &= P(-1<z<2) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times0.68+\dfrac{1}{2}\times0.95 \\ &= 0.815 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{probability} = 81.5\%$$

The can has a height of $13$ cm, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{288_q23_1}

The area of the label is $234\text{ cm}^2$.

Find the diameter of the can, correct to two decimal places.
items.sol:
The label covers the curved surface, so use the curved surface area of a cylinder.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{curved surface area}&=2\pi rh\\ 234&=2\times\pi\times r\times 13\\ 234&=26\pi r\\ r&=\dfrac{234}{26\pi}\\ &\approx 2.8648\end{aligned}$$

The diameter is twice the radius.

$$\begin{aligned}d&=2\times 2.8648\\ &\approx 5.73 \text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ d\approx 5.73 \text{ cm}$$

items.part:
Two hikers decide to leave a campsite ($C$) to visit some natural landmarks in the area. One hiker walks $16$ km on a bearing of $65^\circ$ to see a lake ($L$); the other hiker walks $26$ km on a bearing of $285^\circ$ to reach the top of a mountain ($M$).
Show that the angle between the mountain and the lake is $140^\circ$.
items.sol:
Let $N$ be the point due north of $C$. A bearing of $285^\circ$ is measured clockwise from north.

$$\begin{aligned}\angle MCN&=360^\circ-285^\circ\\ &=75^\circ\end{aligned}$$

The bearing of $L$ gives

$$\angle NCL=65^\circ$$

$$\begin{aligned}\angle MCL&=\angle MCN+\angle NCL\\ &=75^\circ+65^\circ\\ &=140^\circ\end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Two hikers decide to leave a campsite ($C$) to visit some natural landmarks in the area. One hiker walks $16$ km on a bearing of $65^\circ$ to see a lake ($L$); the other hiker walks $26$ km on a bearing of $285^\circ$ to reach the top of a mountain ($M$).
Calculate the distance between the mountain and the lake, correct to the nearest kilometre.
items.sol:
Apply the cosine rule in triangle $MCL$, with $d=ML$.

$$\begin{aligned}d^2&=26^2+16^2-2\times 26\times 16\times\cos 140^\circ\\ &\approx 1569.3490\\ d&\approx 39.6150\\ &\approx 40 \text{ km}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ d\approx 40 \text{ km}$$

items.part:
Two hikers decide to leave a campsite ($C$) to visit some natural landmarks in the area. One hiker walks $16$ km on a bearing of $65^\circ$ to see a lake ($L$); the other hiker walks $26$ km on a bearing of $285^\circ$ to reach the top of a mountain ($M$).
Hence, using your answer from part (c) and the sine rule, find the bearing of the lake from the mountain, correct to the nearest degree.
items.sol:
Apply the sine rule in triangle $MCL$, where $\theta=\angle CML$ is opposite $CL=16$.

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{16}&=\dfrac{\sin 140^\circ}{40}\\ \sin\theta&=\dfrac{16\sin 140^\circ}{40}\\ \theta&=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{16\sin 140^\circ}{40}\right)\\ &\approx 14.8989^\circ\\ &\approx 15^\circ\end{aligned}$$

The bearing of $L$ from $M$ is found from

$$\begin{aligned}\text{bearing}&=180^\circ-(15^\circ+75^\circ)\\ &=90^\circ\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing is } 090^\circ$$
