The average flow rate of Stephanie's shower head is $14$ litres per minute. Stephanie has two $8$-minute showers each day. The cost of water usage is \$2.55 per kilolitre.

Calculate the yearly cost of Stephanie's showers, correct to the nearest cent.
items.sol:
Find the water used per year in litres, then convert to kilolitres.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{usage per year}&=14\times 8\times 2\times 365\\ &=81\,760 \text{ L}\\ &=81.76 \text{ kL}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{cost per year}&=81.76\times 2.55\\ &=208.488\\ &\approx \$208.49\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{cost}\approx \$208.49$$

items.part:
Frances achieved a score of $84$ on a test. The class scores were normally distributed. The mean of the class scores on the test was $72$. Frances's $z$-score was $1.5$.
What was the standard deviation of the class scores on the test?
items.sol:
Use the $z$-score formula $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

$$\begin{aligned}1.5&=\dfrac{84-72}{s}\\ s&=\dfrac{84-72}{1.5}\\ &=8\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the standard deviation is } 8$$

items.part:
Frances achieved a score of $84$ on a test. The class scores were normally distributed. The mean of the class scores on the test was $72$. Frances's $z$-score was $1.5$.
The class scores were standardised to a mean of $78$ and a standard deviation of $6$.

Determine Frances's new moderated score for the test.
items.sol:
Frances's $z$-score is unchanged, so use the new mean $78$ and standard deviation $6$ in $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

$$\begin{aligned}1.5&=\dfrac{x-78}{6}\\ x-78&=9\\ x&=87\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the moderated score is } 87$$

items.part:
Frances achieved a score of $84$ on a test. The class scores were normally distributed. The mean of the class scores on the test was $72$. Frances's $z$-score was $1.5$.
If $120$ students completed the test, how many students would be expected to receive a moderated mark less than $66$?
items.sol:
Find the $z$-score of $66$ using the moderated mean $78$ and standard deviation $6$.

$$\begin{aligned}z&=\dfrac{66-78}{6}\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$

By the empirical rule, $2.5\%$ of scores lie below $z=-2$.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{number of students}&=2.5\%\times 120\\ &=3\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ 3 \text{ students}$$

items.part:
Chris has eight blue socks and seven white socks in his drawer. He is rushing while getting ready for work and, without looking, randomly selects two socks from the drawer.

What is the probability that Chris chooses two socks that are the same colour?
items.sol:
There are $15$ socks in total. The socks are the same colour if both are blue or both are white (without replacement).

$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{same colour})&=P(BB)+P(WW)\\ &=\dfrac{8}{15}\times\dfrac{7}{14}+\dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{6}{14}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{15}+\dfrac{1}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{7}{15}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P=\dfrac{7}{15}$$

Domenica is a furniture maker who builds and sells wooden coffee tables. She has a fixed cost of \$360 to cover the equipment that she uses, and the materials for one table cost her \$180. She sells each table for \$200.
The cost ($C$) associated with the number of coffee tables made ($n$) and the income from selling the coffee tables ($I$) can be modelled by two equations.

Write the TWO equations using the variables $C$, $n$ and $I$.
items.sol:
Let $C$ be the cost, $n$ the number of coffee tables and $I$ the income.

Cost is the fixed cost plus $\$180$ per table, and income is $\$200$ per table.

$$\begin{aligned}C&=180n+360\\ I&=200n\end{aligned}$$

Cost line $C=180n+360$ is the solid line, with intercept $360$. Income line $I=200n$ is the dashed line, through the origin.

items.sol:

items.part:
Domenica is a furniture maker who builds and sells wooden coffee tables. She has a fixed cost of \$360 to cover the equipment that she uses, and the materials for one table cost her \$180. She sells each table for \$200.
Calculate how much profit Domenica will earn when she makes $30$ coffee tables.
items.sol:
Profit is income minus cost.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{profit}&=\text{income}-\text{cost}\\ &=200n-(180n+360)\\ &=20n-360\end{aligned}$$
For $n=30$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{profit}&=20(30)-360\\ &=\$240\end{aligned}$$

Sean purchased 500 Coles Myer shares at \$3.20 per share.

Sean is a paid a dividend of 26 cents per share, and then immediately sells the shares for \$4.80 each.

Brokerage fees were $1.5\%$ of the purchase price and sale price.

What is Sean's total profit?
items.sol:
Purchase, including brokerage of $1.5\%$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= 500 \times 3.20 = \$1600 \\ \text{Brokerage} &= 1.5\% \times 1600 = \$24 \end{aligned}$$
Sale, including brokerage of $1.5\%$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sale} &= 500 \times 4.80 = \$2400 \\ \text{Brokerage} &= 1.5\% \times 2400 = \$36 \end{aligned}$$
Total cost:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total cost} &= 1600 + 24 + 36 \\ &= \$1660 \end{aligned}$$
Total income:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Dividend} &= 0.26 \times 500 = \$130 \\ \text{Total income} &= 130 + 2400 = \$2530 \end{aligned}$$
Profit:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Profit} &= 2530 - 1660 \\ &= \$870 \end{aligned}$$

Each week the distance is multiplied by $1.1$.

\begin{itemize}
\item 5 x Steak and Gravy (S)
\item 3 x Garlic Prawns (P)
\item 2 x Cashew Tofu (T)
\end{itemize}
Show that the probability of the two dishes being the same is $\dfrac{14}{45}$?
items.sol:
The dishes are the same if both are S, both P or both T.
$$\begin{aligned} P(SS) &= \dfrac{5}{10}\times\dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{20}{90} \\ P(PP) &= \dfrac{3}{10}\times\dfrac{2}{9} = \dfrac{6}{90} \\ P(TT) &= \dfrac{2}{10}\times\dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{2}{90} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same}) &= \dfrac{20}{90}+\dfrac{6}{90}+\dfrac{2}{90} \\ &= \dfrac{28}{90} \\ &= \dfrac{14}{45} \end{aligned}$$

A student was asked to solve the following simultaneous equations.

$$\begin{aligned} y &= 3x - 7 \\ x - 2y + 6 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

After graphing the equations, the student found the point of intersection to be $(4, 5)$?

Is the student correct? Support your answer with calculations.
items.sol:
Substitute $x = 4$, $y = 5$ into each equation.

For $y = 3x-7$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= 3(4)-7 \\ &= 5 \\ &= \text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$
For $x-2y+6=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= 4-2(5)+6 \\ &= 0 \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
The point satisfies both equations.

$\therefore$ Yes, the student is correct.
items.final: Yes, the student is correct; (4, 5) satisfies both equations

Substitute $x=75$ into the equation from part (d).

items.part:
An eagle flying above a field, looking for prey, sees a rabbit. When the eagle is at an altitude of 85 metres, the angle of depression from the eagle to the rabbit is $42^\circ$.

The rabbit's only chance of survival is to escape into its burrow. The burrow is $k$ metres to the right of the rabbit and has an angle of elevation of $23^\circ$ to the eagle, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1246_q16_1}
What is the distance, $d$, between the eagle and the rabbit? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
items.sol:
In the right-angled triangle formed by the eagle, the ground directly below it and the rabbit, the angle of depression equals the angle of elevation $42^\circ$ at the rabbit.
$$\sin 42^\circ = \dfrac{85}{d}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \dfrac{85}{\sin 42^\circ} \\ &\approx 127.0 \text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

items.part: Robbie put \$360 into an account which paid simple interest. After 18 months, Robbie has \$440. What rate of interest did Robbie get for this account? Give your answer to one decimal place.
items.sol:
The interest earned is $\$440 - \$360 = \$80$, and $18$ months is $1.5$ years. Using $I = Prn$,
$$80 = 360 \times r \times 1.5$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} r &= 0.1481\ldots \\ &\approx 14.8\% \text{ p.a. (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

Three years ago, chicken breast fillets were \$9.85 per kilogram. How much would you expect to pay today?
items.sol:
Each year's price is multiplied by the growth factor for that year's inflation rate.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Price} &= 9.85 \times 1.0323 \times 1.035 \times 1.0316 \\ &\approx \$10.86 \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
The investment is compounded half-yearly for $2.5$ years, so there are $5$ periods at $3\%$ per period. The table factor for $5$ periods at $3\%$ is $1.159$. The present value is the future value divided by this factor.

items.sol:
The dividend yield is the dividend divided by the market value of the shares, as a percentage.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Yield} &= \dfrac{120}{1500 \times 2} \times 100 \\ &= 4\% \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Max and Angus each invest \$9\,500 for three years. Max's investment earns simple interest at the rate of $7.2\%$ per annum. Angus' investment earns interest at the rate of $7.2\%$ per annum compounding monthly.

At the end of three years, correct to the nearest cent, who has more money and by how much?
items.sol:
Max (simple interest):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 9500 + 9500 \times 3 \times 0.072 \\ &= \$11\,552 \end{aligned}$$
Angus (compound interest, $\dfrac{7.2\%}{12}$ per month for $36$ months):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 9500 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{0.072}{12}\right)^{36} \\ &= \$11\,782.87 \end{aligned}$$
The difference is
$$11\,782.87 - 11\,552 = \$230.87$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Angus has more, by } \$230.87$$

Joseph and Lee are both in the same Maths class. Each week there is a quiz out of 20 that they must complete. Their average mark for the five quizzes is 12 and 15 respectively.

Will Lee be able to achieve his goal of an average of 17 for all seven quizzes? Support your answer with appropriate calculations.
items.sol:
The total needed for an average of 17 over 7 quizzes is
$$17 \times 7 = 119$$
The current total is
$$5 \times 15 = 75$$
So Lee needs $119 - 75 = 44$ marks in the 2 quizzes.

The maximum possible is $2 \times 20 = 40$ marks.

$$\therefore \text{No, it cannot be done.}$$
items.final: No, it cannot be done (needs 44 marks but maximum is 40).

items.part:
Sinclair is concerned about the kangaroo population in the local community. He captures 144 kangaroos and tags them. A couple of months later he collects 15 kangaroos and found 10 of them were tagged.

What is his estimate of the kangaroo population using the capture-recapture method?
items.sol:
Using the capture-recapture proportion,
$$\dfrac{P}{144} = \dfrac{15}{10}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 144 \times \dfrac{15}{10} \\ &= 216 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the estimated population is } 216 \text{ kangaroos}$$

Sydney is 3 hours ahead of Hong Kong, so convert the departure time to Sydney time.
$$2\text{ pm (HK)} = 5\text{ pm (Sydney)}$$
The plane arrived at 7 am the next day, which is $14$ hours after 5 pm.
$$\text{Total time} = 14\text{ hours}$$
Subtract the 3 hour stop-over.
$$\text{Flying time} = 14 - 3 = 11\text{ hours}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Total flying time} = 11\text{ hours}$$

items.part:
Nicholas used his credit card to purchase a plane ticket valued at \$2149 on 17th October 2020. He made no other purchases on his credit card account in October. He paid the October account in full on 21st November 2020.

The credit card account has no interest free period. Compound interest is charged daily at a rate of $19.45\%$ per annum, including the date of purchase and the date the account is paid.

How much interest did he pay, to the nearest cent?
items.sol:
Interest is charged daily from 17 October to 21 November, including both dates, which is $36$ days.

The daily rate is $\dfrac{0.1945}{365}$. Using the compound interest formula $FV = PV(1+r)^n$:
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= 2149\left(1 + \dfrac{0.1945}{365}\right)^{36} \\ &= \$2190.61 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest} &= \$2190.61 - \$2149 \\ &= \$41.61 \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
The January 2020 price is $102\%$ of the January 2019 price.

What was the original purchase price of the appliances? Give your answer correct to the nearest dollar?
items.sol:
Using the declining balance formula $S = V_0(1-r)^n$:
$$19\,770 = V_0(1 - 0.15)^3$$
$$\begin{aligned} V_0 &= \dfrac{19\,770}{(1-0.15)^3} \\ &\approx \$32\,192 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The original price was } \$32\,192 \text{ to the nearest dollar.}$$

items.sol:
The dividend from the company with $1200$ shares is found from shares $\times$ dividend yield $\times$ price.
$$1200 \times 0.06 \times 8.50 = \$612$$
The dividend from RKW is the rest of the total.
$$856.80 - 612 = \$244.80$$
Let $n$ be the number of RKW shares.
$$\begin{aligned} n \times 0.045 \times 6.80 &= 244.80 \\ n &= 800 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Tom has } 800 \text{ shares in RKW.}$$

Each entry in the table that is not a dash is an edge, with its length as the weight. The edges are:

From the network, $E$ is joined only to $A$, so every route from $E$ starts $E \to A$ (46 km). In the table this is the only link from $E$.

From $A$ the only other edge goes to $D$, and from $D$ the edge $DC$ reaches $C$ (the route through $B$ is longer, since $D$ to $B$ to $C$ is $19+43=62$ km).
$$\begin{aligned} E\text{ to }A\text{ to }D\text{ to }C &= 46+22+7 \\ &= 75 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the shortest journey is } E-A-D-C, \text{ of length } 75 \text{ km}$$

The degree of a vertex is the number of paths joined to it. Counting the edges at each vertex:
$$\begin{aligned} A&: AB, AC &&\text{degree } 2 \\ B&: BA, BC, BD, BF &&\text{degree } 4 \\ C&: CA, CB, CF, CE &&\text{degree } 4 \\ D&: DB, DF, DE &&\text{degree } 3 \\ E&: ED, EC &&\text{degree } 2 \\ F&: FB, FD, FC &&\text{degree } 3 \end{aligned}$$
Check: the sum of degrees is $18$, which is twice the $9$ edges.

The completed table is:

$A=2,\ B=4,\ C=4,\ D=3,\ E=2,\ F=3$

A minimum spanning tree joins all $6$ vertices with $5$ edges and no cycles, using least total length. Use Kruskal's algorithm: add the shortest edge that does not form a cycle.
$$\begin{aligned} AB&=30 &&\text{accept} \\ AC&=40 &&\text{accept} \\ BF&=70 &&\text{accept} \\ DE&=80 &&\text{accept} \\ CF&=85 &&\text{reject (cycle } C,A,B,F) \\ DF&=90 &&\text{accept (joins } D,E \text{ to the rest)} \end{aligned}$$
This gives $5$ edges, so the tree is complete.
$$\text{Total length} = 30+40+70+80+90 = 310 \text{ m}$$

Timothy inherits \$30 000 and invests it into an account earning an interest rate of $0.45\%$ per month. Each month, immediately after the interest has been paid, Timothy withdraws \$400.

The amount in the account immediately after the $n$th withdrawal can be determined using the recurrence relation

$$A_n = A_{n-1}(1.045) - 400,$$

Where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ and $A_0 = 30\,000$.

Use the recurrence relation to find the money in the account immediately after the third withdrawal.
items.sol:
Apply the recurrence relation $A_n = 1.045A_{n-1} - 400$ three times, starting from $A_0 = 30\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 30\,000(1.045) - 400 = 30\,950 \\ A_2 &= 30\,950(1.045) - 400 = 31\,942.75 \\ A_3 &= 31\,942.75(1.045) - 400 = 32\,980.17375 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after the third withdrawal the account holds } \$32\,980.17$$

items.part:
Jodie mixes petrol and oil in the ratio of $40:1$ for her leaf blower.
Jodie pours 5 litres of petrol into an empty container to make fuel for the blower

How much oil should be added to make sure the ratio of petrol to oil is correct?
items.sol:
Petrol : oil $= 40 : 1$, so the oil is $\dfrac{1}{40}$ of the petrol.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{oil} &= \dfrac{5}{40} \\ &= 0.125 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0.125 \text{ L (125 mL) of oil}$$

items.part:
Jodie mixes petrol and oil in the ratio of $40:1$ for her leaf blower.
Jodie has 4.1 litres of fuel left in his container after filling the leaf blower.

She wishes to use this fuel in her lawnmower. However, the lawn mower requires a petrol to oil mix in the ratio of $25:1$.

How much oil should be added to the container to ensure the fuel is in the correct ratio for her lawnmower?
items.sol:
The fuel is in the ratio $40:1$, which is $41$ parts in total.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{oil} &= \dfrac{1}{41} \times 4.1 = 0.1 \text{ L} \\ \text{petrol} &= 4.1 - 0.1 = 4.0 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
For the ratio $25:1$ the oil needed is
$$\dfrac{4.0}{25} = 0.16 \text{ L}$$
Oil to add:
$$0.16 - 0.1 = 0.06 \text{ L}$$
$$\therefore\ 0.06 \text{ L (60 mL) of oil should be added}$$

items.part:
Five boxes with varying weight are arranged from lightest to heaviest, left to right.

\exfigure{235_q21_1}

The following data is given about the boxes.

Mode: 0.6 kg\quad Mean: 1.2 kg\quad Median: 0.9 kg\quad Range: 1.5 kg

What is the weight of the contents of box 4?
items.sol:
Let the weights in order be $b_1\le b_2\le b_3\le b_4\le b_5$.

The median is the middle value, so $b_3 = 0.9$.

The mode is $0.6$ kg, which must occur at least twice. It is the smallest value, so $b_1 = b_2 = 0.6$ (no other value is repeated).

The range is the largest minus the smallest:
$$b_5 = 0.6 + 1.5 = 2.1$$
The mean is $1.2$ kg, so the total weight is
$$5\times 1.2 = 6.0 \text{ kg}$$
Therefore
$$\begin{aligned} 0.6 + 0.6 + 0.9 + b_4 + 2.1 &= 6.0 \\ 4.2 + b_4 &= 6.0 \\ b_4 &= 1.8 \end{aligned}$$
This fits the order $0.9 \le 1.8 \le 2.1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{box 4 weighs } 1.8 \text{ kg}$$

items.part:
40 people were surveyed, $95\%$ of them had between 42 and 54 hours of sleep per week. Results were found to be normally distributed.
How many hours of sleep per week would correspond to a $Z$-score of 1.5 in this survey?
items.sol:
In a normal distribution about $95\%$ of scores lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean.

The interval $42$ to $54$ is symmetric about the mean, so
$$\bar{x} = \dfrac{42+54}{2} = 48$$
and $2\sigma = 54 - 48 = 6$, so $\sigma = 3$.

Using $z = \dfrac{x-\bar{x}}{\sigma}$ with $z = 1.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \bar{x} + z\sigma \\ &= 48 + 1.5\times 3 \\ &= 52.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{a } Z\text{-score of } 1.5 \text{ corresponds to } 52.5 \text{ hours of sleep per week}$$

items.part:
40 people were surveyed, $95\%$ of them had between 42 and 54 hours of sleep per week. Results were found to be normally distributed.
A participant, James, had 56 hours sleep per week.

Explain why it is likely that out of the 40 people, James's $Z$-score would have been highest.
items.sol:
James's $Z$-score is
$$z = \dfrac{56-48}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3} \approx 2.67$$
About $95\%$ of people have $Z$-scores between $-2$ and $2$ (42 to 54 hours), so only about $2.5\%$ of the 40 people (about 1 person) would be above 54 hours.

James, at 56 hours, is above 54 hours with $z\approx 2.67 > 2$, so he is very likely the one person with the highest $Z$-score.

Simple interest: $I = Prn$, with $I = 11.60$, $r = 0.1825$ per year and $n = \dfrac{29}{365}$ years.

From the graph, at $N$ parts the income is $\$120\,000$ and the cost is $\$90\,000$.

Since $I = 20N$:
$$N = \dfrac{120\,000}{20} = 6000$$

items.part:
A new drug study was conducted with 80 people chosen at random to determine whether taking Vitamin $A$ or Vitamin $B$ over a period of 2 months, had any significant effects on lowering cholesterol levels.

40 people were given Vitamin $A$ and the other 40 people were given Vitamin $B$.

All 80 people recorded cholesterol levels between 8 and 10 before the study.

The diagram below shows parallel box plots with the results of the study from the two groups.

\exfigure{235_q27_1}

By comparing the differences in the presented data (in terms of central tendency and spread), what conclusions can be made about the effectiveness of the Vitamins in the study?
items.sol:
Reading the box plots (approximately):

Vitamin $A$: minimum $5.2$, $Q_1 = 6.5$, median $7.6$, $Q_3 = 7.9$, maximum $10$.

Vitamin $B$: minimum $3.2$, $Q_1 = 4.5$, median $5$, $Q_3 = 6$, maximum $8$.

Central tendency: everyone started between $8$ and $10$. Vitamin $B$ has median $5$ compared with $7.6$ for Vitamin $A$, and its whole box and most of its data lie lower. Both groups' medians are below $8$, but Vitamin $B$ lowered cholesterol by much more.

Spread: the ranges are about the same ($4.8$ for both) and the interquartile ranges are similar ($1.4$ for $A$, $1.5$ for $B$), so the variability of results is similar.

Conclusion: both vitamins appear to lower cholesterol, but Vitamin $B$ is more effective as its median and quartiles are much lower, while the spread is similar. (Vitamin $A$ had a maximum of $10$, so for some people it may have had no effect.)
items.final: Both vitamins appear to lower cholesterol, but Vitamin B is more effective (much lower median and quartiles), with similar spread.

\exfigure{235_q28_s1}

The bearings of $S$ and $R$ from $P$ are $260^\circ$ and $140^\circ$, so the angle between $PS$ and $PR$ is
$$\angle SPR = 260^\circ - 140^\circ = 120^\circ$$
In triangle $PSR$, $PS = 25$ and $PR = 40$. Using the cosine rule, $SR^2 = PS^2 + PR^2 - 2\cdot PS\cdot PR\cos\angle SPR$:
$$\begin{aligned} SR^2 &= 25^2 + 40^2 - 2\times 25\times 40\times\cos 120^\circ \\ &= 625 + 1600 + 1000 \\ &= 3225 \\ SR &= \sqrt{3225} \approx 56.8 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ SR \approx 56.8 \text{ m}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{area} \approx 9.75 \text{ m}^2$$

From (a) the area is $11 \text{ m}^2$ (to the nearest square metre), and from (b) the trapezoidal estimate is $9.75 \text{ m}^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{difference} &= 11 - 9.75 = 1.25 \text{ m}^2 \\ \text{percentage} &= \dfrac{1.25}{11}\times 100\% \\ &\approx 11.4\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the trapezoidal rule underestimates the area by approximately } 11.4\%$$

items.part:
The emergency stopping distance ($S$) (in metres) required by a motorist on dry surfaces consists of the reaction distance $R$ plus the braking distance $B$ (both in metres), given by the formulas:

$$R = 0.7v,\qquad B = 0.01v^2 \quad \text{and} \quad S = R + B$$

where $v$ is the speed of the vehicle (in km/h).
Show that when a motorist is travelling at 70 km/h on a dry surface, the braking distance and the reaction distance are equal.
items.sol:
Substitute $v = 70$ into each formula.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 0.7\times 70 = 49 \text{ m} \\ B &= 0.01\times 70^2 = 0.01\times 4900 = 49 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ R = B = 49 \text{ m at } 70 \text{ km/h}$$

items.part:
The emergency stopping distance ($S$) (in metres) required by a motorist on dry surfaces consists of the reaction distance $R$ plus the braking distance $B$ (both in metres), given by the formulas:

$$R = 0.7v,\qquad B = 0.01v^2 \quad \text{and} \quad S = R + B$$

where $v$ is the speed of the vehicle (in km/h).
What is the stopping distance when travelling at 70 km/h?
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= R + B \\ &= 49 + 49 \\ &= 98 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the stopping distance is } 98 \text{ m}$$

The emergency stopping distance ($S$) (in metres) required by a motorist on dry surfaces consists of the reaction distance $R$ plus the braking distance $B$ (both in metres), given by the formulas:

$$R = 0.7v,\qquad B = 0.01v^2 \quad \text{and} \quad S = R + B$$

where $v$ is the speed of the vehicle (in km/h).
If $0.01v^2 = 25$, what is the value of $S$?
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.01v^2 &= 25 \\ v^2 &= 2500 \\ v &= 50 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} R &= 0.7\times 50 = 35 \text{ m} \\ S &= R + B = 35 + 25 = 60 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

The diagram shows a vertical pole $PQ$ and a building $RT$, both standing on level ground.

From the top of the pole the angle of depression of the top of the building is $32^\circ$ and of the base of the building is $68^\circ$.

On a direct line of sight from the top of the pole to the base of the building, the distance is 55 m.

\exfigure{235_q31_1}
Mark the given information on the diagram and explain why $\angle PRT$ is $122^\circ$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{235_q31_s1}

The horizontal through $P$ is parallel to $QT$. So, with alternate angles between parallel lines:

$\angle PTQ = 68^\circ$ (angle of depression of $T$)

$\angle RPT = 68^\circ - 32^\circ = 36^\circ$ (the line of sight to $R$ is $32^\circ$ below the horizontal, the line to $T$ is $68^\circ$ below it)

The building is vertical, so $\angle RTQ = 90^\circ$, giving
$$\angle PTR = 90^\circ - 68^\circ = 22^\circ$$
Angle sum in triangle $PRT$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle PRT &= 180^\circ - 36^\circ - 22^\circ \\ &= 122^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle PRT = 122^\circ$$

items.part:
The diagram shows a vertical pole $PQ$ and a building $RT$, both standing on level ground.

From the top of the pole the angle of depression of the top of the building is $32^\circ$ and of the base of the building is $68^\circ$.

On a direct line of sight from the top of the pole to the base of the building, the distance is 55 m.

\exfigure{235_q31_1}
Use the Sine rule to calculate the height of the building $RT$ correct to the nearest metre.
items.sol:
In triangle $PRT$: $\angle RPT = 36^\circ$, $\angle PRT = 122^\circ$ and $PT = 55$ (opposite $\angle PRT$). Using the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{RT}{\sin 36^\circ} &= \dfrac{55}{\sin 122^\circ} \\ RT &= \dfrac{55\sin 36^\circ}{\sin 122^\circ} \\ &\approx 38.1 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ RT \approx 38 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
The diagram shows a vertical pole $PQ$ and a building $RT$, both standing on level ground.

From the top of the pole the angle of depression of the top of the building is $32^\circ$ and of the base of the building is $68^\circ$.

On a direct line of sight from the top of the pole to the base of the building, the distance is 55 m.

\exfigure{235_q31_1}
How much taller is pole, than the building?
items.sol:
In the right-angled triangle $PQT$, $PT = 55$ is the hypotenuse and $\angle PTQ = 68^\circ$, so $PQ$ is opposite the angle:
$$\begin{aligned} PQ &= 55\sin 68^\circ \\ &\approx 50.99 \\ &\approx 51 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The difference in height is
$$51 - 38 = 13 \text{ m}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the pole is } 13 \text{ m taller than the building}$$
items.final: the pole is $13$ m taller than the building

A company stocks two different grades of sandstone paving blocks.

Grade $A$ is sells for $\$60$ per square metre. Grade $B$ sells for $\$40$ per square metre.

Let $x$ represent the number of square metres of Grade $A$ sandstone blocks and $y$ represent the number of square metres of Grade $B$ sandstone blocks purchased.

Write down two equations for $x$ and $y$, and solve these simultaneous equations graphically. Thus determine how many square metres of each grade of sandstone block were purchased.

\exfigure{235_q33_1}
items.sol:
Total area: $x + y = 50$.

Total cost: $60x + 40y = 2400$, which simplifies (divide by $20$) to $3x + 2y = 120$.

To graph each line, find two points.
$$\begin{aligned} x + y = 50:&\ (0, 50),\ (50, 0) \\ 3x + 2y = 120:&\ (0, 60),\ (40, 0) \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{235_q33_s1}

The lines intersect at $(20, 30)$.

Check: $20 + 30 = 50$ and $60\times 20 + 40\times 30 = 1200 + 1200 = 2400$.
$$\therefore\ 20 \text{ m}^2 \text{ of Grade } A \text{ and } 30 \text{ m}^2 \text{ of Grade } B$$

items.part:
Electromagnetic waves include radio waves, ultraviolet rays and visible light.

The frequency $F$ (measured in cycles/second), of such waves is inversely proportional to their wavelength, $L$ (measured in metres)

A particular colour of visible light has a frequency of $5 \times 10^{14}$ cycles per second when its wavelength is $6 \times 10^{-7}$ metres.
Show that: $F = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{L}$.
items.sol:
Since $F$ is inversely proportional to $L$, $F = \dfrac{k}{L}$ for some constant $k$. Substitute $F = 5\times 10^{14}$ and $L = 6\times 10^{-7}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5\times 10^{14} &= \dfrac{k}{6\times 10^{-7}} \\ k &= 5\times 10^{14}\times 6\times 10^{-7} \\ &= 30\times 10^{7} \\ &= 3\times 10^{8} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F = \dfrac{3\times 10^{8}}{L}$$

items.part:
Electromagnetic waves include radio waves, ultraviolet rays and visible light.

The frequency $F$ (measured in cycles/second), of such waves is inversely proportional to their wavelength, $L$ (measured in metres)

A particular colour of visible light has a frequency of $5 \times 10^{14}$ cycles per second when its wavelength is $6 \times 10^{-7}$ metres.
An infrared wave has a wavelength of $2 \times 10^{-4}$ metres.

What is its frequency? (Write your answer in scientific notation.)
items.sol:
Substitute $L = 2\times 10^{-4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} F &= \dfrac{3\times 10^{8}}{2\times 10^{-4}} \\ &= 1.5\times 10^{12} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F = 1.5\times 10^{12} \text{ cycles per second}$$

Following the arrows from $S$ to $P$:
$$\begin{aligned} &S\text{-}A\text{-}C\text{-}P \\ &S\text{-}A\text{-}C\text{-}F\text{-}P \\ &S\text{-}A\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}P \\ &S\text{-}A\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}F\text{-}P \\ &S\text{-}E\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}P \\ &S\text{-}E\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}F\text{-}P \\ &S\text{-}E\text{-}F\text{-}P \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 7 \text{ paths}$$

The maximum capacity (vehicles per hour) of each road in the network is indicated, and the minimum cut is shown as a dashed line.

\exfigure{235_q35_1}
Explain why the capacity of the minimum cut is 800 vehicles per hour?
items.sol:
The dashed line separates $S$ from $P$. Only roads directed from the $S$ side to the $P$ side are counted: $AC$, $DC$ and $FP$. Road $CF$ points back across the cut, so it is not counted.
$$200 + 300 + 300 = 800$$

The maximum capacity (vehicles per hour) of each road in the network is indicated, and the minimum cut is shown as a dashed line.

What is the maximum flow of vehicles per hour through the network of roads?
items.sol:
By the maximum flow-minimum cut theorem, the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum flow} = 800 \text{ vehicles per hour}$$

items.part:
The diagram below shows a network of directed roads on which vehicles can travel from a shopping centre at $S$ to a park at $P$ in a city suburb.

The maximum capacity (vehicles per hour) of each road in the network is indicated, and the minimum cut is shown as a dashed line.

\exfigure{235_q35_1}
Would the construction of a road directly from $E$ to $P$ with a capacity of 500 vehicles per hour, improve the maximum flow through the network from $S$ to $P$? Justify your answer.
items.sol:
Yes. The new road $EP$ crosses the old minimum cut from the $S$ side to the $P$ side, so that cut now has capacity $800 + 500 = 1300$ and is no longer the minimum.

The roads out of $S$ have total capacity $500 + 400 = 900$, so the flow cannot exceed $900$.

This flow is achievable:
$$\begin{aligned} &S\text{-}A\text{-}C\text{-}P: 200 \\ &S\text{-}A\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}P: 300 \\ &S\text{-}E\text{-}P: 400 \end{aligned}$$
No road is over capacity ($CP$ carries $500 \le 600$, $EP$ carries $400 \le 500$), and the total is $900$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum flow increases from } 800 \text{ to } 900 \text{ vehicles per hour}$$
items.final: Yes; the maximum flow increases from 800 to 900 vehicles per hour

items.sol:
Draw the perpendicular from $X$ to the midpoint $M$ of $YZ$ (the triangle is isosceles, so this bisects $YZ$). Then $YM = 5$.

In right-angled triangle $XMY$, by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$XM = \sqrt{k^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{k^2 - 25}$$
Area using base $YZ$ and height $XM$:
$$A = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 10\times\sqrt{k^2 - 25} = 5\sqrt{k^2 - 25}$$
Area using two sides and the included angle, $A = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$A = \dfrac{1}{2}k^2\sin\theta$$
Equate the two areas:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}k^2\sin\theta &= 5\sqrt{k^2 - 25} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{10\sqrt{k^2 - 25}}{k^2} \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), the area is $5\sqrt{k^2 - 25}$. Set it equal to $60$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5\sqrt{k^2 - 25} &= 60 \\ \sqrt{k^2 - 25} &= 12 \\ k^2 - 25 &= 144 \\ k^2 &= 169 \end{aligned}$$
So $k = 13$ (a length is positive). Then
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{10\times 12}{169} = \dfrac{120}{169}$$
$$\theta \approx 45.2^\circ \text{ or } 134.8^\circ$$
The perpendicular $XM$ bisects $\theta$, so in triangle $XMY$:
$$\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{5}{13}$$
and so $\dfrac{\theta}{2} \approx 22.6^\circ$, which is less than $45^\circ$. Hence $\theta$ is acute, and $134.8^\circ$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ \theta \approx 45^\circ$$

The scale $1:250$ means the real length is 250 times the model length.

items.sol:
Convert the logo to millimetres: $130 \text{ cm} = 1300 \text{ mm}$.

The model lengths are 250 times smaller (scale $1:250$).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{model side} &= 1300 \div 250 \\ &= 5.2 \text{ mm} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the logo on the model should be } 5.2 \text{ mm} \times 5.2 \text{ mm.}$$

The table shows the number of standard drinks in three types of beer available at a restaurant: full-strength, mid-strength and low-strength. The restaurant sells the beer in small and large glasses.

\extable{250_q19_t1}

Geoff is 24 years old and weighs 78 kg. He has dinner with friends at the restaurant, where he drinks three large glasses of full-strength beer and one small glass of mid-strength beer between 7:30 pm and 11:30 pm.

The following formula is used to calculate an estimate for blood alcohol content (BAC) for males.

$$\text{BAC}_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$$
Calculate Geoff's BAC at 11:30 pm, correct to three decimal places.
items.sol:
From the table, the number of standard drinks is
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 3 \times 1.6 + 1 \times 0.8 \\ &= 5.6 \end{aligned}$$
The drinking period from 7:30 pm to 11:30 pm gives $H = 4$ hours, and $M = 78$ kg.

Substitute into the formula:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{BAC} &= \dfrac{10(5.6) - 7.5(4)}{6.8 \times 78} \\ &= \dfrac{56 - 30}{530.4} \\ &= \dfrac{26}{530.4} \\ &\approx 0.049 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{BAC} \approx 0.049$$

The table shows the number of standard drinks in three types of beer available at a restaurant: full-strength, mid-strength and low-strength. The restaurant sells the beer in small and large glasses.

The number of hours required for Geoff to reach a BAC of 0 after he stops consuming alcohol is given by the following formula.

Convert the decimal part to minutes:

A cut separates $S$ from $T$. The capacity is the sum of the capacities of the edges that cross the dashed line from the $S$ side to the $T$ side.

The dashed line crosses the edges $A \to T$, $B \to T$ and $C \to T$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{capacity} &= 20 + 18 + 30 \\ &= 68 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the capacity of the cut is } 68.$$

By the maximum-flow minimum-cut theorem the maximum flow is at most 68, the capacity of the cut. So it is enough to find a flow of 68.

One such flow:
$$\begin{aligned} S \to C &: 25 & D \to C &: 5 \\ S \to D &: 5 & C \to T &: 30 \\ S \to B &: 15 & E \to B &: 3 \\ S \to E &: 23 & B \to T &: 18 \\ E \to A &: 20 & A \to T &: 20 \end{aligned}$$
Every flow is within the edge capacity. Flow is conserved at each vertex: at $C$, $25+5=30$; at $D$, $5=5$; at $E$, $23=20+3$; at $B$, $15+3=18$; at $A$, $20=20$.

The flow into $T$ is
$$30 + 18 + 20 = 68$$
so the flow is 68, equal to the minimum cut.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum flow} = \text{minimum cut} = 68$$

With no flow from $B$ to $A$, the only edge carrying flow out of $B$ is $B \to T$.

The edge $B \to T$ is in the minimum cut, so in a maximum flow it is full (capacity $18$).
$$\text{outflow at } B = 18 + 0 = 18$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the outflow at } B \text{ is } 18.$$

items.sol:

items.part:
Jacinta has a credit card that charges a simple interest rate of $21\%$ per annum. The credit card does not have an interest-free period, and interest is charged up to and including the date of payment.

During one weekend, Jacinta makes the following transactions.

\extable{250_q21_t1}
Jacinta is due to pay her account in full on 9 February.

What will be the total interest payable on Jacinta's transactions?
items.sol:
Interest is charged from the day of each transaction up to and including 9 February, so the number of days is (days remaining in January, including the transaction day) $+\ 9$.

13 January to 9 February:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Days} &= (31-13+1)+9 \\ &= 28 \end{aligned}$$
18 January to 9 February:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Days} &= (31-18+1)+9 \\ &= 23 \end{aligned}$$
Interest is simple interest, $I = Prn$, with daily rate $r = \dfrac{0.21}{365}$.
$$\begin{aligned} I_1 &= 30\times\dfrac{0.21}{365}\times 28 \approx \$0.48 \\ I_2 &= 89\times\dfrac{0.21}{365}\times 23 \approx \$1.18 \end{aligned}$$
Total interest:
$$\begin{aligned} I &\approx 0.4833+1.1777 \\ &\approx \$1.66 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total interest payable} \approx \$1.66$$

For the 2020–2021 financial year, Hara had a total income of \$145 000, and her tax payable was \$33 167 (excluding the Medicare levy).
Calculate Hara's taxable income.
items.sol:
Tax payable is $\$33\,167$. This lies between $\$29\,467$ and $\$51\,667$, so Hara's taxable income is in the $\$120\,001$ to $\$180\,000$ bracket, where tax is $\$29\,467$ plus $37$c for each $\$1$ over $\$120\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 29\,467+0.37(T-120\,000) &= 33\,167 \\ 0.37(T-120\,000) &= 3700 &&(\text{subtract } 29\,467) \\ T-120\,000 &= 10\,000 &&(\text{divide by } 0.37) \\ T &= 130\,000 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{taxable income} = \$130\,000$$

At a schools swimming carnival, the finish times for students under 17 who competed in the 50 m backstroke race are found to be normally distributed with a mean race time of 42 seconds and a standard deviation of 3 seconds.

The standard normal distribution table is shown. The values in the table represent the area under the normal curve to the left of the $z$-score.

\exfigure{250_q33_1}

Using standardised scores and the standard normal distribution table, find the probability that a randomly chosen competitor achieves a finish time between 43 and 46 seconds. Give your answer correct to three decimal places.
items.sol:
Standardise each time using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ with $\mu=42$ and $\sigma=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} z_{43} &= \dfrac{43-42}{3} \approx 0.33 \\ z_{46} &= \dfrac{46-42}{3} \approx 1.33 \end{aligned}$$
From the table, the area to the left of $z=0.33$ is $0.62930$ and the area to the left of $z=1.33$ is $0.90824$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(43<X<46) &= P(z<1.33)-P(z<0.33) \\ &= 0.90824-0.62930 \\ &= 0.27894 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(43<X<46) \approx 0.279$$

Willow's business Fashion Face Masks makes and sells embroidered face masks. Willow purchases plain cloth masks and embroiders them with different patterns.

The cost of each plain mask is \$4 and Willow sells the embroidered masks for \$10 each. Willow invests \$420 in an embroidery machine and a thread kit to make 100 masks.

The production cost and revenue generated from the sale of the embroidered masks can be modelled with two linear equations, as shown in the graph.

\exfigure{250_q34_1}
Using the graph, solve the two equations simultaneously and explain the significance of this solution for Willow's business.
items.sol:
The two lines cross where the revenue and cost graphs meet. Reading from the graph, this is at $70$ masks and $\$700$.

Check with the equations: revenue is $R=10x$ and cost is $C=420+4x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10x &= 420+4x \\ 6x &= 420 \\ x &= 70 \end{aligned}$$
Then $R=10\times 70=\$700$.

The solution is $x=70$ masks, $\$700$. This is the break-even point: when Willow sells $70$ masks, revenue equals cost, so she makes no profit and no loss. After selling more than $70$ masks she makes a profit.
items.final: $x=70$ masks, $\$700$; the break-even point, where revenue equals cost (no profit or loss)

Hanako contributes \$8500 to an investment account every year for 6 years. The account pays $8\%$ interest per annum, compounded annually.

Hanako is considering opening another investment account that pays $8\%$ interest per annum, compounded biannually, for 3 years.

Using the formula $FV = PV(1 + r)^n$, determine the single sum of money that Hanako would need to invest in this account to reach the same future value calculated in part (a).
items.sol:
Compounded biannually means twice a year, so the rate per period is $r=\dfrac{8\%}{2}=4\%=0.04$ and the number of periods is $n=3\times 2=6$.

The future value needed is $FV=62\,355.15$. Substitute into $FV=PV(1+r)^n$.
$$\begin{aligned} 62\,355.15 &= PV(1.04)^6 \\ PV &= \dfrac{62\,355.15}{1.04^6} \\ &\approx \$49\,280.18 \end{aligned}$$
Hanako would need to invest about $\$49\,280$.

Reading the five-number summaries from the box-plot:

Home: minimum $25$, $Q_1=35$, median $65$, $Q_3=80$, maximum $95$.

Away: minimum $20$, $Q_1=25$, median $35$, $Q_3=60$, maximum $80$.

Skewness: the home median ($65$) is closer to $Q_3$ than $Q_1$, with a longer lower tail, so the home distribution is negatively skewed. The away median ($35$) is closer to $Q_1$, with a longer upper part, so the away distribution is positively skewed.

Spread: the home interquartile range is $80-35=45$ and the range is $95-25=70$. The away interquartile range is $60-25=35$ and the range is $80-20=60$. The home scores are more spread out.

Jo delivered catalogues as a job during her summer holidays.

She was paid a rate of \$20 per 1000 catalogues.

On an average day she delivered 4 catalogues to each residence along 45 city blocks.

Each block had on average 40 residences to receive catalogues.
What would she have been paid for a week where she worked on 3 days?
items.sol:
Catalogues delivered per day:
$$\begin{aligned} 4\times 45\times 40 &= 7200 \end{aligned}$$
In 3 days:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\times 7200 &= 21\,600 \text{ catalogues} \end{aligned}$$
She is paid $\$20$ for each 1000 catalogues:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Pay} &= \dfrac{21\,600}{1000}\times 20 \\ &= \$432 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{She was paid } \$432.$$

items.part:
Jo delivered catalogues as a job during her summer holidays.

She was paid a rate of \$20 per 1000 catalogues.

On an average day she delivered 4 catalogues to each residence along 45 city blocks.

Each block had on average 40 residences to receive catalogues.
It took her on average 12 minutes to cover each block.

What hourly rate of pay would be equivalent to her piecework pay rate?
items.sol:
Pay for one average day (7200 catalogues):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{7200}{1000}\times 20 &= \$144 \end{aligned}$$
Time for one day, at 12 minutes for each of 45 blocks:
$$\begin{aligned} 45\times 12 &= 540 \text{ minutes} \\ &= 9 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
Equivalent hourly rate:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{144}{9} &= 16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The equivalent rate is } \$16 \text{ per hour.}$$

items.sol:
Use $A = P\left(1+r\right)^n$, where $r$ is the rate per compounding period and $n$ is the number of periods.

ACA: $r = 0.049$ per year, $n = 3$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 4000(1.049)^3 \\ &\approx \$4617.28 \end{aligned}$$
NSA: $r = \dfrac{0.048}{12} = 0.004$ per month, $n = 3\times 12 = 36$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 4000(1.004)^{36} \\ &\approx \$4618.21 \end{aligned}$$
The NSA account is better. The extra earned is:
$$\begin{aligned} 4618.21 - 4617.28 &= \$0.93 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{He earns about } \$0.93 \text{ more with the NSA account.}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= 2\times 0.82\times 1250 \\ &= \$2050 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{She should choose Option 2, because it is } \$75 \text{ cheaper.}$$
items.final: She should choose Option 2, because it is $75 cheaper.

items.part:
She will fly from Sydney to Broome and stay for two weeks at a resort.
There are two resorts which she likes.

Resort A : Normal rate is \$250 per night, but a discount of 10% for bookings of a week or more.

Resort B : Normal rate is \$260 per night, but a free night is added for every six paid nights booked.

Which resort should she choose and why?
items.sol:
She stays for two weeks, $14$ nights.

Resort A: $10\%$ discount on $\$250$ per night.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= 14\times 250\times 0.9 \\ &= \$3150 \end{aligned}$$
Resort B: every seventh night is free, so she pays for $12$ of the $14$ nights.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= 12\times 260 \\ &= \$3120 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{she should choose Resort B, since } \$3120<\$3150$$
items.final: She should choose Resort B, since $3120 < $3150.

From the top of a tower, which is 60 metres high, Isaac throws a stone upward and allows it to fall under gravity.

The height of the stone is modelled by the equation, $h = 20t - 5t^2 + 60$, where $h$ is the height (in metres) of the stone above ground level and $t$ is the time in seconds since the stone was thrown.
On the grid below, draw the graph of this model and label it as Stone.

\exfigure{264_q24_1}
items.sol:
Find key points of $h = 20t - 5t^2 + 60$.

The $h$-intercept is $h = 60$ at $t = 0$. The stone reaches the ground when $h = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -5t^2 + 20t + 60 &= 0 \\ t^2 - 4t - 12 &= 0 \\ (t-6)(t+2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $t = 6$, as $t \ge 0$.

The axis of symmetry is $t = \dfrac{-20}{2(-5)} = 2$, and the maximum height is
$$\begin{aligned} h(2) &= 40 - 20 + 60 \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$
Table of values:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline h & 60 & 75 & 80 & 75 & 60 & 35 & 0 \end{array}$$
\exfigure{264_q24_s1}

At the same time as the stone is thrown, Jay releases a toy glider from the top of the tower.

The glider drifts down, losing height at a constant rate of 5 metres each second.

Draw the graph modelling the height of the glider on the grid on the previous page and determine the equation which describes the model. Label the graph Glider.
items.sol:
The glider starts at the top of the tower ($h = 60$ when $t = 0$) and loses 5 metres each second, so the height decreases at a constant rate $5$ m/s. This is a straight line with gradient $-5$ and $h$-intercept $60$.
$$h = 60 - 5t$$
Points: $(0, 60)$ and $(6, 30)$.

\exfigure{264_q24_s2}
$$\therefore\ \text{The glider model is } h = 60 - 5t.$$

From the top of a tower, which is 60 metres high, Isaac throws a stone upward and allows it to fall under gravity.

A manufacturing process involves completing nine activities $A$ to $I$.

The network diagram shows the order in which the activities are completed and their duration in minutes.

\exfigure{264_q26_1}
List the activities that make up the critical path and give the minimum time required to complete the manufacturing process.
items.sol:
Label the nodes: $P$ (end of $A$), $Q$ (end of $C$), $R$ (end of $E$, $B$, $F$), $S$ (end of $G$, $H$). Find the earliest start time at each node, taking the longest route.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 12 \\ Q &= 14 \\ R &= \max(12+10,\ 15,\ 14+13) = 27 \\ S &= \max(27+12,\ 14+20) = 39 \\ \text{End} &= \max(12+25,\ 39+12) = 51 \end{aligned}$$
The longest route is $C \to F \to H \to I$:
$$\begin{aligned} 14+13+12+12 &= 51 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Critical path: } C,\ F,\ H,\ I; \text{ minimum time } 51 \text{ minutes.}$$
items.final: Critical path: C, F, H, I; minimum time 51 minutes.

items.part:
A manufacturing process involves completing nine activities $A$ to $I$.

The network diagram shows the order in which the activities are completed and their duration in minutes.

\exfigure{264_q26_1}
The foreman is told that one activity has been delayed by 10 minutes, but he is not concerned, as it will not delay the whole process.

Which possible activities could he have been told about?
items.sol:
A delay of 10 minutes does not delay the process only if the activity has float of at least 10 minutes.

Compare each non-critical activity's float (latest finish minus earliest start minus duration), using the longest path through it:

More simply, compare the longest path through each activity with 51 minutes.
$$\begin{aligned} A,\ E,\ H,\ I &: 12+10+12+12 = 46 \text{ (float } 5\text{)} \\ B,\ H,\ I &: 15+12+12 = 39 \text{ (float } 12\text{)} \\ A,\ D &: 12+25 = 37 \text{ (float } 14\text{)} \\ C,\ G,\ I &: 14+20+12 = 46 \text{ (float } 5\text{)} \end{aligned}$$
Activities $A$, $E$ and $G$ lie on a path of 46 minutes, so a 10 minute delay would make the process 5 minutes longer. $A$ is also on path $A,D$ but its longest path is 46, so its float is 5.

Only $B$ (float 12) and $D$ (float 14) can absorb a delay of 10 minutes.
$$\therefore\ \text{He could have been told about activity } B \text{ or activity } D.$$
items.final: He could have been told about activity B or activity D.

Four family members are living in cities around the world, in different time zones.

\extable{264_q27_t1}
At 2:00 pm on Saturday $14^{\text{th}}$ August, local Parkes time, Roniel rings Siobahn to organise a group chat with the others.

At what local time does Siobahn receive the call?
items.sol:
Parkes is UTC $+10$ and Montreal is UTC $-5$, so Montreal is $15$ hours behind Parkes.
$$\begin{aligned} 2{:}00\text{ pm Sat} - 15 \text{ h} &= 11{:}00\text{ pm Fri} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Siobahn receives the call at } 11{:}00 \text{ pm on Friday } 13^{\text{th}} \text{ August.}$$

items.part:
Four family members are living in cities around the world, in different time zones.

\extable{264_q27_t1}
The group chat begins when Quentin joins at 1:00 pm Sat $21^{\text{st}}$ August local Copenhagen time.

It ends when Tahlia leaves at 3:30 am Friday $20^{\text{th}}$ August local Honolulu time.

How many minutes did the chat last?
items.sol:
Convert both times to UTC.

Start: Quentin, Copenhagen (UTC $+1$), 1:00 pm Sat $21^{\text{st}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 13{:}00 - 1 \text{ h} &= 12{:}00 \text{ UTC on Sat } 21^{\text{st}} \end{aligned}$$
End: Tahliah, Honolulu (UTC $-10$), 3:30 am. Add 10 hours:
$$\begin{aligned} 3{:}30 + 10 \text{ h} &= 13{:}30 \text{ UTC} \end{aligned}$$
As printed, the end is given as Friday $20^{\text{th}}$, which would be before the start. The chat can only end after it begins, so the end is taken as 3:30 am on Saturday $21^{\text{st}}$ (13:30 UTC on the same day as the start).

Duration:
$$\begin{aligned} 13{:}30 - 12{:}00 &= 1.5 \text{ hours} \\ &= 90 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The chat lasted } 90 \text{ minutes.}$$

Reading the plot with Zeros on the left and Cyphers on the right, each has 20 scores. The median is the mean of the 10th and 11th scores.

Zeros in order: $5, 7, 8, 14, 16, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 31, 33, 35, 45, 47, 52$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Median} &= \dfrac{22+24}{2} = 23 \end{aligned}$$
Cyphers in order: $8, 13, 17, 21, 24, 28, 32, 34, 38, 38, 38, 39, 42, 44, 47, 49, 49, 52, 54, 56$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Median} &= \dfrac{38+38}{2} = 38 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The median was greater for Cyphers, by } 38 - 23 = 15 \text{ points.}$$
items.final: The median was greater for Cyphers, by 15 points.

items.sol:
The lower quartile is the median of the lowest 10 scores, the mean of the 5th and 6th scores.

Zeros: lowest 10 are $5, 7, 8, 14, 16, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22$
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 &= \dfrac{16+16}{2} = 16 \end{aligned}$$
Cyphers: lowest 10 are $8, 13, 17, 21, 24, 28, 32, 34, 38, 38$
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 &= \dfrac{24+28}{2} = 26 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The lower quartile of Cyphers (26) is greater than that of Zeros (16), by } 10 \text{ points.}$$
items.final: Cyphers' lower quartile (26) is greater than Zeros' (16), by 10 points.

items.sol:
The upper quartile is the median of the highest 10 scores, the mean of the 15th and 16th scores overall (5th and 6th of the top 10).

Zeros: top 10 are $24, 25, 27, 28, 31, 33, 35, 45, 47, 52$
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 &= \dfrac{31+33}{2} = 32 \end{aligned}$$
Cyphers: top 10 are $38, 39, 42, 44, 47, 49, 49, 52, 54, 56$
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 &= \dfrac{47+49}{2} = 48 \end{aligned}$$
Interquartile range $= Q_3 - Q_1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Zeros: } & 32 - 16 = 16 \\ \text{Cyphers: } & 48 - 26 = 22 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Cyphers had the greater interquartile range, by } 22-16 = 6 \text{ points.}$$
items.final: Cyphers had the greater interquartile range, by 6 points.

items.part:
Maggie has a credit card which has no interest free period

Interest is charged at the end of each month at 16.25% per annum, compounding daily, from the purchase date (included) to the last day of the month (included).

There is a minimum payment of 2.5% of the closing balance after the interest is added.

Maggie started the month of June with a zero balance and made purchases of \$150.00 on $6^{\text{th}}$ June and \$245.90 on $20^{\text{th}}$ June.

Calculate the minimum payment due at the end of June.
items.sol:
Interest compounds daily, so the daily rate is
$$r=\dfrac{0.1625}{365}\approx 0.000445205$$
June has 30 days. Each purchase earns interest from its purchase date to 30 June, both days included.

$\$150.00$ (6 June): $6$ to $30$ June is $25$ days.

$\$245.90$ (20 June): $20$ to $30$ June is $11$ days.

Using $A=P(1+r)^n$ for each purchase:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 150(1+r)^{25} \approx \$151.68 \\ A_2 &= 245.90(1+r)^{11} \approx \$247.11 \end{aligned}$$
Closing balance after interest:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Balance} &\approx 151.68+247.11 \\ &= \$398.79 \end{aligned}$$
The minimum payment is $2.5\%$ of the closing balance:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.025\times 398.79 &\approx \$9.97 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum payment} \approx \$9.97$$

items.part:
The probability tree diagram below shows the probabilities for Jack choosing a colour combination for his T-shirt and shorts. The diagram includes all the T-shirts and all the shorts that he owns.

\exfigure{264_q30_1}
The probability for white T-shirts has been left off the diagram.

Give this probability as a fraction.
items.sol:
The probabilities on the first set of branches add to $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{White}) &= 1-\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{White T-shirt})=\dfrac{1}{6}$$

Multiply along the branches Black T-shirt, then Black shorts.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Black, Black}) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P=\dfrac{1}{10}$$

The same colour means Black and Black, or Blue and Blue. There are no white shorts, so White and White is not possible.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{same}) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{4}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{4}{15} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{30}+\dfrac{8}{30} \\ &= \dfrac{11}{30} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{same colour})=\dfrac{11}{30}$$

Different colours is the complement of the same colour.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{different}) &= 1-\dfrac{11}{30} \\ &= \dfrac{19}{30} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{different colours})=\dfrac{19}{30}$$

A block of land is in the shape of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ shown below. The diagonal $AC$ has been drawn.

\exfigure{264_q31_1}

The following measurement have been taken:

$AD = 75$ m, $BC = 90$ m.

$D$ is 135 m due south of $B$.

$\angle CAD = 53^\circ$ and $\angle ACD = 32^\circ$.
Find the length of $CD$. (Answer correct to the nearest metre.)
items.sol:
In $\triangle ACD$, the angle sum gives
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ADC &= 180^\circ-53^\circ-32^\circ \\ &= 95^\circ \end{aligned}$$
CD is opposite $\angle CAD=53^\circ$ and $AD$ is opposite $\angle ACD=32^\circ$, so by the sine rule
$$\dfrac{CD}{\sin 53^\circ}=\dfrac{75}{\sin 32^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} CD &= \dfrac{75\sin 53^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \\ &\approx 113.03 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ CD\approx 113 \text{ m}$$

items.part:
A block of land is in the shape of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ shown below. The diagonal $AC$ has been drawn.

\exfigure{264_q31_1}

The following measurement have been taken:

$AD = 75$ m, $BC = 90$ m.

$D$ is 135 m due south of $B$.

$\angle CAD = 53^\circ$ and $\angle ACD = 32^\circ$.
Find the size of $\angle CBD$. (Answer correct to the nearest degree.)
items.sol:
In $\triangle BCD$ the three sides are known: $BC=90$, $BD=135$, $CD\approx 113$. Use the cosine rule for the angle at $B$, opposite $CD$.
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle CBD &= \dfrac{BC^2+BD^2-CD^2}{2\times BC\times BD} \\ &= \dfrac{90^2+135^2-113^2}{2\times 90\times 135} \\ &\approx 0.5580 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle CBD &\approx 56.1^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle CBD\approx 56^\circ$$

items.part:
A block of land is in the shape of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ shown below. The diagonal $AC$ has been drawn.

\exfigure{264_q31_1}

The following measurement have been taken:

$AD = 75$ m, $BC = 90$ m.

$D$ is 135 m due south of $B$.

$\angle CAD = 53^\circ$ and $\angle ACD = 32^\circ$.
Give the bearing of $C$ from $B$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{264_q31_s1}

$D$ is due south of $B$, so $BD$ lies along the north-south line through $B$, pointing south ($180^\circ$). $C$ is east of this line, and $\angle CBD\approx 56^\circ$ from the south direction.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing of } C \text{ from } B &= 180^\circ-56^\circ \\ &= 124^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{bearing}=124^\circ\text{T}$$

Two websites give reviews of books.

Both sites give each book a rating out of a possible 100.

A statistician analysed the ratings awarded by the two sites to 100 books and obtained the statistical results below.

\extable{264_q32_t1}
The book “Moonlighting” got a rating of 78 on Bookophile and a rating of 84 on Great Reads.

Convert both these ratings to $z$-scores and determine which website rated the book higher in comparison to other books on the site.
items.sol:
Use $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ for each website.
$$\begin{aligned} z_{\text{Bookophile}} &= \dfrac{78-60}{12} = 1.5 \\ z_{\text{Great Reads}} &= \dfrac{84-76}{8} = 1 \end{aligned}$$
The larger $z$-score is further above the mean for its site.

$\therefore$ Bookophile rated the book higher in comparison to other books on its site, since $1.5>1$.
items.final: Bookophile rated the book higher relative to its site ($z=1.5$ vs $z=1$)

items.part:
Two websites give reviews of books.

Both sites give each book a rating out of a possible 100.

A statistician analysed the ratings awarded by the two sites to 100 books and obtained the statistical results below.

\extable{264_q32_t1}
What percentage of books would have a rating between 60 and 84 on the Bookophile website?
items.sol:
Convert the ratings to $z$-scores for Bookophile (mean $60$, standard deviation $12$).
$$\begin{aligned} z_{60}&=\dfrac{60-60}{12}=0 \\ z_{84}&=\dfrac{84-60}{12}=2 \end{aligned}$$
By the $68$-$95$-$99.7$ rule, $34\%$ lie between $z=0$ and $z=1$, and $13.5\%$ between $z=1$ and $z=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(0<z<2) &= 34\%+13.5\% \\ &= 47.5\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 47.5\% \text{ of books}$$

items.part:
Two websites give reviews of books.

Both sites give each book a rating out of a possible 100.

A statistician analysed the ratings awarded by the two sites to 100 books and obtained the statistical results below.

\extable{264_q32_t1}
Hal chooses a book at random from those reviewed by Great Reads.

What is the probability that it had a rating of 68 or more?
items.sol:
For Great Reads (mean $76$, standard deviation $8$), a rating of $68$ has
$$z=\dfrac{68-76}{8}=-1$$
By the $68$-$95$-$99.7$ rule, $50\%$ of ratings lie above the mean and $34\%$ lie between $z=-1$ and $z=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(z\ge -1) &= 0.50+0.34 \\ &= 0.84 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{rating}\ge 68)=0.84$$

To measure the height of a vertical pole used for a mobile phone antenna, Steph finds a nearby vertical fence post and measures the length of the shadow of both, as well as the height of the fencepost. Both are on level ground.

Her measurements are shown on the sketch below.

Briefly explain why the triangles shown on the diagram are similar.
items.sol:
Both triangles have a right angle, since the pole and the post are vertical and the ground is level. They also share the same angle $\alpha^\circ$, since the sun's rays are parallel. Two angles are equal, so the third angles are equal too.

$\therefore$ the triangles are equiangular, hence similar.

items.part:
The value of the Australian dollar (\$AU) compared to other currencies varies continually. The conversion graph below shows the conversion lines for the highest rate and lowest rate that the \$AU reached in 2020 against the US Dollar (\$US).

\exfigure{264_q35_1}

Ajax is an Australian importer and buys goods from the USA to sell in Australia. He pays \$US39 per bottle for a perfume that he imports.

Bella is an Australian wine exporter and sells mainly to the USA. She charges \$AU80 per case for a popular variety.

Use these examples to compare how Australian importers and exporters are affected when the exchange rate increases from the lowest to the highest rate. Outline who are advantaged and who are disadvantaged by a rise in the exchange rate.
items.sol:
Read both lines on the graph at the values given.

Ajax (importer) pays $\$US39$ per bottle. On the highest-rate line $U=39$ corresponds to about $A=50$. On the lowest-rate line $U=39$ corresponds to about $A=67$.

So the bottle costs Ajax about $\$AU67$ at the lowest rate and about $\$AU50$ at the highest rate, a saving of about $\$AU17$ per bottle.

Bella (exporter) charges $\$AU80$ per case. On the lowest-rate line $A=80$ corresponds to about $U=46$. On the highest-rate line $A=80$ corresponds to about $U=62$.

So the case costs her US customers about $\$US46$ at the lowest rate and about $\$US62$ at the highest rate, an increase of about $\$US16$ per case.

Conclusion: when the exchange rate rises from its lowest to its highest, importers such as Ajax are advantaged, because imported goods cost fewer Australian dollars. Exporters such as Bella are disadvantaged, because their goods cost overseas buyers more, which may reduce sales or force her to cut her Australian dollar price.

items.part:
The diagram shows a network of pipes (edges) and pumping stations (vertices) which connect a Gas Plant and a Gas Storage facility. The capacity of each pipe is given in kilolitres per hour.

To determine the efficiency of the network, five “cuts” have been drawn on the network, labelled $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $\varepsilon$.

\exfigure{264_q37_1}
Find the value of each cut and determine the maximum flow of the network.
items.sol:
The value of a cut is the sum of the capacities of the pipes it crosses, in the direction from the Gas Plant to the Gas Storage.
$$\begin{aligned} \alpha &: 180+220+140 = 540 \\ \beta &: 180+220+140 = 540 \\ \gamma &: 70+90+220+140 = 520 \\ \delta &: 70+90+220+140 = 520 \\ \varepsilon &: 70+90+220+140 = 520 \end{aligned}$$
The maximum flow equals the minimum cut.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum flow}=520 \text{ kilolitres per hour}$$
items.final: Cuts: α=540, β=540, γ=520, δ=520, ε=520; maximum flow = 520 kilolitres per hour

items.part:
The diagram shows a network of pipes (edges) and pumping stations (vertices) which connect a Gas Plant and a Gas Storage facility. The capacity of each pipe is given in kilolitres per hour.

To determine the efficiency of the network, five “cuts” have been drawn on the network, labelled $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $\varepsilon$.

\exfigure{264_q37_1}
What change to the capacity of a single pipe would allow the full inflow to the network from the Gas plant to reach the Gas storage.
items.sol:
The inflow from the Gas Plant is $540$, but the minimum cuts $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are only $520$. Every one of these cuts crosses the pipe $AE$, so $AE$ is a bottleneck.

Increasing the capacity of $AE$ by $20$ makes each of these cuts $540$, so the minimum cut becomes $540$.

$\therefore$ increase the capacity of pipe $AE$ from $220$ to $240$ kilolitres per hour (an increase of $20$). The flow then equals the full inflow of $540$.
items.final: Increase the capacity of pipe AE from 220 to 240 kilolitres per hour (an increase of 20)

items.part:
Mia wants to invest \$42 000 for a total of 5 years. She has three investment options.

\begin{itemize}
\item Option A – simple interest is paid at the rate of $6\%$ per annum.
\item Option B – compound interest is paid at a rate of $5.5\%$ per annum, compounded annually.
\item Option C – compound interest is paid at a rate of $4.8\%$ per annum, compounded quarterly.
\end{itemize}

Determine Mia's best investment option. Support your answer with calculations.
items.sol:
Option A (simple interest):

$$\begin{aligned} I &= 42\,000\times 6\%\times 5 \\ &= \$12\,600 \end{aligned}$$

So $FV=42\,000+12\,600=\$54\,600$.

Option B (compound, annually):

$$FV=42\,000\left(1+\dfrac{5.5}{100}\right)^5=\$54\,892.32$$

Option C (compound, quarterly, $5\times 4=20$ periods at $\dfrac{4.8}{4}\%$ each):

$$FV=42\,000\left(1+\dfrac{4.8}{400}\right)^{20}=\$53\,316.24$$

Therefore Option B is the best investment, as it earns the most interest.
items.final: Option B is the best investment (FV $\$54\,892.32$ vs A $\$54\,600$, C $\$53\,316.24$)

There are 52 weeks in a year, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Annual income} &= 650\times 52 \\ &= \$33\,800 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Annual after-tax income} = \$33\,800$$

Convert every expense to a yearly amount (52 weeks or 26 fortnights in a year).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Board} &= 85\times 52 = \$4420 \\ \text{Car maintenance} &= \$938 \\ \text{Registration and insurance} &= \$1252 \\ \text{Car repayments} &= 249\times 26 = \$6474 \\ \text{Clothing} &= 60\times 26 = \$1560 \\ \text{Entertainment} &= 68\times 52 = \$3536 \\ \text{Fuel} &= 73\times 52 = \$3796 \\ \text{Gym} &= 30\times 26 = \$780 \\ \text{Health insurance} &= \$2159 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Total annual expenditure} = \$24\,915$$

Annual savings are income less expenditure.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Annual savings} &= 33\,800-24\,915 \\ &= \$8885 \end{aligned}$$
Divide by 52 weeks.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Weekly savings} &= \dfrac{8885}{52} \\ &\approx \$170.87 \end{aligned}$$

items.sol:
Break-even is where revenue equals cost, which is where the two lines on the graph cross.

This agrees with the graph, where the lines meet at $n=14$ (about $\$280$).
$$\therefore\ \text{The committee must sell 14 T-shirts to break even}$$

Work out the shortest time from $A$ to each vertex.

What score will Stan have to average, in the last two quizzes, to raise his mean for all 7 quizzes to 12 marks?
items.sol:
After 5 quizzes, Stan's total is $5\times 10=50$ and Ollie's total is $5\times 14=70$.

For a mean of 12 over 7 quizzes, Stan's required total is $7\times 12=84$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Marks needed} &= 84-50 \\ &= 34 \end{aligned}$$
Over two quizzes this is an average of
$$\dfrac{34}{2}=17$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Stan must average } 17 \text{ per quiz}$$

items.sol:
The combined goal is a total of
$$16\times 14=224$$
Stan's total is 84 and Ollie's first five quizzes total 70, so Ollie needs
$$224-(84+70)=70 \text{ marks}$$
in his last two quizzes. Each quiz is worth at most 20 marks, so the most he can score is $40$.

$\therefore$ Since $70>40$, Ollie's task is impossible.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Number of students} &= 2.5\%\times 120 \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \left(x + \dfrac{3}{x}\right)dx$.
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 \left(x + \dfrac{3}{x}\right)dx &= \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} + 3\ln|x|\right]_1^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{2^2}{2} + 3\ln 2\right) - \left(\dfrac{1^2}{2} + 3\ln 1\right) \\ &= 2 + 3\ln 2 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + 0\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{2} + 3\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

The strip width is

\extable{Ts11586_1}

items.part:
The functions $y = \cos x$ and $y = \dfrac{1}{2}$ are drawn below. Find the exact area enclosed between the curve $y = \cos x$ and the line $y = \dfrac{1}{2}$ in the domain $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right]$.

\exfigure{631_q7c_1}
Find the area enclosed between the curve $y = \sqrt{x-2}$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y = 0$ and $y = 3$.
items.sol:
\exfigure{631_q7d_s1}

The area is found by integrating with respect to $y$. Making $x$ the subject of $y=\sqrt{x-2}$ gives $x=y^2+2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^3 (y^2 + 2)\,dy \\ &= \left[\dfrac{y^3}{3} + 2y\right]_0^3 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{3^3}{3} + 2 \times 3\right) - \left(\dfrac{0^3}{3} + 2 \times 0\right) \\ &= 9 + 6 \\ &= 15 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Alternate solution:

\exfigure{631_q7d_s2}

The area under the curve from $x=2$ to $x=11$ is

$$\begin{aligned} \int_2^{11} \sqrt{x-2}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{2(x-2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_2^{11} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}(11-2)^{\frac{3}{2}} - \dfrac{2}{3}(2-2)^{\frac{3}{2}} \\ &= 18 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The rectangle $ABCD$ has area $3\times 11 = 33 \text{ units}^2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 33 - 18 \\ &= 15 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Show that $\left(-2, \dfrac{-2}{e^2}\right)$ is a point of inflection on the curve $g(x) = xe^x$.
items.sol:
Differentiating using the product rule,

$$\begin{aligned} g'(x) &= xe^x + e^x \\ g''(x) &= xe^x + e^x + e^x \\ &= (x+2)e^x \end{aligned}$$

For a possible point of inflection $g''(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} (x+2)e^x &= 0 \\ x &= -2 \end{aligned}$$

The $y$ value is

$$\begin{aligned} g(-2) &= -2e^{-2} \\ &= \dfrac{-2}{e^2} \end{aligned}$$

Test the concavity either side of $x=-2$ (the sign of $g''$ is the sign of $x+2$, since $e^x>0$).

\extable{Ts11593_1}

The concavity changes at $x=-2$.

$$\therefore\ \left(-2, \dfrac{-2}{e^2}\right) \text{ is a point of inflection.}$$

items.part: Find the stationary points of the function $y = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x - 1$ and determine their nature.
items.sol:
Differentiating,

$$y' = 3x^2 - 6x - 9$$

For stationary points $y'=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) &= 0 \\ (x-3)(x+1) &= 0 \\ x = 3 \ &\text{or}\ x = -1 \end{aligned}$$

The $y$ values are

$$\begin{aligned} x=3:\ y &= 27 - 27 - 27 - 1 = -28 \\ x=-1:\ y &= -1 - 3 + 9 - 1 = 4 \end{aligned}$$

So the stationary points are $(3,-28)$ and $(-1,4)$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.

$$y'' = 6x - 6$$

$$\begin{aligned} x=3:\ y'' &= 12 > 0 &&\text{minimum turning point} \\ x=-1:\ y'' &= -12 < 0 &&\text{maximum turning point} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ (3,-28) \text{ is a minimum and } (-1,4) \text{ is a maximum.}$$
items.final: $(3,-28)$ is a minimum and $(-1,4)$ is a maximum.

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sin 2x}{1-\cos 2x}\,dx$
items.sol:
Let $y=1-\cos 2x$, so $y'=2\sin 2x$. The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{\sin 2x}{1-\cos 2x}\,dx &= \dfrac12\int\dfrac{2\sin 2x}{1-\cos 2x}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac12\ln(1-\cos 2x)+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Find $\displaystyle\int \left(x^2-\dfrac{1}{x^2}+\sqrt[3]{x}\right)dx$
items.sol:
Write each term as a power of $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\left(x^2-x^{-2}+x^{\frac13}\right)dx &= \dfrac{x^3}{3}+x^{-1}+\dfrac{3}{4}x^{\frac43}+C \\ &= \dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac1x+\dfrac{3\sqrt[3]{x^4}}{4}+C \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^2e^{2x^3}\,dx$
items.sol:
Let $u=2x^3$, so $du=6x^2\,dx$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1x^2e^{2x^3}dx &= \dfrac16\int_0^1 6x^2e^{2x^3}dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{e^{2x^3}}{6}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{e^2}{6}-\dfrac16 \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Using two trapeziums of equal width, approximate the given integral correct to 4 significant figures $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{\ln(2+x)}\,dx$.
items.sol:
Two trapeziums on $[-1,1]$ give $h=\dfrac{1-(-1)}{2}=1$, so $x=-1,\,0,\,1$.

The function values are $f(x)=\sqrt{\ln 1},\ \sqrt{\ln 2},\ \sqrt{\ln 3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^1\sqrt{\ln(2+x)}\,dx &\approx \dfrac12\left[\sqrt{\ln1}+2\sqrt{\ln 2}+\sqrt{\ln 3}\right] \\ &\approx 1.357 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:

What is the equation of the curve?
items.sol:
Integrate the gradient.
$$y=\int5\sec^2x\,dx=5\tan x+C$$
Substitute $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},2\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= 5\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}+C \\ 2 &= 5+C \\ C &= -3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=5\tan x-3$$

items.part: If $k>0$ is a constant find the integer $n$ such that $\displaystyle\int_k^{3k}\dfrac{6}{3x-k}\,dx=\log_e n$ .
items.sol:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_k^{3k}\dfrac{6}{3x-k}\,dx &= 2\Big[\ln(3x-k)\Big]_k^{3k} \\ &= 2\left[\ln 8k-\ln 2k\right] \\ &= 2\ln 4 \\ &= \ln 16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n=16$$

items.part: Differentiate $\dfrac{x}{1+\ln x}$ .
items.sol:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=1+\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac1x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{1+\ln x}\right) &= \dfrac{(1+\ln x)\cdot1-x\cdot\frac1x}{(1+\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2} \end{aligned}$$

items.part: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{3\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2}\,dx$ .
items.sol:
From part (a),
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{1+\ln x}\right)=\dfrac{\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2}$$
Multiplying by 3,
$$\int\dfrac{3\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2}\,dx=\dfrac{3x}{1+\ln x}+C$$

Write $\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$.
$$\int\cot x\,dx=\int\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx$$
Let $u=\sin x$, so $du=\cos x\,dx$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1}{u}\,du &= \ln|u|+C \\ &= \ln|\sin x|+C \end{aligned}$$

The graph is symmetric about $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so the area on $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right]$ equals that on $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Hence
$$A=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(2\cos x-\cot x)\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{5\pi}{6}}(\cot x-2\cos x)\,dx=2\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(2\cos x-\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\Big[2\sin x-\ln\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= 2\left[2\left(1-\dfrac12\right)-\left(\ln1-\ln\dfrac12\right)\right] \\ &= 2+2\ln\dfrac12 \\ &= 2-2\ln2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=2(1-\ln 2)\text{ units}^2$$

items.part:
The velocity, in cm/s of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the equation $v=4t^3-24t^2+20t$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 3 cm to the right of the origin.
Find an expression for $x$, the position of the particle as a function of time.
items.sol:
Position is the integral of velocity.
$$x=\int(4t^3-24t^2+20t)\,dt=t^4-8t^3+10t^2+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=3$, so $C=3$.
$$\therefore\ x=t^4-8t^3+10t^2+3$$

items.part:
The velocity, in cm/s of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the equation $v=4t^3-24t^2+20t$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 3 cm to the right of the origin.
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=1$.
items.sol:
Substitute $t=1$ into $v$.
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 4(1)^3-24(1)^2+20(1) \\ &= 4-24+20 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore the particle is at rest when $t=1$.

items.part:
The velocity, in cm/s of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the equation $v=4t^3-24t^2+20t$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 3 cm to the right of the origin.
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 2 seconds.
items.sol:
The particle is at rest only at $t=1$ in the first 2 seconds, apart from $t=0$, so it changes direction at $t=1$.

From $x=t^4-8t^3+10t^2+3$, the positions are
$$x(0)=3,\quad x(1)=6,\quad x(2)=-5$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total distance} &= |6-3|+|-5-6| \\ &= 3+11 \\ &= 14 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Some students are given a maximum of 4 minutes to complete a Rubik's Cube. The time spent on the Rubik's Cube, in minutes, can be modelled using the continuous random variable $X$ which has the probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(16-x^2), & 0\le x\le 4\\ 0, & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$
Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{64}$ .
items.sol:
The total probability is 1.
$$\begin{aligned} k\int_0^4(16x-x^3)\,dx &= 1 \\ k\left[8x^2-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^4 &= 1 \\ k(128-64) &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{64} \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Some students are given a maximum of 4 minutes to complete a Rubik's Cube. The time spent on the Rubik's Cube, in minutes, can be modelled using the continuous random variable $X$ which has the probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(16-x^2), & 0\le x\le 4\\ 0, & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$
Calculate $P(X<3)$ .
items.sol: $$\begin{aligned} P(X<3) &= \dfrac{1}{64}\int_0^3(16x-x^3)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{64}\left[8x^2-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^3 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{64}\left(72-\dfrac{81}{4}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{207}{256} \\ &\approx 0.8086 \end{aligned}$$

items.part:
Some students are given a maximum of 4 minutes to complete a Rubik's Cube. The time spent on the Rubik's Cube, in minutes, can be modelled using the continuous random variable $X$ which has the probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(16-x^2), & 0\le x\le 4\\ 0, & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$
Find the median of the above distribution. Give your answer correct to 3 dp.
items.sol:
The median $m$ satisfies $P(X<m)=0.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{64}\int_0^m(16x-x^3)\,dx &= 0.5 \\ 8m^2-\dfrac{m^4}{4} &= 32 \\ m^4-32m^2+128 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $u=m^2$, so $u^2-32u+128=0$.
$$u=\dfrac{32\pm\sqrt{(-32)^2-4(128)}}{2}=27.3137\ \text{or}\ 4.68629$$
If $m^2=27.3137$ then $m=5.226$, rejected since $m\le 4$.

If $m^2=4.68629$ then $m=2.16478\ldots$
$$\therefore\ \text{Median}\approx 2.165$$

items.part: Simplify the ratio $\$4 : \$2.50$

A marine biologist used the capture-recapture technique to estimate the number of fish in a lake. He captured, tagged and released 28 fish. Later he caught 35 at random and found that 4 had been tagged. What is the estimate for the total fish in the lake?
items.sol:
The tagged fraction in the sample equals the tagged fraction in the lake.

$$\dfrac{28}{x} = \dfrac{4}{35}$$
$$\dfrac{x}{28} = \dfrac{35}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{35}{4} \times 28 \\ &= 245 \end{aligned}$$

The estimate is $245$ fish.

items.part: The ratio of cars to motorbikes in a car park is $8:3$ and the ratio of motorbikes to vans is $5:2$. If there are 160 cars, find the total number of vehicles in the car park.
items.sol:
Matching the motorbikes, with cars : motorbikes $= 8:3 = 40:15$ and motorbikes : vans $= 5:2 = 15:6$:

$$\text{cars} : \text{motorbikes} : \text{vans} = 40 : 15 : 6$$

Since $40$ parts $= 160$ cars, $1$ part $= 4$ cars.

items.part:
Jenny's class completes two tests.

For the first test, the mean was 63.2 and the standard deviation was 5.5.

For the second test, the mean was 70 and the standard deviation was 7.5.

Jenny scored 72 on the first test. Calculate the mark that she needed to obtain in the second test to ensure that her performance relative to the class was maintained.
items.sol:
The $z$-score measures position relative to the class, so find $z$ on the first test.

$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{72 - 63.2}{5.5} \\ &= 1.6 \end{aligned}$$

For the second test the same $z$-score is needed.

$$\begin{aligned} 1.6 &= \dfrac{x - 70}{7.5} \\ 1.6 \times 7.5 &= x - 70 \\ x &= (1.6 \times 7.5) + 70 \\ &= 82 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x = 82$$

Convert the heights to $z$-scores using $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$.

$$z = \dfrac{5.99 - 5.36}{3} = 0.21 \qquad z = \dfrac{7.19 - 5.36}{3} = 0.61$$

From the table:

$$\begin{aligned} P(0.21 < z < 0.61) &= P(z < 0.61) - P(z < 0.21) \\ &= 0.72907 - 0.58317 \\ &= 0.1459 \end{aligned}$$

Harrison is above only $29.8\%$ of competitors, so his $z$-score is negative.

By symmetry, find the positive $z$ with $P(z < z_0) = 1 - 0.298 = 0.702$.

$$0.702 \approx 0.7019$$

From the table, $z_0 = 0.53$, so Harrison's $z$-score is $-0.53$.

$$\begin{aligned} -0.53 &= \dfrac{x - 5.36}{3} \\ x &= (3 \times -0.53) + 5.36 \\ &= 3.77 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x = 3.77 \text{ metres}$$
